en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men,
as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory.
[One should meditate on] Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, who is moon-colored, and who has four arms.
One should meditate upon the serene-faced one for the pacification of all obstacles:
Oṃ! I salute Vyāsa, the grandson of Vasiṣṭha, the great-grandson of Śakti, the stainless son of Parāśara, the father of Śuka, and a treasure-house of asceticism.

Salutations to Vyāsa, who is the form of Viṣṇu; salutations to Viṣṇu, who is the form of Vyāsa. Salutations indeed to the treasure-house of Brahman, the descendant of Vasiṣṭha; salutations again and again.
Janamejaya said:
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the sons of Pṛthā were defeated at dice and provoked to anger by the evil-minded sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and their ministers through deceitful means;
they were made to hear harsh words as the latter incited the ultimate enmity.

What did my ancestors, the Kauravas, do? And how did the sons of Pṛthā, who possessed splendor equal to that of Śakra, lose their sovereignty and suddenly fall into misery as they dwelt in the forest?
And who followed them when they had fallen into this supreme calamity?
What was their food, what was their conduct, and where was the dwelling of those great-souled ones?
How did those high-minded men spend twelve years in the forest?
O best of Brahmins, they passed by those heroes who were slayers of their enemies.
And how was it that the princess, the most excellent among all women,
devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, and always truthful in speech— ?
"She who did not deserve such suffering has undergone this dreadful forest-dwelling.
O ascetic, tell me all of this in detail;
I wish to hear the life-story of those possessed of abundant wealth and splendor."
"O Brahmin, as you speak, my curiosity is indeed great.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Thus were the sons of Pṛthā defeated at dice and provoked to anger by those evil-souled ones."
Accompanied by their ministers, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra departed from Hastināpura.
Having then gone out through the gate of Vardhamāna city,
they set forth bearing weapons toward the north together with Kṛṣṇā.
Indrasena and the others, fourteen servants in all,
followed them with swift chariots, taking all the women with them.
Then those tigers among men, O Bhārata, mounted their chariots.
On the bank of the Jāhnavī, they beheld the great banyan tree named Pramāṇa. Knowing that they were departing, the citizens, overwhelmed with grief,
repeatedly censured Bhīṣma, Vidura, Droṇa, and Gautama.
Free from fear, they gathered together and said to one another:
"This entire lineage is no more, nor are we, nor our homes,
where the wicked Duryodhana is protected by the son of Subala."
And with Karṇa and Duḥśāsana, he desires to rule this kingdom.
If not [this], there would be neither family, nor conduct, nor dharma, nor wealth—how then could there be happiness?
For here this wicked man, having sinful allies, seeks to possess the kingdom.
Duryodhana is a hater of his elders, one who has abandoned proper conduct and friends;
he is greedy for wealth, arrogant, base, and naturally pitiless.
This entire earth does not exist where King Duryodhana is present.
"Let us all go gladly to where the Pāṇḍavas are going—
to those high-souled ones who are compassionate, who have conquered their senses and enemies,
who are modest, renowned, and devoted to the practice of dharma."

Having spoken thus, they all approached the Pāṇḍavas and, with palms joined in reverence, said to those sons of Kuntī and Mādrī, "Where will you go? May it be well with you; why do you leave us, who are partakers of sorrow?"
We too shall follow wherever you go,
having heard that you have been defeated by enemies devoid of compassion through unrighteous means;
we are all deeply distressed, and you ought not to abandon us here.
"O friends who are devoted and deeply attached, always intent on what is dear and beneficial,
let us not be utterly destroyed while this kingdom is presided over by a bad king.
Listen, O bulls among men, as we shall describe the virtues and vices."
Just as fragrance perfumes a cloth, water, sesame seeds, or the earth, so too do qualities born of association arise through the influence of the virtuous or the non-virtuous.
For association with the foolish is indeed the source of the net of delusion;
day by day, association with the virtuous is the source of dharma.
Therefore, [one should associate] with those who are wise, aged, of excellent character, and ascetic.

One should associate with the virtuous who are devoted to tranquility—those whose three things are pure: their birth, their learning, and their conduct. One should serve them, for sitting in their company is weightier even than the sacred scriptures.
For even though we are free from any undertaking, we shall surely obtain merit here by associating with virtuous and holy men; whereas evil results from the service of the wicked,
through seeing them, touching them, conversing with them, or sitting together with them.
The practice of dharma declines and men do not achieve success;
the intellect of men diminishes through association with the base. Through association with the mediocre, one reaches mediocrity, and through the best, one attains excellence.
Neither by those who are base, nor by those who are outside the scope [of dharma], nor especially by those who are unrighteous;

those virtues which are celebrated in the world as the source of dharma, pleasure, and wealth, which arise from worldly conduct and one's own nature, which are declared in the Vedas, and are approved by the learned— [these should be practiced].
"Those excellent qualities, both collectively and individually, reside here among you. O virtuous ones, desiring our own welfare, we wish to dwell in your midst.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"We are fortunate that the subjects, headed by the Brahmins, constrained by their affection and compassion, speak of virtues in us that we do not even possess. Therefore,
together with my brothers, I make this request to you all."
It must certainly be done otherwise, out of affection and compassion for us.
My grandfather Bhīṣma, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, my mother,
and most of my friends are in the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).

Therefore, for the sake of our welfare, you must all together, with great effort, protect them who are overwhelmed by grief and torment; having come from afar, they have been bound by the oath of reunion.
I must direct my mind, filled with affection, toward my own kin who have become my trust;
for this indeed stands as the highest of my duties within my heart. By doing this well, I shall find satisfaction and receive due honor.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by that King of Dharma,
those subjects, overcome with grief, raised a terrible cry of distress, exclaiming, "Alas, O King!"
Remembering the virtues of Pārtha, they were afflicted by grief and deeply distressed;
though unwilling, they turned back after meeting the Pāṇḍavas. When the citizens had returned, the Pāṇḍavas mounted their chariots.
They went to the great banyan tree named Pramāṇa on the bank of the Jāhnavī.
Having reached that banyan tree at the close of the day, those heroic Pāṇḍavas stayed there for the night after touching the pure water.
Emaciated by grief, they spent that night subsisting on water alone;
and certain twice-born men followed them there out of affection— some with their sacred fires, others without, accompanied by their circles of disciples and kinsmen.
Surrounded by those expounders of the Veda, the king shone resplendent. At that hour, both beautiful and formidable, as they had kindled their sacred fires,
a conversation arose among them, preceded by the chanting of the Vedas.

With voices as sweet as swans, those foremost of Brahmins comforted the king, the best of the Kurus, passing the entire night with him. Meanwhile, the king remained together with his brothers and all his circles of friends.
The king lay there that night, struck down by pain and grief.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the night had turned into dawn, for those of unwearied deeds—
As they were desiring to go to the forest, the Brahmins, who lived on alms, stood before them.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, said to them:
"For we have been robbed of all our possessions, stripped of our kingdom, and deprived of our prosperity."
Subsisting on fruits, roots, and meat, we shall go to the forest in our distress.
And the forest is full of dangers, abounding in wild beasts and reptiles; I believe that certain suffering will surely befall you there.
"The affliction of Brahmins would bring even the gods to ruin; how much more so me? O Brahmins, turn back from here as you please.
The Brahmins said:
"O King, we are prepared to go wherever you are going.
You ought not to abandon us, your devoted followers who perceive the true Dharma;
for even the gods show compassion toward their devotees."
Especially toward Brahmins who adhere to virtuous conduct.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O twice-born ones, I too always possess supreme devotion toward Brahmins."
But this loss of my companions truly overwhelms me;
for even those brothers of mine who used to bring back fruits, roots, and deer for me are now utterly bewildered by the sorrows born of grief.
"Because of the dragging away of Draupadī and the seizure of their kingdom, these men are already filled with sorrow; I cannot bear to subject them further to such afflictions here.
The Brahmins said:
"O King, let there be no anxiety in your heart regarding our sustenance;
we ourselves shall gather forest-grown foods and follow you.
Through meditation and the recitation of prayers, we shall ensure your welfare."
"And we shall delight together in the forest with agreeable conversations.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"It is even so; there is no doubt that I would delight in the company of the brahmins."
"Because of this deficiency, I see it as a rejection of myself.
How shall I look upon you all, who have brought food yourselves—those who, though unworthy, are suffering out of devotion to me? Fie on those sinful sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra!"
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, that king sat down upon the ground, grieving.
Then a learned brahmin named Śaunaka, who delights in the knowledge of the supreme self, [approached him].
Skilled in both Yoga and Sāṃkhya, he spoke this to the king:
"Thousands of occasions for sorrow and hundreds of occasions for fear assail the fool day after day, but not the wise man."
For wise men like you do not become attached to actions that are contrary to knowledge, fraught with many faults,
and destructive of the highest good; they call that eightfold intelligence the destroyer of all that is not beneficial.
O King, that [wisdom] which is endowed with the Śruti and Smṛti resides within you. Service, listening, comprehension, retention,
as well as reasoning and refutation, discernment, and knowledge of reality— these are the qualities of the intellect.
In times of financial hardship, in difficult terrains, and during calamities involving their own kin,
those such as you do not succumb to physical or mental suffering. Listen, for I shall relate how it was in the past with Janaka.
These verses, which establish the nature of the self, were sung by the Great-Souled One:
"The world is afflicted by two kinds of suffering arising from the mind and the body;
hear now this means for their pacification, both in detail and in brief."

In this body, diseases arise from wind, bile, and phlegm; all sufferings originate from indigestion and likewise from the arising of evil karma. [These arise] from the contact with the undesirable caused by disease, from exhaustion, and from the loss of what is desired.
Physical suffering arises from four causes:
because it is quickly remedied, because one constantly refrains from dwelling upon it,
and because mental and physical ailments are pacified through the dual application of ritual action and yoga.
For this reason, wise physicians first bring about the pacification of the mind in men through pleasant words and the provision of enjoyments;
for by mental suffering, the body is tormented.

One should pacify the mind with knowledge, just as one would extinguish fire with water; for when the mental suffering has been stilled, physical suffering subsides, just as water in a pot is cooled by a heated iron ball.
It is perceived that affection is the root of mental suffering;
through affection, a living being becomes attached and encounters the yoke of suffering. Sufferings have affection as their root, and fears are born from affection.

Sorrow, joy, and likewise exhaustion—all these proceed from affection (*sneha*). From affection arises attachment to the instruments [of perception] as well as attachment to sense objects; both of these lead to what is not beneficial, yet of the two, the former is considered the more serious.
Just as a fire in the hollow of a tree might burn down a tree entirely, root and all, so too,
even a slight fault of passion may destroy one who seeks the Dharma. Yet, one who is detached does not suffer from separation, for he perceives the faults inherent in union.

A person who is free from enmity and devoid of possessiveness attains dispassion. Therefore, one should use wisdom to turn away from attachment toward one's own kin, friends, and the accumulation of wealth, as well as that which arises from one's own body.

Among those who are endowed with knowledge, preeminent, learned in the scriptures, and self-disciplined, affection does not cling to them, just as water does not cling to lotus leaves. A person overcome by passion is dragged away by desire.
Desire arises for him, and from that, craving proceeds.
For craving is most evil among all things; it constantly causes agitation to men, abounds in unrighteousness, is terrible, and leads to further sin.
That which is difficult for the foolish to abandon, which does not age even as one ages,

and which is a disease that ends only with life— that craving brings happiness only when it is relinquished. Indeed, that craving of human beings has no beginning or end, yet it resides within the body.
It destroys what has been produced, like a fire born from a non-womb;
just as fuel meets its destruction by the fire arising from itself,
so too does one of undisciplined soul perish through innate greed.
From kings, from water, from fire, from thieves, and even from one's own kin;
from supplicants and from time— therefore, those who possess wealth always live in fear,
just as living beings always live in fear of death.
For just as meat in the air is devoured by birds, on the ground by beasts of prey, and in the water by fish, so too is a man of wealth preyed upon by everyone; indeed,
for some men, wealth itself becomes a source of misfortune.
A person who is attached to wealth and prosperity does not find true well-being;
therefore, all acquisitions of wealth increase the delusion of the mind,
as do miserliness, pride, arrogance, fear, and anxiety.
The wise know that these are the sufferings of embodied beings arising from wealth:
there is suffering in the acquisition of wealth, as well as in its preservation and its depletion;
there is suffering in its loss and suffering in its expenditure, and people even kill for the sake of wealth.
Wealth is difficult to abandon, and even when protected, it brings no happiness;
it is acquired with great hardship, yet one should not worry about its loss. Fools are intent on discontent, while the wise attain contentment.
There is no end to thirst; contentment is the supreme happiness.
Therefore, the wise regard contentment alone as true wealth in this world.
Youth, beauty, life, and the accumulation of riches are all impermanent.

A wise person should not covet sovereignty or the company of loved ones; therefore, one should abandon accumulations—for who could endure the suffering born of them? Indeed, no one possessing accumulations is seen to be free from affliction.
Therefore, among virtuous men, one who has no desire for wealth is praised;
for him whose striving for wealth is for the sake of dharma, it is better to be without such striving at all.
Indeed, it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, you ought not to harbor such longing for worldly objects;
if you have need for dharma, then become free from desire for wealth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"O Brahmin, this desire for wealth on my part is not for the sake of craving the enjoyment of objects; rather, I seek it for the maintenance of the Brahmins, and not out of greed. For how, O Brahmin, could one such as I, while living in the householder stage of life,"
One should not fail to provide maintenance and protection for one's followers;
indeed, the distribution of shares to all beings is enjoined.
Likewise, the householder must give to those who do not cook for themselves.
Grass, ground, water, and fourthly, kind speech—
these are never lacking in the homes of the virtuous. One should give a bed to the weary and a seat to one who is fatigued from standing.
One should give water to the thirsty and food to the hungry;
one should give sight, one should give thought, and one should give pleasant speech.
Furthermore, rising up, one should offer a seat; this is the eternal dharma.
One should go out to meet [the guest] and perform a formal reception according to the prescribed rule. For the Agnihotra fire, the draft-ox, kinsmen, guests, and relatives,
as well as one’s sons, wife, and dependents, would consume [the householder] with fire if they are not honored.

One should not cook food for one's own sake, nor should one slaughter animals in vain; nor should one eat that which has not been offered according to the prescribed rule. One should scatter [food] on the ground for dogs, for those who cook dogs (outcastes), and for birds.
For this is indeed called the Vaiśvadeva; it is prescribed for both evening and morning.
Therefore, one should always be an eater of *vighasa* and a consumer of *amṛta*.
*Vighasa* is the remains of what has been served to dependents, while *amṛta* is the remains of the sacrifice.
One should give sight, one should give mind, and one should give pleasant speech;
one should follow [the guest] and attend upon him— that is a sacrifice with five sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) for one who gives unwearyingly while traveling on the road.

For one who is weary and has never seen this before, the fruit of his merit is great. For him who lives according to this way of life while remaining in the householder stage, they say his dharma is supreme; what do you think, O Brahmin?
Śaunaka said:
Alas! What great misery! This world is indeed perverse, for that by which the virtuous man is put to shame brings satisfaction to the wicked.
For the sake of the genitals and the stomach, the unwise man creates much waste;
overcome by delusion and passion, he follows the power of the objects of the senses. Even while being conscious, a man is carried away by his alluring senses.
With his consciousness utterly bewildered, like a charioteer with runaway, wicked horses,
when the six sense-faculties encounter their respective objects,
then the mind arises within them, born from prior volitional formations.
When one's mind is impelled toward the objects of the collection of senses,
longing arises in him and active engagement is produced.
Then, by the power of volition, through desire, and with the arrows of sense-objects—

Pierced by it, one falls into the fire of greed; through greed, one falls like a moth into a flame. Then, O Lord of the People, deluded by pleasures and food, one is submerged in the mouth of great delusion and does not recognize oneself.
Thus one falls into saṃsāra, wandering like a wheel through various wombs here by means of ignorance, karma, and craving;
one revolves among all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
Arising again and again in water, on earth, and likewise in the sky—
this is the destiny of the ignorant; now hear from me concerning the wise,
those people who delight in the highest dharma and find their joy in liberation.
Regarding this Vedic injunction, "Perform action" and "Renounce action," one should not practice all these duties out of mere pride.
Sacrifice, study, charity, austerity, truthfulness, forbearance, and self-restraint— [these are the duties].
Non-attachment—this is the eightfold path of Dharma as it is remembered. Among these, the first four-fold group stands on the path of the ancestors;
one should perform what is to be done, not out of self-conceit.
The northern path, however, is that which leads to the gods and is always practiced by the virtuous;
one whose self is purified should traverse it by means of the eightfold path through the connection of right resolve and the proper restraint of the senses.
Through the proper observance of specific vows, through the proper service of the guru,
through the proper application of diet, through the proper acquisition of learning,
through the proper renunciation of action, and through the proper restraint of the mind.
Thus, performing such deeds while desiring to conquer saṃsāra,
those who are liberated from passion and hatred have attained divine sovereignty—
the Rudras, the Sādhyas, the Ādityas, the Vasus, and also the two Aśvins.
Endowed with the sovereignty of yoga, they sustain these creatures;
likewise, O son of Kuntī, you too, having established yourself in abundant tranquility,
should seek perfection through austerity and the perfection of yoga, O Bhārata.
"You have attained success consisting of your father and mother, as well as success born of ritual action.
Now, seek success through asceticism for the sake of supporting the twice-born;
for those who have attained perfection accomplish whatever they desire through their grace."
"Therefore, having undertaken ascetic penance, fulfill the desire of your soul.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by Śaunaka, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, [acted accordingly].
Approaching his family priest in the midst of his brothers, he said this:
"These Brahmins, masters of the Vedas, are following me as I set forth;
yet, burdened by much sorrow, I am not capable of protecting [the kingdom]."
"I am unable to abandon it, yet I lack the power to give it away.
What should I do in this matter? May the Blessed One tell me that.
Having reflected for a moment and sought the proper course through the Dharma, he replied:
Dhaumya, the best among the upholders of dharma, said this to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"In the beginning, created beings were severely oppressed by hunger;
therefore, out of compassion for them, the Sun-god acted like a father."
Having thus consoled him, the God then appointed him to the task of sustaining living beings.
Having traveled to the northern course and drawn up the essences of energy with his rays,
the Sun, returning to the southern course, enters the earth.

Then, upon that field-like [surface], the Lord of Herbs (the Moon), having extracted the splendor of heaven, generated [herbs] by means of water. Infused with the splendors of the moon, the sun, having descended to the earth, is brought forth.
The herbs, possessing the six tastes, are pure; they are the food of living beings upon this earth.
Thus, food consisting of light indeed sustains the life-force of all creatures.
He is the father of all beings; therefore, go to him for refuge.
For high-souled kings, purified by their lineage and their deeds, rescue all their subjects by resorting to abundant austerity—
such as Kārtavīrya Bhīma, Vainya, and Nahuṣa.
For indeed, by those established in austerity, yoga, and meditative concentration, calamities were lifted from their subjects;
likewise, you too, O righteous-souled one, purified by your actions,
should take up austerity and support the twice-born according to dharma, O Bhārata.
Having been addressed with these words by Dhaumya that were appropriate for the occasion,
he— steadfast in his vows, self-restrained, and established in the meditative absorption of renouncing worldly ties—
then taught him the mantra that accomplishes all goals.
The pure-souled Dharmarāja, who was constantly devoted to the supreme eight-syllable mantra dear to those in distress,
performed the highest austerity after worshipping the Sun with offerings of flowers and oblations.
Having plunged into the water, the righteous king stood facing the god; practicing yoga, subsisting on air alone, with his senses conquered,
he touched the water of the Gaṅgā and remained there in breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Having become pure and restrained in speech, Yudhiṣṭhira then began this hymn of praise:
"O Bhānu, you are the eye of the world; you are the self of all embodied beings."
You are the womb of all beings; you are the conduct of those who perform ritual actions.
You are the goal of all followers of Sāṃkhya; you are the supreme refuge of the yogins. You are the gate with its bolt unbarred; you are the destination of those seeking liberation.
By you the world is sustained; by you the world is illuminated;
by you it is purified; and by you it is protected without guile. Having attended upon you at the proper time, the Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas [attain their goals].

Seeking boons, the hosts of Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Guhyakas, and Pannagas follow your divine chariot as it moves along, worshipping with mantras prescribed by their own Vedic branches— that chariot which is honored by the throngs of Ṛṣis.
The thirty-three gods, as well as the hosts of celestial beings in their mansions—
both those with Upendra and those with Mahendra— have attained perfection by worshipping you;
indeed, having honored you, they have reached the fulfillment of their desires.
O supreme Vidyādharas, with divine mandāra garlands,
the Guhyakas, the seven classes of Pitṛs— both those who are divine and those who are human—
having worshipped you alone, quickly attain preeminence.
The Vasus, Maruts, Rudras, and those who are Sādhyas and Marīcipas,
as well as the Siddhas such as the Vālakhilyas and others, have attained preeminence among living beings throughout all seven worlds, including the realm of Brahmā.
I do not consider that being to exist which surpasses the Sun;
there are other beings who are powerful and great,
yet they possess neither such radiance nor such majesty as you do.
All luminaries are in you; you are the lord of all lights.
In you reside truth, goodness, and all states of being characterized by purity.
By your splendor, the discus with its beautiful hub was fashioned by Viśvakarman.
O wielder of the Śārṅga bow, by you the pride of the enemies of the gods was destroyed; taking up the heat of all embodied beings with your rays during the summer,
you release it again along with the essences of all medicinal herbs during the rainy season.

Some clouds scorch, others burn, and others roar; likewise, during your rainy season, they flash with lightning and pour down rain. Neither fire, nor outer garments, nor woolen blankets provide such comfort as you do.
Just as your rays [illuminate] that which is afflicted by cold winds in the world,
you illuminate the earth consisting of thirteen islands with your rays;
for the welfare of even the three worlds, you alone exert yourself.
If you were not to arise, this world would be blind;
wise men would not engage in the pursuit of dharma, artha, and kāma, nor would they perform the rites of consecration, animal sacrifice, offerings, mantras, formal sacrifices, and ascetic penances.

By your grace, the hosts of Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas attain that which is called a day of Brahma, measured by a thousand yugas; you are proclaimed by those who know time to be both its beginning and its end.
Of the Manus, the sons of Manu, and of the non-human world,
you are the Lord of all the lords of the Manvantaras;
when the time for dissolution arrives, [this world] issues forth from your wrath.

The fire of universal destruction stands having reduced the three worlds to ashes; born from your rays, these great clouds of various colors, accompanied by Airāvata and lightning, shall persist until the dissolution of all beings.
Having divided yourself twelvefold, you have attained the state of the twelve Ādityas;
having withdrawn the entire world into the single ocean, you dry it up with your rays.
They call you Indra; you are Rudra, you are Viṣṇu, and you are Prajāpati.
You are Agni; you are the subtle mind; you are the Lord, the eternal Brahman. You are Haṃsa, Savitṛ, Bhānu, Aṃśumālin, and Vṛṣākapi;
you are likewise Vivasvān, Mihira, Pūṣan, Mitra, and Dharma.

You are the thousand-rayed Āditya, the scorching one, and the lord of rays; you are Mārtaṇḍa, Arka, Ravi, Sūrya, the refuge, and likewise the maker of day; you are Divākara, the seven-horsed, the light-haired, and Virocana.
You are praised as the swift-moving, the destroyer of darkness, and the one with green horses. Furthermore,
Lakṣmī attends that man who, free from despondency and free from egoism, performs worship with devotion on either the seventh or the sixth lunar day.
For those who worship and pay homage to you with undivided minds, there are no calamities, nor mental anxieties, nor likewise physical ailments;
they are free from all diseases and liberated from all sins.

Those who possess devotion to Your nature become happy and long-lived. O Lord of Food, it behoves You to grant food with faith to me as well, who am desirous of food and wishing to offer hospitality to all.
And all those attendants of yours who have taken refuge at the edge of your feet—
Māṭhara, Aruṇa, Daṇḍa, and the others— I salute each of them,
as well as Kṣubhā, Maitrī, and the other Mothers of Beings (bhūtamātṛ).
"I bow down to all of them; may they protect me who has come for refuge.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O great king, having been praised in this manner, Bhāskara, the creator of the world,"
Janamejaya said:

Having worshipped him who is the soul of all beings with offerings of flowers and oblations many times according to the prescribed rites, he— his vital breaths restrained and his senses conquered— [proceeded].
How did that king Yudhiṣṭhira, the bull among the Kurus,
propitiate the Sun of wondrous prowess for the sake of the Brahmins?
O Brahmin, if you have affection for me, and if I am worthy of your favor—
"O Blessed One, if there is no secret, then tell it to me now.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Listen attentively, O King, having become pure and composed."
Wait a moment, O Indra among kings, and I shall tell you everything without omission.
Listen, O high-minded one, to those eight hundred holy names as they were spoken by Dhaumya to the great-souled son of Pṛthā.
Sūrya, Aryaman, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, Arka, Savitṛ, Ravi,
Gabhastimat, Aja, Kāla, Mṛtyu, Dhātṛ, and Prabhākara;
earth, water, fire, ether, and wind— these are his ultimate refuge.
Soma, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Budha, and Aṅgāraka;
Indra, Vivasvat, Dīptāṃśu, Śuci, Śauri, and Śanaiścara; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Skanda, Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama.
He is the fire of lightning and the digestive fire within the body; he is the fuel for the fires and the lord of all luminous energies.
He is the banner of dharma, the creator of the Vedas, the limbs of the Vedas, and the vehicle of the Vedas.
He is the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages, and the refuge of all the immortals.
He is the maker of the years,
the Ashvattha tree, the wheel of time, and the source of light;
he is the eternal Purusha, the Yogi, both manifest and unmanifest, the primeval one.

The overseer of the world, the overseer of creatures, the architect of the universe, the dispeller of darkness; Varuṇa, the ocean, the ray of light, the cloud, the life-giver, the slayer of enemies; the refuge of beings, the lord of beings, served by all beings.
The creator, the fire of destruction, the origin of all, free from greed;
the infinite, Kapila, the sun;
the jewel, the golden one, the source of beings, the granter of desires, facing in every direction.
Victorious, vast, the granter of boons, swift-moving, the sustainer of life,
served by all the elements;
Dhanvantari, the comet-bannered one, the primordial god, the son of Aditi.
The twelvefold one, the lotus-eyed, the father, the mother, and the grandfather;
the gate of heaven, the gate of progeny, the gate of liberation, and the celestial realm;
the creator of the body, the tranquil-souled, the soul of the universe, whose face is turned in every direction.
The soul of the moving and the unmoving, the subtle self, endowed with a friendly form—
this indeed is the hundred and eight meritorious names of the high-souled Sūrya, as spoken by the great-souled Śakra.
From Śakra Nārada received it, and after him Dhaumya;
from Dhaumya Yudhiṣṭhira received it and attained all his desires.
It is served by the hosts of gods, ancestors, and yakṣas.
Worshipped by the Asuras, night-stalkers, and Siddhas,
and possessing the radiance of a fine gold fire—
meditate upon that Sun within your mind.
The man who, with a concentrated mind, recites this at sunrise, shall obtain sons, accumulations of wealth and jewels,
and always possess the memory of his past lives.
And he attains supreme mindfulness and intelligence.
That man who, with a pure mind and concentrated attention, recites this hymn of praise to the best of gods;
He is liberated from the ocean of the forest fire of grief and shall obtain all desires as wished for in his mind.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the Sun, being pleased, revealed himself to the Pāṇḍava,
blazing with his own form like a flaming fire.
"O King, you shall obtain all that you have desired."
"I shall provide you with food for twelve years—
fruit, roots, meat, and vegetables prepared in the kitchen.
O lord of men, take this copper vessel given by me."
"O observer of noble vows, as long as the princess of Pañcāla desires food from this vessel,
those four kinds of edibles shall remain inexhaustible for you.
In the fourteenth year from now, you shall regain your kingdom once more."
Having said, "And various kinds of wealth shall be yours," he vanished. Whoever else here recites this hymn with effort and concentration, seeking to obtain a boon, shall likewise succeed.
The Sun shall grant him whatever he desires,
even if it be very difficult to obtain;
and whoever should constantly uphold this or listen to it repeatedly.
One who desires a son obtains a son; one who desires wealth obtains wealth;
and one who desires knowledge obtains knowledge—whether it be a man or a woman—whoever, male or female, recites this daily at both twilights.
Having encountered calamity, one shall be released; the bound shall be released from bondage.
Brahmā gave this [knowledge] in the past to the great-souled Śakra, and Nārada received it from Śakra, and Dhaumya received it immediately thereafter.
Having obtained [this] from Dhaumya, Yudhiṣṭhira attained all his desires;
he will always be victorious in battle and shall acquire vast wealth.
He is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of the Sun.
Having obtained the boon, the son of Kuntī, the knower of dharma, emerged from the water;
the steadfast one grasped the feet of Dhaumya and embraced his brothers.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of the twice-born, by your grace I have obtained what I desired;
having united with Draupadī and beholding her,
the lordly Pāṇḍava then proceeded to the kitchen and prepared the food."

The cultivated fourfold food produced by the forest becomes inexhaustible; that food increases, and with it he feeds the twice-born. And when the Brahmins have eaten, as well as his younger brothers whom he has caused to eat, [he performs the concluding rites].
Yudhiṣṭhira eats what remains, designated as *vighasa*, afterwards;
having fed Yudhiṣṭhira, the daughter of Pṛṣata eats the remainder.
Thus, having obtained [this food] from the Sun, she who possesses a splendor equal to the Sun—
The Lord bestowed upon the Brahmins all the objects of their desire;

and with the family priest at their head, sacrificial rites were performed on auspicious lunar days, under favorable constellations, and during sacred festivals, according to the authority of ritual manuals and mantras.
Then, having had the rites for a successful journey performed by Dhaumya, the Pāṇḍavas set out for the Kāmyaka forest, surrounded by throngs of twice-born brahmins.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the Pāṇḍavas had entered the forest, Ambikā’s son, whose eye was wisdom, being tormented by grief,
[approached] the righteous Vidura of unfathomable intellect.
Seated comfortably, the king spoke these words:
"Your wisdom is as pure as that of Bhārgava, and you understand the supreme and subtle Dharma."
"You are impartial and highly esteemed by the Kauravas;
speak what is beneficial for them and for me as well. Such being the case, O Vidura, tell me what must be done today."
"How might these citizens divide themselves from us?
And how might they not uproot us entirely? I do not desire their destruction."
By that very wicked son of Subala, who desires the welfare of Duryodhana, a cruel deed was committed; an act has been performed that is not pleasing to me.
Since this has indeed been done there, you ought to speak about it.
What else do you consider appropriate at this time, given that the opportunity has arrived?
My heart is breaking at the thought that there is no assistance to be found in righteousness,
where all the sons of Pāṇḍu suffer, having come to the forest.
Vidura said:
"O lord of men, this triad of human goals has its root in dharma;
they say that even this kingdom has its root in dharma."
O King, abiding by righteousness according to your own power,
protect all your sons and the sons of Kuntī;
for that very dharma has been violated in the assembly hall.
Having summoned the son of Kuntī to the game of dice, your son defeated that man true to his word by means of the evil-minded ones, headed by the son of Subala.
O King,
O Kauravya, I perceive a means for the remainder of this ill-conducted [act] of yours, so that your son may be freed from sin.
"May he be liberated and established in the world;
O King, may the sons of Pāṇḍu obtain all that which was granted by you."
This is the supreme dharma: that a king should find contentment with his own and not covet the property of others;
thus his fame shall not perish, and there shall be no dissension among his kinsmen.
If this were done, dharma would not exist;
yet this task is your foremost duty:
to bring them satisfaction and the humiliation of Śakuni.
"O King, if you have such [wealth] remaining for your sons, do this quickly;
O King, if you do not do this in this manner,"
The destruction of the Kurus is certain;
for when Bhīmasena or Arjuna are enraged, they would leave no remnant of the enemy host.
Those whose warrior is Savyasācin, skilled in weapons; those whose bow is Gāṇḍīva, the essence of the world; and those whose warrior is Bhīma, possessed of mighty arms;
What indeed is not obtainable in this world for those who have as their king the Great-Souled Son of Dharma?
What indeed is difficult to attain in this world for them?
It was said by me previously, when your son had just been born, that which was for your benefit at that time:
"Abandon this son, for he is harmful to the lineage."
O King, you did not do this;
now that beneficial advice has been spoken to you, if you do not act upon it, O King, you will suffer remorse later.
If this son of yours approves of this—
sharing a single kingdom with the Pāṇḍavas— then, being well-pleased through that bond of affection, no distress shall surely come upon you.
If you do not accept the son along with his companions,
then another will indeed seize him;
therefore, establish the son of Pāṇḍu in the sovereignty.
O wise one, the destruction of you, along with your son, your circle of kinsmen, and the kings,
is certain to occur in the fourteenth year, O lord of men.
O lion among kings, you will bring about the destruction of your own clan;
therefore, O lord of men, establish Yudhiṣṭhira, the foremost of the righteous, in sovereignty.
For Ajātaśatru is indeed freed from passion;
O King, let him rule this earth according to dharma.
Therefore, O King, let all these rulers of the earth—
"Let them attend upon us immediately, like Vaiśyas;
O King, let Duryodhana, Śakuni,
and the Sūta’s son serve the sons of Pāṇḍu with affection."
"Let Duḥśāsana entreat Bhīmasena and Drupada’s daughter in the midst of the assembly;
you, however, must console Yudhiṣṭhira."
"And having honored him, establish him in the kingdom.
When asked by you, what else should I say?
Having done this, O King, you will have fulfilled your duty."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Vidura, these words which you spoke here in the assembly concerning the Pāṇḍavas and me— "
"That which is beneficial for them is harmful for my people;
all of this does not enter my mind.
But now, from where could this [other matter] possibly be certain?"
Because of what you have said regarding those Pāṇḍavas,
I think today that you are not well-disposed toward me;
for how could I abandon my son for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas?
"Without doubt, they too are my sons;
yet Duryodhana was born from my own body.
Therefore, let him indeed sacrifice his own body for the sake of others."
Who indeed, observing impartiality, would speak thus? Vidura, you tell me everything crookedly;
yet I maintain even greater respect for you.
"Go or stay as you please;
for even when well-consoled, an unfaithful woman abandons [her husband].
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having said this much, O King, Dhṛtarāṣṭra rose up suddenly and entered his inner apartments; meanwhile,
Vidura spoke, saying, "This [plan] will not succeed."
He fled to where the sons of Pṛthā were.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"The Pāṇḍavas, those bulls of the Bharata race, having resolved upon dwelling in the forest..."
Departing from the banks of the Jahnavī with their followers, they proceeded toward Kurukṣetra;
having frequented the Sarasvatī, the Dṛṣadvatī, and the Yamunā,
they went continuously from forest to forest toward the western direction.

Then, on the banks of the Sarasvatī, in the level desert lands of Marudhanvan, they beheld the forest named Kāmyaka, which is dear to the sages. There those heroes dwelt in the forest, abounding in deer and birds.
O Bhārata, while they were being seated by the sages and comforted by them,
Vidura, longing for a sight of the Pāṇḍavas,
then departed for the prosperous Kāmyaka forest by means of a single chariot.
Then Vidura, having traveled to that forest by means of a chariot drawn by swift horses,
beheld Dharmarāja seated in a secluded spot.
Then, together with Draupadī, his brothers, and the brahmins,
that king, who was true to his word, quickly beheld Vidura approaching from nearby.
Then he said to his brother Bhīmasena:
"What indeed will the Kṣattṛ say to us when he meets us? I hope he has not [come] at the word of Saubala."
The summoner approaches for the sake of the gods;
will that petty bird not [use] weapons so as to defeat us once again at the game of dice?
"Summoned by someone with the words 'Come quickly!',
I am not able to retreat from Bhīmasena, nor can the Gāṇḍīva bow ever be brought into doubt."
"Our attainment of the kingdom would be uncertain," [they thought]. Then, O King, all the sons of Pāṇḍu rose up and received Vidura.
Honored by them, that descendant of Ajamīḍha met with the sons of Pāṇḍu as was appropriate;
and those bulls among men comforted Vidura.
Then they asked him the reason for his arrival, and he, in turn, related to them in detail everything that had occurred concerning Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā.
Vidura said:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke to me in private,
O Ajātaśatru, having embraced me and honored me.
Since things have come to this, having attained equanimity,
tell me what is beneficial for them and for me alike—
whatever is appropriate for the Kauravas that has been spoken by me as well.
What is beneficial and wholesome for Dhṛtarāṣṭra— that indeed is wholesome, yet his mind does not accept it;
therefore, I consider nothing else to be appropriate.
"O son of Pāṇḍu, I have spoken of the highest good,
yet the son of Ambikā did not listen to it;
for it was like wholesome food to one who is ill."
That which was being said did not please him;
O Ajātaśatru, he is not led toward what is beneficial,
like a corrupt woman in the house of a learned Vedic scholar.
Speaking thus, he was not pleasing to the bull of the Bharatas,
like a sixty-year-old man to a young maiden;
"O King, the destruction of the Kauravas is certain."
Truly, Dhṛtarāṣṭra does not attain what is beneficial,
just as water poured upon a lotus leaf does not remain; so too, the wholesome advice spoken to him does not stay with him.
Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra, filled with anger, said to me:
"O Bhārata, go wherever you have faith;
I no longer desire you as my companion."
O King, having been abandoned by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, I have come here in haste to rule over this earth or its cities.
All that I have spoken here in this assembly,
let that be held fast, as well as what I shall further declare,
while being joined by my rivals with intense afflictions.
He who, practicing patience, waits for his time while increasing [his power] like a self-possessed man tending a small fire,
he indeed enjoys the earth alone.
O King, he whose wealth is shared with his companions has companions who share in his suffering as well;
this is the means for gathering together one's companions.
They say that upon obtaining a companion, one attains the earth;
therefore, by always speaking the truth,
one immediately becomes dear to the world.
Truth is supreme, O Pāṇḍava, when free from idle chatter;
food should be shared equally with one's companions,
and one should not place oneself before them.
A ruler who conducts himself in this manner prospers with friends, sons, and an abundance of land, elephants, and horses;
he was formerly able to protect this earth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I shall do exactly as you say; having attained this supreme understanding, I will remain vigilant."
"And whatever else is appropriate to the place and time, that indeed should be spoken; I shall perform all of that.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, O Bhārata, when Vidura had departed for the hermitage of the Pāṇḍavas,
the highly wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra was consumed by grief,
reflecting upon the power of Vidura and his role in bringing about peace and war.
Perceiving that the supreme prosperity of the Pāṇḍavas was imminent,
he approached the gate of the assembly hall; bewildered by the memory of Vidura,
his consciousness overwhelmed, he fell down in the presence of the lords of the earth.
The king suddenly fell down, helpless like a tree cut at its roots. Having regained consciousness and risen from the surface of the earth,
the king spoke these words to Saṃjaya, who was standing nearby.
"My brother is my friend and is like Dharma itself in person;
remembering him today, my heart is as if being rent asunder.
Bring that knower of dharma, my brother, back here quickly."
Speaking thus, that king lamented piteously,
tormented by remorse and emaciated by the memory of Vidura.
Out of brotherly affection, O King, he addressed these words to Sañjaya:
"Go, Sañjaya, and find out about my brother Vidura—
whether he still lives after being cast out by me, a sinner, in my wrath. For by that brother of mine, not even the slightest [wrong] was ever done."
"An offense was previously committed against me by that wise one of immeasurable intellect.
How could that supremely intelligent man have incurred such offense from me?
That wise man would not abandon his life; go, Saṃjaya, and bring him back."
Having heard those words of the king and having paid him due respect, Sañjaya said, "So be it," and set out for the Kāmyaka forest.
Reaching that forest where the Pāṇḍavas were dwelling, he arrived there before long.
Then he beheld Yudhiṣṭhira, clad in a garment of deerskin,
seated together with Vidura and thousands of Brahmins,
protected by his brothers like Śatakratu by the gods.
Then Saṃjaya, having approached Yudhiṣṭhira, paid him honor;
he likewise rendered to Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins the respect they deserved.
When questioned by the king regarding his welfare, Saṃjaya sat down comfortably.
He explained the reason for his arrival and spoke these words:
"O Kṣattṛ, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, remembers you.
Go quickly to see him and restore that monarch to life."
Having paid his respects to those best of men, the Pāṇḍavas, the joy of the Kurus, Vidura said:
"O giver of honor, you ought to go at the command of that lion among kings.
Thus addressed, the wise Vidura, who was devoted to his own kin, [prepared to depart].
With Yudhiṣṭhira’s permission, he returned once more to Hastināpura. Having arrived at the king’s palace and paid his respects,
he then attended upon the high-souled monarch like a servant.
The powerful Dhṛtarāṣṭra said to that highly wise one:
"By good fortune you have arrived, O knower of dharma; by good fortune you remember me, O sinless one.
Today, both by night and by day, I am yours for the sake of you, O bull among the Bharatas."
"In my wakefulness, I see my own body appearing in various forms.
Taking Vidura onto his lap and smelling the crown of his head, he said,
"Forgive me for what you were told by me in anger."
The great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, out of affection for his brother, said:
"Yudhiṣṭhira is well and remains together with his brothers;
moreover, O bull of the Bharatas, I spend my nights and days for your sake."
"You alone are always dear to me, a brother endowed with every virtue.
Vidura said:
"O King, I have indeed forgiven you; you are our supreme elder."
For thus have I come quickly, intent upon seeing you;
for men whose minds are fixed on righteousness, O tiger among men, rush to the aid of the distressed, O King— of this there is no need for doubt.
"As my sons were to Pāṇḍu, so are your sons to me;
for today my mind is overcome with the thought that they are miserable.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus conciliated one another, those two brothers of great splendor—
Vidura and Dhṛtarāṣṭra— attained supreme joy.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard that Vidura had arrived and had been pacified by the king, the evil-minded King Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son was consumed with remorse. He summoned Saubala, as well as Karṇa and Duḥśāsana.
Entering, the king spoke these words, shrouded in the darkness born of ignorance:
"This minister of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
highly esteemed, Vidura— the wise friend of the sons of Pāṇḍu who is devoted to their welfare— has returned."
As long as Vidura does not yet turn his mind away from bringing the Pāṇḍavas here, so long must you deliberate on what is for my benefit;
for I shall see how it is that the sons of Pṛthā arrive here by some means.
Once again I shall go to my destruction, destitute and unrestrained; I shall resort to poison, or hanging, or a weapon, or entering the fire,
for I do not have the strength to behold those powerful ones here once more.
Śakuni said:
"O King, O lord of the people, why have you adopted the mind of a fool?
Having gone there after making an agreement, it shall not turn out thus."
"O bull of the Bharatas, all the Pāṇḍavas are established in truthful speech;
O dear one, they will never accept your father's word.
Or, if they do accept it, they will return again to the city."
If the Pāṇḍavas should return again to the city named after the elephant,
having cast aside their agreement, we shall once more make a wager;
all of us shall remain neutral, following the will of the king.
"Beholding many vulnerabilities among the Pāṇḍavas while remaining well-guarded themselves," Duḥśāsana said:
"O highly wise maternal uncle, it is exactly as you say."
"For as you speak to me constantly, your wisdom indeed pleases me.
O King, it shall happen exactly so; it will not be otherwise.
Those heroes will not return without having made an agreement regarding the time."
"And out of delusion they would undoubtedly return to the gambling match again.
Karna said:
"O Duryodhana, we all certainly look upon your desire with favor."
"O King, unanimity is indeed observed among us all.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by Karṇa, King Duryodhana then—
With his mind not at all joyful, he quickly turned his face away.
Then Karṇa, perceiving this, rolled his beautiful eyes in rage toward both Duḥśāsana and the son of Subala.
Extremely enraged, he spoke, exerting himself by his own power:
"O lords of men, listen to that which is my thought!
We all desire to do what is pleasing to the king, with our hands like those of servants."
"Nor are we all able to remain unwearied in his service.
Therefore, taking up our weapons, mounting our chariots, and clad in armor,
let us go together to slay the Pāṇḍavas who dwell in the forest."
When all of them have been pacified and have gone to an unknown destination,
the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and we ourselves shall be free from dispute—
so long as they remain destitute and so long as they remain devoted to grief.
"As long as they are deprived of their friends, so long are they vulnerable; this is my opinion.
Having heard those words of his, honoring them again and again, they all then replied to the son of the Sūta, "So be it!"
"This is the most important duty of the high-souled Kuru king.
Having spoken thus, all of them, filled with rage and having made their resolve, set out in separate chariots in groups to slay the Pāṇḍavas.
Having perceived through his divine vision that they had set out, the pure-souled Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana then arrived; and having seen them,
the Blessed One, who is worshipped by the world, forbade them all.
Approaching him who was seated with the eye of wisdom, he spoke in haste.
Vyāsa said:
"O Dhṛtarāṣṭra of great wisdom, listen to my words."
I shall speak to you for the supreme benefit of all the Kauravas. O mighty-armed one, it is not pleasing to me that the Pāṇḍavas have gone to the forest,
having been defeated through deceit by those who follow the will of Duryodhana.

"O Bhārata, remembering their sufferings when the thirteenth year is complete, they will, filled with rage, discharge their poison upon the Karūṣakas. Why then does this evil-souled son of yours, so dull-witted, act thus?"
Constantly enraged, he seeks to slay the Pāṇḍavas for the sake of the kingdom.
Let this fool be restrained; let your son attain peace. Desiring to kill them while they dwell in the forest, he shall be deprived of his life.
"O one of great wisdom, let that which is right be done, just as the wise Vidura has said, as Bhīṣma has said, as we have said, and as Kṛpa and Droṇa have said;
for war with one's own kin is censured."

O King, do not engage in that which is unrighteous and brings ill repute. For such is the attitude you hold toward the Pāṇḍavas, O Bhārata; if it is neglected, O King, it will lead to great misfortune.
"Or rather, O King, let this dull-witted son of yours go to the forest alone and unassisted, accompanied by the Pāṇḍavas;
for then there will arise between your son and the Pāṇḍavas an affection born of association."
O Lord of Men, if you were one who has already accomplished his task today, then it would be so;
or rather, O Great King, it is heard that whatever character is born with one at birth does not depart until death.
"What does Bhīṣma think, or Droṇa, or even Vidura? Or what do you yourself consider to be the appropriate course of action here, before our purpose passes away?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Blessed One, I too do not approve of this addiction to gambling.
O Sage, I believe that fate, having assailed me, has compelled me to do it.
Neither Bhīṣma, nor Droṇa, nor Vidura approves of this."

Gāndhārī did not desire this gambling match, yet it was set in motion through delusion. O Blessed One, though you know my resolve and am aware of everything, I am unable to abandon the senseless Duryodhana because of my affection for my son.
Vyāsa said:
"O King, son of Vicitravīrya, you have spoken the truth as you have said.
I know full well that a son is supreme; there is nothing superior to a son."
Even Indra was awakened by the falling of Surabhī’s tears;
there is nothing superior to a son, even over other abundant riches.
In this regard, I shall relate to you a great and supreme narrative.

O lord of the people, O King, listen to the conversation between Surabhi and Indra. Long ago, O dear one, when Surabhi—the mother of cows—had gone to heaven, she wept; Indra then felt compassion for her.
Indra said:
"O auspicious one, why do you weep? Is all well with the dwellers of heaven, or perhaps with humans and cattle? This [calamity] will not be a minor matter."
Surabhi said:
"O Lord of the Thirty-three, no calamity whatsoever is seen for you;
however, O Kauśika, I grieve for my son, and for that reason I weep."
"Behold this fierce plowman, my weak little son,
striking him with a goad while he is oppressed by the yoke.
O Lord of the Gods, look upon him as he is utterly exhausted and being beaten."
O Lord of the Gods, I am overcome with compassion and my mind is deeply distressed. There,
one among them is endowed with strength and bears a heavy burden,
while the other possesses little strength or vitality, being emaciated and covered in a network of veins.
"O Vāsava, I truly grieve for that [ox] who carries a burden with great difficulty;
though being struck by the goad and prodded again and again,
he is simply unable to carry that load— behold him, O Vāsava!"
Then, afflicted by grief and deeply distressed, I cried out to him, shedding tears from my eyes with a piteous voice. Indra said:
"O beautiful one, while thousands of your sons are being tormented, why do you feel pity here? Only one son among them is being tormented.
Surabhi said:
"O Śakra, if I had a thousand sons, my compassion would be exactly the same toward each; however, for one who is distressed, O Śakra, there is greater pity for his own son.
Vyāsa said:
O descendant of Kuru, having heard those sweet words of Surabhi, Indra was greatly amazed; he regarded his son as more precious than even his own life.
And right there, he suddenly poured down a torrent of water.
The Lord Pākaśāsana, creating an obstacle for the farmer, said:
"Just as Surabhi has declared, let it be so for you:
O King, among all your sons, your compassion is greater toward those who are distressed."
"O dear son, as my son Pāṇḍu was, so are you to me;
and so too is the highly wise Vidura. Out of affection, O King, I say this to you:
for a long time you shall have one hundred and one sons."
Only five [sons] of Pāṇḍu remain, and they too are dull-witted and deeply distressed;
my mind grieves for those wretched sons of Pṛthā as I wonder how they shall live and how they might even prosper.
"O King, descendant of Kuru, if you desire that the Kauravas remain alive here,
let your son Duryodhana seek peace with the Pāṇḍavas.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sage of great wisdom, it is exactly as you say;
I myself recognize this, as do all these lords of men.
Yet, you consider that which brings about the welfare and happiness of the Kurus to be right."
O sage, Vidura, Bhīṣma, and Droṇa have also said this to me:
"If I am worthy of your favor, and if you have compassion for the Kauravas,
then instruct my wicked-souled son Duryodhana."
Vyāsa said:
"O King, here indeed comes the venerable sage Maitreya,
having followed the Pāṇḍava brothers here with the desire to see us."

"O King, this great seer will instruct your son Duryodhana according to what is right for the sake of peace within your family. O Indra among kings, whatever he says should be carried out without hesitation."
"For if you fail to perform this task, he will curse your son in his wrath.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, Vyāsa departed, and Maitreya appeared.
Seeing that the seer had arrived, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men,
honored him according to tradition and inquired about the purpose of his visit. Together with his sons, the king received him with due hospitality.

Having performed all the rites beginning with the offering of water for the feet (*arghya*), King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, addressed the preeminent sage who was now at rest with great humility: "O Blessed One, has your journey through Kurujāṅgala been pleasant?"
Are the five heroic Pāṇḍava brothers well?
Do those bulls among men wish to abide by their agreement? Will the brotherly affection of the Kurus remain uninterrupted?
Maitreya said:
"While proceeding on my pilgrimage to sacred fords, I arrived at Kurujāṅgala;
there, by chance, I beheld the King of Dharma in the Kāmyaka forest."
O Lord, hosts of sages came there to see that high-souled one, who was clothed in matted hair and deerskin and dwelt in the forest of asceticism; it was there,
O Great King, that I heard of the delusion of your sons.
This calamity in the form of gambling, a great disaster, has now arrived.
Therefore, I have come to you out of concern for the Kauravas;
for, O Lord, my affection and love for you are always exceedingly great.
"O King, while Bhīṣma and you yourself are alive, it is not appropriate that your sons should be at variance with one another, O lord of men; for you yourself, O King,
are the central pillar in matters of restraint and favor."
O joy of the Kurus, why do you overlook this terrible injustice as it arises? O King, because of the conduct of the Dasyus that occurred in your assembly,
you do not shine in this gathering of ascetics.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, turning toward King Duryodhana, who was filled with indignation,
the venerable seer Maitreya spoke to him in gentle words.
"O mighty-armed Duryodhana, best among speakers, O highly wise one, listen to my words as I speak what is for your benefit. Do not bear malice toward the Pāṇḍavas, O King; act for your own welfare."
O bull among men, [this concerns] the Pāṇḍavas, the Kurus, and the world at large;
for all those tigers among men are heroes who fight with great prowess.
All of them possess the strength of ten thousand elephants, and they are firm, with bodies as solid as adamant.
All were devoted to the vow of truth, all were proud of their manliness, and they were the slayers of the enemies of the gods— those *rakṣasas* capable of changing form at will,
including the chief *rakṣasas* such as Hiḍimba and Baka, as well as Kirmīra.
As those great-souled ones were departing from here at night,
a fierce being, blocking their path, stood firm like an immovable mountain.
Bhīma, who delights in battle and is the foremost among the strong, [confronted] him with his might.

He struck him with the "animal-slaying" blow, as a tiger kills a small deer. Behold, O King, how Jarāsaṃdha, that great archer possessed of the strength of ten thousand elephants, was felled in battle by Bhīma during his conquest of the quarters.
Vāsudeva is their kinsman and the son of Pṛṣata is their brother-in-law;
what man subject to old age and death would sit in battle against them?
Therefore, O bull of the Bharatas, let there be peace between you and the Pāṇḍavas.
"O King, follow my words; do not fall under the power of death.
O lord of the people, as Maitreya was speaking thus, he struck the king’s thigh, which resembled the trunk of an elephant, with his hand.
Duryodhana, having smiled, scratched the earth with his foot;
the dull-witted one stood there without saying anything, his face slightly cast down. But seeing him refusing to listen and scratching the ground, [he spoke].
O King, upon seeing Duryodhana, anger took possession of Maitreya. Overcome by that wrath, Maitreya, the best of sages,
being impelled by destiny, set his mind upon cursing him.
Then, having sipped water for purification, Maitreya, his eyes bloodshot with anger, cursed that evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"Since you have disregarded me and do not wish to act upon these words..."
Therefore, receive now the fruit of this arrogance:
a great war shall arise, joined with hostility toward you,
wherein the powerful Bhīma will shatter your thigh with blows from his mace.
When these words had been spoken, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of the earth,
sought to appease the sage, saying, "May this not be so.
Maitreya said:
"O King, if your son attains peace in such a manner, O dear one, the curse shall not take effect; if it is otherwise, it will come to pass.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O king of kings, Duryodhana’s father, feeling ashamed, asked Maitreya: "How was Kirmīra struck down by Bhīma?
Maitreya said:
"I shall not speak, for you are full of malice and your son does not wish to listen.
Once I have departed, this Vidura will tell you everything.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, Maitreya departed as he had come; Duryodhana, agitated by the slaying of Kirmīra, went outside.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Kṣattṛ, I wish to hear of the slaying of Kirmīra; let it be told. How did the encounter between the Rākṣasa and Bhīmasena come to pass?
Vidura said:

Listen to this deed of Bhīma, whose actions transcend those of ordinary men; I have heard it before from them, again and again at the conclusion of their stories— how Bhīma of terrible prowess slew [the son of the king] in Ekacakrā.
His younger brother, of great heroism and vast prowess, was a *rākṣasa* with eyes copper-red with rage, arrogant and superior in strength;
he was shrouded by the ashes of calamity arising from the destruction of his elder brother.
Seeking an opening against Bhīmasena, he wandered this earth;
he heard that the Pāṇḍavas had been defeated at dice and were now on their way from here, O king of kings.
In three days and nights, they reached that forest named Kāmyaka.
O King, it was at the dead of night, when the hour had passed halfway through the deep stillness,
and the man-eating Rākṣasas of terrible deeds were roaming about.
The ascetics and the other forest-dwellers constantly avoided that forest from afar, it is said, out of fear of the man-eater. O Bhārata, as they were entering there, he blocked their path.
A terrifying Rakshasa with blazing eyes appeared, holding a firebrand;
stretching out his massive arms and displaying a fearsome mouth,
he stood blocking the path by which the best of the Kurus were traveling.
With his lips and fangs bared, his eyes copper-red, and his hair blazing upward,
he was like a cloud accompanied by lightning flashes and the rays of the sun,
and filled with crows; emitting a great roar, he was manifesting the illusory power of a rākṣasa.
He let out a vast roar like a rain-bearing cloud. Terrified by that sound, birds from all directions flew away crying out, those dwelling on land together with those dwelling in the water.
That forest, crowded with deer, leopards, buffaloes, and bears fleeing in all directions,
seemed as if it were moving away from his roar.
Its copper-colored sprouts, acting as arms, were struck by the wind from his thighs.
Climbing vines growing at a distance entwined themselves around the trees;
then, at that very moment, an exceedingly fierce wind blew,
and by the dust it raised, the sky became shrouded and its stars were lost.
An unknown great enemy of the five sons of Pāṇḍu,
like an incomparable surge of grief for the five senses,
he saw from afar the Pāṇḍavas clothed in black antelope skins.
He blocked that entrance to the forest like Mount Maināka;
having encountered him, the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇā was terrified and,
out of sheer fear, closed her eyes, for such a sight had never been seen before.
With her hair disheveled by the hand of Duḥśāsana,
she was like a river caught in agitation between five mountains;
as she was fainting there, the five Pāṇḍavas seized her.
While his senses were thus attached to their objects with delight,
Dhaumya then [neutralized] that Rakshasi illusion of terrible appearance by means of various Rakshasa-slaying mantras properly employed.
While the sons of Pāṇḍu were looking on, that powerful one destroyed their illusions.
Having lost his power of illusion, that exceedingly strong one, his eyes wide with rage,
appeared like Death himself— a base being who could assume any form at will.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, possessed of long-standing wisdom, said to him:
"Who are you? To whom do you belong? What may be done for you? Speak.
Thereupon, that Rākṣasa replied to Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma.
"I am indeed the brother of Baka, renowned as Kirmīra;
born in the Paiṭhīna lineage, I am an atheist and a reviler of the Vedas. I dwell in this empty Kāmyaka forest, free from all anxiety."
"Having constantly practiced my diet by defeating men in battle, [he said:
'Who are you that have arrived here in my presence as food?
Having defeated you all in combat, I shall devour you, free from all anxiety.'"
But Yudhiṣṭhira, having heard those words of that evil-minded man,
then declared everything— his lineage, name, and so forth— saying, "O Bhārata,
I am the Pāṇḍava Dharmarāja, if my name has reached your ears."
Accompanied by all his brothers, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and the others,
he— having been deprived of his kingdom and having resolved to dwell in the forest—
has now come to this terrible forest that is your domain.

But Kirmīra said to him: "By good fortune, this which has been long desired by my mind has now been brought about here by the gods. Having fallen into a state of supreme amazement, the Rākṣasa of terrible appearance [spoke].

"For the sake of slaying Bhīmasena, I have constantly traveled the entire earth with my weapon raised, yet I could not find him. By good fortune, this slayer of my brother, whom I have long desired, has now been found."
"O King, by him— relying on the power of his knowledge and appearing in the guise of a Brahmin— my beloved brother Baka was slain at Vetrakīya’s house;
for he possesses no innate strength."
"Hiḍimba, my dear friend who roamed the forest,
was killed by this evil-minded one, and his sister was carried off long ago.
That very fool has now arrived here in this dense forest of mine."
"Now that the time for our wandering has arrived and midnight has set in,
today I shall exact that long-accumulated enmity from him;
I shall satisfy the crane with his abundant blood."
"Today, having become free from debt to my brother and likewise to my friend,
I shall attain supreme peace by slaying this thorn in the side of the Rākṣasas;
provided that Bhīmasena was indeed released by Baka in the past."
"Today, O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall devour him while you look on.
Having slain this Vṛkodara of immense vitality today,
I shall consume and digest him, just as Agastya did the great Asura."
Thus addressed, the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira, true to his promise, replied with anger, "This shall not be! and he rebuked the Rākṣasa. Then the mighty-armed Bhīma, swiftly uprooting a tree—

Then, in the mere twinkling of an eye, Arjuna, the victorious, rendered that bow— ten vyāmas in height and devoid of arrows— ready for use, with the Gāṇḍīva possessing the weight and roar of a thunderbolt.

Having warded off Jishnu, Bhima rushed toward that demon of terrible appearance and spoke these words: "Stay! Stay! O descendant of Bharata. Having spoken thus to him, the enraged Pāṇḍava tightened his girth-belt.
Crushing hand against hand and biting his lips,
the powerful Bhīma, with a tree as his weapon, then rushed at him with speed;
he then brought that [tree], which resembled the staff of Yama, down upon his head.
He brought it down with great force, like Maghavan hurling his thunderbolt;
yet that Rākṣasa appeared unperturbed in the battle,
and he hurled a blazing brand like a flaming thunderbolt.
Then Bhīma, the best among strikers, kicked that hurled firebrand with his left foot; it returned toward the *rākṣasa*. Kirmīra, too, suddenly uprooted a tree and [hurled it] at the Pāṇḍava.
Enraged like Yama, the wielder of the staff, he fought back in battle;
that tree-fight ensued, destroying the trees,
just as in the past between the two brothers Vālin and Sugrīva, both desiring sovereignty.
The trees that fell upon their two heads were shattered in many ways,
just as blue and red lotuses are crushed by two elephants in rut; many trees there were reduced to fragments like muñja grass.
Like scattered rags, they quivered there in that great forest;
O lord of the people, that battle between trees lasted for a short while between the chief of the Rākṣasas and the best of men.
Then, while Bhima stood firm in battle, the enraged Rākṣasa lifted up a rock and hurled it; Bhimasena wavered,
and the Rākṣasa rushed toward him as he was numbed by the blow of the stone.
With rays scattered from his outstretched arms like Rahu upon the sun,
the two of them, having locked together and dragging each other to and fro,
both shone like two bulls engaged in combat.
Between those two there occurred a most tumultuous and exceedingly fierce encounter,
like that of two proud tigers armed with claws and fangs.
Duryodhana was emboldened by his contempt for [the enemy] and by the prowess of his own arms.
Beheld by the eyes of Kṛṣṇā, Vṛkodara grew in strength; then,
rushing forward in indignation, he seized him with his arms like one elephant with rutting temples and face seizing another.
Then the powerful Rakshasa seized him;
Bhimasena, the best among the strong, flung him away with his own strength. From the clashing of the arms of those two mighty warriors at that time, [a great sound arose].
A terrible sound arose in the battle, like the cracking of bamboos.
Then Vṛkodara, having violently seized him by the middle and cast him down,
shook him with force, as a fierce wind shakes a tree.
Seized by the powerful Bhīma in battle, the weak man struggled with all his might and dragged at the Pāṇḍava. Then Vṛkodara, perceiving that he was exhausted, [acted].
With his two arms, he bound him as one binds an animal with a rope;
though he was crying out with a great roar, sounding like a split kettledrum,
the king whirled him around for a long time while he struggled, deprived of his senses.
Perceiving that the Rākṣasa was despondent, the son of Pāṇḍu seized him with force by his two arms and slew him like an animal;
he pressed down upon the waist of that lowest of Rākṣasas with his knee.
Vṛkodara squeezed his throat with both arms; then,
seeing him with all his limbs paralyzed and his eyes rolling wildly,
he threw him down upon the ground and spoke these words.
"O wicked one, you shall not wipe away the tears of Hiḍimba and Baka; you have gone toward the abode of Yama. Having spoken thus, that hero among men—
With eyes rolling in rage, he cast away that Rākṣasa— who was quivering, with his garments and ornaments fallen off, and whose mind was bewildered— deprived of life.
When he, whose form was like a rain-cloud, had been slain,
the sons of the king placed Kṛṣṇā at their head and praised Bhīma for his many virtues.
Then, filled with joy, they departed for the Dvaitavana forest. Thus, O lord of men, Kirmīra was slain in battle by Bhīma at the command of that Dharmarāja, O Kaurava.
Then, having made that forest free of thorns, the unconquered one,
the knower of dharma, dwelt in that habitation together with Draupadī.
And all those bulls of the Bharata race, having comforted Draupadī, remained there.
With delighted minds and out of affection, they praised Vṛkodara. Then, once the Rākṣasa had been crushed and destroyed by the strength of Bhīma’s arms,
the heroes entered that forest, which was now secure and its thorn removed.
As I was traveling along the road, I saw that wicked-souled and terrifying being lying scattered in the great forest, slain by Bhima of fearsome strength;
and there, O Bhārata, I heard of this deed of Bhima.
To the brahmins who had gathered there and were speaking thus,
Vaiśampāyana said:
"In this manner, Kirmīra, the foremost of Rākṣasas, was slain in battle."
Having heard this, the king, intent on meditation, then sighed like one in pain.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard that the Bhojas, along with the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, had gone forth into the forest life, [the king...]
The heirs of the Pañcāla king and Dhṛṣṭaketu, the lord of Cedi, as well as the powerful Dhṛṣṭadyumna, gathered together in the great forest with the Pāṇḍavas who were tormented by grief.
The illustrious son of Śiśupāla and the highly heroic Kekayas— brothers renowned throughout the world—
advanced toward the Pārthas in the forest, filled with rage and resentment.
Keśava, Sātyaki, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata,
together with their ministers, allies, forces, and kinsmen,
went by that path to the forest and said to the Pārthas, "What shall we do?"
Reproaching the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, they said, "What shall we do?
Then all those bulls among Kṣatriyas, placing Vāsudeva at their head,
sat down surrounding the righteous King Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having saluted the best of the Kurus, the despondent Keśava spoke.
Vāsudeva said:
"Of Duryodhana, Karṇa, and the evil-minded Śakuni..."
The earth shall drink the blood of those four, with Duḥśāsana as the fourth;
having slain them in battle, along with their followers,
and having utterly defeated all of them together with the lords of men.
"Therefore, let us all consecrate Yudhiṣṭhira as the King of Dharma;
for he who serves by means of deceit deserves to be slain—this is the eternal law.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Arjuna pacified Janārdana, who was enraged by the assault upon the sons of Pṛthā and seemed as if he wished to consume all creatures,
by recounting Keśava’s previous incarnations to him while he was filled with wrath.
He proclaimed the deeds of that high-souled Satyakīrti—
of that immeasurable person, the Truth, of infinite splendor,
the wise Viṣṇu, Lord of Prajāpati and Protector of the World.
Arjuna said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, in former times you wandered for ten thousand years on Mount Gandhamādana as a sage who lived wherever evening found him."
O Kṛṣṇa, in former times you dwelt at Puṣkara for ten thousand and ten hundred years, subsisting on water alone;
and at the vast Badarī, O Madhusūdana, you remained with your arms raised aloft.
For a hundred years, O Kṛṣṇa, you stood on one foot, subsisting only on air;
with your upper garment cast aside, emaciated and covered with a network of veins,
you remained at the Sarasvatī during the twelve-year sacrificial session.

And then, O Kṛṣṇa, having reached the sacred site of Prabhāsa, which is frequented by holy beings, you, possessed of great splendor, remained for a thousand divine years performing austerities while standing on one foot, steadfast in your vow.
"Vyāsa told me that you exist for the sake of the world's continued activity;
O Keśava, you are the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of all beings, the beginning and the end;
O Kṛṣṇa, you are the repository of austerities and the eternal sacrifice."
O Hṛṣīkeśa, you are the eternal author of yoga and the author of Sāṃkhya;
you are the moral conduct of all yogas and the discipline of heroes.
Having slain the earthly Naraka and having recovered the jeweled earrings, [you have accomplished this].
O Kṛṣṇa, you released the first-born sacrificial horse;
having performed that deed for the sake of the worlds, you, the bull among men and conqueror of all worlds,
slew in battle all the assembled Daityas and Dānavas.
Then, O mighty-armed Keśava, having bestowed the sovereignty over all upon the Lord of Śacī, you manifested among human beings. Having become Nārāyaṇa, you were Hari, O scorcher of foes.
Brahmā, Soma, Sūrya, Dharma, Dhātṛ, Yama, Anala,
Vāyu, Vaiśravaṇa, Rudra, Kāla, space, earth, and the directions—
you are the Unborn One, the teacher of all that moves and is stationary, the Creator, O Puruṣottama.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Janārdana, you of immense splendor indeed performed sacrifices such as the Turāyaṇa and others, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, in the Caitraratha forest;
you offered a hundred times a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
