Then, in each sacrifice, you were present in full portions;
O delighter of the Yādavas, having also attained the status of being a son of Aditi,
you became renowned on earth as Viṣṇu, the younger brother of Indra.
O scorcher of foes, having become a child, you traversed the heavens, the sky, and the earth with three strides by your splendor, O Kṛṣṇa;
reaching the heavens and the firmament, you remain in the abode of the Sun.
O Soul of all beings, you outshone the sun with your own splendor; O Lord Kṛṣṇa, in those various thousands of manifestations, hundreds of asuras who delighted in unrighteousness were slain by you.

The nooses of Mura have been destroyed; Nisunda and Naraka have been slain; and the road leading toward the city of Prāgjyotiṣa has once again been made safe. At Jārūthī, Krātha and Śiśupāla, along with their followers, were offered as oblations.
Bhīmasena, Śaibya, and Śatadhanvan were all defeated;
likewise, with a chariot possessing the roar of a rain-cloud and the splendor of the sun,
you carried off the Bhoja queen after defeating Rukmin in battle.
Indradyumna was slain in anger, as was the Yavana Kaśerumān;
Śālva, the lord of Saubha, was killed by you, and Saubha itself was brought down.
Thus have these been slain in battle; now hear further of others as well.
Likewise, on the Irāvatī, both Gopati and Tālaketu— Bhojas equal to Kārtavīrya in battle— were slain by you.
And that holy Bhogavatī, beloved by the sages, O Janārdana, [was also subdued].

Having brought Dvārakā under your own control, you shall cause it to be carried away by the ocean. O Madhusūdana, O Daśārha, neither anger, nor envy, nor falsehood resides in you; how much less cruelty or crookedness?
O Acyuta, having approached you as you sat in the midst of the mind, blazing with your own splendor,
all the sages begged for protection from fear.
O Madhusūdana, at the end of the age, you withdraw all beings into yourself.
O scorcher of foes, having made the world one with yourself, you sit within your own self;
O Vārṣṇeya, at the beginning of the age, Brahmā— the teacher of all that moves and is stationary, from whom this entire universe originates— was born from the lotus of your navel.
When the two terrible Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
rose up to slay him, Śambhu— the trident-wielder with three eyes— was born from the forehead of Hari, who was enraged by their transgression.
"In this way, Nārada told me that these two lords of the gods have arisen from your own body and are the executors of your commands;
likewise, O Nārāyaṇa, in former times through sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees..."
O Kṛṣṇa, you have performed a great sacrificial session in the Caitraratha forest;
neither those of the past nor those of the future will ever perform such deeds as these which you, O God of great splendor, accomplished even while a child.
O lotus-eyed one, accompanied by Baladeva, you performed [these deeds];
and you also dwelt together with Brahmā in the palace of Vairāja.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to himself, the son of Pāṇḍu, who is the very self of Kṛṣṇa, remained silent; then Janārdana said to Pārtha:
"You are mine alone, and I am yours alone; those who are mine are yours, and those who are yours are mine."
"He who hates you hates me; he who follows you follows me.
You are Nara, O invincible one, and I am Hari, indeed Nārāyaṇa.
We two, the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa, have come from that world to this world."
"O Pārtha, you are not other than I; O Bhārata, I am not other than you. It is impossible to perceive any difference between us, O bull of the Bharatas.
When these words had been spoken by the high-souled Keśava, [the battle continued].
Having spoken thus to his beloved Pāṇḍava,
the lotus-eyed Hṛṣīkeśa, being well-pleased, became silent;
for that assembly of heroes was filled with kings who were then highly agitated.
Surrounded by her heroic brothers headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
the Pāñcālī Kṛṣṇā approached the lotus-eyed one as he sat with the Yādavas, and seeking refuge, she spoke to that protector.

"O Acyuta, you are Vāsudeva among the Vasus and Vāsava [Indra] in many ways; you are the God of gods for all the worlds," so Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana has said. They call you the sole Prajāpati at the beginning of the creation of beings.
Asita Devala said: "O invincible Madhusūdana, you are Viṣṇu, the creator of all beings;
you are the sacrifice and the sacrificer, just as the son of Jamadagni declared."
The seers have declared you to be forgiveness and truth, O Supreme Person;
from truth you were born as sacrifice, just as Kaśyapa has described you. You are the Lord of lords even over the Sādhyas, the gods, and the Vasus.
O Creator of the World, O Lord of the World, just as Nārada has described you—
how you, O tiger among men, sport again and again with the hosts of gods beginning with Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and Śakra, like a child with his toys.
The heavens are pervaded by your head, O Lord, and the earth by your two feet;
these worlds are your belly—you are the eternal Puruṣa. For those whose souls have been purified by austerity and who are heated by the fire of knowledge and penance, [you are the goal].
O best of sages, O Supreme Person, you are the refuge for those sages who have realized the vision of the Self,
for the royal sages who perform meritorious deeds and do not retreat in battle,
and for all those endowed with every virtue.
You are the Lord, you are the All-pervading, you are the Earth, you are the Self-born, and you are the Eternal. The world-protectors, the worlds, the constellations, the ten directions,
the sky, the moon, and the sun— all are established in you.
The mortality of living beings and the immortality of the dwellers of heaven—
O mighty-armed one, all the affairs of the world are established in you. Out of affection for you, O Madhusūdana, I shall relate my sorrow to you.
"You are the lord of all beings, both those who are divine and those who are human.
O Lord Kṛṣṇa, how indeed could a wife of the Pārthas, your friend,
the sister of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and one such as I, be dragged into the assembly hall?"
In my menses, trembling and drenched in blood,
clad in a single garment, I was dragged away in distress into the assembly of the Kurus—
into the midst of the kings in the hall, while I was covered in dust.

And seeing me being dragged along, O Mādhava, wretched and like one who is helpless, the evil-minded sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra laughed aloud. They said to those [others], "These five Pāṇḍavas are like sterile sesame seeds."
"Choose another husband," they all said to me, O Madhusūdana;
"they wished to enjoy me as their slave, O Madhusūdana,
while the sons of Pāṇḍu, the Pañcālas, and the Vṛṣṇis were still alive."
"O Kṛṣṇa, am I not by law the daughter-in-law of both Bhīṣma and Dhṛtarāṣṭra? Yet I have been forcibly reduced to slavery!
I reproach the Pāṇḍavas alone, those mighty ones who are preeminent in battle."
"O Janārdana, fie on the strength of Bhīmasena and fie on the archery of Pārtha, those two who could endure seeing their illustrious lawful wife being tormented by these wretches!"
This path of dharma is eternal, always practiced by the virtuous:
that husbands protect their wives, even when they themselves are weak in strength.
When the wife is protected, the progeny is protected.
When offspring is protected, one's own self is protected;
for one's self is born within her, and thus she becomes a wife. A husband must be protected by his wife; how else could my wife [be born] from my own womb?
"Indeed, these [others] never abandon those who have come to them for refuge;
yet the Pāṇḍavas did not extend such protection to me, who had sought their shelter.
These five princes, born of the five [Pāṇḍavas], possess immeasurable prowess."
O Janārdana, for the sake of looking after them as well, I must be protected:
Prativindhya from Yudhiṣṭhira, Sutasoma from Vṛkodara,
Śrutakīrti from Arjuna, and Śatānīka from the son of Nakula.
The youngest was Śrutakarman; indeed, all of them were of truthful prowess. O Kṛṣṇa, just as Pradyumna is, so too were those great chariot-warriors.
Surely these are the best of archers, invincible in battle by their enemies.
For what reason do they endure the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who are so much weaker?
Their kingdom has been seized through unrighteousness, and likewise, we have all been made slaves. And I was dragged into the assembly hall while wearing but a single garment and in my courses.
Even the stringing of the Gāṇḍīva, which cannot be accomplished by anyone else except for Arjuna, Bhīma, or you, O Madhusūdana— fie on the strength of Bhīmasena, and fie on the Gāṇḍīva of Pārtha!
O Kṛṣṇa, as long as Duryodhana lives for even a moment,
time creates all beings and time destroys all creatures; I consider this to have been ordained by Time, not an increase in your own prowess.
O Madhusūdana, that wicked man who formerly expelled from the kingdom those boys— those students established in their vows— who were accompanied by their mother and were harmless,
caused poison to be mixed into Bhīmasena’s food.
"O Janārdana, that fresh, sharp Kālakūṭa poison, which causes the hair to stand on end when gathered,
has been digested by Bhīma along with his food without any adverse effect, O mighty-armed Puruṣottama, because a portion of it remains."
When Vṛkodara was unsuspecting and fast asleep at the crossing of the Pramāṇa river,
Kṛṣṇa bound him, threw him into the Gaṅgā, and returned.
When the son of Kuntī awoke, he tore his bonds asunder.
The mighty-armed and immensely powerful Bhīmasena arose;
he then caused black, venomous serpents to bite him as he slept in every part of his body, yet that slayer of enemies did not die.
But upon waking, the son of Kuntī crushed all the snakes;
with a mere flick of his hand, he struck down his beloved charioteer.
Furthermore, he burned the sleeping children at Vāraṇāvata.
Who indeed would be capable of doing that— to lie down with the noble lady while she was weeping in fear and spoke thus to the Pāṇḍavas,
having fallen into great calamity and being surrounded by fire?
"Alas! I am destroyed! Where indeed can there be peace from this fire today?
Helpless, I shall perish along with my young sons.
There, the mighty-armed Bhīma possesses prowess equal to the speed of the wind."
Vṛkodara comforted his noble sister and his brothers as well, saying:
"Just as Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā and the best of all who fly, so shall I swoop down; there is no cause for fear here."
Placing the noble lady on his left hip and the king on his right,
and holding the twins upon his shoulders as well as Bībhatsu on his back,
the valiant one suddenly sprang up with speed, carrying them all.

The powerful one liberated his brothers and their noble sister from the fire. Then all those illustrious ones set out at night with their mother and reached the great forest of Hiḍimba’s grove nearby.
Exhausted and deeply distressed, they fell fast asleep there along with their mother.
While they were sleeping, a Rākṣasī named Hiḍimbā approached them;
she saw the Pāṇḍava lying there together with his brothers.
Overcome by passion, she indeed desired Bhīmasena;
having placed Bhīma’s feet upon her own lap,
that beautiful woman, filled with joy, then pressed them firmly with her soft hands.

The powerful Bhima, of immeasurable soul and true prowess, perceived her; and he asked her, "O blameless one, what do you desire here? Thus addressed by Bhima, that Rākṣasī, who could assume any form at will, [replied].
To the high-souled Bhīmasena, she of the pure smile said this:
"Flee from here quickly! My brother, possessed of great heroism, will come to slay you; therefore, go without delay."
Then Bhīma spoke these words to her with pride:
"I shall not tremble before him; I will slay him when he arrives.
I shall fight against this Rākṣasa who has come as your brother."
Having heard what they said, that lowest of Rākṣasas arrived,
possessing a terrifying form and emitting loud roars, fearsome to behold.
Then that angry man-eating Rākṣasa spoke to her.
"With whom are you conversing? Bring him here into my presence;
O Hiḍimbā, we two shall devour him—you should not delay.
With a heart seized by compassion, that wise woman [replied].
Out of compassion, the blameless lady did not wish to tell him that; meanwhile,
that man-eating Rākṣasa, uttering terrible roars,
then rushed impetuously toward Bhīmasena.
Seeing that mighty Rākṣasa approaching, the exceedingly powerful Bhīmasena suddenly rose up and seized him;
rushing toward him in great fury, the strong hero assailed him with immense speed.

The Rākṣasa seized Bhīmasena’s hand with his own; that hand was as firm as a thunderbolt, possessing the impact of Indra’s lightning and a solid, adamantine structure. Grasping it, he suddenly flung his arm at Bhīmasena.
Then Bhimasena, the mighty-armed Vṛkodara, could not endure the Rākṣasa seizing his hand with his own; he grew furious there. A tumultuous battle then took place between Bhimasena and Hiḍimba.
O sinless one, after sporting for a very long time with that Rākṣasa— both being experts in all weapons like the terrible Vṛtra and Vāsava— the mighty Bhīma,
possessed of great heroism, then struck him down when he was rendered powerless.
Then, with palms like thunderbolts and with fists, he struck him.
Thereupon, the mighty-armed Bhīma, assuming a truly massive form,
furiously slew the Rākṣasa, just as the Lord of the Gods slew Vṛtra.
Having slain Hiḍimba, Bhīma then set out with his brothers,
placing Hiḍimbā at their head— the woman from whom Ghaṭotkaca was born.
Thereupon, all those illustrious ones fled together with their mother.
Facing Ekacakrā, surrounded by throngs of Brahmins,
Vyāsa served as their counselor for the journey— dear and well-wishing.
Then the Pāṇḍavas, firm in their vows, departed for Ekacakrā.
There they also encountered a man-eater named Baka, who was possessed of great strength,
terrifying, and equal to Hiḍimba himself;
and Bhīma, the best among strikers, slew that fierce one as well.
Accompanied by all his brothers, he went to the city of Drupada.
While dwelling right there, Savyasācin obtained me,
just as you, O Kṛṣṇa, won Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka.

"O Madhusūdana, thus was I won by Pārtha in fair combat at the svayaṃvara, after he had performed a great feat difficult for others to achieve. Thus have we been tormented by many afflictions and are deeply distressed."
"O Kṛṣṇa, these men, led by Dhaumya, have been dwelling here deprived of their noble lady;
though they possess the prowess of lions and are superior to all enemies in valor,
how can they remain indifferent while I am thus tormented by those who have wronged me?"
Such agonies as these, blazing for a long time, are endured by those who are exceedingly weak— those evildoers of trivial deeds. Indeed, I was born into a great family by means of a divine rite.

"I am the beloved wife of the Pāṇḍavas and the daughter-in-law of the high-souled Pāṇḍu; O Kṛṣṇa, I am that virtuous and excellent woman who has been seized by the hair while the five [Pāṇḍavas], who are like Indra himself, look on, O Madhusūdana."
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇā, who speaks softly, covered her face with her hand— which was as radiant as a lotus bud— and wept;
she had breasts that were full, well-formed, auspiciously marked, and not yet sagging.
The princess of Pañcāla rained down teardrops born of sorrow;
wiping her eyes and sighing again and again,
she spoke these words in anger, her throat choked with tears.
“O Madhusūdana, I have no husbands, nor sons;
I have no brothers, nor father, nor you, nor kinsmen— those who,
like those free from grief, look on with indifference while I am being mistreated by the base.”
My grief does not subside because Karṇa laughed at me then.
O Kṛṣṇa, for four reasons— out of kinship, out of respect, out of friendship, and indeed out of your lordship— I must always be protected by you, O Keśava.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, having heard those words of Draupadī in that assembly of heroes, Kṛṣṇa— filled with wrath and indignation— consoled that woman of excellent limbs with well-chosen words.
Indeed, the women of those with whom you are angry, O passionate lady, will weep thus for them—
covered by the arrows of Bibhatsu, drenched in floods of blood,
slain, and having abandoned life as they lie upon the surface of the earth.

"O lady of faultless limbs, you shall hear from the mouths of your enemies, headed by Duryodhana, what I shall do for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas; do not grieve. I promise you this in truth: you shall become the queen of kings."
"The sky might fall, the Himalayas might shatter, the earth might break into pieces,
and the ocean might dry up— O Kṛṣṇa, my word shall never be in vain.
Having heard those words from Acyuta, Draupadī then offered this reply.
Turning her gaze askance, that princess of Pañcāla looked at her middle husband.
Then, O Great King, Arjuna spoke to Draupadī:
"Do not weep, O lady with beautiful copper-hued eyes; do what Madhusūdana has told you."
"O Goddess, O lady of excellent complexion, it shall be exactly so and not otherwise.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna said:
"I will slay Droṇa, while Śikhaṇḍin shall slay the Grandfather."
Bhīmasena will slay Duryodhana, Dhanañjaya will slay Karṇa,
and the son of Mādrī will kill Śakuni, that gambler with the dice.
Relying upon Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, O lady of pure smiles, we are invincible.
"Even against the two slayers of Vṛtra in battle, how much more so against the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra?
Vaiśampāyana said:
When this was said, the heroes turned toward and approached Vāsudeva.
In their midst, the long-armed Keśava spoke these words.
Vāsudeva said:
"O lord of the earth, you would not have fallen into this distress."
"O King, if I had been present in Dvārakā previously,
I would have come even uninvited to the gambling match by the Kauravas,
O invincible one, and by King Duryodhana, the son of Ambikā."

I would have prevented the gambling, pointing out its many evils, after having summoned Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and Bāhlika; [I would have said to] King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Vicitravīrya: "Enough with this gambling, O Kaurava!"
"O Lord, O Indra among kings, regarding your sons and for your sake,
I shall explain there the faults by which you were deposed from your position, and by which the son of Vīrasena was formerly cast down from his kingdom."

O lord of the people, I shall indeed describe to you that [treatise] by the king Puṣkara, as well as the destruction of one who does not eat [the prescribed food], and the gambling, along with the constant addiction to it,
exactly as they are.
Women, dice, hunting, and drinking— these four vices arising from desire have been declared, O King, by which one is deprived of prosperity. Regarding these matters,
those learned in the scriptures maintain that one must speak out in every instance.
Moreover, those who know the art of gambling observe that one must speak specifically of it:
in this [game], the loss of wealth in a single day is certain, as is calamity;
there is the destruction of riches before they have been enjoyed, and nothing but verbal harshness.

"O Kauravya, O mighty-armed one, I shall speak of this and other related matters that result in bitter consequences regarding the game of dice when I have approached the son of Ambikā. If, being thus addressed by me, he should accept my words,"
O joy of the Kurus, there would have been well-being for the dharma of the Kurus,
O Indra among kings, had he not disregarded my sweet words; and had he done so,
O best of the Bharatas, I would have restrained him by force.
Then, having brought them together, I shall cause dissension among all those so-called friends who are in fact enemies, as well as the members of the assembly and the gamblers;
I shall seize them all and bind them with the nooses of Varuṇa.
"O Kauravya, it was because of my absence from the Anartas at that time that you have met with this calamity caused by the gambling match. Therefore,
O best of the Kurus, O son of Pandu, I have now come to Dvaraka."
"I heard from Yuyudhāna exactly as it happened that you were in distress.
As soon as I heard this, O Indra among kings, my mind became extremely agitated;
desiring to see you, O lord of the people, I have come here in haste."
"Alas, O bull of the Bharatas, we have all fallen into great distress,
we who behold you in calamity along with your brothers.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, O delighter of the Vṛṣṇis, how was it that you were absent? Where did you dwell while away, and what did you do while living abroad?
Kṛṣṇa said:

"O bull of the Bharatas, O best of men, I went to Saubha, the city of Śālva, in order to destroy it; hear from me the reason for that. That king was possessed of great splendor, mighty arms, and great fame."
O best of the Bharatas, at your Rājasūya sacrifice, the heroic Śiśupāla, the son of Damaghoṣa, was slain by me because of the offering;
that evil-minded one, overcome by the power of rage, could not endure it.

O descendant of Bharata, hearing that he had been slain, Śālva was overcome with intense rage; while I remained here, he approached the deserted Dvārakā. O King, there he was fought by the young Vṛṣṇi heroes.
Having mounted the Saubha, which moves at will, that king, a doer of cruel deeds, arrived;
for by the grace of the Lotus-born One, he too was long-lived.
Then, having slain those many young heroes of the Vṛṣṇis at that time—
The evil-minded one destroyed all the city gardens and said, "O mighty-armed one, where has that Vasudeva, the lowest of the Vṛṣṇi clan,
that dull-witted son of Vasudeva, gone?"
"I shall destroy the pride of him who seeks battle in combat. O people of Ānarta, tell me truly where he is; having slain that slayer of Kaṃsa and Keśin, I shall return."

"I shall not turn back without having slain him; by this truth, I touch my weapon. "Where is he? Where is he? thus he ran here and there, desiring indeed to fight with me in battle, that king of Saubha.
Today, out of indignation at the slaughter of Śiśupāla, I shall send that evil-doer, that base betrayer of trust, to the abode of Yama—
that brother of mine who was struck down by my sinful nature.
"I shall slay that King Śiśupāla upon the surface of the earth;
though he was my brother, a child, and a king, he was not slain by me at the front of the battle, nor while he was heedless— I, a hero, shall now kill that Janārdana."
Having lamented in this manner and other ways, O Great King,
that evil-minded king of Mārtikāvata, the descendant of Kuru, ascended to heaven by means of the Saubha chariot that moves at will, leaving me behind, O joy of the Kurus.
Having gone there, O Kauravya, I heard how that evil-minded king of Mārttikāvata had behaved toward me;
and then, O Kauravya, my eyes became clouded with rage.

Having resolved this in his mind, O King, he set his heart upon his slaughter. He considered the oppression and insults he had suffered at the hands of the Ānartas, as well as the swelling arrogance of that evildoer, O Kaurava.
Then, O lord of the earth, I set out for the destruction of Saubha;
while seeking it, I beheld him at Sagarāvarta.
Thereupon, O king, I blew my conch, Pāñcajanya.
Having summoned Śālva to battle, I stood ready for combat;
for a brief moment there was fighting with the Dānavas,
and they were all brought under my control and struck down upon the earth.
O mighty-armed one, this was the task for which I did not come then; as soon as I heard that Hastinapura had been reached and that the gambling match arising from such misconduct had occurred,
I have come quickly, desiring to see you all who are so deeply distressed.
"O lord of men, as soon as I heard that, I came here in haste at that very moment.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Vāsudeva, O mighty-armed one, O high-minded one, [tell me] in detail..."
"Tell me of the slaughter of Saubha, for I am not satiated by the telling.
Vāsudeva said:
"O mighty-armed one, having heard that King Śrutaśravas was slain by me..."
O best of the Bharatas, O son of Pāṇḍu, that evil-minded Śālva besieged the city of Dvāravatī from all sides by means of a stratagem;
indeed, Śālva stood there having arrayed that city in the air.
Then, stationed there, the protector of the earth attacked that city with his entire force; a battle took place there. The city was fortified on all sides, adorned with banners and gateways.
It was equipped with wheels and defensive towers, as well as mechanical engines and miners; it possessed upper chambers, main streets, and watchtowers, along with gatehouses,
grappling hooks, firebrands, missiles, and battering rams.
O best of the Bharatas, O King, it was equipped with spears, drums, cymbals, and small drums; provided with fuel, grass, and *kuśa* grass; furnished with *śataghnīs*, iron clubs, and plows;
and supplied with *bhuśuṇḍīs*, stones, mallets, weapons, and battle-axes.

O bull of the Bharata race, that army was equipped with iron armor and shields, possessed fire, and included *huḍa* and *śṛṅgika* weapons; it was joined according to the rules prescribed in the treatises,
and was furnished with many various materials such as Gada, Sāmba, Uddhava, and others.
O tiger among the Kurus, that force known as the *sārasa* was protected by men who were capable of repelling the enemy—
heroes of renowned lineage whose prowess had been witnessed in battle—
and by the central division (*madhyama-gulma*).
With the thorny bushes cleared away, and by means of horses and foot-soldiers,
Ugrasena, Uddhava, and the others— guarding against negligence— proclaimed throughout the city: "Wine must not be drunk!"
"King Śālva might indeed launch an attack against those who are heedless.
Thinking thus, all those Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas remained vigilant,
as did all the people of Ānarta, including the actors, dancers, and singers.
All those who guarded the stores of wealth were driven out;
all the bridges were demolished and the boats were forbidden from crossing. Furthermore, O Kauravya, the moats were made secure by being firmly braced with stakes.
O best of the Kurus, wells and likewise water-vessels were constructed;
for a distance of one *krośa* on all sides, the uneven ground was leveled,
all the bridges were repaired, and the walls were renovated.
By its very nature it was uneven and difficult to traverse, and by its very nature it was well-protected;
by its very nature it was equipped with weapons, O sinless one, especially at that time. It was well-guarded, well-concealed, and furnished with all kinds of armaments.

O best of the Bharatas, that city was just like the abode of Indra. O King, at the time of the encounter with Saubha, no one entered or departed from the city of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas without a seal.
O Kaurava, O Indra among kings, throughout all the streets and at the crossroads, there was an army abounding in elephants and horses;
it had been provided with wages and food, and supplied with weapons and equipment.
O mighty-armed one, at that time the army was composed of those who had performed great deeds;
there was no one receiving wages for grain, nor anyone whose wages were overdue,
nor anyone supported as a favor, nor anyone whose prowess had not been witnessed.
"Thus, O King, Dvārakā has been well-provided for by those who give profuse sacrificial fees,
and it is well-guarded by King Āhuka, O lotus-eyed one.
Vāsudeva said:
Having approached that place, O Indra among kings, Śālva, the lord of Saubha,
then encamped with his army, which abounded in men and elephants,
on level ground near a vast reservoir of water.
Equipped with the fourfold army and protected by King Śālva,
that force settled there, avoiding cremation grounds, temples of the gods, anthills, and sacred shrines.
By the division of the divisions, six paths were made; O King, there were also nine slopes in Śālva’s camp. It was equipped with all kinds of weapons and filled with those skilled in every weapon.
Thick with chariots, elephants, and horses, crowded with foot soldiers and banners, it was filled with contented and well-fed people, marked by the characteristics of heroes,
and possessed diverse flags, armor, chariots, and bows.
O descendant of Kuru, O bull among men, having established himself in Dvārakā,
he then advanced with speed like the king of birds.
Then, seeing Balarāma approaching, the lord of Śālva—
Having gone out, O Kaurava, the princes who were the delights of the Vṛṣṇis went forth to fight, unable to endure that invasion by King Śālva—
namely Cārudeṣṇa, Sāmba, and the great car-warrior Pradyumna.
All of them, armored and equipped with chariots adorned with various ornaments and banners,
engaged in combat with many of Śālva’s foremost warriors.
Then Sāmba, seizing his bow, [attacked] Śālva’s minister in battle.

Greatly delighted, he fought against Kṣemavṛddhi, the commander of the army. O best of the Bharatas, the son of Jāmbavatī released a vast shower of arrows upon him, just as the thousand-eyed Indra releases rain.
O Great King, that commander of the army endured that tumultuous shower of arrows,
remaining as immovable as the Himalayas;
and then, O Indra among kings, Kṣemavṛddhi likewise [endured it] for Sāmba.
He released a vast net of arrows produced by his illusory power.
Then, having torn apart that illusory net with his own illusory power,
Sāmba showered his chariot with a thousand arrows.

Then Kṣemavṛddhi, the commander of the army, having been pierced by Sāmba and tormented by Sāmba’s arrows, fled away on swift horses. When that cruel commander of Śālva’s army had thus retreated, [the battle continued].
A powerful Daitya named Vegavān rushed toward my son; but when he was attacked, O Indra among kings, Sāmba, the upholder of the Vṛṣṇi lineage, stood firm, O King,
as that hero withstood the force of Vegavān.
O son of Kuntī, that hero Sāmba, whose valor is truth, whirled and swiftly hurled the impetuous mace at Vegavatī.
Struck by it, O King, Vegavatī fell to the earth.
Like a great tree with rotten roots, crushed and broken by the wind,
that heroic and mighty asura fell when struck by the mace;
then my son, having entered the vast army, began to fight.

The Dānava named Vivindhya, a renowned great car-warrior and wielder of a mighty bow, O Great King, engaged in combat with Cārudeṣṇa. Then a most tumultuous battle took place between Cārudeṣṇa and Vivindhya.
O King, it was just as it had been in the past between Vṛtra and Vāsava;
enraged at one another, they struck each other with arrows,
roaring like two mighty lions, O great king.
Then the son of Rukmiṇī, having consecrated with a great mantra that arrow which possessed a brilliance like fire and the sun and was the destroyer of enemies, fixed it upon his bow;
and that great car-warrior, filled with rage, challenged Vivindhya.
O King, my son hurled it, and he then fell down lifeless. Seeing Vivindhya slain and that army thrown into turmoil,
Śālva returned once more on his Saubha chariot, which moves at will.
Then, O mighty-armed one, seeing Śālva stationed upon Saubha while standing on the earth, that entire army residing in Dvārakā became utterly agitated. Thereupon,
O son of Kuntī, having marched out and reorganized that force, [he prepared for battle].
O great king, Pradyumna spoke these words to the Ānartas:
"Let all of you stand firm; let everyone behold me in battle as I forcibly repel Saubha along with its king in this conflict."
"O Yādavas, today I shall destroy the army of the lord of Saubha with iron arrows released from my bow and arms like serpents.
Take heart; you need have no fear, for the king of Saubha perishes this very day."
"Attacked by me, that evil-souled one along with Saubha shall perish.
O son of Pāṇḍu, while Pradyumna was speaking thus with great joy,
O hero, that army halted and fought as they pleased.
Vāsudeva said:
Having spoken thus to the Yādavas, O bull of the Bharatas, the son of Rukmiṇī mounted his golden chariot,
which was yoked with armored bay horses.
Raising his decorated banner bearing the sign of a sea-monster with its mouth wide open,
he pursued his enemies on those horses that seemed as if they were leaping into the sky;
the one of great strength brandished and made resound his excellent bow.
Carrying a quiver and a sword, the hero, with his leather arm-guard and finger-protectors bound on,
brandished a bow that flashed like lightning from hand to hand;
he utterly bewildered all the Daityas dwelling in Saubha.
No one could perceive any interval as he repeatedly drew his bow, fixed his arrows, and struck down his enemies in battle; even the color of his face did not change.
And his limbs remained firm even as he roared with the majestic roar of a lion;
the world heard that foremost, wondrous form of his.
A water-dweller, stationed upon a golden staff,
with wide-gaping mouth and a crusher of all crocodiles, shines forth upon that preeminent vehicle, striking terror into all.
Then, O King, Pradyumna, the crusher of enemies, having quickly emerged with his preeminent banner at the head of Śālva’s army,
rushed toward Śālva himself, intending to provoke a conflict.

O descendant of the Kuru lineage, the enraged Śālva could not tolerate that assault by the heroic Pradyumna in the great battle. Intoxicated by the pride of his wrath, he descended from his celestial car that moves at will.
Śālva, the conqueror of enemy cities, fought against Pradyumna;
the worlds beheld the tumultuous battle between those two heroes, Śālva and the Vṛṣṇi, like that between Bali and Vāsava.
O hero, his chariot was composed of illusion and adorned with gold;
it was equipped with a banner, a flag, a chassis, and quivers. O Lord, that illustrious one indeed ascended that excellent chariot.
O descendant of Kuru, the mighty one released arrows at Pradyumna; then, as if to utterly confound Śālva, Pradyumna swiftly unleashed a rain of arrows in battle by the force of his arms.
Struck by them in battle, that king of the Saubhas could not endure it;
he discharged arrows resembling blazing fire at my son as they were rushing toward him. Those [arrows] falling...
That one of great strength cut down the showers of arrows;
then he discharged other blazing shafts at my son.
O Indra among kings, that son of Rukmiṇī was pierced by Śālva’s arrows.

In that battle, he swiftly released an arrow capable of piercing the vital organs. That feathered shaft, discharged by my son, quickly shattered his armor and pierced his heart; he fell down and lost consciousness.
When that heroic King Śālva had fallen unconscious, the lords of the Dānavas fled, rending the earth as they went.
O lord of the earth, the army of Śālva broke out into cries of "Alas! Alas! (Hāhākṛta).
O King, when the lord of Saubha had fallen down unconscious,
the immensely powerful one then rose up, O Kauravya, and having regained his senses, swiftly released an arrow at Pradyumna.
Pierced by him in that battle, the mighty-armed hero Pradyumna sank down deeply in his chariot at the region of the collarbone,
O great king; having thus struck the son of Rukmiṇī, Śālva—
He let out a lion’s roar, filling the earth with that sound. Then, O Bhārata, when my son had fallen into a swoon,
he quickly released other unassailable arrows once again.
Struck by those many arrows and rendered unconscious by him,
O best of the Kauravas, Pradyumna became motionless on the field of battle.
Vāsudeva said:
When Pradyumna, the foremost of the strong, was afflicted by the arrows of Śālva, the Vṛṣṇis who had entered the army, their resolve shattered, were struck with distress.
Then the entire force of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas broke out into cries of "Alas! and "Woe!"

O King, when Pradyumna had fallen, the enemies were filled with joy. Seeing him thus deprived of consciousness, the skilled charioteer Dāruki then swiftly bore him away from the battlefield on his fleet-footed horses.

When the chariot had not yet gone very far, the driver, urged by that best of car-warriors, regained his senses, took up the bow, and said this to the charioteer: "O Sūta, what is your intention? Why are you driving away with your back turned?"
"This is not said to be the duty of the Vṛṣṇi heroes in battle.
O Sauti, have you perhaps lost your wits upon seeing Śālva in this great conflict, or are you despondent at the sight of the fray? Tell me the truth."
Sūta said:
"O Jānārdana, I felt neither delusion nor did fear enter me;
however, O Keśava’s joy, I consider Śālva to be an excessive burden for you."
"O hero, I shall depart slowly; this evildoer is powerful.
A brave warrior in battle must be protected by his charioteer, even if he is deluded.
O long-lived one, you must always protect me, and I too must protect you."
"Thinking that the charioteer must always be protected, I am withdrawing;
for you are alone, O mighty-armed one, while the Dānavas are many.
Considering the battle to be unequal, O son of Rukmiṇī, I am withdrawing."
Vāsudeva said:
"O Kauravya, while the charioteer was speaking thus, he who bears the dolphin-bannered god (Kāma) then said to the charioteer, 'Turn the chariot back again.'"
"O son of Dāruka, never again,
under any circumstances, should you flee from the battle while I am still alive, O Sūta. He who abandons the fray has not been born into the Vṛṣṇi clan."
He who strikes one who has fallen, or one who says "I am yours," as well as he who kills a woman, an elder, or likewise a child;
or one who is deprived of his chariot, whose limbs are mangled, and whose weapons and arms are broken— [such a man incurs the same fate].
"You were born into the family of charioteers and are well-trained in the duties of a charioteer;
you are a knower of dharma, O Dāruka, even in the battles of the Vṛṣṇis. Knowing the entire history of the Vṛṣṇis at the front of the army,"
"O Sauti, do not retreat under any circumstances!
What will the invincible Mādhava, the elder brother of Gada, say to me when he hears that I have retreated from the field, struck on my back, terrified, and fled from the battle?"
What will the elder brother of Keśava say, clad in blue garments and intoxicated with pride? What will the mighty-armed Baladeva say when he has arrived?
And what will the grandson of Śini say—he who is a lion among men and a wielder of the great bow?
"O Sauti, Samba, the victor in assemblies, has departed from the battle;
as have the invincible Cārudeṣṇa, and likewise Gada and Sāraṇa.
And what will the mighty-armed Akrūra say to me, O charioteer?"
"What will the women of the Vṛṣṇi heroes say when they gather together about me— a man who was once esteemed as a hero, always proud of his manhood—
now that this Pradyumna approaches, terrified and having abandoned the great battle?"
"They will say, 'Fie on him! but they will not say, 'Well done! "O Sūta, even a derisive jest with words from me or one like me is worse than death; therefore, do not withdraw again."
"For Hari, the slayer of Madhu, has departed after entrusting the burden to me;
he has gone to perform the sacrifice for Pārtha, that lion among men of immeasurable splendor.
As for the hero Kṛtavarman, I restrained him even as he was about to set out."

"O son of a Sūta, I shall hold back Śālva; you stay here!"—thinking thus of me, the son of Hṛdika indeed turned back. Having approached him and abandoned the battle, what shall I say to that great car-warrior?
What shall I say of that invincible, mighty-armed, lotus-eyed Person who has arrived, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace;
and of Sātyaki, Baladeva, and all the other Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis?

They constantly vie with me; what indeed shall I say to them? O Sūta, having abandoned this battle and being struck from behind by arrows, removed by you while helpless, I shall not live by any means.
"O son of Dāruka, turn back the chariot quickly!
This must never be done again, even in times of calamity.
O charioteer, I do not value life at all."
"O son of a Sūta, when have you ever known me to be overcome by fear, fleeing from the battle while being struck in the back with arrows,
abandoning the fight like a coward?"
"O son of Dāruka, it is not fitting for you to abandon the battle while I am so intensely desirous of fighting; therefore, go back to where the fray is. Vāsudeva said:
Thus addressed in that battle, O son of Kuntī,
the Sūta’s son spoke these smooth and sweet words directly to Pradyumna:
"O son of Rukmiṇī, I have no fear while driving the horses in combat."
"I am well-acquainted with the warfare of the Vṛṣṇis; there is nothing here that could be otherwise.
O long-lived one, it is traditionally taught that when acting as a charioteer, the warrior must be protected in all circumstances—and you, moreover, are severely afflicted."
"For you, O hero, having been struck severely by an arrow discharged by Śālva and overcome by faintness, I then retreated; now, by chance,
you have regained consciousness from the presence of that chief of the Sātvatas."
"Behold my skill in managing horses, O delighter of Keśava!
Trained by Dāruka, I have been instructed exactly as required;
free from fear, I shall enter this vast army of Śālva."
Having spoken thus, the hero then urged his horses forward in the battle; drawing up the reins,
he then charged with speed,
performing various circular maneuvers, both symmetrical and otherwise.
O King, struck on their left and right sides in every way by the goad and pulled by the raised reins,
those excellent horses shone as if they were leaping into the sky.
O King, perceiving that Dāruka was endowed with such manual dexterity,
they then felt as if they were burning and touched the earth with their feet.
O bull of the Bharatas, he [Dāruka] kept the army of Śālva to his right.
He performed that feat without great effort, yet it seemed like a marvel;
unable to endure being circumambulated in the inauspicious counter-clockwise direction by Pradyumna,
that king of the Saubhas suddenly struck his charioteer with three arrows.
But Dāruka’s son, disregarding that torrent of arrows,
O mighty-armed one, urged on the excellent horses once again.
Then that king of Saubha discharged various kinds of arrows once more.
He released them at my heroic son, the offspring of Rukmiṇī;
but the slayer of enemy heroes, the son of Rukmiṇī, smiling and displaying his manual dexterity, cut them down with sharp arrows before they could reach him.

Seeing those arrows cut down by Pradyumna, the king of Saubha resorted to a fierce demonic illusion (*āsurī māyā*) and discharged more shafts. Recognizing that the weapon of the Daityas was being employed, the one of great strength—

Having severed them in mid-air with the Brahmā weapon, he released other feathered shafts. Those blood-drinking arrows quickly shook off that weapon and pierced him in the head, chest, and mouth; he fainted and fell.
When that base Śālva had fallen, afflicted by arrows,
the son of Rukmiṇī fixed another arrow capable of destroying the enemy—
an arrow worshipped by the entire host of the Daśārhas.
Seeing the arrow, radiant as the blazing sun, being drawn back upon the bowstring amidst blessings, the atmosphere broke out into cries of "Alas! and "Alas! (hāhākṛta).
Then all the hosts of gods, together with Indra and the Lord of Wealth,
dispatched Nārada and the mighty Śvasana.
Having approached the son of Rukmiṇī, those two spoke these words on behalf of the denizens of heaven:
"O hero, this King Śālva must not be slain by you under any circumstances.
Withdraw your arrow; he is not to be killed by you in battle. For there is no man anywhere who cannot be slain by this arrow in combat."

"O mighty-armed one, the son of Devakī, Kṛṣṇa, has been ordained by the Creator as his death in battle; let that not prove false. Thereupon, Pradyumna, filled with supreme joy, [prepared] his excellent arrow.
He withdrew [the arrow] from that best of bows and placed it back into his quiver.
Then, O king of kings, Śālva, extremely dejected and afflicted by Pradyumna’s arrows, rose up and quickly departed with his army.
Abandoned by the Vṛṣṇis and tormented by them, that cruel one, O king of kings, mounted the Saubha and then ascended into the sky. Vāsudeva said:
When the city of Ānarta was liberated, I then departed from there,
O King, once your great Rājasūya sacrifice had concluded.
And I beheld Dvārakā, O great king, shorn of its splendor.
Seeing the absence of Vedic recitation and the *vaṣaṭ*-calls, the lack of ornaments on the noble women,
and the gardens of Dvārakā with their forms unrecognizable,
I was seized by doubt and questioned the son of Hṛdika.
"This city of the Vṛṣṇis is utterly devoid of men and women and lacks its horses;
O tiger among men, what is this? We wish to hear it.
Thus addressed by me, he spoke this in detail.
O best of kings, Hārdikya [reported] both the siege and the liberation from Śālva.
Then, O foremost of the Kauravas, having heard everything in its entirety, I immediately formed the resolve for the destruction of King Śālva.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, having comforted the people in the city,
as well as King Āhuka and likewise Anakadundubhi,
and gladdening all the foremost heroes of the Vṛṣṇis, I spoke at that time.
"O bulls among the Yādavas, you must always remain vigilant in the city.
Know that I am setting out for the destruction of King Śālva;
I shall not return to the city of Dvāravatī without having slain him."
"Having destroyed Śālva and the city of Saubha, I shall see you again.
Let this drum, which terrifies enemies, be struck with the three musical notes.
O bull of the Bharatas, those heroes were thus consoled by me according to the truth.
"03.021.010c All of them, filled with joy, said to me: 'Go forth! Slay the enemies!
03.021.011a Honored by those heroes with joyful hearts through their blessings, and having caused the best of the twice-born to recite auspicious prayers, I bowed my head to Aṅgada."
O King, O tiger among men, having sounded the quarters with a chariot yoked to Sainya and Sugrīva,
and having blown my preeminent conch, Pāñcajanya,
I set forth surrounded by a great army.
With a well-ordered fourfold army appearing victorious,
having traversed many countries and mountains abounding in trees,
as well as lakes and rivers, he reached Mārttikāvata.
There, O tiger among men, I heard that Śālva had departed from the city, having mounted the Saubha; I followed after him, and then,
O king of kings, I beheld the king of the Śālvas nearby.

Then, having reached the ocean within its great-waved belly, O slayer of enemies, Śālva took his stand upon the Saubha at the navel of the sea. Beholding me, he suddenly dispatched his own army into battle.
And when only a small portion of the army remained,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, that evil-minded one beheld me from afar with my arm raised, and as if smiling, he repeatedly challenged me to battle once more.

His city could not be reached by the many arrows released from the Śārṅga bow that pierced his vital organs; therefore, O King, wrath took possession of me. And he too, that base Daitya of sinful nature, O monarch—
The invincible one rained down thousands of streams of arrows upon me;
he overwhelmed my soldiers, my charioteer, and my horses.
Yet, disregarding those arrows, O Bhārata, we continued to fight.
Then, in that battle, hundreds of thousands of straight-knotted arrows were hurled at me by the heroic followers of Śālva. They struck my horses, my chariot, and even Dāruka himself.

The Asuras covered [us] with arrows that pierce the vital organs. O hero, neither the horses, nor the chariot, nor my driver Dāruka could be seen, for they were shrouded by arrows; likewise, I and my soldiers were invisible.
Then, O descendant of Kuru, I too discharged many tens of thousands of consecrated arrows from my bow according to divine rites; yet,
O Bhārata, there was no room for my army there.
For that city of Saubha, suspended in the sky, appeared as if it were only a *krośa* away.
Then all those spectators stood like those in an arena and cheered me loudly with lion-roars and the sound of clapping hands.
Released from my bow in that great battle, those arrows, smeared with blood, entered the limbs of the Dānavas like locusts. Then, a tumultuous roar arose within Saubha.
Being struck by sharp arrows and falling into the great ocean, those Dānavas— whose arms and shoulders were severed and who appeared like headless trunks (kabandhas)—
fell down while uttering terrifying cries.
Even those who have fallen are devoured by the creatures dwelling in the waters of the ocean. Then,
with all my might, I blew into the water-born conch Pāñcajanya, which possesses the luster of cow’s milk, the kunda flower, the moon, lotus stalks, and silver.
Seeing them fallen there, Śālva, the lord of Saubha,
then engaged me in battle with a great illusory warfare (*māyāyuddha*). Then [there appeared] *huḍahuḍas*, spears, javelins, spikes, and battle-axes.
Spearheads, maces, clubs, nooses, lances, iron bludgeons, arrows, sharp-edged spears, and *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons fell incessantly upon me;
I quickly received them with my own illusory power (*māyā*) and destroyed them.
When that illusion was destroyed, he fought with mountain peaks.
Then there was darkness as if it were night, yet it became like dawn;
there was foul weather and fair weather alike, and both cold and heat, O Bhārata.
O Bhārata, he rained down showers of glowing coals and showers of weapons;
thus manifesting his *māyā*, the enemy fought me.
Recognizing all of that, I destroyed it by means of *māyā* alone.

Then that Dānava bewildered me in battle with his illusory power (*māyā*). When that *māyā* had been destroyed by me in the fight, I then, according to the occasion, struck down the Dānava on all sides with arrows in combat.
Then, O great king, the sky became as if filled with a hundred suns;
it was adorned, O son of Kuntī, with a hundred moons and tens of thousands of stars.
Consequently, at that time, neither day nor night nor the directions could be discerned.
Then, having fallen into a state of confusion, I employed the weapon of wisdom (*prajñā-astra*).
Thereupon, that weapon was dispersed by [his] weapon like a tuft of cotton in the autumn wind.
Thus did that tumultuous battle, which made the hair stand on end, proceed.
"O Indra among kings, having regained my vision, I fought the enemy once more.
Vāsudeva said:
"Thus, O tiger among men, did Śālva, the great enemy of kings,"
While fighting with me in battle, he again ascended into the sky.
Then [he hurled] śataghnīs, great maces,
blazing spears, clubs, and swords.
O great king, Śālva, dull-witted and desirous of victory, hurled them at me in anger; I,
however, quickly [struck] those arrows as they came rushing toward me with my own swift shafts.
Quickly warding off those sky-rangers while they were still in the air, I swiftly cut them into two or three pieces with my released shafts;
then a great roar arose in the intermediate space.
Then, with a hundred thousand straight-knotted arrows,
he completely covered Dāruka, the horses, and the chariot.
Thereupon, O hero, Dāruka, as if overwhelmed, spoke to me.
"I must remain standing," [he said], yet, tormented by Śālva’s arrows, I am unable to stand; my limbs are failing me.
Having heard these piteous words of his charioteer, I—

Looking about, I saw the charioteer afflicted by arrows; O best of the Pāṇḍavas, I could see no opening— neither on his chest, nor on his head, nor on his body, nor on his two arms— that was not struck by shafts.
From the pressure of that shower of arrows, his blood flowed copiously,
like a mountain rich in red chalk-ore when rained upon by clouds;
[he was struck] by arrows of various forms, consecrated with divine mantras.
With various missiles and weapons, those stationed in the sky— even though they were invisible—
beheld that charioteer in battle, his hands gripping the reins, sinking down and oppressed by Śālva’s arrows; and I, O mighty-armed one, steadied him.
Then, O Bhārata, a certain man residing in Dvārakā approached my chariot in haste and spoke to me as if out of friendship, O hero—
he was an attendant of that very Āhuka. "O hero, these are the words of Āhuka."
Listen to this, Yudhiṣṭhira, as I speak with a dejected heart and a choked throat:
the heroic Āhuka, the lord of Dvārakā, has sent this message to you through Keśava; understand here what your father’s friend has said to you.
"O descendant of Vṛṣṇi, Śālva has arrived at Dvārakā today;
while you were preoccupied, O invincible one, the son of Śūra was slain by force.
Therefore, enough of this fighting; desist from it, O Janārdana."
"Protect Dvārakā itself; this is your great duty.
Having heard these words of his, I became deeply distressed in mind and could not determine whether I should do one thing or the other.

O hero, O descendant of Kuru, having heard those unpleasant words, he mentally reproached Sātyaki, Baladeva, and the great car-warrior Pradyumna; for I am indeed the protector of Dvārakā and of my father.
Having established protection over them, the mighty-armed Baladeva set out for the destruction of Saubha; does that slayer of enemies still live,
along with Sātyaki, the son of Rukmiṇī, and the heroic Cārudeṣṇa?
Together with Sāmba and the others, I was deeply distressed in mind.
For while these tigers among men were still alive, O tiger among men, the son of Śūra could not have been slain by anyone, even by the wielder of the thunderbolt himself.

"Śūrasuta has clearly been slain, and it is evident that they too have lost their lives—all those headed by Baladeva; such is my firm conviction. Thus, I am reflecting again and again upon that total destruction."
O great king, being extremely dazed, I fought Śālva once more. Then, O great king, I saw the heroic son of Śūra falling from Saubha; at that moment, O hero, a swoon came over me.
O lord of men, the form of my father as he was falling—
like Yayāti when his merit was exhausted and he descended from heaven to the earth—
was such that his turban had fallen away and shattered, and his garments and hair were disheveled.
I appeared as if falling, like a planet whose merit has been exhausted.
Then, O son of Kuntī, the Śārṅga, the best of bows, slipped from my hand;
overcome by delusion, I sank down upon the floor of the chariot.
Then, O Bhārata, my entire army, having seen me seated in the chariot as if lifeless, raised a great cry of "Alas! and lost their senses;
they fell down with their arms outstretched and their legs extended as well.
I saw the form of my father like that of a bird swooping down.
As he fell, O mighty-armed one, those heroes with spears and battle-axes in their hands struck him repeatedly; they caused my heart to tremble.
Then, having regained consciousness after a moment,
O hero, in that great conflict,
I saw neither Saubha there, nor the enemy, nor Śālva.
"I see my aged father, yet he is not there;
therefore, it occurred to my mind that this was an illusion," I decided. Then I awoke once more, scattering arrows by the hundreds.
Vāsudeva said:
"Then, O best of the Bharatas, taking up my beautiful bow,
I struck down the heads of the enemies of the gods from Saubha with my arrows."
I discharged arrows resembling venomous serpents, soaring upward and possessed of fierce energy—
released from the Śārṅga bow and adorned with fine feathers— at the King of Śālva.
Thereupon, O scion of the Kuru lineage, Saubha could no longer be seen.

He vanished through his illusory power (*māyā*), and I was filled with wonder. Then, O Great King, descendant of Bharata, those hosts of Dānavas— with their deformed faces and hair— shouted aloud while I stood there, O Bhārata.
Then, in that great battle, acting with haste for their destruction, I discharged the weapon known as Śabdasāha;
thereupon, the sound ceased. All those Dānavas by whom that sound was uttered were slain.
With arrows resembling the sun, blazing and producing a great sound,
when that noise had ceased, O Great King, another sound arose once more from elsewhere; there too, I discharged my arrows.

O Bhārata, in this manner, those Asuras made all ten directions—across, above, and below—resound with their cries; yet they were all slain by me. Then, having gone to Prāgjyotiṣa, he appeared once again.
O hero, bewildering my eyes with the city of Saubha that moves at will,
the Dānava in the form of a monkey, the bringer of destruction to the worlds,
then suddenly overwhelmed me with a great shower of rocks.
O Indra among kings, being struck on all sides by that rain of mountains, I became like an anthill covered by a mountain. Then,
covered by the mountain, I remained there along with my horses and my charioteer.
O King, together with his banner and piled with mountains, he shall go to obscurity.
Then those foremost heroes of the Vṛṣṇis who were my soldiers at that time fled suddenly in all directions, afflicted by fear.
Then, O lord of the people, a great cry of "Alas! arose from everyone;
indeed, heaven, earth, and the intermediate space were filled with lamentation when I was no longer visible. Then, O King, my friends became despondent in mind.
Overcome with pain and grief, they wept and wailed aloud;
the enemies rejoiced, while those who were not enemies were filled with distress.
Thus, O hero, did he conquer, and afterwards I heard this, O Acyuta.
Then, raising my beloved weapon, the thunderbolt that shatters all rocks, I demolished all those mountains. Thereupon,
oppressed by the weight of the mountains, their breath and movements became feeble.
O great king, my horses seemed to tremble; yet,
seeing me like the sun risen in the sky after tearing through a mass of clouds,
all my kinsmen once again experienced joy.
Then, O King, the charioteer, bowing with joined palms, said to me:
"O Vārṣṇeya, look well at Śālva, the lord of Saubha, who stands there.
Enough of disregarding him, O Kṛṣṇa; exert yourself properly."
"Today, cast away your mildness and your friendship toward Śālva.
Slay Śālva, O mighty-armed Keśava; do not let him live, O Vīra, for an enemy must be slain with every means of prowess, O slayer of foes."
An enemy must not be disregarded by one who is stronger, even if he is weak— not only one who is confined to a seat, but especially one standing in the midst of battle. Therefore,
O tiger among men, O Lord, you must [overcome] him with every effort.

Slay him, O best of the Vṛṣṇi clan; let not time pass you by again. He who conquered the son of Jamadagni after many tens of millions of years—he cannot be slain by others at all, indeed, save for you alone.
"O hero, he is certainly not one who can be subdued by mildness, nor is he your friend, by whom you were challenged to battle and by whom Dvārakā was laid waste.
Having heard these and other such words from the charioteer, O son of Kuntī, I—
Knowing this to be the truth, I set my mind on battle for the sake of slaying King Śālva and destroying Saubha; and I said to Dāruka, "O hero, wait but a moment."

Then, he fixed upon his bow in that battle an irresistible, divine, and indestructible weapon of fire— exceedingly powerful, beloved, all-conquering, and of great splendor— which brings about the end of the Dānavas.
In battle, it is the great reducer of yakṣas, rākṣasas, dānavas,
and hostile kings to ashes;
it is a stainless discus with edges like razors, resembling Kāla, Antaka, and Yama.
"Having consecrated this incomparable weapon, which is the destroyer of enemies,
slay Saubha by your own prowess, as well as those who are my foes therein! Having spoken thus, I hurled it at him in fury with the strength of my arms.

Then, as he was falling through the sky, the form of Sudarśana appeared like that of a second sun blazing at the end of a yuga. Having reached the city of Saubha, which had lost its splendor, [he struck it].
He split it asunder through the middle, like a saw cutting a tall tree;
then Saubha, shattered into two by the power of the Sudarśana,
fell like Tripura when struck by the arrow of Maheśvara.
When Saubha had fallen, my discus returned to my hand;
raising it again with speed, I said, "For Śālva!
Then, in that great battle, Śālva brandished a heavy mace.
He suddenly split it in two and blazed forth with splendor.
When that hero had fallen, the Dānavas, their hearts terrified, cried out "Alas!
Alas! and fled in all directions, tormented by my arrows.
Then, having stationed my chariot near Saubha and blown my conch with joy, I gladdened my friends; [I beheld] that city,
which resembled the peak of Mount Meru, with its watchtowers and gateways destroyed.
Seeing him burning, those women fled in all directions. Having thus slain Śālva in battle and brought down Saubha,
I returned once more to the Ānartas and brought joy to my friends.
For this reason, O King, slayer of enemy heroes, I did not go to the city named after the elephant; for had I gone, O hero, Suyodhana would not be alive,
or else the gambling match would not have taken place.
"What shall I do now, like water that has broken its dam?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed Puruṣottama addressed the Kaurava.
Having taken leave of the Pāṇḍavas, the wise Madhusūdana departed;
the mighty-armed one, having saluted Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira,
was smelled on the head by the king and by Bhīma of the great arms.
Embraced by Arjuna and saluted by the twins, he was honored by Dhaumya and worshipped with tears by Draupadī; then,
having placed Subhadrā and Abhimanyu upon the golden chariot, [he departed].
Honored by the Pāṇḍavas, Kṛṣṇa ascended his chariot,
which was yoked with the horses Saibya and Sugrīva and possessed the splendor of the sun;
having comforted Yudhiṣṭhira, Kṛṣṇa set out for Dvārakā.
Then, when the descendant of Daśārha had departed, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata,
took the sons of Draupadī with him and set out for his own city; likewise,
Dhṛṣṭaketu, the king of Cedi, took his sister and departed.
Having seen the Pāṇḍavas, he went to the beautiful city of Śuktimatī; and the Kekayas also, having been granted leave by the son of Kuntī of immeasurable splendor,
took their leave of all the Pāṇḍavas and departed, O Bhārata.
The Brahmins, the Vaiśyas, and likewise the inhabitants of the realm,
though being urged to depart, could not bear to leave the Pāṇḍavas. That assembly, O Indra among kings, was a sight of truly great wonder.
O bull of the Bharata race, while those high-souled ones were seated in the Kāmyaka forest,
the magnanimous Yudhiṣṭhira, having paid due honor to those brahmins,
commanded his men at the proper time, saying, "Yoke the chariots."
Vaiśampāyana said: When that lord of the Daśārhas had departed,
Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, and Arjuna [remained].
The twins, Kṛṣṇā, and the family priest—
those heroes, having mounted costly chariots yoked with excellent horses, set out together for the forest.
Resplendent like the Lord of Beings,
they set forth after bestowing gold coins, garments, and cows upon those learned in the syllables of instruction and the sacred mantras.
Twenty attendants stood in front, bearing weapons;
they carried bows, armor, yellow arrows,
bowstrings, mechanical devices, and shafts.
Then all of them, taking up the garments, ornaments, and [other belongings] of the princess, went to the lowest part [of the chariot]. The nurses and the maidservants also followed.
Then Indrasena, quickly taking hold of him,
followed closely behind in the chariot;
thereafter, the citizens approached the best of the Kurus.
Those of undaunted spirit performed circumambulations,
and the Brahmins, full of joy, as well as all the leaders of Kurujāṅgala, addressed him with words of greeting.
And he, the King of Dharma, being gracious, greeted them in turn; together with those brothers,
that high-souled lord remained there.
Seeing the multitude of people from Kurujāṅgala,
that high-souled bull among the Kurus felt toward them the same affection as a father feels for his sons.
And they too, toward that best of the Bharatas,
then behaved like sons toward a father.
Then, having encountered a great multitude of people, [the king]...
Surrounding the hero of the Kurus, they stood there crying out, "Alas, O Lord! Alas, O Dharma!
and all of them, overcome with shame, had tears upon their faces.
The lord of the Kurus and ruler of his subjects, having abandoned us as a father abandons his sons— these citizens and all these people of the countryside; he has departed.
"Having abandoned us, where indeed has the King of Dharma departed? Fie on the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, whose mind is so cruel, and on the evil-minded Karṇa along with Saubala!"
O lord of men, those fierce evildoers desire your ruin, even though you are ever devoted to righteousness; yet you,
the Great-Souled One, having yourself established this peerless [kingdom]—
Having abandoned that great city, which shone like the city of the gods and was the abode of Indra, where indeed has the King of Dharma gone, he whose actions are never in vain?
The high-souled Maya constructed that peerless assembly hall, radiant like the assembly hall of the gods;
it was like a divine illusion protected by the gods.
"Where indeed has the King of Dharma gone after leaving us?"— to those who were gathered together, Bībhatsu, of supreme energy and knower of dharma, desire, and wealth,
spoke aloud.
Having dwelt in the forests, the king will take up this dwelling, eclipsing the glory of his enemies;
the foremost of the twice-born, both united and separately, [will attend him].
Having approached the ascetics who understand the meaning of dharma, you should propitiate them and say:
"May our supreme success in our purpose be achieved."
When these words had been spoken by Arjuna,
O King, those brahmins and all the other castes rejoiced together with joy and performed [the rites].
Having circumambulated the best of the upholders of dharma,
he took leave of Pārtha, Vṛkodara,
Dhanañjaya, Yājñasenī, and the twins.
Deprived of joy, they departed for their respective kingdoms with the permission of Yudhiṣṭhira.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, after they had departed, the son of Kuntī, Yudhiṣṭhira, whose soul is dharma and who is true to his promise, addressed all his brothers:
"We must dwell for these twelve years in the uninhabited forest."
"Examine this region in the great forest, abounding in deer and birds,
rich in many flowers and fruits, delightful, auspicious, and frequented by holy men—
a place where we may dwell happily for all these remaining autumns."
When this had been said, Dhanañjaya replied to the King of Dharma,
having honored the high-minded preceptor of men as if he were his own guru.
Arjuna said:
You alone have attended upon the aged great seers;
there is nothing unknown to you in the world of men.
For you, O bull of the Bharatas, have always served the brahmins.
Dvaipāyana and others, as well as Nārada of great asceticism—
he who, having mastery over himself, constantly traverses the gateways to all the worlds,
from the realm of the gods to the realm of Brahmā, and even to that of the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
"You know all the destinies of the Brahmins, there is no doubt;
O King, you also know the powers of them all.
You alone, O King, know the very cause of what is beneficial."
"O Great King, wherever you desire to dwell, there we shall make our home.
This lake named Dvaitavana is frequented by holy people; it is delightful, abounding in flowers and fruits, and inhabited by various birds."
"In this matter, I propose that we spend these twelve years [in disguise];
O King, if this is agreeable to you, or what else do you think?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Pārtha, this which you have proposed is also my own opinion:
let us go to the great and famous sacred lake of Dvaitavana.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Then all those Pāṇḍavas, practitioners of dharma, set out together with many Brāhmaṇas toward the sacred lake of Dvaitavana— Brāhmaṇas who maintained the sacred fire-sacrifices as well as those who were without such fires.
Many Brahmins— ascetics dwelling in the forest, devoted to their own sacred study, engaged in silent recitation, and observant of truth— surrounded Yudhiṣṭhira by the hundreds, firm in their vows.
Having traveled there together with many brahmins, those Pāṇḍavas,
the bulls of the Bharata lineage, entered the holy and delightful Dvaitavana forest,
which was filled with śāla, tāla, āmra, madhūka, and nīpa trees.
At the end of the summer heat, the lord of the realm beheld a great forest filled with *kadamba*, *sarja*, *arjuna*, and *karṇikāra* trees bearing flowers.
Perched upon the crests of great trees,
flocks of peacocks, water-hens, and cakora birds uttered delightful cries.
In that forest, the grove-cuckoos [resounded] along with herds of female elephants accompanying their leaders—
leaders who were fierce with rut and possessed the splendor of mountains.
Having approached the enchanting Bhogavatī in that forest, the lord of the realm beheld vast herds of great elephants.
In that forest, the dwelling place of those who uphold dharma, he beheld many hosts of perfected seers who were self-controlled and wore bark garments and matted hair.
Then, descending from his vehicle, the king—
the best among those whose souls are devoted to dharma— entered that forest together with his brother and his people.
Like Śakra of immeasurable power entering Triviṣṭapa,
hosts of Cāraṇas and Siddhas, desiring to see him who was true to his promise, approached him together.
And the forest-dwellers also stood surrounding that wise lion among kings;
there, he greeted all the perfected ones (siddhas).
Honored in return like a king and like a god,
he— the best among the upholders of dharma— entered together with all those foremost of the twice-born, with palms joined in reverence.
That high-souled one, virtuous in conduct like his father,
was approached by ascetics devoted to dharma and honored by them at the foot of the Puṣpadhara tree.
The king sat down beneath the great tree,
as did Bhīma, Kṛṣṇā, Dhanañjaya,
the twins, and their attendants, surrounding the lord of men.
Having unyoked their mounts and descended,
all those foremost of the Bharatas stood there in attendance upon him,
who was bent over by a canopy of creepers along with the Pāṇḍavas.
The great tree shone with those five high-souled ones, fierce archers who had come to dwell there,
like a great mountain with leaders of elephant herds.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having reached that forest, the sons of the king, though accustomed to comfort, entered upon a life of hardship.
Those who resembled Indra dwelt in those auspicious *sāla* groves along the Sarasvatī;
and the king [honored] all the *yatis* and the sages.
In that forest, the high-souled bull among the Kurus gratified the foremost of the twice-born with abundant roots and fruits.

While the Pāṇḍavas were dwelling in the great forest, their domestic priest— possessed of all-encompassing splendor— performed the ancestral sacrifices as well as those pertaining to the sacred fires.
Dhaumya acted toward the Kurus like a father.
While they were living away from their kingdom,
an ancient seer arrived as their guest.
To that hermitage of the illustrious Pāṇḍavas came Mārkaṇḍeya, whose intense splendor was fully developed;
he arrived with the radiance of a blazing sacrificial fire.
The high-minded Yudhiṣṭhira, the bull among the Kurus,
being possessed of incomparable strength and heroism, honored that great sage who is worshipped by gods, seers, and men.
That all-knowing, high-souled one, having gazed upon Draupadī Kṛṣṇā,
Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, and Arjuna,
remembered Rāma in his mind.
Among the ascetics, he of undiminished splendor smiled;
the King of Dharma, as if dejected, said to him:
"All these ascetics are filled with shame."
"Why do you appear so joyful, as if smiling, upon seeing me while the ascetics look on? Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O dear one, I do not rejoice, nor do I feel pride; neither elation nor arrogance takes hold of me,
even as I behold this calamity of yours today, O Rāma."
I remember Satyavrata, the son of Daśaratha;
and that king, together with Lakṣmaṇa,
lived in the forest by the command of his father.
O Pārtha, in former times, while wandering as an archer,
that high-souled one, who resembles the thousand-eyed Indra, was seen by me on the peak of Mount Ṛṣyamūka.
The sinless son of Daśaratha, the slayer of Maya, Jeta, and Namuci, lived out his term of exile in the forest according to his father’s command, fulfilling his own duty.
He too, equal in splendor to Śakra,
possessed of great majesty and invincible in battles,
abandoned worldly enjoyments and wandered in the forests.
Thinking "power will not perish," one should practice unrighteousness;
for kings such as Nābhāga and Bhagīratha,
having conquered this earth bounded by the oceans...
"By truth alone, O dear one, they conquered those worlds;
one should not practice unrighteousness thinking, 'I am the master of force.
They say that Alarka was virtuous, O best of men;"
Having abandoned his kingdom and wealth, Satyavrata, the king of Kāśī and Karūṣa, fled because he could not protect his army; thus one should not practice unrighteousness.
O best of men, O son of Pṛthā, by honoring that ancient ordinance established of old by the Creator, the virtuous Seven Seers shine in the heavens.
"One should not practice unrighteousness thinking 'I am powerful,' O lord of men! Behold these mighty, horned elephants, as large as mountain peaks."
O best of men, seeing that all beings abide by the command of the Creator, one should not practice unrighteousness, thinking, "I am the master of power. O lord of men, behold all living creatures!
Just as that which was ordained by the Creator according to its own nature acts through its inherent power,
so one should not practice unrighteousness, thinking, "I am the master of my own strength."
Through truth, through righteousness, through conduct befitting your station,
and likewise through a sense of shame, you have transcended all beings;
thus, both your fame and your splendor are blazing.
O Pārtha, O high-souled one, having endured this difficult dwelling in the forest according to your vow, you are like the sun, the source of light.
"Then, O King, you shall take back from the Kauravas that prosperity which was blazing with its own splendor.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken these words in the midst of the ascetics, the great seer addressed Dhaumya and the sons of Pṛthā who were together with their friends.
Then he set out toward the northern direction.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Now, while the high-souled Pāṇḍavas were dwelling in the Dvaitavana forest, [the king] departed.
The great forest became overspread with Brahmins;
being constantly filled on all sides with the sound of Vedic recitation,
the sacred lake of Dvaitavana became equal to the world of Brahmā.
The heart-stirring sound of the *yajus*, *ṛc*, and *sāman* verses, as well as of all prose recitations being uttered in every way,
arose alongside the twang of the bowstrings of the Pāṇḍavas and the Vedic chanting of the wise ones.
The *kṣatra* power, united with the *brahman*, shone forth even more brilliantly.
Then Baka Dālbhya spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma,
as he sat at twilight surrounded by the ṛṣis, O son of Kuntī.

"Behold, O Pārtha, O best of the Kurus, the time for the *homa* sacrifice in the ascetic Brāhmaṇas of the Dvaitavana forest, as the fires blaze forth. Protected by you, these men of firm vows practice their dharma in this sacred place."
The Bhṛgus, the Aṅgirases, the Vasiṣṭhas along with the Kāśyapas,
the highly blessed Āgastyas, and the Ātreyas of supreme vows—
all these Brahmins, the most excellent in the entire world, have assembled here with you.
O Pārtha, listen with one-pointed mind to these words of mine,
O Kaunteya, which I shall speak to you along with your brothers, O Kaurava:
Brahman joined with Kṣatra, and Kṣatra together with Brahman.
When they rise up together, they consume their enemies like fire and wind consuming forests.
My dear son, one who desires to conquer both this world and the next should not wish to remain long without a Brahmin.
Having obtained a twice-born man who has mastered the meaning of the Dharma and is free from delusion, the king drives away his enemies while practicing the dharma that leads to the highest good,
which consists in the protection of his subjects.
Bali found no sanctuary in the world other than the twice-born;
for the Asura, the son of Virocana, was never deficient in his desires, and his prosperity remained inexhaustible.
Having obtained the earth through association with Brahmins,
he perished because he acted wickedly toward them; this earth, along with its abundance, does not belong to one who is not a Brahmin.

He who is disciplined in statesmanship and instructs a king according to the principles of policy will cause that king to long abide in the second caste, and even the ocean-girdled earth will bow down before him.
Just as the strength of an elephant in battle perishes when it is deprived of its goad, so too does the power of the *kṣatra* perish when it is abandoned by the *brāhmaṇas*.
The vision of the *brahman* is incomparable; the strength of the *kṣatra* is peerless.
When these two move together, then the world prospers;
for just as a great fire, fanned by the wind, consumes dry undergrowth,
so does a king, united with a Brahmin, consume his enemies.
Then, the wise man should pursue the cultivation of his intellect by means of the Brahmins,
for the sake of acquiring what has not been acquired and for the increase of what has been acquired; that is,
for the acquisition of the unacquired and the growth of the acquired.
In order to establish a worthy place of pilgrimage,
you should settle a brahmin who is illustrious, learned in the Vedas, wise, and possessed of great erudition.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, your conduct toward the Brahmins has always been supreme;
therefore, your celebrated fame shines throughout all the worlds.
Then all those Brahmins honored Baka Dālbhya.
While Yudhiṣṭhira was being praised, they became even more joyful:
Dvaipāyana, Nārada, the son of Jamadagni (Paraśurāma), Pṛthuśravas,
Indradyumna, Bhāluki, Kṛtacetās, and Sahasrapād.
Karṇaśravas, Muñja, Lavaṇāśva Kāśyapa, Hārīta, Sthūṇakarṇa, Agniveśya, and Śaunaka;
Ṛtavāk, Suvāk, Bṛhadaśva, and Ṛtāvasu.
Ūrdhvaretas, Vṛṣāmitra, Suhotra, and Hotravāhana—
these and many other Brahmins of rigid vows honored Ajātaśatru, just as the ṛṣis honor Purandara.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
having gone to the forest, the Pārthas sat down with Kṛṣṇā in the evening and engaged in conversation, being wholly devoted to sorrow and grief.
"Beloved, beautiful, wise, and devoted to her husband—
then Kṛṣṇā spoke these words to the King of Dharma:
'Surely that wicked man feels not the slightest bit of sorrow for us.'"
O King, there is nothing found in that cruel and evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
who did not say a single word to you when you were clothed in deerskins along with me and all your brothers.
Having sent you away to the forest, that evil-minded and wicked-souled one felt no remorse;
surely the heart of that doer of evil deeds must be made of iron,
since he then addressed such harsh words to you, who are supreme and devoted to dharma.
Unpleasant words and harsh insults in the assembly—
having brought such suffering upon himself, that evil-souled man of sin rejoices along with his circle of friends, though he is accustomed to comfort and undeserving of pain.
O Bhārata, when you departed for the forest clad in deerskin, tears did not fall from the eyes of only four people:
Duryodhana, Karṇa, and the evil-minded Śakuni.
O best of the Kurus, from the eyes of that fierce Duryodhana, his wicked brother Duḥśāsana, and indeed all the other Kurus who were overwhelmed with grief,
tears fell.
