Seeing this bed and that which was yours in former times, I grieve for you, O Great King, who are undeserving of sorrow and accustomed to happiness— seeing also that self-controlled, jewel-adorned throne in the midst of the assembly hall.
Seeing this mat of *kuśa* grass, this grief overwhelms me;
for when I saw you in the assembly hall surrounded by kings,
O King, what peace can there be for my heart that no longer sees you?

O Bhārata, I who once beheld you anointed with sandalwood paste and radiant as the sun, am now bewildered to see you smeared with mud and filth. Indeed, I who formerly [saw] you in bright, costly Kausika garments...

O Indra among kings, I have seen it; I see you now clad in bark garments. And as for that prepared food, fulfilling every desire, which used to be carried from your house by the thousands in golden vessels for the Brahmins—[where has that gone?]
O King, O Lord, food of such excellent quality is given to the ascetics who live without homes, as well as to those householders; yet, O King,
for me who does not see that, what peace can there be for my heart?
In the past, in your home, you honored thousands with all their desires;
you worshipped the twice-born with every provision of their wishes. O great king, those brothers of yours who were young and adorned with polished earrings—
"O lord of men, those who were once fed by cooks with choice foods most exquisitely prepared—
I see them all today living on forest fare in the woods;
my mind finds no peace, for they do not deserve such suffering."
"And as for this Bhīmasena, who dwells in the forest in sorrow and is lost in thought— why does your anger not increase now that the time has come?
For Bhīmasena, O Acyuta, is performing deeds himself."
Seeing one who deserves happiness now suffering, why does your anger not increase?
Having honored him with various vehicles and diverse garments,
why does your anger not increase upon seeing him gone to the forest?
For this powerful Vṛkodara, who is capable of slaying all the Kurus, endures [this] while awaiting your favor— he who,
though possessing only two arms, is the equal of the many-armed Arjuna.
In the discharge of his arrows, he was like Yama, the Ender of Time, due to his swiftness;
by the prowess of his weapons, all the kings were made to bow down and attend upon the Brahmins at your sacrifice, O Great King.

Seeing this tiger among men, Arjuna— who is honored by gods and *dānavas*— now lost in meditation, why does your anger not increase? Having seen Pārtha, who is undeserving of suffering and accustomed to comfort, now dwelling in the forest.
And yet your anger does not increase; because of this, O Bhārata, I am bewildered.
He who, on a single chariot, conquered the gods, men, and serpents—seeing him gone to the forest, why does your anger not swell?
He who, surrounded by wondrous vehicles, horses, and elephants,
forcibly seized the wealth of kings, that scorcher of foes;
he who, with a single impulse, hurls five hundred arrows.

Seeing him gone to the forest— dark-complexioned, tall, young, and the foremost among those who wield shields in battle— why does your wrath not increase? Seeing Nakula in the forest, why does your wrath not increase?
O Yudhiṣṭhira, seeing Sahadeva— the son of Mādrī, handsome and heroic— in the forest, why does your wrath not increase? O King,
why do you endure this?

O lord of men, seeing both Nakula and Sahadeva— those two who did not deserve such suffering— you were grieved, for they were born in the family of Drupada and are daughters-in-law to the high-souled Pāṇḍu.
Seeing me, the sister of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the devoted wife of a hero, now dwelling in the forest, why does your anger not increase? Surely, O best of the Bharatas, you have no anger at all.
"You have clearly abandoned [your duty] for the sake of destruction, just like the Lord of Bhṛgu;
for your mind is not distressed even upon seeing your brothers and me. It is recorded as a traditional saying that there is no Kṣatriya in this world who is devoid of wrath."
Today, O Kṣatriya, I see that very thing reversed in you:
that a Kṣatriya does not display his splendor when the time has come. O Pārtha, all beings always treat such a person with contempt.
Therefore, you must never, under any circumstances, practice forbearance toward your enemies;
for they can be destroyed by your splendor alone—of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, that kṣatriya who does not remain tranquil at the time for forbearance [is likewise lost].
"Unpleasant to all beings, he perishes both here and in the hereafter.
Draupadī said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
And [he heard] the dialogue between Prahlāda and Bali, the son of Virocana—
the lord of the Asuras, possessed of great wisdom, who had mastered the traditional scriptures on dharma—
as Bali questioned his father’s father, Prahlāda, the lord of the Daityas.
"O dear one, is forbearance indeed better, or is it rather energy? O father, resolve this doubt of mine as I ask you;
tell me, O knower of dharma, that which is truly superior here, so that I may be free from uncertainty."
"I shall indeed carry out all that instruction exactly as it is. Thus questioned, the Grandfather, the wise one who knows all certainties, explained everything to him who asked about his doubt.
Prahlāda said:
"O dear one, know this for certain: brilliance is not always superior, nor is forgiveness always superior;
these two are thus distinct."
O dear one, he who is constantly forgiving incurs many faults:
his servants treat him with contempt, and likewise those who are indifferent;
moreover, all living beings never bow down before him.
Therefore, my dear son, constant forbearance is censured by the wise;
for servants, disregarding such a person, resort to him due to his many faults,
and those of small intellect seek to seize his wealth.
Vehicles, garments, ornaments, beds, and seats,
as well as foods, drinks, and all other utensils—
those mindless officials may take these according to their desire.
They do not give what has been assigned as gifts even by their husband's command,
nor do they ever honor him with the honors due to a husband;
for in this world, contempt is more detestable than death itself.
"O dear one, such a forgiving person— even when spoken to with harsh words— is addressed by servants, sons, dependents, and even those who behave like neutrals.
Furthermore, they even seek to treat with contempt the wife of that forgiving man."

And his wives, being mindless, act according to their own whims; likewise, though they are always cheerful, if they incur even the slightest punishment from their lord, they become corrupted, and being corrupted, they cause harm.
These and many other faults always belong to those who possess forgiveness;
now, O son of Virocana, know these to be the faults of those who lack forgiveness:
being constantly shrouded by passion (rajas), whether in an improper place or even in a proper one.
Enraged, he inflicts various punishments by his own power;
yet, shrouded in that very power, he incurs hostility with his friends and becomes an object of hatred both to the world and to his own kin.
Through such contempt, a man incurs loss of wealth, censure, and disrespect, as well as anguish, hatred, greed, and enemies;
by yielding to anger, he inflicts various punishments upon men.

He who approaches both wrongdoers and benefactors with sheer severity quickly falls away from sovereignty, from his very life, and even from his own kin; therefore, the world trembles before him as if from a snake that has entered the house.
How can there be prosperity for one from whom the world is terrified?
For upon seeing even a slight vulnerability in him, the world will surely act with hostility.
Therefore, one should not over-exert one's brilliance, nor should one be constantly mild.
When the proper time arrives, one may be mild or even harsh;
he who is mild at the right time and becomes stern when it is appropriate truly attains happiness both in this world and in the next.

I shall now describe the occasions for forgiveness; listen to them from me in detail—those which the wise have declared should never be abandoned. When one who has previously rendered assistance commits a transgression that is not grave, [one should forgive].

That offender should be forgiven for the benefit he has conferred; likewise, offenders who have acted out of ignorance should be forgiven. Indeed, wisdom is not easily attained by a person in all circumstances.
If those crooked men, having committed an act intentionally, should claim it was done unintentionally,
you should punish them for even a minor offense;
yet, O living being, you must forgive a single offense of everyone.
When a second offense occurs, one becomes liable to be executed even for a very slight transgression.
If some offense has been committed unknowingly,
they say that it must certainly be forgiven after a thorough investigation through careful examination.
One overcomes gentleness with gentleness; one overcomes the cruel with gentleness.
There is nothing that cannot be accomplished by gentleness; therefore, gentleness is sharper than anything else.
Having carefully considered the place and the time, as well as one's own relative strength and weakness.

Having carefully examined both the cause and the effect, as well as one's own power or forbearance, nothing should be done at an improper place or time; rather, the right place and time must be awaited.
Likewise, out of regard for public opinion, an offender should be forgiven.
"These are the times declared to be appropriate for forgiveness;
when circumstances occur otherwise, it is said to be the time for fiery energy.
Draupadī said:
Therefore, O lord of men, I consider this to be the time for your splendor,
while the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra remain greedy and constantly harmful. Indeed, there is no longer any occasion for forgiveness toward the Kurus.
And when the time for brilliance has arrived, you ought to display that brilliance. A person who is treated with mildness becomes contemptuous, while people tremble before one who is harsh;
he who knows how to employ both when the proper time has come is a true lord of the earth.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the auspicious words of Draupadī, spoken with smooth syllables and phrases,
King Yudhiṣṭhira smiled and spoke to Draupadī.
O highly wise lady, you have become angry with the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra for reasons that you consider manifold and significant;
hear from me the arguments regarding how anger is a root-destroying enemy.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Anger is the destroyer of men, and anger, again, is their nourisher. Know this, O highly wise lady: existence and non-existence have their roots in anger."
O beautiful one, he who restrains his anger possesses true being;
he who does not restrain his anger, on the contrary, lacks being.
Therefore, O beautiful one, anger is the cause of non-existence.
Furthermore, O auspicious one, when a man does not constantly restrain his anger,
that most terrible anger leads to his own destruction;
for it is seen here in this world that the ruin of living beings has its root in anger.
How, then, could one such as I give way to anger, which destroys the world?
An angry man may commit sin; an angry man may even slay his elders;
an angry man, with harsh speech, insults even those who are superior.
For when enraged, one never discerns what should or should not be spoken;
there is no deed too base for an angry man, nor is there anything he would not say.
Out of anger, he might slay those who should not be slain, or even honor those who deserve to be executed.
An angry person may even send himself to the abode of Yama;
seeing these faults, the wise have conquered anger,
desiring the highest good both in this world and in the next.
"How could one like me indulge in that anger which the wise have abandoned?
Keeping this in mind, O Draupadī, my wrath does not increase;
for it is through self-control that one protects both oneself and others from great danger."
By not returning anger to one who is angry, one acts as a physician to both.
If a foolish and powerless man, while being afflicted, gives way to anger,
he ultimately destroys himself at the hands of those more powerful men.
When one who lacks self-control gives up his own life, his worlds are destroyed;
therefore, O Draupadī, it is taught that the restraint of anger belongs to the powerless. Likewise, the wise man who is capable yet does not become angry when being afflicted [is likewise noble].
Having destroyed his tormentor, he rejoices in the next world;
therefore, both the strong and the weak,
being wise, should always practice forbearance even in times of adversity.

For the virtuous here praise victory over anger, O Kṛṣṇa; it is the opinion of the wise that for the patient and the good man, victory is eternal. Truth is better than falsehood, and kindness is better than cruelty.
Why would one such as I give way to such anger— which is fraught with many faults, devoid of virtue, and even more grievous than the slaughter of Suyodhana—
merely because the wise and far-sighted call him "the radiant one"?
It is certain that anger does not dwell within him who,
when anger has arisen, repels it with wisdom; those who see reality consider such a person to be truly majestic.
For when enraged, O fair-hipped one, a man does not perceive his duty as it truly is;
an angry man perceives neither his task nor the bounds of propriety.
In his rage, he slays even those who should not be slain, and he strikes even his elders with harsh words.
Therefore, when one must manifest brilliance (*tejas*), anger should be kept at a distance.
For skill, impatience, heroism, and swiftness are the qualities of brilliance;
they cannot be easily attained by one who is overcome by anger.

Having abandoned anger, a person attains true splendor; for when joined with the right time, O highly wise lady, the energy of the angry is extremely difficult to endure. Yet, by the ignorant, anger is constantly designated as "energy."
Passion has been ordained for the destruction of the worlds with respect to human beings;
therefore, a man who conducts himself properly should forever abandon anger. It is certain that one who does not deviate from his own duty is superior to one who is angry.
O blameless lady, if all those who lack wisdom and intelligence have already transcended [this world],
how indeed could one such as I transcend it? If there were no men among humanity who, like the earth itself, are possessed of forgiveness.
There would be no peace among men, for conflict has its root in anger.
For one who is provoked would provoke in turn, and one struck by a superior would strike back;
thus would the destruction of beings occur, and unrighteousness would become widespread.
If every man, when reviled, were to revile in return;
if he who is struck were to strike back, and likewise he who is harmed were to harm in return;
then fathers would slay their sons, and sons would likewise slay their fathers.
Husbands would slay their wives, and likewise wives would slay their husbands. When the world is thus enraged, O Kṛṣṇā, birth no longer exists;
for know, O fair-faced one, that the birth of living beings has its root in union.

O Draupadī, in such a situation, all these subjects would quickly perish; therefore, wrath leads to the destruction and the non-existence of living beings. Yet, it is because those who are as patient as the earth are seen in this world [that the world endures].
Therefore, O beautiful lady, both the birth and the continued existence of living beings are brought about; a man must practice forbearance here in all calamities,
for forbearance is proclaimed to be both the existence and the very birth of beings.
He who, though reviled and struck by a stronger man, remains patient;
he who has eternally conquered anger—he is a wise and supreme person. Even if such a man possesses great power, his worlds are eternal.
But one who is prone to anger and possesses little wisdom perishes both in this world and after death.
In this regard, they cite these verses concerning those who are ever-forgiving,
sung by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa Kāśyapa, O Kṛṣṇe:
Forgiveness is dharma; forgiveness is sacrifice; forgiveness is the Vedas; forgiveness is sacred learning.
He who understands it thus is worthy to forgive everything.
Forgiveness is Brahman; forgiveness is truth; forgiveness is the past and the future.
Forgiveness is austerity; forgiveness is purity; by forgiveness the world is sustained.
Those who possess forgiveness attain those worlds that surpass the realms of the knowers of Brahman, the ascetics, and even the experts in sacrifice.
Forgiveness is the splendor of the spirited; forgiveness is the sacred power of ascetics;
forgiveness is the truth of the truthful; forgiveness is charity; forgiveness is fame.
O Kṛṣṇā, how could one such as I abandon such forgiveness as that?
In that [state] reside both Brahman and Truth, as well as the sacrifices and the worlds;
likewise, the worlds of the performers of sacrifice and those of the patient are enjoyed there. For the patient ones in the world of Brahmā, there are worlds most highly honored.
A wise person should always practice forbearance;
for when one forgives everything, one then attains the state of Brahman.
This world belongs to those who are forbearing, and the next world belongs to those who are forbearing.

Those men whose anger is always subdued by forgiveness attain honor in this world and a blessed state in the next; for them there are the highest worlds beyond. Therefore, patience is considered supreme.
"Thus were these verses concerning those who are ever-forgiving sung by Kāśyapa. Having heard these verses on forgiveness, O Draupadī, be satisfied and do not be angry;
the grandfather Śāṃtanava will honor peace."
The preceptor Vidura, the Kṣattṛ, will speak only of peace;
and Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, will honor peace;
and both Kṛpa and Saṃjaya will likewise speak only of peace.
Somadatta, Yuyutsu, and likewise the son of Droṇa,
as well as our grandfather Vyāsa, constantly speak of peace;
for the king is surely being urged toward peace by these men.
"It is my conviction that he will give away the kingdom, unless he perishes through greed—
at which time this terrible hour has arrived for the destruction of the Bharatas, when Pārtha stands with bow in hand, and Bhīma and the heroic Kṛṣṇa are present."
"It is my conviction that the destruction of the entire world upon this earth is at hand;
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Karṇa—what do you see remaining there?
O beautiful lady, I have always been certain of this even from the very beginning."
"Suyodhana does not deserve [this], and thus he finds no forgiveness;
I, however, am worthy of him, and therefore forgiveness finds me. This is the conduct of those who possess self-mastery; this is the eternal dharma."
"I shall truly practice both forgiveness and compassion.
Draupadī said:
"Homage to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, who have brought about this delusion in you!"
Your mind is otherwise inclined toward the ancestral conduct inherited from your fathers and grandfathers, which must be upheld;
yet the world is fashioned by actions, with its various modes of coming and going. Therefore, one who desires to attain liberation out of greed [for it] must perform the obligatory rites.

In this world, a man does not attain prosperity through righteousness or compassion, nor through patience or uprightness, nor ever through mere tenderness. O Bhārata, if such an unbearable calamity as this has come upon you...
That you do not deserve it, nor do these brothers of yours of great prowess; for neither then nor now, O Bhārata,
have they ever perceived anything dearer than dharma, even more so than life itself in this world.
"Your kingdom is for the sake of dharma alone, and your life is for the sake of dharma;
this the Brahmins, the elders, and even the gods know,
as do Bhīmasena, Arjuna, the two sons of Mādrī, and myself."
"It is my understanding that you would abandon [me], yet you would not abandon righteousness;
for it has been heard by me from the noble ones that 'righteousness protects the king who protects righteousness,' but I think that righteousness does not protect you."

"O tiger among men, your intellect always follows nothing but dharma alone; it constantly pursues it like one's own innate shadow follows a person. Indeed, dharma well-earned by me follows a person like a shadow."
For you did not despise those who were your equals, much less those who were inferior or superior;
yet, despite having obtained the entire earth, your horn did not grow.
[You honored] the twice-born with the utterances of *svāhā* and *svadhā*, and even with various forms of worship.
O Pārtha, you constantly serve the deities and the ancestors;
O Pārtha, the Brāhmaṇas have been perpetually gratified by you with all their desires,
as well as the ascetics seeking liberation and the householders, O Bhārata.
They eat from golden bowls where I serve as an attendant;
yet you give iron vessels to the forest-dwellers. There is nothing in your house that cannot be given to the brahmins.
O King, that which is given every morning and evening at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice— having given that to guests and dependents, you live on what remains;
and having given to dogs and outcastes, you live on what is left over.
The *iṣṭi* sacrifices, the animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*), those performed for specific desires or on specific occasions,
the *pākayajña* offerings, and the regular sacrificial rites—
all these continue even in this great forest, though it is desolate and frequented by bandits.

For one who dwells having departed from his kingdom, your dharma does not decline. You have also performed these great sacrifices— the Aśvamedha, Rājasūya, Puṇḍarīka, and Gosava— with abundant sacrificial fees.
O King, with a clouded intellect during that disastrous defeat at dice,
you were deprived of your kingdom, your wealth, your weapons, your brothers, and even me.
[Yet this was done against one who is] upright, gentle, generous, modest, and truthful.
"How has this intellect born of the calamity of gambling come upon you?
Your mind falls into extreme delusion and is deeply distressed,
having perceived this suffering of yours and such a misfortune as this."
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history,

showing how the world remains under the control of the Lord and not under its own power; for the Creator alone indeed ordains the pleasure and pain, the pleasant and the unpleasant, of all living beings.
The Lord, rising as pure light from the front, bestows everything.
O hero among men, just as a wooden puppet is moved by a man who manipulates its limbs, so too, O King, are these subjects moved.
O Bhārata, like space pervading all beings,
the Lord ordains here both that which is auspicious and that which is evil;
this person is bound by necessity and is not his own master, like a bird tied to a string.
Remaining under the control of the Lord, one is not the master of others nor of oneself;
like a gem strung on a thread, or a bull led by a nose-rope, one follows the command of the Creator, for one is absorbed in Him and offered unto Him.
This human being is not master of himself for any length of time,
like a tree fallen from the bank into the middle of a current.
This ignorant creature is powerless over his own pleasure and pain.
Impelled by the Lord, one goes to heaven or even to hell;
just as the tips of blades of grass fall under the power of a mighty wind,
so do all beings fall under the power of the Creator, O Bhārata.
Engaging in noble deeds or again in evil,
the Lord moves pervading all beings, yet he is not perceived as "this.
This body, known as the field (*kṣetra*), is merely the instrument of the Creator.
By which the omnipresent Lord causes actions to be performed that yield both auspicious and inauspicious fruits—
behold this power of illusion (*māyā*) as it has been fashioned by the Lord, who,
having deluded beings with his own *māyā*, destroys beings by means of other beings.
Things perceived in one way by the sages who have seen the Vedas turn out otherwise,
like the gusts of the wind;
for indeed, men think of various things in quite a different way.
The Lord creates and transforms those things in a manner entirely different [from their own nature],
just as one might cut wood with wood, stone with stone, or even iron with iron— [all] while they themselves are motionless and insentient.
Thus, O Yudhiṣṭhira, that Blessed Lord, the Self-existent Great-Grandfather,
destroys beings by means of other beings, having assumed a disguise;
this Lord, who acts according to his own will, unites them and then separates them.
"O Blessed One, he plays with living beings as a child plays with toys.
O King, the Creator does not behave toward beings like a mother or a father;
rather, he acts as if driven by anger, just like any other ordinary person."
Seeing the noble ones who possess virtue and modesty yet are emaciated by lack of livelihood,
while the ignoble are happy, I am as if overwhelmed with anxiety;
for I see this misfortune of yours and the prosperity of Suyodhana.
O Pārtha, I revile the Creator who looks upon things with partiality—
what fruit does that Creator enjoy for bestowing prosperity upon the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who is cruel, greedy, a transgressor of the noble scriptures, and a destroyer of righteousness?
If an action performed follows the doer and does not reach another,
then surely the Lord is defiled by that sinful deed.
Or, if the evil deed committed does not reach the doer—
"In this world, power alone is the cause; I grieve for those who are weak.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Yājñasenī, these words spoken by you are beautiful, composed of varied phrases, and gentle."
"That which was spoken has been heard by us; however, you speak with atheism. O princess, I do not practice seeking the fruits of dharma;
I simply give what ought to be given, and I sacrifice because it is right to sacrifice."

Whether there be fruit for this or not, O Kṛṣṇā, I perform whatever ought to be done by a man living as a householder to the best of my ability. I practice dharma, O lady of beautiful hips, not for the sake of the fruits of dharma.
Without transgressing the scriptures and observing the conduct of the virtuous,
my mind, O Kṛṣṇa, is fixed upon dharma alone by its very nature.
One who traffics in dharma is base and the lowest among those who speak of dharma.

He who wishes to milk the Dharma does not obtain the fruit of the Dharma; nor does the evil-minded man who, out of atheism, suspects it after having performed it. Do not cast excessive suspicion upon the Dharma because of harsh words or pride.
A man who harbors doubts about the Dharma is destined for rebirth among the animals; he who,
being weak of soul, would doubt the Dharma or the teachings of the sages, shall fall from this ageless and immortal world like a Śūdra from the Vedas.

O illustrious lady, one who studies the Vedas, is devoted to dharma, and is born of noble lineage should be appointed by righteous kings among the elders; for such a person is more wretched than Śūdras, and especially so than thieves.

The dull-witted man who transgresses the scriptures and harbors excessive doubt regarding Dharma has already seen with his own eyes, O King, the seer Mārkaṇḍeya of immeasurable soul and great ascetic power, who attained long life through Dharma.
Vyāsa, Vasiṣṭha, Maitreya, Nārada, Lomaśa, Śuka,
and other perfected sages who are well-disposed through righteousness alone—
you see them all directly before you, endowed with divine yoga.
Capable of both cursing and bestowing grace, and even more venerable than the gods, these men—
whose wisdom is as direct as sacred scripture and who resemble the immortals themselves— always describe dharma alone as my primary duty.

Therefore, O auspicious lady, you ought not to revile or even suspect the Creator and the Dharma itself with a mind deluded by passion. A fool considers all those who have attained certainty to be mad.
One who is suspicious of the Dharma does not find authority in anything else;
puffed up by his own standard of judgment, he indeed despises what is superior. This world, which is witnessed by all people, is bound to the pleasure of the senses.
The fool thinks only this much, yet he goes into delusion elsewhere;
there is no atonement for him who harbors excessive doubt regarding the Dharma. Meditating thus, that wretched sinner does not attain the higher worlds.
For he who transgresses the authoritative means of knowledge, who reviles the meaning of the Vedas and the scriptures,
and who is a fool following after lust and greed, falls into hell;
whereas he whose mind is ever-settled pursues only dharma.
O auspicious lady, he who acts without hesitation attains infinity in the hereafter.
But the fool who transgresses the authority of the seers (*ārṣa*), fails to protect the duties (*dharma*),
and oversteps all scriptures, finds no peace throughout his births.
O beautiful lady, for one who regards neither the words of the seers as authoritative nor the conduct of the cultured,
it is certain that there is neither this world nor the next. O Kṛṣṇā, do not cast doubt upon the dharma practiced by the cultured.
This ancient [teaching] was proclaimed by the seers, who are all-knowing and all-seeing.
O Draupadī, for those going to heaven, dharma alone is the raft and nothing else;
it is like a ship for a merchant seeking to reach the far shore of the ocean.
O blameless lady, if the Dharma practiced by those who walk the path of Dharma were fruitless,
this world would sink into a bottomless darkness;
they would not attain Nirvana, but would live the life of beasts.
They would be joined only with frustration and would not attain any goal at all,
if asceticism, celibacy, sacrifice, Vedic study,
charity, and uprightness were indeed to be fruitless.
If those who practiced the Dharma— those of the past and those of more distant times— had not done so,
this would be a total deception, for ritual actions would then be fruitless;
[this is true] even for the sages, the gods, the gandharvas, asuras, and rākṣasas.

O Kṛṣṇa, for what reason would those lords practice dharma with such reverence? For they practice that eternal dharma, O Kṛṣṇa, having recognized here in this world that the Creator bestows the fruit of certain spiritual welfare.

And this dharma is fruitful; dharma is not said to be fruitless. For the fruits of the sciences as well as of ascetic penances are indeed seen. Know this truly regarding your birth from Kṛṣṇa, just as it has been heard.
"And you also know how the powerful Dhṛṣṭadyumna was born.
This much alone is sufficient as a comparison, O lady of pure smiles:
that a wise man is satisfied even with a small result, knowing that there is indeed fruit for one's actions."
For even with much, the ignorant and witless are never satisfied;
for them there is no happiness born of dharma after death,
nor any fruit arising from their actions, whether meritorious or sinful.
O beautiful lady, the origin and the dissolution [of all things], as well as the secrets of the gods—
no one knows these, for all these creatures are deluded therein;
even in a thousand kalpas, a man may not attain the highest good.
These [realms] are to be guarded by the gods, for the deities possess hidden powers of illusion. Indeed,
those twice-born ones who have emaciated bodies, who are firm in their vows, whose sins have been burnt away by austerity,
and who are endowed with serene minds, truly perceive these.

One should not doubt the Dharma or the deities because results are not immediately seen; one should sacrifice vigilantly and give without malice. That there is a fruit of actions—this is the eternal nature of Dharma.
"Brahmā spoke to his sons that which the seer Kaśyapa knows;
therefore, O Kṛṣṇā, let your doubt perish like the mist. Resolving that 'everything exists,' abandon the state of atheism."
Do not cast doubt upon the Lord, the Sustainer of all beings;
train yourself in him and bow down to him, lest you harbor such a thought as this:
that by his grace, a mortal devoted to him attains immortality.
"O Kṛṣṇa, do not speak disparagingly of the Supreme Deity in any way whatsoever.
Draupadī said:
"O Pārtha, I do not disregard nor do I revile Dharma in any way whatsoever."
"How indeed could I despise the Lord, the Prajāpati? Know me, O Bhārata, to be one who speaks thus only because I am afflicted;
listen to me as I shall lament further with a composed mind."
"O crusher of enemies, one who has been born must indeed perform action in this world;
for only immobile beings live without action, and no other people do.
From the time of drinking from the mother's breast until the time of retiring to bed,"
O Yudhiṣṭhira, mobile beings obtain their livelihood through action;
O bull of the Bharatas, among mobile beings especially,
human beings desire to obtain a livelihood through action both in this world and after death.
O Bhārata, all beings recognize the importance of exertion;
they experience the visible fruits of their actions, witnessed by the world. I see that living creatures subsist upon their own exertion.
Even if Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ were to provide for this crane in the water,
there would indeed be no means of subsistence whatsoever for beings who do not act; therefore,
one should apply oneself to that very [effort] and never fail in any way.
Perform your own duty; do not grow weary. Be armored by your action.

For he who truly understands what must be done—whether such a person exists or does not exist among a thousand—is the one for whom there remains work to be done, both in furthering his cause and in protecting it.
For even the Himalayas would be exhausted if they were consumed without being replenished;
all living beings would perish if they did not perform their work. Likewise, these beings would not increase if action were to be fruitless.
Moreover, we see people performing actions that yield no fruit;
for otherwise, they would not understand how to maintain their livelihood in this world in any way whatsoever.
Both he who in this world relies on destiny and he who is a proponent of chance—
Both of these are outcasts; it is the intellect that engages in action which is praised.
For he who, relying on destiny, remains inactive and sleeps at ease, will perish like an unbaked clay pot in water—he of wicked intellect.

Likewise, one who possesses a mind of forceful effort (*haṭhabuddhi*) but is capable yet performs no action will not live long, being weak like one who is helpless. Furthermore, whatever man may happen to obtain wealth unexpectedly—
People consider that to be achieved by force, yet no one exerts such effort; and whatever a man obtains that is called "destiny," O Pārtha, that is determined to be the work of divine ordinance.

Whatever fruit a person obtains through his own action, seen directly with the eye, that is remembered as *pauruṣa* (human effort). Another, acting by his own nature, obtains objects without [prior] cause.

Know that, O best of men, the fruit is of the nature of inherent disposition (*svabhāva*). Thus, whatever a person obtains through exertion, fate, inherent disposition, or likewise through action— that is the fruit of prior karma.
For even Dhātṛ, acting as the Lord through various causes,
distributes here the fruits of the deeds previously performed by men;
for whatever good or evil this person performs, it is indeed he who ordains it.

Know that this is ordained by the Creator as the arising of the fruit of past actions. This body is the instrument for every action; just as the Creator impels it, so does it act, being without autonomy.
For Maheśvara is the one who directs them toward their respective tasks;
O son of Kuntī, he causes all beings to act, even though they are powerless.
Having first determined the objects of desire with the mind, one subsequently attains them through action.
The wise man himself, acting with prior intelligence, is the cause therein.
O bull among men, it is impossible to count the deeds [performed];
for indeed, the accomplishment of houses and cities has man as its cause.
Just as one finds oil in sesame seeds, milk in a cow, and fire within wood,
so should the wise man discern [the self] through his intellect, as well as the means for its realization. Thereafter, he proceeds toward the instruments of action for the sake of that realization.
In this world, living beings subsist upon that success resulting from their actions.
An action performed by a skillful agent is well-determined as "this was done by one who is skilled," and it is perceived as distinct from that which is performed by one who is unskilled.
The fruit of sacrifices and charitable works would not exist, nor would there be disciple or teacher,
if this person were not the cause in matters accomplished through action.
It is precisely because of his agency that a person is praised for the successful accomplishment of action.

If [the result] is not established, one is even censured; how then can there be the destruction of karma here? Some say that everything arises from force (daiva), others say it is from destiny (diṣṭa), while some say it is born of human effort; thus this is explained in three ways.
Others, however, do not consider the matter to be settled by this much alone;
they hold that everything exists, yet it is invisible—namely, destiny (*diṣṭa*) and chance (*haṭha*).
For indeed, the occurrence of events is seen to proceed from both chance and destiny.
A person obtains results partly from destiny, partly from chance, and partly from one’s own action; there is no fourth cause here—
so declare those who are skillful and knowers of reality.
In the same way, if Dhātṛ, the bestower of desired and undesired fruits upon all beings,
did not exist, there would be no such thing as a miserable person among living beings.
Whatever object a man seeks to obtain, he performs action toward that end.
Each and every action would indeed be fruitful if past deeds did not exist;
yet those men who do not perceive the attainment of success through these three doors,
as well as the attainment of failure, are exactly like the common world.
"One must indeed perform action"—this is the firm resolve of Manu.
Until death one should seek prosperity; one should not consider it unattainable.
For a man who is entirely devoid of effort inevitably comes to ruin.
But that would undoubtedly not happen while you remain inactive;
for in this world, O Yudhiṣṭhira, success generally attends one who acts,
whereas the lazy person never attains the certain accomplishment of results.
But when this [atonement] is impossible, a penance is prescribed;
for once the rite has been performed, O King of kings, one attains freedom from debt. Misfortune enters that man who lies down in indolence.
Having obtained a result that is beyond doubt, the skillful man enjoys prosperity;
those who have cast off doubt choose a state of uncertainty rather than misfortune. Wise men are devoted to action, yet they never remain in a state of total uncertainty.
For at present, this misfortune has befallen us entirely;
yet it would not be without doubt if you were to remain engaged in action.
Or rather, success itself might come to pass, and your greatness would likewise be established.
Whether the deeds of Vṛkodara, Bībhatsu, and the twin brothers,
or those of others, or even our own,
may their success be understood through the distance [of time], just as one perceives the fruit once the action has been performed.
Having broken the earth with a plough, the farmer sows the seed;
then he sits in silence, for Parjanya is the cause therein. If the rain does not favor him, the farmer is blameless in that matter.
"Whatever another person might do, all that has been done by me.
If that results in fruitlessness for us, there is no fault in us anywhere. Having reflected thus, the steadfast man should not reproach himself in that regard.

"O Bhārata, one should not fall into despondency thinking, 'Success does not come to me despite my efforts,' for both success and failure are the two possible outcomes of this action; otherwise, there would be no engagement at all."
For it is through the combination of many factors that an action succeeds;
in the absence of these qualities, the result is deficient or even non-existent. But in the case of no undertaking at all, O Acyuta, neither fruit nor quality is seen.

The wise man, through his intelligence, employs the proper place, time, and means, as well as auspicious rites and blessings for the sake of prosperity, according to his capacity and strength; that task must be performed with vigilance by one who possesses the prowess of an instructor.
In the application of actions, almost all effort is directed toward this end.
However, when a wise man perceives that another is superior to him in many virtues,
he should seek his purpose through conciliation alone and employ action for that person's sake.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should desire the misfortune or even the destruction of such a person,
whether he be as vast as the ocean or as firm as a mountain, let alone one who is subject to the nature of mortals;
for he is constantly intent on exertion in seeking out the vulnerabilities of his enemies.
A man attains freedom from debt both toward others and toward himself;
yet, a person should never despise himself,
for prosperity does not come to one who has humiliated himself, O Bhārata.
O Bhārata, such is the established order of success for the world;
the manifold paths to success have been described according to the divisions of time and circumstances.
Formerly, my father maintained a learned Brāhmaṇa in his household.
O bull of the Bharatas, he explained this matter to my father;
he previously caused my brothers to master the science of polity as proclaimed by Bṛhaspati. I heard that conversation of theirs at that time in our home.
O King Yudhiṣṭhira, as I sat upon my father’s lap, serving him, he spoke to me consolingly when I had arrived there performing my duties. Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Yājñasenī, the exceedingly intolerant Bhīmasena,
sighing in anger, approached the king and said:
"Follow the path of the kingdom that is righteous and worthy of virtuous men."
"For those of us who are destitute of virtue, pleasure, and wealth, what purpose is there in dwelling in this forest of asceticism?
That kingdom was not taken from us by means of righteousness, nor by honesty, nor by prowess;
it was seized by Duryodhana through the employment of fraudulent dice."

Just as a weak jackal, subsisting on leftovers, might seize the prey of powerful lions, so too has our kingdom been snatched away by him who is cloaked in a mere fragment of righteousness while he truly possesses the power of both dharma and desire.
"O King, why do you suffer in these difficult straits after having abandoned your purpose? While we were merely following your lead, our kingdom was snatched away—
even though it was protected by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, whom even Śakra could not have taken."
Like wood-apples on the hands of the club-footed, or like cows to the lame,
our sovereignty has been snatched away while we still live for your sake;
such a great calamity as this has come about simply because you desire what is pleasing to you.

"O Bhārata, we have acted in accordance with one who is devoted to dharma; O bull of the Bharatas, having restrained ourselves under your instruction, we have emaciated our own friends and brought joy to our enemies."
That we did not slay these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra at that very time— having accepted your instruction— that evil deed now torments us. Therefore,
look upon this conduct of yours as being like that of a wild beast.
O King, I do not approve of this path frequented by the unheroic and pursued by those lacking strength—
a path which neither Kṛṣṇa, nor Bībhatsu, nor Abhimanyu, nor Sṛñjaya,
nor I myself, nor both the sons of Mādrī would ever welcome.

"O King, you who are constantly emaciated by vows, crying 'Dharma! Dharma!', have you perhaps, out of despair, fallen into the life of a eunuch? Or will you no longer remember the duty of a Kshatriya, thinking it to be impossible?"
For base men, out of despondency, have fallen into a wretched livelihood;
for base men, having entered into fruitless and all-destructive despair, they sink down like a weak cow in the mud.
"Since the daughter of Dhṛtarāṣṭra is capable of accomplishing all our tasks,
yet remains unable to bring fortune to herself, she instead acts for her own pleasure; therefore, you, who possess foresight and perceive your own manliness, ought to act."
O King, devoted as you are to compassion, you do not perceive the calamity that awaits us.
These sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra consider us—who are capable yet remain forgiving—to be truly powerless; that is what causes us pain, more so than death in battle.
In that case, if we fight straightly and do not retreat,
death in every respect is better, for after passing away we shall attain the higher worlds.
Or else, O bull among the Bharatas, let us slay them ourselves.
"Let us take back all the cattle; even so, it will be for our welfare.
In every respect, this is what must be done by us who follow our own duty, who desire vast fame, and who wish to retaliate against the enmity."

When the characteristics of duty are well understood, there is only praise and no censure for those who fight for their own sake when their kingdom has been seized by others. For that dharma which aims at the emaciation of one's friends as well as oneself is not commendable.

"O King, that which is called calamity is not dharma; it is adharma. For a man who is constantly devoted to dharma yet is weak in dharma, both dharma and artha abandon him in every way, my dear, just as pleasure and pain abandon a dead man."
He whose practice of dharma is for the sake of dharma alone, yet suffers the burden of affliction, is not a wise man;

he does not understand the true purpose of dharma, just as one blind to light cannot perceive the radiance of the sun. And he whose wealth exists solely for the sake of wealth is no expert in the nature of wealth.
He who guards [the king's wealth] like a hired servant in the forest is exactly like that;
for he who, being excessively greedy for wealth, does not attend to the other two [virtues],
is fit to be slain by all beings and is as loathsome as a slayer of a Brahmin.
He who constantly pursues only desire and does not attend to the other two [dharma and artha] loses his friends and is deprived of both dharma and artha.
For one thus deprived of dharma and artha, death at the end of his desires is certain.
For one who indulges in desire, it is like a fish at the drying up of the water;
therefore, the wise never neglect virtue and worldly prosperity,
for that is the very nature of desire, just as fire-sticks are the source of fire.
In every way, wealth has its root in dharma, and dharma is sustained by wealth;
know that these two arise from one another, like the clouds and the ocean. That joy which arises from the union of the touch of objects with wealth—
That desire is a mental construction; it has no physical body.
O King, a man seeking wealth attains great dharma;
one seeking pleasure attains wealth, but nothing other than that which he seeks.
And he who seeks sensual pleasure does not find anything other than pleasure through sensual pleasure;
for one desire is not accomplished by means of another desire—that is merely a fruit.
A wise man understands this to be like the ashes produced from wood through the consumption of its fruit.
"O King, just as a fowler kills these small birds,
such is the nature of unrighteousness for those who inflict injury upon living beings;
he who, out of desire or greed, does not perceive the true course of dharma."
That evil-minded man deserves to be slain by all beings, both in this world and after death.
O King, it is evident that you understand the matter of the possession of wealth;
you also know its natural state as well as its manifold transformations.
For one of weak soul, the acquisition of wealth is more important than its loss or destruction through old age or death;
yet they consider such acquisition to be a misfortune, and this very thing now occurs among us.
The pleasure that arises when the five senses, the mind, and the heart engage with their respective objects— that, in my view, is desire; it is the supreme fruit of actions.
In this very way, having perceived dharma, artha, and kāma as distinct,
a man should not be devoted solely to dharma, nor solely to artha,
nor should he be solely devoted to kāma; rather, he should pursue all of them at all times.
One should practice Dharma first, wealth in the middle, and desire last;
one should follow this sequence every day—this is the rule established by the scriptures.
Alternatively, one may practice desire first, wealth in the middle, and Dharma last.

A friend should follow one in this manner; such is the injunction established by the scriptures. O best of speakers, a wise man who knows the proper time should divide his time accordingly and pursue virtue, wealth, and pleasure all at their appropriate seasons.

O King, for those who seek happiness, either liberation is the supreme good, or its attainment by relying on intelligence and employing the proper means, O joy of the Kurus. Therefore, O King, let that be done quickly, or let the attainment [of liberation] be achieved.
For life for one who wavers between two states is as painful as that of a sick man. Dharma is indeed known to you, and it has been constantly practiced by you;
your friends, recognizing this, urge you toward righteous action.
"O King, charity, sacrifice, honoring the virtuous, the preservation of the Vedas, and straightforwardness— this is the supreme dharma, which bears fruit both in this world and after death.
O King, this cannot be practiced by one who is destitute of wealth."
O tiger among men, even if all other qualities were present, O King, the world has dharma as its root; nothing excels dharma. And dharma, O King, can be practiced through great wealth.
O King, the true goal can never be understood through a life of begging, nor by means of weakness, even for one whose mind is solely intent on dharma; for begging,
by which a twice-born man indeed achieves success, has been forbidden to you.
O bull among men, strive to acquire wealth through valor alone;
for a Kṣatriya, the life of a mendicant is not ordained, nor is the livelihood of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra.
Indeed, for a Kṣatriya in particular, righteousness is his innate strength.
Fulfill your own duty; slay the assembled enemies. O Pārtha, destroy the forest of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons with me as your Pārtha.
The wise who possess true knowledge declare that dharma alone is noble.
Adopt a noble course; you ought not to remain in what is base. Wake up, O Indra among kings! You know the eternal laws (dharmas), yet you are born for cruel deeds because of which the people tremble.
The fruit arising from the protection of your subjects is not to be despised;
O King, this is the eternal dharma ordained for you by the Creator.
Therefore, O Pārtha, if you deviate from it, you will become an object of ridicule in the world.
For deviation from one’s own duty is not praised among men. Therefore,
O son of Kuntī, having adopted the heart of a warrior and casting aside this lax mind, summon your valor and bear the burden like one who is fit for it.
O King, no earthly ruler who was solely devoted to righteousness has ever conquered the earth, nor attained prosperity or royal fortune;
for he had given his tongue over to many petty men of greedy mind.

One obtains a kingdom through deceit, just as a porcupine obtains its food; O bull among the Pāṇḍavas, even the Asuras, though they were previously born brothers and possessed great wealth in every respect, were utterly defeated by the gods through deceit.
"O lord of the earth, knowing that everything belongs to the powerful,
O mighty-armed one, slay your enemies by resorting to supreme deceit;
for there is no archer or warrior equal to Arjuna in battle."

"O King, there may be some man who is my equal or even a wielder of the mace; yet even one who is very powerful engages in battle through *sattva* (inner strength). It is not by physical size nor by mere enthusiasm that one succeeds—be established in *sattva*, O Pāṇḍava."
For truth is the root of wealth; that which is otherwise is false.
It does not persist, just as the shade of a tree in winter does not. Indeed, one who desires superior wealth must abandon [untrue] wealth.

O Kaunteya, let there be no doubt in you regarding this, for it is like a seed. Where a loss equal to the gain is incurred and no profit is obtained, one should not engage in trade there; for that is merely like scratching an ass.

In this very way, O lord of men, when a man abandons a minor dharma and attains a great dharma, he is certain to be called a Buddha. Wise men cause a friend who has become an enemy to be alienated by means of other friends.
One who is weak brings under his control even a strong man whose friends have been divided and who has been abandoned by them. O King, even one who is very powerful engages in battle through courage;
he does not win over all the subjects through mere exertion or through sacrificial offerings.
In every way, even a powerful enemy can be slain by the weak when they are united, just as the honey-thief is slain by bees.
O King, just as the sun protects all creatures with its rays, so too [should one protect] his subjects.
"And you too must eat in that very same manner; thus may you become equal to Savitṛ.
For this, O King, is the ancient austerity, as we have heard it, which was practiced by our grandfathers through the protection of the earth according to the sacred law."

O King, a Kṣatriya does not attain the worlds through asceticism in the same way that he does through battle— whether by victory or otherwise. Indeed, it is said that light might depart from the sun and splendor from the moon, but [the world] would never leave a king who has performed his duty.
"O King, having witnessed this distress of yours, the world has reached such a conclusion;
assemblies have gathered separately, O monarch, occupied with discourse concerning your praises and the censures of the other."
O King, this is even more significant: the Brahmins and your elders,
having gathered here, joyfully proclaim your steadfastness in truth—
that you have never, out of delusion, wretchedness, greed, or even fear, [failed to act rightly].
Not out of desire, nor for the sake of wealth, has any falsehood ever been spoken by you.
Whatever sin a king commits while acquiring the earth,
he later dispels it all through sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
O King, by giving villages and cows by the thousands to the Brahmins,
one is liberated from all sins, just as the moon is freed from darkness.
O descendant of Kuru, almost all the people of the city and the countryside [act thus].

O Yudhiṣṭhira, O great king, people including the old and the young together praise you; they do not praise the policy of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son. It is like milk poured into a dog’s skin-bag, or like the Veda entrusted to a low-born man.
"Truth resides in the thief, strength in a woman, and sovereignty in Duryodhana"—
this proverb, O Bhārata, has long circulated in the world;
even women and children recite it as if it were a sacred text.
"O subduer of enemies, since you have reached this state along with us, alas, we are all truly lost now that you have met with such calamity. Therefore,
please mount the chariot equipped with all its implements."

Hastening forth, let him depart today for Hastinapura, having had the best of the twice-born recite benedictions that bring about his success; surrounded by his brothers, who are skilled in weapons and wield firm bows, let him go forth to achieve his long-cherished purpose.

O hero of great strength, O son of Kuntī, seize the royal fortune from the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— crushing your enemies with your splendor like the slayer of Vṛtra with the Maruts who are like venomous serpents, and like the destroyer of Asuras against the demons.
For no mortal whatsoever could endure the touch of those arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva— feathered with vulture plumes and resembling venomous serpents.
Who could endure [the loss] of their own bodies as they are being carried away by enemies?
O Bhārata, there is no hero, no elephant,
and no noble steed who could withstand the force of my mace when I am enraged in battle—
neither among the Sṛñjayas, the Kaikeyas, nor with the bull of the Vṛṣṇis.
O son of Kuntī, how indeed might we not lose our kingdom in battle? O King, how indeed might you recover the earth that has fallen into the hands of the enemy,
having exerted effort here and being endowed with a great army?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by Bhīmasena, the king of great majesty remained true to his vow.
Immediately thereafter, Ajātaśatru,
endowed with fortitude, spoke these words.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Bhārata, there is no doubt that this is true,
even as you wound me and exhaust me with the arrows of your words;
yet I do not reproach you for this hostility.
For it was through my own misconduct that this calamity has come upon you;
indeed, desiring to seize it, I engaged with the dice to take from the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra his kingdom and his realm.
But that deceitful gambler,
Śakuni, the son of Subala from the mountains, a master of great illusions, played against me for the sake of Suyodhana.
"O Bhīmasena, I saw that wickedness when, while constantly casting heaps of dice in the assembly, he deceived me— who am free from guile— with deceit."
For had one been able to restrain the self upon seeing the dice of the bird exactly as they were—
both odd and even, and favorable to desire—
it would have been possible [to control it].
But anger destroys a man's fortitude; one who is bound by pride and valor, my dear, cannot control himself through human effort.
"O Bhīmasena, I do not find fault with your words;
I believe that it was destined to happen thus.
That king is the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
Desiring the kingdom, he cast us into calamity and brought us to slavery, O Bhīmasena,
where Draupadī became our refuge.
You also know that, when we returned to the assembly hall for the game of dice, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra said this to me: "And you too, O Dhanañjaya, know what he said."
O Prince, for the sake of obtaining a single portion [of the kingdom], you have lived for twelve years in the forest in the presence of the Bharatas,
as was known to Ajātaśatru according to his desire.
Furthermore, you should move about unrecognized,
concealed by a disguise along with all your brothers; for if they hear that you, dear one, are acting in such a manner, [they will be alarmed].
"The spies of the Bharatas will discover you;
therefore, O Pārtha, having decided upon another [disguise], undertake it and remain for as many years as those."
O King, if he has not been discovered by us during this time, having employed his chariot and deluded my men,
I speak the truth here in this assembly of the Kurus: [he is still alive].
O Bhārata, those five rivers are yours alone,
and we, all your brothers as well,
having abandoned our enjoyments, have been won over by you for the sake of time.
"I shall dwell there," that king said long ago;
"So be it," I told him in the midst of the Kurus.
There, our ignoble game of dice took place.
In him all have been conquered and have gone forth;
thus we wander through the lands, appearing wretched as we traverse forests and hardships.
And Suyodhana, not desiring peace,
again fell under the sway of wrath and incited all the Kurus.
And as for those who have come under his influence,
who indeed would abandon that alliance in the presence of the virtuous for the sake of a kingdom?
I consider death to be more grievous for a noble man than this:
that he should rule the earth by transgressing the Dharma.
Had you performed heroic deeds at that very moment;
When you seized the iron mace during the gambling match, desiring to burn up your arms though restrained by Phalguna—
what evil deed would have been committed by you, Bhima, at that time?
Why did you not speak thus earlier, while still aware of your own prowess, before this agreement was made? But now that the time has arrived, you have finally resorted to it.
"Why do you now speak to me so excessively?
O Bhīmasena, my sorrow increases even further; I suffer as if having experienced the taste of poison."
"O Bhīma, when you saw Yājñasenī being dragged away and yet remained patient, that was indeed patience;
but today, O hero of the Bharatas, it is not possible [to remain so]."
Having done what was said in the midst of the Kuru heroes,
wait for the time when happiness arises,
just as a sower of seeds waits for the ripening of the fruits.
For when one who has previously been treated with deceit, having recognized that enmity is now flowering and bearing fruit,
seizes back a great benefit through his own manly effort;
Then that hero lives in the world of the living,
attains complete prosperity in this world,
and I believe his enemies bow down before him.
Friends also attend upon him out of great affection,
and they live in dependence on him just as the gods depend on Indra; furthermore, understand my vow to be true.
I choose dharma over immortality and life,
over kingdom, sons, fame, and wealth;
all these do not approach even a fraction of truth.
Bhīmasena said:
"Having made an alliance with Time, the winged Destroyer,
who is infinite, immeasurable, a current that carries away all things— "
Being mortal and bound by time, O Great King, you consider time to be something perceptible; yet you are like foam in nature and likewise like fruit in nature,
O son of Kuntī, for your life diminishes even with the blink of an eye.
Why should one wait, as if with a needle for powdered collyrium,
unless one were indeed of immeasurable lifespan or a knower of the measure of life? Only one who perceives all things directly would wait for such a time.
"O King, as we wait, thirteen years have passed;
having diminished our lifespan, Time will lead us toward death.
For among embodied beings, death is ever inherent within the body."
Therefore, let us strive for sovereignty even before death;
for time is surely ever-present and immortal for a human being—
he who does not attain discernment remains obscure, merely increasing the earth [with his presence].
He who does not settle his enmities sinks down like an ox;
that man of little strength and effort who does not exact revenge for his enmity— I consider his birth to be fruitless, for he has been born in vain.
O King, his two arms become as if made of gold, and he gains renown on earth;
having slain his enemy in battle, he enjoys wealth acquired by the strength of his own arms. O subduer of foes, if a man slays an enemy who seeks to do him harm, O King—

In a single day he would go to hell; that [hell] is equal to heaven for him. For the torment born of indignation is more brilliant than fire, by which I am so consumed that I can lie neither by night nor by day.
And this Pārtha Bībhatsu, the most excellent at drawing the bowstring,
sits here deeply distressed, surely like a lion in its lair—
he who alone considers himself superior to all the archers in the world.
Like a great elephant restraining its own heat, he [Yudhiṣṭhira] restrains his own offspring;
Nakula, Sahadeva, and their aged mother, the mother of heroes,
sit like those who are dull-witted or mute, desiring only what is pleasing to you.

All those kinsmen, together with the Sṛñjayas, desire what is pleasing; I alone, as well as my mother Prativindhya’s mother, am deeply distressed. Yet, whatever I say here is indeed for the sake of the welfare of all.
For all have met with calamity, yet all still rejoice in battle. O King, no misfortune more wretched than this will ever exist:
that our kingdom, having been snatched away by base and weak men, is now being enjoyed by them.

O scorcher of foes, because of the fault of your character, you are filled with loathing; yet out of compassion, O King, you endure these afflictions, though no one else praises you. You are like a dull-witted, ignorant reciter of the Vedas, O King.

Your intellect, struck down by mere recitation, does not perceive the true meaning of reality. You are compassionate and possess the nature of a Brāhmaṇa; how then were you born into the Kṣatriya order?
For those born in this womb are generally of cruel disposition.

You have heard the duties of kings exactly as Manu proclaimed them— cruel, joined with deceit, and ordained for those lacking self-restraint. O Great King, why do you forgive the evil-minded sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra?

O tiger among men, he whose fame is not celebrated for wisdom, asceticism, or heroism; or for learning, or even for wealth—he is nothing but his mother’s excrement. Why do you sit like a cripple crawling on a bench when there is duty to be performed?

O son of Kuntī, you who wish to subdue us are like one who desires to cover the Himalayan mountain with a single handful of grass, despite being endowed with intelligence, prowess, learning, and noble birth.

O Pārtha, it is not possible for you to move about unrecognized and in secret upon this earth while being renowned throughout it, any more than it is possible for the sun in the sky to move about unseen.
You are like a great *śāla* tree in a marshy place, possessed of branches, flowers, and foliage.
How will Jishnu move about unrecognized, like a white elephant?
And how, O Pārtha, will these two brothers, Nakula and Sahadeva, who resemble lions and are together as youths, conduct themselves?
"This princess Draupadī, of virtuous fame and the mother of heroes, is world-renowned; how will Kṛṣṇā live unrecognized, O son of Pṛthā? And these subjects, O King, know me even as far as children."
I perceive this life in concealment to be like the hiding of Mount Meru;
likewise, many kings and princes have been exiled by us from their kingdoms, yet they remain devoted to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

For even they do not remain peaceful when they have been treated with contempt and cast out; they will certainly seek to harm us, as they desire our welfare [only in name]. They too would employ many people against us in secret.
If they were to find out and tell [our location], it would cause us great fear.
We have lived properly in the forest for thirteen months;
consider them to be that many years in their full measure.
"There is a substitute for the month, as the wise have declared;
let this be done just as they do with rotten *soma* plants.
Or else, O King, [let it be given] to a noble bull that carries its burden well."
By the single act of giving satisfaction through food, one is liberated from sin;
therefore, O King, you must make a firm resolve to slay the enemy. For every Kṣatriya, there is no duty other than combat.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Bhīmasena, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī,
that tiger among men and scorcher of foes, sighed deeply and reflected.
I have heard the duties of kings and those of the various social orders individually;
he who perceives both the future and the present is truly one who sees.
Knowing the course of Dharma, which is so difficult to understand, I recognize its supreme goal.
"How shall I accomplish this by force, like the crushing of Mount Meru? Having reflected for a moment and determined what must be done,
he spoke these words to Bhīmasena without a pause.
"It is exactly so, O mighty-armed Bhārata, as you say. Now, O you who are skilled in speech, attend to these other words of mine:
those acts which are great sins committed through sheer recklessness."

O Bhīmasena, descendant of Bharata, those undertakings that are poorly planned, poorly executed, poorly performed, and poorly deliberated upon fail; however, O mighty-armed one, when they are well-planned, well-executed, well-performed, and well-deliberated,
they succeed, for in such cases destiny is favorable.
But you, out of sheer recklessness and puffed up by pride in your strength, consider this task yourself to be undertaken; hear my words regarding that.
Bhūriśravas, Śala, and the heroic Jalasaṃdha—
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and the heroic son of Droṇa,
as well as the Dhārtarāṣṭras led by Duryodhana— invincible and all masters of weapons— are constantly intent on doing you harm.
The kings and rulers of the earth whom we have previously oppressed have now sought refuge with the Kaurava faction; they have developed affection for them and,
O Bhārata, are now intent on the welfare of Duryodhana rather than ours.
With their treasuries full and endowed with strength, all the Kaurava forces— including their sons, ministers, and soldiers— will strive for protection;
for they have been provided for in every way with shares of wealth and enjoyments.
Those heroes have been especially honored by Duryodhana;
it is my firm conviction that they will give up their lives in battle.
Even though Bhīṣma’s conduct toward us and toward them has been equal.
O mighty-armed one, it is my conviction that Droṇa and the high-souled Kṛpa must necessarily provide sustenance for the king;
therefore, they will renounce even their lives, which are so difficult to give up, in the midst of battle.
All of them are experts in divine weapons, all are devoted to righteousness,
and it is my conviction that they are invincible even by the gods led by Indra.
Among them, however, is the great car-warrior Karṇa, who is impatient and ever-joyful.
Skilled in all weapons, unassailable, and clad in impenetrable armor—
without first conquering all these foremost of men in battle,
Duryodhana cannot be slain by you if you are without allies.

"O Vṛkodara, as I reflect upon it, I find no sleep because of the Sūtaputra’s lightness of hand, which surpasses all wielders of the bow. Having heard these words, Bhīmasena, who is exceedingly intolerant, [was filled with rage].
He became dejected and terrified, and said nothing at all while those two Pāṇḍavas were thus conversing. At that moment,
the great yogi Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, arrived.
Having approached and been duly honored by the Pāṇḍavas,
that best of speakers addressed these words to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, I know the thought within your heart."
O bull among men, O Bhārata, it was by means of my intelligence that I have quickly come here from Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa,
and the son of Droṇa, as well as from Prince Duryodhana and even Duḥśāsana.
"O slayer of enemies, whatever fear revolves within your heart,
I shall destroy it for you by means of a method prescribed by rule.
Having heard this, maintain your fortitude and put it into practice through action."
"O Indra among kings, having thus instructed him, quickly dispel his fever.
Then, having led Yudhiṣṭhira to a secluded place, the son of Parāśara,
who was skilled in speech, spoke these words full of profound meaning.
"O best of the Bharatas, a time more favorable than this has arrived for you,
by which Pārtha Dhananjaya shall overcome his enemies in battle. Accept this success, which I have described, as if it were personified."
I shall declare to you, who have sought refuge, a knowledge named *Pratismṛti*,
by acquiring which the mighty-armed Arjuna will achieve his goal;
let him go to Mahendra and Rudra for the sake of these weapons.
O Pāṇḍava, he is capable of beholding Varuṇa, the Lord of Wealth, and Dharmarāja; for by means of his ascetic power and prowess,
this rishi of great splendor has Nārāyaṇa as his companion.
The ancient, eternal, and divine portion of Viṣṇu, who is everlasting,
having taken up weapons from Indra, Rudra, and the guardians of the world,
that mighty-armed one will perform a great deed.
"O son of Kuntī, O lord of the earth, consider another forest than this one for your dwelling, whatever may be suitable for you; for indeed,
a long stay in one place does not produce joy."
It will cause distress to the peaceful ascetics;
there will be the depletion of wild animals and the destruction of creepers and medicinal herbs.
For you support many Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Having spoken thus to the pure one who had sought refuge, the blessed Lord,
the wise Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī and knower of the truth of yoga, then taught the unsurpassed science of yoga to Dharmarāja.

Having given leave to the son of Kuntī, he vanished right there. But the righteous-souled Yudhiṣṭhira, being wise and self-controlled in mind, retained that Brahman, practicing it repeatedly from time to time.

Urged by the words of Vyāsa, he departed from the Dvaitavana forest and went to the grove named Kāmyaka on the banks of the Sarasvatī. O great king, those who were learned in the syllables of the sacred sciences likewise followed him.
Endowed with ascetic power like the ṛṣis of the lord of gods,
those bulls of the Bharata race then reached Kāmyaka once more,
just as the ṛṣis attend upon the lord of the gods.
Having reached that delightful forest, those high-souled ones, together with their ministers and followers, took up residence there;
O King, those wise men dwelt there for some time.
Heroic warriors devoted to the science of archery, listening to the supreme Veda,
constantly engaged in hunting with pure arrows in pursuit of game,
and making offerings according to the prescribed rites to the ancestors, the gods, and the Brahmins.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, after some time had passed, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma,
remembering the sage’s instruction, spoke these words.
In that secluded place, having smiled and touched with his hand Arjuna, the bull of the Bharatas, who was wise and experienced,
he— the subduer of enemies— reflected for a moment upon their forest dwelling.
In private, Dharmarāja spoke thus to Dhanañjaya:
"O Bhārata, the fourfold science of archery (dhanurveda) is today established in these men: Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, and the son of Droṇa."
They fully understand the Brahma, Daiva, and Asura weapons, along with their methods of employment and neutralization, as well as the discharge of all missiles in their entirety;
all of them have been conciliated by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

They were treated with equal shares and were satisfied; he behaved toward them as toward his own teachers. O Bhārata, all of them attained a state of oneness with the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and his conduct toward all the warriors was always unsurpassed.
When the teachers are honored and satisfied, they indeed bring about peace;
when duly worshipped, they will not fail to exert their power at the proper time.
And today this entire earth is under the sway of Duryodhana.

O Pārtha, together with its villages and cities, its oceans, forests, and mines—by means of this sacred power (*brahman*), my son, everything is sustained. You are our refuge; upon you our burden is placed.
In this matter, O subduer of enemies, I perceive a task that has arrived at its proper time.
My dear friend, I have received a secret instruction (*upaniṣad*) from Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana;
when that is properly employed, the entire world becomes clearly manifest.
Therefore, my dear son, being united with that Brahman and remaining well-composed,
await the favor of the deities at the proper time;
O bull among the Bharatas, apply yourself to fierce asceticism.
Armed with a bow, clad in armor, bearing a sword, and accompanied by a sage and a crane, do not yield the way to anyone; go, O son, toward the northern direction.
For all divine weapons, O Dhanañjaya, reside in Indra.
"Then, out of fear of Vṛtra, the gods surrendered their strength to Indra. You shall obtain all those powers gathered in one place;
seek refuge with Śakra alone, and he will bestow the weapons upon you."

O Pārtha, for you who are disciplined in yoga, there is no doubt in this matter. Today, Dhananjaya alone among the Pāṇḍavas has obtained that preeminent, incomparable, true, and ever-flawless weapon of the virtuous.
O son of Kuntī, the gods never wish to see one who is unrighteous, nor one who has not attained success, nor one who lacks austerity; they do not look upon one who is fickle-minded in any way,
nor one who wails piteously, nor one who is harsh, nor one who is envious, nor one who uses bitter words.
One who is wicked, a boaster, a reviler, a slayer, or one who is full of doubt;

a betrayer of those who trust him, a deceiver, one prone to anger, a speaker of falsehoods; one who eats excessively, an atheist, one who lacks self-control, a betrayer of friends, and one who suspects everyone.
One who reviles others, one who is excessively proud, one who is fierce, greedy, and lustful;
a thief, a drinker of intoxicants, a killer of an embryo, and one who violates the teacher’s bed; one who considers himself highly esteemed, one who is exceedingly cruel, and one who is harsh.
They do not attain these worlds; they are worldless, O Dhanañjaya.
Compassion, pity, truth, and a sense of mercy, self-restraint, steadfastness, fortitude, righteousness, forgiveness, and unsurpassed beauty—[these are theirs].
Compassion, self-restraint, righteousness, reverence for teachers, gratitude,
friendliness, and devotion to the twice-born dwell within you, O Phālguna;
as do impartiality toward all beings, forgiveness, generosity, intelligence, and mindfulness.
Therefore, O Kauravya, you shall meet with Śakra, O Dhanañjaya; for a meeting with one such as you is worthy of praise among the gods,
O bull of the Bharatas, as well as for all friends and brothers.

O dear one, you are the supreme refuge, just as the slayer of Vṛtra is for the Maruts. In that thirteenth year, all your brothers and friends will take refuge in your great strength of arm, O mighty one.
"Go, O Pārtha, subduer of enemies, to your father, the thousand-eyed one; receive from Vāsava the art of grasping with the fist and all celestial weapons.
Thus spoke Maghavan on Mount Śataśṛṅga, O mighty-armed one.
Having smelled the crown of your head while all beings listen,
you shall go to heaven, O dear one, known to all creatures;
having reached the worlds of the merit-makers, that best of victors will rejoice there.
O Pārtha, honored by the thirty gods and having sported very happily in heaven,
you shall return to earth after obtaining the supreme weapons;
for Vāsava, O dear one, witnessed your virtues while you were burning the Khāṇḍava forest.
While all beings were listening, he spoke again and again:
"O Vāsava, best among men, you ought to fulfill that vow.
Having reached some direction from here, become intent upon the practice of asceticism."
"O Kaunteya, you ought to do what is beneficial according to the word of Maghavan.
Having been initiated this very day, go now to see the god Purandara.
Having spoken thus, the lord Dharmarāja instructed him.
Then the elder brother gave leave to his heroic younger brother, who had been initiated according to the prescribed rite and had restrained his speech, body,
and mind, so that he might see the god Purandara at the command of Dharmarāja.
Taking up the bow Gāṇḍīva as well as the two inexhaustible great quivers,
the mighty-armed one, clad in armor with its finger-guards and leather armlets fastened,
offered oblations into the fire and had the Brahmins pronounce blessings with the presentation of gold coins.
The mighty-armed one set forth, grasping his bow,
