sighing and looking upward for the sake of slaying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Seeing the son of Kuntī there with his bow grasped, [the enemy army trembled].
The Brahmins, the Siddhas, and the invisible beings spoke;
the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas, as well as the Gandharvas, said to him:
"May it be well with you; maintain your vow, and may your resolve be fulfilled."
"And may all your desires be fulfilled, O great chariot-warrior.
Having been addressed thus, Pārtha, having saluted them with his palms joined in reverence, paid homage to the domestic priest while his mind was intent on the practice of asceticism.
Then, with a joyful mind, Jiṣṇu paid homage to both those brothers,
the great car-warriors Yudhiṣṭhira and Vṛkodara,
who had approached him quickly with weary hearts.
Both the twins paid their respects to the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow;
having greeted those two heroes, he spoke to the son of Pākaśāsana:
"All the divine weapons must be obtained from Vāsava."
O Kaunteya, obtain whatever weapons you desire in your mind; for all your words shall be firm, faultless, and esteemed by the virtuous.
O Dhanañjaya, you alone among the Pāṇḍavas have now attained this.

O son of Kuntī, the gods do not wish to see one who knows what is unrighteous, nor one who has not attained perfection, nor one who lacks austerity; nor do they wish to see one who is fickle-minded, deceitful,
or one who wails piteously, is envious, or speaks harsh words.
He is deceitful, boastful, a reviler, and a slayer; he is full of doubt, a betrayer of the trusting, a deceiver, wrathful, and a speaker of falsehoods.
He is gluttonous, an atheist, a non-giver, a betrayer of friends, and suspicious of everyone.
One who reviles others, one who is excessively proud, one who is fierce, greedy, or lustful;
a thief, a drunkard, a killer of an embryo, one who violates the teacher’s bed,
and a man who is exceedingly self-conceited and cruel.
They do not attain these worlds; they are worldless, O Dhanañjaya.
Compassion, pity, truth, and sensitivity to suffering, self-restraint, steadfastness, fortitude, righteousness, forgiveness, and unsurpassed beauty—[these are theirs].
Compassion, tranquility, righteousness, reverence for elders, gratitude,
friendliness, and devotion to the twice-born dwell within you, O Phalguna;
as do impartiality toward all beings, mercy, generosity, intelligence, and mindfulness.
Therefore, O Kauravya, you shall meet with Śakra, O Dhanañjaya; for an encounter with one such as you is worthy of praise among the gods,
O bull of the Bharatas, as it is for all friends and brothers.

O dear one, you are the supreme refuge, just as the slayer of Vṛtra is for the Maruts. In that thirteenth year, all your brothers and friends will surely take refuge in the strength of your arms, O one of great power.

"Go, O Pārtha, to your father, the thousand-eyed subduer of enemies; receive from Vāsava the art of grasping with the fist and all celestial weapons. On Śataśṛṅga, O mighty-armed one, Maghavan spoke thus."
Having smelled the crown of your head while all beings listen,
you shall go to heaven, O dear one, known by all creatures;
having attained the worlds of the merit-makers, you shall rejoice, O best among victors.
O Pārtha, honored by the thirty gods and having sported most happily in heaven,
you shall return again to earth after obtaining the supreme weapons. O dear one, while you were burning the Khāṇḍava forest, Vāsava witnessed your virtues.
In the hearing of all beings, he spoke again and again:
"O best of men, you ought to fulfill that vow made to Vāsava.
Having reached some place from here, become intent upon the practice of asceticism."
"O descendant of Kuru, you ought to do what is beneficial according to the word of Maghavan.
Having been initiated, go this very day; you shall behold Purandara. Having embraced them both and taken leave of Kṛṣṇā, O Lord, Bībhatsu departed.
Delighted, he also greeted the foremost of ascetics.
"O son of Kuntī, quickly obtain whatever you desire in your heart," the Brāhmaṇas said to Pārtha, having thus pronounced blessings of victory.

"Accomplish your task, O son of Kuntī; may your victory be certain! As Arjuna, whose thighs were like the trunks of *śāla* trees, advanced like a lion, Kṛṣṇā, seizing the hearts of everyone, spoke these words.
"O mighty-armed Dhanañjaya, son of Kuntī, may all that Kuntī desired for you at your birth be yours,
O Kaunteya, as well as whatever you yourself desire.
May no one ever again obtain birth in our kṣatriya clan."
"Constant salutations to the Brahmins, whose livelihood does not depend on battle.
And this is my supreme sorrow, O Pārtha, that Suyodhana,
seeing me in the assembly of kings, laughed and called me a 'cow'."
Therefore, it is my opinion that this suffering is more grievous than the former:
that which you spoke so much against us in the assembly in a manner so improper. Surely all your brothers must have been kept awake by your words.

They will take delight in recounting your heroic deeds again and again. O Pārtha, neither in enjoyments, nor in wealth, nor even in life shall there be satisfaction or peace of mind for us while you remain on a long journey abroad.

O Pārtha, upon you depend the happiness and sorrow of us all; our very life and death, as well as our kingdom and sovereignty, rest with you. You have been bid farewell by me, O Kaunteya; may you attain well-being, O Pāṇḍava.
"O sinless one, this task must be undertaken by you against those who are powerful. O one of great strength, proceed quickly and without obstacle toward victory!
Homage to the Creator and the Ordainer; go forth in safety and well-being."
May the Dharmas protect you who hate [them], and may Bhāskara, the radiant one, protect you.
May Hrī, Śrī, Kīrti, Dhṛti, Puṣṭi, Umā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī—
may these indeed protect your wealth, O Dhanañjaya, as you travel on your journey.
Honoring the eldest and carrying out the word of his elder brother, he said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, for the sake of peace, I take refuge in the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas along with the hosts of Maruts, as well as the Viśvedevas and the Sādhyas."
Having spoken these benedictions, the illustrious Kṛṣṇā fell silent.
She considered this exile from her sons to be even more painful than her confinement in the forest, her dwelling in the woods, or the seizure of all her possessions.
With palms joined in reverence, Kṛṣṇā paid homage to the gods and addressed the Pāṇḍava with words that were most powerful and auspicious:
"Homage to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ! May you have well-being; go from forest to forest."

"May the *dharmas* favor you, O Pārtha, and may the sun, the source of light, do so as well. May Brahmā and the Brahmins protect you, O Dhanañjaya; for you, honoring the eldest, have followed the word of your elder brother."

O bull among the Bharatas, for the sake of peace, you should take refuge in the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas together with the hosts of Maruts, and likewise the Viśvedevas and Ādityas. May there be well-being for you from those of the intermediate space and those of heaven, O bull among the Bharatas.
Compared to all earthly rulers, whoever may be one's adversaries—
whether from imprisonment, exile to the forest, or even the seizure of all one's possessions—
I consider this to be a greater suffering than the banishment of my sons.

"May I never again be born into a kṣatriya family. I pay homage to the brahmins who do not live by the profession of arms. [For you], O bull of the Bharatas, have been driven from your own home and from the kingdom."
Having taken up residence in the forest, you remain there out of benevolence;
O bull among the Bharatas, people now behold you as you depart— you who are the conqueror of all enemies and who gratified the sacrificial fire.
In this great forest, surely your brothers, your friends,
the *cāraṇas*, and likewise the *ṛṣis*, will recount stories about you— those very things,
O mighty-armed Dhanañjaya, that Kuntī desired for you at your birth.
"May all that be exactly as you desire in your mind. O Pārtha, let the noble lady Pṛthā, the sister of Vasudeva, behold you upon your return, just as Aditi beheld the thousand-eyed Indra."
"Surely all your brothers will find delight in staying awake with your stories, recounting your deeds again and again.
O Pārtha, we have no desire for enjoyments, nor for wealth, nor even for life."
"Or will your mind become despondent while you are away on this long journey? O hero, hope arises within us as you enter the forest.
O Pārtha, for all of us, both happiness and sorrow are established in you."
Life and death, as well as heaven and likewise hell—these you have questioned me about, O Kaunteya. May you attain well-being, O Pāṇḍava;
I shall see you returned again, skilled in weapons and endowed with prosperity.
"May there be well-being for you from the beings of the intermediate space, from those of the earth, O Bhārata,
and from those of the heavens, as well as from any others who would stand as obstacles.
Having spoken these blessings, the illustrious Kṛṣṇā fell silent.
Then, having circumambulated his brothers and Dhaumya,
Arjuna, the mighty-armed son of Pāṇḍu, set forth, holding his beautiful bow and keeping in his heart the fare of Kṛṣṇā’s sidelong glances.
Slowly, O bull of the Bharatas, that hero proceeded toward the northern direction;
O Bhārata, gathering up trees and creepers with his speed,
the one of immense strength went on without clinging to the trees.

As he proceeded with vigor, endowed with the yoga of Indra and exerting his prowess, all living beings moved aside from his path. O dear one, he went to those mountains inhabited by those whose wealth is their asceticism.

That subduer of foes, the high-minded one, having become as swift as thought in his movement and disciplined in yoga like the wind, reached that sacred mountain, the divine Hemavata, frequented by the gods, in a single day.
Having crossed the Himavat and Gandhamādana,
he traversed difficult terrains day and night without weariness; then,
having reached Indrakīla, Dhanañjaya halted there.
Then he heard a voice in the sky saying, "Stay!
Having heard that, the Pāṇḍava cast his gaze in every direction;
after traveling for six days and nights, on the seventh day, the Pāṇḍava—
At Prasthendra-kīla, in that auspicious place, he became devoted to the practice of austerity;
with arms raised, he did not move his limbs at all— Samāhitātman, self-restrained, the son of Sahasrākṣa, the infallible one.
Then Savyasācin saw at the foot of a tree an ascetic,
glowing with Brahmanic splendor, tawny, with matted hair, and emaciated.
Seeing Arjuna standing there, that great ascetic spoke to him.

"Who are you, dear father, who have arrived here armed with a bow, wearing armor and arrows, with your sword-belt fastened, devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya? There is no need for weapons here; this is the abode of those who seek peace."
For these ascetic Brahmins, whose anger and joy have been subdued, there is no need for a bow here, nor ever for battle. Lay down this bow, my son; you have attained the supreme state.
Thus the brahmin repeatedly spoke these words to the hero Arjuna, who possessed infinite splendor, addressing him as he would any other ordinary man;
yet he could not shake him from his fortitude, for his resolve was firmly fixed.
Then that twice-born one, being pleased, spoke to him as if smiling:
"Choose a boon—blessings upon you—I am Śakra, O slayer of enemies.
Thus addressed, Dhanañjaya replied to the thousand-eyed god.
With palms joined in reverence, the heroic scion of the Kuru lineage bowed down and said:
"This is indeed my desired wish; grant me this boon.
O Blessed One, I wish to learn the entirety of the weapons from you today."
Mahendra, his soul filled with joy, replied to him as if laughing:
"O Dhanañjaya, what need have you for weapons now that you have arrived here? Choose boons and celestial worlds; you have attained the supreme goal."
Thus addressed, Dhanañjaya replied to the thousand-eyed one:
"I do not desire the worlds, nor again sensual pleasures, nor divinity— how much less happiness—
and I do not crave the sovereignty over all the immortals, O Lord of the Thirty-three."
"Having abandoned those brothers in the forest and failed to avenge our enmity,
I would incur infamy throughout all the worlds for eternal years.
Thus addressed, the slayer of Vṛtra replied to the son of Pāṇḍu.
Consoling him with gentle words, he who is honored by all the worlds said:
"O dear one, when you behold the three-eyed Śiva, the Lord of Beings and wielder of the trident,
then I shall grant you all the divine weapons in their entirety."
"Exert yourself to behold the god Parameṣṭhin;
O son of Kuntī, through the sight of him, you shall attain perfection and go to heaven. Having spoken thus to Phalguna, Śakra then vanished from sight.
Then Arjuna also remained right there, absorbed in yoga.
Janamejaya said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about Pārtha, whose actions are effortless."
Tell this story in detail,
how that tiger among men, the long-armed Dhananjaya,
having obtained his weapons, entered the uninhabited forest, radiant and fearless.
"Furthermore, O best of those who know Brahman, what did he do while dwelling there?
And how were the Blessed Sthāṇu and the King of the Gods propitiated?
I desire to hear this through your grace, O most excellent of the twice-born."
For you, O omniscient one, know both the divine and the human;
O one of great wisdom, it is said that Arjuna engaged in a most wonderful, hair-raising,
and incomparable battle with Bhava.
Formerly, that best of strikers, undefeated in battles, was one whose very name—
when heard by those lions among men— caused even the hearts of the heroic Pārthas to tremble with grief, joy, and extreme amazement.
Tell me everything else that Pārtha has done; for I do not perceive even the slightest blameworthy act in this victorious Jishnu. Proclaim all those deeds of that hero to me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O dear one, O tiger among the Kauravas, I shall relate to you this divine, great, and wonderful tale concerning that high-souled one."
O sinless one, hear correctly about the encounter of Pārtha with Tryambaka, the God of gods, involving contact through the touch of their bodies;
he of immeasurable prowess went forth at the command of Yudhiṣṭhira.

Taking up that divine bow and sword, the bull among men, the mighty-armed and powerful Arjuna set out for the sake of accomplishing his task— to behold Śakra, the lord of the gods, and Śaṅkara, the god of gods.

O King, the Kauravya son of Indrāṇī, a great chariot-warrior of all the worlds, with a steady mind and firm resolve for asceticism, set out toward the northern direction toward the peak of the Himavat, endowed with the utmost haste.
He entered alone that formidable, thorn-filled forest,
which was endowed with various flowers and fruits, frequented by various birds,
teeming with various herds of wild animals, and inhabited by *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*.
It was adorned by Gandharvas and Apsarases sporting together,
as well as by intoxicated Kimpuruṣas who had gathered at the drinking grounds;
and he was gazed upon from all sides by his beloveds as they turned toward him.
That tiger among men went to see the god who wields the Pināka bow.
Then, as the son of Kuntī departed for the forest devoid of humans,
the sound of conchs and drums arose in the sky.
A truly great rain of flowers fell upon the surface of the earth,
and a vast web of clouds spread out, covering everything on all sides.
Having passed through the forest fastnesses, they drew near to the great mountain.
While dwelling there upon the slopes of the Himalayas, Arjuna then shone resplendently;
he beheld there trees in full bloom, made melodious by the songs of birds,
and rivers with many eddies, resembling blue lapis lazuli.
Resounding with the songs of swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, as well as the cries of cranes,
the calls of male cuckoos, and the notes of *krauñca* birds and peacocks— Arjuna, the great chariot-warrior, was in that place endowed with enchanting forests.

Seeing those rivers of meritorious, cool, and pure water, he became joyful in mind. Then, delighting in that beautiful forest region, the high-minded Arjuna of fierce splendor remained engaged in severe asceticism.
Then, having clothed himself in darbha grass and bark, adorned with a staff and an antelope skin,
he spent one month subsisting on fruits alone for every completed three-night period;
by doubling that same duration of time, he passed through the second month.
For a third month as well, subsisting on food once every fortnight, he consumed only withered leaves that had fallen to the ground. Then,
when the fourth month had fully arrived, after that [he proceeded further].
Subsisting on air alone, the mighty-armed son of Pāṇḍu remained with his arms raised high, without support, standing balanced on the tips of his big toes;
and through his constant practice of this, he became possessed of immeasurable energy.
The matted locks of that great-souled one resembled lightning and a lotus;
then all the great seers went to the god who wields the Pināka bow,
wishing to report that the son of Pṛthā was established in fierce asceticism.
Having prostrated before and propitiated the illustrious blue-throated Lord,
they all reported that deed of Phalguna:
"This Partha of great splendor has taken refuge on the slopes of the Himalayas."

Standing in fierce and difficult-to-cross asceticism, he causes the quarters of the sky to smoke; O Lord of Gods, none of us know what he intends to do. He torments us all; let him be properly restrained.
Having heard those words of the sages whose souls were purified,
Umāpati, the Lord of Beings, spoke these words. Maheśvara said:
"Go quickly, rejoicing and unwearied, by the way you came. I know the resolve dwelling in his mind;
you must not feel any despondency whatsoever regarding Phalguna."
"He has no desire whatsoever for heaven, nor for sovereignty, nor for long life;
whatever he desires, all that I shall surely accomplish for him this very day.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Śarva, those truth-speaking sages,
with joyful hearts, returned to their respective hermitages.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When all those high-souled ascetics had departed,
the blessed Lord Hara, the wielder of the Pināka bow and the destroyer of all sins,
assumed the guise of a Kirāta, resembling a golden tree.
Resplendent in his physical form like a second Mount Meru,
he took up his glorious bow and arrows resembling venomous serpents,
and rushed forth with great radiance like a fire consuming dry grass.
Then the glorious one, together with the goddess Umā— who shared his vows and attire—
was followed by joyful spirits wearing various disguises,
and he himself was disguised in the dress of a Kirāta, accompanied by thousands of women.
O King, descendant of Bharata, that god then shone forth exceedingly;
in an instant, that entire forest became silent,
and the sound of the waterfalls as well as the birds ceased.
Having dispatched the son of Diti, who was either mute or certain of his purpose toward the sons of Pṛthā,
that one of great strength desired to dwell together with my own people regarding what I had intended;
therefore, you have indeed been pierced by Arjuna’s arrows and by mine as well.
"O mighty-armed Dānava, having cast off your body, you shall come to me alone.
Having approached Pārtha, whose actions are effortless,
he beheld the son of Diti named Mūka, who was of wondrous appearance.
Assuming the form of a boar and as if challenging Arjuna,
that one of most wicked soul spoke to him; then Phalguna,
taking up the bow Gāṇḍīva and arrows resembling venomous serpents, [prepared to strike].
Having strung my excellent bow and making it resound with the twang of the bowstring,
since you seek to kill me while I have come here innocent,
therefore I shall first send you to the abode of Yama.
Seeing Phalguna, the firm archer, about to strike him,
Śaṅkara, in the form of a Kirāta, suddenly restrained him,
saying: "This one, who possesses the luster of a dark cloud, was previously sought after by me."
Disregarding those words, Phalguna then launched his attack;
he released a sharp arrow, as powerful as a thunderbolt or a lightning strike. And the immensely radiant Kirāta, at that very same moment, aimed at that same single target.
He discharged an arrow resembling a thunderbolt and like a crest of fire;
those two arrows released by them both fell simultaneously upon Mūka’s broad body, which was as firm as a mountain.
Like the crash of a thunderbolt or the impact of a diamond against a mountain,
such was the collision of those two arrows at that time.
Pierced by many shafts that were like serpents with flaming mouths, he was struck down.
Having once again assumed a terrifying form as a Rākṣasa, he died;
then Jiṣṇu, the slayer of enemies, beheld a man of golden luster,
disguised in the garb of a Kirāta and accompanied by a woman.
With a pleased mind, the son of Kuntī spoke to him as if laughing:
"Who are you that wanders in this empty forest surrounded by a host of women?
O one with the luster of gold, do you not fear this terrible forest?"
"And for what purpose have you pierced this deer, which is my possession? For this rakṣasa was already pursued by me when he arrived here;
whether out of desire or out of contempt, you shall not escape from me alive."
"Indeed, this is not the way of a hunter, which you have practiced today toward me;
therefore, O mountain-dweller, I shall deprive you of your life.
Thus addressed by the son of Pāṇḍu, the Kirāta spoke as if laughing.
He spoke in gentle words to the Pāṇḍava Savyasācin:
"O hero, you should not feel fear on my account regarding our proximity to the forest;
this ground has always been suitable for us while dwelling in the woods."
"Why have you, however, recommended dwelling here, which is so difficult?
We, O rich in asceticism, dwell in this place abounding in living beings;
but you are like the fire, delicate and accustomed to comfort."
Arjuna said:
"How will he wander alone through this desolate region,
taking refuge in the *gāṇḍīva* bow and his iron arrows that resemble fire?"
"I dwell in the great forest like a second son of Pāvaka (Agni). And this creature here has also assumed the form of a deer.
The Kirāta said:

A terrible Rākṣasa, who had come here to kill me, has been slain. Indeed, he was already struck by me with arrows released from my bow; thus, being struck by those shafts, he lies dead and has been led to the abode of Yama.
"This man was my very target; he was already my prey, and by my own hand alone has he been deprived of life. Arrogant in your own strength, you ought not to attribute your own faults to another."
"I have been provoked, O dull-witted one; you shall not escape from me alive. Stand firm! I shall release arrows like thunderbolts.
Exert yourself with all your might and you too, release your arrows!"
Having heard those words of the Kirāta, Arjuna then summoned his wrath and struck him with arrows; thereupon,
with a joyful heart, the Kirāta received those shafts.
"Again and again! he cried; "Gently, gently! he said. "Strike them with these iron arrows that pierce the vital organs.
Thus addressed, Arjuna immediately released a shower of arrows.
Then, enraged and roaring repeatedly, the two of them mangled one another with arrows resembling venomous serpents. Thereupon,
Arjuna unleashed a shower of arrows upon the Kirāta.
Śaṃkara, with a serene mind,
accepted that shower of arrows for a moment; having received it, the wielder of the Pināka stood firm like an immovable mountain, his body unhurt.
Seeing that shower of arrows rendered futile, Dhanañjaya was filled with supreme wonder and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
He thought, "Aha! This one, whose limbs are so delicate, dwells upon the peaks of the Himavat."
"Unflustered, he receives the iron arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Who could this be? He must be a god in person—perhaps Rudra, or a Yakṣa, or the Lord of the Gods; for the assembly of the thirty deities is held upon that best of mountains."
Indeed, no one else is capable of withstanding the force of my thousands of discharged volleys of arrows, except for the god who wields the Pināka bow—
whether he be a god, a yakṣa, or anyone else standing apart from Rudra.
"I shall send him to the abode of Yama with my sharp arrows.
Then, O King, Jishnu, with a joyful heart, released hundreds of iron shafts that pierce the vital organs,
like the sun emitting its rays.
With a serene mind, the Blessed One, the creator of the world, whose hand bears the trident, received them just as a mountain receives a rain of stones. Then,
in an instant, Phalguna’s arrows were exhausted.
Then, seeing that exhaustion of his arrows, he was struck with fear;
but Jiṣṇu thought of the blessed Agni,
by whom two inexhaustible quivers had been given to him previously at Khāṇḍava.
"What indeed shall I discharge from my bow, since my arrows have been exhausted? And yet, this certain man swallows all my arrows entirely.
I shall strike him with the tip of my bow, as one strikes an elephant with the point of a spear."
"I shall lead you to the abode of Yama, the wielder of the staff.
Then, seizing him with the tip of his bow and dragging him with the noose of his bowstring,
the one of great splendor struck him with fists that were like thunderbolts.
The son of Kuntī, the slayer of enemy heroes, fought back with the tip of his bow;
yet even that divine bow of his was swallowed by the mountain-dweller.
Then Arjuna, his bow having been devoured, stood with sword in hand.
Desiring indeed to bring an end to the battle, he rushed toward him with great speed;
then the joy of the Kurus, exerting his prowess, released by the strength of his arms a sharp sword upon his head— a blade that would not stick even in mountains.
Having reached his head, that excellent sword indeed split it asunder.
Then Phalguna fought with trees and stones;
thus he, of massive form, received both the trees and the stones.
Then the illustrious and mighty Pārtha, assuming the form of a Kirāta,
struck the invincible one who appeared as a Kirāta with fists having the touch of thunderbolts, causing smoke to issue from his mouth.
Then, with extremely fierce fists resembling the thunderbolt of Śakra, the Blessed One in the form of a Kirāta struck Phalguna. Thereupon,
a most terrible crackling sound arose.
As the Pāṇḍava and the Kirāta fought with their fists,
there occurred for a brief moment a great battle that made the hair stand on end,
joined by blows of the arms like those between Vṛtra and Vāsava.

Then the mighty Jiṣṇu seized the Kirāta with his chest, and the Kirāta also struck the struggling Pāṇḍava with force. From the crushing pressure of their arms and the friction of their chests, [the mountain shook].
A fire accompanied by glowing coals and smoke was produced within his limbs.
Then Mahādeva, having pressed him down with his own limbs until he was thoroughly crushed,
assailed him with his splendor out of wrath, bewildering his mind.
Then, with his limbs pressed together, he appeared as if he were a single mass;
having meditated thus for a short while, he, being conscious, rose up again.
Thereupon, the Blessed Lord Bhava, the destroyer of desire, was pleased with him.
O Bhārata, Phalguna, being confined within the body by the God of gods,
became breathless, completely restrained by that Great-Souled One;
then Phalguna, the slayer of enemy heroes, revealed himself.
Assuming great fortitude, he challenged Śaṅkara;
then the Blessed Lord Bhava, assuming his own form, spoke. Thereupon, [the other] fell down bewildered, and then Bhava became pleased.
Having remained thus for a moment, that son of Pāṇḍu regained consciousness and rose up again; with his limbs drenched in blood and deeply distressed,
he sought refuge with the Blessed One, the wielder of the Pināka bow, who is the protector of all who seek shelter.

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) made of clay, he worshipped Bhava with a garland. Then the son of Pṛthā, the best of the Pāṇḍavas, beheld that garland resting upon the head of the Kirāta, and he returned to his natural state with joy.
He fell at his feet, and then Bhava became pleased;
Hara, with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, spoke these words to him,
beholding him filled with wonder and his physical frame now emaciated.
The Blessed One said:
"O Phalguna, I am pleased with this incomparable deed of yours;
in this valor and fortitude, there is no kshatriya equal to you."
"O sinless one, today my splendor and prowess are equal to yours.
I am pleased with you, O mighty-armed one; behold me, O bull among men!
O large-eyed one, I grant you vision, for you were once a primordial seer."

"You shall conquer all your enemies in battle, even all the dwellers of heaven. Out of affection for you, I shall grant you that weapon which is irresistible; for you are indeed capable of wielding that weapon of mine in an instant."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Phalguna beheld there the god Mahādeva, the dweller of the mountains, the wielder of the trident, possessed of great splendor, together with the Goddess.
Falling to his knees upon the earth and prostrating with his head,
Pārtha, the conqueror of enemy cities, sought to propitiate Hara.
Arjuna said:
O Kapardin, Lord of all beings, destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes!
O Blessed One, Śaṅkara, you ought to forgive my transgression. O God of gods, Mahādeva, blue-throated one, wearer of matted locks!
I know you, the three-eyed and all-pervading Lord, to be the supreme cause of all causes; I know you, O God, to be the refuge of the gods, and that this entire world has been produced from you.
You are invincible by the three worlds, including the gods, asuras, and humans.
Salutations to Śiva who has the form of Viṣṇu, and to Viṣṇu who has the form of Śiva; salutations indeed to Hari-Rudra, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice;
to Śarva, the one with an eye on his forehead, the bountiful giver, who holds a trident in his hand.
To the protector of the *pināka*, to Sūrya, to Mārjālīya, to the Creator;
I propitiate you, O Blessed One, Great Lord of all beings,
the Lord of the Gaṇas, the Auspicious One of the world, the cause of the causes of the universe.
Desiring to behold Bhava, I have reached this great mountain, which transcends both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, which is supreme and exceedingly subtle, and which is Hara;
it is your beloved, O Lord of Gods, and the most excellent abode of ascetics.
I propitiate you, O Blessed One, who are saluted by all beings: let this transgression of mine not be [counted] against me, O Mahādeva, due to my extreme rashness;
for this conflict with you was committed by me out of ignorance.
"O Śaṅkara, forgive this today from me who has come to you for refuge.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"The one whose banner is the bull, possessed of great splendor, laughed and spoke to him."
Having raised his beautiful arm and embraced Phalguna with both arms, saying "Well done!", the blessed Lord Hara, his soul filled with joy,
the bull-bannered god, spoke again to Pārtha with words of consolation.
Śarva, his matted locks marked by the Gaṅgā, grasped the beautiful, rounded arm of the infinitely radiant Pārtha— its palm copper-colored and its fingers well-formed—
and the Blessed One spoke.
In a former body, you were indeed a man accompanied by Nārāyaṇa;
in Badarī, you performed fierce austerities for many tens of thousands of years.
Whether it be in you or in Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, resides the highest splendor.

By you two, the foremost of men, the world is sustained through your splendor. O Lord, at the consecration of Śakra, the Dānavas were slain by you and Kṛṣṇa as you grasped that great bow which resounded like a rain-cloud.
O Pārtha, O best of men, this is that very Gāṇḍīva bow suited for you, which was swallowed by me after I had employed my illusory power; and here again,
O Pārtha, are your two inexhaustible quivers as they were before.
"And your body shall be free from disease, O joy of the Kurus.
I am indeed pleased with you, O Pārtha of true prowess;
choose from me whatever boon you desire, O bull among men."
"O giver of honor, there is no man equal to you among mortals, nor even in heaven; O subduer of enemies, the kṣatriya power has you as its foremost leader.
Arjuna said:
"O Blessed One, O Bull-bannered Lord, if you would grant me my desire out of affection,
I desire that divine and terrible Pāśupata weapon, O Master—
that which is named Brahmaśiras, belonging to Rudra, and possessed of fearsome power."

When the terrible end of the age has arrived, he withdraws the entire world; yet, O Mahādeva, by your grace, may I conquer Karṇa, Bhīṣma, Kṛpa, and Droṇa in battle, for a great conflict is about to take place.
I shall have a great battle with those endowed with the knowledge of the Brahma-weapon, by which I may consume the Dānavas, Rākṣasas,
as well as Bhūtas, Piśācas, Gandharvas, and Pannagas in combat.
From which thousands of spears, maces of terrifying appearance,
and arrows resembling venomous serpents arise when consecrated—
by means of that [weapon] would I fight against Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Kṛpa.
And by the son of the Sūta, who always speaks harshly in battle—
O Blessed One, O Destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, this has been my primary desire:
that through your grace I might become capable as he is.
The Blessed One said:
"O Pāṇḍava, I shall give you my beloved and great Pāśupata weapon; you are capable of wielding it, discharging it, and even withdrawing it."
Neither Mahendra, nor Yama, nor the King of the Yakṣas, nor Varuṇa, nor Vāyu knows this; how then could human beings know it?
But, O Pārtha, this must never be released rashly against any person whatsoever.
If cast upon one of little power, it would utterly consume the entire world.
There is nothing in the three worlds, including the mobile and the immobile, that is called "unslayable" by him;
he strikes down his targets with his mind, his eye, his speech, and his bow.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard that, Pārtha quickly purified himself and became composed;
having approached the Lord of All, he said, "Please teach me."
Then he taught that weapon, along with its secret methods of withdrawal,
to the best of the Pāṇḍavas— that weapon which was like Death personified—
just as it had attended upon the high-souled three-eyed Lord of Umā.
Then Arjuna, filled with joy, accepted that [gift];
thereupon the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and trees, along with its oceans, woodlands, villages, cities, and mines, began to tremble.
The sounds of conchs and dundubhi drums, and thousands of kettledrums, arose;
and when that moment arrived, a great atmospheric crash occurred.
Then there appeared the fiercely blazing weapon of the Pāṇḍava of immeasurable power.
The gods and dānavas saw him standing by their side in embodied form. And as soon as Phalguna of immeasurable prowess was touched by Tryambaka,
whatever impurity there was in his body all went to destruction.
Then, having been granted permission by Tryambaka with the words, "Go to heaven," Arjuna,
the son of Pṛthā, bowed his head and gazed at the god with joined palms. Thereupon, the Lord, the master of those who dwell in the third heaven, [spoke].
Mahāmati, Giriśa, Umāpati, Śiva,
Bhava— the destroyer of the Daityas and Piśācas— gave that great bow Gāṇḍīva to the best of men.
Then the Lord, together with Umā, left that auspicious and excellent mountain— its ridges and caves white with snow—
which was frequented by great sages and birds.
He ascended into the sky while the best of men looked on.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Even as he was looking on, the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose banner bears the bull, [departed].
The sun vanished from sight, as if having set for the world;
then Arjuna, the slayer of enemy heroes, was filled with supreme wonder,
thinking, "O Bhārata, I have seen Mahādeva face to face."
"I am blessed, I am favored, that Tryambaka Hara,
the wielder of the Pināka bow, the granter of boons, has been seen by me in his embodied form and touched with my hand; I perceive my own self as having achieved its supreme purpose."
"All enemies have been conquered and the purpose has been accomplished"— as Pārtha of immeasurable splendor was reflecting thus,
there appeared one with the hue of lapis lazuli, illuminating all directions.
Surrounded by hosts of aquatic creatures,
the glorious Lord of the Waters arrived at that place— Varuṇa, the self-controlled master of sea-monsters, accompanied by nāgas, rivers, streams, daityas, sādhyas, and deities.
Then the lord Kubera, whose body was like refined gold, arrived in a celestial chariot of great radiance, followed by yakṣas;
appearing with a wondrous sight, he seemed to illuminate the sky.
The illustrious lord of riches came to see Arjuna;
likewise, the glorious and powerful Yama, the end-maker of the worlds,
appeared in person along with the world-creating Pitṛs, both those possessing form and those devoid of form.
Daṇḍapāṇi, whose nature is inconceivable and who causes the destruction of all beings,
Vaivasvata, the King of Dharma, illuminated the three worlds with his celestial chariot, as well as the Guhyakas, Gandharvas, and Pannagas.
Like a second sun when the end of the age has arrived,
they took their stand upon the radiant and variegated peaks of the great mountain and beheld Arjuna there, endowed with ascetic power.
Then, after a moment, the Blessed One Śakra arrived, seated upon the head of Airāvata, accompanied by Indrāṇī and surrounded by hosts of gods,
with a white parasol being held over his head.
Resembling a white cloud, the king of stars shone brightly;
being praised by Gandharvas and by seers whose wealth is asceticism,
he reached the mountain peak and stood there like the risen sun.
Then the wise Yama, the knower of the highest dharma, who dwells in the southern quarter, spoke these auspicious words with a voice like the roar of a cloud:
"O Arjuna, Arjuna, behold us, the guardians of the world, assembled here."
Today we grant you our vision, for you are indeed worthy of being seen.
You are the ancient seer of immeasurable soul, the one of great power named Nara;
by the command of Brahmā, dear son, you have entered into the state of mortality.
Born from Vāsava, you possess great heroism and prowess;
O sinless one, Bhīṣma, whose soul is supremely devoted to dharma, must be overcome by you in battle. Along with you has arisen the Grandfather, endowed with great heroism.
The *kṣatra* class, whose touch is like fire and who is protected by the son of Bharadvāja,
as well as the Dānavas of great heroism who have entered the human state,
and the Nivātakavacas themselves— these must be subdued, O joy of the Kurus.
"O Dhanañjaya, that Karna of great heroism, who is a portion of my father, the god who blazes over all the worlds, must be slain by you. Furthermore,
there are portions of gods, Gandharvas, and Rakshasas who have descended upon the earth."
Slain by her in battle, O Kaunteya, subduer of foes, they shall attain the destination won by the fruits of their own actions, each according to his own merit;
and your imperishable fame, O Phalguna, shall endure in the world.
"For you have personally gratified Mahādeva in the great battle;
together with Viṣṇu, the earth must now be made light.
O mighty-armed one, take up this weapon, the staff that cannot be resisted."
"By means of this weapon, you shall indeed perform a very great deed. Pārtha, the joy of the Kurus, accepted it according to the prescribed rites,
together with its mantras, its ritual procedures, its method of discharge, and its method of withdrawal.
Then Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, dark as a rain-cloud,
established himself in the western quarter and, the powerful one, uttered these words:
"O Pārtha, you are a preeminent Kṣatriya, firmly established in the duty of a warrior."
"Behold me, O large-eyed one with copper-hued eyes; I am Varuṇa, the lord of the waters.
Accept from me, O son of Kuntī, these irresistible nooses of Varuṇa, along with the secret mantras for their casting and withdrawal."
O hero, in that battle of Tāraka, thousands of high-souled Daityas were restrained by me with these [weapons]. Therefore, O being of great essence, through my grace, these have arisen.

"Take this; for even Antaka himself could not escape you when you are an assailant with this weapon. When you range through the battlefield with this weapon, the earth will undoubtedly become devoid of kṣatriyas."
Then Vāsava, the best among those skilled in weapons, duly received from Varuṇa those divine Varuṇa-weapons. Thereafter,
the Lord of Wealth, whose abode is Kailāsa, spoke.
When the divine weapons had been bestowed by Varuṇa and Yama,
O wise and mighty son of Pāṇḍu, I too was pleased,
having encountered you who are likewise unconquered.
O Savyasācin, O mighty-armed one, O eternal primordial deity, you have always been weary alongside us throughout the past kalpas. Yet,
O bull among men, because of my sight of you, I bestow this divine [vision] upon you.
"O mighty-armed one, you shall conquer even the non-human beings who are difficult to defeat. From me as well, receive this weapon, *Antardhāna*, which is dear to me;
let him take up this unsurpassed weapon."
"With this you shall consume the armies of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son;
therefore, accept it—
this weapon that robs [the enemy] of strength, energy, and splendor, which induces sleep, and slays foes."
When the high-souled Śaṅkara destroyed Tripura,
it was then that this weapon was released by him, by which the great Asuras were consumed. And this [weapon] has been prepared by me for your sake, O you whose prowess is truth.
"You are worthy of bearing this, O one whose gravity is like Mount Meru.
Then the mighty-armed Arjuna, the joy of the Kurus,
being of great strength, duly received that divine weapon of Kubera.
Then the king of the gods, his voice sounding like a cloud or a kettledrum, spoke with gentle words to Pārtha, the doer of effortless deeds, consoling him:
"O mighty-armed son of Kuntī, you are the ancient Lord."
He has attained supreme perfection and has directly entered the state of the gods.
O subduer of enemies, a very great task for the gods must indeed be performed by you;
you must ascend to heaven, so prepare yourself, O one of great splendor!
"A chariot yoked with Mātali shall come to this earth for your sake;
there, O Kaurava, I will bestow upon you divine weapons.
Having seen those world-protectors assembled on the mountain peak, [he spoke thus].
The wise Dhanañjaya, son of Kuntī, was filled with wonder.
Then Arjuna, endowed with great splendor, honored the assembled world-protectors according to the prescribed rites with words, water, and even fruits.

Then the gods, having honored Dhanañjaya, departed as they had come, all those deities possessing the speed of thought at will. Then Arjuna, that bull among men, attained great joy, having acquired the divine weapons.
With his heart’s desire fulfilled, he considered himself as one who had accomplished his purpose.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the world-protectors had departed, Pārtha, the destroyer of enemies—
O Indra among kings, he thought of the arrival of the chariot of the king of the gods. Then, while the wise Guḍākeśa was thus reflecting,
a chariot of great splendor, yoked with Mātali, arrived.
Making the sky free of darkness, as if splitting the clouds,
and filling the quarters with roars resembling the sound of great thunderclouds—
swords, terrible spears, and maces of fearsome appearance [rained down].

Divine missiles and spears of great luster, as well as lightning bolts of immense radiance, were present there; likewise, thunderbolts joined with discuses, mallets, and clubs, along with wind-explosions accompanied by portents, resounded with a roar like that of peacock-colored clouds.
There, the Nāgas were of massive body, with flaming mouths and most terrible;
they resembled masses of white clouds and were gathered together like boulders.
There were ten thousand bay horses, swift as the wind.
They saw there the great, dark-blue Vaijayanta banner of immense splendor, which draws that divine chariot composed of illusion that steals away the vision of the eyes;
it was as dark as a blue lotus, with a bamboo shaft adorned with gold.
Seeing the charioteer standing on that chariot, adorned with refined gold, the mighty-armed Pārtha considered him to be a god indeed. While Phalguna was thus reflecting, Mātali—
Bowing down and becoming humble, he spoke these words to Arjuna:
"O glorious son of Śakra! Śakra desires to see you.
May your lordship quickly ascend Indra’s esteemed chariot."
Your father, Śatakratu, the best of the immortals, said to me:
"Let the inhabitants of the celestial realm behold the son of Kuntī who has arrived here.
This is Śakra, surrounded by the gods as well as the hosts of sages."

The Gandharvas and Apsarases are waiting to behold you as you depart from this world for the realm of the gods by the command of Indra, the subduer of Pāka. Ascend with me; having acquired the celestial weapons, you shall return again.
Arjuna said:
"O Mātali, go quickly; mount this most excellent chariot, which is very difficult to obtain even through hundreds of Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices."

This supreme divine chariot cannot be ascended by kings of great fortune who have performed sacrifices with abundant gifts, nor even by gods or dānavas, unless one has practiced intense austerity. This great celestial chariot is not possible to mount without having performed penance.

O virtuous one, while you stand firm upon the chariot with its steady horses, it would be impossible even to see, touch, or mount it— let alone do so. Only after you have ascended shall I follow, just as a man of merit follows the path of the righteous.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of his, Mātali, the charioteer of Śakra,
quickly ascended the chariot and restrained the horses with the reins.

Then Arjuna, the son of Kuntī and joy of the Kurus, with a joyful mind, bathed in the Gaṅgā and, being purified, recited his prayers according to the prescribed rites. Thereafter, he offered libations to the ancestors in accordance with the rules and tradition.
He began to take leave of Mandara, the king of mountains:
"O Mountain, you have always been the refuge for virtuous sages of righteous character and meritorious deeds who long for the path to heaven."
"O Mountain, by your grace, the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas have always attained heaven and move about with the gods, free from all suffering.
O King of Mountains, Great Mountain, refuge of sages, you who are like a sacred ford and a forest!"
"I am departing; I take my leave of you. I have dwelt happily with you.
Your peaks, groves, rivers, and waterfalls, as well as your most sacred bathing places, have been beheld by me many times."
Fruits of exquisite fragrance were eaten here and there,
and streams of highly fragrant water issued forth from my body;
I drank the waters of the springs, which tasted like nectar.
O King of Mountains, O Lord, just as a child dwells in great happiness upon his father’s lap, so have I sported upon your lap,
which is crowded with throngs of *apsarases* and resounds with the chanting of the Vedas.
"O mountain, I have always dwelt happily upon your peaks.
Having spoken thus to the mountain and taken his leave, Arjuna, the slayer of enemy heroes,
ascended his divine chariot, shining like the sun.
With that divine form of the sun and through those wondrous deeds,
the wise joy of the Kurus ascended upwards, filled with great delight. Having passed beyond the range of vision for mortals who roam the earth, he departed.
He beheld thousands of celestial chariots of wondrous form;
there, neither the sun nor the moon shone, nor did fire,
for they were illuminated there by their own merit-earned radiance.
Those luminous forms which are seen here as stars,
though they are vast, appear small like lamps due to their great distance;
those same radiant and beautiful forms, O Pāṇḍava, are seen there.
He saw them shining with their own radiance upon their respective seats;
there, royal sages, perfected beings, and heroes slain in battle,
having won heaven through asceticism, flocked together in hundreds of groups.
Beholding thousands of Gandharvas with a splendor blazing like the sun,
as well as Guhyakas, Rishis, and hosts of Apsarases,
Phalguna was filled with wonder as he gazed upon these worlds that shone with their own radiance.
He questioned Mātali with affection, and he (Mātali) replied to him:
"O Pārtha, these are the doers of good deeds who, O Lord, reside in their own celestial abodes as the forms of stars that you have seen upon the earth."
Then he beheld standing at the gate a white, victorious elephant,
Airāvata with four tusks, like Mount Kailāsa with its peaks.
Having traversed that path of the perfected ones, that best of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas—
He shone as Mandhātṛ, the best of kings, did in former times; that lotus-eyed one surpassed all other kings. Thus did that highly illustrious one proceed there in the heavenly world.
Then he beheld that city of Śakra, Amarāvatī.
Vaiśampāyana said:
He beheld that beautiful city, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
It was adorned with trees that bore the auspicious flowers of every season; there,
he was fanned by a mingled breeze, fragrant with the holy scent of *saugandhika* trees.
And he beheld the divine Nandana grove, frequented by throngs of *apsarases*,
where the trees seemed to beckon with their celestial blossoms;
it cannot be seen by one who has not performed austerities, nor by one who has not maintained the sacred fires.

That world belongs to those who perform meritorious deeds, nor to those who turn their backs in battle; it does not belong to those who do not sacrifice, nor to liars, nor to those devoid of Vedic learning; nor to those whose limbs have not been purified by bathing at sacred fords, nor to those excluded from sacrifice and charity.
Nor can he be seen in any way by those who destroy sacrifices, the base, those addicted to drink, those who violate the teacher’s bed, or those evil-minded eaters of meat.
Beholding that divine forest, resounding with celestial songs, he saw—
The mighty-armed one entered Śakra’s beloved city;
there he then beheld thousands upon tens of thousands of celestial chariots that travel at will, some stationed and others already in motion.
Praised by the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the Pāṇḍava was fanned by holy breezes carrying the fragrance of flowers;
then that bull among men was showered with auspicious heaps of blossoms.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis,
joyfully honored Pārtha, the doer of effortless deeds. He was praised with benedictions and the sounds of celestial musical instruments.

The mighty-armed son of Pṛthā, being praised on all sides, proceeded by the command of Indra along the vast path of the stars, renowned as the *suravīthī*, which resounded with the blare of conchs and drums.
There were the Sādhyas, as well as the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, and the Aśvins;
the Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras, as well as the stainless Brahmarṣis and many royal sages, kings headed by Dilīpa.
Tumburu, Nārada, and the two Gandharvas Hāhā and Hūhū—
the joy of the Kurus approached all of them according to the prescribed rites,
and then he beheld the king of the gods, Śatakratu, the subduer of enemies.
Then the mighty-armed Pārtha, descending from his excellent chariot,
beheld face to face his father, the lord of the gods and subduer of Pāka,
shaded by a beautiful white parasol with a golden handle.
He was being fanned with a whisk scented with divine perfumes,
while being praised by Viśvāvasu and other Gandharvas with hymns and salutations, and by the foremost of the twice-born with recitations from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Then the mighty son of Kuntī approached and bowed his head;
he, in turn, received him with his outstretched arms.
Then [he seated him] upon the holy throne of Śakra, worshipped by the kings of gods and the ṛṣis.
Śakra took him by the hand and seated him nearby;
then the lord of the gods, the slayer of enemy heroes, having smelled the crown of his head,
placed him— who was then bowed low with humility— upon his lap.
Then, by the command of the Thousand-eyed One, that son of Pṛthā,
whose soul was immeasurable, ascended Śakra’s throne like a second Vāsava.
Thereupon, out of affection, the enemy of Vṛtra gazed upon Arjuna’s auspicious face.
He touched him with his hand, which was fragrant with merit, consoling him;
while the winds from the divine yak-tail fans, drawn by the hands of celestial beauties,
gently stroked his long and auspicious arms.

With arms as firm as two golden pillars capable of drawing a bow and hurling arrows, the slayer of Bala, the wielder of the thunderbolt, repeatedly and slowly flexed his arms, his hand marked by the grip of the *vajra*.
Looking at Guḍākeśa as if smiling, the thousand-eyed slayer of Vṛtra, his eyes wide with joy, could not look enough;
seated together upon a single throne, the two of them graced the assembly hall.
The sun and the moon appeared in the sky like those risen on the fourteenth day;
there, the Gandharvas, led by Tumburu and skilled in songs and Sāman chants, sang verses with most beautiful melodies.
Ghṛtācī, Menakā, Rambhā, Pūrvacitti, Svayaṃprabhā,
Urvaśī, Miśrakeśī, Duṇḍu, Gaurī, Varūthinī,
Gopālī, Sahajanyā, Kumbhayoni, and Prajāgarā.
Citrasenā, Citralekhā, Sahā, and Madhurasvarā—
these and other excellent women danced here and there,
lotus-eyed maidens intent on agitating the hearts of the Siddhas.
With broad hips and loins, their breasts heaving,
they captivated the heart, intellect, and mind with the sweetness of their side-long glances and gestures.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Then the gods, together with the Gandharvas, having understood the intention of Śakra, took up the most excellent *arghya* and immediately paid homage to the son of Pṛthā. Having offered water for his feet and water for sipping to the prince, they honored him.

Then they ushered him into the abode of Purandara. Thus honored, Jishnu, the son of Pandu, dwelt in his father’s palace, training himself in the great weapons along with the methods for their withdrawal.
From the hand of Śakra, he took the beloved weapon, the vajra, which is difficult to withstand,
as well as thunderbolts of great roar marked by clouds and peacocks. Having taken up these weapons, the son of Kuntī, the Pāṇḍava, remembered his brothers.
By the command of Purandara, he lived happily for five years. Then, when the time had come and Pārtha had mastered the weapons, Śakra said to him:
"O Kaunteya, learn dancing and singing from Citrasena."
"O son of Kuntī, acquire that musical instrument ordained by the gods which does not exist in the world of men; it will surely lead to your welfare. And Purandara gave Citrasena to him as a friend.
Having united with him, the healthy Pārtha took his delight;
he once again gave orders for songs, instrumental music, and dances. Nevertheless, that powerful hero found no peace on account of the gambling match.
Incensed by the slaughter of Duḥśāsana and [the death] of Śakuni, the son of Subala,
he then experienced incomparable joy here and there,
and attained peerless Gāndharva dance and instrumental music.
Though he was trained in the many qualities of dance and in all the qualities of instrumental music and song,
that slayer of enemy heroes found no peace.
Remembering his brothers and his mother Kuntī,
Indra, having understood that unsurpassed desire of his, [acted accordingly].
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, at the very beginning, Śakra spoke to Citrasena in private:
"O Vāsava, having learned that Pārtha’s gaze is fixed upon Urvaśī,
O King of the Gandharvas, go today, dispatched by me, to the most excellent of the Apsarases."

"O tiger among men, let Urvaśī attend upon Phālguna, so that he may be honored and receive the weapons through my instruction. You must ensure this is done in such a way that he becomes skilled in the company of women."

Having been addressed thus, and having received permission from Vāsava by saying "So be it," the king of the Gandharvas approached the excellent Apsaras Urvaśī. Upon seeing her, he was recognized and greeted with a welcome by her, and he rejoiced.
Seated comfortably, he addressed these words with a smile to her who was likewise seated comfortably:
"Let it be known to you, O lady of beautiful hips, that I have come here sent by the sole king of the triple heaven, who delights in your favor."
But he who is renowned among gods and men for his innate virtues— for his splendor, character, beauty, religious observance, and self-restraint;
who is celebrated for his strength and heroism, highly esteemed, and possessed of brilliant intelligence— [he is the one].
Radiant, endowed with splendor, patient, and free from envy—
he who studies the Vedas together with their limbs and the Upaniṣads, along with the four [Vedas] and the Purāṇas as the fifth,
and who practices service to his teacher, attains an intellect resting upon the eight qualities.
Through his celibacy, his skill, his progeny, and even his age,
he alone was indeed a protector like Maghavan in the third heaven;
he was free from boastfulness, a respecter of others, liberal in his gifts, and sweet-spoken.

He showers his friends with various kinds of food and drink; he is truthful in speech, honored as a speaker, handsome, and free from egoism. He is compassionate toward his devotees, lovely, beloved, and steadfast in his promises.
Equal to Mahendra and Varuṇa by virtue of his multitude of qualities worthy of being prayed for,
let that hero Arjuna, known to you, obtain the fruit of heaven;
permitted by Śakra, let him today take refuge at your feet.
"Therefore, do this, O auspicious one; Dhanañjaya has sought refuge with you.
Having been addressed thus, the blameless Urvaśī smiled, highly esteemed that honor, and replied with joy to Citrasena.

Having heard that true description of his qualities which you have related to me, I would choose that man; why then should I choose Arjuna? This is by the command of Mahendra and out of affection for you.
"And because of the flood of his virtues, O Phālguna, I have become filled with love.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Go indeed as you wish; I shall come back happily."

Then, having dismissed the Gandharva who had accomplished his purpose, the sweet-smiling Urvaśī, longing for the pursuit of Pārtha, performed her bath with delightful ornaments for bathing and radiant perfumes and garlands.
With her mind deeply pierced by the arrows of Manmatha impelled by passion for the beauty of Dhanañjaya, she was set ablaze by love upon that vast,
excellent bed strewn with divine coverlets.
With their minds focused on the mental image of him and their hearts intent on nothing else, they took delight in Phālguna, who had been attained through their longing,
as the moon rose and the onset of night deepened.
Then that woman of broad hips set out toward the palace of Pārtha, shining brilliantly with her mass of hair— soft, curled, and long— which bore clusters of white water-lilies.
With the sweetness of her arching brows and her speech, and also with her loveliness and gentleness,
she went along as if rivaling the moon with her moon-like face;
her two beautiful faces were anointed with divine unguents and smeared with celestial sandalwood paste.
As she walked, her breasts, blossoming with necklaces, swayed;
bent slightly at every step by the exertion of bearing those breasts,
she was exceedingly beautiful with a waist variegated by the garland of the three folds.
Below, it was as vast as a mountain, with hips broad and elevated;
a radiant abode of the God of Love, adorned with a girdle of tinkling bells,
it was a cause of mental agitation even for divine sages.
Her hips, draped in fine garments, shone with faultless beauty; her feet, with concealed ankles and long, copper-colored soles and toes, were likewise resplendent,
their surfaces elevated like the shell of a tortoise and adorned with the marks of small bells.
Through drinking a small amount of sidhu liquor, through her contentment and intoxication,
and through various playful gestures, she became even more beautiful to behold;
that graceful woman proceeded there accompanied by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas.

Even in heaven, which is full of many wonders, she of most beautiful form shone with a very fine upper garment the color of a cloud; her body moved through the sky like a crescent moon veiled by clouds.

Then, traveling with the speed of thought and the wind, she of the pure smile reached the palace of Phalguna, the son of Pandu, in a mere moment. Having arrived at the gate, she announced her presence to those stationed there.
O best of men, the beautiful-eyed Urvaśī approached that spotless and most enchanting dwelling of Arjuna;
O King, with a heart full of apprehension, he went out to meet her in the night.
Upon seeing Urvaśī, Arjuna, his eyes covered with shame,
spoke;
having then offered his salutation, he performed the worship due to his elder.
"I salute you with my head, O best among the foremost Apsarases. What do you command, O Goddess? I stand here as your servant.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Phālguna, Urvaśī then lost consciousness. Urvaśī spoke,
and she then caused him to hear all the words of the Gandharvas.
O best of men, I shall relate to you exactly what was told to me by Citrasena, and how I have come here while the delightful service of Mahendra was being performed.
O best of men, through your arrival, there occurred a supreme festival for heaven,
with the presence of the Rudras and the Ādityas in their entirety,
as well as the assembly of the Aśvins and the Vasus.
And among the assemblies of great seers and the most eminent royal seers, and among the hosts of Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Yakṣas, and Mahoragas,
all were seated according to their rank, status, and power.
O son of Śakra, while the bodies of Agni, Soma, and Ārka blazed with supernatural power,
and while the *vīṇās* were being played by the Gandharvas,
O large-eyed one, as divine and delightful singing proceeded;
O bull of the Kurus, while all the principal Apsarases were dancing,
you, O Pārtha, indeed gazed at me alone with unblinking eyes;
and there, at that sacrificial bath (*avabhṛtha*), you stood in attendance upon the dwellers of heaven.
Permitted by your father, the gods departed for their respective homes;
likewise, all the Apsarases, having been dismissed, went to their own abodes.
Moreover, O Śatrughna, others as well were sent away by your father.
Then Citrasena, commanded by Śakra, arrived in my presence, O lotus-petal-eyed one; and he then spoke to me:
"O lady of excellent complexion, I have been sent here by the Lord of the Gods for your sake."

"Do what is pleasing to Mahendra, to me, and indeed to yourself. O lady of beautiful hips, seek out Pārtha— who is equal to Śakra in battle, a hero endowed with beauty, generosity, and virtue"— thus he spoke then.
Therefore, O sinless one, having been permitted by him and by my father,
I have come into your presence to serve you, O subduer of enemies;
my heart drawn by your virtues, I have fallen under the power of the bodiless god of love.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O hero, this desire of mine has also been long cherished.
Hearing her speaking thus, Arjuna was deeply overcome with shame.
Covering her ears with both hands in the abode of the gods, she said:
"O fortunate one, O lovely lady, may what you say to me be as if unheard by me;
for you are certainly equal to the wives of my preceptor, O fair-faced one."

Just as the highly fortunate Kuntī and just as Śacī, the consort of Indra, are [to me], so too are you, O auspicious lady; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. And since you have been clearly and specifically gazed upon by me, O beautiful one.
"Listen, O lady of pure smiles, to the truth regarding that which was preceded by a cause:
I beheld you there with eyes wide with joy, having recognized you as the mother of the Paurava lineage."
"O auspicious one, O Apsaras, you ought not to think of me otherwise;
you are more venerable than my guru, for you are the one who increases my lineage.
Urvaśī said:
O King of the Gods, we have all been made free from obstruction;
O Hero, you ought not to appoint me here to a position of authority. For whatever sons or grandsons have come here in the lineage of Puru, [they have not been so appointed].
They delight us with their asceticism, and there is no transgression on their part. Therefore, be gracious; you ought not to dismiss me while I am thus distressed.
O bestower of honor, accept me, for I am devoted to you and tormented by love.
Arjuna said:
"Listen to the truth, O lady of beautiful hips, which I shall speak to you, O blameless one.
Let the quarters and the intermediate directions, together with the gods, hear me."
O sinless one, just as Kuntī, Mādrī, and Śacī are to me, so indeed are you today even more venerable to me as the mother of my own lineage.
Go; O woman of excellent complexion, I have sought refuge at your feet with my head bowed.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"For you are to be honored by me like a mother, and I am to be protected by you like a son.
Thus addressed by Pārtha, Urvaśī was overcome with anger.
Trembling, with her brows knit in a frown, Urvaśī then cursed Dhanañjaya.
Urvaśī said:
"Though you were permitted by your father and had come to my home of your own accord..."
"Because you did not welcome me when I had fallen under the power of the arrows of love,
therefore, O Pārtha, you shall be a dancer among women, devoid of manhood.
Vaiśampāyana said:

"You shall be known as 'impotent' and you shall wander about like a eunuch. Having thus pronounced this curse upon Arjuna, with quivering lips and panting, Urvaśī then quickly returned once more to her own home.
Then Arjuna, the subduer of enemies, hastening toward Citrasena,
informed him of everything that had occurred during the night with Urvaśī; thus did the Pāṇḍava relate it to Citrasena.
And there, Citrasena reported everything exactly as it had happened, including the curse, again and again to Śakra. Then,
having summoned his son to a private place, the one whose vehicle is drawn by bay horses (Indra) spoke.
Having consoled him with auspicious words, he spoke with a smile:
"O best of men, O mighty-armed one, today Pṛthā has truly become a mother of a noble son through you, her son; for even the sages have been surpassed by your fortitude."

O giver of honor, that curse which Urvaśī has pronounced upon you will indeed serve your purpose, my dear; it shall be a means of accomplishment for you. O sinless one, you must dwell on the surface of the earth in an unrecognized state.
O hero, you shall spend thirteen years there in that very state; having spent one year in that dancing attire and likewise in a state of impotence, you will thereafter regain your manhood.
Thus addressed by Śakra, Phālguna, the slayer of enemy heroes,
attained supreme joy and did not dwell upon the curse;
he remained together with the illustrious Gandharva Citrasena.
Dhanañjaya, the son of Pāṇḍu, took delight in the celestial abode.
Indeed, for one who constantly hears this account of the son of Pāṇḍu,
no desire for sinful pleasures arises within them.
Having thoroughly heard this formidable and pure conduct of Phālguna, the son of the foremost of the immortals,
those whose faults of pride, hypocrisy, and passion have departed—
The lords of men, having gone to the third heaven, take their delight there.
Once, while wandering about, the great seer Lomaśa went to the abode of Śakra, desiring to see Purandara.
Having approached and paid homage to the king of the gods, the great sage beheld the son of Pāṇḍu seated upon half of Vāsava’s throne. Then,
permitted by Śakra, he sat upon a superior seat.
The best of the twice-born sat down, being honored by the great seers.
Upon seeing Pārtha seated upon Indra’s throne, his thought occurred:
"How indeed has the kṣatriya Pārtha attained the seat of Śakra?"
"But what meritorious deed has he performed, or what worlds has he conquered,
that he has thus attained this station honored by the gods?
Having understood his intention, Śakra, the slayer of Vṛtra, [spoke].
Laughing, the Lord of Śacī addressed these words to Lomaśa:
"O Brahmarṣi, hear that which you desire to say in your mind;
this one is certainly not merely a mortal who has attained the status of a Kṣatriya."
"O Great Seer, this mighty-armed son of mine was born of Kuntī;
he has arrived here for the sake of weapons and for some other reason as well.
Oh, you do not recognize him as that ancient and most excellent of sages!"
Listen to me as I speak, O Brahmin, regarding who he is and what his cause is:
know that these two, Hṛṣīkeśa and Dhanañjaya, are those two ancient and most excellent sages, Nara and Nārāyaṇa.

The two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa, renowned throughout the three worlds, have descended to this earth— the refuge of merit— for the sake of a specific purpose; they are such that they cannot be seen even by the gods or by high-souled ṛṣis.
That holy hermitage, renowned by the name Badarī,
became the dwelling place of the Brahmin Viṣṇu as well as of Jiṣṇu;
from there flowed the Gaṅgā, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
"O Brahmarṣi, by my command those two of great splendor have been born on earth;
being of great heroism, they shall effect the removal of the burden from the earth. For there are certain arrogant Asuras known as the Nivātakavacas."
Deluded by the granting of that boon, they remain hostile toward us; filled with pride in their own strength, they plot to slay the gods,
for they do not take the gods into account because of the boons they have received.
The fierce sons of Danu, dwellers of the netherworld (pātāla) and possessed of great strength—
all the hosts of gods were indeed unable to fight them. He who is that glorious Viṣṇu, the slayer of Madhu, has descended to the earth.
That divine Lord, the unconquered Hari named Kapila,
by the mere sight of whom the high-souled sons of Sagara were destroyed while they were formerly digging into the subterranean realm (rasātala), O Lord.

"O best of the twice-born, a great task must be accomplished by us and Pārtha together in this great battle; there is no doubt that he is capable of slaying the Asuras along with their followers merely by being seen."
All the Nivātakavacas are like serpents in a great lake;
however, Madhusūdana should not be awakened for a trivial matter,
for he is a vast mass of splendor who, once awakened, would consume the world.

This hero is capable of countering all of them together; having slain them in battle, he will return once more to the world of men. And you, by our command, must go for now to the surface of the earth.
"In the Kāmyaka forest you will see the hero Yudhiṣṭhira dwelling there. That righteous soul, true to his promise, should be told in my name:
'Do not feel anxiety for Phalguna; having mastered the weapons, he will return soon.'"
Neither by one whose strength of arm is impure, nor by one unskilled in weapons,
can Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the others be withstood in battle. But Guḍākeśa, of mighty arms and great mind, having mastered the science of weapons, is capable of facing them.
"O lord of men, you have reached the perfection of divine dance, instrumental music, and song; O subduer of enemies, you ought to visit those secluded sacred fords together with all your brothers."
Having bathed in sacred fords, O king of kings, you shall be cleansed of sin, freed from fever, and rid of all impurity; thus, happy and purified, you shall enjoy the kingdom.
And you, O best of the twice-born, [shall follow] him as he wanders upon the surface of the earth.
O foremost of Brahmins, endowed as you are with the power of asceticism, it is right that you protect us;
for fierce Rākṣasas always dwell in mountain fastnesses and in rugged regions— you must always guard us from them.
When Mahendra had spoken thus, Bībhatsu also,
with a disciplined mind, addressed Lomaśa with these words: "O best of men, you must protect the son of Pāṇḍu so that the king may wander through the sacred fords while being guarded by you."
"O Great Sage, act in such a way that he may indeed give the gift. Having promised "So be it," Lomaśa, of great ascetic merit, set out for the Kāmyaka forest and arrived upon the earth.
There he beheld the son of Kuntī, the King of Dharma and subduer of enemies,
surrounded on all sides by ascetics and his brothers.
Janamejaya said:
"O Brahmin, having heard of this most wonderful deed of Pārtha of immeasurable splendor, what did the highly energetic Dhṛtarāṣṭra say?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard from Dvaipāyana, the best of sages, that Pārtha had gone to the world of Śakra, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, spoke these words to Sañjaya:
"O Sūta, I have heard in its entirety the deeds of the wise Pārtha."
"O charioteer, has it also been made known to you exactly as it is,
that my son— heedless regarding vulgar pleasures, dull-witted, and evil in resolve— will, by his own poor judgment, cause the destruction of the earth?"
For that high-souled one whose words are always true even in his private moments,
even the three worlds would belong to him who has Dhanañjaya as his warrior—
when he discharges barbed arrows, iron shafts, and sharp-pointed bolts whetted on stone.
"Who could stand before Arjuna, even Death himself who has transcended old age?
All my evil-minded sons have fallen under the power of death,
for whom a battle with the invincible Pāṇḍavas has now arrived."
Even as I reflect incessantly, I do not see any car-warrior who could rise up against that very wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow in battle—
not even if Droṇa and Karṇa were to oppose him, or even Bhīṣma himself in the fray.

There would be great uncertainty in the world, yet I do not see victory for us. Karṇa is compassionate and prone to negligence; the Teacher (Droṇa) is aged and venerable. But Pārtha is indignant, powerful, impetuous, and of firm prowess.

A most tumultuous battle would ensue, in which none could be defeated; for all are heroes skilled in weapons and have all attained great fame. Indeed, even sovereignty over all the worlds would not be desired by them once they have been defeated.
Peace would surely come through the death of either them or Phalguna;
however, there is no slayer of Arjuna, nor is there any victor over him. How could his wrath, which has arisen against the dull-witted, be appeased?

Equal to the Lord of the Thirty-three, that hero gratified the fire-god at Khāṇḍava; he conquered all the kings at the great Rājasūya sacrifice. O Sañjaya, even the thunderbolt falling upon the summit of a mountain might leave something remaining.
But the arrows discharged by Kiritin, O dear one, will leave no remnant of them;
for just as the rays of the sun scorch all that is moving and stationary here,
so shall the arrows released from the arms of Pārtha consume my sons.
Or rather, afflicted by fear at the sound of Savyasācin’s chariot,
the Bharata army appears as if torn asunder on all sides,
as he scatters and showers forth his arrows.
Standing in battle as an assailant, the diadem-wearing Arjuna is like the all-destroying Antaka sent by the Creator;
he is likewise impossible to overcome.
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, all this that you have spoken regarding Duryodhana is exactly as you have said; it is not false, O lord of the earth."
For those Pāṇḍavas of immeasurable prowess were indeed possessed by wrath upon seeing the illustrious Kṛṣṇā, their lawful wife, led into the assembly hall,
and having heard those words of Duḥśāsana which portended such terrible consequences.
"O great king, it is my conviction that Karna will not sleep;
for you have heard, O great king, how Sthāṇu, the eleven-fold deity, was gratified by Pārtha with his bow in battle."
Assuming the guise of a hunter, the Lord Kapardin himself, the sovereign of all gods, fought with Phalguna out of a desire to test him;
and that one of great splendor also obtained the supreme weapon, the Pāśupata.
There, those world-protectors revealed themselves to Arjuna,
that bull among the Kurus, who was striving with ascetic penance for the sake of celestial weapons. "Indeed, no one else but Phalguna is capable of obtaining these."
O King, what man on earth dares to wear out in battle that hero, who was not worn out by Maheśvara himself when he swallowed him in his vast form, and who has had direct vision of these lords?
This terrible, tumultuous, and hair-raising calamity has been brought about by those who dragged Draupadī and provoked the Pāṇḍavas;
therein Bhīma, his lips quivering, spoke these great words.
Having seen both thighs displayed by Duryodhana to Draupadī, [Bhīma said:
"O wicked one, at the end of thirteen years, I shall break your thighs with my mace which is like a thunderbolt, you who played such foul dice."

All were the best among strikers, all possessed immeasurable splendor, and all were experts in every weapon; they were difficult to conquer even by the gods. I believe that, incited by wrath, [they will prevail] over your sons in battle.
"Endowed with heroism and indignation, the sons of Pṛthā will bring about their end.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sūta, what has been done by Karṇa in speaking such harsh words?"
"Enough of this enmity; it has reached its limit since Kṛṣṇā was brought into the assembly hall.
Even now, my dull-witted sons might still remain, they for whom their eldest brother and superior does not abide in discipline."
O Sūta, that man of little fortune does not even wish to listen to my words,
seeing me deprived of sight, motionless, and unconscious. And as for his dull-witted ministers, Karna, Saubala, and the others—
Those senseless men, moreover, increase his many faults. Even arrows discharged at will by Pārtha of immeasurable splendor would consume my sons; how much more so when they are impelled by his wrath?

Released by the strength of Pārtha’s arms, discharged from his great bow, and empowered by the mantras of divine weapons, these arrows could destroy even the gods— Pārtha, whose counselor, protector, and friend is Janārdana.

That Hari is the Lord of the three worlds; what, indeed, has he not conquered? And this is a most great marvel here, O Sañjaya, concerning Arjuna—that he has encountered Mahādeva with his own two arms; such is the report.
What was done of old by Phalguna and Dāmodara at Khāṇḍava for the sake of assisting Agni is evident to all the world;
yet, in every way, my son no longer exists, along with his ministers and kinsmen.
When Pārtha, Bhīma, and Vāsudeva the Sātvata were enraged,
Janamejaya said:
"O Sage, regarding that which was lamented by King Dhṛtarāṣṭra..."

Having sent the heroic Pāṇḍavas into exile, all of this is rendered useless. For how could a king overlook his own son, Duryodhana, who is small-minded and inciting the wrath of the great car-warriors, the sons of Pāṇḍu?
"Tell me, what was the food of the sons of Pāṇḍu in the forest? Was it wild forest-gathered fare or cultivated grain? May your honor explain this to me. Vaiśampāyana said:
Those bulls among men ate only after first offering the choice portions to the brahmins— both forest-grown food and deer brought down by pure arrows.
While those heroic and great archers were thus dwelling in the forest, [the people]...
