O King, thousands of Brāhmaṇas followed him— both those who maintained sacred fires and those who did not; likewise, ten thousand high-souled Snātaka Brāhmaṇas, masters of the path to liberation, whom Yudhiṣṭhira supported.

Having slain ruru deer, black antelopes, and other sacrificial forest-dwelling animals with his arrows according to the prescribed rites, he presented them to the brahmins. Not a single person there was seen who was discolored or afflicted by disease.
Whether emaciated, weak, dejected, or even fearful,
O twice-born one, no lack of discipline was seen there at that time;
[they regarded him] like beloved sons, kinsmen, or like brothers born of the same womb.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma and best of the Kauravas, provided for them;
and the illustrious Draupadī likewise nourished all her husbands and the twice-born.
Having fed them first like a mother, she then partook of what remained.
King [Yudhiṣṭhira] went to the east, Bhīmasena to the south, and the twins to the west or the north—
those archers, for the sake of the meat of deer.
They constantly approached [him] and brought about his decline;
for while they were dwelling in the Kāmyaka forest,
they were deprived of Arjuna and filled with longing.
"Exactly five years have passed while they were studying, reciting prayers, and offering oblations.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Sighing deeply and hotly, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā,
addressed Sañjaya the charioteer and spoke, O bull of the Bharatas,
having heard of that superhuman and wonderful conduct of theirs.
"O charioteer, my soul overwhelmed by anxiety and grief, and flooded with indignation,
I find no peace for even a moment, neither by night nor by day,
as I reflect upon that terrible misconduct of the past born of the gambling match."
The valor, fortitude, supreme constancy, and extraordinary mutual affection of those brothers, who possessed unbearable prowess—
[all these were seen] in the two illustrious sons of gods, whose splendor was equal to that of the king of the gods.

Nakula and Sahadeva, the two Pāṇḍavas, are fierce in battle; they possess firm weapons, can strike from afar, and are resolute in combat. Quick-handed, firm in their wrath, ever-diligent, and full of vigor.

O Sañjaya, when those two, Bhīma and Arjuna, having placed themselves at the forefront, stand at the head of the battle with the prowess of lions— unbearable like the two Aśvins— I see no remnant of this army remaining here.
For those two sons of gods, both peerless chariot-warriors (*aprati-ratha*) and great car-fighters (*mahā-ratha*) in battle,
being full of indignation, will not tolerate that suffering of Draupadī. Nor will the Vṛṣṇis, those great archers, or the Pāñcālas of mighty energy.
Protected by Vāsudeva, who is true to his promise in battle,
the sons of Pṛthā will consume my army in the fray,
O son of a Sūta, as the Vṛṣṇis are led by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
His momentum cannot be withstood even by mountains in combat;
in their midst, the great archer Bhīma, of terrifying prowess,
will move about with his Śaṅkya mace, which slays heroes.
Likewise, the lords of men were unable to endure the roar of the Gāṇḍīva bow, which was like the crash of a thunderbolt, nor the force of Bhīma’s mace. Therefore,
following the will of Duryodhana, I disregarded the words of my well-wishers.
"I shall remember those things that ought to be remembered, which were not performed by me in the past.
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, this very great transgression was overlooked by you."
Although you were capable, out of delusion you did not restrain your son.
For when Madhusūdana heard that the Pāṇḍavas had been defeated at dice,
Acyuta quickly went to the Kāmyaka forest to comfort the sons of Pṛthā.
Likewise, the sons of Drupada led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
Virāṭa, Dhṛṣṭaketu, and the great car-warriors of the Kekayas—
having seen the Pārthas defeated there— all spoke together.
Everything was known through my spies, and that has been made known to you by me.
Having approached, Madhusūdana was chosen there by the Pāṇḍavas for the charioteership of Phalguna in battle; and Hari said to them, "So be it."
For even Kṛṣṇa, filled with indignation upon seeing the Pārthas in such a state—
with black antelope skins as their upper garments— spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"That prosperity which once belonged to the Pārthas in Indraprastha..."
At the Rājasūya sacrifice, I witnessed that which is very difficult for other kings to attain: there,
all the rulers of the earth were overcome by the fear of the splendor of his weapons—
along with the Vaṅgas, Aṅgas, Pauṇḍras, Uḍras, Colas, Draviḍas, and Andhakas.
Those who dwell along the shores of the ocean, as well as those living in coastal towns—
the Siṃhalas, the Barbaras, the Mlecchas, and those who inhabit the arid wilderness—
as well as hundreds of western kingdoms reaching to the edge of the sea.
The Pahlavas, Daradas, all the Kirātas, Yavanas, Śakas,
Hārahūṇas, Cīnas, Tukhāras, and Saindhavas; as well as the Jāguḍas, Ramaṭhas, Muṇḍas, the kingdoms of women, and the Taṅgaṇas.
O bull among the Bharatas, these and many others—
those whom you [mentioned] and many other very numerous ones who were summoned, O bull among the Bharatas—
I saw them all arrived as servers at your sacrifice.
O descendant of Kuru, that prosperity which has been seized by those fickle and treacherous men—
having taken their very lives, I shall bring it back to you,
along with Rāma, Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins.
O Bhārata, having slain Duryodhana and Karṇa in battle immediately, [he was accompanied] by Akrūra, Gada, Sāmba, Pradyumna, Āhuka, the heroic Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and the son of Śiśupāla.
[If] Duḥśāsana, the son of Subala, or whoever else shall fight against you,
then, dwelling in Hastināpura together with your brothers and having attained the royal fortune of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s lineage, rule this earth.
Then, in that assembly of heroes, while all those present— including Dhrishtadyumna and the others— were listening, the king said to him:
"O Janardana, I accept these words of yours as true."

"O mighty-armed one, you shall slay my enemies along with their followers after the thirteenth year has passed; O Keśava, make this true for me. For this residence in the forest among kings was indeed promised by me."
Having heard those words of the King of Dharma, the members of the assembly,
led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, immediately pacified the indignant Keśava with sweet words appropriate for the occasion.
In the hearing of Vāsudeva, they spoke to the unwearied Pāñcālī:
"O Queen, out of anger toward you, Duryodhana shall lose his life;
we promise this truth to you, O fair-complexioned one—do not grieve."
"O Kṛṣṇā, those who then laughed at you upon seeing you enraged— the flesh of those men shall be devoured by beasts and birds,
and vultures and jackals shall drink their blood."
O Pāñcālī, you shall see their bodies upon the surface of the earth— those very men by whom you were dragged across the floor of the assembly hall as they pulled at your head—
being dragged and repeatedly devoured by carnivorous beasts.
"Those by whom you were tormented there, and those who looked on with indifference—
the earth shall drink the blood of those whose heads have been severed.
Thus did those bulls among men speak various words at that time.
All of them are radiant and heroic, and all bear the marks of battle scars.
Chosen by Dharmarāja after the thirteenth year has passed,
these great chariot-warriors will set forth, placing Vāsudeva at their head.
Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Dhanañjaya; Pradyumna and Sāmba, Yuyudhāna and Bhīma; the two sons of Mādrī and the sons of the king of Kekaya;
The sons of the Pāñcāla king, together with Dharmarāja—
these all, the world-renowned heroes, invincible,
high-souled, along with their followers and their armies.
"Who that desires life would advance against them in battle, as if against enraged maned lions?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O lord of men, what Vidura told me at the time of the gambling match— that if you should defeat the Pāṇḍavas,
this would surely be the end of the Kurus— has come to pass."
"A great and terrifying flood of blood will arise," O Sūta; I believe that it will indeed happen exactly as the Kṣattṛ spoke those words to me in the past.
"Without doubt, this battle will come to pass when the time has arrived for the Pāṇḍavas, just as it was foretold. Janamejaya said:
When the high-souled Pārtha had gone to the world of Śakra for the sake of the weapon,
what did Yudhiṣṭhira and the other Pāṇḍavas do?
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the high-souled Pārtha had gone to the world of Śakra for the sake of the weapon,
those bulls among men dwelt together with Kṛṣṇā in the Kāmyaka forest.
Then, on one occasion, in a secluded and solitary grassy spot, they sat down.
Afflicted by grief, O best of the Bharatas, they sat down together with Kṛṣṇā,
lamenting for Dhanañjaya with tearful throats and deeply distressed;
for sorrow overwhelmed them all because of that separation.
Afflicted by the separation from Dhanañjaya and the loss of their kingdom,
the mighty-armed Bhīma then addressed Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O Great King, O bull among men, that hero has departed at your command."
Arjuna is the one upon whom the lives of the sons of Pāṇḍu are established;
if he were destroyed, the Pañcālas along with their sons, as well as ourselves,
Sātyaki, and Vāsudeva, would undoubtedly perish.

What indeed could be more painful than this: that the radiant Bībhatsu, disregarding many afflictions, must go forth at your command? It is by relying on the arms of that high-souled one that we all [stand firm].
We consider our enemies already defeated in battle and the earth already won,
for it is through the power of that archer that we regard all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with Saubala, as conquered within the midst of the assembly.
"By whose power all those archers, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with Saubala, were not sent to the other world by me in the midst of the assembly;
we, who possess the strength of arms, [shall now act upon] the anger that has arisen within us."
Protected by Vāsudeva, we endure [all this] because you are our root;
for, having slain our enemies led by Karṇa along with Kṛṣṇa,
we shall rule the entire earth conquered by the strength of our own arms.
"O King, we have all been overwhelmed by the fault of this gambling match; though our prowess is undiminished, O monarch, we are far surpassed in strength by these powerful men.
O great king, you ought to consider the duty of a Kshatriya."
"For indeed, O Great King, the forest-dwelling life is not the duty of a Kṣatriya;
the wise know that sovereignty alone is the supreme duty of a Kṣatriya. Therefore, O King, you who know the duty of a Kṣatriya, do not destroy the paths of righteousness."
"O King, let us slay the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra before twelve years have passed;
reflect upon this in your heart. Therefore, arise, O mighty-armed one!"
Having turned Pārtha back from the forest and having summoned Janārdana, O great king,
lord of the people, I shall, with all speed in this great battle, send the Dhārtarāṣṭras— arrayed in their ranks— to the other world.
"I shall slay all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with Saubala,
as well as Duryodhana, Karṇa, and whoever else shall fight against me.
Once they have been subdued by me, you may return from the forest once again."
O lord of the people, if this is done, no fault shall be yours; O subduer of enemies, O dear one, having shaken off the sin committed through various sacrifices,
O great king, we may go to the highest heaven.

"O King, this would indeed be so if the king were not foolish; for you, devoted to righteousness, would be one who does not procrastinate. It is a settled rule that those whose intellects are steeped in deceit must be destroyed by deceit."
For it is not said that there is sin in slaying a deceitful person through deceit;
thus, O Bhārata, is it seen here among those who know the law. Indeed, O Great King, day and night are equal to a year.
"O Lord, O Great King, the word of the Vedas is likewise heard eternally:
'A full year is completed through the kṛcchra penance.
O Acyuta, if the Vedas are authoritative for you, [then this must be done] after a day has passed."
"O subduer of enemies, let it be known that thirteen years are the fixed period; this is the time to slay Duryodhana along with his followers,
O King, before he brings the entire earth under his single control."
O Indra among kings, that which was done by you, who are fond of gambling, has resulted thus;
we have all been cast down into this life of living incognito. I do not see any place where that most wicked man cannot find us.

The evil-minded Suyodhana will not realize that we are being watched by his spies; and once he has learned of all this, that lowest of men will then, through deceit, send us away again into exile in the forest.
If that wicked man should somehow approach us, having seen that we have completed our period of living incognito, he would surely challenge us once again.
O Great King, the game of dice began for you once more.

Furthermore, Your Majesty, being summoned once more by means of dice, you will be defeated; for he is so skilled at dice that he is certain to strip you of your senses. Thus, O Great King, you shall dwell again in the forests.
O Great King, if you ought not to treat us so piteously,
then look after the Vedas and the entirety of the Dharma for as long as you live;
it is a settled rule that those whose intellects are rooted in deceit must be destroyed by deceit.

"Permitted by you, having gone [to him], I shall slay that dull-witted Suyodhana to the best of my ability— just as the fire, driven by the wind, consumes dry grass; therefore, may your lordship grant us leave."
To Bhīma who was speaking thus, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma,
spoke while consoling the Pāṇḍava, smelling his head:
"O mighty-armed one, you will undoubtedly slay Suyodhana."
After thirteen years have passed, together with the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow—
O Pārtha, O Lord, as for what you say to me that the time has arrived,
I cannot bear to speak an untruth, for such a thing does not exist within me.

"O son of Kuntī, even without resorting to deceit, O invincible one, you shall slay Suyodhana along with his followers, for he is of sinful resolve. While Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira was speaking thus to Bhīma, [the earth trembled].
The highly fortunate and great seer Bṛhadaśva arrived. Seeing that practitioner of dharma who had arrived,
the righteous King of Dharma honored him with the madhuparka offering according to the scriptures.
When he was seated and had been comforted, the mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira sat beside him, looked upon him, and spoke at length with great sorrow:
"O Blessed One, my wealth and my kingdom have been taken from me by means of a game of dice."

Having been summoned by gamblers skilled in dice and expert in deceit, those of evil intent used trickery against me, who am unskilled at dice; they even brought my wife— who is dearer to me than life itself— into the assembly hall.
Having defeated me once again at dice, they exiled me to the great forest for a most terrible dwelling in the woods, clad in deerskins;
while I was living in that forest, enduring hardships, I was overwhelmed by supreme sorrow.
And in the section concerning the game of dice, hearing those most cruel words of my distressed friends as they recounted everything beginning with the gambling match,
I remained dwelling in their hearts, remembering and reflecting upon them throughout all the nights.
In whom all living beings find their life-breath within that wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow—
without that great-souled one, I have become as if lifeless. When shall I see Bībhatsu returned again, having mastered his weapons?
"Speaking kindly, noble-minded, endowed with compassion, and untiring"—
thus all these great archers think of Dhanañjaya;
but because of this, I, along with my younger brother, am despondent.
When I have returned from my dwelling in the forest, those evil-minded ones—
Jayanta and his brothers, who take delight in gambling—
will surely challenge me again by force to a game of dice, as they are experts in the art of the dice.
And once challenged again to the game of dice, I am unable to turn back;
I have no wealth for the stake, nor do I possess any riches whatsoever. Reflecting upon all this, I contemplate it day and night.
"There is no man here on earth more miserable than I; is there any king on this earth whose fortune is even more meager than mine,
whom you have previously seen or even heard of?"
"There is no man more miserable than I, such is my thought; nor is there anyone of even lesser fortune, O Great Sage. To the king who was speaking thus, the sage Bṛhadaśva replied:
To him who was speaking thus, afflicted by grief, the venerable seer Bṛhadaśva spoke, dispelling the sorrow of the wise King Dharmarāja. Bṛhadaśva said:
"O Great King, as for what you say— that there is no man anywhere more unfortunate than yourself, O Pāṇḍava—
your mind, O best among the wise, should not be given to despondency."
"Bibhatsu will come and he shall conquer his enemies. O sinless one, if you wish to hear it, I shall tell you here of that king,
O lord of the earth, who was even more sorrowful than you."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the king said to him, "Let the Blessed One speak;
I wish to hear about the king who has reached this state."
Bṛhadaśva said:
Listen attentively, O King, along with your brothers, O Acyuta,
to the account of that lord of the earth who was even more sorrowful than you.
Among the Niṣadhas, there was a protector of the earth named Vīrasena;
he had a son named Nala, who perceived both dharma and artha.
We have heard that this king was defeated by Puṣkara through deceit.
Unworthy of suffering, he dwelt together with his wife in the forest dwelling.
O King, while he lived in the forest, neither his horse, nor his chariot, nor his brother, nor his kinsmen ever remained there with him.
"For you are surrounded by heroic brothers who are equal to the gods, as well as by the foremost of the twice-born who are like Brahmā; therefore, you ought not to grieve.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of speakers, I desire to hear in detail the life-story of the great-souled Nala; you ought to relate it to me. Bṛhadaśva said:

There was once a king named Nala, the powerful son of Vīrasena; he was endowed with desirable qualities, handsome, and skilled in horses. He was a performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, capable, and always distinguished by his virtuous conduct.
He stood at the head of the lords of men like the Lord of the Gods;
surpassing all others in splendor like the sun,
he was a king devoted to Brahman, a knower of the Vedas, and a hero among the Niṣadhas.
He was fond of dice, truthful, and great as the commander of an *akṣauhiṇī* army; he was desired by excellent women, noble, and self-controlled;
he was the protector and the best among archers, like Manu himself in person.
In the same way, there was in Vidarbha a king named Bhīma of terrible prowess;
he was a hero endowed with all virtues, yet though desiring offspring, he remained childless. With great composure, he exerted supreme effort for the sake of progeny.

O Bhārata, a Brahman-sage named Damana approached him. O Indra among kings, that Bhīma, who knew the dharma and desired offspring, gratified that highly resplendent sage with hospitality along with his queen.
Pleased with him and his wife, the highly illustrious Damana granted them a boon: a jewel among maidens and three noble sons—
Damayantī, Dama, Dānta, and the radiant Damana.
Endowed with all virtues, formidable and of terrifying prowess,
the slender-waisted Damayantī attained fame throughout the worlds for her beauty, splendor, glory, majesty, and good fortune.
Then, when she had reached that age, a hundred female attendants, beautifully adorned, waited upon her like Śacī;
there the daughter of Bhīma shone, decorated with all her ornaments.
In the midst of her friends, that lady of faultless limbs was like a flash of lightning from the clouds;
endowed with exceeding beauty, she was like the goddess Śrī herself with her long eyes.
Neither among the gods nor among the yakṣas was there ever anyone so beautiful.
Never before seen nor heard of among other humans, this young woman agitates the mind; she is beautiful even to the gods. And Nala, that tiger among men, is peerless on earth in his beauty.
In his very form, he was like Kandarpa incarnate.
Out of curiosity, they praised Nala in her presence,
and likewise, they praised Damayantī repeatedly in the presence of the King of Niṣadha.

As they constantly heard each other's virtues, O son of Kuntī, an unseen desire arose between them toward one another, and that longing grew within their hearts. At that time, Nala was unable to restrain his passion within his heart.
He dwelt in seclusion in a forest near the inner apartments. Then, after some time had passed, Nala, the best of kings,
beheld swans adorned with ornaments of gold.
As they were wandering in the forest, one of them seized a bird. Then, a creature moving through the air addressed Nala with these words:
"O King, I must not be killed by you; indeed, I shall do what is pleasing to you."
"O Nala, I shall speak of you in Damayantī’s presence in such a way that she will never at any time regard any man other than you,
and so that she will become your wife, O sinless one."
"O tiger among men, I shall perform [this rite]; may you grant me your permission. Having been addressed thus, the lord of the earth then released the swan.
Those swans, having flown up, then went to Vidarbha.

Having gone to the city of Vidarbha, those Garuḍas then alighted in the presence of Damayantī; she then beheld those birds. Seeing them of such wondrous form, she was surrounded by her circle of friends.
Delighted, she proceeded in haste to seize the sky-faring birds.
Then the swans dispersed in all directions throughout the pleasure grove;
thereupon, the maidens pursued those swans one by one.
But the swan toward which Damayantī ran when she was near,
assuming a human voice, then spoke to Damayantī:
"O Damayantī, there is a lord of the earth named Nala among the Niṣadhas."

In beauty he is equal to the Aśvins; no humans are his match. O woman of excellent complexion, if you were to become his wife, your birth would bear fruit, as would this beauty of yours, O slender-waisted one.
"For we have indeed seen gods, gandharvas, humans, serpents, and rākṣasas,
yet never before have we seen anyone such as this.
And you are a jewel among women, while Nala is the best among men."
"The union of one distinguished with another who is distinguished shall be virtuous.
Having been addressed thus by the swan, O lord of the people, Damayantī spoke there to that swan: "Speak likewise of Nala as well."
"Very well," said the bird to the daughter of the King of Vidarbha, O lord of the people;
having returned to the Niṣadha kingdom, he reported everything to Nala:
"For we are gods and Gandharvas, cursed by Indra for a certain reason."
"By touching us with your hands, may we go to liberation.
Having been addressed thus, the King of Niṣadha then immersed the swans;
once touched by the King of Niṣadha, they returned once more to the world of Indra.
Bṛhadaśva said:
But having heard those words of the swan, O Bhārata,
from that time forward Damayantī became ill at ease with respect to Nala.
Then Damayantī became lost in thought, dejected, with a pale face and emaciated; she was then constantly sighing. With her gaze fixed upward, absorbed in meditation, she appeared like one mad.
Then, her complexion turning pale in an instant, her mind possessed by love, she found no pleasure whatsoever in beds, seats, or enjoyments.
She slept neither by night nor by day, crying out "Alas! Alas! again and again.
Her friends recognized through her gestures that she was unwell and appeared distressed.
Then, O lord of men, Damayantī’s circle of friends informed the King of Vidarbha that Damayantī was not well.
Having heard that from the circle of Damayantī’s friends, King Bhīma reflected upon that very great matter concerning his daughter:
"For what reason does my daughter today appear as if she were not quite well?"

Having observed that his daughter had reached the prime of youth, the protector of the earth saw that his duty was to hold a *svayaṃvara* for Damayantī. O lord of the people, he then assembled the rulers of the earth.
"O heroes, let this *svayaṃvara* be experienced," said the lord. Having heard of Damayantī’s *svayaṃvara*, all the kings then approached Bhīma at his formidable command.
Making the earth resound with the noise of elephants, horses, and chariots,
and accompanied by armies adorned with various garlands and ornaments that were a sight to behold,
Bhīma of mighty arms [advanced] before those high-souled kings.
He performed worship for them as was fitting, and they dwelt there, being honored.
At that very time, two ancient and great-souled sages, the best of seers, were traveling from here to the world of Indra.
The two high-souled ones, Nārada and Parvata, both observers of great vows, entered the palace of the king of the gods, having been most honorably received. Having honored them,
the thousand-eyed Indra then inquired after their eternal welfare.
The all-pervading Lord also inquired after their universal well-being.
Nārada said:
"O God, O Lord, we are well in every respect."
"And in the entire world, O Maghavan, the kings are well, O Lord.
Bṛhadaśva said:
Having heard the words of Nārada, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra questioned him.
Those protectors of the earth who know the Dharma, who fight having renounced their lives,
and who meet their death by the sword at the proper time without turning their backs—
this inexhaustible world is theirs, just as it is mine, fulfilling all desires.
"Where indeed are those heroic Kṣatriyas? For I do not see those lords of the earth, my beloved guests, as they approach.
Thus addressed by Śakra, Nārada replied:
"Listen to me, O Blessed One, as to why the rulers of the earth do not see her—
the daughter of the King of Vidarbha, renowned as Damayantī,
who surpasses all women on earth in beauty."
O Śakra, her *svayaṃvara* will take place before long;
kings and princes from all quarters are going there,
seeking her who is like a jewel to the world.
O slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, they especially longed for this distinction.
While this was being told, the world-protectors, together with Agni,
those best of immortals, arrived in the presence of the king of the gods.
Then they all heard those great words of Nārada;
having heard them, they spoke with joy, "We too shall go.
Then, O Great King, they all set out with their attendants and their vehicles.
They went toward Vidarbha, where all the lords of the earth had gathered;
and King Nala too, O son of Kuntī, having heard of the assembly of kings,
set out with an undaunted spirit, devoted to Damayantī.
Then the gods saw Nala standing upon the earth on their path;
by the perfection of his beauty, he stood there like the god of love (Manmatha) himself in bodily form.
Having seen him shining like the sun, those guardians of the world—
They stood there, their thoughts stilled, struck with wonder by the perfection of his form.
Then, O King, the dwellers of heaven, having steadied their celestial chariots in the mid-air and descended from the sky,
spoke to the king of Niṣadha.
"O Nala, O king of kings, O lord of the Niṣadhas, you are devoted to truth! Render us assistance; become our messenger, O best of men.
Bṛhadaśva said:
O Bhārata, having promised them that he would do it, Nala then stood with palms joined in reverence and questioned them:
"Who indeed are you, and who is he for whom I am desired as a messenger?"
"Furthermore, tell me exactly what must be done by me there.
When the King of Niṣadha had spoken thus, Maghavan replied:
"Know us to be the immortals who have come for the sake of Damayantī."
"I am Indra, and this is Agni; likewise, this is the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa), and this, O King, is Yama, the ender of the bodies of men.
Therefore, announce our arrival to Damayantī."
The world-protectors, together with Indra, are approaching you, desiring to see you.
The gods—Śakra, Agni, Varuṇa, and Yama—wish to obtain you. Choose one of them as your husband, O lady.
Thus addressed by Śakra, Nala spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"It does not behove you to send me on this mission, for I am already engaged in a single purpose.
For how can a man, having already formed a resolve [for another], venture to pursue a woman?"
"May the Great Lords forgive me for speaking such words for the sake of another.
Having been addressed thus by the King of Niṣadha, Maghavan spoke again.
The gods said:
"O Nala, having previously promised us, 'I shall do it,' why will you not do so? Go, O Nala, do not delay!
Indeed, you must announce our arrival to Damayantī."
"For by carrying out the command of the immortals, you shall indeed be united with the highest good.
Bṛhadaśva said:
Having been addressed thus by those gods, that prince of Niṣadha spoke again.
"How can I venture to enter houses that are so well-guarded?
Śakra spoke again to the prince of Niṣadha: "Concealed by our *māyā*, you shall certainly enter."
"You shall enter," Śakra spoke to him once more. Having said, "So be it," he went to Damayantī’s dwelling.
There he beheld the princess of Vidarbha, surrounded by her circle of female companions.
She was radiant with her form and splendor, a woman of excellent complexion; her limbs were exceedingly delicate, her waist slender, and her eyes beautiful,
as if she were eclipsing the light of the moon with her own brilliance.
Upon merely seeing that woman of lovely smiles, his desire increased; yet, wishing to fulfill his vow, he restrained the passion within his heart.
Then, those supreme women, seeing the prince of Niṣadha, were filled with agitation.
Overawed by his splendor, they rose from their seats;
filled with wonder and great joy, they praised Nala,
yet they did not speak to him, reflecting instead within their minds.
"Oh, what beauty! Oh, what radiance! Oh, what fortitude this great-souled one possesses!
Who might he be—is he a god, or a yakṣa, or perhaps a gandharva?"—yet they were not even able to address him with a single word.
Overwhelmed by his splendor, all those modest and excellent women were put to shame. Then Damayantī, smiling and speaking with a gentle smile, addressed the heroic Nala in her astonishment.

"Who are you, O hero of entirely faultless limbs, who increases the longing in my heart? You have arrived like an immortal, O sinless one; I wish to know you. How did you come here, and how were you not perceived?"
"For my palace is well-guarded, and the king indeed possesses stern commands. Thus addressed by the princess of Vidarbha, Nala replied to her:
"O blessed lady, know me to be Nala, a messenger of the gods who has come here."
"The gods—Śakra, Agni, Varuṇa, and Yama—desire to obtain you.
O beautiful one, choose one of those gods as your husband.
It was by their very power that I entered here unobserved."
"For as I was entering, no one saw me, nor did anyone stop me.
It is for this purpose, O blessed lady, that I have been sent by the best of the gods.
Having heard this, O auspicious one, form your resolve as you wish."
Bṛhadaśva said:
Having paid homage to the gods, she smiled and spoke to Nala:
"O King, behave toward me according to your faith; what may I do for you?"
"Indeed, both myself and whatever other wealth I possess, O Lord—trust me, let all that be yours; please show me your favor.
O King, those words of the swans burn me."

"For it was on your account, O hero, that I brought these kings together. If you, O bestower of honor, shall reject me who am devoted to you, I will resort to poison, fire, water, or the rope for your sake."
Thus addressed by the princess of Vidarbha, Nala replied to her:
"While the guardians of the worlds are present, how can you desire a mere mortal— [me],
who am [but a servant] of those high-souled lords, the creators of the world?"
They are not even equal to the dust of your feet; let your mind dwell upon them.
For a mortal who acts against the will of the gods meets with death;
therefore, O lady of faultless limbs, save me and choose the best of the gods.
Dustless garments, divine and variegated garlands,
and the finest ornaments— having obtained these from the gods, do indeed enjoy them;
for he who, having contracted this entire earth, swallows it once again.
Who would not choose as her husband Hutāśa, the lord of the gods,
before whom all gathered hosts of beings submit to righteousness out of fear of his rod? Who would not choose him as her husband?

Who would not choose as her husband that high-souled one, whose nature is dharma, the crusher of Daityas and Dānavas, the great Indra of all the gods? If you so desire, let it be done with a mind free from hesitation.
Listen to these words from Varuṇa, the guardian of the world, spoken as a friend. Having been addressed thus by the prince of Niṣadha, Damayantī spoke these words,
her eyes overflowing with tears born of grief.
"O Lord of the Earth, having paid homage to all the gods, I choose you alone as my husband; I tell you this in truth. Then the king spoke to her, who was trembling with her hands joined in reverence.
"O auspicious one, O blessed lady, having come on this mission, let it be carried out accordingly. For how could I, having given my promise especially to the gods,
and having undertaken an effort for the sake of another, now strive for my own interest?"
"If this dharma is for my own benefit, then I too shall act for my own benefit; therefore, O blessed lady, let it be so arranged. Then Damayantī, of pure smiles, spoke these words choked with tears.
Speaking softly, she said to King Nala:
"O lord of men, I have seen a remedy that is free from danger,
by which no fault whatsoever shall accrue to you, O King."
"O best of men, you and all the gods, led by Agni, must come together to the place where my svayaṃvara is held. Then,
O lord of men, I shall [choose] you in the presence of the world-protectors."
"O tiger among men, I shall choose you; thus no fault will arise.
Having been addressed in this way by the princess of Vidarbha, O lord of the people, King Nala returned once more to the place where the gods had assembled.
The world-protectors, together with their lords, saw him approaching in that manner;
and having seen him, they then questioned him about the entire account.
The gods said:
"O King, have you seen Damayantī of the pure smile?
O sinless lord of the earth, tell us everything she said to all of us.
Nala said:
"Commanded by you, I entered Damayantī’s residence,
a vast courtyard surrounded by elderly men bearing staffs;
yet, as I was entering, not a single man there saw me."
"Except for that daughter of the king, [this was achieved] solely through your own splendor. Her friends were seen by me, and I too was observed by them;
all those lords of the gods were filled with wonder upon seeing me."
O best of gods, while you were being described by me, that lady of radiant countenance,
her resolve fixed upon me alone, chose me;
and the young woman said to me, "Let the gods come together."
"O best of men, wherever my *svayaṃvara* takes place with you present,
O supreme among men, I shall choose you in the presence of them all.
In this way, O mighty-armed one, no fault shall accrue to you."
"O wise ones, I have related this entire account exactly as it occurred; you, O lords of the thirty gods, are the ultimate authority.
Bṛhadaśva said:
Then, when an auspicious time had arrived, on a holy lunar day and at a favorable moment,
King Bhīma himself summoned the lords of the earth to the svayaṃvara.
Hearing that, all the protectors of the earth were tormented by desire.
Desirous of winning Damayantī, they arrived in haste;
those kings entered the great arena— which was resplendent with golden pillars and adorned with an archway— like lions entering a mountain.
There, seated upon various thrones, all those lords of the earth wore fragrant garlands and polished gem-studded earrings;
they filled that assembly of kings like Bhogavatī is filled with nāgas.
The king Nala, of virtuous fame, entered together with the gods into that hall,
which was filled with tigers among men like a mountain cave with tigers.
The lords of the gods and gandharvas beheld him, filled with wonder.
And those citizens and country folk who were gathered there,
their arms appeared there plump and like iron maces;
they were well-proportioned and smooth, resembling five-headed serpents.
The beautiful faces of the kings— with their lovely hair-ends, charming noses, and auspicious features— shone like stars in the sky.
Then Damayantī, of radiant countenance, entered the arena.
Stealing away the eyes and minds of the kings with her radiance,
the gaze of those high-souled men fell upon her limbs;
fixed right there, it did not move as they continued to look.

Then, O Bhārata, while the names of the kings were being proclaimed, the daughter of Bhīma beheld five men who appeared to be identical in form. Observing them all standing there with indistinguishable appearances, she—
Then, due to this uncertainty, the beautiful daughter of Vidarbha could not recognize King Nala; for among those whose age, dress, appearance, and form were indistinguishable,
she thought whoever she looked upon was King Nala.
Reflecting with her intellect, that passionate woman then reasoned:
"How indeed might I recognize the gods? How might I know King Nala?
Thinking thus, the princess of Vidarbha was deeply distressed.
O Bhārata, he reflected upon the signs of the gods that he had heard from the elders:
"Those signs of the gods which I have heard from the aged— I do not perceive even one of them here among those standing upon the ground."
Having deliberated in many ways and reflected again and again,
she considered that the time had come to seek refuge with the gods;
and with both speech and mind, she offered her salutation.
With palms joined in reverence toward the gods, she spoke these words while trembling:
"Since I have heard the words of the swans and have chosen the Prince of Niṣadha as my husband,
by that truth may the gods point him out to me."
Just as I do not transgress [the truth] in word or in thought,
by that truth may the gods point him out to me—
him who has been ordained by the gods as my husband, the lord of Niṣadha.
By this truth, O gods, may they reveal him to me,
just as this vow has been undertaken by me for the sake of winning Nala.
May the world-protectors, together with their lords, restore their own true forms.

Having heard that piteous lamentation of Damayantī, and having ascertained her supreme resolve, her truthfulness, and her deep affection for the King of Niṣadha, [Nala] thought: "How may I recognize the virtuous king?"

O Bhārata, the gods performed the purification of the mind, the intellect, devotion, and passion as prescribed, establishing their capacity for wearing the *liṅga*. She beheld all the deities free from perspiration, with steady eyes.
They were adorned with fresh garlands, free from dust, standing without touching the ground;
whereas the King of Niṣadha was accompanied by his shadow, possessed of withered garlands, covered in dust and sweat, standing upon the earth, and revealed by the blinking of his eyes.
Having then observed the gods and the one of virtuous fame, O Bhārata,
the daughter of Bhīma chose the Niṣadhan king according to dharma, O Bhārata;
bashful, the large-eyed maiden grasped the hem of his garment.
She placed an exceedingly beautiful garland upon his shoulder, and that woman of excellent complexion chose him as her husband.
Then, suddenly, a cry of "Alas! Alas! was let out by the lords of men.
"Excellent! Excellent! was the cry uttered by the gods and the great seers, O Bhārata, as they were filled with wonder and praised King Nala.
But as for Damayantī, O Kauravya, the king who was the son of Vīrasena—
With a joyful inner soul, he comforted the woman of beautiful limbs:
"O auspicious lady, because you have chosen this man in the presence of the gods, know me to be your husband; I am devoted to your word."

"O lady of pure smiles, as long as my life-breaths remain within this body, so long shall I be yours; I tell you this truly. Damayantī, having been thus greeted with these words, joined her palms in reverence.
Seeing those gods led by Agni, the two of them, filled with mutual affection,
then mentally sought refuge in those very deities once the son of Niṣadha had been chosen by the daughter of Bhīma. The world-protectors of great majesty [were thus addressed].

With delighted minds, they all granted eight boons to Nala; Śakra, the lord of Śacī, being well-pleased, bestowed upon the King of Niṣadha the power of direct vision at sacrifices and an unsurpassed, auspicious state.
Agni granted the son of Niṣadha his own self-existence wherever he might desire;
the consumer of oblations also gave him worlds and his own splendors. Yama, however, bestowed upon him the essence of food and supreme steadfastness in dharma.
The son of the Sun, being well-pleased, granted him two boons:
that the Lord of Waters would assume whatever form the Nala desired, and a garland rich with the finest fragrances; and all [the gods] gave him a pair of celestial maidens.
Having thus granted him these boons, those gods departed for the third heaven.
O Bhārata, Nala and Damayantī saw all of this, O Great King;
the people beheld it exactly as if it were a dream.
Then King Bhīma held an extraordinary *svayaṃvara*,
O lord of the people, when all the kings had assembled.
Damayantī also beheld that opulent circle of monarchs.
O Bhārata, having scrutinized the prince of Niṣadha, the daughter of Bhīma chose him in accordance with dharma. And the kings, having witnessed her marriage, were filled with wonder;
delighted, they returned home as they had come.

When the lords of the earth had departed, the high-minded Bhīma was pleased and arranged the marriage of Damayantī and Nala. Having stayed there for as long as he desired, the prince of Niṣadha, the best among men, [departed].
Permitted by Bhīma, he went to his own city;
having obtained that jewel among women, King Puṇyaśloka also took delight with her,
just as the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra rejoiced with Śacī.
Exceedingly joyful and radiant like the sun, the heroic king delighted his subjects while protecting them according to dharma;
he also performed the horse sacrifice, just as Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, had done.
And with many other sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, the wise Nala,
resembling an immortal, sported once more with Damayantī in delightful forests and groves.
And the high-minded Nala begot upon Damayantī a son,
Indrasena, and also a daughter, Indrasenā. Thus that lord of men lived, both performing sacrifices and enjoying himself.
The lord of the earth protected the earth, which was filled with wealth.
Bṛhadaśva said:
But when the son of Niṣadha had been chosen by the daughter of Bhīma, the world-protectors of great power—
As they were departing, they saw Dvāpara approaching together with Kali;
he was carrying a jar filled with liquor, secured at the waist by a rope,
while the other carried much meat piled upon burnt wood.
Surrounded by dogs, fierce, deceitful, with a frowning face,
wearing red garments, dark-complexioned, and adorned with red garlands and unguents,
he relates various most dreadful stories there.
Abducting another’s wife, seizing the property of others, excessive indulgence in drinking, betraying trust,
and engaging in gambling, hunting, theft, and impure acts— [these are the vices].
Then Śakra, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, having looked at Kali, said:
"O Kali, tell me where you will go with Dvāpara as your companion.
Thereupon Kali said to Śakra: "To the svayaṃvara of Damayantī."
"I shall go and choose her, for my heart is fixed upon her.
To him Indra replied with a laugh: "That *svayaṃvara* has already concluded;
King Nala was chosen by her as her husband in our presence."
Thus addressed by Śakra, Kali, filled with rage,
then addressed all those gods and spoke these words:
"That she chose him as her husband from among men in the midst of the gods— "
"Surely, a severe punishment would be just for her.
When this was said by Kali, the gods replied:
"Nala has been chosen by Damayantī with our full consent."
Who would not take refuge in King Nala, who is endowed with all virtues,
who knows all duties exactly as they are, who has observed his vows,
and who has studied the four Vedas along with the Purāṇas as the fifth?
He in whose house the gods are eternally satisfied through sacrifices performed according to dharma; he who is devoted to non-violence, truthful in speech, and firm in his vows;
in whom truth, fortitude, generosity, austerity, purity, self-restraint, and tranquility reside.
These things are certain regarding that tiger among men, a king equal to the guardians of the world:
whoever should wish to curse Nala of such a form, that fool would only curse himself and destroy himself by his own hand.
"O Kali, whoever should desire to corrupt Nala, who possesses such virtues,
shall sink into a vast, bottomless, and boatless hell of great suffering.
Having spoken thus to Kali and Dvāpara, the gods departed for heaven.
Then, when the gods had departed, Kali said to Dvāpara:
"O Dvāpara, I do not dare to unleash my wrath against Nala;
I shall dwell within him and cause him to fall from his kingdom, so that he will no longer take delight with the daughter of Bhīma."
"You too, having entered the dice, ought to provide me assistance;
when that dear service is performed for me, you will have done what is right.
Bṛhadaśva said:
Having thus made an agreement with Kali, Kali then went together with Dvāpara to the place where that king of Niṣadha was.
He dwelt for a long time among the Niṣadhas, constantly watching for a weak point.
Then, in his twelfth year, Kali found an opportunity:
while the prince of Niṣadha was performing his twilight devotions after urinating and sipping water,
Kali entered him before he had cleansed his feet.
Having entered into Nala, he went to the presence of Puṣkara and said this to him: "Come, play at dice with Nala;
for you shall surely defeat Nala in the game of dice, being aided by me."
"O King, having conquered King Nala, take possession of the Niṣadhas.
Thus addressed by Kali, Puṣkara spoke to him.
Puṣkara said:
"O hero, one plays for a stake; I have no wealth for a stake. And Nala does not play with one who is destitute of wealth. When Puṣkara had spoken thus, Kali addressed these words:
"In the future I shall become the best of bulls; stake with me on that wager.
Thus addressed by Kali, Puṣkara approached Nala, and Kali, having become a bull, approached Puṣkara with the cattle as his stake.
Having approached the hero Nala, Puṣkara, the slayer of enemy heroes, said repeatedly to his brother, "Let us play with the bull [as the stake]. Thereupon,
the high-minded king could not endure that challenge.
While the princess of Vidarbha looked on, he considered it the time for the wager:
"Once challenged, one should not turn back, even from gambling or even from a bet.
Thereupon, that king suddenly began to play.

Overcome by fate, the lord of men, Nala himself possessed by fate, was then defeated at dice by his brother who was possessed by Kali, losing gold, fine ornaments, vehicles, draft animals, and garments.
But no friend at all was able to restrain him as he played, intoxicated by the madness of the dice and deprived of his senses,
O Bhārata; then all the citizens, together with the ministers, [approached him].
They were coming to see the king in order to dissuade him from his distress;
then the charioteer, having approached, informed Damayantī:
"All these citizens are standing at the gate, having urgent business."
"Let it be announced to the King of Niṣadha that all the subjects are assembled,
unable to endure the calamity of the king who perceives both dharma and artha.
Then, with a voice faltering with tears and emaciated by grief, she spoke.
The daughter of Bhīma, her mind overwhelmed by grief, said to the King of Niṣadha:
"O King, the citizens, accompanied by all the ministers and motivated by devotion to the monarch, are standing at the gate desiring to see you."
"Accompanied by elders, leading brahmins, and merchants,
O King, he has arrived together with us, relying upon your favor;
you ought to see him," he spoke thus again and again.
As that woman of beautiful eyes and slender waist was thus lamenting,
the king, possessed by Kali, did not say anything at all. Then all those ministers and the city-dwellers [approached].
Afflicted by grief and overcome with shame, they departed for their homes thinking, "This man does not exist.
Thus did that gambling match between Puṣkara and Nala proceed, O Yudhiṣṭhira;
for many months, Puṇyaśloka was defeated.
Bṛhadaśva said:
Then Damayantī, though herself sane, saw that the lord of men, Puṇyaśloka,
had lost his senses in the gambling match like one who is mad.
Then, O King, the daughter of Bhīma, overcome by fear and grief,
reflected upon that very great task concerning the monarch. Suspecting that evil deed, she nevertheless desired to do what was pleasing to him.
And finding Nala stripped of all his possessions, she spoke thus to that highly renowned nurse and attendant, Bṛhatsenā—
who was devoted to her welfare, skilled in all matters, loyal, and eloquent.
"O Bṛhatsenā, having summoned the ministers of Vraja by Nala’s command,
report what wealth has been collected and what riches remain," she was thus instructed, O lord of men, by Bṛhatsenā.
She spoke the Queen’s words into the presence of the ministers.
Then all those ministers, having understood Nala’s command, said,
"May this be our good fortune," and returned once more.
Then all those ministers arrived for the second time;
the daughter of Bhīma informed him of this, but he did not welcome it. Seeing her husband not responding to her words, she [looked at him].
Having heard that the dice were constantly being used against Puṇyaśloka, and that Nala had been stripped of all his possessions, Damayantī entered her quarters again, overcome with shame;
she then spoke once more to her nurse.
"O Bṛhatsenā, go again at Nala’s command to the Vārṣṇeya charioteer; bring him here, O auspicious lady, for a great task has presented itself.
Having heard those words spoken by Damayantī, Bṛhatsenā—
He had the Vārṣṇeya brought by trusted servants who carried out his commands.
Then the blameless daughter of Bhīma, knowing the proper place and time, spoke to the Vārṣṇeya with gentle words suited to the occasion.
"You know how the king has always behaved properly toward you;
you ought to provide assistance to him while he is in such a precarious position. For as the king is being defeated here by Puṣkara,"
In such a manner his passion for gambling increased further and further,
so that the dice fell according to Puṣkara’s will;
likewise, the opposite was seen to occur with Nala’s dice.
He does not listen properly to the words of his friends and kinsmen,
and being deluded, he does not welcome my words either,
O charioteer, as if the King’s fortunes were now aflame.
"I truly believe that nothing remains of the great-souled Nala, since the king, deluded as he is, does not welcome my words. O charioteer, I have come to you for refuge; do as I say."
"For my heart is not at peace, thinking that [Nala] might perish at any time.
Therefore, having harnessed Nala's beloved, high-speed horses and having placed this couple upon them, you ought to go to Kuṇḍina."
"Having entrusted my two children and this chariot to my kinsmen,
as well as these horses, you may stay here as you please or go elsewhere.
To these words of Damayantī, Vārṣṇeya, Nala’s charioteer, replied:
He reported everything in full to the chief ministers of Nala.
Having met with them and reached a decision, and being granted permission by the lord of the earth,
he set out for Vidarbha with that army, having placed the couple upon it.
Having left the horses there, along with that excellent chariot, Indrasenā the maiden, and the boy Indrasena, the charioteer—
distressed and grieving for King Nala— took leave of King Bhīma.
Reflecting again and again in my mind, "Where indeed shall I go?
he then wandered on and reached the city of Ayodhyā. Deeply distressed, he approached King Ṛtuparṇa.
And he entered into his service as charioteer, O lord of the earth.
Bṛhadaśva said:
"Then, after the Vārṣṇeya had departed, while Puṇyaśloka was gambling..."
"The kingdom has been taken by Puṣkara, as well as whatever other wealth there was.
O King, laughing at Nala whose kingdom had been seized, Puṣkara said:
"Let the gambling proceed once more; what stake do you have left?"
"Only one of your subjects, Damayantī, remains; everything else has been won by me.
If you think it right, let the wager with Damayantī proceed.
When Puṣkara had spoken thus, Puṇyaśloka was filled with indignation.
His heart seemed to tear asunder, yet he said nothing at all.
Then, looking at Puṣkara, Nala, filled with supreme indignation, said:
"O lowest of men, do I possess any other wealth?"
Having deposited her in the form of a wager, the highly illustrious Puṇyaśloka, being dejected in mind,
then cast off from all his limbs her upper garment, her clothes,
and her ornaments.
Clad in a single garment, unsheltered, and increasing the grief of his friends,
the king then departed, having abandoned his vast sovereignty.
Damayantī, wearing but a single cloth, followed behind him as he went.
The King of Niṣadha lived with her outside the city for three nights.
But Puṣkara, O great king, proclaimed throughout the city:
"Whoever treats Nala properly shall incur my death penalty."
O Yudhiṣṭhira, because of Puṣkara’s words and his hostility,
the citizens did not offer him hospitality;
thus, though worthy of honor, he was not honored in the vicinity of the city.
Having stayed there for three nights, subsisting on water alone, the king,
afflicted by hunger, set out from that place while gathering fruits and roots;
Damayantī followed after him.
But on the manyth day, Nala, being tormented by hunger,
saw some birds with plumage resembling gold.
Then the powerful lord of Niṣadha reflected:
"This food of mine today shall be my sustenance, and this wealth shall be mine.
Then he spread them out with his inner garment;
taking that inner garment of his, they all departed through the air.
Then those birds, as they were flying up, spoke these words to Nala:
"O man of evil intellect, seeing you standing on the ground, naked, dejected, and with your face cast down, we are the dice, desiring to strip away your garment."
"Indeed, no joy has come to us now that you have departed with our garment.
Seeing those dice gone and himself naked,
King Puṇyaśloka then spoke to Damayantī:
O blameless lady, it is through the provocation of these [gods] that I have been fallen from my sovereignty;
afflicted by hunger and distressed, I find no means of sustaining life,
for which reason the Nishadhas did not show me due honor.
"Having become these birds, they are even carrying away my garment.
I have fallen into a state of extreme adversity; I am suffering and deprived of my senses.
Know that I am your husband; listen to these words for your own benefit."
Many of these paths lead toward the southern region,
passing beyond the city of Avanti and the Ṛkṣavān mountain range.
Here is the great Vindhya mountain, and the Payoṣṇī river that flows to the ocean.
These are the hermitages of the great seers, abounding in flowers and fruits;
this is the path to Vidarbha, and this one leads to Kosala. Beyond this lies the region of the southern quarter, the Deccan.
O Bhārata, King Nala, being deeply distressed, addressed these words repeatedly to Damayantī with focused attention; then she,
emaciated by grief, spoke with a voice choked with tears.
Damayantī spoke these piteous words to that prince of Niṣadha:
"O King, as I think again and again upon your resolve, my heart trembles and all my limbs fail me."
How could I abandon you and depart for the lonely forest while you have been stripped of your kingdom and wealth, are naked, and are overcome by hunger and exhaustion—
while you are weary, afflicted by hunger, and longing for that former happiness?

"O great king, in this terrible forest I shall dispel your exhaustion. There is nothing equal to a wife as a remedy for all sufferings; this is the opinion of physicians, and I tell you this truthfully."
Nala said:
"O Damayantī of slender waist, it is exactly as you have said;
for a man in distress, there is no friend or medicine equal to a wife."
"I have no desire to abandon you; why do you fear, O timid one? I might even sacrifice my own life, but never you, O blameless lady.
Damayantī said:
"O Great King, if you do not wish to abandon me here,
then for what purpose is the path to Vidarbha being pointed out?
And I know, O Lord of Men, that you ought not to forsake me."
But if you abandon me with a distracted mind, O great lord,
you will surely cause my grief to increase, O god-like one, for you have repeatedly told me the path, O best of men.
"O King, if this is your intention— that he should go—
then let us both go together to Vidarbha, if you so deem it right.
O giver of honor, the King of Vidarbha will pay you great respect there."
"O King, because you have been honored by him, you shall dwell happily in our home.
Bṛhadaśva said: Having been addressed thus by the queen, Nala then spoke these words.
Nala said:
"Just as that kingdom belongs to your father, so it belongs to me; of this there is no doubt.
Yet, being in such a precarious state, I shall not go there by any means."
"How is it that, having gone forth prosperous and increasing your joy, I shall return impoverished and increasing your grief? Bṛhadaśva said:
Speaking thus again and again to Damayantī, King Nala consoled the auspicious lady, who was covered only by half a garment. Thus,
clad in that single garment, the two of them wandered here and there.
Exhausted by hunger and thirst, they both approached a certain assembly hall. Having reached that hall, the king, the lord of Niṣadha,
sat down upon the ground together with the princess of Vidarbha.
Bereft of his garments, soiled, with disheveled hair and covered in dust,
he, exhausted, slept upon the surface of the earth together with Damayantī;
and then the auspicious Damayantī also fell asleep, overcome by slumber.
Having suddenly encountered this suffering, the delicate and ascetic woman lay down;
and while Damayantī slept, O lord of the people, King Nala— his mind and soul agitated by grief— could not sleep as he had before.
Beholding that seizure of his kingdom, the total abandonment of his friends, and his own ruin in the forest, he fell into deep reflection:
"What would happen to me by doing this? What would happen to me by not doing it?"
"Is death better for me, or the abandonment of this person?
For she is devoted to me and undergoes this suffering on my account;
yet, separated from me, she might perhaps go back to her own kin."
"She will undoubtedly encounter suffering, this peerless woman;
yet in her renunciation there might be doubt, for she might even find some happiness somewhere.
Having thus resolved after deliberating in many ways again and again, he [proceeded].
The lord of men considered it better to release her;
for this illustrious and highly blessed woman, devoted to her husband and my own devotee, could not have been assaulted by anyone on the road through her own splendor.

Thus, at that time, his mind turned away from Damayantī because of the evil influence of Kali regarding her dismissal. He [perceived] his own lack of clothing and her state of being clad in but a single garment.
Having reflected, the king concluded that he must cut away half of her garment;
"How might I cut the cloth so that my beloved does not perceive it?"—
thinking thus, the King of Niṣadha then paced about the assembly hall.
Then, O Bhārata, Nala, running hither and thither,
came upon an excellent sword with its scabbard in the vicinity of the assembly hall.
With that, the scorcher of foes cut away half of his garment and put on the other half.
Having abandoned the sleeping daughter of Vidarbha, he fled away, deprived of his senses.
Then, his heart bound with longing, he returned once more to that assembly hall;
seeing Damayantī in such a state, the lord of Niṣadha wept.
She whom neither Vāyu nor Āditya had previously beheld as my beloved—
she now lies upon the ground in the midst of the assembly like one who is helpless.
This woman of lovely smiles is wrapped in a tattered garment.
Like one who has gone mad, how will that woman of beautiful limbs fare when she realizes [my absence]?
How will the auspicious daughter of Bhīma, being alone and separated from me,
wander through the terrible forest inhabited by wild beasts and serpents?
"May the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the hosts of Maruts protect you, O highly fortunate lady; for you are encompassed by righteousness.
Having spoken thus to his beloved wife, who was peerless in beauty upon the earth, [he departed].
His wisdom stolen away by Kali, Nala set out with resolve. Having gone and gone again, King Nala repeatedly returned to the assembly hall;
drawn away by Kali, he was pulled back by his affection.
At that time, the heart of the suffering man was as if split in two;
like a swing, it repeatedly moved toward the assembly hall and away from it.
Thus, led astray by Kali, Nala fled.
Having abandoned his wife while she slept and lamented piteously at great length, the king— his mind lost and touched by the *kalī* demon, reflecting on this and that—
departed for the empty forest, leaving his wife behind in sorrow.
Bṛhadaśva said:
O King, when Nala had departed, the beautiful Damayantī, her fatigue dispelled,
became aware of it and was terrified in the lonely forest.
Not seeing her husband, filled with pain and grief, she cried out loudly in terror, "O Great King, O Nishadhan!
"Alas, my lord! Alas, Great King! Alas, my master! Why do you abandon me?"
"Alas! I am ruined, I am destroyed, I am terrified in this lonely forest.
Are you not indeed, O Great King, a knower of dharma and one whose word is truth? How is it that, having spoken such a lie, you have gone away, abandoning me while I was asleep?"
"How can you depart, abandoning your submissive wife who is devoted to you—
especially when she has done no wrong and another has wronged her?
O Lord of Men, will you be able to make those words of yours come true regarding me?"

"O bull among men, death has not been ordained for mortals before their time, yet that beloved woman whom you previously mentioned in the presence of the world-protectors still lives even for a moment after being abandoned by you."
"O bull among men, this jest has gone far enough. I am afraid, O invincible one; show yourself, O Lord!
You are seen, you are seen, O King; here you stand, O Nala!"
While I am being tormented by these roots of sorrow,
why do you not answer me, O King, having hidden yourself behind the thickets? Alas, O Indra among kings, how cruel it is that you remain here while I have come to such a state!
"O King, why do you not embrace me as I lament and offer me comfort? I do not grieve for myself, nor for anything else;
yet how is it that you, who were true to your word, have now become one whose truth has vanished by abandoning me?"
"O King, I grieve for you, thinking: 'How indeed will you be all alone?
O King, how will you be at the root of trees in the evening—thirsty, hungry, and exhausted by fatigue—not seeing me?"
Then, afflicted by intense grief and as if consumed by fury,
she ran hither and thither weeping in her misery: "O Lord, speak to me, for I am helpless in this desolate forest!"
Running hither and thither with a mind agitated by grief, the young woman suddenly faints; now she weeps and laments,
and now the young woman leaps up, and now she falls down overwhelmed.
Terrified, she hides for a moment; then she cries out and weeps.
Tormented by intense grief, sighing repeatedly and overwhelmed, that devoted wife, weeping and distracted by sorrow for her husband, [remains there].
Emerging [from the water], the devoted wife, the daughter of Bhīma, spoke while weeping:
"May that being by whose curse the Nishadhan, afflicted with grief, experiences sorrow,
suffer a sorrow even greater than his."

"May that wicked man who has thus treated Nala, whose mind is free from evil, live a life of misery, having encountered a state more painful than this. Thus did the wife of the high-souled king lament."
She searched for her husband in the forest frequented by beasts of prey;
lamenting here and there like one distracted, the daughter of Bhīma ran to and fro, crying out again and again, "Alas, alas! O King!"
Her, who was withering away excessively like a crying osprey,
grieving piteously and lamenting again and again— Sītā,
the daughter of Bhīma, who had arrived suddenly and was standing close by.
A massive python, a serpent overcome by hunger, seized her. While being swallowed by the serpent and overwhelmed by grief,
she did not grieve for herself as much as she grieved for the King of Niṣadha.
"Alas, my lord! Why do you not rush to my aid here in the forest, as I am being seized by this crocodile like one who is helpless?
O Nala, how will you fare when you remember me again?"
"O Lord, how did you come today, having abandoned me in the forest? Having been freed from sin, you have regained your intellect, your mind, and your wealth.
O Nala, you must be weary, afflicted by hunger, and utterly exhausted."
"O tiger among kings, O giver of honor, who will now destroy this toil?
While wandering through the dense forest, a hunter suddenly heard her crying out and rushed toward her with great speed."
Seeing that large-eyed woman thus seized by the serpent,
the hunter, hurrying with great speed, rushed forward;
having overtaken her with haste, that forest-dweller moved swiftly.
With a sharp weapon, he struck him in the mouth;
having slaughtered that motionless serpent, the hunter, who lives by hunting deer,
released her and washed her with water.
O descendant of Bharata, having comforted her and provided her with food, he then asked:
"Whose daughter are you, O fawn-eyed one, and how have you come to this forest?
And how, O beautiful woman, have you fallen into such great distress?"

O lord of the people, O Bhārata, being thus questioned by him, Damayantī related all this to him exactly as it had happened. She was clothed in but half a garment, with her full hips and breasts revealed.
She possessed delicate and faultless limbs, with a face like the full moon;
her eyes were like blossoming lotuses, and she spoke with such sweetness. Her eyes had curved lashes, and she spoke with such sweetness.
Having observed her, the hunter fell under the sway of desire.
Then, afflicted by passion, the hunter began to soothe her with gentle and soft words; the beautiful woman perceived this.
But Damayantī, devoted to her husband, perceiving that wicked man,
was overcome by intense rage and seemed to blaze with fury. That base and evil-minded one, however, remained intent on violating her.
She considered him unassailable, like a blazing crest of fire.
But Damayantī, afflicted by grief and deprived of her husband and kingdom,
when the time for words had passed, cursed him indeed in her rage.
"As surely as I do not think of anyone other than the King of Niṣadha even in my mind, so may this wretched hunter fall lifeless. As soon as these words were spoken by her, that hunter—
Lifeless, he fell upon the earth like a tree consumed by fire.
Bṛhadaśva said:
Having slain the hunter, that lotus-eyed woman set forth.
The forest was terrifying and desolate, resounding with the chirping of swarms of crickets;
it was inhabited by lions, tigers, boars, bears, ruru deer, and leopards;
it was crowded with various flocks of birds and frequented by barbarians and thieves.
It was covered with *śāla*, *veṇu*, *dhava*, *aśvattha*, *tinduka*, and *iṅguda* trees, as well as *kiṃśuka*, *arjuna*, and *ariṣṭa*; it was filled with *candana* and *śālmali* trees,
and crowded with *jambu*, *āmra*, *lodhra*, *khadira*, *śāka*, and *vetra* trees.
It was covered with *kāśmarya*, *āmalaka*, *plakṣa*, *kadamba*, and *udumbara* trees;
it was overspread with *badarī* and *bilva*, crowded with *nyagrodha* trees,
and filled with *priyāla*, *tāla*, *kharjūra*, *harītakī*, and *bibhītaka*.
He saw various mountains bound together by hundreds of diverse minerals, groves resounding with flocks of birds, caves of wondrous appearance,
rivers, lakes, ponds, and various beasts and birds.
She beheld many piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas of terrifying form, as well as ponds, lakes, mountain peaks on all sides, rivers, and oceans— all of wonderful appearance.
There, the daughter of the lord of Vidarbha saw herds of buffaloes,
boars, jackals, bears, monkeys, and serpents;
she was endowed with supreme splendor, fame, steadfastness, and beauty.
Then Vaidarbhi wandered alone, searching for Nala,
like a doe strayed from the herd in that most terrifying forest;
yet that daughter of Bhima did not fear anyone there.
Having reached the dreadful forest, O King, the daughter of Vidarbha, emaciated by the calamity that had befallen her husband, lamented in great distress;
her body overwhelmed with grief for her lord, she sat down upon a rocky surface.
Damayantī said:
"O beloved, O auspicious one, O delight of kings, you ought to remember those words of mine that were spoken by you in my presence as something dear to me."
"O lion-chested one, O mighty-armed lord of the Niṣadhas,
O King, where indeed have you gone, having abandoned me here in this desolate forest?
O hero, [you who would perform] sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha with abundant sacrificial fees..."
"O tiger among men, having performed the sacrifice, why do you act falsely toward me?
O tiger among men, O one of great splendor, that which was spoken by you in my presence— O auspicious one, O bull among kings, you ought to make that true."
"O King, as was said by the swans, those birds of the air, in your presence and in my own,
you ought to consider what they have spoken:
'The four Vedas, with all their limbs and sub-limbs, in their full detail, [are on one side]...'"
O best of men, well-recited [Vedic study] and truth alone are indeed equal;
for when a thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale,
truth outweighed the thousand horse-sacrifices.
Therefore, O Śatrughna, O lord of men, you ought to make true that word which you spoke long ago in my presence, O hero:
"Alas, O hero! Am I not indeed your beloved, O sinless one?"
"In this terrible forest, why do you not answer me?
This fierce king of the forest, of dreadful form and gaping maw, is threatening me; overcome by hunger, why do you not deign to protect me?"
"O fortunate one, you once said to me, 'No other woman is dearer to me than you.
O King, O descendant of Bharata, make those words you spoke previously come true.
O lord of men, I am your beloved wife, now mad and lamenting."
"O Lord, desired by me, why do you not answer me who desires you? O Ruler of the Earth, [why do you ignore] me, who am emaciated, miserable, pale, and soiled,
clad in but half a garment, alone, and lamenting like one who has no protector?"
O large-eyed one, O crusher of enemies, you do not honor me as I weep— me who am worthy of honor, like a solitary doe strayed from the herd,
here all alone in this great forest, O Great King.
"O Great King, why do you not answer me as I speak to you, your own wife—
endowed with noble lineage and virtue, beautiful in all her limbs,
and devoted to you? Why do you not answer me?"
"O best of men, O lord of Niṣadha, I do not see you today on this mountain, nor in this most dreadful forest frequented by lions and tigers— whether you are lying down, sitting, or standing."
O best of men, whether you have departed or not, you increase my grief.
Afflicted by sorrow and emaciated by grief on your account, whom indeed shall I ask:
"Have you seen King Nala here in the forest, having encountered him?"
"Who indeed might tell me today of Nala, who dwells in this forest—
the handsome, high-souled destroyer of enemy armies— that king Nala with eyes like lotuses whom you seek?"
Whose sweet voice shall I hear today saying, "This is he"?
This glorious king of the forest, with four tusks and a massive jaw, approaches as a tiger; I shall question him without hesitation.
Wandering thus, she saw a tiger with massive jaws;
weeping, she said to him: "You alone are the lord here, O ruler of men!
You are the sovereign of beasts and the master of this forest."

"Know me as Damayantī, the daughter of the King of Vidarbha, the wife of Nala, the lord of Niṣadha and slayer of his enemies; I am here alone, piteous, and emaciated by grief, searching for my husband."
"O King of Beasts, comfort us here if you have seen Nala—
[that one] with the shoulders of a lion, the long arms, and eyes like lotus petals.
Or else, O Lord of the Forest, if you do not speak of Nala,"
"O best of deer, devour me and free this grieving woman of her sorrow!
Having heard my lamentation in the forest, this king of beasts himself goes toward this river of clear water that flows to the ocean."
This mountain, a heap of merit, shines with many lofty peaks that touch the heavens, beautiful in their various colors;
it is strewn with diverse minerals and adorned with manifold stones.
Rising high like a banner for this vast forest,
it was filled with lions, tigers, elephants, boars, bears, and deer,
and resounded on all sides with the cries of various birds.
It was adorned with *kiṃśuka*, *aśoka*, *bakula*, and *puṃnāga* trees;
it was beautified by *karṇikāra*, *dhava*, and *plakṣa* trees in full bloom;
and it was graced by rivers filled with birds and by mountain peaks.

"O Blessed One, O best of mountains, renowned for your divine appearance, I shall first ask this king of mountains— who stands like a crest-jewel upon the earth with its radiant form— concerning the monarch."
O refuge of many blessings, O upholder of the earth, let there be homage to you!
Having approached you, I bow down; know me to be a princess, the daughter-in-law of a king and the wife of a king, renowned by the name Damayantī.
The king, the lord of Vidarbha, my father, is a great chariot-warrior;
he is the ruler named Bhīma, the protector of the four social orders,
who has performed the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
That best of kings, with broad and beautiful curved eyes, will be a performer of sacrifices;
he will be devoted to the Brahmins, virtuous in conduct, truthful in speech, and free from malice;
possessed of good character and excellent behavior, he will be of vast fortune, a knower of dharma, and pure.
"The lord who is the rightful protector of Vidarbha, having conquered the hosts of his enemies— he,
O Blessed One, know me to be his daughter, come here to wait upon you.
In Niṣadha, my father-in-law is the best of kings, like a great mountain."
He was renowned by the auspicious name Vīrasena.
That king had a heroic son, illustrious and of true prowess,
who governed his own ancestral kingdom as it had been inherited from his father.
There was one named Nala, the subduer of enemies, renowned as Puṇyaśloka;
he was devoted to Brahmins, a knower of the Vedas, eloquent, a performer of meritorious deeds, a drinker of Soma, and a maintainer of the sacred fires.
He was a sacrificer, a giver, a warrior, and a truly righteous ruler.
Known as Puṇyaśloka, devoted to Brahman and the foremost knower of the Vedas— O best of mountains, know me to be his wife, come here now abandoned by my husband, protectorless, and beset by calamity.
"O best of mountains, while searching for that husband of mine, the most excellent of men,
have you perhaps seen King Nala in this dreadful forest, by these hundreds of peaks of yours that scrape the very sky?"
"Does the wise Nala, who has the stride of a lordly elephant, long-armed, impatient of insult,
valiant, truthful, steadfast, and highly illustrious—
the lord of the Niṣadhas— have perhaps been seen by you?"

O best of mountains, O lord of the earth, if you have seen anywhere that King Nala, my beloved, who is like a mountain in steadfastness— why do you not speak to me, who am alone, lamenting, and sorrowful?
O hero, O valiant one, O knower of dharma, O king true to his promise, why do you not today comfort her with your voice, as one would a distressed daughter? O King,
if it is possible, reveal yourself here in this forest by your own power.

"When indeed shall I hear that speech of the King of Niṣadha, smooth and deep, resembling the roar of a thundercloud, like nectar itself— those auspicious words addressed to the high-souled king as 'O daughter of Vidarbha'?"

"O King, lover of dharma, comfort me who am terrified— me, who follow the essence of the sacred tradition, who am prosperous, and who would destroy my grief. Having spoken thus to that best of mountains, the daughter of the king [wept].

Then Damayantī proceeded further toward the northern direction. Having traveled for three days and nights, that most excellent woman beheld an incomparable forest of ascetics, appearing like a celestial grove.
It was graced by ascetics equal to Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Atri— men who were self-restrained, moderate in diet, endowed with self-control and purity,
and who subsisted on water, air, or even leaves alone.

He beheld a delightful circle of hermitages inhabited by ascetics— highly fortunate sages who had conquered their senses, were clothed in bark and deerskins, possessed restrained faculties, and were longing to behold the path to heaven.
Upon seeing that hermitage, frequented by various deer and inhabited by troops of monkeys as well as ascetics— delighted by various herds of deer and joined by troops of monkeys— she beheld it.
Upon seeing that place frequented by ascetics, she was immediately comforted;
as soon as Damayantī beheld the hermitage, she regained her composure.
She, with beautiful brows, lovely hair, shapely hips, fine breasts, and a face with perfect teeth, [was thus restored].
Radiant, well-established in her grace, moving with a gracefully curved and uplifted gait—
that jewel among women, the highly fortunate and wise Damayantī, beloved of the son of Vīrasena, entered the hermitage grounds.
Then the daughter of Bhīma was comforted by those ascetics with whom she had met;
having saluted the elders in asceticism, she stood bowed low in humility. And she was addressed by all those ascetics, "Welcome to you."
Having performed the worship for her according to the rules, those whose wealth is asceticism said, "Please be seated; tell us, what may we do for you?
That wise woman then paid homage to the sages in accordance with the prescribed rites.
The woman of beautiful form said to them: "O sinless ones, is all well here with your venerable selves—your asceticism, your sacred fires, your duties, and your care for deer and birds;
and also, O you whose bodies are dharma, is all well with your Vedic studies, your yogic practices, and your religious observances?"
"Is it well with you, O highly fortunate ones, and in your practice of your own dharma?
They replied to that illustrious lady, "It is well, O blessed one, in every respect.
