"Speak then, O lady of faultless limbs—who are you, and what do you wish to do?"
"Upon seeing this supreme form and this highest splendor here, great wonder has arisen within us; take heart and do not grieve.
This is either a great deity of this forest or [the spirit] of the mountain."
"O auspicious and blameless one, tell us truly about this river.
She said to those sages, "I am not the deity of this forest,
nor am I the deity of this mountain, O brahmins, nor even the deity of this river."
"Know me to be human, all you whose wealth is asceticism. I shall relate my story in detail; listen to it all from me.
In Vidarbha, there was a king named Bhīma, possessed of great splendor."
"O best of the twice-born, know me all to be his daughter.
The wise lord of Niṣadha, named Nala, is my husband— he is a hero, a conqueror in battle, a learned man, and a ruler of the people, possessed of great fame."
Devoted to the worship of the gods, affectionate toward the twice-born, the protector of the Niṣadha lineage, highly fortunate and of great splendor,
truthful in speech, a knower of dharma, wise, true to his word, and a crusher of enemies.
Devoted to the Brahmins, dedicated to the gods, illustrious, and a conqueror of enemy cities— Nala by name, the best of kings, equal in splendor to the king of the gods,
my husband, large-eyed, with a face like the full moon, and a slayer of foes.
He was the performer of the principal sacrifices, one who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
a slayer of rivals in battle, and possessed a splendor equal to that of the sun and the moon.
Yet, he was [assailed] by certain men of lowest character— wicked and evil-minded— who were skilled in deceit.
Having been summoned by those skilled and deceitful men at dice, the protector of the earth, who was devoted to truth and righteousness, lost his kingdom and his wealth;
and having been exiled from the city, he entered into forest life.
Know me to be the wife of that bull among kings;
I am known as Damayantī, longing for the sight of my husband.
I have wandered through forests, mountains, lakes, and likewise rivers.
Searching everywhere for my husband Nala, who is skilled in battle, high-souled, and accomplished in the use of weapons, I wander here in sorrow through delightful ponds and forests.
"O venerable ones, has the king named Nala, the lord of the Niṣadhas, perhaps arrived at this meritorious grove of ascetics? It is for his sake,
O brahmins, that I have entered upon this most dreadful [state]."
If, within a few days and nights, I do not see King Nala in this terrifying and formidable forest inhabited by tigers and wild beasts,
I shall unite myself with the highest good by casting off this body.

The woman who lives on after her husband’s life has ended is the lowest of women; she is devoid of luster, like the moon in the daytime. What purpose, indeed, is there for my life without that bull among men?
"How shall I fare today, tormented by grief for my husband? To Damayantī,
the daughter of Bhīma, who was thus lamenting alone in the forest,
those truth-speaking ascetics then spoke.
"O auspicious and beautiful one, your future will be fortunate;
we see this through our ascetic power. Before long, you shall behold the Nishadhan, Nala, the lord of the Nishadhas and the slayer of his enemies."
"O daughter of Bhīma, you shall see that best of the upholders of dharma, freed from all feverish distress,
liberated from all sins, endowed with every jewel,
and ruling over that very same preeminent city as a subduer of his enemies."

"O auspicious lady, you shall see your husband, the king of noble lineage, who causes fear to his enemies and destroys the grief of his friends. Having spoken thus to Nala’s beloved queen, the daughter of the monarch, [the sage departed].
Then those ascetics, along with their sacred fires and hermitages, vanished;
seeing that great marvel,
Damayantī, whose limbs were faultless and who was the daughter-in-law of King Vīrasena, was filled with wonder.
The princess of Vidarbha reflected: "What is this that I have seen?
Was it a dream that I beheld? What manner of ordinance has occurred here?
Where indeed are all those ascetics, and where is that circle of hermitages?"
"Where is that delightful river of meritorious waters, frequented by various birds, and those charming mountains adorned with fruits and flowers?
Thus, O tiger among men, the lotus-eyed lady was filled with wonder.
Having meditated for a long time, Bhīma’s daughter Damayantī, who possessed a radiant smile,
became overcome with grief for her husband; distressed and with a pale countenance,
she then went to another place, speaking with a voice choked with tears.
Then, her eyes filled with tears, she lamented upon seeing the aśoka tree;
having approached that best of trees, the flowering aśoka,
which was lovely with its clusters of sprouts and resounded with the songs of birds.

"Oh, how wonderful! This illustrious traveler shines in this forest interior with his many ornaments, like the glorious King of the Draviḍas. Then the daughter of the lord of Vidarbha spoke to that Aśoka tree.

With palms joined in reverence, dejected and longing for the sight of her husband, Damayantī, having approached that great tree, spoke thus: "O Aśoka, dispel the grief of one whose mind is struck down by sorrow."
"Quickly make me bear your name, for through the sight of you, my beloved,
make me free from sorrow at once, O Aśoka of lovely appearance!
Have you perhaps seen the King, who is free from grief, fear, and affliction?"
You have seen my beloved, the subduer of enemies named Nala, the lord of the Niṣadhas and the husband of Damayantī; you saw him clad in half a single garment, his body and skin so delicate.
"O Aśoka tree, act in such a way that I may depart from this forest without sorrow, for this hero has come here afflicted by calamity. O Aśoka, become true to your name by destroying my grief."
Thus, having circumambulated that Ashoka tree three times in her distress,
the noble lady, the daughter of Bhima, proceeded to an even more dreadful region.
There she beheld many mountains as well as many rivers.
Then, searching for her husband, the daughter of Bhīma beheld many delightful mountains, various beasts and birds, as well as caves, mountain ridges, and rivers of wondrous appearance.
Having traveled a great distance, the sweetly smiling Damayantī then beheld a vast caravan, teeming with elephants, horses, and chariots, as it was crossing a lovely,
auspicious river of clear waters.
It was a vast lake of very cool water, surrounded by cane reeds; it resounded with the cries of cranes and kurara birds and was made melodic by the warbling of ruddy geese;
it was teeming with tortoises, crocodiles, and large fish, and adorned with sandy banks and islands.
As soon as she saw that great caravan, the illustrious wife of Nala approached it; that woman of beautiful limbs entered into the midst of the people,
appearing like one mad, afflicted by grief, and clad only in half a garment.
Emaciated, discolored, and soiled, with her hair covered in dust—
seeing her there, some men fled in fear;
some stood lost in thought, while others cried out aloud.
Some laughed at her, while others reviled her;
some felt compassion for her, O Bhārata, and even questioned her:
"Who are you? Whose are you, O auspicious lady? And what do you seek in the forest?"

"Seeing you here, we are distressed; are you perhaps a human? Tell us the truth: do you belong to this forest, to this mountain, or to the quarters of the sky? For you must be a goddess, O auspicious one, and we have come to you for refuge."
"Are you a Yakṣī, or a Rākṣasī, or perhaps a beautiful woman?
In every way, grant us well-being; protect us, O blameless one, so that this caravan may depart from here quickly and in safety."
"O auspicious lady, act accordingly; we have come to you for refuge.
Thus addressed by that caravan, the virtuous Damayantī, daughter of the king, who was grieving over the calamity that had befallen her husband, replied:
The caravan leader, the caravan itself, and whoever else is here— whether young men, elders, children, or those leading the caravan—
know me to be a human woman, the daughter of a lord of men.

"The king's daughter-in-law, the king's wife, longing for the sight of her husband— where indeed has that gambler gone, having cut away half of my garment, leaving me, the daughter of the King of Vidarbha, whose father is my father and whose husband is the King of Niṣadha?"

O beloved, having abandoned his devoted wife as she slept in the forest, you have fallen into adversity; yet noble women protect themselves by their own resolve, for they are born from the very essence of truth— of this there is no doubt.

Where indeed is that poor woman, afflicted by hunger and thirst and wandering in distress? Where does she stay, remembering that dull-witted man? I seek that illustrious and unconquered one named Nala.
"If you know the king, quickly tell me this pleasant news:
of Nala, that tiger among monarchs and slayer of enemy hosts. To her of faultless limbs, the leader of the great caravan spoke.
"O auspicious lady, listen to my words: I am a caravan leader named Śuci.
O lady of radiant smiles, I am indeed the leader of this caravan;
yet, O illustrious one, I do not see the man named Nala."
In this wretched forest, inhabited by non-humans, I see even elephants, leopards, buffaloes, tigers, bears, and deer; yet,
O mortal, apart from you, a human being, I see no one else in this great forest.
"Since we do not see King Nala here,
may Maṇibhadra, the king of the Yakṣas, be gracious to us today.
Then she spoke to all the merchants and to that caravan leader.
"Where indeed will you go? You ought to tell us this, for this is a caravan.
The caravan leader said:
"This caravan belongs to Subāhu, the truthful king of Cedi."
"O daughter of Manu, you shall soon go to the countryside for the sake of gain.
Bṛhadaśva said:
Having heard those words of the caravan leader, she of faultless limbs then—
Eager for a sight of her husband, she went along with him.
Then, after a long time had passed in that vast and dreadful forest,
she came upon a great lake, auspicious on all sides, filled with lotuses and fragrant water-lilies.
The merchants beheld that delightful place, abundant in fodder and fuel,
endowed with many roots and fruits, and filled with flocks of various birds;
seeing it, they found its pure waters to be enchanting and a source of comfort.
With their mounts utterly exhausted, they set their minds on resting;
with the consent of the caravan leader, they entered that excellent forest.
Having reached the western hour, the great caravan stayed there for the night.
Then, at the hour of midnight, when all was silent and still,
while the caravan— exhausted and asleep— was resting, a herd of elephants approached the mountain river,
which was turbid with the flow of their rut.
Then he saw that caravan and the very many elephants belonging to the caravan. Upon seeing those tame elephants,
all the wild elephants then rushed forward with speed, intoxicated with rut and desiring to kill them.
The force of those elephants as they charged was unbearable,
like mountain peaks shattered and falling to the earth;
even as the elephants quivered, their paths were lost amidst the forest-born creatures.

Blocking the path, he suddenly crushed that excellent caravan as they slept upon the ground beside a lotus pond, writhing in agony; the merchants, letting out cries of "Alas! Alas!", sought for refuge.
Running toward the forest thickets, blinded by sleep due to great fear,
some men were killed by teeth, some by hands, and others by feet;
the ground was crowded with cattle, donkeys, camels, horses, and throngs of infantrymen.
Afflicted by fear, they fled, striking one another at that time; emitting terrible cries, they fell to the surface of the earth—
some becoming entangled in trees, others broken, and some falling upon uneven ground.
Thus, having been attacked by many such divine elephants,
the oxen were oppressed by their burdens and overwhelmed by hunger and thirst;
yet, once their burdens were laid down, they attained supreme joy.
Likewise, horses, elephants, donkeys, and young camels,
upon merely seeing that delightful lake, experienced supreme joy;
and immediately thereafter, merchants and travelers did the same here.

They took up residence in their respective dwellings, each according to what was appropriate and according to their rank. Having descended, they attended to those who were settled there, overseeing their conduct, their food, and even their living quarters.
They engaged in various conversations concerning buying and selling;
others praised the hardships of their path, which was beset by calamities,
as they remembered the enjoyments of home and the company of their kinsmen.
03.062.010 Sons, friends, and wives— all fell under the power of sleep;
03.062.011 exhausted by the carrying of burdens for many days, they desired to lie down and were deeply overcome by slumber.
With limbs stretched out, exhausted, they sat as if they were dead. Then, at the hour of midnight, while that caravan was asleep and weary in profound silence, a herd of elephants arrived.

Then he saw that caravan and many elephants belonging to the caravan, resembling mountains, turbid with streams of rutting ichor, blocking the path on the northern bank of the Padminī where they were fast asleep.
And seeing those wild elephants, all the forest elephants then rushed toward them with speed, intoxicated with rut and desiring to kill them;
the force of those attacking elephants was unbearable.
Like deer falling to the earth from the mountain peaks after being struck down,
and even as the elephants quivered, all the other elephants were brought to death in an instant by those young tuskers through their sudden onset.
And that caravan was also crushed, along with its women, children, and elephants;
there arose a tremendous clamor that struck fear into the three worlds,
as well as from the horses, elephants, camels, and donkeys being struck down.

Being trampled by forest elephants, they could not protect one another; they suddenly crushed those who were sleeping and struggling on the ground, while the members of the caravan, crying out "Alas! Alas!", sought refuge.
And many, blinded by sleep, ran headlong into thickets;
some were struck by elephants with their tusks, others with their trunks, and still others with their feet.
Many were killed along with their camels, as the area was crowded with masses of foot soldiers.
Then, fleeing in fear and striking one another, they fell to the surface of the earth uttering terrible cries; some,
clinging to trees, fell down with their limbs shattered upon the uneven ground.
Thus, that entire prosperous caravan company has been destroyed;
my brother is slain, my son is slain, and my companion is slain.
This terrible fire has broken out; save yourselves, run now!
"This heap of jewels has been scattered; why do you run away? Take them!"—thus [cried out].
Damayantī, her face like the moon, stood there with a terrified countenance, amidst the caravan that had been destroyed and the broken aloeswood and sandalwood.
The entire earth shone with those scattered about, like the sky with autumnal stars—
some fallen, some being felled, and others fleeing here and there,
terrified by the released cries and resounding with shouts of "Alas! (hāhākāra).
That forest indeed became terrifying on all sides;
it was like another great wilderness, resembling the dissolution of the world.
Yet, some caravans that were there managed to escape and fled.
They all spoke together: "Of what action is this the fruit?
Surely we did not honor the highly illustrious Maṇibhadra, nor indeed the glorious and powerful Lord Vaiśravaṇa, the sovereign of the Yakṣas."

Either this worship was performed by those who create obstacles for merchants, or else the omen of the birds has turned out contrary; this must certainly be so. Or perhaps the planets have become unfavorable—what else could have come to pass?
But others, dejected and deprived of their kinsmen and wealth, said:
"That woman who today entered the great caravan, appearing like one mad, with a distorted form and assuming a non-human appearance— "

This most dreadful illusion was previously fashioned by her—whether she be a Rākṣasī, a Piśācī, or a Yakṣī, she is exceedingly terrifying. All this evil belongs to her; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
If we see that wicked woman who destroys the caravan and inflicts manifold sufferings,
she must certainly be struck with clods of earth, dust, grass, wood, and fists—
she who brings such hardship to the caravan.
But Damayantī, having heard those most cruel words of theirs, was ashamed, terrified, and agitated; she fled toward the forest and lamented for herself,
fearing those wicked men.
Alas! How great and terrible is the Creator’s fury directed toward me!
I do not perceive any merit; of what karma is this the fruit?
Surely some great evil committed in another birth has fallen upon me.
I have now reached this final and bitter calamity:
the seizure of my husband’s kingdom, his defeat by his own kinsmen,
separation from my husband, and being torn away from my two children.
Nakedness, dwelling in the forest frequented by many beasts of prey— indeed,
that caravan which I unexpectedly encountered in the lonely, dense forest has also been utterly ruined by some stroke of fate.
Fearing great sin and likewise a more grievous calamity, she thought:
"Surely I am such a person; there is certainly no doubt about this.
But because of my own misfortunes, the caravan has surely been struck down."

Where shall I cast myself down? To whom in the forest shall I go for refuge? Through death alone might there be peace; to endure this miserable life is agony. Alas, my protector! Alas, Great King! Alas, my lord, master of my life!
"O giver of honor, do you not recognize me as I lament thus? Uttering many such and other words of lamentation, distressed by her tears,
she ran about through the depths of the dense forest.
Thus, that entire prosperous caravan company was destroyed;
there arose a tremendous clamor that struck fear into the three worlds:
"This terrible fire has broken out! Save yourselves! Run now!"
"This heap of jewels has been scattered; take it! Why do you run away? This wealth is common to all; my words are not false.
Speaking thus, they then fled in fear.
"I shall speak further; listen with focused minds, O timid ones. While that terrible destruction of people was thus proceeding, Damayantī awoke, her heart trembling with fear."
She beheld there a carnage that struck fear into all the world;
having seen that which she had never seen before, the young girl with lotus-like eyes stood up,
overwhelmed by terror, her face and breath constricted.
But those who were liberated there from the caravan, some of them unhurt, all spoke together: "Of what karma is this the fruit?
Surely we did not honor the highly illustrious Maṇibhadra."
Likewise, it is not that the glorious Lord Vaiśravaṇa, the sovereign of the Yakṣas,
has failed to perform worship for those who cause obstacles; nor is it that the fruit of these omens is certain to be contrary.
"The planets have not been unfavorable; what else could this be that has come upon us?
Others, however, spoke dejectedly, having been deprived of their kinsmen and wealth:
"That woman who was in the great caravan today indeed appeared like one mad."
Having entered with a deformed appearance and assuming a non-human form,
she previously fashioned this most dreadful illusion;
she is surely a terrifying Rākṣasī, or perhaps a Yakṣī, or a Piśācī.
All this evil belongs to her; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
If we were to see that wicked woman, who destroys caravans and inflicts manifold sufferings, we would strike her with clods of earth, dust, grass, wood, and our fists.
"We must certainly kill the sorceress (kṛtyakā) of this caravan!
Hearing those most cruel words of theirs, Damayantī—
ashamed, terrified, and agitated— fled toward the forest.
Fearing that sin, she lamented for herself:
"Alas! How great and terrible is the fury of Fate directed toward me! What wholesome deed does it not obstruct? Of what karma is this the fruit?"

I do not recall having committed even the slightest unwholesome deed toward anyone, whether by action, mind, or speech; of what karma, then, is this the fruit? Surely it is some great evil committed in another life that has now fallen upon me.
I have now reached this final and grievous calamity:
the seizure of my husband’s kingdom, defeat by my own kinsmen,
separation from my husband, and estrangement from my two children.
"Helplessness and dwelling in the forest frequented by many beasts of prey. Then,
when the following day arrived, the people who had survived the slaughter emerged from the forest thickets, lamenting the carnage that had been committed.
O lord of men, while her brother, father, son, and friend were being slaughtered in that caravan, Damayantī, of the pure smile,
was not destroyed there in the forest because she was accompanied by the brahmins.

There, the princess of Vidarbha grieved: "What evil deed have I committed, that even this ocean of people who had come to me in the lonely forest has been destroyed by a herd of elephants? It must be due to my own misfortune."
"Surely I must experience great suffering for a very long time; of this there is no doubt. One does not die before one's time has come—this is the instruction of the elders that I have heard.
That I have not been crushed today by a herd of elephants, though I am so distressed..."
For indeed, nothing that happens to men here exists which is not caused by destiny;
nor was any harm ever committed by me, even in my childhood,
whether by deed, thought, or word, such that this suffering has now come upon me.
I think that the world-protectors have assembled here for the sake of the *svayaṃvara*;
it was for the sake of Nala that I rejected those deities there.
Surely, it is by their power that I have met with this separation.
Bṛhadaśva said:
Having thus lamented these and other such sorrows, that beautiful woman,
the devoted wife Damayantī, then uttered those words of lamentation.
Then, together with the surviving Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas,
that tiger among kings departed, devoted to grief and sorrow;
having heard those words of the caravan leader at that time, she of faultless limbs [acted accordingly].
O tiger among kings, she went along with the great caravan like a streak of autumn lightning— afflicted by grief, longing for the sight of her husband,
and covered in dust, though she possessed a pure smile.
Proceeding through that vast forest without even realizing it,
she reached a beautiful lake at the time of the sun’s setting—
a lake of cool water, exceedingly expansive, pure, and many yojanas in extent.
It was completely covered with white water-lilies, resplendent with lotuses and blue lilies,
teeming with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and graced by ruddy geese;
it was adorned with delightful trees growing on its banks, beautified by fruits and flowers.
He shone like a king surrounded by excellent servants;
taking refuge there, that caravan arrived for the purpose of staying.
But the oxen, afflicted by their burdens and overcome by hunger and thirst, [rested].
Having laid down their burdens, they attained supreme happiness;
likewise, the horses, elephants, donkeys, and young camels,
upon merely seeing that lovely lake, experienced the highest relief.

Immediately thereafter, the merchants and travelers here likewise reached their own dwellings according to their respective needs and locations, as well as their established customs regarding food and lodging.
Having descended, they entered the marketplace where people were resting;
there they engaged in various conversations concerning buying and selling,
while others praised the hardships of the forest infested with wild beasts.
Remembering their domestic enjoyments and the company of their kinsmen,
as well as their sons, friends, and wives, they all fell under the power of sleep;
for they had been carrying loads for many days.
Exhausted, with their limbs fallen and deeply overcome by sleep, they sat with their bodies stretched out, weary and as if dead. Then, at the hour of midnight, a great herd of elephants arrived.
Thirsty, he came to that lake for its water;
then he saw that caravan and the many elephants born of the caravan.
Then all those wild elephants, seeing those domestic elephants, [beheld them].
Intoxicated with rut and desiring to kill, they charged forward with speed;
the force of those elephants as they rushed on was difficult to withstand,
like the peaks of mountains shattered and falling to the earth.
Even the elephants in their agitation were unable to withstand those born of the forest;
all the elephants were brought under the power of death in an instant, and that caravan, along with its women, children, and elephants, was utterly destroyed.
A truly great clamor arose, causing terror to the three worlds,
from the galloping horses, as well as the large camels and donkeys,
which were being trampled and crushed by the wild elephants that could not protect one another.
"My brother is slain! My son is slain! My master is slain!
Alas, this fire has broken out; save me, run now!
This heap of jewels is being scattered; seize them! Why do you run away?"
"This wealth is common property; my word is not false. Speaking thus, they flee from there out of fear, yet those who destroy wealth run back once again.
While that terrible destruction of people was thus proceeding,
Damayantī awoke with a mind terrified by fear;
she beheld that carnage which struck terror into all the world.
Having seen that which she had never seen before, the young girl with lotus-like eyes and a moon-like face stood there with a terrified mind,
amidst all the sandalwood and other trees that were shattered and broken.
Scattered about, the entire earth shone like an autumnal sky filled with parched clouds,
as they fell, were being felled, and had already fallen here and there; for that forest appeared terrifying on every side.
Terrified by the sound of cries of distress and resounding with shouts of "Alas!",
that place, crowded with living beings, shone like another great battlefield. Yet, some caravans there who had escaped remained unhurt.
They all spoke together: "Of what action is this the fruit?
Surely we did not honor the highly illustrious Maṇibhadra, nor the glorious lord of the Yakṣas, the powerful Vaiśravaṇa."
Either this worship was performed by those who create obstacles for the merchants,
or else the omen of the birds is certainly contrary;
or perhaps the planets have become adverse— what else could this be that has occurred?
But others, dejected and deprived of their kinsmen and wealth, said:
"That woman who today entered this great caravan, appearing like one insane, with a distorted form and assuming a non-human appearance— "
This most terrible illusion was previously fashioned by her;
she is surely a Rākṣasī, or a Yakṣī, or a terrifying Piśācī.
All this evil belongs to her; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
"If we see that wicked woman, the destroyer of the caravan who has committed many evil deeds,
we shall certainly strike her down with clods of earth, dust, grass, wood, and our fists; for she is the one who works harm against the caravan."
But Damayantī, having heard those most cruel words of theirs, became afraid, terrified, and agitated; she fled toward the forest and lamented for herself,
fearing that evil.

Alas! How great and terrible is the Creator’s fury directed toward me! Why does prosperity not attend me? Of what karma is this the fruit? I do not recall having committed even the slightest unwholesome act against anyone.
"By what action, thought, or word has this fruit of karma arisen? Surely some great evil committed in another life has now fallen upon me;
I have reached this final, miserable calamity."
The seizure of her husband’s kingdom and defeat by her own kinsmen;
separation from her husband and estrangement from her two sons;
nakedness and dwelling in the forest infested with many beasts of prey.
Even that caravan which I encountered by chance in this lonely, dense forest has surely been overcome by the decree of fate; and thus,
they suspect me of being wicked and likewise suspect me of their calamity.
"I am surely such a person; there is certainly no doubt about this.
Indeed, by my own misfortunes, the caravan has been struck down while I was still slow-witted.
Where in the forest shall I throw myself? To whom shall I go for refuge?"
Peace would come through death, rather than maintaining this miserable life.
Alas, my Lord! Alas, Great King! Alas, Master, Lord of my life!
Why do you not speak to me as I lament thus, O giver of honor?
Uttering many such lamentations, her voice faltering with tears,
she ran about through the lonely, dense forest.
Bṛhadaśva said:
Thus, tormented by suffering and emaciated by the calamity that had befallen her husband,
she traveled for a long time until she reached a great city in the evening— the city of Subāhu, the truthful king of Cedi.

She, whose every limb was beautiful, wrapped in half a garment and a rag, entered that excellent city— the lofty gateway of Subāhu. Pale, emaciated, dejected, with disheveled hair and unwashed, she [entered].
The city-dwellers saw her walking like one who was mad;
then, seeing her entering the city of the King of Cedi,
the young sons of the villagers followed after her out of curiosity.
Surrounded by them, she approached the vicinity of the royal palace. From her palace, the queen-mother saw her surrounded by people and said to her nurse: "Go and bring her here into my presence."
The fool is tormented by people, suffering and seeking refuge;
and as for the form I see, which illuminates my house—
she is like the goddess Śrī herself, long-eyed and disguised in the garb of a madwoman.
Having warded off those people and led her up to that most excellent palace floor,
she, filled with wonder, O King, asked Damayantī:
"Even though you are thus possessed by unhappiness, you still bear a most excellent form."
You shine like lightning among the clouds; tell me, who are you and to whom do you belong?
For your form is not human, even though it is devoid of ornaments; O you of divine splendor, you are unaided and yet you do not tremble before men.
Having heard those words of hers, the daughter of Bhīma spoke these words:
"Know me to be a human woman, devoted to my husband,
a *sairandhrī* of noble birth, a servant who dwells wherever she pleases."
My husband, who subsists on fruits and roots, finds his evening shelter wherever he may be;
he possesses innumerable virtues and is ever devoted to me. I, in turn, am always inseparable from that heroic husband, following him like a shadow.
By fate, he became excessively addicted to gambling;
defeated at the game of dice, he went alone into the forest.
[The king saw] that hero, clad in a single garment, like one who was mad and distraught.
Consoling my husband, I followed him into the forest.
O lady of excellent limbs, for some inscrutable reason, that one of immeasurable soul,
being afflicted with grief, abandoned everything and entered the great forest.
Then, seeing him distressed as he entered the forest,
that hero, on one occasion for some other reason while in the woods,
being overcome by hunger and deeply dejected, abandoned even that single [remaining] one.
Following him— clad in a single garment, naked, mad, and deprived of his senses—
I did not sleep at all through many nights.
Then, after a long period of time, he abandoned me somewhere while I was asleep.
Having cut away half of my garment, he abandoned me, though I was innocent. Seeking that husband of mine, burning with grief day and night,
I— failing to see my beloved who shines like the interior of a lotus— remain thus in my heart.
"I do not find my beloved, who resembles an immortal and is the lord of my life and wealth," said she of faultless limbs; having spoken thus to the queen-mother as well,
she stood there, her eyes filled with tears, trembling and deeply distressed.
To her, whose eyes were overflowing with tears and who was thus lamenting so much, the distressed mother of the king—herself even more distressed than Bhīma’s daughter—spoke:
"Dwell with me, O blessed one; my affection for you is great."
"O blessed lady, my men will search for your husband;
or perhaps he himself will come here, wandering from place to place.
While dwelling right here, O blessed lady, you shall find your husband."
Having heard the words of the king's mother, Damayantī spoke these words:
"O mother of a hero, I am willing to dwell with you on certain conditions:
I shall never eat the remnants of others' meals, nor shall I perform the washing of feet."
"I shall not converse with any other men under any circumstances. If anyone should solicit me, that man must be punished by you;
moreover, O dull-witted one, he shall be put to death by you more than once—this is the vow I have undertaken."
"If I may see the brahmins for the sake of searching for my husband—
if this can be done here, I shall dwell [with you] without doubt;
otherwise, the thought of dwelling anywhere does not occur to my heart."
With a joyful heart, the queen-mother said this to her:
"By good fortune, I shall fulfill all of this; such is your vow.
Having spoken thus to the daughter of Bhīma, O lord of the people, the queen-mother—
O Bhārata, she spoke thus to her daughter named Sunandā:
"Sunandā, recognize this Sairandhrī, who possesses celestial beauty;
let her be your companion, for she has reached your own age."
"Rejoice with her yourself, with a mind free from anxiety. Then,
exceedingly joyful, Sunandā returned home,
taking Damayantī with her and surrounded by her female companions.
Being thus honored there, Damayantī rejoiced;
well-provided with all her desires, she then dwelt there free from anxiety.
Then, O Indra among kings, Sunandā, her countenance radiant with joy, [spoke].
Then, accompanied by Sairandhrī, she went to her own dwelling;
thereafter, Damayantī lived happily with Sunandā,
provided with all her desires, yet longing for the sight of her husband.
O King, she lived together with the princess Sunandā,
that beautiful-eyed woman constantly thinking of the heroic Nala. O King, listen to me as I recount the wondrous life-story of Nala.
Bṛhadaśva said:
O lord of the people, having abandoned Damayantī,
King Nala saw a great forest fire burning in the dense jungle.

There, in the midst of the fire, he heard the voice of some being crying out repeatedly and loudly, "O Nala! O Puṇyaśloka, come to my aid! And Nala, saying "Do not fear," entered into the middle of that fire.
He beheld the king of serpents lying coiled in a circle.
Then that serpent, trembling and with palms joined in reverence, said to Nala:
"O King, O monarch, know me to be the serpent Karkoṭaka."
"I deceived a Brahman seer who was innocent and of great ascetic power;
O lord of men, he, overcome by anger, cursed me:
'Stay, like an immobile thing, for as long as Nala remains anywhere!'"
"For you shall lead me from here, and thus you will release me from the curse wrought by me.
I am unable to move even a single step from his curse;
I shall instruct you in what is for your welfare—you ought to save me."
"I shall be your friend; there is no serpent equal to me. I will also become light for you; take me quickly and go.
Having spoken thus, that lord of serpents became the size of a thumb.
Taking him, Nala proceeded toward a region free from forest fires;
having reached an open space cleared of the black-pathed fire,
the serpent Karkoṭaka spoke again to him as he was wishing to release the snake.
"O Nala, go counting some of your own steps;
there, O great king, I shall bestow upon you the highest welfare.
Then, as he began to count, he bit his tenth step.
As soon as he was bitten, that form vanished instantly.
Seeing himself thus transformed, Nala stood there in amazement;
then the lord of the earth beheld the serpent assuming its own true form.
Then the Naga Karkotaka, consoling Nala, said:
"I have made your form invisible so that people shall not recognize you.
[This concludes the section concerning the Naga Karkotaka, Damayanti, and Nala.]
The recitation of the royal seer Ṛtuparṇa destroys the Kali age.
Because of him, O Nala, you have been transformed by great suffering;
that poison of mine shall dwell within you as pain.
"O Great King, as long as he does not release you while his limbs are covered with poison, so long shall he dwell in suffering within you. By him,
O Lord of Men, you— who are sinless and undeserving— have been wronged."
Out of anger, you were displeased with him, yet protection has been granted to you by me.
O tiger among men, O lord of men, by my grace you shall have no fear from fanged beasts, nor from enemies, nor even from those who know the Veda.
"O King, you shall suffer no pain caused by poison,
and in battles, O Indra among kings, you shall always obtain victory.
Go from here, O King, saying, 'I am the charioteer Bāhuka.'"
"He shall go to the presence of Ṛtuparṇa, for he knows the skill of dice;
O Lord of Niṣadha, let him go this very day to the lovely city of Ayodhyā.
That king will surely give you the secret of the dice in exchange for the secret of horses."
Born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, he will be a glorious friend to you. When you become a knower of the senses, you shall then be united with the highest good;
you shall also be reunited with your wife, so do not set your mind on grief.
"O lord of men, I tell you this truth: regarding my kingdom, my two sons, and my own true form— if you should desire to see them,
then you must remember me and put on this garment."

"Covered by this garment, you shall regain your true form. Having spoken thus, he then gave him a pair of divine garments. O Kaurava, having thus instructed Nala and given him the clothes, [he departed].
Then, O King, the Naga king vanished right there.
Bṛhadaśva said:
When that Naga had disappeared, Nala, the son of Niṣadha, proceeded on his way.
On the tenth day, he entered the city of Ṛtuparṇa.
He presented himself before the king, saying, "I am Bāhuka;
there is no one on earth equal to me in the art of driving horses."
In times of financial difficulty and in matters requiring specialized skill, I am indeed to be consulted;
furthermore, I know the preparation of food better than others. Whatever crafts exist in this world, and whatever else is exceedingly difficult to perform—[I know them all].
"O Ṛtuparṇa, I shall strive to do all that; take me with you.
Having been addressed thus by Nala, O lord of the earth, King Ṛtuparṇa, looking at him with a very pleased mind, spoke.
Ṛtuparṇa said:
"Stay, Bāhuka; may it be well with you. You shall accomplish all this.
My mind is especially intent upon swift travel."
Therefore, apply that yoga by which my horses may become swift;
you shall be the superintendent of the horses, and your salary shall be ten thousand coins. Furthermore, these two, Vārṣṇeya and Jīvāla, shall attend upon you constantly.
"You shall enjoy yourself together with these two; indeed, dwell with me, O Bāhuka.
Bṛhadaśva said:
Having been addressed thus by him, Nala dwelt there, being honored.

In the city of Ṛtuparṇa, together with Vārṣṇeya and Jīvala, that king dwelt there constantly reflecting upon the princess of Vidarbha; every evening, he would always recite this single verse: [The verse follows: "O gambler, where is the gambler? Where has the gambler gone? Where does the gambler sleep? Where does he dwell?"
"Where indeed does that poor woman lie now, afflicted by hunger and thirst and exhausted? Remembering that dull-witted man, whom does she attend to this day?
To the king who was speaking thus in the night, Jīvaka replied:
"Why do you grieve for her constantly? I wish to hear it, Bāhuka.
O long-lived one, whose wife is she for whom you thus lament? To him, King Nala replied: "She belongs to a certain man of dull intellect."
There was a woman who was highly esteemed by him, and he was exceedingly devoted to her.
For some reason, that dull-witted man was separated from her; and being thus separated, the foolish-souled one wandered about, tormented by unhappiness.
Burning with grief, he wandered day and night without ceasing;
at night, remembering her, he would sing a single verse.
Wandering over the entire earth, he eventually reached a certain place.
One who is unworthy dwells there, remembering that suffering all the more;
yet that woman, though following that man into the forest even in the midst of hardship,
if she lives— which is difficult— she has been abandoned by him due to his meager merit.
She is alone, a young girl unacquainted with the paths and unsuited to such a state;
overcome by hunger and thirst, she will find it difficult to survive in this vast and dreadful forest, which is constantly infested by wild beasts.
"O worthy one, she was abandoned by that man of little merit and dull intellect"—
thus did the King of Niṣadha dwell in the palace of that king, living in concealment while remembering Damayantī.
Bṛhadaśva said:
When Nala had been deprived of his kingdom and, along with his wife, had fallen into servitude,
Bhīma dispatched brahmins with the desire to find Nala.
And Bhīma, having given them abundant wealth, commanded them:
"Search for Nala and my daughter Damayantī. When this task is accomplished and the Lord of Niṣadha is discovered," [he shall reward you].
"I shall give a thousand cows to whoever brings those two back to you;
I shall also grant an agrahāra, a village equal in size to a city,
as well as silver, gold, and likewise male and female slaves."
"If Damayantī and Nala cannot be brought here,
even upon merely learning of them, I shall give a thousand cows as a reward.
Having been told this, those brahmins departed joyfully in every direction.
Searching through cities and kingdoms for the Nishadhan together with his wife,
they did not see Nala or the daughter of Bhima anywhere at all. Then, in the lovely city of Chedi, there was a certain brahmin named Sudeva.
Searching about, he then saw the princess of Vidarbha in the royal palace— emaciated, pale, and soiled, wholly devoted to grief for her husband,
standing there together with Sunandā during the king’s recitation of the auspicious day.
With her incomparable form only faintly visible,
she was like the radiance of a fire enveloped by a mass of smoke;
beholding that large-eyed woman, who was exceedingly soiled and emaciated—
Inferring that she was the daughter of Bhīma by establishing it through various reasons,
Sudeva said:
"Just as this woman was seen by me previously, so too is her form now."
Today I have attained my purpose by beholding her who is like the Goddess Śrī, the beloved of the world—
she with a face like the full moon, dark-complexioned, with lovely rounded breasts,
a goddess who makes all directions bright and free from darkness with her radiance.
With eyes like the petals of a beautiful lotus, she was like Rati, the consort of the God of Love;
beloved by the entire world, she was like the radiance of the full moon. She appeared as if she had been drawn from the lake of Vidarbha by the stroke of fate.
Her limbs were smeared with the mire of dust like a lotus stalk;
she was like a full-moon night when the moon has been seized by Rāhu;
distressed by grief for her husband and miserable, she was like a river whose current has dried up.
With its lotus leaves scattered and its birds terrified,
it was like a lotus pond distressed by the trunks of elephants;
she was delicate, with well-formed limbs, and worthy of a jeweled inner chamber.
Like a lotus stalk recently uprooted being scorched by the heat, she was endowed with beauty, nobility, and virtue; though worthy of adornment, she remained unadorned,
like a new crescent moon in the sky shrouded by dark clouds.
Deprived of the enjoyments she desired and separated from her beloved kinsmen, she sustains this wretched body out of longing for a sight of her husband;
for indeed, a husband is a woman’s supreme ornament, even in the absence of all other ornaments.
Separated from him, she does not shine, even though she is naturally beautiful. Nala performs a truly difficult feat in that, though deprived of her,
he maintains his own body and does not perish from grief.
Seeing her— she with the dark ends of her hair, with eyes as long as a hundred-petaled lotus, who deserves happiness yet is now so distressed— even my mind is pained.
When indeed will this beautiful woman reach the further shore of her suffering?
Like the virtuous Rohiṇī from her reunion with the Moon,
the Nishadhan king will surely attain joy upon regaining her,
just as a king fallen from his kingdom rejoices upon recovering the earth.

The King of Niṣadha is worthy of the daughter of Vidarbha, who is endowed with virtues and age equal to his and joined with a family of equal lineage; and this dark-eyed woman is likewise worthy of him, that immeasurable one possessed of heroism and strength. It is fitting that she be united with him by me.
To console my wife, who longs for the sight of her husband— I shall now comfort her, whose face resembles the full moon,
who has never before experienced such sorrow, and who is now afflicted by grief and absorbed in meditation.
Bṛhadaśva said:
Having thus reflected upon her through various reasons and characteristics,
the brahmin Sudeva then approached the daughter of Bhīma and spoke to her.
"O princess of Vidarbha, I am Sudeva, your brother’s beloved friend. At the command of King Bhīma, I have come here to search for you.
Your father, O Queen, as well as your mother and your brothers, are all well."
The two long-lived ones are well there, as are your children;
however, King Bhīma, your mother, your brothers,
and your circle of kinsmen sit as if their life-force has departed because of you.
Seekers and Brahmins were wandering the earth by the hundreds;
but having recognized Sudeva, O Yudhiṣṭhira, Damayantī then questioned all her friends in turn.
And she wept bitterly, O King— the princess of Vidarbha, emaciated by grief—
upon suddenly seeing Sudeva, the beloved and most excellent of brahmins belonging to her brother.
Then Sunandā beheld her weeping and wasted by sorrow.
O Bhārata, while she was conversing in private with Sudeva, she sent word to her mother: "The Sairandhrī is weeping bitterly;
go and find out about her, if you think it right."
Then the mother of the lord of Cedi went from the king’s inner apartments to where that young woman was with the brahmin. O lord of people, having summoned Sudeva, the queen-mother—
His wife asked: "Whose daughter is this beautiful woman, and whose wife is she?
How did this lovely-eyed lady become separated from her kinsmen or her husband? And how was she discovered by you, O Brahmin, while she was in such a state?"
"I desire to know all this from you completely and without remainder;
tell it to me in truth, for I, who am of divine form, am asking.
Thus addressed by her, O King, Sudeva, the best of the twice-born—
Seated comfortably, he related the facts exactly as they were to Damayantī.
Sudeva said:
"The King of Vidarbha is the righteous-souled Bhīma, possessed of formidable prowess."
This is his beautiful daughter, renowned as Damayantī;
and the king named Nala, the son of Vīrasena, known as the Niṣadhan,
is her husband— this auspicious wife of that wise Puṇyaśloka.
"Defeated at dice by his brother and stripped of his kingdom, that lord of the earth went away with Damayantī; he has not been discovered anywhere.
Therefore, we are wandering this earth for the sake of Damayantī."
This young girl has been found in your son’s residence;
there is no human woman here who is her equal in beauty. Moreover, between her eyebrows, there is an excellent, natural mole.
He who was seen so many times before is no longer perceived by me, having vanished;
that one who resembled a lotus and was seen in Śyāmā has vanished from my sight,
for she is now covered by impurity, like the moon by a thin cloud.
This [body] was fashioned by the Creator as a mere sign for the sake of manifesting his glory;
it does not shine brightly, like the crescent of the moon obscured on the first day of the lunar fortnight,
yet its form does not lose its beauty even when its body is covered with impurities.
Even though it is unconditioned, it shines forth clearly like gold.
By this body and by this very mole,
I have recognized this lady, just as a hidden fire is revealed by its heat.
Bṛhadaśva said:
Having heard those words of Sudeva, O lord of the people,
Sunandā cleansed the impurity that concealed the mole.
With that blemish removed,
Damayantī then shone like the moon in a cloudless sky;
and seeing the blemish, O Bhārata, both Sunandā and the queen-mother were filled with wonder.
Weeping, they embraced her and stood for a moment;
then, shedding their tears, the king’s mother slowly spoke these words:
"By this mole, you are revealed as the daughter of my sister."
Both I and your mother, O beautiful one, were daughters of the high-souled Sudāman, the lord of Daśārṇa and a king of great spirit;
she was given to King Bhīma, while I was given to Vīrabāhu.

But you were seen by me when you were born in the city of Daśārṇa, in your father’s house. O beautiful lady, this place is just like your father’s house; for as is my sovereignty, so too is yours, O Damayantī.
O lord of the people, Damayantī, with a joyful heart,
having saluted her mother’s sister, spoke these words:
"Even though I am unrecognized, I have indeed lived here in happiness."
Provided with all desires and always protected by you, your dwelling will be from happiness to greater happiness; of this there is no doubt.
O mother, you ought to grant me leave, for I have been away from home for a long time.
For my two young sons have been taken there and are living there, bereft of their father and tormented by grief; how indeed will they fare without me?
If you wish to do anything at all that is pleasing to me here, [then act accordingly].

"I wish to go to Vidarbha; quickly provide me with a vehicle. Having said "So be it" to her, O King, the delighted maternal aunt, with the consent of her son, then provided her with a great force for protection.
Then,
O best of the Bharatas, the queen mother dispatched Damayantī, preceded by the brahmins, in a magnificent palanquin carried by men, provided with excellent food, drink, and clothing.
Then, before long, that auspicious woman arrived in Vidarbha;
and all her kinsmen, being overjoyed,
honored her upon seeing that all their relatives were well, as were those two children.
O lord of the people, the illustrious and auspicious Damayantī worshipped her mother and father, as well as all her circle of friends, the deities, and the brahmins,
according to the highest ritual injunctions.
The king, delighted merely upon seeing his daughter, gratified Sudeva with a thousand cows, a village, and wealth. Having spent that night there in her father’s house, the beautiful woman [set out].
Having rested, O King, she spoke these words to her mother.
Damayantī said:
"O mother, if you wish me to live, I tell you the truth."
"Indeed, she was intent on bringing back that hero among men, Nala.
Bṛhadaśva said:
"Thus addressed by Damayantī, that queen became deeply distressed."
O King, choked with tears, she did not utter a word in reply. Seeing her in such a state, the entire inner apartment then broke out into cries of "Alas! and wept most bitterly.
Then, O great king, Damayantī, your daughter, spoke these words to Bhīma while grieving for her husband: "O King,
casting aside her shame, she herself spoke thus to me."
"Let your servants strive to find Puṇyaśloka.
Thus urged by her, the king dispatched obedient Brahmins to all directions, saying: "Exert yourselves in the search for Nala."
Then, by the command of the lord of Vidarbha, those bulls among brahmins,
having seen Damayantī, said, "We are now departing. Thereupon,
the daughter of Bhīma spoke these words to them in all kingdoms:
In various assemblies of people, speak again and again:
"O dear gambler, where have you gone after cutting off half of my garment and abandoning me, your devoted beloved, as I slept in the forest?"
Just as she was instructed, she remains there waiting for you;
that young woman, though severely burning with grief, is covered only by half a garment.
O King, she weeps constantly because of that sorrow.
"O hero, show me favor and grant me a reply;
you must say this and more, so that you might show compassion toward me—
for it is the fire, fanned by the wind, that consumes the forest."
In that same way, the fire of grief constantly burns my heart. For a wife must always be supported and protected by her husband;
why then has both of these been lost to you, who are a knower of dharma?
"You were always renowned as wise, well-born, and compassionate;
yet you have now become devoid of compassion, I suspect, due to the exhaustion of my good fortune. O great archer, O bull among men, show mercy toward me!"
"Compassion is the supreme dharma; indeed, I have heard this from you alone.
If anyone should answer you who speak thus, that man must be known in every way—who he is and where he dwells."
O best of the twice-born, having heard your words, whatever reply that man may give, you must quickly take those words and report them to me,
so that he may not discover you while you are traveling under Bhīma’s command.
They must likewise return without weariness;
whether he be prosperous or even destitute,
or whether he be desirous of wealth, his intentions must be understood.

Thus addressed, O King, those brahmins departed in every direction to search for Nala, who was then in such a state of misfortune. They searched through cities, kingdoms, villages, cowherd settlements, and hermitages.

O King, though they searched for Nala, the twice-born ones did not find him. And all those brahmins, O lord of the people, repeated those words here and there exactly as they had been spoken by Damayantī.
Bṛhadaśva said: Then,
after a long time, a twice-born man named Parṇāda returned to the city and spoke these words to the daughter of Bhīma:
"O Damayantī, while searching for the King of Niṣadha day and night,
Bhāṅgasvari went to the city of Ayodhyā and presented himself there.
And in the presence of the great assembly, he was made to hear your message by me."
"O lady of excellent complexion, the highly fortunate Ṛtuparṇa [was told] exactly as I had said.
Having heard that, King Ṛtuparṇa did not say anything at all,
nor did any member of his retinue, even though I spoke to them repeatedly."
But when I had been dismissed by the king, a certain man spoke to me in private:
"There is a man of King Ṛtuparṇa named Bāhuka;
he is the charioteer of that lord of men, deformed and short-armed."
Skilled in swift travel and an expert in preparing delicious food,
he sighed deeply and wept again and again; after inquiring after my welfare, he then spoke these words.
Even when they encounter adversity, women of noble family protect themselves by their own virtue; being truthful, they have conquered heaven without a doubt,
for even when separated from their husbands, they never give way to anger.
Excellent women wear their very lives as the armor of their conduct.
Since she was abandoned by him while he was in a state of distress, deluded, and fallen from happiness,
she ought not to be angry for that reason.
A dark-complexioned woman ought not to be angry at one who, seeking a means of subsistence, has had his garment carried off by birds and is consumed by mental agonies—
seeing her husband reduced to such a state, whether she has been treated with honor or dishonor.
"Śyāmā ought not to be angry with one who has been deprived of his kingdom and stripped of his fortune.
Having heard those words of his, I have come here in haste;
having heard this, you must inform the king and act as you see fit.
O lord of the people, having heard this from Parṇāda, Damayantī, her eyes filled with tears,
approached her mother in private and said:
"This purpose of the Brahmin must not be in vain in any way whatsoever."
"O mother, this matter must not be made known to Bhīma by any means whatsoever.
In your presence, I shall instruct Sudeva, the best of the twice-born,
so that King Bhīma may not discover my intention."
If you wish to do what is pleasing to me, you must strive in such a way that Sudeva may quickly bring my kinsmen here;
by that very auspicious means, let Sudeva depart without delay.
"O mother, let us go from here to the city of Ayodhyā to bring back Nala,
the subduer of enemies, who is currently residing in the palace of Ṛtuparṇa;
and after he has rested, we shall then fetch Parṇāda, the best of the twice-born."
The beautiful lady, the princess of Vidarbha, honored him with abundant wealth;
having indeed worshipped him with great riches, she said to him:
"O Brahmin, when Nala has arrived here, I shall give you even more wealth."
"Indeed, you have done much for me, more than anyone else could;
for, O best of the twice-born, I shall soon be reunited with my husband.
Having been addressed thus, he honored her with most auspicious blessings.
Having accomplished his purpose, that high-minded man returned to his home.
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, having summoned that brahmin, Damayantī,
filled with pain and grief, spoke to him in the presence of her mother.
"O Sudeva, having gone to the city, speak these words to King Ṛtuparṇa, the ruler of Ayodhyā: 'Desiring another husband,
Damayantī, the daughter of Bhīma, will once again hold a svayaṃvara.'"
Kings and princes from all quarters are going there;
since the time has been calculated, it will take place tomorrow.
If you deem it appropriate, O subduer of enemies, go quickly.
"At sunrise, she will choose a second husband;
for it is not known whether that hero Nala is alive or even dead.
Having been told this by her, [the messenger] went and spoke thus to the king.
Then, O great king, the brahmin Sudeva spoke to Ṛtuparṇa.
Bṛhadaśva said:
Having heard the words of Sudeva, King Ṛtuparṇa—
Having summoned his charioteers, headed by Vārṣṇeya,
the king related to them what had occurred and what had been heard from the brahmin; and he also called Bāhuka and spoke of Damayantī’s svayaṃvara.
Consoling him with gentle words, he replied to Bāhuka:
"I wish to go to Vidarbha for Damayantī’s svayaṃvara;
O knower of the nature of horses, do you think it can be done in a single day, Bāhuka?"
When Nala had been addressed thus by that king, O son of Kuntī, his heart was rent with grief; and the high-minded one brooded deeply, thinking:
"Could it be that Damayantī, deluded by sorrow, has done this?"
"Could this great stratagem have been devised for our sake?
Alas, the wretched princess of Vidarbha wishes to commit a cruel act;
she has been deceived by me, a base, sinful, and undisciplined man."
"The nature of women in this world is fickle, and my own fault was grievous;
even so, she might have acted thus, helpless and her affection gone,
the slender-waisted woman being agitated by grief for me and driven by despair."
One should never act in such a manner, especially when one has offspring;
having gone there, I shall discover the truth and what is beneficial,
and I shall fulfill the desire of Ṛtuparṇa as well as my own purpose.
Having thus resolved in his mind, Bāhuka, with a dejected heart and palms joined in reverence, spoke these words to King Ṛtuparṇa:
"I promise you truly, O lord of men, that you shall go."
"O tiger among men, O King, [we shall reach] the city of Vidarbha in a single day.
Thus addressed, the king then laughed and said to Bāhuka:
"If it shall indeed be so tomorrow, what desire of yours shall I fulfill?"
Then, O King, Bāhuka, having entered the stable by the command of King Bhāṅgasvari, conducted an examination of the horses. Urged repeatedly by Ṛtuparṇa, Bāhuka [proceeded].
Desiring to examine horses and having deliberated upon them again and again,
he found those that were lean yet capable on the road,
endowed with energy and strength, and possessed of noble lineage and good character.
Devoid of [inauspicious] marks and lacking in deficiencies, with broad nostrils and large jaws, pure with the ten whorls, born in the Indus region, and possessing the speed of the wind—
though appearing lean in their limbs on the road, they were peerless in swiftness.
Seeing them, the king, filled with a touch of anger, said:
"What is this you seek to do? You are surely mocking us!
How can these horses of mine carry [you], when they possess such meager strength and vitality?"
"And how can such a long journey be traversed by horses like these?
Bāhuka replied, "These horses will go to Vidarbha; of this there is no doubt."
"Or if you think otherwise, O King, tell me which others I shall employ for you:
one on the forehead, two on the head, two each on the sides and the flanks,
two each on the chest, and one indeed at the point of departure."
Ṛtuparṇa said:
"O Bāhuka, you alone are a knower of the true nature of horses and you are skilled;
therefore, yoke quickly those which you consider capable."
Bṛhadaśva said:
Then that skilled man yoked to the chariot four excellent horses, endowed with noble lineage and good character, and possessed of great speed.
Then the king, filled with haste, mounted the yoked chariot;
thereupon those excellent horses knelt upon the ground with their knees.
Then, O lord of the people, the illustrious Nala, the best of men and a king, [proceeded].

He comforted those horses, which were endowed with energy and strength; then Nala, having raised them up by their reins, desired to depart, having mounted the charioteer Vārṣṇeya and exerted his utmost speed.
Driven by Bāhuka according to the prescribed method, those excellent horses seemed to leap into the sky, as if to bewilder the charioteer.
Seeing those horses thus carrying him with the speed of the wind, he was amazed.

The wise lord of Ayodhyā was filled with the utmost wonder upon hearing that sound of the chariot and that restraint of the horses; Vārṣṇeya reflected on Bāhuka’s expertise in the knowledge of horses.
"Could this be Mātali, the charioteer of the king of the gods?
For such great marks are seen upon the heroic Bāhuka.
Or could he be Śālihotra, the knower of the true nature of the breeds of horses?"
"Having assumed this most beautiful human form,
could this perhaps be King Nala, the conqueror of enemy cities?
This must surely be that monarch who has arrived," she reflected thus.

Or rather, whatever knowledge Nala knows, that very same [knowledge] Bāhuka possesses; for I perceive the learning of Bāhuka and Nala to be equal. Moreover, I consider his age to be the same as Nala’s.
"This is not Nala of great heroism; however, he must be someone possessing his knowledge [in disguise].
For high-souled beings wander this earth in concealment, joined by divine destiny and the physical deformations described in the scriptures."

"But there may be a difference in my mind regarding the deformity of my limbs; for it is my thought that I might be diminished in stature. My age and stature would be equal [to his], but there would be a reversal in appearance."
"In the end, I consider Bāhuka to be Nala, endowed with all virtues.
Having reflected thus repeatedly, O Great King, Vārṣṇeya, the charioteer of Puṇyaśloka, pondered deeply within his heart.
But King Ṛtuparṇa, O Indra among kings, rejoiced while reflecting upon Bāhuka’s knowledge of horses, together with his charioteer Vārṣṇeya; he marveled at his strength,
prowess, energy, and that skill in managing horses.
Beholding that supreme effort, he attained the highest joy.
Bṛhadaśva said:
He [traversed] the rivers, the mountains, the forests, and the lakes.
Moving like a bird gliding through the sky, he traversed the distance in no time at all.
As the chariot thus sped along, King Bhāṅgasvari,
the conqueror of enemy cities, then beheld his upper garment fallen behind.
Then, as the cloth fell, the high-minded king, acting with haste, said to Nala, "I shall seize it";
"O one of great intelligence, restrain these horses of great speed."
"O Vārṣṇeya, bring this cloth back to me," [the king said].
Then Nala replied to him, "Your cloth has fallen far away;
it has passed beyond a yojana, and it cannot be recovered by you again."
When Nala had spoken thus, O King, King Bhāṅgasvari then encountered a fruit-bearing *bibhītaka* tree in the forest.
Seeing it, the king addressed Bāhuka in haste:
"O Sūta, you too behold my supreme strength in calculation.
No one knows everything; there is no one who is omniscient. There is no single person in whom knowledge is ever fully perfected."
"O Bāhuka, all the leaves and fruits on this tree—
every single one of them belonging to this lord of the forest— have been counted by me;
and those that have fallen here amount to one hundred and one."
On one leaf there is more than one leaf, and on one fruit there is one arm;
on these two branches as well, there are ten thousand leaves,
and eighty thousand are indeed to be observed among the leaves and fruits.
"Furthermore, there are five crores of leaves on both branches.
You must pluck these two branches and whatever other smaller twigs there may be;
once the two branches have been stripped away, the others that were smaller twigs [will follow]."
"From these two [oxen], two thousand and one hundred less five fruits [have been obtained].
Then, leaping down from the chariot, Bāhuka said to the king:
'O King, O crusher of enemies, you boast as if in my absence.'"
"I shall make this evident by splitting open a *bibhītaka* fruit;
O King, then there will be no uncertainty for you regarding the calculation.
O Great King, I shall count the seeds of the *bibhītaka* right before your eyes."
Indeed, I do not know whether this will happen or not;
however, O lord of men, while you watch, I shall count its fruits.
Let the Vārṣṇeya hold the reins of the horses for just a moment.
The king said to the charioteer, "This is no time for delay.
Bāhuka, however, exerting the utmost effort, replied to him,
"Wait for a moment, or if you are in a hurry, sir, then depart yourself."
"This is the auspicious path; proceed with Vārṣṇeya as your charioteer," Ṛtuparṇa said to him, consoling him, O joy of the Kurus:
"You alone are the driver; there is no other on earth, Bāhuka."
"O expert in horses, for your sake I wish to go to Vidarbha;
I have come to you for refuge, so you ought not to create an obstacle.
And I shall fulfill your desire, whatever you shall tell me, O Bāhuka."
"If you will show me the sun once you have gone to Vidarbha today, then,
O Bāhuka, having counted this *bibhītaka* tree,
I shall go to Vidarbha; do as I say."
"As if unwillingly, the king said to him, 'Count it!
'O sinless one, a single portion of the branch was assigned by me;
O knower of the truth of horses, count that and thereby bring me joy.'"
Then, O King, Bāhuka, in great haste, proceeded to count even a single branch of that tree;
having quickly descended from the chariot, he began to strip that tree [of its fruit].
Then, filled with wonder, he said this to the king:
"Having counted them, the fruits were exactly as you described.
O King, I have witnessed this most marvelous power of yours."
"O King, I wish to hear that science by which this is known.
Then the king, who was eager to depart, said to him:
"Know me to be one who knows the heart of the dice and am skilled in calculation."
Then Bāhuka said to him, "Give this knowledge to me,
and you too, O bull among men, receive from me the secret of horses.
Thereupon King Ṛtuparṇa, because of the gravity of his business, [addressed] Bāhuka.
Out of greed for the knowledge of horses, he spoke these words: "So be it.
Take this supreme heart of dice as you desire.
O Bāhuka, let my deposit, the heart of horses, remain with you."
Having spoken thus, Ṛtuparṇa, that best of men, being pure and single-minded, bestowed the science upon Nala. As Kali emerged from the body of him who now knew the secret of the dice, [he departed].

Constantly vomiting the fierce poison of the Karkoṭaka snake from his mouth, the fire of that curse issued forth from him as he was thus afflicted. Emaciated by that, the king remained for a long time lacking self-control.
Kali rendered him deformed, lusterless, and afflicted;
then Kali, his soul freed from poison, assumed his own form.
Enraged, Nala, the lord of Niṣadha, desired to curse him.
Terrified and trembling, Kali spoke to him with palms joined in reverence:
"Restrain your anger, O King; I shall grant you supreme fame.
In the past, Indrasena’s mother, being enraged, cursed me."
But when I was abandoned by you,
O King of kings, I was then deeply afflicted; O unconquered one, I dwelt with you in great misery,
burning day and night with the poison of the king of serpents.
I have come to you for refuge; hear these words of mine:
those men in the world who shall praise you without weariness, for them there shall never be any fear born of me.
"O King, those men who shall proclaim [the story] of Nala will have no mental, physical,
or verbal suffering whatsoever, provided that you do not curse me for having come to you for refuge while afflicted by fear."
Thus addressed, King Nala restrained his anger.
Then Kali, filled with fear, quickly entered a *bibhītaka* tree.
Due to the taint of association with Kali, that *bibhītaka* tree became impure.
But Kali was not seen by anyone else as he conversed with the King of Niṣadha. Then, O King, the King of Niṣadha, the slayer of enemy heroes, was freed from his fever;
for when Kali had vanished, he counted the fruits of the dice.
Filled with supreme joy and endowed with great splendor,
that radiant one mounted his chariot and set forth with swift horses; meanwhile,
the *bibhītaka* tree became ill-omened due to its association with the Kali age.
From that time forth, O Indra among kings, O son of Pāṇḍu,
in this world Nala urged on those excellent horses again and again as they leaped like birds,
with a heart full of joy.
The high-minded king set out toward Vidarbha; and when Nala had departed, Kali also went home. Then, O lord of the earth, King Nala was freed from his fever.
"O King, he was liberated from Kali, though deprived of his physical form.
Bṛhadaśva said:
"Then, in the evening, [the king] reached Vidarbha, he whose valor is truth."
The people announced Ṛtuparṇa to King Bhīma. At Bhīma’s command, the king entered the city of Kuṇḍina,
making all ten directions resound with the noise of his chariot.
Then Nala’s horses heard that rattling sound of the chariot there;
hearing it, they rejoiced just as they had in the presence of Nala before.
And Damayantī also heard that sound of Nala’s chariot.
Just as at the arrival of the rainy season, when the clouds roar with a deep sound,
[the people] were struck with supreme wonder upon hearing that great noise,
just as in the past when Nala’s horses were controlled by Nala.
The daughter of Bhīma perceived the sound of the chariot as being exactly like that [of the gods], and so too did the horses;
even the peacocks on the palace roofs and the elephants in their stables,
as well as the horses there, heard the roar of the king’s chariot, O lord of the earth.
Hearing the roar of the chariot, O King, those elephants and peacocks raised their faces and trumpeted and shrieked, as if beholding the rising of a cloud.
Then Damayantī said:
"Just as that sound of the chariot seems to fill the earth, it gladdens my heart; this must be King Nala. If I do not see that Nala today, whose face has the luster of the moon—"
"O Hero, I shall undoubtedly perish before one of incalculable virtues,
unless today I enter the space between the arms of that hero, which are so pleasant to the touch; then I shall undoubtedly perish."
"If that Nishadhan, whose voice is like the roar of clouds and who shines with the luster of gold, does not come to me today, I shall undoubtedly perish. If he,
who possesses the prowess of a lion and the strength to restrain a rutting elephant..."
The lord of kings does not come; I shall undoubtedly perish.
I do not recall any falsehood, nor do I recall any harm done, nor any stale word from that great-souled one, even in moments of casual conversation.

The Lord of Niṣadha is powerful, patient, heroic, gentle, self-controlled, and has conquered his senses; yet in private he behaves like a coward toward those who are not lowly. As I remember his virtues, being devoted to him day and night, [I am tormented].
"My heart is breaking from this grief, separated as I am from my beloved.
Bṛhadaśva said:
"O Bhārata, thus lamenting, she was like one who had lost her senses."
He ascended the great palace out of a desire to see Puṇyaśloka. Then, in the middle courtyard, he beheld King Ṛtuparṇa seated upon his chariot together with Vārṣṇeya and Bāhuka.
Then the descendant of Vṛṣṇi and Bāhuka descended from that excellent chariot; having unyoked those horses, they both set the chariot down.
Then King Ṛtuparṇa descended from the seat of the chariot.
O great king, he approached Bhīma of terrible prowess;
then Bhīma received him with the highest honor.
Thus honored by that king, Ṛtuparṇa, the lord of men, [remained there].
While dwelling there in the delightful Kuṇḍina, that lord of the earth looked about repeatedly, yet he did not see anything at all. Then,
he met with the king, the lord of Vidarbha.
Having arrived suddenly and unexpectedly, he did not recognize the woman’s mantra.
O Bhārata, when asked by the king, "What is your business? Welcome to you!", that monarch did not realize that he had come for the sake of his daughter.
That wise King Ṛtuparṇa, whose prowess was truth,
did not see any king or prince at all;
there was neither mention of a *svayaṃvara* nor any gathering of brahmins.
"And there is no other undertaking for me regarding the ritual of a self-choice marriage (svayaṃvara).
Then, reflecting thus in his mind, the King, the lord of Kosala, said to him while saluting him: "I have come."
King Bhīma, too, smiling, reflected within his mind:
"The reason for his coming must be more than a hundred *yojanas* away;
having bypassed other kings, he has arrived here as one who offers his salutations."
Having passed through many villages, he did not find out the matter as it truly was;
for the purpose of his arrival had been designated as a minor task.
Later, in the future, I shall know whatever the cause may be.
"This is not so," said the king; having honored him, he dismissed him, saying again and again, "Rest, for you are weary.
Thus honored by the pleased monarch, he was delighted in spirit and joyful.
Followed by the king’s messengers, he entered the assigned dwelling. O King,
once King Ṛtuparṇa had departed together with the prince of the Vṛṣṇis,
Bāhuka mounted the chariot and went to the chariot-shed.
Having released those horses and tended to them according to the scriptures,
and having himself comforted them, he sat down on the floor of the chariot.
But Damayantī, afflicted with grief, saw King Bhāṅgasvari.
The daughter of Vidarbha thought of the Sūta’s son, the Vārṣṇeya, and likewise Bāhuka: "Whose is this sound of a chariot?
It is as great as Nala's, yet I do not see the King of Niṣadha."
Surely that very science must have been learned by the descendant of Vṛṣṇi;
therefore, the roar of his chariot was as great as that of Nala.
Or perhaps even Ṛtuparṇa is just like King Nala.

"Then this sound of a chariot is perceived as being like that of the King of Niṣadha. Having reflected thus, O lord of the people, Damayantī dispatched a messenger to search for the King of Niṣadha, O monarch.
Damayantī said:
"Go, Keśinī, and find out who this chariot-driver is,
sitting upon the seat of the chariot, deformed and with short arms."
"O auspicious one, having approached him with a composed mind and gentle words, you should ask this man about his welfare according to the truth, O blameless lady.
For I have a great doubt in this matter: could this be King Nala?"
"Thus my mind is satisfied and my heart is at peace. At the conclusion of your conversation, you should speak these words of Parṇāda to him,
and you, O lady of beautiful hips, blameless one, must understand his reply."
Bṛhadaśva said:
Having departed thus with a composed mind, the messenger spoke to Bāhuka;
meanwhile, the auspicious Damayantī, remaining on the palace terrace, watched him.
Keśinī said:
"Welcome to you, O lord of men; I declare that all is well with you.
O bull among men, listen carefully to the words of Damayantī."
"When did you set out, and for what purpose have you come here?
Tell that according to the facts, for the princess of Vidarbha wishes to hear it.
Bāhuka replied:
"O beautiful lady, the illustrious King Kausalya has heard that the second *svayaṃvara* of Damayantī will indeed take place tomorrow.
Having heard this, the king has set out with horses capable of traveling a hundred *yojanas*."
"With horses as swift as the wind and preeminent, I shall be his charioteer.
Keśinī said:
"Now, who is this third one among you; from where does he come, and to whom does he belong?"
"And whose [son] are you, and how was this task assigned to you?
Bāhuka replied:
"I am indeed the charioteer of Puṇyaśloka, known by the name Vārṣṇeya."
O blessed lady, when Nala had fled, I approached Bhāṅgasvari;
for I am skilled with horses and well-versed in the art of cooking,
and I was personally chosen by Ṛtuparṇa for the roles of charioteer and cook.
Keśinī said:
"O Vārṣṇeya, does he know where King Nala has gone?
Perhaps something might have been told to you by him, O Bāhuka."
Bāhuka said:
"Having left Nala’s two sons right here with that man of evil deeds, he departed from there as he pleased; he does not know the prince of Niṣadha."
"O illustrious lady, there is no other man who knows Nala;
the lord of the earth wanders in this world in disguise, his true form concealed. For only Nala himself knows him, as does she who is closest to him."
"Indeed, those signs never indicate Nala.
Keśinī said:
"That brahmin who first went to Ayodhyā at that time—"
Repeatedly uttering these words of a woman:
"O gambler, where have you gone after cutting off half my garment,
O dear one, leaving behind your devoted beloved sleeping in the forest?"
"O King, she remains there exactly as instructed, waiting for you,
burning day and night while covered only by half a garment.
Because of that suffering, O ruler of the earth, she weeps incessantly."
"O hero, show her favor and grant her a reply;
O high-minded one, relate that pleasant narrative to her,
for the blameless daughter of Vidarbha desires to hear those very words."
"Having heard this reply given by you in the past, the princess of Vidarbha now wishes to hear it once more from you. Bṛhadaśva said:
O descendant of Kuru, when Nala had been addressed thus by Keśinī,
his heart was distressed and his eyes filled with tears. Restraining his own grief, the lord of the earth burned with anguish.
With a voice choked with tears, he spoke these words once more:
"Even when fallen into adversity, women of noble family protect themselves by their own resolve; they are truthful and have won heaven for themselves—of this there is no doubt."
Even when deprived of their husbands, virtuous women never become angry; clad in the armor of good conduct, they sustain their lives in this world.
