Thus it was for her who, seeking the means of subsistence, had her garments carried away by birds.
A young woman ought not to be angry with one who is being consumed by mental agonies—
seeing her husband thus transformed, fallen from his kingdom, deprived of fortune, hungry, and overwhelmed by calamity, whether she has been treated with honor or dishonor.
O Bhārata, as Nala spoke these words in extreme distress, he was unable to restrain his tears and wept aloud. Then Keśinī went and informed Damayantī.
"All that has been told, as well as his transformation," Bṛhadaśva said:
"But Damayantī, having heard that, was utterly overcome by grief."
Suspecting him to be Nala, she said this to Keśinī:
"Go again, Keśinī, and perform further tests on Bāhuka;
standing near him, observe his conduct as he speaks."
And whenever he should do anything there, O beautiful lady,
you must observe his movements as he exerts himself;
nor, O beautiful lady, should even fire be given to him by way of obstruction.
"Water must not be given when one begs for it; rather, it should be given properly and without haste.
Having considered all this, report my conduct to him, as well as whatever signs—whether divine or human—you observed regarding Bāhuka."
"And whatever else you may see, that too must be told by you to me. Having been addressed thus by Damayantī, Keśinī then departed quickly;
and having observed the signs of one skilled in horses, she returned once more.
She reported all that had occurred exactly as it happened to Damayantī,
including the divine and human signs that had been observed regarding Bāhuka at that time.
Keśinī said:
"O Damayantī, never before have I seen or even heard of a human being such as this, who is so firm and pure in his conduct. Even when he encounters a low passage, he never bends down."
But upon seeing him, it would expand according to his desire and move about at ease;
even in a narrow space, a very great opening would arise for him.
And for the sake of Ṛtuparṇa, there was food of many kinds.
And a great quantity of animal meat was sent there by the king;
for the purpose of washing it, a water-jar was prepared there,
and when he looked into that jar, it was already full.
Then, having washed [the vessel] and placed it upon the fire, Bāhuka took a handful of grass, blew into it, and set it alight; thereupon the bearer of oblations suddenly burst into flames.
Having seen that most wonderful thing, I have come here in amazement.
Moreover, O auspicious lady, another great marvel was observed by me:
even when touching fire, he is not burned at all.
By his will, the water flowed swiftly toward him, drawn in as if by attraction;
moreover, I beheld another great marvel:
that he took flowers in his hands and crushed them gently.
Then, those flowers, being pressed by his hands,
became even more fragrant and bristled with life;
having seen these wonders beyond imagination, I have come here in haste.
"O large-eyed one, [observe] the gestures of Bāhuka in my presence.
Bṛhadaśva said:
But Damayantī, having heard of those actions of the Puṇyaśloka, [reflected].
She thought that Nala had arrived, indicated by his actions and movements.
Suspecting that her husband was Nala in the form of Bāhuka,
she, weeping, spoke again to Keśinī in gentle words.
"Go again, O beautiful woman, and taking the cooked meat from the kitchen prepared for the negligent Bāhuka, bring it here.
She went and, while Bāhuka was busy, took that meat away.
O descendant of Kuru, Keśinī, acting for her mistress's benefit, immediately gave that very hot food to Damayantī; she had previously tasted much of the meat prepared by Nala.
Having eaten and realizing it was Nala the cook, she cried out in extreme distress. Then, falling into a state of great desolation and washing her face,
O Bhārata, she sent the couple away along with Keśinī.
Recognizing Indrasenā along with her brother, Bāhuka then ran toward them;
the king embraced her and took her onto his lap. Bāhuka, however, approached his two sons, who resembled the children of the gods.
His soul overwhelmed by intense grief, the King of Niṣadha wept aloud; having repeatedly displayed such agitation,
he suddenly cast aside his two sons and spoke thus to Keśinī:
"O blessed lady, this pair is so very similar to my two sons;
upon seeing it, I suddenly shed tears.
People might suspect you of wrongdoing because of your frequent visits here."
"We are but guests in this land; go, O blessed lady, may you be safe.
Bṛhadaśva said:
"But having observed all the transformations of the wise Puṇyaśloka,"
Having arrived quickly, Keśinī announced [the news] to Damayantī. Then Damayantī, afflicted by grief and eager with the hope of finding Nala, sent Keśinī once more into the presence of her mother.
"I have examined Bāhuka many times with the suspicion that he is Nala;
however, I have one doubt regarding his appearance, which I wish to know for myself.
O mother, either let him enter, or you should grant me permission."
"Whether it be known or unknown to my father, let it be arranged.
Thus addressed by the princess of Vidarbha, that queen spoke to Bhīma;
and the king gave his consent to that intention of his daughter.
O bull of the Bharatas, having been permitted by both her father and mother,
she ushered Nala into the place where her quarters were located.
Upon suddenly seeing Damayantī, King Nala—
Overcome by grief and suffering, he became bathed in tears. Seeing Nala thus afflicted at that time, Damayantī,
that woman of excellent complexion, was seized by intense sorrow.
Then, O great king, Damayantī— clad in saffron robes, her hair matted, and covered in dust and mire— spoke these words to Bāhuka:
"O Bāhuka, have you ever before seen anyone named Dharmajña?"

What man, other than Nala of virtuous fame, would depart after abandoning his innocent and beloved wife in the lonely forest— she who was exhausted and bewildered by fatigue? Having left behind that woman sleeping in the wilderness, who else but Nala would go away?
What offense have I committed against that lord of the earth,
that he has abandoned me while I was overcome by sleep in the forest and departed? He who previously chose me, setting aside even the gods themselves in person.
How could you abandon her who was devoted to you, full of longing, and blessed with a son— her hand taken by fire in marriage, remaining faithful to the words of the swans,
and to whom you had pledged the truth, "I shall support you"? Where has that promise gone?
O subduer of enemies, as Damayantī was speaking all this,
a great amount of sorrow-born water flowed painfully from her eyes—
that water which issued from those eyes with their black pupils and red corners.
Seeing the overflowing water, Nala, afflicted with grief, said this:
"O timid one, that my kingdom was lost was not something I did myself;
that was done by Kali, as was the fact that I abandoned you."

O best among the upholders of dharma, in former times you were struck by a curse while dwelling in the forest, distressed and grieving for me as I was naked. That Kali resided within my body, burning there due to your curse.

"O beautiful one, by my truth, he has been burnt by the poison of Karkoṭaka; scorched by your curse, he remains constantly as if placed within a fire. He has been utterly conquered by my resolve and my ascetic power."
"O auspicious one, we must indeed reach the end of our suffering through this.
That wicked man has departed after releasing me; therefore, I have come here, overwhelmed by grief and sorrow, drenched in streams of tears."
"O lady of broad hips, it is for your sake; indeed, I have no other purpose.
How could a woman ever abandon a husband who is devoted and faithful to her, and choose another, as you have done, O timid one?"
By the king's command, messengers roam the entire earth, saying:
"The daughter of Bhīma will indeed choose a second husband according to her own will and as she desires, as if he were suited to herself."
Upon hearing this, Bhāṅgasvari quickly approached and said:
"How can a wife abandon her husband and live in seclusion?
But Damayantī, having heard that lamentation of Nala’s, [remained silent].
With palms joined in reverence, trembling and afraid, she spoke these words:
"In the palace of King Bhīma, may Vaidarbhī and Nala dwell together, seeking each other's happiness with joyful resolve."
Damayantī said:
"O auspicious one, you ought not to suspect me of sin;
for, O Lord of Niṣadha, it was I who, having rejected the gods, chose you."
"O King, for the sake of seeking you out, Brāhmaṇas have gone everywhere through the ten directions, singing my words in verses. Then,
O monarch, a learned Brāhmaṇa named Parṇāda [found you]."

He went to the city of Kosala, to the residence of Ṛtuparṇa. When that speech was properly delivered by him and the reply was likewise received, this means for bringing you back from Niṣadha was seen by me.

"O lord of the earth, O ruler of men, there is indeed no one else in this world besides you who is capable of traveling a hundred yojanas in a single day by means of horses. And so, O protector of the earth, I revere these two feet of yours."
"As long as I do not perform even in my mind any act that is unrighteous, this wind,
the witness of all beings and the ever-moving one, wanders through this world;
let him take away my life-breaths if I have committed any sin."
The sun of piercing rays always moves beyond the world;
may he take away my life-breaths if I commit any sin.
The moon moves within all beings like a witness.
"May he take away my life-breaths if I have committed any sin.
These three gods indeed sustain the entire triple world;
let them speak according to the truth today and let them abandon me."
When this had been said, the Wind then spoke from the atmosphere:
"O Nala, she has committed no sin; I tell you the truth.
O King, Damayantī’s abundant treasure of virtue is well-guarded."
"We have been her witnesses and guardians for three full years;
moreover, she has devised this incomparable stratagem for your sake.
For there is no other man here who could travel a hundred [leagues] in a single day except you."
"O lord of the earth, Bhaimī has been won by you, and you have been won by Bhaimī;
you should entertain no doubt in this matter—unite with your wife.
While Vāyu was speaking thus, a rain of flowers fell from the sky.
The celestial drums resounded and an auspicious breeze blew.
Having witnessed that most wonderful sight, O Bhārata, King Nala,
the subduer of enemies, then dispelled that doubt regarding Damayantī.
Then the lord of the earth put on that dustless garment;
remembering the king of the nāgas, he regained his own body. Seeing her husband then in his true form, the daughter of Bhīma—
Embracing Puṇyaśloka, the blameless woman cried out loudly;
King Nala, shining as he had before,
likewise embraced the daughter of Bhīma and greeted his two children with due affection.
Then, placing his face upon her own breast, she of the beautiful countenance,
overcome by that grief, sighed deeply with her long eyes;
likewise, she of the pure smile, embracing him whose limbs were smeared with dirt, [remained there].

O King, for a very long time she stood there, bathed in tears, before that tiger among men. Then, O monarch, the mother of the princess of Vidarbha affectionately related to Bhīma everything exactly as it had happened between Damayantī and Nala.

Then the great king said, "I shall see Nala tomorrow morning, once he has performed his purificatory rites and has rested comfortably together with Damayantī. Then the two of them spent the night together, recounting their past history.
O King, they dwelt there joyfully for four years, wandering through the entire forest; then,
in the fourth year, having reunited with his wife and having successfully accomplished all his desires, he attained supreme delight.
Damayantī, too, having recovered her husband, was greatly refreshed,
like the earth with its crops half-grown when it receives water. Having thus been reunited with him, her exhaustion was dispelled.
With her fever of longing stilled and her spirit heightened by joy,
the daughter of Bhīma shone like a night that has attained its desire when the cool-rayed moon has risen.
Bṛhadaśva said: Then,
having passed that night, King Nala, well-adorned and accompanied by the princess of Vidarbha, beheld the lord of the earth at the proper time.
Then Nala, with a disciplined mind, paid homage to his father-in-law;
thereafter, the beautiful Damayantī also bowed down to her father.
Bhīma received him with the utmost joy, as if he were his own son.
Having honored them as was fitting, the lord consoled Damayantī, the devoted wife, who was there together with Nala;
the ruler of the earth favored her with great hospitality.
King Nala, having accepted that hospitality according to the prescribed rites,
duly informed him of his own service rendered.
Then, there arose in the city a very great sound of joy.
Seeing Nala returned in such a manner, the people were filled with joy; they adorned the city with garlands of flags and banners,
and at that time, the royal highways were sprinkled, swept clean, and made rich with flowers.
At every gate of the citizens, flower-garlands were arranged,
and all the temples of the deities were honored with worship.
Then Ṛtuparṇa heard that Nala was there, disguised as Bāhuka.
The lord of men rejoiced at being reunited with Damayantī.
Having summoned him, King Nala asked that monarch for forgiveness;
and he, esteemed for his wisdom, forgave him by means of reasoned arguments.
Honored by the protector of the earth, who was filled with wonder,
that knower of truth and best among speakers addressed these words to the prince of Niṣadha:
"By good fortune, you have been reunited with your own wives," he said, thus congratulating him.
"O Nala, O Lord of Niṣadha, have I perhaps committed some offense against you while you were living in my house in concealment? Whether these acts were done intentionally or unintentionally,"
"You ought to forgive those improper acts committed by me.
Nala said:
"O King, you have not committed even the slightest offense against me."
"Even though this has been done, I feel no anger; indeed, I must forgive you.
For you were formerly my friend and my kinsman, O lord of men. From now on, however, you ought to bring even greater joy to me."
From this point forward, however, you ought to forgive me with even greater affection. Fully provided for all my desires, I have lived happily under your care;
O King, I have always been more comfortable in your house than in my own.
"And this very knowledge of horses belonging to you now resides within me;
O King, if you so desire, I wish to impart it to you.
Bṛhadaśva said:
Having spoken thus, the king of Niṣadha gave the science to Ṛtuparṇa,
and he accepted it according to the prescribed ritual.
Then, having received the heart of horses, King Bhāṅgasvari—
O lord of men, having given the secret of the dice to the sovereign of Niṣadha,
the king took another charioteer and indeed returned to his own city.
Once Ṛtuparṇa had departed, King Nala remained there, O lord of the people.
He dwelt in the city of Kuṇḍina for what seemed no very long time.
Bṛhadaśva said:
O son of Kuntī, having stayed there for a month, that prince of Niṣadha took leave of Bhīma.
With a small retinue, he departed from the city toward the Niṣadhas,
traveling in a single splendid chariot accompanied by sixteen elephants,
fifty horses, and six hundred foot soldiers.
Making the earth tremble as it were, the high-minded lord of the earth, acting with haste and extreme agitation, entered with great speed. Then Nala, the son of Vīrasena, having reached Puṣkara—
He said, "Let us play again; I have acquired much wealth, as has Damayantī, and whatever other property I have amassed.
This indeed is my stake; but your stake, Puṣkara, is the kingdom."
"Let the game of dice proceed once more; this is my firm resolve. May you be blessed; let us stake our very lives against one another.
Having won, I shall take back the other's property, whether it be the kingdom or wealth."
A counter-stake must be offered, for it is said that the highest prize is wealth.
If you do not desire that [ordinary] game of dice, let the game of battle proceed;
O King, let there be peace through a duel between chariots, whether for you or for me.
"This kingdom is to be enjoyed by our lineage;
it must be sought back by whatever means possible, even by any [other] method—such is the instruction of the elders.
O Puṣkara, let your mind be made up today for one of these two courses."
"Whether at dice or in battle, let the bow be bent by deceit or by force.
Thus addressed by the King of Niṣadha, Puṣkara, as if laughing and considering his own victory certain, replied to the lord of the earth.
"By good fortune, O Nala, you have acquired wealth for the counter-stake;
by good fortune, the evil deed of Damayantī has come to an end;
and by good fortune, O King, slayer of enemies, you remain alive together with your wife."
"Moreover, O best of men, it is by good fortune that your mind is set upon gambling;
for with this wealth won, the daughter of Vidarbha, adorned in her finery,
will clearly wait upon me like an Apsaras waiting upon Śakra in heaven."
"O Nala, I have indeed been constantly remembering you and waiting for you;
my pleasure in gambling with those who are not my friends has ceased. Yet today, having won this faultless woman of noble form, Damayantī—"
"I shall have fulfilled my purpose, for she has always dwelt in my heart.
Having heard those words of his, which were largely incoherent ravings,
the enraged Nala desired to cut off his head with his sword.
Smiling, yet with eyes copper-red with rage, the king then said to him:
"What stake do you propose? You shall speak only after you have won.
Thereupon, the gambling match between Puṣkara and Nala began.
With a single throw of the hand— blessings be upon you— that Nala defeated him,
having staked even his life along with his entire collection of jewels and treasures.
And having conquered Puṣkara, the king spoke these words while laughing:

"This entire kingdom of mine is undisturbed and its thorns have been removed. But you, O lowest of kings, are not even able to look upon the daughter of Vidarbha; for you and your followers, O fool, have fallen into her service."
"That deed by which I was formerly defeated was not done by you;
that deed was done by Kali, but you, O fool, do not perceive it.
I shall never, under any circumstances, attribute a fault committed by another to you."
"Live as you please; I relinquish my life-breaths to you. Likewise, I bestow upon you my entire store of provisions and my own share.
And likewise, O hero, my affection for you remains—of this there is no doubt."
"O Puṣkara, brotherly affection for you shall never leave me; you are indeed my brother—live for a hundred years! Having thus consoled his brother, Nala, whose prowess is truth, [departed].
Having embraced him again and again, he sent him back to his own city.
Thus consoled by the King of Niṣadha, O King, Puṣkara then saluted the illustrious Nala with joined palms and replied to him.
"May your fame be inexhaustible; live happily for ten thousand years, O King, you who have granted me my life and a dwelling place.
Thus honored by the king, that monarch then stayed there for a month.
O King, O bull among men, Puṣkara, filled with joy and surrounded by his kinsmen, set out for his own city with a vast army and well-disciplined attendants,
shining like the sun with his physical splendor.
Having dispatched Puṣkara, who was wealthy and in good health,
the illustrious king entered his city, which was exceedingly adorned. Having entered, the lord of Niṣadha comforted the citizens.

The citizens and the people of the countryside, their hair standing on end with joy, all spoke with palms joined in reverence, led by the ministers: "O King, today we have found peace, both in the city and in the countryside."
Having arrived once more to pay homage, like the gods approaching Śatakratu,
he then comforted all his ministers and the people of the realm; and he remained constantly attentive toward their welfare, like a father.
Bṛhadaśva said:
When the city was peaceful and joyful, and a great festival had commenced,
the king brought Damayantī back with a large army.
O bull of the Bharatas, having heard that the king of virtuous fame was established in his kingdom, King Bhīma was filled with supreme joy; then,
with a delighted heart, the king set out together with a vast army.

The slayer of enemy heroes, Bhīma of immeasurable soul and terrible prowess, honored Damayantī and sent her forth to the wise Puṇyaśloka. His daughter he dispatched as well, after having treated her with great respect.
When the princess of Vidarbha had arrived along with her sons, King Nala lived in joy, like the lord of the gods in the Nandana grove. Thus, he attained great renown among the kings in Jambūdvīpa.
Having recovered his kingdom, the highly illustrious one dwelt once more in his own realm;
he performed various sacrifices according to the prescribed rites, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Likewise, O Indra among kings, you too shall soon be reunited with your friends.
O bull of the Bharata race, O lord of the earth, Nala— the conqueror of enemy cities and best among men— has encountered such suffering through gambling along with his wife; yet,
O ruler of the world, he has endured this great hardship all alone.
Terrible suffering was endured, and yet prosperity was attained once more;
moreover, O Pāṇḍava, you, together with your brothers and Kṛṣṇā,
take delight in this great forest while constantly reflecting upon dharma alone.
O King, you are constantly attended by highly fortunate Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
[This occurred] when the secret of the dice was revealed to Akṣa in the presence of Ṛtuparṇa.
King Nala made his request, and Kali gave his promise;
the narration of the serpent Karkoṭaka, of Damayantī, of Nala,
and of the royal seer Ṛtuparṇa is the destroyer of Kali.
This history is also said to be the destroyer of the Kali age. O King, for that man who constantly recites this or hears it, there exists no fear whatsoever caused by the Kali age.

O Lord of the People, what can the Kali age do to a man who is constant in dharma, disciplined, ever devoted to honesty, self-controlled, and generous? Having heard this, one such as you is able to find consolation.
This very same [account] was proclaimed here by Vyāsa;
and O King, an unsurpassed boon was granted to the king by Kali when he had gained access to the secret of the dice in the presence of Ṛtuparṇa.
O Bhārata, this verse was recited by Nala for the destruction of Kali:
"Constantly reflecting upon the instability of human effort, find solace in both its gain and its loss; do not grieve."
O King, having heard this ancient history, you ought not to worry;
O Great King, you ought not to despair in the face of calamity.
When fate is unfavorable and human effort has become fruitless, the wise who rely upon their inner strength do not despond;
and those who shall recount this great life-story of Nala [shall likewise find no cause for despair].
They shall indeed hear this constantly, and misfortune shall not possess them;
wealth shall accrue to them, and they shall attain blessedness.
Having heard this ancient and eternally supreme history, one attains these benefits.
He shall obtain sons, grandsons, and cattle, as well as preeminence among men;
he will be free from disease and full of joy—of this there is no doubt.
As for the fear you perceive, it will cause him to summon me once again.

"O King, I shall destroy for you that reputation of being an 'expert in dice. O you of true prowess, I know the entire secret heart of the dice; it will be transmitted to me, of this there is no doubt."
"Be born [again], O Kaunteya; I am pleased and speak thus to you.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the king, with a joyful mind, spoke to Bṛhadaśva.
"O Blessed One, I wish to know the *akṣahṛdaya* (the secret of the dice) in its true essence.
When the son of Kuntī had spoken thus, the great sage Bṛhadaśva then imparted the *akṣahṛdaya* to the high-souled Pāṇḍava.
Having heard this story concerning the life of Nala in such a manner, King Pāṇḍava became free from sorrow;
and having taken his leave of all the Pāṇḍavas, Bṛhadaśva departed.
Having given [the horse], the great ascetic went to the Aśvaśiras [tīrtha] to perform his ablutions.
When Bṛhadaśva had departed, he heard that Savyasācin Pārtha was engaged in fierce austerities, subsisting on air alone, O wise one.
To the Brahmins and ascetics gathering from here and there,
and to those assembled from the best of holy fords and mountains,
the mighty-armed Pārtha, firm in his vows, undertook a penance difficult to achieve.
"Never before has anyone else been seen who possesses such fierce asceticism as Dhanañjaya Pārtha— this ascetic of restrained vows,
a solitary sage, glorious like Dharma personified."
O King, having heard that [his brother] was suffering in the great forest, the Pāṇḍava Kaunteya grieved for his beloved brother Jaya;
with a burning heart, he sought refuge in the great forest.

Yudhiṣṭhira questioned the Brāhmaṇas of various learnings; having received the secret of the dice, O King, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, became joyful in mind while joined by Bhīmasena and the others.
Seeing his brothers gathered together but not seeing Arjuna there, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, became overwhelmed with tears;
and burning with grief, the son of Kuntī spoke to Bhīmasena.
O Bhīma, when indeed shall I see Pārtha, your younger brother, here? For it is on my account that the best of the Kurus performs such difficult penance;
when, then, shall I reveal to him the secret knowledge of the dice?
"O Lord, having heard that the secret of the dice has been acquired by me,
that tiger among men will undoubtedly be filled with joy.
Janamejaya said:
03,079.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
03,079.002 Regarding the greatness of the sacred fords (tīrtha) as described by Pulastya, once, during a pilgrimage to those holy sites, the venerable sage Nārada— 03,079.003 [arrived].
While wandering among the sacred fords (*tīrtha*), he arrived there at Yudhiṣṭhira. Having bowed down with humility, Yudhiṣṭhira questioned him.
Nārada said:
03,079.001*0368_05 The meritorious enumeration of the sacred fords (tīrtha) was [given] to the high-souled Nārada.
03,079.001*0368_06 "I shall relate that to you; listen, O best among the upholders of dharma."
"O Blessed One, when my great-grandfather, the son of Pṛthā, had departed from Kāmyaka,
what did the Pāṇḍavas do without that Savyasācin? For he, the great archer and conqueror of armies, was their refuge."
Just as Viṣṇu is among the Ādityas, so does he appear to me;
and Śaṅkara is likewise among the Rudras,
as is Mahendra among the thirty gods.
"How did those heroic grandfathers fare in the forest, deprived of him who was equal to Indra in prowess and never retreated in battles?
Vaiśampāyana said:
But when Savyasācin, the son of Pāṇḍu, had departed from Kāmyaka, O dear one,
those Kauravas became devoted to grief and sorrow;
they were like jewels whose strings have been snapped, or like birds whose wings have been clipped.
Then all the Pāṇḍavas became dejected in mind,
and that forest, deprived of him whose deeds were untiring,
became like the Caitraratha grove when it is bereft of Kubera.
Without that tiger among men, O Janamejaya, the Pāṇḍavas then dwelt in the Kāmyaka forest, failing to find any joy;
those great car-warriors, exerting their prowess for the sake of the Brāhmaṇas, remained there with their pure arrows.
Slaying various kinds of sacrificial deer, O best of the Bharatas,
those tigers among men and subduers of enemies constantly gathered forest food and,
having collected it, offered it to the Brahmins.
Thus those bulls among men dwelt there, filled with longing;
all of them were dejected in mind, O King, now that Dhanañjaya had departed.
Then the princess of Pañcāla [thought of] her middle husband, the hero who had been away from home.

Remembering the best of the Pāṇḍavas, she spoke these words: "Without that best of the Pāṇḍavas— who was equal to Arjuna himself, though possessing only two arms compared to his many-armed counterpart— the forest does not appeal to me."
"O Lord of the Earth, without him whose splendor is equal to that of Śakra, I see this earth as if it were empty here and there; and yet,
this forest with its blossoming trees is full of great wonders."
Without that Savyasācin,
who resembles a dark blue cloud and possesses the prowess of an elephant in rut—
that lotus-eyed one— this Kāmyaka forest does not please me as it once did.
"O King, whenever the sound of his bow was heard, sounding like a thunderclap, I found no peace while remembering that Savyasācin. Hearing her thus lamenting, the slayer of enemy heroes— "
O great king, Bhīmasena said this to Draupadī:
"O blessed lady of slender waist, what you say so pleasing to the mind gladdens my heart like the tasting of nectar."

His two arms were long, symmetrical, and muscular, resembling iron clubs; they were rounded, marked by calluses from the bowstring, and capable of wielding swords, weapons, and maces; adorned with golden neck-ornaments and bracelets, they were like five-headed serpents.
Without that tiger among men, this forest is as if its sun has vanished;
for relying upon that mighty-armed one, the Pāñcālas and the Kurus do not fear even the armies of the gods when they are prepared for battle.

"Relying upon the arms of that high-souled one, we all considered our enemies already conquered in battle and the earth already won. Without that hero Phalguna, I find no peace of mind in the Kāmyaka forest."
"I see this earth as if it were empty here and there,
and I see all the directions as if shrouded in darkness.
Then Nakula, the son of Pāṇḍu, spoke with a throat choked with tears.
Nakula said: "He who,
having gone to the northern quarter and conquered hundreds of mighty Gandharva chiefs in battle, obtained horses— that son of Vāsava."
On the field of battle, they recount his divine deeds; O King,
what pleasure can there be in the forest without him, that best of warriors, whose celestial horses,
variegated like partridges and swift as the wind, were once his?
Out of affection, he gave it to his brother during the great Rājasūya sacrifice. Without that one of terrible bow, the younger brother of Bhīma—
who is like an immortal— now I have no desire to dwell in the Kāmyaka forest.
Sahadeva said:
"He who, having conquered great chariot-warriors in battle, formerly brought wealth and maidens to the king at the great Rājasūya sacrifice."
He of immeasurable splendor, who alone, having defeated the assembled Yādavas in battle with the approval of Vāsudeva, carried off Subhadrā; and by whom,
having seized half the kingdom from the high-souled Drupada—
O Bhārata, the teacher’s fee was paid to the preceptor Droṇa; yet, O great king,
seeing Jiṣṇu’s seat empty in his dwelling,
my heart never finds peace.
"O subduer of enemies, I desire to depart from this forest;
for without that hero, this forest is no longer delightful to us.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Eager for Dhanañjaya, those illustrious great car-warriors, the Pāṇḍavas, dwelt in that forest together with Draupadī. While the brothers, along with Kṛṣṇā, were thus longing for Dhanañjaya...
Having heard these words, even Dharmarāja became despondent.
Then he beheld there the high-souled celestial sage Nārada,
blazing with Brahmanic splendor and possessing a radiance equal to a kindled fire.
Seeing that he had arrived, the King of Dharma, together with his brothers,
rose up and paid homage according to the prescribed rites to that great-souled one.
Surrounded by those brothers, the illustrious best of the Kurus shone with splendor.
Possessing exceedingly radiant splendor, he shone like Śatakratu among the gods.
And just as Sāvitrī did not abandon the Vedas, so the virtuous Yājñasenī,
in accordance with dharma, did not forsake the Pārthas, just as the radiance of the sun does not leave Mount Meru.
Having brought water for honor and water for the feet, he paid homage to the Imperishable One;
Nārada, of great splendor, then addressed him, saying, "May it be well with you. Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, having beheld that best of celestial sages—

The joy of the Kurus honored him according to his merit and in accordance with the prescribed rites. Having accepted that worship, the venerable seer Nārada comforted the son of Dharma in a manner that was most appropriate, O sinless one.

And he spoke to the high-souled Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira: "Speak, O best among the upholders of dharma; what is your purpose? What may I give to you? Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, together with his brothers, bowed down.
With palms joined in reverence, he addressed these words to Nārada, who was equal to a god:
"O illustrious one, honored by all the worlds, since you are pleased with me,
O observer of noble vows, I consider my purpose already accomplished through your grace."
"O sinless one, if I, together with my brothers, am worthy of your favor,
you ought, O best of sages, to sever the doubt residing in my heart:
for what merit does he gain who, devoted to sacred fords, circumambulates the earth?"
"O Brahmin, you ought to tell me in its entirety what the fruit of that is.
Nārada said:
"Listen attentively, O King, descendant of Bharata, to how it was [explained] by Bhīṣma."
All this was indeed heard from the presence of Pulastya:
formerly, on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, Bhīṣma, the best among the upholders of dharma,
dwelt like a sage, having undertaken his ancestral vow.
O great king, in that auspicious and holy place frequented by celestial rishis,
at Gaṅgādvāra— a site served by gods and gandharvas—
the one of supreme luster and great splendor offered libations to the ancestors and the gods.
And he gratified the sages with rites prescribed by rule. Then, after some time, while engaged in silent recitation,
that great ascetic beheld Pulastya, the best of sages, appearing like a marvel.
Seeing him of fierce asceticism, blazing as if with splendor,
he experienced incomparable joy and was filled with supreme wonder;
O Great King, descendant of Bharata, he honored him as he stood before him.
Bhīṣma, the best among the upholders of dharma,
having purified himself and composed his mind, took the *arghya* offering upon his head according to the prescribed rite and announced his name to that most excellent of Brahman-sages.
"I am Bhīṣma; may it be well with you. O observer of noble vows, I am your servant.
Merely by the sight of you, I have been liberated from all sins.
Having spoken thus, O great king, Bhīṣma, the best among the upholders of dharma, [fell silent].
Restraining his speech and joining his palms, Yudhiṣṭhira remained silent.
Seeing him thus disciplined and emaciated by the recitation of the Vedas according to his vows,
that great ascetic then spoke in a sweet voice.
The sage Pulastya, who knows the dharma, spoke these words with a delighted mind;
the muni became pleased in heart toward Bhīṣma, the best of the Kuru lineage.
Pulastya said:

"O knower of dharma, O illustrious one, I am entirely satisfied with this humility, self-restraint, and truthfulness of yours. O sinless one, such is your dharma, which is grounded in devotion to your father."
"Because of that, my son, you see me here, and I have great affection for you.
I am Bhīṣma, whose sight is never in vain; tell me, what may I do for you?
O sinless best of the Kurus, I shall grant you whatever you ask."
Bhīṣma said:
"O highly fortunate one, honored by all the worlds, since you are pleased,
I consider my purpose already accomplished, for I have beheld the Lord."

"O best among the upholders of dharma, if I am worthy of your favor, I shall speak of a doubt residing in my heart; you ought to explain it to me. O Blessed One, I have a certain doubt regarding dharma concerning sacred fords (tīrthas)."
"I wish to hear from you that explained in detail:
O sage of immeasurable prowess, what is the fruit for one who circumambulates the earth? Tell me that, O brahmin-sage, O you whose wealth is asceticism."
Pulastya said:
"Indeed, I shall declare to you that which is the ultimate refuge of the sages;
listen with a one-pointed mind, my dear son, to what the fruit is at the sacred fords."
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained,
and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and fame— he enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
One who has desisted from accepting gifts, who is contented, self-controlled, and pure— [enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords].
He who has turned away from egoism enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords; he who is free from guile, without worldly undertakings, moderate in diet, with senses conquered,
and liberated from all faults— he enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
O Indra among kings, he who is free from anger, truthful in character, firm in his vows,
and who treats all beings as himself, enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords (tīrtha).
The seers have proclaimed the sacrifices here in the Vedas according to their proper sequence.
And the fruit, according to its true nature, both here and after death in every respect—
these sacrifices, O lord of the earth, cannot be attained by one who is poor;
for sacrifices require many implements and an extensive array of various materials.
These are attained by kings or by men who are prosperous in some way; they are not attained by those whose resources are insufficient for their aims, who are solitary, or who lack unity.
But that method which can be achieved even by the poor, O lord of men—
O best among warriors, understand that this merit is equal to the fruits of sacrifices;
O best of the Bharatas, this supreme secret of the seers is that visiting sacred fords (tīrthas) is more meritorious even than sacrifices.
Without fasting for three nights and without visiting sacred fords,
and without giving gold and cows, one is born poor by name.
Having performed sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees, [one attains prosperity].
One does not obtain that fruit by visiting other sacred fords which one obtains in the world of men by entering the ford of the God of gods, renowned throughout the three worlds,
known by the name Puṣkara— therein a man of great fortune should enter.
O lord of the earth, O joy of the Kurus, ten thousand crores of sacred fords (tīrthas) are present at Puṣkara during the three junctions of the day;
there dwell the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts.
O Lord, Gandharvas and Apsarases are always present there,
where the gods, Daityas, and Brahmarṣis likewise performed austerities;
having practiced many specific types of penance, those of great power attained those stations.
O Great King, those endowed with divine yoga and great merit,
even for a wise person who merely desires them in their mind, all sins are purified by the Puṣkara lakes, and such a person is honored in the vault of heaven.
O highly fortunate one, at that sacred ford (tīrtha), the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) always dwelt with supreme delight, honored by both gods and dānavas.
O highly fortunate one, at Puṣkara, the gods, preceded by the sages, [performed their rites].

Endowed with great merit, they have fully attained spiritual perfection (*siddhi*). The wise declare that for one who performs an ablution there, devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, it is ten times the merit of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
Even if one dwelling in the Puṣkara forest feeds but a single Brahmin,
by that deed, O Bhīṣma, he rejoices both in this world and after death. Or, even if he sustains himself only on vegetables, roots, and fruits;
A man of faith, free from malice, should indeed give that to a Brāhmaṇa;
by that alone, a wise man obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
Moreover, he should cause the Brāhmaṇas to pronounce blessings even with a vessel of water.
"O best of kings, they say that even by such worship, one becomes fit for infinity after death;
whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, these do not go to a degraded womb once they have bathed in the sacred ford of the Great-Souled One."

O bull of the Bharata race, for one who especially visits Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika, his merit increases there inexhaustibly. Furthermore, he who remembers the Puṣkaras morning and evening with palms joined in reverence—
O Bhārata, by that [act] one would have bathed in all sacred fords;
and a man would attain the imperishable worlds in the abode of Brahmā.
Whatever sin has been committed since birth, whether by a woman or a man—
By merely bathing at Puṣkara, everything [sinful] is utterly destroyed.
Just as Madhusūdana is the primordial source of all the gods,
even so, O King, Puṣkara is said to be the foremost of all sacred fords (tīrthas).

Having dwelt for twelve years at Puṣkara, self-restrained and pure, one obtains the merit of all sacrifices and goes to the world of Brahmā. But he who maintains the *agnihotra* sacrifice for a full hundred years—
Or if one should dwell for a single Kārttikī [full moon] at Puṣkara, that is exactly equal [to the former]. There are three white peaks and three springs;
these Puṣkaras were perfected from the beginning, and we do not know the reason for that.
It is difficult to go to Puṣkara; it is difficult to perform penance at Puṣkara;
it is difficult to give gifts at Puṣkara, and to dwell there is indeed very difficult.
Having stayed for twelve nights, self-restrained and restricted in diet, [one attains great merit].
Turning clockwise, one should enter Jambūmārga.
Having entered Jambūmārga, which is frequented by gods, sages, and ancestors,
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.

Having stayed there for five nights, a man who is capable of eating only at every sixth meal-time does not fall into an evil state, but attains the highest perfection. Returning from Jambūmārga, one should go to the hermitage of Taṇḍulikāśrama.
One does not fall into an evil rebirth and is honored in the heavenly world.
Having reached the lake of Agastya and being devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods,
O King, one who fasts for three nights obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Subsisting on vegetables or even fruits, one attains the station of Kumāra upon reaching Kaṇva’s hermitage, which is graced by prosperity and honored by the world;
for that, O bull of the Bharatas, is the ancient and meritorious Dharmāraṇya.
Merely upon entering it, one is indeed liberated from all sins;
having worshipped the ancestors and the gods, self-restrained and restricted in diet,
one enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice that fulfills all desires.
Then, having performed a circumambulation, one should go to Yayātipatana;
there, indeed, one obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
From there, one should go to Mahākāla, self-restrained and restricted in diet.
Having touched the waters at Koṭitīrtha, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
From there, O knower of dharma, one should go to the holy place of Umāpati,
known by the name Bhadravaṭa, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having approached Īśāna there, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
and by the grace of Mahādeva,
O best of men, one attains the status of a Gaṇapati, prosperous, without rivals, and endowed with glory.
Having gone there, one shall indeed attain sovereignty over kings;
then, having reached the Narmadā river, renowned throughout the three worlds,
and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Having reached the southern Sindhu, a student of sacred knowledge who has conquered his senses attains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and ascends a celestial chariot.
Having reached the Carmaṇvatī, self-restrained and restricted in diet, he likewise attains merit.
Permitted by Rantideva, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
From there, O knower of dharma, one should go to Arbuda, the son of Himavat,
where, O Yudhiṣṭhira, there was formerly a fissure in the earth.
There lies the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, renowned throughout the three worlds;
by staying there for a single night, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Having touched the waters at Piṅgatīrtha while practicing celibacy and having subdued the senses, one gains great merit.
O tiger among men, one enjoys the fruit of a hundred *kapilā* cows;
from there, one should go to that sacred ford (*tīrtha*) frequented by the gods. Having bathed there, a man shines like the stainless moon.
Then, O knower of dharma, one should go to Prabhāsa, world-renowned,
a sacred ford (tīrtha) worshipped by hosts of gods and frequented by sages,
where the Fire-god himself is eternally present.
O hero, Agni, whose charioteer is Anila, is the mouth of the gods. Having bathed in that most excellent tirtha, pure and with a restrained mind,
a human being obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices.
Then, having gone to the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean,
one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows and is glorified in the heavenly world,
O bull of the Bharatas, shining eternally with splendor like fire.
Having bathed there, O Indra among kings, one who possesses a radiance equal to the stainless sun and has stayed for three nights should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
he shines like the moon and obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice.

Then, O best of the Bharatas, one should go to the sacred ford (tīrtha) called Varadāna, where Viṣṇu was granted a boon by Durvāsas, O Yudhiṣṭhira. Having bathed at Varadāna, a man obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Then, self-restrained and restricted in diet, one should go to Dvāravatī.
Having bathed at Piṇḍāraka, a man may obtain much gold. O highly fortunate one, in that sacred ford there are those marked with the signs of lotuses.
Even today, O subduer of enemies, those seals are seen; that is a marvel. O joy of the Kurus, lotuses marked with tridents are seen there;
O bull of the Bharatas, the presence of Mahādeva is right there.
O Bhārata, having reached the confluence of the Sāgara and the Sindhu,
and having bathed with a restrained mind at that sacred ford of the Lord of Waters,
one should offer libations to the ancestors, the gods, and the sages, O bull of the Bharatas.
He attains the world of Varuṇa, shining with his own splendor.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the wise declare that by worshipping the god Śaṅkukarṇeśvara, one obtains ten times the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having circumambulated it clockwise, O bull of the Bharatas,
one should proceed to the tīrtha renowned throughout the three worlds, O best of the Kurus,
which is famous by the name Dṛmī and grants liberation from all sins.
Where Brahmā and the other gods worship Maheśvara,
having bathed there and worshipped Rudra who is surrounded by hosts of deities,
a man casts off all sins committed since birth.

O best of men, there is also Dṛmī, which is praised by all the gods; having bathed there, O tiger among men, one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice. It was there, O highly wise one, that Viṣṇu, the powerful Lord, achieved victory.
O King, having previously performed purification by slaying those who were thorns to the gods,
one should then proceed, O knower of dharma, to the celebrated Vasudhārā.
For by merely going there, one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice.
O best of the Kurus, a man who, having bathed with a restrained mind,
offers libations to the gods and the ancestors, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
And here, O bull of the Bharatas, is a supreme and most meritorious sacred ford belonging to the Vasus.
Having bathed and drunk there, one becomes esteemed by the Vasus. Known as Sindhūttama, it destroys all sins;
having bathed there, O best of men, one obtains much gold.
Having reached Brahmatunga, pure and with a restrained mind,
a man of virtuous deeds becomes free from passion and attains the world of Brahmā. There is also the shrine of Kumārikā belonging to Śakra, frequented by the Siddhas.
Having bathed there, a man would quickly attain the world of Śakra. And right there is the sacred ford (tīrtha) of Reṇukā, frequented by the gods;
having bathed there, a brahmin becomes as stainless as the moon.
Then, having gone to Pañcanada, self-restrained and restricted in diet,
one obtains the five sacrifices that have been enumerated in due order.
From there, O knower of dharma, one should go to the supreme station of Bhīmā.
O best of the Bharatas, having bathed there at Yoni, a man,
O King, shall become the son of a goddess, his body adorned with earrings of refined gold,
and he shall obtain the great merit of giving a hundred thousand cows.
Having reached Mount Muñja, renowned throughout the three worlds,
and having paid homage to the Grandfather (Brahmā), one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
From there, O knower of dharma, one should go to the supreme and pure holy site (tīrtha).
Even today, where golden and silver fish are seen,
O best of men, by bathing there one obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
with one's soul purified of all sins, one shall go to the supreme goal.
O Bhārata, having reached the Vitastā and satiated the ancestors and the gods, a man obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. Furthermore,
in Kaśmīra itself is the abode of the Nāga Takṣaka.
The place known as Vitastā is renowned for liberating one from all sins. From there, one should go to Maladā, which is famous throughout the three worlds;
having performed the ritual ablution according to the rules during the evening twilight, one should proceed.
O lord of men, one should offer a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) to the seven-flamed fire according to one's ability;
the wise declare that such a gift to the ancestors yields inexhaustible merit.
The seers, the ancestors, the gods, and the hosts of *gandharvas* and *apsarases* [are the recipients].
Guhyakas, kinnaras, yakṣas, siddhas, vidyādharas,
and men; rākṣasas, sons of Diti, Rudras, and Brahmā, O lord of men—
having undertaken the supreme initiation for a period of a thousand years, they remained self-restrained.
Pleasing Viṣṇu and likewise cooking the sacrificial oblation (*caru*),
he praised Keśava with seven *ṛc*-verses each;
and Keśava, being pleased, bestowed upon them the eightfold sovereign power (*aṣṭaguṇaiśvarya*).
O Lord of the Earth, having granted him other desired objects of enjoyment,
the god vanished right there like lightning among the clouds.
O Bhārata, because of that, it became famous in the worlds by the name Saptacaru.

"O Indra among kings, an oblation to the seven-flamed fire is superior to a hundred thousand cows, a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices, and a thousand Aśvamedha sacrifices. Having turned back from there, one should then enter Vastrapada."

Having approached Mahādeva, one obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha). Having reached Maṇimanta, O King, a self-controlled celibate student (brahmacārī) who has stayed for a single night obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Then, O Indra among kings, one should go to Devikā, world-renowned,
where, O bull of the Bharatas, the origin of the Brahmins is heard of;
and there is the station of the Trident-bearer, famous throughout the three worlds.
O bull of the Bharata race, having bathed in the Devikā and worshipped Maheśvara, and having offered *caru* there according to one's ability,
a man obtains the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled.
There is the holy ford (tīrtha) of Rudra called Kāmākhya, frequented by celestial rishis;
having bathed there, O Bhārata, a man quickly attains perfection. Having gone to Yajana and Yājana, as well as to Brahmavālukā, [one likewise attains success].
Having performed the ritual placement of flowers (*puṣpanyāsa*) and touched the water there, one shall no longer grieve over death.
They say that the Devikā river, five *yojanas* long and half a *yojana* wide,
is sacred and frequented by divine sages.
Then, O knower of dharma, one should proceed in due order to Dīrghasattra,
where the gods headed by Brahmā, the Siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis,
firm in their vows, attend the long sacrificial session with ritual fees.

O Indra among kings, O subduer of enemies, by merely going there, a person obtains the fruit of the long sacrificial session (*dīrghasattra*) as well as the *rājasūya* and *aśvamedha* sacrifices. Thereafter,
one should proceed to Vinaśana, self-restrained and restricted in diet.
The Sarasvatī flows invisibly where she reaches the back of the Maruts;
she is seen at Camasa, Śivodbheda, and Nāgodbheda.
Having bathed at Camasodbheda, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Having bathed at Śivodbheda, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. Having bathed at Nāgodbheda, a man attains the world of the Nāgas.
And having reached the difficult-to-attain tīrtha called Śaśayāna, O Indra among kings, [he obtains great merit].
O Bhārata, O great king, there are lotuses disguised in the form of hares upon the Sarasvatī; for throughout the year,
O best of the Bharatas, they always bathe there on the full moon day of Kārttika.
Having bathed there, O tiger among men, one shines forever like the moon;
and one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows, O bull of the Bharatas.
Having reached Kumārakoṭi, O joy of the Kurus, one should remain self-restrained.

There, devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, one should perform an ablution; one thereby attains the Gavāmaya sacrifice and uplifts one's entire lineage. From there, O knower of dharma, one should proceed with a concentrated mind to Rudrakoṭi.
Long ago, O Great King, ten million sages were gathered there,
lying down in great joy with a longing to behold the God,
each thinking, "I shall see the Bull-bannered One first; I shall see him first!"
O King, descendant of Bharata, it is said that the sages set out in this manner. Then,
O lord of the earth, the Lord of Yoga himself, having applied his yogic power,
acted for the sake of destroying the anger of those sages of purified souls.
A crore of Rudras was created and stood before the sages;
each of them thought individually, "I have seen him earlier than you.
Mahādeva was pleased with those sages of fierce splendor.
O King, out of supreme devotion, he granted them this boon:
"From this day forward, there shall be an increase in your righteousness.
Having bathed there at Rudrakoṭi, O tiger among men, a man becomes pure."
One obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and uplifts one's entire lineage.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the world-renowned confluence, which is greatly meritorious; there people worship Janārdana at the Sarasvatī.
O Indra among kings, where Brahmā and the other gods, the ṛṣis, the siddhas, and the cāraṇas go on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra—
having bathed there, O tiger among men, one obtains much gold.
With his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the world of Brahmā,
O lord of men, where the sacrificial sessions (*satra*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) have been completed;
having reached the conclusion of those sessions, he obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Pulastya said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the highly praised Kurukṣetra;
all living beings who go there are liberated from their sins.
"I shall go to Kurukṣetra; I dwell in Kurukṣetra"—whoever should constantly speak thus is also liberated from sins. Even the dust particles of Kurukṣetra, when raised by the wind, [purify].
Even those who have performed evil deeds are led to the highest state. Those who dwell in Kurukṣetra— situated to the south of the Sarasvatī and to the north of the Dṛṣadvatī— dwell in heaven itself.
O hero Yudhiṣṭhira, one should dwell there for a month on the Sarasvatī,
where the gods headed by Brahmā, the ṛṣis, Siddhas, Cāraṇas,
Gandharvas, Apsarases, Yakṣas, and Pannagas reside, O lord of the earth.
O Bhārata, they go to the Brahma-field, which is of great merit. O Yudhiṣṭhira, even for one who merely desires Kurukṣetra in their mind,
their sins are utterly destroyed and they go to the world of Brahmā.
O best of the Kurus, having gone to Kurukṣetra endowed with faith,
a person obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Thereafter, O King, [he should visit] the mighty gatekeeper Macakruka.
Having paid homage to the Yakṣa, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
From there, O knower of dharma, one should proceed to the unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu,
known as Satata, O king of kings, where Hari is ever present.
Having bathed there and worshipped Hari, the source of the three worlds,
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. From there, one should go to the Pāriplava tīrtha, renowned throughout the three worlds.

A person obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices; having reached the sacred ford (tīrtha) of the Earth, one gains the merit of giving a thousand cows. Then, O lord of men, the pilgrim should go to Śālūkinī.
Having bathed at Daśāśvamedhika, one obtains that very same fruit. Having reached Sarpadarvī, the supreme tīrtha of the Nāgas,
one attains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and finds the world of the Nāgas.
Then, O knower of dharma, one should go to the gatekeeper Tarantuka;
having stayed there for one night, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Then, being self-restrained and restricted in diet, one should go to Pañcanada.

Having touched the waters at Koṭitīrtha, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice; having reached the tīrtha of the Aśvins, one is born endowed with beauty. From there, O knower of dharma, one should go to the supreme tīrtha of Vārāha.

O tiger among men, having bathed there where Viṣṇu formerly stood in the form of a boar, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. Thereafter, O king of kings, one should enter the Somatīrtha at Jayantī.
O bull of the Kurus, having bathed at Ekahaṃsa, a man obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice; and having reached Kṛtaśauca, the pilgrim obtains the merit of a thousand cows.

A man who has performed his purification attains Puṇḍarīka; then he goes to the place named Muñjavaṭa belonging to the wise Mahādeva. Having stayed there for one night, he shall attain the status of a leader of Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya).
And right there, O Great King, is the Yakṣī renowned throughout the world;
by approaching her, O Indra among kings, one shall attain the meritorious worlds.
That is the celebrated gateway to Kurukṣetra, O bull of the Bharatas.
Having circumambulated it clockwise, the pilgrim, composed in mind,
bathes at Saṃmita— one of the Puṣkara lakes— where the high-souled Rāma, son of Jamadagni, performed his ablutions, and there he worships the ancestors and the gods.
O King, one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done and gains the merit of the horse sacrifice.
Thereafter, O lord of men, the pilgrim should go to the lakes of Rāma,
where, O king of kings, by means of his swift power and blazing splendor, Rāma [performed his deeds].
Having destroyed the kṣatriyas by his prowess, five lakes were established;
we have heard, O tiger among men, that they were filled with blood,
and thus all the ancestors as well as the grandfathers were gratified.
Then those ancestors, being pleased, said to Rāma, O lord of the earth:
"O Rāma, Rāma, O highly fortunate descendant of Bhṛgu, we are gratified with you,
O powerful one, because of this devotion to your ancestors and because of your prowess."
"Choose a boon— blessings be upon you— what do you desire, O one of great splendor?
Thus addressed, O king of kings, Rāma, the best among strikers,
spoke these words with palms joined in reverence to his ancestors stationed in the sky.
"O sirs, if you are pleased with me, and if I am worthy of your favor,
I desire through the grace of my father to have my ascetic power restored once more;
for by me, overcome by anger, the kṣatriya order was destroyed."
"Then may I be freed from my sins through your power,
and may these lakes of mine become famous on earth as sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrtha).
Having heard these auspicious words of Rāma, his ancestors then [replied].
Filled with supreme joy and overflowing with delight, they replied to Rāma:
"May your ascetic power increase even further, especially through your devotion to your father;
and as for the fact that the kṣatriyas were exterminated by you while overcome by wrath—"

"Then you shall be liberated from those sins, and they too shall be cast down; moreover, these lakes of yours will undoubtedly attain the status of sacred fords (*tīrtha*). Whoever bathes in these lakes and offers libations to the ancestors,"
"His ancestors, being truly pleased, will grant him on earth that which is difficult to obtain—
the desired wish of his heart and the eternal world of heaven. Having thus granted these boons to Rāma, O King, his ancestors then—
Having addressed the descendant of Bhṛgu, they then vanished on the spot, filled with joy.
Thus are the holy lakes of Rāma belonging to the high-souled Bhārgava; having bathed in these lakes of Rāma, one who observes celibacy and auspicious vows [attains merit].
O Indra among kings, by worshipping Rāma there, one obtains much gold. O best of the Kurus, having reached Vaṃśamūlaka,
the pilgrim who bathes at Vaṃśamūlaka, O King, shall uplift his own lineage.
O best of the Bharatas, having reached that sacred ford (tīrtha) which purifies the body,
there is no doubt that one who has bathed in that ford attains purification of the physical frame;
and with a purified body, he goes to the most excellent and auspicious worlds.
Then, O king of kings, one should go to the tīrtha renowned throughout the three worlds,
where in former times the worlds were uplifted by the powerful Viṣṇu. Having reached that world-uplifting tīrtha, famous in the three worlds, [one attains merit].
O King, having bathed in that best of sacred fords (*tīrtha*), one rescues one's own people;
and having reached Śrītīrtha, one obtains supreme prosperity. Having bathed there with a restrained mind...
Having honored the ancestors and the gods,
and having reached Kapilātīrtha, being celibate and composed,
he bathed there and likewise worshipped the deities and the ancestors.
A person who,
having reached Sūryatīrtha, bathes with a restrained mind,
worships the ancestors and the gods, and is devoted to fasting, obtains the fruit of giving a thousand tawny cows.
He attains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the world of the Sun. Having reached Govābhavana in due order, the pilgrim performing an ablution there obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
O best of the Kurus, having reached Śaṅkhinī there, the pilgrim who bathes in the goddess’s sacred pool attains supreme beauty. From there, O king of kings, one should go to the gatekeeper Arantuka.
There is the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) of that high-souled lord of the *yakṣas* on the Sarasvatī;
having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Thence, O knower of dharma, O lord of men, one should go to Brahmāvarta.
Having bathed at Brahmāvarta, a man shall attain the world of Brahmā. From there, O knower of dharma, one should go to the unsurpassed Sutīrthaka,
where the ancestors are eternally present together with the gods.
There, devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, one should perform an ablution;
one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice and goes to the world of the ancestors.
Then, O knower of dharma, having reached Ambuvaśya in due order, one attains the same result.
O best of the Bharatas, having bathed at the sacred fords of Kośeśvara,
one is liberated from all diseases and is glorified in the world of Brahmā. And right there, O Bhārata, is the Mātṛtīrtha, where one who has bathed—
O King, one's progeny increases and one attains infinite prosperity.
Thereafter, self-restrained and restricted in diet, one should go to Śītavana;
O great king, that sacred ford there is vast and difficult to find elsewhere.
O lord of men, by the mere sight of it, one purifies a single person with a staff;
O Bhārata, by sprinkling water on the hair there, one becomes pure. O great king, that sacred bathing place (tīrtha) is known as Śvānalomāpaha.
O tiger among men, O best of the Bharatas, at that place where learned brahmins devoted to sacred fords attain the supreme goal after bathing;
and at the ford called Śvānalomāpanayana, O best of the Bharatas.
O best of the twice-born, they remove [the sins of] dog-hair through breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma);
and with their souls purified, O king of kings, they go to the supreme goal.
And at that sacred ford (tīrtha), O lord of the earth, there is also the Daśāśvamedhika.
Having bathed there, O tiger among men, one shall go to the supreme goal. From there, O king of kings, one should proceed to Mānuṣa, which is world-renowned;
there, O King, black deer were once tormented by a hunter.
Having plunged into that lake, they attained human form. Having bathed at that sacred ford (*tīrtha*), a man who is celibate and has conquered his senses,
with his soul purified of all sins, is glorified in the heavenly world.
O Lord of the Earth, just one *krośa* to the east of Mānuṣa,
there is a famous river named Āpagā, frequented by the Siddhas.
There, the man who offers food made of *śyāmāka* grain—
By dedicating [the gift] to the gods and the ancestors, the fruit of that merit is great:
when a single Brahmin is fed there, it is as if ten million have been fed.
Having bathed there and having likewise worshipped the deities and the ancestors, [one attains great reward].
Having stayed for one night, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme abode of Brahmā,
known on earth as Brahmodumbara, O Bhārata.
O bull among the Kurus, O king of kings, having bathed there in the pools of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣi) and at Kedāra of the high-souled Kapiṣṭhala,
one should then approach Brahmā, pure and with a restrained mind.
With his soul purified of all sins, he attains the world of Brahmā.
Having reached the field of Kapiṣṭhala, which is very difficult to attain, he,
whose impurities have been burnt away by austerity, obtains the power of invisibility.
Then, O king of kings, one should go to Saraka, renowned throughout the world;
having approached the bull-bannered god on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one indeed obtains all desires and goes to the heavenly world.
O descendant of Kuru, there are three crores of holy fords (tīrthas) at Saraka;
likewise, O lord of the earth, there are ten million Rudras at the well and in the lakes.
And right there, O best of the Bharatas, is the holy ford Ilāspada.
Having bathed there and having worshipped the ancestors and the gods, O Bhārata,
one does not meet with an evil fate and obtains the merit of a Vājapeya sacrifice. And by bathing at Kiṃdāna, O lord of the earth, as well as by reciting prayers there, a man [attains the same].
O Bhārata, by performing libations at Kalaśī with faith and with senses subdued, a man obtains immeasurable merit from both giving gifts and the recitation of prayers,
and he attains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.

To the east of Saraka, O best of the Kurus, is the sacred ford of the high-souled Nārada, renowned as Anājānma. Having bathed in that ford and having cast off his life-breaths there, O Bhārata, a man [attains liberation].
Permitted by Nārada, one attains worlds that are difficult to reach.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight, one should enter Puṇḍarīka;
having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice.
From there, one should go to Triviṣṭapa, renowned throughout the three worlds. There flows the holy river Vaitaraṇī, which liberates one from sin.
Having bathed there and having worshipped the trident-bearing god whose banner is the bull, [one attains merit].
With his soul purified of all sins, he shall go to the supreme goal.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Phalakīvana,
where, O King, the gods always take refuge in the Phalakīvana forest.
They perform extensive austerities for many thousands of years;
by bathing there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. Having bathed in the Dṛṣadvatī and having offered libations to the deities, a man [attains this reward].
O Bhārata, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices;
and by bathing at the sacred ford (tīrtha) of all the gods, O best of the Bharatas,
a human being attains the fruit of a thousand cows, O Indra among kings.

Having bathed at Pāṇikhāta and offered libations to the deities, a man obtains the merit of the Rājasūya sacrifice and goes to the world of the ṛṣis. From there, O king of kings, one should proceed to the supreme holy site of Miśraka.
O Indra among kings, we have heard that at that place, the high-souled Vyāsa mixed all the sacred fords (tīrthas) together for the sake of the twice-born, O tiger among men;
for that man who bathes in Miśraka bathes in all the sacred fords.
Having bathed and worshipped the ancestors and the gods at Miśraka,
one should then proceed to Vyāsavana, self-restrained and restricted in diet.
Having bathed at Manojava, a man obtains the merit of a thousand cows.

Having gone to Madhuvatī, a man who is pure should bathe at the holy ford of the Goddess; being self-restrained and pure, he should worship the gods and the ancestors. Permitted by the Goddess, he shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.

O Bhārata, he who bathes at the confluence of the Kauśikī and the Dṛṣadvatī while restricted in his diet is indeed liberated from all sins. Beyond that is the place named Vyāsasthalī, where the wise Vyāsa [resided].
O Indra among kings, one who, tormented by grief for a son, has resolved to abandon the body,
is then raised up again by the gods;
by approaching that sacred spot, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.

O best of the Kurus, having reached Kiṃdatta and offered a *prastha* of sesame seeds, one goes to the supreme perfection, freed from all debts. Having bathed at the Vedītīrtha, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Ahaśca and Sudina—these two tirthas are very difficult to attain. By bathing in them, O tiger among men, one may reach the world of the Sun.
From there, one should go to Mṛgadhūma, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having bathed there in the pool of the Gaṅgā and having worshipped Mahādeva, the wielder of the trident, a person obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having bathed at Devatīrtha, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Then one should go to Vāmanaka, renowned throughout the three worlds;
having bathed there at Viṣṇupada and worshipped Vāmana,
with one's soul purified of all sins, one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, O tiger among men, having bathed at Pavana’s lake, the supreme sacred ford of the Maruts, a man purifies his own lineage; by bathing there,
he is glorified in the world of Vāyu.
O lord of men, having bathed in the lake of the immortals among the gods,
one is glorified in the heavenly world by the power of the immortals;
mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot, one goes forth together with the gods.

O Indra among kings, O best of men, by bathing according to the prescribed rites at Śāliśūrpa in the river Śālihotrī, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows. And there is the sacred site of Śrīkuñja on the Sarasvatī, O best of the Bharatas.

O King, having bathed there, a man obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. Then, O best of the Kurus, having reached Naimiṣakuñja, it is said, O Indra among kings, that the sages of Naimiṣa, whose wealth is their asceticism, [reside there].
In ancient times, they set out for Kurukṣetra, making a pilgrimage to the sacred fords their primary goal.
Having bathed there at that sacred site, a man obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice (vājimedha).
After that, O best of the Bharatas, Kuñja was established upon the Sarasvatī.
03.081.093c There shall be a place for the sages that provides great satisfaction;
03.081.094a having bathed in that bower, a man obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows. 03.081.094b O knower of dharma, from there one should go to the unsurpassed Kanyātīrtha.
Having bathed at Kanyātīrtha, a man obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
From there, O tiger among men, one should go to the supreme abode of Brahmā;
having bathed there, even a man of inferior caste attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
And a Brahmin of purified soul shall attain the supreme goal. From there, O best of men, one should go to the unsurpassed Somatīrtha;
having bathed there, O King, a man shall attain the world of Soma.
O lord of men, one should then go to the Saptasārasvata tīrtha,
where the great ṛṣi Maṅkaṇaka, world-renowned for his perfection, attained success.
O King, we have heard that in ancient times Maṅkaṇaka [was pricked] by the tip of a blade of kusha grass.

O King, it is said that when his hand was wounded, vegetable juice flowed from it. Upon seeing that vegetable juice, the great ascetic brahmin-sage, overcome with joy, began to dance with eyes wide open in wonder.
Then, O hero, when he began to dance, everything both stationary and moving also danced, for all were deluded by his splendor;
even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, O King, as well as the sages whose wealth is asceticism, were overcome.
"O Great God, O Lord of Men, I have indeed petitioned you on behalf of the seer:
'O Lord, you ought to act in such a way that he does not dance.
Thereupon, having begun to dance with a heart overcome by joy—"
For the sake of the welfare of the gods, the Lord addressed the sage:
"O great seer, knower of dharma, for what reason are you dancing? Or what is the cause of this joy in you today, O bull among sages?"
The sage said:
"O best of the twice-born, do you not see, O God, the vegetable juice flowing from my hand as I stand upon the path of dharma, practicing asceticism?"
"Seeing whom, I indeed began to dance, filled with great joy.
Pulastya said:
"The God, laughing, spoke to that sage who was deluded by passion:"
"O Brahmin, I do not feel any wonder; behold me!
Having spoken thus, O best of men, the wise Mahādeva, O king of kings, struck his own thumb with the tip of his finger, O sinless one.
Then, O King, ashes resembling snow issued forth from the wound.
Seeing that, O King, the sage was filled with shame and fell at his feet, saying:
"I consider no other god to be greater or more supreme than Rudra."
O wielder of the trident, you are the refuge of the world of gods and asuras.
This entire universe, the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving, was created by you.
O Blessed One, at the end of the eon, all beings enter into you alone.
"Even by the gods you cannot be fully known, much less by me;
for within you, O sinless one, all the gods beginning with Brahmā are seen.
You are indeed everything, the creator and the instigator of all the worlds."
"By your grace, all the gods rejoice here, free from fear from any quarter.
Having thus praised Mahādeva, that ṛṣi bowed down.
The ṛṣi said:
"O Mahādeva, by your grace, may my ascetic merit indeed never diminish.
Pulastya said:
"Then the God, his soul delighted, spoke these words to the Brahmarṣi:"
"O Brahmin, may your ascetic power increase a thousandfold through my grace.
O great sage, I shall dwell here in this hermitage together with you.
And those who, having bathed at Saptasārasvata, worship me—"
For them, nothing whatsoever shall be difficult to attain in this world or in the next;
they will go to the world of Sarasvatī, of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva vanished right then and there.
Then one should go to Auśanasa, renowned throughout the three worlds,
where the gods headed by Brahmā, the sages rich in asceticism,
and the blessed Kārttikeya indeed assemble at the three junctions of the day, O Bhārata.
Out of a desire to do what was pleasing to Bhārgava,
she manifested her presence there at the sacred ford Kapālamocana, which liberates one from all sins;
having bathed there, O tiger among men, one is released from all evils.

Then, O bull among men, one should go to Agnitīrtha; having bathed there, one attains the world of Agni and uplifts one's entire lineage. Right there, O best of the Bharatas, is the tīrtha of Viśvāmitra.
O Great King, having bathed there, one is born into the state of a Brahmin;
having reached the source of Brahman, pure and with a restrained mind,
O tiger among men, one attains the world of Brahmā after bathing there.
It purifies one's lineage up to the seventh generation; of this there is no doubt.
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the tirtha renowned throughout the three worlds, known as Pṛthūdaka, which belongs to Kārttikeya, O monarch.

O Bhārata, for one who has merely bathed there, evil is destroyed. One devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods should perform an ablution there, whether [the sin] was committed through ignorance or knowledge, by a woman or by a man.
O Bhārata, whatever inauspicious deed has been committed by one with human intellect— all that perishes for him as soon as he has bathed;
moreover, he obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world.
They say Kurukṣetra is meritorious, and the Sarasvatī is more meritorious than Kurukṣetra;

the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) of the Sarasvatī are more meritorious than the river itself, and Pṛthūdaka is more meritorious than those sacred fords. He who casts off his body at Pṛthūdaka, the most excellent of all sacred fords, [attains the highest goal].
At Pṛthūdaka, one intent on silent recitation need not be tormented by the thought of death tomorrow.
This has been sung by Sanatkumāra and the high-souled Vyāsa;
it is also firmly established in the Veda, O King—therefore, one should go to Pṛthūdaka.
O best of men, there is no sacred ford more meritorious than Pṛthūdaka.
It is pure, holy, and purifying; of this there is no doubt.
Having bathed there, even people who have committed sins go to heaven.
O best of men, the wise have thus spoken regarding Pṛthūdaka;
and right there, O best of the Bharatas, is the sacred ford Madhusrava.
By bathing there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Then, O best of men, one should proceed in due order to the sacred ford of the Goddess,
the world-renowned confluence of the Sarasvatī and the Aruṇā.
Having fasted for three nights and bathed there, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
A man obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices;
he purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation, O bull of the Bharatas. And there, O perpetuator of the Kuru race, is the sacred ford known as Avatīrṇa.
In ancient times, this was created by Darbhin for the sake of showing compassion toward the learned (vipras).
Whether through vows and the initiation ceremony (upanayana), or through fasting, a twice-born man who is endowed with ritual acts and mantras shall undoubtedly become a Brāhmaṇa.
