O bull among men, even one devoid of ritual action and mantras becomes a Brahmin who has fulfilled his vows by bathing there; this has been seen in the ancient lore. Furthermore, the four oceans were brought together there by Darbhin.
O tiger among men, one who bathes in these [tirthas] shall not fall into an evil state;
he obtains the fruits of giving four thousand cows.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the tirtha known as Śatasahasraka.

Right there are two world-renowned sacred fords (tīrthas) called Sāhasraka; by bathing in both, a man obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows. Furthermore, whether it be a gift or a fast, its merit becomes multiplied a thousandfold.
Then, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Reṇukātīrtha. There, devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, one should perform an ablution;
with one's soul purified from flowing sins, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Having touched the waters at Vimocana, with his anger conquered and his senses subdued,
he is completely liberated from all the faults incurred through the acceptance of gifts.
Then, remaining celibate and with his senses subdued, he goes to Pañcavaṭa.
Endowed with great merit, one is honored in the world of the virtuous;
where Sthāṇu himself, the Lord of Yoga who bears the bull as his banner, resides—
by worshipping that Lord of Gods, one attains perfection through the mere act of going there.
The sacred ford named Aujaṣa shines with its own splendor;
there, Guha was then consecrated as the commander-in-chief of the gods by Brahmā and the other deities, as well as by the sages whose wealth is their asceticism.
O best of the Kurus, to the east of Aujaṣa is Kurutīrtha. Having bathed at Kurutīrtha, a man who is celibate and has conquered his senses,
with his soul purified of all sins, attains the world of the Kurus.
Then, self-restrained and restricted in diet, one should go to Svargadvāra;
one attains the world of heaven and goes to the world of Brahmā. From there, O lord of men, the pilgrim should proceed to Anaraka.
O King, having bathed there, a person shall not fall into an evil state. O lord of the earth, O best of men, Brahmā himself is always seated there together with the gods, led by Nārāyaṇa.
O Indra among kings, O upholder of the Kuru lineage, there is the very presence of Rudra’s consort;
by approaching that goddess, one shall not meet with misfortune.
And right there, O great king, is Viśveśvara, the lord of Umā.
Having approached Mahādeva, one is liberated from all sins;
and having approached Nārāyaṇa, the lotus-navelled subduer of enemies,
O Great King, one shines resplendently and attains the world of Viṣṇu.
O bull among men, having bathed at that sacred ford (tīrtha) of all the gods,
he is freed from all sufferings and shines forever like the moon. Thereafter, O lord of men, the pilgrim should proceed to Svastipura.
Having circumambulated it clockwise, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
having reached that purifying *tīrtha*, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods,
whereby a person attains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O bull of the Bharata race, O lord of the earth, right there is the Gaṅgā-hrada and a well;
in that well, O king, there are thirty million sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having bathed there, O King, a man attains the heavenly world.

Having bathed in the Āpagā river and worshipped Maheśvara, a man attains the status of a Gaṇapati and uplifts his own lineage. Thence he should go to Sthāṇuvaṭa, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having bathed there and stayed for a night, one shall attain the world of Rudra.
Then one should go to Badarīpācana, the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha;
having fasted there for three nights, a man should eat jujube fruit.
O lord of men, he who has correctly subsisted on jujube fruits for twelve years becomes equal to one who has fasted for three nights, O king,
once that pilgrim has reached the Indramārga.
By fasting for a day and night, one is glorified in the world of Śakra. Having undertaken a fast for a single night,
a man who is self-controlled and truthful in speech is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Then, O knower of dharma, one should go to the tīrtha renowned throughout the three worlds,
where the hermitage of the high-souled Āditya, that mass of splendor,
is located; having bathed in that tīrtha, a man shall attain a great station.

Having bathed in that *tīrtha* and having worshipped Vibhāvasu, a man goes to the world of Āditya and uplifts his entire lineage. O bull of the Kurus, a man devoted to sacred fords who bathes in Somatīrtha—

A man attains the world of Soma; there is no doubt about this. Thereafter, O knower of dharma, one should go to the most meritorious and purifying tīrtha of the high-souled Dadhīca, which is renowned throughout the world, O King.
O King, at that sacred ford where Sārasvata Aṅgiras, the treasure-house of asceticism,
dwells, a man who bathes obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and attains the state of Sarasvatī; of this there is no doubt.
Then, O King, one who is self-restrained and observant of celibacy should go to Kanyāśrama; having fasted for three nights and being devoted to fasting,
he shall obtain a hundred divine maidens and go to the world of Brahmā.
Then, O knower of dharma, one should go to the sacred ford called Sannihitī,
where the gods headed by Brahmā and the sages whose wealth is asceticism,
endowed with great merit, assemble month after month.
Having touched the water at Saṃnihitī when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu,
one has eternally performed a hundred horse-sacrifices.
Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist on earth and those that move through the intermediate space— [all are attained by this].
O lord of men, on the new moon day, the rivers, streams, lakes, all springs, wells, embankments, and sacred shrines will undoubtedly assemble together.
Because she led [the people] to the sacred fords (*tīrtha*), she is thus renowned on earth as Saṃnitā. Having bathed and drunk there, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
Furthermore, on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) when the sun is seized by Rāhu, at that very place—
Listen to the fruit of merit for that mortal who performs a *śrāddha*:
whatever fruit is obtained from a thousand horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*) properly performed, a man attains that very same fruit simply by bathing after having performed the *śrāddha*.
They arrive month after month at Saṃnihitī; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever evil deed has been committed by a woman or a man, all of that perishes as soon as one has bathed; of this there is no doubt.
By means of a lotus-colored vehicle, he goes to the world of Brahmā. Then, having saluted the Yakṣa gatekeeper Arantuka and touched the Koṭirūpa [tīrtha], one obtains much gold.
And right there, O best of the Bharatas, is the Gaṅgāhrada tīrtha;
having bathed there, O knower of dharma, being celibate and composed,
one obtains the eternal fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Naimiṣa is sacred on earth, and Puṣkara is sacred in the intermediate space;
yet Kurukṣetra excels even over all three worlds.
Even the dust of Kurukṣetra, when raised by the wind, [is purifying].
Even those who have performed evil deeds are led to the supreme goal. Those who dwell in Kurukṣetra— situated to the south of the Sarasvatī and to the north of the Dṛṣadvatī— dwell in Triviṣṭapa.
"I shall go to Kurukṣetra; I dwell in Kurukṣetra.
By uttering even this single word, one is liberated from all sins.
Kurukṣetra is the altar of Brahman, a sacred place frequented by the Brahman-sages.
O King, those who dwell there are not to be grieved for in any way—
those who reside in the region between Tarantuka and Āruntuka,
and between the lakes of Rāma and Macakruka.
"This is Kurukṣetra, Samantapañcaka;
it is called the northern altar of the Grandfather.
Pulastya said:
Then, O knower of dharma, one should go to the ancient Dharmatīrtha,
where the illustrious Dharma performed supreme asceticism;
by him that meritorious tīrtha was established and marked with his own name.

O King, having bathed there, a man of virtuous character and concentrated mind purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation; of this there is no doubt. From there, O knower of dharma, one should proceed to the excellent Kārāpaṭana.
Having traveled with great difficulty and bathed there with a concentrated mind,
one obtains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the world of the sages.
O King, from there a person should proceed to the Saugandhika forest.
Where the gods beginning with Brahmā, the sages whose wealth is asceticism,
the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Kiṃnaras, along with the great serpents (Mahoragas) dwell—
merely by entering that forest, one is liberated from all sins.
Therefore, O King, that most excellent of rivers, the supreme among streams,
the goddess Sarasvatī of great merit, flows forth from the Plakṣa tree;
one should perform ablutions there in the water issuing from the anthill.
Having worshipped the ancestors and the gods there, one obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
There is a very rare sacred ford (tīrtha) there named Īśānādhyuṣita;
it is certain that it is located six throws of a wooden pin (śamyā) away from an anthill.

O tiger among men, by bathing there one obtains the merit of giving a thousand tawny cows and the merit of a horse-sacrifice; this has been seen in ancient times. O Bhārata, [one should visit] Sugandhā, Śatakumbhā, and Pañcayajñā.
Having approached it, O best of men, one is glorified in the heavenly world. Having reached the sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Triśūlakhāta at that very place, O Bhārata,
one should perform an ablution there, devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods.
Upon casting off the body, he attains the state of Gaṇapati; of this there is no doubt.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the station of the Goddess, which is very difficult to attain and renowned throughout the three worlds as Śākambharī.

O King, it is said that for a thousand divine years, she, firm in her vows, took as her food only vegetables once every month. Sages whose wealth was their asceticism arrived there, drawn by their devotion to the queen.
O Bhārata, they say that hospitality was offered to them with vegetables alone;
therefore, the name Śākambharī became established for her.
Having reached Śākambharī, one who is self-controlled and observant of celibacy—
Having stayed for three nights, self-restrained and pure, one should subsist on vegetables;
O Bhārata, whatever fruit is properly obtained by one who subsists on vegetables for twelve years, that same fruit belongs to him who acts according to the will of the Goddess.
From there, one should go to Suvarṇākṣa, renowned throughout the three worlds,
where in ancient times Viṣṇu propitiated Rudra for the sake of his grace and obtained very many boons that are extremely difficult even for the gods to attain.
And he was addressed by the gratified Destroyer of Tripura, O Bhārata:
"Moreover, Kṛṣṇa, you shall become even more beloved to us than anyone else in the world;
and the entire universe shall have you as its mouth—of this there is no doubt."
Having gone there, O Indra among kings, and having worshipped the bull-bannered god (Śiva),
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and attains the status of a Gaṇapati. From there, a man should go to Dhūmāvatī, fasting for three nights.
One obtains the desires sought after by the mind; of this there is no doubt.
O lord of men, to the south of the Goddess is Rathāvarta;
there, O knower of dharma, one who is faithful and has conquered his senses should ascend.
Indeed, through the grace of Mahādeva, one shall go to the supreme goal;
having performed a circumambulation, O bull of the Bharatas,
one should proceed to the place named Dhārā, O highly wise one, which destroys all sins.
Having bathed there, O tiger among men, O lord of men, one does not grieve. Then, O knower of dharma, having paid homage to the great mountain,
one should proceed to Puṣkara, which is said to be eighty hundred *yojanas* from heaven.
O King of kings, the wise declare that there are eighty [yojanas] from Dharmapṛṣṭha,
sixty from Prayāga, and twelve from Kurukṣetra;
Gaṅgādvāra and Triviṣṭapa are indeed situated together.
Gaṅgādvāra is undoubtedly equal to Svargadvāra;
there, with a concentrated mind and pure, self-restrained heart, O great king, one should perform ablutions at Koṭitīrtha.

One obtains the merit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice and uplifts one's entire lineage; by staying there for a single night, one gains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. By offering libations at Saptagaṅgā, Trigaṅgā, and Śakrāvarta, one attains great merit.

By honoring the gods and the ancestors according to the prescribed rites, one is glorified in the world of merit. Then, having bathed at Kanakhala and fasted for three nights, a man obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world.
O lord of men, the pilgrim should go to Kapilāvata;
by staying there for a single night, one obtains the merit of [giving] a thousand cows.
O king of kings, this is the site of the high-souled Kapila, the king of the Nāgas.
O best of the Kuru lineage, there is a sacred ford renowned throughout all the worlds; O lord of men,
one should perform an ablution there at the Nāga-tīrtha,
and a person obtains the merit of giving a thousand tawny cows.
Then one should go to Lalitikā, the supreme tīrtha of Śantanu;
having bathed there, O King, a man shall not meet with an evil fate. And that man who bathes at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the [Yamunā] likewise attains this merit.
One obtains the merit of ten horse-sacrifices and uplifts one's entire lineage.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to Sugandhā, renowned throughout the world;
with one's soul purified of all sins, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

O lord of men, the pilgrim should then proceed to Rudrāvarta; by doing so, O best of men, he obtains the merit of a thousand cows. Having bathed there, O King, a man is glorified in the heavenly world.
O best of men, by bathing at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Sarasvatī,
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world.
Having gone to Bhadrakarṇeśvara and having worshipped the deity according to the prescribed rites, [one attains the same].
One does not fall into an evil state of existence, but goes to the heavenly world.
Then, the pilgrim should proceed in due order to Kubjāmraka;
he obtains the merit of a thousand cows and goes to the heavenly world.

O lord of men, the pilgrim should go to Arundhatīvaṭa; having bathed there, O King, a man is glorified in the heavenly world. Having touched the waters at Sāmudraka and fasted for three nights, a man—
The celibate practitioner who is composed attains the merit of the horse sacrifice;
he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows and uplifts his entire lineage.
Then, as a celibate student (brahmacārī) with a concentrated mind, one should go to Brahmāvarta;
there one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) and goes to the heavenly world.
Having gone to the source of the Yamunā and having performed ablutions in the Yamunā, one attains the same reward.
Having obtained the fruit of the horse sacrifice, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
Having reached the ford known as Darvīsaṃkramaṇa, which is renowned throughout the three worlds,
one attains the fruit of the horse sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world.
Having gone to the source of the Sindhu river, which is frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
and having stayed there for five nights, one obtains much gold. Then, a man, having reached the altar (vedī) that is most difficult to access—

One obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the state of Uśanas. Having reached the Ṛṣikulyā and the Vāsiṣṭha [tirtha], O Bhārata— and having passed beyond the Vāsiṣṭha— all castes become twice-born.
Having bathed in the Ṛṣikulyā, a man attains the world of the Ṛṣis;
having bathed there, a man becomes free from stain,
and having worshipped the gods and the ancestors.
If a man dwells there for a month subsisting on vegetables, O lord of men,
that person obtains the fruit of the twelve-day sacrifice (Dvādaśāha).
Having reached Bhṛgutuṅga, one obtains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (Vājimedha).
Having gone to Vīrapramokṣa, one is liberated from all sins.
And having reached the sacred ford (tīrtha) of Kṛttikā and Maghā, O Bhārata,
the performer of meritorious deeds obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices.

Then, having reached the unsurpassed Vidya-tirtha at twilight and having performed ablutions there, one becomes a master of all branches of knowledge. One should dwell for one night at Mahashrama, which grants liberation from all sins.
Abstaining from food at one time, he dwells in auspicious worlds. Having spent a month in Mahālaya fasting for six meals out of seven,
his soul purified of all sins, he shall obtain much gold.
Having beheld the divine station of Maheśvara, which is worshipped by the gods, a person who has crossed over delivers ten ancestors and ten descendants;
having accomplished his purpose in all duties, that man shall not grieve for death.
Then, having gone to Vetasikā, which was frequented by the Grandfather (Brahmā),
one rescues ten descendants and ten ancestors of one's lineage;
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the destination of Uśanas.

Then, having reached Sundarikātīrtha, which is frequented by the Siddhas, one becomes a possessor of beauty; this has been seen in ancient times. Thereafter, having gone to Brāhmaṇī, one should remain celibate and have the senses subdued.
By means of a lotus-colored vehicle, one reaches the world of Brahmā.
From there, one should go to the holy Naimiṣa forest, frequented by the Siddhas;
there Brahmā dwells eternally, surrounded by hosts of gods.
For one who merely desires to go to Naimiṣa, half of their sin perishes;
but as soon as a man has entered it, he is liberated from all sins. A wise man, devoted to sacred fords, should dwell there in Naimiṣa for a month.
O Bhārata, whatever sacred fords exist on earth are all present at Naimiṣa; there, one who is self-restrained, disciplined in diet,
and performs ablutions obtains the fruit of the Gavamaya sacrifice, O Bhārata.
O best of the Bharatas, he who, devoted to fasting, gives up his life at Naimiṣa purifies his lineage even unto the seventh generation;
dwelling in the heavenly world, he shall rejoice— so say the wise.
O best of kings, Naimiṣa is eternally meritorious and pure;
having reached Gaṅgodbheda and fasted there for three nights,
a man obtains the Vājapeya sacrifice and becomes one with Brahman.
Having reached the Sarasvatī, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
one rejoices in the worlds of Sarasvatī—of this there is no doubt.
Thereafter, one should go to the Bāhudā, remaining celibate and composed.
Having stayed there for one night, a person is honored in the heavenly world;
that mortal obtains the fruit of the Devasatra sacrifice.
Thence, one should go to the holy Cīravatī, frequented by those most meritorious.
Devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, one obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
having reached Vimalāśoka, one shines like the moon,
and by staying there for a single night, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
From there, one should go to Gopratāra, the supreme tīrtha on the Sarayū,
where Rāma went to heaven along with his servants, army, and mounts;
having cast off his body, he ascended to the celestial realm by the power of that sacred ford.
O descendant of Bharata, by the grace of Rāma and through his own resolve,
a man who bathes at that sacred ford of Gopratāra, O lord of men,
becomes purified of all sins and is glorified in the heavenly world.
O descendant of Kuru, by bathing at Rāmatīrtha on the Gomatī,
a man obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and purifies his lineage. O best of the Bharatas, there is also a tīrtha there known as Śatasāhasrika.
Having performed ablutions there, self-restrained and restricted in diet,
one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows, O bull of the Bharatas.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Bhartṛsthāna.
A man obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice by bathing at Koṭitīrtha and worshipping Guha, O King;
that man becomes radiant and gains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Then, having gone to Vārāṇasī and worshipped the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva),
a man who bathes in the Kapilā-hrada obtains the fruit of a Rājasūya sacrifice. O best of the Kurus, the pilgrim who reaches Avimukta [obtains the same].
By beholding the God of gods, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
by casting off his life-breaths right there, a human being attains liberation,
O King of kings, having reached that difficult-to-attain tīrtha of Mārkaṇḍeya.
One obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu; at the world-renowned confluence of the Gomatī and the Gaṅgā,
one obtains the merit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and uplifts one's entire lineage.
Especially in Vārāṇasī, O mighty-armed one, where Śiva, the Lord of All, together with the Goddess, plunges into the Gaṅgā— there a wise man, celibate and composed, should dwell for a month.
The sin committed throughout one's entire life is purified in a single month;
then, O Bhārata, having reached Gayā while practicing celibacy and with senses subdued, one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice simply by going there.
There is the place known as Akṣayavaṭa, renowned throughout the three worlds;
O Lord, whatever is given there to the ancestors becomes indeed inexhaustible.
Having touched the waters of the Mahānadī, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
One shall attain imperishable worlds and uplift one's entire lineage.
Then, one should go to the Brahma-lake, adorned by the Forest of Dharma;
having reached it, one obtains the merit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice as soon as the night has turned to dawn.
O king of kings, in that lake stands the sacrificial post of Brahmā;
by circumambulating that post, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
From there, O king of kings, one should proceed to Dhenukā, which is world-renowned.
O King, having stayed there for one night, he who gives a cow made of sesame seeds—his soul purified of all sins—will certainly go to the world of Soma.
O great king, the sign of that place remains even today; of this there is no doubt.
A tawny cow with her calf roams about on that mountain; even today, O Bhārata, the footprints of that cow with her calf are still visible.
By touching water at those footprints, O Indra among kings, O best of monarchs—

Whatever inauspicious karma there may be, O Bhārata, that is destroyed. Thereafter, one should go to Gṛdhravaṭa, the abode of the wise deity; having approached the bull-bannered god, one should bathe there with ashes.
By a Brāhmaṇa, the twelve-year vow would be completed;
for the other castes, however, all sin is destroyed. Then one should go to Mount Udyanta, which resounds with songs.
O bull among the Bharatas, the footprint of Savitṛ is seen there;
a Brāhmaṇa of firm vows should perform his twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) there, and by doing so,
he shall have performed them for twelve years.
And right there, O bull of the Bharatas, is the famous Yonidvāra;
by visiting that place, a person is liberated from the cycle of rebirth.
A man who dwells at Gayā during both the dark and the bright fortnights [attains this merit].
O King, it purifies the family up to the seventh generation; of this there is no doubt.
One should desire many sons, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā, the sin committed throughout one’s entire life is purified in a single month.
Then, having reached Gayā, being celibate and composed in mind,
one should either perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice or set free a dark-colored bull.
Thereafter, O King, the ruler of men who frequents sacred fords should proceed to Phalgu.
One obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and attains great perfection.
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should proceed with a concentrated mind to Dharmapṛṣṭha,
where Dharma dwells eternally, O great king Yudhiṣṭhira.

There, having drunk the water of the well and bathed therein, one becomes pure; having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, freed from sin, one shall go to heaven. There also is the hermitage of the great seer Mataṅga, whose self was purified through meditation.
Having entered that glorious hermitage which destroys fatigue and sorrow,
a person obtains the fruit of the Gavāmaya sacrifice.
He whose eight parts— the tail, the hump, and the head— are white...
The chest and the head—these four are called the *nīḍa* of that bull. O righteous-souled one, having gone there, one obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
By visiting that place, one then obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
Then, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme holy ford of Brahmā.
Having worshipped Brahmā of immeasurable splendor there, O king of kings,
a person obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Then, O lord of men, the pilgrim should go to Rājagṛha; having performed ablutions at the Taporas, he rejoices like Kākṣīvat. There, a pure man should partake of the daily offering of the Yakṣiṇī.
By the grace of the Yakṣiṇī, one is released from the sin of killing a fetus.
Then, having gone to Maṇināga, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
That man who eats the daily offering at Maṇināga [obtains this reward].
Having eaten there and visited the Maṇi-tīrtha, a person—
even if bitten by a venomous serpent— will not succumb to its poison;
by staying there for one night, he is liberated from all sins.
From there, O King, one should go to the forest of the Brahman-sage Gautama;
having bathed in the lake of Ahalyā, one shall attain the supreme goal. Having approached Śrī, O King, one obtains the highest prosperity.
O knower of dharma, there is a well there renowned throughout the three worlds;
having performed an ablution there, one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice (vājimedha).
Furthermore, there is the well of the royal sage Janaka, which is worshipped by the gods.
Having performed an ablution there, one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu. Thence, one should go to Vinaśana, which liberates from all sins;
one obtains the Vājapeya sacrifice and goes to the world of Soma.

Then, O knower of dharma, having entered the Vipāśā, O sinless one, he rejoices in the world of Guhya, O great king; of this there is no doubt. But having reached the Gaṇḍakī, which arises from the waters of all sacred fords (tīrtha), [he attains the same].

He obtains the Vājapeya sacrifice and goes to the world of the Sun. Then, O knower of dharma, having entered the ascetic grove of Adhivaṃśya, he rejoices among the Guhyakas, O great king; of this there is no doubt.

Having reached the river Kampanā, which is frequented by the Siddhas, one attains Puṇḍarīka and goes to the world of the Sun. Then, having reached the river Viśālā, renowned throughout the three worlds, one attains Puṇḍarīka and goes to the world of the Sun. Then, having reached the river Viśālā, renowned throughout the three worlds...
One obtains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world.
Then, O lord of men, having reached the Māheśvarī Dhārā,
one obtains the merit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice and uplifts one's entire lineage.
Having reached the lotus pond of the gods, a pure man does not fall into an evil state and obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
practicing celibacy with a concentrated mind, he shall go to the abode of Maheśvara.
Having bathed at the station of Maheśvara, one obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice. There, O bull of the Bharatas, a crore of sacred fords is renowned,
O king of kings, [concealed] by a wicked-minded asura in the form of a tortoise.
O King, it was carried away and brought back by the powerful Viṣṇu. O Yudhiṣṭhira, one who performs an ablution there at Tīrthakoṭi attains the Puṇḍarīka merit and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Then, O king of kings, one should go to the abode of Nārāyaṇa,
where Hari always dwells in close proximity, O Bhārata;
there the gods headed by Brahmā and the sages whose wealth is asceticism reside.

The Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras worship Janārdana at the place renowned as Śālagrāma, belonging to Viṣṇu of wondrous deeds; having approached the imperishable Viṣṇu, the lord of the three worlds and the giver of boons.
One obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. O knower of dharma, there is a well there that liberates one from all sins;
the four oceans are always present within that well.
O Indra among kings, having sipped water there, one shall not fall into an evil state;
and by approaching Mahādeva and the imperishable Viṣṇu, the giver of boons,
one shines like the moon, O Yudhiṣṭhira, being liberated from all debts.

Having touched the water at Jātismara, pure and with a restrained mind, one attains the memory of past births by bathing there; of this there is no doubt. Having gone to Vaṭeśvarapura, one should worship Keśava.
One obtains one's desired objects through fasting; of this there is no doubt.
There stands the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, renowned throughout the three worlds.
Then, having gone to Vāmana, which releases one from all sins.
Having paid homage to the god Hari, one shall not fall into an evil state. Having gone to Bharata’s hermitage, which liberates one from all sins,
one should resort there to the Kauśikī river, which destroys even the greatest of crimes.
A person obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. From there, O knower of dharma, one should go to the excellent Campakāraṇya.
Having stayed there for one night, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Then, having reached Jyeṣṭhila, a most highly esteemed sacred ford,
and having fasted for one night, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
There, one beholds the Lord of All (Viśveśvara), possessed of great splendor, together with the Goddess.
O bull among men, one attains the worlds of Mitra and Varuṇa;
having fasted there for three nights, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Having reached Kanyāsaṃvedya, self-restrained and restricted in diet, one should remain there.
O bull of the Bharatas, one attains the worlds of Manu Prajāpati;
O Bhārata, those who provide food and drink for a maiden,
the sages of rigid vows declare that such merit is inexhaustible.
Having reached Niścīrā, which is renowned throughout the three worlds,
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. As for those men who bestow gifts at the confluence of the Niścīrā—
O tiger among men, they go to the world of Brahmā; of this there is no doubt.
There lies the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, renowned throughout the three worlds.
Performing an ablution there, one obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Having reached Devakūṭa, which is frequented by hosts of Brahman-sages,
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and uplifts one's entire lineage.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the lake of the sage Kauśika.
O hero, O bull of the Bharata race, one should dwell for a month on the Kauśikī river, where Viśvāmitra, the son of Kuśika, attained supreme perfection;
by staying there for a month, one acquires the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Whoever should dwell in that great lake, the best of all sacred fords (tīrtha),
shall not fall into an evil state of existence and shall obtain much gold.
And having approached Kumāra, who dwells at Vīrāśrama—
A man obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; there is no doubt about this.
Having reached Agnidhārā, which is renowned throughout the three worlds, he obtains the merit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and does not return from heaven.

Having gone to Pitāmaha-saras, which is situated upon the king of mountains, one who performs an ablution there shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. From that lake of Pitāmaha flows forth the purifier of the world.
Right there is the Kumāradhārā, renowned throughout the three worlds;
having bathed there, one realizes of oneself, "I have accomplished my purpose," and by fasting at the sixth mealtime, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin.

Then, O knower of dharma, one intent on visiting sacred fords (tīrtha) should proceed to the peak of the Great Goddess Gaurī, renowned throughout the three worlds. Having ascended it, a faithful man should enter the breast-lakes (stanakuṇḍa).

Having touched the Stanakuṇḍa, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. Performing an ablution there, devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, one attains the Horse Sacrifice and goes to the world of Śakra.
Having reached Tāmrāruṇa with a concentrated mind as a celibate student,
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Śakra.
And having reached the well at Nandinī, which is frequented by the gods, [one obtains the same].
O best of the Kurus, one obtains that merit which belongs to the Naramedha sacrifice;
having attained the fruit of the Vājimedha, he goes to the world of Śakra. This occurs after bathing at the confluence of the Kālikā, where the Kauśikī and Aruṇā meet.
Having fasted for three nights, the wise man is liberated from all sins;
having reached the Urvaśī-tīrtha and then the hermitage of Soma,
and having bathed at the hermitage of Kumbhakarṇa, that man is honored upon the earth.

Having bathed at the holy Kokāmukha while practicing celibacy and observing strict vows, one attains the memory of former births; this has been witnessed in ancient times. Upon reaching Mṛgatuṅga, the twice-born becomes free from sin.
With his soul purified of all evil, he goes to the world of Brahmā. By reaching the Nandā even once, the twice-born becomes perfected in self;
with his soul purified of all evil, he goes to the world of Śakra.
Having reached Ṛṣabha Island, which is to be served by the slayer of Krauñca,
and having touched the waters of the Sarasvatī, one shines resplendent while stationed in a celestial chariot.
O great king, there is the Auddālaka tīrtha, frequented by sages.

One should perform an ablution there; one is liberated from all sins. Having reached the holy Dharmatīrtha, frequented by Brahmanical sages, a man obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, having reached Campā and performed water-libations in the Bhāgīrathī,
and having visited Daṇḍārka, one obtains the merit of a thousand cows.
From there, one should go to the holy Laveḍikā, which is frequented by the meritorious.
One obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and is honored while seated upon a celestial chariot.
Pulastya said:
Now, having reached the excellent sacred ford known as Saṃvedya at the time of twilight...
By touching the water there, a wise man becomes purified; of this there is no doubt.
O King, by the grace of Rāma, this sacred ford (tīrtha) was established in ancient times. Upon reaching that Lohitya, one obtains much gold.

Having reached the Karatoyā, a man who fasts for three nights obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice when the ritual prescribed by the Grandfather (Brahmā) has been performed. Furthermore, O king of kings, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean—
The wise declare that this is ten times more meritorious than the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
O Bhārata, he who reaches the other island of the Gaṅgā and bathes there,
O King, having fasted for three nights, shall obtain all his desires.
Then, having gone to the river Vaitaraṇī, which liberates one from sin,
and having reached the sacred ford Viraja, a man shines like the moon after fasting for three nights.
He obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice,
becomes preeminent in a meritorious family, and casts off all evil;
having gained the fruit of a thousand cows, that man purifies his lineage.
Dwelling at the confluence of the Śoṇa and the Jyotirathī,
pure and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O joy of the Kurus, [one likewise gains this] at the source of the Śoṇa and the Narmadā.
Having touched the waters at Vaṃśagulma, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice (vājimedha).
O lord of men, having reached the Ṛṣabha tīrtha in Kośalā,
a man who fasts for three nights obtains the fruit of a vājapeya sacrifice.
Having reached Kālatīrtha in Kośalā, one should perform ablutions;
there is no doubt that one obtains the fruit of [giving] eleven bulls.
A man who, having performed ablutions at Puṣpavatī, fasts for three nights, [obtains the same].
One should obtain the fruit of a thousand cows and uplift one's entire lineage.
Then, having bathed at the Badarī-tīrtha with a restrained mind,
one attains a long life and goes to the heavenly world.
Likewise, having reached Campā and performed water-libations at the Bhāgīrathī,
and then proceeding to the place called Daṇḍa, one obtains the merit of donating a thousand cows.
From there, one should go to the holy Lapeṭikā, which is adorned with merit.
One obtains the Vājapeya sacrifice and is honored by all the gods.
Then, having reached Mahendra, which was frequented by the son of Jamadagni,
a man who bathes at Rāmatīrtha shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice (vājimedha).

Vaśiṣṭha, the best of sages, and Durvāsas of great asceticism [are there], O joy of the Kurus; and Mataṅga’s Kedāra is right there as well. Having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Having reached Śrīparvata, one should perform ablutions on the riverbank;
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world.
On Śrīparvata dwells Mahādeva, of great splendor, together with the Goddess.
Brahmā, surrounded by the thirty gods, dwelt there with supreme delight. Having bathed there in the Devahrada, pure and with a restrained mind,
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and attains supreme perfection.

Having gone to Mount Ṛṣabha among the Pāṇḍyas, which is worshipped by the gods, one obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and rejoices in the vault of heaven. Thence one should go to the Kāverī, which is surrounded by hosts of Apsarases.
O King, by bathing there, a man obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows. By bathing at the confluence of the Kāverī, the merit becomes tenfold.
Upon reaching Setutīrtha, one casts off even the sin of killing a Brahmin.

Then, on the shore of the ocean, one should perform ablutions at Kanyātīrtha; having performed ablutions there, O Indra among kings, one is liberated from all sins. Then, one should reach Gokarṇa, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
O Indra among kings, in the midst of the ocean is that which is worshipped by all the worlds,
where Brahmā and the other gods, the sages whose wealth is asceticism,
as well as bhūtas, yakṣas, piśācas, kinnaras, and great serpents reside.
Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, humans, as well as Pannagas,
rivers, oceans, and mountains, all worshipped the Lord of Umā.
Having worshipped Īśāna there and fasted for three nights, a man—
One obtains the merit of ten horse-sacrifices and attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas;
by staying there for twelve nights, a man becomes one who has perfected his self.
From that very place flows the station of the Gāyatrī, renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having stayed there for three nights, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
O lord of men, this is a visible proof before the eyes of the Brahmins:
even one born of mixed lineage who recites the Gāyatrī [attains such merit].
O King, whether it be a *gāthā* or even a *gītikā*, it becomes perfected for him;
however, for one who is not a Brāhmaṇa, the *Sāvitrī* perishes as he recites it.
But having reached the difficult-to-attain pool of the brahmin-sage Saṃvarta—
One becomes a possessor of beauty and is born truly fortunate.
Then, having reached the Veṇṇā, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
such a man obtains a celestial chariot yoked with peacocks and swans.

Then, having reached the Godāvarī, which is constantly frequented by the Siddhas, one obtains the merit of the Gavamaya sacrifice and shall attain the world of Vāsuki. Having bathed at the confluence of the Veṇṇā, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Bāhudā, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice (vājimedha).
Having bathed at the confluence of the Varadā, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
Having reached Brahmasthāna and stayed there for three nights, a man [attains the same].
One obtains the fruit of a thousand cows and goes to the heavenly world.
Having reached Kuśaplavana, being celibate and composed,
and having bathed after staying for three nights, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Then, O King, at the delightful Devahrada, which arises from the waters of the Kṛṣṇaveṇṇā,
as well as at Jātimātrahrada and likewise at Kanyāśrama—
where the king of the gods went to heaven after performing hundreds of sacrifices.
O Bhārata, by merely going there, one obtains the merit of a hundred Agniṣṭoma sacrifices;
by bathing in the Sarvadevahrada, one gains the fruit of a thousand cows;
and by bathing in the Jātimātrahrada, a man becomes a rememberer of his past births.
Then, having reached the highly meritorious Payoṣṇī, the best of rivers,

one who is devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows. Having arrived at the Daṇḍaka forest, O great king, one should perform ablutions there.
O Bhārata, by merely bathing there, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows;
having gone to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga and that of the high-souled Śuka,
a man does not meet with misfortune and purifies his lineage.
Then one should go to Śūrpāraka, which was frequented by the son of Jamadagni;
having bathed at Rāmatīrtha, a man shall obtain much gold.
Having bathed at Saptagodāvara, being self-restrained and restricted in diet, [one attains the same].
One attains great merit and goes to the world of the gods;
then, self-restrained and restricted in diet, one should proceed along the path of the gods,
whereby that man obtains the merit of a divine sacrifice.

Having reached the Tuṅga forest, the sage Sārasvata, a celibate who had conquered his senses, formerly taught the Vedas there. It was there that the son of the sage Aṅgiras [recovered] the Vedas that had been lost.
O Bhārata, he sat upon the upper garments of the great ṛṣis;
and by means of the syllable *oṃ*, properly and correctly uttered according to rule,
whatever each had previously practiced appeared before him.
There were the ṛṣis and the gods— Varuṇa, Agni, Prajāpati,
the god Hari Nārāyaṇa, and likewise Mahādeva—
as well as the illustrious Grandfather (Brahmā) of great splendor, together with the gods.

He appointed the highly effulgent Bhṛgu to perform the sacrifice. Then the blessed one duly performed for all those sages the re-establishment of their sacred fires according to the rites prescribed by rule.

O best of kings, having been duly gratified there with their portions of clarified butter, the gods and the sages departed for the three worlds at their pleasure. Then, O most excellent monarch, he entered that forest of Tuṅgaka.
All the evil of either a woman or a man is utterly destroyed;
there, O King, a wise man, self-restrained and restricted in his diet, should dwell for one month. Such a person goes to the world of Brahmā and purifies his lineage.
Having reached Medhāvikā, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
at that place, one should perform an ablution in the river Pāpapramocanī.
A celibate practitioner who has conquered his senses,
having fed the Brāhmaṇas,
attains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and gains memory and intelligence.
Then, having gone to the world-renowned mountain Kālañjara and bathed there in the Devahrada, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. O King,
one may perfect the self there on Mount Kālañjara.
A man shall be glorified in the heavenly world; of this there is no doubt.
Then, O lord of the people, having reached the Mandākinī river, which liberates one from sin, on Citrakūṭa, the best of excellent mountains.
Performing an ablution there, devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods,
one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and shall go to the supreme destination. From there, O king of kings, one should proceed to the unsurpassed Bhartṛsthāna.
O King, O best of men, wherever the god Mahāsena is ever present, a man achieves success merely by going there. By bathing at Koṭitīrtha, a man obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.

Then, O king of kings, the monarch intent on pilgrimage should proceed; he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows and a most abundant reward. Having performed a circumambulation, the man should go to Jyeṣṭhasthāna.
Having approached Mahādeva, he shines like the moon.
There, O great king, O bull of the Bharata race, is a famous well;
there the four oceans dwell, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having sipped water there, O Indra among kings, and having performed a circumambulation,
a man of self-restraint, purified, shall go to the supreme goal.
From there, O best of the Kurus, one should go to the great city of Śṛṅgaverapura.
O great king, at that very ford where Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, crossed in ancient times—
having bathed there, O mighty-armed one, a man is liberated from his sins. Furthermore,
a man who, being celibate and composed, bathes in the Gaṅgā...
He becomes cleansed of all evil and attains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Then, O lord of men, one should go to Muñjavaṭa, the abode of the wise deity;
having approached Mahādeva and worshipped him, [one gains great merit].
By circumambulating it clockwise, one attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas;
by bathing at that Tīrtha on the Jāhnavī, one is liberated from sins. From there, O Indra among kings, one should go to Prayāga, which is praised by the sages.
There, the gods headed by Brahmā, the quarters along with their presiding lords,
the world-protectors, the Sādhyas, the Nairṛtas, and likewise the Pitṛs,
as well as the supreme ṛṣis led by Sanatkumāra, [were present].
The Brahman-sages headed by Aṅgiras, as well as other [sages],
likewise the Nāgas, Suparṇas, Siddhas, and those who move in celestial chariots;
the rivers, the oceans, and the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
And the Lord Hari sits there, preceded by Prajāpati.
There are three sacrificial fire-pits there, in the midst of which flows the Jāhnavī,
having issued forth from Prayāga and honored by all sacred fords.
There, the daughter of the Sun, renowned throughout the three worlds,
the Yamunā, who purifies the world, joined with the Gaṅgā.
The region between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā is considered the hips of the Earth.
The sages know Prayāga to be the end of the hips and the lap;
likewise, Pratiṣṭhāna along with Kambala and Aśvatara,
as well as the tīrtha Bhogavatī, are declared to be the sacrificial altar of Prajāpati.
There, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the Vedas and the sacrifices, having taken embodied form,
wait upon Prajāpati, as do the sages of great vows;
likewise, O King, the gods and those who wander with the wheel perform sacrifices with ritual rites.

"Therefore, O Bhārata, there is nothing more meritorious than that in the three worlds; O Lord, Prayāga excels all other holy fords (tīrthas). By merely hearing of that sacred ford, or even by chanting its name,"
By touching even the earth there, a man is liberated from sin;
he who, firm in his vows, performs an ablution at that confluence,
obtains the merit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
For this is the sacrificial ground of the gods, highly honored even by them;
what is given there, O Bhārata, however minute it may be, becomes great.
It is not from the words of the Vedas, my dear, nor even from the words of the world [that this is known].
"Your mind should be set upon departing for Prayāga as the place of your death.
O joy of the Kurus, it is proclaimed that ten thousand holy sites (tīrthas) and another sixty crores are present right here."
Whatever merit lies in the knowledge of the four Vedas and whatever merit lies in those who speak the truth,
one obtains all that simply by bathing at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
There, moreover, is the supreme sacred site (tīrtha) of Vāsuki named Bhogavatī.
Whoever should perform an ablution there would obtain the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
There, O joy of the Kurus, is the tīrtha known as Haṃsaprapatana, renowned throughout the three worlds,
as well as Daśāśvamedhika on the Gaṅgā.
There is indeed a distinction at Kanakhala, and at Prayāga it is supremely great.
Even if one has committed a hundred forbidden acts, if one performs the ritual sprinkling with the Gaṅgā,
all of that the water of the Gaṅgā consumes, just as fire consumes fuel.
In the Kṛta age, all places are meritorious; in the Tretā age, Puṣkara is remembered [as the foremost];
in the Dvāpara age, Kurukṣetra; and in the Kali age, the Gaṅgā is remembered. One should perform austerities at Puṣkara and bestow gifts at Mahālaya.
On Mount Malaya one should enter the fire; on Bhrigutunga, one should undertake fasting unto death.
By bathing at Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra, the Gaṅgā, and in Magadha, a living being delivers seven generations of ancestors and likewise seven of descendants.
When her name is proclaimed, she purifies sin; when seen, she bestows well-being;
and when entered and drunk, she purifies one’s lineage unto the seventh generation—so long as a human’s bone touches the water of the Gaṅgā.

O King, that man is glorified in the heavenly world for as long as it takes to visit sacred fords and holy shrines; having worshipped them and acquired merit, he becomes a partaker of the realm of the immortals.
There is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā, and no god superior to Keśava;
there is nothing higher than the Brahmins—thus spoke the Grandfather (Brahmā). The Gaṅgā is equal to Kurukṣetra wherever one bathes in her.
O great king, wherever the Gaṅgā flows, that region is a forest for asceticism;
it should be known as a field of perfection (siddhakṣetra) situated upon the banks of the Gaṅgā.
This is the truth regarding the twice-born, the virtuous, and one's own son.
One should whisper into the ear of friends and of a devoted disciple:
"This is righteous; this is meritorious; this is pure; this is blissful;
this leads to heaven; this is delightful; this is the supreme purifier."
This secret of the great seers, which liberates one from all sins,
brings about stainless purity upon being studied in the midst of the twice-born;
it is glorious, conducive to heaven, meritorious, a subduer of rivals, and auspicious.
The recitation of the lineage of holy places (*tīrtha*) is indeed the supreme producer of intelligence.
A sonless man obtains a son, and one without wealth shall acquire riches. A king conquers the earth, and a merchant (*vaiśya*) attains wealth.

A Śūdra who recites this attains his desired objects, while a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas gains the same by reciting it. Furthermore, whoever constantly hears this merit-bestowing account of sacred fords, remaining ever pure,
shall remember many past births and rejoice upon the heights of heaven.
Those sacred fords that are accessible as well as those proclaimed to be inaccessible—
one should visit them mentally with the intent of beholding all sacred fords.
These [were frequented] by the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the Ādityas, the Maruts, and the Aśvins.
These places have been resorted to by sages who were like gods and who sought the fruits of their meritorious deeds.
Therefore, O Kauravya of noble vows, you too should go to these sacred fords according to this rule; being self-restrained, merit increases through merit.
Through previously cultivated causes, through faith, and through the study of the sacred scriptures,
those holy fords are reached by the virtuous who follow the example of the wise.
One should go together with the virtuous Brahmins who know the true meaning of the treatises.

O Kauravya, neither one who lacks vows, nor one of undisciplined soul, nor one who is impure, nor a thief, nor a man of crooked mind bathes in sacred fords; yet you, always observing right conduct and perceiving the true purpose of dharma, do so.
O dear one, your ancestors and all your great-grandfathers have been delivered;
O King, knower of dharma, the gods led by your grandfather, together with the hosts of sages, have been constantly gratified by your righteousness.
"And you shall indeed attain the worlds of the Vasus, O equal of Vāsava;
and, O Bhīṣma, you shall obtain great and eternal fame upon the earth.
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus and granted leave, the venerable rishi Pulastya,
being pleased with a joyful mind, vanished on that very spot.
And Bhīṣma, O tiger among the Kurus, was one who perceived the true meaning of the essence of the scriptures.
And at the word of Pulastya, he indeed traversed the earth.
Thus was this highly fortunate Tīrthayātrā established at Pratiṣṭhāna; it is of great merit and grants liberation from all sins.
Whoever shall travel across the earth according to this rule will enjoy,
after death, the foremost fruit of a hundred horse-sacrifices. And from this, O Pārtha, you shall obtain eightfold the highest dharma.

"O Bhīṣma, foremost of the Kurus, just as you obtained [merit] in the past, so too do you now; because you are the leader of the sages, the fruit for you is eightfold. O Bhārata, these sacred fords are infested by hosts of Rākṣasas."
O joy of the Kurus, there is no other way [to liberation] except through you. He who,
having risen at dawn, recites this account of the deeds of the divine sages, which encompasses the significance of all sacred fords, shall be liberated from all sins.
There, the foremost sages— Vālmīki, Kāśyapa,
Ātreya, Kauṇḍinya, Viśvāmitra, Gautama,
Asita, Devala, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Gālava— were always present.
Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha, and the sage Uddālaka;
Śaunaka with his son, and Vyāsa, the best among those who recite prayers; Durvāsas, the foremost of sages, and Gālava of great asceticism.
"All these excellent sages, whose wealth is their asceticism, are waiting for you;
accompanied by them, O great king, visit these sacred fords.
This indeed is the celestial sage named Lomaśa, of immeasurable splendor."
"He shall reunite with you; follow him, and together with me, O knower of dharma, visit these sacred fords. You shall attain great fame, just as King Mahābhiṣa did."
Just as the righteous-souled Yayāti and as King Purūravas,
so do you, O tiger among the Kurus, shine by your own dharma;
just as King Bhagīratha and the renowned Rāma.
In that way, you shine above all kings like the sun with its rays;
as Manu did, as Ikṣvāku did, as the highly illustrious Pūru did,
and as the immensely powerful Vainya did, so too are you renowned.
Just as in the past the slayer of Vṛtra,
the king of the gods, having utterly consumed all his rivals, protected the three worlds free from affliction,
so shall you, having brought about the destruction of your enemies, protect your subjects.
"O lotus-eyed one, having obtained the earth conquered through your own dharma,
you shall attain fame through righteousness just like Kārtavīryārjuna.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus consoled the king, the blessed seer Nārada,
taking leave of that high-souled one, vanished on the spot.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the righteous-souled one, likewise remained reflecting upon that very matter.
He reported to the sages the merit associated with visiting sacred fords (*tīrthayātrā*).
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having ascertained the opinion of his brothers and of the wise Nārada, [Dhṛtarāṣṭra]...
King Yudhiṣṭhira said to Dhaumya, who was like a grandfather:
"That tiger among men, Jishnu, of true prowess,
mighty-armed and immeasurable soul, has been sent away by me for the sake of obtaining celestial weapons."
For he is a hero, devoted and capable, O ascetic, skilled and exceedingly proficient in weapons, a lord like Vāsudeva himself. Indeed,
O Brahmin, I am the one who brought both these Kṛṣṇas, the destroyers of enemies, here.
I recognize that the valiant and majestic Vyāsa likewise knows these two lotus-eyed ones of the three ages, Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya;
Nārada also knows this, and he has always declared it to me.
Likewise, I too recognize the two sages, Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
thinking that he was capable, I dispatched Arjuna.
This son of a god, no inferior to Indra, is indeed capable of facing the lord of the gods.
Desiring to see and obtain celestial weapons from Indra, he was sent forth; meanwhile,
the two great car-warriors Bhīṣma and Droṇa, as well as Kṛpa and the invincible son of Droṇa—
those of mighty strength— were chosen by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra for battle.
All were knowers of the Vedas and heroes; likewise, all were skilled in the use of weapons.
All were renowned as great chariot-warriors (*mahāratha*), and all had overcome fatigue.
And there was one of great strength who constantly desired to fight with Pārtha.
And that Karna, the son of a Sūta and a great car-warrior skilled in celestial weapons—

[he who was] like a fire with the force of the wind from the speed of his horses, whose flames were arrows and whose roar was the slapping of his palms; he was a cloud of dust raised by the wind of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons, with the heat of his weapons as its scorching glow.
Like the fire at the end of a Yuga unleashed by Time, he will undoubtedly consume my army as if it were dry grass; fanned by the wind of Kṛṣṇa, he is a great cloud of divine weapons.
Bearing white horses like cranes, blazing with the *gāṇḍīva* bow as a rainbow,
this risen cloud that is Arjuna will extinguish the blazing fire of Karṇa with his constant showers of arrows in battle.
That conqueror of enemy cities, Bībhatsu, shall directly and in truth receive all the divine weapons from Śakra;
it is my firm conviction that he is more than a match for them all.

There is no counter-action for him; rather, his action is the counter-action against his enemies in battle. We shall all behold that son of Pāṇḍu, Dhanañjaya, who has mastered the weapons; for Bībhatsu does not falter when he has taken up a burden.
"O best of men, without that hero, we find no peace of mind in this Kāmyaka forest with Kṛṣṇā; therefore,
please lead us to another pure forest that abounds in food and fruit."
"Tell us of some delightful place frequented by those of meritorious deeds,
where we might dwell for some time and wait for the hero Arjuna, whose prowess is truth, as those longing for rain wait for a cloud."
"O Brahmin, tell us of various hermitages you have heard of from the twice-born, as well as lakes, rivers, and delightful mountains; for we find no pleasure in anything without that Arjuna."
"Let us dwell no longer in this Kāmyaka forest; let us go toward another direction.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Seeing all those Pāṇḍavas eager [to leave] and dejected in heart, he spoke.
Then Dhaumya, who was equal to Bṛhaspati, spoke to comfort them:
"O bull of the Bharatas, O King, listen as I describe to you the holy hermitages approved by Brahmins, as well as the quarters, sacred fords, and mountains."
O King, by hearing this as it is being recited, you shall indeed become free from grief;
O Lord of Men, together with Draupadī and your brothers,
and through the mere hearing of these [accounts], you, O Pāṇḍava, shall attain merit.

O best of men, O King Yudhiṣṭhira, having gone a hundredfold further from those very places toward the eastern direction in the past— frequented by hosts of royal sages— I shall describe that delightful region to you according to my memory.
O Bhārata, in that region frequented by divine sages is the place named Naimiṣa,
where there are various most meritorious tīrthas belonging to the gods; there also flows the holy and delightful Gomatī, which is resorted to by divine sages.

There is the sacrificial ground of the gods and the *śāmitra* altar of Vivasvat. On that [land] is the holy Gayā, the best of mountains, honored by royal sages, where the auspicious Brahmasaras is frequented by the celestial seers.
O tiger among men, for this purpose the ancients proclaim:
one should desire many sons, so that even if but one should go to Gayā,
or perform a horse sacrifice, or set free a dark-colored bull.
He delivers ten ancestors and ten descendants through his continuous lineage.
Right there is the Mahānadī river, as well as, O sinless one, Gayaśiras,
where that banyan tree known as Akṣayyakaraṇa is praised by the brahmins.
O Lord, where food offered to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible,
and where that great river named Phalgu with its holy waters flows,
and also the Kauśikī, O bull of the Bharatas, which abounds in roots and fruits.

03.085.009e Viśvāmitra, whose wealth was his asceticism, arrived at the place where he attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa. 03.085.010a There is the holy river Gaṅgā, upon whose bank, my dear, Bhagīratha performed many sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
O descendant of Kuru, they speak of Utpalāvata among the Pañcālas,
where Viśvāmitra, the son of Kuśika, performed a sacrifice together with Śakra; there,
the blessed son of Jamadagni likewise sang his lineage in verse.
Having witnessed that superhuman power of Viśvāmitra,
the descendant of Kuśika drank the *soma* together with Indra in Kanyakubja;
thereafter, he withdrew from the status of a *kṣatriya* and declared, "I am a *brāhmaṇa*."

O hero, [go to] the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, world-renowned, which is a purifier cherished by the seers, meritorious, sanctifying, and supreme; where in former times the Grandfather, the soul of all beings, performed sacrifice.
Therefore, O best of the Bharatas, it is renowned as Prayāga;
and there, O king of kings, is the great and excellent hermitage of Agastya,
which is likewise a forest of ascetics adorned with those who practice penance.
O King, Hiraṇyabindu is said to be on Mount Kālañjara;
O King, this auspicious and excellent mountain is more meritorious than all other mountains. O descendant of Kuru, there is also the mountain named Mahendra, belonging to the high-souled Bhārgava.
O son of Kuntī, it was there that the Grandfather performed sacrifice in ancient times;
where the holy Bhāgīrathī served as the sacrificial assembly hall, O Yudhiṣṭhira;
and where, O lord of people, that sacred place known as Brahmaśālā is situated.
It is crowded with those whose sins have been shaken off, and the sight of it is meritorious; it is pure, auspicious, renowned in the world as eternal,
and is the great and supreme hermitage of Mataṅga known as Kedāra.
The delightful mountain Kuṇḍoda abounds in roots, fruits, and water;
it was there that the thirsty Nala found both water and relief.
There also lies the beautiful Devavana, graced by ascetics.
O Great King, I have described to you the Bahudā river and the Nandā on the mountain peak,
as well as the sacred fords, rivers, mountains,
and holy sanctuaries located in the eastern direction.
Listen to me regarding the meritorious sacred fords (*tīrtha*) in the other three directions;
listen to my description of the sacred fords in those directions according to my understanding—
[including] rivers, mountains, and meritorious shrines.
Dhaumya said:
"O Bhārata, listen now to the meritorious tīrthas in the southern region,
as they are being described by me in detail according to my understanding, O Bhārata."
In that auspicious direction where the holy river Godāvarī is said to flow— abounding in groves, rich in water, frequented by ascetics,
and beautiful— and where both the Veṇṇā and Bhīmarathī rivers, which remove the fear of sin, are located.
O bull of the Bharatas, in that place crowded with deer and birds and adorned with the dwellings of ascetics, there flows the river Payoṣṇī belonging to the royal seer Nṛga—
a river of many waters and beautiful bathing-ghats, frequented by the twice-born.
Moreover, in this regard, the great yogi Mārkaṇḍeya, possessed of great ascetic power,
sang a genealogical verse concerning Nṛga, the lord of the earth:
"We have heard that it occurred before our very eyes while Nṛga was performing a sacrifice."
Indra was exhilarated by the Soma, and the twice-born were gratified by the sacrificial fees at the Payoṣṇī river,
at the supreme bathing-place (tīrtha) of Vārāha for the sacrificer—
whether it be drawn up from the earth or wafted there by the wind.
The water of the Payoṣṇī removes even the sins committed until the end of one's life. There,
where the stainless and lofty horn of the Trident-bearer rises above heaven,
a mortal, having beheld his own self-established [form], shall go to the city of Śiva.
On one side are all the rivers, including the Gaṅgā and others, with their vast accumulations of water;

on the other side is the holy Payoṣṇī, for she is considered by me to be superior even to all sacred fords (tīrthas). The Maruts are the attendants, and the celestial dwellers are the members of the sacrificial assembly.
The sacred grove of Māṭhara is auspicious and abounds in roots and fruits;
and there, O best of the Bharatas, is the sacrificial post on Mount Varuṇasrotasa. Likewise, on the northern side of the Praveṇī, is the holy hermitage of Kaṇva.

The forest retreats of the ascetics have been described according to the sacred tradition. O dear one, O Bhārata, there is the altar of the high-souled Jamadagni at Śūrpāraka, as well as the delightful Pāṣāṇatīrtha and Puraścandrā.
O son of Kuntī, among mortals there is Aśokatīrtha with its many hermitages;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, there is Agastyatīrtha and Vāruṇatīrtha among the Pāṇḍyas;
and, O bull among men, the sacred Kumārīs are said to be located in the Pāṇḍya country as well.
O son of Kuntī, I shall now describe the Tāmraparṇī; listen to it. It is there, O Bhārata, that the gods performed great austerities at the hermitage known throughout the three worlds as Gokarṇa.

O dear one, that lake is cool, abundant with water, meritorious, and auspicious; it is extremely difficult for men of undisciplined souls to reach. Right there, the fire of *tṛṇasoma* abounds with fruits and roots.
On Mount Devasabha is the holy hermitage of Agastya’s disciple; there stands the glorious Vaiḍūrya mountain, auspicious and composed of jewels,
as well as the hermitage of Agastya itself, abounding in roots, fruits, and water.
O lord of men, I shall also describe the meritorious shrines, hermitages, rivers, mountains, and lakes in Surāṣṭra; for there, O brahmins, they speak of the ritual immersion in the *camasa* vessel.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, there is also the Prabhāsa tīrtha on the ocean, the resort of the thirty gods;
there is the auspicious Piṇḍāraka, frequented by ascetics,
and the great mountain peak Ujjayanta, which swiftly bestows success.
In this regard, O Yudhiṣṭhira, listen to an ancient verse recited by Nārada, the most excellent of celestial sages:
"On a sacred mountain in the Surāṣṭra region, frequented by beasts and birds..."
Having performed austerities at Ujjayanta, he is honored in the vault of heaven;
this glorious Nārāyaṇa, whose abode is the Ocean of Milk,
has left his serpent-couch and come to the city of Mathurā.
03.086.021a Blessed is Dvāravatī, where Madhusūdana resides;

for he is the ancient God in person, for he is the eternal Dharma. 03.086.022a Those Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas, and those people who are knowers of the supreme self (adhyātma), [regard it as such].
They speak of the high-souled Kṛṣṇa as the eternal Dharma;
for Govinda is said to be the supreme purifier among all purifiers. Blessed Viṣṇu is auspiciousness, and Madhusūdana is auspiciousness.
Auspicious is the lotus-eyed one; auspicious is he whose banner bears Garuḍa. He is the most meritorious even among merits, and the auspiciousness among all things auspicious.
The lotus-eyed one is the eternal God of gods of the three worlds.
The immutable Self, the Great Soul, the Knower of the Field, the Supreme Lord—
Hari, the inconceivable Madhusūdana, dwells right there.
Dhaumya said:
In the western direction, indeed, among the Avantis, I shall describe to you those sacred and meritorious shrines that are located there—
[lands] endowed with groves of *priyaṅgu* and mango trees, and garlanded with thickets of reeds.
O Bhārata, there flows the holy river Narmadā, whose current runs toward the sea.

Whatever sacred fords (*tīrtha*), holy shrines (*āyatana*), rivers, forests, and great mountains exist in the three worlds, as well as the gods together with Pitāmaha (Brahmā), [are all present there].

O best of the Kurus, O Bhārata, on the Narmadā, together with Siddhas, Ṛṣis, and Cāraṇas, they always come to bathe in the waters for the sake of a flood of merit. There, the holy abode of the sage Viśravas is renowned.
There, on the auspicious and holy Vaidūryaśikhara, the best of mountains, Kubera, the lord of wealth who is borne by men, was born;
there the trees bear divine flowers and fruits and possess green foliage.
On the peak of that mountain, O King, there is a lake belonging to that wise one, filled with blossoming lotuses and frequented by gods and Gandharvas;
many wonders, O great king, are seen there upon that mountain.

O conqueror of enemy cities, there is a river belonging to that royal seer, possessing auspicious bathing places and flowing with pools; it is meritorious, divine, resembling heaven, and eternally frequented by celestial sages. It is the holy Pārā, known as the Viśvāmitra-nadī.
On its bank, in the midst of the virtuous, Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, fell; yet he regained the worlds and the eternal dharmas. There, O dear one, are the Puṇyahrada lake and Mount Maināka.
O hero, Yudhiṣṭhira, there is a mountain named Asita, abounding in roots and fruits; there, O Pāṇḍava, is the meritorious hermitage of Kakṣasena,
and the hermitage of Cyavana, which is famous everywhere.
O Lord, there men achieve success through even slight austerity.
O Great King, that is the Jambūmārga hermitage of the sages of purified souls, O best of those who seek peace, which is filled with multitudes of deer and birds.
Then, O King, there is Ketumāla, which is most meritorious and constantly filled with ascetics; and Medhyā, O lord of the earth; and Gaṅgāraṇya;
and the famous and holy Saindhavāraṇya, frequented by the twice-born.
O Bhārata, there is the sacred lake of the Grandfather named Puṣkara,
a beloved hermitage of the Vaikhānasa Siddhas and Ṛṣis;
even Prajāpati sang here for the sake of praise.
O best of the Kurus, O foremost of the virtuous, regarding Puṣkara, there is this verse:
"Even for a wise man who merely desires Puṣkara in his mind,
his sins are utterly destroyed, and he rejoices in the vault of heaven."
Dhaumya said:
O tiger among kings, I shall proclaim to you those meritorious places and sacred shrines that truly exist in the northern direction.
Listen attentively, O Lord, as I speak;
O Hero, receiving my discourse generates auspicious faith.
Sarasvatī is a purifier, possessing pools and garlanded with forests.
O Pāṇḍava, where the Yamunā flows with great speed toward the ocean,
there is the most holy and auspicious tirtha called Plakṣāvataraṇa,
where the twice-born, having performed sacrifices to Sarasvatī, go for their ritual ablutions.
O sinless one, the divine and auspicious Puṇya is called Agniśiras,
where Sahadeva performed sacrifice by the throw of a *śamyā*, O Bhārata;
and it is for this very purpose, Yudhiṣṭhira, that this song of Indra is sung.
This verse circulates in this world, being sung by the twice-born:
"The sacrificial fires kindled along the Yamunā by Sahadeva—
those hundreds of hundreds of thousands [of fires] for which hundreds of thousands were given as sacrificial fees."
In that very place, King Bharata, the highly illustrious universal monarch (*cakravartin*), performed twenty-seven horse-sacrifices (*hayamedha*).
He was one who fulfilled the desires of the twice-born; this, dear one, I have heard in the past.
The hermitage there is exceedingly meritorious, and its lake is renowned as Sāraka. O Pārtha, the river Sarasvatī is constantly honored by the virtuous;
it is there, O great king, that the Vālakhilya rishis performed sacrifices in ancient times.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, there the Dṛṣadvatī is renowned as most meritorious; and there,
O best of men, is the Pāñcālya named Nyagrodha, who is called "Meritorious," along with Dālbhyaghoṣa and the high-souled Dālbhya, who dwells upon the earth.
O son of Kuntī, the hermitage of that one of infinite fame, of excellent vows, and immeasurable power, is known as holy and renowned throughout the three worlds.
There, O lord of men, are the two most meritorious [sages], Vaivarṇya and Varṇa.

O best of the Bharatas, both of them were knowers of the Vedas, recognized by the Vedas, and masters of both knowledge and the Vedas; they constantly performed meritorious sacrifices with ritual offerings. In ancient times, the gods, including Indra and Varuṇa, met with them on many occasions.

At Viśākhayūpa they performed austerities; therefore, that place is indeed most meritorious. There, the great seer Jamadagni—highly fortunate and of great renown—the subduer, offered sacrifice upon the holy and delightful Palāśaka trees.
There, all the best of rivers, having brought their respective waters, stood surrounding that most excellent of sages in person; and there,
O Great King, Viśvāvasu himself sang.
O hero, having witnessed this verse and the prowess of that high-souled one as he was sacrificing to the gods,
all the rivers arrived and gratified him with honey.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, at Gaṅgādvāra, the Gaṅgā swiftly broke through that mountain— the best of all peaks— which was adorned by Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Apsarases, and which served as the abode of Kirātas and Kiṃnaras.
O King, that merit-bestowing place is renowned as being frequented by hosts of Brahman-sages; likewise, O Kauravya, there is the holy Kanakhala where Sanatkumāra dwells,
and the mountain named Puru, where Purūravas was born.
O King, where Bhṛgu performed his austerities, attended by hosts of great sages— that great mountain is known as the hermitage of Bhṛgutuṅga.
And whatever has been, whatever is to be, and whatever is now, O bull among men, [all that is there].
Nārāyaṇa, the Lord Viṣṇu, the eternal Supreme Person—
near his highly illustrious and holy Badarī, which is vast,
there is a sacred hermitage renowned and celebrated throughout the three worlds.
O King, along the wide Badarī, there flows the Gaṅgā carrying warm water and another carrying cool water, with sands of gold,
where the highly fortunate and immensely powerful ṛṣis and gods dwell.
Having reached that place, they eternally pay homage to the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Wherever the divine Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Supreme Self, resides, O Pārtha, there lies the entire world, as well as all sacred fords and sanctuaries.
That is merit, that is the Supreme Brahman, that is the sacred ford, that is the forest of asceticism;
that is the supreme, highest God, the Lord of lords of beings,
the eternal, the ultimate, the Sustainer, and the Supreme Goal.
Knowing which, the wise who possess the vision of the scriptures do not grieve; there dwell the celestial seers, the perfected ones, and all those whose wealth is austerity,
where the primordial god, the great yogi Madhusūdana, resides.
That merit is even greater than other merits; let there be no doubt in you regarding this.
O King, lord of the earth, these meritorious tīrthas and shrines on earth have been proclaimed, O best of men.
These [tirthas] have been frequented by the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the Ādityas, the Maruts, the Aśvins,
and by high-souled ṛṣis who are equal to Brahmā. Wandering through these, O son of Kuntī, together with the foremost of Brahmin ṛṣis.
"And with your highly fortunate brothers, you shall cast off your longing.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O descendant of Kuru, while Dhaumya was thus speaking..."
Then the rishi Lomaśa, possessed of great splendor, arrived there.
The king, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, together with his followers and those brahmins,
rose to greet that illustrious man, just as the immortals rise in heaven for Śakra.

Having honored him according to custom, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, asked the reason for his arrival and the purpose of his journey. Thus questioned by the son of Pāṇḍu, the high-minded one was filled with joy.
He spoke in gentle words, as if gladdening the Pāṇḍavas:
"O son of Kuntī, I wander through all the worlds at will;
having gone to the abode of Śakra, I beheld there the Lord of the Gods."
And there I saw your heroic brother, Savyasācin,
seated upon half of Śakra’s throne; O tiger among men, seeing Pārtha in such a state, great was my wonder.

"There the Lord of the Gods said to me, 'Go to the sons of Pāṇḍu. Thus, at the command of Puruhūta and the high-souled Pārtha, I have come here swiftly, desiring to see you along with your younger brothers."
"I shall tell you something pleasing, my dear son, O delighter of the Pāṇḍavas.
Together with your brothers and Kṛṣṇā, O King, listen to that,
since you, O bull among the Pāṇḍavas, requested the mighty-armed one for the sake of weapons."
That great and peerless weapon was obtained by Pārtha from Rudra;
that which is named Brahmashiras, acquired through ascetic penance from Rudra,
that fierce weapon risen from the nectar of immortality was obtained by Savyasācin.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, descendant of Kuru, he [received] that thunderbolt along with other weapons such as the staff (daṇḍa), together with their mantras, methods of withdrawal, expiations, and auspicious rites,
from Yama, Kubera, Varuṇa, and Indra.
Pārtha, of immeasurable prowess, studied celestial weapons;
and from the son of Viśvāvasu, he duly and according to the prescribed rules mastered singing, dancing, the Sāman chants, and instrumental music.

Thus, having mastered the science of weapons and acquired the Gāndharva Veda, Bībhatsu— the son of Kuntī and the youngest brother of your younger brother— dwells in happiness. This is for the purpose of which the best of the gods spoke these words to me.
And I shall tell you that; listen to me, Yudhiṣṭhira.
You will go to the world of men, of this there is no doubt.
O best of the twice-born, speak there to Yudhiṣṭhira these words on my behalf.
"Your brother Arjuna, having mastered the weapons, will soon return after having accomplished a great task for the gods that was impossible even for the inhabitants of heaven to achieve. Meanwhile,
you, together with your brothers, should devote yourselves to ascetic penance."

Indeed, there is nothing superior to austerity; through austerity one attains greatness. And I know Karṇa as he truly is, O bull of the Bharatas—he who is true to his word, possessed of great energy, great heroism, and great strength.
Unequaled in great battles, skilled in great warfare, a heroic wielder of the great bow, a master of mighty weapons, of excellent complexion,
resembling the son of Maheśvara, the lordly son of the Sun.

Likewise, that mass of knowledge and innate, formidable prowess does not equal even a sixteenth part of Pārtha in battle. And as for that fear which dwells in your mind because of him, O subduer of enemies—
And I shall take that back as well once Savyasācin has arrived here.
