Furthermore, O hero, regarding whatever is in your mind concerning this pilgrimage to the sacred fords (tīrthayātrā),
Lomaśa will undoubtedly tell you all of it.
"O Bhārata, whatever fruit associated with asceticism may be found in sacred fords,
that which this great seer declares should be accepted as unerring.
Lomaśa said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, listen also to what Dhanañjaya said:
'Unite my brother Yudhiṣṭhira with the glory of righteousness, for you, O one whose wealth is asceticism, know the supreme laws of dharma and the various forms of austerity.'"
"You know the eternal dharma of illustrious kings; therefore,
you should endow this Pāṇḍava with that supreme purifier which you know exists for men, through the merit of sacred fords."
"Just as that king should visit sacred fords and give away cows,
so must he act with his whole soul"— this is what Vijaya said to me.
Protected by you, he shall travel to all the sacred fords in every direction.
He must be protected from the *rākṣasas* in difficult and treacherous places,
just as Dadhīca protected Devendra and Aṅgiras protected Ravi;
likewise, O best of the twice-born, protect the son of Kuntī from the *rākṣasas*.
"For there are many *yātudhānas* and *rākṣasas*, as large as mountains;
protected by you, they shall not overcome the sons of Kuntī even from nearby.
Thus, at the word of Indra and by the command of Arjuna, I [have come].
"O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, I have come to you; perform meritorious deeds! Protecting you from all dangers, I shall travel with you.
O joy of the Kurus, the sacred fords have already been visited by me twice before."

"This is the third time I shall behold those very same [sages] together with you, O Yudhiṣṭhira. This pilgrimage to the sacred fords (tīrthayātrā), which removes all fear, was undertaken by royal sages who performed meritorious deeds, such as Manu and others, O Great King."

O Kauravya, neither the crooked, nor one of undisciplined soul, nor the ignorant, nor the evildoer bathes in sacred fords, nor does a man of devious mind. But you, O knower of dharma, are always righteous-minded, a knower of dharma, and true to your promise.
"Released from all sins, you shall become even more so than King Bhagīratha, or kings such as Gaya and others;
just as Yayāti was, O son of Kuntī, so too shall you be, O Pāṇḍava."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Out of joy, I cannot find anywhere an answer to these words;
for whom indeed would the King of the Gods remember—what could possibly be superior to him?"
Who indeed could be superior to him who has you as his companion, whose brother is Dhanañjaya,
and whom Vāsava remembers?
And as for what the Blessed One has said to me regarding the visiting of sacred fords (tīrthas)—

"By the word of Dhaumya, this resolve was already made by me previously. Therefore, O Brahmin, whenever you deem it time for our departure to visit the sacred fords, I shall go then; this is my firm and supreme determination."
Vaiśampāyana said:
To that Pāṇḍava who had resolved upon departing, Lomaśa said:
"Be light, O great king; being light, you shall travel at your own will."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Let those Brāhmaṇas who subsist on alms and those ascetics turn back,
for they are unable to endure the afflictions of hunger, thirst, fatigue from the road, exhaustion, and cold."
May all those twice-born ones who eat delicacies turn back; may all those who crave cooked foods, syrups, drinks, and meats,
as well as those who follow after the cooks, likewise turn back.
I have provided for them as is fitting with livelihoods and means of subsistence; let those citizens who have followed me, led by their devotion to the king,
also go to the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

He will grant at the proper time whatever wages are appropriate for each of you. If that lord of men should fail to provide the livelihood due to you, the King of Pañcāla will grant it to you for the sake of our dear interests and welfare.
03.090.022 Vaiśampāyana said: 03.090.022a Then, for the most part, the citizens, burdened by heavy sorrow, as well as disciplined brahmins and ascetics, departed toward Nāgapura.

Out of affection for the King of Dharma, the king who was the son of Ambikā received all of them according to the prescribed rites and gratified them with wealth. Then the king, the son of Kuntī, together with the young Brahmins—
And being well-pleased with Lomaśa, he dwelt for three nights in the Kāmyaka forest.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, as the son of Kuntī was departing, the Brahmins dwelling in the forest [followed him].
Having approached him then, O King, they spoke these words:
"O King, you shall go with your brothers to the sacred fords,
accompanied by the high-souled celestial seer Lomaśa."
"O Great King, O Pāṇḍava, you ought to lead us as well;
for without you, O Kaurava, those difficult and rugged passes infested with beasts of prey could not be traversed by us."
"O lord of men, these sacred fords (*tīrthas*) are inaccessible to men of little strength.
You are brave brothers, always the best among archers;
protected by you heroes, we too shall go."

"Indeed, through your grace, O protector of the earth, lord of the people, we shall obtain the auspicious fruit of sacred fords and religious vows. Protected by your prowess, purified, and bathed in the holy waters, [we shall attain our goal]."
"O King, by visiting these sacred fords (*tīrtha*), may we become cleansed of sin.
You too, O Bhārata, [have visited] those of the lord of men Kārtavīrya,
as well as those of the royal seer Aṣṭaka and Lomapāda."

O King, having bathed in sacred fords, you will surely attain those worlds so difficult to reach— having visited the holy sites beginning with Prabhāsa and the mountains beginning with Mahendra— as well as the realms of the heroic universal monarch Bharata.
"O protector of the earth, we wish to see the Gaṅgā and other rivers, as well as the Plakṣa and other great trees, together with you;
for the sacred fords and shrines have been protected by you heroes."
"O lord of men, if you have any affection for the Brahmins, quickly carry out our word; thereby you shall attain the highest good.
For, O mighty-armed one, the sacred fords are always [beset] by those who create obstacles to asceticism."
They are infested by *rakṣasas*; you ought to protect us from them.
O Indra among kings, the holy fords (*tīrthas*) have been described by Dhaumya, by the wise Nārada, and by the celestial sage Parvata.
O lord of men, travel according to the prescribed rites to all those places which the celestial seer Lomaśa, of great ascetic merit, has described; and,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, visit in their entirety the rivers frequented by sages.
His sins shaken off and protected by us as well as by Lomaśa,
he was thus honored by them; surrounded by his heroic brothers, Bhīmasena and the others, he was overwhelmed with tears of joy.
"So be it," said that bull among the Pāṇḍavas to all those sages. Having taken leave of Lomaśa and his domestic priest Dhaumya,
that self-controlled best of the Pāṇḍavas then set out together with his brothers.
And Draupadī, of faultless limbs, set her mind upon departing.
Then the highly blessed Vyāsa, as well as Nārada and Parvata—
those wise ones— arrived at Kāmyaka to see the Pāṇḍava.
King Yudhiṣṭhira paid them honor according to the prescribed rites.
Having been thus honored, those illustrious ones then spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, O Bhīma, and you twins, practice uprightness in your minds."
"Having indeed performed purification through the mind, go to the sacred fords pure;
for the Brahmins say that the restraint of the body is a human vow,
while the twice-born say that a purified mind and intellect constitute a divine vow."
"O lord of men, for heroes whose minds are undisturbed, this alone is sufficient.
Establishing yourselves in a mind of loving-kindness, go to the sacred fords purified. You, being pure in your thoughts through vows of bodily restraint,"

"By undertaking this divine vow as prescribed, you shall obtain the fruit thereof. Having promised "So be it," the Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇā, all performed the rites for auspiciousness by the sages, both celestial and human.
Having clasped the feet of Lomaśa, Dvaipāyana,
Nārada, O king of kings, and the celestial ṛṣi Parvata,
those heroes, together with Dhaumya and other forest-dwellers, [proceeded].
When the month of Mārgaśīrṣa had passed, they set out from there under the asterism Puṣya;
taking up their ascetic gear, wearing rags, skins, and matted hair,
and equipped with impenetrable armor, they then wandered among the sacred fords.
Accompanied by Indrasena and other servants with fourteen chariots, as well as others occupied with the kitchen and various attendants,
they were equipped with weapons, their swords girded, and possessed of quivers and arrows.
O Janamejaya, facing the east, the heroic Pāṇḍavas set forth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of divine sages, I do not consider myself to be devoid of merit."
I am thus tormented by suffering as no other lord of the earth;
I consider others to be devoid of virtue and not even devoted to dharma. And yet, O Lomaśa, by what sign do they prosper in this world?
Lomaśa said:
"O King, O Pārtha, you should not feel any sorrow whatsoever on this account,
that people who delight in unrighteousness should prosper through unrighteous means."
A man prospers through unrighteousness and for a time beholds auspicious things;
he then conquers his rivals, but finally perishes along with his very roots— O best of kings, this is how kings flourish through righteousness.
They oppress all their rivals, and their kingdom increases.
For I have seen, O lord of the earth, that even the Daityas and Dānavas,
though they grew great through unrighteousness, eventually met their destruction.
O Lord, all this was witnessed by me long ago in the age of the gods: the gods delighted in righteousness, while the asuras abandoned righteousness;
the gods entered sacred fords, whereas the asuras did not enter them, O Bhārata.
Arrogance first entered those doers of unrighteousness;
from arrogance pride arose, and from pride anger was born. From anger came shamelessness, and from that, lack of modesty; thus their virtuous conduct perished.
Then, because they were shameless, devoid of modesty, of base conduct, and their vows were in vain,
Fortune, Prosperity, and Dharma soon abandoned them.
O King, Fortune went to the gods, while Misfortune went to the asuras.
Then Kali also entered those Daityas and Dānavas who were possessed by misfortune and whose minds were struck down by pride. Thus,
those Dānavas were possessed both by misfortune and by Kali.
O son of Kuntī, for those who were overcome by pride, devoid of ritual action, senseless,
and overwhelmed by arrogance, destruction arrived before long;
thus the Daityas, stripped of their glory, went to total ruin.
O King, those who take pleasure in unrighteousness are possessed by misfortune; whereas the gods, being virtuous in character, resort to the oceans, rivers, lakes,
and sacred shrines.
O Pāṇḍava, by means of austerities, sacrifices, gifts, and blessings,
they abandoned all their sins and attained the highest good.
For thus, those who are generous and perform their duties in every way [attain this].
The gods went to the sacred fords (tīrthas) and thereby attained supreme prosperity;
likewise, O Indra among kings, you too, having bathed in the sacred fords along with your younger brothers, shall regain that fortune. This is the eternal path.
For just as King Nṛga, Śibi the son of Uśīnara,
Bhagīratha, Vasumanas, Gaya, Pūru, and Purūravas— these,
constantly practicing austerity, [attained their goals] through the contact with water; ||| 03,092.017a–03,092.018a ||| so too did they.
O lord of the people, by visiting sacred fords and by beholding great-souled beings,
they attained fame, merit, and wealth;
likewise, O Indra among kings, you too have obtained vast prosperity.
Just as Ikṣvāku moved about with his sons, people, and kinsmen,
and as Mucukunda, Māndhātṛ, and King Marutta likewise attained holy fame through the power of their asceticism, so too did the gods.
The celestial sages know this in its entirety, and you too shall come to know it;
however, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, being overcome by pride and delusion,
will before long perish like the Daityas— of this there is no doubt.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O protector of the earth, those heroes, dwelling together here and there in that manner, eventually arrived at the Naimiṣa forest in due course.
Then, O King, having performed their ablutions at the sacred fords of the Gomatī, the Pāṇḍavas gave away cattle and wealth, O Bhārata; and there,
they repeatedly gratified the gods, the ancestors, and the brahmins.
O protector of the earth, at Kanyātīrtha, Aśvatīrtha, and Gavāṃtīrtha,
as well as at Vālakoṭi and having stayed on Mount Vṛṣaprastha, all the Pāṇḍavas performed their ablutions in the Bāhudā river.
O lord of the earth, at Prayāga, the sacrificial ground of the gods,
they bathed their limbs and performed supreme austerities;
those who were true to their vows stayed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.

Free from sin and high-souled, they bestowed wealth upon the learned brahmins. Then, O King, descendant of Bharata, the sons of Pāṇḍu, together with the brahmins, proceeded to the sacrificial altar of Prajāpati, which was frequented by ascetics.
There those heroes dwelt and performed supreme austerities,
constantly gratifying the twice-born with offerings of forest produce.
Then they went to the mountain honored by the knower of dharma.
By the royal seer Gaya, a performer of meritorious deeds and one of incomparable splendor,
[was established] the lake Gayaśiras, where there is also the holy Mahānadī river—
the lovely Vānīramālinī, adorned with sandbanks.
The divine Pavitrakūṭa, which supports the sacred earth; that most meritorious holy ford (tīrtha), frequented by sages, the supreme Brahmasaras,
where the venerable Agastya went toward Vaivasvata.
And he dwelt there himself, O King, where eternal Dharma resides;
it is the source, O Lord of Men, of all rivers,
where Mahādeva, the wielder of the Pināka bow, is eternally present.
There those heroic Pāṇḍavas performed the Cāturmāsya sacrifices with a great sacrifice of the sages at the site of the Great Akṣayavaṭa, where,
in that imperishable sacrificial ground of the gods, the fruit is indeed inexhaustible.
With resolute minds, they observed fasts there;
hundreds of Brahmins, rich in asceticism, gathered at that place and then performed the Cāturmāsya sacrifice according to the Ṛṣi’s ritual injunction.

There, the Brahmins— constant in sacred knowledge and austerity, masters of the Vedas, and seated in the assembly— uttered holy discourses concerning those great-souled ones. There, one who had performed the ceremonial bath upon completing his studies and remained steadfast in the vow of lifelong celibacy (kaumāra-vrata) [was present].
Śamaṭha said: "O King, [I shall tell you of] Gaya Āmūrtarayasa.
The son of Āmūrtarayasa was Gaya, the most excellent of royal sages.
O Bhārata, listen to me as I recount his meritorious deeds."
O King, he whose sacrifice took place here was one of abundant food and many sacrificial fees; there were mountains of food by the hundreds and thousands,
as well as hundreds of streams of clarified butter and rivers of curd.
Thousands of streams of highly precious condiments were given day after day to those who requested them;
furthermore, O King, the brahmins ate other food that was exquisitely prepared.
There, at the time of the sacrificial gifts, the sound of the Vedic recitation reached the heavens;
O Bhārata, nothing else could be discerned because of that sound of the Vedas.
O King, as that merit spread, it pervaded the earth, the quarters, the sky, and the atmosphere.
It was filled with sound, and that too was a great marvel. There,
O bull of the Bharatas, men sang songs,
radiant and satisfied with excellent food and drink in every region.
"Who today at Gaya’s sacrifice desires to eat living beings,
where twenty-five mountains remain as leftovers from the meal?
Such things former men have not done, nor will others do them hereafter."
When the royal seer Gaya of immeasurable splendor performed his sacrifice,
how indeed were the gods so thoroughly satiated by the oblation of Gaya that they would be able to accept any offerings whatsoever given by others?
Just as the grains of sand in the world, or the stars in the sky,
or the drops of rain falling from a cloud cannot be numbered by anyone,
so too can the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) at Gaya’s sacrifice not be counted.
"O descendant of Kuru, such [beings] were very numerous at the sacrifice of that high-souled one near this lake.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then King Kaunteya, who bestows abundant sacrificial fees, set forth;
having reached the hermitage of Agastya, he dwelt at Durjayā. There, the king, the best among speakers, questioned Lomaśa.
For what reason was Vātāpi subdued here by Agastya? What was the power of that Daitya, the destroyer of men?
And for what reason did anger arise in the high-souled Agastya?
Lomaśa said:
"O joy of the Kurus, in ancient times there was a Daitya named Ilvala in the city of Maṇimatī, and Vātāpi was his younger brother."
The son of Diti spoke to that Brahmin endowed with ascetic power:
"May your holiness grant me one son equal to Indra.
But that Brahmin did not grant him a son comparable to Vāsava.

Then that asura became violently enraged at the brāhmaṇa. From that time forward, O king of kings, that best of asuras, full of wrath and possessed of illusory power, transformed his brother into a goat.
And Vātāpi, assuming the form of a ram, could take any shape at will in an instant;
having prepared him, he would feed him to the brahmins, desiring to kill them.
He would summon with his voice anyone who had gone to the abode of Vaivasvata.
Having resumed his body, he was seen alive once again.
Then, having prepared the Asura Vātāpi in the form of a well-cooked goat and having fed him to that Brāhmaṇa, he summoned him back once more.
Having heard those words uttered by the great Ilvala in a loud voice, the powerful and highly illusory Atimāya, that thorn to the Brāhmaṇas,
quickly pierced the side of that Brāhmaṇa, the great Asura.
O King, lord of the people, Vātāpi emerged laughing.
O King, having thus fed the Brahmins again and again,
that evil-minded Daitya Ilvala caused them to be destroyed.
And at that very time, the venerable Agastya beheld the ancestors hanging head-downwards in a pit. He asked those who were hanging there, "For what purpose are you here?"
"For what purpose are you hanging here head-downwards in this pit? they asked. Those expounders of the Veda replied to him: "We are your own ancestors."
"Having reached this pit, we hang here, longing for offspring. If you would beget for us an excellent child of Agastya,
there would be our liberation from this hell, and you too would attain the supreme goal through a son."
The radiant one, devoted to truth and righteousness, said to them:
"O fathers, I shall fulfill your desire; let the fever of your minds depart.
And then he begot an excellent descendant of Bharata.
And his ancestors, O King, obtained the worlds they desired.
Then the venerable seer, reflecting upon the continuity of his progeny,
saw no woman worthy of him for the sake of bearing his offspring.
For the seer named Pratapa, having bestowed an excellent boon,
gathered together the most preeminent limbs of various beings and, with those corresponding parts, fashioned a supreme woman.
The sage of great asceticism gave her, whom he had created for his own purpose, to the King of Vidarbha, who was longing for a son;
there that fortunate woman was born like a flash of lightning from the clouds.
Radiant with beauty, the fair-faced girl grew up.
O Bhārata, upon seeing her as soon as she was born, the King of Vidarbha, the lord of the earth,
announced it to the twice-born with great joy.
O lord of the earth, all those brahmins rejoiced;
and those twice-born ones gave her the name Lopāmudrā.
O great king, she grew up, possessing a most excellent form.
Like a blue lotus in the water, or like the beautiful flame of a fire,
she was radiant; O Indra among kings, when she reached her youth, one hundred well-adorned maidens and a hundred female slaves attended upon that auspicious lady, obedient to her will.
Surrounded by a hundred female servants and in the midst of a hundred maidens,
that radiant girl sat like Rohiṇī in the sky, O Lord;
and though she had reached the prime of youth, she was endowed with excellent character and conduct.
No man dared to refuse her out of fear of that great-souled one.
That maiden Satyavatī, who surpassed even the Apsarases in beauty,
pleased her father as well as her own kin with her virtuous character.
Seeing the young Vaidarbhī thus endowed with such qualities, her father reflected in his mind, "To whom shall I give my daughter?
Lomaśa said:
When Agastya considered her capable of the life of a householder,
he approached the King of Vidarbha, the lord of the earth, and said:
"O King, my mind is set upon marriage for the sake of obtaining a son."
"I choose you, O protector of the earth; grant Lopāmudrā to me.
Thus addressed by the sage, the protector of the earth was bewildered;
he was unable to refuse, yet he did not wish to give her away.
Then that lord of the earth, having approached his wife, said:
"This powerful great seer, being enraged, might consume us with the fire of his curse.
Seeing the lord of the earth thus distressed along with his wife, [the sage spoke].
Approaching him at that time, Lopāmudrā spoke these words:
"O protector of the earth, you ought not to undergo suffering on my account.
Give me to Agastya; save yourself through me, O father."

At the word of his daughter, O lord of the people, that king then gave Lopāmudrā to the high-souled Agastya according to the prescribed rites. Having obtained Lopāmudrā as his wife, Agastya addressed her.
"Cast off these costly garments and ornaments. Then she,
whose thighs were like plantain stalks and whose eyes were long, cast away those beautiful, precious, and fine garments.
Then she took up rags, bark garments, and deerskins; and the large-eyed lady undertook the practice of the same vows as his.
Then the venerable and most excellent of sages arrived at Gaṅgādvāra.
He undertook severe asceticism together with his devoted wife;
out of love and great respect, she then attended to her husband.
And the lord Agastya felt the highest affection for his wife.

Then, after a long time had passed, O lord of the people, the venerable Ṛṣi beheld Lopāmudrā, radiant with asceticism, having just bathed. He was moved by her service, her purity, and her self-restraint.
Delighted by her splendor and beauty, he summoned her for sexual union.
Then that beautiful woman, with palms joined in reverence and appearing somewhat bashful,
spoke these affectionate words to the Blessed One.
"Without doubt, a husband took a wife for the sake of offspring;
O sage, you ought to perform that same pleasure toward me which I feel for you.
O Brahmin, just as I had a bed in my father’s palace,"
Upon such a bed as this, you ought to come to me;
I desire to approach you, adorned with garlands and ornaments,
as you yourself are adorned with celestial jewels according to your pleasure.
"Otherwise, I would not have appeared here wearing bark and saffron robes;
O brahmin-sage, this ornament is by no means impure.
Agastya said:
"O Lopāmudrā, O beautiful one of slender waist, truly there are no riches with me such as those which belong to your father, O blessed lady. Lopāmudrā said:
"O Lord, you are the master here to withdraw everything by means of your ascetic power—
whatever wealth exists in the world of living beings in even a single moment.
Agastya said:
"It is exactly as you have said; however, it causes the depletion of my ascetic merit (*tapas*). Therefore, impel me in such a way that my ascetic merit may not be destroyed.
Lopāmudrā said:
"O ascetic, very little time remains of my season;
I do not wish to approach you in any other way whatsoever,
nor do I wish to violate your dharma, O ascetic."
"You ought to fulfill this for me according to my desire.
Agastya said:
"O blessed lady, if this desire has been firmly resolved by your mind..."
"O destroyer of my Dharma!
If this desired pleasure has been obtained, I shall practice the Dharma as it was seen and as I remember it."
"Come now, I shall depart, O blessed lady; remain here and do as you wish.
Lomaśa said:
"Then, O descendant of Kuru, that Agastya went away to beg for wealth."
Śrutarvāṇa, the protector of the earth, whom the kings considered superior even to the Vedas—
that monarch, having learned of [Agastya’s] arrival, approached the pot-born sage at the border of his realm and, together with his ministers, received him with great honor.
Having brought the *arghya* offering to him according to the prescribed rule, the lord of the earth, with palms joined in reverence and composed, asked about the purpose of his arrival:
"For what reason have you come, O Brahmin? I am blessed by your coming."
Agastya said:
"O lord of the earth, know that I have come to you as a seeker of wealth;
grant me a portion according to your ability, without harming others."
Lomaśa said:
Then the king presented to him his full accounts of income and expenditure.
Therefore, O learned one, take from this whatever wealth you deem fit.

Then, having observed that income and expenditure were equal, the twice-born man of equanimous mind considered that there was suffering for living beings in every way due to the act of acquisition. Taking Śrutarvāṇa with him, he then went to Vadhryaśva.
And he received them both at the edge of his domain according to the prescribed rites;
Vadhryaśva offered them water for their hands and feet,
and having obtained their permission, he inquired about the purpose of their visit.
"Speak as you wish, O best of sages; I am blessed by your arrival.
Agastya said:
"O lord of the earth, know that we two have come here desiring wealth."
"Give us a share according to your ability, without harming others.
Lomaśa said:
"Then the king reported to them that his income and expenditures were equal."
Then, having understood what remained after those provisions were gathered,
the twice-born man, being even-minded, observed that income and expenditure were equal;
he considered that in every way, the taking of these things would cause suffering to living beings.
Then Agastya, Śrutarvan, Vadhryaśva the lord of the earth, and Trasadasyu went to the great wealth of Trasadasyu, the son of Purukutsa;
and Trasadasyu received them all according to the prescribed rites.
Having approached at the border of his domain with his retinue, O Great King,
that best of kings of the Ikṣvāku line honored them according to custom;
then, once they were rested, he inquired about their purpose.
Agastya said:
"O lord of the earth, know that we have come here desiring wealth;
according to our ability, grant us a share without harming others."
Lomaśa said:
Then the king presented to them a full account of their income and expenditure;
having understood this, you should take whatever remains as a surplus.
Then, having seen that income and expenditure were equal, the twice-born one of equanimous mind considered that,
in every respect, there would be suffering for living beings due to the collection [of taxes].
Thereupon, all those kings, having assembled together, [approached] that great sage.
Having looked at one another, O great king, they said this:
"O Brahmin, this is indeed the wealthy Dānava Ilvala on earth;
let us all approach him today and beg for wealth."
At that time, it was their desire to beg food from Ilvala;
then, O King, they all together rushed toward Ilvala.
Lomaśa said:
03.097.001a But Ilvala, having learned that those kings had arrived together with the great seers, honored them at the border of his territory along with his ministers.
03.097.002a Then that best of asuras offered them hospitality.

O Kauravya, when all those royal sages saw that the great asura Vātāpi had been consecrated with the funeral rites while still in the form of a ram, they became despondent and lost heart. It is said that this was done by his brother Saṃskṛta.
Then Agastya, the best of sages, said to those royal seers:
"You must not despair; I shall consume the great asura. Then, having ascended the seat of honor, the great muni sat down.
Ilvala, the lord of the Daityas, approached him as if laughing;
meanwhile, Agastya himself consumed the entire Vātāpi.
While eating, he said with a smile, "I have a great appetite for food."
"O Vātāpi, wake up and display your strength and splendor!
As long as this one, who is difficult to conquer through ascetic power, does not pass you by, so long must you prevail.
Then Vātāpi exerted his force in order to burst open his belly.
The radiant Kumbhayoni, of great ascetic power, became aware of this.
That venerable seer, fierce in his vigor and penance, roared aloud:
"O Vātāpi, you are old; by me you have been destroyed for the peace of the world!"
Having said this, he struck his own belly with the tip of his hand.
Thus enraged three times, appearing as if blazing with splendor,
the Asura Ilvala, having finished eating, issued a summons to him.
Then, O dear one, a wind issued forth from the great-souled Agastya with a mighty sound,
like the thundering of a cloud;
he spoke again and again, saying, "Vātāpi, come forth!"
Laughing, Agastya, the best of sages, said to him, "O King,
how could that asura possibly escape once he has been digested by me? And Ilvala became despondent upon seeing the great asura digested.
With palms joined together, he spoke these words along with his ministers:
"For what purpose have you come? Tell me, what may I do for you?
Then Agastya replied to Ilvala with a smile.
"O Asura, we all know you as the Lord, the master of wealth.
These men are not very wealthy, yet my need for riches is great. Grant us a share according to your power, without harming others."
Then, having saluted that seer, Ilvala spoke these words:
"If you know what I intend to give, then I shall bestow wealth upon you.
Agastya said:
"O Asura, ten thousand cows for each one of the kings—
just as much gold you wish to give, O great Asura;
from that, twice as much shall be mine, as well as a golden chariot."
"O great Asura, these two horses, swift as thought, are what you wish to give.
Lomaśa said:
"But Ilvala said to the sage, 'Everything is yours, exactly as you have told me.'"
Agastya said:
"O great Asura, as for that golden chariot of which you spoke to me, we do not know it;
nor has any untruthful word ever been spoken by me before."
"I shall give all of this—gold, cows, and whatever wealth there is. Let the chariot be examined immediately; it is clearly made of gold.
Lomaśa said:
When that chariot was being examined, O son of Kuntī, it became made of gold.
Thereupon the Daitya, greatly distressed, gave even more wealth. And the two horses Vivāja and Suvāja were yoked to that chariot.
Those two swiftly brought back those riches toward Agastya’s hermitage;
O Bhārata, they reached all the kings along with Agastya in what seemed like the blink of an eye.
But Ilvala, having followed after him, desired to kill Agastya.
The one of great splendor reduced the great asura to ashes with the syllable *huṃ*.
Those two horses, swift as the wind, carried them to the hermitage of the sage.
Then, permitted by Agastya, the royal sages departed.
And the sage performed everything that Lopāmudrā desired.
Lopāmudrā said:
"O Blessed One, you have accomplished all that I longed for."
"Produce for me at once an offspring of exceeding prowess.
Agastya said:
"I am pleased, O auspicious and beautiful lady, with your conduct."
I shall now speak to you regarding the deliberation concerning your offspring; listen to it.
May you have a thousand sons, or a hundred equal to ten, or ten equal to a hundred, or even one who is equal to a thousand.
Lopāmudrā said:
"O one whose wealth is asceticism, let there be for me one son equal to a thousand;
for indeed, one who is wise and virtuous is better than many who are not."
Lomaśa said:
Having promised "So be it," the sage united with her at the appointed time— she who was of similar character, full of faith, and devoted to him.
Then, having conceived that embryo, he departed for the forest itself.
While he was gone to the forest, the embryo grew for seven autumns. When the seventh year had passed, that great poet was born.
O Bhārata, there was one named Dṛḍhasyu, who seemed to blaze with spiritual power;
that highly illustrious man constantly recited the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches and the Upaniṣads. To that seer was born a son, a great and radiant rishi.
While still a child, that radiant youth brought a load of firewood in his father's house; therefore, he became known as Idhmavāha. Seeing him engaged in such labor, the sage then rejoiced.
In this way, he begot that most excellent descendant of Bharata;
and his ancestors, O King, obtained the worlds they desired.
There is the famous hermitage of Agastya, endowed with flowers of every season.
O Great King, by the splendor of that wise one,
Vātāpi, the son of Prahrāda, who was renowned on earth and possessed an evil mind as a slayer of Brahmins, was thus destroyed by Agastya.
"O King, thus has this hermitage of his been destroyed—this delightful place endowed with many virtues, O King. Here is the holy Bhāgīrathī; may you bathe in it as you please."
Like a banner stirred by the wind, she shines resplendent in the vault of the sky;
like a terrified queen of serpents constantly deceived upon mountain peaks and rocky plateaus in the depths.
Flooding the entire southern quarter like a mother,
she who was formerly fallen from the matted locks of Śambhu became the beloved queen of the ocean.
Lomaśa said:

"O Yudhiṣṭhira, bathe as you please in this most meritorious river; understand this, O Great King, for it is renowned throughout the three worlds: this is the sacred ford (tīrtha) of Bhṛgu, frequented by hosts of great seers."
At the place where Rāma, having touched the water, regained the splendor that had been taken from him—
here, O Pāṇḍava, you together with your brothers and Kṛṣṇā ought to regain the splendor that has been seized by Duryodhana.
And how it was again brought back by Rāma, who had previously been at enmity with him.
Vaiśampāyana said:
There, that Pāṇḍava [Dhṛtarāṣṭra] was together with his brothers and with Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī).
Having bathed, O Bhārata, he offered libations to the gods and the ancestors.
The form of that sacred ford shone with a brilliance even more radiant than the blazing sun;
and it became utterly invincible to his enemies, O bull among men.
And the son of Pāṇḍu, O king of kings, questioned Lomaśa:
"O Blessed One, for what reason was Rāma’s form taken away, O Lord?
Lomaśa said:
Tell me, who am asking you, how this was brought back.
Listen, O Indra among kings, to the account of Rāma and the wise Bhārgava. A son named Rāma was born to the high-souled Daśaratha.
Viṣṇu, indeed, for the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa, [appeared] in his own body;
we then beheld him born in Ayodhyā as the son of Daśaratha.
Furthermore, there was Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu, the son of Ṛcīka and Reṇukā.
Having heard this from Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, whose deeds are effortless,
Rāma, filled with curiosity, returned again to Ayodhyā,
taking up that divine bow which is the destroyer of kṣatriyas.
Desiring then to test the prowess of Rāma,
the son of Daśaratha, Daśaratha, having heard of him, went to the edge of his domain and dispatched his son Rāma as an envoy before him.
Seeing him standing there with his weapon raised,
Rāma, as if smiling, O son of Kuntī, spoke these words:
"O Indra among kings, O Lord, this bow has already been mastered by me."
"O King, apply yourself with effort if you are able.
Thus addressed, he said, "O Blessed One, you ought not to revile me;
nor am I inferior in the duty of Kṣatriyas toward the twice-born."

"Especially among the Ikṣvākus, there is no boasting regarding the strength of one's arms. To him who was speaking thus, Rāma then addressed these words: "Enough with this pretext; stretch the bow, O Rāghava!"
Then, O Bhārata, Rāma Dāśarathi, out of wrath, seized from the hand of Rāma— the bull among Kṣatriyas— the divine bow;
he strung that bow as if in sport.
And that heroic one, smiling, produced the sound of the bowstring;
at that sound, all living beings were terrified as if by a thunderbolt.
Then Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, spoke to Rāma.
"O Brahmin, this has been bestowed; what else may I do for you?
To that high-souled one, Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, gave a divine arrow, saying, "Let this be drawn back as far as the ear."
Having heard this, Rāma spoke as if blazing with wrath:
"It is heard and indeed forgiven; yet you are filled with pride, O Bhārgava, for you have acquired power especially from among the Kṣatriyas."
"By the grace of my grandfather, you surely insult me with that [speech]. Behold me in my own form; I grant you sight.
Then Bhārgava Rāma indeed beheld Rāma’s body.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and Sādhyas together with the hosts of Maruts; the Pitṛs and Hutāśana (Agni), as well as the lunar mansions and the planets;
the Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, and all the rivers and sacred fords.
The Vālakhilya sages, eternal and identical with Brahman;
the celestial rishis in their entirety; likewise the oceans and the mountains;
and the Vedas together with the Upaniṣads, along with the *vaṣaṭ*-calls and the sacrifices.
O Bhārata, the *sāman* chants endowed with consciousness, the science of archery (*dhanurveda*),
masses of clouds, rains, and lightnings, O Yudhiṣṭhira—
then that Blessed One, Viṣṇu, indeed released that arrow.
O Bhārata, the surface of the earth was strewn with dry thunderbolts and great meteors; it was covered by a massive rain of dust and showers from the clouds,
as well as by earthquakes, atmospheric crashes, and immense roars.
Having rendered Rāma agitated and having drawn away his entire splendor,
that flaming arrow, impelled by Rāma’s arm, sped forth. But he, having fallen into a state of agitation, regained his consciousness.
Rāma, his life-breath restored, paid homage to the splendor of Viṣṇu;
permitted by Viṣṇu, he returned once more to Mount Mahendra.
Yet, remaining there, that great ascetic dwelt in fear and shame.
Then, when a year had passed, seeing that Rāma was standing there with his vigor gone, devoid of pride, and afflicted by grief, the ancestors said to him:
"O son, this was certainly not done properly by you after encountering Viṣṇu."
For he is always worthy of worship and honor in the three worlds.
Go, my son, to the holy river named Vadhūsara;
by performing ablutions there at its sacred bathing-places, you shall regain your body.

That sacred ford is named Dīptoda, where your great-grandfather Bhṛgu performed supreme austerities during the age of the gods, O Rāma. Rāma did exactly that, O son of Kuntī, at the word of his father.
And having attained supreme splendor at this sacred ford, O son of Pāṇḍu,
such was what was obtained, O dear one, by Rāma of unwearied deeds after he had formerly approached Viṣṇu, O great king.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of the twice-born, I desire once more to hear in detail the deeds of that wise great seer Agastya.
Lomaśa said:
"O King, listen to this divine, wonderful, and superhuman story concerning the power of Agastya, O great monarch, whose soul is immeasurable."
In the Kṛta age, there were terrible Dānavas, intoxicated by battle, known as the Kāleya clans, who were exceedingly cruel. Having taken refuge with Vṛtra, they stood with various weapons raised.
They ran about on all sides toward the gods, headed by Mahendra.
Then, in ancient times, the thirty deities made an effort to slay Vṛtra;
placing Purandara at their head, they approached Brahmā.
To all of them, who stood with palms joined in reverence, Parameṣṭhin said:
"O gods, everything that you intend to accomplish is known to me.
I shall declare the means by which you will slay Vṛtra."
"There is a great ṛṣi of noble intellect renowned as Dadhīca.
Go to him all together and request a boon;
that righteous-souled one will grant it to you with a well-pleased inner heart."
All of you together, desiring victory, should say to him:
"For the sake of the welfare of the three worlds, please give us your own bones. Having cast off his body, he will indeed grant his own bones.
"Let a firm and most terrible thunderbolt be fashioned from her bones—
a great weapon, sharp, six-sided, with a fearsome sound, and the slayer of enemies.
With that thunderbolt, indeed, Śatakratu shall slay Vṛtra."

"All this has been told to you; therefore, let it be carried out quickly. Thus addressed, the gods then took leave of the Grandfather (Brahmā) and, placing Nārāyaṇa at their head, went to the hermitage of Dadhīca.
On the far bank of the Sarasvatī, it was covered with various trees and creepers; it resounded with the humming songs of bees as if with *sāman*-chanters,
and was filled with the cries of male cuckoos mingled with the calls of *jīvañjīvaka* birds.
It was frequented here and there by buffaloes, boars, sṛmara deer, and even yaks, all free from the fear of tigers;
as well as by female elephants and male elephants with temples and faces flowing with rut.
It resounded on all sides with those who had plunged into the lake and were sporting there,
and it echoed with the great roars of lions and tigers;
and it was also filled with others dwelling in caves and mountain clefts who remained hidden therein.
In those various locations, they arrived at the most beautiful and delightful hermitage of Dadhīca, which was as magnificent as heaven itself;
there they beheld Dadhīca, whose splendor was equal to that of the sun.
O King, blazing with splendor like the Grandfather (Brahmā) himself in his majesty,
the gods saluted and bowed down at his feet,
and they all requested a boon as had been instructed by the Supreme Lord.
Then Dadhīca, supremely gratified,
addressed those best of gods, saying:
"O gods, I shall today do that which is for your benefit."
"I shall even cast off my own body. Having spoken thus, that best of bipeds, having mastered his senses, suddenly relinquished his life-breaths.
Then those gods took the bones of the deceased according to the instructions;
and the deities, appearing joyful, [prepared] for victory.
Having approached Tvaṣṭṛ, they spoke of that matter;
and Tvaṣṭṛ, having heard their words,
was joyful in appearance and, being self-restrained, applied himself with great effort.
He fashioned the thunderbolt of exceedingly fierce form;
and having made it, he joyfully said to Śakra: "O God, with this most excellent thunderbolt..."
Reduce the fierce enemy of the gods to ashes this very day;
then, having slain your foe, rule happily over all the heavens as a dweller of the celestial realm together with your hosts.
Thus addressed by Tvaṣṭṛ, Purandara,
being delighted and composed, took up the thunderbolt.
Lomaśa said:
Then the wielder of the thunderbolt, protected by the powerful deities,
approached Vṛtra, who stood encompassing both heaven and earth and was guarded on all sides by the massive-bodied Kālakeyas.
With weapons raised like mountains with peaks,
O best of the Bharatas, a great battle then ensued between the gods and the Dānavas for a moment, causing terror to the three worlds.
From the swords raised and struck down by the arms of heroes,
there arose a most tumultuous sound as they fell upon the bodies;
and from the heads falling from the sky onto the surface of the earth, [the same noise arose].
O protector of the earth, they appeared like palm fruits fallen from their stalks;
those Kāleyas, clad in golden armor and armed with iron clubs,
rushed against the gods like mountains scorched by a forest fire.
The gods were unable to withstand the force of those rushing together with such speed; broken, they fled in fear. Seeing them fleeing in terror, the thousand-eyed Purandara [intervened].
As Vṛtra grew in power,
a great despondency overcame the god Purandara himself, who was terrified by the fear of the Kāleyas;
he quickly went for refuge to the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Seeing Śakra overcome by dejection, the eternal Viṣṇu bestowed his own splendor upon Śakra, increasing his strength. Then,
seeing Śakra revitalized by Viṣṇu, the hosts of gods [were filled with joy].
Then those stainless Brahman-sages each contributed their own respective energy.
Thus replenished by Viṣṇu and the deities,
as well as by the highly fortunate ṛṣis, Śakra became powerful once more.
Knowing that the lord of the thirty gods was established in his strength,
Vṛtra let out great roars;
by his thundering, the earth and the quarters [of the sky] [trembled].
The sky, the heavens, and even the mountains trembled;
everything shook when Mahendra heard that great and terrible roar.
Immersed in fear, O King, he quickly released that great thunderbolt for his slaughter;
struck by Śakra’s thunderbolt, he fell.
The great asura, wearing a golden garland,
was like a massive, preeminent mountain;
he was Mandara, released from the hand of Viṣṇu.
When that best of Daityas was slain, Śakra, overcome with fear, fled to enter a lake;
he did not even consider releasing the thunderbolt from his hand.
And even though Vṛtra had been slain, he did not perceive it because of his fear;
all the gods were joyful and greatly delighted,
and the great ṛṣis praised Indra.
They beheld Vṛtra slain upon the earth,
scattered like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt;
and all the Daityas, having assembled in haste, [beheld him likewise].
The gods struck those who were tormented by the slaughter of Vṛtra;
being thus slaughtered by the thirty deities at that time,
they entered the ocean, afflicted by fear.
And having entered the immeasurable ocean,
which was teeming with large fish and filled with jewels,
they then held a consultation together.
Intending the destruction of the three worlds,
some there, knowing how to determine the course of thought, described various means for that purpose.
As they deliberated there, through the application of sequence and time,
a terrible thought arose in those who were endowed with knowledge and asceticism: "Those who exist [are possessed of these qualities]..."
Their destruction must first be accomplished;
for all the worlds are sustained by austerity; therefore, hasten to bring about the exhaustion of their ascetic power.
"Indeed, whoever there may be upon this earth who are ascetics, knowers of dharma, and experts in that field—
let them be slain without delay."
When they were destroyed, the world was destroyed;
for thus all those whose intellects had lost their sense were exceedingly delighted at the destruction of the world.
Having taken refuge in that difficult-to-access ocean, the mine of jewels and abode of Varuṇa, which is full of great waves;
Lomaśa said:
Taking refuge in the ocean, that storehouse of waters belonging to Varuṇa,
the Kāleyas set themselves to work for the destruction of the three worlds. Enraged, they constantly devoured sages during the night.
Those who were in the hermitages and in sacred shrines—
eighty-eight brahmins and nine other ascetics in the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha— were devoured by those evil-minded ones.
Having gone to the holy hermitage of Cyavana, which was frequented by the twice-born,
they ate the food of a hundred sages who subsisted on fruits and roots. In this manner they spent their nights, and during the day they entered the ocean.
Those wicked Kāleyas, devouring the ascetics rich in penance—
even those disciplined students in the hermitage of Bharadvāja who subsisted on air or water— twenty of them were struck down together.
In this manner, all those hermitages were then run through by the Dānavas during the night; intoxicated and relying on the strength of their arms,
the Kāleyas, impelled by fate, slaughtered many throngs of twice-born ones.
O best of men, human beings did not perceive those Daityas as they were thus engaged among the ascetics performing austerities;
those cruel ones roamed the earth for the destruction of the world.
At dawn,

the sages were seen lying upon the surface of the earth, emaciated by their restricted diet, their bodies deprived of life— devoid of flesh, blood, marrow, and entrails, with their joints disarticulated.
The earth was strewn and covered with heaps like those of conch shells—
with overturned jars, broken *sruva* ladles,
and likewise scattered *agnihotra* fires; thus the ground became completely overspread.

The world became devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, with sacrifices, festivals, and rituals destroyed; it was despondent, oppressed by the fear of the Kāleyas. Thus, O lord of men, human beings were being utterly wasted away.
Terrified and intent on saving themselves, they fled in all directions out of fear;
some entered caves, while others took refuge in mountain torrents;
others, agitated by the thought of death, abandoned their lives out of terror.
There, certain great archers, heroes exceedingly proud of their prowess, exerted the utmost effort in their search for the Dānavas;
yet they did not find them, as those beings had taken refuge in the ocean.
They underwent supreme exhaustion and met with utter ruin;
when the world had fallen into a state of desolation and the performance of sacrifices and festivals had perished,
the gods, O lord of men, experienced the highest distress.
Having assembled together with Mahendra, they held a consultation out of fear;
placing the invincible Vaikuṇṭha, Nārāyaṇa— the unborn, all-pervading Lord who is the refuge of those seeking shelter— at their head, they sought him as their protector.
Then those gods assembled together and said to Madhusūdana:
"O Lord, you are our creator, protector, and sustainer of the world;
all this that exists, both moving and unmoving, has been created by you."
O lotus-eyed one, it dissolves back into you alone. Long ago, O lotus-eyed one, when the earth had perished within the ocean,
you assumed the form of a boar and lifted it up for the sake of the world.
O Supreme Person, the first Daitya, Hiraṇyakaśipu, who possessed great heroism, was slain by you after you assumed the body of a man-lion (Nārasiṃha); likewise,
the great Asura Bali, who was incapable of being killed by any living beings, was also subdued by you.
Having assumed the form of a dwarf, you caused the great archer Asura, renowned as Jambha— the cruel disturber of sacrifices— to fall from the three worlds;
he was struck down by you alone.
Such deeds as these are beyond counting;
for us who are terrified by fear, you are our refuge, O Madhusūdana.
Therefore, O God, Lord of gods, we inform you for the sake of the world.
"Protect the worlds, the gods, and Śakra from great danger;
you alone are firm in your vow to rescue those who have come for refuge.
The gods said:

From this giving, all four classes of beings subsist; when they are nourished, they in turn nourish the dwellers of heaven with *havya* and *kavya* offerings. For thus do the worlds continue to exist, mutually dependent upon one another.
"By your grace we have been free from anxiety and protected by you alone; yet now this supreme terror has come upon the worlds. We do not know by whom these brahmins are being slain at night."
And when the brahmins have perished, the earth will go to ruin;
then, when the earth has perished, the triple heaven will go to ruin. Through your grace, O mighty-armed Lord of the World, all the worlds [shall endure].
"Protected by you, they shall indeed not meet with destruction.
Viṣṇu said:
"O gods, the entire cause of the destruction of living beings is known to me."
I shall also tell you, so listen with your fevers dispelled:
there was a most terrible host known as the Kāleyas;
relying upon Vṛtra, they oppressed the entire world.
Seeing Vṛtra slain by the wise thousand-eyed Indra,
they entered the abode of Varuṇa in order to preserve their lives;
having entered the terrible ocean, which was infested with crocodiles and sharks.
For the sake of destroying the worlds, they slay the sages here at night;
yet they cannot be brought to destruction, for they have taken refuge in the ocean. You must therefore deliberate upon a plan for the drying up of the ocean.
"Who else besides Agastya is capable of drying up the ocean?
Otherwise, they cannot be overcome without the drying up of the sea.
Having heard these words uttered by Viṣṇu, the gods [reflected].
Placing Viṣṇu at their head, they approached Brahmā;
having bowed down before him, they reported that very matter to him—
the Kāleyas, who were resolved upon the destruction of all the worlds.
Having heard those words of theirs, the eternal Lotus-born One,
being exceedingly pleased, spoke these meaningful words to the thirty gods:
"O gods, all the machinations of the Dānavas are known to me."

The death of humans and others has been brought about by the Kāleyas, impelled by Time; destruction has overtaken those who have been struck down by Time. I shall now declare the means for the drying up of the ocean.
There is one renowned as Agastya, the son of Varuṇa, who is perfectly composed.
Approach him together and request this matter of yours;
for he, possessed of great splendor, is capable of drinking up the great ocean in an instant.
"And when the ocean has been brought to exhaustion, you shall slay the Kāleyas.
Having heard these words of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, the gods,
having obtained the command of Parameṣṭhin, went to the hermitage of Agastya.
There they beheld the high-souled son of Varuṇa, blazing with splendor,
being waited upon by sages like the Grandfather [Brahmā] by the gods.
Having approached that high-souled and unshakable son of Mitrā-Varuṇa, they...
Praising with their own deeds that mass of asceticism dwelling in the hermitage,
the gods said:
"In former times, you were the refuge of the worlds when they were tormented by Nahuṣa."
And that thorn of the world, having been deprived of his sovereignty over the gods for the sake of the world,
grew suddenly out of anger like the excellent mountain Bhāskara; yet,
not transgressing your word, the Vindhya mountain does not increase in height.
When the world was shrouded in darkness and all creatures were oppressed by death,
they attained supreme peace only by taking refuge in you as their protector.
For us, who are constantly terrified by fear, the Blessed One is our eternal refuge.
"Therefore, being afflicted, we entreat you for a boon, for you are indeed a granter of boons.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"For what reason did the Vindhya mountain suddenly grow, overcome with anger?"
"I wish to hear this in detail, O Great Sage.
Lomaśa said:
"The king of mountains, the great mountain Maru, the golden peak—"
At both sunrise and sunset, the sun used to circumambulate [Mount Vindhya] from the right.
Seeing this, Mount Vindhya then spoke to the sun:
"Just as Meru is constantly circumambulated by you..."
"And a circumambulation is performed; therefore, O Bhāskara, do this for me.
Thus addressed, Sūrya then replied to the lord of mountains:
"O Mountain, I do not perform this circumambulation by my own will."
"This is the path ordained by me, by which this world was created.
Having been addressed thus, O scorcher of foes, the mountain suddenly grew in fury and desired to block the course of the sun and the moon.
Then all the gods together,
including Indra, having assembled at the king of great mountains,
restrained him by means of skillful stratagems.
And he did not heed their words;
then they approached the sage dwelling in the hermitage,
an ascetic and the most excellent among the upholders of dharma.
Together, those gods spoke to Agastya, who blazed with most wonderful power, regarding that matter. The gods said:

"This Vindhya, the king of mountains, following the dictates of anger, obstructs the path of the sun and moon as well as the course of the constellations. O best of the twice-born, no one else is capable of restraining him."
"O highly fortunate one, since there is no one but you, therefore restrain him.
Lomaśa said:
Having heard those words of the gods, the brahmin approached the mountain.
Approaching the Vindhya mountain, he spoke while standing there with his wife:
"O best of mountains, I desire that a path be granted by you;
I wish to go toward the southern quarter for a certain purpose."
"Wait for me until my return;
O Lord of Mountains, once I have returned, you may grow as you desire.
Having made this agreement with Vindhya, that crusher of enemies—
Even today, the son of Varuṇa does not return from the southern region.
All this has been told to you— how it is that the Vindhya mountain does not grow—
as you asked me concerning the power of Agastya.
O King, listen as I relate how the Kāleyas were destroyed by all the gods after they had obtained a boon from Agastya. Having heard the words of the thirty deities, the son of Mitra and Varuṇa spoke.
"For what purpose have you come? What boon do you desire from me?
When he had spoken thus, all the gods, led by Purandara, replied to that sage with their palms joined in reverence.
"O great seer, O high-souled one, we desire that you act thus: while the great ocean is being drunk up,
we shall then slay [the demons] along with their followers."
Having heard the words of the thirty gods regarding those enemies of the Suras known as the Kāleyas, the sage said, "So be it;
I shall fulfill your desire and bring great happiness to the worlds."
Having spoken thus, he of noble vows then went to the ocean, the lord of rivers,
together with the ṛṣis perfected by austerity, as well as the gods,
humans, serpents, gandharvas, yakṣas, and kimpuruṣas.
Desiring to witness that marvel, they followed the high-souled one.
Then, together, they approached the ocean of terrifying roar,
which seemed to dance with its waves and leap with the wind.
Seeming to laugh with its masses of foam and stumbling through its caves,
filled with various crocodiles and teeming with flocks of diverse birds—
the gods, together with Agastya, along with the gandharvas and great serpents, [approached it].
And the highly fortunate sages approached the great ocean.
Lomaśa said:
"Having reached the ocean, the venerable sage, the son of Varuṇa..."
He spoke to the assembled gods and the sages who had gathered there:
"For the sake of the welfare of the world, I shall indeed drink up the abode of Varuṇa;
let that which is to be performed by you be carried out swiftly."
Having spoken these words, the infallible son of Mitra and Varuṇa,
filled with wrath, drank up the ocean while all the worlds looked on.
Seeing the ocean being drunk, the gods, together with Indra, [were struck with wonder].
They were filled with supreme wonder and honored him with hymns of praise:
"You are our protector and the creator of the worlds, the progenitor of the universe.
By your grace, may the world, together with the gods, not go to destruction."
The high-souled one was being honored by the gods while the musical instruments of the gandharvas resounded on all sides,
and he was being showered with divine flowers.
He made the great ocean waterless. Seeing the great ocean rendered waterless, all the gods were exceedingly delighted.
Seizing their divine and excellent weapons,
those of undaunted spirit struck down those Dānavas;
being slaughtered by the high-souled gods, they [perished].
Then, those of great strength, swift, and roaring—
the inhabitants of heaven— could not endure the force of those high-souled ones who possessed such momentum.

Being slaughtered by the thirty gods, O Bhārata, those Dānavas of terrifying roar waged a most tumultuous battle for a mere moment. Having previously been consumed by the ascetic power of the sages whose souls were purified, they were now overcome.
Striving with all their might, they were slaughtered by the gods; adorned with golden neck-ornaments and wearing earrings and armlets,
they looked beautiful after being slain, like *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom.

Then, O best of men, some of the Kāleyas who remained after the slaughter split open the goddess Earth and took refuge in the depths of Pātāla. Having seen the Dānavas slain, the gods [addressed] the bull among sages.
They praised him with various words and spoke these words:
"O highly blessed one, through your grace, great happiness has been attained by the worlds;
and by your splendor, the Kāleyas of cruel prowess have been slain."
"O mighty-armed one, O creator of the world, fill the ocean!
Release back into it that water which was drunk by you.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, the bull among sages, replied.
To those gods gathered there together with Purandara, Agastya said:
"That water has indeed been drunk by me; therefore, let another means be devised by you who have exerted yourselves for the purpose of filling the ocean."
Having heard these words of the great seer of purified soul,
the gods together were both astonished and despondent;
having taken leave of one another and bowed to that bull among sages, they departed.
O Great King, all the subjects departed as they had come;
the thirty gods, together with Viṣṇu, approached the Grandfather after deliberating again and again on how to fill the ocean.
Then those thirty gods, together with Viṣṇu, approached Dhātṛ and,
with palms joined in reverence, all spoke regarding the filling of the ocean.
Lomaśa said:
Then Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, spoke to those assembled gods,
O King, consoling them with a resonant voice:
"Go, all you deities, according to your pleasure and as you desire."
After a long period of time, the ocean will return to its natural state;
when, making his kinsmen the cause, he brings the Gaṅgā down from the great king Bhagīratha, then it will be full once more.
Having heard the words of the Grandfather, all those most excellent among the gods,
awaiting the proper time, departed as they had come.
[He] will fill the ocean, the reservoir of waters, with floods of water.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Brahmin, how indeed did the kinsmen [behave], and what was the cause in this matter, O sage? And how was the ocean filled through the exertions of Bhagīratha?"
"O ascetic, O Brahmin, I desire to hear this supreme account of the deeds of kings in detail as it is being told by you. Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by the high-souled Dharmarāja,
the lord of brahmins related the majesty of the great-souled Sagara.
Lomaśa said:

In the lineage of the Ikṣvākus was born a king named Sagara, endowed with beauty, character, and strength; he was powerful yet childless, O Bhārata. Having utterly destroyed the Haihayas and the Tālajaṅghas, he—
Having brought other kings under his control, he ruled over his own kingdom.
He had two wives, O best of the Bharatas, who were proud of their beauty and youth: Vaidarbhī, O bull of the Bharatas, and Śaibyā.
Desiring a son, that king performed very great austerities;
O Indra among kings, he resorted to Mount Kailāsa together with his two wives. Engaged in yoga, he practiced those immense austerities.
He approached the high-souled one— the three-eyed destroyer of Tripura,
Śaṃkara, Bhava, Īśāna, the wielder of the trident, the bearer of the Pināka bow,
Tryambaka, Śiva, the fierce lord, the multiformed husband of Umā.

Having seen that granter of boons— the ancient Lord of the Immortals, the undecaying one who supports the world-systems, the sky-clad one whose chariot is the bull, the inconceivable and wondrous yogi—
the king, together with his two wives, [beheld him].
Having prostrated himself, the mighty-armed one requested a boon for the sake of a son.
Hara, being pleased, spoke to that best of kings and his wife:
"O King, at the very moment you chose me here for this boon,"
"O best of men, sixty thousand sons, heroes proud in battle, shall be born to you from a single wife;
and all of them together, O king, shall meet their destruction."
"A single hero shall be born as the sole bearer of his lineage.
Having spoken thus, Rudra vanished on the spot;
and King Sagara returned to his own abode.
Accompanied by his two wives, dear son, Sagara then passed his time with a most joyful heart, awaiting the moment obtained through the boon of Śambhu. Then,
O best of men, those two lotus-eyed wives of his—
Both Vaidarbhī and Śaibyā became pregnant.
Then, in due course of time, Vaidarbhī gave birth to a gourd-like fetus,
while Śaibyā gave birth to a son, a boy of divine form.
Then that king set his mind on casting away the gourd;
at that moment, he heard a voice from the sky with a deep resonance:
"O King, do not act rashly; you ought not to abandon your sons."
Having extracted the seeds from the middle of the bottle-gourd, let them be carefully preserved,
portion by portion, in vessels that have been warmed and filled with clarified butter. Then, O King, you shall obtain sixty thousand sons.
"O lord of men, the birth of a son has been ordained for you by Mahādeva through this sequential process; let not your mind think otherwise. Lomaśa said:
Having heard this from the sky, O best of kings, that monarch, O bull of the Bharatas, then acted exactly as he had been told, placing faith in it; and so,
O lord of men, the king took each seed one by one.
Then, he placed those portions into jars filled with clarified butter;
intent on protecting his sons, he assigned a nurse to each one.
Thereafter, after a long time, they arose endowed with great strength.
O King, sixty thousand sons were born to that royal sage of incomparable splendor through the grace of Rudra;
they were fierce, performers of cruel deeds, and roamers of the sky.
And because of their great numbers, they held all the worlds—
including the immortals— in contempt; those heroes, exulting in battle, oppressed the thirty gods as well as the Gandharvas and Rākṣasas, and indeed all living beings.
Then, being tormented by the oceans of dull-witted intellects, the worlds,
together with all the deities, went for refuge to Brahmā. The illustrious Grandfather of all the worlds spoke to them:

"Go now, all you thirty gods, together with the worlds, each as you came. Before long, O Suras, there will be a great and most terrible destruction of the oceans through the deeds performed by yourselves."
"Having encountered Kapila, they will undoubtedly perish.
O lord of men, having been addressed thus, the gods and the worlds then took leave of the Grandfather and departed as they had come.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, after a long time had passed,
the heroic King Sagara was consecrated for the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). His horse roamed the earth, well-guarded by his sons.
O King, with all their great energy, they moved about at will;
having reached the ocean, which was waterless and terrifying to behold,
he vanished right there while being guarded with great effort.
Then, my dear, those ocean-dwellers, believing the supreme horse had been stolen,
returned and reported to their father that the invisible steed had been carried away. Addressed by him, they were told, "Search for the horse in all directions."
Searching the earth together with its oceans, forests, and islands,
they then obeyed their father’s command and, O great king, sought that horse in all directions across the entire surface of the world.
Then all those oceans, having come together with one another,
did not find the horse nor the thief of the horse.
Having approached their father, they then spoke before him with palms joined in reverence.

Then, O King, all the rulers of the earth stood together with the oceans; the entire world— along with its seas, forests, islands, rivers, streams, caves, mountains, and forest regions— stood there in its entirety.
"O King, O ruler of the earth, we have searched at your command,
yet we have found neither the horse nor the thief of the horse.
Upon hearing their words, that king was overwhelmed with rage.
Then, O King, he spoke these words to them all, who were under the power of fate:
"Go back so that you may not return; search again for the horse fit for the sacrifice. For without that sacrificial horse, my sons, you must certainly not come back."
Having received that message, the sons of Sagara then once again began to search the entire earth. Then those heroes beheld the earth torn asunder.
O protector of the earth, having reached the ocean and the tracks of the horses,
the sons of Sagara then began to dig into that cave and the sea with spades and pickaxes.
Being dug up by the united sons of the ocean, that abode of Varuṇa suffered extreme distress as it was being torn apart on all sides; likewise,
the asuras, uragas, rākṣasas, and various other creatures [were afflicted].
Being slaughtered by the oceans, they uttered cries of distress;
with severed heads, mangled bodies, split knees, bones, and skulls,
living beings were seen by the hundreds and thousands.
Thus, as they were digging toward the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters,
a very great length of time passed, yet the horse was not seen. Then, O lord of the earth, in the north-eastern region of the ocean—
As the earth was being torn apart by the sons of Sagara, who were arrogant in their strength,
they split open the netherworld (pātāla) and, filled with rage,
beheld the horse wandering there upon the surface of the ground.
And having seen the high-souled Kapila, that unsurpassed mass of splendor,
blazing with ascetic power like a fire with its flames,
all the oceans then became filled with joy.
Lomaśa said:
O King, having seen that horse, their hair stood on end with joy;
impelled by Time, they disregarded the high-souled Kapila.
Enraged and desiring to seize the horse, they rushed forward. Then, O great king, the best of sages, Kapila— whom they call Vāsudeva, the best of sages— became incensed.
Opening his eyes and emitting his splendor upon them,
that one of great majesty, the best of sages, simultaneously consumed those sixty thousand dull-witted Sāgaras.
Seeing them reduced to ashes, Nārada, of great ascetic merit,
went into the presence of Sagara and reported that to him.
Having heard those terrible words emerging from the mouth of the sage, the king—
For a moment he became despondent and reflected upon the words of Sthāṇu;
overwhelmed by the grief arising from the death of his son,
he comforted himself with his own mind and turned his thoughts back toward the horse.
Then, O tiger among the Bharatas, having summoned his grandson Aṃśumān— the son of Asamañjas— he spoke these words:
"Those sixty thousand sons of mine possessed immeasurable splendor."
Having encountered the fire of Kapila, they met their death on my account.
And even your father, O sinless one, was abandoned by me, dear friend,
as I sought to protect righteousness and desired the welfare of the citizens.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O one rich in asceticism, tell me why Sagara, that tiger among kings, abandoned his own son, a heroic youth who was so difficult to give up."
Lomaśa said:
"Sagara had a son known as Asamañjas, whom Śaibyā bore; he, indeed, [used to throw] the children of the citizens..."
O Lord of the Earth, as he was playing here and there, he would suddenly seize those who were crying out while running,
and having caught the weaklings by their hooves, he threw them into the river.
Then the citizens, overwhelmed by fear and grief, gathered together.
Standing with palms joined in reverence, they all entreated Sagara:
"O Great King, you are our protector from the fears of enemy armies and the like;
therefore, you ought to protect us from this terrible fear of Asamañjas."
Having heard the terrible words of the citizens, the best of kings became despondent for a moment and said this to his ministers:
"Let my son Asamañja be banished from the city this very day."
"If this is to be done as dear to you as it is to me, let it be carried out quickly.
O lord of men, having been thus addressed by the king,
those ministers acted with haste exactly as they had been instructed and commanded by the monarch.
All this has been told to you, how the son was exiled by the high-souled Sagara, who desired the welfare of the citizens;
and what was said to the great archer Aṃśumat by Sagara.
"I shall tell you all of that; listen to me as it is being recounted.
Sagara said:
"Because of the abandonment of your father and the death of your sons..."
"O dear grandson, I am tormented by the failure to recover the horse; therefore,
being consumed by grief and bewildered by the obstacle to my sacrifice, rescue me from hell by bringing back the horse."
Lomaśa said:
Thus addressed by the high-souled Sagara,
Aṃśumat went in sorrow to that place where the earth had indeed been torn asunder.
He entered the ocean by that very same path, and there he beheld the high-souled Kapila and that horse. Having seen him— a mass of splendor and the ancient, most excellent of sages— [he approached].
Having bowed his head to the ground, he announced his purpose to him.
Then the highly effulgent Kālīpa was pleased with Aṃśumat;
and that righteous one said to him, "O Bhārata, I am a granter of boons."
There, for the sake of performing a sacrifice, he first chose the horse;
secondly, he chose water out of a desire to purify his ancestors.
To him spoke the highly effulgent Kapila, the bull among sages:
"I shall grant you whatever you request, O sinless one—may prosperity be yours!
For in you are established forbearance, righteousness, and truth as well.
By you Sagara has achieved his purpose, and by you your father has become a true father of sons."
And by your very power, the sons of Sagara shall go to heaven;
having become like locusts in the fire of my wrath, they shall ascend.
Furthermore, your grandson shall bring the triple-pathed river down from the third heaven.
"O bull among men, having propitiated Maheśvara for the sake of purifying the oceans, take back the sacrificial horse— may prosperity be yours—
and let the sacrifice of the high-souled Sagara be completed, my son."
Thus addressed by the high-souled Kapila, Aṃśumat took the horse and returned to the sacrificial enclosure of the great-souled one. Then,
he paid homage at the feet of the high-souled Sagara.
He was kissed on the head by him as well, and he reported everything to him—
exactly as it had been seen and heard, including the destruction of the oceans—
and he informed him that the horse had arrived at the sacrificial enclosure.

Having heard that, King Sagara abandoned the grief born of his sons; and having honored Aṃśumat, he brought that sacrifice to completion. With the sacrifice finished, Sagara was honored by all the gods.
He appointed the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, as his son. After ruling the kingdom for a very long time, the lotus-eyed one,
having entrusted the burden of state to his grandson, then departed for the third heaven.
O great king, the righteous Aṃśumat also ruled the earth girt by the oceans,
just as his grandfather had done.
To him was born a son named Dilīpa, who was a knower of dharma.
Having entrusted the kingdom to him, Aṃśumat also passed away.
Then Dilīpa, having heard of the great destruction of his ancestors,
was consumed by grief and reflected upon their fate.
The king made a very great effort to bring down the Gaṅgā,
yet despite striving to the best of his power, he did not succeed in making her descend;
that royal seer, Dilīpa, then succumbed to the law of time.
To him was born a son, illustrious and devoted to righteousness,
renowned as Bhagīratha— truthful in speech and free from malice.
Having consecrated him in the kingdom, Dilīpa retired to the forest.
O bull of the Bharatas, O descendant of Bharata, by virtue of his union with the perfection of asceticism, that high-souled King Bhagīratha, who was devoted to truth and righteousness,
departed from the forest for the third heaven through the course of time.
Lomaśa said:
That king was a great archer, a universal emperor, and a mighty chariot-warrior;
he was the delight of the eyes and minds of all the world.

The mighty-armed one heard from the high-souled Kapila of the terrible destruction of his ancestors and their failure to attain the third heaven. With a grieving heart, he entrusted the kingdom to his ministers.
O lord of men, having purified his sins through austerity and desiring to propitiate Gaṅgā, that best of men went to the side of the Himavat to perform penance;
there he beheld the Himavat, the most excellent of mountains.
Adorned with peaks of various forms containing mineral ores,
it was embraced on all sides by clouds hanging from the wind;
and it was graced by rivers, groves, and mountain slopes filled with water.
It was frequented by lions and tigers lurking in caves and mountain clefts,
and by birds of variegated plumage warbling various songs—
namely, bhringarajas, swans, datyuhas, and water-fowls.
It was filled with peacocks, woodpeckers, cuckoos, and jīvajīvaka birds; with cakoras and black-eyed pigeons, as well as with birds that love their young;
and it was crowded with lotus ponds in its delightful water-bodies.
It was adorned with the sweet cries of cranes,
its rocky surfaces frequented by *kiṃnaras* and *apsarases*,
and its trees rubbed on all sides by the tips of the tusks of the elephants of the quarters.
It was frequented by Vidyādharas, filled with various jewels,
and inhabited by serpents with virulent poison and flaming tongues;
in some places it resembled gold, and in others it was like silver.
In one place, he went to the Himavat, which resembles a mass of collyrium;
there, that best of men, having undertaken severe asceticism,
subsisted on fruits, roots, and water for a thousand years.
When a thousand divine years had passed, the great river Gaṅgā herself appeared to him in personified form. Gaṅgā said:
"What do you desire from me, O Great King? And what shall I give to you? Speak that, O best of men; I shall carry out your word.
Lomaśa said:
Thus addressed, King Bhagīratha then replied to the daughter of Himavat, O King; having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, he said:
"O giver of boons, O great river, my grandfathers were [consumed] by Kapila."
Searching for their horse, sixty thousand sons of the great-souled Sāgara were led to the abode of Vaivasvata;
having encountered the fiery splendor of Kapila, they met their death in an instant.
For those who have thus perished, there is no dwelling in heaven as long as you do not sprinkle those bodies with water; until then,
my ancestors shall not reside in heaven.
"As long as there is no passage for them, O Great River, so long [is it for] those sons of Sagara.
O highly fortunate one, lead my ancestors, the sons of Sagara, to heaven;
for their sake, O Great River, I entreat you indeed."
Having heard these words of the king, Gaṅgā, who is honored by the worlds, spoke these words to Bhagīratha with great pleasure:
"O Great King, I shall do as you have requested; there is no doubt in this matter."
"O King, no one in the three worlds would have been able to sustain my momentum as I fell, displaced from the sky,
were it not for Maheśvara, the blue-throated one, the foremost among the gods."
O mighty-armed one, propitiate Hara, the granter of boons, through ascetic penance;
for that god will bear me upon his head when I have fallen,
and he will fulfill your desire out of a wish for the welfare of the ancestors.
"Lord Śambhu, the creator of the worlds, was propitiated through ascetic penance. Having heard these words, O King, the great king Bhagīratha went to Mount Kailāsa and gratified Śaṅkara.
Then, having met him at a certain juncture of time,
