O King, the lord of the earth requested the descent of the Gaṅgā; and the king obtained from him the boon of sustaining the Gaṅgā.
With the aim of securing a residence in heaven for his ancestors, that best of men—
Lomaśa said:
Having heard the words of Bhagīratha and for the sake of pleasing the inhabitants of heaven...
"So be it," the Blessed One replied to the king. "O mighty-armed one, best of kings, for your sake I shall sustain this auspicious, divine, and holy river of the gods as she falls from the sky."
Having spoken thus, O mighty-armed one, he approached the Himavat mountain,
surrounded by his terrible attendants who were brandishing various weapons.
Then, standing there, he spoke to Bhagīratha, the best of men.
"O mighty-armed one, entreat the daughter of the King of Mountains, that river,
for the sake of purifying your ancestors. O lord of men,
I shall hold that best of rivers as she falls from heaven."
Having heard these words uttered by Śarva, the king, becoming self-restrained and bowing low, meditated upon Gaṅgā. Then,
the beautiful river of holy waters was meditated upon by the king.
Seeing Īśāna standing there, she suddenly descended from the sky. Seeing her thus fallen, the gods, together with the great seers,
Gandharvas, serpents, and Rākṣasas, gathered there out of a desire to see her.
Then Gaṅgā, the daughter of Himavat, fell from the sky—
filled with agitated great whirlpools and teeming with fish and crocodiles.
O King, Hara sustained that Gaṅgā, the girdle of the heavens.
O King, that garland, as if made of pearls, fell upon the region of her forehead and spread out in three ways,
like rows of swans with waters turbid with masses of foam.
In some places winding in broad curves, stumbling here and there,
and draped in the garment of her own foam, she moved like an intoxicated woman;
in other places, she roared with the sounds of her waters, uttering a supreme cry.
In some places, as if contracting the sky on all sides with her whirlpools,
she created many such transformations; then, falling from the heavens and reaching the surface of the earth, she spoke to Bhagīratha.
"O Great King, show me the path by which I shall go;
O Lord of the Earth, I have descended to this world for your sake.
Having heard these words, King Bhagīratha set forth.
O best of men, the knower of dharma brought those bodies of the high-souled Sāgaras to the river, near the presence of the ancestors and the gods,
for the sake of purification by means of its holy waters.
Having performed the retention of the Gaṅgā, Hara, who is honored by the worlds,
went to Kailāsa, the best of mountains, together with the gods.
And having reached the ocean along with the Gaṅgā, O King, [he stayed there].

With great force, he filled the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa. Because she was held by Jahnu and then released by him, she was remembered as the Jāhnavī; and the king then adopted Gaṅgā as his own daughter.
There, his desires fulfilled, he offered water for the ancestors.
Thus, everything has been told to you regarding how Gaṅgā, flowing through the three paths,
was brought down to earth for the purpose of filling the ocean.
O King, just as the Kāleyas were struck down by the Thirty-three gods,
and just as the ocean was drunk for a specific purpose by the Great-souled One,
and just as Vātāpi, that slayer of Brahmins, was brought to his destruction, O Lord.
"O Great King, that which you ask me regarding Agastya," Vaiśampāyana said,
"then the son of Kuntī proceeded by stages, O bull of the Bharatas."
Having reached the mountain Hemakūṭa, which is free from all affliction, the king beheld the two rivers Nandā and Aparanandā, which remove both sin and fear,
and saw there many inconceivable and wonderful phenomena.
Where the clouds and thousands of stones became as speech,
the people, despondent in mind, were unable to ascend it;
where the wind blew constantly and the god rained perpetually.
The sound of Vedic recitation is heard there, yet no one is seen; flies and gadflies swarm there, obstructing his ascetic practice. Despair arises within him, and he begins to long for home.
"The Lord, the bearer of oblations, is seen both evening and morning.
Having observed such various and wondrous phenomena, the Pāṇḍava again questioned Lomaśa concerning that marvel.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, O you of great splendor, tell me all this in detail regarding that which is wonderful upon this mountain of great power."
Lomaśa said:
"O crusher of enemies, O King, listen with an attentive mind as I relate to you this which was previously heard by us."
On this mountain peak Ṛṣabhakūṭa, there lived an ascetic named Ṛṣabha.
A practitioner of austerities with a lifespan of many hundreds of years, he was exceedingly prone to anger.
When addressed by others, he would indeed speak to the mountain out of wrath.
"If anyone here should utter a word, you must then hurl stones at him. Having summoned the wind, that ascetic said,
"Do not make a sound," and any man who speaks is thus restrained by the cloud.

"O King, such were these deeds performed by that great seer; some were done out of anger, while others were prohibited. O King, there is a traditional account that in ancient times the gods approached Nandā."
The men, desiring a vision of the gods, pursued them with haste. But the gods, led by Śakra, not wishing to be seen,
made this region difficult of access by means of mountain obstructions.
From that time forth, O son of Kuntī, men have never been able even to look upon this mountain, much less ascend it;
this great mountain cannot be seen by one who has not performed austerities.
Or even to ascend it, O Kaunteya; therefore, be restrained in speech.
Here, all the gods have always performed the most excellent sacrifices;
their emblems are seen even today, O Bhārata.
"O lord of the people, this Durvā grass appears like Kuśa grass, and this ground seems as if strewn with it;
these many trees here, O ruler of men, take the form of sacrificial posts (yūpa),
and even today, O Bhārata, both gods and sages dwell here."
For them, the fire-god is seen both in the evening and in the morning.
O son of Kuntī, for those who have bathed here, their sin is instantly destroyed.
Therefore, O best of the Kurus, perform the ritual ablution together with your younger brothers.
Then, with your limbs bathed in the Nandā, you shall proceed to the Kauśikī,
where Viśvāmitra performed fierce and unsurpassed austerities.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having bathed his limbs there together with his attendants,
the king went to the holy and beautiful Kauśikī river, whose waters are auspicious.
Lomaśa said:
O bull of the Bharata race, this is the holy celestial river Kauśikī;
here also shines the delightful hermitage of Viśvāmitra.
And there is the hermitage of the high-souled Kāśyapa, known for its sanctity.
His son was the ascetic Ṛśyaśṛṅga, whose senses were fully restrained;
by the power of his austerity, he caused Vāsava to send rain during a drought out of fear of him, so that the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra poured down rain.
Born of a deer, that radiant lord was the son of Kaśyapa;
he performed a great miracle in the realm of Lomapāda,
for whom the king gave his daughter Śāntā once the crops had been turned back [from famine].
Lomapāda [gave] his daughter Sāvitrī, as Savitṛ [gave his daughter].
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How was Ṛśyaśṛṅga, the son of Kaśyapa, born from a deer?"
How was he endowed with ascetic power despite this forbidden union?
And for what reason did Śakra, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, send rain when a drought had set in, out of fear of that wise boy?
Of what nature was that princess of tranquil vows,
who captivated the heart of him who had become like a deer?
And when the royal seer Lomapāda was heard of as being righteous—
"How indeed was it that the subduer of Pāka did not send rain upon his realm?
O Blessed One, you ought to tell me all this in detail and exactly as it happened— the deeds of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, for I am eager to hear."
Lomaśa said:
Of the brahmin seer Vibhāṇḍaka, whose soul was purified by asceticism,
who possessed unfailing potency, and who was equal in splendor to Prajāpati—

Listen, my son, to how the powerful Ṛśyaśṛṅga was born: that child of great splendor, though young, was held in high esteem by the elders. Having reached Mahāhrada, the son of Kaśyapa remained established in ascetic penance.
The ṛṣi, esteemed by the celestial ṛṣis, was exhausted from his long-term austerities;
upon seeing the apsarā Urvaśī, his seed spilled. O King, as he was performing ablutions in the water, a doe then drank it.
O King, having become thirsty, she drank water and became pregnant.
She had previously been told by the Blessed Brahmā, the creator of the world:
"Having become a deer, you shall give birth to a sage and be liberated."
Because the ritual was unfailing and because destiny had ordained it,
a great ṛṣi was born to him from that deer;
named Ṛśyaśṛṅga, he grew up in the forest alone, ever devoted to asceticism.
O King, on the head of that high-souled one there was a horn of a rishya deer;
because of that, he then became celebrated as Ṛśyaśṛṅga. No human other than his father had ever been seen by him before.
Therefore, O King, his mind was constantly fixed upon the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
At that very time, however, there was a friend of Daśaratha known as Lomapāda, who was the lord of the Aṅgas.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, through the transgression of that king’s theft and misconduct,
it is heard that he falsely committed an offense against the Brahmins;
for even though he was a knower of dharma, O Bhārata, his inner being had been struck down by fate.
Then that lord of the earth was abandoned by the brahmins;
and because of the high priest’s misconduct,
the thousand-eyed Indra did not send rain at his will, and consequently the subjects were indeed afflicted.
The lord of the earth questioned those wise brahmins, endowed with ascetic power and capable of making the lord of the gods send rain:
"How might Parjanya pour down rain? Let a means be devised."
Urged by him, those wise men each spoke their own opinions;
however, one eminent sage there addressed the king:
"O Indra among kings, the brahmins are angry with you; perform an act of atonement."
"O King, bring here the sage's son, Ṛśyaśṛṅga— he who dwells in the forest,
is ignorant of women, and delights in uprightness.
O King, if that man of great asceticism should enter your domain,"
"The rain-cloud shall pour forth immediately; of this I have no doubt.
O King, having heard these words and having made amends for himself, he departed and returned once the twice-born were appeased.
Seeing that the king had arrived, the subjects welcomed him;
and he, ever acting for their welfare, received them like a father.
Then the lord of Aṅga summoned his ministers, who were experts in counsel.

He made an effort toward the arrival of Ṛśyaśṛṅga through the determination of counsel; and together with those ministers— who were unswerving, well-versed in the scriptures, proficient in worldly affairs, and fully established in political science— he devised a plan.
Then the lord of the earth summoned the foremost courtesans—
prostitutes skilled in every art— and that king spoke to them:
"Bring here by some means the seer’s son, Ṛśyaśṛṅga."
Having enticed and gained the confidence of those beautiful women,
he directed them toward the seduction of that boy;
and those women, terrified by fear of the king and fear of a curse, [acted accordingly].
Pale and despondent, they declared that the task was impossible;
however, thereupon one aged woman spoke thus to the king:
"O Great King, I shall strive to bring back that man whose wealth is his asceticism."
"You ought to grant permission for my desired wishes;
then I shall be able to seduce the seer's son, Ṛśyaśṛṅga.
The king granted her every intention.
And he bestowed abundant wealth and various kinds of jewels. Then, O lord of the earth, taking with her certain women endowed with beauty and youth, she departed straightway for the forest.
Lomaśa said:
O descendant of Bharata, she established a hermitage on the boat for the sake of accomplishing the king's purpose, both by the command of the monarch and through her own intelligence.
Adorned with artificial trees bearing various flowers and fruits,
and endowed with diverse shrubs and creepers that yield delicious fruits according to one's desires,
it was exceedingly delightful and truly captivating to the mind.

He constructed a delightful boat-dwelling hermitage, the sight of which was like a marvel. Then, having moored that boat not far from the hermitage of Kāśyapa, he had it attended by men for the purpose of providing recreation for that sage.
Then the courtesan, having instructed her daughter in what was to be done,
and seeing an opportunity regarding Kāśyapa, sent forth that woman who was highly esteemed for her intelligence.
Having gone there, she approached the presence of him who was constantly devoted to asceticism.
Having reached that hermitage, she saw the son of the seer.
The courtesan said:
"O sage, is all well with the ascetics?"
I hope you have an abundance of roots and fruits,
and I hope you find delight in this hermitage;
for I have come now specifically to see you.
I hope the asceticism of the forest-dwellers prospers;
I hope your father’s splendor remains undiminished;
and I hope, O Brahmin, that he is pleased with you.
"Is your Vedic recitation being performed? Rishyashringa replied,
"You are prosperous and shine like a light."
I consider you worthy of salutation;
I shall gladly offer you water for your feet and,
according to dharma, fruits and roots as well.
"Sit as you please upon this comfortable seat of kuśa grass covered with a black antelope skin;
where is your hermitage, and what is the name of this [place]?"
"O Brahmin, you indeed observe a vow like a god.
The courtesan said:
"O son of Kaśyapa, my hermitage is beautiful;"
Beyond this mountain, which is three yojanas wide,
our own custom is that we do not offer salutations;
nor do we touch water for washing the feet.
"I am not to be saluted by you; rather, you are to be saluted by me. O Brahmin, such is my vow; you are to be embraced by me.
Ṛśyaśṛṅga said:
"I shall give you ripe fruits:
bhallātaka, āmalaka, parūṣaka, iṅguda, and dhanvana."
Do as you wish with those who are dear to you; indeed, out of my desire to be of service, take what you wish and fulfill whatever desire I have for you.
Lomaśa said:
Having set all those aside,
she then gave him highly precious foods to eat.
Those highly flavorful fruits of Ṛśyaśṛṅga were exceedingly beautiful and indeed gave him great delight;
and she presented him with fragrant garlands.
Then he rejoiced in variegated and radiant garments and the finest drinks;
he played, sported, and laughed aloud.
She played with a ball at his side, like a flowering creeper bending under its own weight,
her limbs rubbing against his limbs.
And he repeatedly embraced Ṛśyaśṛṅga, bending down and breaking off the blossoming *sarja*, *aśoka*, and *tilaka* trees.
As if bashful yet overcome by passion,
she sought to seduce the son of the great seer,
having gazed upon the deformed Ṛśyaśṛṅga.
Repeatedly pressing her body against him and looking back at him, she departed slowly,
using the performance of the *agnihotra* sacrifice as a pretext.
When she had gone, Ṛśyaśṛṅga became intoxicated with passion and lost his senses;
he was empty, his heart having gone entirely toward her.
Sighing, he became distressed in appearance;
then, in a moment, his tawny-brown eyes were covered with hair from the tips of his nails down to his skin.
Vibhāṇḍaka Kāśyapa, devoted to sacred study and endowed with the concentration of virtuous conduct, appeared;
having approached, he saw his son seated there.
Vibhāṇḍaka spoke dejectedly to his son, who was meditating alone with a troubled mind, sighing repeatedly with his gaze fixed upward:
"My son, why are the sacrificial fuel-sticks not being prepared?
Have you performed the Agnihotra sacrifice today? Are the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles well-polished, and is the sacrificial cow ready?"
"Have you today made [the cow] have her calf?
For you do not seem as you did before, my son; you are lost in thought and distracted."
"Why are you so exceedingly dejected here today? I ask you: who has come here today?
Ṛśyaśṛṅga said:
A matted-haired ascetic, a celibate student, has arrived here;
he is neither short nor too tall, wise,
golden-hued, and with eyes as broad as lotuses.
Resplendent like the son of the gods,
possessing a perfected form and shining like the sun, his eyes were exceedingly bright white and black, like those of the cakora birds.
His matted locks are blue, radiant, fragrant,
very long, and tied with golden cords;
moreover, they serve as an ornament upon his neck.
He shines like lightning in the sky;
and two lumps below his throat are hairless and very beautiful.
His waist was slender at the navel region,
and his hips were of exceeding proportions; thus, covered by the hem of his bark garment, they shone forth.
Just as this golden girdle of mine [shines],
so too does another wondrous and beautiful garland of golden luster shine upon her.
Just as a rosary is held at the throat and sways upon the chest when worn by you,
there was another thing of wondrous appearance.
A tinkling sound emanates from his feet,
and likewise from his hands,
which are bound with jingling ornaments like this rosary of beads.
As he struggled,
those garments of his, wonderful to behold, made sounds like intoxicated swans in a lake.
These forms of mine are not like those;
her face is wondrous to behold,
and her speech seems to gladden the heart.
And his voice was like that of the male cuckoo;
as I hear it, my inner soul is distressed,
just as a forest in the middle of the month of Mādhava.
Just as it blows when stirred by the wind,
so too, O dear one, does he, possessing the most excellent fragrance,
blow while being attended by the wind.
His matted locks, well-restrained and neatly parted,
shine symmetrically divided upon his forehead;
and his ears appear as if adorned with variegated circular ornaments.
When it was covered by those possessing beautiful forms,
its fruit likewise became variegated;
then he struck it with his right hand.
Having reached that ground, it rises up again and again with a wondrous form on high;
and having struck it, that [being] rolls about.
Reeling like a tree shaken by the wind— O dear one, upon seeing him, a supreme joy and delight arose within me, as if he were my own son among the immortals.
He embraced my body once more, and grasping my matted locks, he bent my face down;
placing his mouth against my mouth, he made a sound.
That caused great joy to arise within me;
yet he did not value the water for washing his feet,
nor these fruits which I had brought.
He said to me, "I am one who observes such a vow," and he gave me other fresh fruits; those fruits were consumed by me.
These are not equal to them in taste,
nor is their bark like this;
they do not possess cores such as these have.
That one of noble form indeed gave me waters of exceeding flavor to drink;
having drunk them, my joy became even greater.
It seemed to me as if the earth were shaking;
these variegated and fragrant garlands were fastened upon him with silk ribbons.
Having scattered these [offerings] here, he departed for his own hermitage, shining with ascetic power;
by his departure, I have been rendered distraught.
My body is burning intensely all over;
I wish to go quickly to his presence,
for he is constantly revolving here.
"I shall go to him alone, father;
what indeed is that practice of his vow? I wish to perform it together with him."
Just as that man of fierce deeds practices asceticism,
such is the desire in my heart; my mind is tormented if I do not see him.
Vibhāṇḍaka said:
"O son, these are Rākṣasas who roam about in that form of wondrous appearance."
O dear one, those of incomparable form and exceedingly terrible always contemplate obstacles to asceticism,
yet they also possess beautiful forms.
They entice them with various means and cause them to fall from happiness and from the higher worlds;
such are the fierce deeds [of those who prey] upon sages in the forests.
A sage of restrained self, seeking in every way the worlds of the virtuous, should never associate with those who take delight in creating obstacles for ascetics.
O sinless son, those practices of austerity performed by the wicked are themselves evil;
they are like wines that must not be drunk.
"These flower garlands, variegated, radiant, and fragrant, are certainly not prescribed for sages.
Lomaśa said:
Having restrained his son with the words, "Those are rākṣasas," Vibhāṇḍaka set out on that hunt;
yet when he did not find them after three days, he returned.
Then he returned to the hermitage when Kāśyapa had gone out again to gather fruits according to the ascetic rule.
Then she went again to seduce him;
as soon as the sage Ṛśyaśṛṅga saw that courtesan, he was filled with joy.
Then, appearing agitated,
he rushed toward her and said, "Let us go to your hermitage before my father returns."
Then, O King, having caused Kāśyapa’s only son to enter by means of yoga and having released the boat,
they tempted him with various stratagems.
Having moored that exceedingly bright boat within sight of the hermitage, they approached the presence of the lord of Aṅga.
Starting from the riverbank, he likewise created a wonderful forest named Rājāśrama;
and having settled him within the inner apartments, the king—
He suddenly beheld the god raining down, the only son of Vibhāṇḍaka,
as the world was being filled with water.
O King, when Ṛṣyaśṛṅga had arrived,
Lomapāda, his desires fulfilled,
gave his daughter Śāntā to Ṛṣyaśṛṅga.
And he devised means to retaliate against his anger,
including the dragging of cattle across the paths;
meanwhile, King [Daśaratha] was traveling toward Vibhāṇḍaka’s hermitage.
The great seer Vibhāṇḍaka, longing for his son, commanded many cattle and heroic cowherds:
"When he asks you [about me]," he said.
He should be addressed by you with palms joined in reverence:
"O Great Seer, cattle and the cultivation of land belong to your son; what indeed may be done that is pleasing to you?"
"We are all your slaves, bound by your word. Having thus provided the remedy for the pacification of his anger, the king then became happy.
Then that sage, prone to fierce anger,
returned to his own hermitage bringing roots and fruits;
yet, searching there, he did not find his son.
He saw it and then became violently enraged;
then, being torn apart by anger,
he suspected some plot of the king.
Desiring to set it ablaze, he went toward Campā,
intending to consume that king of Aṅga and his territory.
Exhausted and hungry, that descendant of Kaśyapa [approached] them.
Having reached the prosperous villages,
he was duly honored by those cowherds and stayed there that night like a king.
Having received an exceedingly great reception from them,
he said, "O gentle ones, whose [disciples] are you, renowned as you are?
Then they all approached him and spoke.
"This wealth is ordained for you and your son;
likewise, these cowherds and these farmers [are yours]. Being honored in every region," he said.
Hearing those sweet lamentations,
his passion largely stilled and filled with joy,
he approached the Lord of Aṅga who stood before him.
Honored by that bull among men,
he beheld his son there like the god Indra in heaven,
and he also beheld his daughter-in-law Śāntā there.
Just as he had seen Saudāminī rising up,
and having seen the villages, the cowherd settlements, and his son,
his supreme anger was pacified by Śāntā.
O lord of men, Vibhāṇḍaka showed the highest favor toward that king;
having entrusted his son there, the great seer—
He, whose splendor was equal to that of the sun and fire, said:
"Once a son has been born, you should depart for the forest after having performed all that is pleasing to this king."
"O King, having done exactly so for this monarch," having said this to Ṛśyaśṛṅga,
the high-souled Vibhaṇḍaka [was addressed] by King Romapāda.
Having been honored, the great seer, with a joyful heart,
went to the forest frequented by the best of sages;
Ṛśyaśṛṅga acted according to those words.
And he went to where his father was; and Śāntā attended upon him properly,
as favorable as Rohiṇī is to Soma in the sky.
Just as Arundhatī was to the fortunate Vasiṣṭha, or Lopāmudrā to Agastya,
or as Damayantī was to Nala;
Just as Śacī is to the wielder of the thunderbolt, and Nāḍāyanī and Indrasenā likewise, so too,
O descendant of Ajamīḍha, is she ever submissive to Mudgala.
O you whose fame is equal to the rising moon after the departure of Rāhu,
just as Sītā was to the high-souled son of Daśaratha,
so was Draupadī to you, O son of Pāṇḍu.
Likewise, O lord of men, Śāntā, filled with affection, attended upon Ṛśyaśṛṅga while he dwelt in the forest;
this is his sacred hermitage that shines forth.
Adorning the great lake of Puṇyakīrti,
having bathed here, fulfilled in purpose, and purified— O King, proceed now to other sacred fords.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O Janamejaya, the Pāṇḍava set out from the Kauśikī river and visited all the sacred shrines in their proper order.
O King, having reached the ocean at the confluence of the Gaṅgā,
he performed his ritual ablutions in the midst of five hundred rivers.
Thereafter, the lord of the earth proceeded along the shore of the sea.
Accompanied by his brothers, O Bhārata, the hero set out toward Kaliṅga.
Lomaśa said:
"O son of Kuntī, these are the Kaliṅgas, where the river Vaitaraṇī flows."
Where even Dharma, having sought refuge with the gods,
performed sacrifice; this northern bank, frequented by the twice-born, is graced by the mountain and is the site where the sages have performed their sacrificial rites.
By the level path that leads to the gods, those who have ascended to heaven—
here indeed, in ancient times, other sages also performed sacrifices with ritual offerings.
It was right here, O Indra among kings, that Rudra seized the sacrificial animal during a sacrifice.
"O Indra among men, Rudra said, 'This animal is my portion.
When the animal had been taken away, O bull of the Bharatas, the gods then said to him:
'Do not covet the property of others; do not transgress all the laws of righteousness.'"
Then they praised Rudra with words of auspicious form;
having gratified him with a sacrifice, they then honored him, saying:
"This, O Rudra, is indeed your portion; do not destroy this sacrifice of ours."
"‘This is your sacrificial animal,’ so said the assembled gods. Thereupon, having released the animal, he departed by the path of the gods.
In this regard, O Yudhiṣṭhira, learn from me this traditional account concerning Rudra."

Out of fear of Rudra, the gods ordained this eternal portion for him— the foremost share from all shares, free from decay. Any man who touches water while singing this verse here [attains that same state].
"The path of the gods is his, and his vision indeed becomes clear.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Then all the Pāṇḍavas, as well as Draupadī, [crossed] the Vaitaraṇī river."
Having descended, those highly fortunate ones offered libations to their ancestors.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, O you whose wealth is asceticism, having merely touched the water of this river—"
"I have departed from the human realm; behold, O Lomaśa!
By your grace, O observer of noble vows, I perceive all the worlds.
This is the sound of the high-souled Vaikhānasas engaged in silent recitation."
Lomaśa said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, lord of the people, this place where you hear this sound is indeed three hundred thousand yojanas away; remain silent."

O King, son of Kuntī, this beautiful forest of the Self-Existent One shines forth, where the powerful Viśvakarman performed sacrifice; for it was at that sacrifice that the earth was given to the high-souled Kaśyapa.

O son of Kuntī, as soon as the southern region, including its mountains and forest tracts, had been assigned by the Self-born One, the Earth sank down; and being enraged, she spoke these words to the Lord, the Sovereign of the World: 03,114.018c–03,114.019c: "The southern region, together with its mountains and forest tracts, was indeed assigned by the Self-born One. But as soon as it was given, O Kaunteya, the Earth sank down. And she, filled with anger, addressed this to the Lord, the Master of the World."
"O Blessed One, you ought not to give me away to any mortal; this gift of yours would be in vain. I shall go to the netherworld (rasātala).
Having spoken thus, the Earth departed for the netherworld.

O best of the Kurus, O descendant of Bharata, she sank down even though she was being entreated. Seeing her despondent, the venerable seer Kaśyapa then sought to appease the Earth, O lord of the people.
Then, O Pāṇḍava, the earth was gratified by his ascetic power;
emerging once more from the water, she stood manifest in the form of an altar.
This very altar, O King, characterized by its established form, shines forth here.
"O Great King, by ascending this, you shall indeed become possessed of great heroism.
O King, this very altar, having reached the ocean, rests there;
ascend it—blessings be upon you—and cross the ocean alone."
And I shall perform for you a rite of well-being,
so that you may ascend her today; for once she has been touched by a mortal, she will then [enter] the ocean.
This altar enters [the ocean], O descendant of Ajamīḍha.
Om! Salutations to the Protector of the Universe; salutations to You, the Supreme One of the Universe. O Lord of Gods, manifest Your presence here in the salt-water ocean.
"Agni, Mitra, the womb, and the divine waters;
you, O Viṣṇu, are the seed and the navel of immortality.
Speaking these words of truth, O Pāṇḍava;
Ascend this altar with vigor; Agni is your womb and Iḍā is your body— you are the depositor of seed and the navel of the immortal Viṣṇu.
O Pāṇḍava, reciting this truthful speech,
one should then plunge into the Lord of Rivers;
for otherwise, O best of the Kurus, he is a divine being, the lord of the waters.
O son of Kuntī, even with the tip of a blade of kusha grass, one must not touch the great ocean.
With clarified butter as its sacrificial grass and clarified butter as its source, it is beyond reproach;
it is indeed the reservoir of those very waters.
Whatever sin a man commits throughout hundreds of thousands of births,
he is liberated from all those sins by bathing in the salt waters.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having performed the rites for auspiciousness, the high-souled Yudhiṣṭhira went toward the ocean,
having carried out all of his instructions.
Having reached Mount Mahendra, he stayed there for the night.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having dwelt there for that single night, the lord of the earth—
Together with his brothers, he rendered the highest honor to the ascetics.
And Lomaśa pointed out all those ascetics there to him—
the Bhṛgus, the Aṅgirases, the Vasiṣṭhas, and the Kāśyapas.
Having approached them and saluted them with palms joined in reverence, that royal seer questioned the heroic Akṛtavraṇa, a follower of Rāma:
"When, indeed, will the blessed Rāma show himself to the ascetics?"
"For that very reason, I wish to see the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Akṛtavraṇa said:
"You have already been made known to Rāma, who knows his own self."
"Rāma’s affection for you will soon allow him to see you;
ascetics behold Rāma on the fourteenth and the eighth days of the lunar fortnight.
When this night has passed, it will be the fourteenth day."
"There you shall see Rāma, wearing a black antelope skin and matted hair.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"You have followed the heroic and mighty son of Jamadagni."
"You, who have direct perception of all past deeds,
please explain how and for what reason all the Kṣatriyas were defeated by Rāma in battle."
Akṛtavraṇa said:
"O tiger among kings, O Bhārata, I shall relate to you a great and supreme narrative concerning one born in the lineage of the Bhṛgus."
The life-story of Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, which is equal to that of the gods,
and also that of Kārtavīrya, the lord of the Haihayas, O Bhārata;
and how Arjuna, the lord of the Haihayas, was slain by Rāma.
O Pāṇḍava, lord of the earth, by the grace of Dattātreya, he possessed three hundred and seven arms, as well as a golden celestial chariot and sovereignty over all beings on the earth.
The chariot of that great-souled one possessed an unimpeded course;
with that chariot, by virtue of the boon he had received, the heroic one constantly crushed the gods, the yakṣas, and the ṛṣis on all sides.
He oppressed all living beings on every side.
Then the gods and the sages of great vows assembled and spoke to Viṣṇu, the god of gods, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, whose prowess is truth.
"O Blessed One, O Lord, slay Arjuna indeed for the sake of protecting the living beings. Furthermore,
by means of a divine celestial chariot, the lord of the Haihayas once again overpowered Vāsava as he was sporting with Śacī."

Then, O Bhārata, the Blessed Lord, together with Śakra, deliberated for the sake of Kārtavīrya’s destruction regarding that task for the welfare of all beings which had been reported by the Lord of the Gods.
Having promised all of that, the Blessed One, honored by the world,
went to the delightful Badarī, his own hermitage circle.
At that very time, however, there was a lord of the earth upon the earth.
Akṛtavraṇa said:
"O King, there was once a great monarch of immense power in Kanyakubja;
he was the son of Kuśika, born into that lineage."

Renowned in the world as Gādhi, he went to dwell in the forest. While he was living in the forest, a daughter was born to him who was like an Apsaras; she had eyes like a hundred-petaled lotus and was peerless on earth in her beauty.
O Bhārata, Ṛcīka of the Bhṛgu lineage then sought her hand in marriage.
Thereupon, the king said to that brahmin of rigid vows:
"There is a certain custom established by our ancestors that has been practiced in our family."
"O best of the twice-born, know that the bride-price consists of a thousand swift, white horses, each with one black ear; and you,
O Bhārgava, must not say to the Blessed One, 'Let it be given.'"
"And this daughter of mine must be given by me to a high-souled man such as you.
Ṛcīka said:
"I require horses that are white, swift, and each with one black ear."
"I shall give you a thousand horses; my wife and my sons shall be yours.
Akṛtavraṇa said:
"O King, having promised 'So be it,' he spoke to Varuṇa."
"Let one thousand swift, white horses, each with one black ear, be given to me as my bride-price.
Varuṇa then gave him those one thousand horses.
That place became famous as Aśvatīrtha, where those horses emerged;
at Kanyakubja on the Gaṅgā, Gādhi then gave his daughter Satyavatī to him, and the gods were the wedding guests.
Having obtained the thousand horses and having seen those celestial beings,
they were filled with supreme wonder and praised him alone in heaven.
Having rightfully obtained that wife, Ṛcīka, the best of the twice-born, [departed].

He took his pleasure with that woman of slender waist, according to his desire and as he pleased. O King, when the marriage had been performed, the best of the Bhrigus came to see him and his wife; seeing his son, he rejoiced.
Then the husband and wife, having honored their guru— who was seated and worshipped by the hosts of gods— sat beside him with palms joined in reverence.
Thereupon, the blessed Bhṛgu, being well-pleased, spoke to his daughter-in-law.
"Choose a boon, O blessed one, for I am the giver of what you desire.
She then propitiated that preceptor for the sake of her son;
and he bestowed his grace both upon herself and upon her mother.
Bhṛgu said:

"When you and your mother have both bathed after your menstrual periods for the sake of the *puṃsavana* rite, you two should embrace separate trees— you an *udumbara* tree and she an *aśvattha* tree."
"O blessed lady, these two *carus* are for your mother and for you alone;
having brought the entire universe under my control, I have prepared them with great effort.
You must consume them with care," he said, and then vanished from sight.
O King, in their embrace, however, they committed a reversal;
at times Bhṛgu would arrive and he would perceive that reversal.
Then, after a long period of time had passed, the Blessed One [returned].
Having learned this through his divine knowledge, the Blessed One returned once more.
Then the highly resplendent Bhṛgu spoke to his daughter-in-law Satyavatī:
"O blessed lady, the sacrificial porridge was consumed, and the tree was embraced."
"O fair-browed one, you have been deceived by me through my deceptive power.
Your son shall indeed be a Brāhmaṇa following the conduct of a Kṣatriya;
your son, O mother, shall be a great Kṣatriya who follows the conduct of a Brāhmaṇa."
"He will be of great heroism and established on the path of the virtuous.
Then she propitiated her father-in-law again and again, saying, "May my son not be like this; rather, may my grandson be so."
"So be it," she replied to him, O Pāṇḍava, and having been thus gratified,
she awaited the proper time and bore that fetus with great care.
Then, when the time had come, she gave birth to a son, Jamadagni.
Endowed with splendor and luster, that delight of the Bhṛgus grew in brilliance through his study of the Veda; possessed of great energy,
O son of Pāṇḍu, he surpassed many sages.
O bull of the Bharatas, the entire science of archery and the fourfold weapons appeared to him, who possessed a splendor like that of the sun. Akṛtavraṇa said:
Jamadagni, of great ascetic power, was devoted to the study of the Vedas;
he then performed austerities and, through his self-restraint, brought the gods under his control.
As that brahmin-sage was performing penance, the gods, together with Indra, spoke to him.
"For what purpose do you perform austerities, O Brahmin? What desire do you seek?
Thus addressed, the best of the brahmin-sages replied to the gods:
"I perform austerities for the sake of heaven, and may my worlds be imperishable."
Having heard those words of his, the gods then said to him:
"The world does not come into being for one who lacks progeny, even if he has performed hundreds of righteous deeds.
Having heard those words of the thirty gods, O best of the Kurus...
Having approached King Prasenajit, the lord of men,
he requested Reṇukā in marriage, and that king gave her to him.
Then, having obtained Reṇukā as his wife, the delighter of the Bhṛgus—
Dwelling in the hermitage, he practiced austerities together with that devoted wife.
To them were born four sons, with Rāma as the fifth; of all of them, Rāma, though the youngest born, was the most distinguished.
When all her sons had gone out to gather fruits for their food,
Reṇukā, firm in her vows, once went to bathe.
She [encountered] the king named Citraratha, a ruler of the Mārttikāvatakas.
O King, Reṇukā saw him approaching by chance;
seeing Padmamālin sporting in the water with his wife, and beholding his prosperity, Reṇukā then began to envy him.

Because of that transgression, she became senseless in the wet water; terrified, she entered the hermitage, where her husband indeed perceived her as she had fallen from the sky into the great lake of the Narmadā.
Having crossed [the river] with great effort, O bull of the Bharatas, she departed.
Seeing her fallen from her composure and deprived of her Brahmanic splendor, the highly energetic and valiant one censured her with the cry of "Fie! (dhik).
Then the eldest son of Jamadagni, known by the name Rumaṇvat,
as well as Suṣeṇa, Vasu, and Viśvāvasu, arrived.
The Blessed One urged them one after another to slay their mother.
Overwhelmed by confusion and deprived of their senses, they said nothing at all.
Then, out of anger, he cursed them; thus cursed, they lost their consciousness and quickly became like beasts and birds, resembling inert matter.
Then Rāma, the slayer of enemy heroes, returned later to the hermitage.
Jamadagni, of great ascetic power and immense wrath, said to him:
"Kill this sinful mother; and do not, my son, feel any remorse."
O King, having been addressed thus by his preceptor Jamadagni in anger,
Rāma then took up an axe and struck off his mother's head.
Then, O great king, [the wrath] of that high-souled Jamadagni—
His anger departed suddenly, and being pleased, he said this:
"O dear one, at my word you have performed this difficult task. Choose, O knower of dharma, as many boons as you desire from the depths of your heart."
O Bhārata, he chose his mother’s restoration to life, the loss of memory regarding the slaying,
freedom from contact with that sin, the natural state of his brothers,
invincibility in battle, and a long life.
And Jamadagni of great asceticism granted all those desires.
Once, O Lord, while his sons had likewise gone out,
the heroic Kārtavīrya, the lord of the Anūpas, arrived there.
When he arrived at that hermitage, the seer’s wife honored him;
yet, intoxicated by the pride of battle, he did not welcome such hospitality. Then, having violently driven away the sacrificial cow from that hermitage by force, he departed.

He carried off the calf while she was crying out and broke down the great trees. When Rāma arrived, his father himself told him what had happened; and seeing the cow lowing piteously, anger took possession of Rāma.
Overcome by fury, he rushed toward Kārtavīrya;
then, displaying his prowess in battle, the descendant of Bhṛgu, the slayer of enemy heroes,
severed his arms— which resembled iron clubs— with sharpened, broad-headed arrows.
O King, having taken up that beautiful bow capable of withstanding a thousand [weights],
he was overcome by Rāma through the law of time;
having returned and reported that deed to his father, he departed for the forest.

Then Arjuna’s heirs, provoked to anger by Rāma, rushed toward Jamadagni while he was staying in his hermitage, even though Rāma was not there. They slew that great hero, who was an ascetic and was not fighting.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, after Jamadagni had caused the sons of Kārtavīrya to be slain with arrows, those subduers of enemies departed as they had come, while he cried out repeatedly like one who is helpless, "Rāma! Rāma!"
When they had departed and Jamadagni had likewise passed away,
the descendant of Bhṛgu approached the hermitage with fuel in his hand.
Seeing his father thus fallen under the power of death, the hero—
Thus, being in such a state and deeply distressed, he lamented for one who deserved no such fate.
Rāma said:
"O father, you have been slain by those base and foolish men because of my own transgression."

O dear one, how could such a death have befallen that knower of dharma, who was walking the path of the righteous and innocent toward all living beings, like a deer in the forest struck by the arrows of the descendants of Kārtavīrya?
"What sin indeed was not committed by those by whom you, established in asceticism,
being an old man and not fighting, were slain with hundreds of sharp arrows? What indeed will they say there to their ministers and friends?"
"Having slain this single man who was not fighting, who knew the dharma,
and who was without shame," Akṛtavraṇa said:
"O King, having lamented thus piteously and at great length in various ways..."
The one of great asceticism performed all the funeral rites for his father;
Rāma, the conqueror of enemy cities, cremated his father in the fire and,
O Bhārata, vowed the slaughter of the entire kṣatriya order.
Enraged, exceedingly powerful, heroic, and valiant, he alone— resembling Death itself— took up his weapon and slew the sons of Kārtavīrya,
as well as those kṣatriyas who followed them, O bull among kṣatriyas.
And Rāma, the best of strikers, crushed them all;
having cleared the earth of the kṣatriya caste twenty-one times,
the Lord created five lakes of blood at Samantapañcaka.
There, that scion of Bhrigu’s lineage offered libations to the ancestors;
he beheld Carcika in person, and he (Carcika) restrained Rama.
Then, with a great sacrifice, the powerful son of Jamadagni—
He gratified the Lord of the Gods and gave land to the officiating priests;
O lord of the people, he also gave a golden altar to the high-souled Kaśyapa,
having made it ten fathoms long and nine high.
With the permission of Kaśyapa, the brahmins then divided that land into pieces; O King, because of that, they became known as the Khāṇḍavāyanas.
Having bestowed the earth upon that high-souled Kaśyapa, he—

On this Mahendra, the king of mountains, he who possesses immeasurable valor dwells, having undertaken most great asceticism; he is endowed with great strength and prowess. Thus did his enmity arise with the Kṣatriyas who inhabit the world.
And the earth was also conquered by Rāma of immeasurable splendor.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, on the fourteenth day, according to the agreement, the high-minded Rāma—
He revealed himself to those brahmins and to Dharmarāja along with his younger brothers.
That lord, the king of kings, together with his brothers, paid him homage;
that best of monarchs also performed the highest worship for the twice-born.
Having honored the son of Jamadagni, and having been honored by him in turn,
the lord Mahendra, after staying that night on Mahendra, the best of mountains, set out facing the south.
Having addressed Rāma,
the righteous-souled Vaiśampāyana said:
"That high-souled one, proceeding to the sacred fords..."
The king beheld all those auspicious and delightful places adorned with brahmins here and there along the ocean, O Bhārata.
Having performed his ablutions among them,
he— virtuous, accompanied by his younger brothers, and surrounded by kings, sons, and grandsons— [reached] the most meritorious and praiseworthy river that flows to the ocean.
The son of Pāṇḍu, the descendant of Parīkṣit, went there;
having bathed even there, the high-souled one offered libations to the ancestors and the gods.
Having bestowed his wealth upon the foremost of the twice-born,
he went to the Godāvarī, which flows toward the ocean; then, O King, being cleansed of sin, he proceeded among the Draviḍas.
Having reached the ocean, the merit of the world,
he beheld the holy and purifying Agastyatīrtha, and then the hero saw the Nārītīrthas.
There, having heard of that deed of Arjuna, the foremost of archers, which was unbearable for his enemies,
he was being honored by throngs of supreme sages.
The son of Pāṇḍu attained supreme joy,
his limbs consecrated by bathing in those sacred fords,
accompanied by Kṛṣṇā and joined by his younger brothers.
Honoring the prowess of Arjuna,
the lord of kings rejoiced upon the earth;
then, having bestowed thousands of cows as gifts;
At those sacred fords, being delighted along with his brothers, he recounted the gift of cattle by Arjuna, that best of cloud-bearers.
Then, together with his younger brother, he entered the holy Kāverī, whose waters are infinite and which is constantly frequented by divine hermitages.
With his fatigue, grief, and sins destroyed, he rejoiced,
O King, as he visited those sacred fords of the ocean and many other holy places.
Traveling by stages with his desires fulfilled,
he beheld the most holy Śūrpāraka;
there, having passed over a certain region of the ocean;
He reached a forest renowned throughout the earth,
where in former times the gods performed austerities and likewise the most meritorious kings offered sacrifices.
There, he of the long and muscular arms beheld that sacrificial altar of the son of Ṛcīka, the foremost of archers, surrounded by throngs of ascetics.
Then that lord of the earth [honored] her, who was surrounded [by them], meritorious, and worthy of worship— she who belonged to the Vasus,
the hosts of Maruts, and likewise to the Aśvins.
Of Vaivasvata, Āditya, and Dhaneśvara;
of Indra, Viṣṇu, and the all-pervading Savitṛ; of Bhaga, Candra, and Divākara.
O King, that high-souled one was the father of the waters, of the host of Sādhyas, of Dhātṛ, of the Pitṛs,
and likewise of Rudra along with his attendants.
Of Sarasvatī and the host of Siddhas,
of Pūṣan and whatever other immortals there may be, as well as their holy shrines;
The king beheld those most enchanting places,
where various fasts had been observed and great treasures of jewels had been bestowed.
Having bathed his limbs at all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*),
he returned once more to Śūrpāraka by way of that very ford of the ocean.
Setting out once again with his sisters and great brahmins renowned throughout the earth,
he arrived at the sacred site of Prabhāsa.
There, having been consecrated, Pṛthu with his red eyes,
together with his younger brothers, gratified the hosts of gods and the ancestors, and likewise Kṛṣṇā.
And those brahmins, together with Lomaśa,
spent twelve days subsisting on water and air, performing their ritual ablutions day and night.
Having kindled fires on all sides,
he, the most excellent among the upholders of dharma, practiced austerities;
as he was engaged in that fierce asceticism, they watched him.
Both Rāma and Janārdana—
the two foremost of all the Vṛṣṇis— along with their armies, heard [the news] and went to Yudhiṣṭhira, the descendant of Ajamīḍha.
Those Vṛṣṇis, beholding the sons of Pāṇḍu lying upon the ground with their limbs smeared with filth,
and seeing Draupadī as well, who did not deserve such a fate;
Deeply distressed, they cried out in piteous lamentation;
then [he beheld] Rāma, Janārdana,
the son of Kṛṣṇa (Sātyaki), Sāmba, and the grandson of Śini (Yuyudhāna).
Approaching the other Vṛṣṇis as well, he of undaunted spirit offered them worship according to dharma;
and they too, having honored all the Pārthas in return, [departed].
O King, having been thus honored by the sons of Pāṇḍu, they sat down surrounding Yudhiṣṭhira,
just as the hosts of gods surround Indra.
He, being supremely pleased, related to them all the conduct of those others, their dwelling in the forest,
and how Pārtha had gone to Indra for the sake of weapons.
Kṛṣṇa announced the son of the king of the gods.
Having heard his words, they were reassured;
and seeing them as well, who were exceedingly emaciated, they were likewise comforted.
The high-souled Daśārhas shed tears born from their eyes, arising from the pain of grief.
Janamejaya said:

"Having reached Prabhāsa-tīrtha, what did the Vṛṣṇis and the Pāṇḍavas do? And what conversations took place among them there, O ascetic? For they were all high-souled and proficient in all the scriptures."
The Vṛṣṇis, the Pāṇḍavas, and their friends [reunited] with one another.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having reached Prabhāsa-tīrtha, the holy ford of the great ocean...

The Vṛṣṇis stood surrounding the heroic Pāṇḍavas. Then Rāma, the wielder of the plow who wears a forest garland, whose luster is like cow’s milk, the kunda flower, the moon, lotus stalks, and silver, addressed the lotus-eyed one.
O Kṛṣṇa, for a living being, the practice of dharma does not lead to prosperity, nor does adharma lead to ruin,
in a place where the high-souled Yudhiṣṭhira remains with matted hair.
Clad in bark garments, he dwells in the forest and suffers;
yet Duryodhana rules the earth,
and the earth yields no chasm for him.
"An unrighteous act performed is weightier than righteousness"—
thus might a man of small intellect think,
even as Duryodhana continues to grow in power.
While Yudhiṣṭhira was unhappy, having been deprived of his kingdom, home, wealth, and wife, and while the son of Pṛthā was likewise humiliated by the small-minded Duryodhana;
"What indeed should be done today?"— such was the doubt mutually engendered among the people by the subjects;
for this king is one whose origin lies in righteousness.
Devoted to dharma, firm in truth, and a generous giver—
how indeed could Pārtha, having fallen away from dharma, thrive even if he were deprived of his kingdom and happiness?
How is it that Bhīṣma, Kṛpa the brahmin, Droṇa, and the king— the elders of the lineage—
attain happiness by sending the sons of Pṛthā into exile?
Shame on the evil-minded leaders of the Bharatas!
What indeed will that sinful leader of the earth say when he meets his ancestors in the hereafter?
Thinking, "I have acted rightly toward my sons," he did not, in his mind, perceive that he had unjustly deposed his sinless sons from the kingdom.
"What indeed have I done that I am thus born sightless upon the earth among kings— having even exiled the son of Kuntī from the kingdom?"
Surely, on the ground of the world of the ancestors,
the son of Vicitravīrya, together with his sons, beheld those who were prosperous, possessing the luster of gold, born of the earth, and in full bloom.
Having indeed committed a cruel deed, he beheld those with broad shoulders and large red eyes;
surely he did not hear them as he questioned them.
For he fearlessly dispatched Yudhiṣṭhira, who had taken up arms, along with his younger brothers, into the forest;
he who [conquered] the prosperous armies of his enemies.
Though unarmed, the long-armed one could slay [the foe] merely by hearing the roar of Vṛkodara; indeed, at that sound,
the armies discharge excrement and urine.
Emaciated by hunger, thirst, and the journey, yet full of vigor,
he approached with various weapons and arrows in hand,
remembering this most terrible dwelling in the forest.
"It is certain to me that he shall leave nothing remaining;
for by his heroism and strength, no one on earth among men shall ever be his equal."
With his body emaciated by cold, heat, wind, and sun,
he should not leave any remnant of his enemies alive in battle;
having conquered the kings of the east with a single chariot, [he should proceed].
He who was Vṛkodara, the powerful Atiratha who returned safely from battles with his followers,
now suffers in the forest, clothed in bark garments.
Behold today this Sahadeva, who defeated the god-like kings of the south assembled at Dantakūra.
That hero, skilled in battle, who with a single chariot [conquered] the kings toward the western quarter, though appearing as an ascetic in the guise of a *tapasvin*.
This very man, who once triumphed over Nakula in battle, now wanders through the forests with matted hair, his body covered in dirt, subsisting on roots and fruits.
Today my mind perceives itself as deeply dejected,
even though King Atiratha’s sacrifice has been so successful—
that daughter who sprang up from the surface of the sacrificial altar.
How does she, who is worthy of happiness, endure this most painful dwelling in the forest today—
she who belongs to the Wind-god, the foremost of the Trivarga?
How is it that the sons of these gods— the lord of the gods, or the two Aśvins—
though worthy of happiness, now wander in the forest with little joy?
For when the son of Dharma had been defeated and driven away along with his wife, brothers, and followers,
and while Duryodhana was growing ever more powerful;
"How is it that the earth, along with its mountains, does not sink?
Sātyaki replied,
"O Rāma, this is no time for lamentation."
Whatever is best in that regard, that alone we shall all do— whatever may be for the constant welfare of this King Ajamīḍha.
For we act without having transgressed the proper time,
even though Yudhiṣṭhira has not said anything;
for those in this world who possess a protector—
They do not undertake action on their own initiative,
but rather become protectors in the affairs of others,
just as Śaibya and the others were for Yayāti, O Rāma.
O Rāma, those leaders who undertake their affairs in this world according to their own judgment are truly possessed of a protector—
those foremost of men.
Why do they not encounter hardship like those who are unprotected— this [Arjuna], Rāma, Janārdana,
Pradyumna, and Sāmba, all joined together with me?
He dwells in the forest together with his sisters;
having obtained as their protectors the lords of the three worlds,
let the army of the Daśārhas set forth this very day.
Let the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, equipped with abundant and various weapons and variegated armor, go to the abode of Yama along with his kinsmen, overwhelmed by the power of the Vṛṣṇis.
For you alone, by your mere wrath, could envelop even this earth—
let alone the wielder of the Śārṅga bow— so slay the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with his followers.
Just as Mahendra, the lord of the gods, [slew] Vṛtra,
so too is Pārtha my brother, my friend, and my teacher; he is like the very self of Janārdana.
That for which men desire a virtuous son, and for which a teacher desires a disciple whose speech is not contrary— that highest goal for which they strive has been attained.
He performs supreme and irresistible deeds;
having struck down all his showers of weapons with my own superior weapons, I shall overcome him in battle.
O Rāma, my head has been struck from my body by excellent arrows resembling serpent venom and fire,
and I have also been cut with a sharpened sword in battle.
Having forcibly crushed his head from his body,
I shall then slay all his followers,
as well as Duryodhana and all the Kurus.
O son of Rohiṇī, let the inhabitants of the earth, filled with joy, behold me here with my weapons grasped,
alone slaying the foremost warriors of the Kurus in battle.
Like the fire of destruction at the end of time consuming a great forest, Kṛpa, Droṇa, Vikarṇa, and Karṇa were unable to withstand the sharp arrows released by Pradyumna.
"I know the prowess of your son;
this son of Kṛṣṇa is just as he appears when standing on the battlefield. Sāmba, with his two arms, [could seize] along with the charioteer and the chariot—"
Having violently subdued Duḥśāsana,
[he said]: "There is nothing that the son of Jāmbavatī cannot accomplish in battle, for he is fierce in combat."
For by this boy alone, the army of the Daitya Śambara was suddenly repelled;
that wicked one was slain in battle by him alone.
Unrivaled in battle, his form like that of Indra;
just as when he is mounted upon that chariot with the green banner belonging to Purandara.
With rounded thighs and exceedingly long, thick arms,
by him was Aśvacakra slain in battle;
what man indeed could stand before Sāmba in combat?
One should indeed hold fast to the interval between the two arms,
so that having entered the interior of Death,
a person does not emerge again at the time of death.
Having attained such warrior glory and having thus penetrated his inner ranks in battle,
who indeed would return alive?
Vāsudeva [beheld] those two great car-warriors, Droṇa and Bhīṣma,
as well as Somadatta surrounded by his sons,
and all the armies.
It will be consumed by the nets of fire from his arrows;
for what indeed is there in all the worlds, including the gods, that is unbearable to Kṛṣṇa?
Then Aniruddha, sword and shield in hand, [encountered] the peerless wielder of the discus in battle, who had taken up his weapons and held excellent arrows in his grasp.
Let him cover this earth with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— slain, deprived of consciousness, and with their heads severed—
so that it is strewn like a sacrificial altar covered with *kuśa* grass at Vedic rites.
Gada, Ulmuka, Bāhuka, Bhānu,
Nītha, Śūra, Niśaṭha, Kumāra,
Sāraṇa, and Cārudeṣṇa— all fierce in battle.
Let them spread abroad deeds worthy of their lineage—
the assembled armies of Kṣatriyas and Śūrasenas, together with the foremost warriors of the Vṛṣṇis, Bhojas, and Andhakas.
Composed in meditation, King Yudhiṣṭhira— the great-souled one among those who protect, the most excellent of those who uphold the Dharma and bear renown— rightly governed the earth.
Having slain those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle, may he attain abundant fame in the world; thereafter,
let Abhimanyu rule the earth.

O best among the upholders of dharma, as long as the high-souled Yudhiṣṭhira fulfills his vow, just as it was declared by that foremost of the Kurus regarding the game of dice; so long shall he endure.
"Once the enemies have been conquered by the arrows released by us,
then the King of Dharma shall enjoy the earth, cleared of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and with the Sūta's son slain."
"For this is our most important task, leading to glory.
Vāsudeva said:
"O Mādhava, this is undoubtedly true."
"O being of undaunted spirit, we accept your word;
yet the bull among the Kurus would by no means desire land that has not been won by his own two arms."
For Yudhiṣṭhira would never abandon his own dharma out of desire, fear, or greed;
nor would Bhīma, Arjuna, or the two twins, those great chariot-warriors (atiratha).
In the same way, this Kṛṣṇā, the daughter of Drupada,
is here; for both Vṛkodara and Dhanañjaya are indeed peerless on earth in battle.
Why did he not rule the entire earth,
being honored by the two sons of Mādrī,
when that high-souled lord of the Pañcālas was present?
If Śakuni, the lord of Cedi, and we ourselves fight against the enemies with valor,
then Suyodhana will surely abandon the world of the living.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Mādhava, this which you say is not surprising;
however, truth is what must be protected by me most of all, not the kingdom."
But Kṛṣṇa alone knows me as I truly am, and I likewise know Kṛṣṇa as he truly is;
when that time comes, O hero among men—
Then, O Mādhava, this hero of the Śinis shall witness your prowess in battle; and you,
O Keśava, shall conquer Suyodhana.
"Let the heroes of the Daśārhas depart today;
I am firmly supported by my protectors, the lords of the world of men.
O immeasurable ones, practice heedfulness regarding the Dharma."
"I shall see them again, gathered together in happiness.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus addressed one another and saluted each other accordingly;
Having embraced all the elders and children,
the heroes of the Yadu clan went to their own homes,
while the king also traveled along the sacred fords.
Then, having dismissed Kṛṣṇa,
the King of Dharma went to the holy river Payoṣṇī, which possesses excellent bathing places and was honored by the King of Vidarbha.
Accompanied by his brothers and servants, along with Lomaśa and his son Soma, he dwelt there by the Payoṣṇī river, which had waters mixed with the juice of the *soma* plant.
Being praised with excellent hymns by the joyful and eminent twice-born ones, that Great-Souled One was extolled.
Lomaśa said:
O King, it is heard that here Purandara was gratified with Soma by Nṛga while he was performing a sacrifice; being thus satiated, he attained a state of intoxication.
For here, together with the gods, Indras, and even the Prajāpatis, [he was honored].

King Āmūrtarayas, having performed many kinds of great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, gratified the Lord who wields the thunderbolt with Soma juice here in seven horse-sacrifices.
In his seven sacrifices, everything was made of gold:
whatever materials were prescribed for the ritual, whether derived from trees or from the earth—
such as the rings for the sacrificial posts, the stakes, the cups, the pots, the plates, the *sruk* ladles, and the *sruva* spoons.
In those very sacrifices of his, seven renowned applications were performed:
upon each single sacrificial post (*yūpa*), seven *caṣāla* ornaments were placed on top.
In his sacrifices, those sacrificial posts shone brilliantly, made entirely of gold.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the gods, including Indra, raised him up by themselves. During those foremost sacrifices of that lord of the earth, Gaya,
Indra was intoxicated with Soma, and the twice-born were gratified with sacrificial gifts.
The twice-born received countless enumerations,
as numerous as the grains of sand in the world, or as the stars in the sky, or as the drops of rain from a downpour— countless by anyone.
In that same way, O great king, that wealth which Gaya bestowed upon the sacrificial assistants during those seven sacrifices was indeed incalculable;
for this which has been proclaimed here would indeed be calculable.
That sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of the liberal giver could not be counted;
with golden cows fashioned by Viśvakarman,
he gratified the Brahmins who had assembled from various directions.
O lord of the people, as the high-souled Gaya performed his sacrifice here and there, the earth was left with little remaining space except for the sacrificial altars (*caityas*).
By that deed, O Bhārata, he attained the worlds of Indra.
He who touches the waters of the Payoṣṇī shall attain the same world as that [sage].
Therefore, O sinless Indra among kings, having touched the waters here together with your brothers, O protector of the earth, you shall be cleansed of all evil.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having bathed in the Payoṣṇī river together with his brothers, that best of men [visited] Mount Vaiḍūrya and the great river Narmadā.
Having set out with that aim, the best of the Pāṇḍavas, the lord of the earth, departed;
the radiant and sinless one arrived together with his brothers.
Then the venerable rishi Lomaśa recounted everything to him.
O lord of the people, he traveled with his brothers to various delightful sacred fords (tīrthas) according to their suitability and his own pleasure,
repeatedly bestowing wealth upon thousands of Brahmins.
Lomaśa said:
"O son of Kuntī, having beheld the Vaiḍūrya mountain and descended into the Narmadā, one attains the same world as the gods and likewise as kings."
This, O best of men, is the junction between the Tretā and the Dvāpara ages;
having reached this place, O son of Kuntī, one is liberated from all sins. This region, dear one, is renowned as the site of Śaryāti’s sacrifice.
There, the descendant of Kuśika drank Soma directly along with the Aśvins;
then the descendant of Bhṛgu, the great ascetic Cyavana, became enraged at Mahendra,
and that lord paralyzed Vāsava.
And he also obtained Sukanyā as his wife, who was like a princess.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How was the blessed Pākaśāsana (Indra) obstructed by him?"
For what reason did the descendant of Bhṛgu, a man of great asceticism, become angry?
And how, O Brahmin, did he cause the two Nāsatyas to become drinkers of the Soma juice?
May your lordship relate all this to me exactly as it happened.
Lomaśa said:
"The son of the great seer Bhṛgu was Cyavana by name, a descendant of Bhrigu;
that one of great splendor performed austerities near this lake."
O Pāṇḍava, lord of the people, that one of great splendor stood for a very long time in one spot in the heroic posture, as motionless as a pillar;
that seer became covered with creepers and turned into an anthill.
After a long time, O King, he was completely covered by ants;
thus surrounded on all sides like a lump of clay, O King, that wise man continued to perform his austerities, enveloped by the anthill.
Then, after a long time, a king named Śaryāti came to this most excellent and delightful lake in order to sport. He had four thousand women as his wives.
O descendant of Bharata, he had only one daughter, the beautiful Sukanyā by name.
Adorned with all her ornaments and surrounded by her companions,
she approached the anthill of Bhārgava while wandering about.
And she, the one with beautiful teeth, wandering there among the delightful trees and searching about, sported surrounded by her companions—
she who was endowed with beauty, youth, passion, and intoxication.

He broke the branches of the forest trees that were in full bloom. The wise descendant of Bhṛgu beheld her— alone, separated from her companions, clad in a single garment, and adorned— as she moved like a flash of lightning.
Beholding her in that secluded place, he of supreme luster took his delight;
yet the Brahman-sage, though endowed with the power of asceticism,
had a parched throat and spoke to that auspicious woman, who indeed did not hear him.
Then Sukanyā, seeing the two eyes of Bhārgava within the anthill,
being overcome by the power of deluded intellect out of curiosity, said, "What indeed is this? and pierced his two eyes with a thorn.
When his eyes were pierced by her, he became filled with supreme rage;
then he obstructed the excrement and urine of Śaryāti’s army.
When the excrement and urine were thus blocked, the army suffered from the pain of abdominal distension.
Beholding the Tathāgata, that king questioned him:
"By whom has an offense been committed here today against the high-souled Bhārgava, who is constantly devoted to asceticism, advanced in years, and especially prone to anger?"
"Whether it was done knowingly or unknowingly, speak the truth without delay.
All the soldiers said to him, "We do not know of any harm we have done;
may you discover that by whatever means necessary, according to your will."
Then that protector of the earth himself questioned his circle of friends with both gentle and stern words, yet they did not acknowledge [the truth].
Then, seeing that army afflicted by misery and suffering from a lack of food, he [acted].
Then Sukanyā spoke thus to her distressed father:
"While I was wandering here, a glowing creature was seen in an anthill;
it appeared like a firefly, and I pierced it from close range."
Having heard this, Śaryāti quickly ran toward the anthill;
there he beheld the descendant of Bhṛgu, advanced in asceticism and advanced in years,
possessing a radiance equal to that of the moon and the sun.
Then the lord of the earth, with palms joined in reverence, requested for the sake of his army those who were advanced in knowledge and advanced in age:
"Whatever has been done by this girl out of ignorance, you ought to forgive it."
"And I give this very maiden to you, O you of firm vows;
desiring her as a wife, accept her and be gracious, O Bhārgava.
Then Cyavana, the descendant of Bhṛgu, spoke to the protector of the earth.

"O King, pierced by the contempt of this woman who is full of pride, and having accepted your daughter— who is endowed with beauty and nobility yet driven by greed, delusion, and force— I [have come here]."
"I shall forgive you, O protector of the earth; I tell you this truly. Having understood the words of the seer, Śaryāti, without hesitation, gave his daughter to that high-souled Cyavana.
Having accepted that maiden, Cyavana became truly gracious;
having obtained his favor, the king returned once more with his army.
And the blameless Sukanyā, having obtained a husband who was an ascetic, [was filled with joy].
She constantly attended upon him with affection, through asceticism and self-restraint; serving the sacred fires and guests, free from malice,
that lady of beautiful countenance quickly propitiated Cyavana.
Lomaśa said: "Then,
after some time had passed, O King, the two Aśvins of the gods beheld Sukanyā there, having performed her ablutions and being uncovered."
Seeing her, whose limbs were beautiful like the daughter of the King of the Gods,
the two Nāsatyas, the Aśvins, rushed toward her and said this:
"Whose daughter are you, O lady of lovely thighs, and what are you doing in the forest?"
"We desire to know you, O blessed lady; therefore, tell us, O beautiful one.
Then Sukanyā, properly adorned, spoke to those two best of gods:
"Know me to be the daughter of Śaryāti and the wife of Cyavana."
"I am established in this world of men by the name Sukanyā;
with my whole being, I am ever devoted to my husband.
Then the two Aśvins, smiling, spoke to her once again.
"How is it, O auspicious lady, that you have been given by your father to one who has traveled so far? You shine in the midst of the forest like a flash of lightning;
indeed, O beautiful woman, we do not see anyone even among the gods who is your equal."
O blessed lady, though devoid of ornaments and lacking the finest garments, you beautify the forest even more, even without decoration;
whereas one adorned with every ornament and wearing the finest robes—

"You would shine, O lady of faultless limbs, but not thus covered in filth and mud. Why, O auspicious one, having become such as you are, do you serve a husband worn out by old age and deprived of the enjoyments of desire?"

"O lady of pure smiles, you are incapable of protecting or supporting [us]. It would be better for you to abandon this Cyavana and choose one of us two as your husband. O you who resemble a celestial child, do not let your youth go to waste."
Thus addressed, Sukanyā spoke these words to those two gods:
"I am devoted to my husband Cyavana; do not suspect me thus.
They both replied to her again: "We are the two foremost physicians of the gods."
"We shall make your husband young and endowed with beauty;
therefore, choose one of us three as your husband.
O lady of lovely countenance, invite him on this condition."

O King, having approached the descendant of Bhṛgu at their word, she spoke the message that had been addressed by them concerning the son of Bhṛgu. Having heard that, Cyavana said to his wife, "Let it be done."
Having been thus permitted by her husband, she said,
"Let it be done. Hearing those words of hers, the Aśvins said to that princess, "Let your husband enter the waters."
Then Cyavana, desiring that form, quickly entered the water;
O King, O Lord, the two Aśvins also entered that lake.
After a moment, they all emerged from that lake.

All of them bore divine forms, were young, and wore polished earrings; they possessed identical appearances and increased the joy of the mind. Together, they all said: "O auspicious lady, choose whichever one you prefer."
"O blessed one, O woman of excellent complexion, it is our desire that you choose either one of the Aśvins or Cyavana as your husband, O wise lady; or,
O most beautiful one, choose whomever you yourself desire."
Having observed them all standing there, each assuming an identical form,
the goddess determined with her mind and intellect and chose her own husband:
"If in my heart I have desired no other husband besides my own," [then let him be revealed].
"By that truth, may the two gods grant me a husband.
When the virtuous woman had spoken thus, the two Nāsatyas, the best of the gods,
revealed themselves to Sukanyā as the son of Bhṛgu.
Then the gods, being highly pleased, gave that Cyavana his husband. Having obtained a wife and the desired youth and beauty,
the immensely radiant Cyavana joyfully spoke these words to the two Nāsatyas:
"Just as you have made me, though now old, endowed with beauty and possessed of youth, and have provided me with this wife,
therefore I shall, out of affection, make both of you drinkers of the Soma."
"While the King of the Gods looked on, I tell you both this truth.
Having heard this, the two of them returned to heaven with joyful hearts; and Cyavana and Sukanyā, too, sported together like the gods.
On that very bank of the lake, they both assumed their supreme forms.
Lomaśa said:
Then, having heard that Cyavana had been restored to his youth, Śaryāti...
Accompanied by his army, he approached the hermitage of Bhārgava with great joy.
Upon seeing Cyavana and Sukanyā, who were like the children of gods,
King Śaryāti rejoiced as if he had obtained the entire earth.
Honored by that seer, the high-minded lord of the earth sat down together with his wife and engaged in auspicious conversation. Then, O King, the descendant of Bhṛgu spoke to him, consoling him.
"O King, I shall perform the sacrifice for you; prepare the necessary materials.
Thereupon, O great king, Śaryāti, the lord of the earth, being exceedingly delighted, honored those words of Cyavana.
On an auspicious day fit for sacrifice, one rich in the fulfillment of all desires, Śaryāti caused an excellent sacrificial ground to be prepared. There,
O King, Cyavana Bhārgava officiated as the priest for him.
And there were wonders there; learn of them from me.
At that time, Cyavana was about to take the soma for the two divine Aśvins;
Indra sought to prevent him as he was taking their cup.
Indra said:
"It is my opinion that neither of these two, the Nāsatyas, is worthy of the Soma; as physicians for the sons of the gods, they do not deserve it by virtue of their work."
Cyavana said:
"O Maghavan, do not despise these two high-souled ones, who possess supreme beauty and wealth, and who have made me ageless like a god."
"Except for you and the other gods, how indeed would they not deserve the sacrifice?
O Indra, Lord of the Gods, know that even the two Aśvins are deities.
Indra said:
"Being physicians and laborers, endowed with the power to assume any form at will, how do these two,
as they wander among mortals in the world, deserve the Soma here?
Lomaśa said:
When Vāsava repeated these very words,
Bhārgava then disregarded Śakra and seized the vessel;
for he was about to take that Soma, the most excellent portion belonging to the Aśvins.
Having observed this, the god Indra, the slayer of Bala, spoke these words:
"If you yourself take up the *soma* for the sake of these two,
I shall hurl at you my thunderbolt, which is of terrible form and unsurpassed."
Thus addressed, that descendant of Bhṛgu, looking at Indra with a smile,
duly took up the excellent cup of Soma for the Aśvins.
Then the Lord of Śacī hurled his terrible thunderbolt at him.

As he was about to strike, Bhārgava paralyzed his arm; having paralyzed it, Cyavana, possessing great splendor and seeking to accomplish a magical rite (*kṛtyā*), offered oblations into the fire with mantras, intent on harming the god.
Then, through the power of that sage’s asceticism, a *kṛtyā* was produced:
a great Asura named Mada, possessed of immense heroism and a massive body,
whose form could not be described even by the gods and asuras.
No equal to him in stature is found here in this world;
his mouth was formidable and large, with sharp-pointed teeth,
one jaw of his rested upon the earth and the other reached up to heaven.
His four long fangs were each a hundred yojanas in length,
while his other teeth were ten yojanas long;
they had the appearance of ramparts and looked like the points of spears.
His two arms were like mountains, ten thousand *yojanas* long and equal in size;
his eyes resembled the sun and the moon, and his face was like that of the God of Death.
He licked his mouth with a tongue as flickering and restless as lightning.
With his mouth wide open and a terrifying gaze, as if swallowing the world by force,
he rushed furiously toward Śatakratu, intending to devour him,
making the worlds resound with a great and dreadful roar.
Lomaśa said:
Seeing that Mada approaching with his terrible face, like Death himself with a gaping mouth, intent on devouring him, the god Śatakratu [Śakra]—
With his arms paralyzed by fear and repeatedly licking the corners of his mouth,
the King of the Gods, oppressed by dread, then spoke to Cyavana:
"O Bhārgava, from this day forward, these two Aśvins are worthy of the Soma."

"O Brahmin, I tell you this word as the truth regarding what is to come: let this undertaking of yours not be in vain; let it be the highest dharma. And I know, O brahmin-sage, that you will not act falsely."
"O Brahmin, just as these two Aśvins have been made worthy of Soma by you today, so too should you unite me with the highest good. Furthermore,
O Bhārgava, act so that your own prowess may shine forth even more."

"Thinking, 'May the fame of Sukanyā and of her father spread throughout the world,' I have therefore ordained this manifestation of your prowess. Here, the gods, the ancestors, and the great seers dwell with a desire for pleasure."
"O one of great wisdom, those of great power honor your sacrifice;
therefore, grant me your favor so that this may be as you desire.
When the high-souled Cyavana was thus addressed by Śakra, [he replied:]
That wrath departed quickly, and he released Purandara;
O King, the valiant one then distributed Mada— created again and again— in drink, among women, in dice,
and in hunting.
Having thus cast out Mada and gratified Śakra with the moon,
