and having caused that king to perform sacrifices for the gods together with the Aśvins, he—
best among speakers— proclaimed his prowess throughout all the worlds.
He sported in the forest with the devoted Sukanyā;
even today, people here sing the verses of that wise man,
and by hearing them, men do not suffer the loss of their sight.

O King, this lake resounds with the voices of the twice-born and shines forth; those who, having eaten here, shall remember Śaryāti, Sukanyā, Cyavana, Śakra, and the two Aśvins— their sight shall never fail.
"Here, together with your uterine brothers, satisfy the ancestors and the gods;
today, satisfy the ancestors and the gods with water and purifying milk.
Having seen this, O protector of the earth, O descendant of Bharata, and having seen Sikataksha as well—
Having reached the Saindhava forest, O King, behold the sacred streams;
at all the Puṣkaras, touch the water, O great monarch,
and by reciting the mantras of Sthāṇu, you shall attain perfection, O Bhārata.
O best of men, this is the junction between the Tretā and the Dvāpara ages;
for it is seen here, O Pārtha, as the destroyer of all sins. Perform your ablutions here, O you who destroy all sins.
Ārcīka Mountain is indeed the dwelling place of the wise;
it possesses ever-ripening fruit and perpetual streams, being the supreme abode of the Maruts.
And these hundreds of shrines, O Yudhiṣṭhira, belong to the Thirty Gods.
This is the sacred ford of the Moon (Candramas), which the seers (ṛṣis) attend; likewise, the Vaikhānasa seers and the Vālakhilyas do so as well. There are three holy peaks and three springs.
"O son of Kuntī, we do not know the reason why these [tirthas] were established from the beginning;
having circumambulated them all, touch them as you desire.
O son of Kuntī, Śantanu and Śunaka, the lord of men, were also here."
Both Nara and Nārāyaṇa have attained their eternal abode;
here, the gods and the ancestors eternally rest with the great seers. On Mount Ārcīka they performed austerities; worship them, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
O lord of the people, here indeed the ṛṣis partook of the sacrificial porridges; here is the Yamunā of inexhaustible current, and here Kṛṣṇa is devoted to ascetic penance;
and here, O crusher of enemies, are the twins, Bhīmasena, and Kṛṣṇā.
"And we all shall go there, emaciated and devoted to great austerities.
O lord of men, this is the sacred spring of Indra,
where Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and Varuṇa have ascended upwards."
O King, here they dwelt—patient and supremely righteous;
this auspicious and excellent mountain belongs to those who are friendly and upright in intellect.
O King, this is that Yamunā, frequented by hosts of royal sages.
O King, this sacred place, built with various sacrifices, removes the fear of sin;
here, O son of Kuntī, the great archer King Māndhātṛ himself performed sacrifice, as did Sahadeva Somaka, the best among givers.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Great Brahmin, how was Māndhātṛ, that tiger among kings and best of monarchs, the son of Yuvanāśva, born— he who was renowned throughout the three worlds?"
And how did he of immeasurable splendor reach that supreme pinnacle,
under whose control the three worlds were as they are under the control of the high-souled Viṣṇu?
I wish to hear this life-story of that wise one.
O sinless one, as you recount the story of Māndhātṛ of true fame—
how he acquired the title "Māndhātṛ," how he possessed a splendor equal to Śakra, and how that hero of unrivaled valor was born— you are indeed skilled in speaking.
Lomaśa said:
Listen attentively, O King, to how that high-souled monarch was born and what the life-story of that wise one was like.
Just as the name Māndhātṛ is indeed celebrated throughout the worlds,
so too was Yuvanāśva, the lord of the earth born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku;
he, O protector of the earth, performed sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees.
Having performed a thousand horse-sacrifices and various other principal sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
that high-souled royal sage of firm vows remained childless.
Having entrusted that kingdom to his ministers, he became a constant dweller in the forest.
Having disciplined himself by himself according to the method prescribed in the scriptures,
O King, on one occasion that monarch was distressed by fasting.
With his heart parched by thirst, he entered the hermitage of Bhṛgu. On that very night, O king of kings, the high-souled great seer, the joy of the Bhṛgus,
performed a sacrifice for the sake of obtaining a son for the son of Sudyumna.
A great jar, filled with water purified by mantras,
stood there already prepared, O Indra among kings,
so that his wife, having drunk from it, might give birth to a son equal to Śakra.
O King, having placed that jar upon the altar— containing the water which had been duly consecrated according to the rules— those great seers lay down to sleep;
and Sudyumna’s son, overcome by the exhaustion of the night-long vigil, passed them by.
With his throat parched and afflicted by thirst, the king, seeking water,
entered that hermitage exhausted and begged for a drink.
As he cried out with a parched throat, being weary at that time, [the ascetic spoke].
At that time, no one heard anything other than the warbling of a bird.
Then, seeing that jar filled with water, the king rushed toward it with speed; having drunk the water, he cast it aside.

Having drunk the cool water, the wise lord of the earth, who had been afflicted by thirst, attained relief and became exceedingly happy. Then those sages, together with the king, regained their consciousness.
They all beheld that water-jar devoid of water;
having assembled together, they asked, "Whose deed is this?
Yuvanāśva then truly acknowledged, "It was mine."
Then the Blessed One Bhārgava said to him, "This is not proper;
for these waters were set aside for the sake of a son and have been prepared through my ascetic power. Indeed, having undertaken severe austerity, I have infused the Veda into them."
"O royal sage of great strength and prowess, for the sake of a son for you— one who is mighty, heroic, and endowed with the power of asceticism,
who by his valor could send even Śakra to the abode of Yama."
"O King, by this method I have brought about this situation for you.
O King, the drinking of water that you performed today was indeed improper;
however, it is not possible for us to make it otherwise now."
"Surely this which you have done was brought about by fate;
for those waters, O Great King, which were drunk by you while you were thirsty— waters consecrated with rites and mantras and charged with the power of my asceticism— "
"From them, you shall yourself give birth to a son of such prowess. We shall perform for you there a most wonderful sacrifice, so that you,
O valiant one, shall give birth to a son equal to Śakra."
"Nor shall you experience the exhaustion born of carrying a fetus.
Having heard these words of his, the king replied, "So be it.
"And, O Great King, there shall be no separation for you from your life-breaths."
Then, when a hundred years had passed for that high-souled king,
a son of great splendor emerged, having burst forth from his left side like a second sun;
yet death did not overcome him.
That became like a marvel for King Yuvanāśva.
Then Śakra, possessed of great splendor, approached, desiring to see him.
Thereupon the gods asked Mahendra: "What will she bear?"
Then Śakra placed his index finger into the child's mouth;
thus addressed by the wielder of the thunderbolt, "He shall suckle me," the inhabitants of heaven,
together with Indra, gave him the name Māndhātṛ.
O protector of the earth, having tasted the *pradeśinī* finger given by Śakra, that child then grew to thirteen *kiṣkus* in height;
the Vedas, along with the science of archery (*dhanurveda*), and divine weapons attended upon that lord.
O Great King, as soon as he thought of them, they all appeared from every side:
the bow named Ājagava, the arrows made of horn,
and the impenetrable armor, which immediately came to his aid.
O Bhārata, having been consecrated by Maghavan Śakra himself,
he conquered the three worlds through righteousness, just as Viṣṇu did with his strides.
The wheel of that high-souled one rolled forth unopposed.
Precious gems presented themselves of their own accord to that royal seer.
O lord of the earth, this entire earth, filled with wealth, belongs to him;
by him many various sacrifices were performed with abundant sacrificial fees.
Having built many shrines and attained abundant merit,
O King, he of great splendor and immeasurable radiance obtained half of Śakra’s throne.
By that wise man, who was ever devoted to righteousness, the entire earth was [conquered] in a single day.

By his mere command, the earth, together with its mines of jewels and its ports, was conquered; O Great King, the earth bounded by the four oceans was covered by the altars of his sacrificial rites accompanied by liberal fees, such that nothing remained unconquered.
"O great king, it is said that ten thousand padmas of cows were given by that high-souled one to the brahmins.
By that high-souled one, during a twelve-year drought— "
While the wielder of the thunderbolt looked on, he rained down arrows for the sake of increasing the crops;
by him, the great lord of Gāndhāra, born of the lunar dynasty,
was struck down with shafts like a roaring great cloud.
By that high-souled one, O King, the fourfold creatures were conquered;
by his ascetic power and his splendor, the worlds were likewise established.
This is the sacrificial ground of that one who possesses the radiance of the sun.
Behold this most meritorious region in the midst of Kurukṣetra!
Likewise, O Indra among kings, by practicing righteousness and protecting the earth like King Māndhātṛ, you too shall attain the heavenly world.
"O protector of the earth, all this great life-story of Māndhātṛ, as well as his preeminent birth about which you questioned me, has been related to you in its entirety. Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by the great seer Lomaśa, that son of Kuntī,
O Bhārata, immediately asked further concerning Somaka.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of speakers, what was the nature of that King Somaka’s vigor? I wish to hear truly of his deeds and his power.
Lomaśa said:
Yudhiṣṭhira, there was once a righteous king named Somaka. O King, he had a hundred wives who were all his equals.
That lord of the earth, with great effort, [sought] a son among them.
Even after a long time, he did not obtain any [son]. Once, while that old man was striving with great effort,
a son named Jantu was born among those three hundred women.
O lord of the people, as soon as he was born, all his mothers sat surrounding him,
constantly placing their desires and enjoyments behind them,
thinking in their minds, "This is my own biological son."
Then, O King, once an ant bit the boy on his buttock; bitten by it, the child cried out from that pain. Thereupon, all those mothers, deeply distressed, raised a loud cry.
Surrounding the creature together, they raised a tumultuous clamor;
the lord of the earth, seated in the midst of his assembly of ministers along with the sacrificial priests, suddenly heard that cry of distress.
Then the king asked, "What is this? and the Kṣattṛ related to him exactly what had occurred regarding his son. Rising in haste, Somaka, together with his ministers, [set out].
Having entered the inner apartments, the subduer of enemies comforted his son;
and having consoled his son and emerged from the inner apartments,
O King, the monarch sat down together with the sacrificial priests and his ministers.
Somaka said:
"Fie upon having an only son in this world; it would be better to have no son at all. Because living beings are perpetually subject to affliction, having an only son is nothing but grief."
"O Brahmin, O Lord, having examined them thoroughly, I, desiring sons, married this hundred of wives; yet none of them has offspring.
Somehow, this one son, Jantu, was born to me."

O best of the twice-born, as my youth has passed away along with that of my wife, what indeed could be more painful than this for one who strives in all things? For the lives of these women and my own depend solely upon this one son here.
"Is there perhaps some action so ordained by which a hundred sons might be born— whether by a great rite, a small one, or even a difficult task? The officiating priest replied:
"There indeed exists such a rite by which a hundred sons may be born.
O Somaka, if you are able to perform it, then I shall explain it to you. Let it be done without hesitation; then you will obtain sons."
Somaka said:
"Whether it be a deed that ought to be done or one that ought not to be done, by which a hundred sons may be obtained—know that it is already accomplished; let the Blessed One explain it to me."
The officiating priest said:
"O King, perform a sacrifice with Jantu through me when the ritual is extended;
then, a hundred illustrious sons will be born to you before long."
When the omentum is being offered as an oblation, your mothers, having inhaled the smoke,
will then give birth to sons of great heroism for you; moreover,
in that very same woman, another son shall be born to you again.
"And on his left side, there will be a golden mark.
Somaśarman said:
"O Brahmin, whatever is to be done and in whatever manner, perform each of those things accordingly."
"Out of a desire for a son, I shall do everything you say.
Lomaśa said:
Having heard this, that Brāhmaṇa, a master of the Vedas, who wore the armor of the Soma plant...
Then he caused Somaṅka to perform a sacrifice with that Jantu;
but his mothers, filled with compassion, forcibly drew their son away, wailing "Alas, we are undone! while overcome by intense grief.
The mothers, seizing him by his right hand, pulled him back;
but the officiating priest, seizing him by his left hand, likewise pulled him away.
Having dragged their son from them like distressed female ospreys, they were cast aside.
Having dissected him according to the prescribed rite, he offered his omentum as a libation.
O descendant of Kuru, while the omentum was being offered, the mothers, having smelled the fragrance,
fell suddenly to the earth in distress.
And then all those wives of the king conceived;
O lord of the people, O Bhārata, after ten months had passed, a full hundred sons were born to Somaka from all of them.
O Bhārata, Jantu was born as the eldest son from his very mother;
he was beloved by them more than their own biological sons.
And he possessed this mark: a golden spot on his left side.
Among those hundred sons, he was the foremost, endowed with all virtues;
he was renowned throughout the earth as a king who was always devoted to righteousness. Then, that preceptor of Somaka departed for the supreme world.
Then, after some time had passed, Somaka also went to the other world. There he beheld him being cooked in a terrible hell.
He asked him: "O twice-born one, for what reason are you being cooked in this hell?"
Then his preceptor, being severely scorched by the fire, said to him:
"O King, you were made to perform a sacrifice by me; this is the fruit of that action.
Having heard this, the royal seer spoke to Dharmarāja.
"I shall enter here; let my officiating priest be released. For on my account, O illustrious one, he is being cooked by the fires of hell.
Therefore, I will cast myself into hell; let my teacher be set free."
Dharma said: "O King, no one other than the doer ever enjoys the fruit of an action;
O King, if this fruit were to be enjoyed by anyone other than you, how could that possibly be?"
"O best among givers, these fruits of yours are visible here;
yet you must incur the sin of his misdeed so that your father may be released.
Somaśravas said:
"I do not desire the meritorious worlds without this teacher of Brahman;
I wish to dwell with him alone,
whether in the abode of the gods or in hell, O Dharmarāja, for I am equal to him in my deeds."
"O God, let this fruit of merit and demerit be equal for both of us. Dharma said:
"If this is what you desire, O King, then enjoy the fruit of this together with him."
"At the same time as him, you shall afterwards attain a happy state.
Lomaśa said:
"The lotus-eyed king did everything exactly as he was told."

His sins being exhausted, he was liberated from that state along with his preceptor; and together with that very brahmin preceptor, he— being dear to his teacher— again attained his own auspicious worlds won by his own merit.
"This is his holy hermitage, which shines forth here before us;
by dwelling here for six nights with patience, a man attains a happy rebirth. O Indra among kings, we too shall dwell in this place, free from all anxiety."
"O best of the Kurus, remain self-restrained for six nights and prepare yourself.
Lomaśa said:
"O King, it is said that Prajāpati himself performed a sacrifice at this very place."
In ancient times, there was a sacrificial session known as the *iṣṭīkṛta*, lasting for a thousand years. Ambarīṣa Nābhāga performed it along the Yamunā;
through those sacrifices and his asceticism, he attained supreme perfection.
O Bhārata, even today their desired emblems are seen;
O Great King, this earth is indeed strewn with their emblems,
and these trees, O Lord of the People, are many that shine by themselves.
Gods and sages indeed assemble here constantly;
those fires are seen in the evening and likewise in the morning as they perform their ablutions.
O son of Kuntī, for those who have bathed here, sin is instantly destroyed.
Therefore, O best of the Kurus, perform the consecration ceremony together with your younger brothers. Then, having bowed down and bathed your limbs, you shall proceed to the Kauśikī river,
where Viśvāmitra indeed performed unsurpassed ascetic penance.
Then, having bathed his limbs there together with his retinue, King [Lomapāda]—
to whom Lomaśa said— went to the holy, beautiful river Kauśikī, which has abundant waters.
This very river, O Bhārata, is the sacred one named Kauśikī;
here shines the delightful hermitage of Viśvāmitra,
and also the hermitage of the high-souled Kaśyapa, known for its merit.

"O King, this region is the most meritorious of all the sacrificial grounds of Nahuṣa's son, Yayāti, O son of Kuntī, where, having performed ten *padma* sacrifices, he bestowed [the earth] upon the members of the assembly— Yayāti, the sovereign lord of immeasurable power."
"Behold here this sacrificial ground of one who vied with Śakra!
See the earth covered with fires of various forms,
as if sinking under the weight of Yayāti’s sacrificial rites."
This is the Śamī tree with its single leaf, and this is that supreme Śaraka forest.
Behold these lakes of Rāma; behold the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa.
This is the place of the son of Arcīka as he wandered the earth through his yogic powers.
O protector of the earth, hear from me, O joy of the Kurus, as I recite the genealogy concerning the departure of the one of immeasurable splendor to Rūpyā,
just as the Piśācī spoke while describing it with mortars as her ornaments.
"Thinking that there might be obstacles for those who dwell here permanently,
you wish to stay with your sons after eating curds at Yugandhara, staying at Acyutasthala, and likewise bathing at Bhūtilaya."
Having stayed here for one night, if you should stay a second,
your conduct during the day will indeed be thus, but your conduct at night will be otherwise.
Knowing this to be so, O high-minded one, stay for the night.
"O best of the Bharatas, we shall dwell here for the night;
for this, O son of Kuntī, O Bhārata, is the gateway to Kurukṣetra. It was right here, O King, that the royal son of Nahuṣa performed sacrifices."
Where Yayāti, rich in many jewels, attained joy along with Indra—
this is called Plakṣāvataraṇa, the sacred ford on the Yamunā;
the wise indeed call this the gateway to the vault of heaven.
O dear one, here the supreme ṛṣis, having performed sacrifices with the Sārasvata rites and possessing sacrificial posts and mortars, go to the ritual bath at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
It was right here that King Bharata released the sacrificial horse.
O King,
having repeatedly performed sacrifices with the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha), you have rightfully obtained the earth, which is variegated like a black antelope skin.

Right here, O tiger among men, Marutta is performing an excellent sacrificial session (*sattra*), protected by Saṃvarta, the foremost of divine sages. By touching the water here, O king of kings, one beholds all the worlds.
"And by touching [the water], O Bhārata, one is purified from evil deeds.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having bathed there together with his brothers, he was praised by the great ṛṣis."
The best of the Pāṇḍavas spoke these words to Lomaśa:
"O you whose valor is truth, through my ascetic power I behold all the worlds;
while remaining here, O best of the Pāṇḍavas, I see Śvetavāhana."
Lomaśa said:
"O mighty-armed one, it is even so; the supreme ṛṣis behold here, after bathing, the three worlds together with all things mobile and immobile, as they are endowed with ascetic power."

Behold this holy Sarasvatī, filled with those who have sought her as their sole refuge; by bathing here, O best of men, one shall be cleansed of all evil. Here, the celestial sages performed sacrifices dedicated to Sarasvatī.
O son of Kuntī, both the ṛṣis and likewise the royal sages [have said]:
"This altar of Prajāpati extends five yojanas on all sides;
this is the field of the high-souled Kuru, who was devoted to sacrifice."
Lomaśa said:
"O Bhārata, mortals here perform austerities and go to heaven;
O King, men desiring death come here by the thousands."
For thus was the benediction uttered by Dakṣa when he performed sacrifice in the past:
"Those men indeed who shall die here are surely conquerors of heaven.
This is the meritorious Sarasvatī, a divine river abounding in water.
O lord of the people, this is the place called Vinaśana on the Sarasvatī, which serves as the gateway to the kingdom of the Niṣādas; through hatred for whom the Sarasvatī [dries up],
yet those whose sins have been exhausted attain auspicious worlds— of this there is no doubt.
"O hero, I have entered the earth so that the Niṣādas may not recognize me.
This is indeed Camasodbheda, where the Sarasvatī becomes visible; here the divine, holy rivers flowing to the ocean turn toward her."

This is the great ford of the Sindhu, O subduer of enemies, where Lopāmudrā, having approached Agastya, chose him as her husband. This is the ford known as Prabhāsa, which shines with the brilliance of the sun.

This supreme sacred ford (tīrtha), known by the name Viṣṇupada, is seen here; it is dear to Indra, meritorious, purifying, and a destroyer of sins. Therein lies the place called Gayāśiras, which brings satisfaction to the ancestors.
There are many sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and temples of the deities,
as well as all the hermitages (*āśrama*) of the sages, all auspicious and consisting of heaven itself; there is the sacred ford named Gayāśiras, which removes the fear of sin.
"O protector of the earth, bow down to this sacred field according to the prescribed rites;
here the Mountain of the Gods (Meru) is seen, the abode of all holy fords (tīrthas). And here flows the beautiful Vipāśā river, supremely purifying."
Right here, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, out of grief for his son,
bound himself and threw himself into the Vipāśā, yet he rose up again.
Here too is seen Mount Arbuda, the abode of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
O subduer of enemies, behold this entire region of Kaśmīra, which is meritorious and inhabited by great seers; look upon it together with your brothers.
O king of kings, behold the Vitastā, which liberates one from all sins.

O Bhārata, it was inhabited by great sages and possessed cool, perfectly pure waters; here occurred the conversation between all the northern ṛṣis and Nahuṣa, as well as that between Agni and Kāśyapa.
"O Great King, this gateway to the mind shines forth;
it was made in the midst of this mountain by the illustrious Rāma.
This is indeed the celebrated Vātika-ṣaṇḍa, where truth is his prowess."
That gate which leads to the Videhas and the north did not close;
O bull among men, this is another marvel in this land,
O son of Kuntī, that even when the age had declined, Śarva remained here together with his attendants.
And together with Umā, he appears to those who possess the power to assume any form at will.
Indeed, in this beautiful lake during the month of Caitra, the officiating priests, seeking auspicious results, properly worship Pinākin along with his retinue.
Having bathed here in this lake with faith and with senses subdued, one whose sins are exhausted attains auspicious worlds; of this there is no doubt.
This is the place named Ujjānaka, where Yavakrī attained peace.
And there is the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, who dwells with Arundhatī;
this is the Kuśavān lake where the lotus *kuśeśaya* grows;
and here is the hermitage of Rukmiṇī, where she, free from anger, attained peace.

O son of Pāṇḍu, you have heard the summary of the meditative concentrations (samādhis). O great king of immeasurable prowess, you shall see that great mountain Bhrigutunga, as well as Maṇḍavā and Saṃdhyā.
On both sides of the river Yamunā, near the rivers Jalā and Upajalā,
it was there that Uśīnara, having performed sacrifices, surpassed even Vāsava;
and Vāsava himself attended that assembly of his, O lord of the people.
O descendant of Bharata,
Indra and Agni, both granter of boons, approached the king Uśīnara, that high-souled one, desiring to test him; having become a hawk and a pigeon respectively, they came to his sacrifice.
O King, having reached the thigh of the monarch out of fear of the hawk, the pigeon,
afflicted by terror and seeking refuge, then hid himself there. Listen now, O King, to what the hawk said to him on that occasion.
The hawk said:
"O King, all the rulers of the earth say that you alone are a righteous soul;
why then do you desire to perform an act that is contrary to dharma?"
"O King, the eating of one who is oppressed by hunger is ordained. Do not destroy dharma out of greed for dharma; you have already abandoned dharma.
The king said:

"O great bird, this pigeon has come into my presence terrified, seeking protection from you; desiring to save his life, he has approached me. Thus it is with this pigeon who has arrived here seeking safety."
O hawk, what do you see as the highest dharma in failing to give?
This pigeon is seen quivering and terrified;
seeking life from my presence, its abandonment is censurable.
For whoever should kill a twice-born man or a cow, the mother of the world,
and whoever abandons one who has come for refuge— their sin is indeed equal. On one side are all the sacrifices, completed with the bestowing of excellent sacrificial fees.
The preservation of life for a living being terrified on one side [by a hawk].
The hawk said:
"O lord of the earth, all beings come into existence through food."

Living beings grow by means of food; by it they live. It is possible to live for a long time even when one’s wealth is difficult to give up, but it is not possible to subsist for long after abandoning food.
"O lord of the people, today my life-breaths, deprived of their food,
will abandon this body and go upon the path from which there is no return. When I have died, O righteous-souled one, my wife and children will perish."

"By protecting the pigeon, you will lose many lives. That which obstructs righteousness is not righteousness; that is false righteousness (*kudharma*). But that righteousness which is non-opposing is true righteousness, O you of true valor."
O protector of the earth, having determined the relative weight and lightness among conflicting duties,
one should practice that dharma wherein no contradiction exists; for,
in deciding between dharma and adharma, one must understand the gravity or insignificance of each.
"Since one side is greater, O King, therefore make your decision regarding dharma.
The king said:
"O best of birds, you speak words endowed with much that is auspicious."
"O Suparṇa, king of birds, you are undoubtedly a knower of dharma,
for you speak many wonderful things consistent with righteousness. I perceive that there is nothing unknown to you."
How can you consider it right to abandon one who seeks refuge? For one who is hungry, food that has appeared is indeed like a rescue;
O bird, this effort of yours is for the sake of food.
"Moreover, it is possible for you to provide food in another way, even more abundant than this:
let a bull, or a boar, or a deer, or even a buffalo,
or whatever else you desire, be prepared for your sake today."
The hawk said:
"O great king, I do not eat boars, nor oxen, nor various kinds of wild animals; what need have I for such food?"
"But as for that food ordained by fate for me, O bull among Kṣatriyas—release this very pigeon to me, O protector of the earth!
Hawks devour pigeons; this is the eternal law."
"O King, do not, having recognized the path, climb the trunk of a plantain tree.
The king said:
"Rule indeed over the prosperous kingdom of the Śibis, O you who are honored by the flocks of birds!"
"O best of birds, I have given all this away like a king; O hawk,
whatever else you desire, I shall give it all to you—
do not kill this bird who has come to you for refuge."
"O best of birds, tell me that deed by which you might avoid me; I shall do it, for I will not give up the pigeon. The hawk said:
O Uśīnara, O lord of men, if you have such affection for this dove,
then cut off your own flesh and weigh it against the dove;
O King, when your flesh becomes equal in weight to the dove’s, [then you may give it].
"Then that should be given to me; that will be my satisfaction.
The king said:
"O hawk, I consider this a favor that you make such a request of me."
Therefore, today I shall give you my own flesh, weighed upon a scale;
for if this body is not employed for the benefit of living beings,
then why is it being tended to in vain day after day?
Lomaśa said:
Then, O son of Kuntī, that king, the supreme knower of dharma, having cut off his own flesh, weighed it against the pigeon, O lord.
While being weighed on the scale, the dove outweighed [the flesh];
yet King Uśīnara cut away his flesh again and gave it,
until no more flesh remained that was equal in weight to the dove.
Then, with his flesh cut away, he himself ascended the scale.
The hawk said:
"I am Indra, O knower of dharma; this dove is Agni, the carrier of oblations."
Desiring to know the dharma, we have come to your sacrificial enclosure,
O lord of the people; this radiant fame of yours, arising from the flesh that was cut from your limbs, shall surpass all the worlds.
"O King, as long as men shall speak of you in the world, so long shall your fame and your worlds endure eternally. Having spoken thus to the king, he ascended once more to heaven.
The righteous Uśīnara, having covered heaven and earth with his dharma and shining with a magnificent form, ascended to the third heaven.
Lomaśa said:
Having spoken thus to that lord of donors, O King, Indra and Agni then restored their own bodies to their full form and departed for the abode of the thirty gods.
That was the residence of that high-souled king, O son of Pāṇḍu.
Behold this merit-bestowing place that grants liberation from sin along with me;
here indeed, O King, the eternal gods and sages are constantly seen by meritorious and high-souled Brahmins.
Lomaśa said:
"He who is spoken of on earth as Śvetaketu, the son of Uddālaka, the foremost in intelligence and a knower of mantras;"
O lord of men, behold his holy hermitage,
endowed with trees that always bear fruit;
it was here that Śvetaketu beheld [the Lord] in person.
"I shall know Sarasvatī who has assumed a human body"—
thus did Śvetaketu speak to Sarasvatī as she was engaged in conversation.
At that time, there were two foremost knowers of Brahman, maternal uncle and nephew:
Aṣṭāvakra and the son of Kahoḍa.
O King, both Auddālaki Śvetaketu and the king of Videha were brahmins, maternal uncle and nephew.
Having entered the sacrificial arena during the dispute,
they subdued the immeasurable Bandī.
"Wait here, O son of Kuntī, together with your younger brother."
Having entered his most holy hermitage—
of whom they say Aṣṭāvakra was the grandson, and who [was the father] of Bandī at Janaka’s sacrifice.
The disputant, the foremost of Brahmins, though still a child,
approached him and, having defeated him in debate, submerged him in a river.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Of what power was that brahmin who, being thus engaged, subdued Bandin? And on what subject did their dispute then arise?
O Lomaśa, tell me the truth of all this: how did Aṣṭāvakra come to be in the presence of the King of Videha, and by whom was he begotten? Tell me that in its entirety.
Lomaśa said:
O King, there was a disciplined disciple of Uddālaka named Kahoḍa.
Desirous of learning and obedient to the will of his teacher,
he pursued his studies for a long time;
yet the brahmins and his fellow students treated him with contempt.
And having understood that offense, the Guru, perceiving the supreme disciplehood of that very disciple and the transformations of his daughter at that time, [acted accordingly].
To him he immediately granted both sacred learning and his own daughter Sujātā as a wife;
in her, a fetus was conceived that was like unto fire.
Then, while his father was studying, he said to him:
"Father, you have been studying all night; this does not seem to be proceeding correctly."
"O Father, by your grace I have studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs and all the sciences; therefore, even while still in this very womb, I speak thus."
"This does not seem to proceed correctly from you.
Thus rebuked in the midst of his disciples, the great seer cursed him out of anger while he was still in the womb.
"Since you speak while remaining within my womb,
therefore you shall be crooked eight times. He was indeed born thus, truly crooked.
The great seer Aṣṭāvakra was indeed renowned;
Śvetaketu was his maternal uncle,
and he was his equal in age.
Then, being oppressed by her son growing within her womb, Sujātā,
having gone into private, spoke these words to her husband:
"O Great Seer, having gratified my husband with wealth while seeking riches myself, how shall I act if I am destitute?
This month of mine is now the tenth."
"And you have no wealth at all,
my lady, by which I might overcome this calamity. Thus was Kahoḍa addressed by his wife.
Then, for the sake of wealth, he approached Janaka;
at that time, having been defeated in debate by Bandī, that brahmin was submerged here in the waters.
Then Uddālaka,
having heard from the charioteer that he had likewise been submerged in the waters during the debate,
spoke there to Sujātā.
"This matter must be concealed from Aṣṭāvakra," she thought;
and she protected it even from Sumantra,
so that the Brahmin did not hear of it even after he was born.
Aṣṭāvakra regarded Uddālaka as his father, and Śvetaketu as his brother;
then, in the twelfth year, Śvetaketu—
He seized Aṣṭāvakra by the hand as he sat on his father’s lap weeping and dragged him away,
saying, "This is not your father's lap."
Whatever ill-spoken words he had uttered then remained in his heart as a source of great suffering;
returning home, he went to his mother weeping.
He asked this: "Where indeed is my father?
Then Sujātā, appearing deeply distressed and fearing the curse, related everything to him.
"Having understood all that truth from his mother," that brahmin said to Śvetaketu,
"Let us go to the sacrifice of King Janaka."
"His sacrifice is heard to be full of many wonders;
we shall hear the dispute of the Brahmins there,
and we shall also eat the finest food."
"And we two shall possess discernment;
for the sound of the Veda is auspicious and gentle.
Thus spoke the uncle and the nephew as they departed.
As Aṣṭāvakra encountered the king on the road while King Janaka’s sacrifice was being successfully conducted,
he spoke these words as he was being pushed aside.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"The path of the blind, the path of the deaf,
the path of women, and the path of the burden-carrier."
"The path belongs to the king when he does not encounter a brahmin;
but when they do encounter one another, the path belongs to the brahmin alone.
The king said:
"This path is now opened for you by me; go as you wish by whichever way you desire.
Indeed, there is no fire that is too small."
"Even Indra always bows down before brahmins.
Lomaśa said:
"Having been addressed thus by his maternal uncle, he [set out] together with him."
Having reached that sacrificial hall by the path he desired,
and being stopped at the gate, he spoke these words to the doorkeeper.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"O father, we have come here to see the sacrifice;
our curiosity has indeed grown very strong."
"We two have arrived as guests seeking entrance;
we desire your permission, O gatekeeper. We two have come here to behold the sacrifice of Indradyumna."
"O gatekeeper, desiring indeed to speak with and behold the lord of Janaka, do not for a moment join him with anger, as if with a most grievous disease."
And do not overcome us two while we are tormented by disease— you, who have arrived here as a maternal uncle and a nephew, both young and foolish.
"The two gatekeepers must be released at this moment.
The gatekeeper said:
"We are the executors of Bandi's commands."
Listen to these words being spoken by me:
"Indeed, children do not enter here; only the aged, learned, and foremost of the twice-born brahmins enter."
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"O gatekeeper, if entry here has been granted to the elders, it is only right that I should enter as well."
For we are aged and have fulfilled our vows; by the power of the Vedas, we are worthy of entry. We are also devoted to service and have conquered our senses.
We have reached the ultimate goal even in the acquisition of knowledge.
They say one should not despise a person because they are young;
even a small fire burns when touched.
The gatekeeper said:
"Utter the Sarasvatī, which is cherished by the Vedas, the single-syllabled, the multiformed, and the sovereign."
"O fool, look at your own self!
Why do you boast? Success in debate is difficult to attain. Aṣṭāvakra said:
Growth is not known to occur through the growth of the body,
just as a gall-nut on a *śālmali* tree grows even though the tree itself remains short and small in stature.
And for that which is fruitless, there is no state of being old.
The gatekeeper said:
"In this world, the young indeed seek counsel from the elders."
They grasp [knowledge] over time and thus become elders;
for knowledge cannot be attained in a short time.
Why, then, do you, a child, speak as if you were an elder?
Aṣṭāvakra said:
One does not become an elder merely because his head is gray;
even a child who possesses true wisdom—the gods recognize him as an elder.

The seers have established that dharma is not by years, nor by grey hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen; he who is learned in the Vedas is great among us. Desiring to see him, I have come to the royal assembly to meet Bandī.
"O gatekeeper, announce me to the king who wears a garland of lotuses.
Today, O door-keeper, you shall see me speaking as the debate with the wise grows intense."
"O gatekeeper, today you shall see us debating with the wise;
and when the debate has intensified, let the Brahmins, perfected in knowledge, behold even Bandin defeated."
Together with the king and the chief priests—
whether they be of high or low station—
let all of them now remain silent.
The gatekeeper said:
"How can you, a mere child of ten years, enter this sacrifice that is accessible only to those who are disciplined and learned?"
"You shall not enter Bandin without having obtained his consent;
I will strive for your entry through skillful means, so exert yourself properly toward gaining entrance."
This king stands here at Saṃśravaṇa; praise him with refined speech, and he,
filled with affection, will grant you permission.
"And whatever you desire upon my entry," Aṣṭāvakra said:
"O King, best among the Janakas!"
You are worthy of honor; everything is prosperous within you.
You are indeed the performer of sacrificial deeds, or perhaps Yayāti alone was such a king in former times.
The learned Bandī, having defeated those versed in the Vedas in debate and feeling no doubt that they were broken,
was [confronted] by the trustworthy men dispatched by you.
"We have heard that he drowns everyone in water. Having heard this from the presence of the Brahmins, I have indeed come here to engage in a theological debate.
"Where is that Bandi, so that I may encounter him and destroy him, as the sun destroys the stars?
The king said:
"You hope to defeat Bandin without knowing the power of your opponent's speech;
it is only possible to speak thus by those who have understood his prowess."
And he has been seen by the Brahmins who are skilled in debate;
you hope indeed to defeat Bandin without having understood the power of this Bandin.
Previously, those brahmins who had gathered together did not shine, like stars before the sun,
as they were desirous of defeating the bard.
Having reached his presence, O dear one, their splendor vanished;
their pride of learning departed,
how then could they have expanded upon their speech before the assembly?
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"He has indeed been challenged by those like me;
having been made a lion by them, he speaks thus without fear."
"Having encountered me today, he shall lie slain like a cart with broken axles on the road.
The king said:
"He who knows the meaning of that which has six navels, twelve axles, twenty-four joints,
and three hundred and sixty spokes— he is the supreme seer.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"May the wheel that moves eternally— having twenty-four joints, six hubs, twelve rims, and three hundred and sixty spokes— protect you. The king said:
"Like two mares joined together at the swoop of hawks in the sky, who among the dwellers of heaven conceived their embryo, and whose embryo did they bring forth? Aṣṭāvakra said:
"O King, let it not be that in your house there shall certainly be conceived, by the wind-god as his charioteer, even a child of your enemies, nor shall they bring him forth. The king said:
"What is it that does not close its eyes while sleeping? What is it that does not move after being born? Whose heart is there not? And what grows by its own speed? Aṣṭāvakra said:
"A fish does not close its eyes while sleeping; an egg, once born, does not move;
a stone has no heart; and a river increases by its own current.
The king said:
I do not consider you a mere human, but a being of divine nature;
you are no child, for in my estimation you are an elder. No one is found equal to you in the eloquence of speech.
"Therefore, I grant you passage; here is Bandi.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"O King, here among those assembled with Ugrasena..."
When these peerless kings had assembled,
there was indeed no room for further dispute among the speakers,
like the cries of swans in a great body of water.
"O you who pride yourself on being a superior debater, today you shall not speak to me,
having entered this wager like the arrival of rivers before a fire of kindled brilliance."
"Be firm here today for me, O bard!
The bard replied:
"Do not awaken a sleeping tiger."
Like a venomous serpent licking the corners of its mouth after being struck by a foot, it will strike your head;
know this: you shall not escape without being bitten.
He who, out of pride, though possessed of a sturdy frame yet exceedingly weak, strikes at a mountain,
his very hand, along with its nails, is shattered.
Indeed, no wound at all was seen upon Śaila;
all the kings of Mithilā were like the mountains to Maināka, or like calves compared to a bull that has ceased to give milk.
Having thus taken his seat for this dialogue with Bandin,
Aṣṭāvakra, desiring to engage him, repeatedly laughed while censuring him,
just as Mahendra is the foremost among the gods.
Just as the Gaṅgā is the most excellent among rivers,
so are you alone the most excellent among kings; therefore,
bring Bandin into my presence.
Lomaśa said:
O King, Aṣṭāvakra, roaring in the assembly and filled with wrath, spoke to Bandī.
"When these words have been spoken, speak your reply;
and I shall also speak my reply to your words.
Bandi said:
Fire is but one, yet it is kindled in many ways;
the sun is but one, yet it illuminates all this. The slayer is but one hero, the king of the gods.
Yama is the sole lord of the ancestors.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"Indra and Agni indeed move about as two friends."
The two divine seers Nārada and Parvata,
the two Aśvins, and the two wheels of the chariot—
these two pairs of husband and wife were ordained by the Creator.
Bandyu said:
"This progeny is indeed born three times through ritual action;
when three [priests] are engaged, they carry out the Vājapeya sacrifice."
"The Adhvaryu priests perform the three daily libations;
they say there are three worlds and three lights.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
The fourfold assembly of Brahmins is the abode; these four, when joined together, carry out this sacrifice—
the four directions and the four social classes.
"Even a cow is always said to have four feet," Bandī replied, "and the *paṅkti* meter has five feet; there are five fires."
The sacrifices are five, and likewise the five sense organs; the five *pañcacūḍās* are seen in the Veda,
and in the world is renowned the meritorious *pañcanada*.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
Some say that the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is sixfold at the establishment of the fires;
these very six are the seasons of the wheel of time.
"There are six sense organs and also the six Kṛttikās;
the six Sādyaska sacrifices are seen in all the Vedas.
Bandī said:
Seven are the domestic animals, seven the wild;
seven meters carry out a single sacrifice.
There are seven seers and likewise seven offerings.
And the lute is celebrated as having seven strings.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
Eight śāṇas carry one śatamāna.
Likewise, the śarabha, the slayer of lions, has eight feet;
we have heard that among the deities there are eight Vasus,
and the sacrificial post for every sacrifice is ordained to have eight corners.
Bābhravya said:
"Nine indeed are the *sāmidhenī* verses prescribed for the ancestors; likewise, they speak of the ninefold yoga of creation."
"The Bṛhatī is declared to consist of nine syllables;
the combination of nine always attains its calculation.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
Ten tens are said to be a hundred in this world; they say ten hundreds make a full thousand. Women who are pregnant carry the fetus for exactly ten months.
"The Daśerakas, the Daśas, and the Daśārṇas.
Bandī said:
"There are eleven sets of eleven animals."
In this context, there are exactly eleven sacrificial posts;
there are eleven modifications of the vital breaths;
and eleven Rudras are said to exist among the gods in heaven.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"They say that a year consists of twelve months; it is one quarter of the Jagatī meter, which has exactly twelve syllables."
The twelve-day sacrifice is said to be the archetype of ritual;
here, the wise speak of the twelve Ādityas.
Bandī said:
"The thirteenth lunar day is said to be most formidable,
as is the earth consisting of thirteen islands.
Lomaśa said:
Having said this much, the bard fell silent;
Aṣṭavakra uttered the second half of the verse:
"Keśin wandered for thirteen days."
They say that the *Aticchandas* meters consist of thirteen syllables and so forth. Then a great roar arose upon hearing that the son of the Suta had become silent.
At that time, Aṣṭāvakra was facing downward, intent on meditation,
even as he was being raised up while such a tumultuous situation prevailed.
Then, at the grand sacrifice of King Janaka,
all the brahmins, joyful and with palms joined in reverence, approached Aṣṭāvakra to honor him.
Aṣṭāvakra said: "Indeed,
it is said that learned Brāhmaṇas,
having been defeated by him in debate, were submerged in water."
"Let this Bandi obtain those very same dharmas today; seize him and drown him in the waters!
Bandi said:
"I am the son of King Varuṇa;
there, indeed, a twelve-year sacrificial session was held.
O Janaka, that session was simultaneous with yours."
For that purpose, these foremost of the twice-born were dispatched by me;
having all gone there to witness Varuṇa’s sacrifice, they are now returning here once more.
"I shall honor Aṣṭāvakra, who is worthy of worship,
for whose sake I shall meet my father.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
Those brahmins were submerged in the waters of the ocean,
defeated by speech and overcome by their own intelligence;
then, by means of that very intelligence, he drew forth that speech.
Just as the virtuous carefully choose their words,
so may Agni Jātavedas, while burning the houses of the wicked,
release them with his brilliance and not consume them.
While their foolish sons speak piteously,
the virtuous gather such words [of reproach] as you hear from the *śleṣmātaka* tree, which has lost its luster.
Or rather, do these praises intoxicate you?
O Janaka, like an elephant being pierced by goads,
you do not listen to these words of mine.
Janaka said:
"I hear your speech, which is divine in form;
you are truly non-human and manifest as one of divine form."
"Since you have conquered Bandin in debate,
this Bandin is now released at your pleasure.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"O King, there is no purpose for me in this Bandi remaining alive;
if Varuṇa is his father, then drown him in the reservoir of water.
Bandi said:
"I am the son of King Varuṇa;
I have no fear of being submerged in the water.
In this very moment, he shall behold his father."
Lomaśa said:
"Then those brahmins, including Aṣṭāvakra who had long been lost to view, were honored by the high-souled Varuṇa."
They all rose up from the presence of Janaka.
Kahoḍa said:
"O Janaka, it is for this purpose that people desire sons through their actions."
"O Janaka, that which I was unable to accomplish, my son has accomplished for me;
indeed, a strong son may be born to the weak, a wise son to the foolish, and a learned son to the ignorant."
Bandi said:
"O King, may Antaka himself, with his sharp axe, strike off the heads of your enemies in battle; may prosperity be yours."
The great *ukthya* hymn and the foremost *sāman* were chanted there at that sacrificial session (*satra*), and the Soma was duly drunk;
and the pure ones joyfully accepted their respective portions.
Lomaśa said: "O King, when all the gods had then assembled here at Janaka’s sacrifice..."
When those brahmins had become exceedingly radiant,
Bandi, then permitted by King Janaka,
entered the waters of the ocean.
Having honored his father and being duly honored by those brahmins in return, Aṣṭāvakra returned once more to that foremost hermitage.
Having defeated Bandin together with his maternal uncle,
the father then said to Aṣṭāvakra in the presence of his mother:
"Enter this river Samangā quickly."
He spoke thus to her and entered her;
immediately her limbs became symmetrical,
and she became the sacred river Samangā.
In her, one who has bathed is indeed released from sin;
you too, along with your brothers and your wife, enter her for bathing, drinking, and immersion.
O son of Kuntī, having stayed here happily with your brothers and the brahmins, you have been well-pleased; now,
with single-minded devotion to pure deeds, visit other holy places.

O descendant of Ajamīḍha, you shall travel together with me; having shaken off all evil and freed from fatigue, you shall drink at other sacred waters and bathe in the excellent bathing places of the holy rivers.
"With a pure disposition and firm devotion, you shall wander together with me.
Lomaśa said:
"O King, here appears the river Madhuvilā, also known as Samaṅgā."
This is the place called Kardamila, the consecration site of Bharata.
It is said that the Lord of Śacī, having slain Vṛtra and being afflicted by misfortune,
bathed here in the Samaṅgā river and was liberated from all sins.
O bull among men, this is the place of destruction within the belly of Maināka,
where in ancient times Aditi cooked that food for the sake of her sons.
O bull among men, having ascended this king of mountains, [you shall proceed].
"You shall dispel ill repute, infamy, and misfortune.
O King, these are the Kanakhala mountains, beloved by the seers;
here flows the Ganges, the great river, O Yudhiṣṭhira."
"The blessed Sanatkumāra attained supreme perfection here.
O descendant of Ajamidha, by bathing in this [river], you shall be liberated from all sins. [There is also] the lake of waters known as Puṇya and the mountain Bhṛgutuṅga."
O son of Kuntī, together with your ministers, silently touch the waters of the Gaṅgā;
the delightful hermitage of Sthūlaśiras appears here.
O son of Kuntī, abandon both pride and anger in this place.
O son of Pāṇḍu, here shines the glorious hermitage of Raibhya,
strewn with various flowers and adorned with fruits and blossoms;
it resounds with the cries of various birds and is the supreme abode of ascetics.
"O Great King, this is the hermitage of Raibhya, a man of meritorious deeds,
where the wise Yavakrīta, the son of Bharadvāja, perished.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How was the powerful seer Bharadvāja joined [with his wife]?
And for what reason did Yavakrīta, the son of the seer, perish?
O Lomaśa, I wish to hear all this exactly as it happened."
I take great delight in the deeds being recounted of those who are like unto gods.
Lomaśa said:
Bharadvāja and Raibhya were companions.
Those two dwelt there in the forest for a very long time, taking great delight in one another.
Now, O Bhārata, Raibhya had two sons, Arvāvasu and Parāvasu, while Bharadvāja’s son was Yavakrī.
The learned Raibhya was accompanied by his offspring, while the other was an ascetic;
and between them, O Bhārata, there was incomparable affection from their childhood onwards.
Then Yavakrī, seeing his father treated with disrespect despite being an ascetic, [was filled with resentment].
O sinless one, seeing Raibhya honored by the brahmins along with his sons,
that radiant man was consumed with grief and overwhelmed by anger;
thereupon, O Pāṇḍava, he performed severe austerities for the sake of attaining knowledge of the Vedas.
While heating his body over a great, well-kindled fire,
that man of great asceticism produced intense heat within Indra.
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, Indra approached Yavakrīta.
"O you who are worshipped by the hosts of gods, for what reason have you undertaken this supreme austerity? Yavakrī replied: "The Vedas have indeed not been studied by the twice-born."

"O Pākaśāsana, I performed this supreme austerity so that [these things] might appear to me; this undertaking of mine was for the sake of Vedic study. O Kauśika, through this austerity, I desire to know all branches of knowledge."
"O Lord, the Vedas can be obtained from the mouth of a preceptor only after a long time;
therefore, this supreme effort has been undertaken by me.
Indra said:
"O brahmin-sage, this is not the path by which you wish to go. O brahmin, what is the use of this obstruction? Go and study at the mouth of a teacher.
Lomaśa said:
Having spoken thus, Śakra departed, O Bhārata; Yavakrī too, of immeasurable prowess, again exerted himself in asceticism. Tormenting himself with fierce penance, O King, that great ascetic—
We have heard that he greatly tormented the Lord of the Gods.
Then, approaching that great sage who was thus performing such intense austerity,
the god who shatters the forces (Indra) indeed restrained him once more.
"This undertaking you have begun is impossible; this was not done with wisdom on your part.
Indeed, the Vedas shall manifest themselves to both you and your father.
Yavakrī said:
"O King of the Gods, this which I desire shall not be done in this way. With great discipline, I shall perform most terrible penance; having offered limb after limb into the kindled fire,"
Or I shall offer it, O Maghavan; understand this.
If you do not fulfill this desire of mine here, O King of the Gods, then all my wishes [shall remain unfulfilled].
Lomaśa said:
Having understood that resolve of the high-souled sage,
the wise one reflected with his intellect upon the means for the purpose of restraining him.
Then Indra assumed the form of an ascetic Brahmin,
aged many hundreds of years, weak and afflicted with consumption;
he took on the appearance of Yavakrīta as he was accustomed to performing his purificatory rites at the sacred ford.
There, on the Bhāgīrathī, he built a bridge with sands.
When that best of the twice-born would not act upon his words as he spoke them,
Śakra then began to fill the Gaṅgā with sands.
He incessantly cast handfuls of sand into the Bhāgīrathī,
beginning the construction of a bridge as an illustration for Yavakrīta;
and Yavakrīta beheld him thus striving in his endeavor to bind the river.
Laughing, that bull among sages spoke these words:
"O Brahmin, what is this that is happening? And what is it that you intend to do?
For this great effort being made is utterly useless."
Indra said:
"I shall dam the Gaṅgā with a bridge; the path will become easy to travel.
For people, my dear, suffer greatly as they cross it again and again."
Yavakrī said:
"This great torrent cannot be bound by you in any way whatsoever. Desist from what is impossible and undertake a task that is possible."
Indra said:
"Just as this austerity has been undertaken by you for the sake of the Veda, so too is this burden that we have undertaken impossible [to fulfill]."
Yavakrī said:
"O Lord of the Thirty-three, O Subduer of Pāka, if you consider this undertaking of mine to be as futile as yours."
"O Lord of the hosts of gods, let that which is possible for me to do be performed;
and grant me other boons by which I shall surpass all others.
Lomaśa said:
To him, Indra, who had been addressed by that one of great asceticism, granted the boons he requested:
"The Vedas shall manifest themselves to you, together with your father, according to your desire; and whatever other wish you may long for, O Yavakrī, let it be fulfilled—now you may go."
Having attained his desire, Yavakrī then approached his father and said:
Yavakrī said:
"O father, the Vedas shall indeed manifest themselves to both me and you."
"We shall surpass all others; thus have the boons been obtained by me.
Bharadvāja said:
"O dear one, having obtained the boons as you desired, pride will surely arise within you."
"Filled with pride and wretched, you will surely perish quickly.
In this regard, they cite these verses uttered by the gods:
'In ancient times, O son, there was a powerful seer named Bālādhya.'"

Distraught by grief for his son, he performed most difficult austerities, praying, "May my son become immortal," and he obtained that very thing. Yet, while the gods showed him favor, it was not equal to that of the immortals.
"No mortal exists who shall have a lifespan determined by external signs.
Bāladhi said:
"O best of gods, just as these mountains stand forever..."
"May my son's life become inexhaustible because of that.
Bharadvāja said:
"Then a son was born to him, wise yet always prone to anger."
Having heard that, he became arrogant and began to treat the sages with contempt.
While wandering this earth and acting with such insolence toward the munis,
he encountered the wise Dhanuṣākṣa, who was possessed of great heroism.
The wise one acted against him, and that powerful one cursed him, saying, "Become ashes! Yet, though thus addressed, he did not turn into ashes.
But Dhanuṣākṣa, seeing that Medhāvin was unharmed, [was struck with wonder].

The Sage, having personally understood the cause of that, assumed the form of a buffalo and shook the mountains with his horns; consequently, this [city] was reduced to ashes. The valiant one caused it to be demolished by buffaloes for that specific purpose.
When the omen had vanished, the infant suddenly died;
then the father, taking up his dead son, began to lament.
Seeing him thus wailing like one in deep distress, the sages spoke once more.
They spoke with a verse previously declared in the Vedas; learn that from me: "A mortal is not able to overcome destiny by any means whatsoever.
Dhanuṣākṣa split the mountains with his buffalo-headed arrows.
Having thus obtained these boons, the boy, full of arrogance and impetuous, will surely perish before long, just as you have not done. This Raibhya is of great prowess, and his two sons are likewise.
Therefore, my son, you should act with vigilance so that he does not approach you;
for if he is provoked to anger, O son,
that great sage— learned, ascetic, and irascible— is capable of afflicting you in his wrath.
Yavakrī said:
"I shall do so; O father, do not grieve in any way whatsoever.
For just as you are venerable to me, so too is Raibhya my father."
Lomaśa said:
Having spoken thus tenderly to his father, Yavakrī, free from fear,
took delight in the highest joy while treating the other sages with contempt.
Lomaśa said:
Then, while wandering about without fear from any quarter, Yavakrī went toward the hermitage of Raibhya in the month of Mādhava.
In that sacred hermitage adorned with flowering trees, O Bhārata, he beheld his daughter-in-law wandering about like a Kinnarī. Yavakrī said this to her: "Attend upon me."

Shameless and his mind stolen by desire, he approached her who was possessed of modesty; she, having recognized his character and fearing that curse as well as the majesty of Raibhya, said "So be it" and departed.
Then, having reached the hermitage,
O Bhārata, she who was devoted to her husband was requested by Yavakrīta; having led him to a secluded spot, she then caused him to be immersed in water.
Then, O subduer of enemies, Raibhya returned to his own hermitage.
Seeing his daughter-in-law, the wife of Parāvasu, weeping and distressed,
he comforted her with gentle words and questioned her, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
That beautiful woman related to him everything that Yavakrī had said,
as well as her own deliberate response to Yavakrī;
and even as Raibhya was listening to Yavakrī’s conduct, [he became enraged].
Then a great anger arose, as if burning his mind. At that time, the ascetic, overcome by fury and exceedingly wrathful,
tore out a single lock of matted hair and offered it into the well-consecrated fire.
Then a woman appeared, equal to her in beauty;
then, plucking out another lock of matted hair, he offered it again into the fire.
From that, a Rākṣasa was born, with terrible eyes and a fearsome appearance.
Then those two said to Raibhya, "What task shall we perform?
The rishi, enraged, said to them, "Let Yavakrī be killed. Having replied, "So be it," the two departed with the intent to slay Yavakrī.
Then, having assumed the form of Raibhya’s daughter-in-law, she approached Yavakrīta;
and Yavakrīta, believing her to be Raibhya’s daughter-in-law, went toward her.
Thereupon, the *kṛtyā* created by the high-souled one stood before him.
O Bhārata, having deluded him, he seized his water-pot; then,
seeing Yavakrīta defiled and deprived of his water-pot,
that Rākṣasa rushed forward with his spear raised.
Seeing him approaching with a trident in his hand, intent on killing him,
Yavakrī suddenly rose and fled toward a lake. Seeing that the lake was devoid of water, Yavakrī hurried away once more.
He went toward all the rivers, but they too were dried up. Being driven by the terrible Rākṣasa with a spear in his hand,
he fled in fear toward his father’s *agnihotra* fire.
O King, as he was entering, Yavakrīta was forcibly seized at the gate by a blind Śūdra guard;
thus restrained by the Śūdra, that Rākṣasa [stood there].
He struck him with a trident, and he fell down with his heart pierced.
Having killed Yavakrīta, that Rākṣasa approached Raibhya;
permitted by Raibhya, he lived together with that woman.
Lomaśa said:
O son of Kuntī, Bharadvāja, having performed his daily study and rituals and taking up a bundle of sacrificial fuel, entered his own hermitage.
In former times, all the fires used to rise up in greeting upon seeing him;
but now that his son has been slain, those fires no longer attend him.
Bharadvāja did not even perceive the ritual impurity arising from the death of his son.
Having observed this anomaly in the Agnihotra sacrifice, that man of great asceticism then spoke to the blind Śūdra who was sitting there as the guardian of the house:
"O Śūdra, why is it that my fires do not rejoice at the sight of me?"
"And are you not as you were before? Is all well here in this hermitage? Has my dull-witted son gone to Raibhya?
Tell me this quickly, for my mind finds no peace."
The Śūdra said:
"O dull-witted one, that son of yours has surely gone to Raibhya;
for thus he lies slain by a powerful Rākṣasa."

As he was being dragged away by that spear-handed Rākṣasa, I restrained him at the entrance of the fire-sanctuary with my two arms. Then he was slain here; indeed, being impure, he surely desired water.
For he was quickly assailed by the Rākṣasa with a spear in hand.
Lomaśa said:
But Bharadvāja, having heard those unpleasant words of the Śūdra, [was moved].
Taking up his lifeless son, he lamented in great distress:
"Surely you performed austerities for the sake of the Brahmins,
so that the Vedas might be revealed to those twice-born ones who had not yet studied them."
Likewise, you who are of virtuous character toward high-souled brahmins and free from harm toward all beings have nevertheless resorted to harshness; O dear one,
you were forbidden by me from visiting the hermitage of Raibhya.

That man of great splendor, though knowing me to be old and having only one son, has indeed gone away under the sway of anger— that evil-minded wretch who resembles the Destroyer Yama at the end of time. (3.138.012c–013)
"Having encountered this grief for my son through the deed of Raibhya,
O son, I shall abandon my life-breaths— which are most dear to me on earth— without you.
Just as I, a sinner, shall cast off my body through grief for my son."
Likewise, an eldest son might quickly harm the innocent Raibhya;
indeed, those men who by birth have no son are truly happy,
for they wander about at ease, never having experienced the grief of losing a son.
But who indeed could be more wretched than those whose minds are utterly distraught by grief for a son, and who,
in their affliction, curse their beloved friends?
For I have seen my son dead and cursed my dear friend.
"Who indeed shall experience such a calamity as this for a second time? Having lamented thus in many ways, Bharadvāja cremated his son and subsequently entered the well-kindled fire.
Lomaśa said:
At that very time, however, the illustrious and powerful King Bṛhaddyumna, for whom Raibhya was the officiating priest, was performing a sacrificial session.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, the two sons of Raibhya, Arvāvasu and Parāvasu,
were chosen as assistants for the sake of the sacrificial session by the wise Bṛhaddyumna;
having been granted permission there by their father, they both departed.
Now Raibhya was at the hermitage, as was the wife of Parāvasu. Then Parāvasu went alone to his home to look for them;
there in the forest, he saw his father clothed in a black antelope skin.
In the final watch of the night, blinded by sleep even though darkness still remained,
he mistook his father as he was moving through the dense forest for a deer.
Thinking him to be a deer, the son indeed killed his father.
Then, desiring to protect his body and having no other intention,
Parāvasu approached and saw his father slain;
having killed his father through ignorance, mistaking him for a deer.
O King, having lamented in many ways for the sake of the high-souled Raibhya,
he performed all the funeral rites for him, O Bhārata;
then, returning to that sacrificial session, he spoke these words to his brother.
"You alone are not capable of carrying out this task in any way whatsoever.
For my father was killed by me, who mistook him for a deer. Therefore, for our sake, perform the vow that purifies the sin of killing a Brahmin."
"For I am indeed capable of performing this rite alone, O sage.
Arvāvasu said:
"May you indeed perform the sacrificial session for the wise Bṛhaddyumna."
"Restraining my senses for your sake, I shall perform the penance for the murder of a Brahmin.
With single-minded focus, he went to the forest to perform the vow for the murder of a Brahmin.
Having heard that, Arvāvasu subsequently prescribed the means of atonement.
Lomaśa said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having reached the further shore of that Brahman-murder,
the sage Arvāvasu then returned once more to the sacrificial session.
Then Parāvasu, seeing his brother approaching,
spoke these words to Bṛhaddyumna while he was seated in the assembly:
"Let this slayer of a Brahmin not enter to witness your sacrifice."
"Even by a mere glance, a slayer of a Brahmin would afflict you; of this there is no doubt.
Lomaśa said:
"O Lord of the Viśas, having heard that, the king then spoke to his messengers."

O King, as he was being driven away by the servants, Arvāvasu said again and again, "I have not committed this Brahman-murder. Though addressed repeatedly by the servants as "Brahman-killer," O Bhārata, he spoke thus.
He did not at all admit that he himself had committed the murder of a Brahmin;
"This was done by my brother, while I merely protected it," he said. Speaking thus out of anger, he was addressed by those servants.
The great ascetic Brahmarṣi departed silently for the forest itself;
having undertaken fierce penance,
that best of the twice-born took refuge with the Sun and composed the secret Veda of Sūrya.
Then the imperishable one himself, who eats first, beheld him in embodied form.
O King, the gods were pleased with the deed of Arvāvasu;
they chose him as their chief and cast Parāvasu out.
Then the gods, led by Agni, granted him a boon;
and he chose as his boons the restoration of his father to life and the freedom from sin for himself, as well as the lack of recollection regarding the killing of his father and brother.
The best of the twice-born [Vasiṣṭha] recounted the rise of both Bharadvāja and Yavakrīta, as well as the establishment of the solar Veda;
and the gods said to him, "So be it," and granted him boons.
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, they all appeared before him;
thereupon Yavakrīta spoke to the gods, headed by Agni:
"The Veda has been mastered by me, and the vows have been observed."
"O best of immortals, how indeed was Raibhya able to strike down me, an ascetic engaged in study, by such a method? The gods said:
"Do not speak thus, O sage Yavakrīta, as you say. For in the past, you mastered the Vedas easily without a teacher;
but this man has pleased his teachers through his own arduous labor."
After a long time, through great effort, he attained the supreme state of Brahman.
Lomaśa said:
Having spoken thus to Yavakrīta, the gods, led by Agni, [departed].
Having restored them all to life, they returned once more to heaven.
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, Yavakrīta indeed practiced the vow of celibacy for eighteen years and thirty more.
"This is his sacred hermitage, where the trees always bear flowers and fruit;
by staying here, O tiger among kings, you shall be liberated from all sins.
Lomaśa said:
O Bhārata, you have passed beyond Uśīrabīja, Mount Maināka, and Śveta;
O Kaunteya, O King, you have also passed beyond Kālaśaila. Here, O bull of the Bharatas, shines the Gaṅgā divided into seven streams.
There is a beautiful, stainless place where the sacrificial fire is perpetually kindled.
Indeed, this cannot even be seen today by a human being;
therefore, practice concentration with undistracted minds, and you shall behold these sacred fords.
"This play-ground of the gods is seen, marked with their footprints.
You have passed beyond it, O son of Kuntī, as well as Mount Kālaśaila. We shall now enter Mount Śveta and Mount Mandara."
There dwells the Yakṣa Māṇicara and Kubera,
the king of the Yakṣas; there are eighty-eight thousand swift-moving Gandharvas, as well as Kimpuruṣas, O King, and four times as many Yakṣas.
Possessing many forms and shapes and bearing various weapons,
they attend upon Maṇibhadra, the lord of yakṣas, O best of men;
their supernatural power is exceedingly supreme, and they are equal to the wind in speed.

"O Pārtha, those mountains are difficult to traverse; they are protected by powerful beings and guarded by Yātudhānas, who could even displace the King of the Gods from his firm station. Therefore, O dear one, apply yourself to supreme concentration."
"O son of Kuntī, we shall encounter the other ministers of Kubera and the fierce and friendly Rākṣasas; therefore, be diligent in your prowess. O King, Mount Kailāsa extends for six hundred yojanas."
O Bhārata, where the gods assemble and where Viśālā is located,
O Kaunteya, there dwell innumerable Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kiṃnaras,
as well as Nāgas, Suparṇas, and Gandharvas, heading toward the abode of Kubera.
"Enter into them today, O Pārtha, through asceticism and self-restraint,
while being protected by me, O King, and by the strength of Bhīmasena. May King Varuṇa and Yama, the victor in assemblies, grant you well-being."
May the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, and the mountain, grant you [well-being];
may the Maruts together with the two Aśvins, the rivers, and the lakes grant it;
and may there be well-being from the gods and Asuras, and from the Vasus, O one of great splendor!
O Goddess Gaṅgā, on the peak of Indra’s mountain of Jāmbūnada gold, I hear your roar; O fortunate one, protect this man from the mountains.
O Daughter of the Mountain, grant protection to this king, the descendant of Ajamīḍha honored by all, as he enters these mountains.
Having spoken thus regarding the river that flows to the ocean, that brahmin instructed Pārtha, saying,
"Be vigilant," on that best of all rivers which bestows auspiciousness.
03,140.014f*0678_02 [This is] for Yudhiṣṭhira, who has brothers here. 03,140.015 YudhiṣṬHIRA said:
03,140.015a "This agitation of Lomaśa is unprecedented."
"Protect Kṛṣṇā all together; do not be negligent!
For this region is considered by him to be most difficult to traverse;
therefore, practice the highest purity here."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then he spoke to Bhīma of noble prowess:
"O Bhīmasena, protect Kṛṣṇā with vigilance."
"O dear one, since Arjuna is absent and away from here,
you alone must attend to Kṛṣṇā during these times of hardship.
Then the high-souled one, having approached the twin sons of Yama...
Having smelled their heads and stroked their limbs, the king, his voice choked with tears, said to them:
"Do not fear; come back, remaining vigilant."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Vṛkodara, it is possible to traverse through hidden beings and powerful rākṣasas by means of fire and ascetic power."
"O son of Kuntī, restrain your hunger and thirst by means of your strength;
therefore, O best of the Kurus, rely upon both physical power and skill.
You have heard the words of the Ṛṣi concerning Mount Kailāsa."
"O son of Kuntī, observe with your intelligence how Kṛṣṇā will go—
whether with Sahadeva and Dhaumya, O lord,
or with the cooks, the stewards, and all the attendants."

"O Bhima of long eyes, you should return together with all those who have come by chariot and horse, and with whatever other Brahmins there may be who are unable to endure the hardships of the road. As for us three, we shall go on foot, eating light food and restrained by our vows."
Nakula, myself, and Lomaśa of great asceticism—
concentrated and awaiting my arrival at Gaṅgādvāra—
dwell here protecting Draupadī until my return.
Bhīma said:
"O Bhārata, the princess, afflicted by fatigue and stricken with grief,
this auspicious lady continues to go forth indeed out of a desire to see the one of white steeds."
Not seeing that hero here, she is thus deeply afflicted;
how much more so when she does not see Nakula, you, and that heroic Dhanañjaya?
And your own intense distress increases as you do not see him.
O Bhārata, what need is there to speak of the high-souled Guḍākeśa, who never retreats in battles? How much more so regarding Sahadeva, myself, and Kṛṣṇā?
Let the chariots turn back at will, as well as all the attendants.
"Wherever you, sir, consider us to be— whether as cooks or as kitchen overseers—
I certainly do not wish to abandon you here at any time,
even on this mountain crowded with *rākṣasas* and amidst its difficult and rugged terrains."
And this illustrious princess, firm in her vows,
O tiger among men, would not venture to turn back without you;
likewise, this Sahadeva is constantly devoted to you.
He will never turn back, for I truly know his mind.
Moreover, O Great King, all of us here are longing with eager desire to see Savyasācin; therefore, we shall go together.
"If this mountain, with its many caves, cannot be traversed by chariots, we shall proceed on foot; O King, do not be despondent. I myself will carry Pāñcālī wherever she is unable to go."
"Such is my thought, O King; do not be despondent.
Both those heroes, the delighters of Mādrī, though so delicate, I shall carry across the difficult terrain even if they become unable to proceed."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhīma, may your strength increase as you speak thus,
you who venture to carry Draupadī over such a long journey."

"May it be well with you; such a thing as this has never been seen elsewhere. May your strength, fame, righteousness, and glory increase, since you are capable of leading away these two brothers along with Kṛṣṇā."
"O mighty-armed one, may you have no exhaustion, and may there be no defeat for you.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the charming Kṛṣṇā spoke these words while smiling.
"I shall go; you should not feel any distress on my account, O Bhārata.
Lomaśa said:
"The Gandhamādana mountain can be reached through ascetic power."
"O Kaunteya, we shall all devote ourselves to ascetic penance (tapas).
O King, Nakula, Sahadeva, Bhīmasena,
you, and I— O Kaunteya— we shall behold the one who has white horses (Śvetavāhana)."
Vaiśampāyana said: O King,
while conversing in this manner, they joyfully beheld the vast kingdom of Subāhu, which abounded in elephants and horses.
Crowded with Kirātas and Taṅgaṇas, teeming with hundreds of Kuṇindas,
frequented by the immortals on the Himavat, and filled with many wonders—
Subāhu, seeing them, received them with honor.
At the border of the Kuṇinda kingdom, the lord received them with affection;
there they were all honored by him and dwelt happily. When the sun was bright, they set out toward the Himavat mountain.
O King, having entrusted Indrasena and the other servants, as well as the stewards,
cooks, and all the attendants of Draupadī to the king,
the lord of Kuṇinda, those great chariot-warriors [departed].
With great prowess, those descendants of Kuru proceeded on foot alone.
All those Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇā, moved slowly from that place,
filled with joy and longing to see Dhanañjaya.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhīmasena, both the twins, and O princess of Pañcāla, listen:
there is indeed no destruction of a living being; behold us, though we wander in the forest."
That you say to one another, "We are weak and exhausted," yet resolve,
"Let us go even though it is impossible," out of a desire to see Dhanañjaya—
that burns my limbs like fire consumes a heap of cotton.
And because I do not see the hero Dhanañjaya nearby,
that thirst for his sight— which has driven me, along with my younger brothers, to dwell in the forest— burns me all the more, O hero, as does the violation of Yājñasenī.
