"O Vṛkodara, I do not see Nakula’s elder brother, Pārtha, who is of immeasurable energy, unconquerable, and a wielder of a formidable bow; because of him, I am tormented. [I long for] the delightful sacred fords, forests, and lakes."
"I wander together with you out of a longing to see him.
O Vṛkodara, for five years I have not seen the hero Dhananjaya, who is true to his word; because I do not see Bibhatsu, I am consumed by grief."
"I do not see that dark-complexioned Guḍākeśa, who moves with the prowess of a lion and possesses mighty arms; because of him, O Vṛkodara, I am tormented.
He is skilled in weapons, proficient in battle, and the peerless standard for all archers."
"I do not see that best of men, O Vṛkodara, and because of that I am tormented—
seeing Dhananjaya, who has the shoulders of a lion, moving among the hosts of enemies like the wrathful Destroyer at the end of time, or like an elephant in rut with temples flowing."
He who is not inferior to Śakra in heroism and wealth, the elder of the twins, Pārtha, whose horses are white and whose prowess is immeasurable;
he who is equal to Nārāyaṇa in battle, true to his word, and firm in his vows.
O Bhīma, as long as I do not see him, there is no peace for my heart;
overcome by great suffering caused by my own irreversible deeds,
I do not see that Phalguna, the invincible one with the fierce bow.

He who is always of a forgiving nature, even when insulted by one of the slightest stature— he who bestows peace and fearlessness upon those who have entered the straight path— is [the enemy] of one who acts crookedly and seeks to strike him down through deceit.
Even for the wielder of the thunderbolt himself, he would be like deadly poison;
yet toward even an enemy who has sought refuge,
that powerful and compassionate Bībhatsu— of immeasurable soul and great strength— is a giver of fearlessness.
He was the refuge of us all, the crusher of our enemies in battle, the gatherer of all jewels, and the bringer of happiness to every one of us—
by whose prowess those celestial jewels formerly belonged to me.

O hero, O Pāṇḍava, Suyodhana has undergone many births in great numbers; it was by the strength of his arms, O brave one, that my assembly hall of old was renowned throughout the three worlds as being composed of every kind of gem.

I do not see that Phalguna, who is equal to Vāsudeva in prowess, equal to Kārtavīrya in battle, unconquerable and undefeated in war; nor do I see Saṃkarṣaṇa of great heroism, nor you, O Bhīma, who are invincible.
That slayer of enemies was born with the prowess of Vāsudeva;
in the strength of his arms and in his majesty he was equal to Purandara; in speed he was like Vāyu, in countenance like Soma, and in wrath like eternal Death.
O hero, O mighty-armed one, all of us, desiring to see that tiger among men,
shall enter Mount Gandhamādana,
where the vast Badarī tree stands and the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa is located.
We shall behold that supreme mountain, which is constantly inhabited by yakṣas;
we shall go on foot, performing great austerities, to the delightful Kubera-nalinī, which is guarded by rākṣasas.
"O Vṛkodara, this region cannot be traversed by one who has not performed austerities,
nor by one who is cruel, greedy, or lacking in tranquility, O Bhārata.
We shall all go there, seeking the footsteps of Bhīma and Arjuna."
Armed with weapons and girded with swords, together with Brahmins of great vows, O Pārtha, one who is unrestrained encounters flies,
mosquitoes, gadflies, tigers, lions, and reptiles;
but one who is self-controlled does not see them.
"Restraining our senses and limiting our food, we shall enter Mount Gandhamādana, desiring to behold Dhanañjaya.
Lomaśa said:
All the mountains shall be witnesses, as shall the rivers together with their cities and forests;
the glorious sacred fords (tīrthas) shall likewise bear witness, for the water has been touched by his hands.
This path shall lead him to the divine Mount Mandara.
"Be composed and free from anxiety, all you Pāṇḍavas;
this abode of the gods shall indeed be your destination. It is the dwelling place of divine sages who perform meritorious deeds."

"O gentle one, O King, this auspicious and holy great river flows forth from Badarī; it is frequented by hosts of celestial sages. It is constantly attended by the high-souled Vālakhilyas who move through the air."
Honored and approached by the high-souled Gandharvas,
the chanters of Sāman hymns, whose voices were auspicious, sang the Sāman there;
as did Marīci, Pulaha, Bhṛgu, and likewise Aṅgiras.
There, the best of gods, accompanied by the hosts of Maruts, recites his daily prayers;
the Sādhyas and the two Aśvins likewise run around him at that time,
as do the Moon together with the Sun, and the luminaries along with the planets.
Following this river according to the division of day and night,
O highly fortunate one, at Gaṅgādvāra, the bull-bannered Lord bore its water upon his head so that the world might endure.
"O dear ones, you all must go with a disciplined mind and pay homage to this divine lady, the Bhagavatī.
Having heard those words of the high-souled Lomaśa, [they did as instructed].
With disciplined minds, those Pāṇḍavas paid homage to the celestial Gaṅgā.
Having offered their salutations, all those Pāṇḍavas, who walk the path of dharma,
set out once more, filled with joy, together with all the hosts of sages.
Then those best of men saw, shining from afar, a white mass resembling Mount Meru scattered in every direction;
and perceiving that the Pāṇḍavas desired to question him, Lomaśa—
The knower of speech spoke these words: "Listen, O sons of Pāṇḍu!
This which you behold standing there, O best of men—vast, magnificent, and resembling the peak of Mount Kailāsa—is a mountain-like expanse."
These are the bones of the great-souled Daitya Naraka;
resting upon the mountain crags, they shine like a mountain itself,
[preserved] by the ancient god Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self.
O dear one, the Daitya has been slain by him who desires the welfare of the king of the gods;
that high-minded one, performing austerities for ten thousand years,
seeks the station of Indra through his asceticism, Vedic study, and prowess.
By the great power of his asceticism and by the strength of the speed of his arms,
that son of Diti was ever invincible and overawed others;
yet he, having recognized his strength and his practice of vows in righteousness, [remained steadfast].
Overcome by fear and agitated, O sinless one, Śakra then meditated in his mind upon the imperishable god Viṣṇu;
and the omnipresent, glorious Lord arrived and stood there resplendent.
All the ṛṣis and the inhabitants of heaven also praised him.
Upon seeing him, the Blessed Lord Havyavāhana, whose splendor was blazing,
became shorn of his luster, overwhelmed by his brilliance.
Having seen that boon-granting god Viṣṇu, the lord of the hosts of gods,
the wielder of the thunderbolt bowed down with palms joined in reverence and, having paid his respects,
Viṣṇu spoke.
Then he spoke these words regarding the truth from which his fear arose:
"O Śakra, I know your fear of the lords of the Daityas and of Naraka;
therefore, by means of deeds perfected through austerity, you seek the station of Indra."
Therefore, out of affection for you, O Lord of the Gods, I shall certainly separate him from his body— even though he has achieved perfection through asceticism— though wait but a moment.
Then Viṣṇu, of great splendor, took away his consciousness with his hand.
Then he fell to the earth like the king of mountains struck down;
this heap of bones belonging to him who was slain by the master of illusion is indeed the second further deed of Viṣṇu that is made manifest.
"The entire earth was lost and submerged in the netherworld (pātāla).
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
It was raised up again by him, in the form of the single-horned boar."
O Blessed One, relate this story in detail according to its true nature:
how was the earth, which had then vanished,
raised up once more for a hundred *yojanas* by that Lord of the Gods, O Brahmin?
And by what means is the earth, the auspicious and highly fortunate goddess who causes all crops to grow, made firm for the world? And by whose power has she traveled a hundred yojanas?
"By whom was this entire treasury of the Supreme Self’s prowess displayed?
O best of the twice-born, I wish to know all of this according to its true nature.
Lomaśa said:
For you are indeed the refuge for hearing all of this in detail; therefore,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, listen here with full attention as I relate in its entirety everything about this discourse concerning which I have been questioned by you.
Long ago, O dear one, while the Kṛta Yuga was prevailing— then free from fear—
the ancient Primordial God (Ādideva) exercised the office of Yama.
As that wise God of gods was performing the duties of Yama, [the following occurred].
There, O Acyuta, no one dies nor is anyone born;
yet flocks of birds increase, as do cattle,
cows, and sheep, and oxen, horses, and deer— all of them become flesh-eaters.
Likewise, O tiger among men, O scorcher of foes,
human beings increase by the thousands and tens of thousands like water;
while this terrifying confusion, dear one, is thus occurring.
Overburdened, the Earth traveled a hundred *yojanas*;
with all her limbs distressed and her consciousness overwhelmed by the weight,
she sought refuge and took shelter with Nārāyaṇa, the supreme god.
The Earth said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace indeed may I remain here for a very long time;
yet, being overwhelmed by this burden, I am unable to endure."
"O Blessed One, you ought to remove this burden of mine.
Lomaśa said:
"O God, I have come to you for refuge; O All-pervading Lord, show me favor."
Having heard those words of hers, the imperishable Lord, the Blessed One,
being delighted, spoke these words uttered with melodious syllables:
"O upholder of the earth, you need not feel fear on account of this burden."
"I shall act in such a way that you will become light.
Having thus dismissed her, the earth, who was adorned with mountains as earrings,
he then became a boar of great splendor, possessing a single horn.
As if instilling fear with his two blood-red eyes,
and emitting smoke through his splendor, he grew in that region;
having seized the earth with one radiant horn, he held it aloft.
O hero, that Imperishable One draws up a hundred *yojanas* [of water];
as it was being drawn up, a great agitation arose,
and all the gods and the sages whose wealth is asceticism were thrown into turmoil.
Alas! Alas! cried out everyone; the three heavens, the sky, and the earth were likewise filled with lamentation.
Not a single being remained composed, whether god or human.
Then [he beheld] Brahmā seated there, as if blazing with splendor.
The gods, together with the hosts of sages, approached him in great numbers.
Having drawn near to Brahmā, the lord of the gods and witness of the world,
they all stood with palms joined in reverence and then uttered these words.

All the worlds are agitated, and everything mobile and immobile is thrown into confusion; O Lord of the Thirty-three, a great upheaval of the oceans is manifesting. This entire earth has sunk a hundred yojanas.
"By what cause, and by whose power, has this world been thrown into such agitation?
Brahmā said:
"Tell us quickly; we have all lost our senses here."

There is no fear of the Asuras for you anywhere at all. Listen, O immortals, to that by which agitation arises even when [the elements] have been created: it is he who is all-pervading, glorious, and established as the imperishable Self.
By his power, a commotion is manifested in the triple heaven;
this entire earth, which had traveled a hundred yojanas,
was drawn back again by that Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self.
As she was being lifted up, a great agitation arose.
The gods said:
"O sirs, know this: let your doubt be severed."
"Where is that being who joyfully uplifts the earth?
Brahmā said:
"O Blessed One, tell us of that place; we shall go there."
"Come, may prosperity be yours; go and behold him stationed in the Nandana grove.
Here the illustrious and blessed Suparṇa shines forth;
it is the Blessed One, the creator of the worlds, appearing here in the form of a boar."
He appears like the fire of cosmic destruction as he lifts up the surface of the earth;
upon his chest, the Śrīvatsa mark shines forth clearly.
Behold, all you gods, this being who is free from all affliction.
Lomaśa said:
Then, having seen the Great-souled One, and having heard [his words] and taken leave of him, the immortals departed.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Placing the Grandfather at their head, the gods departed as they had come.
But having heard that story, O Janamejaya, all the Pāṇḍavas,
following the path directed by Lomaśa, proceeded with great joy.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Those heroes, possessing great prowess, were equipped with bows, quivers, and arrows; they had fastened their leather arm-guards and finger-protectors, and were armed with swords.
Having taken leave of the best of the twice-born, those foremost of all archers,
O King, set out for Gandhamādana accompanied by the princess of Pañcāla;
they traversed lakes, rivers, mountains, and forests.
And on the mountain peak, they saw trees with dense shade and regions where flowers and fruits were ever-present, frequented by hosts of divine sages;
there the heroes, subsisting on roots and fruits, established their inner self within the Self.
They traversed regions of diverse forms and rugged difficulties,
beholding many various species of wild animals, as well as places frequented by ṛṣis, siddhas, and gods, and beloved by gandharvas and apsarases.
Those high-souled ones entered the mountain frequented by kinnaras. As the heroes were entering Mount Gandhamādana,
O lord of the people, a fierce wind and a great rain appeared.
Then a great cloud of dust arose, thick with leaves,
and shrouded the earth, the atmosphere, and the heavens in darkness.
When the sky was covered by the dust, nothing at all could be discerned.
And they were unable to speak to one another,
nor could they see each other, their vision obscured by the darkness,
O Bhārata, as they were being dragged along by the wind filled with stone dust.
A great sound arose from the trees broken by the wind as they fell violently to the ground, and from other plants growing upon the earth;
one wondered, "Is the sky falling? Is the earth being rent asunder? Are the mountains crumbling?"
Thus they all thought, deluded by the wind;
searching with their hands for the trees, anthills, and uneven ground immediately ahead, they hid themselves in fear of the wind.
Then the mighty Bhīmasena, raising his bow and taking Kṛṣṇā with him, stood together, taking refuge beneath a tree. And Dharmarāja and Dhaumya hid themselves in the great forest.
Taking the *agnihotra* fires with them, Sahadeva remained on the mountain; Nakula, the other brahmins, and the great ascetic Lomaśa,
having taken refuge among the trees, hid themselves here and there in fear.
When the wind had subsided and that dust was settling,
a rain of large droplets quickly descended;
there was a loud *caṭacaṭā* sound, as if thunderbolts were being hurled.

Then those lightnings, with flickering luster, moved across the clouds; thereafter, showers accompanied by stones fell incessantly there, driven by a swift wind and enveloping everything on all sides.
Then, O lord of the people, the waters flowing toward the ocean appeared turbid and frothy on all sides as they were being scattered; carrying abundant water, they were covered with rafts of foam.
Making a great noise, they rushed about, uprooting the trees;
when that rain had ceased and the wind had subsided,
the waters receded into the lowlands and the sun appeared.
They all departed slowly and then gathered together again, O Bhārata;
those heroes set out once more for Mount Gandhamādana.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, as soon as the high-souled Pāṇḍavas had set out,
Draupadī sat down, for she was unaccustomed to traveling on foot;
she was exhausted, overwhelmed by grief, and afflicted by that wind and rain.
Due to her extreme delicacy, the illustrious Pāñcālī fainted;
falling into a swoon, that dark-eyed woman clung with both her rounded and shapely arms to her thighs.
Grasping her thighs, which were together and resembled the trunks of elephants,
she suddenly fell to the ground, trembling like a plantain tree.
As that woman of beautiful hips fell, she clung to him like a clinging creeper.
The heroic Nakula, having rushed forward, seized her.
Nakula said:
"O King, this dark-eyed maiden is the daughter of the king of the Pañcālas."
Exhausted, she has fallen upon the ground; look upon her, O Bhārata!
Unworthy of such suffering, this woman of gentle gait has encountered supreme misery. O Great King, comfort her, for she is emaciated by fatigue.
Vaiśampāyana said:
But at his words, the king, deeply overcome with grief,
as did Bhīma and Sahadeva, suddenly rushed forward.
Beholding her, pale-faced and emaciated, the righteous son of Kuntī took her onto his lap and, overcome with grief, lamented:
"How is it that she, who is accustomed to well-spread beds in secure dwellings..."
The woman of excellent complexion, who deserves only happiness, lies fallen upon the ground;
how is it that her delicate feet and her face, which has the luster of a lotus,
have now turned dark for my sake— she who is worthy of the finest things?
"What is this that has been done by me, a fool driven by the desire for gambling,
having taken Kṛṣṇā to roam in the forest teeming with herds of wild beasts?
Will the princess of Pañcāla find happiness upon obtaining the Pāṇḍavas as her husbands?"
Thus, though she was given away by her father, King Drupada, this large-eyed woman has failed to obtain all that; emaciated indeed by toil and grief,
she lies fallen upon the ground through the deeds of my own sin.
While Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, was thus lamenting,
all the best of the twice-born, headed by Dhaumya, arrived there;
they comforted him and honored him with blessings.
They recited mantras that destroy demons and performed the prescribed rites;
while the supreme ṛṣis were chanting the mantras for the sake of pacification,
the Pāṇḍavas repeatedly touched him with their cool hands.
And as she was being fanned by a cool breeze mixed with water,
the princess of Pañcāla, having found comfort, gradually regained her senses.
Then, taking hold of the distressed Kṛṣṇā, he placed her upon a bed of deerskins.
Then, once she had regained consciousness, they caused the ascetic woman to rest;
the twins gently massaged her feet, which had red soles and auspicious marks, with their hands that were covered in calluses.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, comforted her and,
that best of the Kurus, spoke these words to Bhīmasena:
"O Bhīma, there are many mountains that are rugged and difficult to traverse due to the snow."
"O mighty-armed one, how indeed will Kṛṣṇā move about among them?
Bhīmasena said:
"O King, [you must protect] yourself, the princess, and the twins, those bulls among men."
"I myself shall lead you, O Indra among kings; do not set your mind on despair.
Or else, O sinless one, this bird born of me, Ghaṭotkaca, who is equal to my own strength, shall carry us all at your command."
Having heard these words of Bhīmasena, Dharmarāja, honoring Bhīma and being well-pleased, spoke thus: "So be it.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Permitted by the King of Dharma, he called to mind his Rākṣasa son; and the righteous Ghaṭotkaca, as soon as he was remembered by his father,
then stood before him with joined palms after having saluted the Pāṇḍavas.
The mighty-armed one, whose prowess is truth, was greeted by those brahmins and spoke to Bhīmasena, his father:
"I have been remembered by you; desiring to serve, I have come quickly."
"Command me, O mighty-armed one; I shall do everything without a doubt.
Having heard that, Bhīmasena embraced the Rākṣasa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhīma, let this bull among Rākṣasas— knowing the Dharma, powerful,
heroic, devoted, and like a son born from your own breast— immediately take his mother;
for by your strength, O Bhīma of most terrifying prowess, I am [protected]."
"Unharmed, together with the princess of Pañcāla, I shall go to Gandhamādana.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having understood his brother's words, Bhīmasena [spoke to] Ghaṭotkaca.
That tiger among men commanded his son, the crusher of enemies:
"O son of Hiḍimbā, your mother Aparājitā is exhausted;
you, my dear, are capable of going anywhere at will and are strong—carry her, O bird."
"Place it upon your shoulder— blessings be upon you— and travel through the air amidst us at a low altitude, so that you do not cause her pain.
Ghaṭotkaca said:
"The King of Dharma, Dhaumya, the princess, and likewise the twins—
even I alone am sufficient to carry you, how much more so today when I have companions!
There are also hundreds of other heroic birds capable of changing their forms at will."
"O sinless one, they will all speak together with the Brahmins;
I shall proceed very slowly, carrying the daughter of Drupada.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, that hero Ghaṭotkaca, positioned in the midst of the Pāṇḍavas, carried Kṛṣṇā; and the other Pāṇḍavas as well were carried by others.
Lomaśa, of incomparable splendor, traveled along the path of the Siddhas.
By his own natural splendor, like a second sun,
those Rākṣasas of terrible prowess took all those Brāhmaṇas and departed at the command of the Lord of Rākṣasas.
Thus beholding those most delightful forests and groves, they proceeded toward the vast Badarī; meanwhile,
those heroes were pursued by those exceedingly powerful Rākṣasas of swift movement.
Being carried along, they traveled swiftly over a great distance as if it were short;
they beheld lands teeming with hosts of Mlecchas and abounding in various mines of jewels, as well as the foothills of mountains covered with diverse minerals.
They were frequented on all sides by *kiṃpuruṣas* and *gandharvas*,
crowded with hosts of *vidyādharas*, joined by monkeys and *kiṃnaras*,
as well as by *kiṃpuruṣas* and *gandharvas* everywhere.
They were surrounded by *sṛmara*s, *camara*s, monkeys, and *ruru* deer, as well as by boars, *gavaya*s,
and buffaloes; they were frequented by various other animals of pleasing appearance.
They were strewn with networks of rivers, filled with the warbling of various birds, frequented by many kinds of wild animals, graced by monkeys,
and likewise endowed with trees and intoxicated birds.
Having traversed many countries as well as the Northern Kurus,
they beheld Kailāsa, the best of mountains, filled with various wonders. In its vicinity, they saw the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
They beheld that Badarī tree, endowed with divine trees that always bore flowers and fruit; it had a rounded trunk, was enchanting to the mind,
possessed glossy and dense shade, and was endowed with supreme splendor.
It was endowed with glossy, dense, and soft leaves, beautiful,
with wide-spreading branches, extensive, and possessed of exceeding luster;
it was densely covered with divine, sweet, and abundant fruits.

It was a divine land, constantly frequented by hosts of great sages, flowing with streams of honey, always filled with various flocks of birds ever joyful with intoxication, and situated in a region free from gadflies and mosquitoes, abounding in roots, fruits, and water.
In a place covered with blue grass, frequented by gods and gandharvas,
on a level stretch of ground naturally formed and auspicious,
in a region where the touch was as soft as snow and free from thorns, she was born.

Having approached her together with those bulls among brahmins, all those high-souled ones then slowly descended from the shoulders of the Rākṣasa. Then they reached that holy hermitage inhabited by Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
O King, the Pāṇḍavas, together with the foremost of the twice-born, beheld that holy place,
which was free from darkness, untouched by the rays of the sun,
devoid of the afflictions of hunger, thirst, cold, and heat, and the destroyer of sorrow.

It was crowded with throngs of great seers and endowed with Brahmanic splendor; it was difficult to enter, O Great King, for men excluded from dharma. It was divine, honored with offerings and oblations, well-swept, and anointed.
It was resplendent on all sides with offerings of celestial flowers,
filled with spacious fire-sanctuaries and auspicious sacrificial ladles and vessels,
and adorned with large water-jars and kneading troughs.
It was a refuge for all beings, resounded with the chanting of the Vedas, divine, worthy of being sought for shelter, and a destroyer of fatigue;
it was endowed with splendor, indescribable, and adorned by the conduct of the gods.

[He saw] great seers who subsisted on fruits and roots, self-controlled, clothed in bark and black antelope skins, equal to the sun and fire, whose souls were purified by austerity, intent on liberation, and who were ascetics with their senses restrained.

Accompanied by his brothers, the wise Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, who was self-restrained and pure, approached those sages of great splendor— highly fortunate exponents of the Veda who had become one with Brahman.
Endowed with divine knowledge, all those great seers, having seen that Yudhiṣṭhira had arrived, approached him with great joy; they,
who were intensely devoted to the study of the Vedas, offered him their blessings.
Delighted, those [sages], who were like fire, offered him hospitality according to the prescribed rites,
providing pure water, flowers, roots, and fruits. Then, he accepted with affection that hospitality presented by the great seers.
Then, having received it with self-restraint, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,
together with Kṛṣṇā, was delighted by that holy place which resembled the abode of Śakra, possessed a divine fragrance, was enchanting, and was like heaven itself.
O sinless one, Acyuta entered that place endowed with splendor together with his brothers and with brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
there, that righteous-souled one beheld the shrine worshipped by gods and celestial rishis.
Beholding that abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, graced by the Bhāgīrathī, those Pāṇḍavas, tigers among men, took their delight there;
it was a divine place where honey-dripping fruits grew and which was frequented by hosts of great seers.
Having approached it, those high-souled ones dwelt there together with the brahmins;
filled with joy, those great-souled ones then took delight there,
gazing upon Mount Maināka, which was filled with various flocks of birds.
Having reached Hiraṇyaśikhara and that auspicious Bindusaras,
as well as the Bhāgīrathī with its excellent bathing-places, whose waters are cool, pure,
and auspicious; and having reached that holy river of the gods, the vast and sacred Badarī.
Beholding that place, which was strewn with gems and coral, adorned with trees,
covered with celestial flowers, and increasing the joy of the mind,
the high-souled Pāṇḍavas sported there.
In that region frequented by celestial rishis, which was extremely difficult to access,
the sons of Kuntī, established in supreme purity, then offered libations to the gods and the rishis with the holy waters of the Bhāgīrathī.

There, those heroes, bulls among men, who possessed the splendor of the immortals, dwelt together with the brahmins, repeatedly offering libations to the gods and the ancestors. Beholding the playful sports of Kṛṣṇā there, they remained.
There, those tigers among men, the Pāṇḍavas, took delight in various [pleasures].
Vaiśampāyana said:
There, those tigers among men remained established in the highest purity.
The heroes dwelt there for six nights, desiring to see Dhanañjaya; and the Pāṇḍavas remained sporting and enjoying themselves in that delightful,
excellent forest, which was pleasing to all beings.
It was adorned on all sides by trees beautiful with blossoming flowers and bent down by the weight of their fruit; they were crowded with flocks of male cuckoos, possessing dense,
glossy leaves, and were delightful with their cool shade.
Beholding various lakes with clear waters,
shining everywhere with lotuses and water-lilies,
the Pāṇḍavas took delight there at those beautiful sights.
A wind, fragrant with merit and pleasant to the touch, blew there,
gladdening all the Pāṇḍavas, along with Kṛṣṇā and the foremost of the twice-born. Then, by chance, a wind blew from the northeast.
A divine lotus with a thousand petals, radiant as the sun, was carried along;
the princess of Pañcāla beheld that pure water-born flower, beautiful and of celestial fragrance, which had been brought by the wind and fallen upon the ground.
Having reached that unsurpassed *saugandhika* lotus, which was both beautiful and fragrant,
she was exceedingly joyful, O King, and then spoke to Bhīmasena:
"Behold, Bhīma, this divine, most radiant, and unsurpassed flower."
"O scorcher of enemies, this [grove] of mine, endowed with fragrance and beauty, is a delight to my mind;
yet I shall give it to Dharmarāja.
O bull among men, having taken many other flowers—"
"O Pārtha, if I am dear to you, bring back these many things for my sake to the Kāmyaka hermitage once more;
I wish to take them back to that hermitage in Kāmyaka."
Having spoken thus to Bhīmasena, the blameless Pāñcālī then took those various flowers and went toward Dharmarāja;
for that bull among men had already discerned the queen’s intention.
Desiring to please his beloved, Bhīma of terrible prowess,
facing the very wind from which that flower had come,
went quickly, wishing to seize other flowers as well.
Grasping a bow with a golden back and arrows resembling venomous serpents,
all living beings beheld him, the wielder of the great arrow and bow, like an enraged king of beasts or an elephant in rut.
Neither exhaustion, nor dejection, nor fear,
nor agitation ever overcame Pārtha, the son of Mātariśvan,
as he relied upon the strength of his own arms in pursuit of Draupadī’s welfare.
Free from fear and delusion, the powerful one rushed toward the mountain;
that destroyer of enemies roamed that auspicious peak, frequented by kinnaras, which was covered with trees, creepers, and shrubs, and possessed surfaces of dark-blue stone.
Variegated with minerals, trees, beasts, and birds of diverse colors,
and filled with every kind of ornament, it was like an uplifted arm of the earth;
[he dwelt] upon the ridges of Mount Gandhamādana, which are delightful in all seasons.
With his eyes fixed upon her intention, reflecting it within his heart,
he of immeasurable prowess went forth, with his ears, mind, and sight bound by the songs of the male cuckoos and the humming of the bees.
Inhaling the intense fragrance arising from the flowers of all seasons, the one of great majesty was unrestrained like a rutting elephant in the forest,
while being fanned by the most meritorious scent of various blossoms.
His fatigue dispelled by his father, his hair standing on end with joy,
he was cooled by the breeze from Mount Gandhamādana, which was as refreshing as his father’s touch;
it was a place frequented by hosts of yakṣas, gandharvas, gods, and brahmin-sages.
Then the subduer of enemies stirred it up for the sake of flowers;
it appeared as if smeared with fingers by means of the unevenly cut sections—
pure divisions of minerals consisting of gold, antimony, and silver.
It seemed to dance along with its companion-like clouds clinging to its sides; it was covered as if by pearl necklaces by the waters falling from its cascades;
it possessed delightful river-bowers, waterfalls, and interior caves.
With peacocks dancing to the sound of the anklets of apsarases,
its rocky surfaces were rubbed by the tips of the tusks of the elephants of the quarters;
it appeared as if its garments had slipped away due to the waters flowing from its rivers, which could not be agitated.
He was gazed upon with curiosity by deer who remained calm, holding mouthfuls of young grass, staying nearby, and ignorant of fear;
and he repeatedly shook the networks of creepers with the force of his thighs.
Playing along the way, the illustrious son of Kuntī, the son of Vāyu, proceeded;
the handsome-eyed youth, tall as a golden palm tree and possessing the powerful build of a lion, was intent on fulfilling the beloved one’s desire.
He has the stride of an elephant in rut, the speed of an elephant in rut,
the copper-hued eyes of an elephant in rut, and he is the restrainer of elephants in rut. [He is gazed upon] by those seated at his side, who turn their heads and display various gestures.
He was gazed upon by invisible female yakṣas and gandharvas;
in the marketplace of the maidens of yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and nāgas,
the Pāṇḍava seemed as if he were selling a new incarnation of beauty.
He wandered upon the delightful ridges of Mount Gandhamādana,
recollecting the many various sufferings inflicted by Duryodhana,
and being intent on doing what was pleasing to Draupadī while she dwelt in the forest.

He thought: "Now that Arjuna has gone to heaven and I have returned, how indeed will the noble Yudhiṣṭhira act regarding the flowers? Surely that best of men, out of affection and because of his lack of trust in the forest,"
"Yudhiṣṭhira will not release Nakula and Sahadeva.
Thinking, "How indeed might the acquisition of the flowers be accomplished quickly?",
that tiger among men set forth with great speed, like the king of birds.
Making the earth tremble with his feet like a thunderclap during the change of seasons,
terrifying the herds of elephants, and crushing the packs of lions and tigers, the mighty Vṛkodara rushed forward with the speed of the wind.
Uprooting great trees and striking them down with his chest, the powerful son of Pāṇḍu dragged away creepers and vines with force,
like an elephant seeking to climb higher and higher toward the mountain peak.
Roaring most violently like a rain-cloud accompanied by lightning,
the immensely powerful Bhīmasena let out a tremendous cry.
O Lord, by that terrible sound and the twang of his bow, [the world was filled].
The cave-dwellers abandoned their caves, the tigers hid themselves, and the den-dwelling beasts sought refuge; terrified, herds of deer fled in every direction.
The bears let go of the trees, and the monkeys abandoned their mountain retreats.
Great lions yawned and buffaloes glared about; terrified by this, the elephants, surrounded by their females,
abandoned that forest and went to another great forest.
Herds of wild boars and forest-dwelling buffaloes,
as well as packs of tigers and jackals, roared together with the gayals;
so too did the rathāṅgas, dātyūhas, swans, kāraṇḍavas, and plavas.
The parrots, male cuckoos, and cranes fled in all directions, deprived of their senses;
likewise, other proud elephants and mighty buffaloes did the same.
Then the long-armed one beheld [them] upon the ridges of Mount Gandhamādana.
The immensely powerful one approached with speed that most beautiful grove of plantains, extending for many yojanas,
intending to agitate it like a rutting great elephant breaking various trees.
Uprooting plantain trunks as tall as many palm trees,
Bhīma, the best among the strong, swiftly hurled them in every direction;
there, the powerful Pāṇḍava created a great heap of trees.
Possessing great majesty, he crushed them like a proud lion;
then many and mighty creatures fled,
including herds of ruru deer and elephants, as well as buffalo and those dwelling in the water.
Then, casting them aside, the mighty and illustrious son of Pāṇḍu quickly entered the forest, filling the quarters with his roar;
and the Pāṇḍava blew his resonant conch shell with all his strength.
Enraged lions and tigers rushed toward Bhīmasena,
their minds bewildered by fear, discharging excrement and urine;
with gaping mouths, they were most fierce and let out exceedingly terrifying roars.

Then the son of Vāyu, Bhīma, relying on the strength of his own arms, out of anger struck elephant with elephant; the powerful Pāṇḍava, the subduer of foes, overpowered lion with lion and slew others with blows of his palms.
Being struck down by Bhīma, all those lions, tigers,
and hyenas fled in terror and discharged excrement and urine;
then the mighty one, having cast them aside, quickly entered.
The illustrious son of Pāṇḍu filled the quarters with his sound as he entered the forest;
by that fierce noise and by the roar of Bhīmasena,
all the beasts and birds dwelling within the depths of the woods were struck with terror.
Suddenly hearing that sound uttered by the beasts and birds,
thousands of water-birds with wings wet from the water flew up together.
Beholding those flocks of aquatic birds, the bull of the Bharatas—
Following after them, he beheld a vast and beautiful lake, which,
being fanned by clusters of golden plantain trees swaying gently in the breeze, seemed as if it were being cooled without being disturbed, with those trees spreading along its shores.
Then, having quickly descended into that lake abounding with lotuses and water-lilies,
the exceedingly powerful one, like a wild great elephant, sported with great strength;
after sporting there for a long time, he of immeasurable splendor emerged.
Agitating the waters like a fierce elephant in rut,
the son of Pāṇḍu then plunged with speed into that forest filled with many trees and blew his resonant conch shell with all his might.
And the powerful Bhīma, making the quarters resound, slapped his arms;
by the sound of that conch, by the roar of Bhīmasena,
and by the fierce sound of his arms, the caves of the mountain seemed to cry out.
Then, having heard the sound of the conch and the repeated roaring,
and having heard the sound of trees being shattered upon the mountain,
Rāma’s beloved friend, who was stationed on the side of Mount Gandhamādana, [spoke].
Then that monkey named Hanumān lashed his tail;
as he repeatedly and effortlessly shook it,
the ten directions seemed to resound with the noise of that tail.
Then the earth and the mountains seemed to tremble at that loud sound of the slapping,
which was like the crash of a thunderbolt;
hearing it, the lions sleeping in the mountain caves let out a great roar.
O Bhārata, even the elephants, terrified by the fear of the lion’s roar,
let out a great cry that filled the mountain;
then, hearing that sound, the bull among monkeys who had been sleeping awoke.
The great-bodied monkey named Hanumān yawned;
having recognized his brother Bhīmasena, the monkey Hanumān then blocked the path leading to heaven for the sake of Bhīma.
Thinking, "Let him not indeed go by this path," he sat down on the narrow track adorned with groves of plantain trees,
effectively blocking that road for the sake of protecting his brother Bhīma.
Thinking, "The son of Pāṇḍu will receive either a curse or an insult," the monkey remained thus within the middle of the plantain grove;
staying in the midst of the plantain grove, he then fell under the power of sleep.
By that great sound, the Great Monkey was awakened;
yawning widely like the towering banner of Śakra,
he lashed his tail with a roar equal to Indra’s thunderbolt.
At the roar of his tail, that mountain emitted it from the mouths of its caves on all sides, like a cow releasing a belch while bellowing;
and from the sound of the lashing of his tail, that great mountain shook.
With its peak whirling, it shattered on all sides;
then, with the roar of its tail drowning out the sound of the rutting elephant,
it roamed across the variegated mountain ridges.
Upon hearing that roar, which sounded like the thundering of a great cloud, the elephants trumpeted, the lions roared, and the beasts and birds were struck with terror.
Hearing it, Bhīmasena’s hair stood on end in thrill.
Seeking the source of that sound, he wandered through the grove of plantain trees;
then, in the midst of the plantain grove, upon a broad slab of rock,
the mighty-armed one beheld the lord of the monkeys standing there.
Difficult to behold like a mass of lightning, tawny like a mass of lightning,
resembling a mass of lightning, and as flickering as a mass of lightning; with his thick,
short neck resting upon his crossed arms.

Because his body was composed primarily of the aggregates (*skandha*), his waist and hips were slender; and he was resplendent with a tail that rose upward like a banner, its tip slightly curved, covered in long,
bristling hair.
With red lips, a copper-colored tongue and mouth, and red ears, his eyebrows were quivering;
his fangs were bared, shining with white, sharp tips,
like the radiant moon with its rounded edges.
Adorned with white splendors issuing from within its mouth,
it resembled a heap of *aśoka* flowers mixed with a profusion of filaments;
standing in the midst of golden plantain trees, it possessed great radiance.
Blazing with his own form like a radiant fire,
gazing fearlessly with honey-tawny eyes,
that best of monkeys was a hero of immense body and great strength.
Seeing him standing there like the Himalayas, blocking the path to heaven,
the mighty-armed Bhima of terrible prowess approached him with speed, being alone in that great forest.
Bhīma, possessed of terrible strength, having entered that grove of plantain trees,
saw a monkey sleeping on a narrow path;
he then let out a lion’s roar to awaken the ape.
At that sound, the beasts and birds of Bhīma were terrified;
but Hanumān, the great being, slightly opening his eyes,
then looked on with a disdainful glance through his honey-tawny eyes.
Then the glorious monkey, the son of the Wind, addressing the high-spirited son of Kuntī who was standing nearby with a smile, said to that man:
"For what reason have I, who was sleeping soundly, been awakened by you while suffering from pain?"
"Surely compassion must be shown toward all beings by one who possesses knowledge;
we, having taken refuge in the animal realm, do not know the Dharma.
It is humans, endowed with intelligence, who show compassion toward living creatures."
"How can wise men such as you engage in cruel deeds that defile the body, speech, and mind, and destroy righteousness? You do not understand dharma; you have not attended upon the elders."
"Because of your small-mindedness, you are exterminating the wild deer;
tell me, who are you, or for what purpose have you come to this forest,
which is devoid of human beings as well as men?"
"O bull among men, tell me where you must go today;
beyond this point, this mountain is impassable and extremely difficult to climb. O hero, there is no way here except by the path of the Siddhas."
"This is the path to the world of the gods, forever inaccessible to mortals. Out of compassion and friendship, O mighty one, I restrain you;
beyond this point, it is not possible for you to go. Rest, O Lord."
"Welcome in every way here today, O bull among men!
Eat these roots and fruits that are like nectar, and then return, if you will accept my words."
"Do not meet your death in vain.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard these words of that wise lord of monkeys, [he replied].
Then the heroic Bhīmasena, the crusher of enemies, spoke:
"Who are you, and for what reason have you assumed the form of a monkey?
A Kṣatriya, the social order immediately following the Brāhmaṇas, questions you."
The Kaurava of the Lunar dynasty, borne in the womb of Kuntī,
was the son of Pāṇḍu known as Bhīmasena, the son of Vāyu.
Having received those words of Bhīmasena with a smile, he—
Hanumān, the son of Vāyu, addressed the son of Vāyu:
"I am a monkey; I will not grant you passage as you desire. Go back, turn away, lest you meet with destruction."
Bhīma said:
"Whether it be slaughter or something else, I shall not question you, O monkey. Stand up and give me the way; do not meet with destruction."
Hanumān said:
"I have no strength to rise up, for I am afflicted by disease.
If you must certainly go, then proceed by leaping over me."
Bhīma said:
"The Supreme Self is devoid of qualities; it remains pervading your body.
I do not disregard or transgress that which is to be known through wisdom."
"If I could not find that creator of beings through the sacred scriptures,
I would leap over you and this mountain, just as Hanumān leaped across the ocean.
Hanumān said:
"Who is this named Hanūmān by whom the ocean was leaped over?
I ask you, O best of the Kurus; let it be told, if it can be done.
Bhīma said:
My brother, praised for his virtues and endowed with intelligence, courage, and strength,
is renowned throughout the Rāmāyaṇa as a heroic bull among monkeys;
it was by him that [the bridge] extending a hundred yojanas was built for the sake of Rāma’s wife.
The ocean was crossed in a single stride by that lord of monkeys;
he is my brother of great heroism, and I am his equal in splendor. In strength, prowess, and battle, I am capable of subduing you.
"I have arrived at this place for some particular reason. Arise! Give me way, or else witness my prowess today;
I shall send you to the abode of Yama for failing to obey my command."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having recognized that he was intoxicated by his own strength and arrogant because of the prowess of his arms,
Hanumān laughed at him in his heart and spoke these words.
"Be gracious; I have no power to rise up due to my old age, O sinless one.
Out of compassion for me, please move aside this tail and depart.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When Hanumān had spoken thus,

the formidable Bhīma, proud of the strength of his own arms, thought in his mind that [the enemy] was deficient in heroism and prowess; and seizing him by the tail with speed, he [prepared to drag him away], though he was lacking in heroism and prowess.
"Today, right here, I shall lead this monkey to the very presence of the Ender (Antaka).
Thus addressed, the powerful Bhīma of terrible prowess then seized him with his left hand, smiling with contempt.
And Bhīma was unable to shake the tail of the great monkey;
he raised it up again with both arms, as high as the bow of Indra,
yet even though he possessed great strength, Bhīma could not lift it with his two arms.

With his eyebrows raised, his eyes rolling, and his face knit with a frown, Bhīma’s limbs became covered in sweat; yet, despite his efforts, he was unable to lift it. Though the glorious one exerted himself, he remained shaken by the weight of the tail.
Standing at the side of the monkey, Bhīma remained with his face cast down in shame.
Then the son of Kuntī, having prostrated himself with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words:
"Be gracious, O tiger among monkeys; may my ill-spoken words be forgiven."

Whether you are a Siddha, a god, a Gandharva, or a Guhyaka, please tell me truthfully when asked: who are you that have assumed the form of a monkey? O mighty-armed one, if it is not a secret, and if it is something I may hear, [please speak].
"O sinless one, I question you as a disciple; I have come to you for refuge.
Hanumān said:
"O subduer of enemies, since you have such curiosity to know me..."
Listen to all of that in its entirety, O joy of the Pāṇḍavas. I was born in the womb of Kesarin by Vāyu, the life-breath of the world; O lotus-eyed one, I am the monkey named Hanumān.
O crusher of enemies, all the leaders of the monkey troops approached those two kings of all the monkeys— Sugrīva, the son of the Sun, and Vālin, the son of Śakra—
who were possessed of great heroism.
Between Sugrīva and that high-souled brother [Vālin], there was a friendship like that between the wind and fire;
in prowess, there was no one equal to those two.
Having been humiliated by his brother for a certain reason,
Sugrīva lived for a long time on Mount Ṛśyamūka together with me.
Then there was the heroic son of Daśaratha, the mighty one named Rāma.

Viṣṇu, having assumed a human form, wandered upon this earth. Seeking to please his father, that best of archers, accompanied by his wife and younger brother and bearing his bow, took refuge in the Daṇḍaka forest.
His wife was carried off by force from Janasthāna by Rāvaṇa,
the powerful lord of the rākṣasas, that evil-minded one,
who had assumed the form of a deer variegated with gold and jewels.
Having deceived the highly intelligent Rāghava by means of a deer-form,
that Rāghava— his wife having been carried off— searched for his consort together with his brother,
and on a mountain peak he beheld Sugrīva, the bull among monkeys.
Through him, a friendship arose with that high-souled Rāghava.
Having slain Vālin, he established Sugrīva in the kingdom. He dispatched the monkeys to search for Sītā.
He dispatched monkeys by the hundreds and thousands. Then,
O bull among men, together with those tens of millions of monkeys, I set out toward the direction in which we had previously departed.
"O mighty-armed one, while searching for Sītā,
news concerning Sītā was obtained there;
it was related by Saṃpāti that she was in the abode of Rāvaṇa."

Then, O son of Pāṇḍu, for the sake of accomplishing the task of Rāma of unwearied deeds, I learned of the news from the vulture Saṃpāti and suddenly leapt across the ocean, which was a hundred yojanas wide.
Having crossed the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, by my own prowess,
I beheld Sītā, the daughter of King Janaka, who resembles a daughter of the gods;
and that goddess was seen by me in the residence of Rāvaṇa.
Having met with that goddess Vaidehī, the beloved of Rāghava,
and having completely burnt Laṅkā along with its palaces, walls, and gate-towers,
I returned once more, making my name known there indeed.
Having quickly understood my words, the lotus-eyed Rāma,
having constructed a bridge over the great ocean— a feat never before accomplished by others—
crossed the vast sea surrounded by tens of millions of monkeys.
Then, having slain all those rākṣasas in battle, the heroic Rāma killed that host of rākṣasas— Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the world cry out—
and having slain the lord of the night-stalkers along with his brothers, sons, and kinsmen.
Having consecrated Vibhīṣaṇa as the righteous, devoted, and affectionate lord of the Rākṣasas in the kingdom of Laṅkā— one who is kind to those who follow him—
his wife was recovered, like the lost Vedic revelation brought back once more.
Accompanied by that same virtuous wife, the highly illustrious Rāma, the joy of the Raghus and lord of his enemies, departed from there with great haste and dwelt thereafter in his own city,
Ayodhyā.
Then, once Rāma had departed, I, a hero, made this request;
I, that very person, entreated the lotus-eyed Rāma for a boon, O hero, slayer of enemies:
"O hero, as long as the story of Rāma shall exist in the worlds..."
"I shall live for that long," he said, "and let it be so. O subduer of enemies, O Bhīma, by the grace of Sītā, divine enjoyments appear here before me at all times, exactly as I desire.
For ten thousand years and ten hundred years, Rāma exercised sovereignty; thereafter, he departed for the third heaven.
Therefore, O sinless one, the Apsarases and Gandharvas are always present here, my dear.
Singing of that hero’s deeds, they delight me. Moreover, O joy of the Kurus, this path is inaccessible to mortals;
therefore, I have blocked this path of yours, which is frequented by the gods.
"O Bhārata, may no yakṣa or even a rākṣasa assail or curse you as you travel by this path;
for this is the divine path of the gods, and humans do not go there."
"For the very purpose for which you have come, that lake is indeed right nearby.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed, the mighty-armed and powerful Bhīmasena—
Then, having prostrated with joy and a delighted mind, he spoke in gentle words to Hanumān, the lord of monkeys, his brother:
"There is no one more blessed than I, since I have beheld my noble elder."

"Your favor toward me is very great, and I am satisfied by the sight of you. However, O noble one, I desire that you do for me today this kindness which you performed back then while leaping across the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters."
"O Hero, I wish to behold that peerless form;
thus shall I be satisfied and I shall have faith in your words.
Thus addressed, the radiant Hari smiled and spoke.
That form cannot be seen by you, nor by anyone else;
for at that time, another temporal state prevails, which does not exist now.
Therefore, O best of men, it is difficult for me to show my form today.
The time in the Kṛta Yuga was one thing, another in the Tretā, and yet another in the Dvāpara;
this present time is one of destruction, and today that former nature of mine no longer exists.
The earth, rivers, trees, mountains, Siddhas, gods, and great ṛṣis—[all have changed].
They conform to time according to the conditions in each age;
O bull among men, as time after time arrives for human beings,
their strength, stature, and power indeed decline and arise again.
"Therefore, enough of your seeing that form, O scion of the Kuru lineage!
I shall conform to the age, for time is indeed difficult to overcome.
Bhīma said:
"Tell me the enumeration of the ages (yugas), as well as the conduct in each age;
[tell me] the states of dharma, desire, and wealth, as well as stature, valor, existence, and non-existence.
Hanumān said:

"O dear one, that age is called Kṛta, wherein the eternal Dharma exists. In that supreme age, everything is already accomplished and nothing remains to be done. Therein, virtues do not decline, nor do living beings perish."

Then, by the power of time, that age known as Kṛtayuga attained its characteristic qualities. O dear one, in the Kṛtayuga there were no gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, or Pannagas, nor was there buying or selling.

In that age, there were no Sāman, Yajus, or Ṛk verses, nor was there any ritual action performed by humans; rather, dharma consisted solely of renunciation, directed toward the fruit of meditative contemplation.
During that conjunction of the ages, there were neither diseases nor the decay of the senses.
There was no malice, nor weeping, nor pride, nor slander;
there was no conflict, whence could there be lethargy? There was no hatred, nor any transformation of mind; there was no fear, no distress, no envy, and no selfishness.
Then there was the supreme Brahman, the ultimate goal of yogins,
the Self of all beings, the white Nārāyaṇa;
and there were Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, each possessing their characteristic marks.

In the Kṛta Yuga, the subjects were devoted to their own respective duties; they shared the same stage of life, the same conduct, the same knowledge, and equal strength. For at that time, the social orders (varṇas), performing identical duties, attained their religious merits.
United by a single Veda, with identical ritual procedures and mantras,

they followed distinct duties while remaining devoted to the single Dharma of the one Veda; through their actions conjoined with the four stages of life and performed in accordance with the proper time.

Through union with the fruit of desirelessness, they attain the supreme goal. This dharma, characterized by the performance of action, is joined with self-discipline; in the Kṛta age, it was eternal for the four castes and possessed four quarters.
This is called the Kṛta Yuga, which is devoid of the three qualities (guṇas). Now learn from me about the Tretā as well, in which the sacrificial session (sattra) proceeds.
Dharma decreases by one quarter, and Acyuta turns red.
Men were devoted to truth and dedicated to the performance of ritual duties;
consequently, sacrifices proceeded, as did various religious rites and activities.
In the Tretā age, intentions were directed toward spiritual states, resulting in the fruits of ritual actions and gifts.

In the Tretā Yuga, people were devoted to austerity and charity; established in their own duties and performing sacred rites, they did not indeed deviate from dharma. In the Dvāpara Yuga as well, dharma proceeds diminished by two parts.
Viṣṇu indeed attains the state of being drunk, and the Veda itself becomes fourfold;
thereafter, others are knowers of the four Vedas, and likewise others are knowers of three Vedas, knowers of two Vedas, knowers of one Veda, and others are even devoid of the Ṛgveda.
Thus, as the scriptures have become divided, ritual action is practiced in many ways; and when people engage in austerity and charity, they become characterized by passion (rājasī).
Furthermore, due to the lack of knowledge regarding the single Veda, those Vedas were made manifold.
Due to the decline of truth in this world, some remained established in truth;
however, for those falling away from truth, many diseases arose,
as well as desires and calamities brought about by the gods at that time.
Afflicted by these, men perform intense austerities;
others, desiring sensual pleasures or heaven, perform sacrifices.
Thus, having reached the Dvāpara age, living beings decline through unrighteousness.

O son of Kuntī, in the Kali Yuga, Dharma stands upon only one foot. Having reached this age of darkness, Keśava becomes dark-hued; likewise, Vedic conduct, religious duties, and sacrificial rites fall into decline.
Calamities, diseases, lassitude, the defects such as anger and the like,
as well as secondary afflictions, mental anxieties, and physical ailments prevail;
and as the ages revolve, dharma turns away once again.
But when the Dharma turns away, the world likewise turns away;
when the world has perished, the states that cause the world to proceed go to their destruction. The dharmas brought about by the end of the age transform the objects of aspiration.

This is what is called the Kali Yuga, which will soon commence; however, those who are long-lived continue to follow the patterns of the preceding ages. And as for your curiosity regarding my knowledge, O subduer of enemies—
What purpose can there be for a wise man in things that are useless?
All this that you asked me has been explained to you. O mighty-armed one, may you attain well-being; you may now depart.
Bhīma said:
"Without seeing your former form, I will not depart by any means;
if I am worthy of your favor, show yourself to me in your own true nature."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been thus addressed by Bhīma, the monkey smiled and revealed that form which he had assumed for the crossing of the ocean.
Desiring to do what was pleasing to his brother, he indeed assumed a truly magnificent form—
that very same appearance he had previously possessed when crossing the ocean.
Thereupon, his body increased exceedingly in both length and breadth.
Shrouding that grove of plantain trees with his immeasurable radiance,
that monkey, having reached the height of the mountain,
stood there with his massive body uplifted like a second mountain.
With copper-colored eyes, sharp fangs, and brows knitted over his gaze,
the monkey stood brandishing his long tail, pervading all directions.
Beholding that immense form of his brother, the joy of the Kurus—
Then Bhīma was struck with wonder and rejoiced again and again. Seeing him— who was like the sun in brilliance, like a mountain of gold,
and like the sky ablaze— Bhīma closed his eyes.
And Hanumān, as if smiling, addressed Bhīmasena:
"O sinless one, you are capable of seeing only this much of my form here;
I can increase even further than this, as much as I desire in my mind."
His form increases exceedingly in power against his enemies; seeing that wondrous, most formidable body of Hanumān, which resembled the Vindhya and Mandara mountains,
the son of the Wind was struck with amazement.
Then Bhīma, his hair standing on end with joy, replied with palms joined in reverence to Hanumān, who stood before him with an undaunted spirit:
"O Lord, the immense proportions of this body of yours have been seen."
"O you of great prowess, withdraw yourself by your own self;
for I am unable to behold you, who are like the risen sun,
immeasurable and unassailable as Mount Maināka."
O hero, a very great wonder has indeed arisen in my mind today,
that while you were standing by his side, Rāma himself went against Rāvaṇa.
You alone were capable of conquering that Laṅkā, along with its warriors and its vehicles.
Relying on the strength of your own arms, you are capable of destroying him by your power;
for there is nothing that cannot be attained by you, O son of the Wind-god. Rāvaṇa, together with his hosts, is no match for you alone in battle.
Thus addressed by Bhīma, Hanumān, the bull among monkeys,
then replied with words in a voice that was both affectionate and deep:
"O mighty-armed descendant of Bharata, it is exactly as you say."
"O Bhīmasena, that lowest of Rākṣasas was no match for me; however,
had I slain him— the thorn in the side of the worlds— Rāghava’s fame would have perished, and therefore I overlooked it."

Having slain the lord of the rākṣasas along with his host, that hero brought Sītā back to his own city and established his fame throughout the world. Therefore, O one of vast wisdom, go forth, devoted to the pleasure and welfare of your brother.
"Protected by Vāyu, you shall travel a path that is secure and free from harm. O best of the Kurus, this is the way to the Saugandhika forest;
there you will behold the garden of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), guarded by Yakṣas and Rākṣasas."
"You must not gather these flowers yourself by force;
for the deities are especially to be honored by a man,
O bull of the Bharatas, through offerings, oblations, prostrations, and mantras."
"O Bhārata, the deities indeed grant their favor through devotion.
My son, do not act rashly; uphold your own duty. Abiding in your own duty, understand and learn the supreme dharma."
For indeed, without knowing the Dharma and without serving the elders,
the Dharma cannot be truly understood even by those equal to Bṛhaspati;
wherein unrighteousness is called righteousness, and righteousness is designated as unrighteousness.
It must be understood through its distinctions, for therein the unintelligent are deluded:
Dharma arises from right conduct; from Dharma the Vedas have emerged;
from the Vedas sacrifices are produced; and by sacrifices the gods are established.
The deities are sustained by sacrifices prescribed in the rules of Vedic conduct, and human beings are sustained by the principles of statecraft taught by Bṛhaspati and Uśanas; [furthermore,
they are sustained] by trade, mining, commerce, agriculture, and the rearing of livestock.
Everything is sustained by livelihood through these duties performed by the twice-born.
For those who understand, the threefold knowledge consists of the triple Veda, livelihood, and the science of government;
by these, when properly applied, the course of the world is maintained.

If that performance of dharma did not exist on earth— apart from the dharma of the three Vedas and also apart from the science of government (daṇḍanīti)— this world would become lawless; for if these subjects do not abide by the dharma of their livelihoods (vārtā), they will perish.
For when these three duties are properly performed, offspring indeed flourish.
Dharma is the nectar of the twice-born, and it is one and common to all castes.
Sacrifice, study, and giving—these three are recorded as being common to all.
For Brāhmaṇas, both officiating at sacrifices and teaching, as well as the acceptance of gifts, are prescribed;
for Kṣatriyas, protection is indeed their duty, and for Vaiśyas, the duty is cultivation and supporting others. Service to the twice-born is said to be the duty of Śūdras.
Those who dwell with their preceptors are likewise deprived of the duties of begging for alms, fire-sacrifices, and vows;
O son of Kuntī, your duty here is the protection of righteousness. Therefore, being humble and with senses restrained, take up your own dharma.

Having consulted with elders who are virtuous, wise, and endowed with sacred learning, he who remains steadfast governs by means of punishment; yet one addicted to vice is overcome. When a king proceeds correctly through the proper application of restraint and favor, [the kingdom prospers].

Then the boundaries of the world become well-established. Therefore, in one's own territory, in difficult terrain, and regarding the forces of both enemies and allies, one must constantly ascertain through spies their position, growth, and decline.

For kings, there are four means: wise counsel, valor, restraint and favor, and skill in accomplishing their tasks; [these are achieved] through conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, punishment, and indifference.
Tasks to be accomplished should be carried out through both concise and detailed application.
O bull of the Bharatas, all policies are rooted in counsel, as are spies;
success comes through well-deliberated policies, so one should deliberate with those who are experts in such matters.

One should not discuss secrets with a woman, a fool, a greedy person, a child, or one who is frivolous, nor with those who exhibit signs of insanity; for all their faults are committed by them, and enmity is firmly established therein.
He should deliberate with the learned and have tasks executed by those who are capable; he should employ affectionate men for the application of policy and avoid fools in all matters.
He should employ righteous men in religious duties and wise men in matters of statecraft.

One should employ eunuchs among women and the cruel in cruel tasks. One must discern the intelligence of one's own people and of others regarding what ought and ought not to be done, as well as the relative strength and weakness of one's enemies in their undertakings.
With discernment, he should provide support for those who have entered the right path,
and he should also carry out restraint against the ill-behaved and those who transgress the bounds of propriety.
When the king proceeds correctly in both restraint and support, [the world prospers].
Then the boundaries of the world become well-established.
This terrible and difficult-to-follow duty has been ordained for you, O Pārtha:
[win over] friends with conciliation, a Brāhmaṇa with gifts, and artificial [allies] with [other means].
One should subdue enemies through division and accomplish the welfare of subjects through the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Abiding in discipline, protect them according to the distribution of their respective duties,
just as Brahmins go to heaven by means of austerity, dharma, self-control, and sacrifice.
Through the duties of giving and hospitality, Vaiśyas indeed attain a happy state;
through service to the twice-born, Śūdras obtain the highest goal. Likewise, the Kṣatriya goes to heaven by means of restraint and protection on earth.
For those who have properly administered punishment, being free from desire and hatred,
ungreedy, and devoid of anger, go to the same world as the virtuous.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, contracting that vast body which had been enlarged at will,
the monkey again embraced Bhimasena with both arms.
O descendant of Bharata, as Bhima was thus quickly embraced by his brother, [he felt great joy].
His fatigue vanished, and everything became auspicious; Atibala thought, "In strength, there is no one equal to me anywhere.
Then Hari spoke again, his eyes filled with tears:
Addressing Bhīma with affection, his voice faltering with tears, he said:
"Go, O hero, to your own dwelling; I am to be remembered in the course of your conversations.
But for the sake of accomplishing our task quickly, go now, O son of Pāṇḍu."
"O hero of immeasurable prowess, O best of the Kurus, you must remember me in your conversations; though I am here, let it not be disclosed to anyone by you,
O mighty one, that I have been sent from the abode of the Giver of Wealth."
"May the celestial and Gandharva women come here at this time and place;
my eyes have also been made fruitful, for I have been reminded of Rāghava—
Viṣṇu himself, named Rāma, the delighter of the hearts of the world."
O Bhīma, having gone with you to touch that human body— which is the sun to the lotus-face of Sītā and the sun to the darkness of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa—
let this sight of us, O hero, son of Kuntī, not be in vain for you.
"O Bhārata, honoring our brotherhood, choose a boon.
If it is that I must go to the city named after the elephant and slay the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, however base they may be, then I shall do so."
O Bhārata, tell me how you intend to slay the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
for either that city must be crushed by me with a mountain crag,
or Duryodhana himself shall be bound and brought before you this very day.
"O one of great strength, I shall fulfill this desire of yours today.
Having heard those words of that high-souled one, Bhīmasena,
with a joyful heart, replied to Hanumān.
"O bull among monkeys, you have already accomplished everything for me.
May it be well with you, O mighty-armed one; I beg your forgiveness, be gracious to me.
With you as our protector, O heroic one, all the Pāṇḍavas are truly well-provided for."
"By your very splendor alone, we shall conquer all our enemies.
Thus addressed, Hanumān spoke to Bhīmasena:
"Out of brotherhood and out of friendship as well, I shall do what is pleasing to you."
O hero of great strength, when you have plunged into the army of the enemies, which is crowded with arrows and spears, and let out a lion’s roar,
then I shall augment your cry with my own voice.
"Upon merely hearing this, those enemies will become despondent in battle;
and standing upon Vijaya’s banner, I shall release terrible roars that will take the lives of your foes. Having said this, he vanished.
"By this [path], you shall slay him with ease. Having thus addressed the joy of the Pāṇḍavas, Hanumān then pointed out the way to Bhīma.
Let there be no fever of pride in your mind;
for I have placed my very life-force within my tail,
which is a fit weapon for taking the lives of enemies.
When that best of monkeys had departed, Bhīma, the foremost among the strong,
traveled through the vast Gandhamādana mountain by that same path,
recollecting his form and his peerless splendor upon the earth.
Remembering the majesty and power of the son of Daśaratha,
he then traversed those delightful forests and groves,
agitating them in his desire for the *saugandhika* lotuses.
Forests variegated with full-blown lotuses and in bloom,
as well as lakes and rivers likewise adorned with various flowers.
O Bhārata, he beheld on all sides lakes and rivers variegated with full-blown lotuses, frequented by various birds,
and herds of intoxicated elephants mired in mud.
Then, masses of clouds seemed to be raining as he beheld them;
and on the path, the glorious one, seeing deer with trembling glances accompanied by their mates in the forest, eating mouthfuls of young grass, quickly passed by.
Bhīmasena, free from fear, boldly plunged into the mountain frequented by buffaloes, boars, and tigers;
[he entered it] with trees whose branches were bent down by flowers and tender with copper-colored new shoots.

Passing along the road, he bypassed lotus-pools whose banks were pleasant with groves and which were frequented by intoxicated bees; they seemed like women in the forest making gestures of salutation with their hands folded like lotuses, as they were shaken by the wind.

With his mind and gaze lingering upon the flowering mountain ridges, Bhīma proceeded even more swiftly, carrying the words of Draupadī as his provisions for the journey. Then, as the day drew to a close, the forest was filled with roaming deer.
He beheld the vast river with its pure golden lotuses,
filled with intoxicated *kāraṇḍava* ducks and adorned by *cakravāka* birds;
it appeared like a garland of stainless lotuses fashioned for that mountain.
In that river, the Great Being beheld a vast Saugandhika forest,
which produced great joy and possessed a radiance like that of the rising sun. Upon seeing it, that son of Pāṇḍu felt his heart's desire was fulfilled.
With his mind, he went to his beloved, who was distressed by her dwelling in the forest.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having gone to that beautiful lotus-lake guarded by Rākṣasas, he...
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, in a beautiful forest,
he saw [the hermitage] situated near Kubera’s abode by a mountain torrent, bordered by dark-green meadows and surrounded by variegated trees.
Exceedingly delightful, with vast shade, covered by various trees and creepers,
strewn with green lotuses, divine, and possessing golden lotuses;
it was crowded with flocks of various birds, possessed excellent landing-stairs, and was free from mud.
Extremely delightful, with excellent waters, born upon mountain ridges,
a source of purity for the world, auspicious, and wonderful to behold—
there, the son of Kuntī [drank] that cool, light, and auspicious water of nectar-like flavor.
The Pāṇḍava beheld that pure, auspicious, and abundant water. He saw that delightful lotus pond, filled with fragrant lotuses and covered with golden blossoms of supreme scent.
With excellent stalks of vaidūrya, variegated and captivating,
stirred by *haṃsa* and *kāraṇḍava* birds and scattering pure pollen—
[there stood] the pleasure grove of the high-souled Kubera, king of the yakṣas.
It was highly honored by the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and gods;
it was frequented by divine sages, Yakṣas, and Kimpuruṣas;
and it was protected by Rākṣasas, Kiṃnaras, and Vaiśravaṇa himself.
And upon seeing that, the mighty Bhimasena, son of Kuntī,
became exceedingly joyful at the sight of that celestial lake.
And by the king’s command, the Rākṣasas named Krodhavaśas [were stationed there].

Hundreds of thousands [of beings], equipped with various weapons and accoutrements, were guarding [it]. But as soon as they saw the son of Kuntī— Bhīma, the hero of terrible prowess, clad in deerskins and wearing golden armlets— [they were struck with awe].
They cried out to one another as that tamer of foes approached, armed with weapons, girt with a sword, and free from fear, seeking Puṣkara:
"This tiger among men, equipped with arms and clad in a deerskin..."
"What you have come here desiring to do, that you ought to ask us here.
Then they all approached the mighty-armed Vṛkodara and asked him, who was endowed with splendor: "Who are you? You should tell us."
"You wear the garb of a sage and you appear clad in bark garments;
O one of great luster, tell me for what purpose you have arrived.
Bhīma said:
"O Rākṣasas, I am Bhīmasena, the Pāṇḍava who follows immediately after the son of Dharma. Having reached the vast Badarī together with my brothers, Pāñcālī saw there a peerless *saugandhika* lotus."
"Surely she has been carried away from here by the wind; she must surely desire many [other men].
O night-stalkers, know this: I am the one who stands devoted to the pleasure of that faultless-limbed lawful wife, having arrived here for a meal of flowers."
The Rākṣasas said:
"O bull among men, this is the beloved pleasure-garden of Kubera. It is not possible for a mortal man, subject to the laws of death, to sport here."
O Vṛkodara, here the celestial sages, yakṣas, and gods,
having addressed the foremost of yakṣas, drink and sport; and likewise,
O Pāṇḍava, the gandharvas and apsarases also sport here.
With the permission of the great-souled Kubera, the lord of the yakṣas,
any wicked person here who, out of disrespect for the Lord of Wealth,
should desire to sport [with his property] unjustly, will undoubtedly perish.
"Disregarding him, you wish to take these lotuses from here by force;
how then can you call yourself the brother of Dharmarāja?
Having heard those words of theirs, the Pāṇḍava, though being restrained, [proceeded].
"Having addressed the king of the Yakṣas, you may then drink and take [the lotus];
otherwise, you will not be able to look upon the Puṣkara at all.
Bhīma said:
"O Rākṣasa, I do not see that Lord of Wealth here nearby;
and even if I were to see the great king, I would not venture to beg him. For kings do not beg—this is the eternal law."
"And I do not wish to abandon the duty of a warrior in any way.
Yet this lovely lotus pond has sprung up from a mountain cascade;
it did not come into being upon reaching the palace of the high-souled Kubera."
"For this [wealth] is indeed common to all beings as well as to Vaiśravaṇa. Since things are thus shared, who ought to ask whom?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to all the *rākṣasas*, Bhīmasena plunged in;
the mighty-armed and immensely powerful one entered that lotus pond like an elephant in rut entering a lake.
The hero entered that lotus pool like a rutting elephant.
Then that powerful one was forbidden by the Rākṣasas with words from all sides—“Do not do this! Do not do this!”—as they angrily rebuked him;
yet, disregarding those Rākṣasas, he of terrible prowess [proceeded].
The one of great splendor plunged in, and they all tried to restrain him;
yet, while the rākṣasas looked on, he forcibly seized the lotuses. Those heroes could not endure his taking of those excellent lotuses.
Disregarding them all, the powerful Bhīmasena, established in his own manliness, suddenly seized the lotuses.
"Seize him! Bind him! Cut him down! [they cried].
"Let us cook and eat Bhīmasena!
shouting thus in their rage, they pursued him swiftly,
brandishing their weapons with eyes rolling in fury.
Then, seizing a heavy great mace bound with golden bands and resembling the staff of Yama, that swift warrior rushed toward them.
Then he cried out, "Stay! Stay!
whereupon they suddenly rushed at him, brandishing weapons such as *tomaras* and *paṭṭiśas*.
Desirous of killing him, those fierce and most terrible beings, subject to wrath,
surrounded Bhīma on all sides;
yet that powerful one was born of Kuntī by means of the Wind-god.
A hero, impetuous, and a slayer of his enemies,
he is always devoted to truth and righteousness;
in prowess, he is unassailable by his foes.
Having destroyed their various paths and the weapons of his enemies, that high-souled hero struck down the warriors according to their prowess.
More than a hundred [of them], having seen his heroism and strength near the lotus pond— namely,
the power of his knowledge as well as the strength of his arms— [were amazed].
Unable to withstand [him] from all sides, their foremost heroes having been slain, they suddenly retreated;
being torn asunder right there, they quickly [fled].
Taking to the sky with their senses bewildered,
those Krodhavaśas, tormented by Bhīma and utterly broken, fled toward the peaks of Mount Kailāsa.
Having displayed his prowess and conquered the hosts of enemies in battle— just as Śakra subdues the multitudes of Dānavas and Daityas—
that conqueror of foes plunged into that lotus pond.
Then, out of desire, he took the lotuses;
having drunk that water which was like nectar,
he once again became possessed of supreme vigor and splendor.
Then, having uprooted them, he took the *saugandhika* lotuses of supreme fragrance;
thereupon, those who were under the sway of anger gathered together.
Driven by Bhīma’s terrible strength,
they, being exceedingly dejected, reported to Dhaneśvara exactly what Bhīma’s prowess and power were like in battle.
Having heard those words of theirs, the god laughed and then spoke to the Rākṣasas:
"Let Bhīma take as many lotuses as he desires."
"This was known to me for the sake of Kṛṣṇā.
Then, having taken leave of the Lord of Wealth,
they went to the foremost of the Kurus, their anger subsided.
And they beheld Bhīma in that lotus pond,
sporting alone according to his pleasure.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, he took up those many precious, divine,
stainless garments of various forms;
meanwhile, O King, in the presence of Yudhiṣṭhira—
Then a great, swift wind arose from below, dragging along pebbles;
harsh to the touch, it manifested, inciting the battle.
