A massive meteor, blazing with great radiance, fell down accompanied by a thunderous crash.
The sun became lusterless, its rays obscured and shrouded in darkness;
a terrifying thunderous crash occurred as Bhīma exerted his prowess,
and the earth trembled while a rain of dust fell.
The quarters of the sky became blood-red, and beasts and birds uttered harsh cries;
everything was shrouded in darkness, and nothing could be discerned.
Furthermore, many other terrifying portents arose there.
Beholding that marvel, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma and best among speakers, said: "Prepare yourselves— may you be blessed, O Pāṇḍavas, who are fierce in battle— who is it that will overcome us?"
"From the forms I perceive, our prowess is close at hand.
Having spoken thus, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the Dharmarāja, then looked all around; not seeing Bhīma, he [continued his search].
There, the subduer of enemies, standing near Kṛṣṇā and the twins,
questioned his brother Bhīma, who performs terrible deeds in battle:
"O Pāñcālī, does Bhīma perhaps desire to perform some specific task?"
Or perhaps the hero, who is fond of daring deeds, has already committed some rash act;
for these portents, foreboding a great battle, have appeared on all sides, manifesting intense fear without cause.
To him who was speaking thus, the high-minded Kṛṣṇā replied,
the queen with the beautiful smile, desiring to do what was pleasing to her beloved.
"O King, as for that *saugandhika* flower which was brought by the wind— "
Out of affection for Bhīmasena, I have now brought this about;
furthermore, I told that hero: "If you see even many [of them], take all of them and return quickly."

"O King, that mighty-armed Pāṇḍava has surely gone from here toward the north-eastern direction to fetch those [gems] for my sake. Having been addressed thus by her, the king then spoke these words to the twins:
"Let us go together quickly to where Vṛkodara has gone.
O Rākṣasas, carry the Brahmins according to their exhaustion and their weakness.
And you too, O Ghaṭotkaca, who resemble an immortal, carry Kṛṣṇā."
"It is clear to my mind that the terrible one has entered far from here;
a long time has passed for him, and he is equal to the wind in speed. He is powerful and like the son of Vinatā in leaping across the earth."
"He may even leap into the sky or descend at his will;
O night-rangers, we shall track him down through your power before he commits an offense against the perfected ones who discourse on Brahman."
Having said, "So be it," all of them, headed by the son of Hiḍimbā and knowledgeable regarding the location of Kubera’s lotus pond, O bull of the Bharatas,
then took the Pāṇḍavas along with those numerous brāhmaṇas.
Accompanied by Lomaśa himself, they set forth with joyful hearts. Having traveled together, they all beheld in that forest a most enchanting lotus pond filled with blossoming lotuses.
And they saw that great-souled Bhīma stationed on its bank,
as well as the large-eyed Yakṣas who had been slain—
their bodies, eyes, arms, and thighs shattered, and their necks crushed to pieces.
And he beheld that formidable, high-souled one stationed on her bank,
filled with rage, with fixed eyes and bitten lips,
standing upon the riverbank having raised his mace with both arms.

At the time of the destruction of all creatures, seeing him like Death himself with staff in hand, Dharmarāja embraced him again and again and spoke in gentle words: "O son of Kuntī, what is this that has been done?"
"Alas, this was a rash act—may you be blessed—which is displeasing even to the gods.
You must never do such a thing again, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me.
Having thus instructed the son of Kuntī and having accepted the lotuses, [he departed].
In that very lotus pond, those who resembled immortals sported.
At that very time, however, the guards of that garden— possessing massive bodies and grasping rocks as weapons— appeared.
And those Rākṣasas of fearsome appearance cried out to one another;
wandering in the forest, they had all come to the lotus-lake of King Kubera with agitated minds and troubled inner selves.
They approached the high-souled Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma;
having seen the King of Dharma, as well as the celestial seer Lomaśa,
Nakula, Sahadeva, and other preeminent brahmins.
O Bhārata, all of them, bowing with humility, prostrated themselves;
and being consoled by the King of Dharma, those night-rangers became appeased.
Then those bulls among men were recognized as being known to Kubera.
The best of the Kurus dwelt there for no very long time, enjoying themselves.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While the righteous King Yudhiṣṭhira was thus residing there,
Accompanied by Kṛṣṇā and the twice-born, he spoke thus to his brothers:
"We have seen sacred and auspicious holy sites (tīrthas),
as well as various forests that bring delight to the mind."
These were formerly traversed by the gods and by high-souled sages;
they have been duly honored by the twice-born according to their specific order,
as well as the ancient conduct and the deeds performed by the seers.
In various auspicious hermitages, they listened to the life stories of royal sages and diverse, virtuous tales; there,
they especially performed ritual ablutions together with the twice-born brahmins.
The gods were constantly honored by you with flowers and water,
and the ancestors were also gratified with whatever roots and fruits were available,
upon all the delightful mountains and lakes.
And in the highly meritorious ocean, he was well-sprinkled by great-souled ones; likewise,
at various delightful sacred fords, he was well-sprinkled along with the twice-born, including the Ilā, Sarasvatī, Sindhu, Yamunā, and Narmadā.
Having passed beyond Gaṅgādvāra, there are many auspicious mountains;
the Himavat mountain itself, filled with various flocks of birds; the vast Badarī was seen, as well as the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.

O best of the twice-born, a divine lotus pond, worshipped by the Siddhas and celestial rishis, was seen; and all the sacred shrines were shown in their proper sequence and with their specific distinctions by the high-souled Lomaśa.
"How, O Bhīma, shall we go to this meritorious abode of Vaiśravaṇa, frequented by the Siddhas? May our path vanish!
While the lord of kings was speaking thus, an incorporeal voice spoke.

"O King, it is not possible to proceed further from this hermitage of Vaiśravaṇa along this difficult path; return by the same way you came to the place of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, which is renowned as Badarī."
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, you shall go to the delightful hermitage of Vṛṣaparvan, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas and abounding in flowers and fruits;
and having passed that, O Pārtha, you should dwell in the hermitage of Ārṣṭiṣeṇa.
Then, O son of Kuntī, you shall behold the abode of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada). In the meantime, a pure wind, carrying divine fragrances,
blew pleasantly and refreshingly, cool and raining down a shower of flowers.
Having heard that divine voice from the sky, all were struck with wonder—
especially the sages, the brahmins, and the kings.
Having heard that great marvel, the twice-born Dhaumya then spoke.
"O Bhārata, it is not possible to say anything further; let it be so.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira accepted those words.
Having returned once more to that hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, he remained there.
Surrounded by all his brothers, Bhīmasena and the others,
as well as the Pāñcālīs and the Brāhmaṇas, they then dwelt happily on the ridges of Mount Gandhamādana, awaiting Bībhatsu.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
while those Pāṇḍavas were living there on that king of mountains, full of confidence and together with the twice-born ones, they waited in expectation of the arrival of Pārtha.
When those Rākṣasas had departed and the son of Bhīmasena as well,
there arrived at that time a Rākṣasa known by the name Jaṭāsura,
who happened upon them by chance while they were separated from Bhīmasena.
The Rākṣasa carried off Dharmarāja, the twins, and Kṛṣṇā.
Janamejaya said:
"O Brahman, how did the Rākṣasa [carry off] Dharmarāja, the twins, and Kṛṣṇā?"
"Where has Bhīma gone, and where has that thorn of the Rākṣasas departed?
O foremost of Brahmins, O sinless one, you ought to tell me this account. [He was] a Brahmin skilled in mantras, the best among those who know all weapons."
"I am the disciple of Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, whose deeds are effortless," saying this,
he would constantly attend upon the sons of Pāṇḍu,
examining the quivers and the bows of the Pārthas.
Seeking an opportunity, he who was known by the name Jaṭāsura—
that evil-minded man of wicked intent— acted with regard to the abduction of Draupadī.

O Indra among kings, the joy of the Pāṇḍavas provided for his sustenance; yet that wicked man did not perceive him, like a fire covered by ashes. When Bhīmasena, the subduer of enemies, had departed for the sake of hunting, [the king remained there].
Seeing Ghaṭotkaca with his followers fleeing in all directions,
and seeing those great seers, headed by Lomaśa, who were composed in meditation, as well as the ascetics who had gone out to bathe and gather flowers;
Assuming another form— deformed, terrifying, and immense—
and seizing all his weapons, that evil-minded one set out, taking hold of Draupadī and the three Pāṇḍavas.
Then Sahadeva, the son of Pāṇḍu, having exerted himself to escape from there,
displayed his prowess, seized the enemy’s sword, and released his captor;
he then cried out to Bhīmasena, by whom that mighty warrior had been led away.
As he was being carried away, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, said to him:
"O fool, your dharma is perishing, yet you do not perceive it! Whatever others there may be among men, even those belonging to the animal realm—"

They observe the Dharma, and the Rākṣasas especially; for the Rākṣasas have the Dharma as their root, and they know the Dharma to be supreme. Having examined all this, you ought to abide by your agreement.
The gods, the seers, the perfected ones (siddhas), and the ancestors, as well as the rākṣasas,
gandharvas, yakṣas, and rakṣases; likewise birds and beasts, and even those born of animal wombs, down to the insects and ants.
Human beings depend on you for their livelihood, and therefore you depend on them;
for by the prosperity of this world, your own world prospers.
And when this world grieves, the deities grieve after it.
When they are honored according to the prescribed rites with offerings to the gods and ancestors, they flourish.
O Rākṣasa, we are the guardians and protectors of the kingdom;
if the kingdom is not protected, whence can there be prosperity, and whence can there be happiness?

"A king must never be disregarded by a *rākṣasa* when he is innocent; nor is there even the slightest transgression on our part, O eater of men. We offer to the deities and others according to our ability, subsisting only on the remains of sacrificial food."
One should always be intent on honoring teachers and Brahmins as authoritative;
one must never act with malice toward friends, nor ever toward those who trust one, nor toward those whose food one eats or in whose house one finds shelter.
O you of evil intellect, having been honored in our shelter, having dwelt there in comfort, and having eaten our food, how can you wish to abandon us?
Thus indeed is one whose conduct is in vain, whose growth is in vain, and whose intelligence is in vain.

You deserve a futile death; today you shall not meet with such a fate. But if you are of wicked mind and devoid of all righteousness, then give us back our weapons and take Draupadī by means of battle.
But if you perform this deed without understanding its consequences, O Rākṣasa,
you will obtain only unrighteousness and infamy in the world by touching this human woman today.
"Having stirred this poison together, you have swallowed it with a jar.
Thereupon, Yudhiṣṭhira became a burden to him;
his body overcome by that weight, he was no longer so swift of foot.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira said to Draupadī and Nakula:
"Do not fear the foolish Rākṣasa; I have taken away his power of movement. The mighty-armed son of the Wind-god will be here before long."
"When this very moment has arrived, the Rākṣasa shall no longer exist.
But Sahadeva, seeing that Rākṣasa of deluded mind,
O King, spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī.
"O King, what duty indeed is there for a Kṣatriya greater than this:
that he should either give up his life facing the enemy in battle or conquer his foes? O scorcher of enemies, he is fighting us, and we are fighting him."
"O mighty-armed one, let us achieve our purpose; for this, O King, is indeed the proper time and place.
O you of true prowess, the moment for the duty of a Kṣatriya has arrived. Whether victorious or being struck down, we shall attain a happy state."
"O Bhārata, if the sun were to set today while this Rākṣasa still lived, I would never again say, 'I am a Kṣatriya.
Ho there, Rākṣasa! Stay! I am Sahadeva, the son of Pāṇḍu!"
"Either kill me and take them away, or you shall sleep here today slain.
While he was speaking thus, the mighty-armed Bhīmasena appeared by chance, like Vāsava wielding the thunderbolt.
There he saw his two brothers and the illustrious Draupadī; and he saw Sahadeva standing on the ground, then striking down the Rākṣasa—
the deluded Rākṣasa whose mind was struck by Fate and who had strayed from the path.
Seeing his brothers being led away and Draupadī as well, while he himself was wandering here and there, thwarted by fate,
the mighty Bhīma summoned his wrath and spoke these words to the Rākṣasa:
"You were recognized by me previously while you were acting under the guise of examining weapons; however,
I had no desire to kill you then because you were disguised in the form of a Brahmin and did not speak anything unpleasant to us."
How could I kill you, who act only toward what is dear and never do anything unpleasant, a guest in the form of a Brahmin and innocent of any fault—
even if I were to consider you a Rākṣasa, he who would kill such a person would go to hell?
"Death by time does not come for you while you are still unripe;
surely you have now become ripe, since such a thought as this has been given to you by Time, the performer of wondrous deeds, regarding the abduction of Kṛṣṇā."

He too, having met his time, shall likewise not exist today; this hook has been swallowed by you, suspended on the line of Time. Like a fish with its mouth pierced in the water, how will you escape from me today?
"The region toward which you have set out is one your mind has already traveled to;
you shall not go there, for you shall instead tread the path of Baka and Hiḍimba.
Thus addressed by Bhīma, the Rākṣasa was impelled by Time.
Terrified, he abandoned them all and stood ready for battle;
with his lower lip quivering in rage, he spoke again to Bhīma:
"O fool, O wicked one, I am not lost in the directions; my delay was for your sake."
"I have heard of all those Rākṣasas who were slain by you in battle;
today, with your weapon, I shall perform their water-libation rites.
Having been addressed thus, Bhīma then licked the corners of his mouth.
As if smiling out of rage, resembling the Destroyer Kāla himself, he spoke the words "Stay! Stay! with eyes bloodshot with anger;
desiring a clash of arms, he rushed toward the Rākṣasa.
Then the Rākṣasa, repeatedly opening his jaws and licking the corners of his mouth, rushed furiously toward Bhīma who stood there seeking battle,
just as Bala once rushed toward the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Bhimasena also stood firm, having challenged him to a wrestling match;
and the Rakshasa, full of confidence, likewise desired a hand-to-hand combat.
As that most terrible wrestling match between the two was then proceeding,
Both sons of Mādrī, filled with rage, rushed forward together;
Vṛkodara, the son of Kuntī, checked them both while laughing and said, "I am capable of dealing with this Rākṣasa; behold me!"
"O King, I swear by myself, by my brothers, by my righteousness, by my good deeds,
and by my sacrifices— that I shall slay this Rākṣasa.
Having spoken thus, those two heroes challenged one another.
The two, the Rakshasa and Vrikodara, locked together with their arms;
there occurred a violent clash between the enraged Bhima and the Rakshasa in that battle,
like the encounter between a god and a Danava who would not yield to one another.
Repeatedly uprooting trees, those two of great strength struck one another, roaring like two clouds at the end of the summer heat;
the best among the strong shattered massive trees with their thighs.
Mutually enraged and each desiring victory over the other,
that battle with trees took place between the brothers Vālin and Sugrīva— those lions among monkeys— just as it had occurred long ago.
Brandishing trees again and again for a moment,
they both struck each other while roaring repeatedly.
When all the trees in that place had been felled, [the battle continued].
Heaped up by the hundreds with a desire to slay one another,
O Bhārata, those two of great strength then took up rocks and fought for a moment like two lords of mountains against massive clouds.
Fierce and of formidable appearance, those two impatient warriors struck one another with great force, as if with thunderbolts;
and having struck each other again, they remained proud of their strength.
Then, seizing each other with their arms, they dragged one another like two elephants;
with most terrible fists, they struck at one another,
and a loud crackling sound arose from those two great-souled warriors.
Then, clenching his fist like a five-headed serpent,
Bhīma struck the neck of the Rākṣasa with great force.
Thereupon, that Rākṣasa, struck by Bhīmasena’s arm, became exhausted.
Perceiving him to be utterly exhausted, Bhimasena approached;
then the mighty-armed one, who resembled an immortal, lifted him up by force with his two arms and crushed him against the surface of the earth.
Then, overcome with rage, the Pāṇḍava pressed him violently with both arms and crushed all his limbs; striking him with his elbow,
he severed his head from the body.
With its lips bitten and eyes rolled back,
Jaṭāsura’s head— smeared with blood and its lower lip gnawed— fell, severed by Bhīmasena’s strength like fruit falling from its stalk.
Having slain him, that great archer approached Yudhiṣṭhira,
just as the Lord [Śiva] approached the lord of the Dānavas;
that tiger among men, the Pāṇḍava, became as if filled with joy.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, Dhaumya, Kṛṣṇā,
and the twins likewise beheld the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena approaching;
and having gathered around Dhaumya and the Pāṇḍava Yudhiṣṭhira, they stood together.
The invincible Vṛkodara embraced the twins as well;
and seeing Jaṭāsura slain, Pāñcālī honored the steadfast Bhīma with joy, just as Śacī honors Purandara.
Honored by the virtuous and having saluted the Brahmins,
Bhīma, that bull among the Bharatas, became joyful, having conquered his enemies;
he was praised by those foremost of the twice-born, like Vāsava by the Maruts.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When that Rākṣasa had been slain, the lordly King Kaunteya returned once more to the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa and took up residence there.
Having gathered all those brothers together with Draupadī at that time, he spoke these words, remembering his brother Jaya:
"Four years have passed while we were wandering in the forest in safety."
Having been assigned his task, Bībhatsu reached the king of mountains, Śveta, the best of peaks, at the beginning of the fifth year—
a place adorned with groves of flowering trees and intoxicated cuckoos and bees.
It was perpetually adorned with festivals by peacocks and *cātaka* birds,
and frequented by tigers, boars, buffaloes, *gavaya* oxen, deer,
as well as predatory beasts of fierce form and *ruru* antelopes.
With blossoming thousand-petaled lotuses, as well as hundred-petaled ones and blue water-lilies,
and with fully bloomed lotuses and blue lotuses as well—
[a place] of great merit, pure, and frequented by gods and asuras.
And there too, he was announced by those desiring to meet him;
and an agreement was made by that Pārtha of immeasurable splendor:
"I shall dwell for five years as a seeker of knowledge," he said to me previously.
"There we shall see the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, the subduer of enemies, who has acquired celestial weapons, returned from the world of the gods to this world.
Having said this, the Pāṇḍava addressed all the Brahmins.

And he explained the very reason for that to those ascetics. Delighted with him of fierce austerities, those brahmins circumambulated Pārtha and expressed their approval with auspicious and favorable words.

"O bull among the Bharatas, O knower of dharma, having soon crossed over this affliction— which will result in happiness— by means of the duty of a Kshatriya, you shall protect the earth. Then the king accepted those words of the ascetics.
The scorcher of foes set out together with those brahmins and his brothers;
the illustrious one was accompanied by Draupadī as well as the son of Hiḍimbā and the others,
followed by the Rākṣasas and protected by Lomaśa.
Sometimes he traveled on foot, and sometimes he was carried by Rākṣasas;
here and there, that one of great splendor and firm vows remained with his brothers.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, reflecting upon his many sufferings, [proceeded].
He set out toward the northern direction, which was teeming with lions, tigers, and elephants,
gazing upon Mount Kailāsa and Mount Maināka,
as well as the foothills of Gandhamādana and the mountain-peak Meru.
On the seventeenth day, they reached the sacred plateau of the Himavat, passing many auspicious rivers high above the mountain;
O King, the Pāṇḍavas beheld Gandhamādana nearby.
On the sacred slopes of the Himalayas, abounding with various trees and creepers,
and covered by flowering trees growing near the whirlpools of the water,
stood the most holy hermitage of Vṛṣaparvan.
Approaching that righteous royal sage, the subduers of enemies,
the Pāṇḍavas, their fatigue dispelled, paid homage to Vṛṣaparvan.
That royal sage greeted those bulls of the Bharatas as if they were his own sons.
Honored there, those subduers of enemies dwelt for seven nights.
When the eighth day arrived, they took leave of that world-renowned ṛṣi Vṛṣaparvan and resolved to depart.
Having introduced those Brahmins one by one to Vṛṣaparvan as his own kinsmen, treated them with great honor, and entrusted them to him as a deposit at the appropriate time,
he then handed over the remainder of his personal belongings to that high-souled one.
Then those Pāṇḍavas deposited their excellent garments and beautiful ornaments in that hermitage of Vṛṣaparvan;
he was a knower of the past and the future, skillful, and conversant with all duties.

That knower of dharma instructed those bulls among the Bharatas like his own sons. Having received permission, those high-souled heroes set out for the northern direction together with Kṛṣṇā and great-souled brahmins.
As they were departing, the lord of the earth, Vṛṣaparvan, followed after them;
having then presented the Pāṇḍavas to the brahmins, that one of great splendor comforted the sons of Kuntī with blessings and saw them off.
Having pointed out the path, Vṛṣaparvan turned back;
then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī whose prowess is truth, set forth on foot with his brothers through that forest frequented by various herds of wild animals.
Dwelling on mountain ridges thick with various trees,
the Pāṇḍavas entered the white mountain on the fourth day—
a beautiful peak resembling a mass of great clouds, shrouded in mist.
And he saw the mountain, delightful with its jewels and gold, rising in various heights; the lovely plateau of the Himavat, abounding in caves and waterfalls,
filled with rocks, birds, and branches, and crowded with creepers and trees.
Having reached the path as described by Vṛṣaparvan,
they proceeded according to the directions, beholding various trees and extremely inaccessible caves high upon the mountain.
Those many [places] which were very difficult to traverse, they crossed with ease:
Dhaumya, Kṛṣṇā, the sons of Pṛthā, and the great seer Lomaśa;
they went there together, and no one was left behind.
Resounding with the cries of deer and birds, crowded with various species of birds, frequented by troops of monkeys, and exceedingly beautiful,
it was a holy great forest containing lotus ponds and marshes.
Those of great prowess approached the great mountain Mālyavat,
which is the dwelling place of herds of elephants and teems with packs of lions and tigers;
it is the abode of kinnaras and frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas.
With their hair standing on end from joy, they beheld Mount Gandhamādana,
frequented by Vidyādharas and likewise by Kinnarīs;
it was crowded with elephants and lions, and filled with powerful śarabhas.
Resounding with the roars of śarabhas and inhabited by various wild beasts,
it was then frequented by other animals of gentle cries;
that forest of Gandhamādana was like the Nandana grove.
Rejoicing, the heroic sons of Pāṇḍu, who gladden the mind and heart, entered in due order that forest of auspicious groves; the heroes,
accompanied by Draupadī and those high-souled brahmins.
They heard the beautiful, auspicious sounds uttered from the mouths of birds— sounds that were sweet, exceedingly melodious, pleasing to the ear, intoxicatingly soft, and capable of generating joy;
[they saw trees] rich with the weight of fruit in every season and radiant with flowers in every season.
They beheld trees bent down by the weight of their fruit—
mangoes, hog-plums, blossoming coconut palms,
and *tinduka* trees, as well as *ajāta*, *jīra*, pomegranates, and citron trees.
Panasa, likuca, mocā, kharjūra, āmravetasa,
pārāvata, and likewise kṣaudra and delightful nīpa trees;
as well as bilva, kapittha, jambu, kāśmarī, and badarī.
Plakṣas, udumbaras, vaṭas, and aśvatthas, as well as milky trees;
bhallātakas, āmalakas, harītakas, and bibhītakas; iṅgudas, karavīras, and tindukas with their large fruits.
On the ridges of Mount Gandhamādana, he saw these and various other trees laden with delicious fruits that were like nectar,
as well as campakas, aśokas, ketakas, and bakulas.
Puṃnāgas, saptaparṇas, karṇikāras along with ketakas, pāṭalas, lovely kuṭajas, as well as mandāras, indīvaras,
pārijātas, kovidāras, and likewise devadāru trees.
Śāla, tāla, and tamāla trees, as well as priyāla and bakula;
śālmali, kiṃśuka, aśoka, śiṃśapā, and tarala trees;
and [forests] with cakoras, śatapatras, bhṛṅgarājas, and parrots.
It was inhabited by cuckoos, sparrows, green pigeons, and pheasants,
as well as by priyavratas, cātakas, and various other birds,
all warbling most sweetly and pleasing to the ear.
And there were various lakes with clear waters,
completely covered on all sides by white water-lilies, lotuses, red lotuses, blue lotuses, kahlāra lilies, and kamala lilies.
It was filled on all sides with water-dwelling birds: kadamba ducks, ruddy geese, ospreys,
water-fowls, kāraṇḍava ducks, gallinules, swans, cranes, cormorants,
and others as well.

They beheld the lotus-pools resounding with the sweet songs of joyful bees, who were languid with intoxication from the nectar-liquor of the red lotuses and stained crimson by the pollen and filaments falling from the hearts of the blossoms.
Beholding those delightful sights upon the ridges of Mount Gandhamādana,
which were likewise adorned on all sides with clusters of lotuses,
they saw peacocks together with their mates within the bowers of creeping vines.
Having intensely agitated those [peacocks] with passion by the loud sound of the clouds like the music of trumpets,
and having made them sing a sweet melody of *kekā* cries,
they spread their variegated tails with playful grace, languid with intoxication.
They beheld variegated peacocks, the dancers of the forest, performing their dances;
they saw others sporting happily with their beloved mates,
stationed upon mountain ridges thick with climbing vines and creepers.
And they saw certain species of birds perched exultantly upon the branches,
their plumage spread out in grand display as if wearing variegated crowns,
and they beheld them rejoicing within the hollows of the trees.
Then he saw wild *sindhuvāra* flowers, like the lances of the God of Love,
scattered with golden blossoms upon the mountain peaks;
and he saw *karṇikāra* trees arranged like exquisite ear-ornaments.

Then they saw *kurabaka* trees in full bloom along the forest avenues— trees that, joined together with lovely creepers and clusters of flowers, bore the weight of the forest and possessed a splendor beyond the reach of ordinary burdens.

They beheld those shining tilaka trees, which, like clusters of Kāma’s arrows that stir longing for the power of desire, appeared as if they were noble arrangements fashioned by the very groves of forest trees themselves.
Likewise, he beheld delightful *sahakāra* trees, which resembled the arrows of the Bodiless One (Kāma), resplendent with clusters of blossoms and the humming of bees;
they were adorned with flowers resembling gold and, in other places, resembling forest fires.
With trees red as collyrium and others resembling lapis lazuli,
as well as *śāla*, *tamāla*, *pāṭalī*, and *bakula* trees,
they appeared like garlands draped across the peaks of the mountains.
Thus, in due order, those heroes looked all around at that place crowded with herds of elephants, filled with lions and tigers,
resounding with the roars of śarabhas, and echoing with various cries.
On the ridges of Mount Gandhamādana, the rows of forests became rich with fruits and flowers of every season; they turned yellow, possessing a radiant luster,
for there were none there that were thorny, nor any there that were without blossoms.
On the ridges of Mount Gandhamādana, the trees bear glossy leaves and fruits;
look at these lotus ponds, sweet with the humming of bees and filled with blooming lilies, being agitated by elephants together with their mates.
Behold this other lotus pond, garlanded with lotuses and water-lilies,
like another Śrī herself, embodied and wearing a wreath;
in this most excellent forest, these [trees] are rich with the fragrance of various flowers.
The forest ranges shine as they are sung to by bees;
they possess the luster of pure crystal and are frequented by white-winged birds,
royal swans, and the warbling of cranes.
Beholding lakes and rivers upon the mountain ridges,
the heroic sons of Pṛthā entered, in due order, that peerless and beautiful forest;
there Kṛṣṇā beheld various enchanting trees.
Then, standing nearby, he spoke with affection to Bhīmasena:
"There are lotuses and water-lilies of various kinds, waters pleasant to the touch,
fragrant garlands, and succulent fruits."
All the Pāṇḍavas, their eyes wide with wonder, entered delightful lakes and most enchanting trees,
[scented] by the fragrance of lotuses, water-lilies, kahlāras, and puṇḍarīkas.
Being served in that forest by a breeze of pleasant touch,
Yudhiṣṭhira then spoke these words of affection to Bhīma:
"O Bhīma, oh, how glorious is this forest of Gandhamādana!"
The flowering trees shine most brilliantly upon the mountain ridges;
these and many other forest-born trees are there, along with creepers of various forms, laden with clusters of leaves, flowers, and fruit.
These trees, with their blossoms in full bloom and filled with flocks of male cuckoos, are radiant.
As Yudhiṣṭhira gazed upon those trees on that best of mountains,
he spoke these sweet words to Bhīmasena.

"Behold, Bhīma, these beautiful regions, the pleasure-grounds of the gods, on every side. Having attained a superhuman state, O Vṛkodara, we have reached perfection. And here are the finest trees, covered with many flowering creepers."
O Pārtha, they look beautiful as they cling together upon the ridges of Gandhamādana;
O Bhīma, hear the roar of the peacocks as they move about together with their peahens, calling out on the mountain slopes.
Chakoras, woodpeckers, intoxicated cuckoos, and mainas—
these winged birds cling to these great trees in full bloom.
O Pārtha, the birds perched upon the tops of the trees are red, yellow, and crimson.
Many *jīvajīvaka* birds gaze at one another from all sides upon the green and reddish-brown meadows;
cranes, too, are seen among the mountain cascades.
The *bhṛṅgarāja*, *upacakra*, and *lohapṛṣṭha* birds utter sweet songs that are pleasing to the minds of all beings;
and there are elephants with four tusks, radiant as lotuses, accompanied by their female mates.
These [streams], as high as many palm trees, having fallen from mountain peaks and various springs, agitate this great lake which has the luster of lapis lazuli;
these torrents of water are falling down.
With a radiance like that of the sun, O Bhīma, resembling dense autumnal clouds,
various silver ores beautify the great mountain;
in some places they have the hue of collyrium, and in others they resemble gold.
In some places there were deposits of yellow orpiment and vermilion;
there were caves of realgar resembling masses of twilight clouds,
and in other places there were red chalk minerals with the luster of the blood of a hare.
Resembling white and black clouds, with a radiance like the rising sun,
these beings of great splendor and many forms beautify the mountain;
they are Gandharvas together with their beloveds, just as Vṛṣaparvan described.
O Pārtha, they are seen upon the mountain peaks together with the Kimpuruṣas; O Bhīma, the sound of songs, rhythmic clapping,
and chants is heard in many ways, enchanting to all beings.
Behold the great Gaṅgā, the holy and auspicious river of the gods, frequented by flocks of swans and served by sages and kinnaras; she is adorned with mineral ores, streams, kinnaras, deer,
and birds.

O Kaunteya, subduer of enemies, behold this king of mountains, which is frequented by Gandharvas and Apsarases, by delightful groves, and by beasts of prey of various forms with a hundred heads on every side.
Those heroes, their minds filled with joy, had attained the unsurpassed goal;
yet those subduers of enemies were not satiated by the sight of that lord of mountains.
Together with Draupadī, those heroes remained there along with those high-souled brahmins.

Then they beheld the hermitage of the royal seer Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, which was filled with flowering and fruit-bearing trees. Thereupon, they saw him, emaciated by intense asceticism and covered with a network of veins.
They approached Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, who had reached the further shore of all dharmas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Yudhiṣṭhira, having approached him whose sins were consumed by asceticism, [paid his respects].
Delighted, he greeted them by bowing his head while announcing their names.
Then Kṛṣṇā, Bhīma, and the two illustrious twins,
having touched the royal seer with their heads, stood surrounding him.
In the same way, Dhaumya, the priest of the Pāṇḍavas and knower of dharma,
approached that rishi of rigid vows according to the prescribed rule;
and that muni, the knower of dharma, recognized him by means of his divine vision.
He said, "Be seated," to the sons of Pāṇḍu, the best of the Kurus. Having honored the wise bull among the Kurus,
the one of great asceticism questioned him, who was seated with his brothers, concerning his well-being.
Do you not set your heart on falsehood, and do you abide in righteousness? O Pārtha, does your conduct toward your mother and father not falter?
Are all your elders, the aged, and the learned honored by you?

O Pārtha, I trust you do not set your heart upon sinful deeds? O best of the Kurus, I trust you know how to requite good deeds and how to punish evil deeds according to justice, and that you do not boast about it.
I hope that the virtuous rejoice, being honored by you as they deserve;
I hope that even while dwelling in the forests, you continue to follow the path of dharma;
and I hope, O Pārtha, that Dhaumya does not suffer on account of your conduct.

O Pārtha, do you follow the conduct of your father and grandfather through charity, righteousness, austerity, purity, uprightness, and forbearance? O Pāṇḍava, do you travel along the path trodden by the royal sages?
"When a son or a grandson is born into their respective families, the ancestors dwelling in the world of the fathers both grieve and rejoice. [They wonder:
'What evil deed of his will we ourselves have to suffer for?'"
And what auspicious merit must we obtain for his sake?
Father, mother, likewise fire, the preceptor, and the self as the fifth—
for him by whom these are honored, O Pārtha, both worlds are conquered.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, you have spoken this determination of dharma correctly and appropriately;
according to my ability and in accordance with what is right, I shall perform this rite."
Subsisting on water and subsisting on air, floating through the sky,
sages delight upon that best of mountains during the changes of the moon; there,
those full of desire, devoted to one another, enjoy themselves with their beloveds.
O King, many kimpuruṣas are seen standing upon mountain peaks,
wearing dustless garments made of silk and wool;
O Pārtha, many hosts of gandharvas and apsarases are also seen there.
The hosts of Vidyādharas, wearing garlands and of pleasing appearance,
as well as the hosts of Mahoragas, Suparṇas, Uragas, and others,
are heard [singing] upon this mountain during the junctions of the lunar phases.
O bulls of the Bharata lineage, the sound of kettledrums, small drums, conchs, and clay drums— all of that must be heard by you while remaining right here;
you must not, under any circumstances, set your minds on going there.

"O best of the Bharatas, it is not possible to go further than this; for this is the pleasure-ground of the gods, and that realm is inaccessible to mortals. O Bhārata, even a man whose actions are slightly fickle [cannot enter here]."
All beings hate them and Rākṣasas strike them down.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having ascended this peak of the mountain,
the path of the most perfected ones and the celestial sages becomes visible.

O Pārtha, slayer of enemies, beyond this point, the Rākṣasas strike with iron pikes and other weapons anyone who goes here out of restlessness. [There] Naravāhana is surrounded by Apsarases in great prosperity.
"O dear one, here indeed Vaiśravaṇa is seen at the junctions of the lunar phases upon the mountain peak;
all beings behold that lord of all *rakṣasas* seated there like the risen sun."

O best of the Bharatas, this is the mountain peak garden belonging to the gods, dānavas, and siddhas, as well as to Vaiśravaṇa; here Tumburu sits in attendance upon the Giver of Wealth during the junctions of the lunar phases.
"O dear one, the sound of songs and the chanting of the Sāmans is heard on Gandhamādana.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, such wonderful sights as these, my son,
all living beings behold here many times during the junctions of the lunar phases."

"O best of the Pāṇḍavas, dwell here enjoying all kinds of edibles and succulent fruits until you behold Arjuna. My son, once you have arrived here, you must by no means act restlessly in any way whatsoever."
A fickle man becomes hateful to all beings.
Having lived here according to your desire and having spent your time according to your faith,
O best of weapon-bearers, you shall thereafter protect the earth.
Janamejaya said:
"In that hermitage of Ārṣṭiṣeṇa were all my great-souled ancestors, the sons of Pāṇḍu, who possessed divine prowess."
For how long did they dwell on Mount Gandhamādana?
What did those heroes, all possessed of exceeding strength and prowess, do there?
And what were the foods consumed by those great-souled ones while they were there?
Tell me, O best of beings, what happened while those heroes of the world were dwelling there;
and describe to me in detail the prowess of Bhīmasena,
and whatever that mighty-armed one did on that Himalayan mountain.

O best of the twice-born, while he was dwelling constantly on that mountain inhabited by Dhanada, there was indeed no further battle with the yakṣas. Did he perhaps have meetings with Vaiśravaṇa as well?
"For it was there that the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) came, as Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa told you.
O one rich in asceticism, I wish to hear this in detail;
for I can never have enough of hearing about their deeds."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard this instruction for their own welfare from him of incomparable splendor,
those bulls of the Bharata race constantly acted accordingly.
They partook of the food fit for sages,
as well as succulent fruits and even the meat of deer slain by pure arrows—
all pure on the slopes of the Himalayas— and various kinds of honey.
Thus those Pāṇḍavas, the bulls of the Bharata lineage,
dwelt there. As they lived in that manner, listening to the various words spoken by Lomaśa, the fifth year arrived.
Having said, "I shall present myself at the time of action," Ghaṭotkaca,
O Lord, departed beforehand accompanied by all the Rākṣasas,
while those high-souled ones were dwelling in the hermitage of Ārṣṭiṣeṇa.
Many months passed as they beheld this great marvel;
and as the Pāṇḍavas took their pleasure and sported there,
the highly fortunate sages and Cāraṇas were filled with joy.
Those perfected souls of restrained vows came to see the Pāṇḍavas;
those best of the Bharatas engaged in various divine conversations with them.
Then, after a few days had passed, [they went] to the one dwelling in the great lake.
The Suparṇa suddenly carried off the powerful Great Naga;
the great mountain shook and the massive trees were crushed. All beings and the Pāṇḍavas beheld that marvel.
Then, from the summit of that best of mountains, the wind bore along all manner of fragrant and auspicious garlands. There,
together with his friends, the Pāṇḍavas [gathered] those divine flowers.
They beheld the five colors and the illustrious Draupadī.
Then, at that time, Kṛṣṇā spoke these words to Bhīmasena,
the mighty-armed one, as he sat comfortably in a secluded mountain region.
O bull of the Bharatas, by the mighty wind of the Suparṇas, blowing with the speed of the wind, flowers of five colors—
divine in hue, celestial, and carrying divine fragrances— are cast down.
O bull among the Bharatas, my mind seems to rejoice at their fragrance;
O scorcher of enemies, by the mere sight, touch, and scent of them, this mental anguish of mine vanishes as if it were never there.
"Having worshipped the deities with such divine, auspicious flowers that carry a celestial fragrance, I desire union with you.
But this especially auspicious lotus, O tiger among men— "
Endowed with fragrance and beauty, increasing my delight,
it was witnessed by all beings as I set out toward the river Aśvarathā,
accompanied by Vāsudeva and beloved by Vāsudeva.
O lord of men, at Khāṇḍava, by your brother who is true to his promise,
the Gandharvas, Uragas, Rākṣasas, and even Vāsava were held in check;
the fierce practitioners of illusion were slain, and the Gāṇḍīva bow was obtained.
Your splendor is also exceedingly great, and your great strength of arm is unbearable and unassailable, equal to the power of Indra himself;
by the force of the strength of your arms, all the rākṣasas have been terrified.
O Bhīmasena, let them abandon the mountain and flee in the ten directions;
then, free from fear and delusion, let your friends behold the auspicious summit of that best of mountains, adorned with variegated garlands.
O bull of the Bharatas, they should always provide food in that very manner.
O Bhima, my mind has been set upon this for a long time;
relying on the strength of your arms, I wish to see the mountain peak.
"O tiger among men, O best of the Bharatas, I desire to see such a flower brought before my very eyes by you quickly. Then that scorcher of foes felt himself as if cast down by Draupadī.

The mighty-armed Pāṇḍava— possessing the gait of a lion or a bull, glorious, noble, with a golden luster, high-minded, powerful, proud, honorable, and heroic— could not endure it, just as a fine bull cannot endure a blow.
Red-eyed, with broad shoulders and the gait of an elephant in rut,
possessing the fangs of a lion and massive shoulders, he rose up like a young *śāla* tree;
high-souled, with all limbs beautiful, a neck like a conch shell, and mighty arms.
He grasped his gold-backed bow, his sword, and his quivers;
like an exultant lion or a rutting elephant,
the powerful one, free from fear and delusion, rushed toward the mountain.
All living beings beheld him approaching like a lion or like an elephant in rut, bearing arrows, sword,
and bow; the Pāṇḍava, taking up his mace, increased the joy of Draupadī.
Free from fear and delusion, he ascended the king of mountains. Neither exhaustion, nor cowardice, nor dejection,
nor envy ever affected Pārtha, the son of Mātariśvan.
Having reached that single path, which was rugged and fearsome to behold,
the one of great strength ascended the peak that rose many palm trees high. There he [beheld] the Kinnaras, great serpents, sages, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas.
Gladdening the peak of the mountain, the one of great strength reached it;
there, O bull of the Bharatas, that best of the Bharatas beheld the abode of Vaiśravaṇa,
adorned with houses made of gold and crystal.
It was encircled on all sides by a golden wall,
possessing the luster of every kind of jewel, endowed with every type of garden,
rising high above the mountains, and adorned with watchtowers and battlements.
It was adorned with gates, arches, turrets, and the waving of banners, and decorated on all sides by graceful women dancing excessively,
as well as by flags fluttering in the wind.
Supporting himself on the tip of his bow with his arm bent,
he gazed with weariness toward the city of the Lord of Wealth;
born from Gandhamādana, he brought joy to all living beings.
There, a most pleasant breeze blew, carrying all kinds of fragrances;
there were inconceivable and various trees of supreme beauty, bearing wonderful clusters of blossoms in many diverse colors.
The bull of the Bharatas beheld the auspicious abode of the lord of the Rākṣasas, which was covered with a network of jewels and adorned with variegated garlands; there,
with mace, sword, and bow in hand, he stood ready, having utterly renounced his life.
The mighty-armed Bhīmasena stood firm like an immovable mountain;
then he blew his conch shell, which caused the hair of his enemies to stand on end,
and by making the sound of his bowstring and the slapping of his palms, he bewildered all living beings.
Then, with their hair standing on end,
the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and gandharvas rushed toward that sound in the presence of the Pāṇḍava,
bearing maces, iron clubs, swords, spears, tridents, and battle-axes.
Held aloft by the arms of the yakṣas and rākṣasas, they shone brilliantly.
Then, O Bhārata, a battle commenced between them and him,
a tumultuous roar like that of lions roaring in their fury.
Then Bhīma, with arrows of even more terrifying velocity, cut down the spears, tridents, and battle-axes hurled by those massive-bodied beings—
both those moving through the air and those standing upon the ground, as they roared.
The mighty one pierced the limbs of the Rākṣasas with arrows;
then, O Bhārata, blood fell from them like rain from thick clouds. That great shower of blood rained down upon the mighty warrior.
Streams [of blood] fell from the bodies of the *rākṣasas* on all sides—
streams produced from the bodies of those *rakṣasas* who held maces and iron clubs in their hands—
as they were released in many ways by the terrifying strength of the arms of the *yakṣas* and *rākṣasas*.
Severed bodies and heads were seen scattered about;
all living beings beheld the handsome Pāṇḍava being overwhelmed by the Rākṣasas, like the sun obscured by masses of clouds.
Like the sun with its rays, that mighty-armed, powerful hero of true prowess struck all his enemies with arrows capable of slaying foes;
they were being terrified by him and were uttering loud cries.
None of the rākṣasas could perceive any confusion in Bhīmasena.
With all their limbs mangled by his arrows and tormented by the fear of Bhīmasena,
they let out a terrible cry of distress, their great weapons scattered about.
Casting aside their maces, spears, swords, javelins,
and battle-axes, they fled toward the southern direction, terrified by the one of firm bow.
There stood the broad-chested and long-armed [hero], with spear and mace in hand.
There was a Rākṣasa named Maṇimān who was a friend of Vaiśravaṇa; that one of great strength displayed his authority and his prowess. Seeing them turned back, he spoke as if smiling:
"Many have been defeated in battle by a single man;
having reached the abode of Vaiśravaṇa, what will you say to the Lord of Wealth?
Having addressed them all thus, that Rākṣasa turned back.
With a spear, a trident, and a mace in his hands, he rushed toward the Pāṇḍava.
As he charged with speed like an elephant in rut,
Bhīmasena struck him in the side with three calf-toothed arrows.
Maṇimān also, filled with rage, seized a massive mace;
the one of great strength whirled it around and hurled that huge, most terrible mace, which resembled a flash of lightning, at Bhīmasena through the sky.
Bhimasena struck him with many arrows sharpened on stone;
yet all those arrows, upon encountering his mace, were shattered,
for they could not withstand the force of the mace's momentum.
Understanding the practice of mace-fighting,
that heroic one of terrible prowess frustrated his opponent’s blow.
Then [the other] hurled a most dreadful iron spear with a golden shaft.
In that very interval, the wise Rākṣasa then hurled it;
that most terrible weapon, blazing with fire and emitting a fearsome roar, pierced Bhīma’s right arm and suddenly fell to the earth.
Deeply pierced by that spear, the great archer of immeasurable prowess,
the Kuru prince skilled in mace-fighting, seized his mace—
bound with bands of gold and increasing the terror of his enemies.
Grasping that mace made entirely of refined iron and roaring loudly, Bhīma rushed with speed toward the mighty Maṇimān;
and Maṇimān, for his part, seized a blazing great spear.
Roaring with great force, he who was skilled in mace-fighting shattered the spear with the tip of his mace and rushed swiftly toward Bhīmasena,
like Garuḍa swooping down upon a serpent.
Leaping into the air and suddenly brandishing his mace,
the long-armed one roared at the head of the battle and hurled it.
Then Bhīma struck that night-stalker Maṇimant with the mace.

He suddenly struck him on the head; he fell down and died, like a thunderbolt released by Indra with the speed of the wind. Having slain the Rākṣasa and reached the earth, it fell like a magical incantation (*kṛtyā*).
All living beings beheld that Rākṣasa of terrible strength struck down by Bhīmasena, like a bull by a lion. Seeing him slain upon the ground, the remaining night-stalkers...
Making a terrifying sound of distress, they fled toward the eastern direction.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Hearing those various sounds, the caves of the mountain were being devoured.
Ajātaśatru the son of Kuntī, both sons of Mādrī,
Dhaumya, Kṛṣṇā, the brahmins, and all their friends likewise became despondent,
for they could not see Bhīmasena.
Having given Draupadī to Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, those great car-warriors,
the heroes, then ascended the mountain together, equipped with their weapons.
Then, having reached the mountain peak, the great car-warriors looked about.
Those great archers beheld Bhīmasena, the subduer of enemies,
as well as the massive-bodied Rākṣasas— once trembling and now lifeless—
who had been struck down by Bhīmasena despite their great strength and terrible ferocity.
That mighty-armed one, wielding his mace, sword, and bow, shone resplendent after slaying all the Dānavas in battle, like Maghavan himself. Then, having passed him by, they embraced Vṛkodara.

There the sons of Pṛthā sat down, having attained that unsurpassed state. With those four great archers, the mountain peak shone like heaven with the highly fortunate world-protectors, the best of gods.
Having seen the abode of Kubera and the Rākṣasas struck down,
the brother addressed his seated Pāṇḍava brother:
"O Bhīma, whether out of recklessness or delusion, this evil deed has been committed."
"O hero, this false speech is not worthy of you, like that of a sage. Those who know the Dharma understand that one must not do what is hated by the king;
O Bhīmasena, this act which you have committed is hateful to the gods."
O Pārtha, he who disregards both material gain and dharma and sets his mind upon evil will certainly reap the fruit of those sinful actions;
O Pārtha, among all deeds, one is not released from sin.
"Alas, this was a rash act—may you be blessed—which is displeasing even to the gods!
You must never do such a thing again, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me. Having spoken thus, that righteous brother addressed his steadfast brother.

Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, who possessed great splendor and was skilled in discerning the true nature of matters, ceased speaking and reflected upon that very purpose, regarding the mighty-armed Bhīmasena of invincible prowess.
Then those Rākṣasas who remained after being slain by Bhīmasena gathered together and set out toward the abode of Kubera;
with great speed and immense velocity, they reached the residence of Vaiśravaṇa.
Afflicted by the fear of Bhīmasena, they uttered a terrible cry of distress;
having laid down their weapons and arms, exhausted and with their equipment smeared with blood,
their hair disheveled, O King, they spoke to the lord of the Yakṣas.
O Lord of Wealth, all those Rākṣasas who were your vanguard— fighters with maces, iron clubs, swords, javelins, and spears— have been slain by that mortal who,
with sheer force, crushed the mountain.
Accompanied by him alone in battle, the hosts of the Krodhavaśas were slain—
those foremost among the lords of the Rākṣasas and the Yakṣas, O Lord of Wealth. Struck down, O God, they lie there lifeless, their vital breath departed.
"The mountain has been won, we have been released, but Maṇimān, your friend, has been slain by a human. A deed has been done; now ordain what must follow.
Hearing this, the lord of all the hosts of yakṣas became enraged.
With eyes bloodshot with anger, the Lord of Wealth, having heard that Bhīma had committed a second offense, became enraged and spoke these words:
"Let [the chariot] be yoked! he said to the lord of the Yakṣas.
Then they yoked to that supreme chariot, which resembled a dense mass of clouds and rose as high as a mountain peak, horses of the Gandharva breed;
those excellent steeds were endowed with every quality and possessed clear, bright eyes.
Endowed with splendor, strength, and speed, adorned with various jewels,
and harnessed to the chariot, they shone like swift arrows ready to cross over.
Then those great yakṣas saw the Lord of Wealth enraged.
They gladdened one another with gestures portending victory; then the Blessed One, the king of kings, of great splendor, mounting that great chariot,
set forth while being praised by gods and gandharvas.
As that high-souled lord of all the yakṣas and treasures departed,
those fierce-looking beings followed the great-souled Dhanada;
they were red-eyed, golden-hued, massive in body, and possessed of great strength.
Ten million heroic yakṣas, equipped with weapons and girded with swords, quickly surrounded him and stood by;
drawing the very sky along, they arrived at Mount Gandhamādana.

Then they reached that great mountain peak, beautiful and protected by the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), which was covered with a vast network of kesara flowers; there the Pāṇḍavas arrived in the presence of the approaching Great Lord of Riches.

With their hair standing on end with joy, the Pāṇḍavas beheld that pleasant sight. But Kubera, seeing the sons of Pāṇḍu— those great-souled mahārathas who had taken up their bows and swords— was then filled with delight.
"All these tigers among men possess energy equal to that of Purandara.
Desiring to accomplish the work of the gods, he was pleased in his heart.
With great speed, they sprang up like birds from the mountain peak.
Led by the Lord of Wealth (Dhaneshvara), they stood close to them;
then, O Bhārata, having observed that he was joyful in mind toward the Pāṇḍavas, the Yakṣas and Gandharvas remained there, free from any change of expression.
And the high-souled Pāṇḍavas— Nakula, Sahadeva, and the son of Dharma who knows righteousness— having bowed down to the Lord, the Giver of Wealth,
those great chariot-warriors considered themselves as if they had committed an offense.
They all stood with palms joined in reverence, surrounding the Lord of Wealth.
The Master of Riches ascended the magnificent Puṣpaka chariot, fashioned by Viśvakarman, which was provided with an excellent couch and seat and adorned with variegated borders.
As he sat there, thousands of yakṣas and rākṣasas— of massive body, with spike-like ears and great speed— took their seats around him;
likewise, hundreds of gandharvas and hosts of apsarases did the same.
They stood surrounding him, just as the gods attend upon Śatakratu;
wearing a beautiful golden garland upon his head, Bhīmasena,
with arrows, sword, and bow in hand, gazed up at the Lord of Wealth.

In that situation, even as he gazed upon Kubera standing there, eager for battle and taking up sharp arrows, he felt neither fear of the terrifying one nor exhaustion despite being wounded by the rākṣasas.
Seeing Bhīma, the one who is carried by men (Kubera) spoke to the son of Dharma:
"O Pārtha, all beings know you to be devoted to the welfare of living creatures;
therefore, dwell here on the mountain peak with your kinsmen, free from fear."

O Pāṇḍava, you should not harbor anger toward Bhīmasena; these men were already slain by Time long ago, and your younger brother was merely the instrument. Furthermore, you should not feel shame regarding this act of violence that has been committed.
The destruction of the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas was previously witnessed by the gods;
I have no anger toward Bhīmasena, O bull of the Bharatas,
for I was already gratified by this deed of Bhīma long ago.
Having spoken thus to the king, he addressed Bhīmasena:
"O dear one, O best of the Kurus, this rash act which you have committed for the sake of Kṛṣṇā does not dwell in my mind, O Bhīma."

"O Vṛkodara, disregarding me and the gods, you brought about the destruction of the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas by relying on the strength of your own arms; therefore, I am pleased with you, for today I have been liberated from that terrible curse."

"O joy of the Pāṇḍavas, in the past I was cursed by the great seer Agastya when he was provoked to anger by some offense of mine; this [act] has been performed as an atonement for that. Indeed, my suffering was witnessed by him long ago."
"O slayer of enemies, there is no fault of yours here in any way whatsoever.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, how were you cursed by the high-souled Agastya?"
"O Lord, I wish to hear the cause of this curse of yours;
and it is a source of wonder to me that you were not consumed at that very moment by the wrath of that wise one, along with your army and your followers."
Vaiśravaṇa said:
"O lord of men, there was a council of the deities at Kuśavatī;
I went there, surrounded by three hundred great padmas."
On that path, I then beheld Agastya, the best of sages, performing fierce austerities on the bank of the Yamunā, while yakṣas of terrible form bearing various weapons [surrounded him].
Crowded with flocks of various birds and adorned with flowering trees,
they saw him standing with arms upraised, facing the sun—
a mass of splendor blazing like a kindled fire.
O Bhārata, my illustrious friend, the lord of the Rākṣasas named Maṇimān, while traveling through the sky, spat upon the head of that great ṛṣi out of foolishness, ignorance, pride, and delusion.
In his anger, as if burning all the quarters of the world, he said this to me:
"O Lord of Wealth, since this evil-minded one has committed this insolence against me while you were looking on, disregarding me— [he shall suffer for it]."
Therefore, along with these armies, you shall meet your death at the hands of a human;
and you too, O evil-minded one, shall suffer distress once these troops have been slain.
Only by seeing that very man will you be liberated from your sin.

"Your armies, along with these sons and grandsons endowed with strength, shall not incur this terrible curse; go, and he will carry out your command. This curse was incurred by me previously from that best of sages."
O great king, he was liberated by your brother Bhīma.
Vaiśravaṇa said:
"Yudhiṣṭhira, steadfastness, skill, [knowledge of] place and time, and prowess—[these are the means]."

This fivefold rule pertains to the ordinances for worldly affairs. O Bhārata, in the Kṛta Yuga, men were steadfast and skillful in their respective duties, and they were knowers of the methods of valor.

O best of Kṣatriyas, a Kṣatriya who is steadfast, who knows the proper time and place, and who understands the application of all duties, indeed rules the earth. O Pārtha, it is the man who conducts himself in this manner in all his actions.
That hero gains fame in this world and a happy state after death;
having exerted his prowess while seeking the right place and time, Śakra,
the slayer of Vṛtra, attained sovereignty over the triple heaven together with the Vasus.
But he who, out of sheer impetuosity, does not look at the precipice—
the evil-souled one of wicked intellect who pursues only evil—
perishes both here and after death, being ignorant of the distinction between actions.
One who does not know the proper time, who is of very dull intellect, and who fails to distinguish between different courses of action,
perishes both in this world and after death due to his futile undertakings and improper conduct— especially those wicked-souled, deceitful men who persist in acts of violence.
For those who desire to seize all power, their resolve becomes sinful;
he is ignorant of dharma, arrogant, childish in intellect, and impatient.
O bull among men, instruct this Bhīmasena, who is fearless.
Having heard those words regarding the gathering of the Pāṇḍavas,
Dhanada rose up and immediately set out with them;
having reached King Yudhiṣṭhira, Kubera addressed him.
Having reached the hermitage of the royal seer Ārṣṭiṣeṇa,
dwell there during the first fortnight of the dark half of the month, free from sorrow and fear.
Alakā is inhabited by Gandharvas along with Yakṣas and Rākṣasas.

O lord of men, let all those joined with me and the inhabitants of the mountain protect you, O mighty-armed one, together with these best of the twice-born; and here on this mountain, Vṛkodara stands ready for acts of daring.
"O King, best among the upholders of dharma, let him be properly restrained by you.
O Indra among kings, from this point forward, the forest-dwellers shall behold him,
attend upon him constantly, and protect him in every way."
O bull among men, my messengers shall attend upon you, bringing many delicious foods and drinks,
just as Jiṣṇu attends upon Mahendra and Vṛkodara attends upon Vāyu.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, just as you, my dear son, were born through yoga as a natural son of Dharma,
and just as both the twins are his own sons endowed with his own nature like the two Aśvins,
so too must all of you here be protected by me.
Phalguna, the younger brother of Bhimasena, who knows the distinctions of the true meaning and understands the specific characteristics of all dharmas, is well in heaven;
for whatever supreme attainments are considered foremost in the worlds, he possesses them all.
O dear one, from their very birth, all these qualities have resided in Dhanañjaya:
self-restraint, generosity, strength, intelligence, modesty, fortitude, and supreme energy—
these too reside in that great being of immeasurable splendor.
The victorious one does not perform a contemptible act out of delusion, O Pāṇḍava;
nor do men among men report any false words spoken by the son of Pṛthā.
He is the enhancer of the fame of the Kurus, along with the gods, ancestors, and gandharvas.
O Bhārata, honored in the abode of Śakra, he mastered the celestial weapons;
he was that Śantanu of great splendor, your father’s grandfather, who brought all the rulers of the earth under his control through righteousness.
O Pārtha, he is pleased with Pārtha, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow in heaven; and that one of great heroism, standing like the bearer of his lineage,
has honored the ancestors, the gods, and the Brahmins, being himself of great renown.

O King, that sovereign overlord Śaṃtanu, your great-grandfather, who conquered heaven and now dwells in the realm of Śakra, has brought seven principal great clouds toward the Yamunā and inquires after your welfare.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard these words spoken by the Giver of Wealth (Kubera),
the Pāṇḍavas were then filled with great joy.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, Vṛkodara, having set aside his spear, mace, sword, and bow, paid homage to Kubera. Thereupon,
the Lord of Wealth, the protector, spoke to him who had come for refuge.
Be the destroyer of the pride of your enemies and the increaser of the joy of your friends. O dear son, dwelling on the mountain peak with your kinsmen,
be a source of prosperity and always show honor to the Suparṇas, the Pitṛs, and the gods.
Look straight, not crooked; speak the truth, not falsehood.
Look far, not near; look beyond, not what is behind. Dwell in your own delightful dwellings, O scorers of enemies!
"O bulls of the Bharata race, the yakṣas will provide you with all desired objects.
Very soon, Guḍākeśa Dhananjaya— that bull among men who has mastered the use of weapons— will arrive, having been sent by Maghavan himself."
Having thus instructed Yudhiṣṭhira, whose deeds were supreme,
the lord of the Guhyakas departed for the sunset mountain, the best of excellent peaks,
with [his chariot] covered with elephant-blankets and adorned with various jewels.
Thousands of yakṣas and rākṣasas followed in vehicles;
the roar of the excellent horses as they proceeded along the path of Airāvata toward the abode of Kubera was like the clamor of birds.
Those steeds of the Lord of Wealth swiftly ascended into the sky,
as if dragging along the clouds and drinking in the wind. Then those lifeless bodies of the rākṣasas—
By the command of the Lord of Wealth, they were drawn away from the mountain peak;
for that very time had been designated by the wise Agastya as the period of their curse,
and therefore they were all slain in battle along with Maṇimān.
But the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
free from anxiety and honored by all the Rākṣasas, dwelt happily during that night in those dwellings.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, at sunrise, O subduer of enemies, Dhaumya, having performed his daily rites,
approached the Pāṇḍavas together with Ārṣṭiṣeṇa.
They, in turn, paid homage to the feet of both Ārṣṭiṣeṇa and Dhaumya.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, they all honored those Brahmins.
Ārṣṭiṣeṇa embraced the bulls of the Bharata race like his own sons;
then Dhaumya took Yudhiṣṭhira by the right hand.
Gazing toward the eastern direction, the great seer spoke these words:
"O Great King, there stands Mount Mandara, the king of mountains, shining brilliantly as it covers the earth extending to the edge of the ocean."
"O Pāṇḍava, Indra and Vaiśravaṇa protect this quarter, which is adorned with mountains, forest edges, and groves. This,
they say, belongs to King Mahendra and Vaiśravaṇa."
"O dear one, the seers who know all dharmas are wise and dwell there;
therefore, the subjects indeed wait upon the rising sun,
as do the seers who know dharma, the Siddhas, the Sādhyas, and the deities."
King Yama, whose nature is righteousness and who is the lord of all living beings,
dwells in this southern direction, which is the destination for deceased beings.
This is the holy Saṃyamana, a place of most wonderful appearance.
The palace of the King of the Dead (Yama), endowed with supreme supernatural power, is that mountain-king reaching which,
O King, the sun establishes itself through truth; this,
the wise call "Asta."
Dwelling upon this king of mountains and in the great ocean, King Varuṇa protects all living beings;
this illustrious one stands there, illuminating the northern quarter.
O highly fortunate one, Mahāmeru is auspicious and the refuge of those who know Brahman;
upon it resides the assembly of Brahmā as well as Prajāpati, the soul of all beings, who emits everything that exists, whether moving or stationary.
Those whom they call the mind-born sons of Brahmā, with Dakṣa as the seventh—
their abode is the auspicious and healthy Mahāmeru;
it is here that they are established, and from here they arise again.
"O dear one, the seven celestial rishis, headed by Vasiṣṭha,
always behold that stainless region, the supreme peak of Meru,
where the Grandfather dwells together with the gods who are self-satisfied."
They call him the eternal source of the nature of all beings,
the god Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Lord who is without beginning or end;
from the abode of Brahmā, his transcendent station shines forth.

And the gods behold with effort that divine, auspicious abode of the high-souled Viṣṇu, consisting of radiant energy, blazing more intensely than the sun or fire; O King, it is difficult for even gods and dānavas to look upon because of its own inherent splendor.
In the east, O dear one, the abode of Nārāyaṇa shines resplendently upon Mount Meru;
there, the Lord of Beings, the self-existent source of all nature,
illuminates all creatures and blazes forth with sublime glory.
"O dear one, O best of the Kurus, neither the Brahman-sages nor even the great sages attain this destination of the ascetics here; indeed,
having reached all those luminaries, they do not even shine."
There the Lord himself, whose nature is undepressed, shines forth resplendently;
there the ascetics go with devotion to Hari, Nārāyaṇa,
being endowed with supreme austerity and purified by auspicious deeds.
Those great-souled ones who have attained perfection through yoga, being entirely free from darkness and delusion,
go there and do not return again to this world, O Bhārata—
[to] the self-existent, great-souled, eternal God of gods.
"O highly fortunate Yudhiṣṭhira, this place is indeed permanent, imperishable, and undecaying; for it is always the abode of the Lord, O bowing one.
Day after day, the sun and the moon revolve around this Meru as their fixed point."
O best of the Kurus,
O sinless one, O great king, all the luminaries without exception revolve from every direction, keeping the king of mountains to their right as they move in circumambulation.
Drawing all these luminaries toward him, the Blessed One, the Sun, whose nature is free from darkness, performs his circumambulation;
then, having reached the setting point and passed beyond the twilight, the Maker of Day [proceeds].
This light-maker resorts to the northern quarter;
O Pāṇḍava, having circled Mount Meru,
the divine Savitṛ, who is devoted to the welfare of all beings, proceeds again facing the east.
Dividing the month into many parts at the junctions of the lunar phases,
the blessed Moon likewise moves together with the constellations;
thus he revolves tirelessly around Mount Mahāmeru.
And Soma, dividing time in many ways at the junctions of the lunar phases,
nourishes all beings and returns again to Mount Mandara;
likewise, the god who destroys darkness nourishes the world with his rays.
The sun traverses this unobstructed path;
desiring to send forth the cold seasons, it resorts to the southern quarter. Thereupon, Time brings the cold season upon all living beings.
By its brilliance, the sun, having withdrawn its light from both stationary and moving beings, takes up their vital energies;
thereafter, sweat, exhaustion, drowsiness, and lassitude come upon men.
For living beings, sleep is constantly and repeatedly indulged in. Thus,
having blocked this indefinable path,
the radiant and blessed one again creates the rains, bringing all creatures to life.
Increasing the growth of both the stationary and moving beings through rain, wind, heat, and pleasant conditions,
he of great splendor returns once more.
Thus, O Pārtha, he moves tirelessly through this wheel of time.
Drawing all beings along with him, Savitṛ revolves;
his movement is continuous, O Pāṇḍava, for he does not stand still.
Having indeed taken away the vital energy of beings, he releases it once again.
"O Bhārata, distributing the lifespan and the karma of all beings,
this omnipresent Lord always creates days and nights, as well as the *kalās* and *kāṣṭhās*.
Vaiśampāyana said:"
As those great-souled ones, established in their virtuous vows, dwelt upon that king of mountains,
they experienced both delight and joy.
To those who long for the sight of Arjuna— those endowed with heroism, of perfectly pure being,
radiant, and preeminent in truth and fortitude—
Many joyful hosts of Gandharvas and great ṛṣis approached him as he was surrounded by trees laden with flowers.
Having reached the best of cities, the supreme delight of the mind arose for those great chariot-warriors,
just as it did for the hosts of Maruts upon reaching heaven.
Beholding the peaks and plateaus of the great mountain, which resounded with the cries of peacocks and swans and were strewn with flowers;
Having attained supreme joy on the mountain,
they remained there upon that best of mountains, which had its banks and shores fashioned by Kubera himself.
They saw lotus ponds frequented by *kādamba*, *kāraṇḍava*, and swans, filled with lotuses,
as well as pleasure grounds of magnificent appearance.
Adorned with most wonderful garlands and possessing a natural splendor,
those exquisite jewels were truly enchanting,
as if they belonged to King Vaiśravaṇa, the Giver of Wealth.
It was covered with great trees of many colors and fragrances, reaching up to the rows of clouds,
where those for whom austerity is paramount constantly dwell.
They were unable even to conceive of the peak of that best of mountains,
owing to its own splendor as well as the power of the great medicinal herbs.
O hero among men, no distinction whatsoever existed between day and night for him who remained established [in that state],
[governing] all things mobile and immobile.
The fire of immeasurable power brings all things into being;
those heroic lions among men, remaining there, beheld both its rising and its setting.
O heroes, being thus enveloped, you did not perceive the coming and going of the sun's darkness, nor its rising and setting, even as you gazed upon that dispeller of gloom.
With networks of rays, they illuminate the intermediate and main directions;
they are devoted to sacred study, constant in their ritual observances,
preeminent in dharma, and pure in their vows.
Established in truth, those great chariot-warriors waited for the arrival of that one whose vow is truth;
let there be joy here for all who have gathered together.
"May Dhananjaya, skilled in weapons, soon [return];
speaking these supreme blessings,
those sons of Pṛthā became intent upon asceticism and yoga.
Beholding the diverse forests on the mountain and constantly thinking of Kirīṭin,
night and day became one for them.
In just one year he became identical in appearance [to his father];
as soon as that high-souled Jiṣṇu, with Dhaumya’s permission, had matted his hair and gone forth into the forest.
At that very moment, they felt no joy;
how could there be pleasure for those whose minds were fixed upon him?
Yet, by the command of their brother Yudhiṣṭhira, [they proceeded].
When that Jishnu, who moves with the gait of an elephant in rut, departed from Kamyaka forest and went forth from the woods,
at that very moment they were struck by grief.
At that very moment, having renounced all desires, the Pārthas went forth into the homeless life;
yet at that time, they became overcome with grief as they thus reflected upon him, the one with white horses.
Then, O Bhārata, as Vāsava approached that mountain seeking weapons, a month passed with great difficulty for the descendants of Bharata.
Having dwelt for five years in the abode of the Thousand-eyed One,
he obtained all the divine weapons from the Lord of the Gods—
the Āgneya, Vāruṇa, Saumya, Vāyavya, and Vaiṣṇava.
Having obtained those [weapons]— the Aindra, Pāśupata, Brāhma, Pārameṣṭhya, and that of Prajāpati,
as well as those of Yama, Dhātṛ, Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Vaiśravaṇa—
from the Thousand-eyed One, he paid homage to Śatakratu.
Having been granted permission by him and having performed a circumambulation,
Arjuna then returned to Gandhamādana, joyful and exceedingly delighted. Then, on a certain occasion, [he saw] a vehicle yoked with horses...
Seeing that great chariot of the mahārathas suddenly arrive, possessing the brilliance of lightning,
joy arose among those who were thinking of Arjuna.
Blazing suddenly and illuminating the atmosphere, that chariot held by Mātali shone like a great meteor situated within the clouds.
Like the smokeless, blazing crest of a fire,
he who wore the diadem was seen standing there,
garlanded and adorned with excellent ornaments.
Dhanañjaya, possessing the power of the wielder of the thunderbolt,
arrived at the mountain blazing with splendor;
having reached that mountain, he was adorned with a diadem and garlands.
Having descended from that great Indra’s vehicle,
he first saluted the feet of Dhaumya,
and immediately thereafter those of Ajātaśatru.
He also paid homage at the feet of Vṛkodara;
having been saluted by the two sons of Mādrī,
he met with Kṛṣṇā and comforted her.
He bowed down at his brother's feet;
there was supreme joy among them who had been reunited with that immeasurable one.
And he too, adorned with a diadem and garlands, beheld them and rejoiced, praising the king who,
mounted upon it, had slain seven hosts.
Approaching that steed of Indra, the slayer of Namuci and son of Diti, the sons of Pṛthā, undaunted in spirit, circumambulated it clockwise.
Extremely delighted,
they offered Mātali the highest honor, equal to that shown to the king of the gods,
and all those inhabitants of heaven treated him according to custom.
The sons of the Kuru king questioned him,
and Mātali greeted them in return;
having instructed them like a father his sons, he spoke to them.
He departed on his chariot of incomparable splendor back to the presence of the Lord of the Three Worlds;
once that bestower of boons had mounted his divine steed and departed, [the world was left behind].
The son of Śakra, the crusher of all enemies,
renowned like the thousand-eyed Indra in person,
the glorious Jiṣṇu, having cast off his own body—
The high-souled one gave away the great treasures of excellent form presented by Śakra—
ornaments possessing the brilliance of the sun.
Then, being pleased with his beloved Sutasoma’s mother,
he [bestowed gifts] upon those bulls among the Kurus and upon those whose splendor was equal to the sun and fire.
Sitting in the midst of the foremost of brahmin-sages,
he related everything exactly as it had happened,
including how the preeminent weapons had indeed been granted by the gods.
Proclaiming this while dressed in garments of bark and rags:
"In this manner have the weapons been mastered by me—
directly from Śakra, from Vāta, and from Śiva."
Likewise, by virtue of his moral conduct and meditative concentration,
the gods, together with Indra, were delighted by me.
In brief, he was indeed one of purified karma.
Having announced his entry into heaven to them,
Kirīṭin, accompanied by the two sons of Mādrī,
