slept contentedly in that dwelling.
Then, when the night had dawned, Dhanañjaya, together with all his brothers, paid homage to Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma.
Vaiśampāyana said:

At that very moment, O Bhārata, there arose a tumultuous sound of all kinds of musical instruments belonging to the dwellers of heaven in the sky, as well as the sound of chariot rims and the ringing of bells.

Beholding from all sides the various beasts of prey and birds with their heads turned toward the sound, those best of the Kurus were filled with joy as they saw Śakra approaching through the sky accompanied by the Maruts.
Then the Gandharvas and Apsarases followed from all sides on celestial chariots as radiant as the sun, toward that subduer of enemies, the king of the gods.
Then he [ascended] the [chariot] yoked with bay horses and adorned with gold.
Mounting his chariot that roared like a cloud, blazing with supreme splendor,
Purandara, the king of the gods, swiftly approached the sons of Pṛthā;
having arrived, the thousand-eyed one indeed descended from his chariot.
Upon seeing that high-souled one, the illustrious Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira,
together with his brothers, approached the king of the gods;
and then, he who bestows abundant sacrificial fees honored him according to the prescribed rites.
Having honored the immeasurable-souled one with rites prescribed by rule as was fitting,
the radiant Dhanañjaya prostrated before Purandara and stood near the king of the gods, bowing like a servant.
Beholding Dhananjaya standing nearby, humble and composed, Kuntī’s son Yudhiṣṭhira, possessed of great splendor,
was filled with joy as he looked upon the matted-haired, sinless one who was devoted to asceticism and served the King of the Gods.
Then, filled with great joy at the sight of Phalguna,
he became supremely delighted, honoring the King of the Gods. [He saw] that king, whose mind was no longer dejected, overflowing with joy.
The wise Purandara, king of the gods, spoke these words:
"O King, O Pāṇḍava, you shall rule this earth.
May you attain well-being, O son of Kuntī; return once more to the Kāmyaka hermitage."
O King, all weapons have been obtained from me by the son of Pāṇḍu through his diligent efforts;
I have had my favor won by Dhanañjaya.

"He cannot be conquered even by the three worlds. Having spoken thus to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, the thousand-eyed Indra departed for the third heaven, joyful and being praised by the great seers.
He who, being wise and composed, studies this account of the meeting of the Pāṇḍavas— residents of the house of Dhaneśvara— with Śakra,
while remaining a celibate student for one year, self-controlled and firm in his vows, [attains the highest reward].
He shall live for a hundred autumns, free from affliction and in great happiness.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When Śakra had departed as he had come, Yudhiṣṭhira was reunited with his brothers.
And with Kṛṣṇā, Bībhatsu honored the son of Dharma;
and having smelled the head of the Pāṇḍava as he offered his salutation,
Arjuna, filled with joy, spoke to him in a voice faltering with emotion.
"O Arjuna, how did this time pass for you in heaven?
How were the weapons obtained, and how was the king of the gods propitiated?
O Bhārata, I trust that those weapons have been mastered by you correctly?"

"Is the Lord of the Gods pleased with you, and did Rudra grant you his weapons? How was Śakra seen by you, or the Blessed One who wields the Pināka bow? How were the weapons obtained, and how were they propitiated by you?"
"O subduer of enemies, as the Lord Śatakratu spoke to you,
saying, 'I have done what is pleasing for you,' what was that pleasing deed performed by you?
O one of great splendor, I wish to hear this in detail."

O sinless one, tell me all this in its entirety, O Dhanañjaya: how Mahādeva and the king of the gods were pleased with you, and also how that which was pleasing to the wielder of the thunderbolt was accomplished by you, O subduer of enemies.
Arjuna said:
Listen, O great king,
to the manner by which I beheld the god Śatakratu and the blessed Lord Śaṅkara.
"O King, O crusher of enemies, having studied that science which was spoken by you,
and being commanded by you, I have set out for the forest to perform austerities. Having gone from Kāmyaka to Bhṛgutuṅga, I have established myself there in penance."
Having stayed for one night, I saw a certain brahmin on the road.
He asked me, "O son of Kuntī, where are you going? Tell me. To him, O joy of the Kurus, I told everything exactly as it was.

O best of kings, having heard those truthful words of mine, that brahmin honored me, O King, and became filled with affection for me. Then, being pleased, he said to me: "O Bhārata, apply yourself to asceticism."
"O ascetic, before long you shall behold the lord of the gods. Then, at his word, O great king, I ascended the snowy mountain and performed austerities for a month, subsisting on roots and fruits.
The second month also passed while I subsisted on water;
then, O joy of the Pāṇḍavas, during the third month I remained without food;
and during the fourth month, I stood with my arms raised upward.
Yet my life-force did not diminish, and that seemed like a marvel. When the fourth [watch] had arrived and the first day had passed,
a being in the form of a boar approached me.
Striking the earth with his snout, scratching it with his feet, sweeping the ground with his belly, and rolling over again and again—
after him followed another great being, stationed in the form of a Kirāta.
Then, having encountered that being which was equipped with a bow, arrows, and a sword, and followed by a host of women,
I took up my bow and my two inexhaustible great quivers and struck that hair-raising creature with an arrow.
At that very moment, the Kirāta, having drawn his powerful bow, struck me even more firmly, as if shaking my very heart.
But he said to me, O King: "This is my prior possession."
"Having abandoned the laws of the hunt, for what reason have you struck him? I shall now destroy your pride with these sharpened arrows; stand firm!
Thereupon, that large-bodied and massive creature rushed toward me.
Then he covered me, as if a mountain, with great arrows;
and I, in turn, overwhelmed him with a vast shower of shafts.
Then, with feathered arrows of blazing points that had been consecrated with mantras, [I struck him].
I pierced him back, as one might strike a mountain peak with thunderbolts;
his form then became divided into a hundred and a thousand parts,
and I struck all those bodies of his with my arrows.
O Bhārata, O great king, those bodies were seen once again as a single mass; I shattered them yet again. Becoming minute with a large head, and then large with a minute head, I moved about.
O King, having become one, he then turned toward me in battle;
when I was unable to overcome him with my arrows in that combat,
O bull of the Bharatas, I then employed the Vāyavya weapon.
And I was unable to slay him; that was like a marvel. When that weapon had been repelled, great was my astonishment.
And then, O Great King, I [prepared] once more with even greater distinction.
In that battle, I overwhelmed the being with a great multitude of missiles;
employing the *Sthūṇākarṇa*, the iron net, a fierce rain of arrows,
the mountain-missile, and a shower of stones, I advanced against him.
O sinless one, laughing, he swallowed all those weapons of mine. When they had all been neutralized, I discharged the Brahmā weapon.
Thereupon, he was overwhelmed on all sides by blazing arrows.
And as it was being accumulated by me with the great weapon, it increased;
then the world was tormented by the splendor produced from me,
for in an instant the quarters and the sky were illuminated on all sides.
That weapon as well, the one of great splendor, he destroyed in an instant.
Then I fell to the earth;
thereupon, that being laughed.
O King, when the Brahmā weapon was neutralized, a great fear entered me. Then, taking up my bow and my two inexhaustible quivers,
I suddenly struck that being, but he devoured those weapons as well.

When all my missiles had been destroyed and my weapons devoured, a hand-to-hand struggle ensued between me and that being. We engaged in physical exertion with our fists and struck one another with our palms.
That being struck me down, and I fell motionless to the earth;
then, having laughed, that being vanished right there.
Thereupon, I fell into reflection: "I shall worship him once again."
Having thus gathered flowers, while I was about to worship the Lord Śaṅkara on the sandy bank, I saw that Kirāta holding flowers;
and then, as he was repeatedly worshipping with other flowers again and again.
Having seen all those [omens] upon the head of the Kirāta, O Great King, I thought, "This is Mahādeva," and I bowed down to him again and again while he,
together with his wives, appeared to me like a marvel.
Having done this, O Great King, the Blessed One, the Lord of the Thirty-three, abandoned his form as a Kirāta and assumed another divine form for himself, wearing wondrous celestial garments.
Assuming his divine form, Maheśvara stood there;
then the Blessed One, whose banner is the bull, was seen in person—
accompanied by Umā, with tawny eyes, many-formed, and bearing the Pināka bow.
Approaching me in battle as I stood facing him in that very manner, he,
the wielder of the trident, said, "O scorcher of foes, I am pleased with you. Then, taking that bow and the two quivers of inexhaustible arrows, [he gave them to me].
The Blessed One granted it to me alone and said, "Choose a boon.
"I am pleased with you, O son of Kuntī; tell me, what shall I do for you?
Tell me, O hero, whatever is in your heart, and I shall grant it to you."
"Abandoning immortality, tell me what is in your mind.
Then, with palms joined in reverence and my mind fixed upon the divine weapons,
I bowed my head to Śarva and spoke these words.
"If the Blessed One is pleased with me, and this is the boon I desire,
I wish to know whatever weapons exist among the gods. To this,
the three-eyed Blessed One said to me, "I shall grant them."
"O Pāṇḍava, my own Raudra weapon shall attend upon you.
And the Lord, being pleased, bestowed upon me the Pāśupata weapon;
and having given me that eternal weapon, Mahādeva spoke.
This must never be employed against human beings under any circumstances;
for if it were cast upon one of little power, it would utterly consume the world.
O Dhanañjaya, it may be employed by you with force only when you are being oppressed by a powerful foe.
And you should employ it in every way for the neutralization of weapons;
that divine weapon, which is unassailable and a check to all other weapons,
stands before me in embodied form by my side, now that the bull-bannered god is pleased.
It is the eradication of enemies and the destruction of opposing armies;
it is unassailable and difficult to overcome even for gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas.
Having been granted permission by him, I sat down right there.
And even as I was looking on, the god vanished right there.
Arjuna said:
"Then, O Bhārata, I spent that night there in great joy."
By the grace of the high-souled Tryambaka, the God of gods,
I spent the night; and having performed my morning rites,
I beheld that best of the twice-born whom I had seen previously.

And to him, O Bhārata, I reported everything exactly as it had occurred, saying, "I have come before the Blessed Mahādeva. O Indra among kings, that best of the twice-born spoke to me with great pleasure.
"O sinless one, you have seen Mahādeva as no other has;
having met with all the world-protectors, beginning with Vaivasvata,
you shall see the Lord of the Gods, and he will grant you weapons."
Having spoken thus, O King, and having embraced me again and again,
that brahmin, resplendent like the sun, departed as he pleased. Then,
in the afternoon of that day, a holy breeze began to blow.
As if creating this world anew, O slayer of foes,
divine and fragrant garlands, fresh and beautiful,
appeared nearby at the foot of the Śaiśira mountain.
Divine musical instruments, sounding most melodiously on all sides,
and enchanting hymns of praise dedicated to Indra were heard;
likewise, there were throngs of Apsarases and Gandharvas present there.
In every way, they sang songs before the God of gods;
and there, the hosts of Maruts arrived by celestial paths,
as did those who follow Mahendra and dwell in the abode of the gods.

Then Marutvān, accompanied by Śacī and all the immortals, arrived there with his well-adorned steeds yoked to chariots drawn by bay horses. At that very moment, Kubera, who is borne by men, also arrived.
O King, he revealed himself to me, endowed with supreme splendor;
I beheld Yama stationed in the southern quarter,
and Varuṇa and the king of the gods situated in their respective places.
O great king, those bulls among the gods, having comforted me, said:
"O Savyasācin, behold the world-protectors standing here. For the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods' mission, you have beheld Śaṅkara."
"Receive weapons from us as well," they said from all sides.
Then, O Lord, having become purified and having prostrated before those bulls among the gods,
I duly received those great weapons.
"O Bhārata, having received the weapons from the gods, I was then granted permission by them.
Then all the gods departed as they had come, O subduer of enemies;
and Maghavat, the lord of the gods, mounted his resplendent chariot."
The Blessed One, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, spoke these words as if smiling:
"O Dhanañjaya, even before your arrival here, I already knew you;
therefore, O bull of the Bharatas, I shall now reveal myself to you."

"For in the past, you have repeatedly performed ablutions at sacred fords (tīrtha), and this penance was practiced by you long ago; therefore, O Pāṇḍava, you shall go to heaven. Yet, even further, most formidable penance must still be practiced."
"The display of weapons and the practice of asceticism are difficult and terrible," [he said]. The Blessed One spoke of everything regarding the attainment of ascetic power:
"O destroyer of enemies, you must certainly go to heaven."
"By my command, Mātali shall convey you to the third heaven. For you are already known to the gods and the high-souled ṛṣis,
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, even while staying here performing most difficult austerities."
Then I said to Śakra, "Be gracious to me, O Blessed One;
I choose you as my teacher for the sake of weapons, O Lord of the Thirty-three.
Indra said:
"O dear one, O scorcher of foes, you shall perform a cruel deed, for you are skilled in weapons. O Pāṇḍava, may you attain that desire for which you sought these weapons.
Arjuna said:
Then I said, "O slayer of enemies, I shall not employ divine weapons against mortals unless it is for the purpose of neutralizing their own weapons.
O Lord of the gods, bestow those divine weapons upon me."
"And afterwards, O bull among the gods, may I obtain the worlds conquered by my weapons.
Indra said:
"O Dhanañjaya, these words were spoken by me to you for the sake of testing you."
"O Bhārata, these words of yours are well-founded for my own son. Go to my abode and learn from me all the weapons—
those of Vāyu, Agni, the Vasus, Varuṇa, and the Maruts."
O bull of the Kuru race, all the weapons here— those of the Grandfather (Brahmā), those of the Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, as well as all those of Viṣṇu and the Nairṛtas— are centered in me.
Arjuna said:
Having spoken thus to me, Śakra vanished right there. Then I beheld Indra’s chariot, yoked with bay horses, standing before me.
O King, that divine, illusory, and meritorious chariot which had been brought by Mātali—
when the world-protectors had departed, Mātali then said to me:
"O one of great splendor, Śakra, the king of the gods, desires to see you."
"You have attained perfection, O mighty-armed one; perform your supreme task.
Behold the worlds of those who have performed meritorious deeds; go to heaven in your own body.
O Bhārata, the thousand-eyed King of the Gods desires to see you."
Thus addressed by Mātali, I took leave of the Śaiśira mountain,
circumambulated it clockwise, and ascended that supreme chariot;
he then urged on the horses, which possessed the speed of thought and the wind.
Mātali, the expert in the science of horses who bestows abundant sacrificial fees,
looked at my face as I stood there;
then, O King, as the chariot was whirling about, that charioteer, filled with wonder, spoke these words.
"Today this appears to me as a most wonderful and marvelous marvel,
that you have remained unmoved by foot while mounted upon this divine chariot;
for even the King of the Gods has always been observed by me here [to move]."
O bull of the Bharatas, while the horses were reeling during that first upheaval,
you remained standing right there on the swaying chariot, O upholder of the Kuru lineage;
this strength of yours appears to me to surpass even that of Śakra.
Having spoken thus, O King, Mātali entered the sky and showed me the abodes of the gods and their celestial chariots, O Bhārata. Then that chariot, yoked with tawny steeds, ascended upwards.
O best of men, the sages and the deities themselves worship it;
thereafter, I beheld the worlds of the celestial rishis, which move at will,
as well as the power of the Gandharvas and Apsarases of immeasurable splendor.
Mātali, the charioteer of Śakra, out of affection showed me the many groves of the gods, such as Nandana and others; thereafter,
I beheld Amarāvatī, the palace of Śakra.
Adorned with celestial trees that yield the fruits of every desire and with precious jewels,
that city is not illuminated by the sun, nor is there cold, heat, or fatigue there;
O King, neither dust, mud, nor darkness exists there, nor does old age.
O Great King, O subduer of enemies, neither grief, nor dejection, nor change of complexion was observed there among the denizens of heaven; nor was there any exhaustion,
O Lord of the people, nor were anger, greed, or anything inauspicious present there.
In that abode of the gods, living beings are eternally contented and joyful;
there, the trees possess green foliage and yield flowers and fruits perpetually; and there are various lotus ponds filled with fragrant *padma* and *saugandhika* blossoms.
There, a cool, fragrant, life-giving, and pure breeze blew;
the ground was variegated with all kinds of jewels and adorned with flowers;
and there were many beautiful beasts and birds with sweet voices.
And there many immortals were seen traveling in celestial chariots.
Then I beheld the Vasus, the Rudras, the Sādhyas together with the hosts of Maruts, as well as the Ādityas and the two Aśvins; I paid homage to them all.
They recognized me by my heroism, fame, splendor, and strength,
as well as by my mastery of weapons and my victory in battle;
then I entered that delightful city, frequented by gods and gandharvas.
With palms joined in reverence, I approached the thousand-eyed King of the Gods;
Śakra, the best among givers, being pleased, offered me half of his seat,
and Vāsava, out of great respect, touched my limbs with his own.

There, O Bhārata, I dwelt in heaven together with the gods and Gandharvas for the sake of weapons, practicing the mastery of arms, O giver of many sacrificial fees. And Viśvāvasu’s son, Citrasena, became my friend.
And he, O King, caused me to master the entire science of Gandharva music. Then, O King, having acquired the weapons and being highly honored,
I dwelt happily in the abode of Śakra, endowed with every object of desire.

O scorcher of enemies, O Bhārata, hearing the abundant sounds of singing and musical instruments, and seeing the most excellent Apsarases dancing, one should disregard all that and understand it as it truly is.
Having accepted [the weapons] with great intensity, I remained fixed upon those very *astras*.
Thereupon, the thousand-eyed Lord was pleased by that desire of mine.
O King, as I dwelt in this manner, this period of time passed away in heaven.
Arjuna said: Then,
once I had mastered the weapons and was confident, the rider of the tawny steeds (Indra) touched my head with both his hands and spoke these words.
You cannot be conquered in battle even by the hosts of gods today,
let alone by men of unrefined soul in the world of mortals;
for you are immeasurable, invincible, and likewise peerless in battles.
"For you are indeed invincible in battle by all the gods and asuras alike.
Then the god spoke again, his hair standing on end with joy:
"O hero, in combat with weapons, there shall be no one equal to you."
O best of the Kurus, you are always vigilant, skillful, truthful, and have conquered your senses; you are devoted to the Brahmins, skilled in weapons, and a hero.
You have acquired fifteen weapons.
"O Pārtha, by these five methods you have no equal:
O Dhanañjaya, you know the application, the withdrawal, the repetition, the atonement, and the counteraction in every respect."
"O scorcher of foes, this time has arrived for you to fulfill your preceptor’s purpose. Promise that you will do it, and then I shall know what is supreme.
Thereupon, O King, I spoke these words to the king of the gods:
"If it is possible for me to do, know that it is already done.
Then, O King, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra said to me with a smile:
"There is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds today that is impossible for you to accomplish."
The Dānavas named Nivātakavacas, who are my enemies,
dwell in a fortress situated within the depths of the ocean.
They are said to number thirty million, equal in form, strength, and splendor.
"O son of Kuntī, slay them there; it will serve as your teacher’s fee. Then Mātali presented to me a divine chariot of great splendor, yoked with horses whose hair was like that of peacocks.
And he bound this supreme diadem upon my head;
he also gave me body-ornaments resembling his own form,
as well as this impenetrable armor, excellent and pleasant to the touch.
He also fixed this undecaying string upon the Gāṇḍīva bow. Then I set out in that resplendent chariot,
with which the Lord of the Gods formerly conquered Bali, the son of Virocana.
Then, O lord of the people, all the gods were awakened by that sound;
thinking me to be the king of the gods, they gathered around me.
And having seen me, they asked, "What will you do, Phalguna?"
I spoke to them as it truly was: "In this battle, I shall do this;
know, O highly blessed ones, that I am setting forth seeking the slaughter of the Nivātakavacas. O sinless ones, grant me your auspicious blessings."
Then, O lord of the earth, those thirty gods, being pleased, praised me with excellent words, just as they praise the god Purandara;
for by means of this chariot, Maghavan conquered Śambara in battle.
With this chariot, Maghavan conquered Namuci, Bala, Vṛtra, as well as Prahlāda and Naraka, along with many thousands, millions, and hundreds of millions of Daityas in battle.
O Kaunteya, by means of this [conch], you too shall conquer the Nivātakavacas in battle through your prowess, just as the self-controlled Maghavan did in former times;
and this is the most excellent of conchs, by which you shall defeat the Dānavas.
By this [conch], the worlds were conquered even by the high-souled Śakra.
As it was being offered by the gods, I accepted Devadatta, that water-born shell,
for the sake of victory while being praised at that time by the immortals.
Equipped with a conch, armor, and arrows, and grasping my bow, I set out for the most formidable abode of the Dānavas, desiring to fight. Arjuna said:
Then, being praised here and there by the great seers, I beheld the formidable ocean, the imperishable lord of waters;
its waves were foamy, scattered, gathered together, and towering high.
And here waves were seen, like moving mountains;
thousands of ships filled with jewels were there on all sides,
shining as they moved about like celestial chariots in the sky.
Timiṅgila fish, tortoises, as well as timitimiṅgila fish and makaras are seen here, appearing like mountains submerged in water;
and thousands of conch shells are submerged in the waters on all sides.
Just as stars are seen at night when shrouded by thin clouds,
so too did thousands of heaps of jewels float there;
and the wind blew fiercely, and it was like a marvel.
Having crossed that supreme ocean of great velocity,
I beheld nearby that city of the Daityas, teeming with Dānavas.
There, Mātali quickly descended to the surface of the earth.
Then, having firmly grasped that chariot, he who was skilled in the management of chariots rushed forward;
making the city resound with the roar of the chariot, he charged toward it.
And hearing that sound of the chariot, like the thundering of a cloud in the sky—
Thinking me to be the king of the gods, the Dānavas became greatly agitated;
with their minds all bewildered, they stood holding bows and arrows,
as well as spears, swords, axes, maces, and clubs in their hands.
Then the Dānavas, their hearts filled with terror, closed the gates; having established defenses within the city, not a single person could be seen.
Then, taking up the loudly sounding conch Devadatta, he—
Having approached the city of the Asuras, I blew that [conch] slowly. That sound, having struck against the heavens, produced an echo;
and even the greatest beings were terrified and hid themselves away.
Then all the Nivātakavacas, armored on all sides with various protections and holding diverse weapons in their hands,
[advanced] with great iron spears, maces, and even clubs.
O Bhārata, with sharp-edged spears, swords, and chariot wheels,
with *śataghnīs*, *bhuśuṇḍīs*, and various well-adorned scimitars held aloft,
the sons of Diti appeared by the thousands.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, after deliberating in many ways upon the paths for the chariot, Mātali urged those horses forward on level ground;
because they were swift-moving and had been driven by him, they attained great speed.
At that time, I did not see anything at all, and that seemed like a marvel to me.
Then those Dānavas there fiercely urged on their numerous throngs of warriors, all of whom possessed distorted voices and forms.
At that great sound, hundreds of thousands of fish, resembling mountains, leaped into the ocean with their lives departed. Then,
with great speed, the Dānavas rushed toward me.
Releasing sharp arrows by the hundreds and thousands,
O Bhārata, that tumultuous and most terrible battle between them and me proceeded, bringing about the end of the Nivātakavacas.
Then the celestial rishis, the hosts of dānava rishis,
the brahman rishis, and the siddhas all assembled for that great battle.
Desiring victory, they addressed me with appropriate and sweet words.
The sages praised him with words, just as they had praised Indra during the Tārakāmaya war.
Arjuna said:
"Then, O Bhārata, all the Nivātakavacas [rushed] with speed."
Taking up their weapons in battle, those great car-warriors rushed toward me together, shouting as they blocked my path. Surrounding me on all sides, they overwhelmed me with showers of arrows.
Then other Dānavas of great prowess, with spears and battle-axes in their hands, hurled spikes and *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons at me. That immense shower of spikes was thickly crowded with maces and javelins.
Being discharged incessantly by them, they fell upon my chariot;
others, the Nivātakavacas, rushed toward me in battle—
fierce strikers with sharp weapons and arms, terrible in form like Death itself.
With various swift and straight-flying arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva, I struck each one of them with ten in the fray;
they were all turned back by those stone-sharpened shafts discharged by me.
Then, swiftly urged by Mātali, those horses,
possessing the speed of the wind, moved through many chariot-paths there;
well-restrained by Mātali, they crushed the sons of Diti.

A hundred times a hundred bay horses were yoked to that great chariot; then, urged by Mātali, they moved about as if they were few. By the stamping of their hooves and the sound of the chariot wheels, [the earth shook].
By the falling of my arrows, those asuras were slain by the hundreds; likewise, others who still held their bows, their life-breaths departed,
were dragged away there by their horses whose charioteers had been killed.

Those strikers, obstructing all the cardinal and intermediate directions, slaughtered [the enemy] with various weapons; therefore, my mind was distressed. Then I beheld the most wonderful prowess of Mātali.
Since he held back those swift horses so effortlessly,
O King, I then cut down those Asuras in battle— along with their weapons— by the hundreds and thousands with light and variegated missiles.
O slayer of enemies, as I moved there with every effort in this manner,
Mātali, the heroic charioteer of Śakra, became filled with joy.
Then, those [demons] were struck down by those horses and by that chariot.
Some went to their destruction, while others retreated;
as if vying with us in battle,
the Nivātakavacas obstructed me from all sides with great showers of arrows.

Having struck them down with the force of arrows, I pierced those thousands with supreme, blazing, and swift weapons capable of neutralizing shafts. Then, with light and variegated arrows consecrated by the Brahmā-weapon, I [struck them].
I swiftly struck them down with arrows by the hundreds and thousands.
Then, being thus oppressed, those great asuras, possessed by fury,
together assailed me with showers of arrows, spears, and swords.
Then, O Bhārata, I invoked that supreme weapon of fierce energy, beloved by the King of the Gods, named Mādhava. Thereupon,
[he discharged] thousands of swords, tridents, and javelins.
With the power of my weapons, I cut those [missiles] into a hundred pieces as they were released by them; having severed their weapons,
I then pierced all of them from every side with ten arrows each out of rage.
For from the Gāṇḍīva bow in that battle, arrows issued forth like swarms of bees; Mātali marveled at them.
And those arrows of his, due to their great number, were like locusts.
They powerfully showered me with [missiles], but I dispersed them with my own arrows. Then,
being struck, those Nivātakavacas again surrounded me on all sides with great showers of arrows.
Having struck down their arrow-velocities with my own weapons that destroy arrows, I pierced them by the thousands with blazing, supreme, and swift shafts;
their severed limbs began to shed blood.
Like the peaks of mountains excessively rained upon during the monsoon,
those Dānavas, being struck by my swift, straight-flying arrows whose touch was like Indra’s thunderbolt, became utterly agitated.
With their bodies and entrails split into a hundred pieces and the power of their weapons exhausted,
the Nivātakavacas then fought me with illusory powers (māyā).
Arjuna said:
Then a truly massive shower of stones appeared from all sides;
consisting of trees as large as mountains and most terrifying, it oppressed me severely.
Thereupon, with arrows resembling thunderbolts, impelled by the weapon of Indra, I [countered it].
In the battle, I pulverized each one of them into a hundred pieces with my swift [arrows].
As that shower of stones was being crushed, fire was produced;
there, the stone-dust fell like masses of flame.
Then, with the Vāruṇa weapon, I shattered that shower of stones. When the shower of stones had been destroyed, a much greater shower of water appeared before me in streams as thick as axles.
Thousands of streams of water, falling from the sky with fierce power,
completely enveloped the firmament, the cardinal directions, and the intermediate quarters. By the falling of these torrents and by the roar of the wind, [the world was overwhelmed].
Due to the roaring of the Daityas, nothing could be discerned at all. The torrents of rain, joined together in the sky and upon the earth in every direction,
bewildered me as they fell incessantly upon the ground.

There, I discharged that blazing and terrible divine weapon, the Viśoṣaṇa, taught by Indra; by it, that water was dried up. When the shower of stones had been struck down by me and the shower of water dried up, [the battle continued].
O giver of honor, the Dānavas released illusions of fire and wind.
Then, I extinguished the fire on all sides with the water-weapon (*salilāstra*),
and I restrained the force of the wind with the great mountain-weapon (*śailāstra*).
When she had been repelled, O Bhārata, the Dānavas, intoxicated by battle, simultaneously unleashed various illusions. Then there appeared a massive, hair-raising rain.
That illusory rain, consisting of weapons of terrible form— of fire, wind, and likewise stones— afflicted me in battle; then,
a fierce and intense darkness appeared on all sides.
When the world was shrouded by a terrible and harsh darkness,
the horses turned away from their course and Mātali stumbled;
the golden whip fell from his hand onto the ground.
O bull of the Bharatas, being terrified, he repeatedly asked me, "Where are you?
While he was thus deprived of his senses, a sharp fear entered me;
and he, too, being devoid of knowledge and trembling, spoke this to me.

O Pārtha, O sinless one, in ancient times there occurred a truly great battle between the Suras and the Asuras for the sake of the nectar of immortality, and that was witnessed by me. Furthermore, a truly great battle took place at the slaying of Śambara.
There too, I performed the duty of charioteer for the King of the Gods;
likewise, during the slaying of Vṛtra, the horses were guided by me.
And I also witnessed the most terrible battle with the son of Virocana.
O Pāṇḍava, I have also witnessed these and other most terrible battles involving Bala, Prajñāda,
and others; yet, O Pāṇḍava, I have never before been devoid of knowledge.
"The destruction of living beings has certainly been ordained by the Grandfather;
for this war is not appropriate except for the dissolution of the world.
Having heard those words of his, he steadied himself by means of his own self.
Desiring to bewilder the illusory power of the Dānavas,
I spoke to the terrified Mātali: "Behold the strength of my arms,
the power of my weapons, and the might of my bow Gāṇḍīva."
"Today, by means of the illusion of my weapon, I shall destroy this most terrible illusion and that fierce darkness; do not fear, O charioteer, remain firm.
Having spoken thus, O lord of men, I unleashed the illusion of my weapon.
For the benefit of the inhabitants of heaven, that [weapon] was the deluder of all enemies;
yet when those various illusions were being suppressed, the lords of the Asuras,
possessed of immeasurable power, again created many kinds of illusions.
Again it became light, and again it was swallowed by darkness;
the world vanished from sight and again sank into the waters. When light returned, Mātali [drove] with the well-restrained bay horses.
He moved about with his preeminent chariot in that hair-raising battle.
Then the fierce Nivātakavacas rushed toward me;
seeing an opening, I dispatched them to the abode of Yama.
Likewise, because of the weakness of humans, the great Asuras disregarded the city's invulnerability to the gods and its very impenetrability;
thus it remained during that battle which brought an end to the Nivātakavacas.
I could not suddenly see all those Dānavas, for they were shrouded by illusion.
Arjuna said:
"Those Daityas fought me while remaining invisible through their illusory power."
By the power of my weapons, I fought even those who were invisible;
arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva, properly impelled by mantras,
severed their heads wherever they might be.
Then, being slain by me in battle, the Nivātakavacas suddenly withdrew their illusions and entered their own city. When the Daityas had retreated and visibility was restored, [the gods rejoiced].
There I saw Danavas slain by the hundreds of thousands;
their weapons and ornaments were crushed to pieces there,
and their limbs and armor lay scattered in heaps.
There was no space for the horses to move even a single step;
suddenly leaping up, they then remained suspended, traveling through the intermediate space.
Then the Nivātakavacas completely covered the sky.
For invisible, they rushed forward, hurling masses of rock;
others, having gone beneath the earth, O Bhārata, seized the feet of the horses and the wheels of the chariots— those terrible Dānavas.
Restraining my two bay horses while I was fighting,
they covered me and my chariot on all sides with mountain peaks— some being piled up and others falling down.
That region where we were situated became like a cave,
as it was covered by mountains and because my horses had been brought under control;
I experienced the utmost distress, which Mātali perceived.
Perceiving that I was afraid, he spoke these words:
"Arjuna, Arjuna, do not fear; discharge the thunderbolt weapon.
Then, having heard those words of his, I discharged the thunderbolt.

O lord of men, having reached an immovable position and consecrated the *gāṇḍīva* bow with mantras, I released iron arrows, sharpened and possessing the touch of a thunderbolt, which were the beloved weapon of the king of the gods.
Then all those illusions and those Nivātakavacas were entered by those arrows, impelled by the thunderbolt and having become like thunderbolts themselves.
Struck by the force of the thunderbolts, those Dānavas resembled mountains.
Embracing one another, they fell upon the surface of the earth;
but those Dānavas who had seized the chariot horses within the ground,
the arrows, having entered them, dispatched to the abode of Yama.
With the slain Nivātakavacas cast down like mountains,
that region was completely covered as if by scattered peaks.
There was no injury whatsoever to the horses, nor to the chariot, nor to Mātali.
And that was seen by me then; it was like a marvel.
Then, O King, Mātali, smiling, addressed me:
"O Arjuna, this prowess which is observed in you is not found even among the gods."
When the hosts of asuras had been slain, their wives everywhere in that city wailed like female cranes in autumn. Then,
together with Mātali, I entered that city.
Terrifying the wives of the Nivātakavacas with the roar of his chariot,
he saw those ten thousand horses resembling peacocks and that chariot radiant as the sun; then the women fled away in crowds.

The sound produced by those ornaments as they were shaken by the terrified women was then like the sound of rocks falling upon mountains. Then those Daitya women, seized with fear, entered their own dwellings.
Adorned with many jewels and made of gold,
I beheld that supreme city of wondrous appearance; then,
seeing it to be more distinguished than the city of the gods, I questioned Mātali.
"Why do the deities not enter such a place as this? I perceive that it is indeed superior to the city of Purandara.
Mātali said:
"O Pārtha, in ancient times this city of ours belonged to the king of the gods. Then the gods were driven away from here by the Nivātakavacas.
Having performed intense and great penance, they propitiated the Grandfather."
"This has been chosen as a dwelling place, and there shall be safety from the gods in battle.
Then the Blessed One, the Self-Existent, was urged by Śakra:
"May the Blessed One ordain this, out of a desire for his own welfare."
Then the Blessed One said to Vāsava,
"O slayer of Vṛtra, it has been ordained that you yourself shall be the end of these, though by another body.
Thereupon, for the sake of their slaughter, Śakra gave his weapons to you.
"Indeed, those who have been slain by you could not have been killed even by the gods;
rather, through the transformation of Time, you, O Bhārata,
arrived here as their bringer of death, and thus it was accomplished by you."
"O Indra among men, Mahendra has caused you to receive that supreme and great power of mighty weapons for the sake of destroying the Dānavas. Arjuna said:
Then, having entered the city and slain those Dānavas,
I returned once more with Mātali to that abode of the gods.
Arjuna said:
As I was returning, I then beheld another great city, divine and moving at will, with a splendor equal to fire and the sun;
it was adorned with trees made of jewels and with brilliant, beautiful birds.
It was inhabited by the Paulomas and Kālakeyas, who were ever-rejoicing;
it was equipped with gate-towers and watchtowers, possessed four gates, and was difficult to assail.
Made of every kind of jewel, it was divine and its appearance was like a marvel.
It was surrounded by trees endowed with flowers and fruits, made of divine jewels; likewise, it was filled with celestial birds that were most enchanting,
and with Asuras who were ever-joyful, armed with spears, lances, and clubs.
Surrounded on all sides by those wearing garlands and holding bows and mallets in their hands, I beheld that city of the Daityas, wondrous to behold; and seeing it,
O King, I asked Mātali, "What is this that is seen?"
Mātali said:
"The daughter of the Daityas named Pulomā and the great Asurī Kālakā performed supreme austerities for a thousand divine years."

At the conclusion of their ascetic penance, Svayambhū then granted a boon to the two of them. They chose as their boon, O king of kings, that their sons should experience little suffering and be incapable of being slain by gods, *rākṣasas*, or *pannagas*.
This city is delightful, moving through the sky, and radiant with the merit of its makers;
it is endowed with all kinds of jewels and is unassailable even by the immortals,
along with their hosts of yakṣas, gandharvas, pannagas, asuras, and rākṣasas.
O best of the Bharatas, this divine celestial chariot, endowed with all objects of desire, free from sorrow and disease, was created by Brahmā for the sake of the Kālakeyas;
it moves through the sky, devoid of any immortals.
O hero, that great city known as Hiraṇyapura is inhabited by the Kālakeyas and the Pauloma Dānavas;
it is guarded by the great Asuras, the Kālakeyas and the Paulomas.
O King of kings, O Dhanañjaya, these Dānavas— who are always joyful, incapable of being slain by any of the gods, and who dwell here free from anxiety and desire—
are invincible even by the Suras and Asuras.

"Human death was ordained for them by Brahmā in the past. O Pārtha, even these Kālakañjas, who are difficult to approach and possessed of great strength, you must swiftly bring to destruction in battle with the Vajra weapon."
Arjuna said:
"O Lord, having learned that they were incapable of being slain by either gods or asuras, I then spoke joyfully to Mātali: 'Go straight to this city.'"
"Until I bring about the destruction of the enemies of the Lord of the Thirty-three with my weapons— indeed, there are no wicked haters of the gods who are not to be slain by me"—
he then quickly bore me near to Hiraṇyapura.
On that divine chariot yoked with tawny horses, Mātali [approached];
and those Daityas, adorned with various ornaments and garments, seeing me,
rushed forward with great speed, mounted on their chariots and clad in armor.
Then the lords of the Dānavas, enraged and possessed of fierce prowess, struck me with *nālīka*, *nārāca*, *bhalla*, *śakti*, *ṛṣṭi*, and *tomara* weapons; I,
for my part, warded off that great rain of missiles with a mighty shower of my own.
O King, relying on the power of his knowledge, he unleashed a great rain of weapons;
moving through the battlefields of the chariots, he threw them all into confusion,
so that those Dānavas, utterly bewildered, began striking one another down.
As they were thus bewildered and rushing at one another, I struck off their heads by the hundreds with my flaming arrows. Being slaughtered, those Daityas then took refuge once more in that city.
Resorting to a demonic illusion, they leapt into the sky along with their cities;
then, with a great shower of arrows,
I blocked their path and obstructed the movement of those Daityas.

That divine city, moving through the air, capable of going anywhere at will, and possessing celestial splendor, was maintained by the sons of Diti according to their pleasure through the granting of a boon;
having descended into the interior of the earth, it would rise up once again.
Again he quickly moved sideways and again plunged into the waters;
that city, resembling Amarāvatī, could travel at will,
O lord of men, and I countered it with various kinds of weapons.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, with a net of arrows and by means of divine weapons, I checked that city along with the Daityas;
it was mangled by my straight-flying iron shafts.
O King, he fell upon the great city of the Asuras, which had been shattered;
struck by my iron arrows, swift as thunderbolts,
those Asuras, impelled by Time, wandered about in confusion, O King.
Then Mātali, as if falling swiftly from the front,
quickly descended to the earth with that chariot possessing the splendor of the sun.
Then sixty thousand chariots belonging to those indignant warriors [followed].
O Bhārata, those who desired to fight with me turned back against me;
I struck them down with sharpened arrows feathered with vulture plumes,
and they retreated in battle like the waves of the ocean.
Reflecting that these could not be overcome by human combat,
I then employed all my weapons in succession;
thereafter, those thousands of chariot-warriors who fought with diverse skills—
My divine weapons struck back as if with ease,
while those great car-warriors, moving along various chariot-paths,
were seen by the hundreds and thousands in that battle.
Wearing variegated crests and head-ornaments, with diverse armor and banners,
and adorned with various jewels, they truly gladden my heart. But I, in battle, [shall overcome] them with showers of arrows discharged by means of celestial weapons.
I was unable to cause them pain,
yet they afflicted me; being tormented by those many who were skilled in weapons and proficient in battle, I was distressed in that great conflict, and a great fear came upon me.
Then, utterly exhausted, I questioned Mātali:
"Why are these [demons] not slain by my floods of arrows, consecrated with divine mantras and most terrible? Tell me the truth as I ask you."
He said to me, "O bull of the Bharatas, you are a match for them;
therefore, aiming at their vital points, strike them down.
Having heard this, O king of kings, I was greatly delighted and spoke to him.
"Turn back the chariot quickly and behold these who have been struck down.
Thus addressed, Mātali turned the chariot there;
then, perceiving that they were broken in battle, the Dānavas were filled with joy.
Then, O Great King, they cried out with a loud voice in groups:
"This Pāṇḍava has not been broken by anyone at the forefront of battle;
he has been broken by us in combat! Thus did they speak then.
Then, having become self-restrained and bowing down in the battle, I paid homage to Rudra, the god of gods; and having offered salutations to that Great Soul and said,
"May there be well-being for all beings," I invoked the great weapon.
Then I beheld that divine Pāśupata weapon, known as Raudra, which destroys all enemies and is honored by all the worlds;
[I beheld] from it a three-headed man with nine eyes.
Three-faced and six-armed, blazing with hair like the fire of the sun,
with his head adorned by great serpents licking [his face], O slayer of enemies,
he is the god who has compassion for his devotees and wears a serpent as a sacred thread.
Then, O bull of the Bharata race, having seen that terrible, fierce, and eternal weapon [of Rudra] joined with the Gāṇḍīva bow,
he paid homage to the three-eyed Śarva of immeasurable splendor.

O Bhārata, he released it for the sake of the defeat of the lords of the Dānavas. As soon as it was released, O lord of the people, there appeared by the thousands the forms of deer, lions, and tigers.
Of bears, buffaloes, and serpents, as well as of cows,
elephants, sṛmaras, and śarabhas in every respect,
and likewise of bulls, boars, and cats.
Of those with the faces of bears, horses, and rams, as well as of owls; of those having the forms of fish and crows, moving about with various faces;
and of jackals, *pretas*, and *bhuruṇḍas* in their entirety.
Of leaping tigers, boars, and śarabhas;
likewise of vultures, garuḍas, and crocodiles;
and similarly of trees, mountains, and oceans.

In battle, [he encountered] the gods, the ṛṣis, and the gandharvas in their entirety; likewise the piśācas together with the yakṣas, as well as the enemies of the gods (asuras), the guhyakas, and the nairṛtas.
Of the fish-faced and elephant-faced beings, as well as the owls;
of the multitudes of fish and tortoises with various weapons and swords in their hands;
and likewise of the *yātudhānas* bearing clubs and mallets.
With these and many others assuming various forms,
the entire world was pervaded when that weapon was released—
beings with three heads, four tusks, four faces, and four arms.
Those assembled Dānavas were repeatedly struck by [beings] endowed with many forms, who consume flesh, fat, and marrow,
and possess the brilliance of the blazing sun and the splendor of the thunderbolt and lightning.

O Bhārata, with other arrows made of the essence of stone that tear asunder enemies, I struck down all the Dānavas in a mere moment. Driven away by the weapons of the Gāṇḍīva, they fell from the sky, their lives departed.
Having seen this, I bowed again to the Creator, the slayer of Tripura;
and having observed those adorned with divine ornaments crushed by the Raudra weapon,
the charioteer of the gods attained supreme joy.
"That deed you have performed is unbearable, difficult even for the gods to approach;
seeing it, Mātali, the charioteer of Śakra, honored me.
And with palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words, being filled with joy."
Seeing those thousands of Dānavas slain by me in battle, [I thought: "Indeed, this deed which has been accomplished by you is unbearable even for the gods and asuras;
for even the Lord of the Gods would not be able to perform such a feat in combat."
"O Dhanañjaya, Śakra was surely pleased with you long ago, O destroyer of cities! For this great celestial city, which could not be slain by gods or asuras,
has been shattered by you, O hero, through the power of your own prowess, weapons, and asceticism."
Then, when that city had been destroyed and the Dānavas slain,
all the women rushed out from the city, wailing aloud;
with their hair disheveled, they were distressed and sorrowful like female ospreys.
Screaming like female ospreys, distressed and crying out again and again,
they fell upon the earth mourning their sons, fathers, and brothers;
weeping with piteous voices, they wailed, now deprived of their lords.

Striking their breasts with their hands, their garlands and ornaments fallen away, that city of the Dānavas— filled with grief, shorn of its splendor, and overwhelmed by sorrow and dejection— did not shine, its luster destroyed and its lord slain.
The city became invisible, appearing like a city of Gandharvas, like a lake whose serpents have been slain, or like a forest of withered trees;
yet Mātali swiftly brought me there with a joyful heart.
Having destroyed Hiraṇyapura, the abode of the king of the gods, which had been prepared for battle, and having slain the great Asuras as well as the Nivātakavacas,
I then returned to Śakra.
O Lord of the Gods, O one of great splendor, Mātali recounted all my deeds in detail exactly as they had occurred:
the destruction of Hiraṇyapura and the neutralization of the illusions.
And the slaughter in battle of the mighty Nivātakavacas,
as well as the wondrous and hair-raising destruction of the Kālakeyas—
having heard of that, the blessed thousand-eyed Purandara was delighted.
Accompanied by the Maruts, the glorious one then exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
Having embraced me with affection and smelled the crown of my head with a smile, the king of the gods then comforted me again and again.
Together with the gods, he spoke these very sweet words:
"O Pārtha, you have performed this deed in battle that surpasses both gods and asuras; and by slaying my enemies, O son of Pṛthā, you have accomplished a great service for your preceptor."

In this very way, O Dhanañjaya, you must always remain steadfast in battle; with an undeluded mind, you must employ your weapons. For in combat, you are indeed invincible to gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas alike.

O son of Kuntī, the righteous-souled Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, shall rule the earth— which has been conquered by the strength of your arms— along with its hosts of Yakṣas, Asuras, Gandharvas, flocks of birds, and serpents.
Arjuna said: Then,
having shown me favor, the king of the gods spoke these words at that time to me, who was full of confidence and whose arrow wounds had healed.
"O Bhārata, all divine weapons abide within you;
no human on earth is capable of overcoming you—
not Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, or Śakuni, together with the kings."
"O son, when you stand in the midst of battle, all others are not worth even a sixteenth part of you.
Furthermore, the lord Maghavan gave me this body-protecting,
impenetrable divine armor and a golden garland."
And the god gave me the conch Devadatta, which produces a great sound;
and Indra himself placed this divine diadem upon my head.
Then [he gave] divine garments and divine ornaments.
"Śakra gave these radiant and magnificent [garments] to me.
Thus honored there, O King, I dwelt happily in the sacred abode of Indra together with the young Gandharvas."
Then Śakra, together with the immortals, spoke to me with affection:
"O Arjuna, it is time for you to depart, for your brothers are indeed remembering you.
Thus, O Bhārata, five years passed in the abode of Indra.
"O King, remembering the strife born of the gambling match, I lived there;
then, having reached Gandhamādana, I beheld you upon the summit of this mountain, surrounded by your brothers."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By good fortune, O Bhārata, you have obtained the weapons of Dhanañjaya;
by good fortune, you have propitiated the King, the Lord and Master of the gods."

"By good fortune, O scorcher of foes, the Blessed Lord Sthāṇu has been seen by you in person along with the Goddess; and by good fortune, O sinless one, he has been gratified by you through fair combat.
And by good fortune, O bull of the Bharatas, you have been reunited with the world-protectors."
"By good fortune we all prosper; by good fortune you have returned!
Today, O son of Kuntī, I behold this entire goddess-like earth, garlanded with cities, conquered and restored to me by you."
I consider even the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra to have been brought under your control;
yet, O Bhārata, I desire to see those divine weapons with which you thus slew the heroic Nivātakavacas.
"Mahābala and Mahāmāyā were both struck down by him alone in battle.
Arjuna said:
"Tomorrow at dawn, you shall behold all his divine weapons in their entirety."
"The terrible Nivātakavacas, by whom I was struck down, have been slain by me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus related his arrival there, Dhanañjaya—
Accompanied by all his brothers, he spent that night there.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When that night had passed, the righteous King Yudhiṣṭhira—
Having risen, he performed his necessary duties together with his brothers.
Then he urged Arjuna, the delighter of his brothers, saying:
"O son of Kuntī, display those weapons by which the Dānavas were conquered by you."
Then, O King, Dhananjaya the Pandava,
possessed of great splendor and established in supreme purity, displayed those divine weapons given by the gods according to the prescribed rule, O Bharata.

Having paid homage to the three-eyed god and to Vāsava, the son of Pāṇḍu, Dhananjaya, resplendent, mounted his royal chariot— which had mountain-peaks for its pole-tips, trees for its side-ornaments, beautiful bamboo poles, and triple bamboo shafts.
Then, well-armored with that resplendent coat of mail,
the mighty-armed son of Kuntī took up the bow Gāṇḍīva and the water-born conch Devadatta, shining brilliantly as he proceeded in due order.
He proceeded to display those divine weapons.
Then, as he was about to employ those divine weapons,
the earth, being trodden by his feet, trembled along with its trees.
The rivers were agitated, as was the great ocean;
even the mountains crumbled, and the wind ceased to blow.
The thousand-rayed sun did not shine, and the fire did not blaze.
The Vedas did not manifest in any way for the twice-born. And those creatures who had gone beneath the earth, O Janamejaya,
rising up while being oppressed, surrounded the Pāṇḍava.
Trembling with their palms joined in reverence and their faces covered, they all,
being scorched by those various weapons, then entreated Dhanañjaya.
Then the Brahman-sages, the Siddhas, and the celestial rishis likewise [praised him].
All mobile beings stood still,
as did the preeminent royal sages, the denizens of heaven,
the yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and likewise the birds.
And all the beings who move through the sky remained there.
Then the Grandfather (Brahmā), all the world-protectors,
and the Blessed Mahādeva together with his attendants, arrived at that place.
Then, O Great King, the wind scattered various divine and fragrant garlands all around the Pāṇḍavas from every side;
and the Gandharvas, impelled by the gods, sang diverse songs.
O King, throngs of Apsarases danced in groups,
and delightful, sweet celestial instruments were played.
At that tumultuous time, Nārada, impelled by the gods, [arrived].
Having approached Pārtha, O King, he spoke these words worthy of being heard:
"Arjuna, Arjuna, do not employ the divine weapons, O Bhārata;
these are never to be used against one who lacks a basis."
Then that great-souled one of purified intellect made this earnest request to the best of mountain lords:
"One who is not afflicted by distress should never employ a spell of empowerment."
O descendant of Kuru, there is indeed a very great fault in the improper employment of these weapons. O Dhanañjaya, if they are guarded according to the traditional precepts,
they will undoubtedly become powerful and bring you happiness.
O Pāṇḍava, O Ajātaśatru, if these [weapons] were left unprotected, they would lead even the three worlds to destruction; do not act thus ever again,
for you shall behold them in the midst of battle.
As these were being employed by Pārtha for the destruction of his enemies,
all the gods and others who had gathered there, O bull among men, then turned back from Pārtha and departed as they had come.
O descendant of Kuru, when all those [ascetics] had departed, the Pāṇḍavas dwelt joyfully in that very forest together with Kṛṣṇā. Janamejaya said:
When that foremost of chariot-warriors had returned from the abode of the slayer of Vṛtra, having acquired the celestial weapons—
what did the sons of Pṛthā do after that?
Having met with the heroic Dhanañjaya,
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Those lords of men remained in those very forests;"
Together with Arjuna, who was equal to Indra,
those heroes sported upon that most excellent and beautiful mountain, having gone to the pleasure-garden of the Lord of Wealth.
Beholding those peerless dwellings and pleasure groves surrounded by various trees,
the king of men, armed with his bow, roamed about in many ways.
Thus the diadem-wearing Arjuna remained constantly vigilant regarding his celestial weapons;
meanwhile, the sons of the king of men obtained their residence through the grace of King Vaiśravaṇa.
O King, they did not envy living beings,
and that time became auspicious for them as they stayed together with Pārtha for a single night.
They dwelt there for four years,
and those previous six, making ten years in total; these passed auspiciously for the Pāṇḍavas as they lived in the forests.
Then the impetuous son of Vāyu and Jiṣṇu,
having sat down beside the king,
as did the two heroic twins who were like the king of the gods, spoke.
O King of the Kurus, staying in seclusion, we desire to make your promise true— both for your benefit and your pleasure—
and to do what is dear to you.
Therefore, let us abandon the forests and pursue Suyodhana along with his followers to slay him;
we have now completed this eleventh year of our exile.
Having deceived that Suyodhana, who is of base intellect and character, we— who deserve happiness but have been deprived of it by him—
shall attain a life of ease during our period of living incognito.
O King, by your command, they roam the forests free from fear, having cast aside their pride;
they have been captivated by living in your proximity.
Having spent that year in secret, they will not know us to be in a remote place;
thus we may rescue that lowest of men in comfort.
Having returned the enmity, along with its fruit and its flowers,
to that Suyodhana, the lowest of men and lord of men, who is surrounded by his followers;
Therefore, O Dharmarāja, take this earth; for those who roam upon this mountain that resembles heaven,
O god among men, it is possible to dispel their sorrow.
And your merit-scented fame, O Bhārata,
would perish throughout the worlds of mobile and immobile beings,
had you obtained that kingdom of the bulls among the Kurus.
Great things can indeed be achieved through ritual action,
O lord of men; yet this which you receive from Kubera can be attained by you constantly.
"O Bhārata, set your mind upon the slaughter of your enemies and the suppression of those who have committed offenses;
O King, their fierce energy would not withstand yours."
Even if Vajrapāṇi were to meet them face to face,
those two would never feel any distress; nor would Dharmarāja, even if he were to encounter the gods themselves.
Both he who has Garuda as his emblem and the grandson of Śini have exerted themselves for the sake of accomplishing your purpose;
indeed, they are both matchless in strength, just like Kṛṣṇa.
In the same way, O King, that hero of the Śinis set out for the sake of accomplishing your purpose,
just as Kṛṣṇa did with those Yādavas.
In the same way, O best of gods among men, we two and the two heroic twins, skilled in their application,
have made our primary effort toward achieving your purpose.
"Having encountered the enemies, we shall make them equal.
Then, having understood their intention, that high-souled and most excellent son of Dharma [Yudhiṣṭhira]—
He who knew the meaning of dharma and possessed supreme vigor performed a circumambulation of the abode of Vaiśravaṇa,
bidding farewell to his dwellings, rivers, and lakes.
And Dharmarāja, observing the path by which all the *rakṣasas* had come,
gazed once more toward the mountain.
Having completed his duties, accompanied by his friends,
and having conquered his enemies and regained his kingdom,
O Lord of Mountains, he once again fixed his soul upon asceticism.
"I am your beholder," he thought;
then the lord of the Kurus, surrounded by all his younger brothers and the twice-born, proceeded by that very same path.
And Ghaṭotkaca likewise carried them along with their attendants through mountain cascades; then,
as they set out, the great ṛṣi was filled with joy.
Having instructed all his sons like a father,
Lomaśa, with a joyful mind, departed for the most holy abode of the celestial dwellers.
Instructed by him and by Arṣṭiṣeṇa,
the sons of Pṛthā visited delightful sacred fords, penance groves, and other great lakes.
Beholding it, those foremost of men proceeded toward the best of mountains, which was endowed with cascading springs.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"The best of mountains, possessed of flowing waterfalls;"
As they abandoned their pleasant dwellings along with the elephants of the quarters, the kinnaras, and the birds,
those bulls of the Bharata race felt no joy.
Then,
upon beholding Kailāsa, beloved by Kubera, a great joy once again arose among those bulls of the Bharata race.
He saw mountain ranges shining like clouds,
lofty elevations obstructing the mountains,
cow-pens of the peaks, and rows of mountain-dams.
Having observed many precipices here and there, as well as high ground and low ground, and likewise other great forests, the heroes [proceeded].
Beholding those places frequented by deer, birds, and elephants,
those foremost of men— archers bearing swords— advanced with joyful hearts.
Delightful forests, lakes, rivers,
mountain caves, and mountain recesses—
these were their constant dwellings.
Having dwelt for many nights in that difficult place, those bulls among men reached Kailāsa, which is of inconceivable form.
They reached that most delightful and preeminent hermitage of Vṛṣaparvan;
having come together with King Vṛṣaparvan, they...
Honored by him and freed from delusion, they related in detail their journey, reporting everything concerning Vṛṣaparvan exactly as it had occurred.
Having stayed there for one night in that holy hermitage frequented by gods and great seers,
they proceeded toward the vast Badarī.
Then those heroes of great majesty, the foremost of men who had attained the state of Nārāyaṇa, dwelt there once again in comfort.
Free from sorrow, they beheld the lotus-lake beloved by Kubera, frequented by gods and *siddhas*;
and having seen that lotus-lake, they were freed from grief.
The sons of Pāṇḍu, the foremost heroes among all men,
rejoiced upon reaching that dwelling in Nandana,
just like fearless sages of the twice-born.
Then those heroes among men,
having spent a month happily at Badarī, all returned together by the very same path by which they had come.
[He conquered] the territory of Subāhu, the Kirāta king,
as well as the Cīnas, Tukhāras, Daradas, and Sadarvas; and the lands of Kuṇinda, abounding in many jewels.
Having crossed the difficult region of the Himalayas,
those heroes among men beheld the city of Subāhu;
and having heard that the sons and grandsons of kings had arrived there.
When Subāhu arrived with his entire retinue within the kingdom,
that king went out to meet him filled with joy; and the bulls among the Kurus greeted him with welcome.
Having met with King Subāhu,
they were joined by all the charioteers headed by Viśoka,
as well as Indrasena and the attendants.
Those who were stationed in the kitchen under the supervision of the cooks stayed there for one night in comfort,
taking with them the charioteers and all the chariots.
Having dismissed Ghaṭotkaca along with his followers,
they then proceeded toward the king of mountains by the Yamunā; on that mountain, which was rich in springs, they stayed.
Having reached the sacrificial post at Viśākha on the mountain peak, which was pale red like the dawn and covered with fine woolen cloths, those heroes among men then made their dwelling there.
Having traveled safely through that great forest, which resembled the Caitraratha grove and was frequented by boars, deer, and birds,
those who were devoted to hunting proceeded on.
They spent a year wandering there in that forest.
There they encountered a serpent of exceeding strength,
afflicted by hunger and possessing a form as terrible as Death itself.
Vṛkodara, his inner soul afflicted by despair, delusion, and pain within a mountain cave,
became the island of refuge for Vṛkodara.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the best among the upholders of dharma and possessed of infinite splendor, liberated him whose every limb was encircled by a crocodile.
Then, as the twelfth year approached,
the Kurus were eager to roam in the forest;
from that grove, which was as radiant as Caitraratha.
Blazing with splendor and endowed with ascetic power,
they then departed for the vicinity of the desert,
being ever devoted primarily to the delight of the science of archery.
Having reached the Sarasvatī, they desired to dwell there;
from that lake, they proceeded toward the Dvaitavana forest. Seeing them settled in the Dvaitavana, [the sages approached].

Then the residents there, endowed with austerity, self-restraint, right conduct, and meditative concentration— those who carried grass and water vessels and used stone mortars for grinding— approached him.
Plakṣas, akṣas, rohitakas, and vetasas; snuhās, badaris, khadiras, and śirīṣas; bilvas, iṅgudas, pīlus, śamīs, and karīras.
Growing on the banks of the Sarasvatī,
they became like sacrificial offerings for the deities, beloved by yakṣas, gandharvas, and great ṛṣis.
Moving along the Sarasvatī filled with joy,
the sons of the god-like king sported happily.
Janamejaya said:
O Sage, how did the immensely powerful Bhīmasena, who possessed the strength of ten thousand elephants and,
proud of his might, had challenged the son of Pulastya, the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), to battle, experience such intense fear from that python?
Having caused the slaughter of the foremost Yakṣas and Rākṣasas in the Nalinī grove,
you speak of that crusher of foes as being overcome by fear and fallen into distress;
I wish to hear this, for my curiosity is indeed great.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, while those fierce bowmen were dwelling in that forest of many wonders,
they arrived at the hermitage of the royal seer Vṛṣaparvan.
By chance, Vṛkodara, bow in hand and with his sword girded,
beheld that delightful forest frequented by gods and Gandharvas;
he then saw the auspicious regions of the Himavat mountain.
[He saw] those [forests] frequented by celestial rishis and siddhas, served by throngs of apsaras,
and resonating here and there with the cries of cakoras, cakravākas, jīvajīvaka birds, cuckoos, and bhṛṅgarājas.

Beholding mountain rivers filled with trees that always bore flowers and fruit, tender to the touch like snow, providing abundant shade, and delighting the mind and the eye— rivers resembling lapis lazuli gems.
With waters cool to the touch like snow and teeming with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks,
the forests of *devadāru* trees— interspersed with yellow sandalwood and towering *kālīyaka*— resemble the snares of the clouds.
Pursuing the hunt across level lands and desert wastes,
that one of great strength moved about, piercing wild animals with his pure arrows.
Bhīmasena, however, by his might, [seized] a large fanged beast of renown.
In that forest,
the mighty-armed Bhīma of terrible prowess, possessing the strength of a hundred elephants, slaughtered deer, boars, and buffaloes here and there.
Possessing the strength of a hundred elephants and the endurance of a hundred men,
with the prowess of a lion or a tiger, that one of great power uprooted and violently shattered the trees in that forest.
Making the regions of the earth and the forests resound,
crushing the mountain peaks and roaring free from fever,
he even uprooted trees and filled the entire world with his roar.

Then Bhimasena, whose pride had long been nurtured in the forest, fell down with great force again and again, yet remained undaunted, slapping his arms, shouting his war-cries, and clapping his hands.
The great elephants and the mighty lions,
out of fear, abandoned their caves at the roar of Bhīmasena;
some were running here and there, some stood still, and others sat down.
Seeking deer, he roamed fearlessly through that most terrible forest;
there, that tiger among men, Bhimasena of great strength, moved about on foot like a forest-dweller.
Having entered the great forest, he of great being and prowess uttered wonderful roars, terrifying all living creatures. Then,
by that terrifying sound, the serpents dwelling in their caves were struck with fear.
Having been overtaken by speed, he proceeded slowly in pursuit;
then the mighty Bhīmasena, resembling the foremost of the immortals,
beheld a massive, hair-raising serpent.
Having entered a mountain fastness, he had blocked the cave with his body;
his stature was as vast as a mountain range, his coils were like the orbs of the sun and moon,
his limbs were variegated with diverse skins, and his complexion was like turmeric.
With a cavernous mouth, four tusks,
and gleaming, intensely copper-colored eyes, he repeatedly licked the corners of his mouth;
terrifying to all beings, he resembled Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time.
Standing there as if threatening with the sound of his hissing and roar,
a hungry python, a serpent-like predator, suddenly approached Bhīma and seized him by both arms with force.
As soon as Bhīmasena was touched by him,
his consciousness suddenly failed due to the power of that boon;
for the strength he possessed was equal to that of ten thousand elephants.
That strength of Bhīmasena’s arms was unequaled by any foes; yet,
having been thus subdued by that serpent,
the radiant Bhīma, quivering slowly, was unable to move.
Possessing the strength of ten thousand elephants, with the shoulders of a lion and mighty arms, he was seized;
yet, deluded by the granting of a boon, he abandoned his courage.
For he exerted himself with intense effort to liberate himself.
And that hero was not able to resist him in any way.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus the radiant Bhīmasena fell under the power of the serpent.

He reflected upon the serpent’s exceedingly wonderful and great power, and said to the great serpent: "O snake, tell me what you desire; who are you, O best of serpents, and what will you do with me?"
"I am Bhīmasena, the Pāṇḍava, born immediately after Dharmarāja.
Possessing strength equal to ten thousand elephants, how was I brought under your control?
Lions with manes, tigers, buffaloes, and likewise elephants—"
O best of serpents, Dānavas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas of great strength have repeatedly encountered me and been slain by me in battle;
they were unable to withstand the force of my arms.

Is it the power of knowledge, or perhaps a boon granted by you? Even though I am exerting myself, I have been brought under your control. It is my firm conviction that the prowess of men is truly unreal.
"O Naga, just as this great strength of mine has been thwarted by you,"—
to the hero Bhima, the doer of tireless deeds, who was speaking thus,
the serpent coiled itself all around with its massive body.
Having seized that mighty-armed one,
the serpent then released his two stout arms and spoke these words:
"By good fortune, O mighty-armed one, you have today been provided as food for me by the gods while I was hungry."

"By good fortune, O subduer of enemies, the dear lives of embodied beings have been spared after this great length of time. Listen now, O best of men, for I must certainly explain to you how I came to attain this state of being a serpent."
"Having reached this state through my anger toward wise men,
I tell you this story of a serpent, desiring to reach the end of the curse. You have surely heard of the royal seer named Nahuṣa."
Among your ancestors, you alone were the first son to perpetuate the lineage of Āyu;
through ascetic penances, sacrifices, learning, noble birth,
and valor, I have attained incomparable sovereignty over the three worlds.
Then, the intoxication that destroys all kings entered me; a thousand of the foremost sages carried my palanquin. Thereafter, I was brought down from it by the high-souled Agastya.
See this destiny of mine, which has brought me to such a state!
O dear one, no one can overcome destiny through wisdom, nor by strength, energy, or power,
nor even by the strength of allies.
Now, if wisdom and valor were the causes of prosperity,
then for those possessed of wisdom and valor there would never be a lack of prosperity;
yet we see that even those who are wise and brave lead lives of suffering.

The timid and the foolish are happy; therefore, fate is indeed the cause. Thus, having disregarded the Brahmins due to the curse of Agastya, I have fallen into this state; behold this destiny of mine!
For that sage, having been entreated by me, fell from his supreme celestial mansion;
filled with compassion, he spoke these words: "Bring an end to my curse. Whoever shall answer the questions posed to you in accordance with the Dharma..."
After some time has passed, he will release you from the curse; moreover,
by my grace, there shall be no loss of memory for you,
and even a powerful being, once seized by you, will come under your control.

"If I were to consume you today— even though you are invincible, approaching with a most pleasing appearance— behold what kind of power I possess! For no one who has fallen into my grasp ever escapes from me by any means."
"O best of men, O foremost of the Kauravas, it was not by a mere serpent dwelling in an animal womb that you were seized at the sixth hour, whether as an elephant or even a buffalo; this is my boon."
As I was falling swiftly from the summit of my celestial chariot, from the very seat of Śakra, I cried out,
"O Blessed One, best of sages, put an end to my curse!
To me, that radiant one, overflowing with compassion, spoke.
"O King, that mighty one whom you have ensnared falls into delusion;
yet, O King, after the lapse of some time, your liberation shall come.
Then I fell to the ground, and my memory did not desert me."
"I possess the traditional lore of the Purāṇas exactly as it was received by me. That specialist who shall answer the questions you have posed will deliver you from the curse," so said the Ṛṣi to me.
"O King, for any living being, even one that is stronger or superior, once seized by you,
there will swiftly come a loss of courage;
thus have I heard from those compassionate ones."
Then those twice-born ones, having conceived affection for me, vanished.
Thus, O one of great splendor, I—a perpetrator of most wicked deeds—dwell in this impure hell; having attained this serpent birth, I await my time.
The mighty-armed Bhīmasena said to that serpent:
"I am not angry with you, O great serpent, nor do I reproach myself;
for whether it be destined or not, man is subject to both happiness and suffering."
Whether it comes or whether it departs, one should not let the mind be distressed by that. Who is able to turn back destiny through human effort?
I consider destiny alone to be supreme; human exertion is useless.

Behold how, through the stroke of fate, I have today reached this state here without apparent cause, relying as I did on the strength of my own arms. Yet, I do not grieve for my ruined self as much as I do for this.
Just as they will see their brothers cast into the forest, deprived of their kingdom,
and this Himavat mountain so difficult to traverse and teeming with yakṣas and rākṣasas,
they will fall down in utter distress while looking for me.
Or, having heard that he has perished, they will become devoid of effort;
for those who are virtuous in character were oppressed by me, greedy for the kingdom.
Or perhaps the wise Arjuna will not fall into despair.
Skilled in all weapons and unassailable by gods, gandharvas, or rākṣasas,
that mighty-armed one of great strength is capable, by his own power, of displacing even the king of the gods from his station in a single day.
How much more so for the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that player of foul dice,
hated by all the world and devoted to deceit and greed; and I grieve for my wretched mother as well, who yearns for her son.

"O serpent, how will all those desires of mine— which she constantly aspired for me, that I might possess a greatness superior to others— become fruitless through my destruction when I am left without a protector?"
Nakula and Sahadeva,
the twin sons who are obedient to their elder brother, though always proud as men and supported by the strength of my arms,
will become devoid of energy, their heroism and prowess having failed them.
"Because of my destruction, they will be utterly despondent"— such was the thought that occupied my mind.
Thus Vṛkodara lamented at length in many ways, yet,
restrained by the coils of the serpent, he was unable to move.
But Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, became unsettled in mind as he contemplated those terrible portents that foreboded undesirable events;
