for a jackal stood to his right, uttering a harsh and inauspicious cry.
In that hermitage,
a quail of terrible appearance, with one wing, eye, and foot, was seen crying out in terror toward the blazing quarter of the sky; vomiting blood, it shrieked discordantly as it faced the sun.
A harsh and violent wind blew, dragging along gravel;
all the cries of beasts and birds were inauspicious;
and a black crow behind him cawed, "Go! Go!"
Again and again his right arm throbbed;
likewise his heart and his left foot twitched,
and an ominous change occurred in his left eye.
O Bhārata, that wise Dharmarāja, apprehending a great danger, questioned Draupadī, "Where is Bhīma?
Pāñcālī then informed him that Vṛkodara had been gone for a long time.
He related everything about how [the king] had gone from here to hunt deer. Having heard that, the mighty-armed king, his mind deeply agitated, set out in haste accompanied by Dhaumya.
"Draupadī must be protected," he said to Dhanañjaya;
he then gave Nakula and Sahadeva instructions regarding the twice-born.
Having traced his footsteps from that very hermitage, the lord [departed].
O son of Kuntī, he searched for Bhīmasena in the great forest.
Having set out toward the eastern direction, he saw the earth marked with signs belonging to Bhīma, indicating the presence of great leaders of elephant herds.
Then, seeing thousands of deer and hundreds of lions fallen in the forest, the king entered their path.
As that hero, swift as the wind, was rushing after the deer, he followed the trail.

Having gone along that path, he saw by those signs trees broken by the wind from his thighs and cast aside on the way; he beheld them then in a mountain glen filled with harsh winds, crowded with leafless trees.
In a parched, waterless region, thick with thorny trees, strewn with stones, stumps, and shrubs— a place most difficult to traverse and ruggedly uneven—
his younger brother was likewise seized by the lord of serpents and rendered motionless.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having approached his beloved heroic brother, who was coiled around by the body of a serpent, Yudhiṣṭhira spoke these words.
"O son of Kuntī, how did you come to encounter this calamity,
and who is this best of serpents, resembling the expanse of a mountain?
Having observed the King of Dharma, the younger brother [addressed] his elder brother.
He related all that had occurred, beginning with his capture.
Bhīma said:
"Noble sir, this great being has seized me for the purpose of food."
The royal seer named Nahuṣa remains as if endowed with life.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O long-lived one, let this brother of mine, who possesses immeasurable prowess, be released."
The serpent said:
"We shall give you another kind of food to ward off hunger;
this prince, who has come to my mouth, was obtained by me as food."

"Depart; you must not stay here. Tomorrow you too shall become my prey. O mighty-armed one, this is my vow: whoever enters my domain, dear friend, shall become my food—and you too are within my domain."
"O younger brother, after a long time I have today obtained this food;
I shall not release it, nor do I desire anything else.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Whether you be a god, a Daitya, or a serpent—if you are indeed a serpent, O snake, speak the truth; Yudhiṣṭhira questions you.
And for what purpose, O serpent, was Bhīmasena swallowed by you?
"O serpent, what must be brought or what must be known for you to feel satisfaction?
What food shall I provide, and how might you release him? The serpent replied:
"O sinless one, O lord of men, in former times I was a king named Nahuṣa,
the fifth son of Āyu after Soma, renowned for my sacrifices,
asceticism, Vedic study, and self-restraint."
Having attained unrivaled sovereignty over the three worlds through my prowess,
that lordship having been secured, pride then took hold of me;
for a thousand twice-born men carried my palanquin.

"O lord of the earth, intoxicated by the pride of sovereignty, I then insulted the twice-born; consequently, I have been reduced to this state by Agastya. Yet, O Pāṇḍava, my wisdom has not abandoned me even until this day."
"O King, it is solely through the grace of that high-souled Agastya that this food has been obtained by me at the sixth meal-time;
I shall not release him, nor do I desire any other."
"If you answer the questions I have uttered,
then I shall afterwards release your brother Vṛkodara.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Speak, O serpent, according to your desire; I shall give you an answer.
Moreover, O snake, if I am able, I shall bring you joy.
Whatever is to be known here by a Brahmin, that you alone know."
"Speak, O best of the upholders of dharma, that truth which you must tell me; O king of serpents, having heard it, I shall give you my reply. The serpent said:
"03.177.014d All gods as well as the celestial sages (brahmarṣis) praise dharma.
Therefore, O sinless one, explain dharma to me in brief.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Truth, self-restraint, austerity, purity, contentment, modesty, forgiveness, and uprightness;
the serpent said:
knowledge, tranquility, compassion, and meditation—this is the eternal dharma.
"What is declared to be truth, O King, and what is proclaimed as self-restraint?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What would be the characteristic of austerity, and what is that which is called purity?"
"Truth is declared to be that which is beneficial to living beings; self-restraint is the taming of the mind;
austerity is abiding in one's own duty; and purity is the avoidance of mixing with others.
The serpent said:
"What is declared to be the highest contentment? And what is proclaimed as modesty?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is declared to be the highest forbearance? And what is cited as straightforwardness?"
Contentment, renunciation of sense-objects, modesty, and desisting from what should not be done;
the serpent said:
forbearance, endurance of the pairs of opposites, and straightforwardness, which is equanimity of mind.
"What is declared to be knowledge, O King, and what is proclaimed as tranquility?
What is said to be the supreme compassion, and what is cited as meditation?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Knowledge is the awakening to the meaning of reality; tranquility is the peace of the mind.
The serpent said:
Compassion is the desire for the welfare of living beings; meditation is a mind free from sense-objects.
"What is the invincible enemy of men, and what is the endless disease?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What kind of person is remembered as virtuous, and what kind is remembered as non-virtuous?"

Anger is an enemy difficult to conquer; greed is an endless disease. A virtuous person is one who seeks the welfare of all beings; an unvirtuous person is remembered as being merciless. The serpent said:
"O King, what is declared to be delusion (*moha*), and what is proclaimed to be pride (*māna*)?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is to be understood as indolence (*ālasya*), and what is here called sorrow (*śoka*)?"
Delusion (*moha*) is the state of being bewildered regarding the Dharma; pride (*māna*) is the conceit of selfhood.
The serpent said:
Indifference toward the Dharma is laziness (*ālasya*); sorrow (*śoka*), however, is said to be ignorance (*ajñāna*).
"What is declared by the sages to be steadfastness? What is that which is called fortitude?
What is declared to be the supreme ablution? And what is that which is called giving in this world?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Steadfastness in one's own duty is stability; fortitude is the restraint of the senses.
The serpent said:
"Bathing is the abandonment of the impurities of the mind; charity is the gift of fearlessness."
"O Lord of Men, who is to be known as a wise man, and who is a fool?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is the cause of this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), and what is its supreme inner torment?"
One whose soul is fixed on dharma is to be known as wise; an atheist is called a fool.
Desire is the cause of saṃsāra, and envy is the supreme torment of the heart.
The serpent said:
"O Lord of Men, what is declared to be *ahaṃkāra* (egoism), and what is that which is called *dambha* (hypocrisy)?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is declared to be *abhyasūyā* (malice), and what is that which is called *paiśunya* (slander)?"
Deluded knowledge, egoism, hypocrisy, and the raising of the banner of righteousness;
the serpent said:
"Indeed, hatred of dharma, envy, backbiting, and the reviling of others."
"Dharma, artha, and kāma are mutually contradictory. Since they are eternally opposed, O King, how indeed could there be their union?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
When a husband is content with his wife and likewise a wife with her husband,
in whatever family this is constant, there indeed is certain prosperity. When both husband and wife are subject to each other’s will, [that family prospers].
The serpent said:
"At that time, there was a convergence of all three— dharma, artha, and kāma—
by virtue of [his] birth, lineage, conduct, Vedic study, and sacred learning."
"By what does one attain the status of a Brahmin? Pray, declare this with certainty.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O dear one, neither birth, nor lineage, nor Vedic study, nor sacred learning [is the cause]."
The causes for being twice-born are indeed conduct alone; O dear one, many sages who took refuge in the wombs of animals,
remaining devoted to the practice of their own dharma, have gone from here to the world of Brahmā.

What is the use of much study for one who is evil-minded, like that of an actor? He has truly studied and heard the scriptures who puts them into practice; for otherwise, it is like water in a skull or milk in a dog's skin.
Learning becomes corrupted by a defect in its source, as does that which is devoid of right conduct.
Right conduct must be protected with effort; wealth comes and goes. One who is diminished in wealth is not truly diminished, but one who is ruined in conduct is utterly destroyed.
Of what use is a noble lineage, however vast, to one who is evil-minded?
Do worms not breed within fragrant flowers?
Therefore, O Great King, know that conduct is the defining characteristic of a Brahmin.

Even one who knows the four Vedas, if he is of evil conduct, is considered more sinful than a Śūdra. But the gods know him as a Brāhmaṇa who is devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice, self-controlled, restrained by contentment, pure, and habituated to austerity and the study of the Veda.
The wise one who endures all dualities, who is free from all attachments,
who is friendly and intent on the welfare of all beings— the gods know him as a *brāhmaṇa*.
Clothed in whatever may be, seated in whatever manner, he remains steadfast.
The gods know him as a brāhmaṇa who sleeps wherever he may be;
the gods know him as a brāhmaṇa who fears social crowds as he would a snake, honors as he would death, and women as he would a corpse.
The serpent said:
"O King Yudhiṣṭhira, who may be a brāhmaṇa, and what is that which is to be known? Speak, for we judge you to be one of supreme intelligence by your words."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O lord of serpents, where truth, generosity, forgiveness, good conduct, kindness, self-restraint, and compassion are seen, he is remembered as a Brāhmaṇa."

O bull among men, O Indra among kings, he constantly seeks out the virtues of others and never grasps at their faults, even when they exist; he is ever compassionate toward the wretched and always affectionate toward the virtuous.
The serpent said:
"The gods know him as a true Brahmin who is constantly devoted to giving.
O Indra among kings, tell me with care: what is the proper time for the performance of *śrāddha* and the giving of gifts?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"O best among those who know how to ask questions, you are considered by me to be all-knowing. Regarding that matter where one should indeed see a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas and devoted to meditation—"
The serpent said:
"One should consider wealth as superior; that is the proper time for performing *śrāddha* and giving gifts.
O King Yudhiṣṭhira, tell me what is the supreme object of knowledge."

O mighty-armed one, we infer from your words that you are omniscient. O Serpent, what do you wish to say regarding that supreme Brahman which is to be known— that which is neither suffering nor pleasure— and having gone where they no longer grieve?
The serpent said:
"The fourfold social order, authoritative evidence, truth, and indeed the Veda exist; even among Śūdras there is truth, generosity, and freedom from anger."
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, compassion, non-violence, and pity—
whatever you have described as that which is to be known, free from suffering and free from pleasure, O lord of men—
I perceive that there is no other state apart from those two."
"O lord of men, recount all of those in their entirety.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"This characteristic would be found in a Śūdra, yet it is not present in a twice-born man."
A Śūdra is certainly not a Śūdra, nor is a Brāhmaṇa a Brāhmaṇa;
O serpent, where this conduct is observed, he is remembered as a Brāhmaṇa.
Where this is not present, O serpent, one should designate him as a Śūdra.
Furthermore, as for what you have said— that there is no object of knowledge to be known,
and that even beyond those two there is no state—
O Serpent, this is indeed your view; yet nothing exists that is devoid of those two.
Just as between cold and heat there may be that which is neither hot nor cold, even so, O serpent, there exists a state somewhere that is free from both pleasure and pain;
this is my view, though you may think otherwise.
The serpent said:
"O King, if a Brāhmaṇa is regarded by you only through his conduct,
then his birth is useless, O long-lived one, as long as his deeds are not observed."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O great serpent, O high-minded one, it is my opinion that in this human state, birth is difficult to discern due to the intermixture of all the social orders."
When all men procreate offspring with all women,
then for men, speech, sexual union, birth, and death are equal.
This is the authority of the Ṛṣis, as expressed even in the words "ye yajāmahe."
Therefore, those who perceive the truth know that moral conduct (*śīla*) is the most excellent.
Before the umbilical cord is severed, the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) is prescribed for the male child;
after that, the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), and following that, the tonsure ceremony (*caula*) is prescribed.
Thereafter, the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) for the twice-born is prescribed according to the rule;
in that rite, the Sāvitrī is said to be his mother, while the teacher is called his father.
For as long as he is not born into the Veda, he is indeed equal to a Śūdra in his conduct.
Regarding this very conflict of opinions, Svāyambhuva Manu declared:
"O Lord of Nagas, if the castes have fulfilled their duties but do not possess proper conduct, then a powerful confusion of castes (*saṃkara*) is observed therein."
"O great serpent, O best of serpents, I have previously described to you that Brāhmaṇa in whom refined conduct is now desired.
The serpent said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, your words have been heard by me, who has known all that is to be known. Why would I ever devour your brother Vṛkodara?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"You are such a person in this world, having mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas;
tell me, by performing what action may one attain the unsurpassed goal?
The serpent said:
"O Bhārata, my opinion is that one who gives into a worthy recipient, speaks pleasant words, speaks the truth, and is devoted to non-violence shall go to heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O serpent, between generosity and truth, which is seen to be weightier?
And let the relative gravity or lightness of non-violence and kindness also be declared.
The serpent replied:
Devotion to giving, truthfulness, non-violence, and kindness—
because of the relative gravity of these duties, their relative importance is observed.
Indeed, in certain instances of the application of giving, truthfulness itself is superior.
O Indra among kings, even a small gift is superior to truthful speech;
likewise, O great archer, lord of the earth, non-violence is seen as weightier than pleasant words, yet pleasant speech is desired even more than that.
"O King, let it be so immediately as you have requested;
tell me whatever else you desire, and I shall speak.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How, O serpent, can there be a journey to heaven, and how can the fruit of actions be certain for one who is bodiless? Tell me also of the objects of the senses.
The serpent said:
"O King, three destinies are indeed observed according to one's own actions:
human existence, residence in heaven, and birth as an animal; thus it is threefold.
Among these, from the world of humans, by means of gifts and other virtues, one who is untiring..."
Through causes associated with the purpose of non-violence, one enjoys heaven;

but through contrary causes, O Indra among kings, one becomes a human being. Likewise, O dear one, one may enter the womb of an animal; the specific distinctions in this regard shall now be explained.
One who is possessed by desire and anger, and endowed with violence and greed,
falls away from the human state and is born in the womb of an animal. Once the distinct existence in the animal womb has ended, birth in the human state is ordained.
Likewise, even the state of divinity is seen to result from cows and horses;
thus, O King, this living being, driven by its karma, wanders through all these destinies,
yet it establishes itself eternally in the Great Self.
"Being born again and again, the powerful Self, possessing a body, experiences [the results];
O dear one, it is detached from the purpose of fruit, yet it brings about the manifestation of the characteristics of living beings.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O serpent, tell me truly and without distraction: what is the basis for that [consciousness] regarding sound, touch, form, as well as taste and smell?
Why, O high-minded one, do you not perceive these objects simultaneously?"
"O best of serpents, let all this that was asked be told.
The serpent said:
"O long-lived one, that which is the substance of the self, associated with its dependence upon the body—"

Presided over by the instruments, it experiences enjoyments according to its lot. O bull among the Bharatas, understand from me that knowledge, intellect, and mind are the instruments in its engagement with enjoyment.

"O dear one, the self of beings (bhūtātman), having emerged from the field (kṣetra) and abiding in the locus of the sense objects, sequentially ranges over these objects by means of the mind. And here too, O tiger among men, the mind of a living being is directed."
Therefore, its simultaneous apprehension here is not possible.
O tiger among men, that Self, residing between the eyebrows,
projects the intellect— both supreme and inferior— upon various objects.
"And after the intellect, sensation is perceived by the wise;
this indeed, O tiger among kings, is the process for the contemplation of the Knower of the Field.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Tell me also the supreme characteristic of the mind and of the intellect;
this is prescribed as the highest task for those who know the inner self.
The serpent said:
O dear one, the intellect (buddhi) follows the self (ātman) and is established through its emergence;
for this perception (saṃjñā) is dependent upon it, and the rule regarding its seeking is thus. There is no injunction of qualities for the intellect, but the mind (manas) possesses qualities.

Intellect (buddhi) arises toward an object, whereas the mind (manas) is indeed already present; this, my dear, is the distinction between the mind and the intellect that I have declared. You too have understood this—what do you think of it?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best among the wise, how excellent is this auspicious insight of yours!
You have already known all that is to be known; why then do you question me?"
The serpent said:
"O dear one, best among those who know how to ask questions, all your questions have been answered in their entirety.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Now I release this brother of yours, Vṛkodara. Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the righteous-souled one, having embraced his brother Bhīma who had been released by Nahuṣa, honored Nahuṣa in return.
Nahuṣa, too, liberated from the sage’s curse and with a joyful mind,
assumed a divine form and, being illustrious, replied to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"It is indeed the Vedic revelation that contact with the virtuous is meritorious."
"Look, I have been released by you, a virtuous man, because of my crawling away. Indeed, it is said that men, having practiced righteousness, obtain excellent sons in this world.
By what righteousness was this son obtained by you?"
"O King, it is not only the subjects who are blessed to have you as their ruler;
even Dharma is blessed, O knower of righteousness, since you are such a son to him. Many kings devoted to dharma have been seen and heard of."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, I have neither heard of nor seen a monarch like you who knows the dharma.
I am fortunate, O highly blessed one, that you are pleased with my virtues."
Those who are like you, O god-like one, do not take pleasure in the misfortune of one such as me.
However, O dear one, best of kings, my curiosity is great;
therefore, I ask you out of friendship and not out of malice.
Nahuṣa said: "How did delusion overcome you, who know the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures and are worshipped by the Lord of the Three Worlds, as if you were an ordinary man?"

O son of Kuntī, prosperity deludes even a man who is endowed with learning, virtue, and other qualities, who is righteous, established in austerity, and highly wise; for there is no king whatsoever who remains [unaffected] despite being of low birth and conduct.
O Indra among kings, pride finds no place in the mind of one in whom it does not arise;
for just as heat is certain in fire, motion in the wind,
and coolness in the moon, so too is pride certain in sovereign power.
The eye clouded by the darkness of sovereign power does not see that which is stainless;
only later, when it has been anointed with the collyrium of downfall, does it attain purity.
It is my conviction that one dwelling in the bliss of heaven does not perceive this.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, when I was possessed by the delusion of sovereign power, I fell; now, having regained my full awareness, I awaken you. For who is not wise enough to speak of or to understand that which is beneficial for both worlds?
Even sages would not be wise if they were to follow after such actions;
therefore, O lord of men, you must accomplish what is desired for both worlds.
This secret has been told to you in its entirety, O mighty-armed one.
The twice-born, who are honored by the Lord of the Three Worlds, must not be treated with contempt;
they should be worshipped like gods with gifts, honors, and acts of reverence—
by whom the fire was made all-consuming and the great ocean was rendered undrinkable.
The moon is subject to waning; who would not perish by provoking them?
Who could prosper while harming those who, when provoked, might create other worlds and other world-protectors, or turn gods into non-gods?
Those upon whom the worlds and the gods always depend,
for whom the Veda itself is wealth— who that desires to live would harm them?
Just as fire, whether consecrated or unconsecrated, is a great deity.
"Thus, both the learned and the unlearned regard the Brāhmaṇa as the supreme deity.
How then did delusion overcome you, who are all-knowing and a dweller in heaven? And how did you come to be among the serpents? You ought to explain this."
"Thus, I have a great doubt regarding one of such wondrous deeds.
The serpent said:
"Even a man who is highly wise and brave is deluded by supernatural power (ṛddhi)."
"It is my conviction that everyone dwelling in pleasure does not perceive it;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I myself, overcome by intoxication through the delusion of power,
have fallen, but now awakened, I am alerting you."
"O Great King, O scorcher of foes, you have accomplished my purpose;
by conversing with you, a virtuous man, my most grievous curse has been exhausted.
For in former times, I was traveling through the heavens in a celestial chariot."
Intoxicated by my own pride, I did not think of anyone else;
all the inhabitants of the three worlds— the brahmin-sages, gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kiṃnaras— paid me tribute.
"O lord of the earth, whatever living being I behold with my eye, I swiftly take away its splendor; for such is the power of my gaze.
Indeed, a thousand Brahman-sages once carried my palanquin."
"O King, that misconduct caused me to fall from my royal fortune.
For there, while I was carrying [the sage], the seer Agastya was touched by my foot;
though he was unseen, he spoke to me in anger: 'Be destroyed! Become a serpent!'"
Then, fallen from the top of that celestial chariot and stripped of my ornaments,
as I was falling, I perceived myself to have become a female serpent with my head turned downward.
I entreated that brahmin, saying, "May there be an end to this curse."
"O Blessed One, you ought to forgive me for having acted out of ignorance.
Then, filled with compassion as I was falling, he said this to me:
"Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, shall release you from the curse."

"O lord of men, O great king, when the fruit of your terrible pride and power has been exhausted, you shall obtain the fruit of merit. Upon seeing that power of asceticism, O King, wonder arose within me."
"Brahman and the state of being a Brahmin—that is what I have urged you toward:
truth, self-restraint, austerity, yoga, non-violence, and constancy in giving. These, O King, are always the means for men to achieve their goal; neither birth nor lineage matters."
"O mighty-armed one, this brother of yours, Bhīma, has been released unharmed.
May it be well with you, O Great King; I shall return again to heaven.
And now, O tiger among men, this auspicious time has arrived."
"Therefore, O Pārtha, for this reason, a great service has been rendered to me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Then, at that very moment, a celestial chariot capable of moving at will indeed appeared."
With a great crash, that supreme being fell down there.
Having spoken thus, King Nahuṣa abandoned his serpent body,
assumed a divine form, and departed for heaven itself.
The righteous Yudhiṣṭhira, reunited with his brother Bhīma and accompanied by the illustrious Dhaumya, returned once more to the hermitage. Then,
he related everything exactly as it had happened to all the assembled twice-born ones.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, related all of that. Having heard it, O King, all those twice-born ones, his three brothers,
and the illustrious Draupadī were deeply ashamed.

But all those best of the twice-born, desiring the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas, said to Bhīma, "Do not do this," censuring his rashness. The Pāṇḍavas, however, beheld the mighty Bhīma released from danger.
They brought forth joy and sported, filled with delight.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"The season that brings an end to the summer heat is one that bestows happiness upon all living beings."
While they were dwelling right there, the rainy season arrived;
then, dark clouds with great roars, covering the sky and the directions,
rained down continuously day and night.
Then, by the hundreds and thousands, the dwellings of the end of the heat appeared,
their masses of solar radiance departed, yet possessing the pure luster of lightning;
the earth was overgrown with young grass and filled with intoxicated gadflies and reptiles.

Sprinkled with water, the earth became free from smoke and dust, and its ruddiness subsided; nothing at all could be discerned when everything was completely covered by the waters— neither the level nor the uneven ground, nor the rivers, nor the stationary objects.
With their waters agitated and their great roar, the swift-flowing rivers, hissing as if breathing,
beautified the forests at the end of the summer heat;
various sounds were heard from them as they roared within the edges of the woods.
As the boars, deer, and birds were being struck by the rains,
the *stokaka* birds, the peacocks, along with flocks of male cuckoos,
flew about in intoxication, as did the arrogant frogs.
Likewise, the auspicious rainy season, with its many varied forms and resounded by clouds,
passed away for those wandering in the desert wastes;
then the autumn arrived, filled with flocks of cranes and swans.
With its mountain slopes and forests having reached full maturity, with its rivers of clear water,
and with the stainless sky and stars, that autumn season became auspicious for those high-souled Pāṇḍavas, who were surrounded by deer and birds.
Beholding the nights, free from dust and cool as clouds,
resplendent with clusters of planets, constellations, and the moon, auspicious and bearing cool waters, adorned with white water-lilies and lotuses;
They beheld rivers and lotus-pools beautifully adorned,
with banks resembling the sky and thickets of *nīpa* trees and wild rice;
as they traveled along the Sarasvatī, which possessed sacred bathing places, joy arose within them.
Those heroes, armed with firm bows, rejoiced as they beheld the auspicious Sarasvatī, her waters clear and her banks full. For them,
that most holy autumnal night at the junction of the lunar phases was truly sacred.
O Janamejaya, the Pāṇḍavas dwelt right there during the month of Kārttika, together with virtuous and great-souled ascetics;
O best of the Bharatas, they all engaged in that supreme yoga.
When that night had dawned, the Pāṇḍavas, together with Dhaumya,
set out for the Kāmyaka forest accompanied by charioteers and kitchen-stewards.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having reached Kāmyaka, the sons of Kuntī, led by Yudhiṣṭhira,
were offered hospitality by the hosts of sages and sat down together with Kṛṣṇā.
Then, while those sons of Pāṇḍu were dwelling there in full confidence...
Many Brahmins surrounded him there from all sides.
Then, a certain twice-born man, a dear friend of Arjuna, said:
"The mighty-armed Śauri, self-controlled and noble-minded, will arrive here."
"For you, O leaders of the Kurus, have been known by Hari as having arrived here;
indeed, Hari has always desired to see you and seeks your welfare. Moreover, Mārkaṇḍeya, of great asceticism, is one who has lived for many years."
"Endowed with self-study and austerity, he will quickly join you.
Even as he was speaking thus, Keśava,
the best of chariot-warriors, appeared before him on his chariot yoked with Sainya and Sugrīva.

Like Maghavan accompanied by Paulomī, the son of Devakī, together with Satyabhāmā, approached, desiring to see the best of the Kurus; having descended from his chariot, Kṛṣṇa [honored] Dharmarāja according to the prescribed rites.
The wise one, filled with joy, paid homage to Bhīma, the best among the strong;
he honored Dhaumya and, having been saluted by the twins,
embraced Guḍākeśa and comforted Draupadī.
Seeing the hero Phalguna, his beloved, returned after a long time,
that scion of the Daśārhas embraced the subduer of enemies again and again;
likewise, Satyabhāmā also embraced Draupadī.
She was the beloved wife of the Pāṇḍavas and the dear queen of Kṛṣṇa.
Then all those Pāṇḍavas, together with their wives and their family priest,
honored the lotus-eyed one and surrounded him on every side.
But the wise Kṛṣṇa, having met with Pārtha Dhananjaya, the terror of the asuras,
shone like the high-souled Lord of Beings.
Then the Lord, adorned with a diadem and garlands, having met Guha in person,
related all that had occurred in the forests to the elder brother of Gada.
Having spoken thus according to the facts, the slayer of Madhu questioned him again:
"And how are Subhadrā and Abhimanyu?
Having honored him in the prescribed manner, he [spoke].
Having sat down there together with the sons of Pṛthā, Kṛṣṇā, and the family priest, he spoke to King Yudhiṣṭhira, praising him.
O Pāṇḍava, dharma is superior to the acquisition of a kingdom;
O King, they say that austerity alone is for its sake.
Practice your own dharma with truth and uprightness.
This world and the next have been conquered by you, who first studied the Vedas while observing vows,
and who attained the entire science of archery in its perfection.
Having acquired wealth through the duty of a Kṣatriya,
you have indeed performed all the ancient sacrifices;
yet, you find no delight in vulgar pleasures.
O lord of men, you do nothing out of desire,
nor do you abandon dharma out of greed for wealth;
therefore, by your very nature, you are a king of dharma.
O King, charity, truthfulness, austerity,
faith, tranquility, fortitude, and forgiveness—
you do not abandon these even in times of calamity, O King.
Having obtained kingdoms, wealth, and enjoyments—
this, O Pārtha, was always your supreme delight—
when the multitude of people from Kurujāṅgala [was present].
Who else but you, O Pāṇḍava, could have endured seeing Kṛṣṇā helpless in the assembly hall, where dharma, legal procedure, and conduct had vanished?
Without doubt, having all your desires fulfilled,
you shall soon protect the subjects rightly;
we here [are yours] for the subjugation of the Kurus.
If your vow has been fulfilled,
O lion of the Daśārhas, [then look upon] Dhaumya, Kṛṣṇā, Yudhiṣṭhira, the twins, and Bhīma.
"By good fortune and through your auspicious grace, the diadem-wearing Arjuna has returned joyful and skilled in weapons," he said;
and he also spoke to Kṛṣṇā Yājñasenī.
"By good fortune, you have been reunited with Dhananjaya and the Lord of the Daśārhas along with his friends," Kṛṣṇa spoke thus.
O Kṛṣṇa, those boys were preeminent in their delight in the science of archery, devoted to truth, virtuous in character,
and always practiced the meditative discipline (samādhi) followed by the righteous.
O Yājñasenī, O Kṛṣṇā, your sons wander about, being invited to rule over kingdoms and realms by their father and your brothers.
The children found no pleasure in the houses of Yajñasena nor in those of their maternal uncles;
with auspicious intent, they were facing toward Ānarta alone.
Having gone and entered the city of the Vṛṣṇis, O Kṛṣṇa, your sons, who are preeminent in their delight in the science of archery, no longer envy even the gods.
Just as you yourself ought to employ proper conduct toward them,
so too does the noble Kuntī always act toward them with constant vigilance.
And so it was again with Subhadrā,
just as it was with Aniruddha, as it was with Abhimanyu,
as it was with Sunītha, and just as it was with Bhānu.
Likewise, O Kṛṣṇa, the son of Rukmiṇī is both the instructor and the refuge for your sons;
he is a hero in the wielding of maces, swords, and shields.
In the sciences of weaponry, training, and the management of chariots and horses,
the prince Abhimanyu, being tireless, was constantly and correctly instructed by that teacher.
Having properly instructed him in the training and having bestowed weapons upon them like a preceptor,
he likewise did so for your sons and for Abhimanyu.
The son of Rukmiṇī finds satisfaction in valor; O Yājñasenī, when your sons set out observing the pleasure-park, he is pleased.
Each one of them was followed there by chariots, vehicles, and elephants;
then Kṛṣṇa spoke to the King of Dharma.
The warriors of the Daśārhas, the Kukuras, and the Andhakas—
all these obey your command;
they shall remain wherever you desire, O King.
O King, let your warriors, acting as drivers for your cause, perform their duty with chariots and elephants;
let them turn back, driven by the wind-like force of their bows.
O lord of men, this army of yours— consisting of elephants, infantry, horses, and chariots— is prepared for your purposes, like the honey-bearing hosts led by Halāyudha.
"O Pāṇḍava, let Suyodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the foremost among evildoers, be sent away along with his followers and his circle of friends."
"O lord of men, stay at will upon the path to Saubha and its ruler,
just as the agreement you made in the assembly hall."
Let the city of Hastināpura, along with its soldiers, await you and the warriors of the Daśārhas,
who are free from anger and cleansed of all sin.
Having dwelt wherever you desire at will,
you shall then, free from sorrow, reach the prosperous city of Nāgapura together with its kingdom— first of all.
Then, having understood that intention exactly as it was spoken by the Supreme Person, the high-souled Dharmarāja praised it and looked upon him.
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke thus to Keśava:
"Without doubt, O Keśava, you are the refuge of the Pāṇḍavas; for the sons of Pṛthā have you as their shelter."
At the arrival of that time, you shall again perform that deed; of this there is no doubt. And the time has passed according to your promise.
Having duly completed their twelve years of living incognito in secluded places,
O Keśava, the sons of Pāṇḍu have now come to you.
May this very same wisdom always attend you, O Keśava; for the sons of Pāṇḍu remain established in truth,
together with their kinsmen, their wives, and their constant practice of dharma.
"Indeed, the Pārthas, along with their kinsmen, have taken refuge in you.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Bhārata, while the descendant of Vṛṣṇi and the King of Dharma were speaking thus,"
Then, after some time, the righteous-souled Mārkaṇḍeya, advanced in asceticism, having lived for many thousands of years, appeared;
he was free from old age and death, endowed with the qualities of beauty and nobility, and possessed of great austerity.
He appeared joined with them in such a way that he seemed to be the twenty-fifth principle.
And at Mahāvarāhakoti, tens of thousands of Brahmās reflected upon that Great-Souled One, Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa.
When that aged ṛṣi, who had lived for many thousands of years, arrived,
all the brahmins and Kṛṣṇa along with the Pāṇḍavas paid him homage.
When that best of ṛṣis was honored and seated at his ease, they attended upon him.
In accordance with the opinion of the Brāhmaṇas and the Pāṇḍavas, Keśava spoke these supreme words;
the Pāṇḍavas and the assembled Brāhmaṇas were intent on listening,
as were Draupadī, Satyabhāmā, and myself.

"O Mārkaṇḍeya, recount to us the meritorious stories of the past, the eternal codes of virtuous conduct, and the histories of kings, women, and sages. While they were seated there, the celestial sage Nārada also arrived.
The pure-souled one arrived to visit the Pāṇḍavas;
then all those bulls among men approached that high-souled and wise sage with water for his feet and the guest-offering (arghya), according to the prescribed rule.
Then the celestial sage Nārada, perceiving that they had taken their seats,
approved of the story as Mārkaṇḍeya was telling it.
Knowing the proper time, that Nārada spoke to him as if with a smile.
"O Brahman-sage, tell us what you wish to say regarding the Pāṇḍavas.
Thus addressed, Mārkaṇḍeya, the great ascetic, replied:
"Wait a moment; there is much that remains to be told."
Thus addressed, the Pāṇḍavas together with those twice-born ones stood still for a moment,
gazing at that great sage as they would look upon the sun at midday.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Perceiving that the great sage was desirous of speaking, the Kuru king,
the son of Pāṇḍu, urged him on for the purpose of initiating the discourse:
"You [are the authority] regarding the gods, the Daityas, and the high-souled sages."
He is the eternal knower of the conduct of all royal sages;
he is considered by us to be worthy of service and worship, and has been long desired by us.
And this son of Devakī has arrived as our protector.
Indeed, such is my thought upon seeing myself fallen from happiness and beholding the ill-behaved sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra prospering on every side:
that a person is the agent of their own actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious.

How is it that the agent enjoys the fruit of his own action, for is he not the Lord? Or rather, O best of those who know Brahman, does what is done here by men follow them into pleasures and pains in this very life, or perhaps into another body?

O best of the twice-born, when an embodied being has cast off the body and is being sought out by its auspicious and inauspicious deeds, how does it become joined [with them] after death or in this world?
Is this a matter pertaining to this life alone, or rather to the next world?
"O Bhārgava, where do the karmas of a deceased being reside?
O Sage, you ought to explain all this to me exactly as it occurred.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O best among those who speak rightly, this follow-up question is worthy of you;
that which is to be known has been known by you, yet you ask for the sake of establishing it.
In this matter, I shall explain it to you; listen here with a one-pointed mind."
Just as a man experiences pleasure and pain both here and in the hereafter,
so did the first-born Prajāpati create for embodied beings stainless and pure bodies governed by dharma.
O joy of the Kurus, those ancient and meritorious men of the past— whose resolves were unfailing in power, who were firm in their vows and speakers of truth, and who had become one with Brahman—
all traveled to the celestial vault at will, accompanied by the gods.
Then they all returned again, moving according to their own will;
those men lived according to their own will and died according to their own will. They were subject to few afflictions, free from disease, successful in their aims, and without calamity.
They were beholders of the hosts of gods and of the great-souled ṛṣis;
they were direct perceivers of all dharmas, self-controlled, and free from envy.
For thousands of years they lived, and likewise each had a thousand sons.
Then, after some time had passed, those men who moved upon the surface of the earth became overcome by desire and anger; living by means of deceit and fraud,
and overwhelmed by greed and delusion, they were thereafter abandoned by the gods.
By means of impure actions, the wicked go to the animal realm and the hells;
being cooked again and again within the various cycles of existence,
they have futile desires, futile intentions, and futile knowledge, being devoid of discernment.

Desiring all objects of pleasure, they are nihilists who have broken the moral barriers; being full of doubt toward everything, they have become partakers of afflictions and are generally characterized by unwholesome deeds.
Those of low birth, afflicted by many diseases, evil-minded, and lacking in majesty,
become short-lived sinners whose results arise from the fruits of their fierce deeds; they crave all sensual pleasures, are nihilists, and have broken the moral barriers.
O son of Kuntī, when a person has passed away, their destination here is determined by their own actions.
Where does the treasury of karma of both the wise man and the one of inferior intellect reside? Abiding where does it experience the fruit of its well-done deeds or otherwise?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"This follow-up question is worthy of you; listen to it in its true essence, O Bhārata.
Regarding that vision which you have had, listen now to the explanation of it."
With this initial body created by the gods, this human being accumulates a great store of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds. At the end of his lifespan, he abandons this worn-out physical frame.
Birth occurs simultaneously in the womb; there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Therein, one's own previously committed karma always follows one like a shadow;
it lies down with one when lying down and stands by one when standing.
Formerly committed karma pursues a man as he runs; then,
whether he is worthy of happiness or worthy of suffering,
that creature, joined by the decree of destiny, is born with auspicious marks.
Or, by means of the vision of knowledge, one is seen as free from grasping due to impurities.
This, O Yudhiṣṭhira, has been described as the course of those lacking wisdom;
hereafter, learn of the supreme course of those possessing knowledge.
Those humans who have performed austerities, who are devoted to all the scriptures,
firm in their vows, dedicated to truth, and intent on serving their gurus;
who are of good character, pure by nature, patient, self-controlled, and possessed of great splendor.
Having entered into auspicious wombs, they generally possess auspicious marks;
because their senses are conquered, they are self-controlled; because of their purity, they have few ailments; and due to having little suffering or fear, they remain free from calamities.

Those great-souled seers, whose intellects perceive through direct experience and sacred scripture, perceive with the eye of knowledge their own self and the supreme self in every state— whether passing away, being born, or dwelling within the womb.
Having reached this land of action, they go again to the abode of the gods by performing auspicious deeds through wisdom, O bull of the Bharatas—
partly by destiny, partly by chance, and partly by their own actions.

O King, men attain these [results]; let there be no other doubt in your mind. O best of speakers, Yudhiṣṭhira, listen also to this illustration regarding what I consider to be the supreme good in the world of men.
For some here, but not in the next world; for some there, but not here;
for some both here and there; and for some neither there nor here—those who possess abundant wealth.
They always delight, their limbs beautifully adorned.
O destroyer of the best of enemies, this world belongs to them who are constantly devoted to the pleasures of the body, but not to that [other] world.

Those who are disciplined in yoga, devoted to austerity, habituated to the study of sacred texts, and who wear away their bodies through practice— having conquered their senses and being intent on the welfare of all beings;
O slayer of enemies, this world does not belong to those who practice righteousness first and,
having acquired wealth through righteousness, bestow it at the proper time.
Having obtained wives, they perform sacrifices;
for them, there is both this world and the world beyond.
But those who possess neither knowledge, nor austerity, nor charity—
Moreover, the deluded do not strive for progeny,
and being unfortunate, they do not attain happiness; for them,
neither this world nor the next exists.
All of you are beings of exceeding heroism, endowed with divine vigor and possessed of firm frames; you have descended from that world to this earth.
Having well-studied the sciences for the sake of the gods' work,
these heroes performed great deeds,
being disciplined in austerity, self-restraint, conduct, and deportment.
Having fully gratified the gods, the sages, and all the hosts of departed spirits according to the highest ritual,
he went to the supreme heaven, the abode of those who have performed meritorious deeds.
"You shall attain [your goal] in due course through your own actions.
O Indra among the Kauravas, let there be no doubt in you upon seeing this suffering of yours, though you are worthy of happiness."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the sons of Pāṇḍu spoke to the high-souled Mārkaṇḍeya:
"We wish to hear of the greatness of the foremost of the twice-born; let it be told."
Thus addressed, the Blessed One Mārkaṇḍeya,
of great ascetic power, immense splendor, and learned in all the scriptures, spoke:
"There was a king, the founder of the Haihaya dynasty and conqueror of enemy cities."
The powerful prince, endowed with beauty, went out on a hunt;
while wandering in the forest thick with grass and creepers,
he saw nearby a sage wearing a black antelope skin as his upper garment.
Slain by him in the forest while he was indeed thinking [it] to be a deer,
he was distressed after performing that deed; his consciousness struck by grief,
he went into the presence of the Haihayas of celebrated soul.
O lord of the earth, that prince with eyes like lotus petals then related to those kings exactly what had occurred; indeed,
that delicate protector of the earth [was born] from the Hehaya monarchs.
O dear one, having heard that the sage— who subsisted on roots and fruits— had been harmed, and having seen him there, they all became dejected in mind;
searching here and there, they all asked, "Whose son is this?"
And those Aṛiṣṭanemis went directly to the hermitage of Tārkṣya. Having saluted that high-souled sage of rigid vows, they all stood before him; and the sage then offered them worship.
They said to that high-souled one, "O sage, we do not deserve hospitality from you,
for by our own fault in action, a brahmin has been killed by us.
That brahmin-seer said to them, "How was a brahmin killed by you?"
"Where is he? Speak together; behold the power of my asceticism!
They, however, having related all of that to him exactly as it had happened, gathered there and found that the rishi was dead.
Searching for him with shame, their minds wandering as if in a dream,
the sage Tārkṣya, the conqueror of enemy cities, spoke to them there:
"Could this be that Brāhmaṇa who was destroyed by you?"
"O kings, for this son of mine is endowed with the power of asceticism.
Upon seeing that sage,
O lord of the earth, they were struck with the utmost wonder and exclaimed, "This is indeed a great marvel!"
"For this man was seen dead; how did he regain his life? Is this the power of asceticism by which he has been restored to life again?
O brahmin-sage, we wish to hear this, if indeed it is something that may be heard."
He said to them, "O kings, death has no power over us.
I shall explain the cause to you in brief, along with the application of its reasoning:
we are pure in conduct, diligent, and devoted to the worship of the twilights."

O best of kings, we eat pure food, possess pure wealth, and are endowed with the vow of celibacy; by this, death has no power over us. We recognize only the truth and do not set our minds upon falsehood.
We perform our own duty; therefore, we have no fear of death. We speak only of what is wholesome for these Brahmins; we do not speak of their misconduct, and therefore we have no fear of death.
Having fed our guests with food and drink and our dependents with abundant meals, we eat what remains; therefore, we have no fear of death.
We are patient, self-controlled, of a forgiving nature, and devoted to sacred fords and acts of charity.
Because we dwell in a land of merit, we have no fear of death;
because we dwell in a land of splendor, we have no fear of death. O you who are free from envy, this has indeed been related to you only in brief.
"Go all together; you have no fear of evil.
"So be it," they all replied, honoring the great sage, and those kings returned to their own countries rejoicing, O bull of the Bharatas.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen further from me regarding the greatness of the Brāhmaṇas.
Here, a royal seer named Vainya was consecrated for the horse sacrifice.
We have heard that Atri then set out to go there for the sake of wealth;
however, he did not pursue it further because of his observation of the manifestation of dharma. Having reflected, that man of great luster resolved instead to go to the forest.
Having summoned his lawful wife and his sons, he spoke to them as follows:
"We shall obtain an exceedingly great and secure fruit;
let your departure for the forest, which is superior in merit, be pleasing to you all immediately."
His wife, adhering strictly to righteousness, replied to him:
"Go to the high-souled son of Vena and request a great amount of wealth;
that royal sage, while performing a sacrifice, will give wealth to you who ask for it."
Therefore, O brahmin-sage, having taken and accepted this great wealth,
and having distributed it among your servants and sons, depart then as you desire.
This indeed is declared by those who know dharma to be the supreme dharma.
Atri said:
"O highly fortunate lady, it was told to me by the high-souled Gautama that Vainya is endowed with dharma and artha, and is possessed of vows of truth."
"But there dwell twice-born men who are my detractors;
for as Gautama told me, I do not venture there.
Yet, in that place, one may speak auspicious words endowed with virtue, pleasure, and wealth."
"If they were to speak otherwise than what I have said, then those words of theirs would indeed become meaningless. O highly wise lady, I shall go; your speech pleases me.
Vainya will give me cows and a vast accumulation of wealth."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, the one of great asceticism went quickly to the sacrifice of Vainya.
And having reached the sacrificial ground, Atri praised that king.
Honoring him with words joined with auspiciousness, he spoke these words:
"O King, son of Vena, you are the lord and the first ruler upon earth;
the hosts of sages praise you, for there is no one other than you who knows the Dharma."
There, the rishi of great asceticism, filled with wrath, spoke these words to him:
"O Atri, do not speak thus again; your intellect is not composed.
Here, Mahendra, the lord of creatures, shall indeed stand as our foremost."
Then Atri also replied to Gautama, O Indra among kings:
"This very person is the Ordainer, just as Indra is Prajāpati.
You alone are deluded by ignorance; you truly possess no wisdom."
Gautama said:
"I know; I am not deluded, while you, desiring to speak, are bewildered.
You wish to praise [the Self], longing for prosperity, by relying on the vision of that [Self]."
"You do not know the supreme dharma, nor do you understand its purpose;
you are but a child and a fool, though you are old for some reason.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
While those two were thus disputing, they stood within the sight of the sages;
those who had assembled at his sacrifice asked,
"How was this entrance granted to these two into the assembly of Vainya?"
"Calling out loudly, for what purpose have you two stood here?
Then Kāśyapa, whose soul was supremely righteous and who knew all dharmas,
informed those two disputants that they had arrived.
Then Gautama spoke to the members of the assembly, those best of sages:
"O bulls among the twice-born, hear the question we have discussed;
Atri has stated here that the son of Vena is the Creator, and regarding this, we have a great doubt."

Then, as soon as they heard those words spoken by Gautama in the assembly of Vainya, the high-souled sages rushed swiftly toward Sanatkumāra, the knower of dharma, in order to have their doubts resolved.
03.183.020 All, having bowed down, questioned him just as those who drink soma question Brahmā.
03.183.021 Having heard their words, that one of great asceticism replied to them accordingly, with speech consistent with both dharma and artha.
Sanatkumāra said:
Brahman joined with the Kṣatriya, and the Kṣatriya joined with Brahman—
united, they burn their enemies just as fire and wind consume the forests.
The king is indeed the first dharma and the lord of subjects;
he alone is Śakra, he is Śukra, he is Dhātṛ, and he is Bṛhaspati;
he is Prajāpati, Virāj, Samrāj, Kṣatriya, Bhūpati, and Nṛpa.
Who would not deserve to worship him who is praised with these words:
"The one whose source is ancient, the victor in battle, the joyful one,
Bhava, the golden-eyed leader, the tawny Sahajit"— thus is the King addressed.
Satyānryu, Yudhājīva, and Satyadharman were the promulgators of righteousness;
out of fear of unrighteousness, the seers bestowed power upon the Kṣatriya,
he who was created of old by Brahmā for the protection of all creatures.

He who effects the restraint of the wicked is called a king. He in whom truth, indignation, compassion, protection, and the discernment of dharma and adharma exist, and who possesses spies, is designated as a king.
By us, the Brahmins, the Kshatriya power is sustained, and by the Kshatriya, the imperishable Brahmanic order;
just as the sun among the gods in heaven dispels darkness with its brilliance,
even so does the king on earth forcefully dispel unrighteousness.
Therefore, because the authority of the scriptures is observed, the latter position— that the king is the primary [authority]—
is established;
for that which was previously declared by Atri as "the king," is exactly so and not otherwise.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, his purpose accomplished, that high-minded king was filled with joy;
pleased, he spoke to Atri, who had previously praised him.
"O brahmin-sage, because you have declared me here to be the eldest among all men, and equal to all the gods, and indeed the most excellent,
therefore I shall bestow upon you various and abundant riches."
A thousand dark-complexioned maidservants, well-clothed and adorned;
ten crores of gold and likewise ten loads of refined gold—
these I give to you, O Brahmin, for in my view you are omniscient.
Having accepted all of that according to the prescribed rules, the high-minded Atri,
radiant and of great ascetic power, returned to his own home;
and having joyfully bestowed the wealth upon his sons, he remained self-restrained.
Having resolved upon asceticism, he departed for the forest itself.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
And in this very place, O conqueror of enemy cities, was sung by Sarasvatī—
O Hero, listen to what was asked by the wise Tārkṣya, the sage.
Tārkṣya said:
"O blessed lady, what indeed is the highest good for a person in this world?"
Tell me everything, O lady of beautiful limbs: how acting does one not fall away from one's own duty?
Instructed by you, may I not fall away from my own duty.
"How should one offer oblations into the fire or worship it?
At what time and by what means would dharma not perish?
O fortunate lady, explain all of this."
"So that I may wander through the worlds free from passion.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Thus was he questioned by him with affection;"
Beholding Tārkṣya— the Brahmin endowed with supreme intelligence, devoted to service, possessed of righteousness, and well-disposed—
Sarasvatī spoke these words:
Sarasvatī said:
He who knows Brahman according to its proper place,
who is constant in private Vedic study, pure, and vigilant—
He indeed shall go to the city of the gods; together with the immortals, he shall attain a state of joy. There, indeed, are delightful, vast, and sorrowless [regions].
The lotus ponds are in full bloom, most meritorious, free from mud, filled with fish, and possessing excellent landing-places;
they are covered with golden lotuses.
On their banks sit those of meritorious deeds,
being honored by various Apsarases who are adorned and possess most fragrant scents.
Those who give cows attain the highest world with great joy, being as golden-hued [as the rays of the sun];
having given a bull, they go to the world of the Sun.
By giving a garment, one goes to the world of the Moon;
by giving gold, one attains immortality; and by giving a cow that is well-behaved and easy to milk, [one attains the same].
And one who has auspicious qualities, as well as one who flees from battle,
dwells in the heavenly world for as many years as there are hairs on her body.
He who gives a bull of good disposition,
a bearer of the plough, possessed of infinite vigor, capable of bearing the yoke, strong, and young;
He who indeed gives away a tawny cow (kapilā) along with a cloth, accompanied by a bronze milking vessel, and provided with wealth and an upper garment, attains the ten worlds of the giver of a cow.
Then, having become a cow of plenty through those various virtues,
that cow approaches the man who gave her;
as many hairs as there are upon the cow, [so many years shall he enjoy the fruit].
For that long one obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow;
he rescues his sons, his grandsons, and his entire lineage up to the seventh generation in the world beyond.

To a twice-born man, one who gives a cow made of sesame seeds— accompanied by a sacrificial fee, with beautiful golden horns, a bronze milking vessel, and a costly upper garment— [attains great merit].
The worlds of the Vasus are easily attained through one's own deeds for one falling into the hell of intense darkness, which is crowded with *dānavas*.
Like a boat driven by the wind upon the great ocean,
the gift of cows carries one across to the next world;
so too does he who gives a maiden in marriage as a *brahmadeya*.
He who makes a gift of land to a brahmin and bestows a gift according to the prescribed rule attains the world of Purandara.
O Tārkṣya, he who, being of good vows and virtuous character, offers oblations into the fire for seven years,
purifies seven generations of descendants and seven of ancestors.
"By their own deeds, [they see] their ancestors.
Tārkṣya said:
"What is the ancient vow of the Agnihotra?"
Tell me, O lady of beautiful form, as I ask you:
instructed by you today, may I here learn that ancient vow of the Agnihotra.
Sarasvatī said:
Neither one who is impure, nor one whose hands are unwashed,
nor one ignorant of the Veda, nor one lacking wisdom, should offer the oblation.
For the gods are desirous of food and lovers of purity;
they do not accept an oblation from one who lacks faith,
nor should one employ a man unlearned in the Vedas for the offering to the gods.
For such a person pours [the offering] in vain upon another; Tārkṣya, he has said that one who is not a śrotriya is incomplete;
indeed, such a person would not offer the agnihotra sacrifice.
Those who, full of faith and devoted to the vow of truth, offer oblations into the fire and eat only what remains after the sacrifice,
reach the world of cows, which is fragrant with merit.
They behold the supreme God and also the ultimate Truth.
Tārkṣya said:
[They behold] that which has become the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) regarding the existence of the other world.
O fortunate one, having reflected upon your intellect that has deeply entered into the arising of karma, and upon the goddess Prajñā herself, I ask you: who indeed are you, O lady of beautiful form?
Sarasvatī said:
"I have come from the Agnihotra sacrifice in order to sever the doubts of the foremost among the brahmin seers."
"Through my union with you, I have spoken this truth exactly as it is, remaining established in reality. Tārkṣya said:
Indeed, there is no one like you;
for you shine forth exceedingly, like the goddess Śrī,
and your form is divine and supremely beautiful.
"And you bear the goddess Prajñā, O fortunate one.
Sarasvatī said:
"O best among the foremost of bipeds; those things which are most excellent—"
O learned one, they provide me with nourishment in sacrifices; by those very offerings, O Brahmin, I become fully grown, refreshed, and beautiful.
And whatever substance is employed—
whether derived from trees, made of iron, or of earth—
is endowed with divine form and wisdom.
"Know, O wise one, that success comes through that alone.
Tārkṣya said:
"Considering this to be the supreme good;"
The sages strive with full confidence; tell me of that supreme state free from sorrow,
the ultimate liberation into which the wise enter.
"That which the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga call the supreme, the highest,
the ancient— that I do not know.
Sarasvatī said:
Those who know the Vedas have indeed taken refuge in him— the supreme one, more supreme than the supreme, the ancient one renowned from of old—
through the merits of Vedic study, charity, vows, and yoga.
Then, in the midst of those whose wealth is austerity, who are free from sorrow and liberated,
a sacred-scented cane tree shines forth,
pure and possessing a thousand branches.
From its root flow rivers with delightful streams of honeyed water;
from branch to branch flow great rivers resembling sands.

O Sage, that supreme station is where roasted grains, cakes, meat, vegetables, and constant offerings of milk-rice form a mire, and where the gods, headed by Agni and including Indra along with the hosts of Maruts, performed sacrifices with the most excellent rites.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then that Pāṇḍava spoke again to Mārkaṇḍeya,
"Tell me here the life-story of Manu Vaivasvata."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, O tiger among men, the son of Vivasvat was a supreme ṛṣi of great prowess, possessing a splendor equal to that of Prajāpati.
By his vital energy (*ojas*), brilliance (*tejas*), fortune (*lakṣmī*), and especially by his asceticism (*tapas*),
Manu surpassed both his father and his grandfather.
With his arms raised, that lord of men remained in the vast Badarī forest.
Standing on one foot, he performed intense and very great austerity;
likewise, with his head hanging down and his eyes fixed and unblinking,
he then practiced that formidable penance for ten thousand years.
Once, while he was performing austerities on the bank of the Vīriṇī, wearing wet bark garments and matted hair, a fish approached him and spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, I am a small fish; I have fear of the powerful."
Therefore, O observer of noble vows, you ought to protect me from the fish;
for the strong fish especially devour the weak, according to our eternal, ordained way of life.

"Therefore, you ought especially to rescue me, who am sinking in this great flood of fear; I shall repay your kindness with a deed in return. Having heard the words of the fish, he was overwhelmed with compassion.
Vaivasvata Manu himself took hold of that fish with his own hand;
having brought the fish to the edge of the water, Vaivasvata Manu placed it,
which possessed a luster like the rays of the moon, into a water-jar.

There he grew, O King, the fish being treated with the highest honor; and Manu, in particular, maintained toward him an affection like that for a son. Then, after a long time, that fish became truly enormous.
It is said that he did not remain even in the water of the Aliñjara;
then the fish, seeing Manu, spoke to him once more:
"O Blessed One, please provide another place for me today."
Then, having lifted him from that jar, the blessed sage Manu led that fish at that time to a great pond; there,
O conqueror of enemy cities, Manu cast it in.
Then that fish grew again for many groups of years;
the pond was two *yojanas* in length and one *yojana* in width, yet,
O lotus-eyed one, the fish could no longer fit within it.
O son of Kuntī, O lord of the people, the fish could no longer move about in the pond.
Then, seeing Manu, the fish spoke to him once again:
"O blessed one, O virtuous one, O lord, take me to the queen of the ocean."
"I shall dwell there by the Gaṅgā, or however you think best, dear father;
for I must remain under your command without resentment,
O sinless one, since it is through you that I have attained the highest prosperity."
Thus addressed, the blessed and self-controlled Manu led the fish to the river Gaṅgā; there, the infallible one personally cast it into the water.
O subduer of enemies, the fish grew there for some time.
Then, seeing Manu once more, the fish spoke these words:
"O Lord, because of my great size, I am unable to move about in the Gaṅgā;
please be gracious, O Blessed One, and take me quickly to the ocean."
Then, O Pārtha, Manu himself took that fish out from the waters of the Gaṅgā and led it to the ocean, where he released it;
although it was a very large fish, it remained within the mind of Manu at that time.
It was indeed easy to grasp at will, and its touch and fragrance were pleasant;
when that fish was thrown into the ocean by Manu,
it then spoke these words to him as if smiling:
"O Blessed One, you have indeed provided me with every protection in particular.
Now, however, hear from me what task must be performed by you when the time has come.
O Blessed One, before long, this earthly realm—both the stationary and the moving—"
"O highly fortunate one, everything indeed shall go to dissolution;
this time for the total cleansing of the worlds has arrived.
Therefore, I awaken you today to that which is your unsurpassed benefit."
For all that is moving and all that is stationary, for everything that stirs and everything that does not stir, a most terrible time has arrived.
You must have a sturdy ship constructed, equipped with masts and oars.
O great sage, you should ascend that [boat] together with the seven seers;
and all the seeds previously mentioned by me,
you should place upon that boat, well-protected and sorted according to their kinds.
"And standing upon the ship, O beloved of the sages, you should wait for me.
I shall come with my horn; by that, O ascetic, I am to be recognized.
This must be done by you; having been asked, I now depart."
"Those vast waters cannot indeed be crossed by me without you;
nor should this word of mine be doubted, O Lord.
"I shall do so," he replied to that fish.
Having taken leave of one another, they both departed as they pleased. Then, O great king, Manu, having taken all the seeds exactly as instructed by the fish, crossed over to the ocean at that time.
O hero, subduer of enemies, with that beautiful boat,
O lord of the earth, Manu then began to think of that fish;
and that fish, O conqueror of hostile cities, knowing his thought, [spoke].
O best of the Bharatas, Śṛṅgin then arrived there quickly. O lord of kings, seeing that fish in the ocean of waters,
he was like a horned mountain rising up as described.
Then, O tiger among men, Manu placed a noose made of *vaṭā* fiber upon the head of the fish at that peak;
bound by that noose, O conqueror of enemy cities, the fish remained there.
With great speed, he drew the boat across the salt waters;
by that boat, O lord of men, he crossed the ocean,
which seemed to dance with its waves and roar with its waters.
Agitated by great winds upon that vast ocean,
O conqueror of enemy cities, that ship reeled like a drunken, fickle woman;
neither the earth, nor the cardinal directions, nor the intermediate points could be discerned.
O bull among men, both the sky and the heavens were entirely composed of water.
O best of the Bharatas, when the world had thus become so chaotic,
the Seven Ṛṣis, Manu, and the fish were seen together.
Thus, O King, for many groups of years, that fish tirelessly drew the boat through that mass of water,
O bull among men, until it reached the highest peak of the Himalayas.
Then, O descendant of Kuru, that fish drew the boat toward himself;
thereupon, the fish spoke slowly and with a smile to those sages:
"Bind the boat to this peak of the Himalayas without delay."
O bull of the Bharatas, having heard the words of the fish, those sages quickly tied that boat there upon a peak of the Himalayas;
and that peak of the Himalayas is known by the name Naubandhana.
"O Kaunteya, O bull of the Bharatas, know that it is renowned even today.
Then Animiṣa spoke to those sages assembled there:
'I am Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures; nothing higher than me can be found.'"
In the form of a fish, you and I were liberated from fear;
and by Manu, all creatures— including gods, asuras, and humans—
along with all worlds, both that which moves and that which is immobile, are to be created.
"Through most intense asceticism, his intuitive insight shall arise;
by my grace, he will not fall into delusion regarding the creation of progeny.
Having spoken these words, the fish vanished in an instant.
Desiring to create offspring himself, Manu Vaivasvata became bewildered regarding the creation of beings; he then performed great austerities,
and endowed with that great ascetic power, he proceeded to create.
O bull of the Bharatas, Manu himself duly [governed] all creatures. Thus has this ancient narrative known as the *Mātsyaka* been fully proclaimed;
this tale recounted by me removes all sins.
The man who would constantly hear from the beginning this account of Manu’s conduct shall be happy, successful in all his aims, and go to the heavenly world.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, once again, the righteous King Yudhiṣṭhira, endowed with humility, questioned the illustrious Mārkaṇḍeya:
"O great sage, you have witnessed the ends of many thousands of ages."
Moreover, there is no one here equal to you in lifespan,
except for the high-souled Brāhmaṇa Parameṣṭhin; O best among the knowers of Brahman, there is no one at all who is your equal in longevity.
In this world where there is no intermediate space and which is devoid of gods and dānavas,
you alone, O brāhmaṇa, attend upon Brahmā during the dissolution. And when the dissolution has concluded and the Grandfather has awakened, [you remain].
O brahmin-sage, you alone behold here the fourfold classes of beings being created exactly as they were by the Supreme Lord, who,
having become wind, made the quarters and scattered the waters here and there.
O best of the twice-born, the Teacher of the World, the Grandfather of all the worlds, was propitiated by you directly through supreme meditative absorption; furthermore,
O Brahmin, you have on many occasions established your own authority.

Having entered through formidable austerity, you have conquered the Creator; you are proclaimed as preeminent in the hereafter, resembling the lap of Nārāyaṇa. O Viṣṇu, the Lord who creates the universe has been made one with you alone.

In the past, you beheld with your own eyes the divine extraction of the ear-ornament by Brahmā, who can assume any form at will, through his two eyes endowed with jewels and ornaments. Therefore, neither Death, the ender of all, nor Old Age, which destroys the body, [can prevail].
O brahmin-sage, by the grace of the Supreme Lord, nothing shall enter you;
for when there is neither sun, nor fire, nor wind, nor moon,
neither the intermediate space nor the earth remains— nothing whatsoever exists.
When that world had become a single ocean, with all things mobile and immobile destroyed,
when the hosts of gods and asuras had perished and the great serpents were utterly annihilated,
[he beheld] the one of immeasurable soul reclining upon a lotus, whose abode is the lotus.
"You alone attend upon Brahmā, the lord of all beings.
O best of the twice-born, all this that occurred previously is known to us through direct perception;
therefore, we wish to hear the narrative concerning the nature of all causes."
"For you alone, O best of the twice-born, have experienced this many times;
there is nothing in all the worlds that is forever unknown to you. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Come, I shall tell you this after having paid homage to the Self-Existent One— the ancient, eternal, and undecaying Person,
who is unmanifest, most subtle, devoid of qualities, yet the very self of all qualities.
This Janārdana, with his broad and long eyes, clad in yellow garments—
he is the creator and the transformer, the maker of all beings and all states of existence;
he is inconceivable, a great marvel, and the supreme purifier.
He is the being without beginning or end, the universe itself, inexhaustible and immutable.
He is the agent who is not himself created, and he is the cause of all human endeavor. For even the gods do not know him whom this Puruṣa knows.
"O best of kings, all this that has occurred is truly a marvel,
O tiger among men, at the beginning of the destruction of the entire world.
They say that the Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years."

Its dawn consists of as many hundreds [of years], and its twilight follows thereafter; the Tretā Yuga is said here to consist of three thousand years. Its dawn consists of as many hundreds [of years], and its twilight follows thereafter.
Likewise, the Dvāpara age is two thousand years in duration;
its morning twilight is two hundred years, and following that, its evening twilight is likewise two hundred years. Then, the Kali Yuga is recorded as being one thousand years long.
Its dawn lasts for a hundred years, and after that, its twilight;
understand that the measure of the dawn and the twilight is equal.
And when the Kali Yuga has come to an end, the Kṛta Yuga begins once more.
This period of twelve thousand [years] is proclaimed as what is called a *yuga*.
A thousand such periods is declared to be one day of Brahmā.
Indeed, the entire universe revolves in every respect within the abode of Brahmā.
O tiger among men, the wise know that to be the dissolution of the worlds. But when only a small portion remains at the end of the Yuga, O bull of the Bharatas—
at the end of the thousand [ages]— all men for the most part become speakers of untruth.
O Pārtha, at that time, substitutes for sacrifice, substitutes for giving, and even substitutes for religious vows will prevail;
Brahmins will perform the work of Śūdras, and Śūdras will become accumulators of wealth.

When the Yuga has passed, even the Brahmins will conduct themselves here according to the dharma of the Kshatriyas; having ceased their sacrifices and Vedic study, and being deprived of the offering of rice-balls and water, they will become eaters of all things in the Kali Yuga.
"O dear one, Brahmins will cease their silent recitations (*ajapa*), while Śūdras will become devoted to recitation;
when the world has thus turned upside down, that is the precursor to its destruction.
O lord of men, there will be many Mleccha kings upon the earth."
O best of men, the wicked Āndhras, Śakas, Pulindas, Yavanas, Kāmbojas, Aurṇikas, Śūdras, and likewise the Abhīras will be false teachers, devoted to lying.
At the end of the age, O tiger among men, O descendant of Bharata, there will likewise be such signs:
at that time, O lord of men, no Brāhmaṇa whatsoever will live according to his own dharma,
and even the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas will be established in improper occupations.
People will have short lifespans, meager strength, and little splendor or prowess; their bodies will be small and lacking in essence, and they will likewise speak little truth.
The inhabited lands will become largely desolate, and the quarters of the world will be overrun by wild beasts and predators.
When the end of the age has arrived, those who practice celibacy do so in vain; likewise, Śūdras address others as "Bho," while Brāhmaṇas address others as "Ārya.
O tiger among men, at the end of the age, there will be many such creatures.
O lord of the people, all fragrances do not possess such power when combined with the sense of smell; nor, O tiger among men, do tastes possess such sweetness.
[The people] will have many offspring but short bodies, and they will be devoid of virtuous conduct and proper behavior.
O King, at the end of the Yuga, women will have their vulvas on their faces;
the countryside will have its spines in its market-stalls, crossroads will have their spines in the phallic emblems of Śiva,
and women will have their spines in their hair, O King, at the end of the Yuga.

They say that "aṭṭa" means food, while "vikraya" is said to mean a stake. The Veda is proclaimed as "śiva," and the crossroads are the Brahmins. Hair is called "bhaga," and they subsist by selling it.

O lord of men, cows will likewise yield little milk; trees will bear few flowers and fruits and swarm with many crows. This shall be the lot of those who are stained by the murder of a Brahmin and those who utter false accusations.
O protector of the earth, the twice-born indeed accept gifts from kings;
yet, overcome by greed and delusion, and shrouded by the false banner of dharma,
they roam the quarters of the earth for the sake of alms, O protector of the earth.

Out of fear of the burden of taxes, householders will become thieves, concealing themselves under the guise and appearance of sages, and they will live off trade. At that time, men will also wear their nails and hair falsely.
Out of greed for wealth, O tiger among men, there are those who are celibates in name only;
they follow useless conduct in the hermitages, they are drinkers of intoxicants, and they violate the bed of their guru.
They strive only for worldly ends that increase flesh and blood.

O tiger among men, at the end of the age, hermitages will become negligent regarding matters pertaining to the next world, filled with extreme nihilism, crowded with many heretics, and praising the qualities of others' food.
