O Bhārata, the Lord Pākaśāsana does not rain according to the seasons; consequently, all seeds do not sprout properly at that time,
and the people become impure, delighting in violence.
O sinless one, the fruit of unrighteousness then becomes excessive;
O Indra among kings, the fruit of righteousness perishes everywhere.
And so it is, O protector of the earth, for whoever may be endowed with dharma.
He should indeed be considered short-lived, for there is no dharma whatsoever in him;
people most frequently sell their merchandise with false measures,
O tiger among men, and merchants moreover become full of many deceits.

The righteous decline, while the wicked people prosper; there is a loss of strength for dharma, and likewise, adharma becomes powerful. At that time, the most virtuous men are short-lived and impoverished.
At the end of the age, those who act contrary to the Dharma will be long-lived and prosperous;
at the end of the age, those who act contrary to the Dharma will frequent the monasteries within the cities; and furthermore, people will conduct their affairs by means of most unrighteous methods.

Even with only a small accumulation of wealth, men become rich and filled with pride; O King, being possessed of deceitful conduct, they mostly resolve to seize the vast amounts of wealth entrusted to them by others out of trust.
"Thinking, 'This does not exist,' shameless men behave [in this way];
even man-eating beings, birds,
and likewise wild beasts lie down in the parks and shrines of cities."
O King, women who are seven or eight years old bear children;
sons are born to men of ten or twelve years of age.
Likewise, by their sixteenth year, men have already turned grey.
The exhaustion of the lifespan of human beings occurs very swiftly,
O Great King, when the age has declined; the character of the young arises in the old,
and the character of the old arises in the young.
Then women, having deceived their husbands in secret, act perversely—
even those of ill character— straying with slaves and even with animals;
likewise, O King, the wives of heroes and other women take refuge with men.
They violate even their living husbands;
and when that end of a thousand yugas has arrived and the span of life has come to its exhaustion,
O Great King, a drought lasting many years occurs.
Then, O lord of the earth, those beings of little strength and great hunger mostly meet their destruction upon the earth. Thereafter, O ruler of men, by seven blazing suns, they are consumed.
O Bhārata, all the water in the oceans and rivers is drunk up; and whatever wood or grass there is, whether dry or wet,
O bull of the Bharatas, it is seen to be entirely reduced to ashes.
Then, O Bhārata, the Saṃvartaka fire, together with the wind,
enters the world that has previously been dried up by the suns. Then, having pierced the earth, it enters the subterranean realm (rasātala).
It produces great terror among the gods, dānavas, and yakṣas;
burning the world of the nāgas and whatever else exists here upon the earth,
O protector of the earth, it destroys everything below in an instant.
Then that inauspicious wind and that fire of universal destruction (saṃvartaka) burn for hundreds and thousands of tens of thousands of yojanas,
together with the gods, asuras, and gandharvas, along with the yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
Then that all-pervading Lord, blazing, consumes the entire world.
Thereupon, great clouds of wondrous appearance, resembling herds of elephants and adorned with garlands of lightning, arise in the sky.
Some were dark like blue lotuses, some resembled white water-lilies;
some had the hue of *kāraṇḍava* birds, and some the luster of vermilion; some were like the filaments of a lotus, and some were yellow clouds.
Some resembled turmeric, while others were like the eggs of crows; some resembled poverty (or were pale), some were yellow,
some had the luster of lotus petals, and some had the brilliance of vermilion.
Some clouds have the form of excellent cities, some resemble herds of elephants,
some are like collyrium, and some are shaped like sea-monsters;
with their bodies entwined by garlands of lightning, these clouds indeed arise.
O Great King, then all the clouds, terrible in form and resounding with a fierce roar, pervaded the vault of the sky;
thundering like mountains, O Protector of the Earth.
By them, O Great King, this entire earth— with its mountains, forests, and mines— is filled and overwhelmed by a flood of water. Then,
O Bull among Men, those terrible clouds began to roar.
Urged by the Supreme Lord, they swiftly inundate everything,
raining down vast waters that fill the earth and extinguish the most terrible, inauspicious, and fierce fire.

Then, during that upheaval, those clouds, impelled by the Great-Souled One, poured down for twelve years, filling [the earth] with torrents of rain. Thereupon, O Bhārata, the ocean transgressed its own shore.
The mountains crumble and the earth itself shatters;
those clouds, suddenly whirled about from all sides, vanish after enveloping the vault of the sky, struck down by the force of the wind.

Then, O lord of men, the self-existent God whose abode is the primordial lotus, having swallowed that terrible wind, O Bhārata, goes to sleep. When all mobile and immobile beings have perished, there remains only that single, dreadful ocean.

O protector of the earth, when the hosts of gods and asuras had perished, and the world was devoid of yakṣas and rākṣasas, without humans, without beasts of prey, and without trees, and when the intermediate space of this world had vanished, I wandered alone and full of resolve.
O best of kings, wandering through the terrible waters of the single vast ocean,
I did not see any living beings and fell into a state of extreme despondency.
Then, O lord of men, having traveled a very great distance while floating, I...
Exhausted, I found no refuge anywhere, though I remained unwearied. Then, O lord of the earth, at one point amidst that flood of water, I beheld a truly immense and vast banyan tree.
O lord of men, O protector of the earth, he was seated upon a couch spread with divine coverings on a wide branch of that tree,
O great king, his face like the full moon.
"O Bhārata, I beheld a child with eyes as wide as full-blown lotuses;
then, O protector of the earth, a very great wonder arose within me:
how could this infant lie here when the world had come to its destruction?"
Even while reflecting through ascetic power, O lord of men, though I know the past, the present, and the future, I could not perceive that child;
he who had the luster of the flax flower and was marked with the *śrīvatsa*.
At that time, he appeared to me like the very abode of Lakṣmī herself.
Then that boy, whose eyes were like lotuses, who bore the Śrīvatsa mark, and who was radiant, spoke these words to me that were pleasing to the ear.
"I know you are weary, dear one, and longing for rest.
O Mārkaṇḍeya, descendant of Bhṛgu, stay here as long as you wish;
O best of sages, enter my inner body."

"Stay, sir; your dwelling is prepared, and I have shown you favor. When I was thus addressed by that boy, O Bhārata, I then felt a sense of world-weariness toward this long life and the human condition.
Then, by that boy, his mouth was suddenly opened;
by the turn of fate, I was helplessly made to enter his mouth.
Then, O lord of men, I suddenly entered his belly.
I see the entire earth, crowded with kingdoms and cities,
including the Gaṅgā, Śatadru, Sītā, Yamunā, and Kauśikī;
the Carmaṇvatī, Vetravatī, Candrabhāgā, and Sarasvatī.
O Bhārata, [he visited] the Sindhu and the Vipāśā, as well as the river Godāvarī, the Vasvokasārā, the Nalinī, and the Narmadā;
and the river Tāmrā, the Veṇṇā, which possesses holy waters and brings auspiciousness.
The Suveṇā, the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, and the great river Irāmā;
the Vitastā, O great king, and the great river Kāverī;
the Śoṇa, O tiger among men, as well as the Viśalyā and the Kampunā.
O best of men, as I wandered about, I beheld these and other rivers upon the earth within the belly of that Great-Souled One; thereafter,
I saw the ocean, inhabited by hosts of aquatic creatures.
O destroyer of enemies, I then beheld the sky, which was a mine of jewels, a great reservoir of water, and resplendent with the moon and sun;
it blazed with splendors equal in brilliance to fire and the sun.
And I see the earth, O King, adorned with forests,
along with its mountains, woods, and islands, crowded with hundreds of submerged [beings].
At that time, O King, the Brahmins indeed perform sacrifices with many offerings.
The Kṣatriyas are engaged in pleasing all the social orders;
the Vaiśyas carry out agriculture according to the law, O lord of men; and likewise, the Śūdras are devoted to the service of the twice-born.
Then, O King, as I was wandering within the belly of that great-souled one,
I beheld the Himavat and the Hemakūṭa mountain;
I also beheld Niṣadha and Śveta, which is covered in silver.
I see Mount Pāriyātra,
and I also see Naiṣadha;
O protector of the earth, I see Mount Gandhamādana as well.
O tiger among men, I see Mandara and the great blue mountain; O great king, I see Meru, the golden mountain,
as well as Mahendra and the supreme Vindhya mountain.
I also beheld Mount Malaya and Mount Pāriyātra;
these and many other mountains, as many as there are on earth,
all adorned with every kind of jewel, were seen by me within his belly.
O lord of men, O ruler of the world, I then roamed about there, beholding lions, tigers, boars, and elephants, as well as whatever other creatures exist upon the earth.
O tiger among men, having entered his womb and moving through the quarters,
I beheld Śakra and all the hosts of gods,
as well as the Sādhyas, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Guhyakas, and the Pitṛs.
O lord of the earth, [he saw] the serpents, the *nāgas*, the *suparṇas*, as well as the *vasus* and the two *aśvins*;
the *gandharvas*, *apsarases*, *yakṣas*, and the *ṛṣis*, O ruler of men;
and the hosts of *daityas* and *dānavas*, and the *kāleyas*, O king.
The sons of Siṃhikā, as well as whatever other enemies of the gods there were,
and whatever else— whether stationary or moving— I had ever seen in the world,
all that I beheld within the belly of that great-souled one.
Subsisting on fruit as I wandered throughout this entire world at that time, I did not see the end of his body anywhere, even after more than a hundred years spent within his body.
O lord of the people, O protector of the earth, as I was constantly running about, reflecting and wandering there for many groups of years,
I did not reach the end of that great-souled one, O King.
Then, at that time, I duly sought refuge in him alone—
the most excellent god, the giver of boons— both in thought and in deed.
Thereupon, O King, I suddenly emerged with the speed of the wind.
O best of men, from the open mouth of that Great-Souled One,
O lord of the people, he then sat upon a branch of that very banyan tree,
O tiger among men, having taken up the entire universe.
In that very same guise of a boy, O tiger among men, I saw him of immeasurable splendor seated there, marked with the Śrīvatsa sign. Then,
O hero, that boy spoke to me as if laughing:
"O best of sages, Mārkaṇḍeya, tell me: have you now dwelt at ease within this body of mine, which bears the Śrīvatsa, is radiant, clad in yellow garments, and possesses great splendor?"
Then, in a mere moment, my vision appeared renewed once more. Having seen that Lord of the Gods of gods, I, the sage, spoke these words:
"I beheld myself liberated from that [bondage], having regained my consciousness."
O dear one, his well-set feet have copper-colored soles; they are well-formed and adorned with soft, reddish toes. Having grasped them with my head bowed in devotion, I have indeed paid him homage.
Having beheld the immeasurable power of that one of boundless luster,
and having approached with effort, making a reverent salutation with joined palms,
I saw that lotus-eyed god, the soul of all beings.
With palms joined in reverence, I bowed to him and spoke these words:
"O Lord, I desire to know you and this supreme illusion of yours.
O Blessed One, I have entered your body through your mouth."
I have seen all the worlds in their entirety within your belly;
O Lord, the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas, as well as the yakṣas, gandharvas, and nāgas, and the entire world of moving and stationary beings, abide within your body.
And by your grace, O Lord, my memory does not fail me as you run constantly within my body. Yet,
O Great Lord, though I am unwilling, I have emerged at your will.
"O lotus-eyed one, O blameless one, I desire to know you:
having become a child here in person, why do you remain? Having swallowed this entire universe, you ought to explain this to me."
"For what purpose, O sinless one, is the entire world situated within your body?
And for how long a time, O subduer of enemies, will you remain here?
O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear this out of a longing for the Brahmins."

"O lotus-petal-eyed Lord, you have explained this great and inconceivable matter exactly as it is, just as I have witnessed it. Thus addressed by me, the glorious God of gods, of great splendor, [spoke].
Consoling me, that best of speakers addressed these words:
The God said:
"O Brahmin, even the gods do not know me in truth as they wish."
Out of affection for you, however, I shall explain how I emit this [universe].
O brahmin-sage, you are devoted to the ancestors and have come to me for refuge;
therefore, I am manifest to you in person, and your celibacy is great.
The waters are called *nārāḥ*; this name was given by me. Because they are my eternal abode (*ayana*), I am called Nārāyaṇa.
I am named Nārāyaṇa, the source, eternal and undecaying.
O best of the twice-born, I am the creator and the destroyer of all beings; I am Viṣṇu, I am Brahmā, and I am Śakra, the lord of the gods;
I am King Vaiśravaṇa, and likewise Yama, the lord of the departed spirits.
I am Śiva and Soma, and Kaśyapa the Lord of Creatures;
I am the Ordainer and the Disposer, and I am the Sacrifice, O best of the twice-born. Fire is my mouth, the earth my feet, and the moon and sun my eyes.
The sky is my head, space and the quarters are my ears, and the waters born of perspiration are likewise [my fluids].
The atmosphere together with the directions is my body, and the wind is established within my mind.
By me, hundreds of sacrifices have been performed, many of them accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Those learned in the Vedas worship me while I am present at the place of sacrifice; likewise, the lords of Kṣatriyas and the kings upon earth, desiring heaven,
worship me, as do the Vaiśyas who seek to conquer the heavenly world.
Becoming Śeṣa, I alone support this earth, which extends to the four oceans and is adorned by Meru and Mandara;
in former times, having assumed the form of a boar, this world was [upheld] by me.
O Brahmin, while sinking in the waters, she was rescued by my power. And I, O best of the twice-born, having become the submarine fire (vaḍavāmukha),
drink up the agitated waters and release them once again.
The Brahmins are my mouth; the Kṣatriyas are my arms; the Vaiśyas reside in my thighs; and the Śūdras serve my feet through their respective duties and successive stages.
The Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, Yajurveda, and Atharvaveda likewise [are my limbs].
These emerge from me alone and enter back into me;
they are ascetics for whom peace is supreme, who have restrained their selves and seek liberation,
being free from desire, anger, and hatred, detached, and cleansed of all impurity.
Established in being, free from egoism, and always skilled in the knowledge of the inner self, the wise Brahmins worship me alone, constantly meditating upon me.
I am the light that brings dissolution; I am Yama, the bringer of all things.

I am the sun that brings about the dissolution of the world; I am the wind that brings about the dissolution. O best of the twice-born, know that these forms of stars which are seen in the vault of the sky are my own forms.
Know that all the oceans, the mines of jewels, in every direction,
are my clothing, my bed, and my dwelling;
they have been well-arranged by me alone for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
"O best of beings, know that desire, anger, joy, fear, and likewise delusion— all these are indeed my own forms,
O Brahmin, which men attain by performing auspicious deeds."
Truth, generosity, fierce austerity, and non-violence toward living beings—
these have been ordained by me according to my own method for those who dwell within my body;
their consciousness being overwhelmed by me, they act not out of their own desire.
O wise one, those twice-born who study the Veda correctly, perform various sacrifices, possess tranquil souls, and have conquered their anger,
attain that which cannot be attained by men of evil deeds.

Know that state of mine, which yields great fruit, to belong to those of well-performed deeds; you yourself should recognize it as attainable by men whose selves are purified, and not by those overcome by greed, who are wretched, ignoble,
and of undisciplined soul.
The path practiced by yogis is difficult for the utterly deluded to attain. Whenever there is a decline of dharma, O best of beings,
and a rise of adharma, then I manifest myself.
For when Daityas devoted to violence— who are incapable of being slain by the best of the gods—
and likewise fierce Rākṣasas arise in this world,
then I shall be born in the homes of those who perform auspicious deeds.
Having entered a human body, I pacify everything;
having created gods, humans, gandharvas, serpents, and rākṣasas,
as well as all stationary beings, I withdraw them all by means of my own creative power (māyā).

Furthermore, at the time of action, I, having reflected upon a body, create one for myself; entering a human body for the purpose of establishing the boundaries [of dharma]. My color is white in the Kṛta age, and yellow in the Tretā age.

When it is red, the Dvāpara age has arrived; likewise, when it is black, the Kali Yuga occurs. At that time, three parts indeed belong to unrighteousness, O best of sages, when my complexion becomes black.
And when the time of the end has arrived, becoming Time itself most terrible,
I alone destroy the three worlds in their entirety, including all things mobile and immobile. I am the three-pathed one, the soul of all, who brings happiness to all the worlds.
The Conqueror, all-pervading, infinite, Hṛṣīkeśa, the wide-striding one— O Brahmin, I alone lead the wheel of time; indeed, I am formless,
the pacifier of all beings, and the one who exerts effort for the sake of all worlds.
And in all the worlds, my devotees worship me in every way. O best of sages, O chief of brahmins, my self has been thus rightly dedicated toward all beings, yet no one knows me.
"O twice-born one, whatever suffering you have experienced on my account,
O sinless one, all of that shall lead to your happiness and your ultimate welfare.
And whatever, whether stationary or moving, has been seen by you in this world,"
"O best of sages, this self of mine has been ordained in every way;
half of my body is the Grandfather of all the worlds.
I am named Nārāyaṇa, the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace."
O brahmin seer, for as long as it takes for a thousand cycles of the ages, I, the soul of the universe and the grandfather of all worlds, sleep; in this manner,
O best of sages, I remain here throughout all time.
Though not an infant, he appeared in the form of an infant until Brahmā was awakened. O Brahmin, this boon has been granted to you by me, who am in the form of Brahmā,
being repeatedly well-pleased and honored by the hosts of brahmin-sages.

Seeing everything as a single ocean, with all things mobile and immobile destroyed, I perceived that you were despondent; therefore, I showed you this world. When you entered the interior of my body, you beheld it thus.
Seeing the entire world and being struck with wonder, you did not understand;
therefore, O brahmin-sage, you were quickly expelled from my mouth by me.
And I have declared to you my own self, which is difficult even for gods and asuras to comprehend.
"O brahmin-sage, as long as that Blessed One Brahmā, the great ascetic, does not awaken, you may move about here at your ease with full confidence;
but once he has awakened, O Grandfather of all the worlds,"
"O best of the twice-born, having become one with my body, I shall indeed create space,
earth, light, wind, and water,
as well as whatever else remains in this world, both stationary and moving."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, O dear one, that most wonderful deity vanished;
and I behold these various creatures fashioned in many different ways.
O King, O best of the Bharatas, O foremost of all upholders of dharma, this wonder was witnessed by me when that dissolution of the age had arrived:
how the Soul of the Sūta withdrew himself from the fourteenfold categories of existence.
"O tiger among men, that god with lotus-like eyes whom I beheld long ago— having entered the Supreme Self and sleeping, his intellect thus limited— that very Janārdana is this relative of yours."
Indeed, by virtue of this very boon, memory does not desert me;
and, O son of Kuntī, I possess long life as well as the power to die at my own will.
This is that very Kṛṣṇa, the descendant of Vṛṣṇi, the ancient Person, the all-pervading Lord.
The mighty-armed Hari, whose nature is inconceivable, sits as if at play;
he is the Sātvata, the creator, the ordainer, and the destroyer,
bearing the Śrīvatsa on his chest, Govinda, the Lord of the Lords of Creatures, the Sovereign.
Upon seeing this tiger among the Vṛṣṇis, this memory has come to me:
[the memory] of the primordial god, the unborn Viṣṇu, the Puruṣa clad in yellow garments;
Mādhava is indeed the father and the mother of all beings.
"Go to him for refuge, O bulls among the Kauravas; he is the one worthy of being sought as a protector.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been addressed thus, those sons of Pṛthā and the twins, those bulls among men, [went to him].
Together with Draupadī Kṛṣṇā, they paid homage to Janārdana. And he,
O tiger among men, consoled them with most beautiful and gentle words, honoring them as they deserved according to tradition.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, again questioned the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya regarding the future destiny of the world during the imperial sovereignty;
"O best of speakers, we have heard from you that which is truly wonderful."
O Sage Bhārgava, regarding what occurred at the beginning of the age concerning creation and dissolution,
I have a further curiosity even now in this Kali Yuga:
amidst these confused states of dharma, what indeed will remain?
What will be the vigor of men there, what will be their food and conduct,
what will be their lifespan, and what will they wear at the end of the Yuga? And reaching what limit will the Kṛta age be restored once again?
"O Sage, speak in detail; you speak of many wonderful things here.
Thus addressed, that best of sages, the great muni, spoke once more, delighting the tiger among the Vṛṣṇis and the Pāṇḍavas.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Listen, O King, to that which was seen by me in the past, as well as what was heard and experienced, O Indra among kings, born of the grace of the God of gods."

O bull of the Bharatas, learn from me as I describe the future course of events for all the world, occurring when a turbid age has arrived. In the Kṛta age, dharma was complete in its four quarters, free from deceit and artifice.
In ancient times, Dharma was established among human beings as a bull with all four feet intact;
however, pierced by the foot of Adharma, it remained established with only three parts.
In the Tretā age, it is said that Dharma is mixed with one half of Adharma. In the Dvāpara age, it is likewise described as being thus intermingled.
O best of the Bharatas, when the age of darkness (Tāmasa Yuga) has arrived, unrighteousness stands having overwhelmed the worlds with three parts; meanwhile,
righteousness attends upon human beings with only a fourth part.
"O Pāṇḍava, understand from me that the lifespan, vigor, intelligence, strength, and splendor of human beings diminish with each successive age.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this applies to kings, Brahmins, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras alike."
Men who use the banner of righteousness as a mere pretext will practice dharma through deceptions;
truth will be diminished in the world by men who consider themselves wise. Due to that loss of truth, their lifespan will become short.

Due to the exhaustion of their lifespan, they will not be able to train in knowledge; being devoid of knowledge and lacking discernment, greed will also overcome them. Men will become deluded, dominated by greed and anger, and attached to sensual pleasures.
Bound by enmity and desiring to kill one another,
the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas will become intermingled with each other;
devoid of austerity and truth, they will become equal to Śūdras.
Those at the end will become those in the middle, and those in the middle will become outcasts;
such will the world be when the end of the age has arrived.
Linen will be the finest of garments, and *koradūṣaka* grain the best of crops.
At the end of the Yuga, men will have wives as their friends;
they will live by the sale of fish and meat,
and even milk goats and sheep when cows have disappeared— at the end of the Yuga.
Even those who are always firm in their vows are possessed by greed; indeed,
these men rob one another and cause mutual injury.
At the end of the age, those who do not chant prayers, the nihilists, and thieves will come to be;
they will sow medicinal herbs on the banks of rivers with spades, yet at the end of the age, even those herbs will yield but meager fruit for them.
Those men who are always firm in their vows regarding ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and rites for the gods (*daiva*),
they too, possessed by greed, will eat one another here;
the father will be the eater of the son, and likewise the son of the father.
At the end of the Yuga, forbidden foods will be consumed;
even those observing vows and householders alike will eat at night at the end of the Yuga. Thus shall they act in the Kali age, deluded by the scriptures.

The Brahmins, revilers of the Vedas, will not observe their vows; deluded by the doctrine of causality, they will neither perform sacrifices nor offer oblations. Bewildered by the doctrine of causality, they will direct their efforts toward lowly pursuits.

In low-lying places they will practice agriculture; they will yoke cows to the plow, and men will make even yearling calves pull the burden. Sons will commit the murder of their fathers, and likewise, fathers will commit the murder of their sons.
Free from agitation and speaking with great eloquence, he shall not encounter censure.
The entire world will become like a barbarian, devoid of ritual action and abandoned by sacrifice;
likewise, it will be joyless and without festivals.
For in this world, men— of little heroism and strength, arrogant, and devoted to greed and delusion— will generally seize the wealth of the wretched, of those with many kinsmen, and of widows.
Content with the giving of such stories, even wicked men will accept [such teachings], embracing sinful conduct; and,
O son of Kuntī, kings of evil intellect will cause [others] to be slaughtered.
At the end of the age, the Kṣatriyas will become thorns to the world— fools who imagine themselves wise, intent on killing one another,
unprotective, greedy, and arrogant with pride and conceit.
At the end of the age, O Bhārata, people will take pleasure solely in the use of force; repeatedly attacking the virtuous, they will mercilessly enjoy their wives and wealth even as they weep.

No one will ask for a maiden in marriage, nor will a maiden be given away; when the end of the age has arrived, women will be taken by force. And kings, their minds deluded, will be discontented and seize the wealth of others.
When the end of the Yuga has arrived, they will seize everything by every possible means;
O Bhārata, the entire world will become barbarized,
and when the end of the Yuga has arrived, hand will rob hand.
In this world, truth is obscured by those men who consider themselves wise:
the elderly possess the intellects of children, while children possess the wisdom of the elderly; the timid pride themselves on being heroes, while heroes despair over their timidity.

When the end of the age has arrived, they do not trust one another; the entire world, established in greed and delusion, is to be carried away in a single day. Unrighteousness increases greatly, and righteousness does not prevail.

O lord of men, at the end of the age, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas will no longer remain; the world will then become a single caste. A father will not tolerate his son, nor likewise will a son tolerate his father.
And no wife whatsoever will perform service to her husband;
when the end of the age has arrived, people will resort to those regions where barley is the food and likewise where wheat is the food.
O Lord of the People, when the end of the age has arrived, men and women will eat whatever they please and will no longer tolerate one another;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the entire world will become like barbarians.
For men will no longer satisfy the ancestors with funeral offerings;
no one will be a listener to anyone, and no one will be a teacher to anyone.
At that time, O lord of men, the world will be swallowed by darkness.
At that time, the maximum lifespan will be sixteen years;
then, when the end of the age has arrived, they will relinquish their lives.
Furthermore, girls will give birth at the fifth or even the sixth year.
At that time, O King, men will be born at seven or eight years of age; and then,
O tiger among kings, at the end of the Yuga, neither woman toward her husband nor man toward his wife will find satisfaction.
At the end of the age, there will be those with meager wealth who bear false emblems, and violence will prevail; no one will give anything to anyone.
The countryside will have its markets as its only source of sustenance, and crossroads will be dominated by jackals.
At the end of the age, women will have hair as stiff as thorns;
there is no doubt that in the final period, men will become barbarians— cruel, omnivorous, and fierce in all their deeds.
At the time of buying and selling, O best of the Bharatas, everyone will practice deception against one another out of greed for livelihood;
and likewise, without possessing true knowledge, they will perform their ritual acts.

When the end of the age has arrived, all people will act according to their own whims; by their very nature, they will be performers of cruel deeds and will be suspicious of one another as the destruction of the age approaches.
Without remorse, they will destroy groves and trees;
there will be a destruction in the world of the lives of embodied beings. Thus, overcome by greed, they will roam this earth.
The Brahmins will exist, yet they will consume the property of Brahmins;
the twice-born, crying out "Alas! and afflicted by fear, oppressed by the Śūdras, and finding no protector, will indeed wander this earth.
When men become fierce, cruel, destroyers of life, and harmers of living beings,
then the age will come to an end;
they will take refuge in rivers, mountains, and rugged terrains.
O descendant of the Kuru lineage,
O King, those best of the twice-born fled in terror like crows when oppressed by robbers;
they were constantly tormented by wicked kings with the burden of taxes.
O protector of the earth, having abandoned their fortitude during this terrible dissolution of the age,
those who serve the Śūdras will perform improper acts;
the Śūdras will proclaim the Dharma, while the Brāhmaṇas will sit as their attendants.
And there will be listeners established in authority;
yet this world will become perverted, with high and low reversed,
fallen away from the practice of Dharma, and possessed by greed and delusion.
At the end of the age, they will worship *eḍūka* shrines and abandon the deities; Śūdras will perform services, and not the twice-born,
in the hermitages of the great seers and in the dwellings of the Brāhmaṇas.
In the shrines of the gods, at sacred monuments, and in the abodes of the nāgas,
the earth will be marked by mounds of earth rather than adorned with temples;
when the age has declined, that is the sign of the end of the yuga.

When men will be fierce, devoid of dharma, eaters of flesh, and drinkers of liquor, then the age shall be shortened. O King, when flower is placed upon flower and fruit is placed upon fruit, [then the age shall be shortened].
O Great King, when that [age] comes to an end, the Yuga will be contracted;
when the Yuga has passed, the rain-god Parjanya will fail to rain at the proper time,
and then the religious rites of human beings will be performed out of order.
Then the low-born will enter into conflict with the Brahmins,
and before long the earth will be overrun by barbarians;
out of fear of the burden of taxes, the Brahmins will flee in the ten directions.
The rulers of men will also act unjustly;
the provinces, indistinguishable from one another, will be afflicted by droughts,
and people who subsist on fruits and roots will take refuge in hermitages.
In such a world thrown into confusion, there will be no established order;
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas will abandon their sacred duties,
and disciples, acting contrary to what is pleasing, will not abide by the instructions.
Immediately thereafter, the teacher’s deposit shall remain;
friends, relatives, and kinsmen will depart according to their worldly interests,
and at the end of the age, there will be the destruction of all beings.
All the directions are ablaze, the constellations are wavering,
the luminaries are unfavorable, and the winds are turbulent; moreover,
many falling meteors portend great terror.
Accompanied by six others, the sun will scorch; there will be tumultuous roars and conflagrations in every direction, and at that time,
the sun will be obscured by headless trunks at both its rising and setting.
At that time, when the end of the Yuga has arrived, the thousand-eyed Indra will rain out of season; the crops will not grow,
and women will constantly speak cruelly, harshly, and take pleasure in weeping.
At that time, during the dissolution of the age, women will no longer abide by the words of their husbands; sons will slay their mothers and fathers,
and women, relying on their sons, will destroy their husbands.

O Great King, Rāhu shall approach the sun out of season; and at the end of the age, the consumer of oblations (the fire) shall blaze forth on all sides. At that time, travelers will beg for food and water.
Cast out, they will find no place to dwell and lie upon the road; when the end of the age has arrived,
the elephants, crows, birds, beasts,
and twice-born ones will utter harsh words like portents of destruction.
When the end of the age has arrived, men will then abandon their friends, kinsmen, people, and even their own retinues; they will likewise forsake countries,
directions, towns, and cities.
When the end of the age has arrived, people will gradually take refuge [in these practices];
crying out to one another with most dreadful words such as "Alas, father! Alas, son!", the people will wander over the earth.

At the end of the age, there will be *śūdras* who address others as "bhoḥ," and *brāhmaṇas* who delight in the vulgar; they will be crowded with people of heretical sects when the tumultuous conflict occurs at the end of the age.
The world, preceded by the twice-born, will gradually come into being;
then, after another interval of time, for the sake of the world's increase once more,
destiny will again become favorable by chance.
When the moon, the sun, as well as Tiṣya and Bṛhaspati,
shall come together in a single zodiacal sign, then the Kṛta age will begin; the rain-clouds will pour forth in due season, and the stars will be auspicious.
The planets will also move clockwise and follow their natural courses; they will move to the right and proceed in accordance with their proper orbits,
moving clockwise as they honor one another.
There will be security, abundance, health, and freedom from disease.
Impelled by Time, a twice-born man named Kalki Viṣṇuyaśas,
possessed of great heroism, great intelligence, and great prowess, shall arise.
He was born in the village of Saṃbhala in an auspicious brahmin household;
by his mere thought, all vehicles, weapons, warriors, armaments, and armor shall attend upon him.

He shall become a universal monarch (cakravartin) who conquers through righteousness; he shall bring this turbulent world to a state of clarity. Arisen as a radiant brahmin, noble-minded, he will bring about the end of the age of decay.
For he is the one who brings about the end of this entire age;
surrounded by Brāhmaṇas, that twice-born one will then exterminate all the lowly Mleccha hordes wherever they may be found.
The high-souled king, endowed with excellent conduct and devoted to the welfare of his subjects—
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Then, having brought about the destruction of the thieves, he gave this earth to the twice-born."
Having established the auspicious boundaries ordained by the Self-Existent One, he will duly perform the great horse sacrifice (Vājimedha);
then, his merit and fame having been realized, he will retire to the forest in his old age.
The humans dwelling in this world will follow that same conduct; and when the destruction of the thieves has been accomplished by the Brahmins, there will be security.
[They shall take up] black antelope skins, spears, tridents, and other weapons.
Establishing [the law] in various regions and conquered territories, being praised by the best of Brahmins and honoring those foremost of the twice-born,
Kalki will traverse the earth, ever intent on the destruction of the Dasyus.

"Alas, father! Alas, son!"—uttering such exceedingly cruel words as these while crying out piteously, he will bring those dasyus to utter destruction. Then, O Bhārata, there shall indeed be the destruction of unrighteousness and the increase of righteousness.
When the Kṛta age has arrived, people will likewise be devoted to ritual action;
there will be groves and shrines, ponds and wells, various lotus-pools, and temples for the deities.
In the Kṛta Yuga, various sacrificial rites will flourish;
there will be virtuous Brāhmaṇas, sages devoted to austerity,
and people who abide in truth, including those in the stages of life along with the heretics.
All seeds that are sown shall indeed sprout,
O Indra among kings, and all crops shall flourish in every season;
men will be devoted to acts of giving, to vows, and to religious observances.
In the Kṛta Yuga, brahmins devoted to the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), desiring dharma and filled with joy,
will protect this earth according to dharma;
and vaiśyas will be devoted to their proper occupations.
Brahmins were devoted to the six duties, Kṣatriyas were devoted to protection,
and Śūdras were devoted to serving the three other castes;
such was the dharma in the Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages.
And that which was proclaimed by you regarding the final age,
O Pāṇḍava— the calculation of the ages known to all the world—
all this, concerning the past and the future, has been narrated to you by me.
Having recollected the Purāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu and praised by the sages, I—
who have lived for a long time— have thus seen and experienced the paths of saṃsāra many times; these I have described to you.

And furthermore, O Acyuta, this other matter has been told by me in its entirety and according to the truth, along with my brothers; listen to my words for the sake of liberation from your doubt regarding dharma.
"O best among the upholders of dharma, you must always unite yourself with dharma;
for a king whose soul is rooted in dharma rejoices both in this world and after death. And listen, O sinless one, to these auspicious words which I shall speak to you."
"You must never show contempt for a Brāhmaṇa;
an enraged Brāhmaṇa could destroy even the worlds by his mere resolve.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Mārkaṇḍeya, the wise king, the foremost of the Kurus and possessed of supreme luster, spoke these most excellent words:
"O sage, in what dharma should I abide while protecting my subjects?"
"And how should I conduct myself so that I do not fall away from my own dharma?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of sages, having heard this, what ought I to do?"
"And how shall this conquered world be protected?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"One who is compassionate toward all beings, intent on their welfare, affectionate, and free from malice—"
Devoted to the protection of your subjects as if they were your own children,
practice righteousness, abandon unrighteousness, and worship the ancestors and the gods.
Whatever you have done through negligence, rectify it by means of proper giving.
Enough of relying on pride; always remain dependent [on others]. Having conquered the entire earth, be joyful and happy.
This dharma, pertaining to both the past and the future, has been proclaimed to you.
There is nothing on earth, past or future, that is unknown to you; therefore, my dear son, do not take this distress to heart. Wise men, my dear, are not deluded even when oppressed by time.
O mighty-armed one, this is the time even for all the dwellers of heaven;
for all creatures, O dear one, are bewildered when impelled by Time.
Let there be no hesitation in you regarding what I have said to you, O sinless one.
For if you speak these words with excessive suspicion, there will be a violation of dharma on your part. O bull among the Bharatas, you are born in the renowned lineage of the Kurus;
therefore, perform all this through deed, mind, and speech.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of the twice-born, I shall diligently carry out with effort that speech which you have spoken, O Lord, for it is captivating to the ear and in accordance with the Vedas."
"O chief of Brahmins, I have no greed, no fear, and no envy.
O Lord, I shall indeed do everything that you have commanded of me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, having heard those words of the high-souled Pāṇḍava,
the Pāṇḍavas, together with the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, were filled with joy,
as were all those bull-like Brahmins who had assembled there.
Having thus heard the auspicious discourse of the wise Mārkaṇḍeya, they were filled with wonder upon the narration of the ancient lore. Janamejaya said:
"Furthermore, you ought to speak again of the greatness of the Brahmins,
just as the great ascetic Mārkaṇḍeya described it to the Pāṇḍavas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O son of Pāṇḍu, you ought to speak further regarding the great majesty of the Brāhmaṇas," he said to Mārkaṇḍeya.
Then Mārkaṇḍeya replied:
"Listen to this unprecedented account of the conduct of the Brāhmaṇas."
Listen, I shall relate this ancient history of the Brahman-sages.
In Ayodhyā, there was a king named Parikṣit, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, who went out on a hunt.
While he was pursuing a deer on a single horse, the deer led him far away.
Then, exhausted from the journey and overcome by hunger and thirst, he saw a dark grove of trees in a certain place;
he entered it.
There, seeing an exceedingly beautiful lake in the middle of that grove, he plunged into it together with his horse.
Then, having recovered, he threw the lotus stalks before his horse and sat down on the bank of the lotus pond.
As he lay there, he heard the sound of sweet singing.
Having heard it, he reflected:
"I do not see any human beings here;
whose singing voice is this?
Then he saw a maiden of most exquisite beauty, gathering flowers and singing.
Then she approached the king.
The king said to her,
"Whose daughter are you, O fortunate one?"
She replied,
"I am a maiden.
The king said to her:
"I am a suitor for you," he said;
then the maiden replied,
"I can be obtained by you on one condition."
"It is not otherwise," [she said].
Then the king asked her about the agreement (*samaya*),
and thereupon the maiden spoke as follows.
"Water must not be shown to me," he said.
The king replied, "Very well," and having approached her, he sat with her.
While the king was sitting right there, the army followed after him.
Having followed step by step behind the king, he stood surrounding him. Once the king had recovered his composure, he departed in that very same palanquin without it being opened.
Upon reaching his own city, he remained there enjoying himself in private with her.
He saw nothing else at all.
Then the chief minister questioned the women who were moving about near him, asking,
"What is the purpose here?"
Then those women said, "We see something unprecedented; no water is being brought here.
Then the minister, having caused a waterless grove to be made—abounding in noble trees with many roots, flowers, and fruits—approached the king in secret and spoke to him.
"This forest is vast and waterless;
let us enjoy ourselves here.
At his word, he entered that forest together with that very queen.
Once, while he was living with her in that delightful forest,
the king, afflicted by hunger and thirst and exceedingly exhausted, saw a bower of *atimukta* creepers.
Having entered it together with his beloved, the king beheld a pond filled with pure water and well-constructed with a floor of plaster.
As soon as he saw her, he stood upon that very bank together with the queen.
Then the king said to the queen,
"Come, descend into the water of the pond."
Having heard those words, she descended into the pond and submerged herself; she did not emerge again. While searching for her, the king could not find her.
Having drained the pond and seeing a frog at the mouth of a hole, he became enraged and commanded:
"Let a slaughter of all frogs be carried out!
Whoever seeks my favor shall attend upon me with offerings of dead frogs."
Then, while that terrible slaughter of frogs was being carried out in all directions, fear seized the frogs.
Terrified, they reported everything as it had happened to the king of the frogs.
Thereupon, the king of the frogs, assuming the guise of an ascetic, approached the king.
Approaching him, he said:
"O King, do not fall under the sway of anger;
grant me your favor."
"You ought not to carry out the slaughter of these innocent frogs.
"Do not seek to kill the frogs; O Acyuta, restrain your anger.
And on this point there are two verses:
The great abundance of wealth belonging to those who lack discernment is being squandered.
Promise me this: once you have encountered them, you will not give way to anger. Enough of your committing unrighteousness; what is the use of killing these frogs?
To him who spoke thus, the king—his soul overwhelmed with grief for his beloved people—said:
"I cannot endure this;
I shall slay them."
"My beloved was devoured by these wicked-souled ones;
frogs must be killed by me in every way. O wise one, you ought not to obstruct me."
Having heard those words, his senses and mind distressed, he said:
"Be gracious, O King;
I am the king of frogs, named Āyu."
"That daughter of mine, named Suśobhanā,
is of such immoral conduct;
indeed, many kings have previously been deceived by her."
The king said to him:
"I am a seeker after her;
let her be given to me."
Then her father gave her to the king and said to her,
"Serve this king."
He said to his daughter:

"Since you have deceived the kings, therefore your offspring shall be non-Brahmanical because of your untruthfulness. And that king, having learned of this, his heart bound by the qualities of her charms as if he had attained sovereignty over the three worlds, bowed down and honored her with a voice choked with tears of joy.
He said to the frog king,
"I am favored.
And that frog king, having taken leave of his son-in-law, departed by the way he had come.
Then, after some time, three sons were born to that king: Śala, Dala, and Bala.

Thereupon, at the proper time, his father consecrated the eldest, Śala, in the kingdom and, having fixed his soul upon asceticism, departed for the forest. Then, on one occasion, Śala went out hunting.
Having overtaken the deer, he pursued it in his chariot and said to the charioteer,
"Drive me quickly!"
Thus addressed, the charioteer said to the king:
"Do not persist in this pursuit;
it is impossible for you to capture this deer, even if the two Vāmya horses were yoked to your chariot."
Then the king said to the charioteer:
"Tell me about the two Vāmyas,
or else I shall kill you."
Thus addressed, being terrified by fear of the king and fearful of Vāmadeva’s curse, he told the king:
"Vāmadeva’s two horses, Vāmīs, are as swift as thought.
Then the king once more raised his sword and said to him, "Speak quickly!"
"I shall kill you," the charioteer said to him, terrified by fear of the king.
Then the king spoke to him as he was saying this:
"Go to the hermitage of Vāmadeva."
Having gone to the hermitage of Vāmadeva, he said to that seer:
"Venerable sir, a deer pierced by me is fleeing;
I wish to overtake it."
"Please give me the two Vāmyas," he said.
The seer replied to him,
"I shall give you the two Vāmyas."

"Since you have accomplished your task, you must quickly return these two horses to me. Having accepted those two horses and taken leave of the ṛṣi, he departed toward the deer in a chariot yoked with the two Vāmīs. As he was going, he spoke to his charioteer.
"These two horse-jewels are not suitable for Brahmins;
they must not be returned to Vāmadeva. Having spoken thus, he captured the deer, returned to his own city, and stationed the two horses in the inner apartments.
Then the seer thought:
"The young prince, having obtained a beautiful wife, is enjoying himself;
he does not return her to me."
"Alas, what misery!"—
having thus resolved in his mind, when the month was complete, he said to his disciple:
"Go, Ātreya."
"Tell the king:
'If it is sufficient, give back the two mules belonging to the preceptor.
Having gone there, he spoke thus to the king.
The king replied to him:
"This is the vehicle of kings;
Brāhmaṇas are not worthy of such jewels."
"Furthermore, what need have the brahmins for horses? Please, let us go back. Having gone there, he reported this to his teacher.
Having heard those unpleasant words, Vāmadeva, his soul overcome with anger, approached the king himself and urged him for the sake of the horse. But the king did not give it. Vāmadeva said:
"O King, give me the two Vāmīs;
for you have accomplished a task that could not be achieved by others.
Let Varuṇa not strike you down with his terrible nooses."
Existing between the Brahmin and the Kshatriya,
the King said:
"The two oxen are well-vowed, excellent, and well-tamed."
"O Vāmadeva, this is the vehicle of the Brahmins.
Go with these two wherever you desire, O Great Seer;
for the Vedas indeed carry one such as you."
Vāmadeva said: "O King, the Vedic meters that exist in this world indeed carry one like me to that other world."
"But in this world, O King, this is my vehicle, as it is for others like me. The king said:
"Either let four donkeys carry you,
or excellent mules, or swift bay horses; go by them, for this is the vehicle of a Kṣatriya."
"Know that these two are mine and not yours.
Vāmadeva said:
"They say this is a formidable vow for a Brāhmaṇa."
O King, let these great, iron-bodied beings of terrible form, bearing sharpened spears, carry you away in four directions while you are still alive here.
"Or perhaps four most terrible *yātudhāna*s have been dispatched by me, desiring your death.
The king said:
O Vāmadeva, those who know you as a Brāhmaṇa and yet seek to strike you with word, mind, or deed— may they,
along with their disciples, fall down here.
Driven by my words, with sharp spears and swords in their hands—
Vāmadeva said:
"O King, having accepted these two Vāmya mares of mine..."
"Come to me again with the thought, 'I shall give,' and quickly bestow upon me your two excellent Vāmya horses.
The king said:
If it be possible for you to live,
hunting is not fit for Brāhmaṇas;
yet from this day forward, I shall no longer command you to practice untruth.
"By fully dedicating myself to your very command,
O Brahmin, may I likewise attain the world of merit.
Vāmadeva said:
O King, Brahmins do not engage in reproach through speech, mind, or deed; rather,
the wise man who thus pursues the Brahman through austerity [is truly such].
"Indeed, by that he becomes excellent while living.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O King, when this had been spoken by Vāmadeva,"
Rākṣasas of terrible form rose up;
being struck by them with spears in their hands, the king then spoke these words aloud.
O Brahmin, whether it be the Ikṣvākus,
or Dala, or even other subjects, if they were subject to my will, I would never relinquish Vāmadeva’s two Vāmyas.
"Those who are virtuous in their conduct do not act in such a manner.
Even as he was speaking these words, that lord of the earth was struck by the *yātudhānas* and quickly fell to the ground.
Then, having learned that the king had been struck down,
the Ikṣvākus went there and consecrated that brahmin in the kingdom.
Vāmadeva spoke these words:
"A portion must indeed be given to the Brāhmaṇas;
O King, this is seen as the rule in all matters of dharma."
"O lord of men, if you fear unrighteousness,
give me the two Vāmyas immediately this very day.
Having heard these words of Vāmadeva, [the king replied:]
In his rage, that king said to the charioteer:
"Bring me a single arrow of variegated form, smeared with poison and kept ready."
"By whom Vāmadeva was pierced so that he lay there,
being bitten by dogs and appearing in a state of agony.
Vāmadeva said:
"O lord of men, I know that your son Śyenajit was born ten years ago to the queen;
slay him at my command, for he has been sent forth by me."
"Quickly [strike] my beloved with arrows of terrible form.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O King, having been addressed thus by Vāmadeva..."
That arrow of fierce brilliance, once released, struck the prince within the inner apartments;
having heard that report, Dala spoke these words.
"O Ikṣvākus, behold! I shall do what is pleasing to you;
having overpowered this brahmin, I shall slay him today. Let another one of fierce splendor be brought forth!"
"Behold my prowess today, O lords of the earth!
Vāmadeva said:
"This arrow of terrible form which you [hold]..."
O lord of men, you are fitting to me an arrow smeared with poison; you will not be able to release this excellent shaft, nor even to fit it to the string.
The king said:
"O Ikṣvākus, behold me seized!
Indeed, I am not able to release this arrow."
"And I do not venture to bring about his destruction;
let the venerable Vāmadeva indeed live!
Vāmadeva said:
"Touch this queen with an arrow;
then you shall be released from that sin.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the king did exactly so;
thereupon the princess spoke to the sage,
"O Vāmadeva, I shall join him as is fitting."
Day after day, lying down,
she praised [the Brahmins] while seeking truthful words from them;
O Brahmin, may I likewise attain the world of merit.
Vāmadeva said:
"O lady of auspicious eyes, the royal family has been saved by you;
choose an incomparable boon, and I shall grant it to you."
"O princess, govern these kinsmen and this vast kingdom of Ikṣvāku,
O blameless one; for you, O virtuous lady, are steadfast and pure of heart."
"O fair-browed one, let your mind always be directed toward the Dharma, and expect a boon from me;
for you must always protect the Bull."
The princess said:
"O Blessed One, I choose this one boon alone:
let my husband be released from his sin this very day."
"O Brahmin, may my son thrive in conduct and intellect; may he live today through your grace. Bless him, along with his sons and kinsmen, with auspiciousness."
"O foremost of the twice-born, this boon has indeed been chosen by me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard these words of the princess, that sage—
"So be it," said the hero of the Kurus.
Thereupon the king became joyful and,
having bowed down, he presented the two Vāmyas to him.
Vaiśampāyana said:
The sages, the brahmins, and Yudhiṣṭhira questioned Mārkaṇḍeya: "By what means did the sage Baka become long-lived?"
But Mārkaṇḍeya said to them all: "The royal sage Baka is a man of great asceticism and long life;
there should be no doubt about this."
O Bhārata, having heard this, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, together with his brothers, questioned Mārkaṇḍeya.
The two great-souled ones, Baka and Dālbhya, are heard of as long-lived;
they are the two ṛṣis, esteemed by the world, who were friends of the king of the gods. (4)
O Blessed One, I desire this meeting between Baka and Śakra;
please explain to me in truth that which is joined with both pleasure and pain. (5)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, when that hair-raising battle between the gods and the asuras had concluded,
Indra became the sovereign of the three worlds.
The rain-cloud pours down properly, and the harvests are most excellent;
the subjects are free from disease, exceedingly righteous, and devoted to the Dharma.
And all the people were joyful, established in their own duties;
seeing all those subjects so joyful, the Destroyer of Bala [Indra] was pleased.
Then, O King, the joyful Śatakratu, the king of the gods, mounting Airāvata, gazed upon those joyful subjects. (9)
He saw various hermitages and diverse, auspicious rivers,
as well as prosperous cities, market towns, and rural districts.
And he established kings who were skilled in protecting their subjects and practitioners of righteousness,
as well as wells, water-stations, ponds, lakes, and reservoirs.
O King, having been served by the best of the twice-born through various vows and observances,
Śatakratu then descended from that delightful [heaven] onto the earth.
O King, in that delightful and auspicious region, thickly covered with many trees, situated toward the beautiful eastern direction near the ocean. (13)
There, in that delightful hermitage frequented by deer and birds,
the king of the gods beheld Baka in that beautiful hermitage.
But Baka, seeing the Lord of the Gods, became firmly pleased in mind;
he then honored him with the offering of water for the feet, a seat, and the guest-offering (arghya), as well as with fruits and roots.
Then, seated comfortably and bestowing boons, the destroyer of Bala,
the god and lord of the thirty-three, spoke this question to Baka.
O sinless sage, for you who have lived for a hundred thousand years, tell me, O Brahmin, what is the suffering of those who live so long? (17)
Baka said:
Living together with those who are unpleasant, separation from those who are dear, and association with the wicked—this is the suffering of those who live for a long time. (18)
The destruction of one's children and wife, as well as that of kinsmen and friends, and dependence upon others—what indeed could be more painful than this? (19)
Nothing else appears to me in all the worlds to be more miserable than a man deprived of wealth, who is utterly despised by others. (20)
Those who live long witness the rise of the low-born into noble families and the decline of the well-born into ruin; they behold both unions and separations.
O Lord Śatakratu, this is indeed evident to you:
how can there be a reversal of fortune for those who were once prosperous but have now fallen into ruin?
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, humans, nāgas, and rākṣasas all undergo reversal; what indeed could be more painful than that? (23)
Those born into noble families suffer when they fall under the sway of base origins;
the poor are despised by the wealthy—what indeed could be more painful than that? This great disparity in the world is seen in its vast extent.
Those of inferior knowledge are seen, while those wise and skilled suffer; human existence here is seen to be beset by manifold suffering and affliction. (25)
Indra said:
"O highly fortunate one, served by hosts of celestial sages, O Brahmin, tell me once again: what is the happiness of those who live for a long time?"
Baka said:
"What indeed could be more blissful than for one who, avoiding bad friends, cooks only vegetables in his home on the eighth or even the twelfth lunar day?"
Where days are not counted, they do not call him a great eater;
even for one who cooks only vegetables, there is indeed happiness in the house of Maghavan. (28)
It is better to eat even fruits and vegetables at home with a dignified spirit, having earned them by one's own effort without depending on anyone else. (29)
But for one who eats in another's house and is constantly humiliated, even food that is very pure is not beneficial; therefore, this is the deliberation of the virtuous.
But he who, like a dog, desires to eat the food of others—fie on that which is eaten by that wretched and evil-minded man! (31)
What indeed could be more blissful than for that best of the twice-born who, having given food to guests, living beings, and ancestors, eats the remaining portions? (32)
Therefore, O Śatakratu, there is nothing else more delicious or pure than this:
that one who eats only after having given to guests does so constantly. (33)
For as many mouthfuls of food as a twice-born man constantly eats, the donor obtains the merit of giving away that many thousands of cows. (34)

Whatever sin has been committed in youth, all that certainly perishes when water, accompanied by a sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*), has passed into the hand of a twice-born (*dvija*) who has partaken [of the meal];
for one sprinkles that water with water, and thus one crosses over that sin in an instant. (35)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having related these and many other auspicious stories,
the lord of the gods took his leave of Baka and departed for the third heaven.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the Pāṇḍavas spoke again to Mārkaṇḍeya:
"The great majesty of the Brāhmaṇas has been recounted."
Now, [the author] states that he wishes to hear about the great majesty of the kṣatriya. //37//
The great seer Mārkaṇḍeya said to them:
"Listen now, O kings, to the great majesty of the royal lineages. (38)
A certain king of the Kurus named Suhotra, having approached the great seers and turned back, beheld King Śibi, the son of Uśīnara, standing upon his chariot and facing him.
Having met one another and exchanged greetings according to their respective ages, and recognizing that they were equals to each other due to the similarity of their virtues,
they both found themselves as one soul with the other and did not yield the path to each other.
Then Nārada appeared there and asked,
"Why do you two stand here blocking each other's path? (41)
The two of them said to Nārada:
"No, O Blessed One; [this is not so] because of the prior agents of karma and so forth."
The path of one who is distinguished, or of one who is capable, is being taught;
and we two have entered into friendship with one another.
And that [knowledge], though extremely excellent due to attentiveness, has fallen away from its proper sequence, with the lower preceding the higher. //42//
Thus addressed, Nārada recited these three verses. (43)

O Kauravya, how could a cruel man not obtain [the fruit of his cruelty] when directed toward one who is mild, O Kaurava; and how could a virtuous man not obtain it when directed toward one who is wicked, nor toward one who is virtuous? (44)
One should perform a deed a hundredfold; there is no doubt regarding this even among the gods.
The lord of the earth, Auśīnara, is indeed of virtuous character.
One should conquer the miser with generosity, the speaker of falsehood with truth;
one should conquer the cruel-doer with forbearance, and the wicked man with goodness.
Both of you are indeed noble.
Let whichever of you it may be now depart;
this is the test.
Having spoken thus, Nārada became silent. //47//
Having heard this, the descendant of Kuru, having circumambulated Śibi and yielded the path to him through his many meritorious deeds,
praised him and departed.
Nārada has also described this great good fortune of the king.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen to this other [account]:
King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, while established in his kingdom, was surrounded by the citizens.
He made them his own. // 50 //
A Brahmin seeking funds for his teacher approached him and said: "O King, I would like to beg for the sake of my teacher according to an agreement. (51)
The king said:
"May the Blessed One explain the proper time."
The Brahmin said:
"O King, a man who is being entreated may commit the greatest act of enmity in the world of the living."
Therefore, O King, I ask you this: how is it that you would give to me today that which is so dear to me?
The king said:
"I do not proclaim my gifts, nor do I listen to requests for wealth that should not be asked for."
Having promised the object to be obtained and having also given it, I become very happy. (54)
"I give you a thousand Rohiṇī cows,
for a Brahmin who comes as a petitioner is dear to me; my mind does not become angry with one who asks."
I never grieve over wealth that has been given away. //55//
Having spoken thus, the king gave a thousand cows to the brahmin;
and so the brahmin obtained a thousand cows. //56//
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O great-souled one, tell me once more of his great majesty," thus spoke the Pāṇḍava.
Then Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O Great King, there were two kings named Vṛṣadarbha and Seduka,
who delighted in the path of policy and were skilled in the use of missiles and hand-to-hand weapons."
Seduka understood the silent vow (upāṃśuvrata) of Vṛṣadarbha even as a child:
that base metal (kupya) must not be given to a Brāhmaṇa. // 59 //
Then, a certain brahmin, accomplished in the study of the Vedas, having offered a blessing to that Seduka, begged for the sake of his teacher, saying:
"May the Blessed One give me a thousand horses. (60)
Seduka said to that brahmin,
"It is not possible for me to give away my teacher's fee;
therefore, go to Vṛṣadarbha."
"O Brahmin, that king is a supreme knower of the Dharma; beg from him,
and he will give it to you."
This was his secret vow.
Then the Brāhmaṇa, having gone into the presence of Vṛṣadarbha, requested a thousand horses. That king struck him with a whip.
The brahmin said to him: "Why do you strike me, who am innocent?"
When he had spoken thus while cursing him, the king said: "O Brahmin, is it because he does not give to you, or is this [lack of giving] due to his status as a Brahmin? (63) O Brahmin.
He said: "O King of Kings, sent by Seduka, I have come into your presence to beg;
instructed by him, I have entreated you. (64)
The king said:
"I shall give it to you tomorrow morning, to whoever comes to me today as an offering."
How could the striking with a whip be in vain for one who is struck? (65)
Having said this, he gave the Brahmin the daily fee for his labor; he took only the price for the extra thousand horses. //66//
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
A conversation arose among the gods [regarding] going to the surface of the earth to see Śibi, the son of Uśīnara, the lord of the earth.
"Let us examine this Śibi properly," they said. (67)
Having said, "So be it," Agni and Indra approached him;
Agni in the form of a dove.
Indra, in the form of a hawk, swooped down upon him for the sake of the meat.
Then the pigeon alighted upon the lap of the king as he sat upon his celestial throne.
Then the domestic priest said to the king:
"Fearing the hawk for the sake of protecting his life, this seeker of life approaches you for refuge."
May he grant wealth;
may the lord of the earth provide atonement for him.
They say the alighting of a dove is terrible. //70//
Then the pigeon said to the king:
"Fearing the hawk and seeking to protect my life, I, who am myself seeking protection for my life, take refuge in you."
Having reached you with my limbs as my means, I, seeking my goal, have become a sage and take refuge in you. Know me to be a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), emaciated by Vedic study,
austerity, and self-restraint.
Know me to be one who speaks without opposition to the Teacher, endowed with such qualities, and free from evil. (71)

I recite the Vedas and I investigate the *chandas*; all the Vedas have been studied by me syllable by syllable. Yet, the gift of a gift to one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) is not truly meritorious.
Do not give me to the hawk; I am not a pigeon. //72//
Then the hawk said to the king: //73//
Or perhaps your dwelling among various states of existence occurred by turns;
you were born before this pigeon,
and then you took this pigeon [as your prey].
O King, do not become an obstacle-maker. //74//
The king said:
"By whom has such a supreme speech, uttered in refined Sanskrit by a bird, ever been heard before?"
Regarding that which the dove speaks and that which the hawk speaks—having understood both, how may it be right? //75//
Rain does not fall upon him during the rainy season;
seed sown by him at the proper time does not sprout.
For he who gives away a frightened person seeking refuge to an enemy—
At that time, though seeking protection, he shall find no protection.
The offspring born become short-lived and perish; his ancestors never grant him a dwelling.
He who delivers a frightened refugee to his enemy—
The gods do not accept his oblation. //77//
The thoughtless man gains food in vain;
he falls swiftly indeed from the heavenly world—
he who gives to an enemy one who has come to him for refuge in fear.
The gods, together with Indra, hurl their thunderbolt at him.
Having cooked a bull together with boiled rice,
may they lead [the offering] back to you from this dove;
in whatever place you take great delight, O hawk.
There, let those Śibis carry my flesh. (79)
The hawk said:
"O King, I would not seek out bulls, nor anything else besides this; there is no meat for me superior to the pigeon."
"This food was given to me today by the gods;
therefore, give it to me, for there is a lack of birds. (80)
The king said:
"Let them lead that bull here, unimpaired; let those men see it as mine alone."
"Take from me this inheritance of one who is possessed by fear; do not harm him, for he is indeed your own."
"I would rather give up my life than give away the pigeon; for this one is gentle. Do you not know this, O hawk?
Do not cause me distress here, O gentle one."
"I will not surrender the pigeon by any means whatsoever. //82//
O Śyena, just as the Śibis, being pleased, might praise me with words of commendation for my deeds, so shall I act only for their benefit.
Instruct me; whatever you say, that I shall do. //83//
The hawk said:
"O King, having cut away flesh from your own right thigh,
provide as much as is equal in weight to this pigeon."
Thus, the pigeon was properly saved from that; the Śibis would praise him, thinking, "A dear deed has been done for me. (84)
Then, having cut a piece of his own flesh from his right thigh, he weighed it on a scale; however, the pigeon remained even heavier. (85)
Again, he cut off another [limb],
for the pigeon was indeed even heavier. Having thus obtained everything, he placed the body upon the scale.
Nevertheless, even so, the pigeon remained significantly heavier. (87)
Then the king himself ascended the scale;
and there was no discrepancy in the king's weight.
Having witnessed this event, the hawk cried out, "I am saved! and vanished.
Then the king said: //90//
The Śibis know you as a dove; O dove, I ask you, O bird, who indeed is the hawk?
No one who lacks mastery could ever do such a thing.
O Blessed One, explain this question to me. //91//
The pigeon said:
"I am Vaiśvānara, the blazing fire whose banner is smoke;
furthermore, I am Śyena, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the lord of Śacī."
"O son of a charioteer, it is well for us to know you, the bull among men;
out of a desire to know you, we have come into your presence. (92)
O King, this piece of flesh which you have cut off with your sword and given to me as my ransom—
this mark of yours I shall make auspicious.
Golden-hued, radiant, and possessing a holy fragrance. //93//
From this side shall be born a man who will be the protector of these subjects, illustrious and highly esteemed by the celestial rishis.
And his name was Kapotaroma. //94//
O King, you shall obtain a son named Śibi, whose hair is like that of a dove and who is born from the earth;
he will possess the sturdy build of a bull, be radiant with glory, and be a preeminent hero among charioteers. (95)
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Mārkaṇḍeya, tell me once more of his great majesty," thus spoke the Pāṇḍava.
Then Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"At the horse sacrifice of Aṣṭaka, son of Viśvāmitra, all the kings indeed arrived."
And his brothers were Pratardana, Vasumanas, and Śibi Auśīnara. //97//
Having completed the sacrifice, he set out on his chariot together with his brothers.
And they, seeing Nārada approaching, saluted him and said, "May your honor ascend the chariot."
Having said "So be it" to them,
he mounted his chariot.
Then, one among them addressed the celestial seer Nārada:
"Having propitiated the Blessed One, I wish to ask him something."
"Ask," the seer said. //101//
He said: "Venerable ones, you are all delighted by every virtue. Now, if the abode of heaven must be reached by four [of you], who would descend? (102)
"This Aṣṭaka shall descend," the seer said. (103)
"What is the reason?
he asked. //104//
Then he said:
"I stayed in the house of Aṣṭaka;
he conveyed me away in a chariot."
Then I saw many thousands of cows, distinguished by their various colors. I asked him, "To whom do these cows belong? He replied:
"These [women] have been bestowed by me"—thus [it is said]. // 108 //
He himself praises that very thing which has been told;
this one shall descend. Now, one must proceed by means of three.
Who shall descend now? 110.
"Pratardana," the seer said. (111)
In that regard, what is the reason? // 112 //
I also dwelt for some time in the house of Pratardana; he carried me away in his chariot. (113)
Then a brahmin might beg of him:
"May your lordship give me a horse. (114)
"I shall give [it] once I have returned," he said to the brahmin.
"Let it be given immediately!"
Thus spoke the brahmin. "Hurry! he said. Having spoken thus to the brahmin, he gave him his right side.
Then another Brahmin, also seeking a horse, arrived. (119)
Having spoken thus to him,
he struck his left heel.
Then he set out;
and once again, another Brahmin seeking a horse arrived.
Then, acting with haste, he unharnessed the left-hand draft animal and gave it to him. As he was departing,
another Brahmin seeking a horse arrived.
He said to him:
"I shall give it once you have passed by. (122)
"Let it be given to me immediately," the brahmin said. (123)
Having given him the horse, as he took up the yoke of the chariot, he declared:
"At present, there is nothing that belongs to the Brahmins."
He who both gives and is envious—
by that very utterance, he shall likewise descend.
Now, if it must be traversed by two [paths], who would descend? (126)
"Vasumān shall descend," thus spoke the seer.
"What is the reason?
he asked. //128//
Then Nārada said:
"While wandering about, I arrived at the house of Vasumanas to offer words of blessing."
It was for the purpose of a flower-chariot that I followed him; when the Brahmins had recited the benedictions, the chariot was shown to the Brahmins.
I praised that chariot.
Then the king said:
"The Blessed One has praised the chariot."
"This is the chariot of the Blessed One. Then, on another occasion, I again approached him,
and once more there was the matter of the chariot.
"This is indeed the perfect [teaching] of the Blessed One," thus the king spoke. (132) Once again, I performed the third recitation of the benediction (*svastivācana*). (133) Then...
While showing me to the brahmins, the king looked at me and said:
"Furthermore, the auspicious recitations for the flower-chariot have been most excellently prepared by the Blessed One. (134)
By this speech of malice one should descend;
but if one must travel alone, who would descend? (136)
Nārada spoke again:
"Śibi should go;
I shall descend. (137)
"What is the reason for this? he asked. //138//
I am not equal to that Śibi. (139)
Then a certain Brahmin said to him:
"O Śibi, I am a seeker of food. (140)
Śibi said to him: "What shall be done?
May your honor command."
Then the brahmin said to him:
"This son of yours named Bṛhadgarbha must be killed;
prepare him for that."
"And provide food;
then I shall wait for you. (142)
Then, having crushed his son,
having prepared him according to the ritual, having placed him in a vessel, and having received him with his head bowed,
he sought out a Brāhmaṇa.

Then, as he was searching for him, someone said to him: "This Brahmin here, having entered your city, is burning your house, your treasury, your armory, your women's quarters, your stables for horses, and your stables for elephants; he is enraged."
Then Śibi, with his facial expression unchanged as before, entered the city and said to that brahmin:
"It is accomplished, Blessed One."
"Food," he said. The brahmin said nothing at all;
out of astonishment, he remained with his face cast downward. Then [the king] propitiated the brahmin.
"O Blessed One, please eat," [he said].
After looking at Śibi for a moment, he said,
"You yourself should eat this."
Regarding this, he says: "In that way. (149)
Śibi, likewise with an undisturbed mind, having honored the skull-bowl and lifted it up, desired to eat.
Then a brahmin took his hand and said to him,
"You have conquered anger."
"There is nothing whatsoever that you should not give for the sake of a brahmin.
The brahmin, in turn, honored that illustrious man.
Looking up,
he saw his son standing before him like a divine youth, adorned and permeated by a holy fragrance. Having accomplished that entire purpose, the brahmin vanished.
The Creator came in that very same guise to test that royal seer. //155//
When he had vanished, the ministers said to the king:
"What was this that you have done, knowing it to be so, while desiring to obtain [the kingdom]? (156)
Śibi said:
"I do not give this for the sake of fame, nor for the sake of wealth, nor out of thirst for enjoyment."
"This path has not been cultivated by the wicked"—thinking thus, I perform all of this. //157//
That which is constantly inhabited by the virtuous is praiseworthy;
therefore, my mind takes refuge in what is praiseworthy. This, indeed, is the most excellent fortune for Śibi.
Therefore, I know this exactly as it is. //158//
Vaiśampāyana said:
The ṛṣis and the Pāṇḍavas questioned Mārkaṇḍeya,
"Is there anyone who has been born much longer than you?"
He said to them:
"There is indeed a royal seer named Indradyumna who, his merit exhausted, has fallen from the third heaven;
thus your fame has been cut off."
He approached me and said,
"Does your honor recognize me?
To him I replied:
"We do not employ elixirs; we undertake the pursuit of our goals through the disciplined austerity of the body.
Thus addressed, that royal seer Indradyumna spoke to me again:
"Is there anyone who has been born much longer than you?"
I replied to him again:
"Because my activities were so distracted, I did not recognize him."
"I am he. He said to me, "There is another who is born much earlier than you. I said to him:
Indeed, there is an owl named Prākārakarṇa in the Himalayas;
he might know you,
for the Himalayas are at a great distance.
"He dwells there.
Having become a horse, he carried me to where that owl was.
Then that royal seer questioned him.
"Do you recognize me?
he asked. Having meditated for a moment, he said to him, "I do not recognize you."
