Thus addressed, the royal seer Indradyumna spoke again to that owl:
"Is there anyone who has been born longer than you?
Being thus addressed, he said to him:
There is indeed a lake named Indradyumna;
in it dwells a crane named Nāḍījaṅgha,
who is older than we.
"Ask him.
Thereupon, Indradyumna took me and the owl and went to that lake where that crane named Nāḍījaṅgha was.
He was questioned by us.
"Do you recognize King Indradyumna?
Having been addressed thus, he reflected for a moment and said,
"I do not recognize King Indradyumna."
Then he was asked by us:
"Is there anyone else who is older than you?
He replied to us: "Indeed, there lives right here in this lake a tortoise named Akūpāra."
"He is much older than I.
"If he should somehow recognize him, let us ask this King Akūpāra.
Thereupon, that crane informed the tortoise Akūpāra.
"We have a certain matter we wish to ask you about;
please come here for a moment.
Having heard this, the tortoise rose from that lake and approached the shore where we were standing.
When he had arrived, we asked him:
"Does your honor know King Indradyumna?
Having reflected for a moment, with eyes filled with tears, a distressed heart, trembling, and nearly unconscious, he spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"Why do I not recognize him?
For I have previously been placed by him a thousand times in the construction of fire-altars;
and this lake was made by the cows given as his sacrificial fee as they passed over it."
"And here I dwell," [he said]. Then, immediately upon hearing this uttered by the tortoise, a divine chariot appeared from the world of the gods,
and voices were heard directed toward Indradyumna.
Heaven has been prepared for you; attain the station that is appropriate for you,
for you are possessed of fame.
"Go without distraction"—
thus the sound of meritorious action touches both heaven and earth;
as long as that sound persists, so long is the man said to exist.
If the ill-fame of any being whatsoever is proclaimed in the world,
he surely falls to the lowest worlds for as long as that report is recited. Therefore, a man on earth should be of virtuous conduct for the sake of ultimate [well-being].
"Abandoning most wicked conduct, one should take refuge in dharma alone.
Having heard this, the king said:
"Wait a moment until I have restored these two elders to their proper places."
Having established me, Prākārakarṇa, and the owl in their respective appropriate places, he departed by that very same vehicle and reached his own proper abode.
"This was experienced by me and seen by Cirajīvin," Mārkaṇḍeya said to the Pāṇḍavas. And the Pāṇḍavas, being pleased, spoke.
"Excellent!
You have done well, sir, in restoring King Indradyumna—who had fallen from the heavenly world—to his own place in heaven once again.
Then he spoke to them:
"But was not the royal sage Nṛga, who was sinking into hell, rescued from that distress and restored to heaven by Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī?
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having heard those words concerning the royal sage Indradyumna at that time, the king..."
O bull of the Bharatas, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, questioned the highly fortunate Mārkaṇḍeya— the aged ascetic, long-lived and stainless— concerning the attainment of heaven.
O knower of dharma, the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas are known to you;
likewise, the various royal lineages and the eternal lineages of the ṛṣis are known.
O best of the twice-born, there is nothing in this world unknown to you.
"O sage, you know the divine narratives of humans, serpents, and *rakṣasas*,
as well as those of the gods, *gandharvas*, *yakṣas*, *kiṃnaras*, and *apsarases*.
O twice-born one, I desire to hear this told to me in accordance with the truth."
"How did the unvanquished Ikṣvāku, known as Kuvalāśva, come by the name Dhundhumāra through such a reversal of circumstances? Vaiśampāyana said:
O Bhārata, having been thus addressed by Yudhiṣṭhira, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya related the narrative of Dhundhumāra. "O best of the Bhṛgus, I desire to know this in its true essence."
"How the name of the wise Kuvalāśva became inverted.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Behold, O King Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall tell you; listen!"
Listen to this most righteous narrative concerning Dhundhumāra; hear, O lord of the earth, how that king Kuvalāśva, the descendant of Ikṣvāku and sovereign of the world,
attained the name Dhundhumāra.
O dear descendant of Bharata, there was a world-renowned great ṛṣi named Uttanka;
O Kaurava, his hermitage was located in the delightful Marudhanva regions.
And Uttanka, O great king, performed most difficult austerities.
Desiring to propitiate Viṣṇu for many groups of years, O Lord,
the Blessed One, being pleased with him, appeared before his very eyes. Upon seeing him, the seer bowed low and praised him with various hymns of praise.

O Lord of great splendor, by you all creatures— gods, asuras, and humans, as well as beings both stationary and moving— were created; likewise, the Brahman, the Vedas, and all that is to be known were created by you.
O God, the sky is your head; the moon and the sun are your eyes;
your breath is the wind, and fire is your energy, O Acyuta;
all the directions are your arms, and the great ocean is your belly.
O God, Madhusūdana, the mountains are your thighs, the sky is your navel;
the goddess Earth is your feet, and the plants are likewise your body hairs.
Indra, Soma, Agni, Varuṇa, the gods, asuras, and great serpents [are your limbs].
Bowing low, they wait upon you, praising you with various hymns;
all beings are pervaded by you, O Lord of the World.
Great seers and yogins of immense power offer praise to you.

When you are pleased, the world is at peace; when you are angry, there is great fear. You alone, O Supreme Person, are the dispeller of all fears, bringing happiness to gods, humans, and all living beings.
O Lord, by three strides you seized the three worlds; and by you was brought about the destruction of the prosperous asuras. By your heroic strides, O God, the deities attained supreme nirvāṇa.
And when you are enraged, O lord of the Daityas, O one of great splendor, the defeat of the Daityas occurs;
for you are indeed the creator and the transformer of all beings here in every way.
By propitiating you, the gods prosper in happiness in every respect.
Thus praised by the high-souled Uttaṅka, Hṛṣīkeśa Viṣṇu said to Uttaṅka: "I am pleased with you; choose a boon. Uttaṅka replied:
"This boon alone is sufficient for me, that I have beheld Hari—
the eternal, divine Person, the creator and Lord of the universe.
Viṣṇu said:
"O best of the twice-born, I am pleased with you because of your lack of greed and your devotion. For you must certainly receive a boon from me, O Brahmin.
Thus was he entreated with a boon by Hari at that time.
Uttaṅka, with palms joined in reverence, chose a boon, O best of the Bharatas:
"If the Blessed One, whose eyes resemble lotuses, is pleased with me,
may my intellect always be fixed upon dharma, truth, and self-restraint."
"And may there be constant practice in devotion toward you, O Maheśvara.
Viṣṇu said:
"O twice-born one, all this shall indeed come to pass for you through my grace."
And you shall perceive the yoga by which, when joined with it, you will accomplish a great task for the three worlds and for the dwellers of heaven;
[you shall do so] for the sake of exterminating the great asura named Dhundhu, who is a threat to the worlds.
He is performing terrible austerities; hear who shall slay him.
For there will be, my dear, a powerful and unconquered king of the Ikṣvāku line, a lord of the earth known as Bṛhadaśva.
His son, pure and self-controlled, is known as Kuvalāśva. Relying on my power of yoga, O brahmin-sage, that best of kings shall, by your command, become Dhundhumāra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus to Uttaṅka, Viṣṇu vanished.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, when Ikṣvāku had passed away, Śaśāda, whose soul was supremely devoted to dharma, obtained this earth and became the king in Ayodhyā. The heir of Śaśāda was the heroic one named Kakutstha.
Anenas’s son was Kakutstha, and Pṛthu was the son of Anenas.
Viṣvagaśva was the son of Pṛthu, and from him Ārdra was born. Yuvanāśva was the son of Ārdra, and Śrāvasta was his offspring.
From him was born King Śrāvastaka, by whom the city of Śrāvastī was founded. The heir of Śrāvastaka was the mighty Bṛhadaśva,
and the son of Bṛhadaśva is known as Kuvalāśva.
Kuvalāśva had twenty-one thousand sons,
all of whom were proficient in the sciences, powerful, and difficult to overcome;
yet Kuvalāśva himself surpassed his father in virtues.
Then, O great king, at that time Bṛhadaśva consecrated Kuvalāśva— heroic and supremely righteous— in that kingdom. Having transferred his royal fortune to his son, King Bṛhadaśva [departed].

The wise slayer of enemies departed for the forest of asceticism to perform penance. Then, O King Yudhiṣṭhira, that best of the twice-born, Uttaṅka, heard that the royal sage Bṛhadaśva had set out for the forest.
Approaching that best of men, the immensely energetic Uttaṅka, whose soul was immeasurable, restrained him— the foremost of all those skilled in weapons.
Uttaṅka said:
"You must provide protection; you ought to perform that task first.
O King, by your grace we shall dwell free from anxiety.
For the earth, O Great-souled King, is being protected by you."
"You shall become free from anxiety; you ought not to go to the forest.
For in this world, a great merit is seen in the protection of subjects, whereas such merit is not seen in the forest. Let not your mind be inclined toward such a course."

O Indra among kings, such a dharma as this—namely, that which was practiced by the royal seers of old in the protection of their subjects—is not seen anywhere else. Subjects must be protected by a king; it is right for you to protect them.
"O King, I am unable to perform my ascetic penances free from anxiety. Indeed,
near my hermitage,
in the level desert lands, there is an ocean filled with sand known as Ujjānaka."
Extending for many yojanas in width and many yojanas in length,
there dwells the fierce lord of the Dānavas, possessed of great heroism and prowess;
he is the son of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, named Dhundhu, who is exceedingly terrible.
O King, he of immeasurable prowess dwells within the subterranean regions;
O great king, having slain him, you ought to go to the forest.
He lies there, having undertaken a terrible ascetic penance for the destruction of the world.
O King, for the destruction of the thirty gods and the worlds as well,
he was invincible to the deities, the Daityas, the Rākṣasas,
the Nāgas, the Yakṣas, and the Gandharvas in every respect.
O King, having obtained that boon from the Grandfather of all the worlds,
destroy him— may prosperity be yours— and let not your mind be otherwise;
you shall attain great, eternal, imperishable, and stable fame.
As that cruel one lies sleeping, hidden beneath the sands,
at the end of every year his breath comes forth;
when that happens, the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembles.
By the wind of his breath, a great cloud of dust was raised,
obscuring the path of the sun for seven days; accompanied by sparks, flames, and smoke, it was indeed most terrible, as was the trembling of the earth.
Therefore, O King, I am unable to remain in my own hermitage;
destroy him, O Indra among kings, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Let the worlds become at peace today once that asura has been slain.
"Destroy with your great arrow that exceedingly fierce Dānava named Dhundhu, who causes one's hair to stand on end and is terrible in unequalled battle;
for it is my conviction that you alone are sufficient for his destruction."
Viṣṇu will augment your splendor with his own splendor.
Furthermore, a boon was previously granted to me by Viṣṇu regarding the slaying of him:
"That lord of the earth who shall slay that fierce great asura..."
"O Indra among kings, having gathered that unassailable Vaiṣṇava splendor which is difficult to withstand upon the earth,
destroy that wicked Daitya of fierce prowess."
"O protector of the earth, the immensely powerful Dhundhu cannot be consumed by one of small energy, even in a hundred years.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus addressed by Uttaṅka, O best of the Kauravas, that unconquered royal sage then spoke to Uttaṅka with palms joined in reverence:
"O Brahmin, this visit of yours shall not be in vain."
"O Blessed One, this is my son, known as Kuvalāśva;
he is steadfast, swift in action, and peerless on earth in valor. He will undoubtedly do all that is pleasing to you."
Surrounded by all his sons, who are heroes with arms like iron clubs, that mighty-armed one will surely slay the great asura Dhundhu. O Brahmin, release me; I have now laid down my weapons.
Having been told "So be it" by that sage of immeasurable splendor,
the royal seer, having commanded his son for the sake of the high-souled Uttaṅka,
saying "Let it be done," departed for the supreme forest.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, O you whose wealth is asceticism, who is this Daitya of such great heroism?
Whose son or grandson is he? I wish to know this."
"O one rich in asceticism, I have never heard of such a Daitya of great power,
by the wind of whose breath the earth with its mountains trembles. O Blessed One, I wish to know this according to the truth."
"O one of great wisdom, O ascetic rich in penance, tell me all this in detail.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Listen, O King, lord of men, to all this exactly as it happened."
O one of great wisdom, I shall relate this to you in detail and exactly as it happened:
when there was a single, terrible ocean and all things mobile and immobile had perished,
and when all beings had been destroyed, O bull of the Bharata race.
O Bhārata, I have seen him who is the source of all beings, the eternal and imperishable Puruṣa, whom the perfected sages call the Great Lord of all worlds— the four-armed one of noble limbs.
The blessed Lord Viṣṇu alone slept upon the serpent Śeṣa, who possesses immeasurable splendor, reclining on his great coils as his bed;
so did the blessed Hari, the creator of the worlds and the highly fortunate Acyuta, O noble one.
As that god lay sleeping, embracing this earth with his great serpent-body, a lotus with a radiance equal to the sun emerged from his navel;
it was there that the Grandfather (Brahmā) was born.
Brahmā, the manifest teacher of the world, possessing the splendor of the sun and moon, appeared upon a lotus;
he was the four Vedas, the fourfold form, and likewise the four-faced one—
invincible through his own power, endowed with great strength and prowess.
Then, after some time had passed, two exceedingly powerful Dānavas,
Madhu and Kaiṭabha, born from the wax of Viṣṇu’s ears and rising a hundred yojanas high, beheld the Lord Hari.
He of great splendor was lying upon a divine couch formed by the coils of a serpent,
extending many yojanas in width and many yojanas in length;
he wore a diadem and the Kaustubha gem, and was clothed in yellow silk garments.
O King, blazing with splendor, brilliance, and beauty,
resembling a thousand suns and appearing as a wondrous sight,
there was then a very great amazement in Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Having seen the Grandfather, whose eyes resemble lotuses, seated upon a lotus,
those two of immeasurable power then terrified Brahmā.
Though being repeatedly terrified by them, the highly illustrious Brahmā—
He shook the lotus stalk, and then Keśava awoke;
then Govinda beheld two exceedingly powerful Dānavas [and] Brahmā of immeasurable splendor.
Seeing those two intoxicated by the pride of their own valor, the god said to them: "Welcome to you both, O mighty ones!
I shall grant you an excellent boon, for joy has arisen within me."
Laughing, O great king, those two immensely powerful great asuras together replied to Hṛṣīkeśa, the slayer of Madhu, saying:
"O God, O best of gods, we both are granters of boons; choose a boon from us."
"O heroes, you two are givers; choose a boon for yourself and speak it without hesitation.
The Blessed One said:
"I accept the boon, O heroes; this is the boon desired by me."
"O heroes, choosing the best [of you], I accept [you] according to my desire;
for you two are endowed with prowess, and there is no man equal to you. You two, whose valor is true, shall attain the state of being slain by me."
"I desire to obtain this wish indeed for the welfare of the world.
Madhu and Kaiṭabha said:
"Never before have we spoken an untruth even in jest, much less otherwise."
"O Supreme among Men, know that we two are devoted to truth and righteousness;
in strength, beauty, valor, and tranquility, there is no one equal to us, nor in righteousness, austerity, generosity, virtuous conduct, integrity, and self-control."
"A great calamity is approaching us, O Keśava;
remedy what has been said, for time is difficult to overcome.
O Lord, O All-pervading One, we two desire that one thing be done by you."
O best among the foremost of gods,
O most excellent of men,
endowed with splendor, we two shall enter into the state of being your sons, O fair-eyed one, in this unobstructed space at the time of your destruction.
"O God, O best of deities, know that this boon has been chosen by us;
let not what was promised to us at that time become false, O Lord.
The Blessed One said:
"Very well, I shall do exactly so; all this shall come to pass.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"But after reflecting, Govinda did not see anything that was unobstructed."
O King, having seen his own two unobstructed thighs upon the earth or in the sky, that slayer of Madhu, the best of gods,
then [struck] the heads of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
The highly illustrious one cut him down with a sharp-edged discus.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Their son was named Dhundhu, possessed of great energy and immense splendor."
He, great in power and prowess, performed intense austerities;
standing on one foot, emaciated and covered with a network of veins, he remained thus.
Brahmā, being pleased, granted him a boon, and he chose a boon from the Lord.
"May I indeed be incapable of being slain by gods, dānavas, yakṣas, serpents, gandharvas, and rākṣasas; this is the boon chosen by me.
"So be it; go," the Grandfather said to him.
Having been addressed thus, he touched his feet with his head and departed.
But Dhundhu, having obtained the boon and possessing great heroism and prowess,
then pursued Viṣṇu, remembering the slaughter of his father.
But that intolerant Dhundhu, having conquered the gods along with the Gandharvas,
repeatedly oppressed all the gods and Viṣṇu most severely.
There was a sea filled with sand known as Ujjānaka.
O bull of the Bharata race, having arrived at that region, that evil-minded one,
O Lord, began to harass Uttaṅka’s hermitage to the utmost of his power;
he remained there, hidden beneath the earth and concealed within the sands.
The son of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, Dhundhu, possessed of terrible prowess,
lies there relying on the power of his asceticism for the destruction of the world,
breathing forth flames of fire near the hermitage of Uttaṅka.
At that very time,
O bull of the Bharatas, King Kuvalāśva, accompanied by his servants, troops, and vehicles, and together with the sage Uttaṅka and his sons, set out, O protector of the earth.
The lordly King Kuvalāśva, together with his sons—
the subduer of enemies accompanied by twenty-one thousand of his powerful sons— [set out].

Accompanied by Uttaṅka, he set out for the dwelling of that Dhundhu. Then the blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the master, entered him with his splendor at the command of Uttaṅka and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
As that invincible hero set forth, a great sound arose in the sky:
"This illustrious son of a king shall become Dhundhumāra.
And the gods showered him from all sides with celestial flowers.
The celestial drums resounded of their own accord,
and a cool breeze blew during the departure of that wise one;
and the Lord of the Gods rained down, making the earth free from dust.
The wild beasts and birds also circumambulated him clockwise,
O Yudhiṣṭhira; and there in that very place where the great asura Dhundhu lay, the celestial chariots of the deities were seen in the sky.
Filled with curiosity for the battle between Kuvalāśva and Dhundhu,
the great ṛṣis, accompanied by gods and gandharvas, watched the encounter.
O descendant of Kuru, he was then empowered by the splendor of Nārāyaṇa.
For the benefit of all the worlds,
that king Kuvalāśva, remaining under the command of Udaṅka, quickly went with those sons in every direction; the lord of the earth caused the ocean to be excavated.
By the sons of Kuvalāśva, after digging for seven days in that very sea of sand, the immensely powerful Dhundhu was discovered;
his great and terrible form lay hidden beneath the sand.
O bull among the Bharatas, at the end of the age, all beings will be consumed by him as if by a fire about to burn;
O lord of men, Dhundhu then blazed with splendor like the sun shining with its radiance.
Then, O great king, Dhundhu, possessing a splendor like the fire of cosmic destruction, took refuge in the western direction and fell asleep, O tiger among kings;
he was surrounded on all sides by the sons of Kuvalāśva.
Assailed by sharp arrows, as well as by maces and clubs,
by spears, iron bars, darts, and bright, whetted swords,
that mighty one, being struck, rose up in a fury.
Enraged, he devoured their various weapons;
vomiting forth fire from his mouth like that of the universal dissolution,
he then consumed all those sons of the king with his own splendor.
Enraged, as if overturning the worlds with the fire born from his mouth,
O tiger among kings, he— like the lord Kapila in ancient times— wrathfully [consumed] the sons of Sagara in an instant; it was like a marvel.
O best of the Bharatas, when they had been consumed by the fire of his wrath,
the highly effulgent King Kuvalāśva approached that awakened high-souled one, who was like another Kumbhakarṇa.
From his body, O great king, a vast amount of water flowed forth;
the king, that lord of men, drank up that fiery energy with water.
By means of yoga, the yogi extinguished the fire with water.

Then, O best of the Bharatas, for the sake of granting fearlessness to all the worlds, the king burnt that Daitya of cruel prowess with the Brahmāstra. Having consumed the great Asura with that weapon, the royal sage Kuvalāśva—
Like another lord of the three worlds, the slayer of enemies and destroyer of foes,
the high-minded King Kuvalāśva then rejoiced after killing Dhundhu;
the mighty-armed Kuvalāśva, having slain Dhundhu, was filled with joy.
Thereupon, he became known by the name Dhundhumāra. Then, all the gods together with the great seers, being delighted, said to him as he stood bowed with palms joined in reverence: "Choose a boon."
Extremely delighted, O King, he spoke these words:
"I would give wealth to the foremost of the twice-born, and I would be invincible even to my enemies;
may I have friendship with Viṣṇu, and may I harbor no malice toward living beings."
"May there be constant delight in the Dharma, as well as an imperishable residence in heaven.
Then that king was told "So be it" by the pleased gods,
by the sages along with the gandharvas, and by the wise Uttaṅka.
Having honored that king with various benedictions,
the gods and the great seers then departed for their own abodes.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, three of his sons remained there at that time.
Dṛḍhāśva, Kapilāśva, and Candrāśva, O Bhārata—
O King, from them descended the lineage of the high-souled Ikṣvākus,
a dynasty of kings of immeasurable splendor, O highly fortunate one.
Thus, O best of men, was that Daitya Dhundhu, the son of Madhu and Kaiṭabha and possessed of great heroism, slain by Kuvalāśva. And King Kuvalāśva became known as Dhundhumāra.
From that time forth, he became endowed with virtues according to his name.
I have related all this to you which you asked of me—
the celebrated narrative of Dhundhumāra, renowned for his deeds.
But this meritorious narrative, which is a complete glorification of Viṣṇu—
any man who hears it shall become righteous in soul and possessed of sons; moreover, by hearing it on the sacred festival days (parvan), he becomes long-lived and steadfast.
And, free from fever, he encounters no fear whatsoever of disease.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira [addressed] Mārkaṇḍeya of great luster.

The best of the Bharatas asked a question regarding dharma that is very difficult to speak upon: "O Blessed One, I wish to hear the supreme majesty of women as it is being described by you, O Brahmin, as well as the subtle dharma according to its true essence."
"For by direct perception, O best of Brahmin-sages, the gods are seen, O most excellent one:
the sun and the moon, the wind, the earth, and fire;
as well as the father, the mother, and cows, O venerable and most excellent one."
O descendant of Bhrigu, whatever else has been ordained for them, I consider all that to be like the duties of a guru; likewise, the service performed by women who have but one husband—
those devoted to their husbands— appears to me to be exceedingly difficult to accomplish.
"O Lord, you ought to tell us of the greatness of women devoted to their husbands.
O best of the twice-born, for women there is no other deity than the husband;
having restrained the collection of the senses and having fully controlled the mind, O sinless one."

"O Blessed One, those women who remain thinking of their husbands as if they were deities— O Lord, O twice-born one, this service rendered by women toward their mothers, fathers, and husbands appears to me to be truly difficult to perform."
"Indeed, I see nothing more difficult than the duty of women,
O Brahmin; for virtuous women, ever devoted,
perform what is truly hard to do— namely, their fathers and mothers."
Those women who have but one husband, those who speak the truth,
and those who carry the embryo within their wombs for ten months— what could be more wonderful than these women who, having come together with the [proper] time, give birth?
O Lord, having encountered extreme anxiety and even incomparable pain,
women give birth to sons with great suffering;
yet, O best of the twice-born, they nourish them with great affection.
Then they also reflect: "What will his character be like?
For those who abide in all cruel deeds and are loathsome, always performing their own actions—that, in my view, is difficult to do."
"O twice-born one, tell me truly the practice of the duty of a Kṣatriya;
for dharma, O Brahmin, is very difficult to attain by one who is cruel and evil-minded. O Blessed One, best among those skilled in answering questions, I desire this answer to my question."
"O best of the Bhṛgu lineage, O observer of noble vows, I desire to hear you; I wish to listen to you.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Ah, I shall explain all of this to you—this question which is very difficult to express."
O best of the Bharatas, listen to me as I speak of this according to the truth:
O dear one, some consider the mother and others the father to be equal;
yet the mother performs what is difficult to do, for she causes her offspring to grow.
Through austerity, worship of the gods, salutation, endurance,
incantations, and various means, fathers strive for sons;
thus, having obtained with great hardship a son who is so very difficult to find—
"O Hero, they constantly wonder, 'What will he become?'—
those who, out of a sense of revulsion for all these current [beings], have performed [meritorious deeds] in them;
and both father and mother, O Bhārata, place their hopes in their sons."
O Indra among kings, he who constantly brings about the welfare of his mother and father— who are the source of his fame, renown, sovereignty, progeny, and likewise his dharma—
and who makes their hopes fruitful, is a knower of dharma.
O Indra among kings, for him whose father and mother are always contented,
there is eternal fame and dharma both in this world and after death.
For women, there is no sacrifice whatsoever, nor the *śrāddha* rite, nor the practice of fasting.

But by that service rendered to her husband, she attains heaven. O King Yudhiṣṭhira, with focused attention, listen to the constant dharma of women devoted to their vows, as set forth in this section.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O Bhārata, there was a certain preeminent among the twice-born, named Kauśika, who was a student of the Vedas, rich in asceticism, devoted to penance, and virtuous in character."
That best of the twice-born was studying the Vedas along with their limbs and secret Upaniṣads;
he stood at the foot of a certain tree reciting the Vedas,
and above that tree a crane settled.
She discharged her excrement upon that Brahmin;
seeing her, the twice-born man was then incensed and harbored an evil thought against her,
O great king— that crane who had perished on the mountain peak.
Overcome by intense anger, the Brahmin glared at the crane; cursed by the sage, she fell to the surface of the earth. Seeing the crane fallen, lifeless, and unconscious, [he was filled with remorse].
Tormented by compassion, the twice-born man lamented for her:
"Driven by the force of passion and hatred, I have committed an improper act.
Having spoken thus many times, the learned man entered the village for alms.
O bull of the Bharatas, while wandering among pure families in the village,
he entered that family where he had previously wandered; there,
as he was begging "Give," he was told by a woman, "Wait."
O best of the Bharatas, while the housewife was still engaged in cleaning the vessel, O King, her husband, severely oppressed by hunger, suddenly entered.
But that virtuous woman, seeing her husband and setting aside that brahmin,
gave her husband water for his feet, water for sipping, and likewise a seat.
Bowing low, the dark-eyed lady also attended to her husband.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, she would always eat the remnants of her husband’s food— whether it were solid meals, snacks, or even very sweet words— and,
following her husband’s every thought, she regarded him as a deity.

Neither by deed nor by thought did she ever neglect him, nor did she eat too much, nor even drink excessively. Devoted to serving her husband, she approached him with her whole being; virtuous in conduct, pure, skillful, and desiring the welfare of the household.
She constantly follows whatever is beneficial for her husband; she is always devoted to serving the gods, guests, and dependents, as well as her mother-in-law and father-in-law,
with her senses perpetually restrained.
Then, seeing that brahmin standing there desiring alms,
the fair-eyed and virtuous woman, who was devoted to serving her husband, remembered him and became ashamed, O best of the Bharatas.
Having taken alms for the brahmin, the illustrious lady went outside.
The brahmin said:
"O beautiful woman, what is this? Having told me to wait, why have you departed?"
"You have kept him confined; you did not release him.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"The Brahmin was consumed by anger, as if blazing with spiritual power (*tejas*)."
Seeing him, O lord of men, that virtuous woman spoke these words with conciliation:
"Forgive me, O best of Brahmins; forgive my womanly dullness. Be gracious to me, O Blessed One; show compassion toward me, O twice-born one."
"O Brahmin, you ought to forgive me; my husband is my supreme deity.
He arrived hungry and exhausted, and he was attended to by me.
The Brahmin said:

"O Brāhmaṇas, you are not superior; rather, your husband has been made superior. While abiding by the duties of a householder, you hold the Brāhmaṇas in contempt—even Indra bows down before them, let alone mere humans on earth."
"O arrogant one, you do not know; you have not heard the words of the elders:
for Brahmins are like fire; when insulted, they can swiftly consume even the entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and islands."
The woman said:
"O Brahmin, I do not hold the wise in contempt; they are equal to the gods.
O sinless one, you ought to forgive this offense of mine."
"I am not a crane, O chief of Brahmins; abandon your anger, O you whose wealth is asceticism.
What will you do to me, enraged as you are by this angry glance?
I know the spiritual power of Brahmins and the great majesty of the wise."
Indeed, out of anger, the ocean was made undrinkable and filled with salt water;
likewise, for those sages of radiant asceticism and purified souls,
the fire of whose wrath still does not subside even today in Daṇḍaka.

Why does this fool treat with contempt the Brahmins of immeasurable power? Because of his contempt for the Brahmins, the evil-minded and cruel great Asura Vātāpi was digested upon encountering the seer Agastya.

Many powers are heard of among those who discourse on Brahman, O Brahmin; the wrath and the grace of these great-souled ones are both exceedingly vast. Yet, O sinless Brahmin, you ought to forgive this transgression of mine.
"O twice-born one, that dharma which consists in service to my husband is what pleases me;
even among all the deities, my husband is my supreme deity.
O best of the twice-born, I shall perform his duty toward him without distinction."
"O Brahmin, behold what kind of fruit comes from service to one's husband!
Indeed, it is known to me that the crane was burned by you out of anger.
O best of the twice-born, anger is the enemy residing within the bodies of men."
"Do not be angry; like a crane, I am not to be killed, for I am devoted to my husband.
The gods know him as a *brāhmaṇa* who abandons anger and delusion, and who speaks the truth here and satisfies his teacher."
The gods know him as a Brahmin who, though harmed, does not harm in return;
who has conquered his senses, is devoted to dharma, intent on the study of the Vedas, and pure;
and under whose control lie both desire and anger.
The gods know him as a true Brahmin who regards the world as equal to himself, who knows the Dharma, who is high-minded, and who delights in all righteous duties;
he who would teach, or study, or perform sacrifices, or officiate at sacrifices for others.
Or he who gives according to his ability— the gods know him as a Brāhmaṇa. And that best of the twice-born who studies the Vedas as a celibate student (brahmacārī),
remaining indeed vigilant in his private recitation (svādhyāya)— the gods know him as a Brāhmaṇa.
One should proclaim whatever is virtuous among the Brahmins; for those who speak thus in accordance with truth, the mind finds no delight in falsehood.
They say that the wealth of a Brahmin consists of Vedic study, self-restraint, and uprightness.
O best of the twice-born, those who know the Dharma say that the eternal restraint of the senses and truthfulness and uprightness constitute the supreme Dharma;
for that eternal Dharma is difficult to discern, yet it is firmly established in truth.
"Dharma is that which has the Veda as its authority; such is the instruction of the elders.
O best of the twice-born, dharma is seen in many ways and is indeed subtle. You too are a knower of dharma, devoted to sacred study, and pure."
"But it is my conviction, O Blessed One, that you do not know phenomena in their true nature.
If you do not know the supreme Dharma, O brahmin, O twice-born one,
then go to the city of Mithilā and ask the Dharma-hunter."

"Devoted to the service of his parents, truthful, and having conquered his senses—a hunter living in Mithilā—he will explain the dharmas to you. Go there, O best of the twice-born; may prosperity be yours, according to your desire."
That hunter, whose soul is supremely devoted to dharma, will sever your doubts.
O blameless one, you ought to forgive all that I have said, even if it was excessive; for women are not to be slain by anyone who knows the dharma.
The Brahmin said:
"I am pleased with you; may it be well with you, O beautiful one, and your anger has passed. For the reproach spoken by you is for my supreme welfare."
"May it be well with you; I shall depart, O beautiful one, and accomplish my purpose.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Dismissed by her, he went forth and returned to his own abode."
Reproaching himself, that twice-born Kauśika said, "O best of men,
you are blessed, O auspicious lady, for such is your conduct.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having reflected upon that wonder told by the woman in its entirety,
that twice-born man appeared as if censuring himself like a wrongdoer;
then, pondering the subtle course of dharma, he spoke.
"One must indeed be full of faith; I am going to Mithilā.
It is said that a self-realized man, a knower of dharma, a hunter, dwells there.
I shall go this very day to question that one whose wealth is asceticism regarding dharma."
Having thus reflected in his mind and placing faith in the woman’s words— relying on the testimony of the crane and her auspicious, righteous speech—
he set out for Mithilā, filled with curiosity.
Seeing delightful rivers along the way,
and passing through forests, villages, and cities, he traveled toward the land protected by Janaka.
Then he went to Mithilā, which was well-protected by Janaka;
it was auspicious, filled with the embankments of dharma, abounding in sacrifices and festivals,
possessed of gate-towers and watchtowers, and beautified by houses and ramparts.
Having entered that delightful city, which was surrounded by many celestial palaces, filled with numerous articles for sale, possessed well-laid-out great highways,
and crowded with horses, chariots, elephants, and many other vehicles;
Passing through that city, which was crowded with joyful and well-fed people and filled with constant festivities, the brahmin observed its many wonders;
and he asked about the Dharma-fowler, who had been described to him by other twice-born men.
Having gone there, he saw that ascetic standing in the midst of the slaughterhouse, selling the meat of deer and buffalo; however,
due to the crowding of buyers, the twice-born man stood to one side.
But having learned that a twice-born man had arrived, he rose up suddenly in agitation and went to where the brahmin was staying on a seat in a secluded spot.
The hunter said:
"I salute you, O Blessed One; welcome to you, O best of the twice-born!
I am a hunter—blessings be upon you—command me, what shall I do for you? You were told by the devoted wife: 'Go to Mithilā.'"
"I know all this, for what purpose you have come here.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"But having heard those words of his, that brahmin was greatly delighted."
"This is the second marvel," the twice-born man thought.
Then the hunter said to the twice-born man, "Indeed, this place is not a proper dwelling for you;
O sinless one, let us go to my home, if it pleases you."
"Very well," the Brahmin replied with great joy,
and placing the twice-born man at his head, he set out toward his home. Having entered his beautiful house, he was honored with a seat.
With that *arghya* offering, that best of the twice-born—
the most excellent of brahmins— accepted the water for his feet and the water for rinsing his mouth from that hunter.
Then, having sat down comfortably, he spoke these words to the hunter.
"This deed does not seem worthy of you;
O dear one, I am deeply pained by your terrible act.
The hunter said:
"This is an action appropriate to my family, inherited from my father and grandfather. Since I am abiding in my own dharma, O twice-born one, do not harbor anger toward me.
I am merely fulfilling my own duty as ordained of old by the Creator."

O best of the twice-born, I serve my elders with great effort; I speak the truth, I do not harbor malice, and I give according to my ability. I subsist on what remains after providing for the gods, guests, and dependents.
I do not revile anything, nor do I despise that which is more powerful;
O best of the twice-born, past action follows the doer.
Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are the means of livelihood for people in this world.
The science of government and the triple Veda—by these the worlds are sustained. Service is ordained for the Śūdra, agriculture for the Vaiśya, and battle for the Kṣatriya;
celibacy, austerity, sacred mantras, and truthfulness always belong to the Brāhmaṇa.

The king governs by righteousness, while his subjects are devoted to their own duties; and those who are negligent in their tasks, he enjoins to their proper work. For one must always stand in awe of kings, for they are the lords of the people.
The greedy destroy one who stands outside his duty, just as hunters kill a deer with arrows.
O brahmin seer, here in the realm of Janaka, no one is found standing outside his duty;
O best of the twice-born, all four castes are devoted to their own respective duties.
This King Janaka, even if his son is ill-behaved, subjects him to punishment if he deserves it; thus he does not harm the righteous.
With his spies well-deployed, the monarch perceives everything through the lens of dharma.
Prosperity, sovereignty, and the power of punishment belong to the Kṣatriyas, O best of the twice-born;
for kings desire abundant prosperity through their own duty,
and the king indeed becomes the protector of all the social orders.

"O Brahmin, when boars and buffaloes have been killed by another, O sage among brahmins, I do not kill them myself; rather, I always sell them. I do not eat meat, for I am one who approaches his wife only during her season."
O twice-born one, even a man who is constantly fasting, or likewise eating only at night,
or even one who is of bad character, becomes possessed of virtue;
and even one who delights in harming living beings becomes righteous once again.
Due to the transgressions of kings, the great dharma becomes corrupted;
unrighteousness increases, and likewise the subjects become degenerate—
becoming Uruṇḍas, Vāmanas, hunchbacks, and those with oversized heads.
Eunuchs, the blind, and the deaf are born, as well as those with pendulous nipples; due to the unrighteousness of kings, there is constant misfortune for the subjects.
Yet this King Janaka perceives everything through righteousness.
O best of the twice-born, this King Janaka protects all his subjects like a father, always favoring those who are devoted to their own duty;
he regards alike those men who praise me and those who revile me.

I satisfy all those kings who live by their own duty and enjoy its fruits through my perfectly executed deeds; for they are skillful and habituated to industrious effort, and do not depend on anything else.
One obtains no fruit whatsoever from the neglect of one's own duty.
Constantly giving food according to one's ability, forbearance, constancy in dharma, honoring others as they deserve, and indeed compassion toward all beings— these are the marks of virtue.
Apart from renunciation, no other virtues remain in a mortal man.
One should avoid false speech and do what is pleasing even when unasked. One should not abandon dharma out of desire, nor out of passion, nor out of hatred.
One should not exult excessively in what is pleasant, nor be distressed by what is unpleasant; one should not be bewildered in times of financial hardship, nor should one abandon dharma.
If there should be any other action to be performed, one should not practice anything else.
Whatever is auspicious one should contemplate, therein one should apply oneself.
One should not be evil toward the evil; one should always be virtuous. The evil person who desires to commit evil is destroyed by his own self.
This is the conduct of the wicked and the crooked, like that of the unrighteous:
those who, thinking "there is no dharma," mock the pure;
lacking faith in dharma, they perish—of this there is no doubt.
The wicked man is always like a great leather bag inflated with air;
O best of the twice-born, only one who possesses the conduct of the virtuous is truly so in every respect. The speech of the foolish and the arrogant is devoid of substance.
The inner self reveals itself like the sun revealing its form by day;
a fool does not shine in the world merely by praising himself,
for even one who possesses learning shines here only when he is free from impurity.
They did not speak in disparagement of anyone, nor did they describe their own praise; no one endowed with virtues was seen manifest on earth.
One who is tormented by wrongful action is liberated from sin.
"Thinking, 'I shall not do this again,' one is liberated from the second;
thinking, 'I shall indeed perform dharma,' one is liberated from the third. By whatever action it may be, O best of the foremost of the twice-born, one is freed from evil in this world."
O Brahmin, this traditional teaching is thus observed regarding dharmas:
one who was previously habituated to righteousness destroys, later on, the evils committed here in the past through lack of awareness.
O Brahmin, dharma drives away from men whatever evil they commit here through negligence;
for having committed evil, a man might think, "I am not [the doer]."
But the gods perceive him as their own inner person;
he who is faithful and free from malice should desire only what is auspicious,
whereas he who reveals the flaws of the virtuous is like one pointing out the holes in a garment.
Not seeing his own faults, that evil man perishes after death. But if a man, having committed a sin, turns toward what is auspicious,
he is released from all evils like the moon from great clouds.
Just as the rising sun indeed dispels all darkness,
so too one who abides in what is auspicious is liberated from all evils. Know, O best of the twice-born, that greed alone is the foundation of all sins.
Therefore, O Brahmin, these two should be primarily avoided by the wise:
men who are greedy and not very learned resolve upon evil; they are unrighteousness appearing in the form of righteousness, like wells concealed by grass.
Self-restraint is their means of purification, and their speech is grounded in dharma; for everything exists within them, yet the conduct of the refined is very difficult to find.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
But that highly wise brahmin asked the Dharmavyādha:
"O best of men, how may I know the conduct of the virtuous? O foremost of those who uphold dharma, I desire to hear this; may prosperity be yours."
"O Great-minded one, O hunter, tell me truly what those five purifiers are that are always present in the conduct of the learned. The hunter said:
O best of the twice-born, sacrifice, charity, austerity, the Vedas, and truth—
these five are ever purifying among the practices of the virtuous,
provided one has brought desire, anger, hypocrisy, greed, and crookedness under control.
Those who are satisfied with what is called *dharma* alone are the cultured (*śiṣṭa*), esteemed as such by the cultured.
For those whose habit is sacrifice and the study of the Vedas, no misconduct exists;
and the observance of proper conduct is indeed the second characteristic of the cultured.
Service to one's teacher, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and generosity—

O Brahmin, these four are always present in the conduct of the disciplined. Having fixed the mind upon the conduct of the disciplined and having established it in every way, [one should practice them].
The satisfaction that he attains cannot indeed be achieved otherwise.
Truth is the secret essence (*upaniṣad*) of the Veda; self-control is the secret essence of truth;
and renunciation is the constant secret essence of self-control within the conduct of the disciplined.
But those men who, possessed by delusion of intellect, find fault with the Dharma,

even a follower of theirs is afflicted when they travel upon a wrong path. However, those who are disciplined, well-restrained, and devoted to the abandonment of [worldly] learning according to the scriptures—
"O Great-Minded One, O hunter, explain this according to reality:
sacrifice, giving, austerity, the Vedas, and truth— [what is their nature], O best of the twice-born?"

These five are always purifiers among the practices of the cultured; men endowed with the conduct of the cultured, having ascended the path of dharma and being devoted to truth and righteousness, attain supreme wisdom.

Devoted to the preceptor’s doctrine, steadfast, and perceiving the true meaning of the Dharma, abandon those who are nihilists, who have transgressed the bounds of conduct, who are cruel, and who abide in evil intent; do so by relying on wisdom and serving those who are righteous.
Having fashioned a boat made of fortitude, cross over the difficult straits of birth— the river whose waters are the five senses and which is infested with the crocodiles of sensual desire and greed.
Through gradual practice, you shall accumulate the great dharma consisting of the application of wisdom.
One should be virtuous in the conduct of the disciplined, like dye upon a white cloth.
Non-violence and truthful speech are the supreme benefit for all beings;
non-violence is the highest dharma, and it is established in truth.
Having established themselves in truth, all activities proceed;
truth alone is most weighty, being practiced by the conduct of the disciplined. Conduct is the dharma of the virtuous, and the virtuous are characterized by their conduct.
Whatever being is of such a nature, it experiences its own respective nature;
the evil-minded person, lacking self-control, incurs defects such as anger, desire, and the like. An undertaking that is joined with righteousness is indeed remembered as *dharma*.
"Improper conduct, however, is unrighteousness"— this is the instruction of the cultured.
Those who are free from anger, free from malice, devoid of egoism and envy, upright, and endowed with tranquility— they possess the conduct of the cultured.
Those who are advanced in the three Vedas, pure, possessed of good conduct, wise,
devoted to serving their gurus, self-controlled, and followers of refined behavior— indeed, for those of undepressed spirit who perform such difficult deeds of conduct, [there is no grief].

For those honored by their own deeds, their dreadfulness completely vanishes. Beholding that wonderful, ancient, eternal, and constant righteous conduct as Dharma through Dharma, the wise go to heaven.
Those who are believers, free from pride, and worshippers of the twice-born; those endowed with sacred learning and virtuous conduct—they are the righteous ones who go to heaven.
The supreme dharma is that declared in the Vedas, and another is found in the treatises on dharma (dharmaśāstra).
The practice of the virtuous is the threefold characteristic of dharma for the wise:
the mastery of the sciences, the immersion in the sacred fords,
and the demonstration of conduct characterized by forbearance, truth, uprightness, and purity.
Always compassionate toward all beings and constantly devoted to non-violence,
the virtuous, who are ever dear to the twice-born, do not speak harsh words.
[They understand] the accumulation of the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious actions.
Those disciplined ones, esteemed by the disciplined, understand the ripening of karma;
they are endowed with logic and virtue, desiring the welfare of the entire world.
Being virtuous, conquerors of heaven, and pure, they are firmly established on the path of the righteous.
Those who are givers, those who share their wealth, those who show favor to the distressed, and those who possess compassion for all beings— they are the refined, esteemed by the refined;
they are worthy of honor by all, as are those whose wealth is sacred learning and likewise those who practice austerity.

Those who are constant in giving attain happy worlds and prosperity even in this life. Yet, those virtuous ones who have associated with the wise, being self-composed, give away their wealth beyond their means, even by causing distress to their wives and servants.
Observing the course of worldly life, as well as dharma and their own welfare,
the virtuous who conduct themselves in this manner prosper for eternal years.
Non-violence, truthful speech, compassion, and straightforwardness— these are their qualities.

Free from malice and free from arrogance, possessing modesty, forbearance, self-restraint, and tranquility; wise, steadfast, and compassionate toward all beings, those virtuous ones, untainted by desire or hatred, are honored by the world.
The wise say that there are indeed three steps that constitute the unsurpassed conduct of the virtuous:
one should not bear malice, one should give, and one should always speak the truth; for the virtuous are compassionate toward all and possess a heart of mercy.
Those great-souled ones who follow the conduct of the virtuous and whose dharma is well-ascertained travel here, perfectly content, upon the supreme path of righteousness;
they are free from malice, patient, peaceful, self-contented, and speak kindly.
The abandonment of desire and anger, the practice of the conduct of the refined,
and the unsurpassed path of the virtuous— which is endowed with action and sacred learning— they constantly follow this conduct of the refined, remaining untiring in their duties.
O best of the twice-born, having ascended the palace of wisdom, you observe the various ways of the world as they delude the great masses—
both those that are exceedingly meritorious and those that are sinful, O most excellent of the twice-born.

"O Brahmin, O bull among the twice-born, all this has been related to you according to my understanding and as I have heard it, placing the virtues of the conduct of the disciplined at the forefront. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the Dharmavyādha spoke to the brāhmaṇa:
"That I perform this terrible deed is undoubtedly so;
but destiny, O Brāhmaṇa, is powerful, for that which was done in the past is difficult to overcome."
"This fault of action is the result of evil deeds committed in the past.
O Brahmin, I am indeed striving for the destruction of this fault. When a rite has been previously ordained by destiny, the slayer becomes merely the instrumental cause."
"O best of the twice-born, we are indeed merely the instrumental cause of this karma.
O twice-born one, for those whose flesh we sell when they have been slain—
even for them there may be merit through the enjoyment of eating it."
Through the honoring of the deities, guests, dependents, and ancestors,
it is heard in the sacred revelation (Śruti) that medicinal herbs, creepers, beasts, wild animals, and birds are the very food of the world.

O best of the twice-born, by the gift of his own flesh, the patient King Śibi, the son of Uśīnara, attained heaven which is so difficult to reach. O twice-born one, this formerly occurred in the kitchen of King Rantideva.
Two thousand animals were slaughtered there every day;
likewise, two thousand cows were slaughtered day after day,
for Rantideva constantly gave food along with meat.
O best of the twice-born, the king’s fame became incomparable;
for it was constantly heard that during the Cāturmāsya sacrifices animals were to be slaughtered, and that the sacred fires themselves were desirous of meat— so indeed the Vedic revelation declares.

"O Brahmin, at sacrifices animals are constantly slaughtered by the twice-born; indeed, having been consecrated with mantras, they attain heaven. If, O Brahmin, the sacrificial fires had not formerly been desirous of meat,"
"O best of the twice-born, meat should never be eaten by anyone;
yet even regarding this, a rule for the consumption of meat has been declared by the sages:
he who always eats after having first offered it to the deities and the ancestors."

If one eats according to the prescribed rule and with due faith, he does not incur sin from that eating; thus it is heard in the Veda: "In this way, one becomes a non-eater of meat. Furthermore, a Brāhmaṇa who approaches his wife during her season remains a celibate student (*brahmacārī*).
Having determined the distinction between truth and falsehood, the rule regarding this matter is now stated:
O twice-born one, in former times, humans were devoured by King Saudāsa when he was utterly overcome by a curse; what do you think of this?
"O best of the twice-born, considering it my own duty (*svadharma*), I do not abandon it;
knowing it was performed in the past, I live by this action. O Brahmin, for one who abandons his own duty, unrighteousness (*adharma*) is seen in this world."
But he who is devoted to his own duty—that is Dharma; this is the certainty.
For the action performed in the past does not release the embodied being;
this rule was seen by the Creator in many ways regarding the determination of karma.
O wise one, it must be considered by one engaged in cruel action:
"How may I perform auspicious deeds? How may I be liberated from defeat?
There would be a manifold resolution for that terrible course of action.

O best of the twice-born, I am always devoted to charity, truthful speech, service to my gurus, the honoring of the twice-born, and righteousness; I have desisted from harsh words and excessive pride.

People consider agriculture to be a virtuous pursuit, yet it is traditionally held that violence is paramount therein. As men plow with their plows, they kill many creatures dwelling in the earth and numerous other living beings; what do you think of this?

"O best of the twice-born, those seeds of grain which they call rice and so forth—all these are living beings; what is your opinion on this? Furthermore, having attacked animals, people indeed kill them and eat them."
"O twice-born one, men cut down trees and even medicinal herbs;
for there are many living beings, O Brahmin, within the trees and within the fruits,
as well as many in the water— what do you think of this?"
"O Brahmin, this entire world is pervaded by living beings who subsist on other living beings;
even fish devour fish—what do you think of that? O best of the twice-born, living beings subsist upon other living beings in many ways."

Living beings there devour one another; what do you think of that? O Brahmin, men there, while walking about, trample with their feet many living creatures dwelling upon the earth; what do you think of that?
Whether sitting or lying down, they kill living beings many times over;
even those possessed of knowledge and discernment do so—what does this seem like to you?
This entire space as well as the earth is devoured by living beings.
And because they do not perceive [the living being], they cause harm; what appears to you in this regard?
For it was said long ago by astonished men that "non-violence" (ahiṃsā) is the rule; for who, O best of the twice-born, does not indeed cause harm while living in this world?

"O best of the twice-born, having reflected deeply upon this matter, there is indeed no one here who is entirely non-violent. Yet, those ascetics devoted to non-violence do indeed commit acts of violence; however, through their effort, it becomes much less."
Even men born in noble families and endowed with great virtues become visible [in their true nature] when they commit most terrible deeds and yet feel no shame;
friends act as enemies toward other friends, and the wicked likewise act as enemies toward the wicked.

Relatives do not rejoice even with their own kinsmen who are acting rightly, because they do not perceive them as such; moreover, those fools who imagine themselves to be wise revile even their elders.
"O best of the twice-born, much that is perverted is seen in the world:
what appears to you regarding that which is endowed with *dharma* and that which is *adharma*? It is possible to speak at length concerning the various actions pertaining to *dharma* and *adharma*."
That which is not contrary to the Vedic dharma, which is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and is auspicious—
he who is devoted to his own duty shall indeed attain great fame.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then Dharmavyādha, the most excellent among all upholders of dharma, spoke again with skill to that bull among brahmins, O Yudhiṣṭhira:
"It has been declared by the elders that dharma is indeed based on the authority of the Vedas."
For the course of Dharma is subtle, possessing many branches and no end.
In a life-threatening situation and at a wedding, an untruth may be spoken;
for an untruth may become truth, and truth indeed may become untruth.
That which is ultimately beneficial to living beings is held to be truth; unrighteousness (*adharma*) arises from its opposite. Behold the subtlety of dharma!
Behold the subtlety of dharma: how it regards even that which one performs as an unwholesome action.
O best of the twice-born, I shall describe to you the entire destiny of the agent who performs either an inauspicious or a auspicious deed;
that [result] a person inevitably attains— of this there is no doubt.
Having fallen into an adverse state, he indeed censures the gods excessively;
the fool does not recognize the faults of his own actions. O best of the twice-born, he is deluded, deceitful, and fickle.
When the reversal of pleasure and pain occurs,
neither wisdom, nor well-guided conduct, nor human effort can protect one;
indeed, a man of evil resolve binds himself with auspicious karma.
Whichever desire one might wish for, that very desire one would obtain,
if the fruit of human action were not dependent on other factors.
Even those men who are self-controlled, skillful, and wise [would fail].
Some who are virtuous are seen to be fruitless, having abandoned all worldly activities;
yet another person, constantly intent on harming living beings and deceiving the world, lives here in comfort.
Prosperity attends someone even while they sit inactive and do nothing; conversely, some who perform many deeds do not attain what they seek.
Even by worshipping the gods and practicing austerities, wretched men greedy for sons [fail to achieve their ends].
Those who, having been carried in the womb for ten months, are born as defilers of their lineage;
and others who, through those very auspicious merits they have acquired, are born into abundance of wealth, grain, and enjoyments accumulated by their ancestors.
"O best of the twice-born, the diseases of human beings are not born of the body;
for the illnesses of humans arise from karma— of this there is no doubt—
and they are afflicted by mental agonies just as small deer are tormented by hunters."

And even those diseases, O twice-born one, are warded off by skillful and expert physicians who have prepared the necessary medicines, just as deer are driven away by hunters; yet there are those afflicted by the disorder of *grahaṇī* who still possess food to eat.
"Behold, O best of the upholders of dharma, they are unable to eat;
many other people, though possessing strength of arm,
suffer and obtain food only with great difficulty, O most excellent of the twice-born."

Thus the world is without a protector, overwhelmed by delusion and grief; it is repeatedly cast into the current and carried away by a powerful force. [If] they were not to die, were not to decay, and all were to have every desire fulfilled—
If one were indeed to possess mastery, no one would behold what is unpleasant;
everyone would strive to go higher and higher above the world,
exerting themselves to the best of their ability, yet it does not happen in that way.
Many are seen to possess identical auspicious birth-stars,
yet a great disparity in the fruits of their actions is observed at the junctions of karma:
some carry the palanquin while others travel seated within it.

"O Brahmin, O best of beings, no one has mastery over the self-grasping of actions performed in this world; indeed, their fruition is clearly seen here. As for this Vedic revelation, O Brahmin, it is said that the individual soul (jīva) is eternal."
In this world, the body of all living beings here is impermanent;
when the body is slain, the destruction of the physical frame occurs,
yet the *jīva*, bound by the fetters of karma, migrates elsewhere.
The Brahmin said:
"O best among the upholders of dharma, how does the living soul become eternal? O foremost of speakers, I desire to know this in its true essence."
The hunter said:
"Indeed, there is no destruction of life when the body is divided;
those fools say, 'He dies,' but that is false."
But the living soul departs, separated from the body; its disintegration of the body is merely the end of its ten-fold state.
For no one else eats the fruit of the action performed.
He alone is the doer who experiences pleasure and pain;
for whatever action has been performed by him, that he surely reaps— there is no destruction of what has been done.
Those of non-meritorious character become meritorious,
and those who have committed evil become the best of men; for a person here follows his own deeds.
Then he is born, having been cultivated by those [qualities].
The Brahmin said:
"How does one come to be in a womb, or how [is it determined] by merit and demerit?"
"O best of beings, how does one go through births that are both meritorious and non-meritorious?
The hunter said:
"This process is observed to be joined with the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*)."

O best of the twice-born, I shall briefly explain to you quickly how one who has accumulated the necessary provisions is born once again: the doer of good is born in auspicious wombs, while the doer of evil is born in sinful wombs.
Through auspicious applications one becomes a god; through mixed ones, a human; through deluding actions, one is born in non-human wombs; and through sinful deeds, one goes downward.
One is constantly assailed by the sufferings of birth, death, and old age.
And as a man is cooked in saṃsāra by the faults created by himself,
having gone through thousands of animal births and even to hell,
living beings revolve [in existence], bound by the fetters of karma.
But a living being, having died, suffers on account of those various actions performed by itself;
in order to counteract that suffering, it enters an unwholesome womb.
Thereupon, it again takes up many other new karmas.

But he is cooked by that [karma] again, like a sick man who has consumed unwholesome food; thus, though not actually suffering, he is constantly afflicted by pain because he perceives it as pleasure. This is due to his failure to sever the bonds [of existence] and the continued emergence of karmic actions.
He wanders through saṃsāra like a wheel, experiencing manifold suffering;
yet, O best of the twice-born, if he has severed his bonds and is purified of his karmas, he undertakes the practice of austerity and yoga.
Through many deeds as well, a human being experiences the worlds;
he attains the worlds of those who have performed good deeds, where having gone, he does not grieve. One of evil conduct, committing sin, does not reach the end of his sin.
Performing merit and abiding in virtuous conduct, one does not reach the end of merit.
Therefore, one should strive to perform merit and avoid sinful deeds;
being free from envy and grateful, one cultivates only auspicious things.
A man obtains happiness, merit, wealth, and heaven;
for one who is refined, self-controlled, disciplined, restrained in soul,
and wise, there is an uninterrupted course of well-being both in this world and in the next.

One should abide by the dharma of the virtuous and perform actions as the learned do. O twice-born one, one should indeed seek a livelihood that does not cause distress to the world; for there are the learned who have attained true knowledge and are experts in the scriptures.
In this world, action performed according to one's own duty ensures that there is no confusion of duties. The wise man delights in his duty and makes his livelihood from it;
he maintains his subsistence through dharma and indeed praises dharma.
O best of the twice-born, when wealth has been acquired by him through dharma,
he waters its very root wherever he perceives virtues; for thus does he become a man of dharma, and his mind becomes serene.

Contented with friendly people, he rejoices both in this world and after death. O best of beings, he obtains sound, touch, form, and pleasant fragrances, as well as sovereignty; they know this to be the fruit of dharma.
O great twice-born one, having obtained the fruit of dharma, he is not satisfied;
being unsatisfied, he attains detachment through the eye of knowledge.
A man who possesses the eye of wisdom does not pursue vice in this world.
He becomes dispassionate according to his desire, yet he does not abandon the Dharma;
seeing that the world is subject to decay, he strives for total renunciation.
Thereupon, he exerts himself toward liberation through the proper means, and not by means that are ineffective.
Thus he adopts world-weariness and abandons evil action;
he becomes righteous and attains supreme liberation.
Austerity is the highest good for a living being; its root is tranquility and self-control.
By means of that, O best of the twice-born, one attains all the desires that one wishes for in the mind;
through the restraint of the senses, through truth, and through self-control,
one attains the station of Brahman, which is supreme.
The Brahmin said:
"O you of restrained vows, what are those things which they call the senses? How should their restraint be practiced, and what is the fruit of that restraint?"
"And how does one obtain the fruit of those [deeds], O best of the upholders of dharma?
I wish to know this dharma in its true essence, O most righteous one.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having been thus addressed by the brahmin, the Dharma-hunter replied to the brahmin; listen to that, O lord of men.
The hunter said:
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of perceiving objects, the mind of human beings first sets out; having reached that object, it experiences either desire or anger.
Thereupon, it strives for that end and undertakes great action.
One cultivates and indulges in the practice of desirable forms and scents;
from that, passion arises, and immediately after that, hatred;
from that, greed arises, and immediately after that, delusion.

For one who is overcome by greed and struck down by passion and hatred, the intellect does not arise toward the Dharma; yet he practices the Dharma through deceit, and he finds pleasure in wealth through deceit.
O best of the twice-born, when wealth is being acquired through deceit,
the intellect finds delight therein and consequently desires to commit sin;
even when restrained by friends and wise men, O foremost of the twice-born.
He speaks what is contrary to the sacred revelation, though it be connected with the revelation;
his threefold unrighteousness increases through the fault of passion. He not only conceives of evil, but speaks it and acts upon it as well.

For one who has turned toward unrighteousness, virtuous qualities perish; those of similar character, being evildoers, become his friends. Through that, he experiences unhappiness and is ruined in the next world.
For one becomes evil-minded in this way; now hear from me how the gain of Dharma occurs:
he who, through wisdom, perceives these faults beforehand, is skilled regarding pleasure and pain and attends upon the virtuous.
From his undertaking of virtuous deeds, wisdom regarding the dharmas arises.
The Brahmin said:
"You speak of the true dharma, of which no speaker is found."
"You possess a divine power so great that you are considered by me to be nothing other than a ṛṣi.
The hunter said:
"The highly blessed Brāhmaṇas are indeed the ancestors who always eat first."
A wise person in this world should strive with all their being to do what is pleasing to them;
O best of the twice-born, I shall tell you what is pleasing to them. Having paid homage to the Brahmins, learn from me the Vedic knowledge (*brāhmī vidyā*).

"O Brahmin, this entire universe is invincible in every respect; it consists of the great elements, and there can be nothing higher than this. The great elements are space, wind, fire, water, and earth."
Wind, conjoined with space, exists within all beings;
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are its qualities. Indeed, through austerity, one attains whatever is desired.
When those [organs] have their senses restrained, that constitutes austerity, and not otherwise. All their qualities also function in mutual relation;
all the preceding qualities are present in each of the three subsequent categories of beings in due order.
The sixth, however, is called volition (*cetanā*), which is designated as the mind (*manas*);
the seventh would be the intellect (*buddhi*), and after that comes the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). Furthermore, there are the five sense organs, as well as *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas*.
Thus, this group of seventeen is designated as the Unmanifest;
well-enveloped here by all the objects of the senses, both manifest and unmanifest,
this collection of twenty-four consists of the qualities (guṇas) of the manifest and the unmanifest.
"03,201.020e All this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
03,202.001 Mārkaṇḍeya said:
03,202.001a Having been addressed thus by the virtuous hunter (Dharmavyādha), O Bhārata, that brahmin..."
He spoke again a story that increased the joy of his mind:
"O Brāhmaṇa, best among those who know the Dharma, regarding those which they call the five great elements (mahābhūtas)..."
"Tell me correctly the qualities of each of these five as well.
The hunter said:
"Earth, water, fire, wind, and space."
I shall describe to you the qualities of all those elements, each possessing an increasing number of attributes:
O Brahmin, earth has five qualities, water has four,
fire has three, and both ether and wind have three.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—
these five qualities belong to the earth, and they are more excellent than all [other qualities]. O best of the twice-born, sound, touch, form, and taste [are likewise found there].
O Brahmin of noble vows, these qualities of water have been proclaimed to you.
Sound, touch, and form are the three qualities of fire;
sound and touch belong to wind, while sound alone belongs to space.
"O Brahmin, these fifteen qualities exist within the five elements;
they reside in all beings, in which the worlds are established.
They do not transcend one another, O twice-born one, and their perfect integration occurs."

But when moving and non-moving beings fall into a state of imbalance, then the embodied soul, in the course of time, migrates into another body. They perish in a sequential order and are born again in a sequential order.
For in various places, the elements composed of the five gross constituents (pañcabhautika) are seen,
by which this entire world— both the stationary and the moving— is pervaded. Whatever is produced by the senses is known as the manifest (vyakta).
It should be understood as unmanifest, graspable by its signs, and beyond the senses. These, however, are the respective perceivers of sound and the other [objects].
When the embodied soul, maintaining these sense organs here in this world, suffers.
He sees himself spread throughout the world and the world within himself;
knowing both the high and the low, though remaining attached, he beholds all beings.
Thus he constantly perceives all beings in all their various states at all times.
For one who has become Brahman, no contact with what is inauspicious occurs;
for one who has transcended the affliction born of delusion, which is rooted in ignorance,
the world is seen through the light of the intellect along the path of the knowable.
The wise Blessed One has declared that the living being is without beginning or end, self-born, eternally imperishable, incomparable, and formless;
all this about which you ask me, O Brahmin, has its root in austerity.
The senses alone constitute both heaven and hell;
when restrained or unleashed, they lead respectively to heaven and to hell.
This is the entire method of yoga, which consists in the mastery of the senses.
For this is the root of all austerity and of hell: by attachment to the senses, one undoubtedly incurs fault;
but by restraining them, one attains perfection.

He who attains mastery over the six eternal faculties within himself, having conquered his senses, is never joined with evils, much less with calamities. The body is seen as the chariot of the person.
They say the self is the driver and the senses are the horses;
with these well-trained horses, one who is skillful and vigilant proceeds happily like a wise charioteer.
He who, being steadfast, holds the reins of the six ever-restless senses within himself, he would be the supreme charioteer.
For when the senses are let loose, they are like horses on their tracks.

One should exercise firmness in the role of charioteer; through firmness, one will surely conquer them. For when the mind follows after the wandering senses, it carries away one's discernment, just as the wind sweeps away a boat upon the waters.
Those who, out of delusion, hold conflicting views regarding the attainment of the fruit in these six [paths],
find the fruit born of meditation by practicing with resolute application toward them.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When the hunter Dharmavyādha had thus spoken of the subtle, O Bhārata,
that Brāhmaṇa, being well-composed, again asked about the subtle.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Tell me truly, according to the facts, as I ask here, the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* exactly as they are.
The hunter said:
"Behold, I shall tell you that which you ask of me.
Understand from me as I speak the qualities of these [three] individually:
among them, *tamas* is characterized by delusion, while *rajas* is their instigator."
And because it abounds in luminosity, *sattva* is said here to be superior.
One who abounds in ignorance is deluded, prone to dreaming, and lacking discernment; he is of evil vision, overwhelmed by *tamas*, wrathful, characterized by *tamas*, and lazy.
O brahmin-sage, that minister who speaks with zeal, yet is full of passion, envious, desirous of knowledge, stubborn, and arrogant, is characterized by *rajas*.
He who is full of clarity, steadfast, free from the desire for further knowledge, and devoid of envy— [is characterized by *sattva*].
The wise man who is free from anger and self-controlled is one of sattvic nature.
Yet, even when awakened as one of sattvic nature, he is distressed by the ways of the world;
for when he understands what is to be understood, he comes to loathe worldly conduct.
For the very form of dispassion first begins to manifest;
the ego becomes mild, and that which is straightforwardness becomes serene.
Then all his mutual pairs of opposites are pacified.
And for him, there is no restriction whatsoever anywhere;
for one born from a Śūdra womb who possesses virtuous qualities,
O Brahmin, attains the status of a Vaiśya and likewise that of a Kṣatriya.
"For one who abides in straightforwardness, the state of a Brahmin is born.
All these qualities have been proclaimed to you; what more do you wish to hear?
The Brahmin said:
"Having reached the earthly element, how does the bodily fire come to be?
And by means of what specific space does the wind circulate?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, regarding this question posed by the Brahmin,
that hunter explained it to the high-souled Brahmin. The hunter said:
The fire, residing in the head, protects the body;
the vital breath (*prāṇa*), existing both in the head and in the fire, performs its functions. The past, the present, and the future—all are established in the vital breath.
That alone is the most excellent among all beings; we worship that light of Brahman. He is the living being, the self of all beings, the eternal Puruṣa;
he is the mind, the intellect, the ego, and the object of experience for all beings.
