Within the body there is the navel; in the navel, fire is established. It is the unmanifest, that which is designated as *sattva*, the individual soul (*jīva*), and indeed Time (*kāla*).
O best of the twice-born, it is both primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*), as well as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself.
He remains awake even during the time of sleep, and within the dream state, he dreams;
he bestows strength upon those who are awake and causes those who are active to act. When he is restrained, O chief of brahmins, one is said to be dead.
Having abandoned the body, the elemental self (bhūtātmā) attains another;
yet here, in this world, it is everywhere sustained by the vital breath (prāṇa),
while the equalizing breath (samāna) follows behind, each relying upon its own respective course.
The fire is situated at the base of the bladder and in the anus;
carrying both urine and feces, the *apāna* wind circulates there.
It is that single [wind] which operates in the three—effort, action, and strength.
Those who are learned in the inner self call that the *udāna* wind; likewise, the wind that is situated in every single joint among the bodies of men is taught to be the *vyāna*.
Skin, flesh, fat, marrow, bone, lymph, and blood are the constituent elements (dhātus).
Fire is spread throughout these elements; impelled by the wind, it circulates, maintaining the nutritional fluids, the elements, and the humors (doṣas).
From the convergence of the vital breaths (prāṇas), however, a further convergence is produced.
That which digests the food of embodied beings should be known as heat and fire.
Between the downward-moving breath (apāna) and the upward-moving breath (udāna), the forward-moving breath (prāṇa) and the pervasive breath (vyāna) are situated.
But when endowed with its substratum, the purifying fire digests [the food] correctly.
Its opening, extending as far as the anus, is likewise known as the rectum;
from that, the channels arise in all embodied beings.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*), carrying the force of fire, is struck back at the end of the rectum;

having returned upward, it again throws the digestive fire (*pāvaka*) upward. The receptacle for digested food (*pakvāśaya*) is below the navel, while the receptacle for undigested food (*āmāśaya*) is situated above it.

All the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are established in the center of the navel of the body. Originating from the heart, they proceed sideways, upward, and likewise downward; ten channels (*nāḍīs*), impelled by the *prāṇa*, carry the essences of food.
This is the path of the yogis by which they go to that supreme state;
the wise ones, having conquered fatigue and mastered their postures, place the self in the crown of the head.
For in this way, the prāṇa and apāna breaths are extended throughout all embodied beings.
O Brahmin, know that those two, together with Agni, are indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the self;
it consists of the eleven transformations, is composed of a collection of constituent parts (*kalā*),
and know it to be truly embodied, eternally characterized by what is won through action.
Know that Self which is established therein, like fire constantly placed within a vessel, eternally self-conquered through yoga;
it is the deity established therein, like a drop of water upon a lotus leaf.

Know him to be the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), eternally victorious through renunciation; know that rajas, sattva, and tamas are of the nature of the individual soul (jīvātman). Know the individual soul to be a quality of the Self, and likewise know the Self to be of the nature of the Supreme.
They say that consciousness is the quality of the living soul;
it acts and causes all things to act.
Beyond that, those who know the field (kṣetra) speak.
He who fashioned the seven worlds—
thus the Self of all beings does not manifest within all beings; however,
it is perceived by those who know through subtle and supreme intelligence.
For by the serenity of the mind, one destroys both auspicious and inauspicious karma;
with a serene self, abiding in the Self, one enjoys infinite happiness.
The characteristic of serenity is like that of one who, being satisfied, sleeps in comfort.
Having indeed abandoned both pleasure and pain, free from dualities and without possessions,
he should shine like a lamp in a windless place, illuminated by skillful means;
constantly applying his mind during the first and last watches of the night.
Eating light food and purified in soul, beholding the Self within the self,
he sees with the lamp of the mind as if with a blazing lamp;
having seen the Self as being without a [separate] self, he is then liberated.
By all means, one must restrain greed and anger;
this is considered the purification of sacrifices and indeed the bridge to asceticism.
One should always protect one's austerity from anger and protect one's prosperity from envy.
One should protect one's learning from both honor and dishonor, and protect oneself from negligence. Compassion is the highest dharma, and forgiveness is the supreme strength.
Knowledge of the self is the highest knowledge, and the vow of truth is the highest vow.

Speaking the truth is excellent; truthful knowledge leads to one's welfare. That which is ultimately beneficial to all living beings is indeed considered the supreme truth. He whose every undertakings are always free from the bonds of desire—
He for whom everything is offered as a sacrifice in renunciation is a true renunciant and he is wise;
since even a heavy burden cannot cause him to fall away while he is practicing it,
one should know that to be the yoga of Brahman, which is designated as the state beyond yoga.

One should not harm any living beings and should conduct oneself with a disposition of friendliness; having attained this life, one should not harbor enmity toward anyone. Possessing nothing, being well-contented, free from expectations, and steady.
This alone is the supreme knowledge, the highest knowledge of the true Self. Having renounced all possessions, become one whose vows are restrained through wisdom;
then, whether here or after death, you shall abide in that sorrowless and immovable state.
The self attached to external objects of touch finds only that pleasure which exists within the self; but he whose self is united with *brahman*-yoga enjoys imperishable happiness.
By the sage who is constant in austerity, self-controlled, and of restrained self—
One who desires to conquer the unconquered should remain unattached amidst attachments;
[seeing] virtue and non-virtue as non-attachment, with a single purpose and without interval—
this, O Brahmin, they call your conduct, the singular state of happiness.
The man who renounces both suffering and happiness attains Brahman and proceeds by means of non-attachment. O best of the twice-born, all this has been told to you in brief, exactly as it was heard.
"All this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, when the entire dharma of liberation had been thus narrated..."
With a firm and joyful mind, the brahmin spoke to the Dharmavyādha:
"Everything you have proclaimed is consistent with justice; indeed, there is nothing regarding the principles of dharma that remains unknown to you."
The hunter said:
"O best of the twice-born, behold that dharma which is manifest before my very eyes,
by which I have attained this perfection, O bull among brahmins."
"Arise quickly, O Blessed One; having entered the inner house, you ought to see my mother and father, O Knower of Dharma.
Thus he spoke, and that Brahmin beheld the parents of the hunter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been addressed thus, he entered and then beheld a most highly honored,
heart-stealing mansion with four courtyards, exceedingly beautiful to the mind.
Resembling a temple of the gods and well-honored by the deities,
it was crowded with couches and seats and endowed with the finest perfumes.
There, his parents, wearing white garments, were honored.
Having finished their meal and being well-satisfied, the two sat upon excellent seats;
but when the Dharmavyādha saw them, he fell at their feet with his head bowed.
The two elders said:
"Arise, arise, O knower of dharma! May dharma protect you.
We are pleased with your purity; may you attain long life, a desired state, and likewise knowledge. Thus, be devoted to the Supreme."
"O son, because we have been constantly and well-honored by you, our virtuous son,
we dwell here in happiness as if we had gone to the world of the gods. Among all the deities, there is no other divinity for you."
Because you are ever-striving, O twice-born one, you are endowed with self-restraint.
Your father, your grandfathers, and likewise your great-grandfathers are constantly pleased, my son, by your self-restraint and by your worship of us.
In thought, deed, and word, your service has never faltered;
nor is any contrary intention seen in you at present,
such as was shown by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, toward his aged parents.
"O dear son, you have performed all of that, and even more distinguished.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the Dharmavyādha introduced that Brahmin to the two of them.
Then the two of them honored that brahmin with a welcome;
and having accepted that hospitality, the twice-born man asked both of them,
"Is all well at home for you both, along with your sons and your servants?"
"And is there always freedom from ailment here in both your bodies?
The two elders replied:
"O Brahmin, we are well in every respect—in our home and among our circle of dependents."
"O Blessed One, have you also arrived here without hindrance?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"The Brahmin, filled with joy, replied to them both, 'Indeed so.'"
The Dharma-fowler, however, spoke these meaningful words to that Brahmin:
"O Blessed One, my father and mother are my supreme deities;
whatever duty is to be performed for the gods, that I perform for them."
Just as the thirty-three gods, all led by Śakra,
are to be honored by the entire world, so too are these two elders of mine;
just as the twice-born bring offerings to the deities.
In the same way, O Brahmin, I perform these rites for them without weariness; these two, my father and mother, are my supreme deity,
O twice-born one, and I always gratify them with flowers, fruits, and jewels.
"These alone are the fires for me which the wise proclaim;
the four sacrifices and the four Vedas—all this belongs to me, O twice-born one.
For their sake are my life-breaths, my wife, my sons, and my kinsmen."
Together with my wife and sons, I constantly perform service for them;
I personally bathe them and likewise wash their feet. O best of the twice-born, I myself provide them with food.
I speak agreeable words, avoiding anything unpleasant;
even if it is joined with unrighteousness, I do what is pleasing to these two.
O best of the twice-born, knowing dharma alone to be supreme, I act accordingly.
"O Brahmin, I always perform service without weariness.
O best of the twice-born, there are five gurus for a man who desires his own welfare:
the father, the mother, the sacred fire, the self, and the teacher."
O best of the twice-born, for him who conducts himself properly toward these [duties],
his sacred fires will be perpetually honored;
this is the eternal dharma for one living the life of a householder.
"O Brahmin, I have related this to you; what more do you wish to hear?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Having introduced both his parents, his two gurus, to the Brahmin..."
Once again, that righteous hunter said to the brahmin:
"I have become one whose vision is active; behold the power of asceticism! Go to Mithilā, for this was the purpose for which you were told by her."
"Devoted to service toward her husband, self-controlled, and of truthful character—
that fowler living in Mithilā will explain the dharmas to you.
The Brahmin said:
"O observer of vows, having recalled the words of my wife— who is devoted to her husband, truthful, and rich in virtue— you are, in my opinion, a man of merit, O knower of dharma.
The hunter said:

O best of the twice-born, O Lord, that which you were told by her regarding me at that time has been clearly seen by that devoted wife; of this there is no doubt. However, O Brahmin, this was shown by me to you out of a desire to favor you.
And hear my words, O dear one, which I shall speak for your benefit, O twice-born:
your mother and father have been treated with neglect by you, O best of the twice-born;
you departed from home without their permission, O blameless one.
That which you have done for the purpose of performing the recitation of the Vedas was improper;
out of grief for you, those two ascetics have become blind in their old age. Go to propitiate them, lest great dharma pass you by.
"You are an ascetic, high-souled, and always devoted to dharma;
yet all this of yours is in vain. Quickly propitiate those two.
Having propitiated them, O best of the twice-born, you will attain that which is for your highest good."
"Have faith in me, O Brahmin; you ought not to act otherwise.
Go now, O brahmin-sage; I shall tell you what is for your highest good.
The Brahmin said:
"Whatever has been spoken by you is all true, without a doubt. I am pleased with you, O knower of dharma, you who are endowed with virtuous conduct and qualities.
The hunter said:
For you are indeed equal to a deity, you who are devoted to the eternal, divine, and ancient dharma that is difficult to attain for those of unrefined soul;
O best of the twice-born, having gone into the presence of your mother and father, you [have performed this].
"Without weariness, quickly perform the worship of your mother and father;
for beyond this, I do not perceive any other duty whatsoever.
The brahmin said:
"By good fortune I have come here; by good fortune I have met with you. Such men who demonstrate the Dharma are rare in this world;
perhaps one such person is found among thousands of men, or perhaps not at all."
"I am pleased with your truthfulness; may it be well with you, O Supreme among Men!
For as I was falling into hell, I have been rescued by you. It must indeed have been destined so that you were seen by me, O Sinless One."
O tiger among men, just as King Yayāti was rescued from his fallen state by his virtuous grandsons, so have I been rescued here by you;
at your word, I shall now perform service to my mother and father.
One who has not disciplined his soul cannot discern the determination of dharma and adharma;
for the eternal dharma is difficult to know by one existing in a *śūdra* womb.
Yet, I do not consider you to be a *śūdra*; there must surely be a reason for this.
"O high-minded one, I desire to know this in its true essence: by what ripening of karma did you attain this status of a Śūdra? O self-restrained one, please tell me everything truly as you wish."
The hunter said:
"O best of the twice-born, Brahmins are indeed not to be transgressed against.
Listen, O sinless one, to all this that occurred in my previous body."
"O son of the best of the twice-born, I was formerly a Brahmin,
well-versed in the study of the Vedas and a master who had reached the further shore of the Vedāṅgas; yet,
O Brahmin, through the faults committed by myself, I have come to this present condition."
"O twice-born one, there was once a certain king who was my friend and devoted to the science of archery; through association with him, I became preeminent in the use of the bow.
At that very time, however, the king went out on a hunt."
Accompanied by the leaders of the warriors and well-surrounded by my ministers,
I then hunted a great many deer there near the hermitage. Then, O best of the twice-born, a terrible arrow was discharged by me as well.
Then, O best of Brahmins, that king, a tiger among men, slaughtered deer, boars, and buffaloes;
thereafter, I too, devoted to the pleasure and welfare of the king, [followed] for the sake of sport.
Slaying choice boars with my straight-jointed arrows in the forest fastnesses, O knower of dharma, I roamed like a hunter armed with a bow, equal to that high-souled king.
O best among those who know the dharma, O twice-born one, it was there, in the vicinity of that hermitage, that I then discharged an arrow as hard as a thunderbolt at a deer;
and by that smooth-jointed shaft, the sage was struck.
Falling to the ground, O Brahmin, he spoke while making the air resound:
"I have committed no offense; by whom has this sin been done?
Thinking him to be a deer, I suddenly approached the sage."
I beheld that rishi pierced by my straight-knotted arrow;
that brahmin of fierce asceticism groaning upon the surface of the earth. And because of having committed this unworthy deed, my mind was deeply distressed.
"Thinking 'this was done by me unknowingly,' I then said to him,
'O Brahmin, you ought to forgive me. Thus addressed by me,
the sage, overcome with anger, then replied to me with these words."
"O twice-born one, you shall become a cruel hunter in the womb of a Śūdra. The hunter said:
"O best among the foremost of the twice-born, I was thus cursed by the ṛṣi at that time."
I propitiated the seer, who was skilled in speech, with these words:
"O Sage, this improper act has been committed by me today through ignorance;
you ought to forgive all of that. Be gracious, O Blessed One."
The seer said:
"The curse shall not be otherwise; this is certain beyond doubt.
Yet, out of compassion, I shall now grant you some favor."
"Though you shall exist in a Śūdra womb, you will indeed be a knower of dharma;
you will perform service to your mother and father, of this there is no doubt.
Through that service, you will attain great perfection."
You shall remember your past lives and you will indeed go to heaven;
having become a righteous hunter devoted to the service of your parents,
when the end of the curse has been reached, you will become a twice-born man once again.
The hunter said:
"O best of men, having been cursed in this way long ago by that rishi of fierce splendor, he also granted me this favor."
O best of the twice-born, I extracted the arrow from him and brought him to my hermitage, yet he was not deprived of his life. I have related all this to you exactly as it happened to me in the past.
"O best of the twice-born, I must also go to heaven from here.
The brahmin said:
"In this way, O man, these sorrows and joys [arise]."
O one of great intelligence, they have attained [this state]; you ought not to feel longing.

For, O dear one, you who know the true nature of your own birth, who understand the reality of the world's course, and who are ever devoted to the Dharma, have performed what is indeed difficult to do.
"O learned one, this defect of your karma is indeed due to the nature of your birth; endure it for a short time, and thereafter you shall become a twice-born Brahmin.
Furthermore, I consider you to be a Brahmin now; there is no doubt in this matter."

A Brahmin who persists in acts leading to a fall from caste, in improper occupations, who is hypocritical and prone to evil deeds, becomes equal to a Śūdra. But that Śūdra who is constantly intent upon self-restraint, truth, and righteousness [is equal to a Brahmin].
I consider him a true brahmin, for by his conduct alone one becomes twice-born;
through the fault of one's actions, however, one attains a terrible and miserable destiny.
O best of men, I consider you to be one whose defects have been entirely exhausted.
"You ought not to feel anxiety, for those like you are free from despondency;
they understand the course of worldly affairs and are ever devoted to dharma.
The hunter said:

One should destroy mental suffering through wisdom and physical suffering through medicines; this is the power of discernment, which the foolish do not attain. [This occurs] from union with the undesired and from separation from the beloved.

Men of small intelligence are joined with mental sufferings; likewise, all beings are joined with and separated from their qualities. Since this is true for all, there is indeed no ground for grief for anyone alone.

Seeing oneself joined with the undesired, one likewise quickly becomes dispassionate; and if one perceives a remedy, one applies it. For one who merely grieves, nothing is achieved; he suffers in vain.
Those men who renounce both suffering and pleasure, those wise ones, satisfied with knowledge, alone thrive in happiness. The foolish are intent on discontent, while the learned attain contentment.
There is no end to discontent, but contentment is the supreme happiness.
Those who have traveled the path do not grieve, for they behold the highest goal. One should not set the mind on despair; despair is the ultimate poison.

It destroys the one of unrefined wisdom, like an enraged serpent slaying a child; for that man whom despondency overcomes when a crisis has arisen, being deprived of his vital energy, no human purpose remains for him.

The fruit of an action that is inevitably performed is clearly seen; for one who has fallen into despondency does not attain anything auspicious. However, one might still perceive a means for liberation from suffering.
One should indeed begin [one's practice] without grieving, remaining disciplined and free from addiction.
But those who have reached that which is beyond the intellect, having reflected upon the non-existence of beings, do not grieve; they are of perfected wisdom, beholding the supreme goal.
"O learned one, I do not grieve; I remain here awaiting my time. By these illustrations, O Brahmin, best of beings, I do not despair.
The Brahmin said:
"You have cultivated wisdom, you are intelligent, and your understanding is vast. I do not grieve for you; you are satisfied with knowledge and a knower of dharma.
I take my leave of you; may it be well with you, and may Dharma protect you."
"But you must practice heedfulness regarding dharma, O best of those who uphold dharma.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"So be it," the hunter replied to him with palms joined in reverence.

Then, having performed a circumambulation, that best of the twice-born set forth. Having departed, that twice-born man, firm in his vows, then performed every service toward his aged parents according to the prescribed rule.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, best among the upholders of dharma, all this that you asked concerning dharma, O dear one— namely,
the greatness of the devoted wife and of the brahmin— has been explained to you in its entirety.
"And service to mother and father, as well as the duty toward the sick, has been proclaimed.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Brahmin, this unsurpassed narrative of dharma is truly most wonderful."

"O best among the upholders of all dharmas, O most excellent of the twice-born, O learned one, because it was so pleasant to hear, these moments have passed for me as if they were but an instant. Yet,
O Blessed One, I am not yet satiated while listening to this supreme dharma."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard this auspicious discourse connected with dharma, Dharmarāja again questioned that ascetic seer Mārkaṇḍeya.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
How did Agni go to the forest, and how did Aṅgiras in ancient times,
having become the great Ṛṣi Agni, carry the sacrificial oblation when the fire had vanished?
"O Blessed One, since Agni is indeed one alone, yet his plurality is seen in ritual acts— this entire matter I wish to know. Also,
how the Kumāra was born, and how he became the son of Agni."
O descendant of Bhṛgu, O great sage, filled with curiosity, I desire to hear from you exactly how he was born from Rudra, in the Gaṅgā, and among the Kṛttikās.
"O Brahmin, you ought to tell me this auspicious ancient history.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
Just as the wrathful Fire-god went to the forest to perform austerities,
and just as the blessed Agni himself became Aṅgiras,
scorching with his own radiance and destroying the darknesses.

In former times, O mighty-armed one, the highly fortunate Aṅgiras, while dwelling in his hermitage, performed supreme austerity, excelling even the carrier of oblations (Agni). Having become thus, he then illuminated the entire world.
Performing austerities, the eater of oblations was scorched by his splendor;
the radiant one became severely exhausted and was unable to perceive anything at all.
Then the blessed carrier of the sacrificial offerings reflected:
"A different fire has been set in motion here for the worlds by Brahmā;
indeed, my own status as fire has vanished while I was performing ascetic penance.
Thinking, "How may I become fire once again? he—
He saw the great sage scorching the worlds like fire; terrified, he crept toward him slowly, and then Aṅgiras said to him: "Quickly become fire once again, you who bring prosperity to the worlds."
You are renowned throughout the three worlds, moving within their various forms;
O Agni, you were created first by Brahmā as the dispeller of darkness. Quickly regain your own station, O chaser of gloom!
Agni said:
"My fame shall perish in the world, for you have been born as the consumer of oblations (Hutāśana). People will know only you as Pāvaka, and not me."
"I deposit my state as fire; you become the first fire, and I shall become the second, the very fire of Prajāpati.
Aṅgiras said:
"Perform merit that leads to heaven for your subjects; become a fire that dispels the darkness. And, O God Agni, make me your first son immediately.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard those words of Aṅgiras, Jātavedas did accordingly.
O King, Bṛhaspati by name was also the son of that Aṅgiras;
and he, knowing him to be the first-born son of Agni, [accepted him].
Approaching him, O Bhārata, the gods asked about the cause of that matter;
being thus questioned by the gods, he then explained the reason,
and the gods accepted those words of Aṅgiras.
"Here I shall proclaim various kinds of fires of great splendor, renowned for their many functions; here, among the Brāhmaṇas, there is a diversity [of these fires].
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O scion of the Kuru lineage, the third son of Brahmā had Āpava as his wife; hear from me now concerning his offspring as well: Bṛhajjyotis, Bṛhatkīrti, Bṛhadbrahmā, and Bṛhanmanas.
O King, Bṛhaspati was possessed of great mantras and great luster; among all those offspring, he was peerless in beauty. The goddess named Bhānumatī was the first daughter of the Aṅgiras.
She in whom passion arose for all living beings is called Rāgī because of that passion; she is the second daughter of Aṅgiras,
whom embodied beings call Kapardisutā, Dṛśyā, and Adṛśyā.
Because of her thinness, she is Sinīvālī, the third daughter of Aṅgiras. She sees with her radiant splendors and is Haviṣmatī because of the oblations;
they call this sixth daughter of Aṅgiras, the auspicious Haviṣmatī.
In the great, radiant sacrifices of the Aṅgirases,
the seventh daughter was known as Mahāmatī; she who,
upon being seen, causes people to exclaim "kuhu-kuhu" in wonder at the Blessed One.
"She whom they call Ekānaṃśā, the daughter of Aṅgiras, known as Kuhū.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"The illustrious wife of Bṛhaspati was the daughter of the Moon."

She gave birth to six meritorious fires and also one daughter. That fire for whom clarified butter is prescribed as the oblation among the *āhutis* is the son of Bṛhaspati, the highly resplendent one named Śaṃyu.
In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, in the Iṣṭi, and in the Aśvamedha, he was the first-born sacrificial animal;
then there was the one powerful Agni, blazing with many fearsome flames. Śaṃyū’s incomparable wife was Satyā, who was truly born of Dharma.

His son was the radiant Agni, and he had three daughters of virtuous conduct. The fire that is worshipped with the first portion of clarified butter in the sacrifice is called Bharadvāja, his eldest son.
At all full-moon sacrifices, the clarified butter raised in the *sruva* ladle belongs to him;
that fire is named Bharata, the second son born of Śamyu.
There are three other daughters of whom Bharata is the husband.
His son was Bharata, and he had one daughter named Bharatī. Bharata was the fire of the patriarch Agni; O best of the Bharatas, he was exceedingly great and beneficial.
The wife of Bharadvāja was Vīrā, and her son was the hero Piṇḍada;
the twice-born say that his sacrifice with clarified butter was performed slowly, like that of Soma.
He who is joined with Soma by means of the second oblation—

The progenitor of chariots, whose sound was like a chariot, he is called Kumbharetas; he begat Siddhi upon Sarayū and enveloped Bhānu with his own splendors. He is constantly invoked in invocations as the bringer of the fire-god’s power.
But he who never falls away, always endowed with fame, splendor, and beauty—
Agni, named Niścyavana, praises the earth alone.
Free from evil, liberated from impurities, and pure, he blazes with his radiance.
His son was the sinless Agni, who is true in his ritual duties;
for he provides atonement for beings who utter insults,
that Agni is named Niṣkṛti (Atonement), and when worshipped, he brings beauty.

The fire named Svana is the son of that [fire] which causes pain; it is the one by which people here, afflicted by sensation, cry out in lamentation. But he who stands having pervaded the intellect of the entire world—

Those who know the supreme self call that purifier by the name Viśvajit; for it is the internal fire residing within which digests the food of embodied beings. In sacrifice, O Bhārata, it is known as Viśvabhuj throughout all the worlds.
Chaste, self-controlled, and always observing extensive vows,
the Brahmins worship him as the purifier (pāvaka) in the domestic sacrifices (pākayajña).
He was renowned by the name Gopati, and a river became his beloved wife.
In that [ocean], all actions are performed by the agents of action.
That which is the most terrible Mare’s Mouth (Vaḍavāmukha) drinks the water;
it is the upward-moving one named Ūrdhvabhāj, and it is the sage who resides within the vital breath.

In whose house the sacrificial oblation is constantly offered through the northern gate, from that [offering] the clarified butter becomes well-sacrificed; he is remembered as the supreme Sviṣṭakṛt. He who is wrath when all beings are at peace is the purifier (pāvaka).
The illustrious Lord Agni himself, possessed of great power, is named Manyumān;
he shines forth as he burns the wild and domestic plants alike.
Then there is the glorious fire named Vṛddhimān, who has arisen of his own accord.
That Krodha, possessed of great splendor, is to be recognized as residing within all embodied beings.
From Krodha was born the essence (rasa), and then his daughter Manyatī;
she is Svāhā, fierce and cruel, who dwells among all creatures.
In the third heaven, there was no one at all equal to him in form;
because of his incomparability, the gods gave that purifier the name Kāma.
Standing upon his chariot, wearing a garland and wielding a bow, he suppressed his anger out of joy.
In battle, he destroys enemies; he is the fire named Amogha. O highly fortunate one, he is named Uktha, praised with the three Ukthas. He generated Mahāvāca, whom they know as Sakāmāśva.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Kāśyapa, Vāsiṣṭha, Prāṇa and his son Prāṇaputraka,
Agni Āṅgirasa, and Cyavana Triṣuvarcaka.
For the sake of a son, they performed intense austerities for many years, thinking:
"May we obtain a most righteous son, equal in fame to Brahmā. Then, he was meditated upon by them with the five great mystical utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*).

He was born full of splendor, radiant, five-colored, and powerful. His head was like a kindled fire, his two arms were like the sun, his skin and eyes had a golden luster, and his shanks were dark, O Bhārata.
He was made five-colored by those five people through their ascetic power;
he is heard of in the Veda as Pāñcajanya, for he established the five lineages. Having performed ascetic penance for ten thousand years, that one of great austerity—
Creating the progeny of the ancestors, he generated the fierce purifier (Agni).
From his head he produced the *Bṛhat* and *Rathaṃtara* [Sāmans], and from his mouth, by his power, the two *Ahar*s.
From his navel he created Śiva, from his strength Indra, and from his breath Vāyu and Agni.
From his two arms were born Anudātta and Viśva, as well as all living beings.
Having created these, he then produced five sons of the Pitṛs:
Praṇidhi, the son of Bṛhadūrja, and Bṛhattara, the son of Kāśyapa.
Bhānu was the son of Aṅgiras, and Vīra was the son of Varcas, belonging to the Saubhara lineage; Prāṇa and Anudātta are also explained as five born of the lineage.
He created fifteen other gods who steal the sacrifice.
Through his ascetic power, he created these five gods who plunder sacrifices: Abhīma, Atibhīma, Bhīma, Bhīmabala, and Bala;
as well as Sumitra, Mitravanta, Mitrājña, and Mitravardhana.
Through austerity, Tapa created these gods who possess the nature of friends;
through austerity, he created these five: Surapravīra, Vīra, Sukeśa, Suvarcas, and the slayer even of the gods.
For these five [senses] are established in three ways, each separately.
While they remain here, they rob those who perform sacrifices from heaven;
they seize their merit and destroy it greatly upon the earth.

Out of rivalry with the fire-carriers, these [demons] strike down and carry off the sacrificial offerings upon the altar; that act of seizing is instigated by those skilled in such deeds. Therefore, they do not approach that place where the sacred fire is stationed.
The fire Cita, carrying the sacrifice, obstructs them with its two wings;
for these [obstacles], once pacified by mantras, do not steal away the desired sacrificial merit.
The son of Bṛhaduktha-tapas has taken refuge upon the earth.
While the Agnihotra is being offered, it is sacrificed upon the earth by the virtuous;
and the Rathantara is recited as Agni, the son of Tapas.
Indeed, the Adhvaryus know his oblation for the sake of Mitravinda.
Together with these ascetics of great fortune and radiant splendor, O King,
that highly illustrious monarch rejoiced with his sons, filled with supreme delight.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The fire named Bharata, endowed with heavy observances, is satisfied and bestows prosperity; he is called Bharata because he sustains all creatures.
The fire named Puṣṭimati likewise grants nourishment when pleased. This one sustains all progeny, and for that reason he is called Bharata.
O best of the Bharatas, that fire which is of great splendor is indeed Pāvaka; he who is named Śiva is devoted to the worship of Śakti, and as Śiva,
he is eternally the bringer of auspiciousness to all who are afflicted by suffering.
Having seen that the fruit of austerity had increased greatly,
the wise Puraṃdara was born as a son, desiring to uplift it.
And from Heat (ūṣman) was born Steam (ūṣmā), who is perceived as fire among living beings.
And Agni, named Manu, also performed the rite for Prajāpati.
Then the Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas call that fire Śambhu;
the twice-born call that blazing, great-radiant fire Āvasathya.
Agni begot here five sons of sacrifice, who bestow vigor, carry the oblations, and possess a luster like gold.
O highly fortunate one, when all was tranquil, Agni, the lord of cattle, became exhausted.
He generated the terrible Asuras and various kinds of mortals;
and Aṅgiras produced Manu as the son of Tapas, as well as Bhānu.
Those Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas call him Bṛhadbhānu.
The wife of Bhānu was Suprajā, while Somajā was the wife of Bṛhadbhās;
they both gave birth to six sons—listen now to the account of their progeny.
At that time, she [Somajā] was together with her daughter.
Then there is Bhānu, the son of Aṅgiras;
they call him Agni Balada, the first son of Bhānu, who bestows bodies upon weak beings.

He who becomes fierce anger toward beings who are peaceful is that fire named Manyumān, the second son of Bhānu. He for whom the sacrificial oblation is prescribed here on the new moon and the full moon days.
The fire here named Viṣṇu is that Aṅgiras named Dhṛtimat;
his *āgrayaṇa* oblation is prescribed to be offered together with Indra. That fire is named Āgrayaṇa, and he belongs to the lineage of Bhānu.
He who was the Niragraha of the constant oblations during the Cāturmāsya sacrifices had a lineage belonging solely to the Sun,
together with four sons. He, moreover,
begot a daughter, Niśā, as well as both Agni and Soma.
Manu’s wife indeed gave birth to five fires;
that illustrious fire, accompanied by Parjanya, is the Vaiśvānara who is worshipped with the foremost oblations during the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
He who is proclaimed as the lord of this entire world is that Agni named Viśvapati, the second son of Manu;
from him the clarified butter becomes well-sacrificed (sviṣṭa), and he is remembered as the supreme Sviṣṭakṛt.
That maiden named Rohiṇī was the daughter of Hiraṇyakaśipu; by her [acceptance], he shone as her husband— he who, as that Prajāpati,
animates the bodies of embodied beings by resorting to their vital breath (prāṇa).

The deity named Saṃnihita is the means for the manifestation of sound-form; he moves between white and black, and he bears the sacrificial fire. Though himself stainless, he is the creator of stains, and he is one who resorts to anger.
And he whom ascetics always call the supreme seer Kapila is that fire named Kapila, the founder of Sāṃkhya and Yoga;
for it is Agni who constantly sustains all beings.
Among the various types of actions here, he is called the foremost fire;
he created these other renowned purifiers on earth,
formidable for the purpose of expiation when the *agnihotra* sacrifice has been defiled.
If the fires should somehow come into contact with one another due to the wind,
an *iṣṭi* sacrifice on eight potsherds must be performed for the fire Śuci.
When the *dakṣiṇāgni* comes into contact with two others, that is indeed the case.
If the fires situated in the dwelling should be touched by a forest fire, an *iṣṭi* sacrifice with an eight-pot-sherd cake must be performed for Agni Vīta;
if the fires should indeed be touched by a forest fire while in their place of entry,
an *iṣṭi* sacrifice with an eight-pot-sherd cake must be performed for Agni Śuci.
If a woman in her menses should touch the Agnihotra fire,
an *iṣṭi* sacrifice with an eight-potherd cake must be performed for Agni Dasyumat.
He who is heard to be dead while still living, like cattle that have passed away—
A sacrifice with an eight-potherd cake should be performed for Agni Abhimat. However,
that Brahmin who, being afflicted, has not offered oblations into the fire for three nights,
should perform a sacrifice with an eight-potherd cake for Agni Uttara.

If the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices of one who has established the sacred fires should fail, an *iṣṭi* offering on eight potsherds must be performed for Agni Pathikṛt (the Fire that makes the way). Furthermore,
if the fire of a woman in childbirth should come into contact with the *agnihotra* fire, [a similar rite is required].
A sacrifice with an eight-potherd cake should be performed for Agni, the possessor of flames.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Āpā was the joyful wife of Sahas, his most beloved.
The lord of the earth and sustainer of the world begot a supreme fire,
whom they call the purifier and lord of all beings;
he is known as the Self and the sustainer of the world among the lineages of the twice-born.
He who is the lord of all great beings here on earth— that Blessed One of great splendor, the Purifier, moves eternally. Known by the name Agni Gṛhapati, he is constantly worshipped in sacrifices.
He who carries the oblation offered by this world is the Purifier;
he is the womb of the waters, highly fortunate, accompanied by his sons, and most wonderful.
He is called the Lord of the Earth, the Sustainer of the World, and the Master of the Great.
Consuming deceased beings, his fire became Bharata; and at the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, that best of rites is fixed for Bharata. That powerful Vanhi is eternally sought after by the gods as the first.
Seeing him approaching, he entered the ocean out of fear; though the gods searched for him in every direction, they could not find him. But Agni, having seen Atharvan, then spoke these words.
"Carry the oblation to the gods; as for me, O hero, I am utterly weak.
O Atharvan, go to Madhva’s abode and do this which is dear to me.
Then Agni, having dispatched Atharvan, went to another place.
The fish informed him [Agni], and the enraged Fire said to them:
"You shall indeed become food for embodied beings in various ways.
Then the Bearer of Oblations likewise spoke these words to Atharvan:
Although he was strongly urged by those words of the god, he did not wish to carry the entire oblation; instead, he completely cast off his body and entered the earth.
Having abandoned that body, he then entered the ground.
Touching the earth, he indeed created the various elements separately:
from his mouth came fragrant fire (*tejas*), and from his bones, deodar cedar;
from his phlegm came crystal, and likewise from his bile, emerald.
His liver was black iron, by which indeed his offspring flourished; his nails were masses of clouds, and the networks of his veins were coral.
O King, various other minerals likewise emerged from his body.
Having thus cast off his body and remained steadfast in supreme austerity,
he was then raised up once more by Bhr̥gu, Aṅgiras, and the others through their ascetic power.
Reinvigorated by that penance, the radiant one blazed forth intensely like a flame.
Seeing the sages, he entered the great ocean out of fear. When he had vanished, the world was terrified; then the celestial rishis took refuge with Atharvan and began to worship that very Atharvan.

Then Atharvan, having beheld the worlds with his own self, created the purifier (fire) and churned up the great ocean while all beings looked on. Thus was Agni previously lost and then recovered by the venerable Atharvan.
Summoned by all beings, he always carries their sacrificial offerings. Thus,
while wandering through various regions and roaming about there, he indeed procreated many wise gods mentioned in the Vedas, who are worthy of sacrificial fires.
Excluding the Sindhu, there are five rivers: the Devikā, the Sarasvatī, the Gaṅgā, the Śatakumbhā, and the Śarayū, along with the river called Gaṇḍakī;
as well as the Carmaṇvatī, the Mahī, the Medhyā, and the Medhātithī.
The Tāmraparṇī, the Vetravatī, and the three Kauśikīs;
the Tamasā, the Narmadā, and likewise the river Godāvarī; the Veṇṇā, the Praveṇī, the Bhīmā, and the Medrathā, O Bhārata.
The Bhāratī, Suprayogā, Kāverī, and likewise the Murmurā;
the Kṛṣṇā, Kṛṣṇaveṇṇā, Kapilā, and the Śoṇa—
these are the rivers proclaimed to be the mothers of the Dhiṣṇyas.
The beloved wife of Adbhuta was his son Viḍūratha;
there were as many Somas as there are Pāvakas said to exist.
And in the lineage of Atri were born the mind-born progeny of Brahmā.
Atri, desiring to create sons, held them within himself;
the sacrificial fires then drew them forth from the body of that Brahman.
Thus have these high-souled fires been described by me to you.
Just as they have arisen immeasurable, glorious, and dispellers of darkness,
know that the majesty of this wonder is proclaimed in the Vedas;
for he alone is the consumer of oblations among them all.
This Lord, the first Aṅgiras, is to be known as truly one alone;
he has issued forth from his body in many ways, just as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice [emanates from its source].
Thus has this great lineage of the fires been recounted by me.
Purified by various mantras, he carries the sacrificial oblation for embodied beings.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O sinless one, I have thus described to you the various lineages of the fires.
"Listen, O descendant of Kuru, to the birth of the wise Kārttikeya.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having heard this auspicious narrative connected with dharma, Dharmarāja [Yudhiṣṭhira]..."
Yudhiṣṭhira again questioned that ascetic sage Mārkaṇḍeya concerning how Kumāra was born and how he became the son of Agni.

I wish to hear how he was born from Rudra, in the Gaṅgā, and among the Kṛttikās; my curiosity is indeed great. I shall relate the story of that wonderful son of immeasurable splendor, who is more marvelous than the marvelous itself.
Born from the wives of the Seven Sages, he was devoted to sacred learning and increased their fame.
In ancient times, when the gods and asuras were striving against one another in battle,
the Dānavas of terrible form always defeated the gods there.
Seeing his army being slaughtered many times by them, Purandara then fell into deep anxiety for the sake of a leader for his own forces.
That one of great strength, seeing the divine army broken by the Dānavas, [was filled with concern].
Relying upon his valor, he protected [her]; by me he is to be known as a true man.
Having gone to Mount Mānasa and reflecting deeply on this matter, he then heard a terrible cry of distress uttered by a woman.
"Let no man run toward me; let him rather protect me! Let him designate a husband for me, or let him himself become my husband.
But Purandara said to her, "Do not fear; there is no danger for you."
Having spoken thus, he then beheld Keśin standing before him,
wearing a diadem and holding a mace, like a mountain rich in minerals; taking that maiden by the hand, Vāsava then said to him:
"O Keśin, in this secluded place, choose me as a maiden who does not desire you! While I am the teacher of the wicked, wielder of the thunderbolt, and exalted by my majesty,
why do you, O performer of ignoble deeds, wish to carry off this maiden?"
"Know me to be the wielder of the thunderbolt; desist from this oppression!
Keśin said:
"O Śakra, release her yourself; she has been sought after by me."
"It is fitting for you to go to your own city while still alive, O subduer of Pāka.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, Keśin indeed hurled his mace at Indra for the purpose of slaying him.
Vāsava cut that [mountain peak] as it was falling toward him with his thunderbolt at its center.
Then Keśin, enraged, hurled a mountain summit at him—
one resembling a massive cloud and filled with flickering flames.
Seeing that mountain peak rushing toward him, O King, Śatakratu split it with his thunderbolt; it fell down upon the earth. And as it was falling, Keśin was struck by that very peak.
Leaving behind that highly fortunate maiden, he fled, greatly tormented.
When that asura had departed, Vāsava spoke to the maiden:
"Who are you? To whom do you belong? And what are you doing here, O fair-faced one?"
The maiden said:
"I am the daughter of Prajāpati, renowned as Devasenā. My sister Daityasenā was previously carried off by Keśin."
"We two sisters, together with our friends,
came here to Lake Mānasa for the sake of pleasure after having obtained permission from Prajāpati. Furthermore, the great asura Keśin constantly seeks to abduct us."
"O Pākaśāsana, the army of the Daityas desires him, but I do not.
O Blessed One, she was carried off by him, yet I have been liberated by your power.
O Lord of the Gods, I desire as my husband one who has been designated by you as invincible."
Indra said:
"You are my mother's sister's daughter, and my mother is the daughter of Dakṣa.
I wish for you yourself to declare your own power."
The maiden said:
"O mighty-armed one, I am weak, but my husband shall be powerful;
by virtue of his father’s boon, he will be honored by gods and asuras."
Indra said:
"O Goddess, what kind of power will your husband possess?
O blameless one, I wish to hear this from your own words."
The maiden said:
"He has been seen as the conqueror of the gods, dānavas, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, uragas, and rākṣasas—those who are wicked; he is possessed of great heroism and great strength."
"But he who shall conquer all beings along with you—
he indeed shall be my husband, devoted to the Brahmanas and a promoter of his fame.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard her words, Indra was deeply distressed and reflected:
"This queen has no husband such as she describes.
Then, he who possesses the splendor of the sun beheld the sun rising on the eastern mountain.
On the mountain of sunrise, he beheld the highly fortunate Soma entering the sun,
the commencement of the new moon (Amāvāsyā), the Raudra moment,
and the battle between the gods and the asuras.
The Lord Śatakratu beheld the eastern twilight joined with dense red clouds, and he saw the abode of Varuṇa with its waters turned crimson,
where offerings had been made by the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases with various kinds of mantras.

Having taken the oblation, he entered the fire and the sun; at that time, the twenty-fourth lunar conjunction (parvan) approached the sun. Likewise, the fierce moon had entered the sun, having come under the sway of fate.
Having observed the very union of the moon and the sun,
and seeing that terrible conjunction, Śakra reflected:
"A dreadful halo is seen surrounding both the sun and the moon."
At the very end of this night, he foretells a great battle;
even this river Sindhu flows violently with a current of blood,
while the female jackal, fire-mouthed, howls facing the sun.
This formidable and great conjunction is endowed with splendor;
this wondrous union of Soma, Vahni,
and Sūrya shall produce a son who would become the husband of this goddess.
"Agni is endowed with all these qualities, and Agni is the deity;
if he were to conceive a child, he would become the husband of this goddess.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One then departed for the world of Brahmā.
Having taken Devasenā by the hand, he paid homage to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
He said, "Please grant this goddess a heroic husband.
Brahmā said:
"O slayer of Dānavas, just as this task has been conceived by you,
so shall that embryo be— mighty and of vast prowess.
O Śatakratu, he shall become the commander-in-chief alongside you."
"And he shall indeed become the heroic husband of this goddess.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Having heard this, he, together with the maiden, paid homage to him."
There, the lord of the gods went to where the celestial rishis were gathered—
the preeminent leaders of the brahmins, headed by Vasiṣṭha, who were firm in their great vows—
at that sacrifice where Soma had been procured through their ascetic power for the sake of their sacrificial portions.
Thirsting [for the water], the gods, led by Śatakratu, departed;
having performed the sacrifice according to the rule before the well-kindled fire,
those great-souled ones offered oblations to all the inhabitants of heaven.
Summoned from the solar disc, that wondrous fire emerged and approached, the lordly Agni, restrained in speech according to the ritual rules;
having arrived at the *āhavanīya* fire, he received the oblations offered by those twice-born ones with sacred mantras.

Having accepted there various kinds of oblations, O best of the Bharatas, the consumer of offerings (Agni) presented them to the sages and the dwellers of heaven. And as he was departing, he saw the wives of those high-souled ones.
Seated in their respective hermitages and bathing at their pleasure, they shone like altars of gold; as stainless as crescents of the moon,
they resembled the flames of sacrificial fires, and all were as wondrous as stars.
With his mind fixed upon them, his senses became agitated;
seeing the wives of the best of the twice-born, Agni fell under the sway of desire. He reflected further: "It is not right that I am thus disturbed."
"I desire those virtuous wives of the best of the twice-born, though they are without desire for me. It is not possible for me to look upon them or even to touch them without cause;
therefore, having entered the household fire, I gaze upon them constantly."
As if touching all those flames with his own crests, which shone like gold,
he rejoiced while gazing upon them, taking refuge in the Gārhapatya fire. Having dwelt there for a very long time, the fire thus came under his control.
Fixing his mind upon those beautiful women and desiring them,
his heart tormented by passion and firmly resolved to abandon his body,
the brahmin went to the forest [to enter the fire] when he could not obtain the wives of the brahmins.
"Then Svāhā, the daughter of Dakṣa, first desired him; from long ago, that beautiful woman had been seeking a flaw in him. But she, the blameless one, could find no flaw in the vigilant god."
Having understood him to be Agni who had come to the forest,
that beautiful woman reflected in truth upon him as he was tormented by desire:
"I shall assume the forms of the wives of the seven seers and [approach] Pāvaka."
"I shall desire him who is afflicted by passion and deluded by their beauty;
when this is done, he will find pleasure and I shall attain my desire.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Śivā was the wife of Aṅgiras, endowed with virtue, beauty, and good qualities. O lord of men, having first assumed her form, that excellent woman, the goddess,
approached the fire and spoke to him.

"O Agni, you ought to desire me, for I am tormented by desire. If you do not do so, consider me as already dead; O Consumer of Oblations, otherwise a very great unrighteousness will surely fall upon you."
"O Consumer of Oblations, I am the wife of Aṅgiras, named Śivā;
having deliberated and reached a firm conclusion, I have arrived here together with my friends.
Agni said:
"How do you know me to be afflicted by desire, and how [do you know] those others whom you have mentioned— all the beloved wives of the seven seers? Śivā said:
"You have always been dear to us, yet we are afraid of you.
Having discerned your mind through its gestures, I have been sent into your presence. I have arrived here for sexual union; quickly fulfill the desire that has arisen."
"O one of great heroism, you ought to go first;
my mothers are waiting for me, O Consumer of Oblations. I shall depart.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then Agni, filled with joy and delight, united with Śivā;
and the goddess, joined with him in love, received his seed in her hand. She thought: "Those who see this form of mine in the forest..."
"They will speak of the fault of falsehood regarding the Brahmin women in the fire;
therefore, protecting myself from this, I shall become a female Garuḍa,
and my departure from the forest will be easy."
Then, having become a Suparṇī, she emerged from the great forest.
She saw a white mountain well-concealed by thickets of reeds,
guarded by wondrous seven-headed serpents whose very glance was poisonous.
It was filled with Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and fierce hosts of spirits,
as well as with Rākṣasīs and many beasts and birds; it was endowed with rivers and springs, and covered with various trees and creepers.
Having gone there quickly to that most inaccessible mountain ridge,
that virtuous goddess, in haste, cast her seed into a golden vessel.
She did so for the sake of the high-souled Seven Sages who remained there.
Having assumed the form of Arundhatī’s wife, she desired the Fire-god;
however, she was unable to assume the divine form of Arundhatī herself,
due to the power of her asceticism and her devotion to serving her husband.
O best of the Kurus, that semen was discharged six times by Agni into that vessel on the first day of the lunar fortnight by the passionate Svāhā;
that spilled seed was gathered there by his own splendor and brought forth a son.
Worshipped by the ṛṣis, that which had been spilled was then led to the state of Skanda;
he became Kumāra, possessing six heads, double the number of ears, twelve eyes, arms, and feet, yet having but one neck and one body.
On the second day he was manifested; on the third, he appeared as an infant;
on the fourth, Guha became complete with all his major and minor limbs.
He was enveloped by a great red cloud accompanied by lightning.
He shone like the risen sun amidst a vast, crimson cloud;
he had taken up that massive, hair-raising bow,
which had been wielded by the Destroyer of Tripura to slaughter the enemies of the gods.

Having taken up that best of bows, the powerful one then let out a roar, as if to confound these three worlds with all their mobile and immobile beings. Hearing that roar of his, which sounded like the rumbling of a mass of great clouds—
The two great serpents, Citra and Airāvata, soared upward. Seeing them swooping down, he, who possessed the splendor of the rising sun,
seized them with two hands and held a spear with another hand.
Then another heir of Agni,
that mighty one, seizing with his arm a large-bodied cock— a rooster of great strength who was clinging to him— let out a terrible roar and sported with it.
With two arms, the powerful one seized that supreme conch shell and blew it,
terrifying even the strongest of beings;
with his other two arms, he struck the sky repeatedly.
Sporting there, Mahāsena shone as he seemed to drink in the three worlds with his faces;
that being of immeasurable soul appeared on the mountain peak like the radiant sun at its rising.
Seated upon the summit of that mountain, he of wondrous prowess remained there.
He of immeasurable soul gazed upon the quarters with his various mouths;
beholding diverse phenomena, he let out a roar once more.
Hearing that roar of his, people fell down in many ways.

Terrified and with agitated minds, they sought refuge in him alone. Those people of various castes who had then taken shelter in that god, the Brāhmaṇas call them his attendants (pāriṣada), endowed with great strength.
Then, having risen and consoled those people, the mighty-armed one drew his bow and discharged arrows at the great white mountain;
with those shafts, he pierced Krauñca, the son of Himavat.
Because of that, the swans and vultures were heading toward Mount Meru;
that mountain shattered and fell down, crying out with intense sounds of distress.
When it had fallen, the other mountains shrieked violently out of fear.
Seeing the Krauñca mountain split asunder and all [the creatures] uttering a terrible cry of distress,
that best of the strong, though he heard that sound of those who were deeply afflicted, was not shaken— O one of immeasurable soul— and raising his spear, he roared.
Then that massive spear, hurled by that high-souled one,
swiftly shattered the formidable peak of Mount Śveta.
Struck by it, Mount Śveta became dejected along with the other mountains.
Terrified of that great-souled one, he leapt up, abandoning the earth;
thereupon the earth was deeply distressed and shattered on all sides,
but having approached Skanda in her affliction, she shone forth once more with renewed strength.
And the mountains, having paid homage to him, returned to the earth.
Then this world worshipped Skanda on the fifth day of the bright fortnight.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When that Great Being was born— possessing a great army and great strength—
various kinds of terrible portents arose;
likewise, there were reversals among women and men, as well as among all pairs of opposites.
The planets blazed, the quarters and the sky were aflame, and the earth shook violently; such were the various events that occurred on the fifth day of the bright fortnight.
Then, O lord of men, a great and terrible battle took place on the sixth day.
But the sages, the creators of the worlds, seeing various kinds of most terrible portents, became anxious and performed rites for peace for the sake of the worlds.
As for those people who dwell in that Caitraratha forest—
They said, "This great misfortune has been brought upon us by Pāvaka,
who, having united with the six wives of the seven seers, has done so," they said.
Others, however, said to Garuḍī, "This misfortune was brought about by you."
When people saw that goddess moving about in her form at that time,
they did not know that such an act had been performed by Svāhā;
for Suparṇī, having heard the words, thought, "This is my son."
Approaching Skanda slowly, she said, "I am your mother. Then,
having heard that a son of great luster had been born, the Seven Sages abandoned their six wives, with the exception of the goddess Arundhatī.
"Then those dwelling in the forest said that he was born from six [seeds] alone;
and Svāhā said to the Seven Seers, 'This is my son.
But I, O King, knew again and again, 'It is not so.'"
But the great sage Viśvāmitra, having performed the sacrifice for the Seven Sages,
followed behind the fire-god Pāvaka— who was tormented by desire— unseen; thus,
he understood all of that exactly as it had occurred.
Viśvāmitra, having first sought refuge with the youth,
composed a divine hymn of praise to Mahāsena,
as well as all thirteen auspicious verses concerning the Kumāras.
The great sage performed for him the birth-rites and other ceremonies;
he also taught the majesty of the six-faced one, the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) for Kukkuta,
the means of accomplishment for the goddess Śakti, and likewise for the attendants.
Viśvāmitra performed this deed indeed for the welfare of the world; therefore, the sage Viśvāmitra became dear to the boy. And the great muni authorized the transformation of Svāhā’s form.
And he said to all the sages, "Women do not commit offenses.
Having heard that truth from him, they abandoned their wives entirely.
Then, having heard about Skanda, the gods spoke together to Vāsava.
"O Śakra, slay Skanda of irresistible power quickly and without delay!
If you do not kill him today,
this one of great strength will seize the three worlds, as well as us and you, O Śakra."
Distressed, he said to them, "This child possesses great strength;
Śakra declares, 'I do not dare to kill a child. They replied, "There is no valor in you, since you speak in such a manner."
"Exerting his prowess in battle, he could even destroy the Creator of the worlds himself.
Let all the Mothers of the world approach Skanda today; let them, possessing the power to assume any form at will, slay him. Having said, "So be it," they departed.
Seeing him powerless, with dejected faces, they reflected, "He is incapable," and thus went to him alone for refuge.
And they said: "You are our son; by us the world is upheld."
"Rejoice in us all, who are overflowing with milk and overwhelmed with affection.
Hearing those words of theirs, the Lord, desiring to drink from their breasts,
honored them and granted them their desires, O Mahāsena.
The strongest among the strong beheld his father Agni approaching.
Honored by him along with the host of mothers,
he stood firm, surrounding Mahāsena and guarding him.
Among all those mothers, however, the woman who had arisen from wrath was the nurse;
with a spear in her hand, she protected Skanda like a son. She was the daughter of the ocean of blood, cruel, and a consumer of blood.
Having embraced Mahāsena, he protected him like a son;
becoming Agni Naigameya, with the face of a goat and many offspring,
he delighted the child as he sat on the mountain as if with toys.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The planets along with their subordinate attendants, the sages, and likewise the Mothers,
as well as the blazing hosts of attendants whose mouths are fire.
"These and many other formidable inhabitants of the triple heaven,
together with the hosts of Mothers, stood surrounding Mahāsena.
Seeing that victory was uncertain, the Lord of the Gods, desiring victory, [prepared himself].
Mounting the shoulders of Airāvata,
the powerful Indra, surrounded by all the hosts of gods and taking up his thunderbolt, set out with the deities; desiring to strike down Mahāsena, he proceeded with great speed.
That divine host was fierce, possessed of great speed, and of immense splendor;
it bore various banners and armor, with diverse mounts and bows,
clothed in excellent garments, graced by beauty, and fully adorned.
Then, as Śakra approached desiring to strike him, the prince advanced against him;
meanwhile, the mighty Śakra, roaring along the path, proceeded swiftly,
heartening the divine army and seeking to slay the son of Agni.
Being thus honored by the thirty gods as well as by the supreme ṛṣis,
Vāsava approached the presence of Kārttikeya.
Then, he beheld Skanda standing at the foot of the great white mountain.
Then the Lord of the Gods, together with the deities, let out a lion’s roar;
Guha too, hearing that sound, bellowed like the ocean.
By that great noise, he appeared like the surging sea.
The unconscious army of the gods wandered here and there;
seeing the gods approaching with the intent to kill him, that son of Agni,
filled with rage, emitted from his mouth vast flames of fire.
Those divine armies, writhing upon the surface of the earth, were consumed by fire;
with their heads, bodies, weapons, and mounts ablaze,
they suddenly appeared like a multitude of variegated stars fallen from the sky.

Being scorched by the fire, those gods abandoned the wielder of the thunderbolt and sought refuge with the son of Agni; thus they attained peace. Then, having been forsaken by the gods, Śakra hurled his thunderbolt at Skanda.
Once released, it swiftly struck the right flank of Skanda and pierced the side of that high-souled one, O great king. From the blow of the thunderbolt upon Skanda, another man was born.
A youth clad in golden armor, wielding a spear and adorned with divine earrings;
because he was born from the entry of the thunderbolt (vajra), he became known as Viśākha.
Seeing that other newborn, who possessed a splendor equal to the fire of cosmic destruction, [the gods were struck with wonder].
Out of fear, Indra then went for refuge to Skanda with palms joined in reverence. O best of beings, Skanda granted safety to him and his army.
Thereupon, the gods were overjoyed and sounded their musical instruments.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen to the account of Skanda’s terrible attendants, who are wonderful to behold;
from the blow of Skanda’s thunderbolt, young boys were born there.
Those cruel ones who carry away infants already born as well as those still in the womb— by the stroke of his thunderbolt, daughters were born to him who possessed great strength;
and the Kumāras appointed Viśākha as their father.
Then, having become the Lord with the face of a goat (Chāgamukha) in that battle,
he was surrounded by all the throngs of Kanyās and his own sons;
and while the mothers looked on, Bhadraśākha and Kauśala [also stood there].
Therefore, people on earth call Skanda the father of Kumāra;
they worship Rudra, Agni, Umā, and the mighty Svāhā in various places,
both those desiring sons and those who already possess sons.
The Fire-god, named Tapas, begot those maidens;
when they approached Skanda, he addressed them, saying, "What shall I do?
The Mothers replied:
"By your grace, may we become the most excellent mothers of the entire world, and may we be worthy of worship; please do this which is dear to us. Mārkaṇḍeya said:

He, the noble-minded one, said, "So be it; you shall become various kinds of beings, both inauspicious and auspicious, again and again. Then, having resolved to adopt Skanda as their son, the group of Mothers departed.
Kākī, Halimā, Rudrā, Bṛhalī,
Āryā, Palālā, and Mitrā— these seven are the mothers of Śiśu.
From these [mothers] was born the son named Śiśu, endowed with great prowess and exceedingly fierce.
The son born from the grace of Skanda is Lohitākṣa, the terrifying one. This group of eight heroes is said to have arisen from the host of Skanda’s mothers;
together with Chāgavaktra, they are proclaimed as a group of nine.
Know that the sixth face of Skanda consists of goats;
O King, it has six heads within it, which are constantly worshipped by the host of Mothers.
Among those six heads, this one is proclaimed here as the most excellent.
"By which he created a divine spear, known as Bhadraśākha. Thus occurred this event of various forms on the fifth day of the bright fortnight;
there, O lord of men, a most terrible battle took place on the sixth.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then Skanda sat down, wearing golden armor and garlands,
with a golden crest and crown, golden eyes, and great radiance.
Clad in red garments, with sharp fangs and a charming appearance,
he was endowed with all auspicious marks and was beloved even by the three worlds. Then [he beheld] that hero, the giver of boons, who was young and wore polished earrings.
The goddess Śrī herself, in her embodied form resembling a lotus,
attended upon him. Endowed with glory and possessed of wide renown, that excellent prince was then seen by all beings seated like the moon on a full-moon night.
The high-souled Brahmins honored that one of great strength;
and then the great seers there spoke thus to Skanda:
"O golden-hued one, may prosperity be yours; become the bringer of welfare to the worlds."
"By you, though born only six nights ago, all the worlds have been brought under your control.
Furthermore, O best of gods, it was by you alone that safety was granted to them.
Therefore, may you become Indra, the one who grants fearlessness to the three worlds."
Skanda said:
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, what does Indra do here for all the worlds?
And how does the Lord of the Gods constantly protect the hosts of deities?"
The sages said:
Indra bestows strength, splendor, progeny, and happiness upon all beings;
likewise, when gratified, the lord of the gods grants all boons.

The slayer of Bala destroys those of evil conduct and bestows [favor] upon those established in righteous conduct; he instructs all beings in their duties. Moreover, he may become the sun where there is no sun, and likewise the moon where there is no moon.
Fire, wind, earth, and water exist by means of their causes;
this is what must be performed by Indra, for in Indra there is vast power.
And you, O hero, are the foremost in strength; therefore, become our Indra.
Śakra said:
"O mighty-armed one, become Indra, bringing happiness to us all! Be consecrated this very day, for you are worthy of it, O best of beings."
Skanda said:
"O Śakra, you yourself rule the three worlds with undistracted mind, devoted to victory; I am your servant, for the status of Indra is not desired by me."
Śakra said:
"O hero, your strength is wonderful; slay the enemies of the gods. The worlds, amazed by your prowess, will hold me in contempt."
"O hero, O best of gods, even if I remain in the position of Indra, people will despise me as one who is devoid of strength and defeated by your splendor; moreover,
they will unremittingly strive to create a rift between the two of us."
O Lord, once you have been divided, the world will fall into a state of duality;
and when the worlds have become twofold and are thus determined,
O one of great power, a conflict will break out between us due to that division of beings.
"There, O dear one, you shall defeat me in battle according to your faith;
therefore, you shall become Indra today—do not doubt it.
Skanda said:
"You alone are the king—blessings upon you—of the three worlds and of myself as well.
O Śakra, what command do I have for you? Tell me that.
Śakra said:
"If these words have been spoken by you with certainty as the truth,
or if you wish to carry out my command, O Skanda, listen,
O one of great strength: be consecrated to the generalship of the gods."
"O one of great strength, at your word I shall become Indra.
Skanda said:
"For the destruction of the Dānavas and for the accomplishment of the purpose of the gods..."
"Consecrate me in the office of generalissimo for the sake of protecting cows and Brahmins.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
He was consecrated by Maghavan together with all the hosts of gods.
He shone exceedingly there, being honored by the great seers.
Having heard those words of Skanda, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra,
together with the hosts of gods and the seers, was delighted with Mahāsena.
Having seated Mahāsena upon a divine throne made of gold, inlaid with jewels, and radiant like the rising sun, Śakra then consecrated him as commander-in-chief with pure, auspicious waters.
That golden parasol being held over him shone like the very orb of a well-kindled fire;
and he wore a divine, golden garland fashioned by Viśvakarman.

Having arrived together with the Goddess, O tiger among men, O scorcher of foes, the illustrious Lord whose banner bears the bull, being highly pleased, personally worshipped that [bow] which had been bound by the glorious destroyer of Tripura.

The twice-born call Agni "Rudra," and therefore he is the son of Rudra; that Kumāra of great splendor is celebrated as one of wondrous appearance. The semen discharged by Rudra became the White Mountain (Śveta-parvata).
He consumed that white [substance], and from that Agni became Guha.
The semen of Pāvaka was deposited by the Kṛttikās upon the white mountain;
and seeing it being honored by Rudra, all the inhabitants of heaven [were amazed].
Therefore, they call Guha the son of Rudra, the best among those possessed of virtues.
For this infant was born after Rudra had entered the fire;
since he was born there, Skanda thus became the son of Rudra.
Born from the splendor of Rudra, Agni, Svāhā, and the six women,
Skanda— the best of the gods— therefore became the son of Rudra. Clad in two stainless red garments, he was the offspring of Pāvaka.
The glorious one, with his radiant body, shines like the sun amidst two red clouds;
and the cock given by Agni stands as his adorned banner,
raised high upon the chariot and shining like the red fire of time.
Whatever movement there is of all beings, as well as their splendor, tranquility, and strength—
that power, which increases the victory of the gods, stood before him;
and then it entered his natural armor and body.
When that god is engaged in battle, these qualities always manifest:
power, armor, strength, splendor, beauty, truthfulness, invincibility,
devotion to Brahman, freedom from delusion, and the protection of his devotees.
O lord of men, all these qualities— the destruction of enemies and the protection of the worlds— were born together with Skanda. Thus, well-adorned, he was consecrated by all the hosts of gods.
He shone, confident and well-disposed, like the sight of the full moon;
he was gladdened by the pleasant sounds of Vedic recitation, by the blasts of divine trumpets,
by the songs of gods and gandharvas, and by all the hosts of apsarases.
Surrounded by these and various other joyful, contented,
and adorned hosts of Piśācas as well as hosts of gods,
that son of Agni was then consecrated by the gods as if he were playing.
The inhabitants of heaven beheld Mahāsena consecrated, just as the sun rises here after having dispelled the darkness. Then all the divine armies approached him by the thousands.
Saying, "You are our husband," they approached him from every direction; then the Blessed One, surrounded by hosts of all beings,
honored and praised by them, comforted them as well.
Then Śatakratu, having consecrated Skanda as the commander-in-chief of the army,
remembered that celestial host which had been liberated by him.
"Surely this man has been ordained by Brahmā himself as her husband."
Having thought thus, he brought forth Devasenā, beautifully adorned.
And the slayer of Bala said to Skanda, "O best of gods,
this maiden was designated by the Self-born as your wife even before you were born."

"Therefore, take according to the prescribed rite the right hand of this goddess— hand that has the luster of a lotus— with your own hand, preceded by the sacred mantras. Thus addressed by the Blessed One, the mighty Mahāsena [acted].

Having seen Devasenā, who had eyes like lotus petals, a slender waist, and great renown; who was exceedingly endowed with beauty, adorned with every ornament, possessed of all auspicious marks, and possessed of a pure smile.
Thus addressed, he took her hand according to the prescribed rite;
then, O best of the Bharatas, the Lord of the Devasenā took hold [of it],
while Bṛhaspati recited the ritual mantras and performed the oblations.
Thus the wise know Devasenā to be the queen of Skanda;
she whom the Brahmins call Ṣaṣṭhī, Lakṣmī, Āśā, the bestower of happiness,
Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Sadvṛtti, and Aparājitā.
By such names as these, the Goddess is celebrated;
when Skanda was obtained as her eternal husband by Devasenā,
then Lakṣmī herself, the Goddess in embodied form, took refuge in him.
"Endowed with glory, Skanda [attained it] on the fifth day; therefore, it is remembered as Śrīpañcamī.
Because he became one who had accomplished his purpose on the sixth, that great lunar day is called Ṣaṣṭhī.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When Mahāsena, who was graced with splendor, had been appointed as the commander-in-chief of the divine army,
the six goddesses— the wives of the seven ṛṣis— approached him;
though they were devoted to dharma and observers of great vows, they had been abandoned by their husbands, the ṛṣis.
Arriving swiftly, they said to the lord, the commander of the divine army:
"O son, we have been abandoned by our husbands, who are equal to the gods;
they were men devoted to dharma and observers of great vows."
Taking sole refuge in you,
O Father, we have been cast down from our meritorious station through causeless anger. Indeed,
it has been said by someone that you were begotten by us.
"Having promised this which was untrue, you ought to save us from it. O Lord, by your grace may heaven be eternal for us;
we desire you and your son as well—by doing this, become free from your debt."
Skanda said:
"O blameless ones, you are indeed my mothers, and I am your son. Whatever you desire, all that shall come to pass for you accordingly."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When this had been said, he [Skanda] asked Śakra, "What is to be done? Being thus addressed by Skanda with the words "Speak," Vāsava then replied.
But Abhijit, the younger sister of Rohiṇī, competing with her,
the goddess, desiring seniority, went to the forest to perform austerities. There I became bewildered— blessings be upon you— the constellation having fallen from the sky.
"O Skanda, consider this supreme time together with Brahmā;
at that time, the period beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā was ordained by Brahmā,
whereas previously it began with Rohiṇī, such was the calculation."
When Śakra had spoken thus, the Kṛttikās went to the third heaven;
that constellation, presided over by Agni, shone in the shape of a wagon.
And Vinatā said to Skanda, "You are my son, the giver of the funeral cake."
"I desire, my son, to dwell with you forever.
Skanda said:
"So be it; salutations to you. Out of affection for your son, please command me."
"O Goddess, you shall indeed dwell here forever, being honored by your daughter-in-law.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the entire host of Mothers spoke these words to Skanda.
"We are the mothers of the entire world, praised by the seers;
we wish to become your mothers—honor us.
Having heard their words, Skanda spoke these words:
Skanda said:
"O mothers, you are indeed mine, and I am your son. Tell me what task must be performed by me that is desired by you."
The Mothers said:
"Those who were previously ordained as the mothers of this world— let that status belong to us, and let it not belong to them."
"O bull among gods, let us become worthy of worship by the world; they are not the ones to be worshipped.
Our progeny has been taken away by them on your account; restore them to us.
Skanda said:
"These subjects have been given; they cannot be served by you.
What other offspring shall I grant you, whatever your hearts desire?
The mothers said:
"We wish to devour the offspring of those mothers; grant them to us, along with their lords who have become separated from you.
Skanda said:
"I give you offspring, though what has been uttered by you is painful. Protect them well—may prosperity be yours—you who have been duly saluted.
The mothers said:
"O Skanda, may you be blessed; we shall protect the subjects as you desire.
O Lord Skanda, it pleases us to dwell with you for a long time.
Skanda said:
As long as the young creatures reach the age of sixteen years,
