I shall harass men with various forms;
and I shall bestow upon you my own fierce and imperishable self.
"By that, you shall dwell in supreme happiness together with him, being duly honored.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Then, from the body of Skanda, a person appeared, radiant as gold."
To devour mortals, that being of great strength rushed forth;
then, overcome by hunger and deprived of his senses, he fell to the ground. Permitted by Skanda, he became a planet (graha) of fierce form.
O best of the twice-born, they call Skandāpasmāra a seizing spirit (graha);
Vinatā is said to be the most terrible Śakunigraha;
and they call Pūtanā a Rākṣasī—one should know her as the Pūtanāgraha.
The night-stalker of terrible form and painful appearance,
the Piśācī of fierce aspect, is called Śītapūtanā; she,
of horrific countenance, carries off the fetuses of human women.
They call Aditi Revatī; her graha is Raivata. That terrible great graha indeed afflicts young children.
They call Diti, the mother of the Daityas, Mukhamaṇḍikā.
Exceedingly delighted by the flesh of porpoises, that unassailable one,
as well as the boys and girls who were said to have been born from Skanda— all those very great grahas, O Kauravya, devour the fetus.
They are proclaimed to be the husbands of those very maidens;
remaining unrecognized, these performers of terrible deeds seize children.
Furthermore, O King, she who is called Surabhi by the wise as the mother of cows—
Then, having ascended that bird, Śakuni devours the infants on the ground together with her.
O lord of men, she who is the mother of dogs, the goddess named Saramā,
likewise always seizes the fetuses of human women.

She who is the mother of trees and dwells in the *karañja* tree is indeed a granter of boons; she is gentle and always compassionate toward all beings. Therefore, men seeking sons bow down to her at the *karañja* tree.
But these other eighteen grahas, who are fond of meat and honey,
remain constantly in the maternity chamber for ten nights (five times two).
When Kadrū, assuming a subtle form, enters a pregnant woman—
There she consumes that embryo, and she gives birth to a nāga;
but she who is the mother of the gandharvas, having taken up the embryo, departs,
and thereafter that human woman is seen on earth with her pregnancy dissolved.
She who sits holding the embryo of the Apsarases as their progenitor—
therefore the wise declare that embryo to be seated there.
She is known as the daughter of the Red Ocean and the nurse of Skanda.
She is indeed worshipped at the Kadamba tree as Lohitāyani;
just as Rudra is among men, so is Āryā among women.
Āryā, the mother of Kumāra, is worshipped separately for the sake of fulfilling desires.
Thus have these great planetary spirits (mahāgrahas) of boys been described by me;

they remain inauspicious until sixteen years of age, after which they become auspicious. This also applies to those groups of Mothers (mātṛgaṇas) that have been mentioned, as well as those male planetary spirits.
All those known as *skandagrahas* should always be recognized by embodied beings;
their pacification should be performed through bathing, incense, and collyrium,
as well as through ritual offerings (*balikarma*), oblations (*upahāra*), and especially through the worship of Skanda.
Thus, O Indra among kings, when all these are properly honored with worship and salutations, they bestow auspiciousness upon men— namely, long life and vigor. Furthermore,
those who become the planetary influences (grahas) over men after the sixteenth year...
Having paid homage to Maheśvara, I shall fully describe those [spirits]:
that man who sees the gods, whether awake or even while lying down, quickly goes mad; they know him to be possessed by a Devagraha.

The man who, whether sitting or lying down, sees his ancestors, quickly goes mad; he should be known as one possessed by a *pitṛ-graha*. He who treats the *siddhas* with contempt is cursed by them when they are enraged.
He who quickly becomes insane should be known as one possessed by a *siddha-graha*.
He who smells various fragrances and tastes diverse flavors quickly becomes insane; he should be known as one possessed by a *rākṣasa-graha*.
When divine Gandharvas touch a man on earth, he quickly becomes insane; that is indeed a Gāndharva seizure.
And when Yakṣas enter a person at the turn of time, [he likewise falls ill].
He quickly goes mad; he should be known as one possessed by a yakṣa-graha.
Whenever piśācas constantly mount a man, he quickly goes mad; they know him to be possessed by a paiśāca-graha.

When the mind of an embodied being becomes deluded due to the aggravation of the *doṣas*, he quickly goes mad; the remedy for this is according to the scriptures. [This occurs] from despondency, from fear, and even from the sight of terrible things.
He, however, quickly becomes insane; his means of recovery is as follows:
one [type of] spirit desires to play, another desires to eat, and yet another desires sexual union—thus is this possession of three kinds.
For up to seventy years, these [disturbances] act as planetary influences upon men;
beyond that, however, the fever of embodied beings becomes equal to a planet itself.
[One who is] self-controlled, pure, and ever-vigilant, with senses not scattered, [is not overcome].
The planets always avoid one who is orthodox and full of faith.
Thus has this summary of the planets regarding human beings been proclaimed to you. The planets do not touch those men who are devoted to the Great Lord, Maheśvara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When Skanda had thus performed this pleasing service for the Mothers, Svāhā then spoke to him: "You are my own legitimate son."
"I desire from you a favor that is most difficult to obtain.
Skanda then said to her, "What kind of favor do you desire?
Svāhā replied:
"O mighty-armed one, I am Dakṣa’s beloved daughter, named Svāhā. From my childhood, I have always felt desire for the consumer of oblations (Agni).
Yet, O son, the Purifier does not truly recognize me as one who loves him."
"I desire, O son, to dwell forever together with Agni.
Skanda said:
"Whatever oblation for the gods (*havya*) or the ancestors (*kavya*) is offered by the twice-born accompanied by mantras,"
"O Goddess, from this day forward, those of good conduct established on the path of truth shall always offer oblations into the fire, saying 'Svāhā' as it is raised;
thus, O beautiful one, Agni shall dwell forever together with you."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus addressed and honored by Skanda, Svāhā was gratified;
united with her husband Pāvaka, she in turn worshipped Skanda.
Then Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, spoke to Mahāsena:
"Go to Mahādeva, your father, the destroyer of Tripura. Having entered Agni through Rudra and Svāhā through Umā,"
For the benefit of all the worlds, you, the unconquered one,
were born when the seed was emitted by the high-souled Rudra into the womb of Umā;
it fell upon the mountain, from which Miñjikā and Miñjika arose.
O highly fortunate one, that pair born there from Rudra was produced in the Lohitoda [lake]; the remnant of the semen fell into it,
while other portions fell among the rays of the sun and yet others fell upon the earth.
Another clung to the trees; thus it fell in five ways. These various forms of hosts, these flesh-eaters who are your terrible attendants, should be known by the wise.
Having said, "So be it," Mahāsena, whose soul is immeasurable and who is devoted to his father, worshipped Maheśvara, his father.
Those five Gaṇas, however, should be worshipped with *arka* flowers by those seeking wealth.
And for the sake of pacifying diseases, one should perform worship to them; likewise,
the pair Miñjikā and Miñjika, born of Rudra,
should always be saluted here by one who desires the welfare of children.
There are female spirits who feed on human flesh, known by the name Vṛddhikās;
these goddesses, born upon trees, should be saluted by those desiring offspring.
Thus, these innumerable hosts of Piśācas are recorded.
"O King, hear from me the origin of the bell together with its banner. Airāvata had two bells known as Vaijayantī;
the wise Śakra, having brought them here, gave them personally to Guha."
Therein, one bell belonged to Viśākha and another to Skanda;
the banner of Kārttikeya and that of Viśākha were red.
These were indeed the playthings bestowed upon him by the gods at that time.
With those very ones, the god Mahāsena, possessed of great strength, took his delight;
surrounded by hosts of Piśācas as well as hosts of gods,
he shone upon the golden mountain, blazing and encompassed by splendor.

With that hero, that mountain of beautiful groves shone like Mount Mandara with its lovely caves when graced by the radiant sun; it was adorned with blossoming forests of *saṃtānaka* trees and forests of *karavīra* flowers.
With groves of *pārijāta* trees and likewise groves of *japā* and *aśoka*, with thickets of *kadamba* trees and even divine herds of deer,
as well as with flocks of divine birds, the White Mountain shone resplendently.
There all the hosts of gods and all the great seers were present;
there were the sounds of celestial drums and the roar of clouds, sounding like the agitated ocean.
There the divine Gandharvas and Apsarases danced.
The great roar of the delighted beings there was heard;
thus the entire world, including Indra, stood upon the White Mountain,
gazing at Skanda with joy and never wearying from the sight.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When the blessed son of Agni was consecrated as the commander-in-chief,
the glorious Hara set out for Bhadravaṭa, joyful at heart.
The Lord, accompanied by Pārvatī, traveled in a chariot with the splendor of the sun,
followed by all the gods led by the thousand-eyed Indra;
to that supreme chariot were yoked a thousand lions.
Urged on by Time, he leapt into the bright sky;
then lions with beautiful manes, as if drinking up the atmosphere and terrifying all moving and stationary beings, went through the heavens roaring.
Upon that chariot, Paśupati shone together with Umā,
like the sun accompanied by lightning in a cloud bearing Indra’s bow.
In front of him was the Lord Dhaneśa, together with the Guhyakas.
Seated upon the radiant Puṣpaka, the one whose vehicle is man proceeded;
and Śakra, mounted upon Airāvata along with the gods,
followed from behind as the boon-granting bull-bannered god went forth.
Adorned with garlands by the Jambhakas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas,
the great Yakṣa Amogha proceeds, stationed upon the right wing. To his right are the gods, the Maruts, who fight with marvelous skill.
They go together with the Vasus and are joined by the Rudras;
and Yama, surrounded on all sides by Death,
proceeds with hundreds of terrible diseases, his body likewise assuming a fearsome form.
Behind Yama follows the terrible, three-pointed,
and sharp trident of Rudra, named Vijaya, which is well-adorned; after it goes the venerable Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, holding his fierce noose.
Surrounded by various aquatic creatures, it moves slowly;
behind Vijaya as well goes the *paṭṭiśa* of Rudra,
encircled by maces, clubs, spears, and other supreme weapons.
O King, the *paṭṭiśa* spear followed behind him, as did the fierce umbrella of great luster;
and his water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) followed as well, surrounded by hosts of great seers.
To his right, a staff shone as it went along, enveloped in splendor.
Accompanied by the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases and honored by the gods as well,
Rudra follows behind them, stationed upon a spotless chariot;
he proceeds, gladdening all the inhabitants of heaven with his splendor.
The sages and the gods, the gandharvas and the serpents,
as well as the rivers, the streams, the trees, and likewise the hosts of apsarases;
the constellations and the planets, and those who are the children of the gods.
And women of various forms followed behind Rudra—
exquisite women of beautiful appearance, showering rains of flowers.
And Parjanya also followed, having paid homage to the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Soma held a white umbrella over his head,
while Vāyu and Agni stood by, each grasping a yak-tail whisk;
and Śakra, O King, followed behind him, surrounded by splendor.
Together with all the royal sages, praising the one who has the bull as his emblem,
Gaurī, Vidyā, Gāndhārī, Keśinī, and Mitrāhvayā—
all these, along with Sāvitrī, follow behind Pārvatī.

There, all the hosts of sciences whatsoever that had been composed by poets followed Hara, each according to its own specific application— those very sciences whose word even the gods, including Indra, obey at the head of their armies.
Taking hold of a banner, that Rākṣasa Graha goes at the front;
he who is always occupied in the cremation ground, the friend of Rudra indeed,
is the lord of Yakṣas named Piṅgala, the bestower of joy upon the world.
Accompanied by these, the god went there at his pleasure;
for neither in front nor behind was his movement fixed.
Mortals here worship Rudra as a deity with virtuous deeds.
"He whom they call Śiva, the Lord, Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow"—
thus all the hosts of gods, with delighted minds,
then worshipped Maheśvara with various kinds of dispositions.
Thus the commander of the divine army, surrounded by the celestial hosts,
followed the Lord of Gods— the son of the Kṛttikās, devoted to Brahman.
Then Mahādeva spoke these great words to Mahāsena:
"Always protect the seventh host of the Maruts without weariness.
Skanda said:
"O Lord, I shall protect the seventh host of the Maruts."
"O God, tell me without delay whatever other task I must perform.
Rudra said:
"O son, I am indeed always to be sought out by you in all matters."
"By seeing me and through devotion, you shall attain the highest welfare.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, Maheśvara embraced him and dismissed him.

Delighted, he sent forth Skanda together with Umā, blazing as if with fiery energy. Then, O great king, when Skanda had been dispatched, a great portent occurred that suddenly bewildered all the gods.
The sky, along with its stars, blazed forth; the world was utterly bewildered.
O Lord, the earth trembled and roared, and the universe became shrouded in darkness.
Then, beholding that terrible sight, Śaṅkara became agitated.
Umā, the highly fortunate one, and the gods along with the great ṛṣis were there;
then, while they stood bewildered, a vast and terrible army appeared, resembling mountains and clouds, equipped with various weapons.
For that [demon], terrible and incalculable, roaring with various cries,
rushed in battle against the gods and the blessed Śaṅkara.
By them, numerous nets of arrows were discharged upon the ranks.
Mountains, *śataghnīs*, spears, iron clubs, and maces—
by those terrible great weapons falling down, the entire army of the gods fled in an instant and was seen with its face turned away.
With its warriors, elephants, and horses cut down, its weapons shattered and its great chariots destroyed, the army of the gods, tormented by the Dānavas, appeared turned away from battle;
being slaughtered by the Asuras like a forest by fires.
It fell like a great forest of trees mostly consumed by fire;
those denizens of heaven, their heads and bodies mangled,
were cast down, and as they were being slaughtered in the great battle, they found no protector.
Then, seeing that army in flight and severely oppressed by the Dānavas, the god Purandara spoke these words to reassure them:
"Cast away your fear; may it be well with you! O heroes, take up your weapons!"
"Apply your minds to valor; let there be no distress in you at all. Conquer these Dānavas of wicked conduct and terrible appearance! Charge against the great Asuras with me—may prosperity be yours!"
Having heard the words of Śakra, the inhabitants of heaven were comforted;
making Śakra their refuge, they fought back against the Dānavas.
Then all those thirty gods and the mighty Maruts [advanced].

The Sādhyas, together with the Vasus, rushed forward with great speed. The weapons and arrows discharged by those enraged warriors into the ranks in that battle drank copiously of the blood from the bodies of the Daityas.
Then those sharpened arrows, having pierced through their bodies,
were seen emerging like serpents from mountains.
Those bodies of the Daityas were thus mangled by the shafts.
O King, they fell upon the earth on all sides like scattered clouds. Then that army of Dānavas, terrified in battle by all the hosts of gods with various arrows, was turned back in retreat.
Then all the gods, joyful and with weapons raised, let out a great shout;
and all the musical instruments were sounded together many times. Thus there was a most dreadful battle, joined by one against another.

A mire of flesh and blood belonging to the gods and the dānavas suddenly appeared as a sign of misfortune for the world of the gods; for thus did the terrible dānavas slaughter the inhabitants of heaven.
Then there arose the blaring of musical instruments and the great sound of kettledrums,
along with the terrible lion-roars of the lords of the Dānavas.
Then, from that formidable Daitya host, one of immense strength emerged.
O King, the Dānava named Mahiṣa, seizing a massive mountain,
appeared like the sun surrounded by clouds;
seeing him with the mountain raised aloft, the denizens of heaven fled in all directions.
Then, O Great King, Mahisha rushed forward and hurled that mountain— possessing a massive body like a rain-bearing cloud filled with water— at the gods.
As that mountain fell, O Ruler of the Earth, it struck the army of the gods.
Ten thousand [demons] were struck down by his terrifying form and fell to the earth.
Then Mahisha, together with those Danavas,
rushed swiftly toward the gods in battle, terrifying them like a lion toward small animals.
Seeing that buffalo charging toward them, the gods, including Indra,
fled in fear from the battle, their weapons and banners shattered.
Then that enraged buffalo swiftly advanced toward the chariot of Rudra.
Having rushed forward, he seized the pole of Rudra’s chariot.
When the enraged Mahiṣa suddenly assailed Rudra’s chariot,
heaven and earth trembled violently and the great seers were utterly bewildered.
And the great-bodied Daityas, resembling clouds, let out a roar;
they were certain that victory had been won by them.
Yet, even though things were thus, the Blessed One did not slay Mahiṣa in battle.
Having summoned his son Guha,
the god, desiring to test his son’s prowess, spoke with a smile:
"Behold, my son, the wickedness of this evil-minded Dānava."
"Kill that one of evil conduct quickly; I wish to behold your power. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Maheśvara embraced Skanda and directed him to subdue Mahiṣa, whose life had reached its end.
When things had come to such a state, the Blessed One then remembered Skanda as the death of that evil-minded one. And Mahiṣa, seeing the terrible chariot of Rudra, let out a roar.
Terrifying the gods and gladdening the Daityas as well,
Mahāsena then arrived, blazing with anger like the sun, while that terrible danger had befallen the gods.
Clad in red garments, adorned with red garlands and ornaments,
with a red face, mighty arms, and golden armor,
the Lord mounted a chariot that shone like the sun and possessed a golden luster.
Seeing him, that army of Daityas suddenly fled from the battle. And then, O king of kings, the mighty Mahāsena discharged that flaming spear, capable of rending Mahiṣa.
That spear, having been released, struck the great head of Mahiṣa;
when the head was split, Mahiṣa fell, deprived of life.
By that falling head, the gateway [was covered] for sixteen yojanas.

Covered by that mountain-like [form], it then became impassable; because of that, the Northern Kurus can now go there at their pleasure. But that spear, having been hurled and then withdrawn, slew enemies by the thousands.
Reaching Skandha’s hand, she was seen by the gods and the Dānavas;
for the most part, O great king, she had been struck down by arrows from the wise Mahāsena during that battle between the gods and the Asuras among the Dānavas.

The remaining hosts of Daityas, terrible and formidable, were struck with fear and terror; slain by Skanda’s attendants, they were devoured by the hundreds. Devouring the Dānavas and drinking their blood, those [attendants] continued on.
In an instant, filled with great joy, they rendered everything free of demons;
just as the sun [dispels] darkness, fire [consumes] trees, and the wind [scatters] clouds,
so did the illustrious Skanda conquer his enemies by his own prowess.
Being honored by the thirty gods and having paid homage to Maheśvara,
the son of the Kṛttikās shone like the sun with its rays spread abroad,
now that Skanda had destroyed his enemies and departed for Maheśvara.
Then Purandara, having embraced Mahāsena, said:
"O Skanda, by you this Mahiṣa has been slain— he who had received a boon from Brahmā,
a Dānava of immense strength who was invincible in battle against the gods."
O best among victors, he for whom the gods were as mere blades of grass—
this very thorn in the side of the gods has been quelled by you, O mighty-armed one. In battle, you have slain a hundred Dānavas who were equal to Mahiṣa.
The enemies of the gods, by whom we were previously tormented, have been slain;
and other Dānavas, by the hundreds, have been devoured by your followers,
O Hero, those most terrifying hosts.
"You shall be invincible in battle against your enemies, like the Lord Umāpati himself.
O God, this shall be your first celebrated deed,
and your fame shall be imperishable throughout the three worlds."
"O son of the gods, the deities shall become subject to your will. Having spoken thus, "Mahāsena," the Lord of Śacī, permitted by the Blessed Tryambaka, returned together with the gods.
Rudra went to Bhadravaṭa, and the inhabitants of heaven returned;
and the gods were told by Rudra, "Behold Skanda as you behold me. Having slain the hosts of Dānavas, he was honored by the great seers.

In a single day, the son of Agni conquered the entire triple world. He who recites this account of Skanda’s birth with a well-concentrated mind shall attain prosperity in this world and go to the same realm as Skanda.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear the names of this Great-Souled One.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O best of the twice-born, whatever [deeds] of his are renowned throughout the three worlds,"—
having been addressed thus by the son of Pāṇḍu in the presence of the sages,
the high-souled Mārkaṇḍeya spoke.
There, the Blessed One Mārkaṇḍeya of great asceticism spoke:
"Skanda, the son of Agni, of radiant fame and free from ailment,
whose banner is a peacock, whose soul is righteousness, the lord of beings, the slayer of Mahiṣa."
The conqueror of desires, the bestower of desires, the beloved, the speaker of truth, the Lord of the world;
the infant, the swift, the pure, the fierce, the one of radiant complexion, the fair-faced;
the unerring, the sinless, the terrible, the dear one, and likewise the moon-faced.
One whose power is blazing, whose self is tranquil, the doer of good, the deluder of the peak;
beloved of the sixth, righteous-souled, pure, affectionate toward his mother;
the husband of the maiden, the divided one, the son of Svāhā, and the son of Revatī.
The Lord, the Leader, Viśākha, and Naigameya, who is difficult to traverse; he of excellent vows, the Playful One, and he who is fond of children's toys;
the Sky-walker, the Chaste One, the Hero, and he born from the Śara reed-thicket.

He who recites these divine names of Kārttikeya— Viśvāmitrapriya (Beloved of Viśvāmitra), Devasenāpriya (Beloved of the Army of the Gods), Vāsudevapriya (Beloved of Vāsudeva), Priya (the Beloved), and Priyakṛt (the Doer of what is Dear)— [shall obtain great merit].
He shall obtain heaven, fame, and wealth; of this there is no doubt.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall praise [the one] who is honored by the gods and the ṛṣis.
O hero of the Kurus, understand these names of Guha— the immeasurable one who possesses power, the six-faced one, the wielder of the spear, and the great warrior.

You are indeed devoted to Brahman, born of Brahman, and a knower of Brahman; you are the lord of Brahman, the most excellent among those who possess Brahman; you are dear to Brahman and share the same vows as the Brāhmaṇas.
You are indeed the knower of Brahman and the leader of the Brāhmaṇas;
you are Svāhā and Svadhā, the supreme purifier;
praised by mantras, you are renowned as the six-flamed one.
You are the year and the six seasons,
the months and half-months, the solstice, and the directions;
you are the lotus-eyed one, whose face is like a lotus.
You have a thousand faces and a thousand arms;
you are the guardian of the world and the supreme oblation;
you are the creator of all gods and asuras.
You alone are the fierce commander of the army; you are the lord, the all-pervading one, and the conqueror of enemies. You are the thousandfold source; you alone are the earth.
You are the delight of thousands and the enjoyer of thousands;
you have a thousand heads and infinite forms;
O Guha, you are thousand-footed and the wielder of the spear.
O Lord, you are the son of Gaṅgā by your own will;
likewise, O Six-faced One, you sport with a cock as the Svāhā-offering for the Kṛttikās.
You are one who assumes various forms at will according to desire;
you are the consecration, Soma, and the Maruts forever;
you are Dharma, Vāyu, the Lord of Mountains, and Indra.
You are the eternal among the eternal, the sovereign even of sovereigns, the wielder of the fierce bow, the creator of cosmic order, and the slayer of the sons of Diti.
Victor over enemies, preeminent among the gods,
you alone possess that supreme, subtle austerity;
you are the knower of the high and the low, you are the highest.
O Great-Souled one, foremost among all the gods, this entire world is pervaded by your splendor— by that of Dharma, of Kāma, and of the Supreme Self.
I have praised you, O Lord of the World, according to my ability; homage be to you, whose eyes and arms are twelve!
Beyond this, I know no further way to describe you.
The wise man who, with a concentrated mind, recites this account of Skanda’s birth, or causes it to be heard by Brahmins, or hears it as uttered by the twice-born,
shall obtain wealth, long life, radiant fame, sons, and likewise victory over his enemies.
Having attained nourishment and contentment, he shall reach the same world as Skanda.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While the brahmins and the high-souled Pāṇḍavas were seated, [the sage spoke].
Then Draupadī and Satyabhāmā entered together;
having entered that holy hermitage, those two supreme women,
laughing and well-pleased, sat down there in comfort.
Having seen one another after a long time, O Indra among kings, those two who spoke kindly to each other recounted various stories concerning the Kurus and the Yadus.
Then Satyabhāmā, the beloved queen of Kṛṣṇa, spoke.
Then Sātrājitī, the slender-waisted wife of Yajñasena, spoke these words in private to Draupadī:
"By what conduct, O Draupadī, do you serve the Pāṇḍavas—
those heroes who resemble the world-protectors, who are young, and highly esteemed?"
"And how is it that they are under your control and do not become angry with you, O auspicious one? For the Pāṇḍavas are always submissive to you, O lady of lovely appearance;
yet they do not harbor resentment toward one another—how is this so, O slender-waisted one?"
They all look to you for guidance; tell me this truth:
whether it be the practice of vows, austerity, ritual bathing, mantras, or medicinal herbs;
the power of knowledge, the power of roots, recitation, burnt offerings, or likewise medicines.
"O Pāñcālī, tell me of that which brings glory and bestows fortune,
by means of which, O Kṛṣṇā, Kṛṣṇa may forever remain under my control.
Having spoken thus, the illustrious Satyabhāmā fell silent.
The highly fortunate Draupadī, devoted to her husband, replied to her:
"O Satyā, you ask me about the conduct of unchaste women;
how could there be any praise for a path practiced by the wicked?"
Such a counter-question or doubt is not fitting for you;
for you are endowed with such intelligence as the beloved queen of Kṛṣṇa. Indeed, the moment a husband learns that his wife is devoted to incantations and roots, [he would abandon her].
One should tremble before her then, as if from a snake that has entered the house.
For one who is agitated, whence can there be peace? For one who lacks peace, whence can there be happiness?
A husband shall never be under the control of a wife by means of incantations.
Even the most terrible diseases sent by enemies,
and the poisons that those wishing to kill administer through the incantations of root-mantras—
whatever a person consumes with the tongue or even applies with the skin [is neutralized].
If powders are administered there, they will undoubtedly and swiftly destroy those afflicted with dropsy,
as well as those with vitiligo, gray hair,
and those rendered impotent by women, or likewise made dull-witted, blind, and deaf.
But those wicked women who follow evil paths bring harm even upon their husbands;
a wife must never, under any circumstances, do anything displeasing to her husband. As for the conduct I maintain toward the high-souled Pāṇḍavas—
Listen to all that I say, O Satyabhāmā of true renown, for it is the truth:
having abandoned egoism, as well as desire and anger at all times,
I always serve the Pāṇḍavas and their wives with constant devotion.
Maintaining her affection and establishing herself within her own self,
she was intent on service, free from pride, and a guardian of her husbands' hearts;
she was ever apprehensive of ill-spoken words, improper postures, or unseemly glances.

I served those great car-warriors, the sons of Pṛthā, who resemble the sun and fire, who are like the moon, who possess fierce energy and majesty, and whose very glance can destroy. They are difficult to sit with, difficult to follow, and even their mere gestures and postures are formidable.
Whether he be a god, a human, or a Gandharva, even if he be young and well-adorned, wealthy or handsome— I consider no other man for myself.
Nor [will I choose one] while my husband has not eaten, has not bathed, or is not lying down.
I neither sleep nor eat, even when among the laborers. Whenever my husband returns home from the field, the forest, or the village,
I rise to greet him and welcome him with a seat and water.
With her household utensils polished, her food refined, and providing meals at the proper time;
restrained, with her grain well-guarded, and her dwelling thoroughly swept;
she does not engage in disrespectful conversation nor associate with wicked women.
I am always agreeable and never indolent. I avoid laughing when there is no cause for mirth, standing frequently at the doorway,
staying for long periods in the refuse heap, or lingering in the pleasure gardens.
I am always devoted to truth and to the abandonment of evil deeds.
I shall avoid excessive talk, lack of contentment, gossip about others' affairs, excessive laughter, excessive anger, and any occasion for wrath.

I am always devoted to truth and to the service of my husbands; in every way, being deprived of my husband is not pleasing to me at all. Even when my husband departs on some matter concerning the household, [I remain faithful].
Wearing only *sumana* flowers as my ornament, I live as one observing a vow;
whatever my husband does not drink, whatever my husband does not eat,
and whatever my husband does not consume, all of that I likewise avoid.
O beautiful woman, acting with constancy according to the instructions, well-adorned, diligent, and devoted to the pleasure and welfare of her husband;
and those duties regarding the household that were previously told to me by my mother-in-law—
I constantly and tirelessly practice that truth:
the offering of alms, the śrāddha rites, the *sthālīpāka* offerings on the festival days (*parvan*),
the honoring and respectful treatment of those worthy of honor, and whatever other duties have been made known to me.
Day and night, without weariness, I follow all of them; I always rely upon discipline and restraints with my whole being—
those who are gentle, virtuous, truthful in character, and observers of the dharma of truth.
I serve my husbands as if they were enraged venomous serpents;
for I consider the eternal dharma of women to be centered upon the husband. He is the god, he is the goal, and there is no other; who would do what is displeasing to him?
I do not surpass my husbands in dress, nor in eating, nor in ornamentation; nor do I ever speak ill of my mother-in-law, remaining always self-restrained.
O fortunate lady, this is through my attentiveness and constant industry.
My husbands are under my control through my service to my elders; I myself, alone, constantly attend upon the noble Kuntī— the mother of heroes and speaker of truth— with baths, clothing, and food.
I never excelled her in matters of clothing, ornaments, or food; nor did I ever speak ill of that Pṛthā, who was like the earth itself.
Formerly, there were always eight thousand Brahmins [fed daily].
In Yudhiṣṭhira’s residence, eighty-eight thousand *snātaka* householders eat from golden plates;
Yudhiṣṭhira maintains each one of them with thirty slave-girls.
Ten thousand others,
whose well-prepared food was carried in golden vessels to the ascetics who had sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas),
were all [established] as Brahmins learned in the Vedas through the granting of agrahāras.
I honored them as was fitting with drinks, clothing, and food.
The high-souled son of Kuntī had a hundred thousand maidservants,
well-adorned, wearing shell-bracelets and armlets, and with golden coins (niṣkas) around their necks.
Wearing costly garlands and ornaments, golden-hued and anointed with sandalwood paste, they bore jewels and gold and were skilled in dance and song;
[he described] their names, their forms, and their food and clothing.
I know all of them indeed, as well as their deeds, both those performed and those left undone.
There are a hundred thousand maidservants belonging to the wise son of Kuntī;
with vessels in their hands, they feed guests day and night.
One hundred thousand horses and one hundred thousand elephants were the retinue of Yudhiṣṭhira while he resided in Indraprastha;
such was the extent of the king’s power when he protected the earth.

I prescribe their enumeration and I hear it; I know everything done and undone by all the women of the inner apartments and by all the servants without exception, down even to the cowherds and shepherds.
"O auspicious lady, I alone know all the king's income, revenue, and expenditure, as well as that of the illustrious Pāṇḍavas;
for those bulls of the Bharata race have entrusted their entire household to me."
O lady of auspicious countenance, they were all devoted to worship and strove diligently.
Abandoning all comfort, I indeed exerted myself day and night toward that burden which was entrusted to me and was unassailable by the evil-minded.
Unassailable like the ocean filled with Varuṇa’s treasures,
I alone know this treasury of my husbands who walk the path of dharma; for both day and night, I am their companion against hunger and thirst.
As I serve the Kauravyas, night and day are equal to me; I awaken first and go to sleep last. This, O Satyavatī, is my constant charm.
"I know how to perform this great act of winning over my husband;
however, I would not perform nor do I desire the conduct of unchaste women.
Having heard those words spoken by Kṛṣṇā, which were consistent with righteousness, [he was pleased].
Satyā, having paid her respects, spoke to the virtuous Pāñcālī:
"O Pāñcālī, O Yājñasenī, I have been overcome; forgive me.
For it is the nature of friends to speak with jesting and playfulness."
Draupadī said:
"I shall describe to you this path, free from fault, for winning over the heart of your husband."
"O friend, by conducting yourself properly toward him,
you will draw your husband away from other women.
O Satyabhāmā, there is no deity such as this."
In all the worlds together with their deities,
all desires are obtainable for him whose master is pleased; yet, if he is angered, he would destroy them.
From that [merit] come offspring and various enjoyments;
beds and seats of wondrous appearance,
as well as garments, garlands, and fragrances.
The heavenly world and a precarious reputation—
happiness is never to be obtained here through happiness;
it is through suffering that a virtuous woman attains happiness.
She should propitiate Kṛṣṇa with friendship,
with constant love, and with personal service, as well as with choice foods and the finest garlands.
Through various applications of courtesy and fragrances,
once he realizes, "I am dear to her," he will embrace you alone with his whole being.
Hearing the voice of her husband at the door,
she rose up and stood in the middle of the house;
seeing that he had entered, she quickly offered him a seat.
And you should honor her with water for her feet;
then, once the maidservant has been sent away,
you should rise and perform everything yourself.
O Satyabhāmā, let Kṛṣṇa know this disposition of yours— that you worship him with your whole soul—
when your husband speaks of it in your presence.
Even though that which is not secret must be protected,
some co-wife of yours might reject Vāsudeva, and because of that, he would become disaffected.
You should feed those who are dear to your husband, those who are devoted to him, and those who are beneficial to him by various means;
[but not] those who are hateful, partisan against him, or harmful to him.
Constantly distance yourself from those who are deceitful and arrogant; having abandoned intoxication and negligence toward men, restrain your inner disposition and embrace silence.
Those two youths, Pradyumna and Sāmba,
must never be attended upon in private by women of noble birth who are free from fault.
Let your friendship be with virtuous women;
those who are fierce, addicted to drink, gluttonous,
thieves, wicked, and fickle are to be avoided.
This brings fame and the experience of fortune; likewise, it leads to heaven and is destructive of enemies.
It is adorned with costly garlands, ornaments, and unguents.
"O you of holy fragrance, worship your husband.
Vaiśampāyana said:
[This was spoken] by the brahmins headed by Mārkaṇḍeya and by the high-souled Pāṇḍavas.
Having sat with them for a while in agreeable conversation, Janārdana,
the slayer of Madhu, Keśava, then made his formal farewells with them in the proper manner and called for Satyā as he was about to mount his chariot.
Then Satyabhāmā, having embraced the daughter of Drupada there,
spoke these heart-warming words, composed according to her true feelings:
"O Kṛṣṇā, let there be no longing for you, no distress, and no sleeplessness."
"You shall regain the earth, conquered by husbands who resemble gods;
for women endowed with such virtue and possessed of such honored marks do not endure suffering for long, O dark-eyed one, as you have."

"I have heard it said that you must certainly enjoy this earth, with its thorns removed, together with your husbands, free from all rivals. Having slain the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and avenged your enmities,"

O daughter of Drupada, you shall see the earth ruled by Yudhiṣṭhira. Those Kuru women who, deluded by pride, mocked you as you were going into exile— you shall soon see them with their ambitions destroyed.
"O Kṛṣṇā, know that all those who have acted unkindly toward you while you were beset by suffering have now set out for the abode of Yama; and likewise,
O Queen, those kings who stand there on their side."

O Kṛṣṇa, the time has come for those lords of the earth, which is difficult to withstand. Your son Prativindhya, as well as the powerful Sutasoma, Śrutakarman the son of Arjuna, and Śatānīka the son of Nakula— [all these have fallen].
And your son Śrutasena, who was born from Sahadeva—
all these heroic sons of yours are well, skilled in weapons,
and as delighted and deeply devoted to Dvārakā as Abhimanyu himself.
Just as you are, so too is Subhadrā; she stands with all her heart in affection for them.
Free from the duality of worldly states, she delights in them and is devoid of distress. She suffers through their suffering and likewise rejoices in their happiness.
Likewise, the mother of Pradyumna devoted herself to them with her whole being;
and Keśava distinguishes them above others, such as Bhānu and the rest.
Moreover, my father-in-law is constantly intent upon providing for their food and clothing.
"O beautiful lady, all the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, beginning with Rāma, cherish him;
for their affection for him is equal to that for Pradyumna. Having spoken such pleasant, heart-warming, and agreeable words out of love,"
She set her mind on going toward the chariot of Vāsudeva;
Kṛṣṇa’s chief queen performed a circumambulation of that Kṛṣṇā,
and the beautiful Satyabhāmā ascended the chariot of Śauri.
Having smiled and consoled Draupadī, the best of the Yadus,
that scorcher of foes, turned back and departed swiftly on his horses.
Janamejaya said:
Thus dwelling in the forest, those foremost of men,
their limbs emaciated by cold, heat, wind, and sun,
reached that lake and the sacred grove.
What did the sons of Pṛthā do after that?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having reached that lake, the sons of Pāṇḍu...
Having abandoned their people and established them [in new settlements],
they then wandered through delightful forests, mountains, and river regions.
Likewise, while those great heroes were dwelling in the forest— devoted to sacred study and rich in ascetic merit—
the ancient knowers of the Vedas approached them.
Then those foremost of men honored them. Subsequently, on one occasion, a Brahmin skilled in storytelling arrived among the Kauravas on this earth.
Having met with them, he then approached King Vaicitravīrya by mere chance;
having sat down, he was received with due honors.
Being thus urged by the aged king, the best of the Kurus, he began to speak concerning those born of Dharma, Vāyu, and Indra, as well as the twins.
And those who were emaciated, their limbs withered by wind and sun,
fallen into the mouth of fierce suffering—
even that city, which had heroes as its protectors, appeared as if it were protectorless.
Then, having heard that account of Kṛṣṇā, who was possessed of the quality of having undergone great suffering,
King Vaicitravīrya was consumed with compassion.
Hearing then that the sons and grandsons of kings were dwelling in the forest, having fallen into a river of sorrow,
he spoke with his inner soul struck by dejection.
Afflicted by sighs and tears,
he somehow regained a measure of steadiness in his speech and reflected upon all that had originated from himself.
How indeed is it that my eldest son, the King of Dharma, Ajātaśatru— who is truthful, pure, and of noble conduct— remains upon the surface of the earth?
Formerly, he who used to sleep upon a heap of ranku-deer skins was awakened by throngs of Magadhan bards,
who constantly praised him as one equal to Indra himself.
Surely he, standing on the surface of the earth, is awakened in the final watch of the night by flocks of birds;
how indeed could his limbs not be emaciated by the wind and the sun?
Vṛkodara, his limbs overwhelmed by rage,
lies upon the earth— his body no longer accustomed to such a state—
resting on the surface of the ground in the very presence of Kṛṣṇā.
Likewise Arjuna, though delicate and high-minded,
remained under the control of King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,
with all his limbs as if burning with grief.
Surely Dhṛtarāṣṭra does not sleep at night out of indignation, seeing the twins, Kṛṣṇā, Yudhiṣṭhira,
and Bhīma deprived of happiness.
Sighing like a serpent of fierce energy,
he surely does not sleep at night out of indignation;
likewise, the twins, though deserving of comfort, are now unhappy.
Like two immortals of perfected form in heaven, they remained awake, certainly unpacified,
though restrained by righteousness and truth.
Equal in strength even to the Wind,
he is the powerful son of the Wind himself; though possessed of fierce energy, he is bound by the noose of dharma.
Sighing deeply and suppressing his indignation, Dhruva rolled upon the ground,
longing for the slaughter of my sons.
Though restrained by truth and righteousness,
he who is superior to others in battle awaits his time;
yet when Ajātaśatru was defeated through deceit—
Those harsh words that Duḥśāsana spoke have entered Vṛkodara’s body and burn his vital organs, like fire consuming fuel.
The Son of Dharma will not harbor evil thoughts,
and Dhanañjaya also follows him;
indeed, he flourishes through his dwelling in the forest.
Bhīma’s anger was like fire fanned by the wind;
being torn apart by that rage,
the hero pressed one hand against the other.
He sighs most fiercely and terribly with hot breath,
as if burning these sons and grandsons of mine;
so too do the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow and Vṛkodara.
Impetuous as the Destroyer at the end of time,
scattering arrows that flash like thunderbolts, they would leave no remnant of the enemy host in battle.
Duryodhana, Śakuni, the Sūta’s son,
and the dull-witted Duḥśāsana perceive only the honey, but not the precipice.
And likewise Vṛkodara and Dhanañjaya.
Having performed an action, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
the doer awaits its fruit.
He is joined to that fruit against his will;
how, then, could there be liberation for the person?
For when the field has been well-plowed and the seed sown...
Even when the god rains at the proper time of the season, there may be no fruit; how then could there be success? I think that this occurs only through destiny.
This was done by Matākṣa, who acted wickedly,
and by the Pāṇḍava, who acts righteously,
as well as by me, who have fallen under the sway of a wicked son.
Just as this is the time of the Kurus' end,
she will surely go into exile even if unbidden,
and she who is pregnant will surely give birth.
Surely the destruction of night occurs at the beginning of the day,
and likewise the destruction of the day at the beginning of the night; why then should they not be made by others as well?
Men might not give their wealth by any means whatsoever, and when the time for wealth arrives, it may turn into misfortune;
how indeed could that be so, and from where would it come?
"How may it not be broken, nor leak, nor overflow?"— thus must it be guarded;
for if it were not guarded, it would shatter into a hundred pieces.
"Surely there is no destruction of what has been done in this world;
for Dhanañjaya has gone from the forest even to the realm of Śakra— behold his prowess!"
Having mastered the four kinds of divine weapons,
he returned once more to this world after having gone to heaven in his very own body.
What man, indeed, would wish to return,
except for those many who have been struck down by Time,
were he to behold the Kurus as they stand on the verge of death?
Arjuna Savyasācin is the wielder of the bow,
and that bow is the Gāṇḍīva, the essence of the world;
and those divine weapons belong to him.
Having heard those words of the king, Duryodhana and Saubala remained in private, wondering who indeed could withstand the power of those three.
Approaching Karṇa, he informed him of everything;
and he too became joyless, his mind being small.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Karna, together with the son of Subala,
spoke these words to Duryodhana at that time:
"O Bhārata, having exiled the heroic Pāṇḍavas by your own prowess..."
"Enjoy this earth alone, as the slayer of Śambara enjoys heaven!
O King, today the entire earth, clothed by the ocean, with its mountains, forests, and forms— along with all things stationary and moving— is yours."

O lord of men, all those kings— the inhabitants of the east, the south, the west, and the north— were made to pay tribute. For she who formerly attended upon the Pāṇḍavas as if she were ablaze with splendor—
O King, today that prosperity has been regained by you along with your brothers—
that very same splendor which, while you were at Indraprastha, we beheld shining upon Yudhiṣṭhira, though we ourselves had recently been emaciated by grief.
"O Indra among kings, she who was seen by you today is indeed your enemy;
for she belongs to King Yudhiṣṭhira through the power of his intellect."
O mighty-armed one, cast down by you, she appears as if blazing.
In the very same way, O Indra among kings, slayer of enemy heroes,
all the kings remain established under your command, saying, "What shall we do?"
O King, today this entire earth, clothed by the ocean,
with its mountains and forests, its villages, cities, and mines— the goddess adorned with various forest regions and flourishing towns— is yours.
O King, filled with various provinces, prosperous, and possessing great power,
you shine like the sun with its rays among the gods in heaven through your manly prowess, being saluted by the twice-born and honored by kings.

O King, surrounded by the Kurus, you shine like King Yama with the Rudras, or like Vāsava with the Maruts, like the lord of the stars (the moon). Those who formerly did not respect your commands and were never afraid of you—
We see those Pāṇḍavas dwelling in the forest, deprived of their royal splendor.
For it is heard, O Great King, that the Pāṇḍavas are residing near Lake Dvaitavana together with forest-dwelling Brāhmaṇas.

"Go forth, O Great King, endowed with supreme glory, scorching the sons of Pāṇḍu with your splendor like the sun with its rays; established in your kingdom, you who are possessed of fortune shall look upon those fallen from their kingdom and bereft of fortune."
O King, behold the sons of Pāṇḍu, who have achieved their goals though they were once unsuccessful; O noble lady, established in great prosperity and endowed with a high lineage,
let the Pāṇḍavas gaze upon you as Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, did.
O Lord of the People, that splendor which both friends and enemies behold shining in a man is indeed effective;
for he who looks upon his enemies while remaining in a state of security is superior to those who are themselves in distress.
Like one standing on a mountain looking down upon those dwelling on the plains— what happiness could be greater than that?
O tiger among kings, one does not find such joy through the acquisition of sons or wealth, nor even through sovereignty, as one finds from beholding the destruction of one's enemies.
What happiness indeed would not belong to him in that hermitage who, having achieved his purpose, might behold Dhanañjaya clothed in bark and deerskin?
For your wives are well-attired, while he is clad in bark and deerskin.
O lord of men, seeing today the radiant splendor of your wives, let them behold the unhappy Kṛṣṇā and let her, deprived of wealth, feel weary once more, censuring herself and her very life.

"For it is not possible for her to feel such dejection in the midst of the assembly as she would upon seeing your wives so beautifully adorned. Having spoken thus to the king, Karṇa, together with Śakuni, [departed].
At the conclusion of those words, O Janamejaya, both of them became silent.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the speech of Karṇa, King Duryodhana then—
Becoming joyful and yet again dejected, he spoke these words:
"O Karṇa, everything that you say is already established in my mind;
however, I shall not obtain permission to go where the Pāṇḍavas are."
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra laments for those heroes,
for he considers the Pāṇḍavas to have become even more powerful through their application of asceticism.
Or perhaps the king will come to understand what we intend to do.
Even while protecting the future in this way, he ought not to grant permission;
for indeed, there is no other purpose in the Dvaitavana forest than the extermination of those enemies of mine dwelling in the woods.
For you know how the Steward (Vidura), when the time for the dice game had arrived,
spoke those words to me, to you, and to the son of Subala;
you know those former words and whatever else was lamented.
Reflecting on this, I cannot determine whether I should go or stay;
for it would indeed be a great joy for me to see Bhīma and Phalguna together with Kṛṣṇā, even though they are suffering in the forest.

I would not obtain such joy even by gaining the entire earth as I have upon seeing the sons of Pāṇḍu clad in bark and deerskins. What indeed could be greater than this, that I [should see] the daughter of Drupada?
"O Karṇa, if the King of Dharma and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava were to see me in the forest clad in saffron robes,
and if they were to behold you endowed with supreme splendor, my life would be worth living."
But I see no means by which we might go to that forest,
nor how the lord of the earth would grant me permission to depart,
especially when he is accompanied by the son of Subala and Duḥśāsana.
"Find a clever means by which we may go to that forest. Having deliberated today on whether to go or otherwise, I shall go to the presence of the king early tomorrow morning."
While I am seated there, along with Bhīṣma, the best of the Kurus,
you should state whatever means you have envisioned, together with the son of Subala.
Then, having heard Bhīṣma and the king regarding their departure—
"I shall make an effort, having conciliated my grandfather.
Having said, "So be it," they all departed for their respective dwellings.
When the night had passed, Karṇa approached the king.
Then Karna, laughing, said this to Duryodhana:
"O lord of men, a stratagem has been devised; listen to it. O king, all the cattle-stations in the Dvaitavana forest are waiting for you."
"Under the pretext of a cattle-expedition (*ghoṣayātrā*), we shall go, of this there is no doubt.
For it is always appropriate to go on a cattle-expedition, O lord of people;
and in this way, O King, your father will surely grant you his permission."
As the two of them were thus discussing their decision for the expedition to the cattle-pen,
Śakuni, the King of Gāndhāra, replied as if smiling:
"I have seen a flawless means for our departure."
"The king will grant us permission and will even urge us on;
all the cowherd settlements in the Dvaitavana forest are waiting for you, O lord of men.
Under the pretext of a journey to the cowherds' encampment, we shall go there without a doubt."
Then they all laughed and clapped one another’s hands;
having reached that very decision, they gazed upon the best of the Kurus.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O Janamejaya, they all beheld Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
having inquired after the king’s welfare and having been questioned by the king in turn, O Bhārata,
the cook named Samaṅga, who had previously been appointed by them, [was brought forward].
Then the cows standing nearby reported this to Dhṛtarāṣṭra; immediately thereafter, O lord of the people, the son of Rādhā and Śakuni spoke to Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the best of kings and ruler of men.
"O Kaurava, in these delightful regions,
the cowherd settlements have now arrived at the time for branding their calves and marking them with the year of birth.
O King, this is also the proper season for your son to go hunting."
"You ought to grant permission for Duryodhana’s departure.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Hunting is excellent, my son, as is the inspection of the cattle."
"One must not place trust in the cowherds," so I remember;
yet we have heard that those tigers among men are nearby there.
Therefore, I do not myself grant you permission to go there.
For they have been defeated through deceit and emaciated in the great forest;
O son of Rādhā, those great car-warriors are constant in their asceticism and fully capable.
Dharmarāja would not become angry, but Bhīmasena is intolerant.
The daughter of Yajñasena is indeed nothing but pure energy;
yet you, filled with pride and delusion, might commit an offense against her,
and then, being endowed with ascetic power, she would utterly consume you with her heat.
Alternatively, those heroes, equipped with weapons and overwhelmed by fury,
together with their swords girded on, might consume you all with the fiery power of their arms. Yet, if you should somehow prevail over them due to your numerical superiority—
That would be an ignoble act in the highest degree, and in my opinion, it is impossible.
For the mighty-armed Dhanañjaya dwelt in the world of Indra;
having obtained the divine weapons there, he has now returned to the forest.
In the past, the earth was conquered by Bībhatsu even while he was unskilled in weapons;
how much more so now that he, a great chariot-warrior, is skilled in arms—would he not slay you? Or rather, having heard my words, you shall remain on your guard there.
Living there in a state of anxiety due to a lack of trust, you will experience suffering;
or else, some soldiers might commit an offense against Yudhiṣṭhira,
and that thoughtless act would bring trouble upon you.
"Therefore, let men who act with discretion go there to remind him;
O Bhārata, I do not favor your going there yourself.
Śakuni said:
O Bhārata, the eldest Pāṇḍava is a knower of dharma, and he made a vow in the assembly that he must dwell for twelve years;
and all those Pāṇḍavas, who practice righteousness, have followed his lead.
"Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, will not harbor anger toward us; furthermore,
our desire to go hunting increases greatly,
and we wish to perform the *smaraṇa* rite, but not to see the Pāṇḍavas."
"And there shall be no one there of ignoble conduct;
nor shall we go to where their dwelling place is.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by Śakuni, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men,
reluctantly gave permission to Duryodhana along with his ministers. Having been granted leave, the son of Gāndhārī then departed together with Karṇa.
Surrounded by a vast army, that best of the Bharatas set forth,
accompanied by Duḥśāsana, the gambler Saubala,
other brothers, and thousands of women.
As the mighty-armed one was departing for the Dvaitavana lake,
all the citizens followed him to that forest along with their wives;
there were eight thousand chariots and thirty thousand elephants.
There were many thousands of foot soldiers and nine thousand horses; there were carts, mobile shops, courtesans, merchants,
and bards, as well as men devoted to hunting by the hundreds and thousands.
Then, O lord of the people, as the king set forth, there arose a great clamor like that of a mighty wind rising in the rainy season. At that time,
King Duryodhana encamped at a distance of only two krośas.
Having set out with all his mounts, he then proceeded to Lake Dvaitavana.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Now King Duryodhana, dwelling here and there in that forest—
He went toward the cowherd settlements and there made his encampment;
in a delightful, well-known place, provided with water and trees,
a region endowed with every excellence, the men constructed their dwellings.
In that same way, he then beheld many separate dwellings situated near them—
those of Karṇa, Śakuni, and all his brothers—
and there he saw cattle by the hundreds and thousands.
The king marked them all with signs and numbers; he branded the calves and recognized those that had already approached their mothers. He also rounded up those cows that had young calves.
Then, having made the call to assembly and identified the three-year-old calves,
that joy of the Kurus, surrounded by cowherds, sported about with delight. And all those citizens and thousands of soldiers likewise followed him.
They sported in that forest according to their pleasure, just like the immortals. Then cowherds skilled in singing, dancing, and instrumental music,
as well as well-adorned maidens, waited upon the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Surrounded by a host of women, the king, greatly delighted, bestowed wealth upon them,
as well as various foods and drinks according to their merit.
Then they all together [slew] hyenas, buffaloes, and deer.
Driving away the gavayas, bears, and boars from all sides,
he pierced them with his arrows and bound the elephants in the great forest; indeed,
he caused the deer to be captured in delightful regions.
O Bhārata, consuming dairy products and various enjoyments,
he beheld forests that were exceedingly beautiful, in full bloom,
frequented by intoxicated bees, and filled with the cries of peacocks.
He proceeded by stages to the holy Lake Dvaitavana,
which was frequented by intoxicated bees, filled with the cries of peacocks,
strewn with *saptacchada* trees, and endowed with *puṃnāga* and *bakula* trees.
Endowed with supreme supernatural power like Mahendra wielding the thunderbolt, O lord of the people,
on that very day King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,
performed by chance the Sadyaska sacrifice, a rite of royal seers.
O best of the Kurus, that wise king, together with learned Brahmins dwelling in the forest, lived according to the divine rule and on forest fare;
having established his residence around that lake, the Kaurava remained there.

Accompanied by his wise and lawful wife Draupadī, as well as Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins, the lord of men then dwelt in the vicinity of the lake. Thereupon Duryodhana, along with his younger brothers, gave orders to his servants.
"O Bhārata, let pleasure-parks and dwellings be constructed quickly," [he said].
Having replied "So be it" to the Kauravya, those executors of his word,
desiring to build those pleasure-parks, went to the Dvaitavana lake.
The vanguard of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s army reached Lake Dvaitavana;
as they were entering through the forest gate, the Gandharvas blocked their way.
O lord of the people, the king of the Gandharvas had already arrived there beforehand.
O King, surrounded by his hosts, he came from the abode of Kubera;
accompanied by throngs of Apsarases and likewise by the sons of the gods,
that lake was filled by him as he, fond of diversion, came for the sake of sport.
Seeing that it had been secured by him, O King, those royal attendants then returned to where King Duryodhana was. Having assembled there, they said, "It is not possible to enter."
"O King, the lake Dvaitavana is guarded by many heroes.
Then, O Bhārata, the Gandharvas informed the king of this.
Having heard their words, he [summoned] his soldiers who were fierce in battle.
"O Kauravya, he sent forth [the command]: 'Drive them away!
Hearing those words of the king, the leaders of his army went to Lake Dvaitavana and spoke thus to the Gandharvas."
"The powerful King Duryodhana, son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, is coming here desiring to sport; therefore, withdraw from this place. Thus addressed, O lord of the people, the Gandharvas laughed aloud.
They replied to those men with these very harsh words:
"The dull-witted King Suyodhana does not perceive you;
he commands us as if we were his subjects, like the gods of heaven."
"You are all on the verge of death and of dull intellect, there is no doubt, you who, being senseless, speak thus to us at his word. All of you, go quickly to where that Kuru king is."
"Go this very day to the abode of Dharmarāja, you who are hateful [to us].
Thus addressed by the Gandharvas,
the leaders of the king's army fled toward where the son of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra was.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then they all, having come together, approached Duryodhana and spoke,
O great king, that which they had to say regarding the Kaurava.
When his army had been checked by the Gandharvas, the powerful son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
filled with indignation, addressed his troops, O Bhārata:
"Punish these men who are ignorant of dharma and act against my will!"
"If Śatakratu is sporting together with all the gods,
we shall sport here continuously, as we please.
Having heard the words of Duryodhana, the mighty sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra [acted accordingly].
All the warriors by the thousands were likewise fully armored;
then, having overwhelmed the Gandharvas, they entered that forest by force,
filling the ten directions with a great lion-like roar.
Then, O Lord, other Gandharvas restrained the Kuru soldiers there with peaceful words alone,
saying, "Do not act rashly! Though they were thus being restrained by the Gandharvas through conciliation, O ruler of the earth, they did not desist.
Disregarding those Gandharvas, they entered that great forest.
When the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with the kings, would not desist from their speech,
all those sky-dwellers then reported it to Citrasena.
The king of the Gandharvas spoke to all those Kauravas, saying,
"Punish these ignoble men," for Citrasena was exceedingly intolerant.
O Bhārata, the Gandharvas were then given permission by Citrasena.
All of them, with weapons raised, rushed toward the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Seeing those Gandharvas swiftly descending with uplifted weapons,
they all fled in battle while the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra looked on.
Seeing all those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra fleeing with their backs turned,
the heroic Vaikartana did not turn his back there. However, he beheld the great army of the Gandharvas rushing toward him.
With a great shower of arrows, the son of Rādhā warded him off;
with razor-edged shafts, *viśikhas*, *bhallas*, calf-tooth-headed arrows, and iron ones,
the joy of the Sūtas struck down hundreds of Gandharvas through his lightness of hand.
Striking off the heads of the Gandharvas, that great chariot-warrior in an instant dispersed the entire army of Citrasena.
Those Gandharvas were being slaughtered by the wise son of the Sūta.
Once more they returned by the hundreds and by the thousands;
in an instant, the earth became filled with Gandharvas,
as Citrasena’s soldiers rushed forward with great speed.
Then King Duryodhana, Śakuni the son of Subala,
Duḥśāsana, Vikarṇa, and the other sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra slaughtered that army with chariots whose roar was like that of Garuḍa.
Furthermore, placing Karṇa at their head, they fought once more;
with the great roar of chariots and the movement of horses,
they hemmed in the Gandharvas, seeking to protect the son of Vaikartana.
Then all the Gandharvas, together with the Kauravas, fell upon one another;
at that time, there occurred a most tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end.
Then those Gandharvas became weakened, afflicted by the arrows.
And the Kauravas cried out aloud upon seeing the Gandharvas afflicted;
and seeing the Gandharvas terrified, the highly indignant Citrasena sprang up from his seat in anger, intent on their slaughter.
Then, employing the weapon of illusion (*māyāstra*), he who was skilled in diverse paths fought on;
the terrible arrows released by him, possessing a radiance equal to the rays of the sun,
completely covered the sky, and no wind blew there.
O Bhārata, elephant-riders fell slain along with their elephants;
likewise, horse-riders with their horses, chariot-warriors with their chariots,
and foot-soldiers fell, slaughtered by showers of arrows.
The Kauravas were bewildered by that illusion of Citrasena.
For then, O Bhārata, every single warrior of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son was surrounded by ten Gandharvas each.
Then, being crushed by that great force,
they fled in fear from the battle to where King Yudhiṣṭhira was,
while the Dhārtarāṣṭra armies were being broken on all sides.
O King, Karṇa Vaikartana stood firm like an immovable mountain;
and Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni the son of Subala,
though severely wounded, continued to fight the Gandharvas in battle.
Then all the Gandharvas, by the hundreds and thousands, charging together with the intent to slay, rushed at Karṇa in battle;
those mighty ones [attacked] with swords, spears, spikes, and maces.
Desiring to slay the Sūta’s son, they surrounded him on all sides;
some cut his yoke, others brought down his standard,
others struck the pole, others the horses, and others the charioteer.
Others [held] the umbrella and the shield, while others likewise held the chariot-seat;
these heroes, led by Citrasena, stood with their weapons grasped.
Others occupied the yoke-pole, and others likewise the two wheels.

Many thousands of Gandharvas struck the chariot to pieces. Then, leaping down from the chariot, the son of the Sūta, wielding sword and shield and with his bow slung over his shoulder, fled away with great strength.
Mounting Vikarṇa’s chariot, he urged the horses forward for the sake of escape.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O great king, when the great car-warrior Karṇa had been routed by the Gandharvas..."
The entire army fled while the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra looked on.
Seeing all those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra fleeing with their backs turned,
O great king, Duryodhana did not turn his back there.
Beholding that great army of the Gandharvas rushing toward him,
that subduer of enemies showered it with a vast rain of arrows. But the Gandharvas, disregarding that rain of arrows, [assailed] his chariot.

Desiring to slay Duryodhana, they surrounded him on all sides; they shattered the chariot into pieces as small as sesame seeds— the yoke, the pole, the fender, as well as the banner and the charioteer, the horses, the triple-bamboo shaft, and the seat.
Having rushed toward Duryodhana, who was fallen on the ground deprived of his chariot, the mighty-armed Citrasena then captured him alive,
O great king, having bound that great car-warrior’s arms with a rope.

Having hoisted him up, O Great King, Citrasena let out a roar. When he had been seized, O Indra among kings, the Gandharvas surrounded Duḥśāsana, who remained on his chariot, and hemmed him in from all sides.
Taking Vivimshati and Chitrasena with them, others fled;
others took Vinda and Anuvinda, as well as all the royal ladies. But the troops of Dhritarashtra’s son were pursued by the Gandharvas.
Then, having previously been routed, they joined together and advanced against the Pāṇḍavas;
the wagons, market-stalls, tents, and all the vehicles and draft animals sought refuge with the Pāṇḍavas while the lord of the earth was being carried away.
"The handsome, mighty-armed, and very powerful son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the king, is being carried away by the Gandharvas; O Pārthas, pursue him!
Duḥśāsana, Durviṣaha, Durmukha, and likewise Durjaya [are also there]."
"Bound by the Gandharvas, the king’s wives are being carried away everywhere!
Thus cried Duryodhana’s ministers, longing for the king;
all of them, distressed and with piteous voices, approached Yudhiṣṭhira.
To those aged ministers of Duryodhana— who were thus distressed and dejected, begging Yudhiṣṭhira for mercy— Bhīmasena spoke,
as they stood there as heroes with weapons grasped, led by Citrasena.
Indeed, having equipped ourselves with great effort and with elephants and horses,
this result has come about differently for us who were acting otherwise;
that which was to be performed by us has been performed by the Gandharvas.
"O father, this was ill-advised by the king who plays with dice so poorly;
it was done for the sake of that evil-minded Duryodhana, who desires to see us in distress.
We have heard that others cause a weak man's enemies to fall."
This superhuman deed has been performed by the Gandharvas before our very eyes.
By good fortune, there exists in this world some man who stands devoted to our welfare, by whom the burden of us who were sitting in despair has been removed, bringing us great comfort.

That evil-minded one desires to see those who endure cold, wind, and heat, and are emaciated by their asceticism, while he himself remains in comfort; such is the conduct of that wicked-souled Kaurava who walks the path of unrighteousness.
Those who follow such conduct witness their own downfall;
for unrighteousness has been committed by him who has trained in this way. But the sons of Kuntī are compassionate; I tell you this regarding their overseers.
To Bhimasena, the son of Kuntī, who was speaking thus in indignation,
King Yudhiṣṭhira replied, "This is not the time for harsh words.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"O dear one, how could you speak such words to us Kauravas, who have come to you seeking refuge, afflicted by fear and fallen into calamity? O mighty-armed one, we must be protected; do not speak thus, O high-minded one."
O Vṛkodara, there arise divisions among kinsmen, quarrels, and persistent enmities; yet the duty of kinship is not destroyed. However, when some outsider seeks to solicit the family of the kinsmen...
The virtuous do not tolerate that external provocation;
when insulted by others, we are one hundred and five,
but when there is mutual conflict, we are only five hundred for you.
"For this evil-minded one knows that we have lived here for a long time;
having treated us with contempt, he has done this unpleasant thing by capturing Duryodhana by force in battle through the Gandharva."
"Because of the violation of women by outsiders, our lineage has been destroyed. Therefore,
for the sake of protecting those who have sought refuge and for the protection of our family, arise,
O tigers among men, and prepare yourselves without delay!"
Arjuna, the twins, and you, O unconquered Bhīma,
must rescue Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, Suyodhana, as he is being carried away.
Here are these chariots, O tigers among men, equipped with all weapons.

Mount these resounding chariots, ever ready for action, which bear the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; they possess stainless golden banners and are equipped with golden standards, held together by charioteers such as Indrasena and others.
"O dear ones, having mounted these [vehicles], strive without weariness to fight the Gandharvas in battle for the sake of Suyodhana’s liberation.
Whatever kṣatriya there may be who has come here seeking refuge— "
One should protect another to the best of one's ability; how much more so you, O Vṛkodara?
For who else here would rush to provide protection when thus urged, surely even upon seeing an enemy who has approached for refuge with palms joined in supplication?
O Pāṇḍava, the granting of a boon, the acquisition of a kingdom, and the birth of a son—these three—and the liberation of an enemy from distress: these four are equal.
We five are now a hundred, as long as we remain together.
"We are five hundred and more who have been humiliated by our enemies. For what could be greater than this, that Suyodhana,
having fallen into such distress, seeks his very life by relying on the strength of your arms?"

"O Vṛkodara, O hero, if you were not here, I would have rushed forward myself; for this sacrifice has been prepared, and I have no doubt about it. When we were being humiliated by our enemies, we were but one hundred and five."

But in the event of mutual conflict, we five shall be equal to those hundred. O Bhīma, you must liberate Suyodhana by means of conciliation alone; O Bhīma, you must release the Kauravas through mild means.
"O joy of the Kurus, you should strive by all possible means;
if that king of the Gandharvas does not yield to conciliation,
you should liberate Suyodhana through mild force."
"O Bhīma, if he does not release the Kauravas through mild combat,
they must be released by all possible means after you have subdued those who stand as obstacles.
For this much alone, O Vṛkodara, is it possible for me to instruct."
"O Bhārata, when a Vaitāna sacrifice has been commenced and is in progress,
it is proclaimed that a very great boon should be granted to the petitioner.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of Ajātaśatru, Dhanañjaya pledged his word to liberate the Kauravas from their teacher’s command. Arjuna said:
"If the Gandharvas do not release the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra through conciliation,
today the earth shall drink the blood of the king of the Gandharvas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, having heard that vow of the truth-speaking Arjuna, the minds of the Kauravas then returned once more [to their resolve]. Thus addressed,
the son of Kuntī spoke these words again.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, remembering our former enmity, he whose eyes were bloodshot with anger thought, "In the past, this evil-minded one intended to burn us in a house of lac"; yet, O hero, we were protected by destiny at that time.
O son of Kuntī, even during the time of the gambling match, many wicked deeds were indeed committed: the assault upon Draupadī, the seizing of her hair,
and the stripping away of her garments in the very midst of the assembly hall.
Suyodhana is now reaping the fruit of the evils he committed in the past.
We ourselves must effect the subjugation of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son;
for that which has been done by another would indeed be an act of hostility toward us who desire friendship.
"But the Gandharva is a benefactor; O King, do not be despondent.
In the meantime, O King, while being carried away by Citrasena, Suyodhana lamented, afflicted by great sorrow."
O Yudhiṣṭhira, O mighty-armed one, best among all upholders of dharma;
O son of Pāṇḍu, O mighty-armed one, bringer of glory to the Kauravas— [rescue] those who, along with their sons and wives, have been forcibly carried off by the Gandharva.
"O best among all upholders of dharma, this Gandharva has carried me away by force!
O tiger among men, O highly illustrious Yudhiṣṭhira, protect me!
O mighty-armed one, he is leading away your brother after having bound him."
"The Gandharvas have bound Duḥśāsana, Durviṣaha, Durmukha, and likewise Durjaya, and they are carrying away all our wives. O best of men, pursue me quickly; protect us!"
"The twins follow me with weapons for my protection;
O Pāṇḍavas, having defeated the Gandharvas by your prowess, dispel this great infamy that has fallen upon the Kuru lineage."
Hearing this lamentation of the Kaurava with its piteous voice, Yudhiṣṭhira became agitated and, overwhelmed with compassion,
spoke these words again to Bhīmasena.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Yudhiṣṭhira, all those bulls among men, led by Bhīmasena, rose up with joyful faces.
Then, O Bhārata, all those great car-warriors donned impenetrable armor adorned with gold and took up various divine weapons.
All those Pāṇḍavas, clad in armor, equipped with chariots, bearing banners and bows, appeared like blazing fires. Those chariots were well-furnished and yoked to swift horses.

Mounting their chariots, those tigers among men then departed with great speed. Thereupon, a great roar arose from the Kaurava armies upon seeing the sons of Pāṇḍu, those great car-warriors, advancing together.
Radiant with victory, those sky-dwellers and swift great chariot-warriors gathered fearlessly in that forest in an instant;
then all the Gandharvas, appearing victorious, turned back.
Seeing the four Pāṇḍava heroes mounted on their chariots in battle,
and beholding them shining like the world-protectors (Lokapālas) prepared for action,
the inhabitants of Gandhamādana stood firm with their armies drawn up in formation.
O Bhārata, having heard the words of the wise Dharmarāja, they gradually began the battle with mildness; however,
the soldiers of the Gandharva king were dull-witted.
At that time, it was possible to lead them toward their welfare through gentle means;
therefore, the invincible Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes,
addressed these words preceded by conciliation to those sky-dwellers on the battlefield.
"Release my brother, King Suyodhana!
This loathsome deed is not worthy of the King of the Gandharvas— neither the violation of another's wife nor this encounter with mortals."
"Release these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who possess great heroism,
and set their wives free at the command of Dharmarāja.
Thus addressed by the illustrious Pāṇḍava, the Gandharvas—
Smiling, they then addressed these words to Pārtha:
"O dear one, we would follow the command of only one person on this earth,
by whose instruction we may act free from all anxiety."
"O Bhārata, let us act exactly as he has commanded;
there is no other instructor for us than that Lord of the Gods.
Thus addressed by the Gandharvas, Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, [replied].
