Then he addressed these words once more to the Gandharvas:
"O Gandharvas, if you do not release the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra through conciliation,
I myself shall liberate Suyodhana by my own prowess."
Having spoken thus, Pārtha Savyasācī Dhanañjaya then loosed sharpened arrows toward those sky-dwellers.
In that same manner, those Gandharvas, fierce in their strength, [assailed him] with a shower of arrows.
The Pāṇḍavas turned toward the Pāṇḍavas, and the celestial dwellers [turned] toward the Pāṇḍavas.
Then, O Bhārata, there occurred a most tumultuous battle between the swift Gandharvas and the Pāṇḍavas of terrible speed.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the Gandharvas, endowed with divine weapons and wearing golden garlands,
surrounded him on all sides, discharging blazing arrows.

O King, the four heroic Pāṇḍavas and thousands of Gandharvas fell upon one another in battle; it was like a marvel. It was as if the chariots of both Karṇa and the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were engaged in combat.

The Gandharvas cut them down by the hundreds, and they likewise struck at them. O King, as those Gandharvas rushed forward in battle by the hundreds, those tigers among men received them with numerous showers of arrows.
Being showered from all sides with volleys of arrows by those moving through the sky,
they were unable to remain near the sons of Pāṇḍu;
then Arjuna, beholding the Gandharvas filled with rage, [acted].
Having observed them, he then proceeded to employ divine great weapons.
O King, as they were rushing toward him, raining down divine weapons upon them,
he dispatched a thousand times a thousand of them to the abode of Yama.
In that battle, Arjuna, preeminent in strength among the Gandharvas, [fought] with the fire-missile;
likewise, Bhīma, the great archer and best among the strong,
O King, slew hundreds of Gandharvas in the encounter with his sharpened arrows.

Likewise, O King, the two sons of Mādrī, fighting with superior strength, surrounded [the enemy] from the front and slaughtered their foes by the hundreds. Being struck down by those high-souled ones with divine weapons, the Gandharvas...
Then, seizing the sky, they flew up toward the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
perceiving them as they were taking flight, Dhananjaya, the son of Kuntī,
hemmed them in on all sides with a vast net of arrows.
Bound by a net of arrows like birds in a cage,
they rained down showers of maces, spears, and swords upon Arjuna in their fury; but he,
the master of great weapons, struck down those showers of maces, spears, and swords.
Dhanañjaya struck the limbs of the Gandharvas with broad-headed arrows;
as their heads, feet, and arms fell,
it appeared like a rain of stones, and fear seized his enemies.
Being struck by the high-souled Pāṇḍava, those Gandharvas,
stationed in the sky, covered him as he stood upon the earth with showers of arrows.
But Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes, [warded off] their showers of arrows.
Having warded them off with his own weapons, the radiant one pierced the Gandharvas in return;
likewise, Arjuna, the joy of the Kurus, discharged the Sthūṇākarṇa, Indrajāla, Saura, Āgneya, and Saumya weapons.
Being scorched by the arrows of Kuntī’s son, those Gandharvas fell into extreme despondency,
like the Daityas before Śakra;
and as they attempted to ascend into the sky, they were held back by the net of his shafts.
As they were spreading forth, they were held back by Savyasācin with his bhalla arrows.
Seeing the Gandharvas terrified by the wise son of Kuntī,
Citrasena seized a mace and rushed toward Savyasācin.
As he rushed forward swiftly with mace in hand in that encounter,
Pārtha cut that mace made entirely of iron into seven pieces with his arrows.
Seeing his mace thus severed into many fragments by the swift archer’s shafts, [he was struck with wonder].
Concealing himself through his supernatural power (*vidyā*), he fought the Pāṇḍava;
standing in the sky, he countered the latter's divine weapons with his own divine weapons.
Then the hero Arjuna warded off those [weapons] with his own divine weapons.
Though being warded off by those weapons by the high-souled Arjuna,
the powerful king of the Gandharvas then vanished through his illusory power (*māyā*). Perceiving that he was striking while invisible, Arjuna [acted].
He struck him with sky-ranging [arrows] consecrated with divine mantras;
then the enraged Arjuna,
assuming many forms, employed the "sound-piercing" technique and brought about the destruction of his invisibility.
While he was being struck by those weapons by the high-souled Arjuna,
his dear friend Citrasena then revealed himself to him and spoke thus to his companion: "Know me as your friend in battle."
Then, observing his friend Citrasena to be weak in battle,
that bull among the Pāṇḍavas withdrew the weapon he had previously discharged.
And all the Pāṇḍavas saw Dhananjaya having withdrawn the weapon.
They brought back the fleeing horses, the arrows, and the bows;
Citrasena, Bhīma, Savyasācin, and the twins,
having inquired after one another's welfare, remained stationed upon their chariots.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Arjuna, that great archer of immense splendor, smiling, spoke these words to Citrasena in the midst of the Gandharva army.
"What have you resolved, O hero, regarding the subjugation of the Kauravas?
And for what reason has this Suyodhana been captured along with his wife?
Citrasena said:
O Dhanañjaya, this intention of the wicked Duryodhana and Karṇa was known by that high-souled one while he was staying there,
upon learning that you were living in the forest and suffering like those undeserving of such hardship.
"These have come to carry away the illustrious Draupadī;
seeing them in such a precarious state while I remain secure,
and knowing their unstable intentions and what they wish to do, the Lord of the Gods spoke to me."
"Go, bind Duryodhana along with his ministers, and bring them here.
And Dhanañjaya must be protected by you in battle, together with his brothers;
for that Pāṇḍava is your dear friend and your disciple."
"By the command of the King of the Gods, I have therefore come here swiftly;
this evil-minded one has been bound, and I shall go to the abode of the gods. By the decree of the Subduer of Pāka, I will lead this wicked soul away."
Arjuna said:
"O Citrasena, let our brother Suyodhana be released at the command of Dharmarāja, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me."
Citrasena said:
"This man is wicked and eternally corrupt; he does not deserve release. He has deceived both Dharmarāja and Kṛṣṇā, O Dhanañjaya."
"This is not what he intends to do; for the son of Kuntī, the King of Dharma who observes great vows, knows this. Having heard it, act as you wish.
Vaiśampāyana said:
They all approached King Yudhiṣṭhira;
having approached him, they reported all of that wicked deed to him.
Having heard those words of the Gandharva at that time, Ajātaśatru [was moved].
He liberated them all and praised the Gandharvas, saying:
"By good fortune, this wicked son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with his ministers, kinsmen, and relatives, has not been slain by all of you, who are so powerful and capable."
"O dear ones, you sky-dwellers have rendered me a great service;
my family has not been disgraced by the liberation of this evil-minded one. Command what you desire; we are delighted by the sight of you."
"Having attained all your desires, depart from here without delay.
Thus permitted by the wise son of Pāṇḍu, the Gandharvas,
led by Citrasena, departed joyfully along with the Apsarases.
Then, having gone to the world of the gods together with the Gandharvas,
Citrasena reported all of that to Śatakratu.
The king of the gods also restored those dead Gandharvas to life.
"Those who were slain in battle by the Kauravas with a divine rain of nectar—
then Citrasena spoke these words in a bold voice:
'Release Suyodhana, along with his younger brothers, his ministers, and his wives!'"
Having heard the words of Citrasena, the Gandharvas quickly liberated the king— who was bound by fetters along with his wives, followers, and ministers— from that forest made of a web of arrows.
Rolling about as well, they all came into the presence of Yudhiṣṭhira;
fallen and ashamed, they then stood with their faces cast downward.
Yudhiṣṭhira, too, looked upon them who had come to such a state with compassion.
Then, having bid farewell to those kinsmen and all the king’s wives,
and having performed that difficult task, the Pāṇḍavas, filled with joy,
were honored by the Kurus along with their women and children— those great chariot-warriors.
Those great-souled ones shone in the midst of the Kurus like sacrificial fires.
Then, having released Duryodhana who was accompanied by his brothers,
Yudhiṣṭhira spoke these words with affection:
"O dear one, never again commit such a rash act anywhere;
for those who commit rash deeds do not prosper in happiness, O Bhārata. May you be well, O joy of the Kurus, together with all your brothers."

"Go to your home as you please, and do not harbor despondency. Thus permitted by the Pāṇḍava, King Duryodhana then paid homage to the son of Dharma and departed like a sick man whose senses have failed.
Torn with shame, he departed toward the city.
Once that Kaurava had gone, the heroic Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī,
accompanied by his brothers, was honored by the twice-born.
Surrounded by all those whose wealth was asceticism, like Śakra surrounded by the immortals,
he dwelt with joy in that Dvaitavana forest.
Janamejaya said:

Of that evil-minded man who was conquered and bound by his enemies and later liberated through battle by the high-souled Pāṇḍavas; who was then established in honor, yet remained constantly boastful, arrogant, and full of pride.
It seems to me that it will be difficult for the wicked Duryodhana— who constantly disregards the Pāṇḍavas because of his human pride and nobility, and who always speaks with arrogance—
to enter Hastināpura.
"O Vaiśampāyana, recount in detail the entry of him who was filled with shame and whose mind was agitated by grief. Vaiśampāyana said:

Dismissed by Dharmarāja, Suyodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with his face cast down in shame, departed in deep distress and dejection. Accompanied by his fourfold army, the king proceeded toward his own city.
Reflecting with a mind struck by grief upon his impending defeat,
he left the vehicles on the road and encamped as he desired on a beautiful and pleasant stretch of ground that abounded in excellent fodder and water.
He stationed the elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry each in their proper place. Then, as the king sat upon a couch radiant as fire,
he appeared like the moon eclipsed by Rāhu at the end of the night.
Approaching Duryodhana, Karṇa then said this:
"By good fortune you live, O son of Gāndhārī; by good fortune we have met again;
by good fortune the Gandharvas, who can assume any form at will, have been conquered by you."
"By good fortune, O joy of the Kurus, I see all your brothers together—
those great car-warriors who, having conquered their enemies, have emerged from the battle desiring victory.
But I was pursued by all the Gandharvas while you were looking on."
I was unable to steady my own army as it was being torn apart;
with my limbs severely wounded by arrows and greatly oppressed, I retreated.
But this, O Bhārata, I consider most wonderful—that you remain here.

I see them— along with their wives, wealth, and vehicles— safe, unhurt, and liberated from that superhuman battle. O Bhārata, there is no man to be found in this world who could have accomplished this.
"O Great King, that which was done by you together with your brothers in battle...
Having been addressed thus by Karṇa, King Duryodhana then spoke with his head bowed,
O King, in a voice choked with tears.
Duryodhana said:
"O son of Rādhā, I do not find fault with your words because you did not know [the truth]. You thought that the Gandharvas, our enemies, had been conquered by me through my own prowess."

O mighty-armed one, the Gandharvas fought with my brothers for a very long time, and a slaughter was wrought on both sides by me. But when those heroes, superior in their illusory powers, took to the sky and continued the fight...
Then our battle with those who move through the sky became equal;
however, being unable to fight back against those who had taken to the air,
we suffered defeat in the encounter and were even taken captive.
Together with our servants, ministers, sons, wives, wealth, and vehicles,
we were carried along the high path of the sky by them in great misery.
Then some of our soldiers and ministers [beheld] the great chariot-warriors.
Approaching the Pāṇḍavas, who grant refuge, they spoke in distress:
"This King Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with his younger brothers,
his ministers, and his wives, is being carried off by Gandharvas stationed in the sky."
"Release that lord of men along with his wife—may prosperity be yours! Let there be no further violation regarding the wives of the Kurus in any way.
Having spoken thus, they emerged from the battle and approached the King of Dharma.
When this had been said, the righteous eldest son of Pāṇḍu then appeased all his brothers and gave orders for their release.
Then those bulls among men, the Pāṇḍavas, arrived at that place.
Though they were capable, those great car-warriors first entreated them with conciliatory words;
but when the Gandharvas, those heroes who move through the sky like roaring clouds, did not release us despite being thus pacified, [they took up arms].
Then Arjuna, Bhīma, and the twin sons of Mādrī, fierce in their strength,
released showers of arrows against the Gandharvas in great numbers.
Thereupon, all the sky-dwellers abandoned the battlefield and departed for heaven.
Dragging us along with them, their minds filled with joy while we were dejected,
I then beheld Dhananjaya on all sides surrounded by a web of arrows, discharging superhuman weapons.
Seeing the quarters of the sky covered by the sharp arrows of the Pāṇḍava,
Citrasena, the subduer of foes and friend of Dhanañjaya, then revealed himself and embraced the Pāṇḍava.
He inquired after their welfare, and they in turn asked after his health. Having thus met one another and cast off their armor,
those heroes— the Gandharvas— then became united with the Pāṇḍavas.
Having come together with one another and filled with supreme joy,
Citrasena and Dhanañjaya honored each other.
Duryodhana said:
Then Citrasena, having approached Arjuna, the slayer of enemy heroes, smilingly spoke these words, free from any sign of weakness:
"O hero, O best of Gandharvas, you ought to release our brothers."
"For these Pāṇḍavas are still alive, it is not right for me to suffer such an insult.
Thus addressed by the high-souled Pāṇḍava, the Gandharva said:
"O Karṇa, we have come forth after deliberating upon this matter."

"We shall see the Pāṇḍavas, who were once happy, now deprived of their wives; those who stood established in their kingdom, now fallen from their position and shorn of their splendor, while we ourselves are enveloped in glory"—
as these words were being uttered by the Gandharva, then...
Filled with shame, I sought a hole in the earth to enter.
Then the Gandharvas, together with the Pāṇḍavas, approached Yudhiṣṭhira and reported our ill-advised conduct to him, as well as that we had been bound.

In the presence of women, wretched, bound, and fallen under the power of my enemies, I have been brought before Yudhiṣṭhira; what indeed could be more painful than this? Those whom I have always treated with contempt, and who have always regarded me as their enemy—[how shall I face them?]
I, a man of evil intellect, was rescued by them, and my life was granted by them. O hero, had I met my death in that great battle,
it would have been better for me than this kind of life.
"May my fame be renowned upon the earth for the slaying of the Gandharva;
may I attain the meritorious worlds that are imperishable in the abode of Mahendra.
But hear now, O bulls among men, that which I have resolved to do today."
"I shall observe a fast unto death here; you all must indeed go home.
Let all my brothers also depart today toward the city, as well as Karna and all my other friends and kinsmen."
Placing Duḥśāsana at their head, let them depart today toward the city;
for I shall not return to the city, having been humiliated by my enemies,
after having been one who stripped the pride from my foes and restored the honor of my friends.
Granted, today at the head of the battle I have been humiliated by my enemies;
indeed, I have been addressed with various insults by my enemies and humiliated.
Without cause, I have been conquered and humiliated by my enemies.
Having become a source of grief to my friends and an increaser of joy for my enemies,
what shall I say when I reach the city named after the elephant?
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, Vidura, and likewise Saṃjaya— [what shall I tell them?]
Bāhlīka, Somadatta, and others who are esteemed by the elders— the Brahmins, the heads of guilds, and those who live as neutral mediators—
what will they say to me, and what shall I say in reply to them?
Having stood upon the heads of my enemies and likewise trampled upon their chests,
how shall I speak to them now, fallen through my own fault? For those who are ill-behaved, having attained prosperity, knowledge, and even sovereign power, [fall away].
O blessed lady, those who are intoxicated with pride like me do not remain for long.
Alas! How painful it is that I, through my own evil intellect and delusion, have committed such a wicked deed that I have now fallen into this state of peril.

Therefore, I shall resort to fasting unto death, for I shall not be able to live. For what conscious man could live, having been dragged from distress by his enemies, mocked by his foes, and stripped of his honor and manliness?
He was looked upon with contempt by the Pāṇḍavas, who were rich in prowess.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus overcome by anxiety, he then spoke to Duḥśāsana.
"O Duḥśāsana, descendant of Bharata, listen to these words of mine:
accept this consecration bestowed by me and become king;
rule over the prosperous earth, protected by Karṇa and Saubala."
Protect your brothers with confidence, as the slayer of Vṛtra protects the Maruts;
let your kinsmen depend upon you, as the gods depend upon Śatakratu. Always provide for the livelihood of the Brahmins without negligence.
May you always be a refuge for your kinsmen and friends;
may you look upon your relatives as Viṣṇu looks upon the hosts of gods. Your elders must be protected by you; go, protect the earth!
Gladdening all his friends and intimidating his enemies,
he embraced him by the neck and said, "You may go.
Hearing those words of his, the dejected Duḥśāsana spoke.

With a throat choked with tears, afflicted by great sorrow, and bowing down with palms joined in reverence, he addressed these words in a faltering voice to his eldest brother: "Be gracious!"— and with a grieving heart, he fell upon the ground.
Distressed, shedding tears from his eyes at his feet, that tiger among men said: "This shall not come to pass;
the earth with its mountains might shatter, and the sky itself might split asunder."
The sun might abandon its own radiance, the moon its cool-rayed nature,
the wind its swiftness, and even the Himavat mountain might wander away;
the water in the oceans might dry up, and even fire might relinquish its heat.
"And I, O King, could not rule the earth without you.
Again and again he spoke these words: "Be gracious!"—O King, you who cause sorrow to your enemies and destroy the grief of your friends.
"You alone shall be the king in our lineage for a hundred years.
Having spoken thus, O Indra among kings, he wept aloud,
grasping the feet of his elder brother, who was worthy of honor, O Bhārata.
Seeing Duḥśāsana and Suyodhana thus afflicted with grief,
Karṇa, overcome with distress, approached them and addressed them:
"O Kauravas, why do you despair like two ignorant commoners?"
Grief never ceases for anyone who grieves;
and since grief does not remove the calamity of one who mourns,
what efficacy do you see in grieving for that which is already being grieved over?
"Take heart; do not grieve for your enemies, for you will not bring them joy.
Being steadfast, you would have conquered the enemies, but by grieving, you did not achieve it. O King, the Pandavas have indeed performed what was to be done: your liberation."
Those who dwell within the king's realm must always do what is pleasing to him;
for while being protected by you, they live free from all anxiety. Since this is the case, you ought not to harbor resentment like an ordinary man.
Your uterine brothers are despondent now that you have resolved upon fasting unto death;
therefore, O lord of men, enough of making all these people sorrowful.
Therefore, O lord of men, enough of making all these people sorrowful.
"Arise, go; may it be well with you! Console your brothers.
O King, today I perceive your lack of fortitude here, as well as the meagerness of your intellect and your lack of discernment regarding what must be done."
"O hero, O crusher of enemies, what is there to marvel at in this, that you have been liberated by the Pāṇḍavas? You have immediately fallen under the power of your enemies,
O Kauravya, as well as of those who live by arms and those dwelling within your realm."
Whether known or unknown, one must perform what is pleasing to the king.
Generally, leading men agitate the enemy host;
they are captured in battles and then released by their own soldiers.
"And those men who live by the army in the king's realm—
having joined with them for the sake of the king, they should strive according to what is right.
If it is thus, O King, that those living in your realm [should act] toward the Pāṇḍavas..."
"Since you have been liberated today by chance, what cause for lamentation is there?
And it was not right, O King, O best of monarchs, that the Pāṇḍavas did not follow behind you as you set out with your own army."
Those who were heroes, powerful, and never retreating in battles—
having previously arrived as messengers to your assembly—
they now see you enjoying the very jewels belonging to the sons of Pāṇḍu even today.
"Behold the Pāṇḍavas established in their strength; they have not sat down to fast unto death.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, enough of this resolve to sit in fasting;
arise, O King—may prosperity be yours—you ought not to give way to anxiety."

"O King, those dwelling within the realm of a monarch must necessarily act in accordance with what is pleasing to him; what cause for lamentation is there in that? O Indra among kings, if you do not act according to these words of mine,"
"O crusher of enemies, I shall remain here, serving at your feet.
O bull among men, I do not have the strength to live deprived of you. But if I were to sit in fasting unto death, O King, I would become an object of ridicule for other kings."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been thus addressed by Karṇa, King Duryodhana then did not even set his mind on rising, for he was resolved upon heaven.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Śakuni Saubala, O King, spoke consolingly to the indignant King Duryodhana as he sat in a vow of fasting unto death.
"O Kaurava, what Karṇa said was indeed spoken rightly; have you not heard it?
Why, out of delusion, do you wish to cast away your life through lack of understanding, O best of kings, having abandoned the flourishing prosperity that I brought back?"
And today I also understand that you have not served the elderly,
since you do not restrain the joy or the dejection that has arisen within you;
such a person perishes even after attaining prosperity, like an unbaked earthen vessel in water.
O Bhārata, prosperity never attends that man who fails to restrain the grief that has come upon him— such a person as one who is excessively timid, overly weak, procrastinating, and negligent.
Prosperity does not attend a king who is overcome by vice and seized by sensual objects.
Since you were honored [when you acted rightly], how could there be grief when things have turned out otherwise?
Do not destroy the noble deed performed by the sons of Pṛthā by succumbing to sorrow.

"O Indra among kings, where you ought to feel joy and where the Pāṇḍavas deserve to be honored, there you grieve; this behavior of yours is contrary to what is right. Be gracious, do not abandon yourself, and being satisfied, remember your own good deeds."

"Bestow the kingdom upon the sons of Pṛthā; attain glory and righteousness. By recognizing this duty, you will not be ungrateful. Establish brotherly affection with the Pāṇḍavas and settle them accordingly."
"Bestow upon them their paternal kingdom, and thereby you shall attain happiness.
Having heard the words of Śakuni and having looked at Duḥśāsana— the hero who had fallen at his feet, overwhelmed by brotherly affection— [Duryodhana spoke].
Lifting up Duḥśāsana, the subduer of enemies, with his well-formed arms,
he embraced him and affectionately smelled the crown of his head;
then, remembering the words of Karṇa and the son of Subala, he—
Then King Duryodhana, having reached a state of supreme despondency,
his soul overwhelmed with shame, fell into utter despair;
and hearing this from his friends, he spoke these words in great anger.

"I have no need for the wealth of dharma, nor for happiness, nor for sovereignty, nor for command, nor even for enjoyments; do not obstruct me, go! This resolve of mine is firm, fixed upon fasting unto death."
"Go all of you to the city; my elders are worthy of worship.
Thus addressed, they replied to the king, the crusher of enemies:
"O Indra among kings, O Bhārata, whatever destiny awaits you shall be ours as well."
"Or how shall we enter the city deprived of you?
Though he was addressed in many ways by his friends, ministers, brothers, and kinsmen, he did not waver from his resolve.
Having spread a mat of *darbha* grass with firm resolve, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
having touched water and become pure, took his place upon the ground,
wearing garments of *kuśa* grass and bark, and established himself in the highest discipline.
Restraining his speech, that tiger among kings, desiring the path to heaven,
performed mental worship and cast aside all external activities;
having made a firm resolve, he then remained in the vow of fasting unto death (*prāyopaveśa*).
Then, having understood his resolve, the fierce Daityas and Dānavas dwelling in Pātāla— who had previously been defeated by the gods—
realized that Duryodhana’s own faction was indeed facing destruction.
Then, those experts in mantras performed the rites arising from the Vaitāna ritual for the purpose of summoning him, using the mantras spoken by Bṛhaspati and Uśanas,
as well as those proclaimed in the Atharvaveda and the rituals prescribed in the Upaniṣads.
Then those women, joined with the chanting of mantras, performed the rite;
with great concentration, they offered oblations of milk into the fire according to the mantras— Brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences and were firm in their vows.

Then, O lord of men, while that sacrifice of the Dānavas was proceeding, the Adhvaryu priests set their ritual work in motion. As that rite reached completion, a most wonderful being, yawning there, appeared.
O King, a magical spirit (*kṛtyā*) arose and said, "What shall I do? Then the Daityas, with hearts full of joy, spoke to that magical spirit,
who had extremely sharp tips on her teeth, was radiant, and had flaming hair.
"Bring King Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son here while he is sitting in the fast unto death.
Having promised "So be it," that *kṛtyā* then departed;
and in the blink of an eye, she arrived at the place where King Suyodhana was.
Having taken the king with him, he entered the subterranean realm (rasātala) and,
within a moment, announced that he had brought him to the Dānavas.
Seeing the king brought there at night, the Dānavas gathered together.
With joyful minds and eyes slightly dilated,
they all then firmly embraced him, inquired after his welfare,
and spoke these words with pride to Duryodhana:
The Dānavas said:
"O Suyodhana, O Indra among kings, O upholder of the lineage of the Bharatas,
you who are constantly surrounded by heroes as well as by high-souled men!"
"Why have you committed this rash act of fasting unto death?
For one who abandons his own life falls into reproach and incurs disgraceful infamy.
Indeed, [one should not engage] in actions that are contrary to duty and fraught with many dangers."
"O King, wise men like you do not attach themselves to those who strike at the very root; restrain this mind of yours, which destroys dharma, artha, and sukha,
which slays fame, majesty, and fortitude, and which increases the joy of your enemies."

"Listen, O Lord, to the truth regarding your own divinity, O King, and concerning the creation of this body; then, regain your fortitude. Long ago, you were obtained by us from the gods through our ascetic penance, [specifically] from Maheśvara."
Your entire upper body was fashioned from masses of adamant,
impenetrable by missiles or weapons; yet your lower body, O sinless one,
was made of flowers by the Goddess, enchanting women with its beauty.
"O best of kings, thus your body is joined with Īśvara;
and by the Goddess as well, O tiger among kings, you are indeed divine and not human.
And the Kṣatriyas of great heroism, led by Bhagadatta—"

Those heroes, skilled in divine weapons, who will cast aside even their compassion for the sake of gods and fight against their enemies, shall destroy your foes. Therefore, enough of your despondency; no fear exists for you.
For indeed, those heroic Dānavas have been born on earth for the sake of assisting you;
other Asuras as well will enter into Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and others,
and possessed by them, they will cast aside compassion and fight against your enemies.

O best of the Kurus, when they are about to strike in battle, they will not spare their sons, nor their brothers, nor their fathers, nor their kinsmen; neither their disciples, nor their relatives, nor the young, nor the old.
Devoid of affection and possessed by demons, when their inner selves are overwhelmed,
these tigers among men will cast affection far away and joyfully strike at their own kinsmen with defiled minds.
Deluded by ignorance and driven by the destiny ordained by fate,
they addressed one another, saying: "You shall not escape from me alive,
even as you discharge all your weapons and missiles, standing firm in your manliness."
Boasting, O best of the Kurus, they will cause the destruction of men;
yet those high-souled Pāṇḍavas, endowed with divine power and great strength, will fight back according to their ability and bring about their slaughter.
O King, the hosts of Daityas and Rakshasas, having been born from the womb of Kshatriyas,
will fight with prowess against your enemies in battle,
using maces, clubs, swords, and various other weapons.
Those heroes of great strength will strike at your enemies;
and as for that fear within you, O hero, arising from Arjuna,
we have indeed devised a means for the slaying of Arjuna.
The soul of the slain Naraka has taken refuge in the form of Karna;
remembering that enmity, O hero, he will fight against Keśava and Arjuna. That man, arrogant in his prowess, will defeat the son of Pṛthā in battle.
Karna, the best among strikers and a great chariot-warrior, will overcome all his enemies; however,
knowing this, the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) will, for the sake of protecting Savyasacin, take away Karna’s earrings and armor by means of a stratagem.
Therefore, hundreds of thousands of Daityas and Rākṣasas have been appointed by us for this purpose;
those who are known as the Saṃśaptakas will slay the hero Arjuna— do not grieve.
"O King, this earth shall be enjoyed by you without rivals through me;
do not lead us into despair, for this is not fitting for you. O Kaurava, if you were to perish, our own faction would be diminished."
"Go, O hero; you must not entertain any other thought whatsoever.
You are our constant refuge, as are the Pāṇḍavas for the gods.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Having spoken thus, the Daityas embraced that elephant among kings; and having comforted that invincible one like a son, O Bhārata, those bulls among the Dānavas steadied his mind and spoke words of affection.
Having granted permission, saying, "Go, and may you attain victory," that very *kṛtyā* then brought back the mighty-armed one to that same place where he had previously sat down to fast unto death.
Having set down that hero and having fully honored the *kṛtyā*,
she, permitted by the king, vanished right there. Then,
when she had departed, King Duryodhana—
"O Bhārata, reflect that all this is like a dream; yet,
remembering those words spoken by the Dānavas,
the evil-minded one thought, 'I shall conquer the Pāṇḍus in battle.'"
Suyodhana considered Karṇa and the Saṃśaptakas to be both intent on and capable of slaying Pārtha, the destroyer of enemies;
such was the firm hope of that evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
O bull of the Bharatas, during the conquest of the Pāṇḍavas,
Karṇa— his mind and soul possessed by the inner self of Naraka—
then formed a cruel resolve for the slaughter of Arjuna.
And those heroic Saṃśaptakas, their minds possessed by Rākṣasas and overwhelmed by passion and darkness, were intent on the slaughter of Phalguna; likewise,
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the others had their minds overcome by Dānavas.

O lord of the people, King Suyodhana was not so affectionate toward the sons of Pāṇḍu; nor did he tell this to anyone— that which had been told to him at night by the Dānavas through the agency of Kṛtyā, concerning what was unrighteous.
At the end of the night, Karṇa Vaikartana, having joined his palms as if smiling, spoke these reasoned words to King Duryodhana:
"One who is dead does not conquer enemies; one who lives beholds prosperity."
"O descendant of Kuru, what blessings can there be for one who is dead, and whence can there be victory?
This is no time for despondency, nor for fear, nor even for death.
Having said this, that mighty-armed one embraced him with both his arms.
"Arise, O King! Why do you lie there? Why do you grieve, O slayer of enemies?
Having scorched your foes with your prowess, how can you wish for death? Or has fear arisen in you upon seeing the valor of Arjuna?"
"I promise you truly: I shall slay Arjuna in battle when the thirteenth year has passed; I swear this by my weapon. O lord of men, I will bring the sons of Pṛthā under your control."
Thus addressed by Karṇa, as well as by the words of the Daityas and the prostrations of the others, Suyodhana rose up;
having heard those words of the Daityas and fixed his mind firmly within his heart.
Then that tiger among men marshalled his army,
thick with chariots, elephants, and horses, and crowded with foot soldiers; O King, that great host set forth like the current of the Gaṅgā.
With white umbrellas, banners, and very pale fly-whisks,
and crowded with chariots, elephants, and infantry, that [army] shone exceedingly,
like the autumnal sky when the thick mass of clouds has vanished and it is yet indistinct.
Crowded with rows of swans and graced by wandering cranes, Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the lord of men, was praised like a supreme sovereign with blessings of victory by the best of the twice-born,
while receiving garlands of joined palms.
Suyodhana went at the head, blazing with supreme splendor,
O king of kings, together with Karṇa and the gambler Saubala;
and all his brothers, Duḥśāsana and the others, followed him.
They were met by the Kurus, as well as by the citizens and the Brahmins—
Bhūriśravas, Somadatta, and the great king Bāhlika—
on chariots of various forms, as well as on horses and excellent elephants.
As that lion among kings departed, the best of the Kurus followed him;
in a short time, O King, they all entered their own city with joyful hearts, led by Duryodhana.
Janamejaya said:
O best of beings, while those high-souled sons of Pṛthā were dwelling in that forest,
what did the great archers, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, do?
"Karna Vaikartana, the mighty Shakuni, as well as Bhishma, Drona, and Kripa— you should explain that to me. Vaishampayana said:
When the Pārthas had thus departed and Suyodhana,
having been liberated by the sons of Pāṇḍu, had returned to Hastināpura,
Bhīṣma spoke these words to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Great King.
"O dear one, I told you previously as you were departing for the penance grove:
'My going there is not pleasing to me,' yet you did not do so.
Therefore, O hero, you have been captured by your enemies through force."
And you were rescued by the Pāṇḍavas, who know the dharma, yet you feel no shame, O lord of the people, son of Gāndhārī! Even before your very eyes, along with your army,
the Sūta’s son fled in fear from the battle with the Gandharvas at that time.
O Indra among kings, O prince, as you and your army were crying out,
he departed from behind, looking back at you again and again;
thus was the prowess of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas witnessed by you.
O mighty-armed one, regarding Karna, the evil-minded son of a Sūta,
he does not possess even a quarter of the qualities of the Pāṇḍavas, O best of kings—
whether in the science of archery, in heroism, or in righteousness, O lover of dharma.
"Therefore, O best among those who know the art of peace, I consider it appropriate for you to make peace with those high-souled Pāṇḍavas for the sake of the prosperity of this lineage.
When he had been thus addressed by Bhīṣma, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men—
Laughing, O King, he suddenly departed along with the son of Subala.
Knowing that he had set out, Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and the other great archers followed the mighty son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Seeing them thus departed, O King, Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kurus,
overcome with shame and embarrassment, went to his own residence.
When Bhīṣma had gone, O great king, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men—

Returning once more to that place, O Bhārata, he consulted with his ministers: "What would be for our welfare? What task remains to be done? How indeed might it be well-performed? Thus he deliberated.
Karna said:
"O Duryodhana, O Kaurava, listen to this which I shall say to you:
Bhishma always censures us and praises the Pandavas."
O mighty-armed lord of men, because of his hatred for you, he also hates me;
and in your presence, O ruler of men, he constantly reviles me. Therefore, O Bhārata, I cannot endure those words of Bhīṣma here.
O crusher of enemies, O King, descendant of Bharata, that which was spoken by Bhīṣma in your presence— concerning the fame of the Pāṇḍavas and your own reproach—
grant me leave, O King, along with my servants, forces, and vehicles.

"O King, I shall conquer the earth with its mountains, forests, and groves. Though the earth has been conquered by the four powerful Pāṇḍavas, I alone shall win it back from them; of this there is no doubt."
Let the evil-minded Bhīṣma, the lowest of the Kuru lineage, behold this;
for he who censures the blameless and praises the unworthy shall today witness my power and condemn himself.
"Grant me leave, O King, for your victory is certain.
I swear this truth to you, O King, by touching my weapon.
Having heard these words of Karṇa, O King, bull of the Bharatas, [Duryodhana was filled with joy].
Filled with supreme joy, the lord of men said to Karṇa:
"I am blessed, I am favored, since you, O one of great strength, always abide in my welfare; today my birth has become fruitful."
"And when you consider yourself, O hero, capable of destroying all enemies, then depart— may prosperity be yours— and instruct me.
Thus was Karṇa addressed by the wise son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
The subduer of enemies gave all necessary orders for the expedition; and that great archer set forth under an asterism presided over by auspicious deities,
on a favorable lunar day and at a propitious hour, while being honored by the twice-born.
Having bathed with auspicious and pure rites and being honored with sacred words,
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Making the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, resound with the roar of his chariot."
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, the great archer Karṇa, surrounded by a vast army, besieged the beautiful city of Drupada;
and through a great battle, he brought that hero under his control.
O best of kings, having conquered Drupada, that lord of men caused him to pay tribute consisting of gold, silver, and various kinds of jewels, as well as taxes;
and those kings who were his followers likewise paid him tribute.
He brought them all under his control and made them pay tribute;
then, having gone to the northern direction, he brought the lords of men there under his sway. Having conquered Bhagadatta as well, the son of Rādhā ascended the mountain.
While fighting with his enemies, he went to the great mountain Himavat;
he traversed all directions and brought all the kings under his control.
Having conquered those of the Himalayas, he made them all pay tribute.
He conquered those kings who were in the realm of Nepal;
then, having descended from that mountain, he rushed toward the eastern direction,
[subduing] the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, Śuṇḍikas, and Mithilas.
Having settled the Magadhas and the Karkakhaṇḍas within his own domain,
he conquered the Āvaśīras, the Yodhyas, and Ahikṣatra;
having thus completely subdued the eastern quarter, he proceeded to the land of Vatsa.
Having completely conquered Vatsabhūmi and the entire Mṛttikāvatī,
as well as Mohana, Pattana, Tripurī, and Kosala—
having subdued all these, he took tribute from them in every way.
Taking his stand in the southern direction and having defeated the great car-warriors, Karṇa,
the son of the Sūta, engaged Rukmin in battle among the southerners.
Having fought a tumultuous battle, Rukmin spoke to the son of the Sūta.
"I am pleased with your valor and strength, O Indra among kings.
I shall not create an obstacle for you; I have fulfilled my promise. Out of affection, I grant you as much gold as you desire."
Having met with Rukmin, Karṇa went to Pāṇḍya and Śaila;
he also encountered the king of Kerala in battle, as well as Nīla,
the son of Veṇudāri, and other foremost among kings.
In the southern direction, he caused all the kings to pay tribute;
then, having gone to the son of Śiśupāla, the delighter of the Sūtas conquered him,
and that one of great strength brought even the neighboring kings under his control.
O bull of the Bharatas, having brought the people of Avanti under his control through conciliation,
he joined with the Vṛṣṇis and conquered the western region as well,
reaching as far as the Yavanas and the Barbaras.

Having conquered the entire earth— east, west, south, and north— the hero caused the kings situated in the western lands, along with the Mlecchas, forest-dwellers, and those living in the mountains, to pay tribute.
Having conquered all the Bhadras, Rohitakas, Āgneyas, and Mālavas, as well as all the tribal confederacies, the son of the Sūta, acting with policy as if smiling,
defeated the Śaśakas and the Yavanas.
Having conquered the hosts of great chariot-warriors headed by Nagnajit,
that great car-warrior, having thus brought the entire earth under his control and having triumphed,
that tiger among men returned to the city named after the elephant (Hastinapura).
O great king, when that mighty archer, who graces the battlefield, had arrived, the lord of men, Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, together with his brothers, father, and kinsmen,
went out to meet him and honored Karṇa according to the prescribed rites.
And the lord of men, being delighted, proclaimed that deed:
"That which I did not obtain from Bhīṣma, nor from Droṇa, nor from Kṛpa, nor from Bāhlika—may you have prosperity; for that has indeed been obtained by me from you."
What is the use of saying more? Listen to my words, O Karna:
I am well-provided with a protector, O mighty-armed one, you being my protector, O best of men;
for all those Pāṇḍavas are not worth even a sixteenth part of you.
Or other kings, O tiger among men, who have risen to ever-greater eminence— O Karna, great archer, look upon Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the illustrious Gāndhārī as Indra looks upon Aditi.
Then, O lord of the people, a tumultuous roar arose, and many cries of "Alas! Alas! were heard in the city named after the elephant. Some praised him, while others censured him.
O lord of men, other kings there likewise remained silent.
Having thus conquered, O Indra among kings, Karṇa— the best of weapon-bearers—
[subjugated] the earth with its mountains, forests, and sky, along with its oceans and pleasure gardens.

O Lord of the Earth, having brought the kings under his control in no very long time, he [ruled] the earth— which was filled with various high and low regions, as well as towns and cities, and islands abounding in marshlands.
Taking that inexhaustible wealth, the son of the Sūta approached the king;
and having entered the inner apartments of the palace, O King, subduer of enemies,
that hero beheld Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with Gāndhārī.
Like a son, O tiger among men, that knower of dharma grasped Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s feet;
and having been embraced by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he was dismissed with affection.
From that time forward, both the king and Śakuni, the son of Subala, [remained devoted].
Vaiśampāyana said:
O Bhārata, they believed that the sons of Pṛthā had been defeated by Karṇa in battle;
yet, O King, lord of men, the Sūta’s son had actually conquered the entire earth.
The slayer of enemy heroes spoke these words to Duryodhana:
"O subduer of foes, having heard all that, you ought to act accordingly. O hero, O best of kings, today the earth is yours, free from rivals."
"Protect her, O high-minded one, as Śakra did after his enemies were slain.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been thus addressed by Karṇa, the king spoke again to Karṇa.
"Nothing whatsoever is difficult for him to attain, O bull among men, who has you as his companion—you who are devoted to him and ready to exert yourself for my sake.
However, I have a certain intention; listen to it exactly as it is."
"Having seen that best of sacrifices, the Rājasūya of the Pāṇḍava, a longing has arisen within me; fulfill it, O son of a Sūta! Having been addressed thus, Karṇa then spoke this to the king.
"O best of kings, today all the rulers of the earth are under your command.
Let the foremost of the twice-born be summoned, and let the necessary materials be gathered according to the rules,
O best of the Kurus, as well as the implements for the sacrifice."

"O King, O subduer of enemies, let the invited officiating priests, who have mastered the Vedas as prescribed, perform the ritual according to the scriptures. Let it be provided with abundant food and drink, and endowed with all excellent qualities."
"O bull of the Bharatas, let the great sacrifice proceed for you as well.
O lord of the people, having been addressed thus by Karṇa, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra summoned his domestic priest and spoke these words.
"Perform for my sake the Rājasūya, the best of sacrifices, which is completed with excellent sacrificial fees, according to the rules and in due order.
Thus addressed, that bull among the twice-born spoke to the king.
Accompanied by the wise brahmins who had assembled there, he said:
"O best of the Kauravas, O supreme among kings, as long as Yudhiṣṭhira lives, it is not possible for that most excellent of sacrifices to be performed within your lineage."
"Your father Dhṛtarāṣṭra indeed lives a long life;
therefore, O best of kings, this sacrifice of yours is contrary to that.
However, O Lord, there exists another great sacrificial session equal to the Rājasūya."
Therefore, O Indra among kings, perform that sacrifice and listen to these words of mine: "O King,
let these rulers of the earth who pay tribute to you deliver their taxes, both gold in its wrought and unwrought forms."
"Therefore, O best of kings, let a plough be prepared for you today;
let the ground of your sacrificial enclosure be ploughed with it, O Bhārata.
There, O foremost of monarchs, let the sacrifice be performed, well-prepared and provided with abundant food."
"Let it proceed according to the rule, for it is indeed unimpeded in every respect. This sacrifice of yours, named Vaiṣṇava, is worthy of virtuous men;
no one except the ancient Viṣṇu has ever performed it."
This great sacrifice vies with the Rājasūya, the best of rituals. It pleases us and will surely bring you prosperity, O Bhārata;
may it proceed without obstacle and may your desire bear fruit.
"Therefore, O mighty-armed one, let this sacrifice of yours proceed.
Thus addressed by those brahmins, the lord of the earth, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
spoke these words to Karṇa, Saubala, and his brothers.
"The entire speech of the Brahmins pleases me, there is no doubt; if it also pleases you, then tell me that without delay. Thus addressed, they all said "So be it" to the lord of men.

Then the king gave instructions to the officials in their proper order; all the artisans were likewise commanded to prepare the plough. O best of kings, everything was carried out exactly as instructed and in due sequence.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then all the artisans and the foremost ministers,
as well as the highly wise Vidura, reported [the matter] to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"O King, O Bhārata, the most excellent sacrifice is prepared and the time has arrived;
and a divine golden plough, of immense value, has been fashioned.
Having heard this, O lord of people, the best of kings, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—
The king gave the command to commence the performance of that sovereign sacrifice.
Thereupon the sacrifice proceeded, well-prepared and provided with abundant food;
and the son of Gāndhārī, having been initiated, performed the rites according to the scriptures and in due order.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra was overjoyed, as were the highly illustrious Vidura,
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, and the renowned Gāndhārī.
He then dispatched swift-moving messengers for the purpose of issuing invitations.
O king of kings, those messengers with swift mounts set out for the kings and likewise for the brahmins as they had been directed.
But as one messenger was departing, Duḥśāsana spoke to him.

"Go quickly to the Dvaitavana forest and invite those sinful Pāṇḍavas, as well as the brahmins in that great forest, according to the proper custom. Having gone to the abode of the Pāṇḍavas, he bowed down to them and spoke.
O great king, Duryodhana, the best of monarchs and joy of the Kurus, is performing a sacrifice after having acquired a vast wealth of riches earned by his own prowess;
kings and Brahmins are coming there from every direction.
"But I have been sent, O King, by the high-souled Kaurava;
the king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of men, invites you:
you ought to go to see that sacrifice which is the king's heart's desire."
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, that tiger among kings, having heard those words spoken by the messenger, said: "By good fortune, King Suyodhana—
the enhancer of his ancestors' fame— is performing the foremost of sacrifices."
"We too shall come, but not at this time by any means;
our agreement must be observed until the thirteenth year.
Having heard these words of the King of Dharma, Bhīma spoke.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the Dharmarāja, shall go forth;
when the lord of men casts him into the fire kindled by missiles and weapons at the sacrifice of battle, after thirteen years have passed.
"When the Pāṇḍava offers the oblation of his wrath upon the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
then you must say to that Suyodhana, 'He will come.
But as for the remaining Pāṇḍavas, O King, they did not say anything unpleasant."
And the messenger reported everything as it had happened to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Then the best of men, the lords of various realms,
and highly fortunate Brahmins arrived at the city of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son.
O lord of men, having been honored according to the scriptures, according to their respective classes, and in due order, they were filled with supreme joy and affection;
and Dhṛtarāṣṭra also, O king of kings, was surrounded by all the Kauravas.
Seeing all the kings who had arrived, the high-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was filled with great joy and addressed Vidura:
"O Kṣattṛ, let every person here be happy, provided with food."
"And let it be arranged so that he may quickly be satisfied at the site of the sacrifice.
Thus commanded, O subduer of enemies, the wise Vidura, who knew the dharma, honored all the social orders according to their respective ranks.

With various kinds of food, both solid and soft, drinks, fragrant garlands, and diverse garments, he joyfully provided for them. Having performed the ritual bath (*avabhṛtha*) according to the scriptures and in the proper sequence, the hero—
Having performed the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), the high-minded King Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
that lord of kings, consoled them and bestowed various kinds of wealth,
and then dismissed the monarchs and the thousands of Brahmins.
Having dismissed the kings, he, surrounded by his brothers and accompanied by Karṇa and the son of Subala, entered Hastināpura.
Vaiśampāyana said:
As he entered, O Great King, the charioteers praised the Imperishable One;
and the people also praised that great archer, the best of kings.
Then the people scattered parched grain and sandalwood powder over him.
"By good fortune, O King, this sacrifice of yours has been completed without obstacle," they said.
But others there, who were talkative, said to that lord of the earth:
"Indeed, this sacrifice is not equal to the sacrifice of Yudhiṣṭhira."
"This [other sacrifice] does not equal even a sixteenth part of that sacrifice.
Thus some wandering mendicants spoke there to that lord of men;
however, his friends said there, "This sacrifice surpasses all others."
For this sacrifice was indeed inaugurated by the wise King Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
Yayāti, Nahuṣa, Māndhātṛ, and Bharata likewise—
having performed this sacrifice, they all became purified and went to heaven.
Hearing these auspicious words from his friends, O bull of the Bharatas,
the king entered the city and his own palace with a joyful heart. Then, O lord of the people, he paid homage at the feet of his mother and father.
Having saluted Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the wise Vidura, and being greeted in turn by his younger brothers— being himself devoted to his brothers—
he sat down upon a preeminent seat, surrounded by his brothers.
Rising up, O great king, the son of the Sūta spoke these words:
"By good fortune, O best of the Bharatas, this great sacrifice has been completed by you,
just as the Pārthas were slain in battle during the Rājasūya."
"O best of men, when he has been brought back, I shall honor you again.
To him, the highly illustrious Mahārāja Dhṛtarāṣṭra replied:
"O hero, this is true regarding those evil-minded Pāṇḍavas."

"O best of men, when those [enemies] have been slain and the great sacrifice, the Rājasūya, has been completed, O hero, you shall honor me once again. Having spoken thus, O Bhārata, the highly wise one embraced Karṇa.

The Kaurava king reflected upon the Rājasūya, the most excellent of sacrifices. That best of monarchs, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, spoke to his friends standing by his side— Rādheya, Saubala, and the others.
"O Kauravas, when shall I, having slain all the Pāṇḍavas, perform that most excellent and costly Rājasūya sacrifice? To him, Karṇa then said: "Listen to me, O elephant among kings."
I shall not wash my feet until Arjuna has been slain;
I shall not eat food prepared with sugar, and I shall observe the vow of an Asura:
when asked by anyone for anything, I shall never say "it does not exist."
Then a great shout was raised by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, those great car-warriors and mighty archers,
when Karṇa had vowed the slaughter of Phalguna in battle;
and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra considered the Pāṇḍavas already conquered.
Then, when the son of the Sūta had spoken, having undertaken his vow,
Duryodhana also, O king of kings, dismissed those bulls among men and entered his palace, as the glorious lord enters Caitraratha.
O Bhārata, all those great archers also went to their own homes;
and Karṇa, having gone to his own house, was filled with joy along with his kinsmen and bestowed wealth upon supplicants like a second Lord of Wealth.
O Great King, incited by the words of the messenger, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the other kings, as well as the Pāṇḍavas, those great archers,
each reflecting upon that very matter, found no happiness anywhere.
Furthermore, O Indra among kings,
the spies have reported the vow of the Sūta’s son regarding the slaughter of Vijaya.
Having heard this, O lord of men, the son of Dharma was deeply agitated.
Considering Karna of wondrous prowess to be clad in impenetrable armor,
and remembering his own afflictions, he found no peace;
with his face cast downward, he stood for a long time, pondering what ought to be done.

As that high-souled one was overwhelmed by anxiety, the thought arose in his mind to abandon the Dvaitavana forest, which was infested with many beasts of prey and wild animals. Meanwhile, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra continued to rule over the earth.
Together with his heroic brothers, as well as Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Kṛpa,
he met with Karṇa, the son of a Sūta who shines in battle,
and was constantly pleased by the gambler Saubala.
King Duryodhana, ever devoted to what was pleasing [to his brothers],
honored the foremost of brahmins with sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
and that scorcher of foes, O King, performed what was most dear to his brothers.
Having resolved in his mind that wealth is for the fruit of what has been given or enjoyed, the hero spoke.
Janamejaya said:
"After having liberated Duryodhana, the mighty sons of Pāṇḍu..."
"What did they do in that forest? You ought to tell me that.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Then, while the son of Kuntī was sleeping at night in the Dvaitavana forest, the deer—"
At the end of their dream, with throats choked with tears, they showed themselves to Yudhiṣṭhira.
To them, as they stood trembling with palms joined in reverence, that lord of kings said:
"Speak what you desire to say; who are you, and what is it that you seek?"
Thus addressed by the illustrious Pāṇḍava, the son of Kuntī,
the deer who had survived that slaughter replied there to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O Bhārata, we are the deer remaining from the slaughter in the Dvaitavana forest."

"O Great King, let us not perish; let the turn for our stay be made. Your brothers are all heroes, skilled in every weapon, yet they have left only a few families remaining of those who dwell in the forest."
"O Mahāmati, we who remain here are like seeds;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, king of kings, may we flourish through your grace.
[He saw them] trembling, terrified, with only their seed-essence remaining.
Seeing the deer, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, was deeply afflicted with grief;
yet the king, who is devoted to the welfare of all beings, said to them, "So be it. "What you say is true," he replied, "and I shall do exactly as you have said."
Having awakened thus at the end of the night, that best of kings,
filled with compassion for the deer, spoke to his assembled brothers:
"During the night, I was addressed by the deer who had survived the slaughter at the conclusion of my dream."
"We have become emaciated; may it be well with you, let compassion be shown toward us.
They spoke the truth: "Compassion must be shown by us toward these forest-dwellers, for our own rain has been withheld for eight months while we have consumed them."
Arjuna said:
"O King, we are dependent upon you; do not hesitate in this matter. O Pārtha, wherever you think best, there we shall go."
Furthermore, let us spend these remaining nights sporting in the delightful Kāmyaka, that best of forests abounding in deer,
which is renowned as the head of the desert region near Lake Tṛṇabindu.
There we shall enjoy ourselves.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been thus addressed by the high-souled Pāṇḍava, those great-souled ones,
the Pāṇḍavas who were skilled in dharma, then departed swiftly.
O King, accompanied by brahmins and those who had lived with them there,
and followed by Indrasena and the other servants,
they then traveled along paths provided with excellent food and pure water.
They beheld the holy Kāmyaka hermitage, filled with ascetics;
then those Kauravas, surrounded by the foremost of Brahmins,
entered that forest like virtuous men entering heaven, O best of the Bharatas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O bull of the Bharata race, as those high-souled Pāṇḍavas dwelt in the forest,
eleven years passed by with great hardship.

For those supreme men, subsisting on fruits and roots though deserving of happiness, endured that highest suffering as they reflected upon the time that had come. But the royal seer Yudhiṣṭhira [endured] that which was born from the transgression of his own actions.
Reflecting upon the supreme suffering of his brothers, that mighty-armed king could not sleep in peace, as if darts had been driven into his heart;
for he contemplated at that time the wickedness arising from the game of dice.
Recalling the harsh words of the Sūta’s son, the Pāṇḍava Arjuna—
dejected, sighing heavily, and bearing the great poison of his wrath—
along with both the twins and the illustrious Draupadī, [remained there].
And that Bhīma, of great splendor and the strongest of them all,
gazing at Yudhiṣṭhira— who had long since become a knower of dharma— as if with resentment, then endured unsurpassed suffering.
Considering that only a short time remained, those bulls among men assumed,
as it were, another form through their displays of energy, indignation, and exertion.
Then, after some time had passed, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, arrived.
The great yogi arrived as an observer of the Pāṇḍavas. Seeing that he had come, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī,
went out to meet the high-souled one and received him according to the prescribed rites.
Sitting before him as he sat, desiring to hear his words with senses restrained,
the joy of the Pāṇḍavas gratified Vyāsa by prostrating himself;
he did so beholding those grandsons of his, emaciated and living on forest fare in the woods.
Out of compassion, the great seer spoke with a voice choked with tears:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, O mighty-armed one, best among the upholders of dharma, listen!
My son, those who have not performed austerities do not attain great happiness."
For a person experiences pleasure and pain in alternation;
no one, O bull among men, attains a state that is not subject to suffering at all. However, a wise man, endowed with supreme intelligence, [remains steadfast].

For one who knows the rising and setting [of all things] neither grieves nor exults; he should enjoy the happiness that comes and endure the suffering that arrives. He should wait for what is brought by time, just as a farmer waits for his crops.
There is indeed nothing superior to austerity; through austerity one attains greatness.
Know this, O Bhārata: there is nothing that cannot be accomplished by austerity.
Truth, straightforwardness, freedom from anger, sharing with others, self-restraint, and tranquility—these are the means.
Freedom from envy, non-violence, purity, and restraint of the senses—
these, O Great King, are the means for men of meritorious deeds. The foolish who delight in unrighteousness are destined for rebirth among the animals.
Having entered a miserable womb, people find no happiness.
This world, my dear, is the field of action; that other world is the field of fruition.
Whatever action is performed here, its result is experienced there.
When a tree is watered at its root, its fruit is seen upon the branches;
therefore, one should discipline the body through austerity and self-restraint,
and one should give according to one's ability, having honored and bowed down [to the recipient].
O King, one who gives at the proper time and to a worthy recipient with a joyful heart, free from envy,
truthful, and upright, shall obtain long life without hardship;
and being free from anger and malice, he attains supreme peace.

One who is self-controlled and ever devoted to tranquility does not experience affliction; nor does one whose soul is subdued suffer when seeing the prosperity of others. Such a man is a sharer with others, a giver, and possesses both enjoyments and happiness.
He becomes non-violent and attains supreme health; by honoring those worthy of honor, he obtains birth in a great family and finds ultimate happiness both in this world and in the next.

One who has conquered the senses does not encounter union with calamities; for even when joined with the law of time (death), his mind remains inclined toward auspicious latent tendencies, and through that connection, he is reborn with a truly virtuous disposition.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, O Great Sage, among the duties of charity and asceticism,
which is said to yield more merit after death, and which is considered more difficult to perform?"
Vyāsa said:
"There is nothing on earth more difficult than giving. For there is a great thirst for wealth, and it is acquired with hardship."
"O King, this is indeed seen directly before our eyes, witnessed by the world:
for the sake of wealth, heroic men enter into great battles, as well as the ocean and the forest, even abandoning their dear lives."
Those on earth who are skilled in the meaning of the treatises practice accordingly;
some men, however, practice agriculture and animal husbandry.
Some men go forth as servants seeking wealth;
yet the relinquishing of that which has been acquired with such hardship is extremely difficult.
Nothing is more difficult than giving; therefore, in my view, generosity is the highest good.

That gift is more difficult to perform; therefore, giving is distinguished. However, one should understand the distinction here: wealth acquired by righteous means should be bestowed upon worthy recipients at the proper place and time.

There is no end to what is given with faith and according to rule to a worthy recipient. But that gift of wealth which is performed through the duty of giving by means of riches acquired unjustly does not protect the doer from great fear.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, even a very small gift given at the proper time to a worthy recipient with a perfectly pure mind is recorded as having infinite fruit after death;
so it was for Mudgala, who was endowed with faith regarding the place, the time, and the recipient.

Having given away a *droṇa* measure of rice, he then attained the supreme state. In this regard, they cite this ancient history concerning the fruit that Mudgala obtained from the renunciation of a *droṇa* of rice.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How was that measure of rice (*vrīhidroṇa*) renounced by that great-souled one?
To whom was it given, O Blessed One, and by what rite? Tell me this."
"The Blessed One has directly perceived the Dharma; indeed, for one whose deeds have pleased him, I consider the birth of that practitioner of the true Dharma to be fruitful.
Vyāsa said:
O King, there lived in Kurukṣetra a righteous man named Mudgala, who subsisted by gleaning ears of grain and single grains, was firm in his vows, truthful in speech, free from malice,
devoted to guests, observant of sacred rites, and followed the way of life of a pigeon.
The great ascetic was performing the sacrificial session known as the *iṣṭīkṛta*. Together with his son and wife, that sage subsisted on food eaten only once every fortnight.
O great king, that high-souled sage remained firm in his vows.
For one fortnight, he earned a *droṇa* of rice by living like a pigeon; performing the *darśa* and *paurṇamāsa* sacrifices, free from all envy,
he sustained his body with the remnants of offerings to the gods and guests.

O great king, Indra himself, the lord of the three worlds, accompanied by the gods, personally accepted his share at every change of the moon. Having observed the time for the ritual, he lived according to the conduct of a sage.
With a joyful inner soul, he gave food to his guests. On that day, as the high-souled one, free from envy, gave away food measured by a *droṇa* of rice,
the remainder increased upon the sight of each guest.
Even hundreds of wise brahmins partake of that [food],
yet through the purity of the sage’s renunciation, that food increases. He heard of that most righteous Mudgala, who was firm in his vows.
Then, O King, Durvāsas, clad in the directions as his garment, approached him; wearing an irregular dress like a madman, O Pāṇḍava,
the sage, with disheveled hair, uttered various harsh words.
Then, having approached that brahmin, the best of sages said:
"O best of sages, know me to have arrived here seeking food.
Mudgala replied to the sage, "Welcome to you."

Having announced water for the feet and water for sipping, he who was firm in his vows, observing the discipline of hospitality, offered the finest food obtained through his ascetic power to the hungry madman,
relying upon supreme faith.
Then that very man, possessed by hunger and driven to madness, ate all of that delicious food; and Mudgala gave it to him. Having consumed all the food, he then [anointed] himself with the leftovers.
Smearing himself with the remainder, laughing, singing, and running about,
he danced and even rushed about as if driven by a deluded mind;
then, having smeared his limbs, he departed by the way he had come.
When the second auspicious festival day arrived in this manner, the wise sage,
having returned, ate all the food of those who lived by gleaning;
yet that silent sage, remaining without food himself, continued to gather gleanings once again.
Yet hunger was unable to bring about any change in that Mudgala;
neither anger, nor envy, nor contempt,
nor agitation entered that best of the twice-born as he gathered gleanings together with his son and wife.
In this manner, the sage Durvāsas,
having made a firm resolve, approached that best of sages who lived by the practice of gleaning at the proper times six times; yet the sage did not perceive even the slightest change in his mind.
He beheld the pure and stainless mind of that being of pure essence. Then, filled with joy, the sage spoke to Mudgala:
"In this world, there is no giver equal to you, who is free from all envy."

Hunger dispels the perception of dharma and takes away one's fortitude; the tongue, following after sense-objects, drags one toward flavors. Life-breath originates from food, and the mind is restless and difficult to restrain.
The one-pointed concentration of both the mind and the senses is indeed asceticism;
to renounce with a pure heart that which has been acquired through toil is difficult.
All of this, O virtuous one, has been properly accomplished by you.

"We are delighted and graced by meeting with you; for it is traditionally held that association with the virtuous always removes all sins. O Great Sage, I consider the sight of you to be the supreme purifier."
Victory over the senses, fortitude, generosity, self-restraint, tranquility,
compassion, truth, and righteousness— all these are established in you. By righteousness alone are all the worlds, including the moving and the unmoving, sustained.

O Brahmin, even the Dharma is upheld by you, whose self is endowed with steadfastness; possessed of a pure essence, there is no one else like you. By your deeds, the worlds have been conquered, and you have attained the supreme goal.
"O you whose vows are well-observed, a great cry of 'Ah, what a gift! has been raised for you by the inhabitants of heaven;
you shall go to heaven in your own body!"—even as the sage Durvāsas was speaking thus, at that time, [the king]...
The divine messenger appeared before Mudgala in a celestial chariot,
yoked with swans and cranes, garlanded with networks of tiny bells, moving at will, variegated, and likewise endowed with divine fragrance.
And he said to that brahmin-sage, "Ascend this celestial chariot won by your deeds;
you have attained supreme perfection, O sage. To the divine messenger who spoke thus, the rishi replied:
"I desire to hear from you the qualities of those who dwell in heaven.
What are the virtues of those living there, what is their austerity, and what is their resolve? O messenger of the gods, what is the bliss of heaven in heaven, and what is its defect?"
The virtuous, who are true to their lineage, say that friendship among the good is formed by walking seven steps together.
Out of respect for our friendship, O Lord, I ask you this:
tell me without hesitation what is both the truth and beneficial in this matter.
"Having heard this, I shall make a firm resolve according to your word.
The divine messenger said:
"O great seer, you have set your mind on what ought not to be done, since you reject the supreme happiness of heaven."
"What has been attained should be highly esteemed; yet you deliberate like one who is ignorant.
O Mudgala, there are delightful gardens such as Nandana and others, adorned on all sides with trees that bear the fruits of every desire."

O Sage, that world which is known as *svaḥ* is situated above; it is the upward-tending path of truth, constantly traversed by those who go to the gods. No man who has not practiced austerity, nor one who has not performed great sacrifices, reaches it.
O Mudgala, neither the untruthful nor the atheists go there; rather,
those who are righteous-souled, self-conquered, tranquil, self-controlled, free from envy,
devoted to the dharma of giving, and heroes marked by the signs of battle— such men go there.
Having performed the highest deeds characterized by tranquility and self-restraint, O Brahmin, they go there to the worlds of the merit-makers, frequented by virtuous men—
the gods, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the Maruts, together with the great ṛṣis.
O Maudgalya, the Yāmas, the Dhāmas, and likewise the Gandharvas and Apsarases—even for the gods, O Maudgalya, that supreme state is desired.
There is neither suffering nor unhappiness there; how, then, could there be passion or hatred, O Sage?
For each of these classes of gods, there are numerous,
radiant, and auspicious worlds, full of splendor and endowed with all objects of desire. The golden [palace] measures thirty-three thousand yojanas.
O Mudgala, there stands Meru, the king of mountains, where the divine gardens such as Nandana and others— sacred places of recreation for those of meritorious deeds— are located; there,
neither hunger nor thirst, nor exhaustion, nor fear of cold or heat exists.
There is nothing loathsome or impure there, nor any diseases whatsoever;
rather, there are pleasant fragrances everywhere and soft touches on all sides. O Sage, the sounds there are indeed captivating to the ear and agreeable to the mind from every direction.
There is neither sorrow nor old age there, nor exhaustion or lamentation.
Such is that world, O Sage, which has its cause in the fruits of one's own karma;
there, men are born by virtue of their own well-performed deeds.

The bodies of those who are reborn here, O Maudgalya, are composed of light and are born solely of karma; they are not born of a mother and father. Furthermore, there is neither sweat, nor foul odor, nor excrement, nor urine.
O Sage, dust does not soil their garments there;
their garlands, divine-scented and delightful, do not wither,
and they are carried about in celestial chariots, O Brahmin— such indeed are they.
Free from envy, grief, and fatigue, and devoid of delusion and avarice,
O great sage, those who have conquered heaven dwell there in happiness.
For such people as these, O bull among sages, [are the inhabitants] of those worlds.
Higher and higher than Śakra’s worlds are those endowed with divine qualities;
beyond that, the auspicious worlds of Brahmā consist of pure radiance,
where the ṛṣis go, O Brahmin, purified by their own virtuous deeds.
There, moreover, are others called the Ṛbhus, deities even among the gods;
their worlds are further beyond, and the deities here worship them.
Those supreme worlds are self-luminous, radiant, and fulfill all desires.
They suffer no torment caused by women, nor do they envy worldly sovereignty. They do not subsist on sacrificial oblations, nor are they consumers of ambrosia.
Likewise, they possess divine bodies, yet they do not have corporeal forms.

The eternal gods of gods do not desire pleasure for the sake of pleasure; they do not undergo change even through the revolutions of the kalpas. For them, whence could there be old age or death? Nor is there joy, affection, or worldly happiness.
"O Sage, there is neither suffering nor pleasure; how then could there be passion or hatred?
O Maudgalyāyana, even for the gods, that supreme state is desired;
it is an unsurpassed perfection difficult to attain, inaccessible to those within the sphere of sensual desires."
These are the thirty-three worlds; the remaining worlds are reached by the wise through excellent observances or through gifts preceded by ritual injunctions.
This very auspicious result, brought about by giving, has been attained here.
O Brahmin, enjoy that which was obtained through your good deeds, your splendor illumined by asceticism. This is the happiness of heaven, as well as its various worlds;
I have described to you the qualities of heaven—now learn from me its defects as well.
There, one experiences the fruit of the karma performed in heaven;
yet no other karma is performed there, for it is consumed by the cutting off of its very root.
In my view, this is the defect therein, as well as the subsequent fall at its conclusion.
O Mudgala, that falling from those whose minds are pervaded by happiness,
and that lack of contentment and the torment felt upon seeing more radiant splendors—
this is difficult for those situated in a lower station.
For those falling down, there is confusion of consciousness and an assault by dust; when the garlands have withered, then fear arises for one about to fall.
O Maudgalya, these terrible defects exist as far as the abode of Brahmā.
In the world of the gods, men who have performed meritorious deeds possess tens of thousands of virtues;
however, O Sage, there is this other, supreme virtue for those fallen from heaven:
through the connection with a residual merit (*śubhānuśaya*), they are reborn among human beings.
Even there, O highly fortunate one, he is born into a state of happiness;
yet, if he does not attain awakening there, he subsequently falls into a lower state.
Having gone there, others return, but the wise practitioners of yoga do not.
Whatever action is performed here is experienced in the next world;
this, O Brahmin, is considered the land of action, while that is the land of results.
All this which you asked me, O Mudgala, has been explained to you.
"O virtuous one, out of compassion for you, let us go quickly; do not delay.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words, Maudgalya reflected upon them with his intellect.
Having reflected, the best of sages said to the messenger of the gods:
"O messenger of the gods, salutations to you; go, dear one, as you please.
I have no need for heaven or its pleasures, which are fraught with great defects."
Falling from there is a great suffering, and the torment is most dreadful; since those who enjoy heaven must fall away from it here, I do not desire heaven.
I long for that place where, having gone, they do not grieve, do not suffer, nor waver.
"Therefore, I shall seek that state alone which is absolute.
Mudgala said:
"But these great defects of heaven have been described by you."
The divine messenger said:
"Tell me of that other world which is entirely free from fault;
