it is above the abode of Brahmā, that supreme station of Viṣṇu."

That which the wise know as the pure, eternal light, the supreme Brahman— O Brahmin, men whose souls are devoted to sense-objects do not go there, for they are assailed by hypocrisy, greed, great anger, delusion, and malice.
"Free from possessiveness, free from egoism, free from dualities, with senses restrained,
and devoted to the yoga of meditation— such men go there.
Having spoken these words, the sage dismissed that messenger of the gods.
Abandoning the practice of gleaning ears of grain, he established himself in supreme tranquility;
becoming one for whom blame and praise were equal, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as the same,
he became constantly devoted to meditation through the purity of the yoga of knowledge.

Having restrained the collection of his senses, he concentrated them within himself; with his mind thus disciplined, he then united himself with the Supreme Lord. Having gained strength through the yoga of meditation and attained unsurpassed supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), he—
He attained eternal perfection, the supreme state characterized by Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, you too ought not to grieve;
though fallen from a prosperous kingdom, you shall regain it through asceticism.
"Suffering follows happiness, and happiness follows suffering;
they revolve around a man in turn, like spokes upon the rim of a wheel.
O you of immeasurable prowess, you shall obtain the kingdom inherited from your father and grandfather."
"Let the fever of your mind depart after thirteen years have passed.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to the joy of the Pāṇḍavas, the blessed Vyāsa—
The wise one returned once more to the hermitage for the sake of ascetic penance.
Janamejaya said:
While those high-souled Pāṇḍavas were thus dwelling in the forest...

While they were delighting in various discourses with the sages, until the time for Draupadī’s meal— during which Sūryadatta provided inexhaustible food and they were gratifying the Brāhmaṇas who had arrived seeking alms.
O great sage, how did all those evil-natured sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, led by Duryodhana, behave toward them, even though they provided them with various kinds of meat from wild forest animals?
"Remaining under the counsel of Duḥśāsana, Karṇa, and Śakuni—
tell this, O Blessed One Vaiśampāyana, to me who asks.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O great king, having heard of their conduct as if they were living in a city, Duryodhana conceived a wicked intent toward them,
along with those such as Karṇa and Duḥśāsana, who were skilled in deceit.
While those evil-minded ones were contemplating various means to bring harm upon them,
the righteous ascetic of great renown named Durvāsas, accompanied by ten thousand disciples, arrived there at his will.
Seeing that most wrathful sage had arrived,
the illustrious Duryodhana, with a humble soul and accompanied by his brothers, honored him with hospitality through courtesy and self-restraint.
Standing like a servant, he himself worshipped him according to the prescribed rites. That best of sages remained there for several days,
and the king attended upon him day and night without weariness.
O great king, Duryodhana was apprehensive because of that curse;
he said, "I am hungry, O lord of men, give me food quickly!
Having spoken thus, he would go to bathe and indeed return after a long time.
Having said, "I shall not eat today; I have no hunger," he would vanish from sight.
Yet, returning suddenly, he would say with great haste, "Feed us! And sometimes, at the dead of night, he would rise up, intent on deception.
Having had food prepared as before, he did not eat it, censuring it;
while he remained thus, when King Duryodhana showed neither agitation nor anger, the sage then became satisfied.
And the invincible one said to him, "O Bhārata, I am the granter of boons;
choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever dwells in your heart. For when I am pleased, there is nothing consistent with dharma that cannot be obtained by you."
Having heard these words of that great seer of purified soul,
Suyodhana considered himself to have been born anew;
for this very matter had already been deliberated upon previously by Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and the others.
Having resolved that "the Sage, being pleased, is to be petitioned," the evil-minded king, filled with excessive joy, requested this boon:
"O Brahmin, just as you have become a guest to me along with your disciples..."
In our lineage, the great king Yudhiṣṭhira is the eldest and most excellent;
that righteous-souled one dwells in the forest surrounded by his brothers. He is virtuous and endowed with noble character; please become his guest.
And when that princess, delicate and illustrious,
that woman of excellent complexion, had fed all the twice-born and her husbands,
and having herself rested and eaten, was seated comfortably;
"If there is any favor to be granted by me, you should go there then.
Having spoken thus to Suyodhana, "I shall do so out of affection for you," Durvāsas, the best of Brahmins, departed from there just as he had come.
Then Suyodhana considered himself as one who had achieved his purpose;
and with great joy, grasping Karna’s hand with his own,
Karna also spoke to the king, who was accompanied by his brothers, out of delight.
"By good fortune, your desire has been fully realized; by good fortune, O Kaurava, you prosper.
By good fortune, your enemies have sunk into an insurmountable ocean of calamity;
the sons of Pāṇḍu have fallen into the fire born of Durvāsas’s wrath."
"By their own great sins, they have indeed gone to insurmountable darkness.
Thus, O King, were Duryodhana and the others, whose intellects were devoted to deceit.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Laughing and with joyful minds, they went each to his own abode. Then, on one occasion, the sage Durvāsas, knowing that the Pāṇḍavas were seated comfortably and that Kṛṣṇā was staying there in that forest after having eaten, [approached them].
He arrived surrounded by disciples numbering ten thousand.
Seeing that guest approaching, the illustrious King Yudhiṣṭhira,
remaining steadfast, went out to meet him together with his brothers.
Having properly seated him on an excellent seat with palms joined in reverence,
and having honored him according to the rules, he invited him with hospitality and said, "O Blessed One, having performed your daily rites, please come quickly."

And that sinless sage also went with his disciples to bathe, reflecting, "How might I feed my disciple together with them? Then the assembly of sages, composed in meditation, immersed themselves in the water.
In the meantime, O King, Draupadī, the best of women and devoted to her husbands, fell into deep anxiety on account of food. And as she reflected, she could find no means for obtaining food.
In his mind, he thought of Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of Kaṃsa:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, O imperishable son of Devakī! O Vāsudeva, Lord of the World, destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before you!"

O Soul of the universe, O Creator of the universe, O Destroyer of the universe, O Imperishable Lord! O Protector of those who have sought refuge, O Herdsman, O Protector of subjects, O Supreme beyond the supreme! I bow to You, the impeller of intentions and thoughts.
O most excellent one, O infinite giver of boons, become the refuge for those who have no other resort.
O Ancient Person, beyond the reach of vital breath, mind, mental activity, and the like;
O Overseer of all, O Supreme Overseer, I have come to you for refuge.
Protect me with compassion, O God, you who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge;
you who are dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with eyes as reddish as the interior of a lotus;
you who are clothed in yellow garments and adorned with the shining Kaustubha gem.
You are the beginning and the end of all beings; you alone are the supreme refuge.
You are the light higher than the highest, the soul of the universe, with faces turned in every direction.
They call you the supreme seed and the treasury of all prosperity.
O Lord of Gods, with you as my protector, there is indeed no fear of any calamities. Just as I was previously delivered from Duḥśāsana in the assembly hall,
so too should you lift me up from this present distress.
Thus praised then by Kṛṣṇā, the god who is affectionate toward his devotees—
the god of gods, the lord of the world, Keśava— perceiving the peril of Draupadī, the Lord left Rukmiṇī on her bed at his side.
Then the Lord of inconceivable movement arrived there in haste. Upon seeing him, Draupadī bowed with supreme joy and spoke to Vāsudeva regarding the arrival of the sage and other matters.
Then Kṛṣṇa said to her, "I am hungry and very distressed;
feed me quickly, O Kṛṣṇā, and afterwards you may do everything else.
Hearing those words, Kṛṣṇā was ashamed and spoke these words.
"O Lord, in this vessel given by Bhāskara, there was food until my meal;
but since I have eaten, O God, no food remains. Thereupon, the lotus-eyed Blessed One spoke to Kṛṣṇā.
"O Kṛṣṇa, this is no time for jesting while I am afflicted by hunger and fatigue;
go quickly, bring my cooking pot, and show it to me. Thus, at his persistent urging, that leader of the Yadus brought the pot.

Then, seeing the leafy vegetables clinging to the rim of the pot, Keśava, the Lord Hari, the Soul of the Universe and the enjoyer of sacrifice, partook of them and said to her: "May the God be pleased by this; may he be satisfied."
"Summon the sages quickly for their meal," he said. Thereupon,
the highly illustrious Sahadeva went in haste to the celestial river to invite the sages, beginning with Durvāsas, who had gone there to bathe.
Having descended into the water, they performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite; seeing the bubbles filled with the essence of *sāman* chants, and being endowed with supreme satisfaction,
they emerged from that water and beheld one another.
Looking toward Durvāsas, all those sages said:
"O brahmin-sage, since we have been made to prepare food by the king and have come here to bathe, we are already satiated up to our throats; what indeed shall we eat?"
Durvāsas said:
"We have prepared food in vain; what can we do about that?
By this futile preparation, a great offense has been committed against the royal sage."
"May the Pāṇḍavas not consume us with their very glance;
remembering the power of the wise royal seer Ambarīṣa, O Brahmins, I am exceedingly afraid of those people who have taken refuge at the feet of Hari."
And all the high-souled Pāṇḍavas were devoted to righteousness;
they were heroes, accomplished in learning, observant of vows, established in austerity,
ever delighted in virtuous conduct, and constantly dedicated to Vāsudeva.
"If enraged, they would surely consume you like fire consumes a heap of cotton.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, without even asking them, the disciples fled quickly.
Having been addressed thus by their preceptor, the sage, all those twice-born ones,
being greatly terrified of the Pāṇḍavas, fled in the ten directions;
Sahadeva, however, saw the best of sages at the Devanadī river.
He wandered here and there among the sacred fords, searching for her;
having heard from the ascetics dwelling there that they too had fled,
he approached Yudhiṣṭhira and reported the news to him.
Then all those Pāṇḍavas, desiring their return, remained there for some time with self-restrained minds, waiting; [for they thought:
"He will come at midnight and deceive us by surprise."
Seeing them thus absorbed in thought, sighing again and again, wondering, "How shall we escape from this hardship brought about by fate?",
the glorious Kṛṣṇa, having become manifest before them, spoke these words.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Pārthas, having learned of your calamity arising from the supreme wrath of the sage, I was thought of by Draupadī and have arrived here in haste."
Not even the slightest fear exists from that seer Durvāsas; terrified by your splendor, he fled long ago. Indeed, those who are ever devoted to righteousness never come to grief at any time.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"I take my leave of you; I shall depart. May prosperity surely attend you. Having heard these words of Keśava, their minds became composed.
Accompanied by Draupadī, the Pārthas, freed from their feverish distress, said to him:
"O Govinda, O Lord, with you as our protector, we have crossed over this insurmountable calamity,
like those who, while sinking in the great ocean, find a boat and reach the other shore."
"May it be well; accomplish your purpose; may prosperity be yours. Thus commanded, he departed for the city.
And the illustrious Pāṇḍavas, O Lord, together with Draupadī, dwelt with joyful hearts, wandering from forest to forest.
"O King, thus have I explained to you that which was asked of me here by you.
Such falsehoods as these, employed by the evil-minded sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra against the Pāṇḍavas while they were dwelling in the forest, proved to be in vain."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Delighting in that forest abounding in deer, those great chariot-warriors,
the best of the Bharatas, sported in Kāmyaka like the immortals.
Beholding various forest regions on all sides,
as well as rows of trees in full bloom that were delightful according to the season,
the Pāṇḍavas, being fond of the hunt, roamed through that great forest.

Those subduers of enemies, who were like Indra himself, spent some time there. Then, those tigers among men, the scorchers of foes, all went simultaneously in the four directions to hunt for the sake of the Brahmin.
Having left Draupadī in the hermitage with the permission of the great seer Tṛṇabindu,
who was radiant in asceticism, and of his priest Dhaumya,
the highly illustrious king of the Sindhus, the son of Vṛddhakṣatra, then departed.
Desirous of marriage, he then set out for the Śālveyas,
accompanied by a vast retinue befitting a king;
together with many other kings, he arrived at Kāmyaka.
There he beheld his beloved wife, the illustrious Draupadī of the Pāṇḍavas, standing at the entrance of the hermitage in the lonely forest,
radiant with her body and possessing supreme beauty.
Illuminating the forest region like lightning amidst dark clouds— thinking,
"Is she an Apsaras, a daughter of the gods, or a divine illusion? they all joined their palms in reverence and gazed upon that faultless woman.
Then Jayadratha, the king of the Sindhus and son of Vriddhakshatra,
was struck with wonder upon seeing her of faultless limbs;
his mind filled with desire, he spoke to King Kotikashya.
"To whom does this woman of faultless limbs belong, or perhaps she is not even human? Since there is no one for me to marry after seeing this most beautiful woman,
I shall take her with me and go to my own abode."
"Go, gentle one, and find out whose she is, who she is, or from where she has come;
for what purpose has this fair-browed woman entered this thorn-filled forest?
Could it be that this woman of noble form, the beauty of the world, has come here for my sake?"
"May she with her long-cornered eyes, beautiful teeth, and slender waist, now be mine;
having obtained this excellent woman, may I too have my desires fulfilled.
Go, Koṭika, and find out who indeed is her protector."
Having heard that, Koṭikāśya, adorned with earrings, leaped down from his chariot;
approaching her, he then questioned her like a jackal confronting a tigress.
Koṭikāśya said:
Who are you, standing alone in this hermitage, beautifying it by bending down a branch of the *kadamba* tree,
shining like a blazing crest of fire at night?
O lady of beautiful brows, being tossed about by the wind, you who are endowed with such exceeding beauty— why indeed do you not fear even in these forests?
Whether you are a goddess, or a daughter of the Danavas, a choice Apsaras, or the wife of a noble Daitya, or perhaps the beautiful daughter of a king of the Nagas—
Or perhaps she is a forest-dweller, or the wife of a night-stalking demon— whether she be the consort of King Varuṇa,
or of Yama, Soma, or the Lord of Wealth.
Have you come from the abode of Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Savitṛ, or the All-pervading One, or perhaps from the residence of Śakra? For you do not ask us who we are.
Nor do we know who your protector is here, O blessed lady;
for, increasing your honor, we ask you about your origin and your lord.
"Tell me truly of your kinsmen, your husband, and your lineage, as well as what business you have here.
I, however, am the son of King Suratha."
Whom men know as Koṭikāśya—
O fair-thighed one, he has his senses under control, delights in assemblies,
serves the elderly, and honors his teachers.
But he who stands there upon the golden chariot, like the oblated fire upon the sacrificial altar— he,
O lotus-eyed one, is the King of the Trigartas.
This hero is named Kṣemaṃkara;
but beyond him stands this great archer,
the most excellent son of the lord of Kuṇinda.
He of the broad and long shoulders,
who dwells constantly on the mountains, gazes at you in great amazement— [he] who dwells on the mountains, [he] who is wide awake.
Nor do we know your protector here;
however, that dark youth who stands near the lotus pond is handsome to behold.
O fair-limbed one, he is the son of King Subala of the Ikṣvāku lineage; he is the slayer of his enemies,
whose followers proceed with their banners raised.
The twelve Sauvīraka princes were all mounted on chariots yoked with chestnut horses,
like blazing sacrificial fires at the altars.
Aṅgāraka and Kuñjaraguptaka;
Śatruñjaya, Saṃjaya, and Supravṛddha; then Prabhaṃkara, Bhramara, and Ravi.
Śūra, Pratāpa, and Kuhara by name—
six thousand chariot-warriors follow him, as do elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers.
"If you have heard of one named Jayadratha,
O blessed lady, he is that very king of the Sauviras;
his other brothers are of undaunted spirit."
These foremost Sauvīra heroes, powerful and youthful, who resemble clouds capable of rending the enemy host, follow the king.
"With these companions, the king approaches,
protected like Indra by the hosts of Maruts;
O lady of beautiful hair, make us known to those who do not know us."
"Whose wife are you, and whose daughter?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the princess Draupadī spoke.
Questioned by that foremost of the Śibis,
she looked down, gently released a branch,
and gathered up her silken upper garment.
"O son of a lord of men, I understand through my intellect that one such as I does not deserve to address you; yet,
there is no other speaker here who can deliver this message to you."
Whether it be another man or even a woman— since I am now alone, O gentle one, I shall indeed speak these words; listen to this.
"How indeed shall I, alone in the forest,
converse with you who are devoted to your own duty? And I know you to be the son of Suratha."
O Śaibya, that which men know as Koṭikāśya, from him I likewise declare [the truth] concerning kinsmen; listen to that.
"I am the daughter of King Drupada;
O Śaibya, men know me as Kṛṣṇā.
As such, I choose these five men as my husbands."
Those who were heard to have gone to Khāṇḍavaprastha—
Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, Arjuna,
and the two sons of Mādrī, those heroes among men— [are there].
Having settled me here and divided the four quarters, the sons of Pṛthā set out on a hunt:
the king toward the east, and Bhīmasena toward the south.
Jaya has gone toward the west and the twins toward the north;
I believe that the time has now arrived for those best of chariot-warriors to come here from all sides.
Honored by them, you shall go wherever you desire; having unyoked your mounts, you may bathe. The high-souled son of Dharma is a dear guest.
"He will be pleased upon seeing you"—
having said this much, that daughter of Drupada, moon-faced and confident, addressed the son of Śaibya.
Reflecting upon their duty toward guests, he entered that excellent leaf-hut.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O Bhārata, when all those kings were seated,
he reported everything that had been said together with Kṛṣṇā; having heard those words, which were true to the facts, as they issued from the mouth of Koṭikāśya.
Koṭikāśya went quickly to the region inhabited by the Sindhu king. Having heard Koṭikāśya’s words, the Sauvīra king spoke to Śaibya:
"When my mind finds delight in her as she speaks these words..."
"O mighty-armed one, how have you turned away from this foremost of women? Having seen her, all other women appear to me like female monkeys; I tell you this as the truth."
"O Śaibya, my mind has been utterly captivated by her mere sight;
tell me about that auspicious woman, if she be human.
Koṭikāśya replied:
This indeed is the illustrious princess Draupadī Kṛṣṇā,
the highly esteemed queen of the five sons of Pāṇḍu;
she is beloved and highly honored by all the sons of Pṛthā as a virtuous woman.
"Having met with her, O Sauvīra, go to the Suvīras in great happiness.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Thus addressed, he replied, 'We shall see Draupadī.'"
Jayadratha, the evil-minded lord of the Sauviras and Sindhus,
having entered the empty hermitage like a wolf into a lion's den, spoke these words to Kṛṣṇā, with six others accompanying him.
"Is it well with you, O lady of beautiful hips? Are your husbands also free from ailment?
And those for whom you desire welfare—are they also indeed free from illness?
Draupadī said:
"O Kauravya, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, is well,
as am I and his brothers, and those others about whom you inquire. Is all well with your kingdom, your realm, your treasury, and likewise your army?"
I hope you govern the wealthy Śibis, the Sauviras, along with the Sindhus,
and those others known to you, in accordance with righteousness; and I hope you are well, O King, together with your ministers and your subjects.
"O prince, accept this water for washing your feet and this seat;
I shall give you fifty deer for your morning meal—
black antelopes, spotted deer, nyankus, common deer, sharabhas, and rabbits."
Rishyas, rurus, shambaras, and many gayals; boars, buffaloes, and whatever other species of wild animals there may be—
Kuntī’s son Yudhiṣṭhira himself will present these to you.
Jayadratha said:
"My morning meal has been made wholesome; every hospitality has been rendered to me. Come, mount my chariot and attain complete happiness."
"You ought not to follow the sons of Pṛthā, who have lost their fortune, fallen from their kingdom, wretched, deprived of their senses, and dwelling in the forest;
for wise women do not remain devoted to a husband whose prosperity has vanished."
One should follow him who is engaged [in his duties]; one should not dwell in the decline of prosperity.
Deprived of prosperity and fallen from their kingdom, they have suffered for eternal years. Enough of your devotion to the sons of Pāṇḍu that leads you to endure such affliction.
"O lady of beautiful hips, become my wife; abandon them and attain happiness.
Together with me, enjoy the entire land of Sindhu-Sauvīra.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been addressed with these heart-trembling words by the King of Sindhu,
Kṛṣṇā, her face knit with a frown, departed from that place;
the slender-waisted woman disregarded his speech and rebuked him.
"Do not speak thus," Kṛṣṇā said to the Saindhava, "be ashamed! Desiring the arrival of her husbands, the blameless woman enticed him with words,
composing her speech most skillfully.
Draupadī said:
"O mighty-armed one, do not speak thus; you do not consider what is right. You are the younger sister of both the Pāṇḍavas and the Dhārtarāṣṭras."
"Her name is Duḥśalā; you, born of a royal lineage, are her husband.
And my brother, O great chariot-warrior, must be protected by you in accordance with what is right.
— Vaiśampāyana.
"Born into a family of the most virtuous, you do not regard righteousness.
Thus addressed, the King of Sindhu spoke this reply:
"You do not know the duty of kings, for women and jewels [are what they seek]."
In this world, the wise declare these to be common property:
one's sister, one's sister’s daughter, and likewise the wife of one's brother; and kings take possession of them, as they are born of royalty.
Vaiśampāyana said:
With his beautiful face marred by the flush of anger,
his eyes reddened, and his eyebrows raised and furrowed—
Having blown his mouth wide open at Suvīra, the lord of the Rāṣṭrapa,
the daughter of Drupada then spoke again to him about those illustrious and great car-warriors who possess fierce venom.
O fool, how are you not ashamed to revile those who are equal to Mahendra, devoted to their own duties,
and established even in the midst of hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas?
They do not declare any blameworthy sin against one who is worthy of praise—
whether he be a forest-dweller or a householder, an ascetic, or one whose knowledge is fully perfected.
"O hero, these dog-like men indeed bark thus; but I think that there is no one at all like you in such an assembly of kṣatriyas."
But he who today, seizing with his hand a rutting elephant— resembling a mountain peak— as it falls toward the mouth of the netherworld, should draw it back again; [that man would be my equal].
Like a staff-bearer driving cattle from the herd, you drive away that one who roams the Himalayan foothills—
you who hope to conquer the King of Dharma.
Out of childishness, you are plucking the whiskers from the face of a mighty lion while it sleeps;
you flee after striking it with your foot.
When you behold the mighty Bhimasena, most terrible and fully grown, enraged like a lion born in mountain caves;
You strike down with your foot the fierce one who is asleep;
you shall sit upon the angry, victorious, and fierce one— like two black snakes, sharp-venomed and double-tongued.
O intoxicated one, you seek to trample me underfoot at the base of my tail— you who desire to fight with the two Pāṇḍavas, those best of men born later.
Just as the bamboo, the plantain, or the reed bear fruit only for their own destruction and not for their own prosperity,
even so am I being guarded by them.
"You shall conceive a fetus like a female crab," [he said].
Jayadratha replied:
"I know this, O Kṛṣṇā; this is well known to me."
Just as those sons of gods among men were,
we cannot be terrified by you today in this same way as we were by Vibhīṣaṇa.
We, however, O Kṛṣṇa, have all been born into seventeen families that are not inferior;
we are superior in six qualities and devoid of [those] lacking.
"We consider the sons of Pāṇḍu to be Draupadī;
therefore, mount a chariot or an elephant immediately,
for we cannot be moved by mere words."
"Or perhaps you, speaking piteously,
might hope for the favor of the King of Sauvīra.
Draupadī said:
Though I possess great strength, I appear here as if weak; for I am regarded by the King of Sauvīra as one who has been subdued by force.
I would call the King of Sauvīra a wretch,
for upon whose path the two Kṛṣṇas travel together as companions, mounted upon a single chariot.
Even Indra could not take it away by any means;
how much less any other miserable mere mortal? This is so when the wearer of the diadem, the slayer of enemy heroes, [is present].
Standing in his chariot, he shall strike the hearts of his enemies; he will enter your army in my absence,
like a fire consuming dry grass during the hot season.
The Vṛṣṇi heroes who follow Janārdana,
all the great archers, and the Kekayas as well—
all these are indeed my princes.
With joyful countenances, they should follow his path;
for the arrows released from the bowstring have the roar of thunder,
while those shot from the Gāṇḍīva possess exceeding speed.
Striking Dhananjaya’s hand,
the terrible [beings] let out a most horrific sound as they [encountered] the great floods of arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva.
When you see Arjuna, endowed with heroic prowess, moving with the swift speed of a swarm of locusts,
then you will reproach your own intellect.
When the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, emitting the sound of conchs and the sound of arm-guards,
repeatedly hurls arrows at your chest;
At that time, what would your mind have been like—
seeing Bhīma rushing forward with mace in hand,
and the two sons of Mādrī charging from all directions?
Seeing them vomiting the poison of wrath born of indignation, you, O base one, shall suffer long-lasting torment—
just as I shall never, under any circumstances, transgress.
By that truth— that you have never even in thought desired other husbands worthy of you— I shall today behold you, brought under control, being dragged away by the sons of Pṛthā.
For I shall not be able to avoid falling into a state of panic while being dragged away by you, a cruel man; indeed,
I have come here to join the foremost heroes of the Kurus.
And she returned again to the Kāmyaka forest.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having gazed upon them, that large-eyed woman—
Scolding those who desired to seize her,
she spoke in fear, "Do not touch me!
and she cried out to Dhaumya, the family priest.
Jayadratha seized her by the hem of her upper garment; she threw him down,
and that wicked man, his body struck by her, fell.
She fell like a tree whose roots have been severed,
while the princess, being seized with great force, sighed repeatedly.
Being dragged away, Kṛṣṇā ascended the chariot; having paid homage at the feet of Dhaumya,
Dhaumya said:

"O Jayadratha, it is not possible for you to take her away without first conquering these great chariot-warriors; consider the ancient duty of a Kṣatriya. Having committed this base act, you will undoubtedly reap a sinful fruit."
Having approached the heroic Pāṇḍavas, with Dharmarāja at their head,
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having spoken thus, as that illustrious princess was being carried away..."
Then Dhaumya followed, walking in the midst of the host of foot-soldiers.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the sons of Pṛthā, having dispersed in all directions...
Having slain deer, boars, and buffaloes,
those who were the most excellent archers on earth moved about both separately and together.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira addressed those brothers in that great forest, which was filled with herds of deer and beasts of prey and resounded with the cries of birds.
Having heard the cries of the beasts as they uttered their words,
he turned toward the direction blazing with the sun and said,
"These beasts and birds speak cruelly."
"Experiencing fierce distress as you are being overwhelmed by enemies in a great battle,
turn back quickly; enough of these deer for us."
For my mind is distressed and burning;
and with my intellect completely obscured, the lord of my vital breaths is agitated within my body along with my anger.
Like a lake from which the serpents have been carried off by Garuda,
or like a kingdom stripped of its sovereign and its fortune—
such is Kāmyaka as it appears to me.
Like jars of wine being drunk by drunkards,
they were carried along by those Saindhava horses, which possessed the speed of a great gale and possessed immense velocity.
Yoked to large, excellent chariots, those heroes among men then turned their faces toward the hermitage; meanwhile,
a jackal let out a loud cry for them.
Turning toward his left side,
the king reflected upon him and spoke to Bhīma and Dhanañjaya.
Just as this beast of low birth speaks, having approached our left side like a jackal,
it is quite evident that he disregards us with his wicked words.
Thinking, "The Kurus have forcibly committed this slaughter," they entered that forest after having hunted in the great wilderness.
Then Indrasena, seeing the young nurse— the beloved’s foster-mother and handmaid— weeping, quickly ran toward her.
Then, leaping down from his chariot,
the lord of men ran toward her and, being deeply distressed at that moment, spoke these words to the nurse’s daughter.
"Why do you weep, fallen upon the earth?
Why does your face wither into such a wretched hue? For the sons of Pāṇḍu have indeed departed for the forest."
"Has no harm been done to us by others anywhere in this forest?"—
thus she asked, becoming greatly agitated upon seeing Indrasena rushing swiftly toward her with the charioteer.
Then, striking her chest with even greater pain, the queen cried out loudly, "I am stolen!"— she who was devoted to her husband and true to her word.
Where has she been taken, or by whom? Tell me the truth; by whom has she been led away to her own destruction, having found a vulnerability in the king’s wife?
I hope that the princess Draupadī, of irreproachable form and large eyes, has not been tormented by wicked men who commit cruel deeds.
Even if the queen has entered the earth, or ascended to heaven, or even into the ocean, she is as dear to the bulls among the Kurus as their own bodies.
For the sons of Pṛthā will surely follow her path,
since Dharmarāja is thus consumed by grief;
for who indeed [could endure it] among such crushers of enemies?

One who, out of delusion, would wish to take away from those who endure afflictions and are unconquered— the most beloved [person], equal to their own life— is like one who seeks to seize a supreme jewel.
Today, the heart of the Pāṇḍavas, though it has a protector, does not perceive that which moves outside;
for whose body will this terrible [weapon] pierce today?
Sharp, excellent arrows shall enter the earth;
O timid one, do not grieve for her,
but know that today Draupadī will return once more.
"Having slain all their enemies without exception,
the sons of Pṛthā will then reunite with Yājñasenī.
Then, having wiped his handsome face, he spoke.
The nurse's daughter Kṛṣṇā was carried off by Jayadratha after he had overwhelmed Indrasena, the charioteer, and treated with contempt those five who were like Indra himself.
"These new tracks remain,
and the trees that were broken do not wither even now; therefore, turn back and follow quickly."
The princess has not indeed gone far;
all of you, who are like Indra, arm yourselves with great and beautiful armor.
"Take up your great and costly bows and arrows, and quickly follow in their tracks;
for they have already been bewildered by the punishment of our reproaches."
With a bewildered mind and a parched mouth,
she offers her body to some unworthy person,
like a sacrificial ladle filled with the finest ghee poured into ashes.
Before long, the oblation will be offered as if into a fire of chaff; before long, it will be cast away like a garland in a cemetery;
and before long, the Soma at the sacrifice will be licked up.
Just as when the people were bewildered by a dog,
and formerly the sons of Pṛthā were struck down at Kāpila,
where a stream of milk was poured— exert yourselves!
In ancient times, having wandered for the hunt in a vast forest, a jackal plunged into a lotus pond; likewise,
one should properly attend to the sacred revelation and the primordial nature at the great sacrifice.
Just as a vulgar person would not destroy it,
for previously, when the sacrificial altar was worshipped with mantra-offerings and the fire had been fed, the crow would settle there.
May no evildoer ever touch your beloved’s fair-nosed, beautiful-eyed, serene face, which is as bright as the radiance of the moon.
A dog might indeed devour the sacrificial cake;
follow these paths quickly,
lest the time should swiftly pass you by here.
"Run quickly from here before that wicked man, the lord of men, goes far away!
Drive him back from the presence of his enemies!"
Like lions protecting their own beloved Lakṣmī,
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O blessed lady, remain silent and restrain your speech."
Do not speak harsh words in our presence;
for kings, or even princes,
when intoxicated by power, fall into deception.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, they departed quickly,
following those very same paths.
Breathing repeatedly like serpents and twanging the strings of their great bows,
they then beheld the dust raised by that army.
Dhaumya, who was being kicked up by the dust raised by the horses' hooves as he stood in the midst of the foot soldiers,
cried out to Bhīma, "Come to his rescue!"
Having consoled Dhaumya, those princes, their spirits deeply dejected, said, "May you go in peace," just as hawks intent upon meat [fly after their prey].
Then, with speed, he charged at that army of those whose prowess was like that of great Indra,
who were enraged by the assault upon Yājñasenī.
His wrath blazed up upon seeing Jayadratha and his beloved standing in his chariot;
and then they cried out against the King of Sindhu.
Vṛkodara, Dhanañjaya,
the twins, and the king— all great archers—
then caused the enemies' directions to become utterly bewildered.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
upon seeing Bhīmasena and Arjuna, a most terrible clamor arose among the indignant Kṣatriyas in the forest.
Beholding the tops of their banners, King Jayadratha himself— the evil-souled one among the bulls of the Kurus—
spoke to Yājñasenī.
"O radiant one, standing upon the chariot with your luster dimmed, these five great chariots are approaching;
O Kṛṣṇā, I believe these are your husbands."
"O lady with beautiful hair, knowing this, declare to us who among the Pāṇḍavas stands upon his chariot, one after another.
Draupadī said:
"O fool, what is the use of these great archers being known to you?
Having performed this most terrible deed that shortens one's lifespan,
here are my husbands, these heroes, gathered together."
"There is nothing remaining for you here in this battle; however,
since I have been asked by you who are about to die, I must tell you everything, for this is the duty."
No distress nor fear of you exists for me as I behold the King of Dharma together with his younger brother,
upon the top of whose banner two drums resound.
Nanda and Upananda are sweet-voiced and well-proportioned;
people who have tasks to accomplish always follow this one who knows how to determine what is right and purposeful according to his own duty.
"He who is as fair as pure Jāmbūnada gold, with a prominent nose, slender and long-eyed—
him they call the most excellent of the Kurus."
"Even this hero among men, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma and my husband, who practices righteousness, would give up his own life for an enemy who has come to him for refuge."
"Go away from him quickly for your own welfare, O fool,
with palms joined and weapons laid aside.
Or else, behold him standing upon his chariot."
With mighty arms like a fully grown *śāla* tree,
his lips bitten together and his brows knit in a frown—
this is my husband, named Vṛkodara.
Well-trained, powerful, and well-disciplined thoroughbreds of great strength carry a hero;
his deeds are superhuman.
The name "Bhīma" has spread throughout the earth;
those who have wronged him do not escape with their lives here,
nor does he ever forget an enmity.
Having brought an end to enmity, he departs;
yet afterwards, he does not attain excessive peace. He is gentle, generous, steadfast, and renowned.
This hero among men, who has conquered his senses, serves the elders,
and is both brother and disciple to Yudhiṣṭhira—
he whose name is Dhanañjaya— is my husband.
He who indeed would not abandon dharma out of desire, fear, or greed, and would not commit a cruel act— he,
possessing splendor equal to Vaiśvānara, is this very man.
The son of Kuntī, the subduer of enemies and the crusher of foes,
who knows the determination of all dharma and artha, is a wise man who removes the fear of those afflicted by terror.
Beloved by his kinsmen, the best among those who bear arms,
his prowess irresistible in great battles—
he whose form is said to be the most excellent on earth;
This very hero Nakula, whom all the Pāṇḍavas protect as dearer than their own lives and who is devoted to them— he is my husband.
He is a hero, grateful, and firm in friendship;
he who crushes the enemy in great battle,
a sword-fighter with light and dexterous hands.
And Sahadeva is great and wise, without equal—
O you of deluded nature, today you shall witness his deed,
like that of Śatakratu among the hosts of the Daityas in battle.
He is a hero, skilled in weapons, wise, and thoughtful;
he acts for the pleasure of King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,
and possesses a splendor equal to that of the moon and the sun.
The youngest of the Pāṇḍavas is beloved,
and there is no man found who is his equal in intelligence;
he is likewise an eloquent speaker among the virtuous and one who knows how to reach certain conclusions.
This very Sahadeva, my husband, is ever brave and impatient; he is wise and learned. He would sooner give up his life or enter the sacrificial fire.
But this wise hero among men, ever devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya and most dear to Kuntī even as her own life, would never speak anything contrary to righteousness.
Like a ship laden with jewels being shattered at the edge of the ocean upon the back of a sea-monster,
so is this army of yours, with all its warriors slain.
"You shall see them agitated by the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Thus have these sons of Pāṇḍu been described,
whom you, out of delusion, set out to treat with contempt.
"If you are released by these [weapons] with your body unharmed,
you shall obtain rebirth while still alive.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the five sons of Pṛthā, each like unto Indra,
leaving behind those terrified foot-soldiers with joined palms,
[advanced] toward the chariot-force shrouded in the darkness of a rain of arrows.
Enraged, they hemmed him in from all sides.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Stand firm! Strike! Run about quickly!"

Thus did the King of the Sindhus urge those monarchs forward. Then, upon seeing Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins along with Yudhiṣṭhira in battle, a most terrible clamor arose among the troops in that conflict.
Despair also arose among the Śibis, Sindhus,
and Trigartas upon seeing those tigers among men, who were like tigers fierce in their strength,
wielding a mace made entirely of śaikya-iron with its surface adorned with gold.
Then Bhīma, seizing his opportunity, rushed toward the ruler of the Sindhus who was impelled by Time.
Thereupon, Koṭikāśya turned back and attacked,
surrounding Vṛkodara with a vast array of chariots.
Though being showered with many spears, *tomaras*, and iron arrows hurled by the arms of heroes, Bhīma did not tremble;
he [overthrew] an elephant along with its rider and fourteen foot soldiers.
Bhīma struck the army of the Saindhava at its head with his mace;
Pārtha, seeking to rescue the Sauvīra king, slew five hundred brave great car-warriors from the mountains at the front of the host.
Then, in that battle, the king himself slew a hundred of the foremost and heroic strikers in the mere twinkling of an eye;
Nakula was seen there, having leaped down from his chariot and wielding a sword.
Repeatedly sowing the heads of the foot-guards like seeds,
Sahadeva, however, having approached on his chariot,
struck down the elephant-warriors with iron arrows as if peacocks were falling from trees.
Then Trigarta, having descended from his great chariot with bow in hand,
slew the four horses of that king with a mace. As he approached on foot, the son of Kuntī, the king, [assailed him].
With a crescent-shaped arrow, Dharmarāja pierced him in the chest.
With his heart shattered, that hero, vomiting blood from his mouth,
fell toward Pārtha like a tree whose roots have been severed.
But the King of Dharma, with Indrasena as his sole companion, leaped down from his chariot;
his horses having been slain, he mounted the great chariot of Sahadeva.
Meanwhile, Nakula, aiming at Kṣemankara and Mahāmukha, [proceeded].
Both of them rained down showers of sharp arrows from both sides;
raining down those shafts like two clouds in the monsoon,
the son of Mādravatī struck each one with a single broad-headed arrow.
Then Suratha, the king of the Trigartas, who was skilled in driving elephants, mounted on the pole of his chariot,
caused Nakula’s chariot to be overturned with his elephant. But Nakula, remaining undaunted, leaped from that chariot with sword and shield in hand.
Taking his position on a high ground, he stood as immovable as a mountain.
Then Suratha, in a fit of rage, urged that excellent elephant toward Nakula for the purpose of slaying him, its trunk raised aloft.
As that elephant moved close by,
Nakula cut off its tusked trunk at the base with his sword.
That elephant, adorned with bracelets, let out a great roar.
Falling headlong to the ground, he crushed the elephant-riders. Having performed that great feat, the heroic son of Mādravatī,
that great car-warrior, reached Bhīmasena’s chariot and found refuge there.
But Bhīma, in the encounter, severed with a razor-sharp arrow the head of King Koṭikāśya as he was charging forward, while his charioteer was urging on the horses;
that king did not realize his charioteer had been slain by the mighty-armed hero.

His horses, their driver having been slain, fled hither and thither in the battle. Approaching him as he stood with his back turned and his driver killed, Bhīma, the son of Pāṇḍu and the best among strikers, slew him with a spear equipped with a hand-grip.
Then, while that tumultuous slaughter of warriors was underway, Aṅgāraka, Kuñjara, Saṃjaya, Guptaka,
Śatruñjaya, Suprabuddha, Śubhakṛt, and Bhramaka [all fell].
Śūra, Parāku, and Kuhaka—these twelve were great car-warriors (mahārathas). There were also the mighty Subalas, the Saindhavas, and the powerful Trigartas;
and the Ikṣvāku warriors, formidable chariot-fighters together with their elephants.
Having targeted Pārtha, they overwhelmed him with showers of arrows;
but then Arjuna, filled with rage, struck down that shower of arrows,
while Dhanañjaya [engaged] all twelve of the Sauviras.
With sharpened broad-headed arrows, he cut down their bows and their heads—
the Śibis, the leaders of the Ikṣvākus, the Trigartas, and the Saindhavas as well.
That great car-warrior slew them in battle as they came within the range of his arrows.
Many elephants with their banners and great chariots with their standards were seen struck down by Savyasācin;
covered over them, they lay upon the earth across the entire battlefield.
Headless trunks and headless heads lay there;
dogs, vultures, herons, ravens, hawks, jackals,
and crows feasted insatiably upon the flesh and blood of the slain heroes.
Thus, with the flames of sharp arrows impelled by the fire of the Gāṇḍīva bow,
the wrathful Pārtha-yājaka quickly consumed the fuel that was the army;
O lord of the earth, [he consumed] the fallen wheels and the yokes as well.
There were heaps of quivers, banners, and standards together with chariots;
likewise, there were piles of arrows, axle-ropes, triple-bamboo poles,
as well as axles, yokes, and goads.
There were heaps of fallen heads wearing earrings and turbans,
as well as arms, crowns, necklaces, and armlets,
along with piles of parasols, fans, and shields.
O lord of the people, heaps of severed bows and shields, as well as spears, swords, staffs, and iron clubs, were seen scattered here and there.
With fallen *mātaṅga*s resembling mountains along with their warriors,
with horses fallen together with their riders and weapons,
and with chariots that had entered [the fray] and foot-soldiers who were slain;
The earth, covered in mud of flesh and blood, became impassable. When those heroes had been slain, Jayadratha, the king of Sindhu,
released Kṛṣṇā and, overcome with terror, became intent on flight.
While his army was being routed like the ocean by sea-monsters, that lowest of men, having set Draupadī down in that chaotic host, fled toward the forest, seeking to save his own life.
But Dharmarāja, seeing Draupadī preceded by Dhaumya, then had her placed upon the chariot by the heroic son of Mādrī. Then that fleeing army retreated once Jayadratha had departed.
Aiming them one after another, Vṛkodara struck with iron shafts.
But Savyasācin, seeing Jayadratha fleeing,
restrained him as he was slaughtering the Saindhava soldiers while Bhīma continued his assault.
Arjuna said:
"I do not see Jayadratha here on this battlefield, he through whose transgression we have encountered this insurmountable distress."
"Seek him alone—blessings be upon you! What is the use of these warriors struck down?
This task is devoid of reward; how do you regard it?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by the wise Guḍākeśa, the eloquent Bhīmasena looked toward Yudhiṣṭhira and spoke these words:
"The enemy's foremost heroes have been slain, and for the most part they have fled in all directions."
"O King, taking Draupadī with you, return from here; O Indra among kings, go together with the twins and the high-souled Dhaumya. Having reached the hermitage, O King, console Draupadī."
"O fool, that king of the Saindhavas shall not escape from me alive,
even if he were situated in the depths of Pātāla with Śakra himself as his charioteer.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O mighty-armed one, even though that ruler of the Sindhus is evil-minded, he must not be slain,
out of consideration for Duḥśalā and the illustrious Gāndhārī.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard that, Draupadī— her senses agitated, angry yet modest, and wise— spoke to Bhīma regarding both her husbands, Bhīma and Arjuna:
"If you wish to do what is pleasing to me, that lowest of men must be slain."
That base wretch of the Saindhavas, wicked-minded and a disgrace to his lineage,
who abducted my wife without provocation and seized my kingdom—
that enemy does not deserve to live, even if he begs for mercy in battle.
When this was said, those two tigers among men went to where the ruler of the Sindhus was;
the king, however, returned with Kṛṣṇā and his family priest.
Having entered the hermitage, he saw that the grass mats and water-jars had been cast about in disorder.
He beheld that place crowded with Brahmins such as Mārkaṇḍeya and others,
who were gathered there lamenting for Draupadī;
the highly wise one, accompanied by his wife and standing in the midst of his brothers, joined them.
Seeing that the king had returned— having conquered those Sindhu-Sauvīras and recovered Draupadī— they were filled with joy. Surrounded by them, the king sat down right there.
The passionate Kṛṣṇā entered the hermitage together with the twins.
Bhīma and Arjuna, having heard that the enemy was only a *krośa* away,
spurred their horses themselves and rushed toward him with great speed.
Moreover, the man Arjuna performed this most wonderful feat there:
that he slew the horses of the King of Sindhu even though they were a *krośa* away.
For he was endowed with divine weapons and remained unperturbed even in a time of distress.
He performed a difficult feat with arrows consecrated by mantras.
Then both heroes, Bhīma and Dhanañjaya,
rushed forward toward the King of Sindhu, who was alone, terrified, agitated in mind, and whose horses had been slain.
But Saindhava, seeing his own horses thus slain, was deeply distressed;
leaping down from his chariot, he set out on foot, intent on flight,
as he beheld Dhananjaya performing deeds of great prowess.
Exerting himself to flee, he rushed toward the forest; but seeing the ruler of the Sindhus exerting his prowess in flight,
the mighty-armed Phalguna pursued him and spoke these words.
"With such valor as this, how can you seek to seize a woman by force?
O prince, turn back; flight is not fitting for you. How is it that you flee from the midst of the enemy, abandoning your followers?"
Though addressed in this manner by Pārtha and by the wise Arjuna, the wicked-souled Saindhava did not turn back.
"Stay! Stay! the powerful Bhīma suddenly rushed toward him.
"Do not kill him! Pārtha said to him compassionately.
Vaiśampāyana said:
But Jayadratha, beholding his two brothers with weapons raised,
fled swiftly and calmly, desiring life and deeply distressed,
toward the crown radiant with jewels that was hidden by creepers.
Seeing him fleeing and hiding within the depths of the forest, Bhīmasena, searching for him as he lay concealed in the undergrowth, agitated by fear,
quickly descended from his chariot adorned with jewels.
As he was fleeing, the powerful Bhīmasena, descending from his chariot,
rushed toward him and, filled with great indignation, seized him by the hair. Raising him up in rage, he crushed him against the surface of the earth.
Seizing the king by the neck, he struck him;
and as he regained consciousness and sought to rise again,
the mighty-armed one kicked him on the head as he was wailing.
Bhīma struck him on the knee and then struck him with his forearm; the king, tormented by that excellent blow, fell into a swoon. But Phalguna restrained Bhīmasena, who was filled with rage.
"O Kaurava, regarding what the King said for the sake of Duḥśalā," Bhīmasena said:
"This man of evil conduct does not deserve to live at my hands."
That lowest of men, who tormented Draupadī though she did not deserve such treatment—
what indeed can I do, since the king is ever compassionate,
and you yourself, with your childish intellect, constantly oppress us?
Having spoken thus, Vṛkodara then struck off his five locks with a crescent-shaped arrow while he was still saying nothing. Having thus confounded the king, Vṛkodara then spoke.
Vṛkodara did not realize that he was thus motionless;
[he said: "O fool, if you wish to live, listen to the condition as I speak it:
'I am a slave'—this must be said by you in assemblies and in courts."
"In this way I shall grant you your life; such is the rule for one conquered in battle.
"So be it," replied King Jayadratha, whose life was in peril, to that tiger among men, Bhīma, who shines in combat.
Then Vṛkodara, the son of Pṛthā, having bound him as he struggled—
unconscious and covered in dust— placed him upon his chariot.
Thereupon, Bhīma, following in the wake of the sons of Pṛthā, mounted that chariot.
Approaching the center of the hermitage, he came before Yudhiṣṭhira;
Bhīma then showed Jayadratha in that condition to him.
Seeing him, the king laughed and said, "Let him be released."
And Bhīma said to the king, "Tell Draupadī that this evil-minded man has indeed entered into a state of servitude to the Pāṇḍavas. Then his eldest brother spoke these affectionate words to him:
"Release this man of base conduct, if we are an authority to you.
Then Draupadī, looking toward Yudhiṣṭhira, said to Bhīma:
"Let this slave be released; he has been made a five-locked servant by you for the king."
Thus addressed by his brother and by Kṛṣṇā, Bhīma then released that great sinner, the unconscious Jayadratha;
having been thus spoken to, Bhīma then set him free from his bonds.
Released, he approached King Yudhiṣṭhira, saluted him, and then,
overwhelmed with emotion, the king paid homage to all those sages. Then the compassionate King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, spoke to him.
Likewise, seeing Jayadratha captured by Savyasācin, [Arjuna said]:
"Go, you are no longer a slave; you are released. Never do such a thing again! O lustful for women, fie on you—a base man with base companions!"
"O evil-minded one, who other than you, the lowest of men, would perform such an act that is contrary to dharma and loathed by the world?
Perceiving that creator of inauspiciousness to be as if devoid of life,"
Beholding him, O best of the Bharatas, that lord of men felt compassion:
"May your intellect increase in righteousness; do not set your mind upon unrighteousness.
Go in safety, Jayadratha, with your horses, chariots, and infantry."

Thus addressed, O Bhārata, the king, overcome with shame, went silently with his face slightly cast down; afflicted by grief, he proceeded toward Gaṅgādvāra. Having sought refuge with the god Virūpākṣa, the lord of Umā, he departed.

Without food and having conquered his anger, he stood balanced on the tips of his big toes and performed extensive austerities; the three-eyed Lord whose banner is the bull was pleased with him and personally accepted his offering.
The god granted him a boon, and he accepted it; hear that [boon]. "I would conquer all five Pāṇḍavas together with their chariots in battle," the king said to the god. "No," the god said to him.
You shall hold back in battle those who are unconquerable and even unslayable,
with the exception of the mighty-armed Arjuna, who is difficult to approach even for the gods—
him whom they call Nara, the supreme lord of the gods.
In Badarī, he who has performed intense austerities, who has Nārāyaṇa as his companion,
and who is unconquerable by all the worlds—
he is protected everywhere and at all times by my Pāśupata weapon.
I gave him the divine, peerless arrow of Pāśupata;
from the world-protectors he obtained those great arrows, the thunderbolt and the rest.
For Viṣṇu is the God of gods, the infinite self, the preceptor of the deities, and the Lord.
The Pradhāna-Puruṣa, unmanifest, the soul of the universe, possessing a universal form—
when the end of the Yuga has arrived, he becomes the fire of time and consumes the world,
including its mountains, oceans, islands, peaks, forests, and groves.
Scorching the worlds of the *nāgas* who roam the depths of Pātāla,
there then appeared in the sky vast clouds of many colors,
roaring with terrible sounds and draped with garlands of lightning.
Rising up and raining everywhere in all directions,
those who control the Saṃvarta-fire then extinguished the fire; they stood there, filling everything on all sides with torrents of water as thick as axles.
Then, when that world had become a single ocean in which all moving and non-moving beings were stilled, when the moon, sun, and wind had perished, and it was devoid of planets and constellations—
at the end of a thousand cycles of the four yugas— the earth was submerged by water.
Then that one called Nārāyaṇa— the thousand-eyed, thousand-footed,
thousand-headed Puruṣa, who transcends the senses— desiring to sleep,
[rested upon] Śeṣa, who was formidable with a thousand hoods and reclining in the posture of a couch.
There, like a thousand gathered masses of sharp rays, that Blessed Lord of immeasurable splendor was then sleeping upon the ocean,
possessing the luster of jasmine, the moon, a pearl necklace, cow’s milk, lotus stalks,
and white water-lilies.
The All-pervading Lord makes his own night pervaded by nocturnal darkness;
yet, when he has increased through the predominance of *sattva*, he beholds the world as empty.
And in this regard, they cite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa:
"We have heard that 'waters' (āpaḥ) are called 'nārāḥ' because they are their source;
and since he dwells within them as their refuge, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
At the very moment of profound meditation, however, for the sake of progeny, the Eternal One..."
O Blessed One, as soon as he had meditated, a lotus emerged from his navel;
then Brahmā, the four-faced one, issued forth from that navel-lotus,
and the Grandfather of the worlds sat down there upon it instantly.
Seeing the entire world as empty and [beings] equal to himself in mind,
he then created nine great sages, headed by Marīci; they, in turn,
created all beings, both mobile and immobile.
The form of Brahmā creates the yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, piśācas, uragas, and humans; the human body (pauruṣī tanuḥ) protects them;
and through the state of Rudra, he pacifies them—these are the three states of Prajāpati.
O Lord of the Sindhu, have you not heard the wondrous deeds of Viṣṇu being recounted by sages and Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas,
when the surface of the earth was entirely submerged in water?
And then, as that single ocean existed within that single void, the Lord moved about like a firefly in the night during the rainy season,
searching everywhere for the earth upon which to establish himself.
Seeing the earth submerged in water, he desired in his mind to lift her up:
"What form should I assume to raise the earth from the waters?
Having reflected thus in his mind, he beheld with his divine eye.
He recalled the boar-form that delights in sporting in the waters; having assumed the body of a boar, which was composed of speech and equal to the Vedas,
ten yojanas in width and a hundred yojanas in length.

Having become the Sacrificial Boar, the Lord— resembling a great mountain in stature, possessing sharp tusks and blazing radiance, with a roar like a mass of great clouds and appearing like a dark blue rain-cloud— entered the waters.
Having lifted up the earth with a single tusk, he settled it in its own place; then once more, the mighty-armed Lord, assuming a form never seen before,
made half his body that of a man and half the body of a lion.
Having gone to the assembly hall of the lord of the Daityas and touched his hand with his own hand,
the primordial being of the Daityas, the enemy of the gods, the son of Diti,
beheld him of unprecedented form and, with eyes bloodshot from anger, [confronted him].

Then Hiraṇyakaśipu, the heroic enemy of the gods and son of Diti, wearing a garland and with a spear raised in his hand— resounding like the thundering of clouds and resembling a mass of dark blue clouds— rushed toward Nṛsiṃha.
Then, having approached, he was violently torn apart by the claws of the powerful Lord of Beasts,
who had assumed a man-lion form;
thus did the Blessed One slay the lord of the Daityas, the destroyer of his enemies.
Furthermore, another lotus-eyed Lord, for the welfare of the world,
was the illustrious son of Kaśyapa, conceived as an embryo by Aditi;
when a full thousand years had passed, she gave birth to that supreme child.
Resembling a dark rain-cloud, with blazing eyes and a dwarf-like form,
holding a staff and a water-pot, adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest,
wearing matted hair and the sacred thread, the Blessed One assumed the form of a youth.

Then the illustrious one went to the sacrificial enclosure of the lord of the Dānavas; accompanied by Bṛhaspati, he entered the sacrifice of the powerful one. Seeing him in his dwarf form, Bali was delighted and spoke.
"I am pleased at the sight of you, O Brahmin; tell me, what shall I give to you?
Thus addressed by Bali, Vāmana replied;
and having said "May it be well," the god, smiling, spoke to Bali.
"O Lord of the Dānavas, grant me three strides of the earth.
Bali, with a gracious mind, gave [the earth] to the brahmin of immeasurable splendor.
Then, as Hari strode, his form became divine and most wonderful.
With three strides, the unshakeable one swiftly seized the earth;
and the eternal god Viṣṇu gave the earth to Śakra. This manifestation of yours, known as Vāmana, has thus been proclaimed.
Because of him, the gods came into being, and the world is called Vaiṣṇava;
for the sake of restraining the wicked and for the protection of dharma,
he descended and was born among men in the house of Yadu.
Thus, that Blessed One Viṣṇu is celebrated as Kṛṣṇa— He who is without beginning or end, the unborn God, the Lord worshipped by the worlds, whom the wise sing of; hear now His deeds, O Saindhava.
He whom they call the unconquered god, the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace— the god who bears the Śrīvatsa mark and is clothed in yellow silk—
is protected by that Kṛṣṇa, the foremost among those skilled in weapons.
With the lotus-eyed Śrīmat Puṇḍarīkākṣa as his companion— possessing incomparable prowess and the slayer of enemy heroes— Arjuna mounts the same chariot;
being thus unassailable, he cannot be conquered even by the gods.
But what human being could defeat Pārtha in battle? Excluding that one man alone, O King, you shall conquer all the rest of Yudhiṣṭhira’s army— the four Pāṇḍavas— as enemies for a single day.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus spoken to the king, Hara— the remover of all sins,
the lord of Umā, the lord of creatures, the destroyer of the sacrifice, and the slayer of Tripura— [departed].

O tiger among kings, Tryambaka— the one who struck out the eyes of Bhaga— is surrounded by terrible attendants of dwarfish, misshapen, and hunchbacked forms, with fierce ears and eyes, all raising various weapons.
Accompanied by Umā, the Blessed One vanished right there.
Therefore, O tiger among men, you shall hold back the Pāṇḍavas when they are deprived of Arjuna;
for once, a boon was granted to you by me.
Having been addressed thus, the king went to his own palace,
and the Pāṇḍavas then continued to dwell in that Kāmyaka forest.
Janamejaya said:
"When Kṛṣṇā had been thus abducted, after they had encountered unsurpassed suffering,
what did the Pāṇḍavas, those tigers among men, do thereafter?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus liberated Kṛṣṇā and having utterly defeated Jayadratha,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, sat down with the hosts of sages in their midst,
while those great ṛṣis listened and lamented.
The son of Pāṇḍu spoke these words to Mārkaṇḍeya:
Yudhiṣṭhira said,
"O Blessed One, you are renowned among the celestial rishis as one who knows the past and the future."
I ask you about my doubt; sever it for me, as it dwells within my heart.
For this daughter of Drupada has arisen from the middle of the sacrificial altar;
she is not born of a womb, highly fortunate, and the daughter-in-law of the high-souled Pāṇḍu.

I believe that time is powerful, as is destiny ordained by fate; and there is the inevitable course of beings, which cannot be transgressed. For how could [this have happened] to our wife, who knows the dharma and practices the dharma?
Such a disposition would touch upon purity as falsehood touches upon theft;
for indeed, no evil has ever been committed by her, nor any blameworthy act anywhere.
By Draupadī alone has the great dharma been perfectly practiced toward the Brahmins.
The foolish King Jayadratha forcibly abducted her;
as a result of that abduction, he suffered the shaving of his head and,
along with his allies, met with defeat in battle.

"Having thus slain that army of the Saindhava king, we brought [the princess] back; yet this abduction of a wife was encountered by us unexpectedly. Furthermore, there is this dwelling in the forest and living by means of hunting."
The destruction of species of wild animals by forest-dwellers,
and the exile of forest-dwellers by their own kinsmen through false resolves— surely there must be some man more unfortunate than I.
"Have you ever seen such a thing before, or even heard of it?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O bull of the Bharata race, incomparable suffering was experienced by Rāma."
There was the calamity of grief for his father and other misfortunes, as well as the great abduction of his wife;
while he dwelt in the forest at his father’s command after his father had passed away,
his wife Jānakī was carried off by a powerful *rākṣasa*.
From the hermitage, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas,
having resorted to his illusory power (*māyā*) and swiftly slain the vulture Jaṭāyu while traveling through the air, carried her away; but Rāma, relying on the strength of Sugrīva, recovered her.
Having built a bridge across the ocean and having burned Laṅkā with his sharp arrows,
the mighty Rāma then slew that enemy who had abducted his wife at the head of the battle, together with the army of monkeys.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: In what family was Rāma born? What was his prowess and what was his valor?
Whose son was Rāvaṇa, and what indeed was the cause of his enmity with him?
"O Blessed One, you ought to relate all of this to me correctly,
exactly as you have seen it all in person without exception;
I wish to hear the life-story of Rāma, whose deeds are effortless."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King, to this ancient history of what occurred in the past,
concerning how Rama, together with his wife, experienced suffering, O Bhārata.
There was a great king named Aja, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage;
his son was Daśaratha, who was pure and constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas. He had four sons who were experts in matters of dharma and worldly affairs.
Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and the mighty Bharata—
of these, Kausalyā was the mother of Rāma, Kaikeyī that of Bharata,
and Sumitrā gave birth to the two sons Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna, who were subduers of their enemies.
Janaka was the king of Videha, O Lord, and Sītā was his daughter, whom Tvaṣṭṛ himself fashioned as the beloved queen of Rāma. Thus has the birth of Rāma and of Sītā been recounted to you.
O lord of men, I shall also explain to you the birth of Rāvaṇa.
The grandfather of Rāvaṇa was the god Prajāpati himself—
the self-existent, the lord and creator of all worlds, possessed of great ascetic power.
He had a beloved mind-born son named Pulastya;
his son was the lord Vaiśravaṇa, born of Gavi.
Abandoning his father, he attended upon the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Out of anger at him, O King, his father created another self from himself. That twice-born one was born as Viśravas, formed from half of his own body,
and he was filled with wrath for the sake of taking revenge upon Vaiśravaṇa.
But the Grandfather, with a delighted soul, granted to Vaiśravaṇa immortality, the lordship of wealth, and the status of a world-protector (lokapāla),
as well as friendship with Īśāna and a son, Nalakūbara.
The Lord gave him the capital city of Laṅkā, inhabited by hosts of Rākṣasas; the celestial chariot named Puṣpaka, which travels at will;
and the sovereignty over the Yakṣas, as well as the status of a king of kings.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The sage named Viśravas, who had become a half-bodied being due to the wrath of Pulastya,
looked upon Vaiśravaṇa with anger.

But the lord of the *rākṣasas*, Kubera, perceived his father to be filled with anger; O King, he constantly strove to propitiate him. That king of kings, whose vehicle is man, continued to dwell in Laṅkā.
He gave three *rākṣasīs* to his father as attendants; O tiger among the Bharatas, they were skilled in dance and song and strove to gratify that high-souled *ṛṣi*.
O lord of the people, Puṣpotkaṭā, Rākā, and Mālinī— those slender-waisted women,
O King, desiring their own welfare and vying with one another—
the high-souled Blessed One, being pleased with them, granted boons.
To each of them were born sons resembling the guardians of the world, according to their desires; from Puṣpotkaṭā were born two sons who became lords of the Rākṣasas,
Kumbhakarṇa and Daśagrīva, whose strength was peerless on earth.
Mālinī gave birth to a single son, Vibhīṣaṇa.
From Rākā was born a pair: Khara and Śūrpaṇakhā.
Vibhīṣaṇa, however, surpassed them all in beauty.
He became highly distinguished, a protector of dharma, and devoted to ritual action.
Daśagrīva, however, was the eldest of them all, a bull among the Rākṣasas,
possessed of great energy, great heroism, and great courage and prowess.
At that time, Kumbhakarṇa was superior to all in strength;
he was a master of illusion, skilled in battle, fierce, and a night-stalker. Khara was valiant with the bow, a hater of Brahmins, and a consumer of flesh.
And likewise the fierce Śūrpaṇakhā, who creates obstacles for those seeking success;
all of them were knowers of the Vedas, heroes, and observers of well-performed vows,
dwelling with their father on Mount Gandhamādana.

Then they beheld Vaiśravaṇa there, whose vehicle is man, seated together with his father and endowed with supreme prosperity. Thereupon, filled with emulation, they resolved their minds upon ascetic penance.
Then they gratified Brahmā with terrible ascetic penance;
for a thousand years, the ten-headed Rāvaṇa stood on one foot, subsisting on air alone, surrounded by the five fires, and perfectly composed in meditation.
Sleeping on the ground, Kumbhakarṇa restricted his food and observed his vows;
Vibhīṣaṇa consumed only a single withered leaf. The wise one took delight in fasting and was always devoted to the chanting of prayers.
During that very time, the noble-minded Khara performed intense austerities,
as did Śūrpaṇakhā; while they were performing those penances,
the two of them served and protected them with joyful hearts.
Vibhīṣaṇa and Daśagrīva performed supreme austerity for ten thousand years, subsisting on air alone, O scorcher of foes;
they practiced it for ten years at Saraka and eight years at the ocean.
They dwelt for thousands of years in this Gokarṇa penance grove;
those two subduers of enemies lived on grass and leaves together with the wild animals.
And in the hermitage of Bādari, O King, they performed supreme austerity.
Those two great ascetics, serving Brahmā with purity,
completed a full thousand years; then the invincible Ten-faced one, having severed his own head, offered it into the fire, whereby the Lord of the World was pleased.
Then Brahmā went there in person and restrained them from their asceticism, enticing each and every one of them individually with the granting of boons. Brahmā said:
"I am pleased with you; turn back and choose boons, my sons!
Whatever you desire—except for one thing, immortality—let that be so. Whatever has been offered into the fire, all of it was done with the great longing for your heads."
In that very way, those [weapons] shall appear in your body according to your desire;
there shall be no deformity in your body, for you shall likewise be able to assume any form at will. You will be the conqueror of your enemies in battle, of this there is no doubt.
Rāvaṇa said:
"Neither from Gandharvas, gods, or Asuras, nor from Yakṣas or Rākṣasas,
nor from serpents, Kiṃnaras, or spirits, shall there be defeat for me."
Brahmā said:
"O blessed one, you shall have no fear from all those who have been mentioned here, except for a human; thus has it been ordained by me."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been addressed thus, the ten-necked one then became satisfied;
for that evil-minded man-eater held human beings in contempt.
Then the Great-Grandfather spoke likewise to Kumbhakarṇa:
"O mighty-armed Kumbhakarṇa of noble vows, choose a boon!
Choose a boon—may prosperity be yours—for I am well pleased with you," he said again and again.
With his consciousness seized by darkness, he chose a profound sleep.
Having said, "It shall be so," [Rāvaṇa] spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa again and again: "Choose a boon, my son; I am pleased with you."
Vibhīṣaṇa said:
"Even when I am beset by the greatest calamity, may my mind never turn toward unrighteousness;
and, O Blessed One, may the Brahma-weapon, though unstudied, manifest itself to me."
Brahmā said:
"O crusher of enemies, since your mind does not delight in unrighteousness despite being born in the womb of a Rākṣasa, I grant you immortality."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O lord of the people, having obtained the boon, the ten-necked Rākṣasa,
having conquered the Lord of Wealth in battle, drove him out of Laṅkā.
Having left Laṅkā, that Blessed One entered Gandhamādana,
accompanied by gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kiṃpuruṣas; meanwhile,
Rāvaṇa, having assailed him, seized his Puṣpaka aerial chariot.
Vaiśravaṇa cursed him: "This shall not carry you;
rather, he who slays you in battle—he alone this shall carry. Having shown contempt for me, your elder, you shall soon cease to exist."
But the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa, mindful of the dharma of the virtuous,
followed him, O great king, endowed with supreme splendor.
The blessed Lord of Wealth, his brother, was pleased with that brother.
The wise one bestowed the generalship over the armies of both Yakṣas and Rākṣasas.
Then the Rākṣasas, man-eaters, and mighty Piśācas all gathered together and consecrated the ten-faced Rāvaṇa as king.
The ten-necked one, who could assume any form at will and fly through the air, was preeminent in strength among both the Daityas and the gods; having assailed them, he seized their jewels.
Because he caused the worlds to cry out (*rāvayām āsa*), he is called Rāvaṇa.
The ten-necked one, whose strength lay in his passions, instilled fear in the gods.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the Brahman-sages, the Siddhas, and likewise the divine royal sages—
Placing the bearer of oblations at their head, they went for refuge to Brahmā.
Then all the gods, led by Śakra,
having assembled together and entrusted their speech to Agni, addressed Brahmā.
Then the blessed Agni, having bowed down to the blessed Grandfather, the Lord of the World, spoke these words with palms joined in reverence. Agni said:
That son of Viśravas, the ten-necked one of great strength,
who was made indestructible by the Blessed One in the past through the granting of a boon—
that one of great power now oppresses all creatures with various forms of cruelty.
"Therefore, O Blessed One, protect us; for no other protector is to be found.
Brahmā said:
"O Vibhāvasu, he cannot be conquered in battle even by the gods and asuras."
Whatever task has been ordained there for the complete subjugation of him,
for that purpose the four-armed Viṣṇu, the best among strikers, has descended at my command; he shall perform this deed.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then the Grandfather (Brahmā), in their presence, spoke these words:
"Together with all the hosts of gods, take birth upon the surface of the earth."
"Beget heroic sons upon the female bears and female monkeys everywhere— sons who are Viṣṇu’s allies and endowed with the power to assume any form at will.
Having been thus addressed by the Blessed One, they accepted that command.
The gods and gandharvas procreated sons in the form of monkeys.
Then, according to their respective portions, all the gods, gandharvas,
and dānavas quickly took pleasure in descending to the earth.
The high-souled ṛṣis, the siddhas, along with the kinnaras and the cāraṇas,
created formidable monkeys who roam the forests;
thousands of them were created, intent on the slaying of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa.
The monkeys were of immeasurable strength, heroic, and able to assume any form at will.
Whatever was the form, dress, and splendor of whichever deity, sons corresponding to those qualities were then born from them.
In their presence, the boon-granting god commanded a Gandharva woman named Dundubhī by name, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods' work. Then,
having heard the words of the Grandfather, the Gandharva woman Dundubhī—
At that time, Mantharā became a hunchbacked woman in the world of men;
and all those foremost of gods, beginning with Śakra,
begot sons upon the excellent women of the monkeys and bears.
They all followed their fathers in both glory and strength—
those breakers of mountain peaks, who used *śāla* trees, *tāla* palms, and stones as weapons;
all of them possessed bodies as firm as thunderbolts, and all were likewise endowed with the force of a rushing torrent.
All of them possess desire and vigor, and are experts in battle;
they have the strength of ten thousand elephants and are equal to the wind in speed.
Some of these forest-dwellers dwell wherever they please.

Having thus arranged all of that, the Blessed One, the creator of the world, instructed Mantharā on exactly what was to be done and in whatever manner it was to be done. Having understood his words, she, swift as thought, acted accordingly.
Wandering here and there, she delighted in fanning the flames of enmity.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The Blessed One has related the births of Rāma and the others individually."
"I have heard all about his deeds from birth onwards, including his marriage and so forth;
O Brahmin, I wish to hear the reason for his departure—
please tell me how the two heroic brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, the sons of Daśaratha, [came to leave]."
O Brahmin, they were sent forth to the forest, as was the illustrious daughter of Mithilā.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Vṛṣṭi, Jayanta, Vijaya, Siddhārtha, and Rāṣṭravardhana—
Aśoka, Dharmapāla, and Sumantra was the eighth; these were the eight ministers of Daśaratha. King Daśaratha, having fathered sons, became filled with joy.
Delighting in ritual action, devoted to dharma, and constantly serving his elders,
those sons of great energy gradually grew up and became masters of the Vedas along with their secret Upanishads, as well as of the science of archery.
O King, when they had practiced the life of celibacy and taken wives,
Daśaratha then became joyful and happy;
among them, Rāma was the eldest, for he indeed delighted the subjects.
