Because of his charm, the wise prince brought delight to his father’s heart. Then that intelligent king, considering himself to be advanced in age,
consulted with his ministers who were knowers of dharma and with his family priests.
O Bhārata, all those best of ministers considered the time to have arrived for the consecration of Rāma as the crown prince;
[they beheld him] with red eyes, mighty arms, and the gait of an elephant in rut.
Long-armed and broad-chested, with dark, curly hair,
that hero blazed with splendor; he was not inferior to Śakra in strength,
had reached the further shore of all dharmas, and was equal to Bṛhaspati in wisdom.
He whose subjects were entirely devoted to him, who was proficient in all branches of knowledge,
who had conquered his senses, and who was pleasing to the sight even of his enemies;
he was the restrainer of the wicked and the protector of those who walk the path of dharma.
O descendant of Kuru, King Daśaratha, beholding his son— who was steadfast, invincible, a conqueror, and unconquered, and who increased the joy of Kauśalyā—
attained supreme delight.
Reflecting upon the virtues of Rāma, the highly energetic and valiant king,
being well-pleased, addressed his family priest, saying, "Blessings to you!
O Brahmin, tonight the moon will enter into the auspicious conjunction with the Puṣya asterism."
"Let the necessary provisions be gathered for me, and let Rāma be invited.
Tomorrow the Puṣya asterism will occur, under which my son Rāma is to be consecrated as the heir apparent by me, together with the citizens and the ministers."
Having thus received the king's command, Mantharā then approached Kaikeyī and spoke these words at that time:
"Today, O Kaikeyī, the king has made your great misfortune known."
"O unfortunate woman, a fierce and enraged venomous serpent will bite you!
Truly fortunate is Kausalyā, whose son shall be consecrated.
For whence comes your good fortune, since your son does not share in the kingdom?"

Having understood those words, she, adorned with all her ornaments and possessing a supreme beauty like the waist of an altar, approached her husband in private and smiled with a pure smile as if laughing.
Manifesting her affection as it were, she spoke these sweet words:
"O King, you who are true to your promise, fulfill that one wish which you granted me; thereby release yourself from this peril."
The king said:
"Lo, I grant you a boon; take whatever you desire.
Who today, though deserving of death, shall not be slain? And who today, though deserving of death, shall be set free?"
"To whom shall I give wealth today, or from whom shall it be taken? Whatever wealth I possess here, other than that which belongs to a Brāhmaṇa,
I am the king of kings upon this earth and the protector of the four castes."
"O auspicious lady, tell me without delay what desire you have longed for.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having understood those words and having accepted the king, she...
Having ascertained his own strength, he then said to him:
"Let Bharata receive that consecration which has been prepared for Rāma; let the descendant of Raghu go to the forest."

"For nine and five years, let Rāma dwell as an ascetic, taking refuge in the Daṇḍaka forest, wearing bark garments, deerskins, and matted hair. Hearing those unpleasant words of the king, which portended a terrible outcome, [Kaikeyī...]
Afflicted by grief, O best of the Bharatas, he did not say anything at all.
Then, perceiving his father thus addressed, the valiant and righteous Rāma set out for the forest so that the king might remain true to his word.

Then the fortunate Lakṣmaṇa, armed with his bow, followed him, as did his wife Sītā— the daughter of Janaka from Videha— may you be blessed. Then, after Rāma had departed for the forest, King Daśaratha...
The body was joined with the law of the passage of time. Having learned that Rāma had departed and that the king had likewise passed away,
Queen Kaikeyī summoned Bharata and spoke these words.
"Daśaratha has gone to heaven, and Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa are dwelling in the forest;
seize this vast kingdom, secure and with its thorns removed.
To her, that righteous-souled one replied, "Alas, you have committed a cruel deed!"

"O mother, you who have killed your husband and destroyed this family out of greed for wealth, having cast infamy upon my head, O defiler of the lineage— may your desire be fulfilled! Having said this, she wept aloud.
Then, having purified his conduct in the presence of all the subjects and having performed the funeral rites for his father according to tradition, Bharata, who is devoted to righteousness,
followed after his brother Rāma, longing to bring him back.
Deeply distressed, he sent Kausalyā, Sumitrā, and Kaikeyī ahead in vehicles, and then set out accompanied by Śatrughna,
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and thousands of other brahmins.
Together with the people of the city and the countryside, longing to bring back Rāma,
he beheld Rāma on Citrakūṭa along with Lakṣmaṇa.
Upon seeing Bharata and hearing of his father’s departure to heaven, that Rāma—
Having duly performed the water libation for him, he spoke to his beloved brother:
"Go, dear one, protect the subjects; I shall protect the truth of my father. [I shall remain here] bearing the bow, wearing the ornament of ascetics."
Having prostrated and joined his palms in reverence, he spoke to the best of the Raghus;
he announced the king’s death and the orphaned state of the people of Kośala,
saying, "O Lord, please take back your own kingdom."
Having heard those words of his, Rāma was deeply distressed;
having bathed, he performed the water-libation rites for his godlike father.
Then Rāma spoke to Bharata, who was devoted to his brother.
"O scorcher of enemies, these sandals shall be the protectors of my kingdom.
To him, Bharata then replied with a prostration, "So be it.
Thus was he dismissed by Rāma, who was carrying out his father's command.
In Nandigrāma, he ruled the kingdom placing his sandals before him;
but Rāma, fearing once more the arrival of the citizens and countryfolk,
entered the great forest toward the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.
Having honored Śarabhaṅga, he took refuge in the Daṇḍaka forest;
then, resorting to the lovely Godāvarī River, he dwelt there. While Rāma was living there, the deed of Śūrpaṇakhā occurred.
He had a great enmity with Khara, who dwelt in Janasthāna;
and for the protection of the ascetics, Rāghava, who is devoted to dharma,
slew fourteen thousand rākṣasas upon the earth.
Having slain both Dūṣaṇa and Khara, who were possessed of great strength,
that wise Rāghava once again made the Forest of Dharma secure.
Having seen this, Śūrpaṇakhā [summoned] fourteen thousand [demons].
Slain in battle by Rāma with sharp arrows while he was on foot, those rākṣasas were destroyed; when they had been killed, Śūrpaṇakhā,
her nose and lips cut off, then went back to Laṅkā, the residence of her brother.
Then, approaching Rāvaṇa, the rākṣasī, fainting with grief and her face smeared with dried blood, fell at her brother’s feet. Seeing her so disfigured, Rāvaṇa was overcome with rage.
Leaping up from his seat in anger, gnashing his teeth against his teeth,
he dismissed his own ministers and spoke to her in private:
"By whom, O blessed lady, has this been done to you, disregarding me and my inconceivable power?"
Who, having encountered a sharp stake, would embrace it with all his limbs? Who, having placed fire upon his head, would sleep in trustful ease?
And who here would touch with his foot a most terrible venomous serpent?
"And who would stand touching the fangs of a maned lion? As he spoke thus, rays of fiery splendor issued forth from his orifices, like those of a tree burning at night through its own hollows.
His sister related to him all of Rāma’s prowess,
including the defeat of the Rākṣasas along with Khara and Dūṣaṇa.
Then, having heard of the slaughter of his kinsmen, Rāvaṇa was impelled by Time (Death).
Desiring the death of Rāma, he turned his mind toward Mārīca. Having then determined his course of action and consoled his sister,
the king, having made arrangements for the city, ascended into the air.
Having crossed over Trikūṭa and Mount Kāla,
he beheld the great ocean, the deep-watered abode of sea-monsters. Having passed beyond that, the Ten-faced one then arrived at Gokarṇa.
To that beloved and tranquil abode of the great-souled wielder of the trident,
Daśānana went to meet Mārīca, his former minister,
who had long ago taken up the life of an ascetic out of fear of Rāma.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then Mārīca, seeing that Rāvaṇa had arrived, was filled with agitation;
he honored him with hospitable offerings such as fruits, roots, and other provisions.
When he was seated at rest, that Rākṣasa sat down beside him and, being skilled in speech, spoke these humble words to the one who was himself an expert in discourse:
"Your complexion does not appear natural; is all well in your city?"
"Do all the subjects serve you as they did before? And what is the purpose of your coming here, O Lord of the Rākṣasas?
Know that whatever you have come for is already accomplished, even if it should be extremely difficult to achieve."
Filled with anger and indignation, Rāvaṇa recounted to him all those deeds of Rāma in brief;
and having heard it in summary, Mārīca spoke thus to Rāvaṇa.
"Enough of your approaching Rāma, for I am indeed well-acquainted with his prowess. For who is capable of enduring the force of the arrows of that great-souled one?
Indeed, it was he, that bull among men, who was the cause of my going forth into exile."
"By what evil-minded person was this gateway to your destruction pointed out to you?
Then Rāvaṇa, filled with rage, spoke to him while threatening him:
"If you do not follow my word, your death is certain."
Mārīca reflected: "Death is better than being disgraced.
Since death is inevitable, I shall do whatever he intends. Then Mārīca replied to the lord of the rākṣasas.

"What assistance must I provide for you? I shall do it, even against my will. To him, the Ten-necked One said: "Go and entice Sītā, having become a deer with jeweled horns and a body variegated with gems."
"Surely Sītā, upon seeing you, will urge Rāma [to act];
and once the descendant of Kakutstha has departed, Sītā will fall under my power. Taking her, I shall carry her away; thereafter, he shall cease to exist."
"Because of separation from my wife, my mind is distressed; please grant me this assistance.
Thus addressed, Mārīca offered water for himself and, deeply sorrowful, followed Rāvaṇa as he went before him.
Then, having gone to the hermitage of Rāma, whose deeds are effortless,
the two of them carried out everything exactly as they had previously planned.
Rāvaṇa, however, became an ascetic, shaven-headed, carrying a water-pot and holding the triple staff.
Having become a deer, Mārīca and [Rāvaṇa] approached that place.
Mārīca, assuming the form of a deer, showed himself to Vaidehī;
impelled by destiny, she urged Rāma toward him for her sake.
Doing what was pleasing to her, Rāma quickly took up his bow,
stationed Lakṣmaṇa for the sake of protection, and set out with the desire to catch the deer.
Armed with his bow, his quiver fastened, and equipped with a sword, leather arm-guard, and finger-protectors, he departed.

Rāma pursued the deer like Rudra pursuing the stellar deer (Tārāmṛga). As the Rākṣasa went on, he vanished and then appeared again; he drew him along a great distance, and only then did Rāma perceive him.
Recognizing him to be a night-stalker, the eloquent Rāghava took up an unerring arrow and struck the one in the form of a deer.
Struck by Rāma’s arrow, he then imitated Rāma’s voice.
"Alas, Sītā! Lakṣmaṇa!"—thus he cried out with a voice of distress.
Then Vaidehī heard those piteous words of his;
she ran toward the direction from which the sound came, and then Lakṣmaṇa spoke to her.
"Enough of your fear, O timid one; who could withstand Rāma?
In a mere moment, O lady of radiant smiles, you shall see Rāma returned.
Having spoken thus, she wept and grew apprehensive for her husband's brother.
Slain indeed by her own feminine nature— she whose ornament was her pure conduct—
that virtuous and devoted wife began to speak harshly to him:
"O fool, this is not the time for that which you desire in your heart."
I might even take up a weapon and slay myself with my own hand;
I might throw myself from a mountain peak, or enter the blazing fire;
or I might drink terrible poison—I shall surely abandon my life this very day.

"Having abandoned my husband Rāma, I would never under any circumstances attend upon you, a base man, any more than a tigress would approach a jackal. Having heard these words, Lakṣmaṇa, who was devoted to Rāghava, [remained silent].
Covering his ears, the man of virtuous conduct set out toward where Rāghava had gone;
grasping at Rāma’s footsteps, that archer pressed forward.
Then Lakṣmaṇa departed, looking back toward Vaidehī.
In the meantime, the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa appeared,
an unworthy being disguised in a worthy form like a fire covered by ashes, concealed in the dress of an ascetic and desiring to carry off that blameless woman.
Rāvaṇa, whose resolve was evil, approached Vaidehī.
Seeing that he had arrived, Janaka’s daughter, who knew what was right,
then invited him with offerings of fruits, roots, and other food.
Disregarding all of that and assuming his own true form,
that bull among Rākṣasas addressed Vaidehī with these conciliatory words:
"O Sītā, I am the king of the Rākṣasas, renowned by the name Rāvaṇa."

My city, named Laṅkā, is beautiful and lies on the far shore of the great ocean. There, you shall shine together with me among excellent women. Become my wife, O lady of lovely hips; abandon that ascetic Rāghava.

Having heard such words as these, Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, covered her ears with her hands; that woman of beautiful hips spoke these words: "May the sky with its stars fall, may the earth shatter into pieces!"
The waters in the ocean might dry up, the moon might abandon its cool rays,
and the sun might relinquish its heat;
even fire might lose its warmth, yet I shall never forsake the joy of the Raghus.
For how could a female elephant, having attended upon a great forest-dwelling lotus-elephant with temples flowing with rut, touch a boar?
For how could she, having drunk *mādhvīka* wine and having drunk honeyed *madhumādhavī* liquor...
"Remember, no woman should ever show greed for sour gruel (*sauvīraka*)," she said,
addressing him thus, and then she entered the hermitage once more,
her lips quivering with anger and her hands shaking repeatedly.
Rāvaṇa pursued that woman of beautiful hips and restrained her;
having threatened her with a harsh voice until she was deprived of her senses,
he seized her by the hair and then ascended into the sky.
Then the vulture Jaṭāyu, whose domain was the mountains, saw that ascetic woman being carried away, crying out, "Rāma! Rāma!
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Jaṭāyu, the son of Aruṇa, was the friend of Daśaratha;
he was the mighty king of vultures whose brother was Saṃpāti.
He then beheld Sītā, his daughter-in-law, held in the embrace of Rāvaṇa.
In his anger, the bird rushed toward Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas.
Then the vulture said to him, "Release her! Release Maithilī!
O night-stalker, how will you carry her away while I am still alive?"
"You shall not escape from me alive if you do not release my wife!
Having spoken thus to the lord of the rākṣasas, he violently tore at him with his claws;
and though he was repeatedly mangled by blows from his wings and beak, [the bird continued his assault].
He shed copious blood like a mountain with its springs;
being struck by the vulture who desired the welfare and pleasure of Rāma,
the ten-faced one, filled with rage, rushed toward that lord of birds.
Taking up his sword, he severed the two wings of that bird;
having struck down the king of vultures, who resembled the peak of a shattered cloud,
the Rākṣasa ascended upward, carrying Sītā in his arms.
Wherever Vaidehī saw a circle of hermitages,
a lake, or even a river, there she dropped an ornament.
On a mountain plateau, she beheld five bulls among monkeys.
There, the high-minded lady cast down a great, divine garment;
blown by the wind, it fell upon those lords of monkeys—
five of them— in their midst, appearing like a flash of lightning amidst the clouds.
Then the proud Lord of Laṅkā, having crossed the great ocean,
settled Sītā in a palace comparable to the Nandana grove;
in a short time, that sky-traveler passed by as if moving through the air.
Then he beheld that delightful city, beautiful and with many gates,
crowded with ramparts and walls, built by Viśvakarman;
the lord of the Rākṣasas, together with Sītā, entered the city of Laṅkā.

Having thus abducted Rāma’s wife, Rāvaṇa went to his own city. While Vaidehī was being carried away in this manner, the wise Rāma, having slain the great deer and turned back, then beheld his brother Lakṣmaṇa.
"How could you abandon Vaidehī in the forest frequented by rākṣasas?"—
thus, seeing his brother, he reproached him, saying, "You have arrived here. Then he spoke of that abduction by the rākṣasa who had assumed the form of a deer.
He was consumed with grief, brooding over his brother’s arrival;
reproaching himself, Rāma quickly approached him and said,
"Lakṣmaṇa, I cannot see whether Vaidehī still lives or not."
Lakṣmaṇa related all of that speech of Sītā to him— those final, unseemly words that Vaidehī had spoken. With a heart burning with anguish, Rāma rushed toward the hermitage.
Then he saw a vulture, slain and resembling a mountain;
suspecting it to be a *rākṣasa*, the descendant of Kakutstha, having powerfully drawn his bow,
rushed toward it along with Lakṣmaṇa.
The radiant king of the vultures spoke to Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa together: "May it be well with you both; I am a friend of Daśaratha.
Having heard those words of his, they grasped their two beautiful bows.
"Who is this that calls our father by name? they both said.
Then they saw him with both wings thus severed;
the vulture told them of his slaughter at the hands of Rāvaṇa for the sake of Sītā.

Rāghava asked the vulture, "In which direction has Rāvaṇa gone? With a nod of his head, the vulture indicated to him, and then he died. Understanding that gesture to mean "to the south," the descendant of Kakutstha [proceeded accordingly].
Honoring his father’s friend, he had him perform the funeral rites;
hearing the voice from the heavens saying, "Oh, how blessed and fortunate is this Jaṭāyu!", he attained a perfection difficult even for the *siddhas* to achieve.
Then, seeing the hermitage site— its grass mats and water-jars cast about, its jars shattered, empty, and frequented by packs of jackals—
the two, overcome by pain and grief and tormented by the abduction of Vaidehī, [were filled with distress].
The two subduers of enemies proceeded southward into the Daṇḍaka forest.
In that vast wilderness, Rāma, together with the son of Sumitrā,
beheld herds of deer fleeing in every direction.
And they heard the terrible roar of the creatures, increasing like that of a forest fire;
and in a moment, they beheld a headless trunk of fearsome appearance,
resembling a cloud or a mountain, with shoulders as broad as a *śāla* tree and mighty arms.
Then, O Bhārata, that Rākṣasa, by chance, seized Lakṣmaṇa— who had broad eyes reaching to his chest and a large belly and great mouth— by the hand; thereupon,
the son of Sumitrā immediately fell into despair.
Looking intently at Rāma, he was drawn toward his face;
dejected, he said to Rāma, "Behold this condition of mine—
the abduction of Vaidehī and this calamity that has befallen me."

There shall be the loss of your kingdom and likewise the death of your father. I shall not see you returned to Kosala, reunited with Vaidehī, established in the sovereignty over the earth inherited from your father and grandfather.

"Fortunate are those who shall behold the face of the noble one, consecrated with *kuśa*, *aja*, *śamī*, and *lava* grass, like the moon emerging from behind a cloud. Thus did the wise Lakṣmaṇa lament in many ways.
Then the descendant of Kakutstha, remaining unperturbed even in the midst of alarms, said to him:
"Do not despair, O tiger among men! While I am standing here, O hero, enhancer of Sumitrā’s joy, no one is capable of overpowering you."
"Cut off his right arm; my left arm has already been severed by him. As he spoke thus, Rāma struck down his arm with an exceedingly sharp sword, lopping it off like the stalk of a sesame plant.
Then the powerful Saumitri struck his right arm with a sword; and beholding his brother Raghava standing there,
Lakṣmaṇa again struck that *rākṣasa* violently in the side.
Then, his life-breath departed, that massive headless trunk (kabandha) fell to the earth.
Emerging from his body,
a person of divine appearance was seen stationed in the sky, blazing like the sun in the heavens.
The eloquent Rāma asked him: "Tell me, who are you? Speak to one who asks. Out of curiosity, what is this marvelous thing that appears so wondrous to me?
To him, the Gandharva replied: "O King, I am Viśvāvasu."
Having incurred the curse of Brahmā, he has entered a womb frequented by Rākṣasas.
Sītā has been carried off by Rāvaṇa, the king who dwells in Laṅkā;
go to Sugrīva, and he will provide you with assistance.
This is Pampā, with its auspicious waters and teeming with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks; it is a lake situated in the vicinity of Mount Ṛśyamūka. Sugrīva dwells here together with his four ministers.
The brother of Vālin, the king of the monkeys who wears a golden garland—
having met with him, you should disclose the root of your sorrow;
being of similar character, he will provide you with assistance.
"This much we are able to say: you shall see Jānakī;
surely the abode of Rāvaṇa is known to the king of the monkeys.
Having spoken thus, that divine person of great luster vanished.
Both those heroes, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, were filled with wonder.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, not far from there, they saw a lotus pond abounding with lotuses and water-lilies.
Afflicted by the sorrow of Sītā’s abduction, Rāma reached Lake Pampā; there,
being attended by a pleasantly cool breeze, fragrant as nectar,
he went in his mind to his beloved in that forest.
Remembering his beloved there, that lord of kings lamented, tormented by the arrows of love. Then the son of Sumitrā said to him:
"O giver of honor, such a state as this ought not to touch you."
Like a disease attacking a man who is self-possessed and of mature character,
you have obtained news of Vaidehī and Rāvaṇa; now,
by means of human effort and your own intelligence, bring that matter to fruition.
"Let us go to Sugrīva, that bull among monkeys, who dwells upon the mountain;
take heart in me, your disciple, servant, and companion.
Thus was Rāghava addressed by Lakṣmaṇa with many such words.
Having spoken thus, he returned to his natural state and became once more the immediate cause of action. Having partaken of the waters of the Pampā and offered libations to their ancestors,
both heroic brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, set forth.
Having approached Mount Ṛśyamūka, which abounded in roots and fruits,
those two heroes then beheld five monkeys upon the mountain peak.
Sugrīva then dispatched a monkey minister to them.
Having first conversed with the intelligent Hanumān, who stood firm like the Himavat mountain, those two then approached Sugrīva;
O King, Rāma then established a friendship with the king of the monkeys.
Then, having heard that Sītā had been abducted and learning all the suffering caused by Vālin, Sugrīva related everything to Rāma of immeasurable splendor.
When his purpose had been made known, they showed him that garment.
Having received that token which Sītā had dropped while being carried away by the monkeys, Rāma himself consecrated Sugrīva, the lord of the leaping monkeys,
in sovereignty over the earth and over the monkeys.
And the descendant of Kakutstha vowed the slaying of Vālin in battle,
while Sugrīva, O King, promised the recovery of Vaidehī;
having spoken thus, they established their agreement and inspired mutual confidence in one another.
Having arrived at Kiṣkindhā, they all stood there, longing for battle.
Upon reaching Kiṣkindhā, Sugrīva let out a roar like the sound of a surging flood.
Vālī could not endure that, but Tārā restrained him.

"Since this powerful monkey Sugrīva is roaring so loudly, I believe he has arrived with a protector; you ought not to go out. Then Vālī, wearing a golden garland, [spoke to] Tārā, whose face was like the lord of stars.
The eloquent lord of monkeys, her husband, spoke these words to her:
"You, who understand the cries of all creatures, look with your discerning intellect:
by what means has this one, who merely bears the name of my brother, arrived here seeking refuge?"
Having reflected for a moment, the wise Tārā, who possessed the radiance of the lord of stars, spoke thus to her husband: "O Lord of Monkeys, listen to everything:
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is a being of great courage whose wife has been abducted."
Having attained a state of equal enmity and friendship with Sugrīva, that wielder of the bow,
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is heard to be dwelling in the forest by his father’s command;
and his brother, the mighty-armed and unconquered son of Sumitrā, is there as well.
The wise one named Lakṣmaṇa stands ready for the accomplishment of our purpose;
and Mainda, Dvivida, Hanumān the son of the Wind,
and Jāmbavān the king of the bears— these ministers of Sugrīva are present.
"All these high-souled ones are wise and possessed of great strength;
relying on the prowess of Rāma, they are sufficient for your destruction. Having set aside those beneficial words spoken by her, the lord of the monkeys—
Jealous and suspecting that Tārā’s mind was fixed on Sugrīva,
he spoke harsh words to her and emerged from the mouth of the cave;
there he addressed Sugrīva, who was standing near Mālyavat.
"O fool, though you have been defeated by me many times and were released because I knew you were a kinsman— even though you are dear to life— why this haste toward death again?
Thus addressed, Sugrīva spoke these reasoned words to his brother:
Thus addressed, Sugrīva laughed loudly at his brother and spoke these reasoned words to his high-souled brother,
as if awakening Rāma, the slayer of enemies, to the fact that the time had arrived.
"O King, for me whose wife has been taken away and whose kingdom has been seized by you, what capacity indeed do I have to live? Know that I have come before you with this intent.
Having spoken thus in many ways, the two of them then fell upon each other.
In the battle, Vālin and Sugrīva, using *śāla* trees, *tāla* trees, and rocks as weapons,
struck one another; both fell to the ground,
both leaped about in various ways, and both struck each other with their fists.
Both heroes, drenched in blood and mangled by nails and teeth, then shone like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom; at that time,
no distinction whatsoever could be seen between them in battle.

Then, having resolved in his mind for the sake of discerning [his identity], Rāma had Hanumān place that garland around Sugrīva’s neck. Adorned with that garland fastened to his neck, the hero shone resplendently.
Like the glorious great mountain Malaya with its garland of clouds,
Rāma, beholding Sugrīva thus marked,
drew his excellent bow toward Vālin as his target.
The expansion of his bow then shone like that of a mechanical engine;
Vālī, struck in the heart by the arrow, was then terrified. With his vital organs pierced and struck down, he vomited blood from his mouth.
He saw Rāma standing nearby together with the son of Sumitrā;
having reproached that descendant of Kakutstha, he fell to the ground in a swoon. Tārā beheld him on the earth like the lord of stars fallen from the sky.

When Vālin was slain, Sugrīva took possession of Kiṣkindhā and of Tārā, whose face was like that of the lord of the stars, now that her husband had fallen. Rāma, however, remained for four months on the auspicious ridge of Mount Mālyavat.
The wise one, attended by Sugrīva, made his dwelling there;
meanwhile, Rāvaṇa, having returned to the city of Laṅkā under the sway of passion,
settled Sītā in a palace comparable to the Nandana grove.
Near the Aśoka grove, which resembled an ascetic hermitage,
that large-eyed lady, wearing the garb of an ascetic, emaciated by thoughts of her husband and devoted to fasting and penance, remained there.
She dwelt there in miserable abodes, subsisting on fruits and roots; meanwhile,
the lord of the rākṣasas stationed female rākṣasīs there for her protection—
women bearing spears, swords, tridents, axes, mallets, and flaming brands.
Two-eyed, three-eyed, and one with an eye on her forehead; long-tongued and tongueless;
three-breasted and one-legged; with three matted locks and a single eye—these and others were there, with blazing eyes and hair as bristly as a camel’s.
They sit surrounding Sītā day and night, unwearied;
those fierce piśācīs of terrible voice, with harsh expressions and syllables, constantly threaten that woman of long-cornered eyes.
"Let us eat her, let us tear her apart, dividing her into pieces as small as sesame seeds—
she who lives here while showing contempt for our husband!
Thus they reviled her, threatening her again and again.
Overwhelmed with grief for her husband, she sighed and said to them:
"Noble ladies, eat me quickly; I have no desire for life without that lotus-eyed one with dark, curly hair."
"Even if I am without food and deprived of the love of life,
I shall wither my limbs like a female serpent dwelling within a palm tree;
yet I would never approach any man other than Rāghava."
"Know this to be my truth; let that which follows now be done. Having heard those words of hers, those harsh-voiced rākṣasīs went to the lord of the rākṣasas to report everything from the beginning.
When they had all departed, a rākṣasī named Trijaṭā—learned in dharma and speaking kindly—consoled Vaidehī:
"Sītā, I shall tell you something; have confidence in me, my friend."
"O lady of beautiful thighs, let your fear depart; listen to these words of mine.
There is a wise and aged bull among the Rākṣasas named Avindhya;
seeking the welfare of Rāma, he spoke to me for your sake."
"Sītā should be addressed with my words, after she has been comforted and reassured:
'Your husband, the powerful Rāma, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, is well;
he has formed an alliance with the king of the monkeys, who possesses splendor equal to that of Śakra.'"
The illustrious Rāghava has done this for your sake and is now fully prepared; O timid one, let there be no fear in you from Rāvaṇa, who is despised by the world,
for you are protected, O blameless lady, by the curse of Nalakūbara.
For this wicked one was cursed long ago for laying hands upon his daughter-in-law Rambhā;
being one whose senses are uncontrolled, he is unable to approach a woman against her will.
Your husband, protected by Sugrīva, will arrive here quickly.
Accompanied by the son of Sumitrā, the wise one will liberate you from this mind.
For I have seen most terrible dreams of evil omen,
portending the destruction of this evil-minded destroyer of the lineage of Pulastya.
For this night-stalker is indeed cruel, evil-minded, and of base deeds;
by his very nature and the defect of his character, he increases the fear of all. With his consciousness struck down by Fate, he vies with all the gods.
In a dream, I indeed beheld signs of his destruction:
the ten-faced one, anointed with oil and with disheveled hair, was sinking into the mud;
he stood as if dancing upon a chariot yoked to donkeys.
And these [demons], Kumbhakarṇa and the others, naked with disheveled hair,
smeared with red garlands and unguents, are being dragged toward the southern quarter.
He, however, bears a white parasol, wears a turban, and is adorned with white garlands and ornaments.
Vibhīṣaṇa alone has ascended Mount Śveta,
as have his four ministers, who are adorned with white garlands and unguents;
they shall deliver us from this great terror.
Rāma, the destroyer of enemies, has delivered you from this fear;
by Rāma’s weapon, the earth together with its oceans has been secured.
Your husband shall fill the entire world with his glory.
I saw Lakṣmaṇa standing upon a heap of bones, eating honeyed milk-rice, while looking in every direction;
and I saw [Sītā] weeping, her limbs wet with blood, protected by a tiger.
"O Vaidehī, you have been seen by me many times going toward the northern direction;
you shall soon experience joy, O Sītā, when you are reunited with your husband Rāghava and his brother."
Having heard those words of Trijaṭā, that young woman with eyes like a fawn’s became hopeful once more of being reunited with her husband,
just as those fierce and most dreadful Piśācīs arrived.
They saw her sitting with Trijaṭā just as before.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then they beheld her, afflicted by grief for her husband, miserable, and wearing soiled garments.

Rāvaṇa, afflicted by the arrows of desire, beheld the devoted wife weeping, her ornaments reduced to mere fragments of jewels, as she sat upon a stone slab surrounded by ogresses; and he drew near to her.
Unconquered in battle by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and kimpuruṣas, he went to the Aśoka grove, deluded by passion;
wearing celestial garments, glorious, and adorned with polished jeweled earrings.
Wearing a crown of variegated garlands, he was like the spring season incarnate;
though adorned with great effort like a wish-fulfilling tree,
he remained terrifying even when decorated, like a tree at a cemetery shrine.
Approaching that slender-waisted woman, the night-stalker appeared like the planet Saturn approaching the star Rohiṇī;
struck by the arrows of the flower-bannered god of love, he addressed that fair-hipped lady.
"‘This is it,’ he said to the young woman, who was as terrified and helpless as a doe;
‘Sītā, this much is sufficient; you have shown enough devotion to your husband. Be gracious, O slender-limbed one, and let your person be adorned.’”
"O lady of excellent hips, adorned with costly ornaments and garments, accept me;
O woman of beautiful complexion, become the foremost among all my women.
For I have daughters of the gods as well as the wives of royal sages."
There are daughters of the Dānavas and also the wives of the Daityas;
fourteen crores of Piśācas abide by my word,
and twice as many man-eating Rākṣasas of terrible deeds.

Then there were three times as many yakṣas who carry out my commands; some of them, O lady, have taken refuge with my brother, the Lord of Wealth. And the gandharvas and apsarases always attend upon me when I am at the banquet hall.
"O lady of beautiful thighs, they attend upon me just as they do my brother.
I too am the son of the brahmin-sage Viśravas, the muni;
my fame is celebrated as the fifth among the world-protectors."

"O beautiful lady, divine foods, both solid and soft, and various kinds of drinks— just as they belong to the Lord of the Thirty-three, so too do they belong to me. Let the evil karma resulting from your dwelling in the forest be exhausted."
"O lady of beautiful hips, become my wife, just as Mandodarī is.
Thus addressed by him, Vaidehī, with her auspicious face turned away,
placed a blade of grass between them and spoke to that night-stalker.

With her exceedingly beautiful thighs drenched incessantly by the unwholesome water of her tears, that young woman, utterly bewildered by despair, somehow managed to steady herself and keep her breasts from falling, though they were pressed together.
Vaidehī, who regards her husband as a deity, spoke these words to that base creature: "O Lord of Rākṣasas, though you have spoken such words repeatedly,
this speech of yours filled with despair has been heard by me, unfortunate as I am."
Therefore, O Bhadrasukha, may it be well with you; let your mind be turned back.
I am the wife of another, unattainable, and ever devoted to my husband. Furthermore, a wretched human woman such as I is not at all a suitable wife for you.
Having violated her against her will, what pleasure will you obtain?
Your father is a Brahmin equal to Prajāpati, born of Brahmā;
how is it that you, who are like a world-protector, do not uphold righteousness?
"How can you not feel shame here, claiming as your brother the lord of kings, the friend of Maheśvara, the master Dhanesvara?
Having said this, Sītā wept, making her breasts tremble.
The slender-limbed woman covered her neck and face with her garment;
as that beautiful lady wept, her long, well-bound braid— dark,
glossy, and black— was seen upon her head like a female serpent.
Having heard those very harsh words spoken by Sītā, the evil-minded Rāvaṇa,
though rejected, spoke these words once more:
"O Sītā, let the god whose banner is the makara indeed torment my limbs with desire."

"I shall not approach you, O woman of beautiful hips and lovely smiles, against your will. What indeed can I do, since even now you remain devoted only to Rāma, who is but food for us, a mere mortal?"

Having spoken thus to her of faultless limbs, that lord of the hosts of Rākṣasas vanished on the spot and departed in his desired direction. Vaidehī, emaciated by grief, remained there surrounded by the female Rākṣasīs.
Being attended by Trijaṭā, she then continued to dwell in that very place.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
But Rāghava, together with Saumitri, was protected by Sugrīva.
While dwelling on the ridge of Mount Mālyavat, he beheld the cloudless sky;
and seeing the spotless moon in the clear firmament,
followed by the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, that slayer of enemies gazed upon it.
Having been suddenly awakened by the cool breeze carrying the fragrance of white, blue, and red lotuses while staying upon the mountain,
he, dejected in mind, addressed the heroic Lakṣmaṇa at dawn.
"Remembering Sītā, who is confined in the abode of the Rākṣasa, the righteous-souled one said:
'Go, Lakṣmaṇa, and find the lord of the monkeys in Kiṣkindhā—
he who is intoxicated by vulgar pleasures, ungrateful, and clever only in his own self-interest.'"
"That lowest of his lineage, that fool who was consecrated by me in the kingdom—
him whom all the monkeys, gopucchas, and bears indeed follow;
for whose sake Vālin was slain by me, O scion of Raghu's family."

O mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa, when you were with me in the grove near Kiṣkindhā at that time, I considered that lowest of monkeys on earth to be ungrateful— that fool who, being in such a state, does not recognize me today.
I think that he does not understand the fulfillment of one's promise; surely, with his small intellect, he disregards me who have done him a favor.
If he remains inactive, he must be sleeping, his soul devoted to sensual pleasure.
"You must lead him along the path of Vālin to the destination of all beings.
Yet, if this bull among monkeys is willing to serve our purpose, then take him and come, O descendant of Kakutstha; be swift and do not delay."
Thus addressed by his brother, Lakṣmaṇa, who was devoted to the words and welfare of his elder,
set forth, taking up his beautiful bow equipped with arrows and strings;
having reached the gate of Kiṣkindhā, he entered unopposed.
Thinking that he was angry, King Hari went out to meet him;
Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, accompanied by his wife and with a humble soul,
received him with affection and honored him with the hospitality he deserved.

Having heard all of that in its entirety, O king of kings, Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, together with his servants and wife, bowed low with joined palms and, being fearless, spoke those words of Rāma to the son of Sumitrā.
Delighted, he spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa, that elephant among men:
"O Lakṣmaṇa, I am neither dull-witted, nor ungrateful, nor merciless.
Listen now to the effort I have made in the search for Sītā."
All the monkeys have been dispatched by me in every direction; they have been disciplined,
and a time limit has been set for all of them to return again within one month— [to see] this earth with its forests, mountains, and cities, clothed by the ocean.
O hero, the earth—with its villages, cities, and mines—must be searched.
That month ought to be completed in five nights;
then, together with Rāma, you shall hear very great and pleasant news.
Thus addressed by that wise lord of monkeys, Lakṣmaṇa,
casting off his anger and with a spirit undepressed, paid homage to Sugrīva. Then he,
together with Sugrīva, approached Rāma, who was stationed on the ridge of Mount Mālyavat.
Having approached him, they reported the success of that undertaking;
in this manner, those lords of monkeys arrived by the thousands,
and at that time the monkeys came together.
The leaders of the monkeys searched the three directions, but not those who had gone to the south;
they then reported to Rāma that the earth, girdled by the ocean, had been searched.
Although those foremost of monkeys had searched the southern quarter, they had neither found Vaidehī nor seen Rāvaṇa;
yet, despite being distressed, the descendant of Kakutstha maintained his life, placing his hopes in them.
When two months had passed and the appointed time was over,
the monkeys then approached Sugrīva and quickly spoke these words:
"That great and flourishing Madhuvana forest, which was guarded by Vālin— "
"O best of monkeys, the son of the Wind-god eats that which was given by you; and likewise Aṅgada, the son of Vālin, and those other bulls among monkeys who were dispatched by you, O King,
to search the southern quarter."
Hearing of their devotion, he considered himself to have accomplished his purpose;
for such is the conduct of servants who have achieved their goal.
That wise leader of the monkeys then reported this to Rāma.
And Rāma, too, by means of inference, considered Maithilī to have been found;
and those monkeys, led by Hanumān, having rested,
approached the lord of the monkeys in the presence of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.

O Bhārata, having observed Hanumān’s gait and the color of his face, Rāma gained further conviction that Sītā had been seen. Those monkeys, headed by Hanumān, were then filled with joy in their hearts.
They prostrated according to custom before Rāma, Sugrīva, and Lakṣmaṇa.
Grasping his bow with an arrow, Rāma spoke to them as they approached:
"Will you restore me to life? Have you fulfilled your purpose?"
"Having slain my enemies in battle and recovered the daughter of Janaka, I shall once again exercise sovereignty over Ayodhyā;
for without having liberated the princess of Videha and without having struck down my foes in war,"
"Deprived of my wife and cast out, I have no desire to live.
To Rāma, who had spoken these words, the son of the Wind replied:
"I bring you pleasant news, O Rāma: that Jānakī has been seen by me."
Having searched the southern quarter, including its mountains,
forests, and mines, we became exhausted when the time had passed; then we beheld a great cave extending for many yojanas, which we entered.

Having traveled a very great distance through a region that was dark, densely wooded, impenetrable, and infested with insects, we then beheld the radiance of the sun; and right there, in the midst of it, we saw a divine mansion.
O Rāghava, it is said that at that time there was the palace of the Daitya Maya;
there, an ascetic woman named Prabhāvatī performed austerities.
By her were provided various kinds of foods and drinks.

Having eaten and regained our strength, we then departed from that place by the path she had described; and as we emerged, we beheld the Sahya and Malaya mountains, as well as the great mountain Dardura, in the vicinity of the salt ocean.
Then, having ascended Mount Malaya and beholding the abode of Varuṇa, they became despondent, distressed, and exhausted, utterly losing all hope for their lives as they gazed upon the great ocean,
which extended for many hundreds of yojanas.
Reflecting upon that abode of whales, crocodiles, and fish, we were deeply distressed;
having then resolved to fast unto death, we sat there. Then, at the conclusion of our conversation, the story of the vulture Jaṭāyu arose.
Then we beheld a bird of terrible form and fearsome aspect, resembling a mountain peak, like a second son of Vinatā. Approaching us, he spoke these words, intending to devour us.
"O, who is this that speaks of my brother Jaṭāyu?
"I am Saṃpāti by name; I am his elder brother, a lord of birds.
Once, out of mutual rivalry, we two flew up toward the assembly of the Sun."
"Then these two wings of mine were burnt, but those of Jaṭāyu were not;
at that time, my beloved brother Gṛdhrapati, who had not been seen by me for a long while,
fell down with his wings scorched upon this great mountain."
"I am unable to see my heroic brother Jaṭāyu.
When he was speaking thus, we informed him that his brother had been killed,
and we briefly reported this calamity of yours as well.
O King, O subduer of enemies, having then heard that most grievous and unpleasant news, Saṃpāti became despondent in heart and questioned us again:
"Who is this Rāma? How is Sītā? And how was Jaṭāyu killed?"
"O best of monkeys, I wish to hear all of this;
I desire to hear from you in detail the entire account of how this calamity befell him, as well as the reason for his fasting unto death."
That king of birds raised us up with these words:
"Rāvaṇa is known to me, and his great city, Laṅkā,
has been seen by me on the far shore of the ocean in a cave of Mount Trikūṭa."
"Vaidehī will be there; of this I have no doubt. Having heard these words of his, O scorcher of enemies, we rose up in haste and deliberated upon a counsel for crossing the ocean.
When no one could resolve to leap across the ocean,
I then entered my father and leaped over the great sea; having slain the water-demoness, I crossed that expanse of a hundred yojanas.
There, in the inner apartments of Rāvaṇa, I beheld the virtuous Sītā; she was devoted to fasting and asceticism, longing for the sight of her husband,
with matted hair, her limbs smeared with dirt, emaciated, wretched, and full of distress.
Having recognized that Sītā by various signs, I approached the noble lady while she was in private and spoke to her:
"O Sītā, I am Rāma’s messenger, a monkey and the son of the Wind-god."
Desiring to behold you, I have arrived here through the air.
The two princes, the brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, are well;
they are protected by Sugrīva, the lord of all the monkeys.
"Rāma, together with the son of Sumitrā, has inquired after your welfare, O Sītā;
and out of friendship, Sugrīva also asks after your well-being. Your husband will soon arrive here along with all the monkeys."
"O Goddess, grant me your confidence; I am a monkey, not a Rākṣasa.
Having reflected for a moment, Sītā replied to me:
"I know you to be Hanumān from the words of Avindhya."
"O mighty-armed one, the Rākṣasa Avindhya, who is honored by the elders, told me that Sugrīva is surrounded by ministers such as yourself. Having said to me, 'Go,' Sītā gave me this jewel."
By him Vaidehī was protected for all this time, blameless as she was;
and for the sake of providing proof, Janaki related this story of the blade of grass shot at the crow on the great mountain Citrakūṭa.
O tiger among men, for the sake of recognition,
you indeed made that wicked-souled crow one-eyed and deformed;
and having caused him to proclaim your identity, you then burnt that city.
When he had arrived, Rāma honored that speaker of pleasant words.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, while Rāma was seated right there together with them...
Then, at the command of Sugrīva, the foremost of monkeys assembled;
surrounded by a thousand crores of swift monkeys,
the illustrious Suṣeṇa, the father-in-law of Vālin, approached Rāma.
Surrounded by hundreds of millions, the two lords of monkeys— Gaja and Gavaya,
both of great heroism— were seen separately;
as was Kumuda, of great heroism and the most excellent among the bulls of the monkeys.
O Great King, the formidable-looking Gavākṣa, a golāṅgūla who dwells on Mount Gandhamādana and is renowned as Gandhamādana, appeared drawing sixty thousand crores [of monkeys].
The wise monkey named Panasa, possessed of great strength, drew along a thousand crores of fierce monkeys;
he also led ten, twelve, thirty-five, and [another] ten crores.
The illustrious and powerful elder among the monkeys named Dadhimukha led a vast army of monkeys of fearsome splendor—
black bears with white markings on their faces, performers of terrible deeds.
Jāmbavān appeared with a hundred thousand crores;
these and many other leaders of monkey hosts,
O great king, arrived in incalculable numbers for the sake of Rāma.
The tumultuous sound of roaring lions, with the hue of *śirīṣa* flowers,
is heard as they rush here and there;
some resemble mountain peaks, while others are like buffaloes.
Resembling autumn clouds, with forests of crushed vermilion,
the monkeys— leaping up, falling down,
and bounding along— some shaking up dust, gathered from all sides.
That great host of monkeys, resembling the full ocean,
then established their camp there with the approval of Sugrīva. Then,
when those lords of the monkeys had assembled from all sides, [the narrative continues].
On an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable constellation, and at a highly honored moment,
the illustrious Rāghava, accompanied by Sugrīva, set forth with that marshaled army as if he were overturning the worlds.
Hanumān, the son of the Wind, was at the head of the army,
while the son of Sumitrā, free from all fear, protected the rear.
There, the two descendants of Raghu shone resplendent, their hands bound with leathern finger-guards and arm-guards.
Surrounded by the great ministers of Hari like the moon and sun by the planets,
that army of Hari, armed with *śāla* trees, *tāla* trees, and stones,
shone forth like a vast field of rice facing the rising sun.

A vast army, protected by Nala, Nila, Angada, Kratha, Mainda, and Dvivida, set out for the accomplishment of Raghava’s purpose; they proceeded toward regions that were highly auspicious according to ritual precepts and abounding in roots and fruits.
Abiding without hindrance upon auspicious mountain peaks that abound in honey, meat, and water,
that army of monkeys then approached the salt-water ocean.
That army, resembling a second ocean and possessing many banners,
reached the forest on the shore and then made its camp there.
Then the glorious son of Daśaratha addressed Sugrīva.
In the midst of the monkey leaders, he spoke these words appropriate for the occasion:
"What means do you consider suitable for crossing the ocean? For this army is vast, and the ocean is difficult to traverse."
There, other monkeys who considered themselves clever declared:
"These monkeys are capable of leaping across the ocean, but not across it entirely.
Some resolved to cross by means of boats, and others by various kinds of rafts.
"No," Rāma replied, consoling them all:
"All the heroic monkeys are not capable of leaping across the ocean, which is a hundred yojanas in width. This is not a final resolve on your part."
There are not enough boats for the army to cross; furthermore, how could one such as I cause harm to merchants? Moreover, our army is vast, and the enemy would surely strike at its vulnerabilities.
"Crossing by means of rafts or floats does not appeal to me at all in this matter.
However, I shall undertake to cross this ocean through strategic means;
by fasting, I shall lie down [in wait], and then he will reveal himself to me."

"If he does not show me the path, then I shall consume him with great, irresistible weapons, blazing more fiercely than fire and wind. Having spoken thus, Rāghava, together with the son of Sumitrā, performed the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśya).

He lay down according to the prescribed rites upon a bed of *kuśa* grass by the ocean; then the glorious god of the rivers and streams, surrounded by hosts of aquatic creatures, appeared to the descendant of Raghu in a dream.
Addressing him with these sweet words, "O son of Kausalyā," he who was surrounded by hundreds of mines of jewels said this:
"Tell me, O bull among men, what assistance may I provide you here?"
"I am Ikṣvāku, your kinsman," Rāma said to him.
Having been addressed thus by the ocean, Rāma then spoke these words:
"O Lord of rivers and streams, I desire a path to be granted for my army."
"By means of which I may go and slay the ten-necked one, that defiler of the Paulastya lineage,
the Rākṣasa who has carried off my wife, along with his followers—
if you do not grant me passage when I entreat you thus,"
"I shall wither you with arrows consecrated by divine mantras.
Hearing these words spoken by Rāma, the Abode of Varuṇa,
standing with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words in distress.
"I do not wish to oppose you, nor am I one who creates obstacles for you.
Listen to these words, O Rāma; having heard them, act accordingly. If I grant passage for your army as it proceeds by your command,"
"Others too shall command me thus by the power of their bows.
However, there is here a monkey named Nala, esteemed for his craftsmanship;
he is the powerful son of the divine Tvaṣṭṛ, Viśvakarman."
"Whatever wood, grass, or even stone you shall throw upon me, I will support all of it; that shall become your bridge.
Having spoken thus, when he had vanished, Rāma said to Nala:
"Build a bridge across the ocean, for in my opinion you are indeed capable of it.
By that means, the descendant of Kakutstha caused a bridge to be constructed,
ten yojanas in width and a hundred yojanas in length.
That which is renowned as the Nala-setu, still celebrated on earth today,
remains like a mountain, upheld in honor of Rāma’s command;
there, the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa approached him.
The high-minded Rāma welcomed that brother of the lord of the rākṣasas, who was accompanied by four ministers, with a greeting of welcome;
yet Sugrīva felt apprehension, thinking that he might be a spy.
When Rāghava was fully satisfied by his actions and by the sincerity of his conduct and gestures, he then honored him and consecrated Vibhīṣaṇa in the sovereignty over all the rākṣasas.
And he made him a follower of the mantras and a friend to Lakṣmaṇa; then,
in accordance with the counsel of Vibhīṣaṇa, O lord of men, he crossed the great ocean with his army by means of that bridge in just one month.
Then, having gone there and reached the many groves of Laṅkā, he caused the monkeys to break apart those numerous and vast gardens. There dwelt the two Rākṣasa ministers of Rāvaṇa, Śuka and Sāraṇa.
The two spies, who were acting for the benefit of Rāvaṇa, arrived to see the army;
Vibhīṣaṇa seized them while they were in the form of monkeys. When those two night-stalkers had assumed their true rakṣasa forms, [Vibhīṣaṇa captured them].
Having shown his army, Rāma then dismissed it;
having stationed that army in the grove, the heroic one sent Aṅgada as an envoy to Rāvaṇa, accompanied by wise monkeys.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having encamped his army in that forest, which abounded in food and water and possessed many roots and fruits, the descendant of Kakutstha protected it according to the prescribed rules.
And Rāvaṇa carried out the defensive measures prescribed by the treatises for Laṅkā;
she was already naturally difficult to assail, with its walls and gateways firm,
and its moats filled with deep water and teeming with fish and crocodiles.
There were seven invincible [towers], bristling with stakes made of khadira wood;
they were difficult to assail due to their ear-protecting mechanisms and were equipped with hollow tubes,
stones, warriors carrying jars of venomous snakes, resin, and dust.
At all the city gates, there were stationary and mobile military outposts equipped with pestles, firebrands, iron arrows, javelins, spears, battle-axes, *śataghnīs*, and mallets smeared with beeswax.
They were numerous in infantry and possessed many elephants and horses. Then Aṅgada, having reached the gateway of Laṅkā,
was recognized by the lord of the Rākṣasas and entered without fear.
In the midst of many millions of rākṣasas, he of great power shone like the sun surrounded by garlands of clouds;
having approached the descendant of Pulastya, who was surrounded by his ministers.
Having called to mind Rāma’s message, the eloquent one began to speak:
"O King, the highly illustrious Rāghava, the lord of Kosala, says this to you:
these words are appropriate for the occasion; accept them and act upon them."
Having encountered a king who has not disciplined his soul and is devoted to unrighteousness,
both the lands and the cities, overcome by that lack of policy, perish.
By you alone, O one who has committed an offense against me, has Sītā been seized by force.
That [destruction] shall come about for the slaughter of other innocent ones,
those forest-dwelling sages who were previously harmed by you while you were possessed by strength and pride, and even the gods who were insulted by you.

Royal sages have been slain and weeping women have been carried off; this is the fruit that has now come upon you for that misconduct of yours. I shall slay you along with your ministers; fight and be a man!
"O night-stalker, behold the power of my bow, though it belongs to a mere mortal!
Let Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, be released; you shall never escape from me.
With my sharpened arrows, I shall rid this world of Rākṣasas."
Having heard these harsh words spoken by the messenger, King Rāvaṇa, overwhelmed with rage, could not endure them. Then,
four night-rangers who were skilled in discerning their master’s gestures [approached].
They seized him by his four limbs, like birds seizing a tiger;
then Aṅgada, having taken those night-rangers who were thus clinging to his limbs, leaped up into the air and entered the palace roof.
As he leapt up with great speed, those night-stalkers fell to the earth,
their hearts shattered and tormented by his blows.
Released from that palace roof-peak, he descended once more.
Having leaped over the city of Laṅkā and approached the presence of his own forces, Aṅgada then went to the lord of Kosala; having reported everything,
that radiant hero rested, being greeted with joy by Rāghava.
Then, with a total assault by the monkeys who were as swift as the wind,
the joy of the Raghus caused the wall of Laṅkā to be breached;
thereafter, Lakṣmaṇa placed Vibhīṣaṇa and the lord of the bears at the forefront.
He crushed the southern city gate, which was difficult to assail; then,
with a hundred thousand crores of bay horses whose bodies were tawny like young elephants and who were skilled in battle, he rushed toward Laṅkā.
Three crores of smoke-colored bears, with arms, thighs, and shanks hanging down between their legs, took their positions; likewise,
there were monkeys leaping up, falling down, and swooping down.
At that time, the sun was not visible, its radiance destroyed by the dust;
[the sky] was filled with monkeys who resembled the blossoms of the śāli rice, possessed the luster of śirīṣa flowers, were like the rising sun, and were as white as reeds.
O King, the Rākṣasas, along with their women and elders, were filled with wonder as they saw the rampart turned tawny on all sides;
they shattered the jeweled pillars and the tops of the towers and turrets.
They scattered the engines, their momentum shattered and crushed; seizing the *śataghnīs* along with their wheels, clubs, and stones,
those of great strength hurled them into the midst of Laṅkā by the force of their arms.
And whatever hosts of night-rangers were stationed on the ramparts at that time,
they fled by the hundreds, pursued by the monkeys.
Then, by the king’s command, the Rākṣasas, who could assume any form at will, [set forth].
Appearing with distorted forms, they went forth in groups of hundreds and thousands,
raining down showers of weapons and putting the forest-dwellers to flight; exerting their supreme prowess, they cleared away the rampart.
The wall, which had been cleared of monkeys, was once again filled by night-stalkers as terrifying to behold as heaps of black beans;
many of the foremost monkeys fell, their limbs pierced by spears.
And the night-stalkers, their bodies crushed by pillars and gateways, fell there;
a hair-to-hair struggle ensued between the rākṣasas and the monkeys,
as those heroes devoured one another with claws and teeth.
Groaning from both sides, the monkeys and rākṣasas there,
though struck down and fallen upon the ground, did not let go of one another;
Rāma, however, rained down nets of arrows like a rain-cloud.

Having reached Laṅkā, those [arrows] struck down those night-rangers. The son of Sumitrā as well, firm with his bow and having conquered fatigue, felled the Rākṣasas stationed within the fortress, aiming at each one in turn with his iron shafts.
Then, by the command of Rāghava, the withdrawal of the armies took place after the assault on Laṅkā had been accomplished; they had achieved their objective and were victorious. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, as those soldiers were settling in, certain groups of Piśācas and minor Rākṣasas, who were followers of Rāvaṇa, attacked them:
Parvaṇa, Pūtanā, Jambha, Khara, Krodhavaśa, and Hari.
Praruja, Aruja, Praghasa, and others like them—
against those invisible and evil-minded ones as they were swooping down, Vibhīṣaṇa, who knew the proper means, employed the destruction of their power of invisibility.
Being seen by those powerful monkeys who leap great distances,
O King, they were struck down on all sides and went to the earth, deprived of life.
Then Rāvaṇa, unable to endure this, set forth accompanied by his army.
Surrounded by the terrible forces of the *rākṣasas* and the *piśācas*,
he who was skilled in the application of the science of war— like a second Uśanas—
arrayed his troops in the *uśanasa* formation and led all the monkeys forward.

But Rāghava, having marched out and seeing the ten-faced one with his army drawn up in formation, countered the night-stalker by arranging his own forces according to the system of Bṛhaspati. Then, having come together, Rāvaṇa fought there with Rāma.
Lakṣmaṇa fought with Indrajit, and likewise Sugrīva with Virūpākṣa; Nikharvaṭa fought with Tāra, Nala with Tuṇḍa, and Paṭuśas with Panasa.

For whoever considered himself capable of withstanding another encountered him; at the time of battle, each fought relying on the strength of his own arms. That clash increased, heightening the fear of the timid.
Like the terrible and hair-raising battle between the gods and asuras in ancient times,
Rāvaṇa struck Rāma with showers of spears, tridents,
and swords; and Rāghava likewise struck Rāvaṇa with sharp, keen, iron-tipped shafts.
In the same manner, Lakṣmaṇa struck the striving Indrajit with arrows that pierce the vital organs,
and Indrajit also pierced the son of Sumitrā with many shafts;
Vibhīṣaṇa struck Prahasta, and Prahasta struck Vibhīṣaṇa.
Free from pain, he rained down sharp arrows with feathers like bird wings;
there occurred a clash of those powerful great weapons by which all the three worlds, including both the moving and the unmoving, were shaken.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then Prahasta, who was fierce in battle, suddenly approached Vibhīṣaṇa and,
letting out a roar, struck him with a mace.
Struck by that mace of terrible velocity, the wise and mighty-armed one did not tremble, remaining as steadfast as the Himavat mountain.
Then, Vibhīṣaṇa seized a massive mace adorned with a hundred bells.
Having consecrated a great spear with mantras, he hurled it toward his head. As it fell with force like a thunderbolt, the Rākṣasa was seen with his head severed, like a tree broken by the wind.
With its head severed, that Rākṣasa, whose life-force had followed [him] through his misconduct, suddenly fell like a tree broken by the wind;
seeing Prahasta, the night-stalker, slain in battle, [he...]
Dhūmrākṣa rushed toward the monkeys with great speed;
his army, resembling a mass of clouds and terrifying to behold, charged forward.
Upon seeing it, the foremost of the monkeys suddenly broke ranks in the battle.
Then, seeing those foremost of monkeys suddenly broken,
Hanumān, that tiger among monkeys, emerged and took his stand. Seeing the son of the Wind standing firm in battle, the monkeys [regained their composure].
With great speed, O King, they turned back from all sides;
then there arose a great, tumultuous,
hair-raising roar from the armies of Rāma and Rāvaṇa as they rushed at one another.
When that terrible battle, mired in blood, had commenced,
Dhūmrākṣa put that army of monkeys to flight with his feathered arrows.
Then the conqueror of enemies [Rāma] [beheld] that great minister of the Rākṣasa as he was charging forward.
Hanumān, the son of the Wind, received [the blow] with speed.
A terrible battle ensued between those two heroes, the monkey and the rākṣasa,
as they sought to conquer one another in combat, like Indra and Prahlāda.
With maces and iron clubs, the Rākṣasa struck the monkey;
and the monkey struck the Rākṣasa with trees complete with trunks and branches.
First he struck him on the head, and then again and again with his tail.

Then the wise Hanumān, son of the Wind-god, with his great *tṛṇarāja* (bamboo) spear— which was as strong as iron and capable of piercing armor— slew Dhūmrākṣa along with his horses, chariot, and charioteer.
Possessed by great impetuosity, O king of kings, he fought the vast army of the Rākṣasas from all sides with showers of rocks. Then,
seeing that Dhūmrākṣa, the foremost of the Rākṣasas, had been slain—
Having gained confidence, the monkeys approached and slaughtered the soldiers;
being struck down by those powerful monkeys who appeared victorious,
the Rākṣasas, their resolve shattered, fled toward Laṅkā out of fear.
Having fled from the city, those night-stalkers who remained after the slaughter reported everything exactly as it had happened to King Rāvaṇa.
Upon hearing from them that Prahasta had been slain in battle, Rāvaṇa—
Sighing very deeply and springing up from his excellent throne, he said to the great archer Dhūmrākṣa and his army, "O bulls among monkeys,
the time for Kumbhakarṇa’s action has arrived."
Having spoken thus, he awakened Kumbhakarṇa, who was lying there in a state of deep sleep, with various musical instruments of great sound;
and having roused him with great effort, he acted while overcome with trepidation.
Then the ten-necked Rāvaṇa spoke to the mighty Kumbhakarṇa, who was sitting at ease, unperturbed, and free from sleep:
"O Kumbhakarṇa, you are blessed, for such is this sleep of yours."
"You do not realize that this is a terrible time of great danger.
Having crossed the ocean by means of a bridge along with his monkeys, this Rāma disregards us all here and is inflicting a great slaughter."
For his wife, Sītā by name, the daughter of Janaka, was indeed carried off by me;
wishing to liberate her, he has arrived after building a bridge across the great ocean,
and by him our great kinsmen, Prahasta and the others, have been slain.
"O crusher of enemies, there is no other slayer of him except you. Therefore,
O best among the strong, having gone forth today clad in armor,
slay all those enemies— Rāma and the others— in battle, O subduer of foes."
"Moreover, Dūṣaṇa’s younger brothers, Vajravega and Pramāthin, shall follow you accompanied by a great force. Having spoken thus to the powerful Kumbhakarṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas—
He gave instructions regarding what was to be done to Vajravega and Pramāthin.
Having said, "So be it," those two heroes, the younger brothers of Dūṣaṇa,
placed Kumbhakarṇa at their head and quickly departed from the city.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, having emerged from the city with his followers,
Kumbhakarṇa beheld that monkey army standing before him, radiant with the pride of victory.
Scanning that army with a longing to see Rāma,
he beheld the son of Sumitrā standing there, bow in hand;
the monkeys quickly approached him and surrounded him on all sides.
Then, emitting terrifying roars, they released weapons made of rocks and trees;
with their many massive bodies, they struck [the enemy],
while others, casting aside their supreme fear, tore them apart with their claws.
Fighting in many ways with various modes of combat,
those monkeys struck the formidable lord of the rākṣasas with diverse weapons.
Being thus assailed, he laughed and began devouring the monkeys.
Seeing that agonizing deed of the Rākṣasa Kumbhakarṇa, Panasa, Gavākṣa, and the monkey Vajrabāhu—
Tāra and the others then cried out in terror.
As he was crying out loudly for Tāra and the other leaders of the monkey hosts,
Sugrīva, free from fear, rushed toward Kumbhakarṇa. Then,
the high-minded one, having pounced upon Kumbhakarṇa with great speed, [attacked him].

With great force, that elephant among monkeys, Sugrīva, struck Kumbhakarṇa on the head with a *śāla* tree. Although that high-souled monkey of immense speed shattered the *śāla* tree upon Kumbhakarṇa’s head, he did not cause him any pain.
Then, having roared and laughed, Kumbhakarṇa— awakened by the touch of the *śāla* tree— took Sugrīva with both his arms and carried him off by force.
As Sugrīva was being carried away by the Rākṣasa Kumbhakarṇa, [he cried out].
As he was walking, he awakened the small-minded one with a blow;
then, having regained consciousness, Sugrīva tore away Kumbhakarṇa’s ears, lips, and nose,
and departed for the monkey army.

Then the powerful Kumbhakarṇa, filled with rage, devoured the monkeys and rākṣasas who were mingled together; he even crushed them under his feet. All the monkeys were being devoured by the rākṣasa Kumbhakarṇa.

Beholding him, the heroic son of Sumitrā, the delighter of his friends, rushed forward. Attacking with great speed, Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, discharged a great arrow with golden feathers at Kumbhakarṇa.
That arrow, having pierced through his armor and his body, went on its way splitting the earth, drenched in blood. Thus,
with his heart shattered, he abandoned the lord of monkeys.
Possessed by a great impetuosity, Kumbhakarṇa, the great archer who held a rock as his weapon, cried out, "Stay! Stay!
and rushed toward the son of Sumitrā, raising up a massive boulder.
As he rushed forward swiftly, [Indra] cut off his two upraised arms with two sharp-edged razors; he then became four-armed.
[Indra] also [cut off] all those arms of his, which were grasping rocks as weapons.
Displaying his lightness of hand with weapons, the son of Sumitrā cut [the demon] apart with razors.
He became possessed of an enormous body, with many feet, heads, and arms.
Seeing this marvel, the son of Sumitrā—cruel and skilled in battle—[acted].
With the Brahmā weapon, the son of Sumitrā incinerated that [demon] who resembled a mass of mountains. Struck by the divine weapon in battle,
he of great prowess fell like a budding tree consumed by a great lightning bolt.
Seeing that swift Kumbhakarṇa, who resembled Vṛtra,
fallen lifeless upon the ground, the Rākṣasas fled in fear.
Seeing those warriors thus fleeing, the two younger brothers of Dūṣaṇa [beheld them].
Having stationed Saumitri, they then charged forward in a fury.
As those two, enraged and crushing with the speed of thunderbolts, rushed toward him, Saumitri roared and received them both with his feathered arrows.
Then, O Pārtha, a tumultuous battle took place that made the hair stand on end between the two younger brothers of Dūṣaṇa and the wise Lakṣmaṇa;
he overwhelmed the two Rākṣasas with a great shower of arrows.
And those two heroes, both enraged, rained down [arrows] upon one another;
for a moment, such was the most terrible combat between Vajravega and Pramāthin, and the mighty-armed son of Sumitrā.

Then Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, seizing a mountain peak, rushed forward and took the life-breaths of the Rākṣasa Vajravega. And the monkey Nīla, with a massive boulder, struck the younger brother of Dūṣaṇa.
Attacking Pramāthin, the one of great strength crushed him;
then there began once more a battle of bitter consequence between the armies of Rāma and Rāvaṇa as they rushed at one another.
By the hundreds, the forest-dwellers slew the Nairṛtas, and the Nairṛtas slew the forest-dwellers;
yet it was mostly the Nairṛtas who were killed there, and not the monkeys.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, having heard that Kumbhakarṇa had been slain in battle along with his followers,
as well as the great archer Prahasta and the exceedingly radiant Dhūmrākṣa,
Rāvaṇa addressed his heroic son Indrajit.
"O slayer of enemies, slay Rāma along with Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa!
For by you, my virtuous son, radiant fame has been acquired,
having conquered in battle the thousand-eyed wielder of the thunderbolt, the lord of Śacī."
"O slayer of enemies, O best among those who wield weapons, slay the foes with these divine arrows granted as boons, which may be either invisible or visible.
O sinless one, Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sugrīva do not even perceive the touch of your arrows."
Who, then, could be capable of withstanding you, let alone your followers?
O sinless one, O mighty-armed one, go and achieve in battle that vengeance for Khara which was not accomplished by Prahasta or Kumbhakarna.
"O son, having slain your enemies along with their armies today with sharpened arrows, gladden me as you did in the past when you bound Vāsava.
Thus addressed, he replied, "So be it," and, having donned his armor, mounted his chariot.
O King, Indrajit quickly advanced toward the battlefield;
there, that bull among Rākṣasas, having clearly proclaimed his name,
challenged Lakṣmaṇa, who is endowed with auspicious marks, to combat.
Lakṣmaṇa also rushed toward him, grasping his bow with an arrow fixed,
terrifying him with the slapping sound of his palms as a lion terrifies a small deer.
A truly great battle ensued between the two of them, both of whom were greedy for victory.
Then, between those two who were experts in divine weapons and intensely rivalrous with one another,
when the son of Rāvaṇa could not gain the upper hand over him with his arrows,
that best of the strong exerted even greater effort.
Then he struck him with javelins of great velocity;
Saumitri cut those approaching weapons down with sharpened arrows.
Severed by those sharp shafts, they fell upon the surface of the earth.
In the battle against Rāvaṇa’s son, hundreds of arrows were shattered into pieces;
then the glorious Aṅgada, son of Vālin, raising a tree with great speed, rushed forward and struck him on the head.

The valiant Indrajit, remaining unperturbed, desired to strike him in the chest with a javelin; however, Lakṣmaṇa shattered that very javelin of his. Then the son of Rāvaṇa [assailed] the heroic Aṅgada who had come close to him.
With his mace, he struck the bull among monkeys on the left side;
disregarding that blow, the powerful son of Vālin,
the conqueror of enemies, angrily hurled a śāla tree trunk at Indrajit.
That tree, hurled in rage by Aṅgada for the purpose of slaying Indrajit,
O Pārtha, struck Indrajit’s chariot along with its horses and charioteer.
Then, leaping down from the chariot whose horses and driver had been killed, he [Indrajit]...
Right there, O King, the son of Rāvaṇa vanished by means of his illusory power.
Knowing that the Rākṣasa possessed many illusions and had disappeared,
Rāma approached that place and protected his army.
Then, aiming at Rāma with arrows for which boons had been granted,
he pierced him in all his limbs as well as the great chariot-warrior Lakṣmaṇa;
those two heroes [saw] him then made invisible by arrows through his concealment by *māyā*.
Both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa fought against the son of Rāvaṇa.
In his rage, he discharged arrows by the hundreds and thousands once more into every limb of those two lions among men.
Searching for him while he remained invisible and incessantly loosed his arrows,
the monkeys entered the sky clutching massive boulders;
yet that invisible Rākṣasa pierced them as well as those two with his shafts.
Striking them violently, that heroic son of Rāvaṇa, shrouded in illusion,
caused those two heroic brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, covered with arrows,
to fall from the sky to the earth like the sun and the moon.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Seeing those two brothers of immeasurable splendor fallen,
the son of Rāvaṇa then bound them once more with arrows granted by boons.

Those two heroes, those tigers among men, bound by Indrajit in battle with a net of arrows, quivered like two birds in a cage. Seeing them fallen upon the ground, covered by hundreds of shafts, [the monkeys were struck with grief].
Then Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, stood there surrounded by the monkeys—
by Suṣeṇa, Mainda, Dvivida, Kumuda, Aṅgada,
Hanumān, Nīla, Tāra, and Nala.
Then, at the word of Samīra, the lord of birds, being summoned by Rāma,
arrived and liberated the two heroes from that most dreadful serpent-bond.
In an instant, O dear one, Garuḍa was seen there, his wings spread.
Upon seeing the king of birds, the serpents fled;
and that great-winged one, having arrived, stroked both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with his hand and then departed by the path he had come.
Then, having arrived at that place, Vibhīṣaṇa, who had accomplished his task,
awakened those two heroes by means of the Prajñā weapon;
and Sugrīva, in an instant, rendered them both free from the shafts.
By means of the great medicinal herb Viśalyā, applied with divine mantras,
those two best of men regained consciousness; with their arrows extracted,
both great chariot-warriors rose up, and in an instant, both were freed from exhaustion and fatigue.
Then, O Pārtha, seeing that Rāma, the joy of the Ikṣvākus, was free from anxiety, Vibhīṣaṇa spoke these words with palms joined in reverence:
"Having taken this water by the command of the King of Kings— "
"O subduer of enemies, a Guhyaka has come from Śveta to your presence. O great king, subduer of foes, Kubera sends this water to you for the purpose of seeing beings who have become invisible."
"By touching one's eyes with this, you shall see invisible beings, as well as whoever else to whom you shall give it.
Saying "So be it," Rāma then accepted that consecrated water.
The high-minded Lakṣmaṇa performed the purification of his eyes,
as did Sugrīva, Jāmbavān, Hanumān, and Aṅgada, as well as Mainda,
Dvivida, Nīla, and most of the other foremost among the monkeys.
And it came to pass exactly as Vibhīṣaṇa had said;
in an instant, O Yudhiṣṭhira, their eyes became supersensuous.
Then the descendant of Pulastya pierced Lakṣmaṇa in the chest with a spear.
Beholding this descendant of Pulastya, Lakṣmaṇa fell into a swoon.
Then, having withdrawn all the monkeys, Rāghava spoke these words in dejection; listen as I relate them to you.
The kingdom has been lost, we dwell in the forest, Sītā has been carried away, and our father is dead; Lakṣmaṇa has fallen into a swoon—what sorrow could be greater than this for us?
Then the wise Hanumān enlightened Rāma regarding Vibhīṣaṇa.

Having summoned the divine herbs, he restored Lakṣmaṇa to life. But Indrajit, having accomplished his task, reported that deed of his own to his father and returned in haste to the head of the battlefield.
As he approached, enraged and desiring once more to fight,
the son of Sumitrā— abiding by the counsel of Vibhīṣaṇa— rushed toward him,
seeking to slay that victor who had not yet performed his daily rites.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, having received his signal, became enraged and struck him with arrows.
A battle then took place between those two, each desiring to conquer the other;
it was exceedingly wonderful and marvelous, like the combat between Śakra and Prahlāda.
