Indrajit pierced the son of Sumitrā with sharp arrows that strike the vital organs,
and the son of Sumitrā in turn pierced the son of Rāvaṇa with arrows whose touch was like fire.
Stricken by the impact of the son of Sumitrā’s arrows, the son of Rāvaṇa was overwhelmed with rage.
He discharged eight arrows, resembling venomous serpents, at Lakṣmaṇa;
but the son of Sumitrā cut down those eight arrows before they had reached him. Before they could reach him, the joy of the Raghus severed them with his own sharp shafts.

With three feathered iron arrows, the son of Sumitrā, the delighter of his friends, checked the life-breaths of that [demon] with the touch of fire. Then Lakṣmaṇa again discharged eight shafts at the Rākṣasa.
Listen as I describe how that hero struck him down:
with one [arrow] he felled from the body his arm that held the bow,
and with a second, he brought to the ground the arm still clutching the iron shaft.
With his third arrow, broad-edged and radiant,
he struck off the beautiful head, adorned with lovely nostrils and shining earrings;
the headless trunk (*kabandha*), its arms and shoulders severed, was terrifying to behold.
He fell to the earth like a tree severed at its roots;
having slain him, that best of the strong struck down the charioteer as well with his weapons. Then the horses brought that chariot into Laṅkā.
Rāvaṇa beheld that chariot bereft of his son;
seeing his son slain, his eyes wild with terror,
Rāvaṇa— afflicted by grief and delusion— prepared to kill Vaidehī.

Taking up his sword, that evil-minded one rushed with speed toward her as she stood in the Ashoka grove, longing for the sight of Rāma. Seeing that wicked resolve of the evil-minded man, Avindhya [intervened].
He pacified the enraged king; hear now the reason why: "Established as you are in a radiant great kingdom, you ought not to kill a woman.
She is already as good as dead, since she is both a woman and held captive in your house."

"It is my conviction that she cannot be destroyed by the destruction of her body; therefore, slay her husband alone—for when he is slain, she will be slain. Indeed, even Śatakratu himself is not your equal in prowess."
"For many times you have terrified the thirty gods, including Indra,
in battle. With these and various other words, Avindhya then pacified the enraged Rāvaṇa, and he accepted his counsel.
Having set his mind on departure and sheathed his sword,
the night-stalker then commanded, "Let my chariot be prepared.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, his beloved son having been struck down, the ten-necked Rāvaṇa became enraged;
mounting a chariot adorned with gold and jewels, he went forth,
surrounded by terrible Rākṣasas with various weapons in their hands.
He rushed toward Rāma, crushing the leaders of the monkey hosts.
As he charged forward in a fury, Mainda, Nīla,
Nala, Aṅgada, Hanumān, and Jāmbavān, together with their armies, surrounded him.
Those leaders of the hosts of bears and monkeys destroyed that army of the Ten-necked one with trees, even as the Ten-necked one looked on.
Then, beholding his own army being slaughtered by the enemies, [he...]
Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, being a master of illusion, employed his magical power;
from his body there emerged hundreds and thousands of Rākṣasas who appeared with arrows, spears, and swords in their hands.
Rāma slew all those Rākṣasas with a divine weapon;
then that lord of the Rākṣasas once again employed his illusory power,
O Bhārata, assuming the forms of both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
The ten-faced Rāvaṇa rushed toward both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Then, O King, those night-stalkers, desiring to strike Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
fell upon them while brandishing their lofty bows.
Seeing that illusion of the lord of the rākṣasas, the joy of the Ikṣvākus,
the son of Sumitrā, remaining unperturbed, spoke these weighty words to Rāma:
"Slay these wicked rākṣasas who are the replicas of yourself."
Having been addressed thus, O Pārtha, Rāma then prepared to depart for Lakṣmaṇa; he struck down those others who were his own reflections.
Then, with a chariot yoked to tawny horses and radiant as the sun—
Mātali, the charioteer of Śakra, approached Rāma in battle.
Mātali said:
"This is the supreme, victorious chariot of Maghavan, yoked with bay horses."
"I have come here for your sake, O Kakutstha, by the command of Śatakratu. By means of this noble chariot, O tiger among men, Śakra has slain hundreds of Daityas and Dānavas in battle."
"Therefore, O tiger among men, with this very chariot by which I [fought] him in battle, slay Rāvaṇa quickly; do not delay.
Having been addressed thus, Rāghava began to doubt the truth of Mātali’s words.
"This is the illusion of the Rākṣasa," Vibhīṣaṇa said to him.
"O tiger among men, this is not the illusion of the evil-minded Rāvaṇa.
Therefore, O one of great splendor, quickly mount this chariot of Indra."
Then Kakutstha, greatly delighted, said "So be it" to Vibhīṣaṇa;
filled with wrath, he swiftly rushed toward the Ten-necked one in his chariot.
As Rāvaṇa was being assailed, all living beings cried out in lamentation.
Lion-roars accompanied by the beating of drums resounded divinely in the sky;
then a great battle commenced between Rāma and Rāvaṇa,
and likewise a great battle took place between the two princes, the sons of the ten-necked king.
Having no other comparison for it,
that night-stalker discharged at Rāma a most terrible spear,
resembling Indra’s thunderbolt and raised like the staff of Brahmā.
Rāma cut that spear apart with sharp arrows in mid-air;
seeing that difficult feat, fear entered Rāvaṇa.
Then, enraged, the ten-necked one quickly discharged sharpened arrows.
For Rāma, there were thousands upon tens of thousands of various weapons;
then there were *bhuśuṇḍī*s, spears, maces, battle-axes,
spears of diverse forms, and *śataghnī*s with sharp edges.
Seeing that distorted illusion of the ten-necked Rākṣasa,
all the monkeys fled in every direction out of fear.
Then [he took] that best of arrows, well-feathered, with a fine point and a golden shaft.
Taking [an arrow] from his quiver, the descendant of Kakutstha charged it with the Brahma-weapon.
Seeing that excellent arrow consecrated by Rāma with the Brahma-weapon,
the gods and Gandharvas, led by Śakra, rejoiced.
Then the Rākṣasas,
along with the gods, Gandharvas, and Kiṃnaras, considered the enemy’s life to have little remaining because of the discharge of the Brahmā weapon.
Thereupon, Rāma released that arrow of incomparable power.
O Bhārata, as soon as it was released by Rāma, who had drawn it back a great distance— that terrible weapon, the end-maker of Rāvaṇa, which was like the raised staff of Brahmā—
it was unerring and irresistible even to the gods, asuras, and pannagas.
Illuminating all directions with his own radiance, he possessed great splendor;
that best of *rākṣasas*, together with his chariot, horses, and charioteer,
blazed up as if enveloped by a fire of immense flames.
Then the thirty gods, along with the gandharvas and cāraṇas,
were overjoyed upon seeing Rāvaṇa slain by Rāma of unwearied deeds;
the five elements abandoned that illustrious Rāvaṇa.
For he has been cast down from all the worlds by the splendor of the Brahmā weapon;
indeed, his bodily constituents— his flesh and even his blood—
were consumed by the Brahmā weapon, and not even ashes were seen.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having slain the base Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas and enemy of the gods,
Rāma, together with his friends and the son of Sumitrā, was filled with joy.
Then, when the Ten-necked one had been slain, the gods, led by the sages,
honored that mighty-armed one with blessings joined with cries of victory;
all the deities praised Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals.

The Gandharvas and the inhabitants of the celestial realm honored Rāma with showers of flowers and words of praise; having done so, they returned as they had come. O Acyuta, that sky then appeared like a great festival.
Then, having slain the ten-necked Rāvaṇa, the illustrious Lord Rāma, the conqueror of enemy cities, bestowed Laṅkā upon Vibhīṣaṇa.
Then, placing Sītā— who was herself preceded by Vibhīṣaṇa— at his front, he set forth.
The highly wise elder minister named Avindhya went forth and spoke to the high-souled descendant of Kakutstha, who was overcome by dejection:
"O Great-souled One, accept the princess Janaki, who is of virtuous conduct."
Having heard these words from him, the joy of the Ikṣvākus descended from his excellent chariot and beheld Sītā, who was overwhelmed with tears. Seeing her,
whose every limb was beautiful, yet emaciated by grief as she sat upon the vehicle, he looked upon her.
To Vaidehī, whose entire body was covered in dirt, who wore matted hair and black garments, Rāma—suspecting she had been violated—said:
"Go, Vaidehī; you are released. That which was to be done by me has been accomplished."

"O blessed lady, had you not found me as your husband, you would have reached old age in the dwelling of a rākṣasa; it was for this reason that I slew that night-stalker. For how could one like me, knowing the certain determination of dharma, ever [remain indifferent]?"
O Maithilī, even for a moment I cannot bring myself to enjoy you today— whether you are of good conduct or bad— once you have passed into the hands of another,
like an oblation licked by a dog.
Then, having suddenly heard those cruel words,
the young queen fell down in distress like a severed plantain tree;
for that flush of joy which had appeared upon her face vanished at once.
In an instant, he was lost again, like a breath upon a mirror.
Then all those monkeys, having heard what Rāma had spoken,
became motionless along with Lakṣmaṇa, as if their lives had departed.
Unable to endure the words spoken by Rāghava, Sītā said to Lakṣmaṇa: "Quickly kindle a fire for me,
so that there may be confidence in Rāma and conviction among the people."
Having understood Rāghava’s intention, Lakṣmaṇa, the subduer of enemies, at that very moment gathered a great heap of wood, kindled the fire,
and approached Rāma’s side, standing there in silence.
Then Sītā, filled with devotion, circumambulated Rāghava while all the worlds— including the women of the gods and the rākṣasas— looked on; and Maithilī bowed down to the deities and the brahmins.
With her palms joined in reverence, she who stood near the fire spoke these words:
"As my heart never departs from Rāghava,
so may the Purifier, the witness of the world, protect me on all sides."
Having spoken thus, the virtuous Sītā circumambulated the fire and entered the blazing flame with a fearless heart. Then the pure-souled four-faced god [Brahmā] appeared in his celestial chariot.
The Grandfather, the creator of the world, appeared before Rāghava;
as did Śakra, Agni, Vāyu, Yama, and Varuṇa;
and the blessed Lord of the Yakṣas, as well as the stainless Seven Sages.
And King Daśaratha, possessing a divine and radiant form,
[arrived] from there in a magnificent, shining celestial chariot yoked with swans;
then that entire atmosphere was crowded with gods and gandharvas.
It shone like the autumnal sky variegated with stars.
Then, rising up in their midst, the illustrious and auspicious Vaidehī spoke these words to Rāma of the broad chest.
"O prince, I do not harbor anger toward you, for I understand the nature of both women and men; listen now to these words of mine.
The wind, which moves eternally, dwells within all living beings."
May he take away my life-breaths if I have committed any sin.
May fire, water, space, earth, and wind likewise take away my life-breaths if I have committed any sin.
"O hero, just as I have never thought of anyone other than you, even in my dreams,
so may you indeed become my husband, as ordained by the gods.
Then a voice arose in the sky, making it heard in all directions:
This was a meritorious and heart-gladdening [speech] for those high-souled monkeys.
Vāyu said:
"O Rāghava, truly I am Vāyu, the one who is always in motion."
"O King, Maithilī is sinless; reunite with your wife.
Agni said:
"O descendant of Raghu, I dwell within the bodies of all living beings."
"O descendant of Kakutstha, Maithilī has not committed even the slightest transgression.
Varuṇa said:
"O Rāghava, the vital fluids (rasas) indeed originate from me within the bodies of all beings."
I indeed tell you this: accept Maithilī.
You alone are the further shore and the supreme shore, possessing the nature of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the Self. O Hari, you are the shoreless shore, forever beyond even all shores.

O Lord of all, you are the one who has crossed to the further shore of Brahman, and likewise, you are the one who leads others to the further shore. You are the supreme among the supreme, the eternal shore, and the shore itself. O Infinite One, you dwell within all beings and are likewise the ultimate reality.
"O descendant of Kakutstha, I am Yama, the King of Dharma, the witness to the deeds of the world,
both auspicious and inauspicious. O Sītā, let this sinless woman be accepted."
Brahmā said:
"O son, this is no cause for wonder in you, who follow the dharma of royal seers;
O virtuous one established on the path of righteous conduct, hear these words of mine."
O hero, this enemy has been struck down by you— among gods, gandharvas, bhogins,
yakṣas, dānavas, and great ṛṣis. Previously, by my grace, he was incapable of being slain by any living beings.
For some reason, that wicked one was overlooked for a period of time;
by him, that evil-minded soul, Sītā was abducted for the sake of his own destruction.
Furthermore, her protection was secured by me through the curse of Nalakūbara.

"For if he were to approach another woman even against her will, his body would surely shatter into a hundred pieces"—so was it said in the past. You should have no doubt in this matter; accept her, O one of great splendor!
"A great service has been performed by you for the gods, O one of immortal luster!
Daśaratha said:
"I am pleased, my child; may it be well with you. I am your father, Daśaratha."
"I authorize you; rule the kingdom, O best of men.
Rāma said:
"I salute you, O Indra among kings, if you are indeed my father."
"By your command, I shall go to the beautiful city of Ayodhyā.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O lord of men, his father, being greatly delighted, spoke to him again.
"Go to Ayodhyā and rule it, O Rāma, whose eyes have red corners!
For the fourteen years are now complete, O you of great splendor.
Then, having paid homage to the gods, he was greeted with joy by his friends.
Like Mahendra joined with his wife Paulomī,
he then bestowed a boon upon Avindhya, O scorcher of foes,
and united the Rākṣasī Trijaṭā with wealth and honor.
Then Brahmā, surrounded by the gods headed by Śakra, said to him:
"O son of Kausalyā, what desired boons shall I grant you today?
Rāma chose steadfastness in dharma and invincibility against his enemies.
And regarding the reappearance of the monkeys slain by the rākṣasas,
when Brahmā had thus spoken those words, "So be it," O great king, the monkeys then rose up, having regained their consciousness.
And the highly fortunate Sītā also granted a boon to Hanumān:
"O son, your life shall endure as long as the fame of Rāma;
moreover, divine enjoyments, brought about by my grace, shall always be yours."
"O golden-eyed one, they will attend upon Hanumān," he said. Then,
while those of unwearied deeds were looking on,
all the gods, led by Śakra, vanished from sight.
But seeing Rāma united with Jānakī, the charioteer of Śakra,
supremely delighted, spoke these words in the midst of his friends:
"Of the gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, humans, asuras, and serpents..."
O you whose prowess is truth, this suffering has been removed by you; the worlds—
including the gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas—
shall speak of you as long as the earth endures.

Having spoken thus and taken leave of Rāma, the best among those who bear arms, he honored him and departed on that chariot which possessed the brilliance of the sun. Then Rāma, placing Sītā at his side, set out together with the son of Sumitrā.
Accompanied by all the monkeys headed by Sugrīva,
and preceded by Vibhīṣaṇa, he established a guard over Laṅkā and once again crossed the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, by means of that bridge.
Traveling by means of the radiant Puṣpaka chariot, which moves through the sky at will and is driven according to his desire, the self-controlled king was surrounded by his principal ministers;
then he reached the shore of the ocean where that monarch had lain down to sleep.
There the righteous-souled one dwelt together with all the monkeys.
Then, at the proper time, Rāghava gathered them together, honored them,
and dismissed them after satisfying them in every way with precious gems.
When those lords of monkeys, the cow-tailed macaques, and the bears had departed,
Rāma, accompanied by Sugrīva, returned once more to Kiṣkindhā,
followed at that time by Vibhīṣaṇa.
Displaying the forest to Vaidehī from the Puṣpaka chariot,
Rāma, the best among strikers, reached Kiṣkindhā and consecrated Aṅgada,
who had accomplished his task, as the crown prince.
Then Rāma, accompanied by those very same men and by the son of Sumitrā,
set out toward his own city by the path by which he had come. Having reached the city of Ayodhyā, the lord of the realm then—
Then, having observed all his gestures and having communicated what was pleasing to him, he dispatched Hanumān as a messenger to Bharata;
and when the son of the Wind had returned, he went once more to Nandigrāma.
There, Rāghava Rāma saw Bharata— his limbs smeared with dirt, clad in bark garments, and accompanied by Śatrughna— seated upon a throne in Nandigrāma, having placed the two sandals before him.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, the valiant Rāghava, together with Saumitri, rejoiced upon meeting with Bharata and Śatrughna;
likewise, Bharata and Śatrughna were then reunited with their elder brother.

Upon seeing Vaidehī, both of them attained great joy. To him who had arrived, Bharata, filled with supreme delight, restored that kingdom which had been treated with due honor, as a trust returned to its owner.

Then, on a day under the auspicious constellation Vaiṣṇava, Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva together consecrated that hero. Having been consecrated, he [Rāma] [honored] Sugrīva, the best of monkeys, along with his circle of friends.
Having honored Vibhīṣaṇa, the descendant of Pulastya,
with various jewels, he— filled with affection and joy—
dismissed him to his home after instructing him on what remained to be done, though it was with great sorrow.
Having honored that Puṣpaka chariot, Rāghava,
the joy of the Raghus, gave it back with affection to Vaiśravaṇa himself.
Then, accompanied by the celestial sages, he proceeded along the Gomatī river.
He performed ten horse-sacrifices of the Jārūthya type, free from all obstacles;
Rāma ruled the kingdom for eleven thousand years, and thereafter he departed for the third heaven.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O mighty-armed one, it was thus that in former times this most terrible calamity, caused by dwelling in the forest, befell Rāma of immeasurable splendor."
Thus has been told to you the entire, unsurpassed *Rāmāyaṇa*. This narrative bestows long life and destroys the sins of those who hear it;
it grants sons and grandsons to men and increases their lifespan and health.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, O son of Dharma, you too, together with your brothers,
should not grieve, O tiger among men; for you are a Kṣatriya, O scorcher of foes,
and you abide on the path that relies upon the strength of one's arms and possesses radiant resolve.
Indeed, not even the slightest trace of wrongdoing is seen in you;
on this path, even the gods and asuras, including Indra himself, might despair. Vṛtra was slain by the wielder of the thunderbolt together with the Maruts acting in concert.

Even the invincible Namuci and the Rākṣasī Dīrghajihvā are his allies; for one who has Dhanañjaya as his brother, all purposes are established here in every respect— what indeed remains unconquered by him in battle?
And here is Bhīma, the best among the strong, of terrifying prowess;
and the two young sons of Mādravatī, the twins, both great archers.
Why do you despair, O scorcher of foes, when you have these as your allies?
"Those who could conquer the army of the wielder of the thunderbolt along with the hosts of Maruts—
even you, O bull of the Bharatas, shall conquer all enemies in battle, accompanied by these great archers who possess the forms of gods."

Moreover, behold this Draupadī, the dark-complexioned one, who was abducted from here by the evil-minded Saindhava, powerful and intoxicated by his own prowess, and now brought back by these high-souled ones after performing a most difficult feat.
And King Jayadratha, having been conquered and brought under control, [was released]; furthermore,
by Rāma alone and without assistance,
Vaidehī was recovered after he had slain the ten-necked Rākṣasa of terrifying prowess in battle.
O King, consider this with your intellect: that for whom monkeys, bears, and likewise black-faced bears are friends, even though they have entered into other species.
Therefore, O tiger among the Kurus, O bull of the Bharata race, do not grieve.
"For high-souled ones such as you do not grieve, O scorcher of foes.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"And those who shall recount this great life-story of Rāma,"
Those who shall listen to this repeatedly, misfortune shall never befall them;
they shall be worthy of honor, and they shall possess great wealth. Having heard this ancient and eternally supreme history, [they shall attain these blessings].
They shall obtain sons, grandsons, and cattle, and they shall attain preeminence among men;
they shall be free from disease and endowed with intelligence—of this there is no doubt.
Those best of men who remember this delightful narrative [shall likewise attain these things].

Together with their sons and grandsons, they rejoice and attain that which is dear to Viṣṇu. Those of virtuous character who hear this, or cause this supreme teaching to be heard, obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
The best of men goes to heaven in a golden celestial chariot;
returning once more to the surface of the earth, he is born endowed with prosperity.
Having heard this narrative, one should find no pleasure in hearing anything else.
Having heard the cry of the male cuckoo, which was like the voice of a crane or a crow,
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Thus was the king consoled by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya."
Having cast off his sorrow, the undepressed Yudhiṣṭhira spoke this once again; having heard the entire Rāmāyaṇa and abandoned his grief,
he addressed Mārkaṇḍeya together with his esteemed brothers.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O great sage, I do not grieve for myself, nor for these brothers of mine,
nor even for the seizure of our kingdom as much as I do for this daughter of Drupada."
At the gambling match, we were tormented by those evil-minded men, yet we were rescued by Kṛṣṇā;
and again, Jayadratha forcibly carried her away from the forest.
Is there any woman, then, who has been seen or heard of before who [endured such]?
"Just as this highly fortunate daughter of Drupada is devoted to her husband.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Listen, O King Yudhiṣṭhira, to the great fortune of women of noble lineage."
All this occurred exactly as it befell the princess Sāvitrī. In the land of the Madras, there was a righteous king, supremely virtuous,
devoted to the Brahmins, a protector of those seeking refuge, true to his word, and one who had conquered his senses.
There was a king named Aśvapati, a performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, skillful, and beloved by the people of both the city and the countryside; he was devoted to the welfare of all beings,
possessed of patience, childless, truthful in speech, and one who had conquered his senses.
Having passed his youth and fallen into deep distress,
he undertook a rigorous vow for the sake of obtaining offspring; at the proper time, he restricted his food, lived as a celibate student, and mastered his senses.
Having offered a hundred thousand oblations with the Sāvitrī mantra, O best of kings,
he then ate sparingly at every sixth mealtime;
he remained under this discipline for eighteen years.
When the eighteenth year was complete, Sāvitrī attained satisfaction;
O King, she then revealed her true form to that monarch,
rising from the *agnihotra* fire and filled with great joy.
Then the boon-granting goddess spoke these words to that king:
"O King, Sāvitrī [spoke] to that Aśvapati while he remained steadfast in his observances,
purified by his celibacy, self-restraint, and discipline."
"O King, O Aśvapati, O King of Madra, I am pleased with you because of your devotion to me with your whole being. Choose a boon as you desire;
however, you must never, under any circumstances, be negligent in your duties toward dharma."
Aśvapati said:
"O Goddess, this undertaking was made by me with the desire for dharma and for the sake of offspring. May I have many sons, O Queen, who shall be the sustainers of my lineage."
"If you are pleased with me, O Goddess, I choose this boon:
for the twice-born have told me that progeny is the highest dharma.
Having spoken thus, Sāvitrī replied to the king.
Sāvitrī said:
"O King, having already known this intention of yours, I spoke to the Grandfather for your sake regarding the matter of a son."

"O gentle one, by virtue of that very grace ordained for you by the Self-Existent One upon this earth, a radiant daughter shall soon be born to you. Furthermore, you must not say anything further to him under any circumstances."
"Indeed, I speak this to you because I am pleased by the grace of the Grandfather.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O King, having assented to Sāvitrī’s words with 'So be it,' the monarch—"
He propitiated her again, saying, "May it be so immediately.
When Sāvitrī had vanished, the king returned to his own home;
and he dwelt in his kingdom with joy, protecting his subjects according to dharma.
After some time had passed, that king, firm in his vows,
conceived an embryo in his eldest queen, who was devoted to righteousness.
O bull of the Bharatas, that embryo was conceived in the princess of Mālava.
He grew like the lord of stars in the sky during the bright fortnight;
and when the time arrived, he gave birth to a lotus-eyed daughter,
at which the king then joyfully performed her rites.

Because she was granted by the pleased Sāvitrī and because the Sāvitrī mantra had been offered as an oblation, the Brahmins and her father gave her the name Sāvitrī. That daughter of the king grew up like the goddess Śrī incarnate.
In time, that maiden reached the bloom of youth;
seeing her with her slender waist and broad hips, like a statue of gold, people thought, "This must be a daughter of the gods who has arrived here."
But no one sought her hand— her eyes like lotus petals, blazing as if with splendor— for she was warded off by her own brilliance. Then,
having fasted and bathed her head, she approached the deities.
Having offered oblations into the fire according to the rules on that auspicious day, he caused the Brahmins to recite benedictions.
Then, having accepted the remaining flowers from the high-souled one,
she approached her father like the goddess Śrī incarnate.
Having saluted her father’s feet and first announced the remainder [of the news],
the beautiful woman stood by the side of the king with palms joined in reverence;
and he beheld his daughter, established in youth and possessing the form of a goddess.
And since she was not being sought after by suitors, the king became distressed.
The king said:
"O daughter, the time for your giving has arrived, yet no one chooses me [as a suitor]."
Seek for yourself a husband who is equal to you in virtues. Whatever man you desire, once he has been presented to me by you, I shall deliberate and bestow him upon you; choose as you wish.
"For I have heard it recited by the twice-born in the treatises on dharma:
'A father who does not give [his daughter in marriage] is censurable, and a husband who does not approach her is censurable. Therefore, O auspicious lady, listen to my words as I speak them."
When her husband has died, a son who does not protect his mother is to be censured.
Having heard these words of mine, hasten to search for your husband; act in such a way that I do not become subject to the reproach of the gods.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having thus spoken to his daughter and the aged ministers, he assigned them an escort and urged them, saying, "You may go."

Having saluted her father’s feet like a modest and high-minded woman, she obeyed her father’s command and departed without hesitation. Ascending a golden chariot, she was surrounded by her aged ministers.
He went to the delightful penance groves of the royal sages; there,
having paid homage by touching the feet of the venerable elders,
O dear one, he visited all those forests in succession.
In this manner, the princess, distributing wealth among the foremost of the twice-born at all the sacred fords (*tīrthas*), proceeded from one region to another. Mārkaṇḍeya said:

Then, O Bhārata, the king, the lord of the Madras, having met with Nārada, sat down in the midst of the assembly during the course of their conversation. Thereafter, [the king] had visited all the sacred fords as well as the hermitages.
Sāvitrī, together with her ministers, arrived at her father’s residence.
Seeing her father seated with Nārada,
the auspicious lady paid homage by bowing her head at the feet of both.
Nārada said:
"O King, where had this daughter of yours gone, and from whence has she come?
For what reason do you not bestow this young woman upon a husband?"
Aśvapati said:
"Indeed, she was sent away for this very purpose and has returned this very day.
Therefore, O divine sage, hear from her who the husband she has chosen."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Urged by her father to speak in detail, that auspicious woman,
having received his words as if they were those of a deity, spoke thus.

Among the Śālvas there was a righteous kṣatriya, a lord of the earth, known by the name Dyumatsena; later, he indeed became blind. While that wise man’s eyes were lost and his son was still young, [the following occurred].
His kingdom was seized by a former enemy through a stratagem during this very vulnerability;
he, along with his wife who had a young child, departed for the forest,
and having reached the great wilderness, that man of great vows practiced austerities.
"His son was born in the city and grew up in the forest of asceticism;
Satyavat, who is worthy of me as a husband, has been chosen by my mind.
Nārada said:
"Alas! O King, a great misfortune has been committed by Sāvitrī, in that she, unaware [of his true nature], chose the virtuous Satyavat.
His father speaks the truth; his mother speaks the truth."
Then the brahmins gave him this name, Satyavān. Horses were dear to the boy, and he would make horses out of clay;
he also drew horses in pictures, and thus he was called Citrāśva.
The king said: "Is that son of a king now possessed of splendor, or is he wise? Is he patient, or is he a hero? Is Satyavat a delighter of his father?"
Nārada said:
He was radiant like Vivasvat, equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect,
as heroic as Mahendra, and endowed with forbearance like the Earth.
Aśvapati said:
"Is the prince Satyavat a giver, devoted to the Brahmins,
handsome, noble, or even pleasing to behold?"
Nārada said:
O Sāṅkṛti, that Rantideva was equal to Śibi Auśīnara in his devotion to giving according to his capacity,
as he was devoted to the Brahmins and truthful in speech.
Noble like Yayāti, pleasing to behold like Soma, and in beauty like one of the two Aśvins, that mighty son of Dyumatsena was generous, radiant,
wise, and endowed with patience.
He is self-controlled, he is gentle, he is a hero, he is truthful, and he has conquered his senses;
he is friendly, he is free from malice, and he is modest and steadfast. In him, uprightness ever abides, and his stability is firm.
In brief, it is thus described by those advanced in asceticism and those advanced in virtue.
Aśvapati said:
"O Blessed One, you describe him to me as being endowed with all virtues."
"Tell me also of his faults, if there be any here.
Nārada said:
"He has but one fault alone, which stands surpassing all his virtues."
And that fault cannot be overcome even by great effort;
he has no other defect than this one, and from this day forward he shall be truthful. After one year, his life being exhausted, he will cast off his body.
The King said:
"Come, Sāvitrī; go now, O beautiful one, and choose another.
A single great defect of his stands there, overwhelming all his virtues."
"Just as the Blessed One Nārada, honored by the gods, has told me:
'He, being short-lived, will cast off his body within a year.
" Sāvitrī said:
A share of inheritance falls but once; a daughter is given away but once;
one says "I give" but once—these three things happen only once.
Whether he be long-lived or short-lived, virtuous or even devoid of merit.

"My husband has been chosen by me once; I shall not choose a second. Having made this resolution with my mind, it is then expressed by speech, and afterwards acted upon through deed; therefore, my mind is my authority."
Nārada said:
"O best of men, the resolve of your daughter Sāvitrī is firm;
there should be no delay in this matter once it has been decided."
"She cannot be moved from this path of dharma by any means whatsoever.
Indeed, the virtues that exist in Satyavat are not found in any other man.
Therefore, I favor the giving away of your daughter."
The king said:
"These words spoken by the Blessed One are indeed true and beyond doubt;
I shall do exactly as you have said, for the Blessed One is my guru."
Nārada said:
"May there be no obstacle in the giving away of your daughter Sāvitrī.
We shall now depart; may it be well with you all."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, Nārada flew up into the sky and departed for the third heaven;
the king, for his part, performed all the marriage rites for his daughter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, reflecting upon that very matter regarding the giving away of his daughter,
the king brought together all the necessary articles for the wedding.
Then, having summoned all the elderly twice-born ones, the officiating priests,
and the family chaplains, he set out with his daughter on an auspicious lunar day. Having reached the sacred forest, the king proceeded to the hermitage of Dyumatsena.
On foot, he approached that royal sage together with the twice-born. There he saw the illustrious king, who was then devoid of sight, seated upon a cushion of kusha grass beneath a shala tree.

Having performed worship for that royal seer according to his merit, the king, with speech well-restrained, made a formal self-introduction. Having offered him the guest-water, a seat, and a cow, that knower of dharma—
"What is the reason for your coming? the king asked the other king.
He then explained everything—the entire purpose and the course of action he had in mind—referring specifically to Satyavat.
Aśvapati said:
"O royal sage, this beautiful maiden named Sāvitrī is my daughter;
O knower of dharma, accept her from me as your daughter-in-law according to the sacred law."
Dyumatsena said:
"We have fallen from our kingdom and taken refuge in forest-dwelling; we wander about, self-restrained, practicing dharma as ascetics."
"How will your daughter, who is unaccustomed to dwelling in a forest hermitage, endure this hardship?
Aśvapati said:
When one understands that pleasure and pain consist of arising and passing away, and that I am indeed the same [in both states],
such speech as this is not appropriate for one like me.
O King, I have come to you with a firm resolve;
out of friendship and affection, you ought not to frustrate my hope. You should not reject one who has approached you so full of love.
"For you are a worthy match for me in union, and I am likewise a worthy match for you. Accept my daughter as your daughter-in-law and as the wife of Satyavat.
Dyumatsena said:
"Even before this, a union with you was desired by me;
however, because my kingdom has been lost, I reflected upon this matter. Yet, this is the very intention that I have longed for from the very beginning."
"Let him return this very day, for you are the guest I have long desired.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Then, having summoned all the twice-born residents of the hermitage,"
The two kings performed the marriage ceremony according to the prescribed rites;
having bestowed his daughter along with suitable gifts and attendants, Aśvapati returned to his own palace filled with supreme joy.
Satyavat, too, having obtained that wife endowed with every virtue, rejoiced;
and she, having obtained him as her husband—her heart’s desire—rejoiced as well.
When her father had departed, she set aside all her ornaments.
He took up only bark garments and saffron-colored robes;
and through his service, his virtues, his humility, his self-restraint,
and by performing every desired task, he brought satisfaction to them all.
She should honor her mother-in-law with all forms of bodily service, such as providing clothing and other necessities;
she should honor her father-in-law through the performance of divine rites and by restraining her speech;
likewise, she should do so with pleasant words, skillfulness, and tranquility.
And she gratified her husband with private attentions.
Thus, O Bhārata, as those virtuous ones dwelt there in that hermitage practicing austerities, a certain period of time passed by.
Whether lying down or standing, day and night,
the words spoken by Nārada remained in Sāvitrī’s mind;
from that time forward, Sāvitrī began to count the days.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, after a long time had passed,
O King, that moment eventually arrived when Satyavat was destined to die.
As Sāvitrī counted day after day as they passed,
those words spoken by Nārada remained constantly in her heart;
reflecting that she was to die on the fourth day, the beautiful woman [continued her vigil].
Having undertaken a vow for three nights, she remained standing day and night.
Hearing of that painful restraint of his daughter-in-law, the king was overcome with grief;
rising up, he spoke these words to Sāvitrī, consoling her.
"O daughter of a king, this undertaking you have begun is exceedingly intense;
for to remain in these three states [of fasting] is indeed extremely difficult.
Sāvitrī said:
"O dear one, you should not grieve; I shall fulfill this vow.
For this has been undertaken with resolve, and resolve is the cause of success.
Dyumatsena said:
"I am not able, by any means, to say to you, 'Break your vow. A person such as I should speak the words, 'Fulfill it.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, the high-minded Dyumatsena became silent;
and Sāvitrī, though remaining there, appeared as if she had become a block of wood.
O bull of the Bharatas, when her husband’s death was to occur on the following day, Sāvitrī—
As she remained there overcome by sorrow, that night passed away;
and today, having offered oblations into the blazing fire and performed her morning rites when the sun had risen to the height of a yoke, she thought, "This is that very day."
Having completed her vow, the illustrious Sāvitrī bathed and became pure;
then, having saluted all the elderly twice-born ones, as well as her mother-in-law and father-in-law, in due order, she stood with joined palms, self-restrained.

Then all those ascetics dwelling in the penance grove uttered auspicious blessings for Sāvitrī’s sake, wishing that she might never be a widow. "So be it," said Sāvitrī, as she became absorbed in the yoga of meditation.
With her mind, she received all those words of the ascetics.
Waiting for that time and that very moment, the princess,
reflecting upon the words spoken by Nārada, was deeply distressed.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, her mother-in-law and father-in-law spoke these words with affection to the princess as she stood in a secluded place. The parents-in-law said:
"Since this vow has been duly completed by you exactly as it was prescribed, the time for food has arrived; let that which follows be done.
Sāvitrī said:
"When the sun has set, I must eat, having fulfilled my desire;
this is the resolve in my heart and the vow I have made.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
While Sāvitrī was speaking thus regarding food,
Satyavān took an axe upon his shoulder and set out for the forest; likewise, he held a sharp tool in his hand.
Taking up his spade, Satyavān set out toward the forest.
Bowing to him, the virtuous Sāvitrī, who was obedient to her husband's will, spoke these words as Nārada had instructed: "My lord, you ought not to go alone."
"I shall come along with you, for I cannot bear to leave you.
Satyavat said:
"O beautiful lady, you have never gone to the forest before, and the path is difficult."
"And being emaciated by vows and fasting, how will you go on foot?
Sāvitrī replied:
"I feel no exhaustion from the fasts, nor do I have any fatigue."
"You ought not to prevent her, for she is resolved to go.
Satyavat said:
"If you have such a desire to go, I shall do what is pleasing to you."
"But if you consult my elders, this fault shall not touch me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Then she, firm in her great vows, approached and spoke to her mother-in-law and father-in-law."
"My husband here is going to the great forest to gather fruit;
I wish to be permitted by my noble mother-in-law and father-in-law to go out with him,
for separation from him is not bearable for me."
Your son has set out for the sake of his guru and the agnihotra sacrifice;
he must not be turned back, for he would only be restrained if he had set out for the forest otherwise. I have not departed from the hermitage for anything less than a full year.
"I have a great curiosity indeed to see the forest in full bloom.
Dyumatsena said:
"Ever since Sāvitrī was given by her father as my daughter-in-law..."
"I do not recall ever having spoken anything improper in response to a request such as this before.
Therefore, let this bride obtain her desire exactly as she has wished;
and, my daughter, you must exercise vigilance on the path of Satyavat."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been permitted by both, that illustrious lady departed with her husband, smiling as it were, though her heart was consumed with grief.
The large-eyed lady beheld on all sides diverse and delightful forests resounding with the cries of peacocks,
as well as rivers carrying holy waters and the finest of flowering trees.
"Look," Satyavat said to Sāvitrī in sweet syllables. Gazing at her husband in every state, the blameless woman, remembering the words of the sage, considered him already dead.
Following her husband, she walked with gentle steps;
as if her heart were divided in two, she awaited that appointed time.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then that valiant man, accompanied by his wife, took some fruits and filled a basket; thereafter, he split pieces of wood. As he was splitting the wood, sweat indeed broke out upon him.
And by that exertion, a pain arose in his head;
afflicted by fatigue, he approached his beloved wife and said:
"By this exertion, a pain has arisen in my head."
"O Sāvitrī, my limbs and my very heart seem to burn;
O lady of measured speech, I perceive myself as if unwell. I feel as though this head of mine were pierced by sharp pangs."
"Therefore, O auspicious lady, I wish to sleep; I have no strength to remain standing.
All the directions seem to be spinning before me, and my mind feels as if it were mounted upon a wheel. Then Sāvitrī, having approached her husband, embraced him.
Placing his head upon her lap, she sat down upon the surface of the earth.
Then that ascetic woman, reflecting on the words of Nārada,
calculated for him the moment, the instant, the hour, and the day.
Thinking, "Alas, that time has now arrived," she remained absorbed in reflection;
and after what seemed like a mere moment, she beheld a man clad in yellow garments,
with his hair tied in a topknot, possessed of a magnificent form and a splendor equal to the sun.
Dark-complexioned yet radiant, with red eyes, a noose in hand, and terrifying to behold,
he stood at Satyavat’s side, gazing intently at him alone. Seeing him, she rose suddenly and gently laid her husband’s head down.
With palms joined in reverence, she spoke in distress, her heart trembling:
"I recognize you as a deity, for this form of yours is indeed superhuman. O God, tell me out of compassion: who are you, and what do you intend to do?"
Yama said:
"O Sāvitrī, you are devoted to your husband and likewise endowed with ascetic merit;
therefore I address you. Know me, O auspicious lady, to be Yama."
"This husband of yours, Satyavat, the son of a king, has reached the end of his life. I shall bind him and lead him away; know that this is what I intend to do.
Sāvitrī said:
"O Blessed One, it is heard that your messengers are coming to lead away human beings;
why indeed have you yourself come here, O Lord?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, the blessed Lord of the Ancestors proceeded to relate everything exactly as he intended to do, for the sake of her pleasure:
"For this man is endowed with righteousness, handsome, and an ocean of virtues."
"He is not worthy of being led by my servants; therefore, I have come here in person.
Then, from the body of Satyavat, Yama forcibly extracted a man the size of a thumb, bound with nooses and brought under his control.

Then that body, its life-force extracted, breath departed, its luster destroyed, and rendered motionless, became unpleasant to behold. But Yama, having bound him in that manner, set out facing the south.
And Sāvitrī, afflicted with grief, followed after Yama; for that ascetic woman of slender waist, having first ensured the protection of her husband’s body,
followed her husband while he was in such a state.
"O highly blessed lady, devoted to your husband, you have attained perfection through your observances and vows.
Yama said:
"Turn back and go, Sāvitrī; perform for him the funeral rites."
"You have discharged your debt to your husband; you have gone as far as it is possible to go. This path, O large-eyed one, is not to be followed by anyone else.
Sāvitrī said:

"Wherever my husband is led, or wherever he goes of his own accord, there I too must go; this is the eternal dharma. Through austerity, service to my elders, affection for my husband, and the observance of vows,"
And by your very grace, my progress has not been obstructed.
Those wise ones who perceive the truth of reality say that friendship is established with seven steps;
honoring this bond of friendship, I shall say something—please listen to it.
But those who possess self-mastery wander in the forest;
through their discernment, they proclaim the Dharma, their dwelling, and their exertion.
Therefore, the virtuous say that Dharma is paramount; through Dharma, according to the view of the wise,
we have all entered upon that path.
"I do not desire a second [birth], nor indeed a third;
therefore, the virtuous say that dharma is the foremost.
Yama said:
"Desist! I am pleased with these words of yours, which are endowed with proper vowels, consonants, syllables, and reasoning. Choose a boon here, even at the cost of your life."
"I grant you every boon, O blameless one.
Sāvitrī said:
"He has been displaced from his own kingdom and has taken refuge in a life in the forest;"
May my father-in-law, who has lost his sight in this hermitage,
regain his vision through your grace and become a powerful king, resplendent like the blazing sun.
Yama said:
"O blameless one, I grant you every boon as you have requested; it shall be exactly so."
"I perceive in you as if the exhaustion of a long journey; turn back, go home, lest you suffer fatigue.
Sāvitrī said:
Whence could there be fatigue for me, since my husband is near?
For wherever my husband is, that is my certain destination; wherever you shall lead my lord, there shall be my destination.
O Lord of the Gods, listen further to my words:
for the virtuous, even a single meeting is considered the highest desire;
beyond that, they declare it to be true friendship.
"Association with a virtuous person is never without fruit;
therefore, one should dwell in the company of the righteous.
Yama said:
"Agreeable to my mind and increasing the wisdom of the learned,
you have spoken words to me that are based on what is beneficial; yet,
[all this is] without the life of this Satyavat."
"Choose a second boon, O beautiful lady.
Sāvitrī said:
"In the past, the kingdom of my wise father-in-law was taken away."
That king shall regain his very own kingdom,
provided he does not abandon his own duty as my preceptor has commanded;
this second boon I choose from you.
Yama said:
"The king shall regain his own kingdom before long, and he shall not fall away from his own duty."
"O daughter of a king, my desire has been fulfilled by me; turn back and go, lest you suffer further exhaustion.
Sāvitrī said:
These creatures are restrained by you through discipline; having disciplined them, you lead them not out of desire.
Therefore, O God, your status as Yama is renowned.
And listen to these words spoken by me:
non-malice toward all beings in action, thought, and speech,
as well as benevolence and charity, is the eternal dharma of the virtuous.
"Such is generally this world: human beings are tender toward those who possess power;
yet even the virtuous show compassion toward enemies when they have fallen into distress.
Yama said:
Just as water would be to one who is thirsty,
so has this speech been uttered by you;
yet it is without the life of this Satyavat.
"Choose a boon here, O auspicious lady, whatever you desire.
Sāvitrī said:
"My father, the lord of the earth, is childless;"
"May my father have a hundred sons born of his own body who shall ensure the continuity of the lineage;
this is the third boon I choose from you."
Yama said:
"O auspicious lady, may your father have a hundred sons, endowed with great luster, who shall ensure the continuity of his lineage."
"O daughter of the lord of men, since your desire has been fulfilled, turn back; for you have come a long way on this path.
Sāvitrī said:
"This is not far for me while in the presence of my husband;
for my mind runs even further ahead.
Thus speaking, as she was walking along, she raised her voice.
Listen further to what I am about to say:
you are the powerful son of Vivasvat;
therefore, you are called Vaivasvata by the wise.
The subjects were delighted by your tranquility and righteousness;
therefore, O Lord, you possess the status of a King of Dharma here.
Even toward oneself, there is not such trust as that which exists in the virtuous.
Therefore, everyone especially desires affection from the virtuous;
indeed, trust toward all beings arises from friendship. Consequently, people place their trust particularly in those who are virtuous.
Yama said:
"O auspicious lady, such words as you have uttered, O beautiful one, have never been heard by me from anyone other than you."
"By this I am pleased; I shall take away his life. Choose a fourth boon and then depart.
Sāvitrī said:
"Let there be a hundred sons for me, endowed with strength and heroism, who shall carry on both my lineage and that of Satyavat here in this world."
This is the fourth boon I choose from you;
O Lord, I choose this boon from Satyavat:
let there be for me a hundred sons, for this is my desire.
Yama said:
"O frail woman, you shall have a hundred sons, endowed with strength and heroism, who will bring you joy."
"O daughter of a king, let there be no further exhaustion for you;
turn back, for you have come a long way from the path.
So be it, O fair-faced one; may you have a hundred sons."
"Turn back quickly; you must not undergo further exhaustion.
Sāvitrī said:
"The practice of dharma is eternally constant for the virtuous."
The virtuous do not falter, nor do they tremble;
for the virtuous, association with the virtuous is never fruitless,
and the virtuous do not follow after fear from the virtuous.
For the virtuous lead the sun by means of truth;
the virtuous sustain the earth through austerity.
O King, the virtuous are the refuge of all that has been and all that is to be.
The virtuous do not falter in the midst of the virtuous,
having realized that this conduct is eternally cherished by the noble; thus,
while acting for the sake of others, the virtuous do not look for any recompense.
Faith placed in virtuous persons is never in vain;
neither does one's purpose perish, nor is one's honor lost,
because this is always certain among the good.
Therefore, the virtuous are protectors.
Yama said:
"In whatever way you speak, it is consistent with dharma."
In whatever way my devotion toward you is most excellent— conducive to the mind, composed of beautiful words, and full of great meaning— choose a peerless boon, O you of steadfast vows.
Sāvitrī said:
"O giver of honor, your liberation cannot be separated from your merit in the same way as it was with the other boons."
"I choose this boon: let this Satyavān live;
for without my husband, I am as if dead.
Separated from my lord, I do not desire happiness."
Separated from my husband, I do not desire heaven;
separated from my husband, I do not desire prosperity;
deprived of my husband, I have no resolve to live.
"The granting of a boon and a hundred sons were mine;
yet by you alone my husband is being taken away.
I choose this boon: let this Satyavān live!"
"Your word alone shall come true.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having said "So be it," Yama, the son of Vivasvat, released those bonds.
The King of Dharma, his soul filled with joy, spoke these words to Sāvitrī:
"O blessed lady, delight of your family, this husband of yours has been released by me, for you,
O virtuous woman, have pleased me with your words consistent with dharma and artha."
He shall be free from disease, easy to lead, and successful; he shall attain a lifespan of four hundred years together with you,
and having performed sacrifices according to dharma, he will achieve renown in the world.
Satyavat shall beget upon you a hundred sons;
all of them shall be Kṣatriya kings with many sons and grandsons, and they shall be eternal here on earth, renowned by your name.

And your father shall have a hundred sons by your mother Mālavī; they shall be known as the eternal Mālavas, possessing many sons and grandsons. Your brothers shall be Kṣatriyas, equal to the gods of the thirty-three.
Having thus granted her the boon, the majestic Dharmarāja turned Sāvitrī back and departed for his own abode. And when Yama had gone, Sāvitrī, having recovered her husband, [returned].
She went to the place where her husband’s lifeless body lay;
beholding her husband on the ground, she approached and embraced him,
and placing his head upon her lap, she sat down upon the earth.
Having regained consciousness, Satyavat addressed Sāvitrī,
looking at her again and again with affection like one who has returned from a journey;
then Satyavat spoke:
"Alas, I have slept for a very long time; why was I not awakened?
And where is that dark-complexioned man who dragged me along?
Sāvitrī said:
"Alas, O bull among men, you have slept for a very long time upon my lap!
That blessed Lord Yama, the restrainer of creatures, has departed. You are rested, O illustrious one, and now awake, O prince."
"If you are able, arise and behold the deep night.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Then, having regained consciousness, he rose like one who had been sleeping happily."
Having gazed upon all the directions and the edges of the forest, Satyavān said:
"O slender-waisted one, I went out with you to gather fruit for my food;
while I was splitting wood, a pain arose in my head."
"O auspicious one, I remember everything: tormented by a headache and unable to remain awake for long, I fell asleep upon your lap;
and while I was embraced by you, my mind was carried away by sleep."
Then I beheld a terrible darkness and a man of great majesty.
O slender-waisted one, if you know what that was, tell me;
was it a dream I saw, or was it indeed reality?

Then Sāvitrī said to him: "The night is deepening, O prince; tomorrow I shall tell you everything exactly as it happened. Arise, arise—blessings be upon you—and behold your parents, O observer of noble vows."
This night has grown deep and the sun has set;
these night-prowlers, speaking with cruel voices, roam about in joy. And the rustling of leaves from the beasts moving through the forest can be heard.
"These jackals, emitting terrible howls, have taken their stand in the south-western direction and are crying out fiercely, making my heart tremble. Satyavat said:
"The forest, enveloped by dense darkness, has a terrifying appearance;
you will not discern the path, nor will you be able to proceed.
Sāvitrī said:
"Now that this forest has been burnt today, a dry tree stands ablaze;
fanned by the wind, the fire is seen here and there.
Therefore, having brought more fire here, I shall set it alight on all sides."
"There are these pieces of wood here; cast away your personal distress.
If you do not venture forth, I perceive that you are afflicted by illness, and you will not find the path in this forest shrouded in darkness."
"Tomorrow at dawn, when the forest is visible, we shall depart with your permission; let us dwell here for this night, O sinless one, if it pleases you.
Satyavat said:
"My headache has ceased and I perceive my limbs to be healthy;
by your grace, I desire to be reunited with my mother and father. For never before have I gone to the hermitage at an improper hour."
When twilight has not yet arrived, my mother keeps me confined;
even when I have gone out during the day, my parents suffer.
And my father, along with the other residents of the hermitage, searches for me.
In the past, I was reproached many times by my mother and father, who were deeply distressed, saying, "You are coming back after a long time.
I reflect now: what must be the condition of those two today on my account?
"When they and I are out of sight, great sorrow will arise;
for previously, while weeping at night, those two aged ones, though deeply afflicted and filled with much affection, spoke thus to me."
"Deprived of you, my son, we cannot live even for a moment.
As long as you survive, my son, our life is certain. You are a staff for us, old and blind; upon you our lineage is established."
"In you [rest] our funeral offerings, our fame, and our lineage.
My mother is old and my father is old; I am indeed their only support. Not seeing me at night, what state will they reach?
I feel resentment toward sleep, on account of which my father and my innocent mother have fallen into peril because of me; and I too have fallen into peril, having been beset by this dire calamity.
"Indeed, without my mother and father, I cannot bear to live.
Clearly, with a troubled mind, my father— whose eye is wisdom—
is at this very hour questioning each resident of the hermitage."
O auspicious lady, I do not grieve for myself as much as I do for my father, nor for my mother, who is so exceedingly frail and has followed her husband;
for because of me, they both will today experience the utmost anguish.

"As long as they live, I shall live depending on them, for they are to be supported by me; I live only so that I may do what is pleasing to them. They are my supreme deity, and they must always be honored by me."
"But for those two, I always maintain this ancient vow.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having spoken thus, that righteous soul, who was devoted to his guru and dear to his guru, remained obedient to him.
Raising his arms, afflicted by grief, he wept aloud. Then, seeing her husband thus emaciated by sorrow,
the virtuous Sāvitrī wiped the tears from his eyes and spoke.
"If I have practiced austerity, if I have given gifts, or if I have offered oblations— by this merit, may this night be auspicious for my mother-in-law, my father-in-law, and my husband. Indeed,
I do not recall ever having spoken an untruthful word, even in jest."
"By that truth, may my parents-in-law remain alive this very day.
Satyavān said:
"I desire to see my parents; go, Sāvitrī, without delay."

"O beautiful lady, I swear by my own soul that I shall not live if I see anything unpleasant happen to my mother or father while they still draw breath; indeed, I would rather see those two elders alive."
"If your mind is set on dharma and if you wish me to remain alive, or if you must do what is pleasing to me, then go to the hermitage nearby.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then Sāvitrī, rising up and binding her hair, the beautiful woman,
raised her husband by embracing him with both arms. And Satyavat, having risen, wiped his limbs with his hand.
Having surveyed all directions, she fixed her gaze upon the grindstone.
Then Sāvitrī said to him: "Tomorrow you shall take the fruits from here;
for the sake of your well-being and security, I myself will carry this axe."
Having hung her heavy burden upon a tree branch and taken up an axe, she returned once more to her husband’s side; then,
that woman of beautiful thighs placed her husband’s arm upon her left shoulder.
Embracing him from the right, she who moved with gentle grace departed.
Satyavat said:
"O timid one, because of my frequent travels, the paths are well known to me."

"By the moonlight visible through the gaps between the trees, I can discern the path by which you two have come and where the fruits were gathered. O auspicious lady, go back by the way you came; do not hesitate."
At this grove of *palāśa* trees, the path divides into two;
go by the path to the north and hasten. I am well and strong, eager to see both my parents.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Speaking thus, the illustrious Satyavān, firm in his vows, set out in haste toward the hermitage together with Sāvitrī.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
At that very time, however, Dyumatsena, having regained his sight in the great forest and with a serene soul, beheld everything with his vision.
Having visited all the hermitages with his wife Śaibyā,
that bull among men fell into the deepest distress on account of his son. They [sought them] in hermitages, rivers, forests, and lakes.
Searching through various regions, the couple wandered about;
whenever they heard any sound whatsoever, they looked up in the hope that it was their son, and cried out, "Satyavān is coming with Sāvitrī! and ran toward it.
With their feet split, harsh, wounded, and drenched in blood,
their limbs pierced by *kuśa* grass and thorns, they ran about like two madmen. Then, all those brahmins dwelling in the hermitage approached them.
Having surrounded him and comforted him, they brought him back to their own hermitage. There, accompanied by his wife and surrounded by aged ascetics rich in austerity,
he was consoled with various meaningful stories concerning former kings.
Then, having recovered their breath once more, the two elders, longing to see their son and remembering his deeds from childhood, were deeply distressed;
they also recalled the various sightings of Sāvitrī.

Emaciated by grief, they both fell into sorrow for one another; and having spoken piteous words again and again, they wept, crying out, "O son! O virtuous daughter-in-law! Where are you? Where are you?"
The Brāhmaṇa Satyavāk spoke these words to them both.
Suvarcas said:
"Since his wife Sāvitrī [possesses] ascetic power and self-restraint..."
"And Satyavān lives thus, endowed with proper conduct.
Gautama said:
"The Vedas along with their auxiliary branches have been studied by me; great ascetic merit has been accumulated by me."

I have observed lifelong celibacy from my youth; my teachers and the sacred fires have been propitiated by me. With a concentrated mind, I have performed all my vows, subsisting on air and fasting, as well as whatever other auspicious practices were mine.
"By this ascetic power, I know everything you intend to do;
understand this truth: Satyavān still lives.
The disciple said:
"Whatever word has issued from the mouth of my preceptor can never be false; thus Satyavān lives.
The sages said:
"Just as his wife Sāvitrī is endowed with all the auspicious marks that prevent widowhood, so shall Satyavat live. Bhāradvāja said:
"Since his wife Sāvitrī is endowed with asceticism, self-restraint, and proper conduct, Satyavat lives accordingly. Dālbhya said:
"Just as your vision has proceeded, and just as Sāvitrī’s vow has been carried out— Satyavān lives, having gone without food.
Māṇḍavya said:
"Just as the beasts and birds cry out when the quarters are peaceful, so too, from your terrestrial report, Satyavat lives. Dhaumya said:
"Endowed with all virtues, just as your son is beloved by the people,
so Satyavān lives, long-lived and possessed of auspicious marks.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus consoled by those ascetics of truthful speech,
he remained as if lost in thought, reflecting upon various matters.
Then, after a moment, Sāvitrī was together with her husband Satyavat.
She arrived at the hermitage at night and entered it full of joy;
seeing her, all those twice-born ones rose up and were filled with delight.
Her mother and father embraced her neck and wept.
The brahmins said:
"O lord of the earth, having seen you today reunited with your son and endowed with sight, we all indeed wish you prosperity."
"By the reunion with your son, by the sight of Sāvitrī, and by the recovery of your own eyesight—by these three blessings you have fortunately increased in prosperity.
Whatever has been said by all of us is exactly so; there is no doubt in this matter."
"And your prosperity shall increase more and more very quickly.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Then, having kindled the fire there, all those twice-born ones indeed—"
O Pārtha, they paid their respects to the lord of the earth, Dyumatsena;
then Śaibyā, Satyavān, and Sāvitrī,
standing together and permitted by all of them, sat down free from sorrow.
Then, O Pārtha, all those forest-dwellers seated with the king, filled with curiosity, questioned the son of the monarch:
"O Lord, why did you not come earlier, accompanied by your wife?"
"Why did you return at the end of the night, and what was the cause for your delay?
O prince, our father, our mother, and we ourselves have all been filled with anxiety.
We know that this could not have happened without a reason; therefore, you ought to tell us everything."
Satyavat said:
"Permitted by my father, I went forth accompanied by Sāvitrī.
Then, while I was splitting wood in the forest, a pain arose in my head."
"I perceive that I have been asleep for a long time due to this sensation;
never before have I slept for such a length of time.
May no distress come upon any of you."
"Therefore, there is no other reason for his arrival at the end of the night.
Gautama said:
"The recovery of sight by your father Dyumatsena has occurred quite unexpectedly."
"You do not know the cause of this; Sāvitrī ought to speak it.
"I wish to hear it, O Sāvitrī, for you indeed know both the high and the low.
"For I know you, Sāvitrī, as one who is like Sāvitrī herself in splendor."
"You know the reason in this matter; therefore, let the truth be told.
If there is no secret here, speak it to us.
Sāvitrī said:
"It is exactly as you understand it; for your conception of this is not otherwise.
There is no secret from me—listen now to the truth of the matter here:
my death was foretold to my husband by the high-souled Nārada."
That very day has now arrived; therefore, I have not abandoned him.
While he was asleep, Yama himself approached him along with his attendants, bound him, and led him away to the direction inhabited by the ancestors.
I praised that omnipresent God with truthful speech;
he granted me five boons. Listen to them from me:
two boons were for my father-in-law—his eyesight and his own kingdom.

I have obtained a hundred sons from my father and a hundred sons for myself; my husband Satyavat has been recovered, and his lifespan is now four hundred years. Indeed, for the sake of my husband’s life, I have steadfastly observed my vow.
"I have related this truth to you in detail— the cause of how this great suffering of mine occurred, which results in future happiness. The sages said:
O lady of virtuous character, you who are steadfast in dharma and merit, it was by you that the royal family— sinking and overwhelmed by calamities in a lake of darkness— was rescued.
"O virtuous lady, it has been rescued again by one of noble birth.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having thus praised and honored her, they...
Having addressed the king and his son, those assembled sages took leave of that excellent woman and, being joyful, departed quickly for their own abodes with auspicious blessings.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When that night had passed and the solar disc had risen,
all those whose wealth is asceticism, having performed their morning rites, assembled together.
The great seers were never satiated as they recounted again and again all that great fortune of Sāvitrī to Dyumatsena. Then, O King, all the subjects arrived from the Śālvas.
They reported that the king had been slain by his own minister;
and having heard that he, along with his allies and kinsmen, had been killed by the minister, they reported the facts as they were, including how the enemy force had fled.
"Furthermore, there was a unanimous consensus among all the people regarding the king:
'Whether he has sight or is sightless, let him be our king.
It was with this resolution, O King, that we were dispatched here."
"These vehicles have arrived, as has your fourfold army.
Set forth, O King—may prosperity be yours! Victory has been proclaimed for you in the city.
Occupy for a long time the station of your fathers and grandfathers."
And seeing that king endowed with such beauty and possessed of vision,
they all fell prostrate with their heads, their eyes wide open in wonder.
Then, having saluted those aged twice-born ones dwelling in the hermitage, [he paid his respects].
Honored by them all, he set out toward the city;
Śaibyā, together with Sāvitrī, departed on a well-upholstered, radiant vehicle drawn by men, surrounded by an army.
Then, out of affection, the family priests consecrated Dyumatsena;
they also anointed his high-souled son as the crown prince.
Then, after a long time, [they performed] for Sāvitrī that which increases her fame...
To him were born a hundred sons, heroes who never retreated in battle; likewise, he had a hundred uterine brothers of great strength, born to Aśvapati, the lord of Madra, by Mālavī.

In this way, Sāvitrī rescued her own self, her father, her mother, her mother-in-law, her father-in-law, and the entire family of her husband from distress. In the very same manner, this auspicious Draupadī is likewise esteemed for her virtuous conduct.
"She will deliver you all, like a virtuous wife devoted to the Sāvitrī mantra.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus was that son of Pāṇḍu consoled by that high-souled one.
Free from sorrow and free from fever, O King, he then dwelt in the Kāmyaka forest.
And that man who hears this supreme narrative of Sāvitrī with devotion shall be happy, successful in all his aims, and shall never encounter suffering.
Janamejaya said:
O Great Brahmin, regarding those words which Lomaśa spoke at that time,
having approached Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu, by the command of Indra—
"And as for that intense fear which you do not mention anywhere—
that too I shall remove once Savyasācin has arrived here.
O best of the wise, what indeed is this great fear regarding Karṇa?"
And that righteous-souled one did not speak of it to anyone.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O tiger among kings, I shall relate this story to you."
"O best of the Bharatas, listen as I answer your question. When the twelfth year had passed and the thirteenth had arrived, Śakra, acting for the benefit of the Pāṇḍavas, prepared to beg from Karṇa."
Then, O great king, having understood the intention of Mahendra, Vibhāvasu, the Sun, approached Karṇa for the sake of the earrings. He found the hero upon a costly bed covered with exquisite rugs.

O Indra among kings, O Bhārata, the Sun-god, filled with supreme compassion and out of affection for his son, appeared at night in a dream to that one who was lying down in full trust, devoted to the Brahmins, and truthful in speech.
Having become a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, Sūrya, endowed with form through his yogic power,
spoke these words to Karṇa in a conciliatory manner for his benefit:
"O Karṇa, my dear son, best among those who uphold the truth, listen to my words."
"O mighty-armed one, as I speak today out of friendship for your supreme benefit, Śakra will approach you, desiring the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas;
O Karṇa, he will come in the guise of a Brāhmaṇa, wishing to take away your earrings."
Your character is known to him, as it is to the entire world:
that when you are asked by the virtuous, you only give and never beg. For you, my son, always give to the brahmins whenever you are entreated.
"Whatever wealth you possess, and whatever else they say you have, you never refuse anyone.
Knowing you to be such as this, Pākaśāsana himself will surely come to beg for the earrings and the armor."
"You must not give those earrings to him as he begs for them;
rather, you should entreat him to the best of your ability, for this is for your own supreme welfare.
O dear one, when he speaks regarding the earrings, you should address him with many reasons."
Desiring the earrings, Purandara repeatedly tried to dissuade him with various kinds of wealth— through jewels, women, enjoyments, and even manifold riches— and by means of many persuasive arguments.
"O Karṇa, if you give away your two auspicious, innate earrings,
you will reach the end of your life and fall under the power of death.
O giver of honor, while you are still endowed with both your armor and your two earrings,"
"Know these words of mine: you are invincible by your enemies in battle. For both of these have arisen from the nectar of immortality and are produced from jewels.
Therefore, O Karṇa, you must protect them if your life is dear to you."
Karṇa said:
"Who are you that speaks thus to me, displaying such supreme friendship?
O Blessed One, tell me if you please: who are you, wearing the guise of a twice-born?"
The Brahmin said:
"O dear one, I am the Thousand-rayed One (the Sun); out of friendship, I point this out to you.
Perform these words of mine, for this is indeed your supreme welfare."
Karṇa said:
"It is indeed my ultimate welfare that today the Lord of the Cowherds, seeking my benefit, speaks as my instructor; listen now to these words of mine."
I propitiate you, the giver of boons, and I speak out of affection:
if I am dear to you, I must not be prevented from this vow.
For the entire world knows this to be my vow, O Vibhāvasu.
"O best of sky-dwellers, I would surely give even my own life to the foremost of the twice-born,
if Śakra were to come to me disguised as a brahmin to beg for the sake of the sons of Pāṇḍu."
"O best of the gods, I shall give you my earrings and my excellent armor,
so that my fame, renowned throughout the three worlds, may not perish. For one such as I, it is not fitting to preserve life at the cost of infamy."
"For death endowed with glory is esteemed by the world.
Therefore, I shall give the two earrings along with the armor to Indra,
if that slayer of Bala and Vṛtra comes to me for the sake of a gift."
To beg my earrings for the sake of the welfare of the sons of Pāṇḍu—
this will bring me fame in the world, while it will bring infamy to him.
For I choose fame in this world, O radiant one, even at the cost of my life.
One who possesses fame attains heaven, but one devoid of fame perishes.
For in this world, fame revives a person like a mother,
whereas infamy destroys the life of an embodied being, even while they are still living.
O Vibhāvasu, Lord of the World, this ancient verse was indeed sung by the Creator himself: "Just as fame is the life-span of a man in this world,
so in the next world, fame alone is the supreme refuge for a person."

In this world, pure fame increases one's lifespan; therefore, by giving away my own flesh, I shall attain eternal fame. And having bestowed gifts upon the Brahmins according to the prescribed rules and ordinances, I shall achieve this end.
Having offered my body as a sacrifice in battle and performed deeds most difficult to accomplish,
or having conquered my enemies in combat, I shall obtain pure fame alone;
for I have granted fearlessness to those who were terrified and seeking their lives in the fray.
"O Destroyer of Svarbhānu, by delivering the aged, the young, and the twice-born from this great fear,
I shall attain supreme fame in the world;
know that even at the cost of my life, my glory must be protected— this is my vow."
"O Lord, having given this unsurpassed alms-offering to Maghavan disguised as a brahmin, I shall go to the supreme goal in the world. Sūrya said:
O Karṇa, best among those who possess life, do not act so as to bring harm to yourself, nor to your friends,
your sons, your wives, your mother, or your father;
do this without endangering the bodies of living beings.
The attainment of glory and enduring fame in the third heaven is desired; yet,
for you who seek eternal fame at the cost of your life, that fame will depart taking your life with it— of this there is no doubt.

O bull among men, while they live, the father, the mother, the sons, and whatever other kinsmen there may be in this world perform their duties; and so too do kings, O tiger among men— understand that all this is accomplished through manly effort.
O you of great splendor, fame is virtuous for a man while he lives;
what use is fame to a deceased embodied being who has been reduced to ashes?
A dead man does not know fame; it is while living that one enjoys fame.
"The fame of a mortal who has died is like a garland upon one whose life has departed. But I speak this to you because you are my devotee and out of a desire for your welfare;
for those who possess devotion to me must be protected—this is also my reason."

"O mighty-armed one, because he is devoted to me with supreme devotion, devotion has likewise arisen in me; therefore, do as I say. Furthermore, there exists here a certain supreme spiritual mystery ordained by the gods."
Therefore, I say this to you: let it be done without hesitation.
O bull among men, you are not able to know the secret of the gods;
therefore, I do not reveal that secret to you, for you shall come to know it in due time.
"I shall speak again what has been said before; listen to that, O son of Rādhā.
Do not give these two earrings to this mendicant who holds a thunderbolt in his hand.
For you, O one of great splendor, shine brilliantly with these two beautiful earrings."
"Like the spotless moon situated between the two Viśākhās in the sky, know this:
fame belongs to a virtuous man while he is alive. Therefore, dear son, you must refuse Purandara when he comes for the sake of the earrings."
Devoted to the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas, you, disguised as a wandering Brahmin,
O sinless one, may repeatedly seek to thwart the King of the Gods' desire for the earrings with various arguments supported by sound reasoning.
O Karna, dispel this thought of Purandara with arguments that are logically sound and adorned with sweetness;
for you, O tiger among men, always vie with Savyasacin.
The heroic Savyasācin will indeed encounter you in battle; however,
Arjuna will not be able to defeat you in combat while you are endowed with these two earrings, even if Indra himself were to become his arrow.
"Therefore, O Śakra, you must not give these two auspicious earrings to him,
if, O Karṇa, you desire to conquer Arjuna in battle.
Karṇa said:
