"O Lord of the Earth, O God of most fierce rays, you know how devoted I am to the Blessed One; I am not devoted to any other god in any way whatsoever.
To me, there are no wives, no sons, no self, and no friends."

"O Lord of Rays, just as you are always beloved by me through my devotion, so too are the high-souled ones beloved by those devotees who are themselves beloved; of this there is no doubt. They bestow their favor upon those they love, and you, O Bhāskara, know this well."

"Karna is my beloved and my devotee, and he knows no other deity in heaven"— thinking thus, the Blessed One spoke for my benefit. Furthermore, having propitiated him again and again, I entreat him once more with my head bowed low.
Thus I speak, O Tigmāṃśu; you ought to forgive me. I do not fear death as much as I fear untruth, especially among all the virtuous twice-born at all times.

Even regarding the gift of my own life, I have no hesitation in this matter. O Sun, let the mental anguish born of anxiety concerning what you have said to me regarding Phalguna, the son of Pāṇḍu, depart from your heart.

"Against Arjuna and against me as well, I shall conquer Arjuna in battle. O Lord, you too know the great power of my weapons, which I have acquired from the son of Jamadagni as well as from the high-souled Droṇa."
"O best of gods, grant me this boon:
should I beg from the wielder of the thunderbolt, I would give him even my own life.
Sūrya said:
"O father, if you give these two auspicious earrings to the wielder of the thunderbolt,
then, O mighty one, you should also speak to him for the sake of victory:
'You must indeed give the earrings to Śatakratu under a solemn vow.'"
"For you are indeed invulnerable to all beings as long as you are endowed with these two earrings.
O child, the slayer of the Dānavas, seeking your destruction in battle, desires to seize those earrings of yours from Arjuna."
Therefore, you too, having propitiated him again and again with truthful and pleasant words,
should entreat Purandara, the lord of the gods, for an unfailing purpose:
"Grant me an infallible spear that destroys enemies."
"O thousand-eyed one, I shall give you my earrings and my supreme armor"—
by this very condition, O Śakra, you should give the earrings to him.
By means of them, O Karṇa, you will slay your enemies in the heat of battle.
"O mighty-armed one, for without slaying his enemies, he does not return again with tribute;
such is the power of the king of the gods, by the hundreds and thousands.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, the Thousand-rayed One suddenly vanished.
But Karṇa, O King, woke up at the end of his dream as if trembling;
and having awakened, O Bhārata, the son of Rādhā reflected upon that dream.
O King, best among speakers, he made this resolve regarding the spear:
"If Indra, the scorcher of foes, comes to me for the sake of the earrings,
I shall give him the spear, as well as the earrings and the armor."
Having risen in the morning and performed his duties, O bull of the Bharatas, he had the Brahmins recite auspicious prayers and proceeded with what was to be done; then,
O tiger among kings, he muttered prayers for a moment according to the prescribed rite.
Then, at the conclusion of his prayers to the Sun, Karṇa reported the dream exactly as it had been seen,
according to its true nature, and just as it had been told by both during the night;
the bull among men then related all of that to him in due order.
Having heard that, the Blessed Lord Sun, the slayer of Svarbhānu,
spoke to Karṇa as if smiling, saying, "So be it.
Then Rādheya, the slayer of enemy heroes, realizing this was the truth, [acted accordingly].
Desiring only power, he indeed waited for Vāsava.
Janamejaya said:
"What was that secret which was not told to Karṇa here by the hot-rayed one (the Sun)?"
"What were those earrings like, and what was that armor like?
And from where did he obtain that armor and those earrings, O best of men?
I wish to hear this; tell it to me, O rich in asceticism."
"O Brahmin, O best of beings, tell me how that secret of Vivasvat was [obtained] and what those two earrings were like; explain both of these to me as they truly are.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O King, I shall now tell you that secret of the Sun-god—
what kind of earrings and what kind of armor he possesses. Long ago, O King, a Brahmin approached Kuntibhoja."
Of sharp brilliance and great stature, bearing a beard, staff, and matted locks,
he was handsome with faultless limbs, as if blazing with splendor;
honey-colored and sweet-spoken, his ornament was the practice of austerity and sacred study.
That man of great asceticism spoke to King Kuntibhoja:
"O one free from envy, I wish to eat alms-food in your house.
You, or your attendants, must not cause me any offense."
"O sinless one, if it pleases you, I shall dwell thus in your house;
I may go and come just as I wish,
and no one, O King, should cause me any offense regarding my bed or seat."
Kuntibhoja spoke these words to him with affection:
"So be it, and even more. Then he said to him again:
"O great Brahmin, I have a daughter, the illustrious Pṛthā by name."
Endowed with virtuous conduct, chaste, self-controlled, and free from pride, she will indeed attend upon you, honoring you and never treating you with contempt;
and through her virtuous conduct, you will attain complete satisfaction.
Having spoken thus and having honored that brahmin according to the prescribed rites,
he approached the large-eyed maiden Pṛthā and said:
"O child, this highly fortunate brahmin wishes to dwell here."
"In my house, I promised him 'so be it' regarding the propitiation of this Brahmin, O child; having placed your trust in you,
you must never at any time make those words of mine false."
"This ascetic and venerable twice-born man is devoted to his Vedic studies;
whatever this one of great splendor may say should be given to him without stinginess.
For Brahmins are supreme radiance; Brahmins are supreme austerity."

Through his salutations to the Brahmins, Sūrya shines resplendent in the sky. For it was because he failed to honor those worthy of honor that the great Asura Vātāpi and likewise Tālajaṅgha were struck down by the staff of the Brahmins' curse.
"O child, this great burden has now been placed upon you;
you must always remain self-restrained and devoted to the service of the Brahmin.
O Nandini, I know your dedication from the time of your childhood."

Among all the brahmins here, as well as among your teachers and kinsmen, and likewise among all your servants, friends, relatives, and mothers, and even toward me, you conduct yourself with due respect, honoring everyone appropriately.
For there is no person here, neither in the city nor in your inner apartments, who is dissatisfied with you,
O lady of faultless limbs, owing to your perfectly proper conduct— even toward your servants. Yet,
I think you ought to give instructions regarding that irascible twice-born man.
"O Pṛthā, because you were but a child, and thinking 'you are my daughter,' you were born in the lineage of the Vṛṣṇis as the beloved daughter of Śūra;
long ago, while still a girl, you were given to me by your father himself out of affection."

The sister of Vasudeva is the foremost among my daughters; having first made a solemn vow, she has thus become my daughter. For she was born into such a family and was raised within that very lineage.
Having attained happiness after happiness, as if coming from one lake to another,
even those of low birth who have somehow attained self-restraint often revert to their former nature due to youthful impulses, O auspicious lady.

O beautiful woman, you were born in the royal house of Pṛthu, and your form is wonderful to behold; for that reason, you are endowed with and possessed of every excellence. Therefore, O beautiful woman, cast aside pride, hypocrisy, and arrogance.
"O Pṛthā, by propitiating that boon-granting Brahmin, you shall be united with prosperity.
Thus, O auspicious and sinless one, you will surely attain what is beneficial. But if that best of the twice-born were to be provoked to anger, my entire lineage would be consumed."
Kuntī said:
"O King, O Indra among kings, I shall attend upon the brahmin with worship, restrained and according to my vow; I do not speak falsely."
"This is indeed my own nature: that I should honor the twice-born. It is both pleasing to you and for my own supreme welfare.
Whether he comes in the evening, in the morning, or even at night,"
"If the Blessed One does not show me anger at midnight,
O King of kings, it will be a great gain for me that I may worship the twice-born while abiding by your command; thus, O best of men, I shall perform what is beneficial."
"Be confident, O Indra among kings; that best of the twice-born shall not meet with any misfortune while dwelling in your house. I tell you this as the truth.
Whatever is pleasing to this brahmin and beneficial to you, O sinless one," [he said].
"I shall strive accordingly, O King, so that the fever of your mind may depart. For the highly blessed Brahmins, O Lord of the Earth, when honored,
are capable of delivering one from calamity, and in the contrary case, of bringing about one's destruction."
Knowing this, I shall satisfy that best of the twice-born;
O King, you shall not suffer distress on my account from that most excellent of brahmins.
For when there is an offense, O Indra among kings, brahmins bring misfortune to monarchs.
"Just as Cyavana in former times became [restored] for the sake of Sukanyā,
so shall I serve that best of the twice-born with supreme discipline,
O lord of men, exactly as you have spoken regarding this Brāhmaṇa."
Having embraced and consoled her who was speaking thus many times,
and having instructed her on what ought to be done both here and there, the king then commanded everything.
The king said:
"O blessed lady, O daughter, this must be done by you without hesitation—
for my sake, for the sake of the family, and likewise for your own sake.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to that maiden, the highly illustrious Kuntibhoja,
who was deeply affectionate toward his daughter, entrusted Pṛthā to that twice-born man, saying:
"O Brahmin, this is my daughter, a young girl raised in comfort."
Whatever offense you may commit, you should not take it to heart;
for the highly fortunate twice-born are generally free from anger toward the elderly, children, and ascetics, even when they are constantly opposed by them.
"Even for a very great offense, forgiveness must be practiced by the twice-born;
O best of the twice-born, an offering should be accepted according to one's ability and according to one's enthusiasm.
When the Brahmin had said, "So be it," the king was delighted in his heart.
He pointed out to him a residence resembling the moonbeams of a swan. There, in the fire-sanctuary, he presented him with a radiant seat and likewise offered all provisions such as food.
Having cast aside both lassitude and pride,
the princess applied herself with supreme effort to the propitiation of the brahmin. There, Pṛthā, devoted to purity, approached the brahmin.
O King, devoted to service day and night without weariness,
she satisfied him— who was worthy of ritual attendance like a god— with proper devotion.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O great king, that maiden, herself firm in her vows, gratified with a pure mind a brahmin who was likewise strict in his observances.
Having said, "I shall return in the morning," that best of the twice-born would sometimes return in the evening, O Indra among kings, or even again at night;
and at all times he was provided with food, edibles, and shelter.
That maiden constantly honored him with ever-increasing hospitality,
such as the offering of food and the provision of beds and seats;
day by day, these services toward him increased and never diminished.
O King, even when subjected to insults, reproaches, and likewise unpleasant speech, Pṛthā did nothing disagreeable to the brāhmaṇa at that time.
When the time was favorable, the twice-born man would come again and again, and many times he would not come at all.
"Even if food is difficult to obtain, let it be given," he said;
and Pṛthā, being well-restrained, reported to him that everything had indeed been prepared,
treating him like a disciple, a son, and a brother.
O Indra among kings, that blameless maiden, by her efforts, produced such delight in that most excellent of the twice-born as was pleasing to him; indeed,
that best of the twice-born was gratified by her character and conduct.
With great attentiveness, he then exerted even greater effort for her sake.
And every morning and evening, O Bhārata, her father asked her:
"Daughter, is the brahmin satisfied with your service?"
The illustrious lady replied to him, "So be it. Thereupon, the high-minded Kuntibhoja attained the highest satisfaction.
Then, when a full year had passed for that best of those who recite prayers, he—
Devoted to her friendship, he did not perceive any fault whatsoever in Pṛthā.
Then, with a joyful mind, that brahmin said to her:
"I am exceedingly pleased, O auspicious lady, with your service, O beautiful one."
"Choose boons, O blessed lady, which are difficult for mortals here to attain, by which you shall surpass all women in fame.
Kuntī said:
"O best of those who know the Vedas, since you, as well as my father, are pleased with me, everything has been accomplished for me; O Brahmin, my boons have been granted.
The Brahmin said:
"If you do not wish to receive a boon from me, O blessed lady of pure smiles,
then take this mantra for summoning the dwellers of heaven;
whichever deity you shall invoke with this mantra," [he said].
"O blessed lady, he will come under your control in whatever way you desire; whether unwilling or willing, he shall not fail to submit to your power.
Like a wise servant, once pacified by counsel, he will bow before your word."
Vaiśampāyana said: O King,
that blameless woman was unable to refuse him—
that foremost of the twice-born— for fear of his curse.

Then, O King, that twice-born one caused her of faultless limbs to receive the collection of mantras heard in the *Atharvaśiras*. Having bestowed them upon her, O Indra among kings, he spoke to Kuntibhoja:
"O King, I have lived happily, gratified by your daughter;
well-provided for and always duly honored in your house. We shall now depart," he said, and vanished.
But when the king saw that the twice-born had vanished right there at that moment,
he was filled with wonder and honored Pṛthā.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When that best of the twice-born had departed, after some time had passed,
that maiden reflected upon the strength and weakness of the collection of mantras:
"Of what nature indeed was this [mantra] given to me by that high-souled one?"
"I shall know his collection of mantras and his power before long.
While she was reflecting thus, she unexpectedly perceived her season;
the young girl became ashamed, having reached her menses while still in the state of maidenhood.
Then, while standing upon the roof of the palace, Pṛthā— who was accustomed to a costly bed—
beheld the rising thousand-rayed sun in its brilliance. As she gazed at it, her mind and sight became fixed there, and she stood motionless.
She was not satiated by the beauty of the sun as it reached the twilight;
her vision became divine, and she beheld a divine sight—
the god clad in armor and adorned with two earrings.
O lord of men, she felt a great curiosity regarding the mantra;
then that beautiful woman performed the invocation of that deity. Having touched water for purification, she then summoned the Sun-god.
Then, O King, the sun-god Divākara arrived in haste—
tawny as honey, mighty-armed, with a neck like a conch shell, as if smiling,
adorned with armlets and a bound crown, as if setting the very quarters of the sky ablaze.
Having divided himself in two through yoga, he arrived and performed his ascetic penance;
then he addressed Kuntī with words of supreme sweetness and conciliation:
"O blessed lady, I have come under your power, compelled by the force of your mantra."
"O Queen, what shall I do, being powerless? Speak, and I shall do it for you.
Kuntī said:
"O Blessed One, please go back to the place from which you came."
"Summoned by curiosity, [she said], 'Be gracious, O Blessed One.
Sūrya replied:
"O slender-waisted one, I shall go just as you tell me."
But it is not right to summon a god and send him away in vain;
for your intention, O fortunate lady, was that a son might be born from the Sun—
one peerless in valor in the world, clad in armor and wearing earrings.
Therefore, O lady with the gait of an elephant, grant yourself to me;
for a son shall be born to you, O beautiful woman, exactly according to your wish. Now, O blessed one of the lovely smile, I shall depart after having united with you.
"If you do not carry out my dear request today, I shall, in my anger, curse both you and your father, the brahmin.
Because of your actions, I shall consume them all; of this there is no doubt."

O fool, I shall today impose the highest discipline upon your father, who does not recognize this transgression of yours, and upon that Brahmin who gave you the mantra without having ascertained his character and conduct.
"For all these gods in heaven, headed by Purandara,
look upon what has been done to them by you as if they were smiling, O beautiful lady.
Behold these hosts of gods, for this divine vision is yours."
"By that very [gift] which was given by me previously, you have seen me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the princess beheld the gods.
All of them, stationed in their own celestial abodes,
were shining, radiant, and great,
just like the sun as it blazes.
Seeing them, the young goddess, as if ashamed and frightened, spoke these words to the Sun:
"O Lord of Rays, go indeed to your own celestial chariot."
This practice is painful because of her maidenhood;
for her father, mother, teachers,
and others have authority over the giving away of this body.
"I shall not violate the dharma in this world;
for women, the protection of the body is honored as their proper conduct.
O Vibhāvasu, you were summoned by me to test the power of my mantras."
"O Lord, you ought to forgive me for that, considering her a mere child out of childishness.
Sūrya said:
"Because she is a child, I have offered this conciliation to you;"
I give [this]; let no other entreaty be accepted. O daughter of Kunti, grant me your own self;
for in this way, O timid one, there shall be peace for you.
Moreover, it is not right for me to depart while my conduct has been false,
O timid one, without having met with you who have been summoned by my mantra, O beautiful lady; for if I go, O lady of faultless limbs, I shall become an object of derision in the world.
"O lady of beautiful hips, if I were to go [to you] in this manner, I would indeed be rejected;
O auspicious one, I would become an object of reproach among all the gods.
Therefore, come together with me, and you shall obtain a son like myself."
"And you, O beautiful lady, shall become preeminent among all the worlds.
Vaiśampāyana said:
But that maiden, speaking many kinds of sweet words, continued:
The high-minded lady was unable to dissuade the thousand-rayed sun;
when the young woman could not refuse the dispeller of darkness,
O King, she became afraid of his curse and then reflected for a long time.

"How might the curse of my innocent father and likewise that of the Brahmin not fall upon me because of me— this blazing fire— were he to be enraged? Even though I am but a child, I have through delusion committed many grave offenses."
One must not overly provoke fiery energies or ascetic powers.
Thus, being seized firmly by the hand today, I am greatly terrified;
how indeed could I perform such an improper act as the self-giving of myself?
O best of kings, terrified by that curse and reflecting deeply at that time,
her limbs overcome by delusion, she smiled again and again and spoke to that god in fear of her kinsmen.
Trembling with shame and terrified by the curse, O lord of the people,
Kuntī said:
"O God, my father lives, as do my mother and other kinsmen."
"While they are still living, this violation of the sacred law would not occur;
O God, if my union with you were to take place outside the prescribed rites, then because of me,
the fame of this lineage would perish in the world."
"Or rather, O best of ascetics, if you consider this to be dharma,
then even without being given away by my kinsmen, I shall fulfill your wish; for,
O invincible one, having surrendered myself to you, I shall remain faithful."
"In you reside the dharma, the glory, the fame, and the lifespan of all embodied beings.
The Sun said:
"O lady of pure smiles, neither your father, nor your mother, nor your elders [are as worthy of honor] as you."
They have power over you, O lady of excellent limbs; may you be blessed, hear my words.
Because she desires all things, O beautiful woman, and because of the verbal root *kan*, she is therefore called a *kanyā* here, O fair-hipped one of excellent complexion, for she is independent.
"O beautiful lady, no unrighteousness has ever been committed by you;
how then could I practice unrighteousness out of a desire for worldly gain?
O woman of excellent complexion, all women and men are indeed unrestrained."
"This is the very nature of the worlds; change is known as something else.
Having united with me, you shall become a maiden once again.
And your son shall be mighty-armed and of great renown."
Kuntī said:
"If I were to have from you a son who dispels all darkness,
one who is heroic, long-armed, and possessed of great strength, wearing earrings and armor,"
"O you of fierce rays, O mighty-armed one, I shall unite with you;
let my union with you, O God, take place according to this agreement.
Sūrya said:
"He will be mighty-armed, wearing earrings and bearing divine armor;
both of these, O blessed lady, shall consist of nectar for him.
Kuntī said:
"If this nectar exists, along with the earrings and the supreme armor,
for my son whom you shall procreate from me— O God,
O Blessed One, let there be union between us as you have spoken."
"He shall possess your valor, beauty, strength, and energy, and he shall be endowed with righteousness.
Sūrya said:
"O Queen, O beautiful lady, the two earrings were given to me by Aditi."
"O timid one, I shall indeed give this supreme armor to you.
Pṛthā said:
"O Blessed One, O God, I shall unite with you."
"O Lord of the Cowherds, if a son should be born to me exactly as you say," Vaiśampāyana said,
"the bird, having replied 'So be it' to Kuntī, entered her."
The enemy of Svarbhānu, whose soul was absorbed in yoga, touched her at the navel.
Thereupon, that maiden became as if overwhelmed by the splendor of the Sun;
then the goddess fell upon the bed, her consciousness clouded.
Sūrya said:
"O lady of beautiful hips, I shall accomplish this; you will indeed give birth to a son, the best among all wielders of weapons, and you shall remain a virgin."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O king of kings, that bashful young woman spoke thus to the sun of great splendor as he was about to depart: "So be it."
Having spoken thus, that daughter of the King of Kunti, bashfully entreating Vivasvat,
fell upon that sacred bed.
Overcome by delusion like a withering creeper,
he bewildered her with his solar splendor and,
through yoga, absorbed her into his own self.
And Bhānu did not violate her;
then the young woman regained her consciousness once more.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O lord of the earth, a fetus was formed within Pṛthā,
like the moon, the lord of the stars, in the sky during the bright fortnight of the tenth lunar day.
Out of fear of her kinsmen, that young woman concealed the pregnancy.
The fair-hipped woman maintained this secret, yet no one among the people discovered it;
for no other woman knew of her,
that foster-daughter, except for herself, as she remained in the maidens' quarters, a young girl skilled in self-concealment.

Then, in due time, that woman of excellent complexion gave birth to a child of divine luster through the grace of that god; even as a maiden, she bore him who was already clad in armor and adorned with earrings blazing with gold.
He had tawny eyes and shoulders like a bull, just like his father;
and as soon as that child was born, O Bhārata, the beautiful woman, having consulted with her nurse, desired to cast away the infant and caused it to be done.
O King, have the artisans quickly prepare a well-fastened and well-constructed chest,
bound with various kinds of floats for the purpose of crossing the water;
likewise, have it provided with beds spread with soft deerskins.
She placed [the child] in a well-lined casket that was smooth on all sides,
filled with beeswax, comfortable, and well-covered; then, weeping, she set it adrift upon the river Aśvanadī.

Knowing full well that conceiving a child was improper for a maiden, O Indra among kings, she lamented piteously out of affection for her son. Then, casting the basket into the waters of the Ashva river, she wept.
Listen to those words which Kuntī, weeping, spoke:
"May there be well-being for you from the beings of the atmosphere and the earth, O son,
as well as from the divine beings and those who dwell in the waters."

May your paths be auspicious, and may there be no adversaries on your way; and likewise, my son, may those you encounter be free from hostile intent. May King Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, protect you in every body of water.
May Pavana, who dwells in the intermediate space and pervades all, protect you there; and may your father, Tapana, the best among those who give heat, protect you everywhere—
he by whom you were indeed given to me as a son through a divine rite.
May the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, and all the Viśvedevas,
as well as the Maruts together with Indra and the quarters along with their presiding deities—
may all these gods protect you in both times of ease and times of distress.
"I shall recognize you even in a foreign land by the sign of your armor. Blessed is your father, the god Bhānu, the source of light,
who shall behold you with his divine eye as you stand amidst the army."
Blessed is that woman who shall regard you as her son,
for you, O god-born one, being thirsty, shall drink from her breast as her son. What dream must she have seen, she who [shall behold] you, radiant as the sun?
Endowed with divine armor and adorned with celestial earrings,
with large eyes as broad as lotuses and radiant with copper-colored palms,
he— possessing a beautiful forehead and lovely hair— will adopt [you] as his son.
"Blessed are those who shall see you, my son, crawling upon the ground,
speaking indistinct and sweet words, covered in dust. Blessed are those who shall see you again at the onset of youth."
Like a maned lion born in the forests of the Himalayas,
O King, having lamented in many such ways most piteously, Pṛthā then cast the basket into the waters of the Aśvanadī.
O King, at midnight, the lotus-eyed Pṛthā, afflicted by grief for her son and longing to see him, wept together with her nurse;
she had placed the basket there out of fear of waking her father.
Then, overcome with grief, she entered the royal palace once more.
But that casket traveled from the Aśvanadī river to the Carmaṇvatī river;
from the Carmaṇvatī it went to the Yamunā, and from there it proceeded to the Gaṅgā.
He arrived at the city of Campā, located in the Sūta territory on the Gaṅgā. That infant, carried within a chest and borne along by the waves,
possessed that divine armor and earrings which had arisen from the nectar of immortality.
She bore that divine embryo, fashioned by fate and ordained by destiny.
Vaiśampāyana said:
At that very time, there was indeed a friend of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
The charioteer named Adhiratha, together with his wife, went to the Jahnavī (Ganges).
O King, his wife was peerless on earth in beauty;
she was the highly fortunate lady named Rādhā, yet she did not obtain a son.
She exerted supreme effort, especially for the sake of offspring; then,
by chance, she saw a basket being carried along,
secured with protective amulets and adorned with auspicious touch-stones.
Bringing her to the vicinity by the waves and billows of the Gaṅgā,
she was turned around many times, again and again, here and there;
then, O King, she was carried away by the wind and the powerful current.
Since the charioteer, accompanied by his wife, had approached and taken refuge in the water,
that beautiful woman, out of curiosity, caused him to seize her as she arrived;
then she indeed informed the charioteer Adhiratha.
Having lifted that chest and drawn it close to the water,
he opened it with mechanical devices; there he saw a boy who resembled the rising sun and was clad in golden armor.
With his face shining, adorned with polished earrings,
he beheld that noble son endowed with supreme beauty, while the boy himself was weeping intensely, hungry, and his face utterly withered.
With eyes wide open in wonder, that charioteer, together with his wife,
placed the boy on his lap and spoke these words to his wife:
"O timid one, O beautiful lady, this is most marvelous, since I have been born from you."
"Having seen him, I think this one is a divine being who has come to us;
surely this son has been granted to me, who am childless, by the gods.
Having said this, O lord of the earth, he gave that son to Rādhā.

Rādhā received him according to the prescribed rites—he who possessed a divine form, whose son shone like the interior of a lotus, a child of the gods endowed with splendor. And then, by divine power, her breast milk flowed forth; such was the certainty.
She nourished him according to the prescribed rites, and he grew up full of prowess;
from that time forward, other biological sons were also born to her. And they performed his naming ceremony, for earrings were seen upon him.
Seeing that boy with earrings,
and seeing that boy wearing golden earrings and clad in excellent armor,
the twice-born then gave him the name Vasuṣeṇa because he was "Karna" (ear-ringed).
Thus he of immeasurable prowess became the son of a charioteer;
the lord was known as Vasuṣeṇa and also as Vṛṣa. That heroic man, the eldest son of the Sūta, grew up among the Aṅgas.
Through a spy, it was known that Pṛthā possessed a divine armor; then,
when her son had grown up in due time, the charioteer Adhiratha,
seeing him, sent him away to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
There he undertook the service of Drona for the purpose of learning the science of archery;
and thus that heroic youth entered into friendship with Duryodhana. From Drona, Kripa, and Rama, he acquired the fourfold collection of weapons.

Having attained renown in the world, he became one of the foremost archers; having entered into an alliance with the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he remained intent on doing what was displeasing to the sons of Pṛthā,
constantly aspiring to fight with the high-souled Phalguna.
For he always had a rivalry with Arjuna, O lord of the people,
and Arjuna likewise with Karṇa, as soon as they saw one another;
this secret, O great king, belonged to Sūrya, there is no doubt.
Yudhiṣṭhira was filled with anguish when he saw that Karṇa, who had been born to Kuntī in the family of charioteers by the Sun, was now equipped with earrings and armor,
and deemed invincible in battle.
But when Karṇa, O Indra among kings, standing in the water with palms joined in reverence, praises the radiant sun at the arrival of midday,
Brahmins seeking wealth approach him there.
At that time, there was nothing whatsoever that he would not give to the twice-born.
At that very moment, Indra, desiring the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas,
approached him in the guise of a brahmin and said, "Give me alms."
"Welcome," the son of Rādhā then replied to him.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Vṛṣa [Karna] addressed the King of the Gods, who had arrived in the guise of a Brahmin.

Seeing him, he said, "Welcome," yet he did not grasp the Brahmin's intention. Then the son of Adhiratha said to that Brahmin, "Shall I give you women with golden necklaces, or villages abounding in herds of cattle?"
The Brahmin said:
"I do not desire here women with golden necks or anything else that increases pleasure; let that be given to those who seek it."
"O sinless one, if you are true to your vow, cut off this innate armor and these two earrings of yours and give them to me. O scorcher of the foe, I desire that these be given by you quickly."
"This is considered by me to be the supreme gain among all gains.
Karṇa said:
"Land, women, cattle, and provisions for many years—"
"O sage, I shall give that to you, but neither the armor nor the earrings.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus entreated by him with many kinds of words, that twice-born man—
O best of the Bharatas, Karṇa requested no other boon;
though consoled to the best of his ability and honored according to tradition,
that foremost of brahmins desired no other boon at all.
O lord of the people, when that best of the twice-born chose no other boon,
except for his natural armor and earrings,
then the son of Rādhā spoke to him once more, as if laughing.
"O Brahmin, my armor is innate, and these earrings are born of ambrosia;
because of them, I am invulnerable in all the worlds, and therefore I will not give them up. [I prefer] a vast sovereignty over the earth, secure and with its thorns removed."
"Accept these from me, O bull among brahmins;
for I shall be vulnerable to my enemies, O best of the twice-born, now that I am deprived of my two earrings and my innate armor."
When the Blessed Lord, the subduer of Pāka, chose no other boon,
Karṇa laughed and spoke these words to him again:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, O Master, you were already known to me from before."
"O Śakra, it is not right for me to grant you a boon in vain;
for you are the Lord of the Gods in person, and a boon should be granted to me by you. Indeed, you are the creator of beings and the lord of all other creatures."
"O Lord, if I give you the earrings as well as the armor,
I shall become vulnerable to death and you, O Śakra, will become an object of ridicule.
Therefore, having made an exchange for the earrings and the excellent armor— "
"O Śakra, grant me my desire; I shall not give otherwise.
Śakra said:
"I was already known to Ravi even before I came into your presence."
"By him all has been told to you; this is so, there is no doubt. 'Let it be as you wish, my dear Karna,' [said Indra], 'just as you desire;
however, with the exception of my thunderbolt (vajra), choose whatever you wish.'"
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Karṇa, being greatly delighted and his heart’s desire fulfilled, approached Vāsava and, coming forward, chose the infallible spear.
Karṇa said:
"O Vāsava, give me your armor and your two earrings,
along with that spear which is unfailing and the slayer of hosts of enemies at the head of the army."
Vaiśampāyana said: Then, O protector of the earth, having reflected for a moment in his mind regarding the matter of the spear, Vāsava spoke these words to Karṇa.
"Give me your earrings and the armor born with your body;
O Karṇa, take from me this spear on this condition:
released from my hand, it shall slay hundreds of enemies unfailingly."
And again, as I slay the Daityas, it returns to my hand; now,
having reached your hand and slain one powerful enemy, this sword,
O son of a Sūta, shall return to me alone— me who am roaring and scorching [the foe].
Karṇa said:
"I desire to slay only one enemy in this great battle— one who roars and scorches me, from whom my fear arises."
Indra said:
"You shall slay one roaring, powerful enemy in battle;
but that single one for whom you strive is protected by a high-souled being."
"He whom those learned in the Vedas call the invincible boar, Hari,
Nārāyaṇa, and the inconceivable— one is protected by that Kṛṣṇa.
Karṇa said:
"O destroyer of the Dānavas, it is exactly as you have said.
I shall slay in battle whatever enemy stands before me as my adversary. Let it be so, O Blessed One; let this be for the sake of my own singular heroism."
"By means of this unfailing and supreme spear, I shall slay that scorning foe;
having cut them off, I will give you the earrings and the armor.
And even when my limbs have been mangled, there shall be no loathsomeness in me."
Indra said:
"O Karṇa, there shall be no loathing for you in any way,
nor any wound upon your limbs, since you do not desire untruth."
"O best of speakers, O Karṇa, with the very same complexion and splendor as your father’s, you shall become once again,
provided that among existing weapons you do not discharge an unfailing one without hesitation."
"Even if you are negligent, you shall be released, and she will fall upon you alone.
Karṇa said:
"Having encountered this supreme danger, I shall release this weapon of Vāsava."
"O Śakra, as you have told me, I tell you this truly.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Then, O lord of the people, having received that blazing spear..."
Taking up a sharpened weapon, he cut all his limbs.
Then the gods, humans, and dānavas [beheld] Karṇa thus cutting himself.
Seeing this, all the hosts of Siddhas raised a shout;
for indeed, there was no change in him born of sorrow.
Then, celestial drums resounded.
A divine rain of flowers fell from on high as they beheld Karṇa, that hero among men, his limbs mangled by weapons yet smiling again and again.
Then, having cut the divine armor from his body while it was still wet, he gave it to Vāsava; likewise,
having carved them out, he gave those two earrings.
Because of that deed, he was Karna Vaikartana;
then the god Vajrapāṇi was delighted upon seeing Karna with his limbs mangled by weapons.
Then Śakra, laughing, having deceived Karṇa and having endowed him with fame in the world,
considered the task of the Pāṇḍavas as already accomplished.
Thereafter, he flew up into the very sky.
Upon hearing that Karṇa had been robbed [of his earrings], all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra became dejected, as if their pride were shattered.
Hearing that the son of the Sūta had been reduced to such a state, the Pārthas dwelling in the forest rejoiced.
Janamejaya said:
Where were those heroic Pāṇḍavas staying? From whom did they hear this pleasant news? And what did they do when the twelfth year had passed?
"May the Blessed One explain all of that to me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having recovered Kṛṣṇā and having put the ruler of the Sindhus to flight;"
Together with the brahmins, they had previously heard from Mārkaṇḍeya at the Kāmyaka hermitage the ancient accounts in detail,
including the life-stories of the celestial rishis.
Accompanied by their chariots and retinues,
together with all the cooks and kitchen-stewards,
those heroes among men returned to the sacred Dvaitavana forest.
Having completely endured the severe forest exile,
Janamejaya said:
"When Kṛṣṇā had been thus abducted, they encountered unsurpassed suffering."
"Having obtained Kṛṣṇā, what did the Pāṇḍavas do next?
Vaiśampāyana said:
"They all subsisted on flowers and fruits, and all of them were moderate in their eating."
When Kṛṣṇā had been thus abducted and [the Pāṇḍavas] had undergone unsurpassed suffering,
listen now to what they did after recovering Kṛṣṇā:
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the steadfast one, departed from the Kāmyaka forest together with his brothers.
Yudhiṣṭhira returned once more to the delightful Dvaitavana forest,
toward the charming hermitage of Mārkaṇḍeya, which abounded in sweet roots and fruits; there they all subsisted on gathered fruits, eating with moderation.
O Bhārata, the Pāṇḍavas dwelt there together with Kṛṣṇā.
While King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, was residing in the Dvaitavana forest,
so too did Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī.

Those self-controlled and righteous-souled subduers of enemies, exerting themselves for the sake of the Brāhmaṇa, underwent great hardship that resulted in ultimate happiness; while dwelling there, those best of the Kurus experienced what followed.
I shall now describe that suffering in the forest which results in future happiness; listen to it. The fire-drill belonging to an ascetic brahmin became entangled in the antlers of a rubbing deer.
O King, having taken that [fruit], the great deer departed in haste;
moving with great speed, he leaped swiftly, disappearing from the hermitage.
O best of the Kurus, seeing him being carried away, that brahmin—
He arrived there in haste, desiring to obtain the *agnihotra* fire.
And while those Pāṇḍavas were dwelling there in the forest, he approached the great chariot-warrior Ajātaśatru as he sat together with his brothers.

O King, at the third watch of the afternoon, while Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira was eating together with Draupadī, the irascible brahmin Durvāsas arrived in the forest, urged on by Duryodhana and himself hungry.

Then, his soul overwhelmed with anxiety, the son of Dharma meditated upon Janārdana; the Blessed One arrived with haste. At that time, after Durvāsas had departed to bathe in the Gaṅgā, [the Lord appeared].
Then, O King, Madhusūdana ate a single leaf of the *śāka* plant.
Out of compassion, he who is affectionate toward his devotees said, "The three worlds are now satiated. Durvāsas, having attained satisfaction, joyfully granted him auspiciousness.
Approaching Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, as he sat in the hermitage of Mārkaṇḍeya,
a certain Brahmin, distressed, quickly spoke these words:
"My fire-drills, together with the wooden block, were suspended upon a tree."
As the deer was rubbing itself, [the jewel] became caught in its horn. Taking it, O King, that great deer departed in haste,
leaping swiftly from the hermitage with great speed.
"O Pāṇḍavas, having gone quickly to that place and having overtaken the great deer, bring it back so that the Agnihotra sacrifice shall not be interrupted.
Having heard the words of the Brāhmaṇa, Yudhiṣṭhira was then deeply distressed.
Taking up his bow, the son of Kuntī rushed forth together with his brothers;
all those bulls among men, armed and armored, rushed forward,
striving for the sake of the Brahmin, swiftly pursuing the deer.
Discharging barbed arrows, reed-tipped shafts, and iron bolts, those great chariot-warriors could not pierce [the deer],
for the Pāṇḍavas, though watching closely from nearby, did not see that great beast as they exerted themselves. It remained invisible to them.
Not seeing the deer, those wise men, exhausted and having met with suffering,
reached a banyan tree with cool shade in the dense forest;
their limbs overcome by hunger and thirst, the Pāṇḍavas sat down together.
While they were seated together, Nakula, filled with grief and indignation, then spoke to his eldest brother, O best of the Kurus:
"In this family, dharma has never before been submerged."
Nor did there come about any loss of wealth through indolence;
we have attained the highest state among all beings. By what means, O King, have we fallen into this doubt?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"There is no limit to calamities, nor is there a fixed cause or reason;
yet it is dharma alone that distributes the fruits of both merit and sin in this world."
Bhīma said:
"O Prātikāmī, you then brought Kṛṣṇā to the assembly hall like a servant;
because I did not slay you there, we have fallen into this danger."
Arjuna said:
"The sharp words spoken by the Sūta’s son, which pierce the very bones—though they were exceedingly harsh, I endured them; because of that, we have fallen into this peril."
Nakula said:
"O Great King, because the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra did not slay me at that time when they were reviling me during the game of dice, they have now fallen into this calamity."
Sahadeva said:
"O Bhārata, because Śakuni defeated you at the game of dice, he was not slain by me there; for that reason, we have fallen into this peril."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira spoke these words to Nakula:
"O son of Mādrī, having climbed the tree, survey the ten directions."
"Look for water nearby, or trees that grow near water;
for these brothers of yours, dear father, are exhausted and thirsty.
Having said, "So be it," Nakula quickly climbed a tree.
By the command of his eldest brother,
the wise one rose from there and,
looking all around at his elder brother, spoke to him.
"O King, I see many trees growing near water, and I hear the cry of cranes; there is undoubtedly water here. Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and upholder of truth, spoke.
"Go, gentle one; go quickly from here and bring water at once. Having said "So be it," Nakula, by the command of his elder brother, ran toward where the water was and reached it with great speed.
Seeing the pure water surrounded by cranes, he then desired to drink; but from the sky, he heard a voice saying:
"Do not act rashly, my son! This is my prior possession."
"O son of Mādrī, answer my questions first, and then drink and take [the water].
But Nakula, being extremely thirsty, disregarded those words and drank the cool water; having drunk it, he fell down dead.
While Nakula was delaying, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī,
spoke to his heroic brother Sahadeva, the subduer of enemies:
"O dear Sahadeva, your elder brother is taking a long time."

"Bring back that very uterine brother of yours, and you yourself bring water. Having said, "So be it," Sahadeva set out in that direction and then beheld his brother Nakula lying slain upon the ground.
Tormented by grief for his brother and oppressed by thirst, he rushed toward the water; then a voice spoke:
"Do not act rashly, my son! This is my prior possession."
"Having answered the questions as you wish, then drink and take [the water].
But Sahadeva, disregarding those words and being parched with thirst, drank the cool water; and having drunk it, he fell down dead.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, said to Vijaya:
"O Bībhatsu, subduer of enemies, your two brothers have been gone for a long time. Bring them back—blessings be upon you—and bring water as well."
"For you, dear one, are the refuge for all of us who are suffering.
Thus addressed, the wise Guḍākeśa, grasping his bow with its arrow and having girded his sword, proceeded toward that lake.
Since those two tigers among men had gone to fetch water, Śvetavāhana saw them there— those two brothers, tigers among men, lying on the surface of the earth, deprived of life.
Seeing them as if they were fast asleep, the lion among men, the son of Kuntī, was deeply distressed; raising his bow, he surveyed that forest,
but he saw no creature there in that great wood.
Then Savyasācin, being exhausted, ran toward water. As he was running, he heard a voice from the sky:
"What is this? This water cannot be obtained by you through force."
"O Kaunteya, if you indeed answer the questions posed by me,
then, O Bhārata, you shall drink the water and carry it away. Though thus forbidden, Pārtha replied, "Show yourself and stop me!"
"Until you are pierced through by my arrows, you shall not speak thus again.
Having said this, Pārtha then rained down arrows consecrated with mantras upon that entire quarter, demonstrating his skill in hitting a target by sound alone.
Discharging *karṇin*, *nālīka*, and *nārāca* arrows, O bull of the Bharatas,
he rained down the sky with numerous volleys of shafts upon that invisible being of immeasurable splendor dwelling in the firmament.
The mighty-armed Dhanañjaya loosed a net of arrows. Then, having turned those masses of shafts discharged from the Gāṇḍīva bow into clouds, he laughed aloud; it was like a marvel.
The Yakṣa said:
"O Pārtha, what is the use of this obstruction? Answer my questions and then drink;
but if you drink without answering the questions, you shall cease to exist."
Thus addressed, Savyasācī Dhanañjaya, the son of Pṛthā, [acted].
Vaiśampāyana said:
"But he, afflicted by thirst, discharged his unerring arrows."
Without even understanding those questions, he drank them and fell down dead.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, spoke to Bhīmasena,
as well as Nakula, Sahadeva, and the unconquered Bībhatsu.
"O Bhārata, they have been gone for a long time seeking water and do not yet return;
bring them back, may you be blessed, and bring the water yourself.
Having said, "So be it," Bhīmasena set out in that direction.
Seeing those tigers among men, his brothers, struck down there,
the mighty-armed Bhīma was pained with grief and tormented by thirst; he thought that this was the work of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas.
Then Vṛkodara, the son of Pṛthā, thought: "I must certainly fight today; first, I shall drink some water. Then that bull among men, thirsting for water, rushed toward it.
Then an invisible voice spoke very clearly to the son of Pāṇḍu.
The Yakṣa said:
"O dear one, do not act rashly; this is my prior possession."
"O son of Kuntī, having answered the questions, then drink and take [the water].
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by the Yakṣa of immeasurable splendor, Bhīma then...

Without even understanding those questions, he fell down as if having drunk [the poison]. Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and son of Dharma, set out to find his brothers who had been gone for a long time.
As they were delaying for a long time, he spoke to them again and again many times: "O sons of Mādrī, why do you delay? Why does the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow delay?
And why does Bhīma, the possessor of great strength, delay there?"
"I shall go to see their abode," having thus resolved, Yudhiṣṭhira,
the son of Kuntī, that king and bull among men, reflected;
then Vaiśampāyana said:

Reflecting thus upon himself by means of his own self, he spoke these words. Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, seeing that his brothers had been gone for a long time and that they were repeatedly delaying, spoke to them again and again.

"What forest is this that we see? What deer could have been seen here?"—having thus mocked the great being, they were cursed by him and fell down; or else those heroes no longer saw the water where they had gone.
"Searching for water in the forest, they have been struck down by Time;
what indeed could be the cause that those bulls among men do not return?
I shall go to see their tracks," having thus resolved, Yudhiṣṭhira—
Vaiśampāyana said:
Reflecting upon these and other such words, that best of kings,
the mighty-armed one, rose up with a burning heart.
Devoid of the noise of people, he entered the great forest,
which was frequented by ruru deer, boars, and birds,
and adorned with trees of dark and radiant hues.
The highly illustrious one proceeded through that forest, which was charming with its ground covered in soft, lush grass, resonant with the songs of bees and birds, and adorned with nets of gold.
The illustrious one beheld that lake, which was as if created by Viśvakarman;
it was filled with clusters of lotuses and surrounded by sindhuvāra,
cane, ketaka, karavīra, and pippala trees.
Then the illustrious son of Dharma, longing to see his brothers and afflicted by fatigue, approached that lake; having seen it, he was filled with wonder.
Vaiśampāyana said:
He beheld his brothers slain, like the world-protectors fallen when the end of the age has arrived— those who possessed a majesty equal to Śakra.
Seeing Arjuna struck down, with his bow and arrows scattered about, he [beheld him].
Seeing Bhīmasena and both the twins motionless, as if their lives had departed,
he sighed long and hot, overwhelmed by tears of grief;
beholding all his brothers fallen, he was filled with anxious thought.
The long-armed son of Dharma lamented at great length:
"O Vṛkodara, O mighty-armed one, did you not indeed vow:
'In battle, I shall shatter the two thighs of Suyodhana with my mace'?"

Now that you, the heroic, high-souled, long-armed enhancer of the Kurus' fame, have been struck down, all those human words I promised— which were contrary to dharma— have become utterly futile for me today.
How could those divine words of yours be false?
And when even the gods said to you at your birth, O Dhanañjaya:
"O Kuntī, this son of yours shall indeed be no inferior to the thousand-eyed Indra."
On the northern Pāriyātra mountain, all beings cried out:
"He shall truly restore their lost prosperity;
there is no one who can conquer him in battle, nor is there anyone whom he cannot conquer."
How has this victorious one of great strength fallen under the power of death? Here lies Dhanañjaya on the ground, having shattered my hope— he,
the protector relying upon whom we endured these sorrows.

How did those two heroic sons of Kuntī, Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya— both of great strength, ever vigilant in battle, destroyers of enemies, and unassailable by any weapons— come under the power of their foes?
Surely my heart is made of the essence of stone,
for it does not shatter even now upon seeing these two, the twins, fallen;
though they were knowers of the scriptures, aware of place and time, devoted to austerity, and endowed with ritual action.
O bulls among men, why do you lie here without having performed a worthy deed? Why do you, whose bodies are unhurt and whose bows are untouched,
lie unconscious upon the ground, though you are unconquered?
Seeing his brothers sleeping soundly like the ridges of a mountain, the high-minded one— perspiring, distressed, and fallen into a state of misery—
said, "This is exactly so," O lord of men, that righteous-souled king.

Standing in the midst of an ocean of grief, the mighty-armed and high-minded one, who understood the distinctions of place and time, reflected on the cause of his distress and what ought to be done, yet he could find no way out through his deliberations.
Then,
having thus lamented in many ways, the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma and offspring of asceticism,
steadied himself and reflected with his intellect: "O heroes, by whom have they been struck down?"
"There is no stroke of a weapon here, nor is there the footprint of anyone;
I believe this is some great being by whom my brothers have been slain.
I shall contemplate with one-pointed mind, or perhaps I shall know by drinking the water."
This terrible calamity has befallen our high-souled brothers all at once;
yet it must have been secretly orchestrated by Duryodhana,
who was constantly instigated by the crooked-minded King of Gandhāra.
Who would trust that hero of evil mind and undisciplined soul, for whom what ought to be done and what ought not to be done are exactly the same?
Or perhaps this is a plot devised by that wicked-souled man using secret agents.
The mighty-armed one reflected in many ways:
"What indeed shall I say to the Teacher? And what to Bhīṣma?
What indeed shall I say to Vidura, who is equal to Bṛhaspati in statesmanship?"
And what indeed shall I say to my mother, who is ever a partaker of sorrow,
when she sees me deprived of my brothers and asks after her son with longing?
When you were with all your brothers, whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra—

"You went to the forest together with the heroes; how have you come back alone? "It did not occur to him that this water had been poisoned, for even though these men were dead, no sign of decomposition appeared."
"The complexion of my brothers' faces is serene," he thought;
"for who else, save for Time, the Destroyer, or Yama, could withstand these best of men, each possessing the strength of a flood?"
With this determination, he plunged into that water;
and as he was immersing himself in that water, he heard from the sky a voice:
the Yakṣa said:
"I am Baka, a consumer of water-weeds and fish;
by me have your younger brothers been led into the power of the departed. You shall be the fifth, O prince."
"If you do not answer the questions of one who asks them, my dear, do not act rashly; this is my prior possession.
But once you have answered the questions, O son of Kuntī, then drink and take [the water]."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Are you the foremost among the Rudras, the Vasus, or the Maruts?
I ask, which god are you? This was not done by Śakuni."
Himavān, Pāriyātra, Vindhya, and Malaya—
by whose splendor were these four mountains cast down to the earth?
O best among the powerful, you have performed a truly great deed.
That you have slain even my four younger brothers, those great archers,
such that neither gods, nor Gandharvas, nor Asuras, nor Rākṣasas could withstand them in a great battle— that is a most wonderful deed you have performed.
I do not know what must be done, nor do I understand what you desire;
a great curiosity has arisen within me, and fear has come upon me,
by which my heart is agitated and a fever has arisen in my head.
"Therefore, O Blessed One, I ask you: who are you that stands here?
The Yakṣa said:
"I am a Yakṣa; may it be well with you. I am not a bird nor a water-dweller."
"By me all these brothers of yours, possessed of great energy, have been slain.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having heard those inauspicious words consisting of harsh syllables, he [was filled with grief].
O King, as the yakṣa was speaking, he approached and stood there;
then, O King, having stepped back from that spot,
he remained standing before the large-bodied yakṣa Virūpākṣa, who was as tall as a palm tree.
The bull of the Bharatas beheld him standing upon the bridge— resplendent like a blazing sun, invincible, and resembling a mountain—
threatening with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, O one of great strength.
The Yakṣa spoke to the son of Kuntī, who was tormented by grief for his brothers.
The Yakṣa said:
"O King, these brothers of yours were repeatedly restrained by me."

"Desiring to take the water by force, they were indeed slain by me. O King, this water must not be drunk by one who wishes to preserve his life here, O Pārtha; do not act rashly, for this is my prior possession."
"O son of Kuntī, having answered my questions, you may then drink and take [the water].
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Yakṣa, I do not desire that which was previously taken by you."
Granted that virtuous men never praise themselves; yet,
O Lord, whatever a man may say in praising his own self according to his own understanding,
I shall answer your questions as best I can— so ask me.
The Yakṣa said:
"What indeed raises up the sun? And who are those that move around it?
Who leads it to its setting, and upon what does it rest?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Brahmā raises up the sun, and the gods move about on all sides of it;
Dharma causes it to set, and it is established in truth.
The Yakṣa said:
By what does one become a master of the Vedas? By what does one attain greatness?
By what, O King, does one have a companion, and by what does one possess wisdom?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Through sacred learning one becomes a master of the Vedas; through austerity one attains greatness;
through fortitude one gains a companion; and through service to the aged one becomes wise.
The yakṣa said:
What constitutes the divinity of brahmins, and what is their dharma like that of the virtuous? What is their human nature, and what is it like that of the wicked?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Their study of the Vedas is their divinity; their austerity is like that of the virtuous. Their death is their human nature; their slander is like that of the wicked.
The Yakṣa said:
What constitutes the divinity of Kṣatriyas, and what is their duty like that of the virtuous? What is their human nature, and what is it like that of the wicked?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Their mastery of archery is their divinity; their sacrifice is like that of the virtuous.
Their fear is indeed their human nature; their abandonment [of others] is like that of the wicked.
The Yakṣa said:
"What is the one Sāman worthy of sacrifice? What is the one Yajus worthy of sacrifice?
And what is that single thing which cuts across the sacrifice, and which the sacrifice does not overstep?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the Sāman worthy of sacrifice; the mind (manas) is indeed the Yajus worthy of sacrifice. Speech alone cuts through the sacrifice, yet the sacrifice does not transcend it."
The Yakṣa said:
"What is the best among those things that fly? What is the best among those that fall? What is the best among those that stand firm? And what is the best among those that speak?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
The rain is the best among those that fall; the seed is the best among those that are sown;
the cow is the best among those that stand firm; and the son is the best among those who speak.
The Yakṣa said:
Experiencing the objects of the senses, wise, honored by the world,
and esteemed by all beings— who does not live while breathing?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
He who does not offer [oblations] to these five— the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself— though he breathes, he does not truly live.
The Yakṣa said:
"What is weightier than the earth? What is loftier than the sky? What is swifter than the wind? And what is more numerous than men?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
The mother is weightier than the earth; the father is loftier than the sky;
the mind is swifter than the wind; and the anxiety of men is more abundant [than all else].
The Yakṣa said:
What is it that does not close its eyes while sleeping? What is it that, once born, does not move?
Whose is there no heart? And what grows by its own speed?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
A fish sleeps without blinking; an egg, once born, does not move;
a stone has no heart; and a river increases by its own current.
The Yakṣa said:
"What indeed is the friend of one traveling abroad? What indeed is the friend of one staying at home? What is the friend of the sick, and what is the friend of one who is dying?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
For one traveling abroad, a caravan is a friend; for one staying at home, a wife is a friend;
for the sick, a physician is a friend; and for one who is dying, charity is a friend.
The Yakṣa said:
Who is the guest of all beings? What indeed is the eternal dharma? What, O Indra among kings, is the nectar of immortality? And what is this entire world?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
The guest is the fire of all beings; he is Soma, the nectar of cows;
he is the eternal, immortal Dharma; and he is Vāyu—this entire world.
The Yakṣa said:
"What is it that wanders alone? Who is born again after being born?
What is the remedy for cold? And what is the great field of sowing?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
The sun moves alone; the moon is born again.
Fire is the remedy for cold, and the earth is the great vessel for sowing.
The Yakṣa said:
"What is the single word for righteousness? What is the single word for fame? What is the single word for heaven? And what is the single word for happiness?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Skillfulness is the sole foundation of righteousness; generosity is the sole foundation of fame;
truth is the sole foundation for attaining heaven; and virtuous conduct is the sole foundation of happiness.
The Yakṣa said:
"What indeed is the self of a human being? What indeed is the friend bestowed by fate? What is his means of subsistence? And what is his ultimate refuge?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"A son is a man's own self; a wife is a friend ordained by fate;
the rain-cloud is his means of subsistence, and giving is his ultimate refuge."
The Yakṣa said:
"What is the best among things that bring prosperity? What is the best among riches?
What is the best among gains? And likewise, what is the best among forms of happiness?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Skillfulness is the best among blessings; sacred learning is the best among riches;
health is the best of gains; and contentment is the highest of pleasures.
The Yakṣa said:
"What is the supreme dharma in the world? What dharma always bears fruit?
By restraining what do people not grieve? And with whom does an alliance never decay?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Compassion is the supreme dharma; the dharma of the three Vedas always bears fruit. One who restrains the mind does not grieve, and his alliance with the virtuous never decays.
The Yakṣa said:
"What indeed, having abandoned, does one become beloved? What indeed, having abandoned, does one not grieve?
What indeed, having abandoned, does one become wealthy? What indeed, having abandoned, would one become happy?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
By abandoning pride one becomes beloved; by abandoning anger one does not grieve. By abandoning desire one becomes wealthy; by abandoning greed one becomes happy.
The Yakṣa said:
"For what purpose is a gift given to a Brāhmaṇa? For what purpose to actors and dancers?
And for what purpose to servants, and for what purpose to kings?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
A gift given to a Brāhmaṇa is for the sake of dharma; to actors and dancers, it is for the sake of fame;
to servants, it is indeed for the sake of their maintenance; and to kings, it is for the sake of protection from fear.
The Yakṣa said:
By what is the world shrouded? By what does it not shine? Why does one abandon friends? Why does one not go to heaven?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
The world is shrouded by ignorance; it does not shine because of darkness. Through greed one abandons friends, and through attachment one does not go to heaven.
The Yakṣa said:
"How may a man be dead? How may a kingdom be dead?
How may a funeral rite (śrāddha) be dead? And how may a sacrifice be dead?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
A poor man is as good as dead; a kingdom without a king is dead;
a Śrāddha ceremony without a learned Vedic scholar is dead; and a sacrifice without a sacrificial fee is dead.
The Yakṣa said:
"What is the direction? What is declared to be water? What is food, O Pārtha, and what is poison?
Tell me the proper time for a śrāddha; then you may drink and take away [the water]."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The quarters, water, space, the cow, food, and desire—[these are the ingredients].
O Yakṣa, what do you think regarding the Brāhmaṇa, the time, or the manner of the Śrāddha?"
The Yakṣa said:
"What is declared to be the characteristic of austerity (*tapas*), and what is proclaimed as self-restraint (*dama*)?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is declared to be the highest forbearance (*kṣamā*), and what is celebrated as modesty (*hrī*)?
Abiding in one’s own duty is austerity (*tapas*); self-control (*dama*) is the subduing of the mind.
Forbearance is endurance of the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*); modesty is the turning away from what ought not to be done.
The Yakṣa said:
“O King, what is declared to be knowledge (*jñāna*), and what is proclaimed as tranquility (*śama*)?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

What is declared to be the supreme compassion? And what is cited as straightforwardness (*ārjava*)? Knowledge is the awakening to the meaning of reality; tranquility (*śama*) is the pacification of the mind.
The Yakṣa said:

Compassion, the desire for the happiness of all, uprightness, and equanimity of mind—what is the invincible enemy of men? And what is the endless disease? What kind of person is considered virtuous, and what kind is considered non-virtuous?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Anger is an enemy most difficult to conquer; greed is a disease that knows no end.
The Yakṣa said:

A virtuous person is one who seeks the welfare of all beings; an unvirtuous person is said to be merciless. O King, what is declared to be delusion (*moha*), and what is proclaimed to be pride (*māna*)?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is to be understood as indolence (*ālasya*), and what is proclaimed as sorrow (*śoka*)?

Delusion (*moha*) is the state of being bewildered regarding *dharma*; mental conceit is the identification with the self (*ātman*). Indolence is the failure to act in accordance with *dharma*, while sorrow is said to be ignorance (*ajñāna*).
The Yakṣa said:
"What is declared by the sages to be steadfastness (*sthairya*), and what is cited as fortitude (*dhairya*)?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What is declared to be the supreme bath, and what is said here to be the supreme gift?
Steadfastness in one’s own duty, stability, fortitude, and restraint of the senses.
The Yakṣa said:
Bathing is the abandonment of the impurities of the mind; giving is indeed the protection of living beings. What man is to be known as a wise person, and who is called an atheist?
Who is a fool, what is desire, and what is traditionally known as envy?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"One who knows the Dharma is to be known as wise; an atheist is called a fool.
The Yakṣa said:
Desire is known as the cause of saṃsāra, and heart-burning is said to be envy. What is declared to be egoism (ahaṃkāra), and what is proclaimed as hypocrisy (dambha)?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is declared to be that supreme destiny (*daiva*), and what is called malice (*paiśunya*)?
Egoism is great ignorance; hypocrisy is the raising of the banner of righteousness. Destiny is said to be the fruit of giving; malice is the censuring of others.
The Yakṣa said:
"Dharma, Artha, and Kāma are mutually contradictory.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How can there be a union in one place for these things that are eternally opposed, when both Dharma and the wife are each subject to the other's will? The Yakṣa said:
Then there is the union of all three—dharma, artha, and kāma.
O bull of the Bharatas, by what means is inexhaustible hell attained?
You ought to answer this question quickly for me as I ask it.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
If one personally invites a Brahmin who is destitute and begging,
and later says, "I have nothing," he shall go to an eternal hell.
He who acts falsely toward the Vedas, the treatises on dharma, the twice-born,
the gods, or the ancestral rites, shall go to an inexhaustible hell; likewise,
he who, despite possessing wealth, is devoid of giving and enjoyment due to greed.
The Yakṣa said:
"O King, he who says that there is nothing after death shall go to an inexhaustible hell,
regardless of his lineage, conduct, Vedic study, or sacred learning."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By what does one attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa? Tell me this with certainty.
"Listen, O Yakṣa, my dear: it is not lineage, nor Vedic study, nor sacred learning."
For there is no doubt that conduct alone is the cause of being twice-born;
conduct must be preserved with effort, especially by a Brāhmaṇa.
One whose conduct is undiminished is not diminished, but one who has failed in conduct is truly destroyed.

Those who merely recite, those who teach, and others who merely contemplate the scriptures—all such are fools and addicted to worldly distractions; he alone is wise who is devoted to action. Even one learned in the four Vedas, if he is of evil conduct, is inferior to a Śūdra.
The Yakṣa said:
"He who is devoted to the agnihotra sacrifice and is self-controlled is remembered as a Brāhmaṇa.
What does one who speaks pleasant words obtain?"
"What does one who deliberates before acting obtain?
What does one who makes many friends obtain?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Tell me, what does one who delights in the Dharma obtain?
One who speaks pleasant words becomes beloved;
one who acts after due reflection achieves greater victory.
"One who makes many friends lives happily.
The Yakṣa said:
"And he who delights in the Dharma attains a [fortunate] rebirth."
"Who rejoices? What is the marvel? What is the path? And what is the news?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Tell me the answers to these four questions: how may deceased kinsmen be restored to life?"
On the fifth or the sixth day, he cooks vegetables in his own home;
free from debt and not living abroad, that wanderer of the waters rejoices. Day after day, living beings here depart for the abode of Yama.
The rest desire immobility; what could be more marvelous than this? Reasoning is unstable, the sacred scriptures are divided, and there is no single sage whose opinion is authoritative.
The reality of Dharma is hidden in the cave;
that path is the one by which the great people have gone. In this cauldron filled with great delusion—
With the sun and fire as its fuel, with day and night as its kindling, and with the months and seasons as the stirring ladle, Time cooks all beings— such is the report.
The Yakṣa said:
"O scorcher of foes, you have explained my questions to me exactly as they are.
Now, however, tell me about the man who possesses all wealth."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
The sound of meritorious action touches both heaven and earth;
as long as that sound persists, so long is a man said to exist.
He for whom the pleasant and the unpleasant are equal, and likewise pleasure and pain;
he who possesses equanimity toward all things—he indeed is called a *puruṣa*. He is free from longing for the past, the present, and the future, and his mind is tranquil.
"Indeed, that man who possesses both the past and the future is truly a possessor of all wealth.
The Yakṣa said:
"O King, you have explained who that man is who possesses all wealth."
"Therefore, among your brothers, let whichever one you desire live.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"This dark-complexioned one with red eyes, who stands tall like a great *śāla* tree—"
"O Yakṣa, let Nakula, who is broad-chested and mighty-armed, live!
The Yakṣa said:
"This Bhīmasena is dear to you, and Arjuna is your ultimate refuge."
O King, why do you wish Nakula to live while he is your rival,
when you have abandoned Bhīma— whose strength is equal to ten thousand elephants— and yet desire Nakula to survive?
In this way, men call him Bhīmasena, your dear one;
yet by what reasoning do you wish for the life of your rival,
upon whose strength of arm all the Pāṇḍavas rely?
"Leaving Arjuna aside, you wish for Nakula to live.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Dharma, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when protected, protects."
Therefore, I do not abandon *dharma*; let not *dharma*, once destroyed, destroy us.
Compassion (*ānṛśaṃsya*) is the supreme *dharma*, and in my view, it is superior even to the ultimate goal (*paramārtha*).
O Yakṣa, I desire to practice compassion; let Nakula live.
"Men have always known me as a king of virtuous character;
I shall not swerve from my own duty, O Yakṣa, let Nakula live.
Both Kuntī and Mādrī were the two wives of my father."
"Both [wives] should indeed have sons; this is the thought that dwells in my mind. Just as Kuntī is to me, so is Mādrī; there is no distinction between them for me.
O Yakṣa, I wish Nakula to live together with his two mothers."
The Yakṣa said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, since you consider compassion to be superior to both wealth and pleasure, therefore let all your brothers live."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, at the word of the Yakṣa, those Pāṇḍavas arose;
and at that very moment, hunger and thirst departed from them all.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I ask you, who are you, O unconquered one, standing upon this lake on a single foot? Which god are you? I do not believe you are a yakṣa.
Are you perhaps the sole lord of the Vasus, or of the Rudras,
or the preeminent leader of the Maruts, or the wielder of the thunderbolt, the sovereign of the thirty gods?
For these brothers of mine are warriors capable of fighting against hundreds and thousands.
"I do not perceive any means by which they could have been struck down;
I observe that their senses are restored to a state of well-being upon awakening.
You are our friend, or perhaps you are our father."
The Yakṣa said:
"O dear one, I am your father, Dharma, of gentle prowess. Know me, O bull of the Bharatas, as having come here desiring to see you."
Fame, truth, self-restraint, purity, straightforwardness, modesty, steadiness,
generosity, austerity, and celibacy— these are my bodies.
Non-violence, equanimity, peace, austerity, purity, and freedom from envy [are likewise].
"Know these to be my gates, for you are always dear to me. By good fortune you are devoted to the five; by good fortune you have conquered the sixfold path:
two at the beginning, two in the middle, and two at the end, pertaining to the hereafter."
"I am Dharma; may you be blessed. I have come here desiring to know you.
I am pleased with your compassion, O sinless one, and I shall grant you a boon. Desire and anger are the first [obstacles], while greed and delusion are the middle ones."
At the end, there is fear and despondency; this is remembered as that sixfold path.
Choose a boon, O Indra among kings, for I am indeed the giver to you, O sinless one.
For those men who are devoted to me, there is no miserable state.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"If a deer should take away the fire-drills along with their base, let his sacred fires not be extinguished; let this be my first boon."
Dharma said:
"O son of Kuntī, O Lord, it was I who, in the guise of a deer, took away the fire-drills belonging to that Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of testing you."
Vaiśampāyana said:
"I shall give," was the very answer the Blessed One gave in reply. "Choose another boon, O you who resemble an immortal; may prosperity be yours."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Twelve years have been spent in the forest, and the thirteenth has now arrived.
During that time, may men not recognize us anywhere as we dwell there."
Vaiśampāyana said:
"I give," was the very answer the Blessed One gave;
and he further comforted Kaunteya, whose prowess is truth.
"O Bhārata, though you roam this earth in your own forms, no one in the three worlds shall recognize you;
this shall be by my grace for this thirteenth year, O best of the Kurus."
"You shall dwell in the city of Virāṭa, hidden and unrecognized.
Whatever form each of you has conceived in your mind, of whatever kind it may be, you shall all assume that very form according to your own will."
"Give this, together with the fire-drills, to a Brāhmaṇa;
for I brought it here in the form of a deer merely for the sake of testing you.
Choose another boon, gentle one; I shall grant it to you."
"I am not yet satiated, O best of men, even while granting these boons to you. Accept, my son, a third boon— great and peerless—
for you, O King, have your origin in me, and Vidura is a portion of myself."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Father, I have beheld you in person as the eternal God of gods. Whatever boon you, being pleased, grant me, that I shall accept."
"O Lord, may I always conquer greed, delusion, and anger;
may my mind be constantly fixed upon generosity, austerity, and truth. Dharma said:
"O Pāṇḍava, you are endowed with all virtues by your very nature;
moreover, you are Dharma himself, and what has been spoken to you shall come to pass.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Dharma, the creator of the world, vanished;
and the wise Pāṇḍavas, having gathered together, slept soundly.
Then all those heroes, their fatigue dispelled, returned to the hermitage.
They gave the Āraṇeya fire to that ascetic Brahmin.
This great account of the reunion and restoration is a source of glory for both father and son.
A man who recites this shall have his senses conquered and become self-controlled;
accompanied by sons and grandsons, he shall live for a hundred years,
neither engaging in unrighteousness nor in causing dissension among friends.
The minds of men who understand this true teaching should never take pleasure in stealing the property of others, violating the wives of others, or in miserliness.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been granted permission according to dharma by him, the Pāṇḍavas, whose prowess is truth,
were to live in concealment for the thirteenth year.
Having sat down together, the wise ones— those ascetics who were devoted to him and dwelling in the forest, firm in their vows—
the high-souled and disciplined sages then spoke to them with palms joined in reverence.
Seeking permission to dwell there, those of firm vows said:
"Everything is known to you all— how we were deprived of our kingdom by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra through deceit, and how we have been rendered destitute in many ways."

We have lived in the forest through hardships for twelve years; the thirteenth year remains as the period for living in concealment. We shall dwell there in disguise; you ought to grant us permission for that.
The evil-minded Suyodhana, Karṇa, and the son of Subala, being our extreme enemies, would act treacherously toward us even while knowing our situation;
yet they are disciplined in conduct and devoted to the citizens and their own kin.
"Indeed, who among those evil-minded ones would be capable of placing trust in them?
Might it be that we shall once again, together with the brahmins,
all remain established in our own sovereignty within our own kingdoms?"

Having spoken thus, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, afflicted by pain and grief, pure and with a throat choked with tears, then fainted. Then all the brahmins, together with his brothers, began to console him.
Then Dhaumya spoke these words of great significance to the king:
"O King, you are learned, self-controlled, true to your promise, and a master of your senses; men such as you do not lose their composure in any calamity whatsoever."
Even the gods have encountered calamities on many occasions while remaining in disguise,
in various places, for the sake of subduing their enemies— such as when the high-souled Indra reached the Niṣadha country and stayed in a hermitage on a mountain plateau.
Having performed deeds in secret for the subjugation of his enemies,
Viṣṇu, having assumed the form of Aśvaśiras,
dwelt for a long time unrecognized within the womb of Aditi for the sake of slaying the Daityas.
You have heard how, having assumed the form of a dwarf— concealed yet possessing the nature of Brahman— his kingdom was seized from Bali by means of his strides;
and how the Brahmarṣi Aurva then dwelt concealed within the thigh.
"O dear one, you have heard everything that was done in the worlds;
and you have also heard, O knower of dharma, what was done by Hari in the slaying of Vṛtra— remaining hidden even as he entered the thunderbolt of Śakra."
And you have heard all that was done for the sake of the gods by Hutāśana, who entered the waters and remained concealed;
likewise, O dear one, by Vivasvat, who remained hidden despite possessing supreme splendor.
While dwelling on earth in every way, all his enemies were utterly consumed;
and while Viṣṇu was indeed dwelling in the house of Daśaratha,
the ten-necked Rāvaṇa was slain in battle by him of terrible deeds in disguise.

"In this way, these great-souled ones, remaining concealed here and there, conquered their enemies in battle; so shall you also be victorious. Thus was the knower of dharma thoroughly gratified by the words of Dhaumya.
Neither by the wisdom of the scriptures nor by his own intellect did Yudhiṣṭhira waver.
Then the mighty-armed Bhīmasena, possessed of great strength and the best among the powerful, spoke to the king, gladdening him with his words.
Out of regard for you, O Great King, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, acting with a mind devoted to dharma, has committed no act of rashness. Sahadeva and Nakula were constantly restrained by me.
Capable of destroying them, those two slayers of enemies possess terrible prowess. We shall not abandon that task for which you will employ us;
may you ordain all of it, and we shall swiftly conquer the foes.
When Bhīmasena had spoken thus, the brahmins, having offered supreme blessings and taken leave of the Bharatas, departed for their respective homes;
they were all eminent knowers of the Vedas, as well as ascetics and sages.
Having uttered their blessings according to tradition and longing for a future meeting,
those five wise Pāṇḍavas, together with Dhaumya,
rose up and set out, O Bhārata, taking Kṛṣṇā with them.
Having traveled a distance of one *krośa* from that place by way of certain signs,
on the following day, those tigers among men,
all of whom were experts in various sciences and proficient in counsel, prepared themselves for their period of concealment.
Knowing the proper times for peace and war, they sat down together for counsel.
